text:
Ice regimes and landfast ice
Ice pixels from both dates are pooled and grouped into four regimes with k-means on standardized normalized HH and HH texture (GLCM contrast, GLCM homogeneity and local standard deviation). HV and the co-/cross-pol ratio are left out because HV is noise-limited on one of the two dates, and distance to coast is left out so the regimes describe the ice, not its location. Pooling keeps the regime definitions identical on both dates. Each feature is clipped at its 1st and 99th percentiles before clustering, so a few extreme texture values along floe and image edges cannot claim a cluster of their own. The cluster with the strongest texture (high GLCM contrast and local variability, low homogeneity) is named rough or deformed ice; the other three are ordered by mean normalized HH from dark to bright. The names follow the stages of development each regime most resembles:









ID
Regime
Typical appearance
Closest WMO stages




0
Open water
dark in normalized HH
ice-free


1
Smooth dark ice
lowest HH among ice, smooth
new ice, nilas


2
Grey ice
moderate HH
grey, grey-white


3
Thin first-year ice
brightest HH among smoother ice, large floes
thin first-year


4
Rough or deformed ice
strongest texture
brash, rafted, ridged


5
Landfast candidate
ice joined to shore, stable between dates
fast ice



A pixel becomes a landfast candidate when it is ice on both dates, belongs to an ice body that touches the coast, lies within 3 km of land, and its normalized HH changed by less than 1.5 dB. These names are interpretations of unsupervised clusters; Section 15 explains how to train a supervised classifier from CIS charts instead.


Code
CLASS_NAMES = ["Open water", "Smooth dark ice", "Grey ice", "Thin first-year ice", "Rough/deformed ice",
               "Landfast candidate"]
CLASS_COLORS = ["#0b3d91", "#c6dbef", "#9e9ac8", "#f0f0f0", "#fd8d3c", "#31a354"]
cmap_cls = ListedColormap(CLASS_COLORS)
norm_cls = BoundaryNorm(np.arange(-0.5, 6.5), cmap_cls.N)
REGIME_FEATURES = ["HH_dB", "GLCM_contrast_HH", "GLCM_homogeneity_HH", "local_std_HH"]
use = [FEATURES.index(n) for n in REGIME_FEATURES]

X_all = np.concatenate([stacks[t][use][:, ice[t]].T for t in range(len(DATES))])
valid = np.isfinite(X_all).all(axis=1)
lo_clip, hi_clip = np.percentile(X_all[valid], [1, 99], axis=0)
mu = np.clip(X_all[valid], lo_clip, hi_clip).mean(axis=0)
sd = np.clip(X_all[valid], lo_clip, hi_clip).std(axis=0)


def standardize(X):
    return (np.clip(X, lo_clip, hi_clip) - mu) / sd


rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
sample = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(valid), size=min(200_000, int(valid.sum())), replace=False)
km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(standardize(X_all[sample]))
z = km.cluster_centers_                                           # standardized cluster centres
roughness = z[:, 1] + z[:, 3] - z[:, 2]                           # contrast + local std - homogeneity
rough_cluster = int(np.argmax(roughness))
others = sorted((c for c in range(4) if c != rough_cluster), key=lambda c: z[c, 0])   # dark to bright HH
cluster_to_class = {c: k + 1 for k, c in enumerate(others)} | {rough_cluster: 4}

ice_class = []
for t in range(len(DATES)):
    cls = np.full(grid.shape, 255, np.uint8)
    cls[ocean] = 0
    X = stacks[t][use][:, ice[t]].T
    ok = np.isfinite(X).all(axis=1)
    lab = np.full(len(X), 3, np.uint8)
    lab[ok] = [cluster_to_class[c] for c in km.predict(standardize(X[ok]))]
    cls[ice[t]] = lab
    ice_class.append(cls)

# Landfast candidates: ice on both dates, attached to the coast, within 3 km, stable HH
dhh = (hh_n.isel(time=1) - hh_n.isel(time=0)).values
both = ice[0] & ice[1]
labels, n = ndi.label(both)
coastal = np.unique(labels[ndi.binary_dilation(land_mask, iterations=2) & both])
attached = np.isin(labels, coastal[coastal > 0])
landfast = attached & (dist_coast <= 3.0) & (np.abs(dhh) < 1.5)
for cls in ice_class:
    cls[landfast] = 5

centers = pd.DataFrame(km.cluster_centers_ * sd + mu, columns=REGIME_FEATURES)
centers["roughness score"] = roughness
centers.index = [CLASS_NAMES[cluster_to_class[c]] for c in range(4)]
centers.loc[CLASS_NAMES[1:5]].round(2)

    ax.imshow(show, cmap=cmap_cls, norm=norm_cls, extent=extent, interpolation="nearest")

text:
Ice concentration
Ice concentration is the fraction of ice-covered ocean pixels in a cell, reported in tenths (0 to 10) to match the CIS egg code. A 1 km grid (20 x 20 pixels) feeds the route analysis and a 5 km grid matches the scale of CIS chart comparison. Cells that are entirely land or coast are left empty.


Code
def ice_concentration(ice_binary, factor):
    # ice_binary: 1 = ice, 0 = water, NaN = land; returns tenths on a coarser grid
    h, w = ice_binary.shape
    blocks = ice_binary[: h // factor * factor, : w // factor * factor]
    return np.nanmean(blocks.reshape(h // factor, factor, w // factor, factor), axis=(1, 3)) * 10


F1, F5 = int(1000 / RES), int(5000 / RES)
CT_CMAP = plt.get_cmap("Blues_r").copy()

ct5 = [ice_concentration(np.where(ocean, ice[t].astype("float32"), np.nan), F5) for t in range(len(DATES))]

        axes[j, t].set(title=f"{d} ice concentration, {label} (mean {np.nanmean(ct):.1f}/10)", xticks=[], yticks=[])

text:
Change between 28 January and 3 February
Both dates are on the same grid and normalized to the same incidence angle, so they can be compared pixel by pixel. Three views summarize the change: a from-to transition table of regimes, the change in ice concentration (positive means more ice), and the HH log-ratio, which in dB is simply the difference of the normalized images. Because the scenes are 6 days apart, these are net changes in ice state (new ice formation, export down the estuary, compaction against the south shore, growth or break-up of landfast ice), not drift vectors. sar.omnibus_test and sar.pairwise_change are not used here because they assume both dates share the same acquisition geometry and number of looks, which two different beams do not.
Read the HH log-ratio with care. Even after normalization it is negative over most of the AOI, because calm open water darkens with incidence much faster than the single first-year-ice slope assumes, and the second scene is about 17 degrees steeper. The log-ratio is therefore most informative within ice (rafting, ridging and floe break-up show as local increases), while the ice masks and concentration maps, which use a threshold per date, are the better guide to where ice appeared or disappeared.

Ice-cost surface and least-cost route
Each pixel gets a navigation cost from its regime, scaled by the local 1 km ice concentration: cost = base_cost(class) x (1 + CT / 10). Land and the coastal fringe are impassable. The base costs below are illustrative for a ferry or cargo ship with a modest ice class; an icebreaker or a Polar Class vessel would use flatter costs, and a pressure penalty can be added along the south shore when northwest winds are compressing the ice.

skimage.graph.route_through_array then finds the cheapest 8-connected path between a start point off Baie-Comeau and an end point off Matane. Both points are snapped to the nearest ocean pixel inside the AOI, and the route is compared with the straight line to measure the detour caused by ice.


Code
BASE_COST = np.array([1, 2, 4, 8, 15, 50], "float32")
START_LONLAT, END_LONLAT = (-68.10, 49.20), (-67.55, 48.93)     # off Baie-Comeau, off Matane
to_utm = Transformer.from_crs(4326, CRS, always_xy=True)
to_ll = Transformer.from_crs(CRS, 4326, always_xy=True)
_, (near_r, near_c) = ndi.distance_transform_edt(~ocean, return_indices=True)


def snap(lon, lat):
    col, row = ~transform * to_utm.transform(lon, lat)
    r = int(np.clip(row, 0, grid.shape[0] - 1))
    c = int(np.clip(col, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1))
    return int(near_r[r, c]), int(near_c[r, c])


def rc_to_lonlat(rows_, cols_):
    x, y = transform * (np.asarray(cols_) + 0.5, np.asarray(rows_) + 0.5)
    return to_ll.transform(x, y)


start, end = snap(*START_LONLAT), snap(*END_LONLAT)
routes, route_rows, costs = {}, [], []
for t, d in enumerate(DATES):
    ct_full = np.kron(np.nan_to_num(ct1[t]), np.ones((F1, F1)))
    ct_full = np.pad(ct_full, ((0, grid.shape[0] - ct_full.shape[0]), (0, grid.shape[1] - ct_full.shape[1])), mode="edge")
    cost = np.full(grid.shape, 1e6, "float32")
    ok = ice_class[t] != 255
    cost[ok] = BASE_COST[ice_class[t][ok]] * (1 + ct_full[ok] / 10)
    costs.append(cost)
    path, total = route_through_array(cost, start, end, fully_connected=True, geometric=True)
    r_, c_ = np.array(path).T
    lon, lat = rc_to_lonlat(r_, c_)
    routes[d] = LineString(zip(lon, lat))
    crossed = pd.Series(ice_class[t][r_, c_]).map(dict(enumerate(CLASS_NAMES))).value_counts(normalize=True)
    straight = np.hypot(start[0] - end[0], start[1] - end[1]) * RES / 1000
    length = (np.hypot(np.diff(r_), np.diff(c_)).sum()) * RES / 1000
    route_rows.append({"date": d, "route length (km)": round(length, 1), "straight line (km)": round(straight, 1),
                       "detour": f"{length / straight - 1:.1%}", "total cost": round(float(total), 0),
                       **{f"% {k}": round(100 * v, 1) for k, v in crossed.items()}})
route_table = pd.DataFrame(route_rows).fillna(0)

This interactive map overlays the AOI, the 1 km ice concentration of both dates (cells shaded from dark blue for open water to white for full ice cover) and the least-cost routes for both dates on Esri World Imagery. Use the layer control (top right) to switch dates on and off, and hover over a cell or a route to read its values. The map is built with folium, so it is saved in the notebook as HTML and displays in Jupyter, JupyterLab, VS Code and nbviewer without a live widget kernel. def to_tif(array, name, factor=1, dtype="float32", nodata=np.nan):
    da = grid.copy(data=np.asarray(array, dtype=dtype)) if factor == 1 else None
    if da is None:
        import xarray as xr
        t_ = transform * Affine.scale(factor)
        ys = t_.f + t_.e * (np.arange(array.shape[0]) + 0.5)
        xs = t_.c + t_.a * (np.arange(array.shape[1]) + 0.5)
        da = xr.DataArray(np.asarray(array, dtype=dtype), dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": ys, "x": xs})
        da = da.rio.write_crs(CRS).rio.write_transform(t_)
    da.rio.write_nodata(nodata).rio.to_raster(OUT_DIR / name)
    return name

title: Sea Ice Mapping for Shipping Routes in the St. Lawrence Estuary with RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM)
text:
Review, validation, and limitations
Validate before use. Download the CIS Gulf of St. Lawrence charts (SIGRID-3 shapefiles) for 28 January and 3 February 2026 or the nearest dates. Compare the 5 km concentration with the chart total concentration (CT) and report bias, RMSE and R². To replace the unsupervised regimes with a supervised classifier, rasterize chart polygons where one stage of development dominates (partial concentration of 8/10 or more) onto the common grid, refine them by visual interpretation of the SAR images, sample a balanced set of pixels per class from the Section 7 feature stack, and train a sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier; train on 28 January and test on 3 February to check transfer across beams. Route results can be checked against AIS tracks for the same days: measure how far real ship tracks are from the modelled route and which regimes ships actually crossed (sar.ship.match_points handles the point matching).
Limitations.

Resolution: 100 m resolution cannot resolve narrow leads, small floes or individual ridges; ridges appear only as texture.
Wind: wind-roughened open water can be mistaken for ice, especially in HH. Pixels are flagged, not removed, because no wind data are bundled.
Young ice: new, grey and grey-white ice have similar backscatter, so confusion between regimes 1 to 3 is expected.
Different beams: SCLNA and SCLND have different incidence angles and noise profiles; normalization reduces but does not remove the difference.
Noise floor: at the 50 to 54 degree incidence of the 3 February scene, HV over most of the AOI is within about a decibel of the NESZ, so that date is mapped from HH alone and wind-roughened water cannot be tested on it. Prefer acquisitions at moderate incidence (below about 40 degrees) when HV matters.
Incidence normalization: a single linear slope is an approximation over a 17 degree difference between the dates; open water and different ice types have different slopes, so residual differences between dates remain.
Geocoding: ellipsoid tie-point geocoding is accurate over water but can be off by a pixel or two on steep coast; the coastal buffer hides this.
Land mask: Natural Earth 1:10m is generalized; small islands, piers and narrow bays may be misclassified.
Time gap: 6 days is too long for ice drift tracking in the estuary; changes are net state changes.
Unsupervised regimes: cluster names are interpretations and cluster boundaries depend on the ice present on these two dates.

title: Sea Ice Mapping for Shipping Routes in the St. Lawrence Estuary with RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM)
text:
Summary and conclusions
This notebook processes two RCM ScanSAR Low Noise GRD scenes end to end with GeoLattice and no external SAR software. rcm.read_rcm_grd_subset reads only the AOI window of each scene, calibrates it to sigma-nought with the product’s gain tables, removes the ScanSAR noise floor and returns ground control points and incidence angles; refined Lee filtering with a measured ENL, geocoding of both dates onto one UTM grid, a land and coastal mask, and incidence normalization with a slope fitted from the data make the two beams comparable. On that common basis the notebook separates ice from open water, groups ice into regimes with texture, computes ice concentration in tenths at 1 km and 5 km, measures net change between 28 January and 3 February, and turns the ice maps into an ice-cost surface and a least-cost route between Baie-Comeau and Matane. The outputs are saved as GeoTIFF, GeoJSON and CSV.
Results for these two scenes. About half of the open estuary inside the AOI was ice-covered on both dates (49.9% of ocean pixels on 28 January and 52.2% on 3 February; mean concentration 5.0 and 5.2 tenths on the 1 km grid), with open water along the north shore off Baie-Comeau and in the west, and denser ice toward the south and east. The total hardly changed, but the ice moved: 18.5% of ocean pixels gained ice and 16.3% lost it between the dates. On 28 January HV stood about 4 dB above the noise floor and agreed with the HH ice map on 88.8% of pixels; on 3 February, at 50 to 54 degrees incidence, HV was at the noise floor and the map relies on HH alone. The least-cost crossing from off Baie-Comeau to off Matane was 62.7 km on 28 January (25% longer than the straight line, 86% in open water) and 67.5 km on 3 February (35% longer, 93% in open water), the second route swinging north through the open lead along the north shore. The large rise in “smooth dark ice” on 3 February should be read with caution: part of it is the steeper viewing geometry, which darkens ice more than the single normalization slope corrects, rather than new ice formation.
The ice/water split and the route are the most robust products. The ice regimes and landfast candidates are interpretations of unsupervised clusters and should be checked against CIS charts, and wind-roughened water should be reviewed with wind data, before the maps are used for navigation. The same workflow extends naturally to a winter time series, to scenes one or two days apart for drift tracking, and to a supervised classifier once chart labels are available.

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
text:
Overview
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow, globally important maritime chokepoint linking the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. It carries energy as well as food and fertilizer trade, so disruption can affect supply chains well beyond the region. The World Trade Organization’s Strait of Hormuz portal documents trade impacts and measures connected with the 2026 Strait situation; its reporting includes measures introduced on or after February 28, 2026. Monitoring vessel presence after April 20 therefore provides useful situational context for observing traffic patterns during this wider period of disruption. The International Maritime Organization reported on 21 April that about 20,000 mariners and 2,000 ships were stranded in the Persian Gulf due to the closure.
Satellite ship-candidate detection can help analysts compare where vessels are visible across selected acquisition dates, identify areas for closer review, and complement maritime reports. Sentinel-1 SAR is useful because it can collect imagery at night and through cloud cover, but each image is only a snapshot, not continuous tracking. This notebook’s April 23, 2026 acquisition is an example observation after April 20—not evidence that a specific incident occurred on that date. GRD detections are unverified radar candidates: they do not establish vessel identity, intent, threat, or route, and should be corroborated with AIS, trusted maritime notices such as UKMTO, and independent image review.

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
text:
Scope and interpretation
The GRD search uses the requested 20–30 April 2026 interval and Planetary Computer’s sentinel-1-grd collection. The catalog supplies georeferenced VV and VH measurement COGs plus calibration/noise XML assets; GeoLattice reads and calibrates only the AOI window. The notebook ranks matching acquisitions by their footprint overlap with the AOI and processes the best-overlapping IW dual-pol scene. A single granule may cover only part of this large AOI, so its coverage is reported and should not be mistaken for complete Strait coverage.
GRDH detections are bright point-like candidates relative to local sea clutter, not a vessel identification product. Coastlines, ports, islands, wakes, sidelobes, and azimuth ambiguities can all create false detections. No pre-CFAR speckle filter is applied because spatial filtering can smear small targets. Sub-look coherence is computed from complex SLC data and is a separate confirmation feature; GRD intensity cannot be used to calculate it. Planetary Computer does not publish an IW SLC collection, so the optional SLC section looks for matching SAFE products already present locally and explains when they are unavailable.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import json
import re
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import rasterio
from rasterio.features import geometry_mask
from rasterio.transform import from_gcps
from shapely.geometry import box, shape

from geolattice.rsense.sar import sentinel1, ship

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})
DATA_DIR = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones/hormuz_strait_sentinel1")
if not DATA_DIR.is_dir():
    DATA_DIR = Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones/hormuz_strait_sentinel1")
AOI_PATH = DATA_DIR / "AOI_hormuz_strait.geojson"
if not AOI_PATH.is_file():
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"Hormuz Strait AOI not found: {AOI_PATH.resolve()}")

aoi = gpd.read_file(AOI_PATH)
if aoi.empty:
    raise ValueError(f"AOI has no features: {AOI_PATH}")
if aoi.crs is None:
    aoi = aoi.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
aoi = aoi.to_crs("EPSG:4326")
aoi_geometry = aoi.geometry.union_all()
WEST, SOUTH, EAST, NORTH = aoi.total_bounds
BOUNDS = (WEST, SOUTH, EAST, NORTH)
# A bounded representative ship-lane window keeps full-resolution CFAR practical.
PROCESSING_BOUNDS = (56.15, 26.35, 56.65, 26.75)
processing_geometry = box(*PROCESSING_BOUNDS)
if not aoi_geometry.covers(processing_geometry):
    raise ValueError("PROCESSING_BOUNDS must lie inside the Hormuz Strait AOI")
print(f"GeoLattice Sentinel-1 ship workflow | AOI: {AOI_PATH}")
print(f"AOI bounds (west, south, east, north): {BOUNDS}")
print(f"Full-resolution processing bounds: {PROCESSING_BOUNDS}")
print(f"Local SAFE products: {len(list(DATA_DIR.rglob('*.SAFE')))}; "
      f"IW SLC products: {sum('_SLC__' in p.name for p in DATA_DIR.rglob('*.SAFE'))}")

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
text:
AOI and acquisition search
The AOI GeoJSON stores coordinates in the required GeoJSON order, longitude then latitude. The STAC search filters to IW scenes with both VV and VH polarization. If matching local SLC SAFE products are present, the notebook first considers GRD scenes from the same platform and acquisition date so sub-look coherence can be demonstrated; it then selects the candidate with the largest projected AOI overlap. Otherwise, it selects the best-overlapping GRD scene. Full-resolution detection is bounded to PROCESSING_BOUNDS, a representative 0.5° by 0.4° ship-lane window inside the larger AOI, to control memory and run time. Change these bounds to investigate another part of the AOI. Repeat the processing for additional scene footprints to cover more area or build a date series.


Code
STAC_URL = "https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1/search"
SEARCH = {
    "collections": ["sentinel-1-grd"],
    "intersects": aoi_geometry.__geo_interface__,
    "datetime": "2026-04-20T00:00:00Z/2026-04-30T23:59:59Z",
    "limit": 100,
}
request = urllib.request.Request(
    STAC_URL,
    data=json.dumps(SEARCH).encode("utf-8"),
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/geo+json"},
    method="POST",
)
with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=60) as response:
    search_result = json.load(response)
items = [
    item for item in search_result.get("features", [])
    if item.get("properties", {}).get("sar:instrument_mode") == "IW"
    and set(item.get("properties", {}).get("sar:polarizations", [])) == {"VV", "VH"}
    and "GRDH_1SDV" in item.get("id", "")
]
if not items:
    raise RuntimeError("Planetary Computer returned no IW GRDH 1SDV scenes for the AOI/date interval")

# Prefer acquisitions that can be paired with a local SLC; otherwise use any catalog match.
local_slc_keys = set()
for safe in DATA_DIR.rglob("*.SAFE"):
    if "_SLC__" not in safe.name:
        continue
    match = re.search(r"_(20\d{6})T", safe.name)
    if match:
        local_slc_keys.add((safe.name[:3], match.group(1)))
paired_items = [
    item for item in items
    if (item["id"][:3], item["properties"]["datetime"][:10].replace("-", "")) in local_slc_keys
]
candidate_items = paired_items if paired_items else items
print(f"Scenes with a same-platform/date local SLC: {len(paired_items)}")

# Rank by overlap area in a local projected CRS rather than by degree-squared area.
aoi_projected = aoi.to_crs("EPSG:32640")
aoi_area = float(aoi_projected.geometry.area.sum())
ranked_items = []
for item in candidate_items:
    footprint = gpd.GeoSeries([shape(item["geometry"])], crs="EPSG:4326").to_crs(aoi_projected.crs).iloc[0]
    overlap_area = float(footprint.intersection(aoi_projected.geometry.union_all()).area)
    ranked_items.append((overlap_area, item))
ranked_items.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0], reverse=True)
overlap_area, selected_item = ranked_items[0]
coverage_fraction = overlap_area / aoi_area
selected_footprint = shape(selected_item["geometry"])
if not selected_footprint.intersects(processing_geometry):
    raise ValueError("Selected scene does not cover PROCESSING_BOUNDS; select another matching acquisition")

print(f"Matching IW GRDH 1SDV scenes: {len(items)}")
print(f"Selected: {selected_item['id']}")
print(f"Acquisition: {selected_item['properties']['datetime']}")
print(f"Platform / relative orbit: {selected_item['properties'].get('platform')} / "
      f"{selected_item['properties'].get('sat:relative_orbit')}")
print(f"AOI area covered by this scene: {coverage_fraction:.1%}")

# Keep an unsigned catalog record for provenance; never save the temporary access token.
record_path = DATA_DIR / "selected_grd_stac_item.json"
record_path.write_text(json.dumps(selected_item, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
footprint_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"scene": [selected_item["id"]]},
    geometry=[shape(selected_item["geometry"])],
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
aoi.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="red", linewidth=2, label="AOI")
footprint_gdf.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="royalblue", linewidth=1.2, label="Selected GRD footprint")
ax.set(title="Hormuz Strait AOI and selected Sentinel-1 GRD footprint", xlabel="Longitude", ylabel="Latitude")
ax.legend()
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
section: Read calibrated VV/VH over the AOI
text:
Read calibrated VV/VH over the AOI
Planetary Computer’s Sentinel-1 GRD assets are cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs with ground control points. GeoLattice read_grd_subset uses these geolocation points together with the scene’s calibration and noise XMLs to return linear sigma0 in the AOI window. Border-noise removal is limited to actual full-scene edges, not the artificial edges of the AOI crop. COG data are read remotely by window, so the full multi-hundred-megabyte measurement assets do not need to be downloaded first. A matching local COG, if present, is preferred; its calibration/noise metadata are still retrieved from the selected STAC item.


Code
from geolattice.rsense.core.io import read_safe

local_grd_safes = sorted(
    safe for safe in DATA_DIR.rglob("*.SAFE")
    if "_GRDH_1SDV_" in safe.name and safe.name.startswith(selected_item["id"])
)
if local_grd_safes:
    safe_index = read_safe(local_grd_safes[0])
    vv_source, vh_source = safe_index["measurement"]["vv"], safe_index["measurement"]["vh"]
    vv_cal, vh_cal = safe_index["calibration"]["vv"], safe_index["calibration"]["vh"]
    vv_noise, vh_noise = safe_index["noise"]["vv"], safe_index["noise"]["vh"]
    print(f"Using local GRD SAFE: {local_grd_safes[0].name}")
else:
    token_url = "https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/sas/v1/token/sentinel-1-grd"
    with urllib.request.urlopen(token_url, timeout=30) as response:
        sas_token = json.load(response)["token"].lstrip("?")

    def signed_asset(key):
        href = selected_item["assets"][key]["href"]
        return href + ("&" if "?" in href else "?") + sas_token

    vv_source, vh_source = signed_asset("vv"), signed_asset("vh")
    vv_cal, vh_cal = signed_asset("schema-calibration-vv"), signed_asset("schema-calibration-vh")
    vv_noise, vh_noise = signed_asset("schema-noise-vv"), signed_asset("schema-noise-vh")
vv_result = sentinel1.read_grd_subset(
    vv_source,
    vv_cal,
    vv_noise,
    bounds=PROCESSING_BOUNDS,
    border_noise=True,
)
vh_result = sentinel1.read_grd_subset(
    vh_source,
    vh_cal,
    vh_noise,
    bounds=PROCESSING_BOUNDS,
    border_noise=True,
)
if vv_result["data"].shape != vh_result["data"].shape:
    raise ValueError("VV and VH AOI windows differ; check that both assets belong to the same GRD item")
vv = vv_result["data"]
vh = vh_result["data"]
gcps = vh_result["gcps"]
print(f"Calibrated AOI window: {vh.shape[0]:,} lines x {vh.shape[1]:,} samples")
print(f"Window in source scene: {vh_result['window']}")
print(f"Finite sigma0 pixels: VV={np.isfinite(vv).mean():.1%}, VH={np.isfinite(vh).mean():.1%}")
print("Sigma0 is in linear power; convert to dB only for display and contrast summaries.")

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
section: Mask land and build a sea-clutter field
text:
Mask land and build a sea-clutter field
A land/coastal exclusion mask prevents shoreline clutter from dominating CFAR. This cell caches Natural Earth’s 1:10m land polygons in the AOI data folder, clips them to the AOI, and applies GeoLattice’s configurable coastal buffer. Natural Earth is suitable for a regional demonstration but may omit small islands, port structures, and newly built features; inspect and improve the mask for operational use.


Code
LAND_PATH = DATA_DIR / "ne_10m_land.geojson"
LAND_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector/master/geojson/ne_10m_land.geojson"
if not LAND_PATH.exists():
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(LAND_URL, LAND_PATH)
land = gpd.read_file(LAND_PATH).to_crs("EPSG:4326")
land_geoms = [
    geom.intersection(processing_geometry)
    for geom in land.geometry
    if geom is not None and geom.intersects(processing_geometry)
]

window_transform = from_gcps(gcps)
inside_aoi = geometry_mask(
    [processing_geometry], out_shape=vh.shape, transform=window_transform, invert=True
)
land_mask = ship.land_mask_for_window(
    gcps,
    vh.shape,
    land_geoms,
    buffer_m=300.0,
    pixel_spacing=10.0,
)
sea = inside_aoi & ~land_mask & np.isfinite(vv) & np.isfinite(vh) & (vh > 0)
if not sea.any():
    raise ValueError("No valid sea pixels remain; inspect AOI overlap and coastline masking")
print(f"AOI sea pixels retained: {sea.sum():,} ({sea.mean():.1%} of the read window)")
print("Land mask includes a 300 m shoreline buffer to suppress coast and harbor clutter.")

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
section: Detect GRD ship candidates with GeoLattice CFAR
text:
Detect GRD ship candidates with GeoLattice CFAR
GeoLattice ship.cfar_tiled evaluates a local background ring in unfiltered VH sigma0. This workflow estimates ENL from the most homogeneous valid sea blocks instead of assuming one nominal value for the whole scene. It also uses a more conservative pixel false-alarm threshold, requires adequate background support, and filters components by mean-power contrast (less sensitive to a single bright speckle pixel than peak contrast). These are screening candidates, not confirmed ships: GRD speckle, sea state, sidelobes, and bright structures can still cause false alarms, while conservative thresholds can miss small or low-contrast vessels. Lower MIN_MEAN_CONTRAST_DB to increase sensitivity after visual review.


Code
PFA = 1e-8
ENL = ship.estimate_enl(vh, sea, block=64, max_cv_quantile=0.2)
OUTER_PIXELS = 101
GUARD_PIXELS = 61
MIN_MEAN_CONTRAST_DB = 12.0
vh_linear = np.nan_to_num(vh, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)
detections, background_db = ship.cfar_tiled(
    vh_linear,
    sea,
    tile=1024,
    method="gamma",
    pfa=PFA,
    enl=ENL,
    outer=OUTER_PIXELS,
    guard=GUARD_PIXELS,
    min_ring_fraction=0.7,
)
targets = ship.extract_targets(
    detections,
    vh_linear,
    np.nan_to_num(vv, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0),
    gcps=gcps,
    background_db=background_db,
    pixel_spacing=10.0,
    min_px=3,
    max_px=500,
    min_mean_contrast_db=MIN_MEAN_CONTRAST_DB,
)
print(f"CFAR parameters: Pfa={PFA:g}, ENL={ENL:g}, guard={GUARD_PIXELS} px, outer={OUTER_PIXELS} px")
print(f"CFAR-positive pixels: {detections.sum():,}")
print(f"Candidates with mean contrast >= {MIN_MEAN_CONTRAST_DB:g} dB: {len(targets):,}")
targets = targets.sort_values("mean_contrast_db", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
targets.head(20)

The GRD catalog item supplies measurement, calibration, and noise assets, but not the original IW annotation needed by GeoLattice to read the pulse repetition frequency and build the incidence-angle grid for azimuth-ambiguity tests. Therefore this remote-COG path does not automatically label ambiguity ghosts. If the matching original GRD SAFE is available locally, use ship.detect_ships_grd (or ship.read_prf, sentinel1.incidence_angle_grid, and ship.flag_azimuth_ambiguities) to add that quality-control step. Candidate tables should be reviewed against imagery and, where possible, independent vessel reports.

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
section: Optional IW SLC range sub-look coherence
text:
Optional IW SLC range sub-look coherence
Range sub-looks split an IW SLC’s processed range spectrum into lower- and upper-frequency images; GeoLattice calculates their local coherence with ship.sublook_coherence. Ships often retain higher coherence between sub-looks than sea clutter. Use an SLC from the same platform, pass, relative orbit, and acquisition as the GRD candidates where possible. This is not coherence between two dates or a replacement for interferometric coherence.
Planetary Computer publishes GRD and RTC collections, not SLC. Place an authorized, matching IW SLC SAFE product in Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones/hormuz_strait_sentinel1 to run the optional cell below. The processing is limited to IW1 and bursts whose range window intersects the AOI; select IW2/IW3 as appropriate for other swath coverage.


Code
SLC_SWATH = "IW1"
slc_safes = sorted(DATA_DIR.rglob("*.SAFE"))
slc_matches = [
    safe for safe in slc_safes
    if "_SLC__" in safe.name and safe.name[:3] == selected_item["id"][:3]
    and selected_item["properties"]["datetime"][:10].replace("-", "") in safe.name
]
if not slc_matches:
    print("No same-platform, same-date IW SLC SAFE found locally.")
    print("Planetary Computer's Sentinel-1 collection does not provide SLC; range sub-look coherence was not computed.")
    print("Add a matching authorized SAFE with annotation/ and measurement/ folders, then rerun this cell.")
else:
    import pandas as pd

    slc_safe = slc_matches[0]
    annotation_path = next(iter(sorted(slc_safe.glob(f"annotation/*-{SLC_SWATH.lower()}-slc-vv-*.xml"))), None)
    measurement_path = next(iter(sorted(slc_safe.glob(f"measurement/*-{SLC_SWATH.lower()}-slc-vv-*.tiff"))), None)
    if annotation_path is None or measurement_path is None:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Could not find {SLC_SWATH} VV annotation and measurement in {slc_safe}")
    ann = sentinel1.read_slc_annotation(annotation_path)
    processing_params = ship.read_processing_params(annotation_path)
    if targets.empty:
        print("No GRD candidates are available to sample for SLC sub-look coherence.")
    else:
        # Process a small neighborhood around the strongest GRD candidate to bound SLC memory.
        target_index = targets["mean_contrast_db"].idxmax() if "mean_contrast_db" in targets else targets.index[0]
        target = targets.loc[target_index]
        delta_lon = 0.015
        delta_lat = 0.015
        target_bounds = (
            max(PROCESSING_BOUNDS[0], float(target.lon) - delta_lon),
            max(PROCESSING_BOUNDS[1], float(target.lat) - delta_lat),
            min(PROCESSING_BOUNDS[2], float(target.lon) + delta_lon),
            min(PROCESSING_BOUNDS[3], float(target.lat) + delta_lat),
        )
        burst_ids, burst_cols = [], []
        for burst_id in range(len(ann["bursts"])):
            cols = sentinel1.burst_window(ann, burst_id, target_bounds, margin=200)
            if cols[1] - cols[0] >= 64:
                burst_ids.append(burst_id)
                burst_cols.append(cols)
        if not burst_ids:
            raise ValueError(f"No {SLC_SWATH} SLC bursts cover the strongest GRD candidate")
        common_cols = (min(c[0] for c in burst_cols), max(c[1] for c in burst_cols))
        coherence_layers = []
        for burst_id in burst_ids:
            burst = sentinel1.read_slc_burst(measurement_path, ann, burst_id, cols=common_cols)
            lower, upper = ship.range_sublooks(burst, processing_params, ann["range_sampling_rate"])
            valid_burst = np.isfinite(burst) & (np.abs(burst) > 0)
            coherence, _ = ship.sublook_coherence(lower, upper, window=(3, 9), valid=valid_burst)
            coherence_layers.append(coherence)
        candidate_coherence = ship.coherence_at_points(
            [target.lat], [target.lon], ann, burst_ids, common_cols, coherence_layers, sea_height=0.0
        )[0]
        targets.loc[target_index, "slc_range_sublook_coherence"] = candidate_coherence
        targets.to_csv(target_path, index=False)
        print(f"Strongest candidate index: {target_index} | sub-look coherence: {candidate_coherence:.3f}")
        print(f"Processed {len(burst_ids)} {SLC_SWATH} burst(s) around a bounded candidate window.")
        print(f"Updated candidate table: {target_path}")
    print(f"SLC source: {slc_safe.name} | swath: {SLC_SWATH}")

text:
View candidate detections on satellite imagery
This interactive Leafmap view overlays the AOI, the full-resolution processing window, and the screened GRD candidate locations on Esri World Imagery. import leafmap

section: Repeat the analysis near Abu Musa
text:
Repeat the analysis near Abu Musa
This second run uses the user-provided southwest and northeast coordinates (SW 26.483593, 54.904882; NE 25.877560, 55.953254), normalized to (west, south, east, north) order. It reuses the selected Sentinel-1 acquisition and the same calibration, shoreline mask, adaptive ENL estimate, and CFAR thresholds, then saves a separate candidate table and maps the results on satellite imagery. The selected scene intersects this region; its footprint covers approximately 99.96% of the requested rectangle, so check the footprint and image edges when interpreting detections.


Code
ABUMUSA_BOUNDS = (54.904882, 25.877560, 55.953254, 26.483593)
abumusa_geometry = box(*ABUMUSA_BOUNDS)
if not aoi_geometry.covers(abumusa_geometry):
    raise ValueError("The Abu Musa analysis bounds must lie inside the Hormuz Strait AOI")
if not selected_footprint.intersects(abumusa_geometry):
    raise ValueError("The selected GRD scene does not intersect the Abu Musa analysis bounds")

vv_abumusa_result = sentinel1.read_grd_subset(
    vv_source, vv_cal, vv_noise, bounds=ABUMUSA_BOUNDS, border_noise=True
)
vh_abumusa_result = sentinel1.read_grd_subset(
    vh_source, vh_cal, vh_noise, bounds=ABUMUSA_BOUNDS, border_noise=True
)
if vv_abumusa_result["data"].shape != vh_abumusa_result["data"].shape:
    raise ValueError("VV and VH Abu Musa windows differ; check that assets belong to the same GRD item")
vv_abumusa = vv_abumusa_result["data"]
vh_abumusa = vh_abumusa_result["data"]
gcps_abumusa = vh_abumusa_result["gcps"]

land_geoms_abumusa = [
    geom.intersection(abumusa_geometry)
    for geom in land.geometry
    if geom is not None and geom.intersects(abumusa_geometry)
]
inside_abumusa = geometry_mask(
    [abumusa_geometry],
    out_shape=vh_abumusa.shape,
    transform=from_gcps(gcps_abumusa),
    invert=True,
)
land_mask_abumusa = ship.land_mask_for_window(
    gcps_abumusa,
    vh_abumusa.shape,
    land_geoms_abumusa,
    buffer_m=300.0,
    pixel_spacing=10.0,
)
sea_abumusa = (
    inside_abumusa & ~land_mask_abumusa
    & np.isfinite(vv_abumusa) & np.isfinite(vh_abumusa) & (vh_abumusa > 0)
)
if not sea_abumusa.any():
    raise ValueError("No valid sea pixels remain in the Abu Musa analysis window")

enl_abumusa = ship.estimate_enl(vh_abumusa, sea_abumusa, block=64, max_cv_quantile=0.2)
detections_abumusa, background_db_abumusa = ship.cfar_tiled(
    np.nan_to_num(vh_abumusa, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0),
    sea_abumusa,
    tile=1024,
    method="gamma",
    pfa=PFA,
    enl=enl_abumusa,
    outer=OUTER_PIXELS,
    guard=GUARD_PIXELS,
    min_ring_fraction=0.7,
)
targets_abumusa = ship.extract_targets(
    detections_abumusa,
    np.nan_to_num(vh_abumusa, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0),
    np.nan_to_num(vv_abumusa, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0),
    gcps=gcps_abumusa,
    background_db=background_db_abumusa,
    pixel_spacing=10.0,
    min_px=3,
    max_px=500,
    min_mean_contrast_db=MIN_MEAN_CONTRAST_DB,
)
targets_abumusa = targets_abumusa.sort_values(
    "mean_contrast_db", ascending=False
).reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Abu Musa bounds (west, south, east, north): {ABUMUSA_BOUNDS}")
print(f"Calibrated window: {vh_abumusa.shape[0]:,} x {vh_abumusa.shape[1]:,} pixels")
print(f"Valid sea pixels: {sea_abumusa.sum():,} | estimated ENL: {enl_abumusa:.3f}")
print(f"CFAR-positive pixels: {detections_abumusa.sum():,}")
print(f"Candidates with mean contrast >= {MIN_MEAN_CONTRAST_DB:g} dB: {len(targets_abumusa):,}")

If a matching local IW SLC was found above, the next cell searches IW1, IW2, and IW3 for the swath that covers the strongest Abu Musa candidate and samples its range sub-look coherence. The coherence value is supplemental; it is not a standalone ship classifier.


Code
if targets_abumusa.empty:
    print("No Abu Musa candidates are available for the optional SLC coherence sample.")
elif not slc_matches:
    print("No matching local IW SLC is available; Abu Musa candidates remain GRD-only.")
else:
    target_abumusa = targets_abumusa.iloc[0]
    target_bounds_abumusa = (
        max(ABUMUSA_BOUNDS[0], float(target_abumusa.lon) - 0.015),
        max(ABUMUSA_BOUNDS[1], float(target_abumusa.lat) - 0.015),
        min(ABUMUSA_BOUNDS[2], float(target_abumusa.lon) + 0.015),
        min(ABUMUSA_BOUNDS[3], float(target_abumusa.lat) + 0.015),
    )
    swath_match = None
    for swath in ("IW1", "IW2", "IW3"):
        annotation_candidate = next(
            iter(sorted(slc_safe.glob(f"annotation/*-{swath.lower()}-slc-vv-*.xml"))), None
        )
        if annotation_candidate is None:
            continue
        annotation_candidate_data = sentinel1.read_slc_annotation(annotation_candidate)
        burst_candidate_ids, burst_candidate_cols = [], []
        for burst_id in range(len(annotation_candidate_data["bursts"])):
            cols = sentinel1.burst_window(
                annotation_candidate_data, burst_id, target_bounds_abumusa, margin=200
            )
            if cols[1] - cols[0] >= 64:
                burst_candidate_ids.append(burst_id)
                burst_candidate_cols.append(cols)
        if burst_candidate_ids:
            swath_match = (
                swath, annotation_candidate, annotation_candidate_data,
                burst_candidate_ids, burst_candidate_cols,
            )
            break

    if swath_match is None:
        print("No IW swath bursts cover the strongest Abu Musa candidate; coherence was skipped.")
    else:
        (swath_abumusa, annotation_path_abumusa, ann_abumusa,
         burst_ids_abumusa, burst_cols_abumusa) = swath_match
        measurement_path_abumusa = next(
            iter(sorted(slc_safe.glob(
                f"measurement/*-{swath_abumusa.lower()}-slc-vv-*.tiff"
            ))), None
        )
        if measurement_path_abumusa is None:
            raise FileNotFoundError(
                f"Could not find {swath_abumusa} VV SLC measurement in {slc_safe}"
            )
        processing_params_abumusa = ship.read_processing_params(annotation_path_abumusa)
        common_cols_abumusa = (
            min(cols[0] for cols in burst_cols_abumusa),
            max(cols[1] for cols in burst_cols_abumusa),
        )
        coherence_layers_abumusa = []
        for burst_id in burst_ids_abumusa:
            burst = sentinel1.read_slc_burst(
                measurement_path_abumusa, ann_abumusa, burst_id, cols=common_cols_abumusa
            )
            lower, upper = ship.range_sublooks(
                burst, processing_params_abumusa, ann_abumusa["range_sampling_rate"]
            )
            valid_burst = np.isfinite(burst) & (np.abs(burst) > 0)
            coherence_layer, _ = ship.sublook_coherence(
                lower, upper, window=(3, 9), valid=valid_burst
            )
            coherence_layers_abumusa.append(coherence_layer)
        coherence_abumusa = ship.coherence_at_points(
            [target_abumusa.lat], [target_abumusa.lon], ann_abumusa,
            burst_ids_abumusa, common_cols_abumusa, coherence_layers_abumusa, sea_height=0.0
        )[0]
        targets_abumusa.loc[0, "slc_range_sublook_coherence"] = coherence_abumusa
        print(
            f"Strongest Abu Musa candidate mean contrast: {target_abumusa.mean_contrast_db:.2f} dB | "
            f"{swath_abumusa} range sub-look coherence: {coherence_abumusa:.3f}"
        )

abumusa_csv_path = DATA_DIR / "grd_ship_candidates_abu_musa.csv"
targets_abumusa.to_csv(abumusa_csv_path, index=False)

vh_abumusa_db = sentinel1.to_db(vh_abumusa)
finite_abumusa_db = vh_abumusa_db[np.isfinite(vh_abumusa_db) & sea_abumusa]
if finite_abumusa_db.size == 0:
    raise ValueError("No finite VH dB values inside the Abu Musa sea mask")
vmin_abumusa, vmax_abumusa = np.percentile(finite_abumusa_db, [2, 98])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 7))
ax.imshow(vh_abumusa_db, cmap="gray", vmin=vmin_abumusa, vmax=vmax_abumusa, origin="upper")
ax.imshow(

if not targets_abumusa.empty:
    ax.scatter(
        targets_abumusa.col, targets_abumusa.row,
        s=18, facecolors="none", edgecolors="cyan", linewidths=0.8,
    )
ax.set(
    title=f"{selected_item['id']} VH sigma0 and candidates near Abu Musa",
    xlabel="Range sample", ylabel="Azimuth line",
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"Saved Abu Musa candidate table: {abumusa_csv_path}")

abumusa_map = leafmap.Map(
    center=((ABUMUSA_BOUNDS[1] + ABUMUSA_BOUNDS[3]) / 2,
            (ABUMUSA_BOUNDS[0] + ABUMUSA_BOUNDS[2]) / 2),
    zoom=9,
    height="700px",
    draw_control=False,
    measure_control=False,
)
abumusa_map.add_basemap("Esri.WorldImagery")
for layer in list(abumusa_map.layers):
    if getattr(layer, "name", None) == "OpenStreetMap":
        abumusa_map.remove_layer(layer)
abumusa_map.add_gdf(
    aoi,
    layer_name="Hormuz Strait AOI",
    style={"color": "#00ffff", "weight": 2, "fill": False},
    zoom_to_layer=False,
)
abumusa_area = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"name": ["Abu Musa analysis bounds"]},
    geometry=[abumusa_geometry],
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
abumusa_map.add_gdf(
    abumusa_area,
    layer_name="Abu Musa analysis window",
    style={"color": "#ff9900", "weight": 3, "fill": False},
    zoom_to_layer=False,
)
if not targets_abumusa.empty:
    popup_fields_abumusa = [
        field for field in [
            "mean_contrast_db", "contrast_db", "vh_peak_db", "vh_mean_db",
            "vh_vv_ratio_db", "n_px", "length_m", "width_m",
            "slc_range_sublook_coherence",
        ]
        if field in targets_abumusa.columns
    ]
    abumusa_map.add_points_from_xy(
        targets_abumusa,
        x="lon",
        y="lat",
        popup=popup_fields_abumusa,
        layer_name="Abu Musa GRD candidates",
        marker_colors=["red"],
        icon_colors=["white"],
        icon_names=["info"],

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
text:
Review, validation, and limitations
The candidate CSV is an initial detection list. Inspect candidates near coastlines, ports, islands, and bright fixed structures; compare VV/VH contrast and size; and check for along-track ghost patterns. If AIS data are available for this region and acquisition time, GeoLattice ship.match_points can compare detections with vessel positions and ship.detection_scores can report precision, recall, and F1. AIS is not bundled here and should only be used after verifying its timestamp, coverage, and position accuracy. Do not treat unvalidated detections or coherence thresholds as confirmed vessel identities.

title: Ship Detection in the Strait of Hormuz with Sentinel-1
text:
Summary and conclusions
This notebook uses GeoLattice to search Sentinel-1 IW GRDH dual-polarization acquisitions, read a georeferenced AOI window with radiometric calibration and noise removal, mask land and coastal clutter, and find candidate vessels using tiled gamma-CFAR on VH intensity. It reports the selected scene’s AOI coverage and saves candidate attributes to CSV. If a matching local IW SLC SAFE is supplied, range sub-look coherence can be sampled at the GRD candidates as an additional feature. The candidate locations are also displayed interactively on satellite imagery with Leafmap. A second analysis and satellite map cover the user-provided Abu Musa area, with a separate candidate CSV.
The catalog’s GRD data are not complex SLC samples, so they cannot support sub-look coherence by themselves. This example selects one scene rather than mosaicking the full multi-orbit catalog. Scene-edge coverage, coastline quality, false alarms, ambiguities, and vessel motion must be reviewed before operational use; independent AIS or manual image interpretation is recommended for validation.

text:
Overview
The supplied sibling flood_mapping.ipynb is empty, so the documented UN-SPIDER steps are the workflow reference.
Unlike a synthetic demo, this workflow reads and calibrates the actual SAFE measurement subsets, co-registers the dates on a common grid, and detects change from pre- and post-flood VH backscatter composites. The available scenes are all ascending, relative orbit 114: May 24 and June 5, 2025 (before), July 11 and August 16, 2025 (after).
Interpretation and limits: The supplied folder contains no DEM, JRC permanent-water, population, or land-cover rasters. The output is therefore a radar-derived candidate flood extent; slope/permanent-water exclusions and exposure/damage estimates are not made. Flood detections can include seasonal or permanent water and other surface changes.

text:
Set dates and Sentinel-1 parameters
Use date windows rather than one acquisition, the same polarization and pass, and the same relative orbit for both periods. Metadata in the local SAFE manifests is checked below. A 30 m common grid keeps this local workflow manageable while retaining the broad flood signal.


Code
# Analysis parameters: date windows, polarization/orbit filters, grid, and detection thresholds.

# 1. Pre- and post-flood date windows. Using a window rather than one date lets step 3 pick
#    every matching local scene, which are then median-composited in step 5 to reduce speckle.
BEFORE = ("2025-05-01", "2025-06-30")
AFTER = ("2025-07-01", "2025-08-31")

# 2. Keep one polarization, pass direction, and relative orbit so every scene compared
#    shares the same viewing geometry; mixing orbits/passes would look like spurious change.
POLARIZATION = "VH"
PASS_DIRECTION = "ASCENDING"
RELATIVE_ORBIT = 114

# 3. Common analysis grid: UTM zone 46N (covers Sylhet) resampled to 30 m pixels.
GRID_CRS = "EPSG:32646"
RESOLUTION_M = 30.0

# 4. Flood-detection tuning: a post/pre backscatter ratio below 0.80 (a >=20% drop in linear
#    sigma-nought) flags candidate new water; a 3x3 median filter suppresses speckle first;
#    detected blobs smaller than 8 pixels are discarded as noise.
RATIO_THRESHOLD = 0.80  # new-water post/pre linear backscatter ratio
SMOOTH_SIZE = 3         # median-filter window in pixels
MIN_PIXELS = 8          # remove isolated detections smaller than this component size
print(f"Before {BEFORE[0]} to {BEFORE[1]}; after {AFTER[0]} to {AFTER[1]}")
print(f"{POLARIZATION}, {PASS_DIRECTION} relative orbit {RELATIVE_ORBIT}; {RESOLUTION_M:g} m grid")

section: Inventory and filter the local scenes
text:
Inventory and filter the local scenes
Read pass direction and relative orbit from each manifest.safe, then retain only scenes inside the selected date periods with the requested polarization and orbit. This avoids comparing different viewing geometries.


Code
# Catalogue every local SAFE product, then keep only the ones matching the chosen orbit,
# pass direction, polarization, and date windows.

# 1. Parse one SAFE product's manifest.safe for its pass direction (ascending/descending)
#    and relative orbit number, by walking the XML tree for the matching tags.
def manifest_metadata(safe_path):
    root = ET.parse(safe_path / "manifest.safe").getroot()
    pass_direction, relative_orbit = None, None
    for element in root.iter():
        tag = element.tag.rsplit("}", 1)[-1]
        if tag == "pass" and element.text:
            pass_direction = element.text.strip().upper()
        elif tag == "relativeOrbitNumber" and element.attrib.get("type") == "start":
            relative_orbit = int(element.text)
    if pass_direction is None or relative_orbit is None:
        raise ValueError(f"Could not read pass/orbit metadata from {safe_path / 'manifest.safe'}")
    return pass_direction, relative_orbit

# 2. Build a catalogue of every *.SAFE folder in DATA_DIR: acquisition date (parsed from the
#    SAFE filename), pass/orbit (from the manifest), available polarizations, and the
#    read_safe() handle used later to locate each band's measurement/calibration/noise files.
scene_catalog = []
for safe_path in sorted(DATA_DIR.glob("*.SAFE")):
    scene_date = datetime.strptime(safe_path.name.split("_")[5][:8], "%Y%m%d").date()
    info = read_safe(safe_path)
    pass_direction, relative_orbit = manifest_metadata(safe_path)
    polarizations = tuple(sorted(p.upper() for p in info["measurement"]))
    scene_catalog.append({
        "path": safe_path,
        "date": scene_date,
        "pass": pass_direction,
        "relative_orbit": relative_orbit,
        "polarizations": polarizations,
        "info": info,
    })

# 3. Display the full catalogue as a table before filtering, for a visual sanity check.
catalog = gpd.pd.DataFrame([
    {"date": s["date"].isoformat(), "pass": s["pass"],
     "relative orbit": s["relative_orbit"], "polarizations": ", ".join(s["polarizations"]),
     "SAFE": s["path"].name}
    for s in scene_catalog
])
display(catalog)

# 4. Keep scenes that match the chosen pass direction, relative orbit, and polarization, and
#    fall inside either the BEFORE or AFTER date window; split the result into pre/post lists.
before_start, before_end = (datetime.strptime(d, "%Y-%m-%d").date() for d in BEFORE)
after_start, after_end = (datetime.strptime(d, "%Y-%m-%d").date() for d in AFTER)
selected = [
    s for s in scene_catalog
    if s["pass"] == PASS_DIRECTION
    and s["relative_orbit"] == RELATIVE_ORBIT
    and POLARIZATION in s["polarizations"]
    and (before_start <= s["date"] <= before_end or after_start <= s["date"] <= after_end)
]
pre_scenes = [s for s in selected if before_start <= s["date"] <= before_end]
post_scenes = [s for s in selected if after_start <= s["date"] <= after_end]
if not pre_scenes or not post_scenes:
    raise ValueError(f"Need scenes in both periods; found {len(pre_scenes)} pre and {len(post_scenes)} post")
print(f"Selected {len(pre_scenes)} pre-flood and {len(post_scenes)} post-flood scenes.")
for item in selected:
    print(item["date"], item["pass"], f"relative orbit {item['relative_orbit']}", item["path"].name)

title: Flood Mapping with Sentinel-1 Data - Sylhet, Bangladesh
section: Calibrate, subset, and co-register the GRD scenes
text:
Calibrate, subset, and co-register the GRD scenes
read_grd_subset reads only the AOI window from each large measurement GeoTIFF, applies the SAFE calibration/noise LUTs, and zeros border noise. create_stack geocodes each window onto one shared UTM grid using its geolocation control points. Values remain in linear sigma-nought units for physically meaningful temporal ratios.


Code
# Read, calibrate, and co-register each selected scene onto one common UTM grid.

# 1. For every selected scene, read only the AOI window (plus a 100 m margin) from the VH
#    measurement GeoTIFF, applying the SAFE calibration/noise LUTs to produce calibrated
#    sigma-nought backscatter and zeroing out border-noise artifacts near the swath edges.
subsets, scene_times = [], []
for scene in selected:
    info = scene["info"]
    pol = POLARIZATION.lower()
    subset = rs.sar.read_grd_subset(
        info["measurement"][pol],
        info["calibration"][pol],
        info["noise"][pol],
        bounds=AOI_BOUNDS,
        margin=100,
        kind="sigmaNought",
        border_noise=True,
    )
    subsets.append(subset)
    scene_times.append(np.datetime64(scene["date"].isoformat()))
    print(f"{scene['date']}: read window {subset['window']}, {subset['data'].shape}, {len(subset['gcps'])} local GCPs")

# 2. Geocode every scene's window onto one shared grid (GRID_CRS, RESOLUTION_M) using its
#    ground control points, stacking the results along a time dimension. This turns scenes
#    read from different raw pixel grids into pixel-for-pixel comparable arrays.
stack = rs.sar.create_stack(
    subsets,
    scene_times,
    bounds=AOI_BOUNDS,
    crs=GRID_CRS,
    resolution=RESOLUTION_M,
    resampling="bilinear",
    name=f"{POLARIZATION.lower()}_sigma0",
)
# 3. Report the stack shape and how much of the grid's bounding box each date actually covers.
scene_coverage = np.isfinite(stack.values).mean(axis=(1, 2))
print("Common stack shape:", stack.shape)
for date, coverage in zip(stack.time.values, scene_coverage):
    print(f"{np.datetime_as_string(date, unit='D')}: {coverage:.1%} valid coverage of grid bounding box")

title: Flood Mapping with Sentinel-1 Data - Sylhet, Bangladesh
section: Build the before/after composites and mask to the AOI
text:
Build the before/after composites and mask to the AOI
A temporal median reduces single-date speckle and transient noise. The 3×3 median filter is then applied by GeoLattice as part of the UN-SPIDER workflow. The AOI polygon is rasterized on the common grid, so pixels outside the supplied boundary do not contribute to detections or area statistics.


Code
# Build the pre-/post-flood composites and mask both to the AOI polygon.

# 1. Temporal median across each period's dates reduces speckle and transient noise that a
#    single scene would carry; stack.sel(...) picks only that period's time slices first.
pre_times = [np.datetime64(s["date"].isoformat()) for s in pre_scenes]
post_times = [np.datetime64(s["date"].isoformat()) for s in post_scenes]
before = stack.sel(time=pre_times).median(dim="time", skipna=True).rename("before_vh_sigma0")
after = stack.sel(time=post_times).median(dim="time", skipna=True).rename("after_vh_sigma0")

# 2. Rasterize the AOI polygon onto the common grid: True inside the AOI, False outside.
#    geometry_mask with invert=True marks pixels covered by the polygon as True.
aoi_projected = aoi.to_crs(GRID_CRS)
aoi_inside = geometry_mask(
    [mapping(geom) for geom in aoi_projected.geometry],
    out_shape=(stack.sizes["y"], stack.sizes["x"]),
    transform=stack.rio.transform(),
    invert=True,
    all_touched=False,
)
# 3. Wrap that boolean grid as a georeferenced DataArray and use it to null out pixels
#    outside the AOI in both composites, so later statistics only count AOI pixels.
aoi_mask = xr.DataArray(
    aoi_inside, dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": stack.y, "x": stack.x}, name="aoi_mask"
).rio.write_crs(GRID_CRS).rio.write_transform(stack.rio.transform())
before = before.where(aoi_mask)
after = after.where(aoi_mask)

# 4. valid_data flags pixels that are inside the AOI AND have a finite value in both
#    composites; it is reused throughout to keep area statistics and exports consistent.
valid_data = np.isfinite(before.values) & np.isfinite(after.values) & aoi_inside
print(f"AOI pixels: {int(aoi_inside.sum()):,}")
print(f"AOI pixels with both period composites: {int(valid_data.sum()):,} ({valid_data.sum()/aoi_inside.sum():.1%})")

title: Flood Mapping with Sentinel-1 Data - Sylhet, Bangladesh
text:
Inspect the radar composites
The maps are calibrated VH sigma-nought displayed in dB. Compare the pre- and post-flood composites before applying the ratio threshold; water commonly appears darker, but vegetation, soil moisture, and acquisition conditions can also change the signal.


Code
# Convert both composites to dB and plot them side by side for a visual before/after check.

# 1. rs.sar.to_db converts linear sigma-nought to decibels (10*log10); the AOI mask keeps
#    pixels outside the study area as NaN so they do not affect the color stretch below.
before_db = rs.sar.to_db(before).where(aoi_mask)
after_db = rs.sar.to_db(after).where(aoi_mask)

# 2. A shared 2nd-98th percentile stretch (computed from both dates' valid pixels) keeps the
#    before/after panels on the same grayscale scale, so darker really means lower backscatter
#    in both images rather than an artifact of two different per-image stretches.
valid_db = np.concatenate([
    before_db.values[np.isfinite(before_db.values)],
    after_db.values[np.isfinite(after_db.values)],
])
vmin, vmax = np.percentile(valid_db, [2, 98])

# imshow defaults to pixel coordinates; use the raster's UTM transform so the
# GeoDataFrame AOI boundary and SAR pixels are drawn in the same map coordinates.
transform = stack.rio.transform()
MAP_EXTENT = (
    transform.c,
    transform.c + transform.a * stack.sizes["x"],
    transform.f + transform.e * stack.sizes["y"],
    transform.f,
)

# 3. Shared helper for every map panel in this notebook: draws a raster in true map
#    coordinates (via MAP_EXTENT) and overlays the AOI boundary in cyan on top of it.
def show_map_image(ax, values, *, cmap, vmin=None, vmax=None, alpha=1.0):
    image = ax.imshow(
        np.ma.masked_invalid(values),
        extent=MAP_EXTENT,
        origin="upper",
        interpolation="nearest",
        cmap=cmap,
        vmin=vmin,
        vmax=vmax,
        alpha=alpha,
    )
    aoi_projected.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="cyan", linewidth=0.8, zorder=4)
    ax.set_xlim(MAP_EXTENT[0], MAP_EXTENT[1])
    ax.set_ylim(MAP_EXTENT[2], MAP_EXTENT[3])
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel("UTM easting (m)")
    ax.set_ylabel("UTM northing (m)")
    return image

# 4. Draw the before/after dB composites side by side with one shared colorbar.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.5), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, image, title in zip(
    axes,
    [before_db, after_db],
    ["Before composite VH (dB)", "After composite VH (dB)"],
):
    view = show_map_image(ax, image.values, cmap="gray", vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)
    ax.set_title(title)
fig.colorbar(view, ax=axes, shrink=0.78, label="Backscatter (dB)")
plt.show()

title: Flood Mapping with Sentinel-1 Data - Sylhet, Bangladesh
section: Detect new water with the backscatter ratio
text:
Detect new water with the backscatter ratio
The GeoLattice un_spider_flood_mapping implementation converts linear backscatter to a post/pre linear ratio, applies a 3×3 median filter, and identifies new-water candidates below 0.80 (at least a 20% decrease). It also removes connected components smaller than eight pixels. No permanent-water or slope mask is passed because those source rasters are not present locally.


Code
# Detect candidate new-water pixels from the post/pre linear backscatter ratio.

# 1. un_spider_flood_mapping implements the UN-SPIDER recipe: compute the post/pre ratio in
#    linear units, apply a 3x3 median filter (SMOOTH_SIZE) to suppress speckle, flag pixels
#    whose ratio falls below RATIO_THRESHOLD as candidate new water, and drop connected
#    components smaller than MIN_PIXELS as likely noise rather than real flood patches.
flood_result = rs.sar.un_spider_flood_mapping(
    before,
    after,
    units="linear",
    ratio_threshold=RATIO_THRESHOLD,
    smooth_size=SMOOTH_SIZE,
    min_pixels=MIN_PIXELS,
)
# 2. Clip the ratio to the AOI, and intersect the flood mask with valid_data so neither
#    out-of-AOI pixels nor pixels missing from either composite are counted as flood.
ratio = flood_result["ratio"].where(aoi_mask).rename("post_pre_sigma0_ratio")
flood_values = np.asarray(flood_result["flood"].values, dtype=bool) & valid_data
flood = flood_result["flood"].copy(data=flood_values).rename("candidate_flood")

# 3. Convert the flagged pixel count to hectares using the grid's pixel area, and report it.
pixel_area_m2 = abs(float(stack.rio.transform().a * stack.rio.transform().e))
flood_pixels = int(flood_values.sum())

print(f"Candidate flood pixels: {flood_pixels:,}")
print(f"Candidate flood area: {flood_area_ha:,.1f} ha")
print("Note: candidate extent is not corrected for permanent water or terrain slope.")

Write the radar-derived flood candidate, post/pre ratio, and the two smoothed dB composites as COGs. The flood raster uses 255 as NoData outside the AOI or where either period lacks valid data. Polygon output is generated from the same clipped candidate mask.

# Export the raster and vector flood products as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs and a GeoPackage.

# 1. The flood mask, as uint8 (0/1), with 255 marking NoData outside the AOI or wherever
#    either period lacked a valid composite value (per valid_data from step 5).
flood_raster = flood.astype("uint8").where(xr.DataArray(valid_data, dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": stack.y, "x": stack.x}), 255)
flood_raster = flood_raster.rio.write_crs(GRID_CRS).rio.write_transform(stack.rio.transform()).rio.write_nodata(255)
ratio_export = ratio.where(xr.DataArray(valid_data, dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": stack.y, "x": stack.x}))

# 2. The smoothed before/after composites (post-median-filter, as used for detection) in dB,
#    with a float NoData sentinel (-9999) marking AOI/coverage gaps for the ratio and dB rasters.
before_export = rs.sar.to_db(flood_result["pre_smoothed"]).where(aoi_mask).rename("before_vh_db")
after_export = rs.sar.to_db(flood_result["post_smoothed"]).where(aoi_mask).rename("after_vh_db")
FLOAT_NODATA = -9999.0
ratio_export = ratio_export.fillna(FLOAT_NODATA).rio.write_nodata(FLOAT_NODATA, encoded=True)
before_export = before_export.fillna(FLOAT_NODATA).rio.write_nodata(FLOAT_NODATA, encoded=True)
after_export = after_export.fillna(FLOAT_NODATA).rio.write_nodata(FLOAT_NODATA, encoded=True)

# 3. Write all four rasters as COGs under OUTPUT_DIR.
rs.write(flood_raster.rename("candidate_flood"), OUTPUT_DIR / "sylhet_flood_extent.tif", nodata=255)

# 4. Vectorize the flood mask into polygons (dropping fragments under MIN_PIXELS again) and

flood_vector = rs.sar.mask_to_polygons(flood, min_pixels=MIN_PIXELS)
if flood_vector.empty:

title: Wild Fire Burned-area Mapping
text:
Overview
Sentinel-2 burn radiometric indices are mathematical combinations of spectral bands from the Sentinel-2 satellite used to detect and measure the effects of fire on vegetation, soil, and land surfaces. They help researchers identify burned areas, estimate burn severity, monitor vegetation damage, and assess post-fire recovery using satellite imagery.

Important Sentinel-2 spectral bands
Sentinel-2 provides 13 spectral bands. Several are particularly useful for burn detection.









Band
Wavelength
Spatial resolution
Relevance to fire




B2 — Blue
490 nm
10 m
Surface and atmospheric information


B3 — Green
560 nm
10 m
Vegetation and surface reflectance


B4 — Red
665 nm
10 m
Chlorophyll absorption and vegetation damage


B8 — NIR
842 nm
10 m
Vegetation structure and canopy damage


B8A — Narrow NIR
865 nm
20 m
Vegetation and canopy characteristics


B11 — SWIR1
1610 nm
20 m
Vegetation moisture and burned surfaces


B12 — SWIR2
2190 nm
20 m
Burn scars, dry vegetation, and surface changes



Key idea: Near-infrared (NIR) reflectance is generally high for healthy vegetation, while shortwave infrared (SWIR) reflectance often increases as vegetation dries or burns. This makes NIR–SWIR combinations particularly valuable for mapping burned areas.
Note that the original spatial resolution of B11 and B12 is 20 m, even when the final index map is resampled to 10 m.


Major Sentinel-2 burn indices and their formulas
The following are widely used indices for burned-area mapping and fire-impact assessment. 

Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR)
Purpose: Detect burned areas and assess changes in vegetation caused by fire.
\[\mathrm{NBR}=\frac{B8-B12}{B8+B12} \]

B8: Near-infrared (NIR)
B12: Shortwave infrared 2 (SWIR2)

Interpretation:

High positive NBR: often healthy, green vegetation.
Low NBR: potentially burned vegetation, bare soil, or dry vegetation.
Negative NBR: surfaces with relatively high SWIR reflectance compared with NIR.

NBR is usually the first index to calculate when mapping wildfire damage.


Differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR)
Purpose: Estimate the magnitude of vegetation change between pre-fire and post-fire images.
\[ \mathrm{dNBR}=\mathrm{NBR}\_{pre}-\mathrm{NBR}\_{post} \]
A commonly used set of approximate dNBR severity classes is shown below. These thresholds are illustrative; classification systems should be adapted to local vegetation and validated with field data.



dNBR
Approximate interpretation




Below −0.25
Substantial post-fire greening or other change


−0.25 to −0.10
Moderate greening


−0.10 to +0.10
Little apparent change


+0.10 to +0.27
Low severity


+0.27 to +0.44
Moderate-low severity


+0.44 to +0.66
Moderate-high severity


Above +0.66
High severity





Normalized Burn Ratio 2 (NBR2)
Purpose: Examine changes in surface and vegetation moisture using two SWIR bands.
\[ \mathrm{NBR2}=\frac{B11-B12}{B11+B12} \]

B11: SWIR1
B12: SWIR2

NBR2 can help distinguish burned surfaces from unburned vegetation and assess changes associated with drying. It is also useful for tracking post-fire conditions, although soil type and background moisture can affect its performance.


Burned Area Index (BAI)
Purpose: Highlight pixels whose red and NIR reflectance resembles the spectral characteristics of burned surfaces.
\[ \mathrm{BAI}= \frac{1}{(0.1-B4)^2+(0.06-B8)^2} \]

B4: Red
B8: NIR

BAI is designed to emphasize pixels near reference reflectance values associated with burned surfaces. Higher values can indicate potential burned areas.
Important: BAI is sensitive to reflectance scaling. The reference values 0.1 and 0.06 assume reflectance is expressed as a fraction (for example, 0.10 rather than 1000 in scaled Sentinel-2 data).


Burned Area Index for Sentinel-2 (BAIS2)
Purpose: Use visible, red-edge, NIR, and SWIR bands to improve burned-area detection.
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{BAIS2}={}& \left(1-\sqrt{\frac{B6B7B8A}{B4}}\right)\\\ &\times\left(\frac{B12-B8A}{\sqrt{B12+B8A}}+1\right) \end{aligned} \]
This index incorporates vegetation red-edge bands B6 and B7, narrow NIR B8A, red B4, and SWIR2 B12. It was developed specifically for Sentinel-2 imagery and can provide additional discrimination between burned and unburned surfaces. 


Mid-Infrared Burn Index (MIRBI)
Purpose: Separate burned surfaces from unburned backgrounds using SWIR reflectance.
\[\mathrm{MIRBI}=10B12-9.8B11+2\]
MIRBI uses the contrast between the two SWIR bands. It is especially useful in some dry environments where burned ground, ash, and dry vegetation have distinct SWIR responses.
Use the reflectance scaling and formulation appropriate to the source of your imagery; MIRBI is not a normalized index and its numerical range depends on the input scale.

title: Wild Fire Burned-area Mapping
section: How to calculate burn indices from Sentinel-2 imagery
text:
How to calculate burn indices from Sentinel-2 imagery
Step 1 — Obtain satellite images
Download Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance imagery from before and after the fire.
Step 2 — Preprocess the images
Mask clouds, cirrus, cloud shadows, and invalid pixels. Ensure both dates use compatible reflectance values, spatial alignment, and projection.
Step 3 — Calculate the indices
Apply the equations to each pixel to create NBR, NBR2, BAI, BAIS2, or MIRBI raster layers.
Step 4 — Map burn extent and severity
Calculate dNBR from the pre- and post-fire NBR layers, classify the change, and validate the result against reference data.
The sections below do this locally with GeoLattice. get_images searches the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC catalog and writes AOI-clipped GeoTIFFs to disk. Scaling, cloud masking, compositing, burn indices, and the GeoTIFF export then run on those files.

title: Wild Fire Burned-area Mapping
text:
Which index should you choose?

For burned-area mapping: Start with NBR and compare it with BAI or BAIS2.
For burn severity: Use dNBR, preferably supported by field observations or an established local classification.
For dry vegetation and soil backgrounds: Test MIRBI and NBR2 alongside NBR.
For vegetation recovery: Track NDVI and NBR across multiple post-fire dates.

My recommendation: Start with NBR, dNBR, and BAIS2, then compare their performance using reference burned-area data. No single index performs best in every ecosystem, and drought, harvesting, bare soil, and seasonal vegetation changes can mimic fire-related spectral changes.

title: Wild Fire Burned-area Mapping
section: Select a wildfire for the case study
text:
Select a wildfire for the case study
The CAL FIRE archive currently reports the following large incidents:
Bug Fire: Lassen and Sierra counties · Started August 8, 2026, 93,733 acres, 100% containment listed in the archive.
Biscar Fire: Lassen County · Started July 18, 2026, 69,355 acres, 98% containment listed in the archive.
Plaskett Fire: Monterey County · Started August 26, 2026, 30,124 acres, 100% containment listed in the archive.
These are the incident acreage figures published by CAL FIRE, not independent satellite-derived measurements. Imagery must be examined to estimate the observed burned footprint. 
For this tutorial, we’ll use the Bug Fire as the example because of its large reported footprint. The same workflow can be adapted to the other fires. A large fire may cover multiple Sentinel-2 tiles, so use a fire perimeter to constrain the analysis rather than downloading an entire satellite scene unnecessarily.

title: Wild Fire Burned-area Mapping
text:
What will we produce?

Satellite imagery: Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance before and after the fire
Burn index rasters: NBR, dNBR, NDVI, and optionally NBR2 and BAIS2
Burned-area maps
A spatial map of candidate burned pixels and severity classes- Estimated hectares and acres, change statistics, and accuracy assessment

A key distinction: burned-area extent and burn severity are different products. Burned area answers “where did the fire burn?” Burn severity estimates the magnitude of ecological and surface change within the affected area.

title: Wild Fire Burned-area Mapping
text:
Set up your Python environment
This tutorial uses GeoLattice for local image download and processing. geolattice.rsense.get_images searches a STAC catalog and saves only the bands you ask for, clipped to the fire perimeter. Later cells read those GeoTIFFs, scale them to reflectance, mask clouds with the Scene Classification Layer, and calculate burn indices.
The dataset is Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance from the Microsoft Planetary Computer. Reflectance bands are stored as integers scaled by 10,000, with a −1000 offset on scenes processed since 25 January 2022. The Scene Classification Layer (SCL) identifies clouds, shadows, water, and vegetation.

Install the required libraries
rsense-access installs the Planetary Computer STAC client that get_images uses. Run this once in the notebook environment:
If you’re using Ubuntu and an existing Python environment, activate your virtual environment before running the installation.


Import GeoLattice and required libraries
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.

text:
Obtain the fire perimeter
A fire perimeter is a polygon outlining the reported extent of a fire. It gives us an area of interest (AOI) so we can restrict satellite processing to the relevant region.
The next cell reads Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones/bug_fire_sentinel2/bug_fire_perimeter.geojson when that file is already present. Otherwise it downloads the Bug Fire polygon from the NIFC WFIGS Interagency Fire Perimeters service: incident name Bug, state US-CA. That record is the Lassen County fire discovered on 8 August 2026, about 93,733 acres. The current-perimeter layer drops incidents after they leave the active list, so the query uses the full interagency archive.
Use this fire footprint as the AOI. A county boundary would download far more imagery than the burn.

Read and inspect the perimeter


Code
import json
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlencode
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd


# This section downloads or loads the fire perimeter for the Bug Fire, checks/cleans the GeoDataFrame, and provides summary info.
# 1. Check for perimeter GeoJSON. If missing, it queries the NIFC ArcGIS service for the Bug Fire perimeter in California, saves as GeoJSON.
# 2. Reads the GeoJSON with geopandas, fixes CRS, and if needed, selects only features from the correct year and largest area.
# 3. Keeps only relevant columns, prints out summary info about the loaded fire perimeter, and displays it as an interactive map.

if "DATA" not in globals():
    DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones/bug_fire_sentinel2")
perimeter_path = DATA / "bug_fire_perimeter.geojson"
perimeter_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# URL for the full archive of fire perimeters (not just active fires)
WFIGS_PERIMETERS = (
    "https://services3.arcgis.com/T4QMspbfLg3qTGWY/arcgis/rest/services/"
    "WFIGS_Interagency_Perimeters/FeatureServer/0/query"
)

# Only download the perimeter if we don't already have it locally
if not perimeter_path.exists():
    # Construct request parameters to select the Bug Fire in CA and get wanted fields as GeoJSON with specified SRID and geometry precision
    query = urlencode({
        "where": "poly_IncidentName='Bug' AND attr_POOState='US-CA'",
        "outFields": ",".join([
            "poly_IncidentName",
            "poly_GISAcres",
            "attr_POOState",
            "attr_POOCounty",
            "attr_FireDiscoveryDateTime",
        ]),
        "f": "geojson",
        "outSR": "4326",
        "geometryPrecision": "5",
    })
    request = Request(
        WFIGS_PERIMETERS + "?" + query,
        headers={"User-Agent": "geolattice-tutorial/1.0"},
    )
    # Fetch the result (timeout set generously), load as JSON
    with urlopen(request, timeout=120) as response:
        payload = response.read()
    downloaded = json.loads(payload)
    # If no features were returned, halt with an informative error
    if not downloaded.get("features"):
        raise RuntimeError(
            "NIFC returned no Bug Fire perimeter for California. "
            f"Save a perimeter GeoJSON at {perimeter_path}."
        )
    # Save the downloaded result
    perimeter_path.write_bytes(payload)
    print("Downloaded Bug Fire perimeter to", perimeter_path.resolve())
else:
    print("Using existing perimeter", perimeter_path.resolve())

# Load the perimeter as a GeoDataFrame
fire_gdf = gpd.read_file(perimeter_path)
if fire_gdf.empty:
    raise ValueError("The perimeter file contains no features.")

# Ensure the GeoDataFrame has a CRS; if not, set it to WGS84
if fire_gdf.crs is None:
    fire_gdf = fire_gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
fire_gdf = fire_gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

# If the fire discovery time is present, parse it and filter for fires in 2026 only
if "attr_FireDiscoveryDateTime" in fire_gdf.columns:
    fire_gdf["discovery"] = pd.to_datetime(
        fire_gdf["attr_FireDiscoveryDateTime"], unit="ms", utc=True
    )
    in_2026 = fire_gdf["discovery"].dt.year == 2026
    if in_2026.any():
        fire_gdf = fire_gdf.loc[in_2026].copy()

# If for some reason multiple features remain, keep only the largest by reported acres
if "poly_GISAcres" in fire_gdf.columns and len(fire_gdf) > 1:
    fire_gdf = fire_gdf.sort_values("poly_GISAcres", ascending=False).head(1)

# Choose a subset of columns to keep for clarity
keep = [
    column for column in (
        "poly_IncidentName", "poly_GISAcres", "attr_POOCounty", "discovery", "geometry"
    )
    if column in fire_gdf.columns
]
fire_gdf = fire_gdf[keep].reset_index(drop=True)

# Print basic info about the fire perimeter for inspection and debugging
print(fire_gdf.drop(columns="geometry"))
print("CRS:", fire_gdf.crs)
print("Number of features:", len(fire_gdf))
print(
    "Bounds (west, south, east, north):",
    tuple(round(float(v), 4) for v in fire_gdf.total_bounds),
)

# Display perimeter as an interactive map (folium/leaflet in a Jupyter notebook)
fire_gdf.explore()
