The 1 km sensors average a whole section of land: on the Westside, one MODIS pixel can hold an irrigated orchard, a fallow field and a road. Anchor pixels at 1 km are therefore less pure than at 30 m, and the extremes of the LST and NDVI scatter shrink.


Thermal sharpening
Thermal sharpening (Kustas et al. 2003; Gao et al. 2012) uses the fact that at any one time and place LST is largely explained by surface properties that a finer sensor sees: vegetation cover, moisture (shortwave infrared) and brightness. The data mining sharpener (DMS) of Gao et al.:

Aggregates the fine reflectance bands to the coarse thermal grid.
Fits a regression (decision tree, random forest or boosting) between coarse LST and the aggregated bands, using the most homogeneous coarse pixels, where the relation is cleanest.
Applies the regression to the fine bands to predict fine LST.
Adds back the coarse residual (observed minus aggregated prediction), so the sharpened image averages exactly to the observed coarse LST (energy conservation).

The sharpened LST is a statistical estimate: it cannot recover temperature contrasts that the reflectance does not explain, such as two identical green fields under different irrigation.


MOD16
MODIS also has its own ET product, MOD16 (Mu et al. 2011), a Penman-Monteith model with surface conductances from LAI and weather, published every 8 days and yearly at 500 m. It uses no thermal band; notebook 11 compares its annual total with Landsat.

text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (registers the .rio accessor)
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.rsense.surface_energy_balance as seb  # energy balance and ET models
import seb_data as sd  # chapter helper: downloads, caches and loads the scenes

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results written by this chapter
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed
print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__, "| data folder", sd.DATA.relative_to(sd.DATA.parents[3]))  # versions and paths

from pyproj import Transformer  # coordinate transformations
from rasterio.enums import Resampling  # resampling methods
from scipy.ndimage import zoom  # bilinear upsampling for a baseline
from geolattice.rsense.optical.sensors import sentinel3 as s3  # Sentinel-3 readers

SITE = sd.WESTSIDE  # Landsat window
LAT, LON = SITE["lat"], SITE["lon"]  # scene centre for sun angles and weather
landsat = sd.load_scene()  # Landsat 8, 5 July 2024
path = OUT / "metric_20240705.nc"  # METRIC result of notebook 06
metric = xr.open_dataset(path).load() if path.exists() else sd.run_metric_scene(landsat)  # read or recompute
metric = metric.rio.write_crs(landsat.rio.crs)  # same UTM 11N grid as the Landsat stack
ref_daily = sd.daily_reference(SITE, "2024-01-01", "2024-12-31")  # daily ERA5 reference ET of 2024


def metric_chain(lst, ndvi, albedo, lai, dem, when, mask, etr_daily):  # METRIC from any sensor's layers
    wx = seb.interpolate_weather(sd.weather(SITE, f"{when:%Y-%m-%d}", f"{when:%Y-%m-%d}")["hourly"], when)  # ERA5 at the overpass
    ea = float(seb.actual_vapour_pressure(t_dew_c=wx["dew_point_2m"]))  # kPa
    u2 = float(seb.wind_2m(wx["wind_speed_10m"], 10))  # m/s
    z = float(dem.median())  # m
    etr_h = float(seb.asce_pm_hourly(wx["temperature_2m"], ea, wx["shortwave_radiation"] * 0.0036, u2, z, LAT, LON, when, reference="tall"))  # mm/h
    cos_t = float(np.cos(np.radians(seb.solar_position(LAT, LON, when)["zenith"])))  # flat ground
    P = seb.pressure_from_elevation(dem)  # kPa
    tau = seb.broadband_transmissivity(cos_t, pressure=P, ea=ea)  # transmissivity
    e0 = seb.surface_emissivity(lai, ndvi)  # broadband emissivity
    anchors = seb.select_anchors(ndvi, lst, albedo_=albedo, mask=mask)  # hot and cold pixels
    rl_in = seb.incoming_longwave(anchors["cold"]["lst"], seb.air_emissivity(tau_sw=float(tau.median())))  # W/m2
    rn = seb.net_radiation(seb.incoming_shortwave(cos_t, tau, dr=float(seb.inverse_relative_distance(when.day_of_year))),
                           albedo, rl_in, seb.outgoing_longwave(lst, e0), e0)  # W/m2
    g = seb.soil_heat_flux(rn, lst, lai=lai, method="metric", ndvi_=ndvi)  # W/m2
    res = seb.run_metric(lst, rn, g, seb.momentum_roughness(lai=lai), float(seb.wind_at_blending_height(u2)), P, etr_h,
                         anchors=anchors, etr_daily=etr_daily)  # METRIC
    return res, anchors, etr_h  # result, anchors and overpass ETr

text:
MODIS at 1 km
sd.modis_1km reprojects the Terra daytime LST (nearest), the nadir reflectance and LAI (averaged from 500 m) and the elevation onto a 1 km UTM grid. QC_Day bits 0 and 1 equal to 0 mark LST of good quality. Day_view_time is the local solar time of the observation.


Code
mo = sd.modis_1km("2024-07-05")  # MODIS inputs, 1 km
good = ((mo.qc.fillna(255).astype(int) & 3) == 0) & mo.lst.notnull() & mo.red.notnull()  # good quality LST and reflectance
solar_h = float(mo.view_time.where(good).median())  # local solar time of the view, hours
when_m = pd.Timestamp("2024-07-05") + pd.Timedelta(hours=solar_h - LON / 15)  # approximate UTC time of the observation

      f"(Landsat: {pd.Timestamp(landsat.attrs['datetime']):%H:%M} UTC)")  # grid and time

title: ET at Other Resolutions: MODIS, Sentinel-3 and Sentinel-2 with Thermal Sharpening
text:
MODIS against Landsat
Landsat METRIC daily ET of the same day, averaged over each MODIS cell inside the Landsat window, is the comparison.


Code
ls_1km = metric.et24.rio.reproject_match(mo.lst, resampling=Resampling.average)  # Landsat daily ET averaged to the MODIS grid
inside = ls_1km.notnull() & res_m.et24.notnull()  # cells inside the Landsat window
stats = seb.compare_to_tower(res_m.et24.where(inside), ls_1km.where(inside))  # MODIS against Landsat
print(f"{int(stats.n)} cells: Landsat mean {stats.mean_obs:.2f} mm, MODIS mean {stats.mean_pred:.2f} mm, bias {stats.bias:+.2f} mm, "
      f"RMSE {stats.rmse:.2f} mm, R2 {stats.r2:.2f}")  # agreement
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.8))  # three panels
win = dict(x=slice(float(ls_1km.x[inside.any("y")].min()), float(ls_1km.x[inside.any("y")].max())),
           y=slice(float(ls_1km.y[inside.any("x")].max()), float(ls_1km.y[inside.any("x")].min())))  # the Landsat window
for a_, v, t in [(ax[0], ls_1km.sel(**win), "Landsat METRIC averaged to 1 km"), (ax[1], res_m.et24.where(inside).sel(**win), "MODIS METRIC, 1 km")]:  # two maps
    im = a_.imshow(v, cmap="YlGnBu", vmin=0, vmax=14); a_.set_title(t); a_.axis("off")  # map
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[:2], shrink=0.8, label="mm/day")  # shared scale
ax[2].scatter(ls_1km.where(inside).values.ravel(), res_m.et24.where(inside).values.ravel(), s=12, alpha=0.6); ax[2].plot([0, 14], [0, 14], "k--", lw=0.8)  # scatter
ax[2].set_xlabel("Landsat, 1 km mean (mm/day)"); ax[2].set_ylabel("MODIS (mm/day)"); ax[2].set_title("Daily ET, 5 July 2024"); plt.show()  # labels


785 cells: Landsat mean 8.25 mm, MODIS mean 11.39 mm, bias +3.14 mm, RMSE 4.31 mm, R2 0.53









MODIS reproduces the broad pattern of the Landsat result (R2 0.53 over 785 cells) but is 3.1 mm/day higher on average. The anchors explain most of it: METRIC assigns 1.05 ETr to the cold anchor, and at 1 km that pixel is a mixture with bare ground in it that cannot evaporate that much; every cell calibrated against it inherits the excess, and the cooler hot anchor narrows the range further. The inputs add to the difference (a different LST algorithm and view time, 8 day LAI, 16 day BRDF reflectance). For water accounting at the scale of irrigation districts MODIS is useful once its calibration is checked against a finer sensor; for individual fields it is not.

title: ET at Other Resolutions: MODIS, Sentinel-3 and Sentinel-2 with Thermal Sharpening
text:
Testing the sharpener on Landsat
The honest way to test a sharpener is to degrade an image whose truth is known. The 30 m Landsat LST is aggregated to 990 m (33 x 33 pixels, averaging emitted power), sharpened back to 30 m with the Landsat reflectance, and compared with the original. Bilinear interpolation of the 990 m image is the baseline the sharpener must beat.


Code
m = landsat.clear.astype(bool)  # clear pixels
n = 33 * (min(landsat.sizes["y"], landsat.sizes["x"]) // 33)  # crop to whole 33 x 33 blocks
L = landsat.isel(y=slice(0, n), x=slice(0, n))  # cropped stack
truth = L.lst.where(L.clear.astype(bool))  # 30 m LST, K
coarse = seb.aggregate_lst(truth, 33)  # 990 m LST, emitted-power mean
fine = L[list(sd.REFLECTANCE)].assign(ndvi=seb.ndvi(L.red, L.nir))  # 30 m predictors: six bands and NDVI
sharp = seb.thermal_sharpen(coarse, fine, factor=33, model="forest", smooth_residuals=False, random_state=0)  # data mining sharpener
bilinear = xr.DataArray(zoom(coarse.values, 33, order=1, mode="nearest")[:n, :n], coords=truth.coords, dims=truth.dims)  # baseline
rows = {}  # accuracy table
for name, est in [("bilinear 990 m", bilinear), ("DMS random forest", sharp)]:  # both estimates
    s_ = seb.compare_to_tower(est, truth)  # against the 30 m truth
    rows[name] = {"RMSE (K)": s_.rmse, "bias (K)": s_.bias, "R2": s_.r2}  # metrics
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3))  # table
print(f"largest difference between the sharpened image averaged to 990 m and the coarse LST: "
      f"{float(np.nanmax(np.abs(seb.aggregate_lst(sharp, 33, emissive=False) - coarse))):.3f} K")  # residual correction conserves the coarse LST
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5))  # three maps
for a_, v, t in zip(ax, [coarse, sharp, truth], ["Landsat LST aggregated to 990 m", "Sharpened to 30 m", "Original 30 m"]):  # three images
    im = a_.imshow(v - 273.15, cmap="inferno", vmin=30, vmax=62); a_.set_title(t); a_.axis("off")  # map
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="C"); plt.show()  # shared scale

title: ET at Other Resolutions: MODIS, Sentinel-3 and Sentinel-2 with Thermal Sharpening
section: Sentinel-3 LST on a grid that nests Sentinel-2
text:
Sentinel-3 LST on a grid that nests Sentinel-2
The SLSTR LST product is a swath with a latitude and longitude for every pixel. The 20 m Sentinel-2 window is cut to whole 50 x 50 pixel blocks, so a 1 km grid with the same origin nests exactly. The swath coordinates are projected to the Sentinel-2 UTM zone (10N) and the valid LST is placed on that 1 km grid by nearest neighbour.


Code
s2 = sd.sentinel2_20m()  # Sentinel-2B L2A, 4 July 2024, 20 m, UTM 10N
folder = sd.sentinel3_lst_folder()  # SLSTR LST files (about 10 MB)
when3 = pd.Timestamp((folder / "datetime.txt").read_text())  # SLSTR acquisition time, UTC
lst3 = s3.read_slstr_lst(folder)  # LST, uncertainty, flags, lon/lat
valid = s3.slstr_lst_mask(lst3)  # no cloud
to10 = Transformer.from_crs(4326, s2.rio.crs, always_xy=True)  # lon/lat -> UTM 10N
xx, yy = to10.transform(lst3.longitude.values, lst3.latitude.values)  # swath coordinates in metres
xx = xr.DataArray(xx, dims=lst3.LST.dims); yy = xr.DataArray(yy, dims=lst3.LST.dims)  # as DataArrays
bounds = (float(s2.x.min()) - 10, float(s2.y.min()) - 10, float(s2.x.max()) + 10, float(s2.y.max()) + 10)  # outer edges of the 20 m window
lst_1km = s3.swath_to_grid(lst3.LST.where(valid), xx, yy, resolution=1000.0, bounds=bounds, crs=s2.rio.crs,
                           method="nearest", max_distance=750.0)  # SLSTR LST on the 1 km grid
print(f"Sentinel-2 at {pd.Timestamp(s2.attrs['datetime']):%H:%M} UTC, SLSTR at {when3:%H:%M} UTC, 4 July 2024")  # times
print(f"20 m grid {dict(s2.sizes)} -> 1 km grid {dict(lst_1km.sizes)}; valid 1 km cells: {int(lst_1km.notnull().sum())}")  # grids

title: ET at Other Resolutions: MODIS, Sentinel-3 and Sentinel-2 with Thermal Sharpening
text:
Sharpening Sentinel-3 with Sentinel-2
The same sharpener now learns from 756 Sentinel-3 cells and the Sentinel-2 bands averaged over them, and predicts LST for every 20 m pixel. Here the residual is smoothed bilinearly before it is added back: the unsmoothed residual conserves the 1 km LST exactly but leaves visible 1 km block edges, while the smoothed one gives up a little of that conservation for a better 20 m pattern. Landsat LST of the next day (5 July, 18:33 UTC), reprojected to the 20 m grid, gives an independent check of the pattern; a bias between the two is expected, since the days, times and LST algorithms differ.


Code
m2 = s2.clear.astype(bool) & (s2.water == 0)  # clear land pixels
pred2 = s2[list(sd.REFLECTANCE)].where(m2).assign(ndvi=seb.ndvi(s2.red, s2.nir).where(m2))  # 20 m predictors
lst_s2 = seb.thermal_sharpen(lst_1km, pred2, factor=50, model="forest", smooth_residuals=True, random_state=0)  # 20 m LST, K (smoothed residual)
ls_on_s2 = landsat.lst.where(landsat.clear.astype(bool)).rio.reproject_match(s2.red, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)  # Landsat LST on the 20 m grid
near = xr.DataArray(np.kron(lst_1km.values, np.ones((50, 50))), coords=s2.red.coords, dims=s2.red.dims)  # 1 km LST repeated at 20 m
rows = {}  # agreement with Landsat
for name, est in [("Sentinel-3, 1 km blocks", near), ("Sentinel-3 sharpened to 20 m", lst_s2)]:  # both estimates
    s_ = seb.compare_to_tower(est.where(m2), ls_on_s2)  # against next-day Landsat
    rows[name] = {"R2 with Landsat": s_.r2, "bias (K)": s_.bias, "RMSE (K)": s_.rmse}  # metrics
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3))  # table
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5))  # three maps
for a_, v, t in zip(ax, [near, lst_s2, ls_on_s2], ["SLSTR LST, 1 km (4 July)", "Sharpened with Sentinel-2, 20 m", "Landsat LST, 30 m (5 July)"]):  # three images
    im = a_.imshow(v.where(m2) - 273.15, cmap="inferno", vmin=30, vmax=62); a_.set_title(t); a_.axis("off")  # map
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="C"); plt.show()  # shared scale

lai2 = seb.leaf_area_index(seb.savi(s2.red, s2.nir, L=0.1)).where(m2)  # LAI (METRIC SAVI curve)

      f"ETrF against Landsat: R2 {s_.r2:.2f}, bias {s_.bias:+.3f}, RMSE {s_.rmse:.3f}")  # agreement

crops = cdl2.where(m2).to_series().value_counts().index[:8]  # the 8 most common classes

title: ET at Other Resolutions: MODIS, Sentinel-3 and Sentinel-2 with Thermal Sharpening
text:
Summary and exercises

MODIS, Sentinel-3 and Landsat trade pixel size against revisit; at 1 km anchors are mixtures, so the calibration spans a narrower temperature range.
METRIC on MODIS at 1 km reproduced the regional pattern of Landsat METRIC averaged to 1 km (R2 0.53) but was 3.1 mm/day higher, because its cold anchor is a mixed pixel given 1.05 ETr.
The data mining sharpener, tested on Landsat degraded to 990 m, halved the RMSE of bilinear interpolation (2.3 against 4.5 K) and, unsmoothed, conserves the coarse LST exactly.
Sentinel-3 LST sharpened with Sentinel-2 to 20 m gave a METRIC ETrF map on a day without Landsat that matched the next day’s Landsat pattern (R2 0.79), with higher ETrF over the driest fields.

Exercises

Repeat the Landsat sharpening test with model="tree" and model="boosting", and with only NDVI as a predictor. Which predictors matter most?
Run METRIC on the Aqua afternoon overpass (MYD11A1). How does ETrF from 13:30 compare with the morning?
Sharpen Sentinel-3 with the 30 m Landsat reflectance of 5 July instead of Sentinel-2. Does the sensor of the predictors matter?
Find the next Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-3 pair after 5 July (9 July) and map ETrF for that day. How much did the fields change in four days?

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text: Banner

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text:
Overview

SSEBop: operational simplified surface energy balance
Senay et al. (2013, 2023) define, for each pixel and day, a cold (wet) limit and a hot (dry) limit of LST:

Cold limit Tc = c Tmax, where Tmax is the daily maximum air temperature and c is calibrated as the typical ratio of LST to Tmax over well watered, dense vegetation (NDVI of at least 0.7).
Hot limit Th = Tc + dT, where dT = Rn rah / (rho cp) is the temperature difference a dry, bare surface needs to carry the clear-sky daily net radiation Rn as sensible heat, with a fixed aerodynamic resistance of 110 s/m.

The ET fraction is the position of LST between the limits, ETf = (Th - Ts) / dT, clipped to 0 to 1.05, and actual ET is ETa = ETf k ETref. Because dT and c come from climate and the image, SSEBop needs no anchor pixels and no wind, and it runs globally (USGS FEWS NET) and in OpenET.


S-SEBI: simplified surface energy balance index
Roerink et al. (2000) observed that in an image with both wet and dry areas the scatter of LST against albedo has a dry edge (the hottest LST at each albedo, decreasing at high albedo where bright soil reflects much of the radiation) and a wet edge (the coolest LST, rising slowly with albedo). With the two edges fitted as lines, EF = (T_H - Ts) / (T_H - T_LE), where T_H and T_LE are the dry and wet edge temperatures at the pixel’s albedo. No weather data are needed for the fraction.


The triangle method
Jiang and Islam (2001) use the LST against fractional cover scatter. The dry edge gives the hottest possible LST at each cover, the coolest pixels the wet limit. A Priestley-Taylor parameter phi runs from phi_max fc at the dry edge to phi_max = 1.26 at the wet limit, and EF = phi Delta / (Delta + gamma).


PT-JPL
Fisher et al. (2008) start from the Priestley-Taylor equation, LE = alpha Delta / (Delta + gamma) (Rn - G) with alpha = 1.26, and split it into canopy transpiration, soil evaporation and interception, each reduced by constraints:








Constraint
Formula
Meaning




fwet
RH^4
wet canopy fraction


fg
fAPAR / fIPAR
green fraction of the canopy


fT
exp(-((Ta - Topt) / Topt)^2)
temperature limit of photosynthesis


fM
fAPAR / fAPARmax
plant moisture


fSM
RH^(VPD / beta)
soil moisture from atmospheric dryness



PT-JPL uses no thermal band: it sees water stress only through vegetation indices and the dryness of the air. Over irrigated land in a dry climate this is its main weakness, because the air above an irrigated field says little about the field’s soil moisture.


Ensembles
Each model’s errors come from different assumptions, so their average is often more accurate than any one of them. OpenET computes, for each pixel and month, the ensemble of its six models after removing up to two outliers with the median absolute deviation (MAD) rule, and publishes the ensemble mean together with each model.

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (registers the .rio accessor)
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.rsense.surface_energy_balance as seb  # energy balance and ET models
import seb_data as sd  # chapter helper: downloads, caches and loads the scenes

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution

          "Fallow": [61], "Grass and shrubs": [176, 152], "Developed": [121, 122, 123, 124]}  # CDL codes per group


def by_group(**layers):  # mean of each layer per crop group

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text:
SSEBop
The c factor compares LST with the daily maximum air temperature over dense vegetation. dT uses the clear-sky daily net radiation of a reference surface (albedo 0.23), computed as in FAO-56, and the fixed resistance of 110 s/m.


Code
tmax_k = a["tmax_c"] + 273.15  # ERA5 daily maximum, K
tc, c = seb.cold_reference_temperature(p["lst"], p["ndvi"], tmax_k)  # cold limit and c factor
ra = float(seb.extraterrestrial_radiation_daily(sd.WESTSIDE["lat"], a["doy"]))  # MJ m-2 d-1
z = p["z"]; rso = (0.75 + 2e-5 * z) * ra  # clear-sky shortwave, MJ m-2 d-1
ea_d = float(seb.actual_vapour_pressure(t_dew_c=a["t_dew_daily_c"]))  # daily vapour pressure, kPa
rnl = 4.901e-9 * ((a["tmax_c"] + 273.16) ** 4 + (a["tmin_c"] + 273.16) ** 4) / 2 * (0.34 - 0.14 * ea_d ** 0.5)  # clear-sky net longwave
rn_cs = (0.77 * rso - rnl) / 0.0864  # clear-sky daily net radiation, W/m2
dT = seb.dt_from_climate(rn_cs, tmax_k, float(p["pressure"].mean()))  # hot - cold limit difference, K
ssebop = seb.run_ssebop(p["lst"], tc, dT, eto=p["etr_daily"], k=1.0)  # ETf and ETa with the alfalfa reference
print(f"c = {c:.4f}, Tc = {float(tc) - 273.15:.1f} C | clear-sky Rn = {rn_cs:.0f} W/m2, dT = {float(dT):.1f} K, Th = {float(tc + dT) - 273.15:.1f} C")  # limits
print(f"pixels at ETf = 0 (hotter than Th): {float((ssebop.etf == 0).mean()):.1%} | at the 1.05 cap: {float((ssebop.etf >= 1.05).mean()):.1%}")  # clipping
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5.5)); im = ax.imshow(ssebop.etf, extent=ext, cmap="YlGnBu", vmin=0, vmax=1.05)  # ETf map
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8); ax.set_title("SSEBop ET fraction, 5 July 2024"); ax.axis("off"); plt.show()  # draw


c = 0.9760, Tc = 38.9 C | clear-sky Rn = 166 W/m2, dT = 16.7 K, Th = 55.7 C
pixels at ETf = 0 (hotter than Th): 32.0% | at the 1.05 cap: 5.9%









SSEBop’s limits come from the weather and a scene-wide c, not from two pixels. Here c is 0.976, so the cold limit (38.9 C) is 3.7 K warmer than METRIC’s cold anchor (35.2 C), and the hot limit (55.7 C) is 4.3 K cooler than METRIC’s hot anchor (60.0 C). The narrower range has two effects: 6 % of pixels, the coolest fields, reach the cap of 1.05, and 32 % of pixels, the hot fallow land and rangeland, are hotter than the hot limit and get zero ET. SSEBop is run here with the alfalfa reference and k = 1 so that all models scale with the same reference; the operational SSEBop of OpenET uses grass reference ET with a scaling factor.

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text:
S-SEBI
seb.ssebi bins the albedo axis, takes the 99th and 1st percentile LST in each bin, fits the dry edge to the bins above the albedo of the hottest bin and the wet edge below it, and returns EF.


Code
from io import StringIO  # read JSON text

ss = seb.ssebi(p["albedo"], p["lst"], p["rn"], p["g"], n_bins=30)  # S-SEBI
bins = pd.read_json(StringIO(ss.attrs["bins"]))  # the bins the edges were fitted to (stored as JSON)
print(f"dry edge T_H = {ss.attrs['a_dry'] - 273.15:.1f} C + {ss.attrs['b_dry']:.1f} albedo | wet edge T_LE = {ss.attrs['a_wet'] - 273.15:.1f} C + {ss.attrs['b_wet']:.1f} albedo")  # edges
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))  # scatter and map
ax[0].hexbin(p["albedo"].values.ravel(), (p["lst"] - 273.15).values.ravel(), gridsize=70, bins="log", cmap="Greys", extent=(0.1, 0.35, 28, 66))  # scatter
xx = np.linspace(0.1, 0.35, 50)  # albedo axis
ax[0].plot(xx, ss.attrs["a_dry"] - 273.15 + ss.attrs["b_dry"] * xx, "r-", label="dry edge"); ax[0].plot(xx, ss.attrs["a_wet"] - 273.15 + ss.attrs["b_wet"] * xx, "b-", label="wet edge")  # edges
ax[0].plot(bins.x, bins.y_max - 273.15, "r.", ms=6); ax[0].plot(bins.x, bins.y_min - 273.15, "b.", ms=6)  # bin percentiles
ax[0].set_xlabel("albedo"); ax[0].set_ylabel("LST (C)"); ax[0].legend(); ax[0].set_title("S-SEBI edges")  # labels
im = ax[1].imshow(ss.ef, extent=ext, cmap="YlGnBu", vmin=0, vmax=1); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8); ax[1].set_title("S-SEBI evaporative fraction"); ax[1].axis("off")  # map
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


dry edge T_H = 69.3 C + -35.9 albedo | wet edge T_LE = 37.4 C + -5.7 albedo









The scatter has the textbook shape: the hottest LST rises with albedo up to about 0.2 (darker surfaces are hotter only when they are also dry) and then falls, as brighter surfaces reflect more sunlight. The dry edge is fitted above that turning point (T_H falls by about 3.6 K per 0.1 of albedo) and the wet edge below it, where it is almost flat near 36 to 37 C. Above an albedo of 0.3 there are no wet pixels, and the wet edge is an extrapolation. EF follows the irrigated fields, but the wet edge is the coolest 1 % of every bin, so the method assumes some pixels at every albedo are fully wet.

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text:
The triangle method


Code
fc = seb.fractional_cover(p["ndvi"])  # fractional cover from NDVI (0.15 bare, 0.85 full)
tri = seb.triangle_method(fc, p["lst"], p["rn"], p["g"], a["t_air_c"] + 273.15, float(p["pressure"].mean()), n_bins=30)  # triangle
print(f"dry edge Tmax(fc) = {tri.attrs['a_dry'] - 273.15:.1f} C {tri.attrs['b_dry']:+.1f} fc | wet limit {tri.attrs['t_wet'] - 273.15:.1f} C")  # edges
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))  # scatter and map
ax[0].hexbin(fc.values.ravel(), (p["lst"] - 273.15).values.ravel(), gridsize=60, bins="log", cmap="Greys")  # scatter
ax[0].plot([0, 1], [tri.attrs["a_dry"] - 273.15, tri.attrs["a_dry"] + tri.attrs["b_dry"] - 273.15], "r-", label="dry edge")  # dry edge
ax[0].axhline(tri.attrs["t_wet"] - 273.15, color="b", label="wet limit"); ax[0].legend()  # wet limit
ax[0].set_xlabel("fractional cover"); ax[0].set_ylabel("LST (C)"); ax[0].set_title("The triangle")  # labels
im = ax[1].imshow(tri.ef, extent=ext, cmap="YlGnBu", vmin=0, vmax=1); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8); ax[1].set_title("Triangle evaporative fraction"); ax[1].axis("off")  # map
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


dry edge Tmax(fc) = 61.9 C -17.7 fc | wet limit 35.8 C









The scatter shows the classic triangle, with a dry edge falling from about 60 C over bare soil toward the wet limit at full cover. The ceiling of EF = phi Delta / (Delta + gamma) is 1.26 Delta / (Delta + gamma), about 1.0 at the air temperature of this day, so the triangle cannot represent fields that draw heat from the air either.

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text:
PT-JPL
PT-JPL needs net radiation, NDVI, SAVI (with the usual L = 0.5), air temperature, vapour pressure and pressure. The optimum temperature for growth Topt is set to 25 C here; Fisher et al. derive it for each pixel from the climatology of the vegetation.


Code
savi05 = seb.savi(p["sr"].red, p["sr"].nir, L=0.5)  # SAVI with L = 0.5
pt = seb.priestley_taylor_jpl(p["rn"], p["ndvi"], savi05, a["t_air_c"], a["ea_kpa"], float(p["pressure"].mean()), g=p["g"], topt_c=25.0)  # PT-JPL
es = float(seb.saturation_vapour_pressure(a["t_air_c"]))  # kPa
rh = a["ea_kpa"] / es  # relative humidity at the overpass
print(f"RH {rh:.2f}, VPD {es - a['ea_kpa']:.2f} kPa -> fwet = {rh ** 4:.5f}, fSM = {rh ** ((es - a['ea_kpa']) / 1.0):.5f}; "
      f"fT = {np.exp(-((a['t_air_c'] - 25) / 25) ** 2):.2f}")  # the atmospheric constraints
by_group(LE_canopy=pt.le_c, LE_soil=pt.le_s, LE_interception=pt.le_i, LE_total=pt.le, LE_metric=metric.le).round(0)  # per crop group

With 9 % relative humidity and a vapour pressure deficit above 6 kPa, PT-JPL’s soil moisture constraint fSM is essentially zero, so soil evaporation vanishes everywhere, including under irrigated orchards whose wetted soil does evaporate. title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
section: Five models on a common footing
text:
Five models on a common footing
The models differ in two ways at once: how they estimate the instantaneous energy partition, and how they scale it to a day (METRIC and SSEBop with reference ET; S-SEBI, the triangle and PT-JPL with net radiation or EF). To compare the first part alone, every model’s instantaneous LE is turned into a reference ET fraction, ET_inst / ETr_inst, and scaled with the same daily alfalfa reference ET. SSEBop’s daily ETf is used directly.


Code
lam = seb.latent_heat_of_vaporization(p["lst"])  # J/kg
to_etrf = lambda le: (3600 * le / lam / p["etr_inst"]).clip(0, 1.3)  # instantaneous LE -> ETrF
fractions = {"METRIC": metric.etrf, "SSEBop": ssebop.etf, "S-SEBI": to_etrf(ss.le), "Triangle": to_etrf(tri.le), "PT-JPL": to_etrf(pt.le)}  # one fraction per model
daily = xr.concat([f * p["etr_daily"] for f in fractions.values()], dim=pd.Index(list(fractions), name="model"))  # daily ET, mm
ra24 = float(seb.extraterrestrial_radiation_daily(sd.WESTSIDE["lat"], a["doy"])) * 1e6 / 86400  # W/m2
rn24 = seb.daily_net_radiation(a["rs_daily_mj"] * 1e6 / 86400, p["albedo"], ra24=ra24)  # 24 h net radiation, W/m2
native = {"S-SEBI": seb.instantaneous_to_daily(ss.ef, method="ef", rn24=rn24)}  # S-SEBI with its own EF scaling
tab = pd.concat({m: by_group(et=daily.sel(model=m)).et for m in fractions}, axis=1)  # mean daily ET per crop group and model
tab["S-SEBI, EF x Rn24"] = by_group(et=native["S-SEBI"]).et  # S-SEBI with its native scaling, for contrast

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text:
An ensemble and its spread
The ensemble follows the OpenET idea: at each pixel, models further than two scaled median absolute deviations from the median are dropped, and the rest are averaged. The spread (range of the remaining models) shows where the models disagree.


Code
med = daily.median("model")  # per-pixel median, mm
mad = 1.4826 * np.abs(daily - med).median("model")  # scaled median absolute deviation
keep = np.abs(daily - med) <= np.maximum(2 * mad, 0.25)  # drop models far from the median (0.25 mm floor for near-identical values)
ens = daily.where(keep).mean("model").rename("ensemble")  # ensemble mean
spread = (daily.where(keep).max("model") - daily.where(keep).min("model")).rename("spread")  # range of the kept models
dropped = (~keep & daily.notnull()).sum(["y", "x"]) / daily.notnull().sum(["y", "x"])  # how often each model is an outlier
print("share of pixels where each model is dropped:", (100 * dropped.to_series()).round(1).to_dict())  # outlier rates
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))  # two maps
im = ax[0].imshow(ens, extent=ext, cmap="YlGnBu", vmin=0, vmax=16); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8, label="mm/day"); ax[0].set_title("Ensemble daily ET"); ax[0].axis("off")  # ensemble
im = ax[1].imshow(spread, extent=ext, cmap="magma_r", vmin=0, vmax=8); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8, label="mm/day"); ax[1].set_title("Spread of the kept models"); ax[1].axis("off")  # spread
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
xr.Dataset({"ensemble": ens, "spread": spread, "models": daily}).to_netcdf(OUT / "ensemble_20240705.nc", encoding={v: {"zlib": True, "complevel": 4} for v in ["ensemble", "spread", "models"]})  # saved for notebook 11, compressed
by_group(ensemble=ens, spread=spread, metric=daily.sel(model="METRIC")).round(2)  # per crop group

PT-JPL is dropped at half of the pixels, because it departs most from the thermal models over irrigated land, and METRIC at a fifth of them, mostly over the crops where it is the only model that represents advection. The ensemble is therefore 2 to 3 mm below METRIC over the crops. The spread of the kept models is smallest over fallow land (about 2.4 mm) and largest over grapes and annual crops (3.6 to 4.2 mm). A large spread is a warning that a single model’s value there is uncertain; notebook 11 asks which models are closer to independent estimates.

title: SSEBop, S-SEBI, the Triangle Method and PT-JPL
text:
Summary and exercises

SSEBop sets its wet and dry limits from Tmax and clear-sky net radiation (here c = 0.976 and dT = 16.7 K) and needs no anchors or wind; its narrow range put 32 % of pixels at zero ET.
S-SEBI and the triangle read their limits from the image scatter; their fraction cannot exceed about Rn - G.
PT-JPL has no thermal input; on this very dry day its soil moisture constraint removed soil evaporation everywhere and it gave much less ET than the thermal models over irrigated crops.
The thermal models agree on the spatial pattern (correlations 0.94 to 0.99) and differ in level; METRIC is highest over crops, and the daily scaling (reference ET or net radiation) roughly halves or doubles daily ET by itself.
An OpenET-style ensemble with a MAD outlier rule dropped PT-JPL at half of the pixels and METRIC at a fifth; its spread map shows where a single model is least reliable.

Exercises

Run SSEBop with the grass reference (p["eto_daily"]) and k = 1.25. How close is it to the run with the alfalfa reference?
Replace Topt = 25 in PT-JPL with 35 C. How much of PT-JPL’s gap to METRIC does the temperature constraint explain?
Fit the S-SEBI edges only on pixels with NDVI below 0.4. What happens to EF over orchards?
Add the SEBAL result of notebook 05 (scaled with reference ET) to the ensemble. Is it dropped as an outlier?

title: SEBAL: Solving for Sensible Heat with Hot and Cold Pixels
text: Banner

title: SEBAL: Solving for Sensible Heat with Hot and Cold Pixels
text:
Overview

The SEBAL assumptions

Linear dT. The temperature difference dT between 0.1 and 2 m above the surface is a linear function of LST: dT = a + b Ts. This replaces an unknown air temperature at every pixel with two numbers for the whole scene.
Hot anchor. At a dry, bare pixel there is no evaporation: LE_hot = 0, so H_hot = Rn - G and dT_hot = H_hot rah_hot / (rho cp).
Cold anchor. At a wet, well vegetated pixel all available energy evaporates: H_cold = 0, so dT_cold = 0.
Constant evaporative fraction. EF = LE / (Rn - G) at the overpass holds for the whole day, so daily ET is EF Rn24 converted to mm, with Rn24 the 24 hour mean net radiation.

With the two anchors, b = (dT_hot - dT_cold) / (Ts_hot - Ts_cold) and a = dT_hot - b Ts_hot.


Why the iteration
rah depends on stability, stability on H, and H on dT, which depends on rah at the hot pixel. SEBAL starts neutral, computes a, b and H for every pixel, updates the Monin-Obukhov length and the corrections, recomputes rah and the anchor dT, and repeats until rah at the hot pixel stops changing (usually 5 to 10 iterations).


Why it works, and where it does not
The linear dT assumption is reasonable because both Ts and the near-surface air temperature are pulled up by the same thing, sensible heat. Because the calibration is internal, biases in LST (from atmospheric correction or emissivity) and in roughness are largely absorbed: what matters is the contrast between pixels, not their absolute temperature. The two anchor assumptions are the weak points:

In arid, advective regions such as the San Joaquin Valley in summer, well watered fields can evaporate more than Rn - G by drawing heat from the air (H < 0). Setting H_cold = 0 then underestimates ET of the wettest fields; METRIC (notebook 06) addresses this.
After rain a bare field still evaporates, so LE_hot = 0 overestimates H across the image.
The anchors must be representative: large, uniform fields, away from cloud edges, at similar elevation.



Automated anchor selection
Allen et al. (2013) automated anchor selection for METRIC with percentile rules, refined in eeMETRIC and geeSEBAL:








Anchor
Pool
Then




cold
NDVI in the top 5 % of the image, albedo between 0.18 and 0.25
the coolest 20 % of that pool


hot
NDVI in the bottom 10 %, between 0.10 and 0.28 (bare soil, not water)
the hottest 20 % of that pool



From each pool GeoLattice keeps the candidates whose local LST standard deviation (3 x 3 pixels) is at or below the pool median, which removes field edges, and picks the pixel whose LST is closest to the pool mean. A land cover screen (for example, alfalfa for the cold pool and fallow for the hot pool) can narrow the pools further.

title: SEBAL: Solving for Sensible Heat with Hot and Cold Pixels
text:
SEBAL with GeoLattice







Function
Purpose

Rn24 for the daily scaling

Learning objectives

State the four SEBAL assumptions and derive a and b from the anchors.
Select hot and cold anchors by hand and with the percentile method, and judge whether they are representative.
Follow the stability iteration until the hot pixel’s rah converges.
Map H, LE, the evaporative fraction and daily ET.
Check the anchor constraints and find pixels where the assumptions break.
Quantify how much daily ET depends on the choice of anchors.



Data
The 5 July 2024 Landsat 8 scene of the Westside San Joaquin Valley (sd.load_scene) with the net radiation, soil heat flux and roughness of notebooks 03 and 04 (sd.energy_inputs) and the ERA5 daily shortwave for Rn24.


Contents

Setup

The stability iteration

Setup

title: SEBAL: Solving for Sensible Heat with Hot and Cold Pixels
text:
Choosing the anchors
seb.select_anchors picks one pixel from each pool. For comparison, a manual pair is chosen the way an analyst would look for extremes: the coolest dense pixel (NDVI above 0.8) and the hottest fallow pixel, each inside a 7 x 7 pixel (210 m) window whose LST varies by less than 0.4 K, at least 300 m from the image edge.


Code
auto = seb.select_anchors(p["ndvi"], p["lst"], albedo_=p["albedo"], candidates=cand)  # automated: closest to pool mean, homogeneous
ndvi_v, lst_v = p["ndvi"].values, p["lst"].values  # arrays
from scipy import ndimage  # local filters

f = np.nan_to_num(lst_v, nan=400.0)  # LST with gaps filled by an impossible value
sd7 = np.sqrt(np.maximum(ndimage.uniform_filter(f ** 2, 7) - ndimage.uniform_filter(f, 7) ** 2, 0))  # LST standard deviation in 7 x 7 windows
uniform = sd7 < 0.4  # LST nearly uniform over 210 m
uniform[:10] = uniform[-10:] = False; uniform[:, :10] = uniform[:, -10:] = False  # stay 300 m away from the image edge
cold_i = np.nanargmin(np.where(uniform & (ndvi_v > 0.8), lst_v, np.nan))  # coolest uniform dense pixel
hot_i = np.nanargmax(np.where(uniform & (ndvi_v < 0.2) & (ndvi_v > 0.1) & ds.cdl.isin([61]).values, lst_v, np.nan))  # hottest uniform fallow pixel
manual = {k: seb.anchor_at(p["ndvi"], float(ds.x[i % ds.sizes["x"]]), float(ds.y[i // ds.sizes["x"]]),
                           ndvi=p["ndvi"], lst=p["lst"], albedo=p["albedo"]) for k, i in [("cold", cold_i), ("hot", hot_i)]}  # anchor records
tab = pd.concat({"automated": seb.anchor_report(auto, rn=p["rn"], g=p["g"]),
                 "manual": seb.anchor_report(manual, rn=p["rn"], g=p["g"])})  # both pairs
tab["crop"] = [sd.cdl_name(ds.cdl.values[r.iy, r.ix]) for r in tab.itertuples()]  # crop of each anchor
tab["lst_c"] = tab.lst - 273.15  # C

Both pairs sit in the expected corners of the scatter; the manual pair, chosen as extremes, lies just outside the main cloud of pixels (a tomato field at 33 C and a fallow field at 63 C). The automated cold anchor is not the very coolest pixel but a typical member of the coolest, densest pool, which is the intent: a single extreme pixel may be a wet spot, a canal or a cloud remnant. The automated run is used from here on; the last section measures how much this choice matters.

title: SEBAL: Solving for Sensible Heat with Hot and Cold Pixels
text:
One calibration step by hand
The first SEBAL step assumes neutral air. With the hot and cold anchors:


Code
hot, cold = auto["hot"], auto["cold"]  # the automated anchors
hy, hx, cy, cx = hot["iy"], hot["ix"], cold["iy"], cold["ix"]  # their rows and columns
u200, P = p["u200"], p["pressure"]  # wind at 200 m, pressure map
ustar = seb.friction_velocity(u200, 200.0, p["zom"])  # neutral u*
rah0 = seb.aerodynamic_resistance(ustar)  # neutral rah between 0.1 and 2 m
H_hot = float(p["rn"][hy, hx] - p["g"][hy, hx])  # LE = 0 at the hot pixel
rho_hot = float(seb.air_density(float(P[hy, hx]), hot["lst"]))  # a first guess of air density
dT_hot = H_hot * float(rah0[hy, hx]) / (rho_hot * seb.CP)  # K
a0, b0 = seb.calibrate_dt(hot["lst"], cold["lst"], dT_hot, 0.0)  # dT = a + b Ts with dT_cold = 0
print(f"hot pixel: Rn - G = {H_hot:.0f} W/m2, neutral rah = {float(rah0[hy, hx]):.1f} s/m, dT_hot = {dT_hot:.2f} K")  # hot anchor
print(f"dT = {a0:.2f} + {b0:.4f} Ts   (dT = 0 at Ts = {cold['lst'] - 273.15:.1f} C)")  # the line


hot pixel: Rn - G = 327 W/m2, neutral rah = 60.5 s/m, dT_hot = 18.94 K
dT = -235.50 + 0.7636 Ts   (dT = 0 at Ts = 35.2 C)


With neutral resistance the hot pixel needs a dT of about 19 K to carry all its available energy as sensible heat. That is too large: hot, dry surfaces are strongly unstable, so their real rah is much smaller and a smaller dT suffices. The iteration finds it.

title: SEBAL: Solving for Sensible Heat with Hot and Cold Pixels
text:
The stability iteration
seb.sensible_heat_iterative repeats the step above with stability corrections until the hot pixel’s rah changes by less than 0.5 %. SEBAL’s anchor rules are the defaults (le_hot=None means 0, le_cold=None means H_cold = 0).


Code
sh = seb.sensible_heat_iterative(p["lst"], p["rn"], p["g"], p["zom"], u200, P, auto)  # SEBAL calibration
hist = sh["history"]  # one row per iteration
print(f"converged: {sh['converged']} after {sh['iterations']} iterations | final dT = {sh['a']:.2f} + {sh['b']:.4f} Ts")  # result
display(hist.round(3))  # the iterations
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.6))  # three panels
ax[0].plot(hist.index, hist.rah_hot, "o-"); ax[0].set_title("rah at the hot pixel (s/m)")  # resistance
ax[1].plot(hist.index, hist.dt_hot, "o-", color="tab:red"); ax[1].set_title("dT at the hot pixel (K)")  # temperature difference
ax[2].plot(hist.index, hist.L_hot, "o-", color="tab:green"); ax[2].set_title("Monin-Obukhov length at the hot pixel (m)")  # stability
for a in ax:  # every panel
    a.set_xlabel("iteration")  # x label
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

SEBAL’s daily ET for the irrigated crops (about 4 to 5.5 mm on average) is far below the alfalfa reference ET of the day (15.6 mm), even though several of these fields are close to full cover and well watered. The next notebook replaces both with the reference ET.

text:
How much do the anchors matter?
seb.monte_carlo_anchors reruns the model for many anchor pairs drawn at random from the pools and stacks the results. Ten draws give a first impression; notebook 11 does a fuller analysis.

    return seb.run_sebal(p["lst"], p["rn"], p["g"], p["zom"], u200, P, anchors=anchors, rn24=rn24).et24  # mm/day


stack, used = seb.monte_carlo_anchors(run, cand, n=10, seed=1)  # ten random anchor pairs
means = stack.mean(["y", "x"]).values  # scene mean ET of each draw
print(f"scene mean daily ET over 10 anchor pairs: {means.mean():.2f} mm, range {means.min():.2f} to {means.max():.2f} mm")  # spread of the mean
spread = stack.std("draw")  # per-pixel standard deviation

title: SEBAL: Solving for Sensible Heat with Hot and Cold Pixels
text:
Summary and exercises

SEBAL calibrates dT = a + b Ts with a hot anchor (LE = 0) and a cold anchor (H = 0), and iterates rah and stability until the hot pixel converges.
The automated percentile pools found an orchard and a hay stubble field as anchors; a manual pair in large uniform fields gives similar values.
At the hot pixel, the stability iteration lowered rah from 60.5 s/m (neutral) to 17.2 s/m in five iterations, and dT_hot from about 19 K to 5.3 K.
SEBAL maps H, LE and EF well, but on this hot, advective day its daily ET for irrigated crops stays far below the alfalfa reference ET, because H_cold = 0 and the Rn24 scaling cannot represent energy drawn from the air.
Ten random anchor pairs from the pools moved the scene mean daily ET between 3.4 and 4.2 mm.

Exercises

Restrict the cold pool to alfalfa (cold_classes=[36]) and the hot pool to fallow (hot_classes=[61]). How do the anchors and the daily ET change?
Run SEBAL on the 8 April 2024 scene. Is the contrast between the anchors larger or smaller than in July, and what does that do to the iteration?
Replace the METRIC soil heat flux with the SEBAL formula (method="bastiaanssen") and rerun. Which crops change most?
Use seb.anchor_at to put the hot anchor in a developed (urban) pixel. What happens to b, and why is that a poor choice?

title: Net Radiation from Landsat: Albedo, Emissivity and Surface Temperature
text: Banner

title: Net Radiation from Landsat: Albedo, Emissivity and Surface Temperature
text:
Overview

The radiation balance
Rn = (1 - albedo) Rs_in + RL_in - RL_out - (1 - eps0) RL_in








Term
Meaning
How it is estimated




Rs_in
incoming shortwave (sun)
Gsc cos(theta) dr tau_sw: solar constant, incidence angle, Earth-Sun distance, transmissivity


albedo
share of shortwave reflected
weighted sum of surface reflectance bands


RL_in
incoming longwave (sky)
eps_a sigma Ta^4, air emissivity from transmissivity


RL_out
outgoing longwave (surface)
eps0 sigma Ts^4 from LST


(1 - eps0) RL_in
sky longwave reflected by the surface
small, a few W m-2





Broadband albedo
Albedo is reflectance integrated over the whole solar spectrum (0.3 to 3 um) and all directions. Landsat measures six narrow bands at one view angle, so albedo is a weighted sum of them. The weights come from radiative transfer simulations: Liang (2001) for many sensors, adapted for OLI by Smith (2010), and Tasumi et al. (2008) for TM and ETM+, which METRIC uses. They differ because they assume different spectra of sunlight and surfaces; typical differences are 0.01 to 0.02.


Shortwave transmissivity
For clear skies, ASCE (2005) and METRIC compute the broadband transmissivity from pressure P, precipitable water W = 0.14 ea P + 2.1 and the sun angle:
tau_sw = 0.35 + 0.627 exp(-0.00146 P / (Kt cos theta) - 0.075 (W / cos theta)^0.4)
with Kt = 1 for clean air. On sloping ground cos theta is replaced by the cosine of the incidence angle on the slope, which depends on slope, aspect, latitude, declination and hour angle.


Land surface temperature from thermal radiance
The thermal sensor measures radiance at the top of the atmosphere, L_sensor. Part of it comes from the atmosphere itself (upwelled radiance Lu), part is sky radiance reflected by the surface ((1 - eps) Ld), and the surface emission is attenuated by the transmissivity tau:
L_sensor = tau eps B(Ts) + tau (1 - eps) Ld + Lu
Solving for the surface emission and inverting Planck’s law with the band constants K1 and K2 (from the scene’s MTL file) gives LST:
B(Ts) = (L_sensor - Lu - tau (1 - eps) Ld) / (tau eps), Ts = K2 / ln(K1 / B(Ts) + 1)
The Collection 2 Level-2 product delivers every term of this equation (ST_TRAD, ST_URAD, ST_DRAD, ST_ATRAN, ST_EMIS), computed from a reanalysis atmospheric profile with MODTRAN and ASTER emissivity, together with the resulting ST_B10.


Emissivity
Broadband emissivity eps0 (for longwave emission) and narrowband emissivity (for the thermal band) both rise from about 0.95 to 0.98 with leaf area. METRIC uses eps0 = 0.95 + 0.01 LAI for LAI up to 3 (Tasumi 2003) and 0.985 for water.

text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (registers the .rio accessor)
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.rsense.surface_energy_balance as seb  # energy balance and ET models
import seb_data as sd  # chapter helper: downloads, caches and loads the scenes

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results written by this chapter
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed
print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__, "| data folder", sd.DATA.relative_to(sd.DATA.parents[3]))  # versions and paths

import requests  # the MTL file
from geolattice.rsense.optical import lst as lstmod  # brightness temperature and single-channel LST

ds = sd.load_scene()  # Landsat 8, 5 July 2024
m = ds.clear.astype(bool) & (ds.water == 0)  # clear land pixels
a = ds.attrs  # overpass weather and geometry
ext = [float(ds.x.min()), float(ds.x.max()), float(ds.y.min()), float(ds.y.max())]  # map extent
GROUPS = {"Tree crops": [75, 204, 76, 211, 212, 217], "Grapes": [69], "Annual crops": [54, 2, 1, 36, 208, 24, 21, 51],
          "Fallow": [61], "Grass and shrubs": [176, 152], "Developed": [121, 122, 123, 124]}  # CDL codes per group


def by_group(**layers):  # mean of each layer per crop group
    df = xr.Dataset(layers).assign(cdl=ds.cdl).to_dataframe().dropna()  # one row per pixel
    out = {g: df[df.cdl.isin(c)].drop(columns=["cdl", "spatial_ref"], errors="ignore").mean() for g, c in GROUPS.items()}  # group means
    return pd.DataFrame(out).T  # one row per group

section: Land surface temperature from thermal radiance
text:
Land surface temperature from thermal radiance
The thermal constants of band 10 come from the scene’s MTL file. With them and the atmospheric terms of Collection 2, the radiative transfer equation of the Overview gives LST.


Code
item = sd.landsat_item(sd.MAIN_SCENE)  # STAC item
mtl = requests.get(item.assets["mtl.json"].href, timeout=60).json()["LANDSAT_METADATA_FILE"]  # metadata
K1 = float(mtl["LEVEL1_THERMAL_CONSTANTS"]["K1_CONSTANT_BAND_10"])  # W m-2 sr-1 um-1
K2 = float(mtl["LEVEL1_THERMAL_CONSTANTS"]["K2_CONSTANT_BAND_10"])  # K
print(f"band 10: K1 = {K1}, K2 = {K2}")  # constants

L, tau, Lu, Ld, eps = ds.trad, ds.atran, ds.urad, ds.drad, ds.emis  # radiance terms from Collection 2
B = (L - Lu - tau * (1 - eps) * Ld) / (tau * eps)  # surface-leaving blackbody radiance
lst_rt = (K2 / np.log(K1 / B + 1)).where(m)  # LST by radiative transfer, K
bt = (K2 / np.log(K1 / L + 1)).where(m)  # top-of-atmosphere brightness temperature, K
lst_sc = lstmod.lst_single_channel(bt, lstmod.emissivity_ndvi(seb.ndvi(ds.red, ds.nir)),
                                   wavelength=lstmod.WAVELENGTH["landsat8_b10"])  # emissivity only, no atmosphere
st = ds.lst.where(m)  # Collection 2 ST_B10
print(f"atmosphere at the overpass: tau {float(tau.mean()):.3f}, Lu {float(Lu.mean()):.2f}, Ld {float(Ld.mean()):.2f} W m-2 sr-1 um-1")  # atmosphere
pd.DataFrame({"median (C)": [float(v.median()) - 273.15 for v in (bt, lst_sc, lst_rt, st)],  # medians
              "minus ST_B10, median (K)": [float((v - st).median()) for v in (bt, lst_sc, lst_rt, st)],  # bias against the product
              "minus ST_B10, 95th pct of |diff| (K)": [float(np.abs(v - st).quantile(0.95)) for v in (bt, lst_sc, lst_rt, st)]},  # spread
             index=["brightness temperature", "emissivity correction only", "radiative transfer (this notebook)", "Collection 2 ST_B10"]).round(2)  # table

Correcting for emissivity alone recovers less than 2 K of that; the other 4.8 K is the atmosphere, which absorbs 17 % of the surface signal (tau 0.83) and adds its own, colder, emission. seb.albedo accepts a Dataset of reflectance bands named blue, green, red, nir, swir16, swir22 and applies a chosen set of weights.

sr = ds[list(sd.REFLECTANCE)].where(m)  # six reflectance bands

alb_tasumi = seb.albedo(sr, sensor="tasumi")  # Tasumi et al. (2008), TM/ETM+ bands mapped to OLI

title: Net Radiation from Landsat: Albedo, Emissivity and Surface Temperature
text:
Albedo against MODIS
MODIS MCD43A4 provides nadir BRDF-adjusted reflectance at 500 m, a daily product fitted from 16 days of observations. Liang’s MODIS weights turn it into broadband albedo, and the Landsat albedo averaged over each MODIS pixel gives a scale-matched comparison.


Code
from rasterio.enums import Resampling  # resampling methods

cat = sd._catalog()  # Planetary Computer
it = list(cat.search(collections=["modis-43A4-061"], bbox=sd.WESTSIDE["bbox"], datetime="2024-07-05").items())[0]  # day 187 tile
names = {1: "red", 2: "nir", 3: "blue", 4: "green", 5: "swir12", 7: "swir22"}  # MODIS band numbers
coarse = alb_liang.rio.write_crs(ds.rio.crs).rio.reproject(ds.rio.crs, resolution=480, resampling=Resampling.average)  # Landsat albedo averaged to 480 m
mod = xr.Dataset({n: rioxarray.open_rasterio(it.assets[f"Nadir_Reflectance_Band{b}"].href).squeeze("band", drop=True)
                  .rio.reproject_match(coarse, resampling=Resampling.bilinear) for b, n in names.items()})  # NBAR on that grid
mod = mod.where(mod < 32767) * 1e-4  # fill value and scale factor
alb_modis = seb.albedo(mod, sensor="modis")  # Liang (2001) MODIS weights
pair = pd.DataFrame({"modis": alb_modis.values.ravel(), "landsat": coarse.values.ravel()}).dropna()  # matched pixels
pair = pair[(pair.landsat > 0) & (pair.modis > 0)]  # valid pairs
stats = seb.compare_to_tower(pair.landsat, pair.modis)  # Landsat against MODIS
print(f"{int(stats.n)} cells of 480 m: bias {stats.bias:+.3f}, RMSE {stats.rmse:.3f}, R2 {stats.r2:.2f}")  # agreement
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5)); ax.scatter(pair.modis, pair.landsat, s=8, alpha=0.6)  # scatter
ax.plot([0.1, 0.3], [0.1, 0.3], "k--", lw=0.8); ax.set_xlabel("MODIS MCD43A4 albedo"); ax.set_ylabel("Landsat albedo, 480 m mean")  # 1:1 line
ax.set_title("Broadband albedo, 5 July 2024"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


3373 cells of 480 m: bias -0.004, RMSE 0.018, R2 0.76









The two sensors agree closely on the spatial pattern, with a small offset between them. Exact agreement is not expected: MCD43A4 is nadir reflectance at local solar noon from a 16 day fit, the Landsat image is one view at 11:33, and the two use different weights. The check rules out gross errors such as a missing scale offset or a wrong band order.

title: Net Radiation from Landsat: Albedo, Emissivity and Surface Temperature
text:
Transmissivity and incoming shortwave
Pressure comes from the DEM, vapour pressure from the ERA5 dew point at the overpass, and the sun angle from the metadata. On flat ground cos theta is the cosine of the solar zenith angle.


Code
pressure = seb.pressure_from_elevation(ds.dem)  # kPa
cos_z = float(np.cos(np.radians(90 - a["sun_elevation"])))  # flat ground
tau_sw = seb.broadband_transmissivity(cos_z, pressure=pressure, ea=a["ea_kpa"])  # clear-sky transmissivity
rs_in = seb.incoming_shortwave(cos_z, tau_sw, dr=a["dr"])  # W/m2
slope, aspect = seb.slope_aspect(ds.dem)  # terrain
cos_t = seb.cos_incidence(sd.WESTSIDE["lat"], pd.Timestamp(a["datetime"]), sd.WESTSIDE["lon"], slope, aspect)  # on the slopes
rs_slope = seb.incoming_shortwave(cos_t, tau_sw, dr=a["dr"])  # W/m2 with terrain
print(f"precipitable water {float(seb.precipitable_water(a['ea_kpa'], pressure.mean())):.1f} mm | tau_sw {float(tau_sw.mean()):.3f}")  # atmosphere
print(f"Rs_in, clear-sky model: {float(rs_in.mean()):.0f} W/m2 (flat), {float(rs_slope.min()):.0f} to {float(rs_slope.max()):.0f} W/m2 with terrain")  # model
print(f"pixels the terrain correction changes by more than 10 W/m2: {float((np.abs(rs_slope - rs_in) > 10).mean()):.1%}")  # how many matter
print(f"Rs_in, ERA5 at the overpass: {a['rs_wm2']:.0f} W/m2")  # reanalysis


precipitable water 11.9 mm | tau_sw 0.784
Rs_in, clear-sky model: 950 W/m2 (flat), 788 to 1024 W/m2 with terrain
pixels the terrain correction changes by more than 10 W/m2: 1.1%
Rs_in, ERA5 at the overpass: 854 W/m2


On this valley floor the terrain correction changes only 1.1 % of pixels by more than 10 W m-2. Its extremes (about 790 to 1,020 W m-2) come from canal banks, road embankments and noise in the 30 m DEM, a few pixels with slopes of a few degrees; the chapter therefore uses flat-ground radiation for the Westside scenes, while the hill-slope correction matters in mountain valleys. The clear-sky model gives about 950 W m-2, roughly 10 % more than ERA5’s value interpolated to the overpass. ERA5 averages over each hour and over a 25 km cell that includes hazier foothill air, so a gap of this size on a cloudless day is typical; the METRIC clear-sky formula is used for the instantaneous balance because it is computed for the exact time and place.

title: Net Radiation from Landsat: Albedo, Emissivity and Surface Temperature
text:
LAI and emissivity
METRIC estimates LAI from SAVI with an empirical curve from southern Idaho crops (Allen et al. 2002), using the soil adjustment L = 0.1 from that calibration, and emissivity from LAI.


Code
savi = seb.savi(sr.red, sr.nir, L=0.1)  # SAVI with L = 0.1 (METRIC)
lai = seb.leaf_area_index(savi)  # m2/m2, capped at 6
e0 = seb.surface_emissivity(lai, seb.ndvi(sr.red, sr.nir))  # broadband, for longwave
e_nb = seb.surface_emissivity(lai, seb.ndvi(sr.red, sr.nir), kind="narrowband")  # band 10
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6))  # two panels
im = ax[0].imshow(lai, extent=ext, cmap="Greens", vmin=0, vmax=6); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8, label="m2/m2")  # LAI map

ax[1].set_xlabel("Collection 2 ST_EMIS (ASTER based)"); ax[1].set_ylabel("METRIC narrowband emissivity from LAI")  # labels
ax[1].set_title("Two estimates of band 10 emissivity"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

The two emissivity estimates agree on the range but not pixel by pixel: ST_EMIS adjusts a multi-year ASTER emissivity with the NDVI of the day, while the METRIC curve uses LAI alone, and it is lower over bare soil (0.95 against about 0.97). title: Net Radiation from Landsat: Albedo, Emissivity and Surface Temperature
text:
Longwave radiation
Outgoing longwave follows from LST and broadband emissivity. Incoming longwave needs the air temperature near the surface; METRIC takes the LST of the cold anchor as a surrogate (a well watered crop is close to air temperature) and the air emissivity from transmissivity, eps_a = 0.85 (-ln tau_sw)^0.09. The Brutsaert (1975) formula with ERA5 air temperature and humidity is an independent estimate.


Code
anchors = seb.select_anchors(seb.ndvi(sr.red, sr.nir), st, albedo_=alb_liang, mask=m)  # cold and hot pixels (notebook 05)
t_cold = anchors["cold"]["lst"]  # K
tau_c = float(tau_sw.values[anchors["cold"]["iy"], anchors["cold"]["ix"]])  # transmissivity at the cold pixel
rl_in = seb.incoming_longwave(t_cold, seb.air_emissivity(tau_sw=tau_c))  # METRIC, W/m2
rl_in_b = seb.incoming_longwave(a["t_air_c"] + 273.15, seb.air_emissivity(ea=a["ea_kpa"], t_air_k=a["t_air_c"] + 273.15))  # Brutsaert with ERA5
rl_out = seb.outgoing_longwave(st, e0)  # W/m2
print(f"cold anchor LST {t_cold - 273.15:.1f} C, ERA5 air {a['t_air_c']:.1f} C")  # the two air temperature surrogates
print(f"RL_in: METRIC {float(rl_in):.0f} W/m2, Brutsaert with ERA5 {float(rl_in_b):.0f} W/m2")  # incoming longwave
print(f"RL_out: {float(rl_out.quantile(0.02)):.0f} to {float(rl_out.quantile(0.98)):.0f} W/m2 (2nd to 98th percentile)")  # outgoing longwave

RL_in: METRIC 384 W/m2, Brutsaert with ERA5 392 W/m2
RL_out: 510 to 665 W/m2 (2nd to 98th percentile)


The two estimates of incoming longwave are within 8 W m-2 (384 and 392): the cold anchor (a well watered almond orchard at 35.2 C) is 4.6 K cooler than the ERA5 air, and the transmissivity-based air emissivity makes up most of that difference. Outgoing longwave varies across the scene by about 150 W m-2, almost all of it from LST: hot fallow fields lose far more energy as longwave than cool crops.

title: Net Radiation from Landsat: Albedo, Emissivity and Surface Temperature
text:
Summary and exercises

Radiative transfer with the Collection 2 atmospheric terms reproduces ST_B10 within 0.15 K; the uncorrected brightness temperature is 6.5 K too cold.
Broadband albedo from OLI bands with Liang’s weights ranges from about 0.15 to 0.30, agrees with MODIS MCD43A4 at 480 m (bias -0.004, RMSE 0.018, R2 0.76), and is 0.006 higher than the Tasumi weights in the median.
Clear-sky incoming shortwave at the overpass was about 950 W m-2; ERA5’s hourly value was about 10 % lower.
METRIC’s incoming longwave (cold anchor LST and transmissivity) agrees with Brutsaert’s formula and ERA5.
Net radiation follows LST more than albedo here: orchards and vineyards had about 80 W m-2 more net radiation than fallow land, mostly because they emit less longwave.

Exercises

Recompute LST by radiative transfer with the METRIC narrowband emissivity instead of ST_EMIS. How large are the differences over fallow land?
Replace the Liang albedo with the Tasumi albedo in Rn. What is the mean change in W m-2, and in daily ET if it all went to LE?
Compute Rn for the 8 April scene. How does it compare with July, and which term changes most?
Use seb.cos_incidence to compute incoming shortwave for a 15 degree south-facing slope and a 15 degree north-facing slope at this overpass time.

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Overview

What the models need








Input
Used for
Source in this chapter




Surface reflectance, 6 bands
NDVI, SAVI, LAI, albedo
Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 SR_B2 to SR_B7


Land surface temperature
H, outgoing longwave, anchors

removing bad pixels
QA_PIXEL (CFMask)

incoming shortwave, reference ET
scene metadata


Elevation
air pressure, slope, lapse rate
Copernicus DEM GLO-30


Land cover
anchor screening, results by crop
USDA Cropland Data Layer 2024


Air temperature, humidity, wind, radiation
reference ET, roughness, stability
ERA5 through the Open-Meteo archive; gridMET daily (notebook 02)





Where errors come from

Clouds and their edges. A thin cloud edge or a shadow is cool and dark, exactly what a cold anchor looks like. One missed cloud pixel picked as the cold anchor shifts every flux in the scene. Masks are therefore dilated by a few pixels.
Scaling. Collection 2 stores integers. Reflectance is DN 0.0000275 - 0.2, temperature DN 0.00341802 + 149.0 K. Forgetting the offset gives reflectance that is too high by 0.2 and albedo that is badly wrong.
Grids. DEM, crop map and Landsat must share one grid. Elevation is resampled bilinearly, categorical crop codes with the nearest neighbour.
Time. Landsat crosses the equator at about 10:00 to 10:15 local solar time; over central California the overpass is near 18:30 UTC. Weather must be taken at that moment, not as a daily mean.



Collection 2 Level-2 in brief
USGS processes every Landsat 8 and 9 scene into surface reflectance (LaSRC) and surface temperature (a single-channel algorithm on band 10 with MODTRAN atmospheric profiles and ASTER emissivity). Both are delivered as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs, so a STAC client can read a small window without downloading the whole 7,600 x 7,800 pixel scene.

Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Finding the scenes
A STAC search returns every Landsat 8 and 9 Level-2 scene that touches the box in 2024. The window lies on path 42 row 35 (and, at its edges, the neighbouring paths), so the search is filtered to that path and row to keep one viewing geometry.


Code
items = catalog.search(collections=["landsat-c2-l2"], bbox=SITE["bbox"], datetime="2024-01-01/2024-12-31",
                       query={"platform": {"in": ["landsat-8", "landsat-9"]}}).item_collection()  # every 2024 scene
scenes = pd.DataFrame([{"id": i.id, "date": i.datetime.date(), "platform": i.properties["platform"],
                        "cloud_cover": i.properties["eo:cloud_cover"]} for i in items])  # one row per scene
scenes = scenes[scenes.id.str.contains("_042035_")].sort_values("date").reset_index(drop=True)  # path 42 row 35 only
print(len(scenes), "scenes on path 42 row 35;", (scenes.cloud_cover < 13).sum(), "with less than 13 % cloud")  # counts
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3))  # one panel
ax.bar(pd.to_datetime(scenes.date), scenes.cloud_cover, width=4,
       color=np.where(scenes.cloud_cover < 13, "#1a9850", "#bdbdbd"))  # cloud cover per date
ax.axhline(13, color="k", lw=0.7, ls="--"); ax.set_ylabel("scene cloud cover (%)")  # threshold
ax.set_title("Landsat 8 and 9, path 42 row 35, 2024 (green: used in this chapter)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


44 scenes on path 42 row 35; 27 with less than 13 % cloud









Landsat 8 and 9 together give an image every 8 days. Winter storms cloud out most January to March and November to December dates; from April to October almost every pass is clear, which is why the Central Valley is a good place to learn these models. The list of chosen scenes is kept in sd.SEASON_2024.

text:
Reading a window and applying scale factors
The main scene is 5 July 2024. Its STAC item lists one asset per band; the metadata give the projection (UTM zone 11N) and the acquisition time.


Code
item = catalog.get_collection("landsat-c2-l2").get_item(sd.MAIN_SCENE)  # one scene
epsg = item.properties.get("proj:epsg") or int(item.properties["proj:code"].split(":")[1])  # its UTM zone
print(item.id, "| EPSG", epsg, "|", item.properties["datetime"])  # identity
print("assets:", ", ".join(sorted(k for k in item.assets if k not in ("rendered_preview", "tilejson"))))  # bands and files


LC08_L2SP_042035_20240705_02_T1 | EPSG 32611 | 2024-07-05T18:33:27.252130Z
assets: ang, atran, blue, cdist, coastal, drad, emis, emsd, green, lwir11, mtl.json, mtl.txt, mtl.xml, nir08, qa, qa_aerosol, qa_pixel, qa_radsat, red, swir16, swir22, trad, urad




Code
from pyproj import Transformer  # coordinate transformations

to_utm = Transformer.from_crs(4326, epsg, always_xy=True)  # lon/lat -> UTM
b = SITE["bbox"]  # west, south, east, north
xs, ys = to_utm.transform([b[0], b[2], b[0], b[2]], [b[1], b[1], b[3], b[3]])  # the four corners in UTM
x0, x1, y0, y1 = min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys)  # window that covers the box

red_dn = rioxarray.open_rasterio(item.assets["red"].href).squeeze("band", drop=True)  # lazy: nothing read yet
print("full scene:", dict(red_dn.sizes))  # whole scene size
red_dn = red_dn.sel(x=slice(x0, x1), y=slice(y1, y0)).load()  # read only the window
print("window:", dict(red_dn.sizes), "| dtype", red_dn.dtype, "| DN range", int(red_dn.min()), "to", int(red_dn.max()))  # what was read


full scene: {'y': 7951, 'x': 7821}
window: {'y': 953, 'x': 926} | dtype uint16 | DN range 7063 to 34414


Only the window (about 3 % of the scene) is transferred. The values are 16-bit integers; the Collection 2 scale factors turn them into reflectance and kelvin. A DN of 0 is fill.


Code
red = (red_dn.where(red_dn > 0) * 2.75e-5 - 0.2)  # surface reflectance, 0 to 1
st_dn = rioxarray.open_rasterio(item.assets["lwir11"].href).squeeze("band", drop=True).sel(x=slice(x0, x1), y=slice(y1, y0)).load()  # ST_B10
lst = st_dn.where(st_dn > 0) * 0.00341802 + 149.0  # surface temperature, K
pd.DataFrame({"DN": [float(red_dn.median()), float(st_dn.median())],  # raw medians
              "physical": [float(red.median()), float(lst.median())],  # scaled medians
              "forgotten offset": [float(red_dn.median()) * 2.75e-5, float(st_dn.median()) * 0.00341802]},  # scale without offset
             index=["red reflectance", "surface temperature (K)"]).round(3)  # table

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Decoding the quality band
QA_PIXEL packs one flag per bit. Bits 0 to 5 mark fill, dilated cloud, cirrus, cloud, cloud shadow and snow; bit 7 marks water. A pixel is clear when none of bits 0 to 5 is set.


Code
qa = rioxarray.open_rasterio(item.assets["qa_pixel"].href).squeeze("band", drop=True).sel(x=slice(x0, x1), y=slice(y1, y0)).load().astype("int64")  # QA_PIXEL
BITS = {"fill": 0, "dilated cloud": 1, "cirrus": 2, "cloud": 3, "cloud shadow": 4, "snow": 5, "clear": 6, "water": 7}  # CFMask bits
flags = pd.Series({name: float(((qa >> bit) & 1).mean()) for name, bit in BITS.items()})  # share of pixels with each flag
(100 * flags).round(3).to_frame("% of window")  # table









% of window




fill
0.000


dilated cloud
0.000


cirrus
0.000


cloud
0.000


cloud shadow
0.000


snow
0.000


clear
100.000


water
0.095







5 July is almost perfectly clear. To see why masks matter, the same decoding on a partly cloudy scene (16 April 2024, 12 % cloud over the whole scene) shows clouds, their shadows and the cool fringes around them.


Code
cloudy = sd.load_scene("LC08_L2SP_042035_20240416_02_T1")  # cached stack of a partly cloudy scene (raw QA not kept)
it2 = catalog.get_collection("landsat-c2-l2").get_item(cloudy.attrs["scene_id"])  # its STAC item
qa2 = rioxarray.open_rasterio(it2.assets["qa_pixel"].href).squeeze("band", drop=True).sel(x=slice(x0, x1), y=slice(y1, y0)).load().astype("int64")  # its QA_PIXEL
cloud = (((qa2 >> 3) & 1) | ((qa2 >> 1) & 1)).astype(bool)  # cloud or dilated cloud
shadow = ((qa2 >> 4) & 1).astype(bool)  # cloud shadow
buffer = ndimage.binary_dilation((cloud | shadow).values, iterations=3)  # three more pixels (90 m) around them
lst2 = cloudy.lst - 273.15  # its surface temperature, C
ring = buffer & ~(cloud | shadow).values  # the 90 m ring the dilation adds
print(f"cloud {cloud.mean().item():.1%}, shadow {shadow.mean().item():.1%}, dilation adds {ring.mean():.1%} of the window")  # sizes
print(f"median LST: clear {float(lst2.where(~buffer).median()):.1f} C | added ring {float(lst2.where(ring).median()):.1f} C | "
      f"shadow {float(lst2.where(shadow).median()):.1f} C | cloud {float(lst2.where(cloud).median()):.1f} C")  # temperatures

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))  # two maps
ax[0].imshow(lst2, cmap="inferno", vmin=0, vmax=45); ax[0].set_title("LST, 16 April 2024 (C)")  # temperature
show = np.where(cloud, 3, np.where(shadow, 2, np.where(ring, 1, 0)))  # 0 clear, 1 ring, 2 shadow, 3 cloud
ax[1].imshow(show, cmap=plt.matplotlib.colors.ListedColormap(["#f0f0f0", "#fdae61", "#4d4d4d", "#4393c3"]), vmin=0, vmax=3, interpolation="nearest")  # masks
ax[1].set_title("clear (grey), cloud (blue), shadow (dark), 90 m ring (orange)")  # legend in the title
for a in ax:  # both maps
    a.axis("off")  # hide axes
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


cloud 16.4%, shadow 9.8%, dilation adds 5.1% of the window
median LST: clear 29.8 C | added ring 28.6 C | shadow 24.8 C | cloud 18.7 C









Clouds and their shadows are far cooler than the clear land, and the ring of pixels the dilation adds is cooler than the clear median too. Those ring pixels look like well watered vegetation to an anchor search. sd.read_landsat excludes every flagged pixel (bits 0 to 5), which already includes CFMask’s own dilated cloud bit; notebook 05 adds a homogeneity test to the anchor search for the same reason.

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Overpass time and sun angles
The scene centre time and the sun elevation and azimuth come with the metadata. seb.scene_geometry reads them from STAC properties or from a Landsat MTL file, and seb.solar_position computes the same angles from the time and position, which is a useful check (and what you need for sensors without these fields).


Code
geo = seb.scene_geometry(item.properties)  # from the STAC properties
pos = seb.solar_position(SITE["lat"], SITE["lon"], geo["datetime"])  # computed at the window centre
local = geo["datetime"] + pd.Timedelta(hours=SITE["utc_offset"])  # Pacific daylight time
pd.DataFrame({"metadata (scene centre)": [geo["sun_elevation"], geo["sun_azimuth"]],  # what USGS reports
              "computed (window centre)": [float(pos["elevation"]), float(pos["azimuth"])]},  # what seb computes
             index=["sun elevation (deg)", "sun azimuth (deg)"]).round(2).assign(  # table
    note=[f"overpass {geo['datetime']:%H:%M} UTC = {local:%H:%M} local", f"day {geo['doy']}, Earth-Sun factor dr = {geo['dr']:.4f}"])  # time and distance









metadata (scene centre)
computed (window centre)

sun elevation (deg)

The metadata refer to the centre of the whole scene, about 90 km from the window centre, so the sun elevation differs by about 0.6 degree and the azimuth by less; the computed angles are the right ones for the window. dr is below 1 in early July because the Earth is near its farthest point from the sun (aphelion), so sunlight is about 3 % weaker than the annual mean.

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Elevation on the Landsat grid
sd.dem_on merges the Copernicus DEM tiles around the window and reprojects them bilinearly to the Landsat grid. Elevation sets air pressure (needed for air density and the psychrometric constant), and slope and aspect change the incoming sunshine on hillsides.


Code
lst_grid = lst.rio.write_crs(epsg)  # the Landsat grid with its CRS
dem = sd.dem_on(lst_grid, SITE)  # elevation on that grid, m
slope, aspect = seb.slope_aspect(dem)  # degrees
pressure = seb.pressure_from_elevation(dem)  # kPa
print(f"elevation {float(dem.min()):.0f} to {float(dem.max()):.0f} m | slope above 5 deg: {float((slope > 5).mean()):.1%} | "
      f"pressure {float(pressure.min()):.2f} to {float(pressure.max()):.2f} kPa")  # ranges
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8))  # two maps
im = ax[0].imshow(dem, cmap="terrain"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8, label="m"); ax[0].set_title("Copernicus DEM on the Landsat grid")  # elevation
im = ax[1].imshow(slope, cmap="magma_r", vmax=10); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8, label="deg"); ax[1].set_title("Slope")  # slope
for a in ax:  # both maps
    a.axis("off")  # hide axes
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


elevation 43 to 140 m | slope above 5 deg: 0.0% | pressure 99.65 to 100.79 kPa









The valley floor is nearly flat, so terrain corrections of radiation are small here; they matter in hilly scenes and are included in notebook 03 for completeness.

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Weather at the overpass
seb.weather_open_meteo returns ERA5 reanalysis from the free Open-Meteo archive (no key): hourly air temperature, humidity, dew point, wind at 10 m, shortwave radiation and pressure, in UTC. ERA5 is a 0.25 degree (about 25 km) product, so it describes the regional air rather than any single field. Notebook 02 compares it with gridMET and discusses what that means over irrigated land.


Code
day = geo["datetime"].strftime("%Y-%m-%d")  # the overpass date
w = sd.weather(SITE, day, day)  # cached Open-Meteo hourly and daily tables
hourly = w["hourly"]  # hourly ERA5, UTC
wx = seb.interpolate_weather(hourly, geo["datetime"])  # linear interpolation to the overpass time
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.6))  # three panels
local_h = hourly.index + pd.Timedelta(hours=SITE["utc_offset"])  # local time axis
for a, col, lab in zip(ax, ["temperature_2m", "shortwave_radiation", "wind_speed_10m"],
                       ["air temperature (C)", "shortwave (W/m2)", "wind at 10 m (m/s)"]):  # each variable
    a.plot(local_h, hourly[col], "o-", ms=3); a.axvline(local, color="r", lw=1)  # hourly series and overpass
    a.set_title(lab); a.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=30)  # labels
plt.suptitle(f"ERA5 on {day} (local time), red line: Landsat overpass"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
wx[["temperature_2m", "relative_humidity_2m", "dew_point_2m", "wind_speed_10m", "shortwave_radiation", "surface_pressure"]].round(2)  # values at the overpass









temperature_2m            39.85
relative_humidity_2m       9.33
dew_point_2m               1.83
wind_speed_10m             2.16
shortwave_radiation      853.79
surface_pressure        1004.11
Name: 2024-07-05 18:33:27.252130, dtype: float64


ERA5 hourly values are averages over the hour ending at the time stamp, so linear interpolation between the two neighbouring hours gives the best estimate at 18:33 UTC. The models need vapour pressure (from the dew point) and wind at 2 m and at the 200 m blending height, where wind is assumed independent of the surface below (notebook 04).


Code
ea = float(seb.actual_vapour_pressure(t_dew_c=wx["dew_point_2m"]))  # vapour pressure, kPa
u2 = float(seb.wind_2m(wx["wind_speed_10m"], 10.0))  # FAO-56 log profile from 10 m to 2 m
u200 = float(seb.wind_at_blending_height(u2, z=2.0))  # over grass, extended to 200 m
es = float(seb.saturation_vapour_pressure(wx["temperature_2m"]))  # saturation vapour pressure, kPa
print(f"vapour pressure {ea:.2f} kPa, vapour pressure deficit {es - ea:.2f} kPa")  # humidity terms
print(f"wind: {wx['wind_speed_10m']:.2f} m/s at 10 m -> {u2:.2f} m/s at 2 m -> {u200:.2f} m/s at 200 m")  # wind profile


vapour pressure 0.70 kPa, vapour pressure deficit 6.62 kPa
wind: 2.16 m/s at 10 m -> 1.61 m/s at 2 m -> 3.12 m/s at 200 m


A vapour pressure deficit above 6 kPa is extreme; typical summer afternoons in the valley reach 3 to 5 kPa. Together with the strong sunshine, it drives the very high reference ET of this day.

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Saving the stack
All layers share one grid, so they go into one xr.Dataset with the overpass weather and geometry as attributes. sd.load_scene does exactly this (plus the thermal radiance terms used in notebook 03) and caches the result as compressed NetCDF; here the hand-built layers are compared with the cached stack.


Code
ds = sd.load_scene(sd.MAIN_SCENE)  # the cached stack (built on first use)
same = {"red": float(np.nanmax(np.abs(ds.red - red.astype("float32")))),  # hand-built vs cached reflectance
        "lst": float(np.nanmax(np.abs(ds.lst - lst.astype("float32")))),  # surface temperature
        "dem": float(np.nanmax(np.abs(ds.dem - dem))),  # elevation
        "cdl": int((ds.cdl != cdl).sum())}  # crop codes that differ
print("largest differences, hand-built vs sd.load_scene:", same)  # should be zero
print(list(ds.data_vars))  # layers
{k: ds.attrs[k] for k in ["scene_id", "datetime", "sun_elevation", "dr", "t_air_c", "ea_kpa", "u10", "rs_wm2", "tmax_c", "tmin_c", "rs_daily_mj"]}  # key attributes

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Every clear scene of 2024
Notebook 10 builds a seasonal ET record from every clear 2024 scene. The stacks are built here in parallel processes (each scene takes one to two minutes to download the first time; later runs read the cache).


Code

title: Building an Analysis-Ready Stack for Energy Balance Models
text:
Summary and exercises

STAC search plus Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs give a small study window from each scene without downloading whole scenes: 27 Landsat 8 and 9 scenes of 2024 passed the 13 % cloud filter on path 42 row 35.
Collection 2 values must be scaled (DN 0.0000275 - 0.2 for reflectance, DN 0.00341802 + 149 K for temperature); the offset matters.
QA_PIXEL bits 0 to 5 flag fill, dilated cloud, cirrus, cloud, shadow and snow. Cloud fringes are cool and would make false cold anchors, so masks are generous.
Elevation (bilinear) and crop codes (nearest) go on the Landsat grid; weather is interpolated to the overpass and wind moved to 2 m and 200 m.
sd.load_scene reproduces all of this and caches one NetCDF per scene. Masks are saved as plain integers without a fill value: a _FillValue of 0 inherited from QA_PIXEL would turn every cloudy 0 into a missing value that reads back as clear.

Exercises

Count, for every 2024 scene, the share of clear pixels inside the window rather than the scene cloud cover from the metadata. Which scenes would you drop?
Dilate the 16 April cloud mask by 1, 3 and 6 pixels and plot the median LST of each added ring. How far from the cloud does the cooling reach?
Compute the sun elevation with seb.solar_position at the four corners of the window. How large is the difference across 28 km?
Download a week of hourly ERA5 around 5 July (sd.weather(SITE, "2024-07-01", "2024-07-08")) and plot the air temperature at every overpass hour. How unusual was 5 July?
