title: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Your Own Data
text:
Overview

What to measure








Quantity
Why it matters
How




accuracy of frozen embeddings
how much the encoder already knows
linear and kNN probes


label efficiency
the reason to use a foundation model at all
accuracy with few labels per class


spatial generalization
maps are used where no labels exist
spatial or grouped cross-validation


speed and memory
cost of mapping a region or an archive
seconds per 1000 chips, peak GPU memory


licence and access
whether the model can be used at all
model card





A fair comparison

Same samples, same folds for every model, including the baselines.
Each model’s own input contract (bands, units, statistics), so no model is handicapped by wrong preprocessing; a deliberately mismatched model shows what that would cost.
Baselines that need no foundation model: simple statistics of the bands, and a small network trained from scratch.
Spread, not just means: the fold-to-fold standard deviation says which differences matter.
Spatial hold-outs wherever the samples have coordinates.



Why probes
A linear probe trains only a linear classifier on frozen embeddings; a kNN probe uses the raw distances. Both are cheap, deterministic and comparable across models. Fine-tuning can change the ranking (notebook 09_11_04 showed a U-Net beating a frozen and a fine-tuned Prithvi on segmentation), so probes measure what the embeddings hold, not the best achievable accuracy.

title: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Your Own Data

Prepare one labelled set for many models, each with its own input contract.

title: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Your Own Data
text:
Task 1: EuroSAT RGB
Two hundred images per class are drawn from EuroSAT. Every model gets the same images, resized to its input size and normalized by its contract: ImageNet statistics for Scale-MAE, 0 to 1 for Satlas NAIP, CLIP statistics for RemoteCLIP and GeoRSCLIP, per-band standardization for DOFA and Panopticon (told the band wavelengths). The SSL4EO ResNet-18 expects thirteen Sentinel-2 bands; it receives the RGB bands with the other ten filled from the nearest of them, as a deliberately mismatched entry.


Code
zf = zipfile.ZipFile(CAP / "EuroSat.zip")  # the archive
files = np.array([n for n in zf.namelist() if n.endswith(".jpg")])  # every image
cls = np.array([n.split("/")[1] for n in files])  # class names
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)  # random generator
pick = np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(cls == c), 200, replace=False) for c in np.unique(cls)])  # 200 per class
rgb64 = np.stack([np.asarray(Image.open(zf.open(f)).convert("RGB"), "float32") / 255 for f in files[pick]])  # (2000, 64, 64, 3)
y_es = cls[pick]  # labels
x64 = torch.as_tensor(rgb64).permute(0, 3, 1, 2)  # (2000, 3, 64, 64)
up = lambda s: torch.nn.functional.interpolate(x64, size=s, mode="bicubic", align_corners=False).clamp(0, 1)  # resize


def norm(x, mean, std):  # channel-wise normalization
    return ((x - torch.tensor(mean)[:, None, None]) / torch.tensor(std)[:, None, None]).numpy()  # (n, 3, s, s)


def standardize(x):  # per-band standardization over the whole set
    return ((x - x.mean((0, 2, 3), keepdim=True)) / x.std((0, 2, 3), keepdim=True)).numpy()  # (n, 3, s, s)


x224 = up(224)  # RGB at 224 px
bands13 = fm.input_spec("ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco")["bands"]  # the 13 bands SSL4EO expects
order13 = [["red", "green", "blue"].index(b) if b in ("red", "green", "blue") else
           ["red", "green", "blue"].index(min(["red", "green", "blue"], key=lambda c: abs(fm.WAVELENGTHS_NM[c] - fm.WAVELENGTHS_NM[b])))
           for b in bands13]  # nearest RGB band for each of the 13
print("SSL4EO bands filled from RGB:", [b for b in bands13 if b not in ("red", "green", "blue")])  # the mismatch

inputs_es = {
    "RGB mean and std (baseline)": {"embeddings": np.c_[rgb64.mean((1, 2)), rgb64.std((1, 2))]},  # 6 numbers
    "colour histogram (baseline)": {"embeddings": np.concatenate([np.stack([np.histogram(im[..., c], 16, (0, 1))[0] for im in rgb64]) for c in range(3)], 1) / 4096},  # 48 numbers
    "scale-mae": {"x": norm(x224, fm.input_spec("scale-mae")["mean"], fm.input_spec("scale-mae")["std"])},  # ImageNet statistics
    "satlas-swinb-naip": {"x": up(256).numpy()},  # 0..1, 256 px
    "remoteclip-vit-b-32": {"x": norm(x224, CLIP_MEAN, CLIP_STD)},  # CLIP statistics
    "georsclip-vit-b-32": {"x": norm(x224, CLIP_MEAN, CLIP_STD)},  # CLIP statistics
    "dofa-base": {"x": standardize(x224), "load": {"bands": ["red", "green", "blue"]}},  # wavelengths from band names
    "panopticon": {"x": standardize(x224), "load": {"bands": ["red", "green", "blue"]}},  # wavelengths from band names
    "ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco (mismatched)": {"model": "ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco",
                                              "x": x224.numpy()[:, order13] * 1.0},  # RGB copied into 13 bands
}
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
bench_es = fm.benchmark_encoders(inputs_es, y_es, cv=5, device=DEVICE, batch_size=64)  # probes, speed, memory
print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")  # total time
bench_es.round(3).sort_values("linear_f1_macro", ascending=False)  # ranked

A small CNN trained from scratch on the same images and folds is the second baseline: four convolution blocks, 20 epochs per fold.


Code
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score  # scores
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold  # same folds as the probes

classes = sorted(np.unique(y_es)); yi = np.array([classes.index(c) for c in y_es])  # class indices


def small_cnn():  # four conv blocks for 64 px RGB
    blk = lambda i, o: torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Conv2d(i, o, 3, padding=1), torch.nn.BatchNorm2d(o), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.MaxPool2d(2))  # one block
    return torch.nn.Sequential(blk(3, 32), blk(32, 64), blk(64, 128), blk(128, 128), torch.nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1),
                               torch.nn.Flatten(), torch.nn.Linear(128, 10))  # network


f1s, t0 = [], time.perf_counter()  # fold scores and timing
for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED).split(yi, yi)):  # same folds as fm.linear_probe
    torch.manual_seed(SEED); net = small_cnn().to(DEVICE)  # fresh network
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(net.parameters(), 2e-3)  # optimizer
    X, Y = x64[tr].to(DEVICE), torch.as_tensor(yi[tr]).to(DEVICE)  # training data
    for ep in range(20):  # epochs
        net.train()  # training mode
        for i in torch.randperm(len(tr)).split(64):  # mini-batches
            xb = X[i].flip(-1) if ep % 2 else X[i]  # flip every other epoch
            loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(xb), Y[i]); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()  # update
    net.eval()  # evaluation mode
    with torch.no_grad():  # inference
        pred = net(x64[te].to(DEVICE)).argmax(1).cpu().numpy()  # predictions
    f1s.append(f1_score(yi[te], pred, average="macro"))  # fold score
cnn_row = pd.DataFrame({"linear_f1_macro": [np.mean(f1s)], "s_per_1000": [np.nan], "embed_dim": [np.nan]},
                       index=["small CNN from scratch (baseline)"])  # one row
print(f"small CNN: macro F1 {np.mean(f1s):.3f} +/- {np.std(f1s):.3f} in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")  # result


small CNN: macro F1 0.693 +/- 0.054 in 14 s


Every foundation model beats both baselines by a wide margin: linear probes on frozen embeddings reach a macro F1 of 0.92 to 0.96, against about 0.65 for six RGB statistics, 0.63 for colour histograms and 0.69 for the small CNN trained from scratch on 1,600 images per fold. (A CNN trained longer, with augmentation, on all 27,000 EuroSAT images reaches far higher; with this small labelled set it cannot.) Panopticon and GeoRSCLIP lead at about 0.96, and GeoRSCLIP embeds a thousand chips in under 2 seconds against 12 for Panopticon and 22 for Scale-MAE. The deliberately mismatched SSL4EO ResNet-18, which received RGB copied into thirteen bands, still reaches 0.92: EuroSAT is forgiving, and the mismatch costs only three to four points here. The kNN scores, which use raw distances, are lower and spread more, because embedding spaces differ in how well plain distance reflects the classes.

title: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Your Own Data
text:
Label efficiency on EuroSAT
Foundation models should matter most when labels are scarce. A logistic regression is trained on 2, 5, 10 and 50 images per class from the first fold’s training images and scored on its test images, five draws each. The embeddings are recomputed once per model.


Code
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression  # classifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline  # scaling + model
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler  # scaling

tr, te = next(StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED).split(yi, yi))  # first fold
EMB = {"RGB mean and std (baseline)": inputs_es["RGB mean and std (baseline)"]["embeddings"]}  # baseline features
for n in ["scale-mae", "satlas-swinb-naip", "georsclip-vit-b-32", "dofa-base"]:  # four models
    spec = inputs_es[n]; e = fm.load_model(spec.get("model", n), device=DEVICE, **spec.get("load", {}))  # load
    EMB[n] = e.embed(spec["x"], batch_size=64); del e; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # embeddings
rows = []  # label efficiency
for k in [2, 5, 10, 50]:  # labels per class
    for rep in range(5):  # draws
        r = np.random.default_rng(rep)  # generator
        idx = np.concatenate([r.choice(tr[yi[tr] == c], k, replace=False) for c in range(10)])  # k per class
        for n, E in EMB.items():  # every input
            clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)).fit(E[idx], yi[idx])  # train
            rows.append({"labels per class": k, "input": n, "F1": f1_score(yi[te], clf.predict(E[te]), average="macro")})  # score
eff = pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby(["labels per class", "input"])["F1"].mean().unstack()  # mean over draws
ax = eff.plot(marker="o", logx=True, figsize=(8, 4.8)); ax.set_ylabel("macro F1 (held-out fold)")  # curves
ax.set_title("EuroSAT: label efficiency"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()  # draw
eff.round(3)

title: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Your Own Data
section: Task 2: early-season crops in the Corn Belt
text:
Task 2: early-season crops in the Corn Belt
The second task repeats the June experiment of notebook 09_11_04 with more encoders: each model reads the 22 June 2025 scene at native resolution with its own contract, its patch features are averaged to 640 m cells, and the cells are probed with folds over 5.8 km blocks. Run time and peak GPU memory are measured for the whole scene. Copernicus-FM, Panopticon and CROMA return pooled vectors only and are left out of this patch-level comparison (notebook 09_11_05 evaluates them at chip level).


Code
s2 = xr.open_dataarray(CUBE / "s2_20m.nc").sel(time="2025-06-22").drop_vars("time").load().rio.write_crs("EPSG:32615")  # June scene
cdl = xr.open_dataset(CUBE / "labels_20m.nc")["cdl"].sel(year=2025).load()  # CDL 2025
CELL = 32; NY, NX = -(-cdl.shape[0] // CELL), -(-cdl.shape[1] // CELL)  # 640 m cell grid
pad = np.full((NY * CELL, NX * CELL), -1, cdl.dtype); pad[:cdl.shape[0], :cdl.shape[1]] = cdl.values  # padded CDL
blk = pad.reshape(NY, CELL, NX, CELL).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(NY * NX, -1)  # pixels per cell
cnt = np.stack([(blk == k).sum(1) for k in (0, 1)], 1); y_cb, pur = cnt.argmax(1), cnt.max(1) / blk.shape[1]  # labels
gy, gx = np.divmod(np.arange(NY * NX), NX); group = (gy // 9) * 10 + gx // 9; ok = pur >= 0.6  # blocks and usable cells


def cells(d):  # patch map -> (cells, D) on the 640 m grid
    f = int(round(d.sizes["y"] / NY))  # patches per cell side
    d = d.coarsen(y=f, x=f, boundary="pad").mean() if f > 1 else d  # average to 640 m
    return d.values[:, :NY, :NX].reshape(d.sizes["embedding"], -1).T  # (cells, D)


CB_MODELS = ["prithvi-eo-2.0-300m", "prithvi-eo-1.0-100m", "terramind-v1-base", "ssl4eo-s12-vits16-dino",
             "ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", "satlas-swint-s2-ms", "dofa-base", "scale-mae"]  # patch-capable encoders
inputs_cb = {"band means (baseline)": {"embeddings": np.nan_to_num(s2.coarsen(y=CELL, x=CELL, boundary="pad").mean().values[:, :NY, :NX].reshape(10, -1).T)[ok]}}  # baseline
cost = {}  # time and memory per model
for n in CB_MODELS:  # every encoder
    e = fm.load_model(n, device=DEVICE)  # load
    if DEVICE == "cuda":  # reset the memory counter
        torch.cuda.synchronize(); torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()  # start clean
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
    E = cells(e.embed_raster(s2, dense=True, norm="model", batch_size=8))  # (cells, D)
    if DEVICE == "cuda":  # wait for the GPU
        torch.cuda.synchronize()  # finish
    cost[n] = {"seconds for the scene": time.perf_counter() - t0, "params (M)": sum(p.numel() for p in e.model.parameters()) / 1e6,
               "peak GPU memory (MB)": torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 2**20 if DEVICE == "cuda" else np.nan}  # cost
    inputs_cb[n] = {"embeddings": E[ok]}  # features of usable cells
    del e; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
bench_cb = fm.benchmark_encoders(inputs_cb, y_cb[ok], groups=group[ok], cv=5).join(pd.DataFrame(cost).T)  # probes + cost
bench_cb[["embed_dim", "linear_f1_macro", "knn_accuracy", "seconds for the scene", "params (M)", "peak GPU memory (MB)"]].round(3).sort_values("linear_f1_macro", ascending=False)  # ranked

title: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Your Own Data
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

A fair benchmark uses the same samples and folds for every model, each model’s own input contract, simple baselines, fold-to-fold spread and spatial hold-outs.
fm.benchmark_encoders gives probe scores, embedding size, parameters, speed and GPU memory in one table, for loaded models and for precomputed baselines.
On EuroSAT RGB and on early-season Sentinel-2 crops the best models differ, and a model fed inputs outside its contract falls behind.
Label efficiency, speed and licence matter as much as the top score.
Rankings from one task or benchmark do not transfer automatically: evaluate on your own data.



Exercises

Add remoteclip-vit-l-14 and dofa-large to the EuroSAT benchmark. Are larger models worth their cost?
Run the EuroSAT benchmark on the CPU only (device="cpu") and recompute the cost plot.

Add a random forest on the 10 band means and NDVI as a third Corn Belt baseline.

title: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space
text:
Overview

Change as distance between embeddings
Classical change detection compares band values or indices between two dates: dNBR for fires, NDWI for water, NDVI for vegetation. Each index targets one kind of change and responds to everything that changes its bands, including illumination, phenology and haze. Embedding change compares what an encoder sees in a patch, so it responds to changes in structure and texture as well as colour, for any kind of change at once. fm.embedding_change returns 1 minus the cosine similarity of the two embeddings in every cell: 0 means no change, larger values mean more change.


One normalization for both dates
Change detection only works if both dates are prepared identically. Standardizing each scene by its own mean and standard deviation removes exactly what a fire changes, the overall brightness of the bands, so the statistics of one date (or the model’s fixed statistics) must be applied to both.


Thresholds and false alarms
A change map is continuous; a burned area map needs a threshold. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and its area (AUC) score the map without choosing one. False alarms come from clouds and shadows, seasonal change in vegetation, and changes the encoder notices that the reference does not record.


Similarity search
An index of embeddings is an archive searchable by example: give one patch, get every patch that looks like it. fm.similarity_map scores every cell of a map against a query, and fm.embedding_search returns the nearest rows of any index. For millions of chips, approximate nearest-neighbour libraries (FAISS, Annoy) replace the exact search used here.

title: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space
section: Before and after the Bug Fire
text:
Before and after the Bug Fire
Both scenes are tile 10TGK: the clearest July or early August scene before the fire and the clearest September scene after it, chosen by the cloud cover recorded in each scene’s metadata. Sentinel-2 stores some bands at 10 m and others at 20 m, so every band is put on the 10 m grid before stacking. The Planetary Computer files hold digital numbers of processing baseline 05.12, which carry an offset of 1000: reflectance is (DN - 1000) / 10000. The scene classification layer (SCL) masks clouds, cirrus and snow, but not “cloud shadow”: its classifier often labels fresh burn scars as shadow, and masking them would remove the fire. The area around the perimeter (with a 3 km margin) is averaged to 20 m to keep the arrays small.


Code
perim = gpd.read_file(FIRE / "bug_fire_perimeter.geojson").to_crs(32610)  # NIFC perimeter, UTM 10N
perim["geometry"] = perim.geometry.buffer(0)  # repair self-intersections in the drawn perimeter
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = perim.total_bounds + np.array([-3000, -3000, 3000, 3000])  # 3 km margin


def clearest(folder, after=None):  # 10TGK scene with the lowest cloud cover (optionally after a date)
    import json  # scene metadata
    scenes = [d for d in (FIRE / folder).glob("*T10TGK*") if after is None or d.name[11:19] >= after]  # candidates
    cc = {d: json.loads((d / "item.json").read_text())["properties"]["eo:cloud_cover"] for d in scenes}  # cloud cover
    return min(cc, key=cc.get)  # the clearest


def read_s2(d):  # 9-band reflectance at 20 m around the fire, clouds masked
    ref = rioxarray.open_rasterio(d / "red.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.clip_box(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)  # 10 m grid
    layers = []  # one layer per band
    for b in S2_BANDS:  # every band (10 m or 20 m on disk)
        a = rioxarray.open_rasterio(d / f"{b}.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True)  # band
        layers.append(a.rio.reproject_match(ref, resampling=0))  # every band on the same 10 m grid
    arr = xr.concat(layers, dim=pd.Index(S2_BANDS, name="band"))  # (9, y, x)
    arr = (arr.astype("float32") - 1000) / 10000  # baseline 05.12 offset and scale
    scl = rioxarray.open_rasterio(d / "scl.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.reproject_match(ref, resampling=0)  # scene classes
    arr = arr.where(~scl.isin([0, 1, 8, 9, 10, 11]))  # drop no data, saturated, cloud, cirrus, snow (keep class 3: burn scars are often labelled shadow)
    return arr.coarsen(y=2, x=2, boundary="trim").mean().rio.write_crs(32610), d.name[11:19]  # 20 m, and the date


pre, d_pre = read_s2(clearest("pre")); post, d_post = read_s2(clearest("post", after="20260901"))  # clearest dates
post = post.assign_coords(x=pre.x, y=pre.y)  # identical grids
print(d_pre, "->", d_post, "|", dict(pre.sizes), "| masked before / after:",
      f"{float(pre.isnull().any('band').mean()):.1%} / {float(post.isnull().any('band').mean()):.1%}")  # summary

ext = [float(pre.x.min()), float(pre.x.max()), float(pre.y.min()), float(pre.y.max())]  # map extent
swir = lambda a: np.clip(np.nan_to_num(a.sel(band=["swir22", "nir08", "red"]).transpose("y", "x", "band").values) / 0.4, 0, 1)  # SWIR false colour
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))  # before and after
for a, (t, da) in zip(ax, {f"before, {d_pre}": pre, f"after, {d_post}": post}.items()):  # two dates
    a.imshow(swir(da), extent=ext); perim.boundary.plot(ax=a, color="yellow", lw=1); a.set_title(f"SWIR-NIR-red, {t}")  # map
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

dNBR, the reference index
The Normalized Burn Ratio uses NIR and SWIR 2; its difference before minus after (dNBR) is the standard burn severity index (Key and Benson 2006). Values above about 0.1 indicate burning.


Code
nbr = lambda a: (a.sel(band="nir08") - a.sel(band="swir22")) / (a.sel(band="nir08") + a.sel(band="swir22"))  # NBR
dnbr = nbr(pre) - nbr(post)  # dNBR, positive = burned
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))  # one panel
im = ax.imshow(dnbr, cmap="inferno", vmin=-0.1, vmax=0.8, extent=ext); perim.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="cyan", lw=1)  # map

title: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space
text:
Embeddings of both dates
Two encoders read both dates: DOFA (wavelength-aware, nine bands) and the SSL4EO ViT-S (thirteen bands, the four missing ones filled from neighbours). For DOFA the per-band mean and standard deviation of the before scene standardize both dates; SSL4EO has fixed statistics, so norm="model" is already identical for both.
The scene is embedded in overlapping chips: 32 pixels (640 m) wide, every 16 pixels (320 m), each resized to the model’s 224 pixel input and pooled to one vector. A first version of this notebook used patch features of 224 pixel chips (dense=True); DOFA’s change map was then dominated by bright lines along chip borders, where a patch sees less context and its features change most between two images. Overlapping pooled chips give every cell the same context on both dates. Masked (cloudy) pixels are filled with the scene mean for the encoder, and chips more than 10 % masked on either date are left out of the maps and the scores.


Code
CH, ST = 32, 16  # chip size and stride in 20 m pixels (640 m chips every 320 m)


def chip_mean(field):  # mean of a 2-D field in the same overlapping chips -> (rows, cols), ys, xs
    c, ys, xs = fm.chip_raster(field.expand_dims(band=["v"]).astype("float32"), chip_size=CH, stride=ST)  # chips
    return np.nanmean(c[:, 0].reshape(len(c), -1), 1).reshape(len(ys), len(xs)), ys, xs  # chip means


masked, ys, xs = chip_mean((pre.isnull().any("band") | post.isnull().any("band")).astype("float32"))  # masked share per chip
usable = masked <= 0.10  # chips clear enough on both dates
mu = pre.mean(("y", "x")).values; sd = pre.std(("y", "x")).values  # statistics of the before scene
fixed = {"method": "standard", "mean": mu, "std": sd}  # one normalization for both dates
fill = pre.mean(("y", "x"))  # value for masked pixels
emb = {}  # embeddings per model and date
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
dofa = fm.load_model("dofa-base", device=DEVICE)  # DOFA
for k, da in {"pre": pre, "post": post}.items():  # both dates
    emb[("DOFA", k)] = dofa.embed_raster(da.fillna(fill), chip_size=CH, stride=ST, norm=fixed, batch_size=128)  # (768, rows, cols)
del dofa
ssl = fm.load_model("ssl4eo-s12-vits16-dino", device=DEVICE)  # SSL4EO ViT-S, DINO
for k, da in {"pre": pre, "post": post}.items():  # both dates
    emb[("SSL4EO", k)] = ssl.embed_raster(da.fillna(fill), chip_size=CH, stride=ST, norm="model", batch_size=128)  # (384, rows, cols)
del ssl; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
change = {m: fm.embedding_change(emb[(m, "pre")], emb[(m, "post")]).where(usable) for m in ["DOFA", "SSL4EO"]}  # 1 - cosine, clear chips
print(f"{usable.size} chips, {usable.mean():.0%} clear on both dates | {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")  # summary


9108 chips, 100% clear on both dates | 241 s


dNBR is averaged over exactly the same chips, and a chip counts as inside the fire when its centre is inside the perimeter.


Code
dn = np.where(usable, chip_mean(dnbr)[0], np.nan)  # dNBR per chip
yy, xx = np.meshgrid(ys, xs, indexing="ij")  # chip centres
inside = gpd.points_from_xy(xx.ravel(), yy.ravel(), crs=32610).within(perim.union_all()).reshape(yy.shape)  # centre inside the perimeter
cext = [xs.min() - 160, xs.max() + 160, ys.min() - 160, ys.max() + 160]  # extent of the chip grid

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5.5))  # three change maps
for a, (t, v) in zip(ax, {"dNBR per chip": dn, "DOFA embedding change": change["DOFA"].values,
                          "SSL4EO embedding change": change["SSL4EO"].values}.items()):  # every map
    im = a.imshow(v, cmap="inferno", extent=cext, vmin=np.nanpercentile(v, 2), vmax=np.nanpercentile(v, 98))  # map
    perim.boundary.plot(ax=a, color="cyan", lw=1); a.set_title(t); plt.colorbar(im, ax=a, shrink=0.75)  # perimeter and scale
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The three maps agree on the burn scar: a large burned area in the west and south and a narrower arm running north-east. The SSL4EO change map is almost a smoothed copy of dNBR (correlation about 0.90 over all chips). The DOFA map shows the same scar with more chip-to-chip noise and some isolated bright chips outside it (correlation about 0.55). Neither encoder was told anything about fire: the change is simply what moved most in their embedding spaces between the two dates.
crumbs: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space

title: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space
section: Scoring change maps against the perimeter
text:
Scoring change maps against the perimeter
The perimeter is an imperfect reference (it includes unburned islands and is drawn from aerial surveys), but it is independent of all three maps. ROC curves show how well each map separates chips inside from chips outside at every threshold.


Code
ok = np.isfinite(dn) & np.isfinite(change["DOFA"].values) & np.isfinite(change["SSL4EO"].values)  # clear chips
maps = {"dNBR": dn, "DOFA embedding change": change["DOFA"].values, "SSL4EO embedding change": change["SSL4EO"].values}  # scores
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5.5))  # ROC panel
auc = {}  # areas under the curve
for n, v in maps.items():  # every map
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(inside[ok], v[ok]); auc[n] = roc_auc_score(inside[ok], v[ok])  # ROC
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{n} (AUC {auc[n]:.3f})")  # curve
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:", lw=1); ax.set_xlabel("false positive rate"); ax.set_ylabel("true positive rate")  # axes
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_title("Inside vs outside the perimeter"); plt.show()  # draw
print(ok.sum(), "clear chips | correlation with dNBR:", {n: round(np.corrcoef(dn[ok], v[ok])[0, 1], 3) for n, v in maps.items() if n != "dNBR"})  # agreement









9108 clear chips | correlation with dNBR: {'DOFA embedding change': np.float64(0.554), 'SSL4EO embedding change': np.float64(0.902)}


dNBR, the index designed for burned areas, separates chips inside the perimeter best (AUC about 0.975). Both embedding change maps reach about 0.90, a good score for a generic signal that knows nothing about fire. They trade off differently: SSL4EO finds most burned chips at very low false alarm rates, then levels off, while DOFA needs more false alarms to find the first burned chips but catches more of the rest. Where a dedicated index exists, it remains the better tool for its own kind of change. Embedding change earns its place for change that no single index describes.
crumbs: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space

title: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space
text:
What separate normalization does
The DOFA change map is recomputed with each date standardized by its own statistics, the default of embed_raster. The fire darkens the after-scene in NIR and brightens it in SWIR, and per-date standardization removes part of exactly that signal.


Code
dofa = fm.load_model("dofa-base", device=DEVICE)  # DOFA again
own = {k: dofa.embed_raster(da.fillna(da.mean(("y", "x"))), chip_size=CH, stride=ST, batch_size=128)
       for k, da in {"pre": pre, "post": post}.items()}  # per-date statistics
del dofa; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
c_own = fm.embedding_change(own["pre"], own["post"]).values  # change map
pd.DataFrame({"AUC vs perimeter": {"one normalization for both dates": auc["DOFA embedding change"],
                                   "each date standardized separately": roc_auc_score(inside[ok], c_own[ok])}}).round(3)  # comparison









AUC vs perimeter




one normalization for both dates
0.904


each date standardized separately
0.723







Standardizing each date by its own statistics drops DOFA’s AUC from about 0.90 to about 0.72. The fire changed the band statistics of the whole after-scene, and separate standardization subtracted much of that change before the encoder saw it. One normalization for both dates is not optional.

title: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space
text:
Seven years of a delta
The Bangladesh delta changes every year as rivers move and new land (char) forms and erodes. Seven dry-season Landsat 8 scenes of path 137 row 45 (2013 to 2020; there is no 2016 scene on disk) have only green, red and NIR bands; DOFA reads those three by wavelength. The scenes cover only part of their grid, so the analysis uses the largest window, 600 pixels (18 km) tall, that has data in every year. All years share the statistics of 2013, and the overlapping chips are 32 pixels (960 m) every 16 pixels (480 m).


Code
years = sorted(DELTA.glob("LC08_L2SP_137045_20*"))  # path 137 row 45 scenes
L_BANDS = ["green", "red", "nir"]  # bands on disk
names_l = {"green": "green", "red": "red", "nir": "nir08"}  # OLI NIR is 865 nm


def read_ls(d):  # Landsat reflectance, 3 bands
    a = xr.concat([rioxarray.open_rasterio(d / f"{b}.tif", masked=True).squeeze("band", drop=True) for b in L_BANDS],
                  dim=pd.Index([names_l[b] for b in L_BANDS], name="band"))  # bands
    return (a * 0.0000275 - 0.2).rio.write_crs(a.rio.crs)  # Collection 2 scale and offset


stack = [read_ls(d) for d in years]  # one array per year
ref = stack[0]  # 2013 grid
stack = [a.rio.reproject_match(ref).assign_coords(x=ref.x, y=ref.y) for a in stack]  # identical grids
labels = [d.name[17:21] for d in years]  # years
valid = np.logical_and.reduce([np.isfinite(a.values).all(0) for a in stack])  # data in every year
H = 600  # window height in pixels
best = (0, 0, 0)  # (width, first row, first column)
for r0 in range(0, valid.shape[0] - H, 10):  # slide the window down
    cols = valid[r0:r0 + H].all(0)  # columns with data on every row
    runs = np.diff(np.r_[0, cols.astype(int), 0]); starts, ends = np.flatnonzero(runs == 1), np.flatnonzero(runs == -1)  # runs of True
    if len(starts) and (ends - starts).max() > best[0]:  # widest so far
        i = np.argmax(ends - starts); best = ((ends - starts)[i], r0, starts[i])  # record it
w, r0, c0 = best  # the window
stack = [a.isel(y=slice(r0, r0 + H), x=slice(c0, c0 + w)) for a in stack]  # crop every year
print("years:", labels, f"| window {H} x {w} pixels ({H * 0.03:.0f} x {w * 0.03:.0f} km)")  # summary

mu, sd = stack[0].mean(("y", "x")).values, stack[0].std(("y", "x")).values  # 2013 statistics
dofa = fm.load_model("dofa-base", device=DEVICE)  # DOFA
E = [dofa.embed_raster(a, chip_size=CH, stride=ST, batch_size=128, norm={"method": "standard", "mean": mu, "std": sd})
     for a in stack]  # one map per year
del dofa; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
yearly = np.stack([fm.embedding_change(E[i], E[i + 1]).values for i in range(len(E) - 1)])  # change between consecutive years
total = fm.embedding_change(E[0], E[-1])  # first to last year
ndwi = lambda a: (a.sel(band="green") - a.sel(band="nir08")) / (a.sel(band="green") + a.sel(band="nir08"))  # water index
dw = chip_mean(ndwi(stack[-1]) - ndwi(stack[0]))[0]  # NDWI change per chip

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(16, 9))  # four panels
fc = lambda a: np.clip(np.nan_to_num(a.sel(band=["nir08", "red", "green"]).transpose("y", "x", "band").values) / 0.3, 0, 1)  # NIR false colour
ax[0, 0].imshow(fc(stack[0])); ax[0, 0].set_title(f"{labels[0]}, NIR-red-green")  # first year
ax[0, 1].imshow(fc(stack[-1])); ax[0, 1].set_title(f"{labels[-1]}, NIR-red-green")  # last year
im = ax[1, 0].imshow(total, cmap="inferno", vmin=0, vmax=float(np.nanpercentile(total, 98))); ax[1, 0].set_title(f"DOFA change {labels[0]} to {labels[-1]}")  # embedding change
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1, 0], shrink=0.8)  # scale
im = ax[1, 1].imshow(dw, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-0.6, vmax=0.6); ax[1, 1].set_title("NDWI change per chip (blue = wetter)"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1, 1], shrink=0.8)  # water change
for a in ax.ravel():  # all panels
    a.axis("off")  # no axes
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
print("correlation of embedding change with |NDWI change|:", round(np.corrcoef(total.values.ravel(), np.abs(dw).ravel())[0, 1], 3))  # agreement


years: ['2013', '2014', '2015', '2017', '2018', '2019', '2020'] | window 600 x 975 pixels (18 x 29 km)









correlation of embedding change with |NDWI change|: 0.809


The window covers 18 x 29 km of the delta, with the lower Meghna channel on the east. Embedding change is concentrated along the main channel, where the river shifted and new land formed, and it follows the water index closely: the correlation between embedding change and the size of the NDWI change is about 0.81. Part of the change in the channel is the colour of the water itself (turbid in 2013, darker and clearer in 2020), which both measures see as change. Inland, the many small paddies and villages change little between dry seasons.
How often each chip changed strongly between consecutive years separates stable land from the active river corridor.


Code
thr = np.nanpercentile(yearly, 95)  # "strong change": the top 5 % of all yearly changes
n_strong = (yearly > thr).sum(0)  # intervals with strong change per chip
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.8))  # map and bar chart
im = ax[0].imshow(n_strong, cmap="magma"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8, label="intervals with strong change"); ax[0].axis("off")  # map
ax[0].set_title(f"Strong change between consecutive years, {labels[0]} to {labels[-1]}")  # title
ax[1].bar([f"{labels[i]}-{labels[i + 1][2:]}" for i in range(len(labels) - 1)], (yearly > thr).mean((1, 2)) * 100)  # share per interval
ax[1].set_ylabel("chips with strong change (%)"); ax[1].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45); ax[1].set_title("Change by interval")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









Chips with strong change in several intervals line the main channel: the active river corridor, where banks erode and chars grow year after year. Inland, strong change is rare and isolated. Among the intervals, 2013 to 2014 has the most strong change and 2014 to 2015 the least, which reflects differences between acquisitions (water level, turbidity, date in the dry season) as much as change on the ground. A change series must be read with the conditions of each image in mind.

title: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space
section: Searching a scene with one example
text:
Searching a scene with one example
The 2020 embedding map is an index of every chip. One example chip is chosen automatically: the chip with the brightest red reflectance among chips that contain at least 10 % water. It turns out to be a stretch of riverbank on the main channel, part land and part water. Every chip is scored by its similarity to it.


Code
e20 = E[-1]  # 2020 embeddings
red = chip_mean(stack[-1].sel(band="red"))[0]  # red reflectance per chip
wet = chip_mean((ndwi(stack[-1]) > 0.2).astype("float32"))[0] > 0.1  # chips with at least 10 % water
iy, ix = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(np.where(wet, red, np.nan)), red.shape)  # brightest chip next to water
query = e20.isel(y=iy, x=ix)  # the example
sim = fm.similarity_map(e20, query)  # cosine similarity of every chip
X = e20.values.reshape(e20.sizes["embedding"], -1).T  # index (chips, D)
idx, score = fm.embedding_search(X, query.values[None], k=40)  # 40 nearest chips
hy, hx = np.unravel_index(idx[0], red.shape)  # their positions
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 5))  # map and similarity
ax[0].imshow(fc(stack[-1]), extent=[0, red.shape[1], red.shape[0], 0])  # 2020 image on the chip grid
ax[0].scatter(hx + 0.5, hy + 0.5, s=25, facecolors="none", edgecolors="yellow", label="40 most similar chips")  # hits
ax[0].scatter(ix + 0.5, iy + 0.5, s=120, marker="*", color="red", label="example"); ax[0].legend(loc="lower left")  # query
ax[0].set_title("2020 and the most similar chips"); ax[0].axis("off")  # title
im = ax[1].imshow(sim, cmap="viridis", vmin=float(np.nanpercentile(sim, 50)), vmax=1); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8)  # similarity
ax[1].set_title("cosine similarity to the example"); ax[1].axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
far = np.hypot(hy - iy, hx - ix) > 4  # hits more than 2 km from the example
print(f"hits with water: {wet[hy, hx].mean():.0%} | more than 2 km away: {far.mean():.0%} | "
      f"red reflectance of hits {np.nanmean(red[hy, hx]):.3f} vs window {np.nanmean(red):.3f}")  # check









hits with water: 100% | more than 2 km away: 75% | red reflectance of hits 0.097 vs window 0.084


The 40 most similar chips all contain water, and three quarters of them lie more than 2 km from the example: the search found riverbanks along the whole main channel, with a few on the western channels, and ignored the inland paddies. This is retrieval by example without any labels: one chip in, every chip of the same kind out. The similarity values themselves are all high (above 0.96) because DOFA’s embeddings of one scene occupy a narrow cone; ranking, not the absolute value, is what matters.
crumbs: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space

title: Change and Similarity in Embedding Space
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

Embedding change (1 minus the cosine similarity of two dates) maps any kind of change at once; for the Bug Fire it is scored against dNBR and the perimeter with ROC curves.
Both dates must share one normalization: the statistics of one date, or the model’s fixed statistics. Separate per-date standardization removes part of the change signal.
Over a seven-scene Landsat series, consecutive-year embedding change highlights the active river corridor of the delta, and the number of years with strong change separates stable land from migrating channels.
An embedding map is a searchable index: fm.similarity_map and fm.embedding_search find every place that looks like one example.



Exercises

Map the Bug Fire with the clearest early-September post-fire date instead. Does the change map depend on how soon after the fire the image was taken?
Choose a threshold on the DOFA change map that matches the burned area of dNBR > 0.1, and map the cells where the two disagree. What are they?
Repeat the delta analysis with path 136 row 45, which overlaps it. Do the two series agree in the overlap?
Use five examples of the same feature as the query (their mean embedding). Is the search more precise?
Install FAISS and replace fm.embedding_search with an IVF index for the seven years of embeddings. How do speed and results compare?



References

Key, C. H. and Benson, N. C. (2006). Landscape assessment: ground measure of severity, the Composite Burn Index, and remote sensing of severity, the Normalized Burn Ratio. USDA Forest Service RMRS-GTR-164-CD.
Johnson, J., Douze, M. and Jegou, H. (2019). Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs (FAISS). IEEE Transactions on Big Data.
Xiong, Z. et al. (2024). DOFA. arXiv:2403.15356.
Wang, Y. et al. (2023). SSL4EO-S12. IEEE GRSM.

title: Very High Resolution: DINOv3-sat, Satlas NAIP, Scale-MAE and SAM 2
text:
Overview

What changes at sub-metre resolution









10 to 30 m (Sentinel-2, Landsat)
0.3 to 2 m (WorldView, NAIP, aerial)




a pixel holds
a mixture of materials
mostly one material


informative signal
spectra and their change over time
shape, texture, shadow, context


bands
10 to 13 including SWIR
usually RGB, sometimes NIR (WorldView-2: 8 bands)


typical outputs
per-pixel classes, indices
objects, outlines, counts


nuisances
clouds, mixed pixels
shadows, off-nadir lean, misregistration



Spectral models trained on Sentinel-2 do not transfer to this scale; the models below were trained on aerial or commercial imagery.


The encoders

DINOv3-sat (Meta, 2025): a ViT-7B trained by self-distillation on 493 million Maxar images, distilled into ViT-L and smaller models. Its dense features are among the strongest available for satellite imagery. The weights are gated: you must accept the licence on Hugging Face and log in.
SatlasPretrain NAIP Swin-B: Swin-v2 trained with labels on 1 m US aerial imagery (NAIP).
Scale-MAE ViT-L: a masked autoencoder trained on fMoW RGB imagery at 0.3 to 3 m with a resolution-aware position encoding.



Dense features
A ViT with 16 pixel patches returns one feature vector per 16 x 16 pixel patch, a map 16 times coarser than the image. embed_raster(dense=True) stitches the patch maps of all chips into one georeferenced map; features can then be sampled at any point by interpolation.


Promptable segmentation
SAM and SAM 2 (Kirillov et al. 2023; Ravi et al. 2024) return the mask of the object under a prompt: a point, a box or a rough mask. They have no notion of classes: a click on a field returns that field’s outline, and a click on a pond returns the pond. With good prompts they delineate objects far more sharply than patch features can, so the two are complementary: features say what, SAM says where exactly.

section: A WorldView-2 scene and its fields
text:
A WorldView-2 scene and its fields
The scene is stored as one 8-band GeoTIFF with digital numbers. The encoders read RGB (bands 5, 3 and 2), scaled to 0 to 1 by the 2nd and 98th percentiles. The field polygons were drawn by hand and labelled crop or fallow.


Code
wv = rioxarray.open_rasterio(WV / "Images" / "multi.tif", masked=True)  # 8 bands, 1.6 m
fields = gpd.read_file(WV / "Labeled_data" / "aoi_trianing.shp").set_crs(wv.rio.crs, allow_override=True)  # polygons (no .prj: same UTM 46N grid as the image)
fields["label"] = fields["Class"].str.strip()  # crop or fallow
lo, hi = [np.nanpercentile(wv.isel(band=[4, 2, 1]).values, q) for q in (2, 98)]  # display stretch
rgb = ((wv.isel(band=[4, 2, 1]) - lo) / (hi - lo)).clip(0, 1).fillna(0)  # red, green, blue in 0..1
rgb = rgb.assign_coords(band=["red", "green", "blue"]).rio.write_crs(wv.rio.crs)  # named bands
print(dict(wv.sizes), "| pixel", wv.rio.resolution(), "|", fields["label"].value_counts().to_dict())  # summary
ext = [float(wv.x.min()), float(wv.x.max()), float(wv.y.min()), float(wv.y.max())]  # extent
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8.5))  # one panel
ax.imshow(rgb.transpose("y", "x", "band").values, extent=ext)  # image
fields.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color=fields["label"].map({"Crop": "yellow", "Fallow": "magenta"}), lw=0.6)  # polygons
ax.set_title("WorldView-2, 1.6 m: crop (yellow) and fallow (magenta) fields"); plt.show()  # draw

title: Very High Resolution: DINOv3-sat, Satlas NAIP, Scale-MAE and SAM 2
text:
Dense features of the scene
Each encoder reads the RGB scene through its contract: fm.prepare(name, rgb, units="unit") says the values are already scaled to 0 to 1 and applies the model’s statistics (ImageNet statistics for Scale-MAE, none for Satlas NAIP). Chips have the model’s own size, and the patch features are stitched into one map.


Code
dense, secs = {}, {}  # feature maps and run times
for n in ENCODERS:  # every available encoder
    enc = fm.load_model(n, device=DEVICE)  # load
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
    x = fm.prepare(n, rgb, units="unit")  # RGB is already 0..1: apply the model's statistics only
    dense[n] = enc.embed_raster(x, dense=True, norm={"method": "none"}, batch_size=8)  # (D, y, x) patch features
    secs[n] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # seconds
    del enc; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory

Inside the empty area the maps show the models’ own structure: Scale-MAE a smooth gradient inside each 224 pixel chip (its position encoding, visible when the content carries no information) and Satlas one block per 256 pixel chip. title: Very High Resolution: DINOv3-sat, Satlas NAIP, Scale-MAE and SAM 2
section: Crop or fallow from patch features
text:
Crop or fallow from patch features
Fields average about 1,200 m², a few patches each. For every polygon the features are interpolated at its centroid (emb.interp), and the baseline is the mean of the 8 WorldView-2 bands in a 5 x 5 pixel window at the same point. Fields are grouped into eight spatial clusters for cross-validation.


Code
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans  # spatial groups

cent = fields.geometry.representative_point()  # a point inside every polygon
cx, cy = xr.DataArray(cent.x.values, dims="f"), xr.DataArray(cent.y.values, dims="f")  # as DataArrays
groups = KMeans(8, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit_predict(np.c_[cent.x, cent.y])  # spatial clusters
y_f = fields["label"].values  # crop or fallow
win = wv.rolling(y=5, x=5, center=True, min_periods=1).mean()  # 5 x 5 pixel band means
X = {"8 band means": win.interp(x=cx, y=cy, method="nearest").values.T}  # baseline features
for n, d in dense.items():  # every encoder
    X[n] = d.interp(x=cx, y=cy, method="linear").values.T  # features at the centroids
ok = np.isfinite(np.c_[tuple(X.values())]).all(1)  # points with all features
rows = {n: {"F1 (linear)": fm.linear_probe(v[ok], y_f[ok], groups=groups[ok])["mean"]["f1_macro"],
            "accuracy (kNN)": fm.knn_probe(v[ok], y_f[ok], groups=groups[ok], k=7)["mean"]} for n, v in X.items()}  # probes
print(ok.sum(), "fields |", dict(zip(*np.unique(y_f[ok], return_counts=True))))  # sample
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)

The labels are unbalanced (469 crop fields, 87 fallow), so macro F1 is the score to read; always predicting “crop” would already give 84 % accuracy. On macro F1 the Scale-MAE features beat the eight band means (about 0.72 against 0.66), while Satlas NAIP falls below them (about 0.57): Satlas sees 51 m cells, coarser than most fields. The kNN accuracy reverses the order, because with this imbalance kNN mostly rewards getting the majority class right, and the eight bands, including the NIR bands the RGB encoders never see, separate green crops from bare fallow well. Fields of a few hundred square metres are at the limit of what 26 to 51 m patch features can describe.

title: Very High Resolution: DINOv3-sat, Satlas NAIP, Scale-MAE and SAM 2
section: DeepGlobe land cover per 8 m cell
text:
DeepGlobe land cover per 8 m cell
DeepGlobe tiles are 2448 pixels at 50 cm with land cover masks. Twenty tiles are embedded; each 16 pixel (8 m) patch is labelled with the majority class of its mask pixels when it covers at least 70 % of them. Tiles are the cross-validation groups, so the probe is tested on tiles it never saw. The baseline is the mean and standard deviation of red, green and blue in each patch.


Code
DG_CLASSES = pd.read_csv(DG / "class_dict.csv")  # class colours
meta = pd.read_csv(DG / "metadata.csv").query("split == 'train'").sample(20, random_state=SEED)  # 20 tiles
code = {tuple(r[["r", "g", "b"]]): k for k, (_, r) in enumerate(DG_CLASSES.iterrows())}  # colour -> class index
feats = {n: [] for n in ENCODERS}; base, lab, grp = [], [], []  # features, baseline, labels, tiles
encs = {n: fm.load_model(n, device=DEVICE) for n in ENCODERS}  # load the encoders once
for t, (_, row) in enumerate(meta.iterrows()):  # every tile
    im = np.asarray(Image.open(DG / row["sat_image_path"]).convert("RGB"), "float32")[:2432, :2432] / 255  # crop to 19 x 128 px
    mk = (np.asarray(Image.open(DG / row["mask_path"]).convert("RGB"))[:2432, :2432] > 128) * 255  # clean mask colours
    cls_px = np.vectorize(lambda r, g, b: code.get((r, g, b), 6))(mk[..., 0], mk[..., 1], mk[..., 2])  # class per pixel
    da = xr.DataArray(im.transpose(2, 0, 1), dims=("band", "y", "x"), coords={"band": ["red", "green", "blue"],
                      "y": -np.arange(2432) * 0.5, "x": np.arange(2432) * 0.5})  # tile as a raster (0.5 m)
    b = cls_px.reshape(152, 16, 152, 16).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(152 * 152, -1)  # mask pixels per 8 m cell
    cnt = np.stack([(b == k).sum(1) for k in range(7)], 1); maj = cnt.argmax(1); pur = cnt.max(1) / 256  # majority class
    keep = (pur >= 0.7) & (maj != 6)  # pure, known cells
    rgbcell = im.reshape(152, 16, 152, 16, 3)  # pixels per cell
    base.append(np.c_[rgbcell.mean((1, 3)).reshape(-1, 3), rgbcell.std((1, 3)).reshape(-1, 3)][keep])  # baseline features
    for n, e in encs.items():  # every encoder
        d = e.embed_raster(fm.prepare(n, da, units="unit"), dense=True, norm={"method": "none"}, batch_size=8)  # patch features
        f = int(round(d.sizes["y"] / 152))  # patches per 8 m cell (1 for 16 px patches, 0.5 for Swin)
        v = d.values if f <= 1 else d.coarsen(y=f, x=f).mean().values  # cell grid
        if v.shape[1] < 152:  # coarser features (32 px Swin cells): repeat to the 8 m grid
            v = np.repeat(np.repeat(v, 152 // v.shape[1], 1), 152 // v.shape[2], 2)  # nearest upsampling
        feats[n].append(v[:, :152, :152].reshape(v.shape[0], -1).T[keep])  # features of kept cells
    lab.append(maj[keep]); grp.append(np.full(keep.sum(), t))  # labels and tile groups
del encs; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
lab, grp, base = np.concatenate(lab), np.concatenate(grp), np.concatenate(base)  # all cells
names = DG_CLASSES["name"].tolist()  # class names
print(len(lab), "cells from", len(meta), "tiles |", pd.Series(lab).map(dict(enumerate(names))).value_counts().to_dict())  # sample
sub = np.random.default_rng(SEED).choice(len(lab), min(len(lab), 20000), replace=False)  # at most 20,000 cells for the probes
res = {"RGB mean and std": fm.linear_probe(base[sub], lab[sub], groups=grp[sub])["mean"]}  # baseline
for n in ENCODERS:  # every encoder
    res[n] = fm.linear_probe(np.concatenate(feats[n])[sub], lab[sub], groups=grp[sub])["mean"]  # probe
pd.DataFrame(res).T.round(3)

At 50 cm and with six land cover classes, the patch features clearly beat simple RGB statistics: a macro F1 of about 0.48 for Scale-MAE and 0.44 for Satlas NAIP, against 0.29 for the mean and standard deviation of red, green and blue in each 8 m cell, with whole tiles held out. Texture and context (roofs and roads for urban land, crowns for forest, the uniform surface of water) are what the encoders add and colour statistics miss. Scores stay moderate because DeepGlobe’s rangeland and barren land look alike, and agriculture covers half of all cells.

title: Very High Resolution: DINOv3-sat, Satlas NAIP, Scale-MAE and SAM 2
text:
Outlining fields with SAM 2
SAM 2 receives the RGB scene once and then one prompt per field. Two kinds of prompt are compared on thirty crop fields: a single click inside the field (SAM returns three candidate masks; the smallest is kept, since a click inside a field may also mean the whole block of fields), and the bounding box of the drawn polygon. Each mask is compared with its polygon by intersection over union (IoU), and the box masks are turned into polygons and exported.


Code
from rasterio.features import rasterize, shapes  # polygons <-> masks
from sam2.sam2_image_predictor import SAM2ImagePredictor  # SAM 2
from shapely.geometry import shape  # GeoJSON -> shapely

pred = SAM2ImagePredictor.from_pretrained("facebook/sam2.1-hiera-large", device=DEVICE)  # SAM 2.1 Hiera-L (cached)
img8 = (rgb.transpose("y", "x", "band").values * 255).astype("uint8")  # the scene as 8-bit RGB
amp = dict(device_type=DEVICE, dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=DEVICE == "cuda")  # mixed precision on the GPU
with torch.inference_mode(), torch.autocast(**amp):  # inference
    pred.set_image(img8)  # encode the scene once
tr = rgb.rio.transform()  # map <-> pixel
crop_fields = fields[fields["label"] == "Crop"].sample(30, random_state=SEED)  # 30 crop fields to prompt
rows, masks_box = [], {}  # scores and box masks
for i, f in crop_fields.iterrows():  # every field
    truth = rasterize([f.geometry], out_shape=img8.shape[:2], transform=tr).astype(bool)  # drawn polygon as a mask
    p = f.geometry.representative_point(); col, row = ~tr * (p.x, p.y)  # click inside the field
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = f.geometry.bounds; (c0, r0), (c1, r1) = ~tr * (x0, y1), ~tr * (x1, y0)  # bounding box in pixels
    with torch.inference_mode(), torch.autocast(**amp):  # inference
        mp, _, _ = pred.predict(point_coords=np.array([[col, row]]), point_labels=np.array([1]), multimask_output=True)  # 3 candidates
        mb, _, _ = pred.predict(box=np.array([c0, r0, c1, r1]), multimask_output=False)  # one mask
    mp = mp.astype(bool)[np.argmin(mp.sum((1, 2)))]; mb = mb[0].astype(bool)  # smallest point mask, box mask
    iou = lambda m: (m & truth).sum() / max((m | truth).sum(), 1)  # intersection over union
    rows.append({"field": i, "pixels drawn": int(truth.sum()), "IoU point": iou(mp), "IoU box": iou(mb)})  # scores
    masks_box[i] = mb  # keep for the figure and export
del pred; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
iou = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("field")  # scores per field
polys = [shape(g) for m in masks_box.values() for g, v in shapes(m.astype("uint8"), mask=m, transform=tr) if v == 1]  # masks -> polygons
out = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"source": ["SAM 2, box prompt"] * len(polys)}, geometry=polys, crs=wv.rio.crs)  # outlines
out.to_file(OUT / "wv2_sam2_fields.gpkg", driver="GPKG")  # export
print("written", OUT / "wv2_sam2_fields.gpkg", "|", len(out), "polygons | median field size", int(iou["pixels drawn"].median()), "pixels")  # export
pd.DataFrame({"median IoU": iou[["IoU point", "IoU box"]].median(), "share with IoU >= 0.5": (iou[["IoU point", "IoU box"]] >= 0.5).mean()}).round(2)  # summary

Code
pick = iou.sort_values("IoU box", ascending=False).index[[0, len(iou) // 2, -1]]  # best, median and worst box result
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))  # three examples
for a, i, t in zip(ax, pick, ["best", "median", "worst"]):  # every example
    g = fields.loc[i].geometry; x0, y0, x1, y1 = g.buffer(40).bounds  # 40 m around the field
    a.imshow(rgb.transpose("y", "x", "band").values, extent=ext); a.set_xlim(x0, x1); a.set_ylim(y0, y1)  # zoom
    a.contour(rgb.x, rgb.y, masks_box[i], levels=[0.5], colors="cyan", linewidths=1.5)  # SAM outline of this field
    gpd.GeoSeries([g]).boundary.plot(ax=a, color="yellow", lw=2)  # drawn polygon
    a.set_title(f"{t}: IoU {iou.loc[i, 'IoU box']:.2f} (cyan SAM, yellow drawn)"); a.axis("off")  # title
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









A single click almost never outlines the field (median IoU about 0.01): the fields are tiny for SAM, a median of about 380 pixels in a scene SAM shrinks to 1024 pixels on its long side, and in this dry-season image neighbouring fields have similar colour, so a click inside a field is ambiguous. A box around the field tells SAM what is meant, and the median IoU rises to about 0.49, with half the fields at 0.5 or better. The best outlines follow the drawn polygon closely (IoU about 0.9); the worst field was drawn over a part of the scene with no image data, where SAM has nothing to outline. In practice boxes come from a detector, from a coarse map or from a cadastre, and SAM sharpens them.

title: Very High Resolution: DINOv3-sat, Satlas NAIP, Scale-MAE and SAM 2
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

Very high resolution imagery is about shape, texture and context; encoders for it are trained on aerial and commercial images (DINOv3-sat, Satlas NAIP, Scale-MAE).
Gated models need a licence and a login; the notebook falls back to freely available encoders.
Dense patch features, sampled at field centroids or aggregated per cell, classify fields and land cover; a simple band-value baseline shows what they add.
SAM 2 outlines objects far more sharply than any patch feature map, but the prompt decides what it outlines: on small, low-contrast fields a single click is ambiguous and a box works much better, and every outline must still be checked against reference polygons.
Features say what, SAM says where exactly: together they turn very high resolution imagery into labelled vector objects.



Exercises

Accept the DINOv3-sat licence, run hf auth login and rerun the notebook. How do its features compare?
Add the WorldView-2 NIR bands: embed bands 7, 5 and 3 (NIR, red, green) as false colour with Scale-MAE. Do crop and fallow separate better?
Prompt SAM 2 with a click plus a box, or with several clicks per field. Which prompt works best for the smallest fields?
Use the dense features to find cells similar to one pond and prompt SAM 2 at each of them to map all ponds in the scene.
Compute the crop-or-fallow probe with features averaged over the whole polygon instead of the centroid.

title: AlphaEarth Foundations: Precomputed Embeddings for the Whole Planet
text:
Overview

Embedding fields
AlphaEarth Foundations (Brown et al. 2025) is a model that learns an embedding field: a function from a place and a time period to a vector. It was trained on more than 3 billion observations from Sentinel-1 and 2, Landsat 8 and 9, GEDI lidar, the GLO-30 elevation model, ERA5 climate, GRACE gravity and text descriptions, with objectives that reconstruct those sources and keep the vectors consistent in space and time. The published product summarises each calendar year at each 10 m pixel.



Property
Value




Earth Engine collection
GOOGLE/SATELLITE_EMBEDDING/V1/ANNUAL


Bands
A00 to A63, 64 float values


Resolution
10 m, in local UTM tiles


Time
one image per calendar year, 2017 onward


Length
every vector has length 1 (unit sphere)


Licence
CC BY 4.0 (check the dataset page)





What unit length means
Because every vector has length 1, the dot product of two pixels is their cosine similarity: 1 for identical, near 0 for unrelated. Similarity search and change detection are therefore a few lines of arithmetic. Averaging pixels shortens the vector, so averaged embeddings are re-normalised before comparing them.


Strengths and limits

Strengths: no model to run; the same representation everywhere; many sensors combined, so clouds matter less; a year of phenology in each vector.
Limits: one vector per year (no within-season maps); the dimensions have no names; the product is computed by Google and its exact inputs cannot be audited pixel by pixel; access through Earth Engine; licence terms apply.



Three ways to get the embeddings









Source
Format
Account
Best for




Source Cooperative GeoZarr mosaic
one global Zarr array, EPSG:4326, ~10 m, chunks of 256 x 256 pixels x 64 bands
none
points and areas up to tens of kilometres


Google Cloud Storage
8192 x 8192 pixel Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs in UTM zones, with overviews
none (“provider pays”)
coarse maps of large regions


Earth Engine
ee.ImageCollection
Earth Engine account and registered Cloud project
server-side analysis



The public files store each value as an 8-bit integer to save space: v = sign(x) * sqrt(|x|) * 127.5, with -128 for no data. fm.alphaearth_dequantize inverts it, x = (v / 127.5) ** 2 * sign(v). Small differences from the Earth Engine floats come from that quantization. This notebook uses the Zarr mosaic; every read is cached in outputs/, so the notebook reruns offline.

Where the embeddings live
The Zarr mosaic is opened lazily: only its metadata is read. Its single array has the dimensions (year, band, y, x); one chunk holds all 64 values of a 256 x 256 pixel block, so a point costs one small request. The Cloud Storage index lists every GeoTIFF tile by year and bounding box.

arr = fm._aef_array()  # the public Zarr array (metadata only)

print("stored int8:", raw, "| as floats:", fm.alphaearth_dequantize(raw).round(4))  # quantization

section: Reading two years for the Corn Belt
text:
Reading two years for the Corn Belt
fm.alphaearth_to_xarray(..., like=grid) reads the box covering the CDL grid from the Zarr mosaic at its native resolution (about 10 m in latitude and longitude) and puts it on the 20 m UTM grid of the Sentinel-2 cube, so every pixel lines up with the CDL. About 2.2 million pixels x 64 values per year; the first run takes several minutes.


Code
cdl_all = xr.open_dataset(CUBE / "labels_20m.nc")["cdl"].load()  # CDL 2020 to 2025 on the 20 m grid
grid = cdl_all.sel(year=2024).rio.write_crs("EPSG:32615")  # target grid
cache = {y: OUT / f"alphaearth_cornbelt_{y}_20m.nc" for y in (2020, 2024)}  # cached reads
ae = {}  # embeddings per year
for y, path in cache.items():  # both years
    if not path.exists():  # read once
        t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
        da = fm.alphaearth_to_xarray(None, y, like=grid)  # (64, y, x) on the CDL grid, from the Zarr mosaic
        da.drop_vars("spatial_ref", errors="ignore").to_netcdf(path)  # cache
        print(y, f"read in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")  # timing
    ae[y] = xr.open_dataarray(path).rio.write_crs("EPSG:32615")  # (embedding, y, x)
print({y: dict(a.sizes) for y, a in ae.items()})  # sizes
norms = np.linalg.norm(ae[2024].values.reshape(64, -1), axis=0)  # vector lengths
print(f"vector length: median {np.nanmedian(norms):.4f}, 1st to 99th percentile {np.nanpercentile(norms, 1):.4f} to {np.nanpercentile(norms, 99):.4f}")  # unit length check

text:
What the 64 dimensions show
Three single dimensions shown as RGB, and the first three principal components of all 64, next to the CDL of the same year.


Code
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap  # class colours
COLORS = ["#e6c229", "#2a9d3c", "#b9e08b", "#d7301f", "#1f5fbf", "#7f7f7f"]  # one per class
ext = [float(grid.x.min()), float(grid.x.max()), float(grid.y.min()), float(grid.y.max())]  # extent
three = ae[2024].isel(embedding=[0, 16, 32]).transpose("y", "x", "embedding").values  # A00, A16, A32
three = (three - np.nanpercentile(three, 2, (0, 1))) / (np.nanpercentile(three, 98, (0, 1)) - np.nanpercentile(three, 2, (0, 1)))  # stretch
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5.8))  # three panels
ax[0].imshow(np.clip(np.nan_to_num(three), 0, 1), extent=ext); ax[0].set_title("A00, A16, A32 as RGB, 2024")  # raw dimensions
ax[1].imshow(fm.embedding_rgb(ae[2024]).transpose("y", "x", "band"), extent=ext); ax[1].set_title("first 3 principal components")  # PCA
ax[2].imshow(np.ma.masked_less(grid.values, 0), cmap=ListedColormap(COLORS), vmin=-0.5, vmax=5.5, extent=ext, interpolation="nearest"); ax[2].set_title("CDL 2024")  # reference
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









Even three raw dimensions show the field pattern, and the first three principal components of all 64 reproduce the CDL almost field for field: one colour for corn, another for soybeans, a third for the grass and wetland strips along the streams, small dots for farmsteads and a thin grid for the roads. Each vector summarizes a whole year of observations, so the crop of the year, not the look of one day, is what dominates it.

title: AlphaEarth Foundations: Precomputed Embeddings for the Whole Planet
text:
Fields like this one
One pixel in the middle of a large 2024 corn field is the query. fm.similarity_map computes its cosine similarity with every pixel; thresholding the map gives “fields like this one”, scored against the CDL corn class.


Code
corn = (grid.values == 0)  # CDL corn pixels
from scipy import ndimage  # distance inside fields
depth = ndimage.distance_transform_edt(corn)  # distance to the nearest non-corn pixel
qy, qx = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(depth), depth.shape)  # the most interior corn pixel
sim = fm.similarity_map(ae[2024], ae[2024].isel(y=qy, x=qx))  # cosine similarity to it
valid = grid.values >= 0  # labelled pixels
auc = roc_auc_score(corn[valid], np.nan_to_num(sim.values[valid]))  # how well similarity ranks corn first
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.8))  # map and histogram
im = ax[0].imshow(sim, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1, extent=ext); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8)  # similarity map
ax[0].plot(float(grid.x[qx]), float(grid.y[qy]), "r*", ms=14); ax[0].set_title("cosine similarity to one corn pixel")  # query
for k, c in [(0, "Corn"), (1, "Soybeans")]:  # two crops
    ax[1].hist(sim.values[grid.values == k], 100, alpha=0.6, label=c, color=COLORS[k], density=True)  # distributions
ax[1].legend(); ax[1].set_xlabel("cosine similarity"); ax[1].set_title(f"by CDL class (AUC corn vs rest {auc:.3f})")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









One pixel is enough. Corn pixels have cosine similarities near 1 to the query, soybean pixels mostly between 0.4 and 0.6, and the similarity ranks corn above everything else with an AUC of about 0.99. A threshold anywhere between 0.75 and 0.85 would give a corn map with no training beyond the single query. This works because a year of observations separates crops with different calendars so well; classes that look alike all year, such as different grass covers, would not separate like this.

title: AlphaEarth Foundations: Precomputed Embeddings for the Whole Planet
text:
Clusters without labels
K-means with six clusters on a random sample of pixels, applied to the whole map, compared with the six CDL groups by the adjusted Rand index (ARI).


Code
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans  # clustering

X = ae[2024].values.reshape(64, -1).T  # (pixels, 64)
okp = np.isfinite(X).all(1) & (grid.values.ravel() >= 0)  # labelled pixels with embeddings
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED); samp = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(okp), 50000, replace=False)  # 50,000 for fitting
km = KMeans(6, n_init=10, random_state=SEED).fit(X[samp])  # six clusters
lab = np.full(X.shape[0], -1); lab[okp] = km.predict(X[okp])  # every labelled pixel
ari = adjusted_rand_score(grid.values.ravel()[okp], lab[okp])  # agreement with the CDL
ct = pd.crosstab(pd.Series(grid.values.ravel()[okp]).map(dict(enumerate(CLASSES))), lab[okp], normalize="columns").round(2)  # cluster composition
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.8))  # clusters and CDL
ax[0].imshow(np.ma.masked_less(lab.reshape(grid.shape), 0), cmap="tab10", interpolation="nearest", extent=ext); ax[0].set_title(f"6 clusters, ARI with CDL {ari:.2f}")  # clusters

title: AlphaEarth Foundations: Precomputed Embeddings for the Whole Planet
text:
Change between 2020 and 2024
fm.embedding_change is 1 minus the cosine similarity of the two years at each pixel. In the Corn Belt most change is crop rotation: a corn field in 2020 is often soybeans in 2024 and the reverse. The change map is compared with the CDL: did the crop group of the pixel change between the years?


Code
chg = fm.embedding_change(ae[2020], ae[2024])  # 1 - cosine, per pixel
c20, c24 = cdl_all.sel(year=2020).values, cdl_all.sel(year=2024).values  # CDL of both years
both = (c20 >= 0) & (c24 >= 0) & np.isfinite(chg.values)  # labelled in both years
rotated = (c20 != c24)  # crop group changed
auc_c = roc_auc_score(rotated[both], chg.values[both])  # change map vs CDL change
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.8))  # change and CDL change
im = ax[0].imshow(chg, cmap="inferno", vmin=0, vmax=float(np.nanpercentile(chg, 98)), extent=ext); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8)  # change
ax[0].set_title(f"AlphaEarth change 2020 to 2024 (AUC vs CDL change {auc_c:.3f})")  # title
ax[1].imshow(np.where(both, rotated, np.nan), cmap="coolwarm", extent=ext, interpolation="nearest"); ax[1].set_title("CDL group changed 2020 to 2024 (red)")  # reference
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
pd.DataFrame({"median change": {f"{a} -> {b}": float(np.median(chg.values[both & (c20 == i) & (c24 == j)]))
              for i, a in enumerate(CLASSES[:2]) for j, b in enumerate(CLASSES[:2])}}).round(3)  # by transition

The change map is almost a binary map of crop rotation: fields that switched between corn and soybeans have a change near 0.5, fields that kept their crop near 0.06 to 0.07. It ranks pixels whose CDL group changed above those that did not with an AUC of about 0.89; the misses are mostly field edges and the thin road and stream lines, where the 20 m CDL and the embeddings disagree on a pixel or two. The annual embeddings make crop rotation history available for every field without classifying any year.

title: AlphaEarth Foundations: Precomputed Embeddings for the Whole Planet
section: AlphaEarth, DOFA and SSL4EO on the same probe
text:
AlphaEarth, DOFA and SSL4EO on the same probe
The 640 m cell probe of notebooks 09_11_03 and 09_11_04, for 2024: corn or soybean cells, folds over 5.8 km blocks. AlphaEarth pixels are averaged per cell; DOFA and SSL4EO patch features come from the 31 August 2024 Sentinel-2 scene, averaged per cell as in notebook 09_11_04.


Code
CELL = 32; NY, NX = -(-grid.shape[0] // CELL), -(-grid.shape[1] // CELL)  # 640 m cells
pad = np.full((NY * CELL, NX * CELL), -1); pad[:grid.shape[0], :grid.shape[1]] = grid.values  # padded CDL
blk = pad.reshape(NY, CELL, NX, CELL).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(NY * NX, -1)  # pixels per cell
cnt = np.stack([(blk == k).sum(1) for k in (0, 1)], 1); y_c, pur = cnt.argmax(1), cnt.max(1) / blk.shape[1]  # labels
gy, gx = np.divmod(np.arange(NY * NX), NX); group = (gy // 9) * 10 + gx // 9; ok = pur >= 0.6  # blocks, usable


def cells(d):  # (D, y, x) -> (cells, D) on the 640 m grid
    f = int(round(d.sizes["y"] / NY))  # pixels or patches per cell side
    d = d.coarsen(y=f, x=f, boundary="pad").mean() if f > 1 else d  # average
    return np.nan_to_num(d.values[:, :NY, :NX].reshape(d.sizes[d.dims[0]], -1).T)  # (cells, D)


s2 = xr.open_dataarray(CUBE / "s2_20m.nc").sel(time="2024-08-31").drop_vars("time").load().rio.write_crs("EPSG:32615")  # Sentinel-2
F = {"band means (baseline)": cells(s2), "AlphaEarth (64)": cells(ae[2024])}  # baseline and AlphaEarth
for n in ["dofa-base", "ssl4eo-s12-vits16-dino"]:  # two encoders
    e = fm.load_model(n, device=DEVICE); F[n] = cells(e.embed_raster(s2, dense=True, norm="model", batch_size=8))  # patch features
    del e; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
bench = fm.benchmark_encoders({k: {"embeddings": v[ok]} for k, v in F.items()}, y_c[ok], groups=group[ok], cv=5)  # same folds
bench[["embed_dim", "linear_f1_macro", "knn_accuracy"]].round(3)

AlphaEarth’s 64 values per cell classify the 2024 corn and soybean cells perfectly (macro F1 1.0, kNN accuracy 1.0). The band means of a single late-August Sentinel-2 date are already almost as good (0.99), and the SSL4EO ViT patch features match them; DOFA’s patch features trail (0.93). title: AlphaEarth Foundations: Precomputed Embeddings for the Whole Planet
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

AlphaEarth Foundations publishes a 64-value, unit-length embedding per 10 m pixel and year since 2017, in Earth Engine and as public Zarr and GeoTIFF copies that need no account; fm.alphaearth_to_xarray and fm.sample_alphaearth read them into GeoLattice.
Dot products are cosine similarities, so “fields like this one”, clustering and change detection need only array arithmetic.
Without any model to run, AlphaEarth separates crops and land cover as well as or better than embeddings computed from a single Sentinel-2 date, because each vector summarizes a year of many sensors.
Change between years in the Corn Belt is dominated by crop rotation, which the change map follows.
The annual summary cannot map within-season events; its dimensions have no physical names.



Exercises

Repeat the similarity search with a query in a soybean field and with one in a town.
Cluster with 10 clusters and name each from its CDL composition table.
Compute the change between consecutive years 2020 to 2024 and find pixels that changed every year.
Read 2017 and 2024 at 100 m for all of Iowa (scale=100, which uses the GeoTIFF overviews) and map the largest changes.
Train a random forest on AlphaEarth to predict the 2024 CDL and apply it to 2025 embeddings. How well does a classifier trained on one year transfer to the next?



References

Brown, C. F. et al. (2025). AlphaEarth Foundations: an embedding field model for accurate and efficient global mapping from sparse label data. arXiv:2507.22291.
Google Earth Engine Data Catalog. Satellite Embedding V1, GOOGLE/SATELLITE_EMBEDDING/V1/ANNUAL.
Gorelick, N. et al. (2017). Google Earth Engine: planetary-scale geospatial analysis for everyone. Remote Sensing of Environment.

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
text:
Overview

Why sensor-agnostic models
A conventional network has a fixed first layer: one set of weights per input band, in a fixed order. A new satellite, a different band set or a radar image needs a new model, or a hack such as copying weights between bands. Three ideas remove that limit:








Idea
How it works
Models




Wavelength-conditioned patch embedding
a small hypernetwork turns each band’s centre wavelength (and bandwidth) into that band’s first-layer weights
DOFA, Copernicus-FM


Spectral cross-attention
every band is a token tagged with its wavelength; attention merges any number of them
Panopticon


One encoder per modality, fused
separate optical and SAR encoders trained so that their embeddings of the same place agree
CROMA


Any-to-any tokens
every modality is tokenized; the model learns to predict any modality’s tokens from any other’s
TerraMind



Copernicus-FM also takes metadata: longitude, latitude, acquisition date and the area of the chip, encoded like extra tokens. TerraMind can generate a missing modality, for example a Sentinel-1 image from a Sentinel-2 image, which it calls “thinking in modalities”.


What flexibility does not give for free
A model that accepts Landsat bands has not necessarily learned that a Landsat pixel and a Sentinel-2 pixel of the same field should give the same embedding. Differences in resolution (30 m vs 20 m), band width and processing shift the inputs, and the embeddings shift with them. Cross-sensor transfer, training on one sensor and predicting on another, is the real test, and it is measured below against a simple band-value baseline.


Radar and clouds
Sentinel-1 sees through clouds; Sentinel-2 does not. CROMA’s joint embedding promises a representation that keeps working when the optical part is degraded. The test below covers half of the test chips with synthetic cloud and compares optical-only, SAR-only and joint embeddings.

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
section: Three sensors, one week, one landscape
text:
Three sensors, one week, one landscape
The Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-1 scenes come from the Corn Belt cubes. The Landsat 8 Collection 2 Level-2 bands are stored as digital numbers; reflectance is DN x 0.0000275 - 0.2. They are resampled to the Sentinel-2 grid with rio.reproject_match. Landsat’s NIR band (OLI band 5, 865 nm) corresponds to Sentinel-2 band 8A, so it is named nir08.


Code
s2 = xr.open_dataarray(CUBE / "s2_20m.nc").sel(time="2025-07-14").drop_vars("time").load().rio.write_crs("EPSG:32615")  # Sentinel-2
s1 = xr.open_dataarray(CUBE / "s1_20m.nc").sel(time="2025-07-20").drop_vars("time").load().rio.write_crs("EPSG:32615")  # Sentinel-1 dB
LS_BANDS = {"coastal": "coastal", "blue": "blue", "green": "green", "red": "red", "nir": "nir08",
            "swir16": "swir16", "swir22": "swir22"}  # Landsat file -> GeoLattice band name
ls = xr.concat([rioxarray.open_rasterio(LANDSAT / f"{f}.tif", masked=True).squeeze("band", drop=True)
                for f in LS_BANDS], dim=pd.Index(list(LS_BANDS.values()), name="band"))  # 7 bands, 30 m
ls = (ls * 0.0000275 - 0.2).rio.write_crs(ls.rio.crs)  # Collection 2 scale and offset to reflectance
ls = ls.rio.reproject_match(s2.isel(band=0), resampling=1).assign_coords(x=s2.x, y=s2.y)  # bilinear onto the 20 m grid
cdl = xr.open_dataset(CUBE / "labels_20m.nc")["cdl"].sel(year=2025).load()  # CDL 2025
for n, da in {"Sentinel-2": s2, "Landsat 8": ls, "Sentinel-1": s1}.items():  # check each sensor
    print(f"{n:11s}", dict(da.sizes), "| bands:", list(da.band.values), f"| missing {float(da.isnull().any('band').mean()):.1%}")  # summary

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5.5))  # three sensors
ext = [float(s2.x.min()), float(s2.x.max()), float(s2.y.min()), float(s2.y.max())]  # extent
for a, (t, da) in zip(ax[:2], {"Sentinel-2, 14 July": s2, "Landsat 8, 15 July": ls}.items()):  # optical
    a.imshow(np.clip(np.nan_to_num(da.sel(band=["red", "green", "blue"]).transpose("y", "x", "band").values) / 0.15, 0, 1), extent=ext)  # true colour
    a.set_title(t)  # title
ax[2].imshow(s1.sel(band="vv"), cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=-2, extent=ext); ax[2].set_title("Sentinel-1 VV (dB), 20 July")  # radar
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

Chips and labels follow notebook 09_11_03: 32 pixel (640 m) chips, the majority CDL class when it covers at least 60 % of the chip, corn and soybeans only, and 5.8 km blocks for spatial folds. The western half of the scene trains and the eastern half tests when a single split is needed.


Code
ny, nx = -(-cdl.shape[0] // CHIP), -(-cdl.shape[1] // CHIP)  # chip grid
pad = np.full((ny * CHIP, nx * CHIP), -1, cdl.dtype); pad[:cdl.shape[0], :cdl.shape[1]] = cdl.values  # padded CDL
blk = pad.reshape(ny, CHIP, nx, CHIP).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(ny * nx, -1)  # pixels per chip
counts = np.stack([(blk == k).sum(1) for k in (0, 1)], 1)  # corn and soybean pixels
major, purity = counts.argmax(1), counts.max(1) / blk.shape[1]  # majority and share
gy, gx = np.divmod(np.arange(ny * nx), nx)  # chip row and column
group = (gy // 9) * 10 + gx // 9  # spatial blocks
ok = purity >= 0.6  # pure corn or soybean chips
west, east = ok & (gx < nx // 2), ok & (gx >= nx // 2)  # single split for transfer tests
y = major  # labels
print(ok.sum(), "chips |", west.sum(), "west |", east.sum(), "east")  # sizes

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
text:
One model, three sensors
DOFA takes any optical band set through its wavelengths. Panopticon takes optical bands by wavelength and radar channels by special negative ids, so it alone reads all three sensors here. Each model embeds each sensor with its default per-band standardization; the probe is the spatial 5-fold linear probe of the previous notebooks, and the baseline is the chip mean of each band.


Code
SENSORS = {"Sentinel-2": s2, "Landsat 8": ls, "Sentinel-1": s1}  # the three inputs
emb, rows = {}, []  # embeddings and probe results
flat = lambda m: m.values.reshape(m.sizes["embedding"], -1).T  # (chips, D)
for model in ["dofa-base", "panopticon"]:  # wavelength-aware models
    enc = fm.load_model(model, device=DEVICE)  # load once
    for sname, da in SENSORS.items():  # every sensor
        if model == "dofa-base" and sname == "Sentinel-1":  # DOFA is used for optical bands here
            continue  # skip radar
        enc.bands, enc.wavelengths = None, None  # let embed_raster read this sensor's bands
        emb[(model, sname)] = flat(enc.embed_raster(da, chip_size=CHIP, norm="model", batch_size=64))  # (chips, D)
        rows.append({"input": model, "sensor": sname,
                     "F1": fm.linear_probe(emb[(model, sname)][ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok])["mean"]["f1_macro"]})  # probe
    del enc; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
for sname, da in SENSORS.items():  # band-mean baseline per sensor
    bm = np.nan_to_num(fm.chip_raster(da, chip_size=CHIP)[0].mean((2, 3)))  # mean of every band per chip
    emb[("band means", sname)] = bm  # keep it for transfer
    rows.append({"input": "band means", "sensor": sname, "F1": fm.linear_probe(bm[ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok])["mean"]["f1_macro"]})  # probe
pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="input", columns="sensor", values="F1")[list(SENSORS)].round(3)  # inputs x sensors
