In mid-July every optical input separates corn and soybeans almost perfectly, Sentinel-2 or Landsat, band means or embeddings: the crops differ strongly in the near and shortwave infrared at this time of year. The radar is the harder input. Band means of VV and VH reach about 0.90, and Panopticon’s radar embeddings about 0.92, a modest gain, while DOFA is not used on radar here. The interesting question is not whether a model can read each sensor, but whether what it learned from one sensor carries over to another.

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
section: From Sentinel-2 to Landsat: cross-sensor transfer
text:
From Sentinel-2 to Landsat: cross-sensor transfer
A logistic regression is trained on Sentinel-2 chips in the west and applied to the eastern chips twice: once on Sentinel-2 (same sensor) and once on Landsat 8 (other sensor). For the band-mean baseline only the six bands both sensors share are used.


Code
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression  # the transferred classifier
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score  # scores
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline  # scaling + model
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler  # feature scaling

common = [list(s2.band.values).index(b) for b in ["blue", "green", "red", "nir08", "swir16", "swir22"]]  # shared S2 bands
common_ls = [list(ls.band.values).index(b) for b in ["blue", "green", "red", "nir08", "swir16", "swir22"]]  # same in Landsat
pairs = {"band means (6 shared bands)": (emb[("band means", "Sentinel-2")][:, common], emb[("band means", "Landsat 8")][:, common_ls]),
         "dofa-base": (emb[("dofa-base", "Sentinel-2")], emb[("dofa-base", "Landsat 8")]),
         "panopticon": (emb[("panopticon", "Sentinel-2")], emb[("panopticon", "Landsat 8")])}  # S2 and Landsat features
rows = []  # transfer results
for n, (A, B) in pairs.items():  # every input
    clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)).fit(A[west], y[west])  # train on S2, west
    same = f1_score(y[east], clf.predict(A[east]), average="macro")  # S2 east
    other = f1_score(y[east], clf.predict(B[east]), average="macro")  # Landsat east
    cos = np.median((A[ok] * B[ok]).sum(1) / (np.linalg.norm(A[ok], axis=1) * np.linalg.norm(B[ok], axis=1) + 1e-12))  # S2 vs Landsat agreement
    rows.append({"input": n, "F1 Sentinel-2 -> Sentinel-2": same, "F1 Sentinel-2 -> Landsat": other,
                 "drop": same - other, "median cosine S2 vs Landsat": cos})  # record
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("input").round(3)  # transfer table

The three inputs behave very differently. A classifier trained on Panopticon’s Sentinel-2 embeddings still reaches about 0.94 on the Landsat embeddings of the same fields. The same classifier on DOFA embeddings collapses to about 0.44, below the band-mean baseline (about 0.73). The cosine column shows why that is surprising: DOFA’s Sentinel-2 and Landsat embeddings of a chip are, on the whole, more alike (0.94) than Panopticon’s (0.73). What matters is not the overall similarity but whether the small direction that separates corn from soybeans is preserved across sensors. In DOFA a shift caused by the different sensor (30 m resampled, broader bands) moves the embeddings across the decision boundary; in Panopticon it does not. Accepting a sensor’s bands is not the same as transferring between sensors, and cross-sensor transfer must always be measured.

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
text:
Copernicus-FM: does metadata matter?
Copernicus-FM accepts, for every chip, its longitude and latitude, acquisition date and area. With metadata=True, embed_raster computes them from the raster coordinates (fm.chip_metadata) and passes them to the model; without it, they are unknown (NaN) and the model ignores them.


Code
cfm = fm.load_model("copernicus-fm", device=DEVICE)  # Copernicus-FM ViT-Base
s2t = s2.assign_attrs(time="2025-07-14")  # acquisition date for the metadata
with_meta = flat(cfm.embed_raster(s2t, chip_size=CHIP, norm="model", metadata=True, batch_size=64))  # lon, lat, date, area
no_meta = flat(cfm.embed_raster(s2t, chip_size=CHIP, norm="model", batch_size=64))  # metadata unknown
del cfm; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
meta = fm.chip_metadata(fm.chip_raster(s2, chip_size=CHIP)[1], fm.chip_raster(s2, chip_size=CHIP)[2], s2.rio.crs,
                        time="2025-07-14", chip_size=CHIP, resolution=20)  # what the model received
print(meta.head(3).round(4))  # first chips
cos = (with_meta * no_meta).sum(1) / (np.linalg.norm(with_meta, axis=1) * np.linalg.norm(no_meta, axis=1))  # agreement
pd.DataFrame({"F1": {"with metadata": fm.linear_probe(with_meta[ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok])["mean"]["f1_macro"],
                     "without metadata": fm.linear_probe(no_meta[ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok])["mean"]["f1_macro"]},
              "median cosine between the two": {"with metadata": float(np.median(cos)), "without metadata": float(np.median(cos))}}).round(3)  # comparison

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
section: CROMA: optical, radar and both under clouds
text:
CROMA: optical, radar and both under clouds
CROMA has separate optical (12 Sentinel-2 bands) and radar (VV, VH) encoders trained to agree, plus a joint embedding. Its input chips are 120 pixels, so the 32 pixel chips are resized to 120. Three embeddings are computed: optical only, SAR only and joint.
To simulate clouds, the optical input of a random half of the eastern chips is replaced by a bright, flat patch: three standard deviations above the scene mean in every standardized band, which is how a thick cloud looks after the same normalization. A classifier trained on clean western chips is then scored on the eastern chips, with and without the clouds.


Code
opt = fm.prepare("croma-base", s2)  # 12 optical bands, standardized over the scene
sar = fm.prepare("croma-base", s1, modality="sar")  # VV, VH, standardized
resize = lambda c: torch.nn.functional.interpolate(torch.as_tensor(c), size=120, mode="bilinear").numpy()  # 32 -> 120 px
Co = resize(fm.chip_raster(opt, chip_size=CHIP)[0])  # optical chips
Cs = resize(fm.chip_raster(sar, chip_size=CHIP)[0])  # radar chips
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)  # random generator
e_idx = np.flatnonzero(east)  # eastern labelled chips
cloudy = np.zeros(len(Co), bool); cloudy[rng.choice(e_idx, len(e_idx) // 2, replace=False)] = True  # half get clouds
Cc = Co.copy(); Cc[cloudy] = 3.0  # bright flat cloud in standardized units
print(f"{cloudy.sum()} of {east.sum()} eastern chips clouded")  # how many

croma = {}  # embeddings per variant
for mode in ["optical", "sar", "both"]:  # three CROMA heads
    enc = fm.load_model("croma-base", device=DEVICE, modality=mode)  # CROMA with that modality
    if mode == "sar":  # radar only: clouds do not matter
        croma[("sar", "clear")] = croma[("sar", "clouds")] = enc.embed(Cs, batch_size=64)  # radar embeddings
    else:  # optical or joint
        kw = {"x_sar": Cs} if mode == "both" else {}  # joint mode also takes the radar chips
        croma[(mode, "clear")] = enc.embed(Co, batch_size=64, **kw)  # clean optical input
        croma[(mode, "clouds")] = enc.embed(Cc, batch_size=64, **kw)  # clouded optical input
    del enc; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory

rows = []  # cloud test
for mode in ["optical", "sar", "both"]:  # every embedding
    clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)).fit(croma[(mode, "clear")][west], y[west])  # train clean, west
    for cond in ["clear", "clouds"]:  # test condition
        pred = clf.predict(croma[(mode, cond)][east])  # predict east
        pc = clf.predict(croma[(mode, cond)][cloudy])  # predictions on the clouded chips
        rows.append({"embedding": mode, "test": cond, "F1 all east": f1_score(y[east], pred, average="macro"),
                     "F1 clouded chips": f1_score(y[cloudy], pc, average="macro"),
                     "clouded chips called corn": (pc == 0).mean()})  # scores and what the classifier says
pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="embedding", columns="test").round(3)  # embedding x condition

On clear chips all three embeddings classify well, radar alone at about 0.91. Under clouds the optical and the joint embeddings fail in the same way: the classifier calls almost every clouded chip the same crop, and macro F1 on those chips falls to about 0.27. The radar-only embedding is unaffected. CROMA’s joint embedding does not fall back on radar by itself when the optical half is corrupted. In practice clouds must be masked, and a radar-only embedding (or a classifier trained with cloudy examples) used where the optical input is unreliable.

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
section: TerraMind: two modalities in, one generated
text:
TerraMind: two modalities in, one generated
TerraMind’s encoder takes several modalities at once as a dictionary. Each is prepared with its own statistics (fm.prepare(..., modality="S1GRD") for radar). Its embeddings of Sentinel-2 alone, Sentinel-1 alone and both together are probed like the others; TerraMind reads 224 pixel chips, so the 32 pixel chips are resized.


Code
resize224 = lambda c: torch.nn.functional.interpolate(torch.as_tensor(c), size=224, mode="bilinear").numpy()  # 32 -> 224 px
X2 = resize224(fm.chip_raster(fm.prepare("terramind-v1-base", s2), chip_size=CHIP)[0])  # S2L2A chips (12 bands)
X1 = resize224(fm.chip_raster(fm.prepare("terramind-v1-base", s1, modality="S1GRD"), chip_size=CHIP)[0])  # S1GRD chips


def tm_embed(enc, inputs, batch=32):  # embed dicts of modalities in batches
    out = []  # embeddings
    for i in range(0, len(next(iter(inputs.values()))), batch):  # batches
        d = {k: torch.as_tensor(v[i:i + batch]) for k, v in inputs.items()}  # one batch per modality
        out.append(enc.encode(d).float().cpu().numpy())  # pooled tokens
    return np.concatenate(out)  # (chips, 768)


tm = {}  # embeddings
for mods, inputs in {"S2L2A": {"S2L2A": X2}, "S1GRD": {"S1GRD": X1}, "S2L2A + S1GRD": {"S2L2A": X2, "S1GRD": X1}}.items():  # variants
    enc = fm.load_model("terramind-v1-base", device=DEVICE, modalities=list(inputs))  # encoder for these modalities
    tm[mods] = tm_embed(enc, inputs)  # embeddings
    del enc; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
pd.DataFrame({"F1": {k: fm.linear_probe(v[ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok])["mean"]["f1_macro"] for k, v in tm.items()}}).round(3)  # probes









F1




S2L2A
1.000


S1GRD
0.916


S2L2A + S1GRD
0.999







TerraMind’s encoder classifies the July crops perfectly from Sentinel-2 and reaches about 0.92 from Sentinel-1 alone, close to Panopticon’s radar embeddings. Adding radar to optical does not improve an already perfect optical score; the value of the radar input lies in scenes where the optical input is missing or cloudy.
The generative TerraMind model turns a Sentinel-2 chip into a Sentinel-1 chip by iterative denoising of radar tokens. It is built from TerraTorch’s model registry. Inputs are standardized with fm.prepare and the output is converted back to dB with TerraMind’s radar statistics.


Code
from terratorch.registry import FULL_MODEL_REGISTRY  # TerraTorch full models

gen = FULL_MODEL_REGISTRY.build("terratorch_terramind_v1_base_generate", modalities=["S2L2A"],
                                output_modalities=["S1GRD"], pretrained=True, standardize=False,
                                timesteps=10).to(DEVICE).eval()  # Sentinel-2 -> Sentinel-1 generator
win = dict(y=slice(400, 624), x=slice(600, 824))  # one 224 pixel (4.5 km) window
x2 = torch.as_tensor(fm.prepare("terramind-v1-base", s2.isel(**win)).values[None]).to(DEVICE)  # standardized S2
torch.manual_seed(SEED)  # the generation is stochastic
with torch.no_grad():  # inference only
    g = gen({"S2L2A": x2})["S1GRD"][0].float().cpu().numpy()  # generated, standardized
sp = fm.input_spec("terramind-v1-base")["S1GRD"]  # radar statistics
g_db = g * np.array(sp["std"])[:, None, None] + np.array(sp["mean"])[:, None, None]  # back to dB
real = s1.isel(**win).values  # the real Sentinel-1
del gen; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory

def corr(a, b, k=1):  # Pearson correlation after k x k averaging
    a = a.reshape(a.shape[0] // k, k, -1, k).mean((1, 3)); b = b.reshape(b.shape[0] // k, k, -1, k).mean((1, 3))  # block means
    m = np.isfinite(a) & np.isfinite(b)  # valid cells
    return np.corrcoef(a[m], b[m])[0, 1]  # correlation

print("mean dB  generated:", g_db.mean((1, 2)).round(2), "| real:", np.nanmean(real, (1, 2)).round(2))  # levels
print("correlation VV, pixels:", round(corr(g_db[0], real[0]), 3), "| 16 x 16 px blocks (320 m):", round(corr(g_db[0], real[0], 16), 3))  # agreement
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))  # input, generated, real
ax[0].imshow(np.clip(s2.isel(**win).sel(band=["red", "green", "blue"]).transpose("y", "x", "band").values / 0.15, 0, 1)); ax[0].set_title("input: Sentinel-2, 14 July")  # input
ax[1].imshow(g_db[0], cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=-2); ax[1].set_title("TerraMind: generated VV (dB)")  # generated
ax[2].imshow(real[0], cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=-2); ax[2].set_title("real Sentinel-1 VV (dB), 20 July")  # real
for a in ax:  # every panel
    a.axis("off")  # no axes
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


mean dB  generated: [ -8.87 -15.35] | real: [ -8.65 -14.78]
correlation VV, pixels: 0.19 | 16 x 16 px blocks (320 m): 0.527









The generated radar image has the right overall level (within about 0.6 dB of the real one in VV and VH), and it places the river and the farmstead correctly, features the optical image shows clearly. It does not reproduce the backscatter of individual fields: pixel correlation with the real image is about 0.2, and about 0.5 after averaging to 320 m blocks. Generation is stochastic, so these numbers change a little from run to run even with a fixed seed on the GPU. The generated image is a plausible radar image of this kind of landscape, not a measurement of these fields six days later. Generated modalities can fill gaps for visualization or as an extra input to TerraMind’s own reasoning, but they are not a substitute for an acquisition.

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
text:
An eight-band WorldView-2 image
WorldView-2 has bands that no Sentinel or Landsat sensor has, such as yellow (608 nm) and a second near-infrared band (949 nm). GeoLattice has no band names for them, so DOFA receives the wavelengths directly. The scene is a 1.6 m image of a Bangladesh landscape; a 448 pixel (720 m) window is embedded in 224 pixel chips with patch features.


Code
WV2_NM = [427, 478, 546, 608, 659, 724, 833, 949]  # WorldView-2 band centres (nm): coastal to NIR2
import geopandas as gpd  # field polygons mark where the image has data
full = rioxarray.open_rasterio(WV2, masked=True)  # the whole scene (no-data around the edges)
cxf, cyf = gpd.read_file(WV2.parents[1] / "Labeled_data" / "aoi_trianing.shp").set_crs(full.rio.crs, allow_override=True).union_all().centroid.xy  # centre of the fields
ix, iy = int(np.abs(full.x - cxf[0]).argmin()), int(np.abs(full.y - cyf[0]).argmin())  # its pixel
wv = full.isel(y=slice(iy - 224, iy + 224), x=slice(ix - 224, ix + 224))  # 448 x 448 window over the fields
print(f"window without data: {float(wv.isnull().any('band').mean()):.1%}")  # check
wv = wv.assign_coords(band=[f"b{i}" for i in range(1, 9)])  # generic band names
dofa = fm.load_model("dofa-base", device=DEVICE, wavelengths=WV2_NM)  # DOFA told the wavelengths
wv_emb = dofa.embed_raster(wv, chip_size=224, dense=True)  # 16 px (26 m) patch features
del dofa; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5.3))  # image and embeddings
v = wv.isel(band=[4, 2, 1]).transpose("y", "x", "band").values  # red, green, blue
ax[0].imshow(np.clip(v / np.nanpercentile(v, 98), 0, 1)); ax[0].set_title("WorldView-2 true colour, 1.6 m")  # image
ax[1].imshow(fm.embedding_rgb(wv_emb).transpose("y", "x", "band"), interpolation="nearest"); ax[1].set_title("DOFA patch embeddings (26 m)")  # embeddings
for a in ax:  # every panel
    a.axis("off")  # no axes
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
print("embedding map:", dict(wv_emb.sizes))  # size


window without data: 29.7%









embedding map: {'embedding': 768, 'y': 28, 'x': 28}


DOFA receives the eight WorldView-2 wavelengths, including the yellow and second near-infrared bands, and produces patch features at 26 m (16 pixels of 1.6 m). The window is a mosaic of small fields, with greener crops in the north-west and paler fallow or harvested fields in the south, and an area without data in the top right. The embedding map follows that division: the greener northern fields and the paler southern fields take different colours, and the empty area (filled with zeros after normalization) is one uniform block, a reminder to mask no-data cells before using the embeddings. Notebook 09_11_09 classifies these WorldView-2 fields with encoders built for very high resolution imagery.

title: One Model for Many Sensors: DOFA, Panopticon, Copernicus-FM, CROMA and TerraMind
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

Wavelength-conditioned (DOFA, Copernicus-FM), spectral-attention (Panopticon), paired-encoder (CROMA) and any-to-any (TerraMind) models read band sets and sensors a fixed-input model cannot.
Reading a sensor is not the same as transferring between sensors: classifiers trained on Sentinel-2 embeddings lose accuracy on Landsat embeddings of the same fields, and the loss has to be measured against a band-value baseline.
Copernicus-FM’s location and date metadata change its embeddings; whether that helps depends on the task.
A joint optical and radar embedding can be compared with optical-only and radar-only embeddings under simulated clouds.
TerraMind generates a plausible radar image from optical input at the level of overall backscatter, but not as a substitute for a real Sentinel-1 acquisition.
Unusual band sets such as WorldView-2’s yellow and NIR2 bands are passed to DOFA as wavelengths.



Exercises

Add Panopticon’s Sentinel-1 embeddings to the transfer table: train on radar, predict on optical. What happens, and why?
Repeat the Copernicus-FM test with a wrong date (for example January). Does the probe notice?
Cloud the western (training) chips as well and retrain. Which CROMA embedding benefits most?
Generate S2L2A from S1GRD with TerraMind (swap modalities and output_modalities) and compare the generated NDVI with the real one.
Embed the WorldView-2 window with Panopticon (pass wavelengths=WV2_NM) and compare its map with DOFA’s.



References

Fuller, A., Millard, K. and Green, J. R. (2023). CROMA: remote sensing representations with contrastive radar-optical masked autoencoders. NeurIPS.
Jakubik, J. et al. (2025). TerraMind: large-scale generative multimodality for Earth observation. arXiv:2504.11171.
Waldmann, L. et al. (2025). Panopticon. arXiv:2503.10845.
Wang, Y. et al. (2025). Towards a unified Copernicus foundation model for Earth vision. arXiv:2503.11849.
Xiong, Z. et al. (2024). DOFA. arXiv:2403.15356.

title: From a GeoTIFF to an Embedding Map
text:
Overview

The input contract of a model
A pretrained encoder learned its weights from data prepared in one way. Five properties of that preparation define its input contract:








Property
Example
What goes wrong if it differs




Bands and their order
Prithvi: blue, green, red, narrow NIR, SWIR 1, SWIR 2
the first layer applies “red” weights to the NIR band


Units
digital numbers (reflectance x 10,000), reflectance 0 to 1, dB for SAR
values are 10,000 times too small or large


Normalization
per-band mean and standard deviation of the pretraining data
features drift away from the range the model has seen


Chip size and resolution
224 pixels at 30 m (Prithvi), 256 at 10 m (Satlas)
objects appear at a scale the model never saw


Time steps
1 to 4 frames (Prithvi-EO-2.0)
wrong tensor shape, or frames read as bands



Wavelength-aware models (DOFA, Copernicus-FM, Panopticon) relax the first property: they build their input layer from the band wavelengths, so any band set works, but units and normalization still matter.


Pooled and patch embeddings
embed_raster cuts a raster into chips and returns one vector per chip (pooled), or with dense=True the grid of patch vectors inside every chip. A chip is the unit the model sees at once: a 224 pixel chip of 20 m Sentinel-2 covers 4.5 km, so its pooled embedding describes a landscape, while 32 pixel chips resized to 224 describe single fields. Resizing changes the apparent ground resolution, another departure from the contract that this notebook makes on purpose and measures.


Why it fails silently
A neural network has no notion of units. A chip in reflectance (0 to 0.5) given to a model that expects digital numbers (0 to 5,000) produces activations near zero, a nearly constant embedding and a probe that barely beats guessing, yet no error is raised. The only defence is to check the contract (fm.input_spec) and to measure, as below.

Embedding Rasters with GeoLattice

fm.embedding_rgb, fm.embeddings_to_frame

Learning objectives

Read the input contract of a model and prepare a raster to match it.
Know the parts of a FoundationEncoder and the difference between pooled and patch embeddings.
Cut a raster into chips and keep their georeferencing.

Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README. It also uses geolattice[rsense-foundation], which no GeoLattice option installs: pip install "geolattice[rsense-foundation]".


Code
import os  # environment variables

text:
The input contract
fm.input_spec returns the contract recorded for a model: the bands in order (GeoLattice names), the units the statistics refer to, the mean and standard deviation, and the chip size. The values come from the TorchGeo weight transforms, the TerraTorch pretraining constants and the model cards.


Code
names = ["prithvi-eo-2.0-300m", "ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", "satlas-swint-s2-ms", "scale-mae",
         "terramind-v1-base", "dofa-base", "panopticon", "ssl4eo-s1-resnet50-moco"]  # models to compare
rows = []  # one row per model
for n in names:  # every model
    sp = fm.input_spec(n)  # its contract
    rows.append({"model": n, "bands": "any (wavelength-aware)" if sp["bands"] is None else ", ".join(sp["bands"]),
                 "units": sp["units"], "statistics": "per-band standardization" if sp["mean"] is None
                 else f"mean {sp['mean'][0]:g}.., std {sp['std'][0]:g}..", "chip": sp["img_size"]})  # summary

Three patterns stand out. Prithvi and TerraMind standardize digital numbers with the statistics of their pretraining archives. SSL4EO and Satlas only divide by a constant (Satlas takes red, green and blue from Sentinel-2’s 8-bit true colour product, which prepare approximates by dividing by 3,000). DOFA and Panopticon accept any bands and have no fixed statistics, so each band is standardized over the scene.

title: From a GeoTIFF to an Embedding Map
text:
Anatomy of a FoundationEncoder
fm.load_model builds the network, downloads the weights on first use and wraps both in a FoundationEncoder. The SSL4EO ResNet-18 is small and quick, so it is a good first example.


Code
enc = fm.load_model("ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", device=DEVICE)  # SSL4EO-S12 ResNet-18, MoCo weights
print(enc)  # name, loader, embedding size, device
print("catalog entry:", enc.spec.architecture, "|", enc.spec.inputs)  # the catalog record it came from
print("network:", type(enc.model).__name__, "|", f"{sum(p.numel() for p in enc.model.parameters()) / 1e6:.1f} M parameters")  # the torch module
x = torch.randn(2, 13, 224, 224)  # two random 13-band chips
print("forward_features:", tuple(enc.forward_features(x).shape))  # raw output: a feature map
print("encode:", tuple(enc.encode(x).shape))  # pooled: one vector per chip


FoundationEncoder('ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco', loader='torchgeo', embed_dim=512, device=cuda)
catalog entry: ResNet-18, MoCo-v2 | Sentinel-2 L1C 13 bands, reflectance / 10000
network: ResNet | 11.2 M parameters
forward_features: (2, 512, 7, 7)
encode: (2, 512)


forward_features returns what the network produces: for a ResNet a 512 x 7 x 7 feature map (the 224 pixel chip downsampled 32 times). encode pools it to one 512 value vector per chip, and embed does the same in batches and returns NumPy. A vision transformer returns tokens instead, and pooling can take the class token or the mean of the patch tokens.


Code
vit = fm.load_model("ssl4eo-s12-vits16-dino", device=DEVICE)  # SSL4EO ViT-Small, DINO weights
tok = vit.forward_features(x)  # (chips, 1 + 196 tokens, 384)
cls_vec, mean_vec = vit.encode(x, pool="cls"), vit.encode(x, pool="mean")  # two pooling choices
print("tokens:", tuple(tok.shape), "| dense grid:", vit.dense_features(x).shape)  # tokens and patch grid
print("cosine(CLS, mean of patches):",
      torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(cls_vec, mean_vec).cpu().numpy().round(3))  # how different they are


tokens: (2, 197, 384) | dense grid: (2, 384, 14, 14)
cosine(CLS, mean of patches): [0.107 0.074]


The 197 tokens are one class token plus a 14 x 14 grid of 16 pixel patches; dense_features drops the class token and reshapes the rest into that grid. The CLS vector and the mean of the patch tokens are different summaries of the same chip, which is why the pooling choice must stay fixed within an analysis.

section: Preparing a raster for a model
text:
Preparing a raster for a model
fm.prepare applies the contract to a raster. For the SSL4EO model the Corn Belt stack lacks three of the thirteen bands (coastal aerosol, water vapour and cirrus); prepare fills each from the band nearest in wavelength and records what it filled. For Prithvi it picks six bands, converts reflectance to digital numbers and standardizes with the HLS statistics.


Code
for n in ["ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", "prithvi-eo-2.0-300m", "satlas-swint-s2-ms", "dofa-base"]:  # four contracts
    p = fm.prepare(n, s2)  # bands, units and normalization for model n
    print(f"{n:26s} bands {p.sizes['band']:2d} | filled: {p.attrs['filled_bands'] or '-':28s} | "
          f"mean {float(p.mean()):6.2f}, std {float(p.std()):5.2f}")  # what prepare did
print("wavelengths (nm) used by DOFA:", fm.band_wavelengths(list(s2.band.values)))  # DOFA reads these


ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco   bands 13 | filled: coastal,watervapor,cirrus    | mean   0.20, std  0.17
prithvi-eo-2.0-300m        bands  6 | filled: -                            | mean  -0.17, std  0.53
satlas-swint-s2-ms         bands  9 | filled: -                            | mean   0.24, std  0.17
dofa-base                  bands 10 | filled: -                            | mean  -0.00, std  1.00
wavelengths (nm) used by DOFA: [490.0, 560.0, 665.0, 705.0, 740.0, 783.0, 842.0, 865.0, 1610.0, 2190.0]


After preparation Prithvi’s values have a mean near zero and a standard deviation near one, as the pretraining data had; the SSL4EO input is reflectance, as SSL4EO expects. Filling missing bands from neighbours is a compromise: the coastal band (443 nm) copied from blue (490 nm) is close, the cirrus band (1375 nm) copied from SWIR 1 (1610 nm) is not, since real cirrus reflectance is near zero over clear land. The probe below shows how much such compromises cost.

title: From a GeoTIFF to an Embedding Map
text:
Chips and their labels
fm.chip_raster cuts the scene into square chips and returns the coordinates of their centres. Here the chips are 32 pixels (640 m), about one field, so each chip can carry one crop label: the majority CDL class, kept when it covers at least 60 % of the chip. The scene edges are padded by reflection so every pixel falls in a chip.


Code
CHIP = 32  # chip size in 20 m pixels (640 m)
chips, ys, xs = fm.chip_raster(s2, chip_size=CHIP)  # (n, band, 32, 32) and chip centres
print("chips:", chips.shape, f"on a {len(ys)} x {len(xs)} grid")  # count and layout


def chip_labels(lab, chip):  # majority class and its share in every chip (row-major order)
    a = lab.values  # class codes, -1 = none
    ny, nx = -(-a.shape[0] // chip), -(-a.shape[1] // chip)  # chips per column and row
    pad = np.full((ny * chip, nx * chip), -1, a.dtype); pad[:a.shape[0], :a.shape[1]] = a  # pad with "none"
    blocks = pad.reshape(ny, chip, nx, chip).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(ny * nx, -1)  # pixels per chip
    counts = np.stack([(blocks == k).sum(1) for k in range(len(CLASSES))], 1)  # pixels per class
    return counts.argmax(1), counts.max(1) / blocks.shape[1]  # majority class and its share


major, purity = chip_labels(cdl, CHIP)  # one label per chip
ok = purity >= 0.6  # chips dominated by one class
gy, gx = np.divmod(np.arange(len(major)), len(xs))  # chip row and column
block = (gy // 9) * 10 + gx // 9  # 9 x 9 chip blocks (5.8 km) for spatial cross-validation
print(ok.sum(), "labelled chips in", len(np.unique(block[ok])), "spatial blocks")  # usable samples
pd.Series(major[ok]).map(dict(enumerate(CLASSES))).value_counts()  # chips per class


chips: (2208, 10, 32, 32) on a 46 x 48 grid
1458 labelled chips in 30 spatial blocks


Corn              940
Soybeans          509
Grass/pasture       5
Developed           3
Wetland/forest      1
Name: count, dtype: int64


Corn and soybeans dominate, as they do in Iowa; developed land and wetland/forest chips are rare, because 640 m chips seldom contain 60 % of either. The blocks group neighbouring chips, so a probe trained in one block is tested in other blocks, not on the field next door.

title: From a GeoTIFF to an Embedding Map
text:
Four models, four embedding maps
embed_raster(norm="model") prepares the scene with the model’s contract, chips it and resizes each 32 pixel chip to the model’s input size. The four models differ in architecture and pretraining data: an SSL4EO ResNet-18, a Satlas Swin-T, DOFA and Panopticon.


Code
MODELS = ["ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", "satlas-swint-s2-ms", "dofa-base", "panopticon"]  # models to compare
emb, secs = {}, {}  # embedding maps and run times
for n in MODELS:  # every model
    e = fm.load_model(n, device=DEVICE)  # load (downloads once)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
    emb[n] = e.embed_raster(s2, chip_size=CHIP, norm="model", batch_size=64)  # (D, 46, 48) map
    secs[n] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # seconds for the scene
    del e; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free the GPU
pd.DataFrame({"embedding size": {n: emb[n].sizes["embedding"] for n in MODELS},
              "seconds for the scene": pd.Series(secs).round(1)})  # sizes and run times

corn = (pad.reshape(len(ys), CHIP, len(xs), CHIP) == 0).mean((1, 3))  # share of corn in every chip
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(24, 4.4))  # six panels
ax[0].imshow(rgb, extent=ext); ax[0].set_title("Sentinel-2 true colour")  # the scene
ax[1].imshow(corn, cmap="YlOrBr", extent=ext, interpolation="nearest"); ax[1].set_title("CDL corn share per chip")  # reference
for a, n in zip(ax[2:], MODELS):  # every model
    a.imshow(fm.embedding_rgb(emb[n]).transpose("y", "x", "band"), extent=ext, interpolation="nearest")  # PCA colours
    a.set_title(n, fontsize=9)  # model name
for a in ax:  # all panels
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









Each model panel shows the first three principal components of its embeddings as colours, one square per 640 m chip. The maps look speckled, and so does the corn share: in this landscape of square-mile sections every chip holds a different mix of corn and soybean fields, so neighbouring chips differ more than distant regions do. The models still disagree with one another. DOFA’s colours vary most smoothly across the scene, while the ResNet, Swin and Panopticon maps change more from chip to chip, a sign that they respond to different contrasts within each chip. A visual impression is not a measure, so a probe follows.
fm.embeddings_to_frame flattens a map to a table, one row per chip with its coordinates, ready to join with labels or to export.

A linear probe with spatial-block cross-validation measures how much crop information each map holds. Only corn and soybeans have at least 20 pure chips, so the probe separates those two; the rare classes would make the macro F1 score meaningless. The baseline is the mean reflectance of the ten bands in each chip.


Code
ok &= np.isin(major, np.flatnonzero(np.bincount(major[ok], minlength=len(CLASSES)) >= 20))  # classes with 20+ chips
y_ok, g_ok = major[ok], block[ok]  # labels and blocks of usable chips
print(ok.sum(), "chips:", pd.Series(y_ok).map(dict(enumerate(CLASSES))).value_counts().to_dict())  # what the probe sees
flat = lambda m: m.values.reshape(m.sizes["embedding"], -1).T  # (chips, D) in chip order
bandmean = np.nan_to_num(chips.mean((2, 3)))  # baseline: mean reflectance per band and chip
res = {"band means (baseline)": fm.linear_probe(bandmean[ok], y_ok, groups=g_ok)["mean"]}  # baseline probe
for n in MODELS:  # every model
    res[n] = fm.linear_probe(flat(emb[n])[ok], y_ok, groups=g_ok)["mean"]  # spatial 5-fold probe
probe = pd.DataFrame(res).T.round(3)  # accuracy and macro F1 per input

In late August corn and soybeans differ so clearly in their spectra that the ten band means already classify almost every chip correctly, so there is little room for any encoder to add information. DOFA and Panopticon reach slightly higher scores than the baseline, Satlas matches it and the SSL4EO ResNet-18 falls below it, with three of its thirteen input bands filled from neighbours. That is a lesson in itself: when a simple spectral baseline nearly saturates, a foundation model brings cost, not accuracy. Notebook 09_11_04 moves to a harder setting (patch embeddings, an early-season date and fewer labels), where the differences between models are larger.

title: From a GeoTIFF to an Embedding Map
text:
What a wrong normalization costs
The same SSL4EO model is run three ways: with its contract (reflectance, the SSL4EO scaling), with reflectance mistaken for digital numbers (values 10,000 times too small), and with per-scene standardization instead of the model’s statistics. The cosine similarity to the correct embeddings and the probe accuracy show the cost.


Code
ssl = fm.load_model("ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", device=DEVICE)  # the SSL4EO ResNet-18 again
variants = {  # three ways of preparing the same scene
    "contract (reflectance)": fm.prepare("ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", s2),  # correct
    "reflectance read as DN": fm.prepare("ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", s2, units="dn"),  # 10,000 times too small
}
variants["per-scene standardization"] = fm.prepare("ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", s2).pipe(
    lambda p: (p - p.mean(("y", "x"))) / p.std(("y", "x")))  # same 13 bands, standardized instead of scaled
E = {k: flat(ssl.embed_raster(v, chip_size=CHIP, norm={"method": "none"}, batch_size=64))
     for k, v in variants.items()}  # embeddings for each variant
ref = E["contract (reflectance)"]  # the correct embeddings
cos = lambda a, b: (a * b).sum(1) / (np.linalg.norm(a, axis=1) * np.linalg.norm(b, axis=1) + 1e-12)  # row cosine
pd.DataFrame({k: {"median cosine to contract": float(np.median(cos(v, ref))),
                  "probe accuracy": fm.linear_probe(v[ok], y_ok, groups=g_ok)["mean"]["accuracy"]}
              for k, v in E.items()}).T.round(3)  # cost of each mistake

contract (reflectance)

The table quantifies two different kinds of damage. Embeddings computed from inputs on the wrong scale point in a different direction from the correct ones (a low cosine similarity), so they cannot be mixed with embeddings computed correctly elsewhere, for example a stored index. The probe accuracy can still look reasonable, because a linear probe re-learns whatever structure is left, and that is exactly what makes the error silent. Per-scene standardization changes the values without changing their order within each band, so it often hurts less, but the embeddings of two scenes standardized separately are no longer comparable.

title: From a GeoTIFF to an Embedding Map
text:
CPU and GPU
Embedding is inference only, so a CPU works; a GPU is faster for large models and large areas. The same 512 chips are embedded on each device.


Code
rows = []  # timings
for n in ["ssl4eo-s12-resnet18-moco", "dofa-base"]:  # a small and a medium model
    for dev in (["cpu", "cuda"] if DEVICE == "cuda" else ["cpu"]):  # available devices
        e = fm.load_model(n, device=dev, bands=list(s2.band.values))  # model on that device
        x = fm.prepare(n, s2).isel(y=slice(0, 32 * 16), x=slice(0, 32 * 32))  # a prepared 512-chip block
        c, _, _ = fm.chip_raster(x, chip_size=CHIP)  # its chips
        c = torch.nn.functional.interpolate(torch.as_tensor(c), size=e.img_size, mode="bilinear").numpy()  # model size
        e.embed(c[:32], batch_size=32)  # warm-up (kernels, memory)
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); e.embed(c, batch_size=64)  # timed run
        if dev == "cuda":  # wait for the GPU to finish
            torch.cuda.synchronize()  # synchronize
        rows.append({"model": n, "device": dev, "chips": len(c), "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0})  # record
        del e  # free memory
t = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # timing table
t["chips per second"] = (t["chips"] / t["seconds"]).round(1)  # throughput
t.round(2)

Saving embeddings with their provenance
An embedding map is only reusable if it records how it was made: the model, its weights, the chip size and the normalization. embed_raster writes these as attributes; the map is saved to NetCDF and read back without loading any model.

m.attrs.update(weights=fm.model_info("dofa-base")["weights"], source="Sentinel-2 L2A 2025-08-26, 20 m",

back = xr.open_dataarray(path)  # read back, no model needed

title: From a GeoTIFF to an Embedding Map
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

Every model has an input contract: bands and order, units, normalization, chip size and time steps. fm.input_spec records it and fm.prepare applies it, filling missing bands from the nearest wavelength and saying which ones it filled.
A FoundationEncoder gives raw outputs (forward_features), pooled vectors (encode, embed), patch grids (dense_features) and georeferenced maps (embed_raster).
chip_raster cuts a raster into chips with their centre coordinates; labels per chip come from the majority class and its share.
Different models produce different embedding maps of the same scene, and a spatial linear probe measures how much task information each holds compared with a simple band-mean baseline.
Wrong units change the direction of the embeddings and may still give a plausible probe score, so the error is silent; per-scene standardization makes embeddings of different scenes incomparable.
A GPU speeds embedding up substantially; saving embeddings with their provenance makes them reusable without the model.



Exercises

Run fm.prepare("terramind-v1-base", s2) and list the filled bands. Which one is the worst substitute, and why?
Repeat the four-model probe with 16 pixel chips (320 m). Which classes gain, which lose?
Use embed_raster(..., dense=True) with the SSL4EO ViT on a 224 pixel chip and plot the 14 x 14 patch map next to the CDL.
Add a fourth normalization variant to the experiment: digital numbers read as reflectance (values 10,000 times too large). What happens to the cosine similarity?
Save the SSL4EO embedding map with its provenance and write a function that refuses to compare two maps whose model or normalization attributes differ.

title: Self-supervised pretraining for Sentinel-2 crop mapping
text:
Overview
Self-supervised learning (SSL) uses that unlabeled imagery to train an encoder without any labels, and a small labeled set is then enough to turn the encoder’s features into a classifier. This tutorial pretrains encoders on unlabeled Sentinel-2 chips over the Iowa corn belt study area (the Corn_belt AOI, about 30 km × 29 km), then measures how useful their features are for crop-type mapping with the USDA Cropland Data Layer (CDL) as the reference.
The imagery is the 20 m Sentinel-2 L2A cube already built by ../09_09_image_classification/09_09_03_02_spatio_temporal_and_multi_sensor_crop_mapping_sentinel_2_sentinel_1_and_landsat_time_series_2020_to_2025.ipynb and cached in Data/08_remote_sensing/08_09_image_classification/Corn_belt/cache_20m: 34 clear-sky acquisitions from May to October, 2020 to 2025, with 10 bands (blue, green, red, three red-edge bands, two NIR bands and two SWIR bands) as surface reflectance, and clouds, shadows and snow set to missing. The CDL labels for every year are cached on the same grid and recoded to six classes: corn, soybeans, grass/pasture, developed, wetland/forest and other.
Four pretraining recipes are compared: SimCLR with ordinary image augmentations, SimCLR and MoCo with seasonal views (two dates of the same place, as in SeCo), and a masked autoencoder (MAE). Each encoder is frozen and scored with a linear probe on held-out geography. A random-weights encoder and the plain band means of each chip are the baselines. The last part shows how pretraining on the test area itself leaks information into the evaluation, and how to check for it.
A CUDA GPU is required. Each pretraining run takes a few minutes on a workstation GPU; on a CPU the notebook would take hours, so the setup cell stops if no GPU is found.

title: Self-supervised pretraining for Sentinel-2 crop mapping

Core concepts

Learning objectives

Read the cached Sentinel-2 cube and CDL labels, cut the scene into chips, and hold out the eastern third of the AOI with a buffer.
Pretrain a ResNet-18 with SimCLR and MoCo, using ordinary augmentations and seasonal views from the same growing season.
Pretrain a convolutional masked autoencoder and inspect its reconstructions.
Freeze each encoder, score the embeddings with a linear probe on held-out geography, and compare them with a random-weights encoder and with band means.
Measure label efficiency and view the embeddings with t-SNE (and UMAP when it is installed).
Check the distance between pretraining chips and test chips, and compare a clean run with one pretrained on the test area.
Save the encoders and write a map of the learned features.

title: Self-supervised pretraining for Sentinel-2 crop mapping
text:
Workflow and GeoLattice functions

Read the cached Sentinel-2 cube and CDL labels, cut the scene into 16 × 16 pixel chips (320 m), and hold out the eastern third of the AOI for testing with geographic_holdout.
Contrastive learning: build a ResNet-18 encoder with make_encoder, look at the nt_xent_loss, and pretrain with pretrain_contrastive (SimCLR and MoCo).
Masked image modelling: build a convolutional masked autoencoder with build_mae and pretrain it with pretrain_masked.
Evaluation: freeze each encoder, compute features with extract_embeddings, score them with linear_probe and classification_report, measure label efficiency, and map the embeddings with t-SNE (and UMAP when it is installed).
Leakage: measure the distance between pretraining chips and test chips with check_geographic_overlap, and compare a clean run with one pretrained on the test area.
Save the encoders and write a map of the learned features as a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF with geolattice.rsense.write.

All SSL functions live in geolattice.rsense.classify.image_classification (imported as ic); PyTorch is needed for the encoders (pip install "geolattice[rsense-dl]").

title: Self-supervised pretraining for Sentinel-2 crop mapping
section: Why self-supervised learning for remote sensing
text:
Why self-supervised learning for remote sensing
Three properties of satellite imagery make SSL attractive:

Labels are scarce, pixels are not. Sentinel-2 alone images every field on Earth every five days, but crop-type labels need field visits or government surveys such as the CDL, which exists only for the United States and only after the season. Most of the archive is unlabeled.
ImageNet features fit poorly. Encoders pretrained on photographs expect three RGB channels, objects seen from the side, and centimetre-scale detail. Sentinel-2 has 10 to 13 bands, a nadir view with no “up”, and 10 to 60 m pixels. Pretraining on the target sensor learns filters for red-edge and SWIR reflectance that ImageNet never saw.
Time gives free augmentations. Contrastive learning needs two “views” of the same thing that should map to similar features. With photographs, the views are made by cropping and colour jitter. A satellite revisits the same place, so two acquisitions of the same location on different dates are natural views: the land is the same, while illumination, atmosphere and crop stage change. This is the idea of Seasonal Contrast (SeCo, Mañas et al. 2021) and of later temporal SSL methods.

Seasonal views need care. If the two dates come from different years, a field can switch from corn to soybeans between them, and the encoder is then trained to ignore exactly the difference that crop mapping needs. In this notebook both views of a pair are therefore drawn from the same growing season, so the crop is the same and only its stage differs.

Imports, paths, and experiment settings
This cell imports PyTorch for the encoders, scikit-learn for the 2-D embedding views, and the GeoLattice image-classification module. It finds the repository so the paths work from any folder inside it, checks that the cached cube and labels are on the local drive, and stops if no CUDA GPU is available. CHIP sets the chip size: 16 pixels at 20 m is 320 m, smaller than a typical Iowa field (about 800 m on a side), so most chips are dominated by one crop. MIN_CLEAR and MIN_PURITY decide which chips are clear enough to use and pure enough to label. BUFFER_M is the gap kept free between the pretraining/training area and the test area.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 6 (every GeoLattice module): pip install "geolattice[all]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
from pathlib import Path  # file paths
import copy  # copy a network
import os  # CPU count
import sys  # Python import path
import time  # timing

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import torch  # PyTorch: encoders and pretraining
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (registers the .rio accessor)
import xarray as xr  # labelled arrays (the Sentinel-2 cube)
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap  # class colours
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA  # colours for the embedding map
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE  # 2-D view of the embeddings
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Dataset  # feed chips to PyTorch in batches

# Prefer this checkout's code when launched from the repository.
ROOT = next((p for p in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents)
             if (p / "pyproject.toml").exists() and (p / "src" / "rsense").is_dir()), None)

    sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "src"))  # import GeoLattice from its src folder

import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing (raster writing)
import geolattice.rsense.classify.image_classification as ic  # chip classification and SSL tools

    raise FileNotFoundError("Start Jupyter from the GeoLattice checkout or one of its subdirectories")  # stop with a clear message
# this notebook's folder
NOTEBOOK_DIR = ROOT / "Tutorials" / "notebooks" / "08_remote_sensing" / "09_11_foundations_models"
# the corn belt study area, shared with chapter 08_09
DATA_DIR = NOTEBOOK_DIR / "../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_09_image_classification" / "Corn_belt"
CACHE_DIR = DATA_DIR / "cache_20m"  # cubes on the 20 m grid, built by notebook 09_09_03_02
S2_PATH = CACHE_DIR / "s2_20m.nc"  # Sentinel-2 reflectance cube (time, band, y, x)
LABEL_PATH = CACHE_DIR / "labels_20m.nc"  # CDL classes per year on the same grid
OUTPUT_DIR = DATA_DIR / "outputs" / "self_supervised"  # encoders and maps written here
OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

# Both cubes are read from the local drive. Notebook 09_09_03_02 builds them from the
# Sentinel_2 scene folders and the CDL rasters (which its download scripts fetch).
missing = [str(p) for p in (S2_PATH, LABEL_PATH) if not p.exists()]  # inputs not found
if missing:  # stop early with the list of missing files
    # stop and name the notebook that builds them
    raise FileNotFoundError("Run 09_09_image_classification/09_09_03_02_spatio_temporal_and_multi_sensor_crop_mapping_sentinel_2_sentinel_1_and_landsat_time_series_2020_to_2025.ipynb first "
                            "to build: " + ", ".join(missing))

if not torch.cuda.is_available():  # pretraining several encoders is impractical on a CPU
    raise RuntimeError("This notebook needs a CUDA GPU (torch.cuda.is_available() is False)")  # stop with a clear message
DEVICE = "cuda"  # every network runs on the GPU

CLASSES = ["Corn", "Soybeans", "Grass/pasture", "Developed", "Wetland/forest", "Other"]  # CDL classes
COLORS = ["#e6c229", "#2a9d3c", "#b9e08b", "#d7301f", "#1f5fbf", "#7f7f7f"]  # one colour per class
K = len(CLASSES)  # number of classes
CHIP = 16  # chip width in 20 m pixels (320 m)
MIN_CLEAR = 0.98  # share of cloud-free pixels a chip needs on a date
MIN_PURITY = 0.6  # share of the chip the majority CDL class must cover to label it
BUFFER_M = 1600  # metres kept free between the training area and the test area
TEST_FRACTION = 1 / 3  # eastern share of the AOI held out for testing
EPOCHS = 100  # pretraining epochs for every method
BATCH = 256  # chips per pretraining batch
SEED = 7  # random seed
ic.set_seed(SEED)  # same initial weights and shuffles on every run
torch.set_num_threads(min(8, os.cpu_count() or 1))  # CPU threads for data preparation
print("GeoLattice checkout:", ROOT)  # repository path
print("PyTorch:", torch.__version__, "| GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))  # versions and device
print("Output folder:", OUTPUT_DIR)  # output folder

PyTorch: 2.14.0+cu132 | GPU: NVIDIA RTX A5500 Laptop GPU
Output folder: /home/zia207/Github/GeoLattice/Tutorials/notebooks/09_remote_sensing/09_09_image_classification/data/Corn_belt/outputs/self_supervised




Read the Sentinel-2 cube and the CDL labels
The cube holds surface reflectance (digital numbers × 0.0001, with the processing-baseline offset already removed) for 34 dates on one 20 m grid; the 10 m bands were averaged onto it. Clouds, cloud shadows, cirrus and snow from the scene classification layer are already set to missing (NaN). The label file holds one CDL map per year, recoded to the six classes, with -1 where the CDL has no data. Both are read fully into memory (about 3 GB).


Code
s2 = xr.open_dataarray(S2_PATH).load()  # (time, band, y, x) surface reflectance, NaN = cloud
labels = xr.open_dataset(LABEL_PATH).load()  # CDL classes per year on the same grid
CRS = labels.spatial_ref.attrs["crs_wkt"]  # map projection (UTM zone 15N)
s2 = s2.rio.write_crs(CRS)  # attach it to the cube

BANDS = [str(b) for b in s2.band.values]  # band names
DATES = pd.DatetimeIndex(s2.time.values)  # acquisition dates
YEARS = [int(y) for y in labels.year.values]  # CDL years
T, C, H, W = s2.shape  # dates, bands, rows, columns
print(f"Sentinel-2 cube: {T} dates x {C} bands x {H} x {W} pixels at 20 m, {s2.nbytes / 1e9:.1f} GB")  # cube size
print("bands:", BANDS)  # band order used by every network
# number of dates in each year
print("dates per year:", pd.Series(DATES.year).value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())
cloud = np.isnan(s2.isel(band=0).values).mean(axis=(1, 2))  # masked share of every date
print(f"masked pixels per date: median {np.median(cloud):.1%}, max {cloud.max():.1%}")  # cloud masking summary


Sentinel-2 cube: 34 dates x 10 bands x 1456 x 1516 pixels at 20 m, 3.0 GB
bands: ['blue', 'green', 'red', 'rededge1', 'rededge2', 'rededge3', 'nir', 'nir08', 'swir16', 'swir22']
dates per year: {2020: 5, 2021: 6, 2022: 5, 2023: 6, 2024: 6, 2025: 6}
masked pixels per date: median 0.0%, max 4.4%




Cut the scene into chips and measure cloud cover
The grid is cut into non-overlapping 16 × 16 pixel chips. For every chip and date, the share of fully valid pixels (all ten bands present) decides whether that chip-date can be used. For every chip and year, the CDL pixels are counted per class: the majority class becomes the chip’s label for that year, and its share is the chip’s purity. A chip on a field boundary has a low purity and is left out of the labelled evaluation set, although it still serves for pretraining, where no label is needed. The chips are stored as 16-bit floats to halve the memory.


Code
NR, NC = H // CHIP, W // CHIP  # chip rows and columns that fit in the grid
cube = s2.values[:, :, :NR * CHIP, :NC * CHIP]  # crop the grid to whole chips
# (time, band, row, y, col, x) -> (chip, time, band, y, x); chip index = row * NC + col
chips = cube.reshape(T, C, NR, CHIP, NC, CHIP).transpose(2, 4, 0, 1, 3, 5).reshape(NR * NC, T, C, CHIP, CHIP)
clear = np.isfinite(chips).all(axis=2).mean(axis=(-2, -1))  # (chip, date) share of valid pixels
chips = chips.astype("float16")  # halve the memory; reflectance needs no more precision
del cube  # free the cropped float32 copy

xs = s2.x.values[:NC * CHIP].reshape(NC, CHIP).mean(axis=1)  # x of every chip centre
ys = s2.y.values[:NR * CHIP].reshape(NR, CHIP).mean(axis=1)  # y of every chip centre
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)  # centre coordinates on the chip grid
coords = np.c_[gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()]  # (chip, 2) map coordinates in metres

cdl = labels.cdl.values[:, :NR * CHIP, :NC * CHIP]  # CDL classes cropped the same way
# (year, row, y, col, x) -> (chip, year, pixels)
cdl = cdl.reshape(len(YEARS), NR, CHIP, NC, CHIP).transpose(1, 3, 0, 2, 4).reshape(NR * NC, len(YEARS), -1)
counts = np.stack([(cdl == k).sum(axis=-1) for k in range(K)], axis=-1)  # (chip, year, class) pixel counts
labelled = counts.sum(axis=-1)  # pixels with a CDL class
major = counts.argmax(axis=-1)  # majority class of every chip and year
purity = counts.max(axis=-1) / np.maximum(labelled, 1)  # share of the majority class
year_index = np.asarray(DATES.year) - YEARS[0]  # CDL year of every date

usable = clear >= MIN_CLEAR  # chip-dates clear enough to use
print(f"{NR} x {NC} = {NR * NC} chips of {CHIP} x {CHIP} pixels ({CHIP * 20} m), "  # number and size of the chips
      f"{chips.nbytes / 1e9:.1f} GB as float16")
print(f"clear chip-dates: {usable.sum()} of {usable.size} ({usable.mean():.0%})")  # how many chip-dates are clear
print(f"chips with purity >= {MIN_PURITY}: {(purity >= MIN_PURITY).mean():.0%} of chip-years")  # how many chips can be labelled


91 x 94 = 8554 chips of 16 x 16 pixels (320 m), 1.5 GB as float16
clear chip-dates: 289677 of 290836 (100%)
chips with purity >= 0.6: 81% of chip-years




Hold out an eastern test region with a buffer
A random split of chips would put test chips right next to training chips from the same fields, so the test score would mostly measure memory of nearby pixels. Instead geographic_holdout puts every chip whose centre falls inside a test rectangle (the eastern third of the AOI) into the test set. A further 1.6 km strip on the western side of that boundary is dropped from training, because fields, soils and farm management are spatially autocorrelated across the boundary. The same western area serves for both pretraining and probe training, so neither the encoder nor the probe ever sees the test area. The section on leakage below checks this and shows what happens without it.


Code
x_split = xs.min() + (1 - TEST_FRACTION) * np.ptp(xs)  # x of the test-area boundary
test_bounds = (x_split, ys.min(), xs.max(), ys.max())  # xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax of the test area
split = ic.geographic_holdout(coords, test_bounds)  # chips inside the box are test, the rest train
train_loc = split.train[coords[split.train, 0] < x_split - BUFFER_M]  # training chips outside the buffer
buffer_loc = np.setdiff1d(split.train, train_loc)  # chips in the buffer strip (never used)
test_loc = split.test  # chips of the test area
print(f"train area {len(train_loc)} chips | buffer {len(buffer_loc)} chips | test area {len(test_loc)} chips")  # chips per region

t_show = int(np.argmax(usable.mean(axis=0) * np.asarray(DATES.month == 7)))  # clearest July date

ext = [s2.x.min().item(), s2.x.max().item(), s2.y.min().item(), s2.y.max().item()]  # map extent
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6.5))  # two panels
ax[0].imshow(np.clip(np.nan_to_num(rgb) / 0.15, 0, 1), extent=ext)  # true colour, 0-15 % reflectance
ax[0].set_title(f"Sentinel-2 true colour, {DATES[t_show]:%d %b %Y}")  # title
cmap_region = ListedColormap(["#3b75af", "#bbbbbb", "#d1495b"])  # train, buffer, test
# region map: west train, buffer, east test
ax[1].imshow(region.reshape(NR, NC), cmap=cmap_region, vmin=-0.5, vmax=2.5,
             extent=ext, interpolation="nearest")  # the three regions on the chip grid
ax[1].set_title("Train area (blue), buffer (grey) and test area (red)")  # title
for a in ax:  # both panels
    a.set_xlabel("UTM easting (m)"); a.set_ylabel("UTM northing (m)")  # axis labels

Seasonal views: the same field on different dates
Before training, every band is standardised with the mean and standard deviation of clear training-area chips, and the few remaining missing pixels are set to zero (the band mean). The figure shows what a seasonal pair looks like. Each row is one chip through one growing season: the bare soil of May, the closed canopy of July and August, and the senescence of September and October. The mid-June scene is hazy: it passed the cloud mask, but thin haze brightens and blues every band. For a contrastive model, any two of these dates are a positive pair: two pictures of the same land, and haze, illumination and crop stage are exactly the differences the encoder is asked to ignore. Corn and soybeans differ mainly in the timing and depth of this cycle, which is why both views of a pair are taken from the same year.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)  # random generator for sampling
pairs = np.argwhere(usable[train_loc])  # (chip, date) positions of clear training chips
pick = pairs[rng.choice(len(pairs), 4000, replace=False)]  # a random sample of them
sample = chips[train_loc[pick[:, 0]], pick[:, 1]].astype("float32")  # (4000, band, y, x)
MEAN = np.nanmean(sample, axis=(0, 2, 3)).reshape(-1, 1, 1)  # per-band mean
STD = np.nanstd(sample, axis=(0, 2, 3)).reshape(-1, 1, 1)  # per-band standard deviation


def normalize(x):  # standardise chips band by band; missing pixels become 0 (the mean)
    return np.nan_to_num((np.asarray(x, "float32") - MEAN) / STD)  # (x - mean) / std, NaN -> 0


def chip_rgb(x):  # true-colour image of one chip (reflectance, not standardised)
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(np.asarray(x, "float32")[[2, 1, 0]].transpose(1, 2, 0)) / 0.15, 0, 1)  # red, green, blue scaled 0-15 % reflectance


SHOW_YEAR = 2023  # season shown in the figure
season = np.flatnonzero(DATES.year == SHOW_YEAR)  # its dates
yi = SHOW_YEAR - YEARS[0]  # its CDL index
examples = []  # one corn chip and one soybean chip, clear on as many dates as possible
for k in (0, 1):  # corn, soybeans
    pure = (major[train_loc, yi] == k) & (purity[train_loc, yi] > 0.95)  # pure chips of that class
    n_clear = usable[train_loc][:, season].sum(axis=1)  # clear dates of each chip in the season
    examples.append(train_loc[np.argmax(np.where(pure, n_clear, -1))])  # the pure chip clear most often
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, len(season), figsize=(2.2 * len(season), 4.8))  # one panel per date
for r, loc in enumerate(examples):  # each example chip
    for c, t in enumerate(season):  # each date of the season
        ax[r, c].imshow(chip_rgb(chips[loc, t]), interpolation="nearest")  # the chip on that date
        ax[r, c].set_title(f"{DATES[t]:%d %b}", fontsize=9)  # date
        ax[r, c].set_xticks([]); ax[r, c].set_yticks([])  # no ticks
    ax[r, 0].set_ylabel(CLASSES[major[loc, yi]])  # CDL class of the chip
fig.suptitle(f"Seasonal views of two 320 m chips, {SHOW_YEAR}: one location, six dates", y=1.0)  # overall title
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

title: Self-supervised pretraining for Sentinel-2 crop mapping
text:
Contrastive learning

The NT-Xent loss
SimCLR (Chen et al. 2020) passes two views of every image through the encoder and a small projection head, giving feature vectors \(z_i\) and \(z_j\). The normalized-temperature cross-entropy (NT-Xent) loss treats the matching view as the correct class among all \(2N - 2\) other views in the batch:
\[\ell_{i,j} = -\log \frac{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(z_i, z_j)/\tau)}{\sum_{k \ne i} \exp(\mathrm{sim}(z_i, z_k)/\tau)}\]
where \(\mathrm{sim}\) is cosine similarity and \(\tau\) the temperature. The loss falls when the two views of one chip are closer to each other than to every other chip in the batch. nt_xent_loss implements it; the cell below shows that matched views give a much lower loss than shuffled ones, and that a lower temperature sharpens the difference.


Code
torch.manual_seed(SEED)  # reproducible random vectors
z1 = torch.randn(256, 64)  # features of 256 "chips", view 1
z2_match = z1 + 0.3 * torch.randn(256, 64)  # view 2: the same chips plus noise
z2_shuffled = z2_match[torch.randperm(256)]  # view 2 paired with the wrong chips
rows = []  # one row per temperature
for tau in (0.1, 0.2, 0.5):  # three temperatures
    rows.append({"temperature": tau,  # loss of matched and shuffled pairs
                 "matched views": float(ic.nt_xent_loss(z1, z2_match, tau)),
                 "shuffled views": float(ic.nt_xent_loss(z1, z2_shuffled, tau)),
                 "chance level, log(2N - 1)": float(np.log(2 * 256 - 1))})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("temperature").round(3)  # show the table

Pretraining datasets: augmented views and seasonal views
Two PyTorch datasets feed the pretraining. Both draw one item per training-area chip location, so every method sees the same number of chips per epoch:

SingleDateChips returns one clear date of a location, chosen at random each time. pretrain_contrastive then makes the two views itself with GeoLattice OverheadAugment: a random 90° rotation or flip (valid because overhead images have no “up”), a random 80 % crop resized back, and mild brightness, contrast and noise jitter. The masked autoencoder uses the same dataset.
SeasonalPairs returns two different clear dates of the same location from one randomly chosen year, each with its own rotation, flip and crop. A batch that is a (view1, view2) pair is used by pretrain_contrastive as is: this is the SeCo-style recipe.

Only locations with at least two clear dates in some year are kept, and new dates are drawn every epoch, so the pairs keep changing.


Code
class SingleDateChips(Dataset):  # PyTorch dataset of single-date chips
    """One random clear date of each location, standardised, as a (band, y, x) tensor."""

    def __init__(self, locs, seed=SEED):  # store the locations and their usable dates
        self.locs = np.asarray(locs)  # chip locations
        self.dates = [np.flatnonzero(usable[l]) for l in self.locs]  # their clear dates
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)  # date sampler

    def __len__(self):  # number of items per epoch
        return len(self.locs)  # one item per location

    def __getitem__(self, i):  # one item
        t = self.rng.choice(self.dates[i])  # a random clear date
        return torch.from_numpy(normalize(chips[self.locs[i], t]))  # the standardised chip


class SeasonalPairs(Dataset):  # PyTorch dataset of seasonal positive pairs
    """Two clear dates of the same location and season (SeCo-style views), each randomly flipped and cropped."""

    def __init__(self, locs, seed=SEED):  # store the locations and their usable dates
        self.locs, self.seasons = [], []  # usable locations and their clear dates per year
        for l in locs:  # every candidate location
            by_year = [np.flatnonzero(usable[l] & (year_index == y)) for y in range(len(YEARS))]  # clear dates of each year
            by_year = [d for d in by_year if len(d) >= 2]  # seasons with at least two clear dates
            if by_year:  # keep the location if one season qualifies
                self.locs.append(l); self.seasons.append(by_year)  # keep the location and its seasons
        self.aug = ic.OverheadAugment(dihedral=True, crop=0.8, seed=seed)  # geometric augmentation
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)  # season and date sampler

    def __len__(self):  # number of items per epoch
        return len(self.locs)  # one item per location

    def __getitem__(self, i):  # one item
        season = self.seasons[i][self.rng.integers(len(self.seasons[i]))]  # a random season
        t1, t2 = self.rng.choice(season, 2, replace=False)  # two different dates in it
        v1 = self.aug(torch.from_numpy(normalize(chips[self.locs[i], t1])))[0]  # view 1
        v2 = self.aug(torch.from_numpy(normalize(chips[self.locs[i], t2])))[0]  # view 2
        return v1, v2  # a positive pair


def make_loader(dataset):  # shuffled batches; drop_last keeps every batch full for the loss
    return DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=BATCH, shuffle=True, drop_last=True,  # batches of BATCH chips
                      generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED))


pretrain_loc = train_loc[[len(np.flatnonzero(usable[l])) >= 2 for l in train_loc]]  # chips with 2+ clear dates
single_ds = SingleDateChips(pretrain_loc)  # single-date chips
pair_ds = SeasonalPairs(pretrain_loc)  # seasonal pairs
print(f"pretraining locations: {len(single_ds)} (single date), {len(pair_ds)} (seasonal pairs); "  # dataset sizes
      f"{len(pair_ds) // BATCH} batches of {BATCH} per epoch")
v1, v2 = pair_ds[0]  # one example pair
print("one seasonal pair:", tuple(v1.shape), tuple(v2.shape))  # (band, y, x) each


pretraining locations: 5187 (single date), 5187 (seasonal pairs); 20 batches of 256 per epoch
one seasonal pair: (10, 16, 16) (10, 16, 16)




Make the encoder and pretrain with SimCLR and MoCo
make_encoder("resnet18", in_channels=10) returns a torchvision ResNet-18 whose first convolution takes the ten Sentinel-2 bands and whose classification head is removed, so the network maps a chip to a 512-number feature vector. No ImageNet weights are loaded: everything is learned from the corn belt chips. ResNet-18 was designed for 224-pixel photographs and shrinks its input 32 times; on a 16-pixel chip the stem convolution and the max-pooling layer would reduce the chip to 4 × 4 pixels before the first residual block. Replacing the max-pooling layer with an identity keeps twice the spatial detail, the usual adjustment for small chips (as for CIFAR images). An untrained copy is kept as the random-weights baseline; a randomly initialised network already gives features that a linear probe can use, so pretraining has to beat it to be worth anything.
pretrain_contrastive adds a two-layer projection head (512 → 512 → 64) and trains both with AdamW. Three runs are made with the same encoder, epochs and learning rate:

SimCLR, augmented views: two augmentations of one date (the classic recipe).
SimCLR, seasonal views: two dates of one season (SeCo-style).
MoCo, seasonal views: the same pairs with MoCo v2: the second view goes through a slowly updated momentum copy of the encoder, and the negatives come from a queue of 4,096 earlier features instead of the current batch, which helps when batches are small.

The projection head is discarded afterwards; the encoder output is what is evaluated.


Code
def new_encoder():  # a fresh ResNet-18 for 10 bands with the same initial weights every time
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)  # identical initialisation for every method
    enc = ic.make_encoder("resnet18", in_channels=C)  # head removed: chip -> 512 features
    enc.maxpool = torch.nn.Identity()  # no max pooling: keep detail on 16-pixel chips
    return enc  # the encoder


encoders, history, minutes = {}, {}, {}  # trained encoders, loss curves and run times
encoders["Random weights"] = new_encoder().to(DEVICE)  # baseline: never trained
runs = {  # name -> (method, dataset)
    "SimCLR, augmented views": ("simclr", single_ds),
    "SimCLR, seasonal views": ("simclr", pair_ds),
    "MoCo, seasonal views": ("moco", pair_ds),
}
for name, (method, dataset) in runs.items():  # each contrastive recipe
    t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
    encoders[name], hist = ic.pretrain_contrastive(  # contrastive pretraining
        new_encoder(), make_loader(dataset), in_channels=C, method=method, epochs=EPOCHS,
        lr=1e-3, temperature=0.2, proj_dim=64, queue_size=4096, momentum=0.99,
        device=DEVICE, seed=SEED, verbose=False)  # pretrain without labels
    history[name], minutes[name] = hist["loss"], (time.time() - t0) / 60  # keep the loss curve and time
    print(f"{name:26s} {EPOCHS} epochs in {minutes[name]:.1f} min, "  # run time and loss
          f"loss {hist['loss'][0]:.3f} -> {hist['loss'][-1]:.3f}")


SimCLR, augmented views    100 epochs in 2.2 min, loss 3.691 -> 1.969
SimCLR, seasonal views     100 epochs in 1.7 min, loss 6.211 -> 3.679
MoCo, seasonal views       100 epochs in 1.5 min, loss 7.259 -> 6.713




Pretraining loss curves
The loss of each run falls as the encoder learns to tell chips apart. The absolute values of different recipes cannot be compared: seasonal views are harder to match than two crops of the same image, and MoCo scores each chip against 4,096 queued negatives instead of the 510 in a SimCLR batch. A falling, flattening curve only says the pretext task is being learned; the linear probe below says whether the features are useful.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))  # one panel
for name, loss in history.items():  # each run
    ax.plot(range(1, len(loss) + 1), loss, label=name)  # its loss per epoch
ax.set(xlabel="epoch", ylabel="contrastive loss", title="Contrastive pretraining loss")  # labels
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # legend, arrange and draw

title: Self-supervised pretraining for Sentinel-2 crop mapping
text:
Masked image modelling

Build and pretrain a masked autoencoder
Masked image modelling takes a different route: hide part of the image and train the network to fill it in. MAE (He et al. 2022) does this with a Vision Transformer; SatMAE and Scale-MAE adapt it to satellite imagery with temporal, spectral and scale-aware position encodings. build_mae gives a small convolutional masked autoencoder that runs on 16-pixel chips: a three-layer encoder (two stride-2 convolutions, 256 output channels) and a two-layer transposed-convolution decoder.
During training, random_mask hides 60 % of the 4 × 4 pixel patches of each chip (patch=4, mask_ratio=0.6), the encoder sees only the visible part, and the loss is the mean squared error on the masked pixels only, so copying the input does not help. To fill a hidden patch, the network has to learn how bands relate to each other and how fields continue in space. pretrain_masked runs the training loop. For linear probing, the encoder’s output is averaged over the chip (the model’s features method), giving 256 numbers per chip.


Code
torch.manual_seed(SEED)  # same initial weights on every run
mae = ic.build_mae(C, width=64, patch=4, mask_ratio=0.6)  # convolutional masked autoencoder (64-128-256 channels)
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
mae, mae_hist = ic.pretrain_masked(mae, make_loader(single_ds), epochs=EPOCHS, lr=1e-3,  # masked-image pretraining
                                   device=DEVICE, seed=SEED, verbose=False)  # reconstruct masked patches
encoders["Masked autoencoder"] = mae  # its encoder is evaluated with the others
minutes["Masked autoencoder"] = (time.time() - t0) / 60  # run time
print(f"masked autoencoder: {EPOCHS} epochs in {minutes['Masked autoencoder']:.1f} min, "  # run time and loss
      f"loss {mae_hist['loss'][0]:.3f} -> {mae_hist['loss'][-1]:.3f} (standardised units squared)")


masked autoencoder: 100 epochs in 0.4 min, loss 0.622 -> 0.175 (standardised units squared)




Look at the reconstructions
Each row shows one test-area chip (never seen in pretraining): the original, the input with the masked patches blacked out, the raw reconstruction, and the reconstruction with the visible patches pasted back. The reconstructions are poor as pictures. The loss is computed only on hidden patches, so the visible parts of the raw reconstruction are never trained to match, and many hidden patches are filled with plausible but invented content, such as a bare-soil field or a road where the original has a uniform canopy. With 60 % of a 16-pixel chip hidden, the remaining pixels often do not say what was there. That is expected: the reconstruction is only the pretext task, and the evaluation below shows that the encoder trained this way still yields the most balanced features of all methods. Good features do not require good reconstructions.


Code
t_peak = int(np.argmax(usable[test_loc].mean(axis=0) * np.asarray(DATES.month == 8)))  # clearest August date
show = test_loc[np.flatnonzero(usable[test_loc, t_peak])[::97][:4]]  # four clear test chips
x = torch.from_numpy(normalize(chips[show, t_peak])).to(DEVICE)  # standardised chips on the GPU
mae.eval()  # evaluation mode
torch.manual_seed(SEED)  # reproducible mask
with torch.no_grad():  # no gradients needed
    _, rec, m = mae(x)  # reconstruction and mask (1 = hidden)
to_refl = lambda a: a.cpu().numpy() * STD + MEAN  # standardised values back to reflectance
panels = {"original": to_refl(x), "masked input": to_refl(x * (1 - m)),  # the four panels per chip
          "reconstruction": to_refl(rec), "visible + reconstructed": to_refl(x * (1 - m) + rec * m)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(len(show), 4, figsize=(9, 2.3 * len(show)))  # one row per chip
for r in range(len(show)):  # each chip
    for c, (title, arr) in enumerate(panels.items()):  # each panel
        img = chip_rgb(arr[r])  # true colour
        if title == "masked input":  # show hidden patches in black
            img = img * (1 - m[r, 0].cpu().numpy()[..., None])  # black out the hidden patches
        ax[r, c].imshow(img, interpolation="nearest")  # draw it
        ax[r, c].set_xticks([]); ax[r, c].set_yticks([])  # no ticks
        if r == 0:  # titles on the first row
            ax[r, c].set_title(title, fontsize=10)  # panel title
fig.suptitle(f"Masked autoencoder on test-area chips, {DATES[t_peak]:%d %b %Y}", y=1.0)  # overall title
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

title: Self-supervised pretraining for Sentinel-2 crop mapping
text:
Evaluation with frozen embeddings

Labelled chips from the CDL
The evaluation uses one peak-season image per year: the July or August date with the most clear chips. A chip is labelled with its majority CDL class of that year when it is clear on that date, at least 60 % pure, and at least 90 % covered by CDL data. Chips in the western training area are the probe’s training set; chips in the eastern test area are the test set; buffer chips are dropped. Corn and soybeans make up most chips, as they cover about 90 % of the AOI, so per-class F1 and macro F1 are reported next to overall accuracy.


Code
peak_dates = []  # the July/August date with the most clear chips, per year
for y in YEARS:  # every year
    cand = np.flatnonzero((DATES.year == y) & np.isin(DATES.month, [7, 8]))  # its July/August dates
    peak_dates.append(int(cand[np.argmax(usable[:, cand].mean(axis=0))]))  # the clearest one
loc_e, t_e = [], []  # chip and date of every labelled sample
for t in peak_dates:  # each peak date
    yi = year_index[t]  # its CDL year
    ok = usable[:, t] & (purity[:, yi] >= MIN_PURITY) & (labelled[:, yi] >= 0.9 * CHIP * CHIP) & (region != 1)  # clear, pure, labelled, not buffer
    loc_e.append(np.flatnonzero(ok)); t_e.append(np.full(ok.sum(), t))  # keep the qualifying chips
loc_e, t_e = np.concatenate(loc_e), np.concatenate(t_e)  # all samples
y_e = major[loc_e, year_index[t_e]]  # their CDL class
tr, te = region[loc_e] == 0, region[loc_e] == 2  # probe training (west) and test (east) samples
X_eval = normalize(chips[loc_e, t_e])  # standardised chips (sample, band, y, x)

print("peak dates:", ", ".join(f"{DATES[t]:%Y-%m-%d}" for t in peak_dates))  # dates used
pd.DataFrame({"train area (west)": pd.Series(y_e[tr]).value_counts(),  # samples per class and area
              "test area (east)": pd.Series(y_e[te]).value_counts()}).reindex(range(K)).fillna(0).astype(int) \
    .set_index(pd.Index(CLASSES, name="class"))

Extract embeddings
extract_embeddings runs a frozen encoder over the chips in batches and returns one feature vector per chip: the ResNet-18 encoders give 512 numbers, and for the masked autoencoder it uses the model’s features method (256 numbers). A non-learned baseline is added: the band means of each chip, ten numbers that hold the chip’s average spectrum. Any useful encoder has to add something to the plain spectrum, such as texture, field structure, or a better use of the red-edge and SWIR bands.


Code
emb = {"Band means": X_eval.mean(axis=(-2, -1))}  # baseline: the average spectrum of each chip
for name, enc in encoders.items():  # every encoder, frozen
    t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
    emb[name] = ic.extract_embeddings(enc, X_eval, batch_size=512, device=DEVICE)  # (sample, features)
    print(f"{name:26s} {emb[name].shape[1]:4d} features for {len(X_eval)} chips in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")  # size and time

SimCLR, augmented views     512 features for 39131 chips in 0.9 s

Linear probe on held-out geography
linear_probe fits a standardised logistic regression on the frozen embeddings of the training area and predicts the test area. A linear classifier cannot build new features, so its score shows how linearly separable the classes already are in each embedding: the standard way to compare SSL encoders. classification_report adds overall accuracy, Cohen’s kappa and macro F1. The scores answer one question for this AOI and these years: how well the features of each encoder separate the six classes in an area that neither the encoder nor the probe has seen.


Code
names = dict(enumerate(CLASSES))  # class id -> name
reports, rows = {}, {}  # full reports and summary rows
for name, E in emb.items():  # each feature set
    t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
    probe = ic.linear_probe(E[tr], y_e[tr], E[te], y_e[te], C=1.0, max_iter=3000)  # fit on west, predict east
    rep = ic.classification_report(y_e[te], probe["predictions"], labels=list(range(K)), class_names=names)  # accuracy, kappa, F1
    reports[name] = rep  # keep the full report
    rows[name] = {"features": E.shape[1], "overall accuracy": rep["overall_accuracy"],  # summary row
                  "kappa": rep["kappa"], "macro F1": rep["macro_f1"],
                  "corn F1": rep["per_class"].loc["Corn", "f1"],
                  "soybeans F1": rep["per_class"].loc["Soybeans", "f1"],
                  "pretraining (min)": minutes.get(name, 0.0)}
probe_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)  # one row per feature set
