title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Statistical and Structural Methods
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

First-order statistics are fast but blind to spatial arrangement; two windows with the same histogram get the same values (see Why texture? Same histogram, different arrangement).
GLCM measures how gray levels co-occur at a given offset. Contrast/dissimilarity, the homogeneity/energy/entropy group and correlation cover most of its information.
GLCM values depend strongly on levels and the quantization range, so compare only images processed with identical settings.
Directional GLCM and GLRLM reveal oriented structures: street grids, ridges, crop rows.
Edge density and lacunarity describe the density and gap structure of primitives; lacunarity is most informative on sparse or binary layers.
Texture from different bands of the same scene is highly redundant; one band (here NIR) is usually enough.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.read, rs.optical.scale, rs.viz.plot_rgb, rs.viz.plot_raster, tx.first_order_stats, tx.glcm_texture, tx.glrlm_texture, tx.edge_density, tx.lacunarity.
Exercises

Compute GLCM texture on NDVI instead of NIR. Which surfaces change their texture signature?
Compute contrast for each of the four angles separately and map the direction of maximum contrast. Does it follow the street grid and the strike of the ridges?
Run tx.glcm_texture with distance=2 and distance=4. How does contrast change over the city?
Threshold NDVI > 0.3 to make a vegetation mask and compute its lacunarity. At which box size does the Las Vegas Wash differ most from the city parks?
Repeat the clustering test with only three features: one first-order, one GLCM and one structural.

References

Canny, J. (1986). A computational approach to edge detection. IEEE TPAMI, 8(6), 679-698.
Galloway, M.M. (1975). Texture analysis using gray level run lengths. Computer Graphics and Image Processing, 4(2), 172-179.
Haralick, R.M., Shanmugam, K. and Dinstein, I. (1973). Textural features for image classification. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC-3(6), 610-621.
Plotnick, R.E., Gardner, R.H., Hargrove, W.W., Prestegaard, K. and Perlmutter, M. (1996). Lacunarity analysis: a general technique for the analysis of spatial patterns. Physical Review E, 53(5), 5461-5468.

title: Large-Area LiDAR Processing: Tiling, Streaming, Parallel Work and the GPU
text:
Overview

Why large-area LiDAR needs a different approach








Problem
Consequence
Remedy




Memory
15 million points with 11 attributes take 0.6 to 1.3 GB in memory depending on the data types; a few tiles exhaust a laptop
Read only the fields needed, process tile by tile, stream files in chunks


Run time
Ground filtering and gridding of hundreds of tiles take hours on one core
Run tiles in parallel (threads or processes), move gridding and raster operations to a GPU


Edges
Filters, interpolation and neighbourhood features see only one side of a tile edge, leaving seams
Process each tile with a buffer of neighbouring points, then trim results back to the tile core


Data transfer
Downloading whole archives to use a small area
Cloud-optimised formats (COPC, EPT) let readers request only a region or a level of detail


Bookkeeping
Many files of different ages, CRSs and densities
A tile index (footprints, point counts, CRS, density) built from the headers before any processing





Tiling with buffers
A tile scheme divides the area into a regular grid of square cores (often the delivery tiles themselves). For each core the processor reads the core plus a buffer of width \(b\) on every side, runs the algorithm, and keeps only the results inside the core. The buffer must be at least as wide as the largest neighbourhood the algorithm uses: the ground filter window, the interpolation search distance, the tree-detection window. Results from neighbouring tiles then meet without seams.


Parallel processing
Tiles are independent once they carry their own buffers, so they can run at the same time. Threads share memory and work well when the heavy work happens inside NumPy and SciPy, which release Python’s global interpreter lock; processes avoid the lock entirely but must copy their inputs. The speed-up is limited by disk reading and by memory: ten tiles in parallel need ten tiles’ worth of memory.


The GPU
Many LiDAR operations are data-parallel: binning points into cells (scatter reductions for min, max, mean and count) and local raster operations such as slope, curvature or TPI apply the same arithmetic to millions of independent elements. On a GPU (with CuPy) they run tens of times faster than on one CPU core. Sequential algorithms such as priority-flood filling and flow routing stay on the CPU.


Cloud-native archives
COPC stores a whole LAZ file as an octree in one file; EPT stores an octree of many files with a JSON description. Both let a reader ask for “points in this box at about this spacing” and download only those parts (see the fundamentals notebook). PDAL pipelines can read EPT directly from the USGS 3DEP archive on AWS, filter on the server side of the stream and write tiles locally.

A tile index from the headers
rs.lidar.las_info reads only the header of each file, so indexing 4.9 GB of tiles takes a fraction of a second. The tile index holds each tile’s footprint, point count, density, elevation range and the share of points by return, and is the starting point for planning any processing.

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
rows = []  # one row per tile
for p in TILES:  # each file
    i = rs.lidar.las_info(p)  # header only
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = i["mins"][0], i["mins"][1], i["maxs"][0], i["maxs"][1]  # footprint
    area = (xmax - xmin) * (ymax - ymin)  # m²

                 "first returns": i["points_by_return"][0] / i["point_count"],  # share of first returns (one per pulse)
                 "version": i["version"], "format": i["point_format"], "geometry": box(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)})

Memory and reading only what is needed
A PointCloud keeps every attribute as a NumPy array. Reading only the fields an operation needs (fields=) saves memory and time: a DEM needs only x, y, z and the classification.

title: Large-Area LiDAR Processing: Tiling, Streaming, Parallel Work and the GPU
text:
Streaming a file in chunks
rs.lidar.read_las_chunks yields a file in pieces of chunk_size points, so statistics can be accumulated without ever holding the whole file in memory. The cell computes the class histogram, the elevation histogram and the return structure of one tile in 2-million-point chunks.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
classes, n_chunks, n_pts = pd.Series(dtype=float), 0, 0  # running class counts
zbins = np.arange(100, 460, 5)  # elevation bins (m)
zhist = np.zeros(len(zbins) - 1)  # running elevation histogram
multi = 0  # running count of returns from multi-return pulses
for chunk in rs.lidar.read_las_chunks(TILES[0], chunk_size=2_000_000,  # one chunk at a time
                                      fields=["classification", "number_of_returns"]):  # one chunk at a time
    classes = classes.add(pd.Series(np.asarray(chunk["classification"])).value_counts(), fill_value=0)  # classes
    zhist += np.histogram(np.asarray(chunk.z), bins=zbins)[0]  # elevations
    multi += int((np.asarray(chunk["number_of_returns"]) > 1).sum())  # multi-return points
    n_chunks += 1; n_pts += len(chunk)  # counters
print(f"{n_pts:,} points in {n_chunks} chunks, {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s | "  # summary line
      f"returns from multi-return pulses: {multi / n_pts:.1%}")  # summary
print("classes:", classes.astype(int).to_dict())  # class counts
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3)); ax.bar(zbins[:-1], zhist, width=5, align="edge")  # elevation histogram
# axis labels and title
ax.set(xlabel="Elevation (m)", ylabel="points", title=f"Elevation histogram of {TILES[0].name}, built chunk by chunk"); plt.show()

title: Large-Area LiDAR Processing: Tiling, Streaming, Parallel Work and the GPU
text:
Processing all tiles in parallel
rs.lidar.process_files reads each file with read_las and applies a function to it, in n_jobs parallel threads. The function below is a small pipeline that turns one tile into the standard products on the tile’s exact 1.5 km grid, so the outputs mosaic without resampling:

DEM at 2 m from the producer’s ground points;
DSM at 2 m from first returns, and the CHM;
heights above ground and area-based forest metrics (p95 height and canopy cover) at 20 m;
a first-return density grid at 10 m.



Code
FIELDS = ["classification", "return_number", "number_of_returns"]  # the attributes the pipeline needs

def tile_products(pc):  # one tile -> dictionary of rasters
    x0 = np.floor(pc.bbox[0] / 1500) * 1500; y0 = np.floor(pc.bbox[1] / 1500) * 1500  # tile origin (1.5 km grid)
    bounds = (x0, y0, x0 + 1500, y0 + 1500)  # exact tile extent
    pc = pc.drop_noise()  # remove noise classes 7 and 18
    dem = rs.lidar.dem(pc.ground(), 2.0, bounds=bounds)  # bare earth
    dsm = rs.lidar.dsm(pc, 2.0, bounds=bounds)  # first-return surface
    chm = rs.lidar.chm(dsm, dem)  # canopy height
    gm = rs.lidar.grid_metrics(rs.lidar.normalize_heights(pc, dem), res=20.0, metrics=("p95", "cover"))  # forest metrics
    dens = rs.lidar.density_map(pc, 10.0, first_returns=True)  # pulses per m²
    # the products of this tile
    return {"dem": dem, "dsm": dsm, "chm": chm, "p95": gm["p95"], "cover": gm["cover"], "density": dens,
            "points": len(pc)}

N_JOBS = min(5, os.cpu_count())  # tiles processed at the same time (limited by memory)
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
results = rs.lidar.process_files(TILES, tile_products, n_jobs=N_JOBS, read_kwargs={"fields": FIELDS})  # all tiles
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0  # wall-clock time
n = sum(r["points"] for r in results)  # points processed
# summary line
print(f"{len(results)} tiles, {n / 1e6:.0f} million points in {elapsed:.0f} s with {N_JOBS} threads "
      f"({n / elapsed / 1e6:.2f} million points per second)")  # throughput


10 tiles, 136 million points in 57 s with 5 threads (2.39 million points per second)

title: Large-Area LiDAR Processing: Tiling, Streaming, Parallel Work and the GPU
text:
Seamless mosaics
rs.lidar.merge_rasters mosaics the per-tile grids. Because each tile was gridded on its own exact extent, the grids align and the mosaic needs no resampling.


Code
mosaic = {k: rs.lidar.merge_rasters([r[k] for r in results]) for k in ("dem", "dsm", "chm", "p95", "cover", "density")}  # mosaics
for k, v in mosaic.items():  # sizes
    print(f"{k:8s} {str(v.shape):14s} cell {abs(float(v.x[1] - v.x[0])):.0f} m | "  # summary line
          f"{float(np.isfinite(v.values).mean()):.1%} filled")  # shape and coverage

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(16, 12))  # four panels
# map: DEM hillshade, 10 tiles
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(mosaic["dem"]), ax=axes[0, 0], cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title="DEM hillshade, 10 tiles")
# map: Canopy height model (m)
rs.viz.plot_raster(mosaic["chm"], ax=axes[0, 1], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=35, title="Canopy height model (m)")
# map: Canopy cover (> 2 m), 20 m cells
rs.viz.plot_raster(mosaic["cover"], ax=axes[1, 0], cmap="YlGn", vmin=0, vmax=1, title="Canopy cover (> 2 m), 20 m cells")
# map: Pulses per m², 10 m cells
rs.viz.plot_raster(mosaic["density"], ax=axes[1, 1], cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=10, title="Pulses per m², 10 m cells")
for a in axes.ravel():  # each panel
    index.boundary.plot(ax=a, color="white", lw=0.6); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # tile outlines
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

The four products cover about 22 km² south of downtown Ithaca: the Six Mile Creek valley, South Hill and the farmland and forest around them. Density stripes follow the flight lines, and empty cells mark water surfaces, which return few laser echoes, and the corners not covered by the ten tiles. The white lines are the tile outlines. Within each tile the DEM was interpolated only from that tile’s own ground points; with dense ground points and a 2 m grid this leaves no visible seams, but algorithms with larger neighbourhoods, such as ground filters, do react to tile edges, as the next section shows.

title: Large-Area LiDAR Processing: Tiling, Streaming, Parallel Work and the GPU
text:
Edge effects and buffered tiles
Many operations depend on neighbours: ground filters compare a point with its surroundings, interpolation fills gaps from nearby points, and tree detection looks for local maxima. At a tile edge these neighbours are missing. rs.lidar.process_tiles cuts a cloud into tiles of size m, gives each a buffer of extra points, runs a function on every buffered tile and trims the results back to the tile cores before merging them.
The experiment: a 1 km square that straddles the boundary between two delivery tiles is processed with SMRF ground filtering and a 1 m DEM on a grid of 250 m tiles, once without a buffer and once with a 40 m buffer, and both are compared with the same DEM computed on the whole square at once.


Code
x_edge = 378000.0  # boundary between two delivery tiles
area = (x_edge - 500, 4697000.0, x_edge + 500, 4698000.0)  # a 1 km square across it
parts = [rs.lidar.read_las(DATA / "Ithaca" / f"u_{t}.las", fields=["classification"]).crop(*area)  # the two halves
         for t in ("3765069650", "3780069650")]
sq = rs.lidar.merge_pointclouds(parts).drop_noise()  # one cloud for the square
print(f"{len(sq):,} points in the 1 km square")  # size

def ground_dem(cloud):  # SMRF ground, then a 1 m DEM
    # SMRF ground, then a 1 m DEM
    return rs.lidar.dem(rs.lidar.smrf(cloud, cell=1.0, slope=0.15, window=18), 1.0)

t0 = time.perf_counter(); whole = ground_dem(sq); t_whole = time.perf_counter() - t0  # reference: all at once
runs = {}  # tiled results
for buf in (0, 40):  # without and with a buffer
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    runs[buf] = rs.lidar.process_tiles(sq, ground_dem, size=250, buffer=buf, n_jobs=4)  # 16 tiles of 250 m
    runs[buf] = (runs[buf], time.perf_counter() - t0)  # keep the time
rows = {}  # one row per run
for buf, (dem_t, sec) in runs.items():  # each run
    d = dem_t.reindex_like(whole, method="nearest") - whole  # difference from the reference
    rows[f"250 m tiles, buffer {buf} m"] = {"max |difference| (m)": float(np.abs(d).max()),  # worst cell
                                            "cells off by > 10 cm": float((np.abs(d) > 0.1).mean()), "seconds": sec}
# reference row
rows["whole square at once"] = {"max |difference| (m)": 0.0, "cells off by > 10 cm": 0.0, "seconds": t_whole}
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(4))  # comparison

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))  # two panels
for ax, buf in zip(axes, (0, 40)):  # each run
    d = runs[buf][0].reindex_like(whole, method="nearest") - whole  # difference map
    rs.viz.plot_raster(d, ax=ax, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1, title=f"Tiled minus whole DEM (m), buffer {buf} m")  # map
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

Without a buffer, the tiled DEM differs from the whole-square result at spots along the 250 m tile boundaries, where the ground filter and the interpolation see only half of their usual neighbourhood. In the south-east, one building cut by a tile boundary is classified differently as a whole and the DEM there is off by up to 12 m. With a 40 m buffer, wider than the 18 m SMRF window plus the interpolation distance, the share of cells that differ by more than 10 cm drops from about 0.7 % to under 0.1 %, and the remaining differences are isolated single cells. The rule is to make the buffer at least as wide as the largest neighbourhood used by any step of the pipeline. Note also that the tiled runs, executed in four threads, were faster than processing the whole square at once.

title: Large-Area LiDAR Processing: Tiling, Streaming, Parallel Work and the GPU
text:
Terrain derivatives on the GPU
With the CUDA backend selected (rs.set_backend("cuda")), GeoLattice raster functions run on CuPy arrays. The cell moves the 2 m DEM mosaic to the GPU and times five local derivatives against the CPU. The first GPU call of each function includes compiling its kernel, so the cell times a second, “warm” call. Point gridding in this version of GeoLattice runs on the CPU (the products above were gridded there).


Code
dem_m = mosaic["dem"]  # 2 m DEM mosaic
ops = {"slope": lambda d: rs.lidar.slope(d), "hillshade": lambda d: rs.lidar.hillshade(d),  # local operations
       "curvature": lambda d: rs.lidar.curvature(d), "TRI": lambda d: rs.lidar.tri(d), "TPI (51 cells)": lambda d: rs.lidar.tpi(d, window=51)}
rows = {}  # timings
rs.set_backend("cpu")  # CPU first
for name, f in ops.items():  # each operation
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); cpu_out = f(dem_m); rows[name] = {"CPU (s)": time.perf_counter() - t0}  # CPU time
if "cuda" in rs.available_backends():  # GPU available
    import cupy as cp  # GPU arrays
    rs.set_backend("cuda")  # switch the backend
    dem_g = dem_m.copy(data=cp.asarray(dem_m.values))  # copy the DEM to GPU memory
    for name, f in ops.items():  # each operation
        f(dem_g); cp.cuda.Device().synchronize()  # first call compiles the kernel
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); out = f(dem_g); cp.cuda.Device().synchronize()  # warm call
        rows[name]["GPU (s)"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # GPU time
    same = float(np.nanmax(np.abs(cp.asnumpy(rs.lidar.slope(dem_g).data) - rs.lidar.slope(dem_m.copy()).values)))  # check
    rs.set_backend("cpu")  # back to the CPU
    tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).T  # as a table
    tab["speed-up"] = tab["CPU (s)"] / tab["GPU (s)"]  # ratio
    display(tab.round(4))  # show it
    # summary line
    print(f"DEM {dem_m.shape} ({dem_m.size / 1e6:.1f} M cells) | largest CPU-GPU difference in slope: {same:.2e}°")
else:  # no GPU
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(4)); print("No CUDA backend: GPU timings skipped.")  # show the table

title: Large-Area LiDAR Processing: Tiling, Streaming, Parallel Work and the GPU
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Index tiles from their headers first: footprints, counts, density and CRS cost almost nothing to read.
Read only the fields a step needs, and stream very large files in chunks when only statistics are required.
Grid each tile on its exact extent so the per-tile rasters mosaic without resampling.
Neighbourhood operations need buffered tiles; the buffer must be wider than the largest window used, otherwise seams appear along tile edges.
Tiles are independent, so they parallelise; memory, not CPU cores, usually limits how many run at once.
Local raster operations run tens of times faster on a GPU; sequential hydrology stays on the CPU.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.lidar.las_info, rs.lidar.read_las (with fields), rs.lidar.read_las_chunks, rs.lidar.process_files, rs.lidar.process_tiles, rs.lidar.merge_rasters, rs.lidar.merge_pointclouds, rs.lidar.write_tiles, rs.lidar.dem, rs.lidar.dsm, rs.lidar.chm, rs.lidar.smrf, rs.lidar.normalize_heights, rs.lidar.grid_metrics, rs.lidar.density_map, rs.lidar.hillshade, rs.lidar.slope, rs.lidar.curvature, rs.lidar.tri, rs.lidar.tpi, rs.set_backend, rs.available_backends, rs.write, rs.viz.plot_raster.
Exercises

Run process_files with n_jobs of 1, 2, 5 and 10 and plot the wall-clock time. Where does the speed-up stop, and why?
Repeat the edge experiment with buffers of 10, 20 and 40 m. What is the smallest buffer that removes the seams for an 18 m SMRF window?

title: Point Cloud Classification with Machine Learning and Deep Learning
text:
Overview

The task
Semantic segmentation of a point cloud assigns a class to every point. It is the 3D counterpart of pixel classification in images, but the input is unordered, irregular and of varying density, so image methods do not apply directly. Two families of methods are in use:

Feature-based machine learning. For every point, describe its neighbourhood with hand-crafted features, then train a standard classifier (random forest, gradient boosting, support vector machine) on labelled points.
Deep learning on points. Networks consume the coordinates and attributes of the points directly and learn their own features.



Hand-crafted point features








Group
Features
What they capture




Height
Height above ground (from a DEM), absolute elevation
Ground versus objects; low versus high vegetation


Return structure
Return number, number of returns
Porous objects (vegetation) versus solid surfaces


Intensity
Echo strength
Material (asphalt, grass, roofing), partly


Covariance (eigenvalue) features
Linearity, planarity, scattering, omnivariance, anisotropy, eigenentropy, change of curvature, verticality, normal z
Local shape: lines, planes, volumes, walls


Multi-scale
The same features at several neighbourhood sizes \(k\)
Objects of different sizes (a roof edge at \(k = 10\), the whole roof at \(k = 50\))



With eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \lambda_3\) of the covariance of the \(k\) nearest neighbours (Weinmann et al. 2015): linearity \(= (\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)/\lambda_1\), planarity \(= (\lambda_2 - \lambda_3)/\lambda_1\), scattering \(= \lambda_3/\lambda_1\), omnivariance \(= (\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3)^{1/3}\), eigenentropy \(= -\sum e_i \ln e_i\) with \(e_i = \lambda_i/\sum\lambda\).


Deep learning on point clouds

PointNet (Qi et al. 2017a) applies the same small multi-layer perceptron to every point, then a symmetric function (max pooling) over all points gives a global feature that does not depend on point order. For segmentation, each point’s own feature is concatenated with the global feature and classified. PointNet sees each point and the whole block, but no local neighbourhoods.
PointNet++ (Qi et al. 2017b) adds hierarchy: it samples centroids (farthest point sampling), groups the points in a ball around each centroid, runs a mini-PointNet on each group, and repeats at coarser levels (set abstraction); feature propagation then interpolates the features back to every point. Like a CNN, it learns local patterns at several scales.
Later networks include KPConv (kernel point convolutions), RandLA-Net (fast random sampling for large scenes), sparse voxel CNNs (MinkowskiNet) and point transformers, available in libraries such as Open3D-ML and torch-points3d.

Networks work on fixed-size blocks: the scene is cut into squares (here 20 m), a fixed number of points is sampled from each, coordinates are normalised within the block, and predictions from overlapping blocks are averaged.


Validation without leakage
Neighbouring points share almost the same features and labels. A random split of points into training and test sets puts near-identical neighbours on both sides and reports accuracies that will not hold in a new area. Here the scene is split spatially: a western training area, a validation strip and an eastern test area separated by gaps.

title: Point Cloud Classification with Machine Learning and Deep Learning
text:
Random forest and gradient boosting
rs.lidar.train_point_classifier computes the features on the training cloud, fits the model (here on 200,000 sampled points) and reports accuracy on a random holdout of the training area. rs.lidar.predict_point_classes then computes the features on the unseen test area and labels its points. The scores on the test area are the honest ones.


Code
train_pc = parts["train"].filter(np.asarray(parts["train"]["label"]) > 0)  # labelled training points
test_pc = parts["test"]  # the unseen eastern area
y_test = np.asarray(test_pc["label"]); scored = y_test > 0  # test labels and scored points

def test_scores(pred, name, seconds):  # metrics on the test area
    p, t = pred[scored], y_test[scored]  # scored points
    f1 = f1_score(t, p, labels=CLASSES, average=None)  # per-class F1
    return {"model": name, "OA": accuracy_score(t, p), "kappa": cohen_kappa_score(t, p),  # overall scores
            "mean IoU": jaccard_score(t, p, labels=CLASSES, average="macro"),
            **{f"F1 {NAMES[k]}": v for k, v in zip(CLASSES, f1)}, "seconds": seconds}

results, fitted, preds = [], {}, {}  # scores, models and predictions
for name, kw in (("random forest", dict(model="rf", n_estimators=200, n_jobs=-1)),  # random forest
                 ("XGBoost", dict(model="xgb", n_estimators=300, max_depth=8, learning_rate=0.1))):  # gradient boosting
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    fit = rs.lidar.train_point_classifier(train_pc, "label", scales=SCALES, sample=200_000, **kw)  # fit
    out = rs.lidar.predict_point_classes(test_pc, fit, field="pred")  # label the test area
    sec = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time for both
    fitted[name], preds[name] = fit, np.asarray(out["pred"])  # keep them
    results.append({**test_scores(preds[name], name, sec), "random-holdout OA": fit["report"]["accuracy"]})  # scores

Which features matter

title: Point Cloud Classification with Machine Learning and Deep Learning
section: PointNet and PointNet++ on the GPU
text:
PointNet and PointNet++ on the GPU
pn.PointBlockDataset cuts the clouds into 20 m blocks and samples 4,096 points per block; each sample has the block-normalised x, y, z and the standardised attributes (height, intensity, return number, number of returns) as channels. With augment=True blocks are randomly rotated about the vertical axis, mirrored and jittered, and samples_per_block=4 draws four different samples per block per epoch. Points with label 0 are ignored in the loss. The validation strip selects the best epoch; pn.predict_point_segmentation sweeps overlapping blocks over the test area and averages the softmax scores of several random passes (votes).


Code
FEATS = ("height", "intensity", "return_number", "number_of_returns")  # per-point channels besides xyz
# training blocks with augmentation
ds_train = pn.PointBlockDataset([parts["train"]], label="label", block_size=20.0, num_points=4096, features=FEATS,
                                ignore=(0,), samples_per_block=4, augment=True, seed=0)  # training blocks
# validation blocks with the training scaling
ds_val = pn.PointBlockDataset([parts["validation"]], label="label", block_size=20.0, num_points=4096, features=FEATS,
                              ignore=(0,), classes=ds_train.classes, stats=ds_train.stats)  # same classes and scaling
# summary line
print(f"classes {list(ds_train.classes)} | training samples per epoch {len(ds_train)} | validation samples {len(ds_val)}")
item = ds_train[0]  # one sample
print({k: tuple(v.shape) for k, v in item.items()})  # its tensors

EPOCHS = 30 if DEVICE == "cuda" else 5  # fewer epochs on a CPU
nets, hist = {}, {}  # trained networks and histories
for name, net in (("PointNet", pn.PointNetSeg(item["points"].shape[0], len(ds_train.classes))),  # vanilla PointNet
                  ("PointNet++", pn.PointNet2Seg(item["points"].shape[0], len(ds_train.classes)))):  # hierarchical
    torch.manual_seed(0)  # same start for both
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    hist[name] = pn.train_point_segmentation(net, DataLoader(ds_train, batch_size=16, shuffle=True),  # training batches
                                             DataLoader(ds_val, batch_size=16), epochs=EPOCHS,  # validation batches
                                             num_classes=len(ds_train.classes), device=DEVICE, log_every=10)
    hist[name]["seconds"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # training time
    nets[name] = net  # keep the best-validation weights
    # summary line
    print(f"{name}: {sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters()):,} parameters, trained in {hist[name]['seconds']:.0f} s")

text:
Where the models go wrong
Mapping the errors in the test area shows where the classes are confused: building edges and walls (between building, vegetation and other), low objects near the ground (between other and ground), and trees overhanging roofs. A cross-section through the area compares the labels with the best model’s prediction.


Code
best = cmp["mean IoU"].idxmax()  # the model with the highest mean IoU
p = preds[best]  # its predictions
wrong = scored & (p != y_test)  # misclassified test points
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(19, 6.5))  # three panels
for ax, (title, lab) in zip(axes[:2], (("Producer labels", y_test), (f"{best} prediction", p))):  # labels and prediction
    for k, col in cols.items():  # each class
        m = lab == k  # its points
        ax.scatter(test_pc.x[m], test_pc.y[m], s=0.1, color=col, label=NAMES[k])  # plan view
    ax.set(title=title, aspect="equal", xticks=[], yticks=[])  # labels
axes[0].legend(markerscale=30, loc="lower left")  # legend
axes[2].scatter(test_pc.x[scored], test_pc.y[scored], s=0.05, color="lightgrey")  # all scored points
axes[2].scatter(test_pc.x[wrong], test_pc.y[wrong], s=0.2, color="red")  # errors
# axis labels and title

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

ym = (y0 + y1) / 2  # a west-east line through the middle of the test area
sec_mask = np.abs(np.asarray(test_pc.y) - ym) < 3  # a 6 m wide slice
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(15, 6), sharex=True)  # two panels
for ax, (title, lab) in zip(axes, (("Producer labels", y_test), (f"{best} prediction", p))):  # labels and prediction
    for k, col in cols.items():  # each class
        m = sec_mask & (lab == k)  # slice points of this class
        ax.scatter(test_pc.x[m] - AREAS["test"][0], test_pc.z[m], s=2, color=col, label=NAMES[k])  # profile
    ax.set(ylabel="Elevation (m)", title=title)  # labels
axes[0].legend(markerscale=5, ncol=4); axes[1].set_xlabel("Distance (m)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
















All four models agree with the producer on most of the ground and the tree canopy (F1 above 0.95 and about 0.9). They differ on the two small classes:

Buildings. The feature-based models are clearly better (F1 about 0.8 for the random forest against about 0.6 for the networks). Buildings are rare in this window: the training area holds a few buildings, most points from one large roof, and the validation strip only about 200 building points, so the networks see few examples and cannot select their best epoch for roofs. Hand-crafted height and planarity features generalise from few examples.
Other. The networks recognise this heterogeneous class (cars, fences, low structures and points the producer left unlabelled) better than the random forest, because they learn context from the whole block rather than from one neighbourhood.

Overall the random forest gives the best mean IoU here, trains in seconds and needs no GPU. Deep networks need far more labelled data (benchmark datasets contain many millions of labelled points from many scenes) and longer training before they overtake well-designed features. Part of the remaining error is in the reference itself: the producer’s labels on the stadium structures and the “other” class are not consistent.

title: Point Cloud Classification with Machine Learning and Deep Learning
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Supervised point classification labels all classes at once from height, return structure, intensity and multi-scale eigenvalue features.
Compute height above ground with a label-free ground filter, so the features do not contain the labels.
Split the scene spatially. A random point-wise holdout puts near-identical neighbours in training and test sets and overstates accuracy.
Random forest and gradient boosting on hand-crafted features are fast, interpretable and strong baselines.
PointNet learns per-point and global features; PointNet++ adds local, multi-scale grouping. Both work on fixed-size blocks and average predictions from overlapping blocks.
Report mean IoU and per-class F1, not only overall accuracy, and inspect errors on maps and cross-sections: reference labels have errors too.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.lidar.read_las, rs.lidar.smrf, rs.lidar.dem, rs.lidar.normalize_heights, rs.lidar.point_feature_table, rs.lidar.train_point_classifier, rs.lidar.predict_point_classes, rs.lidar.write_las, geolattice.rsense.dl.pointnet.PointBlockDataset, PointNetSeg, PointNet2Seg, train_point_segmentation, predict_point_segmentation.
Exercises

Train the random forest with one scale (\(k = 16\)) and with three scales (10, 40, 100). How do mean IoU and run time change?
Remove height from the features. Which class suffers most?
Train PointNet++ with 10 m and 30 m blocks. Which block size suits buildings, which suits ground?
Swap the training and test areas (train east, test west). Are the scores similar?
Apply the random forest trained on Autzen to the UB 2008 campus (about 1 point/m²). Does a model trained on dense data transfer to a sparse survey?

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Overview

Why LiDAR for forests
Canopy height is the strongest single predictor of timber volume and aboveground biomass, and LiDAR measures it directly, to within about a metre for dominant trees. Optical and radar sensors only infer it. National forest inventories in the Nordic countries, forest agencies in North America and carbon projects worldwide use airborne LiDAR to map volume, basal area, biomass, site quality, fuel loads for fire models and habitat structure for wildlife.


Height normalisation
Raw point elevations mix terrain and vegetation. Subtracting the DEM elevation interpolated at each point’s position gives its height above ground:
\[h_i = z_i - \text{DEM}(x_i, y_i).\]
Every forest metric is computed from these heights; errors in the ground classification therefore propagate directly into canopy heights.


The area-based approach (ABA)
The ABA (Næsset 2002) summarises the heights of all returns in a cell or plot with a set of metrics and links them to field measurements with a regression model:








Metric
Definition
Relates to




\(h_{\max}\), \(h_{\text{mean}}\), \(h_{\text{sd}}\)
Maximum, mean and standard deviation of heights
Top height, average height, layering


Percentiles \(p_{25}, p_{50}, p_{75}, p_{95}\)
Height below which that share of returns lies
Volume and biomass (\(p_{95}\) is close to dominant height)


Canopy cover
Share of first returns above a height threshold (often 2 m)
Crown closure, light interception


Coefficient of variation
\(h_{\text{sd}} / h_{\text{mean}}\)
Structural complexity


Foliage height diversity (FHD)
Shannon diversity \(-\sum p_k \ln p_k\) of returns in height layers (MacArthur and MacArthur 1961)
Vertical layering, bird habitat


Effective LAI
\(-\ln(P_{\text{gap}}) / k\) from the gap fraction (Beer-Lambert law)
Leaf area


Canopy relief ratio
\((h_{\text{mean}} - h_{\min}) / (h_{\max} - h_{\min})\)
Shape of the canopy profile



Field plots (typically 200 to 900 m²) are measured on the ground, the same metrics are computed for the LiDAR points inside each plot, a model (linear regression on log-transformed metrics, random forest, etc.) is fitted, and the model is applied to every grid cell of the same size.


Vertical profiles
The share of returns in each height layer, corrected for the light that never reached lower layers, gives a leaf area density profile (MacArthur and Horn 1969):
\[\text{LAD}_k = \frac{1}{k\,\Delta z}\ln\frac{P_{\text{gap}}(z_k)}{P_{\text{gap}}(z_{k+1})},\]
where \(P_{\text{gap}}(z)\) is the fraction of returns below height \(z\) and \(k \approx 0.5\) is the extinction coefficient.


Individual tree detection (ITD)
With enough points per crown (roughly 5 or more per m²), individual trees can be found:

Treetops are local maxima of the CHM. The search window should scale with tree height, because tall trees have wide crowns; a fixed window either merges small trees or splits large crowns.
Crowns grow outward from the treetops with a marker-controlled watershed on the inverted CHM, stopping where crowns meet or the canopy drops below a minimum height.
Per-tree attributes: height, crown area and diameter, and through allometric equations stem diameter, volume and biomass.

Point-based methods assign points to trees directly in 3D and avoid the smoothing of a raster CHM. ITD works best for conifers with distinct apexes; broad, interlocking deciduous crowns are often merged or split.

The analysis uses a 1 km x 1 km block of the Madison survey. The DEM comes from the producer’s ground points (class 2); rs.lidar.normalize_heights adds a height field to every point by bilinear interpolation of the DEM.
The fundamentals notebook showed that this producer used the vegetation codes 3 and 4 by return number, not by height. rs.lidar.classify_vegetation relabels vegetation by height above ground with the ASPRS convention: low (3) 0.5 to 2 m, medium (4) 2 to 5 m and high (5) above 5 m.

section: Canopy height model and canopy cover
text:
Canopy height model and canopy cover
rs.lidar.chm takes the cloud (and builds DSM and DEM internally) or a DSM plus DEM. Its pit_free option removes “pits”, single cells where a pulse travelled deep into a crown and the highest return per cell is far below the canopy surface; they break crowns apart in tree detection. Canopy cover is the share of first returns above 2 m in each cell.
The DSM is gap-filled by interpolation. Over water, which returns no laser echoes, the interpolation stretches the heights of the shoreline trees across the whole lake and creates fake canopy. The small helper mask_empty sets CHM cells with no return within 2 m to zero before any tree analysis. The zoom panels show the 200 m window with the most tall canopy.


Code
from scipy import ndimage as nd  # morphology

def mask_empty(grid, cloud, cells=2):  # set CHM cells with no return within `cells` cells to 0 (water, data gaps)
    hits = rs.lidar.rasterize(cloud, float(abs(grid.x[1] - grid.x[0])), stat="count", bounds=cloud.bbox)  # returns per cell
    near = nd.binary_dilation(hits.reindex_like(grid, method="nearest").fillna(0).values > 0, iterations=cells)  # near data
    return grid.where(near, 0)  # interpolated values far from any return become 0

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
chm_raw = mask_empty(rs.lidar.chm(pc, res=1.0, pit_free=False), pc)  # CHM with pits
chm = mask_empty(rs.lidar.chm(pc, res=1.0, pit_free=True), pc)  # pit-free CHM (median filter)
print(f"two 1 m CHMs in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s | grid {chm.shape} | "  # summary line
      f"canopy > 2 m: {float((chm > 2).mean()):.1%} of the area")  # summary
first = pcn.first_returns()  # one return per pulse
cover = (rs.lidar.rasterize(first.filter(np.asarray(first["height"]) > 2), 10.0, stat="count", bounds=pcn.bbox)  # canopy hits
         / rs.lidar.rasterize(first, 10.0, stat="count", bounds=pcn.bbox)).fillna(0)  # / all first returns

tall = (chm > 10).coarsen(x=200, y=200, boundary="trim").mean()  # share of tall canopy in 200 m windows
wy, wx = np.unravel_index(int(tall.argmax()), tall.shape)  # the most forested window
zoom = dict(x=slice(wx * 200, wx * 200 + 200), y=slice(wy * 200, wy * 200 + 200))  # its pixel ranges
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 4.8))  # four panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(chm, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=32, title="Pit-free CHM (m), 1 km block")  # full CHM
rs.viz.plot_raster(chm_raw.isel(zoom), ax=axes[1], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=32, title="CHM with pits (zoom)")  # pits
rs.viz.plot_raster(chm.isel(zoom), ax=axes[2], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=32, title="Pit-free CHM (zoom)")  # filled
rs.viz.plot_raster(cover, ax=axes[3], cmap="YlGn", vmin=0, vmax=1, title="Canopy cover (> 2 m), 10 m cells")  # cover
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Area-based metrics on a grid
rs.lidar.grid_metrics computes height metrics per cell from the normalised points; rs.lidar.structure_metrics adds foliage height diversity, effective LAI and the canopy relief ratio. A 20 m cell (400 m²) matches a common field plot size.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
# height metrics per 20 m cell
gm = rs.lidar.grid_metrics(pcn, res=20.0, metrics=("hmax", "hmean", "hstd", "p25", "p50", "p75", "p95", "cv", "cover",
                                                   "density"))  # height metrics per 20 m cell
sm = rs.lidar.structure_metrics(pcn, res=20.0)  # FHD, LAI and canopy relief ratio
print(f"area-based metrics for {gm.sizes['x'] * gm.sizes['y']} cells in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")  # timing

# eight metric maps

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Vertical structure
rs.lidar.height_profile bins the returns by height and computes the gap fraction and the leaf area density (LAD) for each layer. The cell selects a tall closed forest stand and an open, low stand by their 20 m p95 values and compares their profiles; rs.lidar.foliage_height_diversity gives the FHD of each.


Code
cells = table.reset_index()  # cell centres and metrics
bx0, by0, bx1, by1 = pcn.bbox  # block extent
cells = cells[(cells.x > bx0 + 10) & (cells.x < bx1 - 10) & (cells.y > by0 + 10) & (cells.y < by1 - 10)]  # whole cells only
tall = cells[(cells.p95 > 25) & (cells.cover > 0.8)].iloc[0]  # a tall closed stand
low = cells[(cells.p95 > 5) & (cells.p95 < 12) & (cells.cover > 0.3)].iloc[0]  # a low, open stand

def stand(c, size=20):  # points of one 20 m cell
    return pcn.crop(c.x - size / 2, c.y - size / 2, c.x + size / 2, c.y + size / 2)  # points within the cell

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5))  # three panels
for (name, c), col in zip((("tall closed stand", tall), ("low open stand", low)), ("C2", "C1")):  # the two stands
    s = stand(c)  # its points
    prof = rs.lidar.height_profile(s, bin_size=1.0)  # vertical profile
    mid = (prof.z_bottom + prof.z_top) / 2  # layer centres
    axes[0].plot(prof.fraction, mid, color=col, label=name)  # share of returns per layer
    axes[1].plot(prof.lad, mid, color=col, label=f"{name}, FHD = {rs.lidar.foliage_height_diversity(s):.2f}")  # LAD
    sec = s.filter(np.abs(np.asarray(s.y) - c.y) < 3)  # a 6 m wide slice through the stand
    axes[2].scatter(np.asarray(sec.x) - c.x + (0 if col == "C2" else 25), sec["height"], s=3, color=col)  # profile view
axes[0].set(xlabel="Share of returns", ylabel="Height above ground (m)", title="Return distribution")  # labels
axes[1].set(xlabel="Leaf area density (m²/m³)", title="MacArthur-Horn LAD profile")  # labels
axes[2].set(xlabel="Distance (m): tall stand left, low stand right", title="Slices through the two stands")  # labels
for a in axes[:2]: a.legend()  # legends
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Treetop detection
rs.lidar.detect_trees finds local maxima of the CHM above min_height. By default the search window grows with height (\(3 + 0.08\,h\) m), so a 30 m tree needs about 5.4 m of separation from a taller neighbour; a fixed window uses the same distance everywhere. The table compares the two on the 1 m CHM and on a 0.5 m CHM.


Code
chm05 = mask_empty(rs.lidar.chm(pc, res=0.5, pit_free=True), pc, cells=4)  # 0.5 m CHM
area_ha = float((chm > 2).sum()) / 1e4  # canopy area in hectares (1 m cells)
rows, tops_all = {}, {}  # results
# detection settings to compare
for name, grid, kw in (("variable window, 1 m CHM", chm, {}), ("fixed 3 m window, 1 m CHM", chm, {"window": 3}),
                       ("fixed 6 m window, 1 m CHM", chm, {"window": 6}), ("variable window, 0.5 m CHM", chm05, {})):  # settings
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    tops = rs.lidar.detect_trees(grid, min_height=5, **kw)  # treetops
    tops_all[name] = tops  # keep them
    rows[name] = {"trees": len(tops), "trees per ha of canopy": len(tops) / area_ha,  # counts
                  "median height (m)": float(np.median(tops.height)), "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(1)  # show the comparison

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 6))  # three panels

    ax.scatter(t.geometry.x, t.geometry.y, s=10, c="red", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)  # treetops

A 3 m fixed window finds many maxima inside single large hardwood crowns (over-segmentation); a 6 m window merges neighbouring small pines (under-segmentation). The variable window is a compromise designed for conifers. Without field data to count real stems, the “right” setting cannot be known; ITD results should always be checked against field plots or very high resolution images.

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Crown segmentation and allometry
rs.lidar.segment_crowns grows a marker-controlled watershed from the treetops over the inverted CHM and returns a label raster and a GeoDataFrame of crown polygons with height, area and equivalent crown diameter \(D = 2\sqrt{A/\pi}\).


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
tops = tops_all["variable window, 1 m CHM"]  # treetops from the default setting
labels, crowns = rs.lidar.segment_crowns(chm, tops, min_height=3)  # watershed crowns
# summary line
print(f"{len(crowns):,} crowns in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s | median area {crowns.area_m2.median():.0f} m² | "
      f"median diameter {crowns.diameter_m.median():.1f} m")  # summary

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6.5))  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(sub, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=32, colorbar=False, title="Crown polygons over the CHM")  # CHM
crowns.cx[xmin:xmax, ymin:ymax].boundary.plot(ax=axes[0], color="white", linewidth=0.6)  # crown outlines
lab = labels.isel(zoom).values  # zoomed labels
shuffled = np.r_[0, np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(int(labels.max())) + 1][lab]  # random colours per crown
axes[1].imshow(np.where(lab > 0, shuffled % 20, np.nan), cmap="tab20", interpolation="nearest")  # crown segments
axes[1].set_title("Crown segments (random colours)")  # title
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


7,561 crowns in 6.4 s | median area 28 m² | median diameter 6.0 m









Allometry. Taller trees have wider crowns. A power law \(D = a\,H^b\), fitted on log-transformed values, describes the relation; a crown that falls far from the curve is often a merged group of trees or a fragment of one. Allometric equations of this kind link LiDAR heights and crown sizes to stem diameter and biomass.


Code
ok = (crowns.height > 5) & (crowns.diameter_m > 1)  # usable crowns
bfit, logafit = np.polyfit(np.log(crowns.height[ok]), np.log(crowns.diameter_m[ok]), 1)  # log D = log a + b log H
a_fit = np.exp(logafit)  # back-transformed coefficient
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.5))  # three panels
axes[0].hist(crowns.height[ok], bins=30, color="C2"); axes[0].set(xlabel="Tree height (m)", ylabel="trees")  # heights
axes[1].hist(crowns.diameter_m[ok], bins=30, color="C1"); axes[1].set(xlabel="Crown diameter (m)")  # diameters
axes[2].scatter(crowns.height[ok], crowns.diameter_m[ok], s=3, alpha=0.3)  # height vs diameter
hh = np.linspace(5, crowns.height.max(), 100)  # heights for the curve
axes[2].plot(hh, a_fit * hh ** bfit, "r-", lw=2)  # fitted power law
axes[2].set(xlabel="Height (m)", ylabel="Crown diameter (m)", title=f"D = {a_fit:.2f} · H^{bfit:.2f}")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Point-based tree segmentation
rs.lidar.segment_trees_points assigns each vegetation point above 2 m to the treetop that is nearest relative to that tree’s expected crown radius (\(0.3\,h\), clipped to 1 to 12 m) and not lower than the point. It works directly in 3D, so points under the canopy surface (lower branches, understorey) can belong to a different tree than the CHM pixel above them. The cell compares the result with the raster crowns.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
pts_seg = rs.lidar.segment_trees_points(pcn, tops, min_height=2)  # tree_id from 3D assignment
pts_rast = rs.lidar.assign_points_to_crowns(pcn, labels)  # tree_id from the crown raster
print(f"point-based segmentation in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")  # timing
tp = np.asarray(pts_seg["tree_id"]); tr = np.asarray(pts_rast["tree_id"])  # the two labelings
veg_pts = np.asarray(pcn["height"]) > 2  # vegetation points
both = veg_pts & (tp > 0) & (tr > 0)  # points labelled by both methods
pair = pd.DataFrame({"pt": tp[both], "rast": tr[both]})  # the two ids of each such point
purity = pair.groupby("pt").rast.agg(lambda v: v.value_counts().iloc[0] / len(v))  # share in the majority raster crown
# summary line
print(f"vegetation points assigned: point-based {np.mean(tp[veg_pts] > 0):.1%}, raster {np.mean(tr[veg_pts] > 0):.1%} | "
      f"median share of a point-based tree's points inside one raster crown: {purity.median():.1%}")  # comparison

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Point clouds of individual trees
With a tree_id on every point, each tree becomes its own small point cloud for per-tree analysis: height, crown base height (the lowest vegetation return), crown volume, intensity statistics for species classification. The cell views the six tallest trees in 3D and computes a few per-tree attributes.


Code
df = pts_seg.to_dataframe()  # points with tree_id and height
df = df[(df.tree_id > 0) & (df.height > 2)]  # vegetation points of segmented trees
per_tree = df.groupby("tree_id").agg(points=("height", "size"), height=("height", "max"),  # per-tree statistics
                                    crown_base=("height", lambda v: np.percentile(v, 5)),
                                    mean_intensity=("intensity", "mean"))
per_tree["crown_length"] = per_tree.height - per_tree.crown_base  # length of the live crown
display(per_tree[per_tree.points >= 30].describe().loc[["count", "mean", "50%", "max"]].round(1))  # summary

top6 = per_tree[per_tree.points >= 30].nlargest(6, "height").index  # the six tallest trees
s = df[df.tree_id.isin(top6)]  # their points
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6)); ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")  # 3D axes

    ax.scatter(g.x - s.x.mean(), g.y - s.y.mean(), g.height, s=3, color=plt.cm.tab10(k), label=f"tree {tid}")  # its points
ax.set(zlabel="Height (m)", title="Points of the six tallest segmented trees"); ax.view_init(15, -60)  # labels and angle

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Effect of point density
The Madison survey has about 1.7 points/m², often only a handful of returns per crown. The 2020 Ithaca survey has about 6.5 points/m². The cell takes the most forested 400 m block of an Ithaca tile, builds its DEM and CHM, and then thins the same points randomly to the Madison density to see what changes.


Code
ith = rs.lidar.read_las(ITHACA_TILE).drop_noise()  # one Ithaca tile (ground classified)
chm5 = rs.lidar.chm(ith, res=5.0)  # coarse CHM to find forest
frac = (chm5 > 10).coarsen(x=80, y=80, boundary="trim").mean()  # share of tall canopy in 400 m blocks
iy, ix = np.unravel_index(int(frac.argmax()), frac.shape)  # the most forested block
bx, by = float(chm5.x[ix * 80]) - 2.5, float(chm5.y[iy * 80 + 79]) - 2.5  # its south-west corner
ith_blk = ith.crop(bx, by, bx + 400, by + 400)  # the 400 m block
dens = rs.lidar.summary(ith_blk)["density_pts_m2"]  # its density
thinned = rs.lidar.thin(ith_blk, method="random", fraction=1.7 / dens)  # thinned to the Madison density

rows, chms = {}, {}  # results
for name, cloud in ((f"Ithaca full ({dens:.1f} pts/m²)", ith_blk), ("Ithaca thinned (1.7 pts/m²)", thinned)):  # two densities
    d = rs.lidar.dem(ith_blk, 1.0)  # same DEM for both (from the full ground points)
    cn = rs.lidar.normalize_heights(cloud, d)  # heights
    c = mask_empty(rs.lidar.chm(rs.lidar.dsm(cloud, 1.0, bounds=ith_blk.bbox).reindex_like(d, method="nearest"), d), cloud)  # CHM
    chms[name] = c  # keep it
    t = rs.lidar.detect_trees(c, min_height=5)  # treetops
    g = rs.lidar.grid_metrics(cn, res=20.0, metrics=("p95", "cover"))  # area-based metrics
    rows[name] = {"points": len(cloud), "trees detected": len(t), "mean CHM (m)": float(c.mean()),  # results
                  "mean p95 (m)": float(g.p95.mean()), "mean cover": float(g.cover.mean())}
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(2))  # comparison table

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))  # two panels
for ax, (name, c) in zip(axes, chms.items()):  # the two CHMs
    rs.viz.plot_raster(c, ax=ax, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=35, title=f"1 m CHM, {name}")  # map
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

Area-based metrics such as p95 and cover hardly change with thinning: they summarise dozens to hundreds of returns per 20 m cell either way. The CHM and tree detection change a lot. At the lower density most 1 m cells contain no return near a crown top, so the DSM is interpolated between a few scattered hits: it is several metres lower on average and bumpy, and the bumps become spurious local maxima, so more “trees” are detected, not fewer. Individual tree methods need dense data (and a CHM cell size matched to the point spacing); area-based methods work with sparse national surveys. (The Ithaca survey was flown in spring, so deciduous crowns may be partly leaf-off; this affects cover in both versions equally.)

title: Forest Structure and Individual Trees from LiDAR
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Every forest metric starts from heights above ground; check that few returns fall below the DEM.
Pit-free CHMs give cleaner crowns; canopy cover is the share of first returns above a height threshold.
Area-based metrics (percentile heights, cover, variability, FHD, LAI) summarise each cell or plot; with field plots they become predictors in biomass and volume models. Many height metrics are redundant.
Height profiles and LAD describe the vertical layering that optical images cannot see.
Treetop detection depends on the search window: fixed small windows over-segment broad crowns, large windows merge small trees; variable windows scale with height.
Watershed crowns and point-based segmentation give per-tree heights, crown sizes and point clouds; allometry checks them and links them to biomass.
Individual-tree methods need dense data; area-based metrics remain stable at low density.

Exercises

Compute grid metrics at 10, 20 and 40 m. How do the mean and spread of p95 and cover change with cell size?
Change the cover height threshold from 2 m to 5 m. Which areas lose most cover?

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
text:
Overview
Every LiDAR product depends on a chain of processing steps, and errors early in the chain propagate into everything that follows:








Step
Question it answers
Typical tools




Quality control
Is the coverage complete and dense enough? Do overlapping flight lines agree? Are the units and classes what the metadata say?
Density maps, swath-overlap differences, class and return tables


Noise removal
Which points are birds, multipath echoes or sensor artefacts?
Statistical and radius outlier filters, elevation bands


Selection and thinning
Which points are needed for this product, and how many?
Class, return and polygon filters; voxel or grid thinning


Ground classification
Which points lie on the bare earth?
Morphological filters (PMF, SMRF), cloth simulation (CSF), TIN densification, machine learning


Surface models
What are the terrain, the top surface and the height of objects above the terrain?
Gridding with min/max/mean statistics, gap filling, DSM minus DEM


Accuracy assessment
How close is the DEM to surveyed ground truth?
Checkpoints, RMSEz, NVA and VVA (ASPRS 2014)




Quality control
Point density. Specifications such as the USGS 3DEP Lidar Base Specification set a minimum aggregate nominal pulse density (for example 2 pulses/m² for quality level QL2) and require that most of the area meets it. A density grid of first returns (one per pulse) shows gaps caused by water, dark roofs, missed flight lines or steep scan angles.
Swath overlap. Neighbouring flight lines overlap, so the same ground is measured twice from different positions. On hard, flat surfaces both lines should agree to a few centimetres. Systematic differences reveal errors in the trajectory or the boresight calibration (strip misalignment). Each point’s point_source_id records the flight line it came from.
Classes and returns. A table of class codes and of returns per pulse is a quick check that the data match the metadata: a vegetated area with almost no multiple returns, or a missing ground class, signals a problem.


Noise
Noise points are far above or below the true surface: birds, low clouds, multipath echoes from water or glass, and range errors near strong reflectors. Two classic filters, both from the Point Cloud Library (PCL):

Statistical outlier removal (SOR). For every point compute the mean distance \(\bar d_i\) to its \(k\) nearest neighbours. Points with \(\bar d_i > \mu + \alpha\,\sigma\) (mean and standard deviation over all points) are outliers.
Radius outlier removal. A point with fewer than \(m\) neighbours within radius \(r\) is isolated and removed.

Outliers can be dropped or reclassified as low noise (class 7) or high noise (class 18) so they stay in the file but are ignored downstream.


Ground classification
Separating ground from non-ground points is the hinge on which every terrain and height product turns. The main families of filters:

Morphological filters. Grid the lowest point per cell and apply a morphological opening (erosion followed by dilation) with a growing window. An opening removes objects narrower than the window, so the opened surface approximates the terrain; cells that rise above it by more than a slope-dependent threshold are objects. The Progressive Morphological Filter (PMF, Zhang et al. 2003) grows the window and the height threshold together. The Simple Morphological Filter (SMRF, Pingel et al. 2013) uses disk-shaped windows up to a maximum radius and a threshold of slope × radius, then interpolates a provisional terrain and labels points within a small tolerance of it as ground. The window must exceed the largest object (the widest roof); the slope must allow for the steepest terrain.
Cloth Simulation Filter (CSF, Zhang et al. 2016). Turn the point cloud upside down and drop a cloth of connected particles onto it under gravity. Stiff springs (high rigidness) keep the cloth flat, so it rests on the lowest points and bridges over buildings and trees (now pointing downwards); soft springs let it follow steep terrain. Points close to the settled cloth are ground.
TIN densification (Axelsson 2000), used in commercial software: start from the lowest points in large cells, build a triangulated surface and add points whose distance and angle to the triangles are small enough.
Machine learning and deep learning classify ground with features of each point and its neighbourhood (see the point classification notebook).

All filters struggle in the same two places: steep slopes and banks, where the terrain itself looks like an object, and dense low vegetation, where few pulses reach the ground and the lowest return is a few decimetres up.


Surface models
A point cloud becomes a raster by binning points into cells and reducing each cell with a statistic:

DEM (DTM). Ground points only, mean or minimum elevation per cell. Cells without ground points (under dense canopy, buildings and water) are filled by interpolation: nearest neighbour, inverse distance weighting (IDW) or linear interpolation on a Delaunay triangulation (a TIN).
DSM. The highest first return per cell: canopy tops and roofs. Empty cells are filled the same way.
CHM (or normalised DSM, nDSM). \(\text{CHM} = \text{DSM} - \text{DEM}\), the height of objects above the ground. Small “pits” (single cells where a pulse went deep into a crown) are removed with a median filter.

The cell size should not be smaller than the point spacing (\(1/\sqrt{\rho}\)) for a DSM, and noticeably larger for a DEM under canopy, where ground points are sparse.
Vertical accuracy. ASPRS (2014) reports the non-vegetated vertical accuracy \(\text{NVA}_{95} = 1.96 \times \text{RMSE}_z\) on open hard surfaces, assuming normally distributed errors, and the vegetated vertical accuracy (VVA) as the 95th percentile of absolute errors under vegetation.

text:
Loading and preparing the two sites
Madison is read in metres and cropped to an 800 m square of mixed forest, roads and water in the south-west of the survey. UB is two neighbouring tiles merged with rs.lidar.merge_pointclouds, reprojected from geographic NAD83 to NAD83 / UTM zone 17N (EPSG:26917) and cropped to a 1 km square around the centre of the campus, which keeps the ground-filter experiments below to a few minutes.


Code
madison = rs.lidar.read_las(MADISON_UTM)  # whole Madison cloud (UTM 15N, metres)
mx0, my0 = madison.bbox[:2]  # south-west corner
mad = madison.crop(mx0, my0, mx0 + 800, my0 + 800)  # an 800 m x 800 m forested block
ub = rs.lidar.reproject(rs.lidar.merge_pointclouds([rs.lidar.read_las(p) for p in UB_TILES]), 26917)  # 2 tiles, metres
ucx, ucy = np.mean(ub.bbox[::2]), np.mean(ub.bbox[1::2])  # centre of the two tiles
ub = ub.crop(ucx - 500, ucy - 500, ucx + 500, ucy + 500)  # a 1 km x 1 km block of the campus
for name, pc in (("Madison", mad), ("UB", ub)):  # the two sites

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))  # two panels
for ax, (name, pc) in zip(axes, (("Madison", mad), ("UB", ub))):  # the two sites
    d = rs.lidar.density_map(pc, 10.0, first_returns=True)  # pulses per m² in 10 m cells
    share = float((d >= 2).sum() / d.notnull().sum())  # share of cells meeting QL2
    rs.viz.plot_raster(d, ax=ax, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=4,  # the map
                       title=f"{name}: pulses/m² (10 m cells), {share:.0%} of cells ≥ 2 (QL2)")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









Neither survey reaches the QL2 pulse density: both were flown with about 1 pulse/m², typical of surveys of their time and enough for a 1 to 2 m DEM. Density doubles where flight lines overlap (the bright stripes) and drops to zero over water and some dark roofs. The table also shows a striking difference in return structure: 42 % of Madison’s pulses produced several returns (leaf-on forest), but only 1 % of UB’s. The 2008 UB system recorded almost exclusively single returns, so return-based rules (for example “trees give multiple returns”) cannot be used on these data.
Flight lines. Colouring points by point_source_id shows the individual swaths and where they overlap.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))  # two panels
for ax, (name, pc) in zip(axes, (("Madison", mad), ("UB", ub))):  # the two sites
    line = rs.lidar.rasterize(pc, 5.0, value="point_source_id", stat="max")  # highest line id per 5 m cell
    ids = np.unique(line.values[np.isfinite(line.values)]).astype(int)  # flight lines present
    rs.viz.plot_raster(line, ax=ax, title=f"{name}: flight line (point_source_id)",  # map of lines
                       categorical={k: (f"line {k}", plt.cm.tab10(i % 10)) for i, k in enumerate(ids)})
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









Swath overlap. rs.lidar.swath_overlap compares, in every cell measured by two or more flight lines, the lowest point of each line and reports the largest difference dz. On UB, the overlap points of the second line were labelled class 12, so the test uses ground (2) and overlap (12) points; on bare, flat ground both lines should agree to about 10 cm.


Code
open_ground = ub.by_class(2, 12)  # ground points and overlap points from the second line
sw = rs.lidar.swath_overlap(open_ground, res=2.0, min_points=2)  # inter-line differences in 2 m cells
slope_ub = rs.lidar.slope(rs.lidar.rasterize(ub.by_class(2), 2.0, stat="mean", bounds=open_ground.bbox))  # terrain slope
flat = (slope_ub.values < 5) & np.isfinite(sw["dz"].values)  # flat cells with a difference value
dz = sw["dz"].values[flat]  # differences on flat ground
print(f"cells measured by ≥ 2 lines: {np.isfinite(sw['dz'].values).sum():,} | on flat ground: {flat.sum():,}")  # counts
print(f"flat-ground line-to-line difference: median {np.median(dz) * 100:.1f} cm, "  # summary line
      f"90th percentile {np.percentile(dz, 90) * 100:.1f} cm")  # agreement between flight lines

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(sw["dz"].where(sw["dz"] < 1), ax=axes[0], cmap="magma", vmax=0.5,  # map of differences
                   title="UB: line-to-line difference dz (m), 2 m cells")
axes[0].set_xticks([]); axes[0].set_yticks([])  # no ticks
axes[1].hist(dz * 100, bins=np.arange(0, 60, 1), color="C0")  # histogram
axes[1].set(xlabel="dz on flat ground (cm)", ylabel="cells", title="Agreement of overlapping flight lines")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


cells measured by ≥ 2 lines: 31,831 | on flat ground: 24,520
flat-ground line-to-line difference: median 1.6 cm, 90th percentile 8.5 cm









On flat ground the two flight lines agree to a median of under 2 cm, and 90 % of the cells to within about 9 cm, as expected from a well-calibrated survey. The larger differences sit on building edges, kerbs and slopes, where a small horizontal offset produces a large vertical difference. A systematic shift across a whole overlap strip would point to a calibration problem.

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
text:
Noise and outliers
A histogram of height above the local ground surface is the quickest way to look for points that do not belong. The cell computes heights from the producer’s ground points and then runs both outlier filters with action="classify", which labels suspected noise as class 7 (below the local surface) or 18 (above it) instead of deleting it.


Code
ground_surface = rs.lidar.dem(ub, 2.0)  # provisional terrain from the provider's ground points
ubh = rs.lidar.normalize_heights(ub, ground_surface)  # height above that terrain for every point
h = np.asarray(ubh["height"])  # heights
# summary line
print(f"points more than 40 m above ground: {(h > 40).sum():,} | more than 2 m below: {(h < -2).sum():,} | "
      f"provider low noise (7): {(ub['classification'] == 7).sum():,}")  # suspicious points

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
sor = rs.lidar.statistical_outlier_removal(ubh, k=8, std_ratio=3.0, action="classify")  # SOR, flagged as 7 or 18
t_sor = time.perf_counter() - t0  # SOR time
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # restart the timer
ror = rs.lidar.radius_outlier_removal(ubh, radius=3.0, min_neighbors=3, action="classify")  # radius filter
t_ror = time.perf_counter() - t0  # radius filter time

rows = {}  # one row per method
for name, out, sec in (("statistical (k=8, 3σ)", sor, t_sor), ("radius (3 m, 3 neighbours)", ror, t_ror)):  # methods
    c = np.asarray(out["classification"])  # new classes
    new = np.isin(c, (7, 18)) & ~np.isin(ub["classification"], (7, 18))  # newly flagged points
    rows[name] = {"flagged": int(new.sum()), "of which > 40 m up": int((new & (h > 40)).sum()),  # results
                  "high noise (18)": int(((c == 18) & new).sum()), "low noise (7)": int(((c == 7) & new).sum()),
                  "seconds": round(sec, 1)}
pd.DataFrame(rows).T  # show the comparison

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5))  # two panels
axes[0].hist(h, bins=np.arange(-5, 70, 0.5), color="grey", log=True, label="all points")  # all heights
axes[0].hist(h[np.isin(c_sor, (7, 18))], bins=np.arange(-5, 70, 0.5), color="C3", log=True, label="flagged by SOR")  # flagged
axes[0].set(xlabel="Height above ground (m)", ylabel="points (log scale)", title="Heights of all and flagged points")  # labels
axes[0].legend()  # legend
noise = sor.filter(np.isin(c_sor, (7, 18)))  # the flagged points
axes[1].scatter(ub.x[::40], ub.y[::40], s=0.1, c="lightgrey")  # a sample of all points as background
sc = axes[1].scatter(noise.x, noise.y, s=4, c=np.asarray(noise["height"]), cmap="plasma", vmin=-5, vmax=50)  # noise
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=axes[1], label="height above ground (m)")  # colour bar
axes[1].set(title="Location of points flagged by SOR", xticks=[], yticks=[], aspect="equal")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The histogram shows why outlier filters must be checked before they are trusted. The points 40 to 55 m above ground form distinct peaks: they are the roofs of the tallest campus buildings, not birds. SOR flags about 5,000 points, but only 22 of them are above 40 m; most lie on building walls, roof edges, light poles and tree crowns, where a survey with 1 point/m² leaves real points far from their neighbours. At this density a global distance threshold cannot tell sparse but real structures from noise, so the flags are kept as a separate class for review rather than deleted. Outlier filters work much better on dense data (several points per m²), and true noise (birds, low clouds) is usually isolated by tens of metres. For the rest of this notebook only the producer’s noise class is removed.


Code
ub = ub.drop_noise()  # drop only the producer's noise class; the SOR flags are kept for review, not applied
mad = mad.drop_noise()  # the same for Madison
print(f"UB after cleaning: {len(ub):,} points | Madison: {len(mad):,} points")  # counts after cleaning


UB after cleaning: 1,028,848 points | Madison: 1,045,509 points

Selecting points: classes, returns, boxes and polygons

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
text:
Thinning
Thinning reduces the number of points, either to make density uniform (overlap strips have twice as many points) or to speed up processing. rs.lidar.thin offers:

voxel: one point per cube of side size, keeping the 3D structure;
grid_min and grid_max: the lowest or highest point per 2D cell, a quick ground or surface sample;
random: a random fraction of the points.

The table shows how many points each method keeps for Madison and how a 1 m DSM built from the thinned cloud differs from the DSM of the full cloud.


Code
dsm_full = rs.lidar.dsm(mad, 1.0)  # DSM from all points
rows = {}  # one row per method
# thinning settings to compare
for name, kw in (("voxel 0.5 m", dict(size=0.5, method="voxel")), ("voxel 1 m", dict(size=1.0, method="voxel")),
                 ("grid_max 1 m", dict(size=1.0, method="grid_max")), ("grid_min 1 m", dict(size=1.0, method="grid_min")),
                 ("random 25 %", dict(method="random", fraction=0.25))):  # thinning settings
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    th = rs.lidar.thin(mad, **kw)  # thin the cloud
    sec = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time taken
    d = rs.lidar.dsm(th, 1.0, bounds=mad.bbox).reindex_like(dsm_full, method="nearest") - dsm_full  # DSM difference
    rows[name] = {"points": len(th), "kept": len(th) / len(mad), "seconds": sec,  # size and speed
                  "DSM bias (m)": float(d.mean()), "DSM RMSE (m)": float(np.sqrt((d ** 2).mean()))}  # effect on the DSM

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
section: Ground classification with SMRF, CSF and PMF
text:
Ground classification with SMRF, CSF and PMF
rs.lidar.classify_ground(pc, method) runs smrf, csf or pmf and writes class 2 for ground and 1 for everything else. The reference is the producer’s classification, restricted to points whose label is unambiguous:

Madison: ground (2) against low and medium vegetation (3, 4);
UB: ground (2) against unclassified (1), which on the campus is mostly buildings and trees. Overlap points (12) carry no ground/non-ground label and are excluded.

Overall accuracy, Cohen’s kappa, ground recall (share of true ground found) and ground precision (share of predicted ground that is true ground) summarise each run.


Code
def scores(pred_ground, ref_ground):  # confusion-matrix scores for a binary ground mask
    tp = np.sum(pred_ground & ref_ground); fp = np.sum(pred_ground & ~ref_ground)  # true and false positives
    fn = np.sum(~pred_ground & ref_ground); tn = np.sum(~pred_ground & ~ref_ground)  # false and true negatives
    n = tp + fp + fn + tn  # number of points
    oa = (tp + tn) / n  # overall accuracy
    pe = ((tp + fp) * (tp + fn) + (fn + tn) * (fp + tn)) / n ** 2  # chance agreement
    return {"overall accuracy": oa, "kappa": (oa - pe) / (1 - pe),  # accuracy and kappa
            "ground recall": tp / (tp + fn), "ground precision": tp / (tp + fp)}  # recall and precision

SITES = {"Madison": (mad, (2, 3, 4)), "UB": (ub, (2, 1))}  # cloud and unambiguous reference classes
METHODS = {"SMRF": dict(method="smrf", cell=1.0, slope=0.15, window=18),  # default-like settings
           "CSF": dict(method="csf", resolution=1.0, rigidness=2),
           "PMF": dict(method="pmf", cell=1.0, max_window=33, slope=0.15)}
rows, ground = {}, {}  # scores and classified clouds
for site, (pc, valid_cls) in SITES.items():  # each site
    c = np.asarray(pc["classification"])  # reference classes
    valid, ref = np.isin(c, valid_cls), c == 2  # points with a clear label, reference ground
    for name, kw in METHODS.items():  # each filter
        kw = dict(kw); method = kw.pop("method")  # separate the method name
        t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
        out = rs.lidar.classify_ground(pc, method, **kw)  # classify ground
        sec = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time taken
        pred = np.asarray(out["classification"]) == 2  # predicted ground
        rows[(site, name)] = {**scores(pred[valid], ref[valid]), "seconds": sec}  # scores
        ground[(site, name)] = out  # keep the classified cloud
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)  # show the comparison

All three filters find nearly all true ground points (recall close to 1); they differ in how many non-ground points they wrongly call ground (precision). On the UB campus kappa drops to about 0.6: buildings wider than the filter window stay in the ground class, as the next sections show. A cross-section through Madison compares the producer’s labels with SMRF’s.

    ax.scatter(sec["distance"][~g], sec.z[~g], s=1, color="#1a9850", label="non-ground")  # vegetation etc.
    ax.scatter(sec["distance"][g], sec.z[g], s=1, color="#8c510a", label="ground")  # ground

Where do the filters disagree with the producer? Mapping the disagreement per 5 m cell shows that the errors concentrate along stream banks and road embankments (steep terrain) and in low, dense vegetation.


Code
c_ref = np.asarray(mad["classification"])  # producer classes
valid = np.isin(c_ref, (2, 3, 4))  # unambiguous points
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5))  # three panels

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
text:
Tuning the ground filters
The most important SMRF parameter is the window, the largest object the filter can remove. On the UB campus the widest buildings are well over 50 m across, so an 18 m window leaves their roofs in the ground class. The sweep below runs SMRF on a 2 m grid with windows from 10 m to 80 m and CSF with the three rigidness settings and scores each run against the producer’s labels.


Code
c_ub = np.asarray(ub["classification"])  # producer classes
valid_ub, ref_ub = np.isin(c_ub, (1, 2)), c_ub == 2  # unambiguous points and reference ground
rows = []  # one row per run
for w in (10, 18, 30, 50, 80):  # SMRF windows (m)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    pred = np.asarray(rs.lidar.smrf(ub, cell=2.0, slope=0.15, window=w)["classification"]) == 2  # classify on a 2 m grid
    rows.append({"filter": "SMRF", "setting": f"window {w} m", **scores(pred[valid_ub], ref_ub[valid_ub]),  # score
                 "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0})
for rg in (1, 2, 3):  # CSF rigidness
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    pred = np.asarray(rs.lidar.csf(ub, resolution=1.0, rigidness=rg)["classification"]) == 2  # classify
    rows.append({"filter": "CSF", "setting": f"rigidness {rg}", **scores(pred[valid_ub], ref_ub[valid_ub]),  # score
                 "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0})
tune = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["filter", "setting"]).round(3)  # as a table

ub_g = rs.lidar.smrf(ub, cell=2.0, slope=0.15, window=best_w)  # rerun with that window

                                     (f"SMRF, window {best_w} m", ub_g))):  # tuned
    dem_w = rs.lidar.dem(cloud, 2.0)  # DEM from that classification
    rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem_w), ax=ax, cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title=f"DEM hillshade: {title}")  # relief
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks

The seconds column shows the price of large windows: the cost of a morphological opening grows with the window area, so SMRF slows down sharply beyond about 50 m, which is one reason to run it on a coarser grid (2 m here) or on tiles. Kappa rises steadily with the SMRF window, from 0.54 at 10 m to 0.80 at 80 m, the largest window tested; CSF improves with rigidness but stays below the wide-window SMRF (0.67). With the 18 m window the large campus buildings survive in the “ground” surface as flat-topped blocks. With the 80 m window most of them are removed, but triangular facets remain inside the largest footprints: a few roof or wall points are still labelled ground, and the linear interpolation spans the gap between them and the surrounding terrain. The stadium stands, built into an embankment, remain in both versions. Windows larger than 80 m would remove more roofs but cost much more time and start to cut off real terrain such as hilltops and road embankments.

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
text:
DEM, DSM and CHM
With ground classified, rs.lidar.dem, rs.lidar.dsm and rs.lidar.chm build the three surfaces on a common grid. chm(dsm, dem) subtracts the terrain and removes single-cell pits with a median filter.


Code
mad_g = ground[("Madison", "CSF")]  # Madison classified by CSF
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
dem = rs.lidar.dem(mad_g, 1.0)  # bare-earth DEM, 1 m, gaps interpolated linearly
dsm = rs.lidar.dsm(mad_g, 1.0, bounds=mad_g.bbox).reindex_like(dem, method="nearest")  # first-return DSM on the same grid
chm = rs.lidar.chm(dsm, dem)  # canopy height model with pits removed
print(f"DEM, DSM and CHM at 1 m in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; grid {dem.shape}")  # timing and size

dem_prod = rs.lidar.dem(mad, 1.0)  # DEM from the producer's ground points
d = dem - dem_prod.values  # CSF DEM minus producer DEM
# summary line
print(f"CSF DEM vs producer DEM: mean {float(d.mean()):+.2f} m, RMSE {float(np.sqrt((d ** 2).mean())):.2f} m, "
      f"|difference| > 0.5 m in {float((abs(d) > 0.5).mean()):.1%} of cells")  # agreement

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem), ax=axes[0], cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title="DEM (hillshade)")  # terrain
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dsm), ax=axes[1], cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title="DSM (hillshade)")  # surface
rs.viz.plot_raster(chm, ax=axes[2], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=30, title="CHM (m)")  # canopy height
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
