CSF DEM vs producer DEM: mean +0.04 m, RMSE 0.20 m, |difference| > 0.5 m in 1.1% of cells









For UB the same steps give a normalised DSM (nDSM): buildings and trees as heights above the campus terrain. Its histogram already separates low objects (cars, shrubs) from buildings and trees.


Code
ub_dem = rs.lidar.dem(ub_g, 1.0)  # DEM from the tuned SMRF classification
ub_dsm = rs.lidar.dsm(ub_g, 1.0, bounds=ub_g.bbox).reindex_like(ub_dem, method="nearest")  # DSM on the same grid
ub_ndsm = rs.lidar.chm(ub_dsm, ub_dem)  # normalised DSM (height of objects)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5.5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1]})  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(ub_ndsm, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=25, title="UB: normalised DSM (m)")  # map
axes[0].set_xticks([]); axes[0].set_yticks([])  # no ticks
v = ub_ndsm.values[np.isfinite(ub_ndsm.values)]  # all heights
axes[1].hist(v[v > 0.5], bins=np.arange(0.5, 40, 0.5), color="C2")  # heights above 0.5 m
axes[1].set(xlabel="Height above ground (m)", ylabel="cells", yscale="log", title="Heights of objects above 0.5 m")  # labels

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
text:
Gap filling and cell size
Under dense canopy and over water, many DEM cells contain no ground points at all. rs.lidar.rasterize with stat="mean" leaves them empty (NaN), and rs.lidar.fill_gaps fills them by nearest neighbour, inverse distance weighting or linear interpolation on a triangulation. The share of empty cells depends strongly on the cell size, which is why DEMs are often built at a coarser resolution than DSMs.


Code
rows = {}  # one row per cell size
for res in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0):  # cell sizes (m)
    raw = rs.lidar.rasterize(mad_g.ground(), res, stat="mean", bounds=mad_g.bbox)  # mean ground elevation per cell
    rows[f"{res} m"] = {"empty DEM cells": float(raw.isnull().mean()),  # share without ground points
                        "empty DSM cells": float(rs.lidar.rasterize(mad_g.first_returns(), res, stat="max",
                                                                      bounds=mad_g.bbox).isnull().mean())}
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3))  # show the table

raw = rs.lidar.rasterize(mad_g.ground(), 1.0, stat="mean", bounds=mad_g.bbox)  # 1 m DEM with gaps
fills = {m: rs.lidar.fill_gaps(raw, m) for m in ("nearest", "idw", "linear")}  # three fills
win = dict(x=slice(150, 450), y=slice(150, 450))  # a 300 m window
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 4.6))  # four panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(raw.isel(win), ax=axes[0], cmap="terrain", title="Mean ground elevation (gaps white)")  # raw grid
for ax, (m, g) in zip(axes[1:], fills.items()):  # each fill
    rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(g).isel(win), ax=ax, cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title=f"Filled: {m}")  # relief
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
text:
Vertical accuracy with checkpoints
A DEM is tested against checkpoints: points whose elevation was surveyed independently, typically with RTK GNSS, on open and flat ground. Here 300 checkpoints are simulated by holding out producer ground points on flat, open terrain (slope < 3°, no canopy within 5 m). The DEM is rebuilt without them and compared with rs.lidar.vertical_accuracy, which reports RMSEz, the mean error and NVA₉₅ = 1.96 × RMSEz.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)  # reproducible sampling
slope1 = rs.lidar.slope(dem_prod)  # slope of the producer DEM
open_cells = (slope1 < 3) & (chm.reindex_like(slope1, method="nearest") < 0.5)  # flat cells without canopy
g = mad.ground()  # producer ground points
gs = rs.lidar.sample_raster(g, open_cells.astype("float32"), "open")  # flag points in open flat cells
cand = np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(gs["open"]) == 1)  # candidate checkpoint indices
pick = rng.choice(cand, 300, replace=False)  # 300 checkpoints
is_cp = np.zeros(len(g), bool); is_cp[pick] = True  # mask of checkpoints
cps = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"z": np.asarray(g.z)[is_cp]},  # checkpoint elevations
                       geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(np.asarray(g.x)[is_cp], np.asarray(g.y)[is_cp]), crs=32615)

rest = mad.filter(~np.isin(np.arange(len(mad)), np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(mad["classification"]) == 2)[pick]))  # withhold them
rows = {}  # one row per DEM
for name, cloud in (("producer ground", rest), ("CSF ground", rs.lidar.csf(rest, resolution=1.0, rigidness=2))):  # DEMs
    for res in (1.0, 2.0):  # two cell sizes
        va = rs.lidar.vertical_accuracy(rs.lidar.dem(cloud, res), cps)  # compare with checkpoints
        # accuracy of this DEM
        rows[(name, f"{res} m")] = {"n": va["n"], "mean error (m)": va["mean_error"], "RMSEz (m)": va["rmse_z"],
                                     "NVA95 (m)": va["nva_95"]}  # results
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)  # show the table

title: LiDAR Processing: Quality Control, Cleaning, Ground Classification and Surface Models
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Check density (first returns per m²) against the specification and look at overlapping flight lines: on flat hard ground they should agree to about 10 cm.
Statistical and radius outlier filters find isolated echoes, but in sparse data they also flag real walls, roof edges and poles; reclassify suspected noise instead of deleting it, and review it.
Thin with the statistic the product needs: grid_max for a DSM, grid_min for a ground sample, voxels to keep 3D structure.
SMRF, CSF and PMF all recover nearly all ground points; their errors concentrate on steep banks and under dense low vegetation. The SMRF window must exceed the widest building.
DEM, DSM and CHM come from the same classified cloud. Linear (TIN) gap filling gives the most natural terrain under canopy; DEM cells should be coarser than DSM cells where ground points are sparse.
Vertical accuracy is reported as RMSEz and NVA₉₅ against independent checkpoints on open ground.

title: Deep Learning for Hyperspectral Classification
text: Banner

title: Deep Learning for Hyperspectral Classification
text:
Overview

Why deep learning for hyperspectral data
Classic classifiers (maximum likelihood, SVM, random forest) see each pixel’s spectrum on its own. Neighbouring pixels carry information too (texture, shape, context: a roof next to a street), and the spectrum has local structure (absorption features) that convolutions can detect. Deep networks learn both from data:








Model
Input
Idea




1D CNN
One spectrum
Convolutions along wavelength learn absorption features


3D CNN
A small cube (bands by p by p pixels)
Joint spectral and spatial kernels


HybridSN (Roy et al. 2020)
A small cube of 15 to 30 PCA components
3D convolutions for spectral and spatial features, then a 2D convolution


Spectral transformer (SpectralFormer style, Hong et al. 2022)
A spectrum split into groups of bands
Self attention between band groups





Pitfalls

Spatial leakage. Neighbouring pixels are almost identical, and patches around neighbouring pixels overlap. If training and test pixels are drawn at random from the same areas, the test measures memorisation, and published accuracies near 100 percent on benchmarks are often inflated this way. Splitting by spatial blocks gives honest numbers.
Few labels. Field labels are expensive; networks with many parameters overfit small training sets, so augmentation (rotations and flips of patches), dropout, weight decay and validation based early stopping matter.
Class imbalance. Benchmarks are dominated by a few classes; overall accuracy then hides poor performance on rare ones, so per class scores and kappa are reported.
Transfer. A network trained on one sensor, date or city rarely works on another without retraining.

title: Deep Learning for Hyperspectral Classification
text:
Deep Learning with GeoLattice
geolattice.rsense.dl.hyperspectral provides block_split (spatial train and test split), the HSIPatchDataset (patches or spectra around labelled pixels, normalised, with optional augmentation), the four model constructors, train_hsi_classifier (AdamW, cosine learning rate, best validation weights), evaluate and predict_hsi_map. Models need PyTorch; a GPU is used automatically when available.

Learning objectives

Split labelled pixels into spatially separate training and test blocks.
Build patch and spectrum datasets with consistent normalisation.
Train and compare 1D CNN, 3D CNN, HybridSN and spectral transformer models against a random forest and SAM.

text:
Datasets and training
Spectral models see the 102 band spectrum of each pixel; spatial models see an 11 by 11 pixel patch of the first 20 principal components (computed on the whole image, which uses no labels). Normalisation statistics come from the training dataset and are reused for validation, test and mapping. Patch datasets for training use random rotations and flips.


Code
pc, _ = hs.pca(pavia, 20)  # 20 principal components
pcc = pc.rename(component="band")  # the dataset and mapping code expect a band dimension
PATCH = 11


def datasets(cube, patch, flat):
    """Train, validation and test datasets sharing the training normalisation."""
    lab = lambda m: np.where(m, gt, 0)  # labels only where the mask is True
    d_tr = dlh.HSIPatchDataset(cube, lab(train), patch=patch, flat=flat, augment=not flat)
    kw = dict(patch=patch, flat=flat, classes=d_tr.classes, stats=d_tr.stats)
    return d_tr, dlh.HSIPatchDataset(cube, lab(val), **kw), dlh.HSIPatchDataset(cube, lab(test), **kw)


spec_ds = datasets(pavia, 1, True)  # spectra
patch_ds = datasets(pcc, PATCH, False)  # PCA patches
print("spectral sample:", spec_ds[0][0]["image"].shape, "| patch sample:", patch_ds[0][0]["image"].shape,
      "| classes:", spec_ds[0].classes)


spectral sample: torch.Size([102]) | patch sample: torch.Size([1, 20, 11, 11]) | classes: [1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9]




Code
models = {
    "1D CNN (spectra)": (lambda: dlh.SpectralCNN1D(102, 9), spec_ds),
    "spectral transformer (spectra)": (lambda: dlh.SpectralTransformer(102, 9, group=6, dim=64, depth=4), spec_ds),
    "3D CNN (PCA patches)": (lambda: dlh.CNN3D(20, 9, width=8), patch_ds),
    "HybridSN (PCA patches)": (lambda: dlh.HybridSN(20, 9, patch=PATCH), patch_ds),
}
histories, nets = {}, {}
for name, (make, (d_tr, d_va, d_te)) in models.items():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    net = make()
    n_par = sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters())
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    hist = dlh.train_hsi_classifier(net, DataLoader(d_tr, batch_size=64, shuffle=True),
                                    DataLoader(d_va, batch_size=512), epochs=80, lr=1e-3, device=DEVICE)
    yt, yp = dlh.evaluate(net, DataLoader(d_te, batch_size=1024), device=DEVICE)  # class indices
    score(name, d_tr.classes[yp], time.perf_counter() - t0)  # back to class codes
    histories[name], nets[name] = hist, net
    print(f"{name}: {n_par:,} parameters, best validation accuracy {max(hist['val_accuracy']):.3f}")

Summary and exercises
Key points

Spatially blocked splits keep test pixels away from training pixels and give honest accuracies; validation pixels from the training blocks are optimistic.
With 200 labels per class a random forest is a strong spectral baseline (0.95); spectral CNNs and transformers add little, while spatial models that see a neighbourhood reach about 0.99 on Pavia.
Per class scores and the confusion matrix show which materials remain confused (similar VNIR spectra), which overall accuracy hides.
Mapping with the best model gives a full scene map and a confidence layer that flags edges, mixed pixels and unknown materials, though softmax confidence is not a calibrated probability.

title: Greenhouse Gas Plume Detection
text:
Overview

Why methane, why imaging spectroscopy
Methane is the second largest contributor to human caused warming, with about 80 times the warming effect of CO₂ over 20 years. A large share of anthropogenic emissions comes from a small number of point sources: leaking wells, compressors, pipelines, flares, coal mine vents and landfills. Finding them requires pixels of tens of metres, which imaging spectrometers such as AVIRIS-NG, EMIT, PRISMA, EnMAP and Tanager provide; Tanager was launched by the Carbon Mapper coalition specifically to find and quantify such plumes.


The physics
Along the light path (sun to ground to sensor) the radiance is attenuated by methane following the Beer Lambert law. A plume adds an enhancement ΔX (in ppm·m: the extra concentration in ppm times the path length in metres) on top of the background column. For small enhancements the change in log radiance is linear:
\[\ln L(\lambda) \approx \ln L_0(\lambda) + k(\lambda)\,\Delta X\]
where k(λ) is the unit absorption spectrum (per ppm·m): the band averaged change in log radiance per unit enhancement, computed from the methane absorption cross sections, the background atmosphere and the sun and view geometry (the air mass factor).


The matched filter
With the background mean radiance μ and covariance Σ, the target is t = μ ⊙ k and the enhancement estimate is (Thompson et al. 2016)
\[\widehat{\Delta X} = \frac{(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{t}}{\mathbf{t}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{t}}\]
the matched filter of notebook 09_05_08 with a physical target, so the score is directly in ppm·m. For pushbroom data in sensor geometry the statistics are computed per detector column; for an orthorectified product they are computed over the scene.


From enhancement to emission rate
The integrated mass enhancement (IME) sums the excess methane mass over the plume: IME = Σ ΔX · 10⁻⁶ · ρ_CH4 · A_pixel. A simple mass balance (Varon et al. 2018) gives the emission rate Q = IME · U / L, with an effective wind speed U (from weather models) and a plume length scale L. Carbon Mapper reports Q = IME · U / fetch, where the fetch is the distance over which the plume was integrated.


Limitations
Bright and dark surfaces with SWIR structure (some soils, paints, oil stains) produce false enhancements; the background statistics must exclude plumes; wind uncertainty usually dominates the emission uncertainty; and the simple k used here ignores water vapour and surface pressure variations.

title: Greenhouse Gas Plume Detection
text:
Methane absorption from HITRAN
HAPI downloads the line list once (about 9 MB) and caches it in Data/08_remote_sensing/08_05_HyperSpectral/hitran. Absorption cross sections are computed on a 0.01 cm⁻¹ grid with Voigt line shapes for a representative lower troposphere (0.85 atm, 280 K).


Code
import contextlib, io  # silence HAPI's log messages
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    import hapi  # HITRAN Application Programming Interface

    HITRAN.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    hapi.db_begin(str(HITRAN))  # use the local cache
    if "CH4" not in hapi.tableList():
        hapi.fetch("CH4", 6, 1, 3950, 4800)  # molecule 6 (CH4), main isotopologue, wavenumber range in cm-1
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    nu, xsec = hapi.absorptionCoefficient_Voigt(SourceTables="CH4", WavenumberRange=[3950, 4800], WavenumberStep=0.01,
                                                Environment={"p": 0.85, "T": 280.0}, Diluent={"air": 1.0},
                                                HITRAN_units=True)  # cross section, cm2 per molecule
print(f"{len(nu):,} wavenumbers in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s | peak cross section {xsec.max():.2e} cm2")
wl_hi = 1e7 / nu  # wavenumber (cm-1) to wavelength (nm)


85,001 wavenumbers in 14 s | peak cross section 3.90e-20 cm2

title: Greenhouse Gas Plume Detection
text:
The unit absorption spectrum
The radiance is read for 2100 to 2500 nm, where methane absorbs. The sun and view zenith angles set the air mass factor (the two way path relative to the vertical). The high resolution transmittance of the background atmosphere (1.9 ppm methane) and of the same atmosphere with an extra 1000 ppm·m are both convolved with Tanager’s band responses; the difference of their logarithms per ppm·m is the unit absorption spectrum.


Code
rad_file = next(GHG.glob("*_ortho_radiance_hdf5.h5"))
rad = hs.read_tanager(rad_file, wavelength_range=(2100, 2500))  # TOA radiance, W m-2 sr-1 um-1
anc = hs.read_tanager_ancillary(rad_file)
sza, vza = float(anc["sun_zenith"].mean()), float(anc["sensor_zenith"].mean())
amf = 1 / np.cos(np.radians(sza)) + 1 / np.cos(np.radians(vza))  # two way air mass factor
print(rad.shape, f"| sun zenith {sza:.1f}, view zenith {vza:.1f}, air mass factor {amf:.2f}")

N_PPMM = 1e-6 * 2.5e25 * 1e-4  # CH4 molecules per cm2 for 1 ppm·m (air number density 2.5e25 m-3)
background = 1.9e-6 * 2.15e25  # vertical background CH4 column (molecules cm-2): 1.9 ppm of the air column
T_bg = np.exp(-xsec * background * amf)  # background transmittance
T_plume = T_bg * np.exp(-xsec * N_PPMM * 1000 * amf)  # with an extra 1000 ppm·m
wl, fwhm = hs.wavelengths(rad), rad["fwhm"].values


def to_bands(T):
    """Band averaged transmittance: Gaussian response of each Tanager band."""
    out = np.empty(len(wl))
    for i, (c, f) in enumerate(zip(wl, fwhm)):
        w = np.exp(-0.5 * ((wl_hi - c) / (f / 2.3548)) ** 2)
        out[i] = (w * T).sum() / w.sum()
    return out


k = (np.log(to_bands(T_plume)) - np.log(to_bands(T_bg))) / 1000  # per ppm·m
print(f"strongest absorption {k.min():.2e} per ppm·m at {wl[np.argmin(k)]:.0f} nm "
      f"(1000 ppm·m darken that band by {100 * (1 - np.exp(1000 * k.min())):.1f} %)")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4))
axes[0].plot(wl_hi, xsec, lw=0.3)
axes[0].set(xlim=(2100, 2500), yscale="log", ylim=(1e-24, 1e-19), xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="cm² per molecule",
            title="HITRAN CH4 cross sections (0.85 atm, 280 K)")
axes[1].plot(wl, k * 1e6, "o-", ms=3)
axes[1].set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="k (10⁻⁶ per ppm·m)", title="Unit absorption spectrum on Tanager bands")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


(81, 1040, 943) | sun zenith 41.4, view zenith 2.8, air mass factor 2.33
strongest absorption -2.14e-05 per ppm·m at 2370 nm (1000 ppm·m darken that band by 2.1 %)









Thousands of individual lines make up the methane band; at Tanager’s 5 to 6 nm resolution they merge into a smooth unit absorption spectrum with its strongest values near 2300 to 2370 nm. A 1000 ppm·m plume darkens the strongest band by about two percent, which is why the detection works through statistics rather than by looking at single spectra.

title: Greenhouse Gas Plume Detection
text:
The enhancement map
The matched filter uses all good bands between 2100 and 2500 nm and the whole scene as background (the product is orthorectified, so the per column option is off).


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
enh = hs.gas_matched_filter(rad, k, window=(2100, 2500), columnwise=False).rio.write_crs(rad.rio.crs)
e = enh.values
med = float(np.nanmedian(e)); sd = float(np.nanmedian(np.abs(e - med)) * 1.4826)  # robust centre and spread
print(f"matched filter in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s | median {med:.0f} ppm·m, robust SD {sd:.0f} ppm·m, "
      f"99.9th percentile {np.nanpercentile(e, 99.9):.0f} ppm·m")
plumes = gpd.read_file(next(GHG.glob("*_ql_ch4_json.geojson"))).to_crs(rad.rio.crs)  # Carbon Mapper plumes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 7))
hs.plot_rgb(hs.read_tanager(rad_file, bands=[55, 37, 17]), (651, 561, 461), ax=axes[0], title="True colour (radiance)")
im = axes[1].imshow(e, cmap="inferno", vmin=0, vmax=2500,
                    extent=[float(enh.x[0]), float(enh.x[-1]), float(enh.y[-1]), float(enh.y[0])])
axes[1].plot(plumes.geometry.x, plumes.geometry.y, "c+", ms=10, mew=1.5, label="Carbon Mapper sources")
axes[1].set_title("CH4 enhancement (ppm·m)"); axes[1].legend(loc="lower left"); axes[1].set_xticks([]); axes[1].set_yticks([])
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1], shrink=0.7)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


matched filter in 0.9 s | median 1 ppm·m, robust SD 292 ppm·m, 99.9th percentile 1513 ppm·m









The background noise of the enhancement map is about 300 ppm·m (the robust standard deviation), and the strongest plumes reach several thousand ppm·m. Elongated plumes stretch downwind (to the south east) from the Carbon Mapper source points in the oil field on the desert plateau. Two artefacts are visible. Fine vertical stripes run along track: each detector column has a slightly different response, and with scene wide statistics on the ortho grid it is not removed (per column statistics in sensor geometry, columnwise=True on a basic product, address this). And the Euphrates and its irrigated valley appear slightly negative, because dark water and wet fields have little SWIR signal and a different spectral shape from the desert that dominates the background statistics.

text:
Comparison with Carbon Mapper
Carbon Mapper’s quick look product is an 8 bit image (scaled values without units) on a grid offset by a pixel or two, so it is reprojected onto the enhancement grid before comparison.


Code
ql = rioxarray.open_rasterio(next(GHG.glob("*_ortho_ql_ch4.tif")), masked=True).squeeze().rio.reproject_match(enh)
q = ql.values
ok = np.isfinite(e) & np.isfinite(q)
print(f"pixel correlation with the quick look: r = {np.corrcoef(e[ok], q[ok])[0, 1]:.2f}")
x0, x1, y0, y1 = plumes.geometry.x.min() - 3000, plumes.geometry.x.max() + 3000, plumes.geometry.y.min() - 3000, plumes.geometry.y.max() + 3000
zoom = dict(x=slice(x0, x1), y=slice(y1, y0))  # area around the sources
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6.5))
for ax, (img, t, vmax) in zip(axes, [(enh.sel(**zoom), "GeoLattice matched filter (ppm·m)", 2500),
                                     (ql.sel(**zoom), "Carbon Mapper quick look (scaled, 8 bit)", np.nanpercentile(q, 99.9))]):
    im = ax.imshow(img, cmap="inferno", vmin=0, vmax=vmax, extent=[x0, x1, y0, y1])
    ax.plot(plumes.geometry.x, plumes.geometry.y, "c+", ms=10, mew=1.5)
    for _, p in plumes.iterrows():
        ax.text(p.geometry.x + 150, p.geometry.y + 150, p["plume_id"][-1], color="c", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_title(t); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.75)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


pixel correlation with the quick look: r = 0.77









The two maps show the same plumes in the same places. The quick look only has values inside Carbon Mapper’s plume masks (everything else is no data), so the correlation of r = 0.77 is measured over those plume pixels: within the plumes, the two retrievals agree on where the enhancement is highest, although the methods differ (Carbon Mapper uses its own processing, target spectra and filtering). The GeoLattice map keeps the full resolution noise and the stripes.

title: Greenhouse Gas Plume Detection
text:
Plumes, IME and emission rates
hs.plume_mask segments the whole map automatically. For a like for like comparison with the published numbers, each Carbon Mapper plume is then integrated the same way: pixels within the plume’s fetch radius that exceed the background by 1.5 robust standard deviations (after a 3 by 3 median filter) and are connected to the source, summed with hs.plume_ime and converted with hs.emission_rate using Carbon Mapper’s wind speed and fetch.


Code
labels, table = hs.plume_mask(enh, sigma=3.0, min_pixels=10)  # automatic segmentation of the whole scene
print(f"automatic plume_mask: {len(table)} candidate plumes above median + 3 MAD")
display(table.sort_values("n_pixels", ascending=False).head(6).round(0))

X, Y = np.meshgrid(enh.x.values, enh.y.values)
smooth = ndi.median_filter(np.nan_to_num(e, nan=med), 3)  # suppress single pixel noise
rows, masks = [], np.zeros(e.shape, int)
for i, p in plumes.iterrows():
    d = np.hypot(X - p.geometry.x, Y - p.geometry.y)  # distance to the source (m)
    cand = (d <= p["fetch"]) & (smooth > med + 1.5 * sd)
    lab, _ = ndi.label(cand)
    touching = np.unique(lab[(d <= 150) & cand])  # components within 150 m of the source
    keep = np.isin(lab, touching[touching > 0])
    masks[keep] = i + 1
    res = hs.plume_ime(enh - med, enh.copy(data=keep.astype(int)), plume=1)  # IME of the masked pixels
    q_ours = hs.emission_rate(res["ime_kg"], p["wind_speed_avg"], p["fetch"])  # kg/h, Carbon Mapper wind and fetch
    rows.append({"plume": p["plume_id"][-1], "quality": p["plume_quality"], "pixels": res["n_pixels"],
                 "IME GeoLattice (kg)": res["ime_kg"], "IME Carbon Mapper (kg)": p["ime"],
                 "Q GeoLattice (kg/h)": q_ours, "Q Carbon Mapper (kg/h)": p["emission"], "Q uncertainty CM": p["emission_uncertainty"]})
res_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("plume")
res_tab.round(0)

Across the twelve plumes the IME correlates with the published values (r = 0.83) and the median ratio is 0.99, a close agreement for an independent retrieval built from HITRAN line data and a simple atmosphere. Plumes A, D, E, F, G, H and L agree within about 20 percent, inside or near Carbon Mapper’s uncertainty bars (grey). The outliers are instructive. I and J are two to three times too high: they sit in the long band of enhancement in the south east, where several plumes merge, and a mask that grows from the source collects their neighbours’ methane too. Separating overlapping plumes is where analyst judgement and plume shape analysis come in. The total over all plumes is about 30 percent higher than Carbon Mapper’s, almost entirely because of I and J.

auto = table.copy()
X0, Y0 = auto["x"].to_numpy(), auto["y"].to_numpy()
dmin = np.min(np.hypot(X0[:, None] - plumes.geometry.x.to_numpy()[None, :], Y0[:, None] - plumes.geometry.y.to_numpy()[None, :]), 1)
auto["distance to nearest CM source (km)"] = dmin / 1000
near = auto["distance to nearest CM source (km)"] < 1.5

      f"elsewhere: {int((~near).sum())}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5))
axes[0].hist(e[np.isfinite(e)], bins=200, range=(-3000, 5000), log=True)
axes[0].axvline(med + 3 * sd, color="r", ls="--", label="median + 3 robust SD")
axes[0].set(xlabel="Enhancement (ppm·m)", ylabel="Pixels", title="Distribution of the enhancement"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].scatter(auto["distance to nearest CM source (km)"], auto["n_pixels"], c=near, cmap="coolwarm", s=15)
axes[1].set(xscale="log", yscale="log", xlabel="Distance to nearest Carbon Mapper source (km)", ylabel="Plume pixels",
            title="Automatic candidates")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


automatic candidates: 45 | within 1.5 km of a Carbon Mapper source: 25 | elsewhere: 20









The enhancement distribution is a Gaussian core (noise) with a long positive tail (plumes and false positives). A fixed threshold keeps many small candidates far from any published source: most are surface artefacts or noise clusters, a reminder that an automatic mask is a list of candidates, not of plumes. Operational systems confirm plumes by their shape, their alignment with the wind, repeated detection on other dates and inspection by analysts.
The emission rate inherits several uncertainties: the noise in ΔX, the choice of mask threshold (at 2 robust SD instead of 1.5 the IME drops for most plumes), the wind speed (an error of 1 m/s at 2 m/s wind is a 50 percent error in Q) and the simplifications in k (one temperature and pressure, no water vapour, a fixed background column).

title: Greenhouse Gas Plume Detection
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Methane plumes darken Tanager radiance by about two percent per 1000 ppm·m in the 2300 nm bands.
A unit absorption spectrum from HITRAN cross sections, the background column and the air mass factor turns the matched filter score into an enhancement in ppm·m.
The GeoLattice enhancement map reproduces Carbon Mapper’s plumes, and IME and emission rates computed the same way agree with the published values within their uncertainties for most plumes.
Surface artefacts produce false enhancements; masks are candidate lists, and wind speed dominates the emission uncertainty.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: read_tanager, read_tanager_ancillary, gas_matched_filter, plume_mask, plume_ime, emission_rate, plot_rgb.

Use only the strongest methane bands (2250 to 2400 nm) in gas_matched_filter(window=...). Does the noise go up or down?
Repeat the IME comparison with thresholds of 1, 2 and 3 robust SD and plot the median ratio.

title: Endmember Extraction and Spectral Unmixing
text:
Overview

The linear mixing model
If materials occupy separate patches of a pixel and light interacts with only one before reaching the sensor, the pixel spectrum is a weighted sum of endmember spectra:
\[\mathbf{x} = \sum_{k=1}^{p} a_k \mathbf{e}_k + \mathbf{n}, \qquad a_k \ge 0, \qquad \sum_k a_k = 1\]
The two constraints (abundance non negativity, ANC, and sum to one, ASC) give four solvers: unconstrained least squares (LS), sum to one (SCLS), non negative (NNLS) and fully constrained (FCLS). Geometrically, the pixels fill a simplex whose vertices are the endmembers. Non linear mixing (multiple scattering between leaves or in sand) is ignored, which is usually acceptable at the 5 to 10 percent level.


Finding endmembers

Pixel purity index (PPI) (Boardman et al. 1995) projects the data on many random directions and counts how often each pixel lands at an extreme.
N-FINDR (Winter 1999) searches for the pixels that span the simplex of largest volume.
Vertex component analysis (VCA) (Nascimento and Bioucas-Dias 2005) repeatedly projects onto a direction orthogonal to the endmembers found so far and takes the extreme pixel.
ATGP (Ren and Chang 2003) takes the pixel with the largest residual after projecting out the targets found so far.

All assume that pure pixels exist. The number of endmembers is usually set near the intrinsic dimension (HySime, VD; notebook 09_05_03).


Variability and large libraries
One spectrum per material is a simplification: vegetation differs in species and condition, roofs in material and age, and illumination varies. MESMA (Roberts et al. 1998) tries many small models, each with one spectrum per class plus shade (a zero spectrum that absorbs brightness differences), and keeps the best fitting model per pixel. Sparse unmixing (SUnSAL, Iordache et al. 2011) uses a large library and an L1 penalty, so that each pixel picks only a few members.

title: Endmember Extraction and Spectral Unmixing
text:
Unmixing with GeoLattice
hs.ppi, hs.atgp, hs.nfindr, hs.vca and hs.extract_endmembers return the endmember spectra, their pixel positions and a SpectralLibrary. hs.unmix solves LS, SCLS, NNLS or FCLS for every pixel (NNLS and FCLS exactly for up to eight endmembers); hs.mesma, hs.sparse_unmix and hs.reconstruct cover variability, large libraries and residual analysis.

Learning objectives

Simulate a mixed scene and measure how well extraction and unmixing recover known endmembers and fractions.
Compare LS, SCLS, NNLS and FCLS and the effect of the constraints.
Extract endmembers from a real scene with N-FINDR and VCA and map their fractions.
Model endmember variability with MESMA and shade.
Unmix with a large library sparsely and count the active members.
Validate fractions against labelled pixels.

text:
A synthetic scene with known answers
Four endmembers (green vegetation, soil, water and clay) on Tanager’s good bands are mixed with spatially smooth random fractions; each corner holds a 4 by 4 block of one pure material, and noise with a standard deviation of 0.005 is added.


Code
probe = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("urban"), window=(slice(0, 1), slice(0, 1)))  # Tanager bands
w = hs.wavelengths(probe)
probe = probe.isel(band=np.flatnonzero(probe["good"].values & (w >= 400) & (w <= 2450)))
names = ["green_vegetation", "soil", "water", "clay_kaolinite"]
E = hs.synthetic_library(np.arange(400.0, 2451.0, 1.0)).resample(probe).subset(names).spectra  # (4, bands)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
H = W = 100
Z = np.stack([ndi.gaussian_filter(rng.normal(size=(H, W)), 4) for _ in range(4)], -1)  # smooth fields
A = np.exp(Z / Z.std() * 1.5); A /= A.sum(-1, keepdims=True)  # fractions that sum to one
for k, (r, c) in enumerate([(0, 0), (0, W - 4), (H - 4, 0), (H - 4, W - 4)]):
    A[r:r + 4, c:c + 4] = np.eye(4)[k]  # pure blocks in the corners
syn = hs.as_cube(np.einsum("yxk,kb->byx", A, E) + rng.normal(0, 0.005, (E.shape[1], H, W)), hs.wavelengths(probe))
print(syn.shape, "| pure pixels per material:", 16, "| mean fractions:", np.round(A.reshape(-1, 4).mean(0), 3))

title: Endmember Extraction and Spectral Unmixing
section: Endmember extraction on the synthetic scene
text:
Endmember extraction on the synthetic scene
Each extractor is asked for four endmembers. Each found spectrum is paired with the closest true endmember by spectral angle.


Code
def match(found, truth):
    """Angle (deg) from each true endmember to its closest found spectrum."""
    f = found / np.linalg.norm(found, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    t = truth / np.linalg.norm(truth, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(t @ f.T, -1, 1))).min(1)


rows, found = [], {}
for name in ["ppi", "atgp", "nfindr", "vca"]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    res = hs.extract_endmembers(syn, 4, method=name)  # spectra, positions and a library
    found[name] = res
    ang = match(res["spectra"], E)
    pure = np.mean([(A[r, c].max() > 0.99) for r, c in zip(res["row"], res["col"])])
    rows.append({"method": name, "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 2), "pure pixels picked": pure,
                 **{f"angle to {n.split('_')[0]} (deg)": a for n, a in zip(names, ang)}})

All four methods pick pure pixels, one in each corner block, and the angles to the true vegetation, soil and clay spectra are below about one degree, the effect of the added noise. Water is the exception at about 19 degrees: its reflectance (a few thousandths beyond 900 nm) is close to the noise level, so even a perfectly pure water pixel has a noisy shape. Averaging several pure pixels, or denoising first, helps dark endmembers. On this easy scene the cheap ATGP is as good as the others; real scenes without pure pixels are harder.

All four solvers fit the spectra equally well, because the noise is the only misfit. They differ in the fractions. Unconstrained LS gives a few percent negative fractions and sums that miss one by about 0.04. NNLS removes the negative values but not the sum error, and its fractions are hardly better. The sum to one constraint is the one that matters here: SCLS and FCLS cut the fraction error by a factor of seven, and FCLS also removes the last negative values. Physically meaningful fractions need FCLS (or SCLS with a shade endmember, used in MESMA below).

Endmembers of a city

title: Endmember Extraction and Spectral Unmixing
text:
Fraction maps and residuals


Code
em_lib = ems["nfindr"]["library"]  # N-FINDR endmembers as a library
ab = hs.unmix(urban, em_lib, method="fcls")  # fully constrained fractions
rec = hs.reconstruct(ab, em_lib, urban)  # modelled spectra
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(17, 8.5))
for ax, n in zip(axes.ravel()[:6], em_lib.names):
    d = describe(em_lib.to_dict()[n])
    im = ax.imshow(ab[n], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.set_title(f"{n}: NDVI {d['NDVI']:.2f}, mean {d['mean']:.2f}"); ax.axis("off")
im = axes[1, 2].imshow(ab["rmse"], cmap="magma", vmax=float(ab["rmse"].quantile(0.99)))
axes[1, 2].set_title("RMSE of the fit"); axes[1, 2].axis("off"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1, 2], shrink=0.8)
r, c = np.unravel_index(int(np.nanargmax(ab["rmse"].values)), ab["rmse"].shape)
axes[1, 3].plot(uwl, urban.values[:, r, c], label="observed"); axes[1, 3].plot(uwl, rec.values[:, r, c], label="modelled")
axes[1, 3].set(title=f"Worst fitting pixel ({r}, {c})", xlabel="Wavelength (nm)"); axes[1, 3].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"mean RMSE {float(ab['rmse'].mean()):.4f} | 99th percentile {float(ab['rmse'].quantile(0.99)):.4f}")









mean RMSE 0.0116 | 99th percentile 0.0215


The maps show how extremes behave as endmembers. The dark endmember (water or deep shadow) takes a large share of nearly every pixel: it acts as shade, absorbing the brightness differences between pixels. The vegetation endmember follows parks and tree lined streets. The four bright endmembers are single unusual pixels (bright roofs and surfaces), and their fractions are near zero almost everywhere except around their own locations. The RMSE map shows the cost: errors of 0.01 to 0.02 over most of the built up area, and the worst fitting pixel has a SWIR shape that none of the six endmembers can reproduce. Six extremes are a poor description of a city’s typical materials; MESMA below uses typical spectra instead.

title: Endmember Extraction and Spectral Unmixing
text:
MESMA: variability and shade
MESMA needs a library with several spectra per class. Here each class gets three image spectra chosen by index rules: green vegetation of low, median and high brightness, impervious surfaces from bright roofs to dark pavement, and the water mean. Up to two classes plus shade are allowed per pixel.


Code
G, R, N, S1 = (hs.band_at(urban, wv).values for wv in (560, 650, 860, 1650))
ndvi, ndwi = (N - R) / (N + R), (G - N) / (G + N)
X = urban.values


def spectra_by_quantile(mask, score, qs):
    """Mean 3 x 3 spectra at the pixels of mask whose score is nearest each quantile."""
    out = []
    for q in qs:
        s = np.where(mask, score, np.nan)
        r, c = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmin(np.abs(s - np.nanquantile(s, q))), s.shape)
        out.append(X[:, max(r - 1, 0):r + 2, max(c - 1, 0):c + 2].reshape(X.shape[0], -1).mean(1))
    return np.array(out)


lib_m = {"vegetation": spectra_by_quantile(ndvi > 0.8, N, [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]),
         "impervious": spectra_by_quantile((ndvi < 0.12) & (ndwi < 0), S1, [0.05, 0.5, 0.97]),
         "water": X[:, ndwi > 0.3].mean(1, keepdims=True).T}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
ms = hs.mesma(urban, lib_m, max_classes=2, shade=True, max_rmse=0.03)
print(f"{len(ms.attrs['models'])} models tried in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s | "
      f"pixels with a model: {float((ms['model'] >= 0).mean()):.1%} | mean RMSE {float(ms['rmse'].mean()):.4f}")
used = pd.Series(ms["model"].values.ravel()).value_counts(normalize=True).head(6)
used.index = [ms.attrs["models"][i] if i >= 0 else "none" for i in used.index]
used.round(3).to_frame("share of pixels")

The model table shows which combinations the pixels chose: most of the window is explained by a vegetation plus impervious mixture, as expected in a city, and the shade fraction absorbs brightness differences between sunlit and shaded parts of a pixel. The class fractions are shade normalised, so they say how much of the non shaded part of a pixel is vegetation. The vegetation map agrees well with the N-FINDR vegetation fraction, but MESMA’s fractions are easier to interpret because each class has a name and several spectra.

title: Endmember Extraction and Spectral Unmixing
section: Sparse unmixing with a large library
text:
Sparse unmixing with a large library
ATGP extracts 30 candidate spectra from the window, more than any analyst would use. Sparse unmixing lets each pixel choose a few of them.


Code
big = hs.atgp(urban, 30)["library"]  # 30 candidate endmembers
t0 = time.perf_counter()
sp = hs.sparse_unmix(urban, big, lam=1e-3, max_iter=600)
print(f"sparse unmixing in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s | mean RMSE {float(sp['rmse'].mean()):.4f} "
      f"(FCLS with 6 endmembers: {float(ab['rmse'].mean()):.4f})")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
im = axes[0].imshow(sp["n_active"], cmap="viridis"); axes[0].set_title("Active library members per pixel"); axes[0].axis("off")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], shrink=0.8)
axes[1].hist(sp["n_active"].values.ravel(), bins=np.arange(0.5, 31.5, 1))
axes[1].set(xlabel="Active members", ylabel="Pixels", title="Sparsity")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


sparse unmixing in 16 s | mean RMSE 0.0023 (FCLS with 6 endmembers: 0.0116)









With 30 candidates the fit is five times better than with six FCLS endmembers, but at this penalty the solution is not very sparse: most pixels use 10 to 15 of the 30 members, and only parks and water use a few. The penalty lam sets the trade off: larger values give sparser, less accurate fits, and a value suited to the scale of the reflectance has to be chosen (see the exercises). Note that sparse unmixing here does not enforce the sum to one constraint.

title: Endmember Extraction and Spectral Unmixing
text:
Checking fractions against labels
The Pavia Centre ground truth labels pure looking pixels of nine classes. Using the mean spectrum of each class as an endmember, FCLS should give each labelled pixel a high fraction of its own class.


Code

pavia = hs.as_cube(arr.transpose(2, 0, 1).astype("float32") / 10000, np.linspace(430, 860, arr.shape[2]))

NAMES = ["water", "trees", "meadows", "self-blocking bricks", "bare soil", "asphalt", "bitumen", "tiles", "shadows"]

title: Endmember Extraction and Spectral Unmixing
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

The linear mixing model with non negativity and sum to one constraints (FCLS) gives physically meaningful fractions; LS, SCLS and NNLS fit as well but violate one constraint or both.
Extractors recover endmembers when pure pixels exist (dark ones stay noisy); on real scenes they return the extremes of the data, which may be rare pixels rather than typical materials.
Residual (RMSE) maps show where the endmember set is incomplete.
MESMA with shade handles variability within classes and brightness differences; sparse unmixing fits better with a large library, but its sparsity depends on the penalty.
Class mean endmembers validated on labelled pixels show which materials a sensor can separate.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: synthetic_library, as_cube, extract_endmembers (ppi, atgp, nfindr, vca), unmix, reconstruct, mesma, sparse_unmix, atgp, read_tanager, drop_bad_bands, band_at, plot_rgb, library.from_dict.
Exercises

Raise the synthetic noise to 0.02 and remove the pure corner blocks. How do the extractors do?
Extract 4, 8 and 12 N-FINDR endmembers for Portland and plot the mean RMSE against the number.
Run MESMA with max_classes=3. Which pixels choose three class models?
Change lam in sparse_unmix to 1e-4 and 1e-2 and compare sparsity and RMSE.
Unmix Pavia with class medians instead of means. Do the confused classes improve?

title: Biophysical and Biochemical Trait Retrieval
text: Banner

title: Biophysical and Biochemical Trait Retrieval
text:
Overview

Three routes from spectra to traits









Approach
How
Strengths
Weaknesses




Empirical
Regress field measured traits on image spectra (PLSR, ML)
Accurate where calibrated
Needs field data; site and date specific


Physical
Invert a radiative transfer model (look-up table or optimisation)
Transferable, no field data
Ill posed (different parameter sets give similar spectra); slow


Hybrid
Train a fast regressor on simulated spectra, apply to images
Transferable, fast, gives uncertainty (GPR)
Only as good as the model’s assumptions and parameter ranges





PROSAIL
PROSPECT (here version D, Féret et al. 2017) models a leaf as a stack of N layers with chlorophyll cab, carotenoids car, anthocyanins ant, brown pigments cbrown, equivalent water thickness cw and dry matter cm. 4SAIL (Verhoef 1984; Verhoef et al. 2007) turns leaf optics into canopy reflectance from lai, the mean leaf angle lidfa, the hot spot parameter, soil brightness and moisture (rsoil, psoil) and the sun and view geometry. Together they reproduce the main features of a canopy spectrum: the red edge moves with cab, the NIR rises with lai, the SWIR falls with cw and the dry matter features follow cm.


Regressors

Partial least squares regression (PLSR) projects the spectra onto a few latent components that covary with the trait. The number of components is chosen by cross validation; variable importance in projection (VIP) scores above about 1 mark influential bands.
Random forests handle non linearity but extrapolate poorly.
Gaussian process regression (GPR) gives a prediction and a standard deviation for every pixel, which flags spectra unlike the training data (Verrelst et al. 2015).



Validation
A model trained on simulations has to be validated against field measurements (destructive LAI, SPAD or extracted chlorophyll, leaf water) before its absolute values are used. Without field data, the honest checks are internal (how well the model inverts independent simulations) and physical (do the maps make sense and agree with indices).

title: Biophysical and Biochemical Trait Retrieval
text:
Trait Retrieval with GeoLattice
hs.prosail_spectrum and hs.prosail_lut run PROSAIL (it needs pip install prosail) and convolve the spectra to a cube’s bands. hs.fit_plsr and hs.fit_regressor return a TraitModel with cross validated metrics and a predict_map method; hs.hybrid_retrieval does the whole hybrid chain in one call; hs.vip_scores explains PLSR models.

Learning objectives

Run PROSAIL and see how LAI, chlorophyll, water and dry matter change a canopy spectrum.
Locate the wavelengths that carry each trait with a global sensitivity analysis.
Build a noisy look-up table on Tanager bands for the scene’s sun and view geometry.
Train and compare PLSR, random forest and GPR models, and interpret VIP scores.
Map LAI, chlorophyll and leaf water with uncertainty by hybrid retrieval.
Flag pixels whose spectra the model was not trained for.



Data







Dataset
Use




Tanager agriculture scene (Gran Chaco, 24 February 2025), 250 by 250 pixel window
Image to retrieve traits from; sun and view angles from the ancillary layers



No field measurements come with the scene, so all accuracy figures here are for simulated data.


Contents

Setup
The PROSAIL forward model
Which wavelengths carry which trait?
A look-up table for the scene
PLSR and variable importance
Random forest and Gaussian process regression
Hybrid retrieval on the Tanager scene
Where can the model be trusted?
Summary and exercises

title: Biophysical and Biochemical Trait Retrieval
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings

from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
from geolattice.rsense import hyperspectral as hs  # hyperspectral cubes, readers and tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_05_HyperSpectral")  # data folder next to this notebook
TANAGER = DATA / "Tanger"  # Planet Tanager sample scenes
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed


def tanager_file(category, product="sr"):
    """Path of a Tanager product (sr or radiance) for a scene category folder."""
    return next((TANAGER / category).glob(f"*/*_ortho_{product}_hdf5.h5"))


print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__)  # library version used for this notebook

import time  # timing

def test_metrics(model, trait):
    """R2 and RMSE of a TraitModel on the held-out simulations."""
    y, p = P[trait].to_numpy()[te], model.predict(Ste)
    return {"R2": 1 - np.sum((y - p) ** 2) / np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2), "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((y - p) ** 2))}

The visible and SWIR of the real forest match dense simulated canopies well, but its NIR plateau is about 0.15 lower (0.35 to 0.40 against 0.45 to 0.50). PROSAIL treats the canopy as a uniform layer of leaves (a turbid medium): it has no tree crowns, no gaps and no shadows between them. In a forest seen at 30 m, shadows between crowns lower the NIR, the region that carries LAI, so the best matching simulation is a much sparser canopy (LAI about 2) with wet, chlorophyll rich leaves, and the GPR, trained on noisy samples, goes lower still. That is exactly what the retrieval reports. PROSAIL based hybrid models are designed for crops and grasslands; forests need models with crown geometry (for example INFORM or DART) or empirical calibration with field data.

title: Biophysical and Biochemical Trait Retrieval
section: Where can the model be trusted?
text:
Where can the model be trusted?
A hybrid model only knows the spectra in its look-up table. The spectral angle from each pixel to its closest simulated spectrum measures how far outside the training space the pixel lies.


Code
X = cube.values.reshape(cube.sizes["band"], -1).T  # (pixels, bands)
ok = np.all(np.isfinite(X), 1)
Xn = X[ok] / np.linalg.norm(X[ok], axis=1, keepdims=True)  # unit vectors
L = hyb["lut"][1]
Ln = L / np.linalg.norm(L, axis=1, keepdims=True)
best = np.full(len(X), np.nan)
for s in range(0, len(Xn), 20000):  # nearest LUT spectrum by angle, in chunks
    best[np.flatnonzero(ok)[s:s + 20000]] = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip((Xn[s:s + 20000] @ Ln.T).max(1), -1, 1)))
angle = best.reshape(cube.shape[1:])
sd = maps["lai_std"].values
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.6))
im = axes[0].imshow(angle, cmap="inferno", vmax=np.nanpercentile(angle, 98)); axes[0].set_title("Angle to nearest LUT spectrum (deg)")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], shrink=0.8)
trusted = angle < 5  # within 5 degrees of a simulated canopy
axes[1].imshow(np.where(trusted, maps["lai"], np.nan), cmap="YlGn"); axes[1].set_title(f"LAI where angle < 5 deg ({trusted.mean():.0%} of pixels)")
m = np.isfinite(angle) & np.isfinite(sd)
axes[2].hexbin(angle[m], sd[m], gridsize=50, bins="log", cmap="viridis")
axes[2].set(xlabel="Angle to nearest LUT spectrum (deg)", ylabel="GPR LAI standard deviation",
            title=f"Spearman r = {spearmanr(angle[m], sd[m])[0]:.2f}")
for ax in axes[:2]:
    ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The river, the town and roads are far outside the table, because PROSAIL simulates only vegetation over soil, and the spectral angle correlates with the GPR standard deviation (Spearman r about 0.77): two independent signs of extrapolation, which mask these pixels well. But 98 percent of the pixels, including the whole forest, pass the 5 degree test. The spectral angle ignores brightness, and the forest’s shape resembles some simulated canopy even though its physics does not. Domain checks catch spectra that are obviously foreign; they cannot catch a model that is wrong for the vegetation type. In practice, choose a radiative transfer model suited to the canopy, restrict the LUT ranges to what is plausible for the crop or biome, and validate with field data (for example by fitting hs.fit_plsr to spectra extracted at field plots with hs.spectra_at).

title: Biophysical and Biochemical Trait Retrieval
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

PROSAIL links leaf biochemistry and canopy structure to reflectance; each trait has its own spectral signature, and some (carotenoids, leaf angle) are weakly expressed.
Global sensitivity analysis on a look-up table predicts which traits can be retrieved.
PLSR, random forests and GPR invert noisy simulations with similar skill for LAI, chlorophyll and water; VIP scores and sensitivity curves explain which bands matter.
Hybrid retrieval maps traits quickly, and GPR adds a standard deviation that flags spectra unlike the training data, but it does not rank errors inside the training space.
Applied to a closed forest, a PROSAIL (turbid medium) model gives plausible patterns but wrong values: crown shadows and gaps make the forest look like a sparse canopy. Spectral angle and GPR uncertainty catch foreign surfaces (water, town) but not a wrong model. Field validation and a canopy model suited to the vegetation remain essential.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: read_tanager, read_tanager_ancillary, drop_bad_bands, prosail_spectrum, prosail_lut, fit_plsr, fit_regressor, vip_scores (through fit_plsr), hybrid_retrieval, index, plot_rgb.

title: Dimensionality Reduction and Band Selection
text:
Overview

Why reduce dimensions

Redundancy: with 5 nm sampling, adjacent bands correlate above 0.99 over most of the spectrum. Storage, computation and many algorithms scale with the number of bands.
The Hughes phenomenon: with a fixed number of training samples, classifier accuracy first rises and then falls as features are added, because covariance and decision boundaries become poorly estimated in high dimensions.
Noise: a few components hold the signal; the rest is mostly noise. Separating them denoises.
Endmembers and detection (notebooks 09_05_07 and 09_05_08) work in a signal subspace whose size must be estimated.



Feature extraction

Principal component analysis (PCA) rotates the data onto orthogonal axes of decreasing variance. It ranks components by variance, not by quality, so a noisy but bright band can dominate.
Minimum noise fraction (MNF) (Green et al. 1988) first whitens the noise, using a noise covariance estimated from neighbouring pixel differences, and then applies PCA. Components are ordered by signal to noise ratio; the eigenvalue minus one is the SNR of each component. Inverting with only the leading components gives a denoised cube.
Independent component analysis (ICA) finds statistically independent, non Gaussian sources, which sometimes isolate single materials better than PCA.



Intrinsic dimension

HySime (Bioucas-Dias and Nascimento 2008) estimates the noise by spectral regression and keeps the eigenvectors whose signal power exceeds the noise power.
Virtual dimensionality (VD) (Harsanyi, Farrand and Chang) counts the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix that are significantly larger than those of the covariance matrix: each such pair indicates a distinct signal source.



Band selection
Feature extraction mixes all bands into new variables; band selection keeps a subset of the original bands, which stays physically interpretable and can guide the design of cheaper sensors. Unsupervised criteria use variance or redundancy; supervised criteria use class labels (mutual information, ANOVA F, random forest importance). A minimum spectral separation avoids picking neighbours that carry the same information.

The correlation matrix is made of large blocks: the visible, the NIR plateau and the SWIR each behave almost as one variable, and adjacent bands correlate above 0.99 nearly everywhere. The weakest links between neighbours are next to the removed absorption windows.

text:
Principal component analysis


Code
pc, pca_t = hs.pca(urban, 20)  # first 20 principal components
cum = np.cumsum(pca_t.explained_ratio)  # cumulative explained variance
print("explained variance of PC1 to PC5:", np.round(pca_t.explained_ratio[:5], 4))
print("components for 99% and 99.9%:", int(np.searchsorted(cum, 0.99) + 1), int(np.searchsorted(cum, 0.999) + 1))

axes[0].set(xlabel="Component", ylabel="Explained variance ratio", title="PCA scree plot")
for k in range(4):
    axes[1].plot(wl, pca_t.components[k], label=f"PC{k + 1}")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


explained variance of PC1 to PC5: [0.6667 0.2845 0.0379 0.0064 0.0013]
components for 99% and 99.9%: 4 12











Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(15, 7.5))
for k, ax in enumerate(axes.ravel()):
    comp = [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 14, 19][k]  # components to show
    ax.imshow(pc.isel(component=comp), cmap="gray", vmin=np.nanpercentile(pc.isel(component=comp), 2),
              vmax=np.nanpercentile(pc.isel(component=comp), 98))
    ax.set_title(f"PC{comp + 1}"); ax.axis("off")
plt.suptitle("Principal component images")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The first component is overall brightness (its loadings have one sign everywhere) and the second contrasts visible and NIR, which separates vegetation from built surfaces. Together the first few components hold more than 99 percent of the variance. Higher components carry less and less structure and more speckle and striping, but because PCA ranks by variance, real but faint features and noise are mixed in the same components.

title: Dimensionality Reduction and Band Selection
text:
Minimum noise fraction
hs.mnf estimates the noise covariance from neighbouring pixel differences, whitens it, and orders the components by SNR.


Code
mn, mnf_t = hs.mnf(urban, 30)  # first 30 MNF components
snr = mnf_t.eigenvalues - 1  # SNR of each component
print("SNR of MNF1 to MNF5:", np.round(snr[:5], 1), "| components with SNR > 1:", int((snr > 1).sum()))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(15, 7.5))
for k, ax in enumerate(axes.ravel()):
    comp = [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 19, 29][k]
    img = mn.isel(component=comp)
    ax.imshow(img, cmap="gray", vmin=np.nanpercentile(img, 2), vmax=np.nanpercentile(img, 98))
    ax.set_title(f"MNF{comp + 1} (SNR {snr[comp]:.1f})"); ax.axis("off")
plt.suptitle("Minimum noise fraction component images")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


SNR of MNF1 to MNF5: [726.9 126.3  61.3  17.   16. ] | components with SNR > 1: 46











Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.semilogy(np.arange(1, 31), np.clip(snr[:30], 1e-3, None), "o-", color="C1")
ax.axhline(1, color="0.5", ls="--")
ax.set(xlabel="MNF component", ylabel="SNR (eigenvalue - 1)", title="MNF eigenvalues")
plt.show()









MNF components are ordered by SNR rather than by variance, and the result here is instructive. The first three components are smooth, large scale patterns with very high SNR: the shift difference noise model sees almost no pixel to pixel change in them, so they look noise free, whatever their origin (residual atmospheric gradients or smooth land cover trends). The street grid and the parks appear from MNF4 on, and the late components show diagonal striping and speckle. The catch is that the shift difference method estimated “noise” from neighbouring pixels, and in a city most of the difference between neighbouring 30 m pixels is real texture. MNF then rates much of the urban detail as noise. The next section shows the consequence.

title: Dimensionality Reduction and Band Selection
text:
Denoising with MNF
hs.mnf_denoise(cube, k) transforms to MNF space, keeps the first k components and transforms back. It is run with both noise models: the default shift difference and the spectral residual model (noise="residual"), which estimates noise from each band’s spectral neighbours and is not fooled by spatial texture. Noise is measured before and after with the residual method from notebook 09_05_02, and the reconstruction error shows how much real signal each version removes.


Code
n0 = hs.estimate_noise(urban, method="residual")  # per band noise before
versions = {"shift noise model": hs.mnf_denoise(urban, 20),  # default noise model
            "residual noise model": hs.mnf_denoise(urban, 20, noise="residual")}
rows = []
for name, den in versions.items():
    rows.append({"MNF denoising (20 components)": name,
                 "median noise before": np.median(n0),
                 "median noise after": np.median(hs.estimate_noise(den, method="residual")),
                 "RMS change to the cube": float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean((den.values - urban.values) ** 2)))})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("MNF denoising (20 components)").round(5))

G, N = hs.band_at(urban, 560).values, hs.band_at(urban, 860).values  # pick a vegetated pixel
r, c = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax((N - G) / (N + G)), N.shape)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.2))
ax.plot(wl, urban.values[:, r, c], lw=2, color="0.5", label="original")
for name, den in versions.items():
    ax.plot(wl, den.values[:, r, c], lw=1, label=f"denoised, {name}")
ax.set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Reflectance", title=f"Vegetated pixel ({r}, {c})"); ax.legend()
plt.show()

Both versions lower the band to band noise, but only the residual model keeps the signal. With the shift difference model the cube changes by about 0.02 in reflectance on average, far more than the noise itself (about 0.001): real urban detail rated as “noise” has been thrown away. Even this vegetated pixel, an easy case, is shifted away from the original in the NIR and SWIR, and darker or mixed pixels change much more. With the residual model the change is about the size of the noise, and the denoised spectrum follows the original without its jitter. MNF is only as good as its noise estimate: the classic shift difference model suits smooth scenes, while textured scenes (cities, mixed agriculture) need a spectral noise model. The choice of k matters too: keep somewhat more components than the intrinsic dimension estimated below, or rare materials are lost.

title: Dimensionality Reduction and Band Selection
text:
Independent components


Code
ic, ica_model = hs.ica(urban, 8, sample=40_000)  # 8 independent components
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(15, 7.5))
for k, ax in enumerate(axes.ravel()):
    img = ic.isel(component=k)
    ax.imshow(img, cmap="gray", vmin=np.nanpercentile(img, 1), vmax=np.nanpercentile(img, 99))
    ax.set_title(f"IC{k + 1}"); ax.axis("off")
plt.suptitle("Independent component images")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









ICA components have no natural order. Some of them pick out a single kind of surface (water, vegetation, particular roofs) more cleanly than any PCA component, because ICA looks for sparse, non Gaussian sources rather than for directions of maximum variance. They are useful features for classification and for finding rare targets.

How many components?
The Pavia Centre cube and its ground truth are loaded here for this and the next section. The 9 classes follow the dataset documentation.

The estimates disagree, and that is typical. Variance thresholds count how many components describe the data’s spread, which says little about how many distinct materials there are. HySime and VD are statistical tests whose answer depends on the noise model and on the number of pixels; with tens of thousands of pixels they find many components significant. Treat them as ranges, not exact answers: here, a few to a few tens of components describe each scene. Notebook 09_05_07 uses such an estimate to choose the number of endmembers.

title: Dimensionality Reduction and Band Selection
text:
Band selection and classification
How much is lost by keeping only ten bands? A random forest is trained on Pavia with all 102 bands, with ten bands chosen in four ways, and with the first ten PCA and MNF components. Training and test pixels come from different 32 by 32 pixel blocks (block_split), so neighbouring pixels never sit on both sides; a random pixel split would inflate the accuracy.


Code

Ten PCA or MNF components classify the held-out blocks slightly better than all 102 bands (overall accuracy about 0.96 to 0.97 against 0.955), and ten bands chosen by decorrelation or random forest importance come within one point of all bands. Mutual information is a little lower because it picks mostly correlated bands on the red edge and NIR plateau. The variance criterion fails (about 0.80): all ten of its bands sit side by side on the bright NIR plateau, where classes spread most but carry the same information. Decorrelation spreads its picks across the blue, the red and the red edge, and the random forest adds a green band, which is why both work well. With this many training pixels the Hughes effect is small for a random forest; it matters more for parametric classifiers and small training sets.

title: Dimensionality Reduction and Band Selection
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Adjacent hyperspectral bands are almost perfectly correlated; the spectrum behaves like a few blocks of variables.
PCA concentrates variance in a few components but ranks noise and signal together; MNF ranks by SNR, but only as well as its noise model allows.
In textured scenes the shift difference noise model treats real detail as noise; MNF denoising with the spectral residual model removes band to band noise and keeps the signal.
Intrinsic dimension estimates (HySime, VD, variance thresholds) disagree; use them as ranges.
A few bands or components retain nearly all the class information; supervised selection with a spectral separation gives interpretable subsets.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: read_tanager, drop_bad_bands, as_cube, pca, mnf, mnf_denoise, ica, estimate_noise, hysime, virtual_dimensionality, select_bands; geolattice.rsense.dl.hyperspectral.block_split.
Exercises

Repeat the PCA scree plot on the snow and ice scene. How many components reach 99 percent?
Denoise with 5, 10, 20 and 40 MNF components and plot the residual noise against k.
Change block_split(block=...) to 8 and 64 pixels. How does the measured accuracy change, and why?
Train with only 300 pixels. Does the gap between all bands and ten bands grow?
Use select_bands(..., method="anova") and compare its bands with mutual information.

title: Reading and Exploring Hyperspectral Data
text:
Overview

Containers and layouts








Format
Typical products
What to look for




HDF5 / HDF-EOS5
Tanager, PRISMA, EMIT (NetCDF4 is HDF5 inside)
Groups and datasets; band metadata in attributes; grid georeferencing in StructMetadata.0


NetCDF
EMIT L1B and L2A
sensor_band_parameters (wavelengths, FWHM, good bands) and a location group with a geometry lookup table


ENVI
AVIRIS-NG, AVIRIS-3, HySpex, many processing chains
A text .hdr with wavelength, fwhm, bbl (bad band list), map info, data ignore value, reflectance scale factor; data in BSQ, BIL or BIP


GeoTIFF
EnMAP (one multiband file), OHS (one file per band)
Band descriptions or tags for wavelengths; side car XML for gains and band centres


Arrays and images
Benchmarks (Pavia), laboratory cameras
Wavelengths come from a separate table or the file names



Band sequential (BSQ) storage is fast for reading whole bands, BIP for reading whole spectra and BIL is a compromise. HDF5 files are usually chunked and compressed, so reading a window or a few bands touches only the chunks that hold them.


Metadata that matters

Wavelengths and FWHM for every band, in nm or µm.
Good band flags (good_wavelengths in Tanager and EMIT, bbl in ENVI): bands to ignore.
Fill values (often -9999 or 0) and no-data masks.
Scale factors and offsets to turn stored integers into radiance or reflectance.
Units: radiance in W m⁻² sr⁻¹ µm⁻¹ (or µW cm⁻² sr⁻¹ nm⁻¹, a factor of 10 apart), reflectance as a fraction or in percent or scaled by 10,000.



Geometry: swath, grid and RPC
Pushbroom data are acquired as a swath: lines along track by samples across track, in sensor geometry. Three ways bring them to a map:

an orthorectified grid delivered by the provider (Tanager ortho, EMIT with its geometry lookup table, PRISMA L2D, EnMAP L2A);
per pixel latitude and longitude (Tanager basic, PRISMA L2B and L2C), resampled by the user;
a rational polynomial camera (RPC) model plus a terrain height (OHS, most commercial satellites), which maps image coordinates to ground coordinates.

Gridding a swath with nearest neighbour keeps the original spectra unchanged, which matters for spectral analysis; bilinear or cubic resampling mixes neighbouring spectra.


Working with large cubes
A full Tanager scene holds about 220 million values. Read only what you need (a window, a bounding box, a wavelength range or a few bands), keep float32, and write analysis ready subsets to ENVI or GeoTIFF once instead of reopening the HDF5 file in every step.

title: Reading and Exploring Hyperspectral Data
text:
Reading Hyperspectral Data with GeoLattice
GeoLattice has one reader per product family and a dispatcher, hs.read_hyperspectral, that picks the reader from the file. All return a cube (band, y, x) (or (band, line, sample) for swaths) with wavelength, fwhm and good coordinates, fill values as NaN and a CRS when known.

Learning objectives

Inspect the structure of an HDF-EOS5 file and find the band metadata.
Read Tanager products whole or by window, bounding box, band list or wavelength range, and know what each costs.
Grid a Tanager swath from its latitude and longitude with hs.swath_to_grid and check it against the provider’s orthorectified product.
Read an OHS scene in sensor geometry and orthorectify it with its RPCs.
Turn a NumPy array or a folder of images into a cube with hs.as_cube.
Explore cubes with band statistics, spectral profiles and composites.
Write subsets to ENVI and read them back.

Reading the whole cube decompresses every chunk and takes a few seconds; a window, a bounding box or a few bands is much faster and smaller. title: Reading and Exploring Hyperspectral Data
text:
Ortho grid and basic swath
The basic product is the same acquisition before orthorectification: lines and samples in sensor geometry, with latitude and longitude for every pixel. hs.swath_to_grid places each grid cell on the nearest swath pixel; with a 30 m grid aligned to multiples of 30 m it lands on the same cells as Planet’s ortho product, so the two can be compared pixel by pixel.


Code
basic = DATA / "20250224_145149_32_4001_basic_radiance_hdf5.h5"  # swath radiance
sw = hs.read_hyperspectral(basic, wavelength_range=(840, 880))  # dispatcher picks read_tanager
print(sw.dims, sw.shape, "| lat:", round(float(sw.lat.min()), 3), "to", round(float(sw.lat.max()), 3))
grid = hs.swath_to_grid(sw, 30.0)  # nearest-neighbour gridding to UTM, 30 m
ortho = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("agriculture", "radiance"), wavelength_range=(840, 880))  # provider grid
print("gridded:", grid.shape, grid.rio.crs, "| ortho:", ortho.shape, ortho.rio.crs)


('band', 'line', 'sample') (8, 501, 607) | lat: -22.275 to -22.095
gridded: (8, 663, 774) EPSG:32720 | ortho: (8, 663, 775) EPSG:32720




Code
a, b = grid.isel(band=4), ortho.isel(band=4)  # one NIR band (about 861 nm) from each
common_x = np.intersect1d(a.x.values, b.x.values)  # shared grid columns
common_y = np.intersect1d(a.y.values, b.y.values)  # shared grid rows
A = a.sel(x=common_x, y=common_y).values  # gridded swath on the common cells
B = b.sel(x=common_x, y=common_y).values  # ortho product on the same cells
ok = np.isfinite(A) & np.isfinite(B)  # cells valid in both
print(f"common cells: {ok.sum():,} | identical values: {np.mean(np.isclose(A[ok], B[ok])):.1%} | "
      f"correlation: {np.corrcoef(A[ok], B[ok])[0, 1]:.4f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.8))
axes[0].imshow(sw.isel(band=4), cmap="gray", vmax=np.nanpercentile(sw.isel(band=4), 99))
axes[0].set_title("Basic swath (line, sample)")
for ax, img, t in [(axes[1], A, "Gridded with swath_to_grid"), (axes[2], B, "Planet ortho product")]:
    ax.imshow(img, cmap="gray", vmax=np.nanpercentile(B, 99)); ax.set_title(t)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


common cells: 368,045 | identical values: 98.9% | correlation: 0.9989









The swath is the image as the sensor saw it, unrotated. After gridding, most cells hold exactly the value of Planet’s ortho product and the correlation is close to one; the rest differ because the two nearest neighbour searches break ties differently near the swath edges and Planet’s processor uses its own terrain model. Gridding your own swath therefore reproduces the provider’s grid, which is useful when only the basic product is available or when a different grid is needed.

section: OHS: band files and RPC orthorectification
text:
OHS: band files and RPC orthorectification
An OHS L1 scene is 32 single band GeoTIFFs of 5056 by 5056 pixels with a shared RPC model and a *_meta.xml. hs.read_ohs stacks the bands in order, attaches the nominal band centres and keeps the RPCs; window= reads a part of the image and ortho=True warps it to a map.

print({k: v for k, v in ohs.attrs.items() if k != "rpcs"})

text:
Arrays and image folders: Pavia and HACARUS
Benchmarks are often distributed as arrays without metadata. hs.as_cube adds the band axis and wavelengths. The Pavia Centre array is (rows, cols, bands), so it is transposed first; its 102 ROSIS bands span about 430 to 860 nm and are treated as evenly spaced.


Code
arr = np.load(DATA / "Pavia/pavia.npy")  # (1096, 715, 102) uint16
pavia = hs.as_cube(arr.transpose(2, 0, 1).astype("float32") / 10000, np.linspace(430, 860, arr.shape[2]))
print(pavia.shape, "| reflectance range:", float(pavia.min()), "to", round(float(pavia.max()), 3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 7.5))
hs.plot_rgb(pavia, (640, 550, 460), ax=axes[0], title="Pavia Centre, true colour")
hs.plot_rgb(pavia, "color_infrared", ax=axes[1], title="Pavia Centre, colour infrared")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


(102, 1096, 715) | reflectance range: 0.0 to 0.8









Pavia Centre is a 1.3 m ROSIS image of the historic centre of Pavia and the Ticino river. The vertical seam about a third of the way across is where the dataset authors removed a strip of pixels without information and joined the two parts. Dividing by 10,000 gives reflectance assuming the common scaling of this benchmark.


Code
def read_png_cube(folder):
    """Stack the *_<wavelength>nm.png band images of a HACARUS scene into a cube."""
    files = sorted(Path(folder).glob("*nm.png"), key=lambda p: float(re.search(r"_(\d+)nm", p.name)[1]))
    wl = [float(re.search(r"_(\d+)nm", p.name)[1]) for p in files]  # wavelength from the file name
    stack = np.stack([np.asarray(Image.open(p), dtype="float32") for p in files])  # (band, row, col)
    return hs.as_cube(stack, wl, name="dn")


lab = {p.name: read_png_cube(p) for p in sorted((DATA / "archive/data").iterdir())}  # all five scenes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 4.2))

Exploring a cube
The urban scene (Portland, Oregon) mixes many materials. A 300 by 300 pixel window is centred on the open water pixel nearest the scene centre, so it holds a stretch of river and the surrounding city; it is read with all bands, then explored with band statistics, composites and spectral profiles.

few = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("urban"), bands=[37, 97])  # green and NIR of the whole scene
g, n = few.values  # 561 and 861 nm
water = (g - n) / (g + n) > 0.3  # open water by NDWI

urban = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("urban"), window=(slice(r0, r0 + 300), slice(c0, c0 + 300)))  # 9 x 9 km
print("window rows", r0, "to", r0 + 300, "| cols", c0, "to", c0 + 300)

def pick(score, q):
    """(row, col) of the pixel whose score is closest to its q-th quantile."""
    return np.unravel_index(np.nanargmin(np.abs(score - np.nanquantile(score, q))), score.shape)


pts = {"water": pick(np.where(ndwi > 0.3, N, np.nan), 0.5),  # typical open water pixel

       "bright roof": pick(np.where(ndvi < 0.1, S1, np.nan), 0.99),  # brightest non-vegetated SWIR
       "dark pavement": pick(np.where((ndvi < 0.1) & (ndwi < 0), S1, np.nan), 0.1)}  # dark, dry, bare

text:
Writing and reusing subsets
ENVI is the simplest interchange format for cubes: a raw binary file plus a text header that keeps wavelengths, FWHM, the bad band list and the map information. hs.write_envi writes a cube, hs.read_envi reads it back (also by window and bands through a memory map), and hs.subset_file cuts a smaller file out of a large one without loading it.

      "| CRS:", back.rio.crs, "| wavelengths kept:", bool(np.allclose(hs.wavelengths(back), hs.wavelengths(urban))))

title: Reading and Exploring Hyperspectral Data
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Hyperspectral containers differ (HDF-EOS5, NetCDF, ENVI, GeoTIFF, arrays, images) but carry the same essentials: wavelengths, FWHM, good bands, fill values, scale factors and georeferencing.
HDF5 chunking makes windows, bounding boxes and band subsets cheap; whole cube reads are not.
Swaths are in sensor geometry. Nearest neighbour gridding from per pixel latitude and longitude (hs.swath_to_grid) reproduces the provider’s 30 m grid for Tanager; RPCs orthorectify OHS.
hs.as_cube turns any array into a GeoLattice cube once the wavelengths are known.
Band statistics, composites and spectral profiles are the first look at any cube; ENVI files make subsets fast to reuse.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: read_tanager, read_hyperspectral, swath_to_grid, read_ohs, as_cube, band_at, wavelengths, band_stats, plot_band_stats, plot_rgb, spectra_at, plot_spectra, spectral_viewer, write_envi, read_envi, subset_file.
Exercises

Time a read of the snow and ice scene with wavelength_range=(2000, 2400) and with bands= set to every tenth band. Which is faster, and why?
Grid the agriculture swath at 60 m with swath_to_grid(sw, 60.0) and compare it with the 30 m ortho product aggregated to 60 m (coarsen(x=2, y=2).mean()).
Orthorectify the OHS window with crs="EPSG:4326" and a resolution of 0.0001°. How many pixels does the result have, and why is it not square?
Write the Portland window as BIP with write_envi(..., interleave="bip") and time reading one full spectrum and one full band from the BSQ and BIP files.

Overview
The table holds canopy cover, greenness, yellowing, plant and panicle counts and height, followed through the season and summarised as growth curves and stage dates. This notebook builds that table from the LUMS rice frames with rs.uav.trait_table and rs.uav.frame_traits, fits logistic curves with rs.uav.fit_logistic, finds stage dates with rs.uav.detect_stages, adds a short thermal water-stress section with rs.uav.cwsi, and closes with one reproducible function that goes from a folder of frames to CSV and GeoPackage outputs and a short report.

Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # control warning messages
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide library warnings

from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import xarray as xr  # labelled arrays
import geopandas as gpd  # GeoPackage export
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
from shapely.geometry import box  # zone polygons

import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing (rs.uav = drone tools)

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_04_uav")
LUMS = DATA / "infrastructure-free-uav-phenotyping"

rs.uav.frame_traits(image, ...) returns a dictionary of standard RGB traits for one frame: canopy cover, mean ExG, VARI and TGI inside the vegetation mask, the senescent fraction (colour rule with the calibrated hue) and, optionally, a plant count. rs.uav.trait_table runs it over every catalogue row.                             min_distance=0.15, sigma=0.03)  # metres
    area = image.sizes["x"] * image.sizes["y"] * image.attrs["gsd_m"] ** 2
    t["plants_per_m2"] = t.pop("plant_count") / area
    return t

title: Season-Long Phenotyping
text:
Growth curves and stage dates
A four-parameter logistic, \(y = \text{base} + \text{amp} / (1 + e^{-r(t - t_{mid})})\), fits most growth traits. rs.uav.fit_logistic(dates, values) returns the parameters, the inflection date and the maximum growth rate; rs.uav.detect_stages(fit) turns the fit into the dates at which 10 %, 50 % and 90 % of the change is reached (onset, mid, plateau). Fitting to all frames, not only the date means, keeps the frame-to-frame spread in the fit.
With flights a week apart and noisy frames, an unconstrained fit can collapse into a step between two flights, with “stages” hours apart. fit_logistic therefore bounds the rate so the 10-90 % transition lasts at least min_transition_days (default: twice the median gap between flights); a transition shorter than that cannot be resolved by the data anyway.
