title: Season-Long Phenotyping
section: Thermal imagery and the Crop Water Stress Index
text:
Thermal imagery and the Crop Water Stress Index
A transpiring canopy is cooler than the air; a water-stressed one closes its stomata and warms up. The Crop Water Stress Index scales canopy temperature \(T_c\) between a wet (fully transpiring) and a dry (non-transpiring) limit:
\[CWSI = \frac{T_c - T_{wet}}{T_{dry} - T_{wet}}\]
rs.uav.cwsi offers three ways to set the limits: statistical (low and high percentiles of canopy pixels), reference (measured wet and dry reference surfaces) and empirical (Idso’s non-water-stressed baseline \(T_c - T_a = a + b \cdot VPD\), with \(b < 0\)).
No thermal camera flew over the LUMS field, so a synthetic thermal frame is built from a real RGB frame: soil and water get soil temperature, the canopy gets the unstressed baseline temperature plus a stress pattern (a dry patch on one side), and a radiometric camera’s raw counts are simulated so that rs.uav.raw_to_celsius can convert them back.


Code
rgb_img = rs.uav.read_frame(sorted((LUMS / "2025-09-12").glob("*.png"))[3], max_dim=960)
veg = rs.uav.exg_plant_mask(rgb_img, min_area=200).astype(bool)
ta, vpd = 33.0, 2.6  # air temperature (°C) and vapour pressure deficit (kPa) at flight time
t_wet_true = ta + 3.38 - 3.25 * vpd  # Idso (1982) wheat-like baseline as stand-in for rice
t_dry_true = ta + 5.0
rows_, cols_ = veg.shape
xx = np.linspace(0, 1, cols_)[None, :].repeat(rows_, 0)
stress_true = np.clip((xx - 0.45) / 0.4, 0, 1) * 0.8  # dry patch towards the right
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
tc = np.where(veg, t_wet_true + stress_true * (t_dry_true - t_wet_true), ta + 9.0) + rng.normal(0, 0.4, veg.shape)
raw = xr.DataArray(((tc + 273.15) / 0.04).round().astype("uint16"), dims=("y", "x"),
                   coords={"y": rgb_img.y, "x": rgb_img.x})  # radiometric counts
temp = rs.uav.raw_to_celsius(raw)  # back to °C (gain 0.04 K/count)
veg_da = xr.DataArray(veg, dims=("y", "x"), coords=temp.coords)
print(f"Ta {ta} °C, VPD {vpd} kPa: true Twet {t_wet_true:.1f} °C, Tdry {t_dry_true:.1f} °C")

methods = {
    "statistical (5-95 %)": rs.uav.cwsi(temp, method="statistical", vegetation=veg_da),
    "reference": rs.uav.cwsi(temp, method="reference", t_wet=t_wet_true, t_dry=t_dry_true, vegetation=veg_da),
    "empirical (Idso)": rs.uav.cwsi(temp, method="empirical", air_temp=ta, vpd=vpd, vegetation=veg_da),
}
truth_c = np.where(veg, stress_true, np.nan)
pd.DataFrame({k: {"Twet": v.attrs["t_wet"], "Tdry": v.attrs["t_dry"], "mean CWSI": float(v.mean()),
                  "RMSE vs truth": float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean((v.values - truth_c) ** 2)))} for k, v in methods.items()}).T.round(3)

The empirical and reference methods are anchored to physics and to measurements and can say how stressed the whole field is.

title: Season-Long Phenotyping
text:
Capstone: one reproducible pipeline
The function below turns a folder of dated frames into a full set of outputs in one call. Every choice made in this module is an explicit argument with its default documented, so a rerun next season, on another field or by another analyst, gives the same numbers.


Code
def phenotype_pipeline(root, out_dir, *, crop="rice", gsd=0.00185, max_dim=1280,
                       exg_threshold=0.10, hue_max=62.0, spacing_m=0.15, zones=(4, 6)):
    """Folder of dated UAV frames -> per-frame and per-date traits, growth fits,
    per-zone GeoPackage and a Markdown report.

    root          : folder with one sub-folder per flight date (YYYY-MM-DD or DDMMYYYY)
    gsd           : ground sampling distance of the full-size frames (m/px)
    max_dim       : frames are read downsized to this longest side for speed
    exg_threshold : fixed ExG cut for canopy cover (Otsu fails after canopy closure)
    hue_max       : green/yellow hue cut for the senescence colour rule (degrees)
    spacing_m     : minimum plant spacing for peak counting (m)
    zones         : (rows, cols) grid of zones per frame for the GeoPackage
    """
    out = Path(out_dir); out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cat_ = rs.uav.build_catalog(root)
    cat_ = cat_[cat_.band == "RGB"].assign(crop=crop).reset_index(drop=True)

    def one(image):
        t = rs.uav.frame_traits(image, threshold=exg_threshold, hue_max=hue_max, count=True,
                                min_distance=spacing_m, sigma=spacing_m / 5)
        t["plants_per_m2"] = t.pop("plant_count") / (image.sizes["x"] * image.sizes["y"] * image.attrs["gsd_m"] ** 2)
        return t

    frames_ = rs.uav.trait_table(cat_, one, max_dim=max_dim, gsd=gsd)
    trait_cols = ["canopy_cover", "ExG_veg_mean", "VARI_veg_mean", "senescent_frac", "plants_per_m2"]
    dates_ = rs.uav.summarize_dates(frames_, trait_cols)
    fits = {}
    for c in ["canopy_cover", "senescent_frac"]:
        try:
            f_ = rs.uav.fit_logistic(frames_.date, frames_[c], limits=(0, 1))
            fits[c] = {"mid_date": f_["mid_date"].date(), "max_rate_per_day": f_["max_rate"], "r2": f_["r2"],
                       **{f"{r.stage}_date": r.date.date() for r in rs.uav.detect_stages(f_).itertuples()}}
        except Exception as e:  # too few dates or no convergence
            fits[c] = {"error": str(e)}
    fits = pd.DataFrame(fits).T

    # per-zone health for the last date's frames, as polygons in each frame's local metres
    polys = []
    for r in frames_[frames_.date == frames_.date.max()].itertuples():
        im = rs.uav.read_frame(r.path, gsd=gsd, max_dim=max_dim)
        lab = rs.uav.health_map(im, mask_method="none", hue_max=hue_max, tile=2048, overlap=0)
        zr, zc = zones
        H_, W_ = lab.shape
        zid = (np.arange(H_)[:, None] * zr // H_) * zc + (np.arange(W_)[None, :] * zc // W_) + 1
        summ = rs.uav.health_summary(lab, zid)
        res = im.attrs["gsd_m"]
        for s in summ.itertuples():
            i, j = divmod(s.zone - 1, zc)
            polys.append({"frame": Path(r.path).name, "date": str(r.date.date()), "zone": s.zone,
                          "plant_cover": s.plant_cover, "senescent_frac": s.senescent_frac,
                          "geometry": box(j * W_ / zc * res, -(i + 1) * H_ / zr * res, (j + 1) * W_ / zc * res, -i * H_ / zr * res)})
    zones_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(polys, geometry="geometry")  # local frame metres, no CRS

    frames_.to_csv(out / "traits_frames.csv", index=False)
    dates_.to_csv(out / "traits_dates.csv", index=False)
    fits.to_csv(out / "growth_fits.csv")
    zones_gdf.to_file(out / "health_zones.gpkg", layer="health_zones", driver="GPKG")
    report = [f"# UAV phenotyping report: {crop}", "",
              f"* Frames: {len(frames_)} over {frames_.date.nunique()} dates "
              f"({frames_.date.min():%d %b %Y} to {frames_.date.max():%d %b %Y})",
              f"* Settings: GSD {gsd * 1000:.2f} mm, ExG cover threshold {exg_threshold}, hue cut {hue_max}°, "
              f"plant spacing {spacing_m} m", "", "## Per-date means", "",
              dates_[["date"] + [f"{c}_mean" for c in trait_cols]].round(3).to_markdown(index=False), "",
              "## Growth fits", "", fits.round(4).to_markdown(), "",
              "Caveats: frames per date come from different locations; cover and senescence come from colour",
              "rules calibrated on this data set; panicle and height traits are not included.", ""]
    (out / "report.md").write_text("\n".join(report))
    return {"frames": frames_, "dates": dates_, "fits": fits, "zones": zones_gdf, "out_dir": out}

title: Season-Long Phenotyping
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Phenotyping is one table: canopy cover, greenness, yellowing, counts and height, with one row per flight date.
A logistic fit supplies onset, mid-point and plateau. Curvature of that curve dates the stages.
CWSI needs canopy temperature, air temperature and a non-stressed baseline. The thermal frame in Section 6 is built because the LUMS folder has no thermal imagery.
The capstone function writes the table, the curves, a GeoPackage and a short report from a folder of frames.

GeoLattice functions used: rs.uav.frame_traits, rs.uav.trait_table, rs.uav.summarize_dates, rs.uav.fit_logistic, rs.uav.detect_stages, rs.uav.growth_rates, rs.uav.cwsi, rs.uav.health_summary.
Exercises

Rerun phenotype_pipeline with exg_threshold=None (Otsu). How do the canopy-cover fit and its stage dates change?
Add a VARI-based cover column to traits and fit a logistic to it. Does VARI date the canopy closure differently from ExG?
In Section 6, raise vpd to 3.5 kPa without changing the canopy temperatures. What happens to the empirical CWSI, and why?
Extend the pipeline to write a plot-level GeoPackage in a real CRS, given an orthomosaic GeoTIFF and plot polygons (rs.uav.plants_per_area, rs.uav.health_summary with rasterised zones).

References

Chaudhry, H., Rana, S. and Jaleel, A. (2026). UAV-based crop reconstruction and trait estimation using RGB imagery without external geospatial infrastructure. Computers and Electronics in Agriculture (accepted).
Idso, S. B. et al. (1981). Normalizing the stress-degree-day parameter for environmental variability. Agricultural Meteorology, 24, 45-55.
Idso, S. B. (1982). Non-water-stressed baselines: a key to measuring and interpreting plant water stress. Agricultural Meteorology, 27, 59-70.
Zhang, X. et al. (2003). Monitoring vegetation phenology using MODIS. Remote Sensing of Environment, 84, 471-475 (logistic phenology and curvature-based stage dates).
Jones, H. G. (1999). Use of infrared thermometry for estimation of stomatal conductance as a possible aid to irrigation scheduling. Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, 95, 139-149.

title: Crop Health: SAM Plant Masks and Senescence Detection
text:
Overview
Mapping yellowing leaves from RGB imagery takes two steps: separate plant from background (in flooded rice the background is water, mud and glare), then split plant pixels into green and senescent. The LUMS study did the first with the Segment Anything Model (SAM), prompted automatically with Excess-Green seed points, and the second with the SegVeg pixel classifier followed by an HSV filter. This notebook rebuilds that pipeline with rs.uav.sam_plant_mask, classify_senescence, hsv_filter, health_map and health_summary, with model-free fallbacks so it runs without downloading any weights.

title: Crop Health: SAM Plant Masks and Senescence Detection
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Build plant masks with ExG + Otsu and understand where they fail.
Generate SAM prompts from colour (positive ExG seeds, negative soil/water/glare points) and run SAM on a frame (sam_plant_mask) or a GeoTIFF (sam_segment).
Classify plant pixels as green or senescent with a colour rule or a SegVeg-style classifier, and clean the result with an HSV filter.
Map health tile by tile over a large image and summarise yellow-leaf fraction per plot.
Follow the senescent fraction through the season.



Data







Data
Type




LUMS rice frames: 28 Aug for early health, then late September and October (Data/08_remote_sensing/08_04_uav/infrastructure-free-uav-phenotyping)
Real (CC BY 4.0)

Real, optional Google Drive download





Contents

Setup
Plant masks from colour
SAM with automatic prompts
Green or senescent?
A SegVeg-style pixel classifier
Large images: tiled health maps and per-plot summaries
The season in yellow
Summary and exercises

title: Crop Health: SAM Plant Masks and Senescence Detection
text:
Plant masks from colour
rs.uav.exg_plant_mask thresholds Excess Green with Otsu and cleans the mask (morphological open/close, small components removed). It is fast and needs no model, but it inherits ExG’s weakness: yellow leaves have low ExG, so they drop out of the “plant” mask, exactly the pixels this notebook is trying to find.


Code
m_exg = rs.uav.exg_plant_mask(img, min_area=300)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.2))
axes[0].imshow(rgb8); axes[0].set_title(f"RGB, {late[2].parent.name}")
axes[1].imshow(rgb8); axes[1].imshow(np.ma.masked_equal(m_exg, 1), cmap="gray", alpha=0.75)
axes[1].set_title(f"ExG plant mask (non-plant greyed): {m_exg.mean():.0%} plant")
for a in axes: a.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

title: Crop Health: SAM Plant Masks and Senescence Detection
text:
SAM with automatic prompts
SAM segments “objects” given prompt points but has no idea what a plant is. LUMS seeded it automatically: positive points where ExG is high and saturated (certainly vegetation), negative points where it is low (soil, water) or bright and grey (glare), spread over the image so no region is missed. health.prompt_points reproduces this; rs.uav.sam_plant_mask runs SAM with those prompts and keeps the mask that covers the most positives and fewest negatives.


Code
pos, neg = health.prompt_points(rgb8, n_pos=80, n_neg=24)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
ax.imshow(rgb8)
ax.scatter(pos[:, 0], pos[:, 1], c="lime", s=25, edgecolors="k", label=f"positive ({len(pos)})")
ax.scatter(neg[:, 0], neg[:, 1], c="red", marker="x", s=30, label=f"negative ({len(neg)})")
ax.legend(loc="lower right"); ax.set_title("Automatic SAM prompts from colour"); ax.axis("off"); plt.show()

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.2))
    axes[0].imshow(m_exg, cmap="Greens"); axes[0].set_title(f"ExG mask {m_exg.mean():.0%}")

title: Crop Health: SAM Plant Masks and Senescence Detection
text:
Green or senescent?
rs.uav.classify_senescence(image, plant_mask) labels each plant pixel 1 = green or 2 = senescent (0 = background). Without a model it uses a colour rule: hue on the green side of yellow (above hue_max degrees) and positive ExG means green.
Calibrate hue_max on your own data. Camera colour processing and crop variety move the hue of “green” a lot. The histogram below shows hue for saturated, reasonably bright pixels on a mid-season date (green canopy) and on 3 October (mixed green and straw): late-season green rice here is olive, at 65-80°, and yellow leaves sit at 45-55°. The package default of 75° would call most olive leaves senescent. Otsu’s method on the late-season hue picks the cut between the two modes.


Code
import cv2
from skimage.filters import threshold_otsu

def plant_hues(paths):
    """Hue (degrees) of saturated, not-dark pixels across frames."""
    out = []
    for f in paths:
        rgb = rs.uav.to_rgb_array(rs.uav.read_frame(f, max_dim=800), uint8=True)
        hsv_full = cv2.cvtColor(rgb, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV_FULL).astype(float)
        m = (hsv_full[..., 1] > 60) & (hsv_full[..., 2] > 70)
        out.append(hsv_full[..., 0][m] * 360 / 255)
    return np.concatenate(out)

h_mid = plant_hues(sorted((LUMS / "2025-09-12").glob("*.png"))[:5])
h_late = plant_hues(sorted((LUMS / "2025-10-03").glob("*.png"))[:5])
h_late_sel = h_late[(h_late > 30) & (h_late < 110)]
HUE = float(round(threshold_otsu(h_late_sel)))
print(f"Otsu hue threshold on 3 Oct plant pixels: {HUE:.0f} degrees")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))
bins = np.arange(20, 130, 2)
ax.hist(h_mid, bins=bins, alpha=0.6, density=True, label="12 Sep")
ax.hist(h_late, bins=bins, alpha=0.6, density=True, label="3 Oct")
ax.axvline(75, color="grey", ls=":", label="package default 75°")
ax.axvline(HUE, color="k", ls="--", label=f"Otsu {HUE:.0f}°")
ax.set(xlabel="hue (degrees)", ylabel="density", title="Hue of plant-like pixels"); ax.legend(); plt.show()


Otsu hue threshold on 3 Oct plant pixels: 62 degrees









Because the ExG mask drops yellow leaves, the classification below runs on a looser mask: anything saturated and not dark (which excludes water, shadow and glare but keeps straw- coloured leaves).


Code
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(rgb8, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
loose = health.clean_mask((hsv[..., 1] > 60) & (hsv[..., 2] > 70), min_area=300)  # saturated, not dark
plant_mask = m_sam if m_sam is not None else loose
labels75, _ = rs.uav.classify_senescence(img, plant_mask)  # package default, 75 degrees
labels, p_green = rs.uav.classify_senescence(img, plant_mask, hue_max=HUE)
labels_hsv = rs.uav.hsv_filter(img, labels, s_min=50, v_min=120)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 7.5))
axes[0, 0].imshow(rgb8); axes[0, 0].set_title("RGB")
axes[0, 1].imshow(labels75, cmap=HEALTH_CMAP, vmin=0, vmax=2); axes[0, 1].set_title("Colour rule, hue_max = 75° (default)")
axes[1, 0].imshow(labels, cmap=HEALTH_CMAP, vmin=0, vmax=2); axes[1, 0].set_title(f"Colour rule, hue_max = {HUE:.0f}° (calibrated)")
axes[1, 1].imshow(labels_hsv, cmap=HEALTH_CMAP, vmin=0, vmax=2); axes[1, 1].set_title("Calibrated + HSV filter")
for a in axes.flat: a.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
pd.concat({"default 75°": rs.uav.health_summary(labels75), f"calibrated {HUE:.0f}°": rs.uav.health_summary(labels),
           "calibrated + HSV filter": rs.uav.health_summary(labels_hsv)}).round(3)

title: Crop Health: SAM Plant Masks and Senescence Detection
text:
A SegVeg-style pixel classifier
SegVeg (Serouart et al. 2022) classifies vegetation pixels as green or senescent with a gradient-boosting model on 14 colour features (RGB, HSV, Lab, chromatic coordinates and more). rs.uav.segveg_features computes them, rs.uav.load_segveg loads the published pickle, and classify_senescence(model=...) accepts any classifier with predict_proba.
The original pickle is not distributed here. To show the plug-in point, the cell below trains a small XGBoost model on pseudo-labels from the colour rule on one frame and applies it to another. It learns to imitate the rule (it cannot be better than its labels); a real SegVeg model, trained on hand-labelled pixels, is what makes this step worth doing.


Code
if SEGVEG_PKL:
    model = rs.uav.load_segveg(SEGVEG_PKL)
else:
    from xgboost import XGBClassifier

    train = rs.uav.to_rgb_array(rs.uav.read_frame(late[0], max_dim=800), uint8=True)
    tlab, _ = rs.uav.classify_senescence(train, None, hue_max=HUE)  # calibrated colour rule on every pixel
    X = rs.uav.segveg_features(train).reshape(-1, 14)
    y = (tlab.ravel() == 1).astype(int)  # 1 = green
    pick = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(y), 60_000, replace=False)
    model = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=120, max_depth=5, learning_rate=0.2, n_jobs=4).fit(X[pick], y[pick])
    print("trained on", len(pick), "pixels;", f"{y.mean():.0%} green")

lab_ml, p_ml = rs.uav.classify_senescence(img, plant_mask, model=model, threshold=0.5)
lab_ml = rs.uav.hsv_filter(img, lab_ml, s_min=50, v_min=120)
both = plant_mask.astype(bool)
print(f"agreement with the colour rule on plant pixels: {(lab_ml[both] == labels_hsv[both]).mean():.1%}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.2))
axes[0].imshow(p_ml, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0, vmax=1); axes[0].set_title("P(green) from the classifier")
axes[1].imshow(lab_ml, cmap=HEALTH_CMAP, vmin=0, vmax=2); axes[1].set_title("Classifier labels + HSV filter")
for a in axes: a.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

section: Large images: tiled health maps and per-plot summaries
text:
Large images: tiled health maps and per-plot summaries
rs.uav.health_map runs mask → classify → HSV filter on overlapping tiles (LUMS: 2048 px with 256 px overlap) and combines tiles with a pixel-wise maximum, so a pixel called senescent by either tile stays senescent. mask_method="sam" uses SAM when sam_checkpoint is given, "exg" the ExG mask, and "none" classifies every pixel and relies on the HSV filter to drop water, mud and shadow (used here, since the ExG mask would remove the yellow leaves). health_summary(labels, zones) reports cover and green/senescent fractions per zone, here a 4 × 6 grid standing in for plots.


Code
full = rs.uav.read_frame(late[2])  # 3840 x 2160
hm = rs.uav.health_map(full, tile=2048, overlap=256, mask_method="none", hue_max=HUE)  # SAM: sam_checkpoint=...
rows_, cols_ = hm.shape
zones = (np.arange(rows_)[:, None] * 4 // rows_) * 6 + (np.arange(cols_)[None, :] * 6 // cols_) + 1
per_zone = rs.uav.health_summary(hm, zones)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4.3))
axes[0].imshow(hm[::3, ::3], cmap=HEALTH_CMAP, vmin=0, vmax=2); axes[0].set_title("Tiled health map")
im = axes[1].imshow(per_zone.senescent_frac.to_numpy().reshape(4, 6), cmap="YlOrBr", vmin=0, vmax=1)
axes[1].set_title("Senescent fraction of plant pixels per zone"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1])
for a in axes: a.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

title: Crop Health: SAM Plant Masks and Senescence Detection
text:
The season in yellow
Senescent fraction for every public frame, with the colour rule on the loose mask (yellow leaves included) and on the ExG mask (yellow leaves largely excluded):


Code
def health_traits(image):
    rgb = rs.uav.to_rgb_array(image, uint8=True)
    hsv_ = cv2.cvtColor(rgb, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
    loose_ = health.clean_mask((hsv_[..., 1] > 60) & (hsv_[..., 2] > 70), min_area=200)
    out = {}
    for name, m in [("loose", loose_), ("exg", rs.uav.exg_plant_mask(image, min_area=200))]:
        lab, _ = rs.uav.classify_senescence(rgb, m, hue_max=HUE)
        s = rs.uav.health_summary(rs.uav.hsv_filter(rgb, lab, s_min=50, v_min=120)).iloc[0]
        out[f"senescent_{name}"] = s.senescent_frac
        out[f"plant_cover_{name}"] = s.plant_cover
    return out

cat = rs.uav.build_catalog(LUMS.parent)
cat = cat[cat.dataset.str.startswith("infra")].assign(crop="rice")
season = rs.uav.trait_table(cat, health_traits, max_dim=1024)
per_date = rs.uav.summarize_dates(season, ["senescent_loose", "senescent_exg"])
display(per_date.round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))

Three things show in the curves:

With the loose mask, senescence is low from 9 to 26 September and rises in October (to about a third of plant pixels on 3 October) as the crop ripens.
The early values (22 Aug to 5 Sep) are not yellow leaves: before the canopy closes, the loose mask also picks up dry soil and weeds between rows, and brown soil has the same hue as straw. A real plant mask (SAM, or a trained classifier) is needed early in the season.
The ExG mask stays near zero all season, because it removes yellow leaves before they can be classified. This is why LUMS used SAM, which segments whole plants regardless of colour.

title: Crop Health: SAM Plant Masks and Senescence Detection
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Health mapping is two splits: plant versus background, then green versus senescent.
ExG + Otsu loses yellow leaves, glare and the boundary with water. SAM, prompted with ExG seeds and with points on soil, water and glare, holds that mask.
The second split is a colour rule, an HSV filter, or a SegVeg-style classifier.
Yellow-leaf fraction per plot, followed through the season, is the trait the map is for.

GeoLattice functions used: rs.uav.exg_plant_mask, rs.uav.sam_plant_mask, rs.uav.sam_segment, rs.uav.classify_senescence, rs.uav.hsv_filter, rs.uav.health_map, rs.uav.health_summary, rs.uav.trait_table, rs.uav.summarize_dates.
Exercises

Set RUN_SAM = True and compare SAM, ExG and loose masks on a late-season frame. Which keeps yellow leaves?
Re-run Section 7 with hue_max 5° above and below the calibrated value. How sensitive is the season curve? Is the early-season level driven by leaves or by dry soil?
Label 200 pixels by hand (green vs yellow) on one frame, train the XGBoost model on them instead of pseudo-labels, and compare with the colour rule.
Turn the 4 × 6 zone grid into polygons and export the per-zone table as a GeoPackage.

title: DEM Correction and Canopy Height
text:
Overview
Without ground control points or RTK, the elevation models from notebook 09_04_03 bend. Structure-from-Motion trades lens distortion against camera height and leaves a dome or bowl, often with a tilt, that can be larger than the crop itself. The LUMS study removed it with RANSAC polynomial fitting (code/dem_post_processing/ransac_flatten.py) and reached R = 0.876 and MAE = 0.177 m against ruler heights. This notebook rebuilds that workflow with rs.uav.ransac_flatten, applies it consistently across dates, derives canopy height and validates plot heights against reference values.

import warnings  # control warning messages

title: DEM Correction and Canopy Height
text:
A season of GCP-free DEMs
Five dates, canopy growing from 0.45 m to 1.0 m. Each date gets its own dome (1.0 to 1.4 m between centre and corners) and tilt, as separate SfM runs never bend identically, plus 2 cm noise. The first date also has a nodata border of -32767, a common photogrammetry fill value.


Code
dates = pd.to_datetime(["2025-09-04", "2025-09-12", "2025-09-19", "2025-09-26", "2025-10-03"])
heights = [0.45, 0.60, 0.75, 0.90, 1.00]  # mean canopy height (m) on each date
domes = [1.20, 1.35, 1.05, 1.25, 1.40]    # dome amplitude (m)
tilts = [(0.40, -0.25), (0.30, -0.35), (0.45, -0.15), (0.35, -0.30), (0.50, -0.20)]
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

dsms, chms_true = [], []
for h, dome, tilt in zip(heights, domes, tilts):
    dsm, chm = rs.uav.synthetic_dem((300, 450), gsd=0.02, canopy_height=h, doming=dome, tilt=tilt,
                                    noise=0.0, seed=7)  # same plots and texture every date
    dsm = dsm + rng.normal(0, 0.02, dsm.shape).astype("float32")  # fresh noise each date
    dsms.append(dsm); chms_true.append(chm)
dsms[0][:, :6] = -32767.0  # nodata strip on the first date
if DEM_PATHS:  # real data replace the synthetic ones
    dsms = [rs.core.read(p).squeeze("band", drop=True) for p in DEM_PATHS]
    chms_true = None

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.6))
im = axes[0].imshow(dsms[1], cmap="terrain"); axes[0].set_title(f"DSM {dates[1]:%d %b} (m)"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0])
im = axes[1].imshow(chms_true[1], cmap="viridis"); axes[1].set_title("True canopy height (m)"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1])
for d, dsm in zip(dates, dsms):
    prof = rs.uav.doming_profile(dsm.where(dsm > -200), axis="x")
    axes[2].plot(prof.x, prof, label=f"{d:%d %b}")
axes[2].set(title="Median elevation across the field", xlabel="x (m)", ylabel="m"); axes[2].legend(fontsize=7)
for a in axes[:2]: a.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









The dome (about a metre) dwarfs the crop (under a metre), and it differs between dates, so subtracting two raw DSMs does not give growth either.

title: DEM Correction and Canopy Height
section: Fitting the trend surface with RANSAC
text:
Fitting the trend surface with RANSAC
A polynomial surface \(z = f(\text{col}, \text{row})\) is fitted to the DEM. Ordinary least squares would be pulled up by the plants; RANSAC repeatedly fits random subsets and keeps the model that most pixels agree with. It locks onto whichever surface is the majority, so with bare alleys between plots (here about 75 % of pixels) it fits the ground. Under a closed canopy it would fit the canopy top instead, which still removes the dome (a level canopy stays level) but gives height relative to the canopy, not the ground.


Code
dem = dsms[1]
rows = []
for deg in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
    surf, info = rs.uav.trend_surface(dem, degree=deg)
    resid = dem.values - surf
    ground = chms_true[1].values == 0
    rows.append({"degree": deg, "inlier_frac": info["inlier_frac"], "trend_range_m": info["trend_range"],
                 "ground_residual_sd_m": float(np.std(resid[ground]))})

Degree 1 (a plane) removes only tilt and leaves 30 cm of dome in the ground. Degree 2 captures the dome and leaves only the 2 cm noise. Degree 3 adds nothing, and degree 4 is worse: with more terms RANSAC’s random minimal samples more often mix ground and canopy pixels, and real fields add furrows and sloping corners a flexible surface would follow. The LUMS script uses degree 2, the default of ransac_flatten.

title: DEM Correction and Canopy Height
text:
One correction for all dates
rs.uav.ransac_flatten(dems, degree=2, reference=0) follows the LUMS script:

mask nodata (edge_threshold, -200 by default) and keep pixels valid in every date;
fit the trend on the reference date only;
subtract the same trend from every date and match each date’s mean to the reference;
normalize="ground" subtracts a season-wide low percentile so bare soil sits at 0 m (normalize="lums" reproduces the script’s 0-5 rescaling instead, which is unitless).



Code
lums = rs.uav.ransac_flatten(dsms, degree=2, reference=0, normalize="ground", ground_percentile=5)
print("fit info:", {k: round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v for k, v in lums.info.items()})
print("ground level removed:", round(lums.ground, 3), "m")


fit info: {'degree': 2, 'inlier_frac': 0.741, 'trend_range': 1.512, 'reference': 0, 'normalize': 'ground', 'match': 'mean'}
ground level removed: -0.174 m


Step 3 hides a trap. Matching each date’s mean to the reference assumes the mean surface does not change between flights, but a growing canopy raises it, so every later date is pulled down by part of its own growth. match="ground" levels the dates on a low percentile (bare soil) instead. A third option is to fit a separate trend for each date, which also handles domes that differ between flights.


Code
shared = rs.uav.ransac_flatten(dsms, degree=2, reference=0, normalize="ground", ground_percentile=5, match="ground")
per_date = [rs.uav.ransac_flatten([d], degree=2, normalize="ground", ground_percentile=5).dems[0] for d in dsms]
variants = {"LUMS (shared, mean match)": lums.dems, "shared, ground match": shared.dems, "per-date trend": per_date}

def ground_err(flat, truth):
    """Bias and spread of flattened bare-soil pixels (should be 0 m)."""
    g = (truth.values == 0) & np.isfinite(flat.values)
    return float(np.mean(flat.values[g])), float(np.std(flat.values[g]))

tab = []
for i, d in enumerate(dates):
    row = {"date": d.date()}
    for name, dems in variants.items():
        b, sd = ground_err(dems[i], chms_true[i])
        row[(name, "bias")], row[(name, "SD")] = b, sd
    tab.append(row)
gt = pd.DataFrame(tab).set_index("date"); gt.columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(gt.columns)

Reading the table:

Mean matching gives bare soil a bias that shrinks date by date (the reference date ends up too high, the late dates are pulled down): exactly the growth it removed.
Ground matching removes that steady drift. What remains (a few centimetres, varying by date, and the larger SD) is the part of each date’s own dome that differs from the reference dome, which no shared trend can remove.
Per-date fitting is cleanest when every flight bends differently. When doming is similar between flights (same drone, altitude and pattern) a shared fit is the safer choice, because it cannot absorb a genuine change in the field into the trend. Inspect the ground residuals before choosing.

for ax, (title, arr) in zip(axes[0], [("raw DSM", dsms[3]), ("shared, ground match", shared.dems[3]), ("per-date trend", per_date[3])]):

    ax.plot(prof.x, prof - float(prof.mean())); ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)

title: DEM Correction and Canopy Height
text:
Canopy height
After normalize="ground", the flattened DEM is height above ground, with a small positive bias because a low percentile of noisy ground sits slightly below the true ground. If a bare-soil DEM from before planting (or a DTM) exists, rs.uav.chm_from_surfaces(dsm, dtm) subtracts it instead; both inputs must be flattened the same way. Here the median of the flattened bare soil stands in for that DTM, which removes the bias.


Code
chm = per_date[3].clip(min=0).where(np.isfinite(per_date[3]))
dtm = per_date[3].where(chms_true[3] == 0)
dtm = dtm.fillna(float(dtm.median()))  # a smooth bare-ground surface (here: flat after correction)
chm2 = rs.uav.chm_from_surfaces(per_date[3], dtm)
for name, c in [("flattened DEM above ground", chm), ("chm_from_surfaces(DSM, DTM)", chm2)]:
    err = (c - chms_true[3]).values
    print(f"{name:28s} bias {np.nanmean(err):+.3f} m, RMSE {np.sqrt(np.nanmean(err**2)):.3f} m")


flattened DEM above ground   bias +0.030 m, RMSE 0.036 m
chm_from_surfaces(DSM, DTM)  bias -0.000 m, RMSE 0.010 m

title: DEM Correction and Canopy Height
text:
Plot heights and validation
Field teams measure plant height with a ruler at a handful of plants per plot. The UAV equivalent is a high percentile of the CHM inside each plot (the canopy top, not the mean, which includes gaps between plants). Plots are found here by labelling the true canopy; with real data you would rasterise plot polygons instead.


Code
zones, n_plots = ndi.label(chms_true[0].values > 0)
print(n_plots, "plots")

def plot_heights(chm_arr, zones, q=95):
    """q-th percentile of canopy height in each plot."""
    return np.array([np.nanpercentile(chm_arr[zones == z], q) for z in range(1, zones.max() + 1)])

rng_field = np.random.default_rng(0)
records = []
for i, (d, t) in enumerate(zip(dates, chms_true)):
    truth = plot_heights(t.values, zones)
    field = truth + rng_field.normal(0, 0.05, truth.size)  # ruler readings: +/- 5 cm
    est = {name: plot_heights(dems[i].values, zones) for name, dems in variants.items()}
    for z in range(n_plots):
        records.append({"date": d, "plot": z + 1, "field_m": field[z], **{name: e[z] for name, e in est.items()}})
val = pd.DataFrame(records)

def scores(obs, est):
    r = np.corrcoef(obs, est)[0, 1]
    return {"R": r, "MAE_m": np.mean(np.abs(est - obs)), "bias_m": np.mean(est - obs), "n": len(obs)}

display(pd.DataFrame({name: scores(val.field_m, val[name]) for name in variants}).T.round(3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.6))
for ax, col in zip(axes, variants):
    for d, g in val.groupby("date"):
        ax.scatter(g.field_m, g[col], s=22, label=f"{d:%d %b}")
    lim = [0, val[["field_m", *variants]].max().max() * 1.1]
    ax.plot(lim, lim, "k--", lw=1); ax.set(xlim=lim, ylim=lim, xlabel="field height (m)", ylabel="UAV height (m)", title=col)
    s_ = scores(val.field_m, val[col]); ax.text(0.03, 0.92, f"R = {s_['R']:.3f}, MAE = {s_['MAE_m']:.3f} m", transform=ax.transAxes)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Without GCP or RTK, a Structure-from-Motion DEM domes, bowls and tilts. The bend can be taller than the crop.
RANSAC fits a polynomial to ground points and subtracts it. Look at the degree and the inliers; a default is not a check.
Use one shared surface across dates when the dome is stable. Fit each date when it is not.
Plot height is a high percentile of the flattened surface. Report it against field heights as R, MAE and bias.

Set plot_gap=0.1 in synthetic_dem (a nearly closed canopy). What does RANSAC fit now, and what happens to the plot heights after normalize="ground"?
Make all five domes equal (1.2 m). Is the shared, ground-matched trend now as good as the per-date one? Is mean matching still biased?
Replace the 95th percentile with the mean and the 99th percentile in plot_heights. Which gives the smallest bias against field heights, and why?

title: RGB Vegetation Indices and Canopy Cover
text:
Overview
Visible-band indices such as VARI, TGI and Excess Green (ExG) are the workhorses of low-cost phenotyping. This notebook computes them with rs.uav.vegetation_indices, reproduces the LUMS make_tgi_vari.py script, turns an index into a vegetation mask and canopy cover with rs.uav.canopy_cover, and builds a first growth curve: rice canopy cover over all 11 public LUMS dates. The last section changes sensor. A five-band wheat mosaic from Barisal, Bangladesh, has red and near-infrared, so ground cover is the perpendicular vegetation index divided by its value at full canopy (Maas and Rajan, 2008), from rs.uav.bare_soil_line and rs.uav.cover_layers.

title: RGB Vegetation Indices and Canopy Cover
text:
Reproducing make_tgi_vari.py
The LUMS script (in code/vegetation_indices/) reads an orthomosaic PNG, computes VARI and the max-normalised TGI in column chunks, and replaces zero denominators with 1e-6. The same arithmetic in plain NumPy:


Code
rgb = rs.uav.to_rgb_array(img).astype(np.float32)  # (rows, cols, 3), 0-1
R, G, B = rgb[..., 0], rgb[..., 1], rgb[..., 2]
den = G + R - B; den[den == 0] = 1e-6
vari_lums = (G - R) / den
mx = np.maximum(np.maximum(R, G), B); mx[mx == 0] = 1e-6
tgi_lums = (G - 0.39 * R - 0.61 * B) / mx

cmp = pd.DataFrame({
    "index": ["VARI", "TGI_MAXNORM"],
    "max_abs_diff": [np.nanmax(np.abs(vari_lums - vi.VARI.values)), np.nanmax(np.abs(tgi_lums - vi.TGI_MAXNORM.values))],
    "pct_pixels_differing_>1e-4": [100 * np.mean(np.abs(vari_lums - vi.VARI.values) > 1e-4),
                                   100 * np.mean(np.abs(tgi_lums - vi.TGI_MAXNORM.values) > 1e-4)],
})

VARI is unstable wherever blue is high relative to red and green (glare on water, white objects), so its histogram has long tails; the script clips nothing, and the histograms below clip to the 1st-99th percentile for display.

Brightness and chromatic normalisation
Clouds passing over during a flight change brightness between frames. Ratio indices (VARI, NGRDI, GLI, TGI_MAXNORM) cancel a uniform scaling; difference indices (ExG, ExGR, TGI) scale with it. normalize=True first converts to chromatic coordinates \(r = R/(R+G+B)\) etc., which makes ExG brightness-invariant too.

Vegetation mask and canopy cover
rs.uav.canopy_cover(index) thresholds an index (Otsu’s method by default, which picks the cut that best separates two modes of the histogram) and returns the mask and the cover fraction. The two curves disagree by 30 to 45 percentage points, and the frames below show why neither is right all season:

Otsu needs two modes. On 22 August the histogram has a plant mode and a soil mode, and Otsu cover (about 31 % on the frame in Section 5) matches what the eye sees. Once the canopy closes in September there is almost no soil left, so the histogram has one broad mode and Otsu splits sunlit from shaded leaves instead. Its cover stalls near 50 % while the field is nearly fully covered, and it drops again on 3 October.
A fixed threshold depends on the background. ExG = 0.10 captures the closed canopy well (about 96 % on 1 October) but early in the season it also counts the greenish, weedy soil between rows, overestimating cover.
The ten frames per date come from different parts of the field, so the error bars mix real spatial variation with the date effect.

In practice, pick the threshold per growth stage, calibrate it once on frames with soil visible and freeze it, or replace thresholding with a trained classifier (notebook 09_04_08).

section: Green ground cover from red and NIR
text:
Green ground cover from red and NIR
The indices above work from red, green and blue. This section uses red and near-infrared on a wheat field at Barisal, Bangladesh, and follows uav-ground-cover.Rmd and uav-ground-cover.py. The soil line is rs.uav.bare_soil_line. PVI, ground cover and WDVI come from rs.uav.cover_layers.
Ground cover (fCover) is the fraction of the ground hidden by green leaves. On a crop it tracks canopy closure, and it is also a clue to erosion and early irrigation: a closed canopy shades the soil and intercepts rain. Maas and Rajan (2008) estimate that fraction from digital numbers. In red-NIR space, bare soil falls on a straight line
\[
\mathrm{NIR} = a_1\,\mathrm{Red} + a_0
\]
Leaves sit off that line, because they reflect NIR and absorb red. The perpendicular vegetation index (PVI) is the distance from the pixel to the line. Ground cover is that distance divided by the distance of a full canopy:
\[
\mathrm{PVI} = \frac{\mathrm{NIR} - a_1\,\mathrm{Red} - a_0}{\sqrt{1+a_1^2}}, \qquad
\mathrm{GC} = \frac{\mathrm{PVI}}{\mathrm{PVI_{FC}}}
\]
The weighted difference vegetation index uses the same slope without the perpendicular term:
\[
\mathrm{WDVI} = \frac{\mathrm{NIR}}{255} - a_1\frac{\mathrm{Red}}{255}
\]
Three mosaics, flown on 12 February, 27 February and 12 March 2015 under the STARS project, are in UAV_BD, with the nine plot polygons in plot_bd_wheat.shp. Each GeoTIFF has five bands and no CRS tag. The plot file is EPSG:32646 and the coordinates match, so the mosaics are read as that CRS. As in the R lesson, band 2 is red, band 3 is green and band 5 is NIR. The values are digital numbers from that camera, so each flight gets its own soil line.


Code
import geopandas as gpd  # plot polygons
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
BD = DATA / "UAV_BD"
PLOTS = gpd.read_file(BD / "plot_bd_wheat.shp")
DATES = {
    "2015-02-12": BD / "multi_bwh_mc_20150212.tif",
    "2015-02-27": BD / "multi_bwh_mc_20150227.tif",
    "2015-03-12": BD / "multi_bwh_mc_20150312.tif",
}
# Band order from uav-ground-cover.Rmd: 2 = red, 3 = green, 5 = NIR.
BANDS = ["b1", "red", "green", "b4", "nir"]
MAXVAL = 255  # landsat::BSL drops digital numbers at or above this
ULIMIT = 0.99  # top fraction of the NIR/red ratio used to find full canopy
GC_CMAP = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    "gc", ["#FF0000", "#FFFF00", "#00FF00", "#008B00"]
)

def load_stack(path):
    """Read one mosaic and attach the plot CRS (the GeoTIFF has none)."""
    da = rs.read(path, band_names=BANDS, masked=True)
    return da.rio.write_crs(PLOTS.crs)

def stretch_linear(band, quantiles=(0.02, 0.98)):
    """2-98% stretch, the limits RStoolbox uses for stretch='lin'."""
    values = band[np.isfinite(band)]
    lo, hi = np.quantile(values, quantiles)
    if hi == lo:
        hi = lo + 1e-9
    return np.clip((band - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1)

stack = load_stack(DATES["2015-02-12"])
print(f"{stack.sizes['y']} rows x {stack.sizes['x']} cols, bands: {', '.join(map(str, stack.band.values))}")
print("CRS", stack.rio.crs)
print("plots", ", ".join(PLOTS.sort_values("ID").Name), "at", PLOTS.Site_name.iloc[0])


703 rows x 601 cols, bands: b1, red, green, b4, nir
CRS EPSG:32646
plots BW1, BW2, BW3, BW4, BW5, BW6, BW7, BW8, BW9 at Barisal



False-colour composite
NIR goes in the red channel, red in the green channel and green in the blue channel, each stretched from the 2nd to the 98th percentile. Leaves are bright in NIR and dark in the red band, so the plots come out magenta. Paths and bare edges, where NIR is low, come out cyan. The white lines are the nine wheat plots.


Code
channels = [stretch_linear(stack.sel(band=name).values) for name in ("nir", "red", "green")]
rgb = np.dstack([np.nan_to_num(channel, nan=0.0) for channel in channels])
alpha = np.isfinite(stack.sel(band="nir").values)
rgba = np.dstack([rgb, alpha.astype("float32")])

left, bottom, right, top = stack.rio.bounds()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5.5))
ax.imshow(rgba, extent=(left, right, bottom, top), interpolation="nearest")
PLOTS.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=0.7)
ax.set_axis_off()
ax.set_title("Barisal wheat, 12 Feb 2015\n(R = NIR, G = red, B = green)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()











Bare soil line
NIR plotted against red forms a triangular cloud. The lower edge is soil: both bands rise together as the soil gets brighter. Vegetation leaves that edge toward high NIR and low red.
rs.uav.bare_soil_line fits the minimum soil line from landsat::BSL. For each integer red value below 255, keep the lowest NIR, then fit a major-axis line (the default in lmodel2, which is what BSL calls). The full-canopy point is taken from the pixels whose NIR/red ratio is above the 99th percentile. Among those, it is the pixel closest to high NIR and low red. The grey cloud in the figure is a sample of pixels; the line is fit on every finite pixel.


Code
red = stack.sel(band="red")
nir = stack.sel(band="nir")
bsl = rs.uav.bare_soil_line(red, nir, maxval=MAXVAL, ulimit=ULIMIT)
print(f"pixels in the fit: {bsl['n_pixels']:,}   red levels: {bsl['n_levels']}")
print(f"a0 = {bsl['intercept']:.3f}    a1 = {bsl['slope']:.3f}    R^2 = {bsl['r_squared']:.3f}")
print(f"full canopy: red = {bsl['top_red']:.0f}, NIR = {bsl['top_nir']:.0f}")

finite = np.isfinite(red.values) & np.isfinite(nir.values)
xs, ys = red.values[finite].ravel(), nir.values[finite].ravel()
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
take = rng.choice(xs.size, size=min(20000, xs.size), replace=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4.5))
ax.scatter(xs[take], ys[take], s=1, c="0.6", linewidths=0, rasterized=True)
line_x = np.array([0.0, MAXVAL])
ax.plot(line_x, bsl["slope"] * line_x + bsl["intercept"], color="red", linewidth=1.5)
ax.scatter([bsl["top_red"]], [bsl["top_nir"]], c="green", s=80, zorder=5)
ax.text(150, 65, f"a1 = {bsl['slope']:.3f}")
ax.text(150, 50, f"a0 = {bsl['intercept']:.3f}")
ax.set_xlim(0, MAXVAL); ax.set_ylim(0, MAXVAL)
ax.set_xlabel("Red"); ax.set_ylabel("NIR")
ax.set_title("Bare soil line, 12 Feb 2015")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Perpendicular vegetation index and ground cover
rs.uav.cover_layers returns PVI, ground cover and WDVI. PVI below 0 lies on the soil side of the line and is set to 0. PVI above 100 is set to 100, as in the R lesson, and the map shows PVI/100. Ground cover is PVI divided by PVI at the full-canopy point, then clipped to 0-1. WDVI is clipped to the same range. The colours are the red-yellow-green ramp from the original figures.


Code
layers = rs.uav.cover_layers(stack, maxval=MAXVAL, ulimit=ULIMIT)
pvi, gc, wdvi = layers.PVI, layers.GC, layers.WDVI
print(f"PVI at full cover = {layers.attrs['pvi_fc']:.2f}")
print(f"GC   min {np.nanmin(gc.values):.3f}   mean {np.nanmean(gc.values):.3f}   max {np.nanmax(gc.values):.3f}")
print(f"WDVI min {np.nanmin(wdvi.values):.3f}   max {np.nanmax(wdvi.values):.3f}")

bd_out = OUT / "uav_bd"
bd_out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name, band in (
    ("pvi", pvi),
    ("pvi_normalized", (pvi / 100).rename("pvi_normalized")),
    ("ground_cover", gc.rename("ground_cover")),
    ("wdvi", wdvi.rename("wdvi")),
):
    rs.write(band, bd_out / f"{name}_20150212.tif")

panels = [
    ((pvi / 100).rename("PVI / 100"), "PVI / 100", None),
    (gc, "Ground cover", (0, 1)),
    (wdvi, "WDVI", None),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.6))
for ax, (band, title, limits) in zip(axes, panels):
    limits_kw = {} if limits is None else {"vmin": limits[0], "vmax": limits[1]}
    band.plot(ax=ax, cmap=GC_CMAP, add_colorbar=True, cbar_kwargs={"shrink": 0.7}, **limits_kw)
    PLOTS.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", linewidth=0.4)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_axis_off()

GC   min 0.000   mean 0.480   max 0.854
WDVI min 0.000   max 0.704











Cover inside the plots, on three dates
Each flight keeps its own soil line, because the digital numbers still carry that day’s brightness. Mean ground cover inside each wheat plot comes from rs.zonal_stats.


Code
rows, gc_maps = [], {}
for date, path in DATES.items():
    da = load_stack(path)
    layers = rs.uav.cover_layers(da, maxval=MAXVAL, ulimit=ULIMIT)
    gc_da = layers.GC
    gc_maps[date] = gc_da
    zonal = rs.zonal_stats(gc_da, PLOTS, stats=("mean",))

        f"{date}  a0 = {layers.attrs['intercept']:.3f}  a1 = {layers.attrs['slope']:.3f}  "
        f"PVI_FC = {layers.attrs['pvi_fc']:.2f}  image mean GC = {float(np.nanmean(gc_da.values)):.3f}"
    )
    for rec in zonal.sort_values("ID").itertuples(index=False):
        rows.append({"date": date, "plot": rec.Name, "gc": rec.GC_mean})

On 12 February, PVI at the full-canopy point is about 117. The map clips PVI at 100, so ground cover on that date tops out near 0.85. On 27 February and 12 March the full-canopy point lies below 100, and some pixels reach 1.
The nine plot means sit above the mean of the whole mosaic, which still includes bare ground outside the plots. From 12 February to 27 February every plot rises: the plot means move from about 0.54-0.63 to about 0.57-0.68. On 12 March every plot is lower, about 0.30-0.43. PVI follows green leaves. title: RGB Vegetation Indices and Canopy Cover
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

VARI, TGI, ExG, ExGR, GLI, NGRDI and CIVE separate plants from soil with red, green and blue alone.
Chromatic normalisation reduces the effect of brightness. A panel or an empirical line is still what turns DN into reflectance.
Otsu on ExG gives a vegetation mask and a canopy-cover fraction. After the canopy closes, a new threshold every date can drift.
A threshold frozen on an early date often makes a cleaner season curve.
With red and NIR, ground cover is PVI divided by PVI at full canopy. Refit the soil line on each date: the digital numbers are not reflectance, and soil brightness moves between flights.

GeoLattice functions used: rs.uav.vegetation_indices, rs.uav.canopy_cover, rs.uav.read_frame, rs.uav.build_catalog, rs.uav.trait_table, rs.uav.summarize_dates, rs.uav.bare_soil_line, rs.uav.cover_layers, rs.read, rs.write, rs.zonal_stats.
Exercises

Repeat Section 6 with VARI (clipped to -1..1) instead of ExG. Does VARI suffer from the same Otsu problem after canopy closure?
Use normalize=True for ExG in cover_traits. Does the frame-to-frame spread shrink?
Find the median Otsu threshold of the 22 Aug frames and apply it, frozen, to every date. Does the resulting curve look more plausible than either curve above?
Pick a threshold for CIVE by looking at its histogram and compare its cover with ExG.
On 12 February, PVI at full cover is above 100, so the clip keeps ground cover below 1. Recompute that date without the clip. How far do the plot means move?
Hold the 12 February soil line fixed and apply it to 27 February and 12 March. Does the March drop in every plot remain?

References

Gitelson, A. A. et al. (2002). Novel algorithms for remote estimation of vegetation fraction. Remote Sensing of Environment, 80, 76-87 (VARI).
Hunt, E. R. et al. (2013). A visible band index for remote sensing leaf chlorophyll content at the canopy scale. International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation, 21, 103-112 (TGI).
Woebbecke, D. M. et al. (1995). Color indices for weed identification under various soil, residue, and lighting conditions. Transactions of the ASAE, 38, 259-269 (ExG).
Meyer, G. E. and Neto, J. C. (2008). Verification of color vegetation indices for automated crop imaging applications. Computers and Electronics in Agriculture, 63, 282-293 (ExGR).
Otsu, N. (1979). A threshold selection method from gray-level histograms. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, 9, 62-66.
Maas, S. J. and Rajan, N. (2008). Estimating ground cover of field crops using medium-resolution multispectral satellite imagery. Agronomy Journal, 100, 320-327. doi:10.2134/agronj2007.0140.

title: Reading and Inspecting UAV Imagery
text:
Overview
Before any index or model, three jobs come first: read the frames into a consistent array layout, throw out the bad ones (blur, over- or under-exposure), and know exactly what is in each folder. This notebook does all three with rs.uav.read_frame, rs.uav.load_pair, the quality-control helpers and rs.uav.build_catalog.

title: Reading and Inspecting UAV Imagery
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Read PNG frames and RGB + NIR pairs into (band, y, x) xarray DataArrays.
Distinguish pixel coordinates from map coordinates and attach a GSD.
Check bit depth and value ranges.
Score frames for blur (variance of the Laplacian) and exposure, and select good frames.
Build a tidy catalogue (crop, date, band, rig, path) of a multi-date collection.
Extract frames from a flight video.



Data







Data
Type

Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide library warnings

from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
from PIL import Image  # inspect raw image files

import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing (rs.uav = drone tools)

section: What is inside a PNG frame?
text:
What is inside a PNG frame?
Look at the file before reading it: size, colour mode and data type tell you the bit depth.


Code
files = {
    "LUMS rice RGB": sorted((LUMS / "2025-08-22").glob("*.png"))[0],
    "Canola RGB": DATA / "Canola dataset/canola_06082019/RGB/5.png",
    "Canola NIR": DATA / "Canola dataset/canola_06082019/NIR/5.png",
}
rows = []
for label, f in files.items():
    with Image.open(f) as im:
        a = np.asarray(im)
        rows.append({"file": label, "size (w x h)": im.size, "mode": im.mode, "dtype": a.dtype,
                     "min": a.min(), "max": a.max(), "MB": round(f.stat().st_size / 1e6, 2)})

title: Reading and Inspecting UAV Imagery
text:
Reading frames into xarray
rs.uav.read_frame returns a (band, y, x) DataArray scaled to 0-1, the same layout used for satellite imagery elsewhere in GeoLattice. Without a GSD the coordinates are pixel centres. With a GSD they are metres in a local, north-up frame whose origin is the top-left corner.


Code
f = files["LUMS rice RGB"]
img_px = rs.uav.read_frame(f)  # pixel coordinates
img_m = rs.uav.read_frame(f, gsd=0.00185)  # metre coordinates (1.85 mm/px)
print(img_px.dims, img_px.shape, img_px.band.values, img_px.dtype)
print("pixel x:", img_px.x.values[:3], "...  metre x:", img_m.x.values[:3].round(5), "...")
print("attributes:", img_m.attrs)


('band', 'y', 'x') (3, 2160, 3840) ['red' 'green' 'blue'] float32
pixel x: [0.5 1.5 2.5] ...  metre x: [0.00092 0.00278 0.00463] ...
attributes: {'source': 'data/infrastructure-free-uav-phenotyping/2025-08-22/frame1123.png', 'gsd_m': 0.00185, 'units_xy': 'm'}


Converting between pixel (row, col) and map (x, y) coordinates uses an affine transform. For a frame read with a GSD it is a simple scale; rs.uav.pix_to_map and rs.uav.map_to_pix handle any transform, including real GeoTIFF orthomosaics.


Code
from affine import Affine  # 2-D affine transforms (as used by rasterio)

T = Affine(0.00185, 0, 0, 0, -0.00185, 0)  # top-left origin, 1.85 mm pixels, y points up
x, y = rs.uav.pix_to_map(T, np.array([0.5, 1919.5]), np.array([0.5, 1079.5]))  # col, row of two pixels
print("map x:", x.round(4), " map y:", y.round(4))
col, row = rs.uav.map_to_pix(T, x, y)
print("back to pixels: col", np.round(col, 2), " row", np.round(row, 2))


map x: [9.0000e-04 3.5511e+00]  map y: [-9.0000e-04 -1.9971e+00]
back to pixels: col [5.0000e-01 1.9195e+03]  row [5.0000e-01 1.0795e+03]


Large frames can be read downsized for previews and quality checks with max_dim; the GSD is adjusted to match.


Code
small = rs.uav.read_frame(f, gsd=0.00185, max_dim=960)
print(small.shape, "GSD now", round(small.attrs.get("gsd_m", np.nan) * 1000, 2), "mm" if "gsd_m" in small.attrs else "",
      "| x spacing:", round(float(small.x[1] - small.x[0]) * 1000, 2), "mm")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
ax.imshow(rs.uav.to_rgb_array(small), extent=[float(small.x.min()), float(small.x.max()), float(small.y.min()), float(small.y.max())])
ax.set(xlabel="x (m)", ylabel="y (m)", title="LUMS rice, 22 Aug 2025 (preview at max_dim=960)")
plt.show()

title: Reading and Inspecting UAV Imagery
text:
RGB + NIR pairs
The crop datasets were taken with two cameras side by side, so each frame has an RGB and a NIR file. rs.uav.load_pair stacks them as bands red, green, blue, nir, resizing NIR to the RGB grid. The cameras do not see exactly the same footprint; the false-colour composite and the edge overlay below show how far apart they are before co-registration (notebook 09_04_05 aligns them).


Code
pair = rs.uav.load_pair(files["Canola RGB"], files["Canola NIR"], register=False)
print(pair.band.values, pair.shape)

def edges(a):
    """Gradient magnitude, rescaled to 0-1 (for overlays)."""
    gy, gx = np.gradient(a)
    m = np.hypot(gx, gy)
    return np.clip(m / np.percentile(m, 99), 0, 1)

g = pair.sel(band="green").values; n = pair.sel(band="nir").values
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.8))
axes[0].imshow(rs.uav.to_rgb_array(pair)); axes[0].set_title("RGB")
cir = np.dstack([n, pair.sel(band="red").values, g])  # colour infrared: NIR, red, green
axes[1].imshow(np.clip(cir / np.percentile(cir, 99.5), 0, 1)); axes[1].set_title("Colour infrared (unaligned)")
axes[2].imshow(np.dstack([edges(n), edges(g), np.zeros_like(g)])); axes[2].set_title("Edges: NIR red, green green")
for a in axes: a.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


['red' 'green' 'blue' 'nir'] (4, 797, 1098)









Where the red and green edges do not coincide (yellow only where they do), the NIR frame is offset from the RGB frame. Any index that mixes NIR with visible bands (NDVI, GNDVI) is wrong at those pixels until the pair is co-registered.

Quality control: blur and exposure
Blur. The variance of the Laplacian measures how much fine detail a frame holds: motion blur and defocus lower it. Exposure. The fractions of near-black and near-saturated pixels flag dark or blown-out frames. rs.uav.frame_quality computes both for many files at once.

q = rs.uav.frame_quality(lums_files, max_dim=1024)
q["date"] = [Path(p).parent.name for p in q.path]
print(len(q), "LUMS frames scored")
q.drop(columns="path").describe().round(3)

A synthetic test shows what the blur score responds to: blurring the same frame step by step lowers it quickly. Note the last row, though: the score is a variance, so it scales with the square of image contrast, and halving the brightness quarters it. A dull, overcast flight therefore scores lower than a sunny one without being any less sharp.


Code
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter, shift  # blur and motion simulation

base = rs.uav.read_frame(lums_files[0], max_dim=1024)
rgb = rs.uav.to_rgb_array(base)
tests = {"original": rgb,
         "defocus sigma=1": gaussian_filter(rgb, (1, 1, 0)),
         "defocus sigma=3": gaussian_filter(rgb, (3, 3, 0)),
         "motion 8 px": np.mean([shift(rgb, (0, s, 0), order=0, mode="nearest") for s in range(8)], axis=0),
         "darker x0.5": rgb * 0.5}
res = pd.DataFrame({k: {"blur": rs.uav.blur_score(v), **rs.uav.exposure_stats(v)} for k, v in tests.items()}).T
res.round(4)

Blur scores depend on scene content (a frame of bare soil is less detailed than one of dense canopy) and on illumination, so thresholds work best relative to the flight: keep frames above, say, half the median score of their own date.


Code
q["blur_rel"] = q.blur / q.groupby("date").blur.transform("median")
q["keep"] = (q.blur_rel >= 0.5) & (q.dark_frac < 0.2) & (q.saturated_frac < 0.05)
print(q.keep.value_counts().to_string())  # the public LUMS frames were already hand-picked
worst = q.sort_values("blur_rel").iloc[0]; best = q.sort_values("blur_rel").iloc[-1]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for ax, r, t in [(axes[0], worst, "least sharp"), (axes[1], best, "sharpest")]:

title: Reading and Inspecting UAV Imagery
section: Extracting frames from a flight video
text:
Extracting frames from a flight video
LUMS recorded 4K video and kept every 6th frame. rs.uav.extract_frames does this and can drop blurred frames on the way. No video ships with the data, so the cell below makes a short clip that pans across one frame (with a few deliberately blurred frames) and then extracts from it.


Code
import cv2  # OpenCV video writing

clip = OUT / "demo_flight.mp4"
src = rs.uav.to_rgb_array(rs.uav.read_frame(lums_files[0]), uint8=True)
h, w = 360, 640
vw = cv2.VideoWriter(str(clip), cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*"mp4v"), 24, (w, h))
for i in range(72):  # 3 s at 24 fps, panning right
    x0 = 20 * i
    fr = cv2.resize(src[400:400 + 1080, x0:x0 + 1920], (w, h), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
    if 30 <= i < 42:  # a gust: motion blur
        fr = cv2.blur(fr, (15, 1))
    vw.write(cv2.cvtColor(fr, cv2.COLOR_RGB2BGR))
vw.release()

frames = rs.uav.extract_frames(clip, OUT / "demo_frames", step=6)
print(len(frames), "frames kept of 72 (every 6th)")
frames.round(3)

title: Reading and Inspecting UAV Imagery
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Most UAV frames are PNG or JPG files with no CRS. Read them to (band, y, x) and attach a GSD when you know one.
Blur (variance of the Laplacian) and exposure scores are the first filter. A frame that fails them should not enter an index or a mosaic.
build_catalog and pair_catalog turn a folder of dates, crops and bands into one table.
extract_frames turns a mapping video into stills and can drop blurred frames while it writes them.

GeoLattice functions used: rs.uav.read_frame, rs.uav.load_pair, rs.uav.pix_to_map, rs.uav.map_to_pix, rs.uav.frame_quality, rs.uav.blur_score, rs.uav.exposure_stats, rs.uav.build_catalog, rs.uav.pair_catalog, rs.uav.extract_frames.
Exercises

Read one Wheat pair with load_pair and make the colour-infrared composite. Is the offset between cameras larger or smaller than in Canola?
Run frame_quality on all frames of canola_06082019. Which frames would you drop with the relative-blur rule? Look at them.
Add a column doy (day of year) to the catalogue and plot frames per crop against doy. Which crops overlap in season?
extract_frames names files by frame index. Change the demo to keep every 12th frame and compute the ground spacing between kept frames for a 1 m/s flight.

References

Pech-Pacheco, J. L. et al. (2000). Diatom autofocusing in brightfield microscopy: a comparative study. ICPR 2000 (variance-of-Laplacian focus measure).
Chaudhry, H., Rana, S. and Jaleel, A. (2026). UAV-based crop reconstruction and trait estimation using RGB imagery without external geospatial infrastructure. Computers and Electronics in Agriculture (accepted).

title: NISAR GUNW: Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram
text:
Overview
It reads the HH unwrapped phase, coherence, connected-component labels, and ionosphere-screen layers from the supplied HDF5 file. GUNW is already geocoded; the AOI is selected from its projected grid.

title: NISAR GUNW: Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Inspect GUNW identification metadata, wavelength from the center frequency, and the frequencyA layer inventory.
Select the coastal Bangladesh AOI window from the 80 m EPSG:32646 coordinate axes.
Read HH unwrapped phase, coherence, connected components, and the ionosphere screen in bounded HDF5 chunks.
Quality-mask and reference the phase with nisar.process_unwrapped_phase, using coherence and connected-component labels.
Convert the referenced phase to relative line-of-sight displacement with the product center frequency.
Inspect the ionosphere phase screen and its uncertainty without applying a correction whose sign is unverified.
Clip phase, displacement, and coherence to the AOI polygon and state why one interferogram is not absolute or vertical motion.



Contents

Processing overview and limitations
Inspect product metadata and layers
Select the AOI and view it on satellite imagery
Read the AOI window in bounded chunks
Quality-mask and reference phase with GeoLattice
Inspect phase quality and ionosphere layers
Clip and map the AOI displacement
Optionally export AOI layers
Summary, exercises and references

title: NISAR GUNW: Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram
text:
Processing overview and limitations
The scene contains an HH pair with a reference acquisition on 2026-09-22 and a secondary acquisition on 2026-10-04, a 12-day interval. The geocoded layers are on an 80 m EPSG:32646 grid. The workflow quality-masks unwrapped phase using coherence and connected-component labels, references phase to a selected stable area, and converts relative phase to line-of-sight (LOS) displacement using the product center frequency.
The reference area defines an arbitrary zero and must be stable; the default GeoLattice selection is only a provisional high-coherence reference within the largest valid component. For scientific results, provide a known stable reference polygon. A single interferogram does not provide absolute deformation or separate deformation from atmosphere, ionosphere, orbit errors, or decorrelation. The ionosphere screen and uncertainty are inspected but not subtracted because the layer metadata does not specify a correction sign convention. Review the matching product specification before applying any correction or assigning toward/away LOS signs.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Import libraries, set plotting defaults, and locate the NISAR GUNW HDF5 scene and AOI file on disk.

from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd  # vector data (the AOI)
import h5py  # read NISAR HDF5 files
import leafmap  # interactive web maps
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import rioxarray  # registers the .rio accessor
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

from geolattice import rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing
from geolattice.rsense.sar import nisar  # NISAR helpers

# 1. Use a slightly higher DPI than the matplotlib default so the phase, coherence, and
#    displacement panels plotted later in the notebook are crisp without being oversized.
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})

# 2. Resolve the data directory so the notebook runs both from the repository root and from
#    its own folder: try the path relative to the repo root first, then fall back to a
#    directory next to the notebook itself.
DATA_RELATIVE = Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/NISAR_bd")
if not DATA_RELATIVE.exists():  # when run from the repository root instead of this folder
    DATA_RELATIVE = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/NISAR_bd")  # use the path from the root
DATA_DIR = DATA_RELATIVE  # the data folder

# 3. Build the path to the GUNW product. The filename itself encodes the acquisition
#    metadata referenced throughout the notebook: track/frame numbers, the HH polarization,
#    and the reference (2026-09-22) and secondary (2026-10-04) zero-Doppler start/end times
#    that define the ~12-day interferometric pair.
SCENE = DATA_DIR / (
    "NISAR_L2_PR_GUNW_031_069_A_013_032_4000_SH_20260922T232058_"
    "20260922T232133_20261004T232058_20261004T232133_P05023_N_F_J_001.h5"
)
AOI_PATH = DATA_DIR / "AOI_coastal.geojson"  # the coastal AOI polygon

# 4. Fail fast with clear messages if the expected inputs are missing, rather than letting
#    later HDF5/GeoPandas calls raise cryptic errors deep in the workflow.
assert SCENE.is_file(), f"NISAR GUNW file not found: {SCENE.resolve()}"
assert AOI_PATH.is_file(), f"AOI GeoJSON not found: {AOI_PATH.resolve()}"  # stop if the AOI file is missing

# 5. Confirm which GeoLattice version and which input files this run is using.
print(f"GeoLattice remote sensing version: {rs.__version__}")
print(f"GUNW: {SCENE.name}")  # the GUNW file
print(f"AOI:  {AOI_PATH}")  # the AOI file

text:
Inspect product metadata and layers
GeoLattice reads the product identification metadata and inventories the frequency-A grid without loading the multi-gigabyte HDF5 raster layers.


Code
# Inspect product identification metadata and the frequency-A grid layout without loading the
# multi-gigabyte raster layers themselves.

# 1. read_identification parses the lightweight HDF5 identification group (mission, product
#    type/level/version, track/frame, orbit pass and look direction, and the reference/
#    secondary acquisition timestamps). inspect_hdf5 walks the frequency-A grid group and
#    returns shape/dtype/attrs for every dataset it contains, again without reading the data.
identification = nisar.read_identification(SCENE, "GUNW")
GRID = "/science/LSAR/GUNW/grids/frequencyA"  # HDF5 path of the frequency-A grid
GRID_INFO = nisar.inspect_hdf5(SCENE, GRID)  # list its datasets

# 2. Print only the identification fields relevant to this workflow: what the product is,
#    which track/frame/orbit geometry it covers, and the reference/secondary acquisition
#    times that define the interferometric pair and its ~12-day interval.
for key in (
    "missionId", "productType", "productLevel", "productVersion",
    "trackNumber", "frameNumber", "orbitPassDirection", "lookDirection",
    "referenceZeroDopplerStartTime", "secondaryZeroDopplerStartTime",
    "referenceZeroDopplerEndTime", "secondaryZeroDopplerEndTime",
):
    if key in identification:  # print only the fields that are present
        print(f"{key}: {identification[key]}")  # field name and value

# 3. Open the HDF5 file directly to pull a few scalar/array values that inspect_hdf5 does not
#    summarize: the map projection EPSG code, the radar center frequency (converted to the
#    wavelength needed later to turn phase into line-of-sight displacement), and the x/y
#    coordinate axes and pixel spacing of the geocoded grid.
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:
    grid = f[GRID]  # the frequency-A grid group
    epsg = int(grid["unwrappedInterferogram/HH/projection"][()])  # EPSG code of the map projection
    center_frequency_hz = float(grid["centerFrequency"][()])  # radar centre frequency (Hz)
    wavelength_m = 299_792_458.0 / center_frequency_hz  # wavelength = c / frequency
    x_axis = grid["unwrappedInterferogram/HH/xCoordinates"][:]  # x coordinate of every column
    y_axis = grid["unwrappedInterferogram/HH/yCoordinates"][:]  # y coordinate of every row
    x_spacing = float(grid["unwrappedInterferogram/HH/xCoordinateSpacing"][()])  # pixel spacing in x (m)
    # pixel spacing in y (m, negative: north-up)
    y_spacing = float(grid["unwrappedInterferogram/HH/yCoordinateSpacing"][()])
    print(f"Center frequency: {center_frequency_hz / 1e9:.4f} GHz")  # centre frequency
    print(f"Radar wavelength: {wavelength_m:.4f} m")  # wavelength
    print(f"Map grid: EPSG:{epsg}; spacing {x_spacing:g} m x {abs(y_spacing):g} m")  # CRS and pixel spacing

# 4. List shape, dtype, and units for the specific layers this notebook will read later
#    (unwrapped phase, coherence, connected-component labels, and the two ionosphere-screen
#    layers), confirming they exist and are sized as expected before committing to the
#    chunked HDF5 reads below.
[(path, info["shape"], info["dtype"], info["attrs"].get("units"))
 for path, info in GRID_INFO.items()
 if any(name in path for name in (
     "unwrappedPhase", "coherenceMagnitude", "connectedComponents",
     "ionospherePhaseScreen", "ionospherePhaseScreenUncertainty",
 ))]

title: NISAR GUNW: Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram
section: Select the AOI and view it on satellite imagery
text:
Select the AOI and view it on satellite imagery
The AOI is transformed to the GUNW map CRS, and its projected bounds select the smallest enclosing row/column window. Leafmap shows the AOI over satellite imagery as geographic context; raster selection is performed using GUNW coordinates.


Code
# Load the AOI polygon, project it into the GUNW map grid to find the row/column window to
# read, and display the AOI over satellite imagery for geographic context.

# 1. Load the AOI GeoJSON and make sure it has features and a defined CRS. GeoJSON is
#    normally WGS84 (EPSG:4326) by convention, so assume that if no CRS is declared.
aoi = gpd.read_file(AOI_PATH)
if aoi.empty:  # the AOI file has no polygon
    raise ValueError(f"AOI contains no features: {AOI_PATH}")  # stop with a clear message
if aoi.crs is None:  # assume WGS 84 when the file has no CRS
    aoi = aoi.set_crs("EPSG:4326")  # set it

# 2. Keep two reprojected copies: aoi_ll in geographic coordinates for the Leafmap basemap
#    display, and aoi_grid in the GUNW product's own map projection (read from the HDF5
#    metadata above) for selecting pixels on the native grid.
aoi_ll = aoi.to_crs("EPSG:4326")
aoi_grid = aoi.to_crs(f"EPSG:{epsg}")  # the AOI in the grid's projection
min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y = aoi_grid.total_bounds  # its bounding box

# 3. Find the smallest contiguous block of rows/columns on the GUNW coordinate axes that
#    encloses the AOI's projected bounding box. Working in grid-native coordinates (rather
#    than resampling) lets step 3 below read only this window from the multi-gigabyte HDF5
#    file instead of the whole scene.
row_indices = np.flatnonzero((y_axis >= min_y) & (y_axis <= max_y))
column_indices = np.flatnonzero((x_axis >= min_x) & (x_axis <= max_x))  # columns inside the AOI
if row_indices.size == 0 or column_indices.size == 0:  # no overlap
    raise ValueError("The AOI does not overlap the GUNW map grid")  # stop with a clear message
row_start, row_stop = int(row_indices[0]), int(row_indices[-1] + 1)  # first and last row (+1)
column_start, column_stop = int(column_indices[0]), int(column_indices[-1] + 1)  # first and last column (+1)
window = (row_start, row_stop, column_start, column_stop)  # the window
# AOI bounds in the grid CRS
print(f"AOI bounds in EPSG:{epsg}: {min_x:.1f}, {min_y:.1f}, {max_x:.1f}, {max_y:.1f}")
# the grid window
print(f"GUNW window: rows {row_start:,}:{row_stop:,}, columns {column_start:,}:{column_stop:,}")
print(f"Window size: {row_stop-row_start:,} x {column_stop-column_start:,} native pixels")  # its size

# 4. Build a Leafmap satellite-imagery view centered on the AOI, purely as geographic
#    context for the reader -- the actual raster selection above already used the projected
#    GUNW coordinates, not this map.
west, south, east, north = aoi_ll.total_bounds
center = ((south + north) / 2, (west + east) / 2)  # map centre (lat, lon)
aoi_map = leafmap.Map(center=center, zoom=8, height="600px")  # an interactive map
aoi_map.add_basemap("Esri.WorldImagery")  # satellite basemap
aoi_map.add_gdf(  # add the AOI polygon
    aoi_ll,
    layer_name="Coastal AOI",
    style={"color": "#ff3b30", "weight": 3, "fillColor": "#ff3b30", "fillOpacity": 0.12},
    hover_style={"color": "#ffff00", "weight": 4, "fillOpacity": 0.2},
    zoom_to_layer=False,
)
aoi_map.add_layer_control()  # layer switcher
aoi_map  # show the map

title: NISAR GUNW: Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram
section: Read the AOI window in bounded chunks
text:
Read the AOI window in bounded chunks
The product’s nested layer groups contain their own coordinate axes and projection. GeoLattice read_l2 supports these nested geocoded layers; this notebook uses HDF5 window reads to avoid loading full-scene arrays. The connected-component fill value is converted to zero so GeoLattice excludes it along with unlabeled pixels.


Code
# Read the AOI window for every needed layer directly from the HDF5 file, in row chunks, so
# the full-scene arrays are never loaded into memory.

# 1. Map each GeoLattice-friendly name used in this notebook to the actual HDF5 dataset name under
#    the HH unwrappedInterferogram group: the unwrapped phase itself, its supporting
#    coherence and connected-component quality layers, and the ionosphere phase screen plus
#    its uncertainty (inspected later as diagnostics only).
LAYERS = {
    "phase": "unwrappedPhase",
    "coherence": "coherenceMagnitude",
    "components": "connectedComponents",
    "ionosphere": "ionospherePhaseScreen",
    "ionosphere_uncertainty": "ionospherePhaseScreenUncertainty",
}

# 2. Read in fixed-size row chunks rather than one HDF5 slice covering the whole AOI window,
#    bounding peak memory use regardless of how large the AOI is. Pre-allocate NaN-filled
#    output arrays for every layer so any pixels not covered end up as NaN rather than zero.
CHUNK_ROWS = 128
row0, row1, col0, col1 = window  # window bounds
window_shape = (row1 - row0, col1 - col0)  # window size
arrays = {name: np.full(window_shape, np.nan, dtype="float32") for name in LAYERS}  # one output array per layer

# 3. Walk the AOI window row-chunk by row-chunk, reading every layer for that chunk in one
#    pass. The connected-component fill value (the sentinel used for pixels that belong to no
#    valid component) is converted to 0 so that, downstream, GeoLattice can treat "no component"
#    and "filled/invalid" consistently when it excludes unlabeled pixels.
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:
    layer_group = f[f"{GRID}/unwrappedInterferogram/HH"]  # the HH unwrapped-interferogram group
    # fill value of the connected-component labels
    component_fill = layer_group["connectedComponents"].attrs.get("_FillValue", 65535)
    for local_start in range(0, window_shape[0], CHUNK_ROWS):  # read the window in chunks of rows
        count = min(CHUNK_ROWS, window_shape[0] - local_start)  # rows in this chunk
        rows = slice(row0 + local_start, row0 + local_start + count)  # source rows
        cols = slice(col0, col1)  # source columns
        target = slice(local_start, local_start + count)  # target rows in the output arrays
        for name, dataset_name in LAYERS.items():  # every layer
            values = layer_group[dataset_name][rows, cols]  # read the chunk
            if name == "components":  # component labels:
                values = values.astype("float32")  # as floats
                values[values == component_fill] = 0  # fill value -> 0 (no component)
            arrays[name][target] = values  # store the chunk

# 4. Wrap each loaded array as a georeferenced xarray.DataArray on the AOI's slice of the
#    native x/y coordinate axes, so downstream GeoLattice processing and rioxarray-based clipping
#    (steps 4-6 below) can operate on them directly.
out_x = x_axis[col0:col1]
out_y = y_axis[row0:row1]  # y coordinates of the window
coords = {"y": out_y, "x": out_x}  # coordinates of the output grid
# unwrapped phase as a DataArray
phase = xr.DataArray(arrays["phase"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="unwrapped_phase")
coherence = xr.DataArray(arrays["coherence"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="coherence")  # coherence
# connected-component labels
components = xr.DataArray(arrays["components"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="connected_components")
# ionosphere phase screen
ionosphere = xr.DataArray(arrays["ionosphere"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="ionosphere_phase_screen")
ionosphere_uncertainty = xr.DataArray(  # its uncertainty
    arrays["ionosphere_uncertainty"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords,
    name="ionosphere_phase_screen_uncertainty",
)

# 5. Sanity-check the loaded window: how much of the AOI has finite (non-NaN) phase and
#    coherence data, and which connected-component labels are actually present.
print(f"Loaded AOI window: {phase.shape[0]:,} x {phase.shape[1]:,} pixels")
print(f"Finite phase fraction: {np.isfinite(phase).mean():.1%}")  # finite phase share
print(f"Finite coherence fraction: {np.isfinite(coherence).mean():.1%}")  # finite coherence share
# component labels present
print(f"Connected-component labels: {np.unique(components.values[np.isfinite(components)])}")

Finite coherence fraction: 100.0%
