title: NISAR GUNW: Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram
section: Quality-mask and reference phase with GeoLattice
text:
Quality-mask and reference phase with GeoLattice
GeoLattice removes pixels below the coherence threshold and pixels without a connected-component label. By default, process_unwrapped_phase uses the largest valid component and its highest-coherence quartile to estimate a phase reference. This is a reproducible demonstration, not proof that the selected pixels are geologically stable. Set REFERENCE_AOI_PATH to a known stable reference polygon to override the automatic selection. Ionosphere correction remains disabled until its sign convention is verified.


Code
# Quality-mask the unwrapped phase, reference it to a stable area, and convert it to relative
# line-of-sight (LOS) displacement using GeoLattice.

# 1. Pixels with coherence below this threshold are excluded as unreliable. REFERENCE_AOI_PATH
#    stays None by default, so GeoLattice falls back to its own automatic reference-pixel
#    selection; set it to a known stable polygon's path for a scientifically defensible
#    reference instead of the provisional one GeoLattice picks.
MIN_COHERENCE = 0.30
REFERENCE_AOI_PATH = None  # Optionally set a path to a stable reference polygon
reference_mask = None  # no reference area by default

# 2. Only runs when a reference polygon path is supplied: load it, reproject it into the GUNW
#    grid CRS, and rasterize it onto the AOI window's pixel grid (geometry_mask with
#    invert=True marks pixels inside the polygon as True) so GeoLattice can average the phase
#    there as the manual zero reference instead of guessing one.
if REFERENCE_AOI_PATH is not None:
    import rasterio  # raster tools
    from rasterio.features import geometry_mask  # rasterise a polygon into a mask
    from rasterio.transform import from_origin  # transform of a north-up grid

    reference_aoi = gpd.read_file(REFERENCE_AOI_PATH)  # the reference area polygon
    if reference_aoi.empty:  # empty file
        # stop with a clear message
        raise ValueError(f"Reference AOI contains no features: {REFERENCE_AOI_PATH}")
    if reference_aoi.crs is None:  # the file has no CRS
        # stop with a clear message
        raise ValueError("Reference AOI must declare its coordinate reference system")
    reference_aoi = reference_aoi.to_crs(f"EPSG:{epsg}")  # into the grid CRS
    # transform of the output grid
    transform = from_origin(out_x[0] - x_spacing / 2, out_y[0] - abs(y_spacing) / 2,
                            abs(x_spacing), abs(y_spacing))
    reference_mask = geometry_mask(  # True outside the reference polygon
        reference_aoi.geometry, out_shape=phase.shape, transform=transform, invert=True
    )

# 3. Hand the phase, coherence, and connected-component layers to GeoLattice. It excludes pixels
#    below min_coherence and pixels with no valid component label, picks (or uses the
#    supplied) reference_mask to zero the phase at a stable area, and converts the referenced
#    phase to LOS displacement using the radar wavelength computed earlier from the center
#    frequency (the standard InSAR relation displacement = phase * wavelength / (4*pi)).
gunw = nisar.process_unwrapped_phase(
    phase,
    wavelength=wavelength_m,
    coherence=coherence,
    min_coherence=MIN_COHERENCE,
    connected_components=components,
    reference_mask=reference_mask,
)
los_displacement = gunw["los_displacement"].rename("relative_los_displacement")  # relative LOS displacement (m)
valid = gunw["valid"]  # quality mask

# 4. Report the reference phase GeoLattice used, the fraction of pixels that survived quality
#    masking, and the displacement range (2nd-98th percentile, to avoid outliers) -- all as
#    relative LOS displacement with respect to the chosen reference, not absolute motion.
print(f"GeoLattice phase reference: {gunw.attrs['reference_phase_rad']:.3f} rad")
print(f"Valid pixels after quality masking: {valid.values.mean():.1%}")  # valid share
print(f"LOS displacement range: {np.nanpercentile(los_displacement, 2):.3f} to "  # displacement range
      f"{np.nanpercentile(los_displacement, 98):.3f} m (2nd-98th percentile)")


GeoLattice phase reference: 0.181 rad
Valid pixels after quality masking: 7.9%
LOS displacement range: -0.064 to 0.169 m (2nd-98th percentile)


The displacement is relative to the selected reference phase, not absolute ground motion. The displayed LOS values inherit the phase-sign convention used by GeoLattice; verify the product documentation before interpreting positive values as motion toward or away from the sensor. Do not treat low-coherence or disconnected components as reliable deformation.

title: NISAR GUNW: Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram
section: Inspect phase quality and ionosphere layers
text:
Inspect phase quality and ionosphere layers
The ionosphere phase screen and its uncertainty are shown as diagnostics only. Their presence does not establish whether to add or subtract the screen from this unwrapped phase; the correction sign and supported use must be confirmed from the matching GUNW product specification.


Code
# Plot a 2x2 panel of phase-quality and ionosphere diagnostics over the AOI window.

# 1. Pair each layer with its display title, colormap, and color limits: the referenced
#    phase and the two ionosphere layers use robust 2nd-98th-percentile stretching (limits
#    left as None), while coherence is fixed to its natural 0-1 range. coherence.where(valid)
#    shows coherence only where GeoLattice kept the pixel after quality masking.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 10))
panels = (  # the panels: image, title, colour map and limits
    (axes[0, 0], gunw["unwrapped_phase"], "Referenced unwrapped phase (rad)", "twilight", None),
    (axes[0, 1], coherence.where(valid), "Coherence, quality-masked", "viridis", (0, 1)),
    (axes[1, 0], ionosphere, "Ionosphere phase screen (rad, not applied)", "coolwarm", None),
    (axes[1, 1], ionosphere_uncertainty, "Ionosphere phase-screen uncertainty (rad)", "magma", None),
)

# 2. Draw each panel: fall back to a robust percentile stretch when explicit limits were not
#    given, render the array, and attach a colorbar. The ionosphere panels are labeled
#    "not applied" as a reminder that this screen is shown for inspection only and has not
#    been subtracted from the phase, since its correction sign convention is unverified.
for ax, image, title, cmap, limits in panels:
    # fixed limits, or a 2-98 % stretch
    vmin, vmax = limits if limits is not None else np.nanpercentile(image.values, [2, 98])
    artist = ax.imshow(image, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, origin="upper")  # show the image
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (m)", ylabel="Northing (m)")  # title and axis labels
    plt.colorbar(artist, ax=ax, shrink=0.78)  # colour bar
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

title: NISAR GUNW: Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram
section: Clip and map the AOI displacement
text:
Clip and map the AOI displacement
The raster window includes the AOI bounding rectangle; rioxarray clips the outputs to the exact GeoJSON polygon. The source grid remains at its native 80 m spacing.


Code
# Clip the windowed rasters to the exact AOI polygon (not just its bounding box) and map the
# referenced phase, LOS displacement, and coherence side by side.

# 1. Attach the GUNW grid CRS to an xarray.DataArray via rioxarray, then clip it to the AOI's
#    actual polygon geometry rather than the rectangular row/column window read earlier.
#    all_touched=True keeps any pixel the polygon boundary passes through, and drop=True
#    discards pixels outside the clipped extent instead of just masking them.
def georeference_and_clip(image):
    # tell rioxarray which dimensions are x and y, and attach the CRS
    return image.rio.set_spatial_dims(x_dim="x", y_dim="y").rio.write_crs(
        f"EPSG:{epsg}"
    ).rio.clip(aoi_grid.geometry, aoi_grid.crs, drop=True, all_touched=True)

# 2. Apply the clip to the referenced phase, LOS displacement, quality-masked coherence, and
#    quality-masked connected components, all on the native 80 m grid.
phase_aoi = georeference_and_clip(gunw["unwrapped_phase"])
los_aoi = georeference_and_clip(los_displacement)  # LOS displacement, clipped to the AOI
coherence_aoi = georeference_and_clip(coherence.where(valid))  # coherence of the valid pixels, clipped
components_aoi = georeference_and_clip(components.where(valid))  # component labels of the valid pixels, clipped

# 3. Map the three clipped layers side by side with a robust percentile color stretch, and
#    overlay the AOI polygon boundary so the clip extent is visible on each panel.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 6))
for ax, image, title, cmap in (  # the panels with their titles and colour maps
    (axes[0], phase_aoi, "Referenced unwrapped phase (rad)", "twilight"),
    (axes[1], los_aoi, "Relative LOS displacement (m)", "RdBu_r"),
    (axes[2], coherence_aoi, "Coherence (quality-masked)", "viridis"),
):
    image.plot.imshow(ax=ax, cmap=cmap, robust=True, cbar_kwargs={"shrink": 0.8})  # show with a robust stretch
    aoi_grid.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="black", linewidth=0.6)  # AOI outline
    ax.set_title(title)  # title
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # equal scale
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

# 4. Report the final clipped grid size, CRS, and native pixel spacing for reference.
print(f"AOI result grid: {los_aoi.sizes['y']:,} rows x {los_aoi.sizes['x']:,} columns")
print(f"CRS: {los_aoi.rio.crs}; source pixel spacing: {abs(x_spacing):g} m")  # CRS and pixel spacing

Summary, exercises and references
Summary

The NISAR GUNW HH product contains a geocoded unwrapped interferogram for acquisitions 12 days apart, with the supplied AOI selected from its EPSG:32646 map grid.
The phase, coherence, connected-component, and ionosphere layers were read from the AOI window in bounded HDF5 chunks.
GeoLattice quality-masked phase using coherence and connected-component labels, referenced it to a stable-area estimate, and converted it to relative LOS displacement using the product center frequency.
The ionosphere screen was inspected but not applied because its correction sign convention was not established from the layer metadata.
The reference area’s stability, phase sign, atmospheric/ionospheric effects, and product version must be checked before interpreting displacement quantitatively.

Conclusion
This notebook demonstrates a memory-bounded GeoLattice workflow for examining NISAR GUNW over coastal Bangladesh. The product is already geocoded, so map-coordinate axes are used to read only the AOI window. Phase-to-displacement conversion yields relative LOS displacement, not absolute or vertical motion. For defensible deformation analysis, select a documented stable reference, validate the product’s phase convention and ionosphere correction, account for atmospheric and orbital errors, and combine independent interferograms or time-series methods where appropriate.

title: NISAR GSLC: Geocoded Single Look Complex Processing
text:
Processing overview and limitations
The source HDF5 contains full-resolution 5 m complex HH and HV images, each about 4.5 billion pixels. This workflow first selects the AOI bounds using the GSLC map coordinate axes, then reads only that window in bounded chunks. A 20 × 20 complex average produces approximately 100 m visualization pixels while retaining a phase estimate; mean intensity is also calculated from the original complex samples before averaging.
This is an exploratory display workflow. The power shown is a GSLC intensity proxy, not a radiometrically calibrated sigma0 or terrain-flattened gamma0 product. Use the paired GCOV product for calibrated geocoded covariance/backscatter analysis. The RGB composite is independently stretched for display and is not quantitative. A single GSLC cannot provide interferometric displacement; that requires a co-registered pair with compatible geometry and a carefully processed interferogram.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Imports, plotting defaults, and locating the NISAR GSLC scene and AOI on disk.

# 1. Standard library and core scientific/geospatial stack. h5py reads the GSLC HDF5
#    directly (so we can stream only the AOI window instead of loading the full ~4.5
#    billion-pixel complex arrays), rioxarray registers the .rio accessor used later to
#    attach a CRS and clip, and leafmap renders the interactive AOI location check.
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd  # vector data (the AOI)
import h5py  # read NISAR HDF5 files
import leafmap  # interactive web maps
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import rioxarray  # registers the .rio accessor
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

# 2. geolattice.rsense exposes shared raster helpers (Lee filtering, dB conversion); the
#    nisar submodule under geolattice.rsense.sar holds the NISAR-specific HDF5 readers used
#    below (read_identification, inspect_hdf5).
from geolattice import rsense as rs
from geolattice.rsense.sar import nisar  # NISAR helpers

# 3. A slightly higher display resolution for the figures drawn later in the notebook.
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})

# 4. Resolve the data folder whether the notebook is run from the repository root or
#    from this tutorial's own directory, then build the path to the specific GSLC
#    granule (coastal Bangladesh) and its companion AOI polygon.
DATA_RELATIVE = Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/NISAR_bd")
if not DATA_RELATIVE.exists():  # when run from the repository root instead of this folder
    DATA_RELATIVE = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/NISAR_bd")  # use the path from the root
DATA_DIR = DATA_RELATIVE  # the data folder
SCENE = DATA_DIR / (  # the GSLC file
    "NISAR_L2_PR_GSLC_031_069_A_013_4005_DHDH_A_20260922T232058_"
    "20260922T232133_P05023_N_F_J_001.h5"
)
AOI_PATH = DATA_DIR / "AOI_coastal.geojson"  # the coastal AOI polygon

# 5. Fail fast with a clear message if the sample data has not been downloaded, rather
#    than letting a later cell raise a confusing h5py/geopandas error.
assert SCENE.is_file(), f"NISAR GSLC file not found: {SCENE.resolve()}"
assert AOI_PATH.is_file(), f"AOI GeoJSON not found: {AOI_PATH.resolve()}"  # stop if the AOI file is missing

print(f"GeoLattice remote sensing version: {rs.__version__}")  # GeoLattice version
print(f"GSLC: {SCENE.name}")  # the GSLC file
print(f"AOI:  {AOI_PATH}")  # the AOI file

section: Inspect the product and geocoded grid
text:
Inspect the product and geocoded grid
The NISAR product-level identification group describes the acquisition, while the GSLC frequencyA group contains complex polarization layers, the valid-sample mask, projected coordinates, and EPSG code. GeoLattice inspect_hdf5 lists dataset metadata without loading the complete image.


Code
# Inspect the product identification group and the frequencyA geocoded grid metadata.

# 1. read_identification pulls scalar acquisition metadata (mission, track/frame,
#    orbit direction, timing, DOI) from the product-level identification group without
#    touching the large image datasets. Print only the keys that are present, since
#    not every field is guaranteed to exist across product versions.
identification = nisar.read_identification(SCENE, "GSLC")
# list the datasets of the frequency-A grid
grid_info = nisar.inspect_hdf5(SCENE, "/science/LSAR/GSLC/grids/frequencyA")

for key in (  # identification fields to show
    "missionId", "productType", "productLevel", "productVersion",
    "trackNumber", "frameNumber", "orbitPassDirection", "lookDirection",
    "zeroDopplerStartTime", "zeroDopplerEndTime", "productDoi",
):
    if key in identification:  # print only the fields that are present
        print(f"{key}: {identification[key]}")  # field name and value

# 2. Open the frequencyA grid group directly to read the handful of attributes needed
#    to plan the AOI subset: the full image shape, which polarizations are present,
#    the projection EPSG code, the pixel spacing, and the 1-D map-grid coordinate axes.
#    Reading these small datasets does not load the full HH/HV complex arrays.
GRID = "/science/LSAR/GSLC/grids/frequencyA"
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:  # open the GSLC file
    grid = f[GRID]  # the frequency-A grid group
    image_shape = grid["HH"].shape  # size of the HH grid
    # polarisations of frequency A (decoded from bytes)
    polarizations = [v.decode() if isinstance(v, bytes) else str(v)
                     for v in grid["listOfPolarizations"][:]]
    epsg = int(grid["projection"][()])  # EPSG code of the map projection
    x_spacing = float(grid["xCoordinateSpacing"][()])  # pixel spacing in x (m)
    y_spacing = float(grid["yCoordinateSpacing"][()])  # pixel spacing in y (m, negative: north-up)
    x_axis = grid["xCoordinates"][:]  # x coordinate of every column
    y_axis = grid["yCoordinates"][:]  # y coordinate of every row
    print(f"Frequency A polarizations: {polarizations}")  # the polarisations
    print(f"Grid: {image_shape[0]:,} rows x {image_shape[1]:,} columns")  # grid size
    print(f"Grid CRS: EPSG:{epsg}; spacing: {x_spacing:g} m x {abs(y_spacing):g} m")  # CRS and pixel spacing

# 3. Summarize the dtype/shape of the datasets most relevant to the rest of the
#    notebook (the two polarization layers, the validity mask, and the coordinate
#    axes), pulled from the inspect_hdf5 listing gathered above.
[(path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1], info["shape"], info["dtype"])
 for path, info in grid_info.items()
 if path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1] in ("HH", "HV", "mask", "xCoordinates", "yCoordinates", "projection")]

title: NISAR GSLC: Geocoded Single Look Complex Processing
text:
Select the AOI window
GSLC xCoordinates and yCoordinates are one-dimensional map-grid axes. Transform the GeoJSON AOI into the product CRS, locate rows and columns intersecting its projected bounds, and retain the precise polygon for a final clip. The interactive Leafmap below displays the AOI on Esri World Imagery; it is a visual location check, while the actual window is computed in the GSLC’s projected CRS. Leafmap is included in the optional geolattice[rsense-viz] dependencies.


Code
# Reproject the AOI into the GSLC's map CRS, find the matching row/column window, and
# show the AOI location on an imagery basemap for a visual sanity check.

# 1. Load the AOI polygon and make sure it carries a CRS (default to WGS84 if the
#    GeoJSON omits one). Keep a lon/lat copy for the Leafmap display and a copy
#    reprojected into the GSLC's own projected CRS (EPSG code read in the previous
#    cell) for the actual pixel-window computation.
aoi = gpd.read_file(AOI_PATH)
if aoi.crs is None:  # assume WGS 84 when the file has no CRS
    aoi = aoi.set_crs("EPSG:4326")  # set it
aoi_ll = aoi.to_crs("EPSG:4326")  # the AOI in longitude/latitude
aoi_grid = aoi.to_crs(f"EPSG:{epsg}")  # the AOI in the grid's projection
min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y = aoi_grid.total_bounds  # its bounding box

# 2. Because xCoordinates/yCoordinates are 1-D map-grid axes (not a 2-D geotransform),
#    the AOI's row/column window can be found directly by boolean-masking the axes
#    against the AOI's projected bounding box, rather than by any raster resampling.
row_indices = np.flatnonzero((y_axis >= min_y) & (y_axis <= max_y))
column_indices = np.flatnonzero((x_axis >= min_x) & (x_axis <= max_x))  # columns inside the AOI
if row_indices.size == 0 or column_indices.size == 0:  # no overlap
    raise ValueError("The AOI does not overlap the GSLC map grid")  # stop with a clear message
row_start, row_stop = int(row_indices[0]), int(row_indices[-1] + 1)  # first and last row (+1)
column_start, column_stop = int(column_indices[0]), int(column_indices[-1] + 1)  # first and last column (+1)
# AOI bounds in the grid CRS
print(f"AOI bounds in EPSG:{epsg}: {min_x:.1f}, {min_y:.1f}, {max_x:.1f}, {max_y:.1f}")
# the grid window
print(f"GSLC window: rows {row_start:,}:{row_stop:,}, columns {column_start:,}:{column_stop:,}")
print(f"Window size: {row_stop-row_start:,} x {column_stop-column_start:,} full-resolution pixels")  # its size

# 3. Render the AOI on an Esri World Imagery basemap purely as a visual location
#    check; this map is in geographic lon/lat and is independent of the projected
#    window computed above, which is what actually drives the HDF5 reads.
west, south, east, north = aoi_ll.total_bounds
center = ((south + north) / 2, (west + east) / 2)  # map centre (lat, lon)
aoi_map = leafmap.Map(center=center, zoom=8, height="600px")  # an interactive map
aoi_map.add_basemap("Esri.WorldImagery")  # satellite basemap
aoi_map.add_gdf(  # add the AOI polygon
    aoi_ll,
    layer_name="Coastal AOI",
    style={"color": "#ff3b30", "weight": 3, "fillColor": "#ff3b30", "fillOpacity": 0.12},
    hover_style={"color": "#ffff00", "weight": 4, "fillOpacity": 0.2},
    zoom_to_layer=False,
)
aoi_map.add_layer_control()  # layer switcher
aoi_map  # show the map

title: NISAR GSLC: Geocoded Single Look Complex Processing
section: Stream and multilook the complex GSLC
text:
Stream and multilook the complex GSLC
Each output pixel is calculated from a small source block. complex_mean is the mean of valid complex samples and retains an averaged phase; mean_power is the mean of source |S|², so it is not biased by phase cancellation. The GSLC mask is valid for values 1 to 254; 0 marks partially focused or invalid interpolation support and 255 is outside the acquisition. Set smaller looks for more detail at higher memory and display cost.


Code
# Stream the AOI window from the HDF5 complex datasets in row-chunks and multilook it,
# producing both an averaged complex sample (for phase) and a mean power (for intensity).

# 1. LOOKS controls the multilook block size: 20 map-grid rows x 20 columns collapses
#    the ~5 m input pixels to roughly 100 m output pixels. OUTPUT_ROWS_PER_CHUNK caps
#    how many output rows are processed per HDF5 read, which bounds peak memory use
#    regardless of how large the AOI window is.
LOOKS = (20, 20)  # (map-grid rows, columns); 5 m input becomes about 100 m output
OUTPUT_ROWS_PER_CHUNK = 4  # multilooked rows computed per read

# multilooked complex values and power of a grid window, read chunk by chunk
def stream_complex_multilook(image_dataset, mask_dataset, window, looks=LOOKS,
                              output_rows_per_chunk=OUTPUT_ROWS_PER_CHUNK):
    """Return block-mean complex samples and mean source power from an HDF5 window."""
    # 2. Snap the requested window down to a whole number of look blocks in each
    #    dimension, since a partial block at the edge cannot be averaged consistently.
    row0, row1, col0, col1 = window
    look_y, look_x = looks  # looks in y and x
    out_rows = (row1 - row0) // look_y  # output rows
    out_columns = (col1 - col0) // look_x  # output columns
    if out_rows < 1 or out_columns < 1:  # window smaller than one look
        # stop with a clear message
        raise ValueError("AOI window is smaller than the selected multilook factors")
    row1 = row0 + out_rows * look_y  # trim to whole looks
    col1 = col0 + out_columns * look_x  # trim to whole looks
    # 3. Pre-allocate the full output arrays as NaN so any output pixel left without
    #    valid input samples is naturally flagged as missing rather than left at zero.
    complex_mean = np.full((out_rows, out_columns), np.nan + 1j * np.nan, dtype="complex64")
    mean_power = np.full((out_rows, out_columns), np.nan, dtype="float32")  # output power array

    # 4. Walk through the output rows in small chunks, reading only the corresponding
    #    band of source rows from the HDF5 dataset each time. This keeps the amount of
    #    full-resolution complex data held in memory at once small and constant,
    #    independent of the overall AOI size.
    for out0 in range(0, out_rows, output_rows_per_chunk):
        count = min(output_rows_per_chunk, out_rows - out0)  # output rows in this chunk
        source0 = row0 + out0 * look_y  # first source row
        source1 = source0 + count * look_y  # last source row
        samples = image_dataset[source0:source1, col0:col1]  # complex samples of the chunk
        mask = mask_dataset[source0:source1, col0:col1]  # the product's validity mask of the chunk
        # 5. The GSLC mask is valid for values 1-254; 0 marks partially focused or
        #    invalid interpolation support and 255 marks pixels outside the acquisition
        #    swath. Also drop any sample whose real/imaginary part is non-finite before
        #    it can contaminate a block average.
        valid = (mask > 0) & (mask < 255)
        valid &= np.isfinite(samples.real) & np.isfinite(samples.imag)  # also drop NaN samples
        # 6. Reshape each chunk so the look_y x look_x block for every output pixel
        #    becomes its own pair of axes, then reduce over just those axes.
        blocks = samples.reshape(count, look_y, out_columns, look_x)
        valid_blocks = valid.reshape(count, look_y, out_columns, look_x)  # validity per look block
        n_valid = valid_blocks.sum(axis=(1, 3))  # number of valid samples per block
        # 7. complex_sum/n_valid gives the mean complex sample (retains an averaged
        #    phase); power_sum/n_valid gives the mean of |S|^2 computed from the
        #    original complex samples, so it is not biased by phase cancellation the
        #    way |mean of S|^2 would be.
        complex_sum = np.where(valid_blocks, blocks, 0).sum(axis=(1, 3))
        # sum of the valid powers per block
        power_sum = np.where(valid_blocks, np.abs(blocks) ** 2, 0).sum(axis=(1, 3))
        complex_mean[out0:out0 + count] = np.divide(  # mean complex value per block
            complex_sum, n_valid, out=np.full_like(complex_sum, np.nan + 1j * np.nan),
            where=n_valid > 0,
        )
        mean_power[out0:out0 + count] = np.divide(  # mean power per block
            power_sum, n_valid, out=np.full_like(power_sum, np.nan, dtype="float32"),
            where=n_valid > 0,
        )
    return complex_mean, mean_power  # return both

# 8. Snap the AOI window from the earlier cell to a whole number of look blocks (the
#    same rule the function enforces internally), so the output row/column counts and
#    the window passed into the function agree exactly.
n_output_rows = (row_stop - row_start) // LOOKS[0]
n_output_columns = (column_stop - column_start) // LOOKS[1]  # output columns
row_stop = row_start + n_output_rows * LOOKS[0]  # trim to whole looks
column_stop = column_start + n_output_columns * LOOKS[1]  # trim to whole looks
window = (row_start, row_stop, column_start, column_stop)  # the final window

# 9. Run the chunked multilook for both HH and HV using the same AOI window and mask,
#    so the two polarizations end up on identical output grids.
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:
    grid = f[GRID]  # the frequency-A grid group
    hh_complex, hh_power = stream_complex_multilook(  # HH complex mean and power
        grid["HH"], grid["mask"], window
    )
    hv_complex, hv_power = stream_complex_multilook(  # HV complex mean and power
        grid["HV"], grid["mask"], window
    )

# 10. Build the output coordinate axes by averaging the original x/y axes within each
#     look block, so the multilooked arrays carry coordinates consistent with the
#     averaging that produced them. Report the overall valid-data fraction as a quick
#     quality check for this AOI.
out_x = x_axis[column_start:column_stop].reshape(n_output_columns, LOOKS[1]).mean(axis=1)
# y coordinate of every output row
out_y = y_axis[row_start:row_stop].reshape(n_output_rows, LOOKS[0]).mean(axis=1)
print(f"Multilooked array: {n_output_rows:,} rows x {n_output_columns:,} columns")  # output size
print(f"Valid HH output pixels: {np.isfinite(hh_power).mean():.1%}")  # valid HH share
print(f"Valid HV output pixels: {np.isfinite(hv_power).mean():.1%}")  # valid HV share

Valid HH output pixels: 100.0%
Valid HV output pixels: 100.0%

title: NISAR GSLC: Geocoded Single Look Complex Processing
text:
Amplitude, intensity, and phase
The mean source power is filtered with GeoLattice Lee filtering in linear units and converted to dB for display. Phase is computed from the averaged complex samples. Phase values are wrapped to (−π, π] and are not displacement: without a second acquisition, flat-earth/topographic removal, coherence weighting, unwrapping, and referencing, they cannot be interpreted as surface motion.


Code
# Derive amplitude, intensity, and wrapped phase from the multilooked complex/power
# arrays, apply Lee speckle filtering and dB conversion to the intensities, and plot
# all four quick looks side by side.

# 1. Wrap the multilooked arrays as labeled xarray DataArrays on the averaged output
#    coordinates. Amplitude is sqrt(mean power); phase is the argument of the averaged
#    complex sample, which is only meaningful because the samples were averaged in the
#    complex domain (not from power alone).
coords = {"y": out_y, "x": out_x}
# HH intensity as a DataArray
hh_intensity = xr.DataArray(hh_power, dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hh_intensity")
hv_intensity = xr.DataArray(hv_power, dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hv_intensity")  # HV intensity
# HH amplitude = sqrt(power)
hh_amplitude = xr.DataArray(np.sqrt(hh_power), dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hh_amplitude")
# HV amplitude
hv_amplitude = xr.DataArray(np.sqrt(hv_power), dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hv_amplitude")
# HH wrapped phase of the averaged complex values
hh_phase = xr.DataArray(np.angle(hh_complex), dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hh_wrapped_phase")
# HV wrapped phase
hv_phase = xr.DataArray(np.angle(hv_complex), dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hv_wrapped_phase")

# 2. Apply GeoLattice's Lee speckle filter to the linear-units intensity (not to the dB or
#    the phase), then convert the filtered intensity to dB only for display. Filtering
#    before the log transform avoids distorting the speckle statistics the filter
#    assumes.
hh_filtered = xr.DataArray(rs.sar.lee(hh_intensity.values, size=5), dims=("y", "x"),
                           coords=coords, name="hh_filtered_intensity")
# Lee speckle filter on HV (5 x 5)
hv_filtered = xr.DataArray(rs.sar.lee(hv_intensity.values, size=5), dims=("y", "x"),
                           coords=coords, name="hv_filtered_intensity")
hh_db = rs.sar.to_db(hh_filtered)  # filtered HH in dB
hv_db = rs.sar.to_db(hv_filtered)  # filtered HV in dB

# 3. Plot filtered intensity (dB, percentile-stretched for contrast) next to wrapped
#    phase (fixed range -pi to pi, cyclic colormap) for each polarization. The
#    percentile stretch is a display choice only; the phase panels use a fixed range
#    because phase is inherently bounded.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 10))
for ax, image, title, cmap, limits in (  # the panels: image, title, colour map and limits
    (axes[0, 0], hh_db, "HH mean intensity (dB)", "gray", None),
    (axes[0, 1], hv_db, "HV mean intensity (dB)", "gray", None),
    (axes[1, 0], hh_phase, "HH multilooked wrapped phase", "twilight", (-np.pi, np.pi)),
    (axes[1, 1], hv_phase, "HV multilooked wrapped phase", "twilight", (-np.pi, np.pi)),
):
    if limits is None:  # no fixed limits: use a 2-98 % stretch
        vmin, vmax = np.nanpercentile(image.values, [2, 98])  # stretch limits
    else:
        vmin, vmax = limits  # fixed limits
    artist = ax.imshow(image, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, origin="upper")  # show the image
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (m)", ylabel="Northing (m)")  # title and axis labels
    plt.colorbar(artist, ax=ax, shrink=0.78)  # colour bar
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw









The intensity display uses percentile limits for readability. These limits affect only the plot. The phase panels show wrapped phase texture and are sensitive to speckle and local scattering; they are not geophysical displacement maps.

title: NISAR GSLC: Geocoded Single Look Complex Processing
section: Attach the CRS and clip to the exact AOI
text:
Attach the CRS and clip to the exact AOI
The GSLC grid is already geocoded. Attach the product EPSG to the downsampled xarray layers, then clip to the AOI polygon. No radar-to-map interpolation is needed for this Level-2 product.


Code
# Attach the GSLC's map CRS to the downsampled layers and clip them to the exact AOI
# polygon (not just the rectangular row/column window used to read the data), then
# plot the clipped HH/HV intensity.

# 1. GSLC is already geocoded onto a projected grid, so no radar-to-map resampling is
#    needed here: set_spatial_dims/write_crs just tell rioxarray which dims are x/y and
#    which CRS they are in, and rio.clip trims the rectangular window down to the
#    AOI polygon's actual shape (all_touched keeps partially covered edge pixels).
def georeference_and_clip(image):
    # tell rioxarray which dimensions are x and y, and attach the CRS
    return image.rio.set_spatial_dims(x_dim="x", y_dim="y").rio.write_crs(
        f"EPSG:{epsg}"
    ).rio.clip(aoi_grid.geometry, aoi_grid.crs, drop=True, all_touched=True)

# 2. Apply the same georeference-and-clip step to both intensity (dB) and phase
#    layers for each polarization, so all four end up on the identical AOI-clipped
#    grid used by the remaining cells.
hh_db_aoi = georeference_and_clip(hh_db)
hv_db_aoi = georeference_and_clip(hv_db)  # HV in dB, clipped to the AOI
hh_phase_aoi = georeference_and_clip(hh_phase)  # HH phase, clipped
hv_phase_aoi = georeference_and_clip(hv_phase)  # HV phase, clipped

# 3. Plot the clipped HH/HV intensity with robust (percentile-based) scaling and
#    overlay the AOI boundary to visually confirm the clip matches the polygon.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))
for ax, image, title in (  # the two images with their titles
    (axes[0], hh_db_aoi, "GSLC HH intensity (dB), AOI"),
    (axes[1], hv_db_aoi, "GSLC HV intensity (dB), AOI"),
):
    # show with a robust stretch
    image.plot.imshow(ax=ax, cmap="gray", robust=True, cbar_kwargs={"label": "dB, display proxy"})
    aoi_grid.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="cyan", linewidth=0.7)  # AOI outline
    ax.set_title(title)  # title
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # equal scale
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

print(f"AOI output grid: {hh_db_aoi.sizes['y']:,} rows x {hh_db_aoi.sizes['x']:,} columns")  # grid size
print(f"CRS: {hh_db_aoi.rio.crs}; source pixel spacing: {x_spacing:g} m")  # CRS and pixel spacing









AOI output grid: 1,120 rows x 1,324 columns
CRS: EPSG:32646; source pixel spacing: 5 m

title: NISAR GSLC: Geocoded Single Look Complex Processing
text:
HH/HV false-color RGB composite
Create a display composite using red = HH intensity in dB, green = HV intensity in dB, and blue = HH−HV in dB (the HH/HV power ratio expressed in decibels). The three channels are contrast-stretched independently from the 2nd to 98th percentile. This is a visualization convention only.


Code
# Build an HH/HV/HH-HV false-color RGB composite for visual comparison of co- and
# cross-polarized response, with each channel independently percentile-stretched.

# 1. Work in plain float32 arrays (not xarray) for the per-channel stretch math. The
#    blue channel is the HH-HV ratio expressed in dB (a subtraction in log units), a
#    common dual-pol visualization convention that highlights contrast between
#    co-polarized and cross-polarized backscatter. valid_rgb marks pixels where both
#    source bands are finite.
hh_values = hh_db_aoi.values.astype("float32")
hv_values = hv_db_aoi.values.astype("float32")  # HV in dB
ratio_values = hh_values - hv_values  # HH minus HV (dB)
valid_rgb = np.isfinite(hh_values) & np.isfinite(hv_values)  # pixels valid in both

# stretch one channel to [0, 1] between percentiles of its valid values
def stretch_channel(values, mask, percentiles=(2, 98)):
    # 2. Compute the stretch percentiles only from valid (finite, AOI) pixels, then
    #    clip and rescale the full array to 0-1 for display. A degenerate channel
    #    (no spread between low and high) is returned as all zeros rather than
    #    dividing by zero.
    finite_values = values[mask]
    if finite_values.size == 0:  # no valid values
        raise ValueError("RGB channel has no finite data inside the AOI")  # stop with a clear message
    low, high = np.percentile(finite_values, percentiles)  # percentile limits
    if high <= low:  # constant channel
        return np.zeros(values.shape, dtype="float32")  # return zeros
    return np.clip((values - low) / (high - low), 0, 1).astype("float32")  # stretch to [0, 1]

# 3. Stack the three independently stretched channels into an (rows, columns, 3) RGB
#    array: red = HH, green = HV, blue = HH-HV ratio in dB. Pixels invalid in either
#    source band are forced to black rather than left with a partial/misleading color.
rgb = np.stack((
    stretch_channel(hh_values, valid_rgb),
    stretch_channel(hv_values, valid_rgb),
    stretch_channel(ratio_values, valid_rgb),
), axis=-1)
rgb[~valid_rgb] = 0  # no-data pixels in black

# 4. Plot the composite in map coordinates (using the AOI-clipped x/y axes as the
#    image extent) with the AOI boundary overlaid for reference.
x = hh_db_aoi.x.values
y = hh_db_aoi.y.values  # northing values
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))  # one panel
# the RGB composite in map coordinates
ax.imshow(rgb, extent=(x.min(), x.max(), y.min(), y.max()), origin="upper", interpolation="nearest")
aoi_grid.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=0.8)  # AOI outline
ax.set(xlabel="Easting (m)", ylabel="Northing (m)",  # axis labels and title
       title="NISAR GSLC dual-pol false-color RGB\nR: HH dB | G: HV dB | B: HH/HV dB")
ax.set_aspect("equal")  # equal scale
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

title: NISAR GSLC: Geocoded Single Look Complex Processing
text:
Summary, exercises and references
Summary

GSLC is a geocoded, complex Level-2 NISAR product; its HH/HV samples retain phase and use a map-projected coordinate grid.
The workflow reads only the AOI window, masks invalid GSLC samples, and performs chunked complex multilooking to reduce memory use.
GeoLattice Lee filtering and dB conversion support intensity visualization, while wrapped phase is displayed separately and remains distinct from displacement.
HH/HV RGB helps compare co-polarized and cross-polarized spatial response, but its percentile stretches are display-only.
For calibrated backscatter and terrain-flattened products, use the matching NISAR GCOV product. For deformation, use a rigorously co-registered multi-date interferometric workflow.

Conclusion
This example demonstrates a practical, memory-bounded way to inspect and visualize a large NISAR GSLC scene over the supplied coastal Bangladesh AOI. Since GSLC is already on a projected map grid, AOI extraction and georeferencing are simpler than for RSLC, while the complex samples still carry phase information. The derived intensity and wrapped-phase quick looks are useful for exploration, but do not replace the calibrated GCOV product or a complete multi-date InSAR analysis.

Overview
NISAR differs from Sentinel-1 in two ways that change the processing: the products come in HDF5 rather than SAFE/GeoTIFF, and most science products are already geocoded (Level-2). Many steps that take a long SNAP chain for Sentinel-1 (calibration, terrain correction, coregistration) are already done. The work shifts toward reading HDF5 correctly, masking, quality control, time series analysis, and corrections such as ionosphere and troposphere.

Reading NISAR HDF5 files (common to all workflows)

Typical file structure
/science/LSAR/
    identification/          # mission, track, frame, orbit direction, dates
    GCOV/ (or GSLC, GUNW, GOFF)
        grids/
            frequencyA/

Steps

Open the file with h5py (or xarray with the h5netcdf engine)
List the structure and confirm layer names
Read the EPSG code from the projection dataset attributes
Read xCoordinates and yCoordinates to build the georeference (pixel centers)
Read the data layer and the mask
Set fill values (often NaN or 0) to missing
Wrap the result in an xarray.DataArray with rioxarray CRS and transform
Clip to your AOI and save as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF or Zarr

title: NISAR Processing
text:
NISAR Data Products: Processing Steps
The eight products form one processing chain. Level 1 stays in radar geometry (slant range × azimuth time), and Level 2 is the same information geocoded to a map grid.
                RSLC (L1, complex, radar geometry)
               /          |             \
          RIFG          ROFF          GSLC (L2) ──> GCOV (L2)
       (wrapped)     (offsets)          |
           |             |           (your own
          RUNW         GOFF (L2)    interferograms)
       (unwrapped)
           |
          GUNW (L2)
Rule of thumb: use Level 2 unless you need custom geocoding, a custom grid, your own unwrapping, or full radar-geometry control. Level 1 gives more control but needs geocoding at the end.
The HDF5 paths below follow the NISAR product specifications. Confirm them in your files with h5py (f.visit(print)), since names and units have shifted between releases.

Steps common to all products

Do the product-specific steps below
Save outputs as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF, Zarr, or NetCDF, with CRS and metadata

title: NISAR Processing
text:
Level 1 products (radar geometry)
Level 1 files keep data on a swaths grid indexed by zeroDopplerTime (azimuth) and slantRange. Geolocation comes from a geolocation grid in the metadata: 3D cubes of map coordinates (x, y) at several heights, plus incidence angle and LOS vectors. You need it, or ISCE3, to put Level 1 results on a map.

title: NISAR Processing
text:
RSLC: Range-Doppler Single Look Complex
What it is: the focused, calibrated complex radar image (amplitude and phase) in slant range and zero-Doppler azimuth. It is the base for every other product.
Key layers - /science/LSAR/RSLC/swaths/frequencyA/HH (and HV, VH, VV): complex64 - .../frequencyA/slantRange, .../zeroDopplerTime - /science/LSAR/RSLC/metadata/geolocationGrid/: coordinateX, coordinateY, incidenceAngle, losUnitVectorX/Y - metadata/orbit, metadata/attitude, metadata/calibrationInformation
When to use: custom InSAR pairs, custom polarimetry, your own GSLC or GCOV with a chosen grid and DEM, research on focusing or calibration.

Path A: Amplitude and backscatter in radar geometry

Read the complex layer for each polarization
Compute power: |s|² (RSLC is calibrated to β⁰)
Convert β⁰ to σ⁰ with the incidence angle: σ⁰ = β⁰ × sin(θ). For hilly terrain, use radiometric terrain correction (RTC) for γ⁰ instead (done by ISCE3 GCOV workflow)
Multilook to roughly square pixels (for example 2 range × 8 azimuth, depending on mode)
Apply a speckle filter
Geocode (see “Geocoding Level 1 products” below)
Convert to dB



Path B: Polarimetry in radar geometry (quad-pol)

Read HH, HV, VH, VV complex layers
Symmetrize: HV_sym = (HV + VH) / 2
Build the scattering vector and C3 or T3 matrix per pixel
Multilook (average the matrix over a window)
Polarimetric speckle filter (Refined Lee)
Decompose (Freeman-Durden, Yamaguchi, H-A-α)
Geocode the outputs



Path C: Interferometry from two RSLCs (ISCE3)

Choose reference and secondary RSLC: same track, frame, frequency, polarization, bandwidth
Get a DEM covering the scene (Copernicus GLO-30)
Write an ISCE3 InSAR run config (YAML) with inputs, DEM, multilook, filter, unwrapper, and ionosphere options
Run python -m nisar.workflows.insar insar_runconfig.yaml
The workflow runs: geo2rdr → coarse resample → dense offsets → rubbersheeting → fine resample → crossmul (interferogram + coherence) → filter → unwrap → ionosphere (split-spectrum) → geocode
Outputs: your own RIFG, RUNW, ROFF, and GUNW, GOFF



Path D: Make your own GSLC or GCOV

Write a run config (input RSLC, DEM, output EPSG, posting, polarizations)
GSLC: python -m nisar.workflows.gslc gslc_runconfig.yaml
GCOV: python -m nisar.workflows.gcov gcov_runconfig.yaml

title: NISAR Processing
text:
RIFG: Wrapped interferogram (radar geometry)
What it is: the complex interferogram from two RSLCs, already coregistered, flattened, and multilooked, with phase still wrapped to (−π, π]. Includes coherence.
Key layers - /science/LSAR/RIFG/swaths/frequencyA/interferogram/HH/wrappedInterferogram (complex) - .../interferogram/HH/coherenceMagnitude - .../pixelOffsets/HH/ (alongTrackOffset, slantRangeOffset, correlationSurfacePeak) - metadata/geolocationGrid
When to use: to look at raw fringes, to apply your own filter and unwrapper, or to estimate ionosphere yourself.

Steps

Read the complex interferogram and coherence
Get wrapped phase: φ = angle(ifg)
Mask pixels with low coherence (for example below 0.3) and fill values
Apply extra multilooking if you want more noise reduction (average the complex values, not the phase)
Filter phase (Goldstein, α about 0.5) to reduce noise before unwrapping
Unwrap: SNAPHU (snaphu-py), using coherence as weights. Mark connected components
Check unwrapping: look for jumps of 2π across component boundaries; use phase closure if you have triplets
Correct ionosphere: split-spectrum (needs sub-band processing from RSLC) or use the RUNW ionosphere layer from the same pair
Set a reference point on stable ground and subtract its phase
Convert to LOS displacement: d = −(λ / 4π) × φ, with λ ≈ 0.24 m (one fringe ≈ 12 cm)
Geocode (see below)

title: NISAR Processing
text:
RUNW: Unwrapped interferogram (radar geometry)
What it is: the RIFG pair after filtering and unwrapping, still in radar coordinates. It includes connected components and usually an ionosphere phase screen.
Key layers - /science/LSAR/RUNW/swaths/frequencyA/interferogram/HH/unwrappedPhase - .../coherenceMagnitude, .../connectedComponents - .../ionospherePhaseScreen, .../ionospherePhaseScreenUncertainty - .../pixelOffsets/HH/ (along-track and slant-range offsets) - metadata/geolocationGrid (incidence angle, LOS vectors, coordinates)
When to use: deformation analysis in radar geometry, stacks for time series in radar coordinates, or when you want to control geocoding yourself.

Steps

Read unwrapped phase, coherence, connected components, and ionosphere screen
Mask pixels with connected component = 0 (not reliably unwrapped) and low coherence
Pick a reference point on stable ground inside the largest connected component; subtract its phase. Components unwrapped separately can have different 2π offsets, so treat them separately or bridge them
Subtract the ionosphere phase screen (check sign convention in attributes)
Correct troposphere (ERA5 via PyAPS, GACOS, or a phase-elevation fit)
Remove residual ramps if present (plane or quadratic fit over stable areas)
Convert to LOS displacement: d = −(λ / 4π) × φ
Optional: project LOS to vertical, assuming vertical motion only: d_U = d_LOS / cos(θ)
Geocode with the geolocation grid or ISCE3
For time series: stack many RUNWs and load into MintPy with the geometry layers (radar-coordinate mode), then invert as in the GUNW workflow below

title: NISAR Processing
text:
ROFF: Pixel offsets (radar geometry)
What it is: sub-pixel image matching (amplitude cross-correlation) between two RSLCs. It measures large displacements in both along-track (azimuth) and slant-range directions, where phase decorrelates or wraps too many times: fast glaciers, large earthquakes, big landslides.
Key layers - /science/LSAR/ROFF/swaths/frequencyA/pixelOffsets/HH/layer1/ (and layer2, layer3, computed with different window sizes) - alongTrackOffset, slantRangeOffset - correlationSurfacePeak, snr - alongTrackOffsetVariance, slantRangeOffsetVariance, crossOffsetVariance - metadata/geolocationGrid

Steps

Choose the layer: small windows give finer detail but more noise; large windows give smoother, more robust results
Read both offset components and quality layers
Check units (meters or pixels) in attributes. If in pixels, multiply by pixel spacing (slant range spacing and azimuth spacing = ground velocity × azimuth time interval)
Mask by quality: low SNR, low correlation peak, high variance
Remove outliers: median filter, compare each value with its neighborhood
Remove bias: subtract the median offset over stable ground (rock outcrops, ice-free areas)
Convert slant-range offset to ground range: d_ground = d_slant / sin(θ)
Convert to velocity: v = offset ÷ Δt (days) × 365 for m/yr
Combine with the other orbit direction (ascending + descending) for 2D horizontal motion; assume surface-parallel flow for 3D
Geocode
Validate with GPS or ITS_LIVE (for glaciers)

title: NISAR Processing
text:
Geocoding Level 1 products
Option 1: ISCE3 (most accurate) - Use isce3.geocode (or the NISAR workflows) with the product’s orbit, Doppler, DEM, and output grid - Handles terrain height, so pixels land in the right place in mountains
Option 2: Geolocation grid interpolation (quick approach) 1. Read coordinateX and coordinateY cubes from metadata/geolocationGrid (indexed by height, azimuth time, slant range) 2. Read a DEM and get the height for each radar pixel (iterate or use mean terrain height for flat areas) 3. Interpolate the cube at each pixel’s azimuth time, slant range, and height to get map x, y 4. Resample the data onto a regular map grid (scipy.interpolate.griddata or pyresample) 5. Assign the CRS from the cube’s EPSG attribute
Option 2 is fine for flat areas and quick looks. Use ISCE3 for quantitative work in hilly terrain.

title: NISAR Processing
text:
Level 2 products (geocoded)
Level 2 files store data on a grids group with xCoordinates, yCoordinates, and a projection (EPSG). No geocoding is needed. Metadata in radarGrid holds 3D cubes of incidence angle, LOS vectors, and slant range on the same map grid.

Reading any Level 2 layer
```python import h5py, xarray as xr, rioxarray
def read_l2(path, product, layer_path): with h5py.File(path, “r”) as f: g = f”/science/LSAR/{product}/grids/frequencyA” data = f[f”{g}/{layer_path}”][:] x = f[f”{g}/xCoordinates”][:] y = f[f”{g}/yCoordinates”][:] epsg = int(f[f”{g}/projection”][()]) da = xr.DataArray(data, coords={“y”: y, “x”: x}, dims=(“y”, “x”)) return da.rio.write_crs(f”EPSG:{epsg}“)

title: NISAR Processing
text:
GSLC: Geocoded Single Look Complex
What it is: the RSLC resampled onto a map grid, with complex values kept, and the phase flattened against the DEM. All GSLCs from the same track and frame share the same grid, so interferograms are a simple pixel-by-pixel multiplication.
Key layers - /science/LSAR/GSLC/grids/frequencyA/HH (complex), plus other polarizations - xCoordinates, yCoordinates, projection, mask - metadata/radarGrid/ cubes

Path A: Interferogram

Choose reference and secondary GSLC: same track, frame, frequency, polarization, bandwidth
Confirm the x and y coordinates match exactly
Crop both to the AOI with the same window
Form the interferogram: ifg = ref × conj(sec)
Check metadata to confirm topographic phase was removed; if not, simulate and remove it with the DEM
Estimate coherence with a moving window (for example 7×7)
Multilook by averaging complex values
Filter phase (Goldstein)
Mask low coherence and mask layer
Unwrap with SNAPHU
Correct ionosphere (use the matching GUNW layer, or split-spectrum)
Reference to a stable point
Convert to LOS displacement
Export as GeoTIFF (already in map coordinates)



Path B: Coherence time series

Form consecutive pairs (12-day or 24-day)
Compute coherence for each pair
Stack into a time series
Use for tillage and harvest detection, forest change, urban damage, flood detection in built-up areas



Path C: Amplitude

Power = |GSLC|²
Multilook and filter
Use for quick-look backscatter (GCOV is better for terrain-corrected γ⁰)

title: NISAR Processing
text:
GCOV: Geocoded polarimetric covariance (γ⁰)
What it is: the terrain-corrected, multilooked, geocoded covariance matrix. Diagonal terms are backscatter γ⁰ in linear power. Off-diagonal terms (complex) are included for quad-pol or when requested. This is the main product for land cover, crops, biomass, and flooding.
Key layers - Diagonals: HHHH, HVHV, VHVH, VVVV - Off-diagonals: HHHV, HHVV, HVVV, etc. - mask, numberOfLooks, rtcGammaToSigmaFactor (names may vary)

Steps

Read the diagonal terms (linear γ⁰)
Apply the mask (layover, shadow, invalid) and fill values
Check numberOfLooks; mask or downweight low-look pixels
Optional: convert to σ⁰ by multiplying with rtcGammaToSigmaFactor
Optional light speckle filter, or a multitemporal filter for stacks
Compute indices in linear units

HV/HH, HH/VV
Quad-pol RVI = 8·HV / (HH + VV + 2·HV)
Dual-pol RVI = 4·HV / (HH + HV)

For quad-pol: build C3 from diagonal and off-diagonal terms, then run Freeman-Durden, Yamaguchi, or H-A-α decomposition
Convert to dB at the end: 10 × log10(γ⁰)
Clip and export



Time series (crops, biomass, flooding)

Collect all GCOV for one track, frame, and orbit direction
Align to a common grid (rio.reproject_match if frames differ)
Stack in xarray with a time dimension
Multitemporal smoothing (Savitzky-Golay or rolling median)
Extract features (mean, percentiles, seasonal amplitude, date of peak HV)
Model or classify (Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM)
Validate with field data, GEDI (biomass), or optical imagery

title: NISAR Processing
text:
GUNW: Geocoded unwrapped interferogram
What it is: the geocoded version of RUNW, with unwrapped phase, coherence, connected components, ionosphere phase screen, and pixel offsets on a map grid. It is the main input for deformation time series.
Key layers - /science/LSAR/GUNW/grids/frequencyA/unwrappedInterferogram/HH/unwrappedPhase - .../coherenceMagnitude, .../connectedComponents - .../ionospherePhaseScreen, .../ionospherePhaseScreenUncertainty - .../pixelOffsets/HH/ (along-track, slant-range) - metadata/radarGrid/ (incidence angle, LOS unit vectors)

Single-pair steps

Read unwrapped phase, coherence, connected components, ionosphere screen
Mask connected component = 0 and low coherence
Reference to a stable point in the main connected component
Subtract the ionosphere phase screen
Correct troposphere (ERA5, GACOS, or phase-elevation fit)
Remove residual ramps
Convert to LOS displacement: d = −(λ / 4π) × φ
Export (already geocoded)



Time series steps (MintPy)

Download all GUNW pairs for one track, frame, and orbit direction
Plot the baseline network and drop pairs with poor coherence or known issues
Set up a MintPy template with NISAR as the processor
Load the stack (smallbaselineApp.py nisar_template.txt)
Choose the reference point (stable, high coherence, ideally GNSS)
Modify the network by coherence thresholds
Correct unwrapping errors (bridging or phase closure, using connected components)
Apply the ionosphere correction
Invert the network to get displacement per date
Correct troposphere and topographic residual
Estimate velocity (linear + seasonal terms)
Mask by temporal coherence (for example above 0.7)
Validate with GNSS



Ascending + descending decomposition

Run time series for both directions
Read LOS unit vectors from metadata/radarGrid for each
Resample both velocity maps to the same grid
Solve per pixel for east and vertical velocity: v_asc = e_asc·v_E + u_asc·v_U v_desc = e_desc·v_E + u_desc·v_U

title: NISAR Processing
text:
GOFF: Geocoded pixel offsets
What it is: the geocoded version of ROFF. Along-track and slant-range offsets with quality layers on a map grid, usually in several layers with different window sizes.
Key layers - /science/LSAR/GOFF/grids/frequencyA/pixelOffsets/HH/layer1 (layer2, layer3) - alongTrackOffset, slantRangeOffset - correlationSurfacePeak, snr, variance layers - metadata/radarGrid/ (incidence angle, LOS vectors, heading)

Steps

Pick the layer (window size) suited to the feature size and noise
Read offsets and quality layers; check units
Mask by SNR, correlation peak, and variance
Remove outliers with a median filter
Remove bias over stable ground
Convert slant-range offset to ground range: ÷ sin(θ), using incidence angle from radarGrid
Rotate along-track and ground-range offsets to east and north using the satellite heading
Convert to velocity: offset ÷ Δt × 365 (m/yr)
Combine ascending and descending for better 2D velocity; assume surface-parallel flow for 3D
Fill small gaps by interpolation
Build time series for glacier speed-up, surge, or earthquake rupture mapping
Validate with ITS_LIVE, GPS, or optical feature tracking

title: Compact-polarimetry (CP)
text: Banner

title: Compact-polarimetry (CP)
text:
Overview
Compact-polarimetry (CP) is a SAR mode where the radar transmits a circularly polarized wave (commonly RH or LH) and receives two orthogonal linear polarizations (Horizontal, RH and Vertical, RV). This enables the construction of a 2×2 complex covariance matrix, capturing much of the information of full quad-pol but at the cost and coverage of dual-pol.

The radar records complex scattering coefficients: SRH and SRV (where RH = Received Horizontal, RV = Received Vertical, both after transmitting Right-Circular polarization).
The covariance matrix [C2] is formed as:
C₂ = | <|S_RH|²>      <S_RH S_RV*>   |
     | <S_RV S_RH*>   <|S_RV|²>      |
or, in markdown math: \[
\mathbf{C}_2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \langle |S_{\mathrm{RH}}|^2 \rangle & \langle S_{\mathrm{RH}} S_{\mathrm{RV}}^* \rangle \\
  \langle S_{\mathrm{RV}} S_{\mathrm{RH}}^* \rangle & \langle |S_{\mathrm{RV}}|^2 \rangle
\end{bmatrix}
\] where ⟨·⟩ indicates spatial averaging (speckle filtering).
From this, you compute Stokes parameters:

\(S_0 = \langle |S_{\mathrm{RH}}|^2 \rangle + \langle |S_{\mathrm{RV}}|^2 \rangle\) (total intensity)
\(S_1 = \langle |S_{\mathrm{RH}}|^2 \rangle - \langle |S_{\mathrm{RV}}|^2 \rangle\)
\(S_2 = 2 \, \operatorname{Re}(\langle S_{\mathrm{RH}} S_{\mathrm{RV}}^* \rangle)\) (real part)
\(S_3 = \pm 2 \, \operatorname{Im}(\langle S_{\mathrm{RH}} S_{\mathrm{RV}}^* \rangle)\) (imaginary part; sign depends on handedness convention)

The degree of polarization is:
\[
m = \frac{\sqrt{S_1^2 + S_2^2 + S_3^2}}{S_0}
\] This describes how “purely” the scene scatters polarization (low m = depolarized, e.g., vegetation).
The ellipticity angle (\(\chi\)) (indicates even vs. odd bounce) is:
\[
\sin 2\chi = -\frac{S_3}{m S_0}
\] Negative means odd-bounce dominant (e.g., double-bounce in urban or flooded areas).
The relative phase (\(\delta\)) between RH and RV is:
\[
\delta = \arctan\left(\frac{S_3}{S_2}\right)
\]

m-χ decomposition: This produces an RGB visualization to distinguish scattering types: - Red channel (Double-bounce): $ $ - Green channel (Volume): $ $ - Blue channel (Surface): $ $
Thus, compact-pol SAR enables physically interpretable, information-rich products using rigorous polarimetric math.
