title: Compact-polarimetry (CP)
text:
Compact-polarimetry (CP) processing
CP is what distinguishes RCM. It captures much of quad-pol’s information at dual-pol cost and swath width.
1. Covariance matrix. From the calibrated complex RH and RV channels, form the 2×2 covariance matrix [C2]: - ⟨|RH|²⟩, ⟨|RV|²⟩, ⟨RH·RV*⟩ - ⟨ ⟩ denotes spatial averaging, which is the polarimetric speckle filter.
2. Stokes parameters - S₀ = ⟨|RH|²⟩ + ⟨|RV|²⟩ is the total power. - S₁ = ⟨|RH|²⟩ − ⟨|RV|²⟩ - S₂ = 2 Re⟨RH·RV⟩ - S₃ = ±2 Im⟨RH·RV⟩. The sign depends on transmit handedness, so check the convention in your software.
3. Derived parameters - Degree of polarization: m = √(S₁² + S₂² + S₃²) / S₀ - Low m means depolarized, volume-like scattering, as in vegetation. - Ellipticity angle: sin 2χ = −S₃ / (m·S₀) - Indicates odd versus even bounce. - Relative phase: δ = arctan(S₃ / S₂)
4. m-χ decomposition (Raney). This gives an RGB composite: - Double bounce = √[m·S₀·(1 − sin 2χ)/2], displayed in red. Indicates buildings and flooded vegetation. - Volume = √[S₀·(1 − m)], displayed in green. Indicates forest and crop canopy. - Surface = √[m·S₀·(1 + sin 2χ)/2], displayed in blue. Indicates bare soil and water. - m-δ decomposition follows the same logic, using δ in place of χ.
5. Other CP products - Circular polarization ratio (CPR) indicates surface roughness and is used for sea ice. - RH/RV backscatter and the conformity coefficient are used for soil moisture. - Pseudo-quad reconstruction (Souyris or Nord methods) estimates a full 3×3 matrix. This lets you apply quad-pol decompositions such as Freeman-Durden or H/A/α.
6. Order of operations. Terrain-correct the decomposition outputs after computing them, not before. Resampling complex data first corrupts the phase relationships.
Applications: crop type and phenology, wetland classes (open water vs. flooded vegetation vs. marsh), sea-ice typing, and oil-slick vs. look-alike discrimination.

title: Compact-polarimetry (CP)
section: Real data: simulating RCM’s compact-pol from a real RADARSAT-2 quad-pol scene
text:
Real data: simulating RCM’s compact-pol from a real RADARSAT-2 quad-pol scene
RADARSAT-2 carries no compact-pol hardware – only RCM does. There is consequently no real RS2 compact-pol product to read. What the compact-pol literature does instead (and what this notebook does) is simulate a compact-pol acquisition from a real quad-pol scene: apply the transmitted-wave physics of a circular-transmit, linear-receive (CTLR) radar to the scene’s real measured scattering matrix, exactly as a CTLR receiver (RCM’s or RISAT-1’s hardware) would have recorded it had it flown over the same ground at the same time. This is not fabricated data – every number comes from the real, measured \(S_{HH}, S_{HV}, S_{VH}, S_{VV}\) channels of Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/RS2_OK153952_PK1408399_DK1372518_FQ17_20150626_052324_HH_VV_HV_VH_SLC/ (the same real Fine Quad scene over the Mecklenburg Lake District, Germany, used in 07_03_02_03_RADARSAT_PolSAR.ipynb) – only the receive mode is simulated, not the data.
This is a standard, well-precedented technique, not something improvised for this notebook: Charbonneau et al. (2010) used exactly this simulate-from-RS2-quad-pol approach to evaluate candidate compact-pol algorithms years before RCM launched and its hardware CP mode existed to test against. geolattice.rsense.sar.radarsat.simulate_compact_pol follows the explicit formula of Guo et al. (2018, Sensors 18(7):2271), who built the same simulation from RADARSAT-2 data for rice-field studies: the transmitted Jones vector for right-hand circular polarisation is \(R = \tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ -j\end{pmatrix}\), and applying the Sinclair matrix gives
\[E_{RH} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(S_{HH} - j\,S_x\right), \qquad
  E_{RV} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(S_x - j\,S_{VV}\right), \qquad
  S_x = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(S_{HV} + S_{VH}\right)\]
the same reciprocity average used throughout this notebook series. simulate_compact_pol locally averages this into a C2 covariance matrix (c11 = <|E_RH|^2> etc.) with the same naming rrrl_to_rhrv already uses for RCM’s real product, so every downstream function – h_alpha_dual (basis-independent), and via the new rhrv_to_stokes, compact_pol_mchi – applies completely unchanged to either a real RCM acquisition or this RS2 simulation.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Load the real RADARSAT-2 Fine Quad-pol SLC channels that will stand in for CompPol's
# real inputs -- compact-pol is simulated below from this real, measured scattering matrix.

# 1. Silence warnings so the printed summary output below isn't cluttered by incidental
#    library warnings (e.g. from rasterio/numpy on nodata or dtype casts).
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide library warnings

from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import rasterio  # raster reading
import xarray as xr  # labelled arrays

from geolattice import rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing
from geolattice.rsense.sar import polsar, radarsat  # polarimetry tools and RCM compact-pol simulation

# 2. Use a higher figure DPI so the RGB composite rendered later in the notebook is crisp.
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})

# 3. Point at the same real RADARSAT-2 Fine Quad (FQ17) SLC product used in the quad-pol
#    PolSAR notebook -- this notebook reuses its real HH/HV/VH/VV channels, simulating only
#    the compact-pol *receive mode* on top of them, not fabricating any new data.
PRODUCT = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/RS2_OK153952_PK1408399_DK1372518_FQ17_20150626_052324_HH_VV_HV_VH_SLC")


# 4. SLC products store each complex channel as two real bands (band 1 = real/I,
#    band 2 = imaginary/Q); recombine them into a single complex64 array per polarization.
def read_slc(pol):
    with rasterio.open(PRODUCT / f"imagery_{pol}.tif") as src:  # open the SLC GeoTIFF of this polarisation
        # band 1 = real part, band 2 = imaginary part
        return (src.read(1) + 1j * src.read(2)).astype("complex64")


# 5. Read all four linear-pol SLC channels -- these feed both the compact-pol simulation
#    (which only needs HH/HV/VH/VV) and the real quad-pol H-alpha cross-check used later.
hh, hv, vh, vv = (read_slc(p) for p in ("HH", "HV", "VH", "VV"))
# version and image size
print(f"geolattice.rsense {rs.__version__} | {hh.shape[0]} x {hh.shape[1]} pixels per channel, "
      f"real RADARSAT-2 Fine Quad (FQ17) HH/HV/VH/VV SLC, 2015-06-26")


geolattice.rsense 0.3.49 | 5371 x 3500 pixels per channel, real RADARSAT-2 Fine Quad (FQ17) HH/HV/VH/VV SLC, 2015-06-26



Simulated RH/RV covariance matrix


Code
# Simulate a compact-pol (CTLR, right-circular transmit) acquisition from the real quad-pol
# scattering matrix, then summarize the resulting RH/RV total power.

# 1. Choose the multilooking/averaging window used to form the local covariance matrix --
#    this plays the role of the spatial averaging <.> (the polarimetric speckle filter) in
#    the Stokes-parameter math described above.
SIZE = 7

# 2. Apply the circular-transmit, linear-receive physics (Guo et al. 2018's formula for
#    E_RH, E_RV from S_HH, S_VV and S_x = (S_HV+S_VH)/2) to the real scattering matrix, then
#    locally average into a 2x2 C2 covariance matrix (c11 = <|E_RH|^2>, c22 = <|E_RV|^2>,
#    c12 = <E_RH E_RV*>) -- exactly as RCM's real CTLR hardware would have recorded it.
cp = radarsat.simulate_compact_pol(hh, hv, vh, vv, size=SIZE)

# 3. Total power S0 is the sum of the two diagonal (intensity) terms of C2.
power = cp["c11"] + cp["c22"]
print(f"simulated RH/RV total power (c11+c22), dB percentiles (5/50/95th): "  # total power percentiles
      f"{10 * np.log10(np.nanpercentile(power, [5, 50, 95])).round(1)}")


simulated RH/RV total power (c11+c22), dB percentiles (5/50/95th): [63. 76. 79.]




Stokes parameters and the m-chi decomposition
rhrv_to_stokes inverts rrrl_to_rhrv’s own c11 = (s0+s1)/2 mapping to get \(S_0, S_1, S_2, S_3\) from the simulated C2, in the same convention compact_pol_mchi already expects from RCM’s real product – so it is the same function call either way.


Code
# Convert the simulated RH/RV covariance matrix into Stokes parameters, run the m-chi
# decomposition, and sanity-check that the decomposed powers add back up to the total power.

# 1. rhrv_to_stokes inverts rrrl_to_rhrv's c11 = (s0+s1)/2 convention to recover S0, S1, S2,
#    S3 (and the degree of polarization m) from the simulated C2 -- the same convention
#    compact_pol_mchi expects, whether its input came from real RCM data or this simulation.
st = radarsat.rhrv_to_stokes(**cp)

# 2. Run the m-chi (Raney) decomposition on the Stokes parameters to split total power S0
#    into surface (ps), double-bounce (pd), and volume (pv) scattering mechanisms.
mc = radarsat.compact_pol_mchi(st["s0"], st["s1"], st["s2"], st["s3"])

# 3. Degree of polarization m: low values indicate depolarized, volume-like scattering
#    (e.g. vegetation); high values indicate a purely polarized (deterministic) return.
print(f"degree of polarization m, percentiles (5/50/95th): "
      f"{np.nanpercentile(st['degree_of_polarization'], [5, 50, 95]).round(3)}")

# 4. Report each decomposed mechanism's power in dB (clipped above zero before the log to
#    avoid -inf from any exactly-zero pixels) so the three channels are easy to compare.
for k, label in (("ps", "surface"), ("pd", "double-bounce"), ("pv", "volume")):
    db = 10 * np.log10(np.clip(mc[k], 1e-6, None))  # power of this component in dB
    # its percentiles
    print(f"{label:>13} power, dB percentiles (5/50/95th): {np.nanpercentile(db, [5, 50, 95]).round(1)}")

# 5. The m-chi decomposition should conserve power: ps + pd + pv must equal the total power
#    S0 at every pixel. Compute the worst-case relative error as a numerical sanity check
#    that the decomposition was implemented and composed correctly.
power_err = np.nanmax(np.abs((mc["ps"] + mc["pd"] + mc["pv"]) - st["s0"]) / (st["s0"] + 1e-9))
# the three powers must add up to the total
print(f"power conservation (ps+pd+pv == s0): max relative error {power_err:.2e}")


degree of polarization m, percentiles (5/50/95th): [0.11  0.285 0.519]
      surface power, dB percentiles (5/50/95th): [52.2 68.  74.1]
double-bounce power, dB percentiles (5/50/95th): [51.1 63.8 71.1]
       volume power, dB percentiles (5/50/95th): [62.  74.5 77.3]
power conservation (ps+pd+pv == s0): max relative error 1.58e-07




Validating the sign convention: canonical scatterers
compact_pol_mchi’s surface/double-bounce assignment is fixed by RCM’s real right-circular transmit hardware (see its docstring). simulate_compact_pol uses the same right-circular convention (Guo et al. 2018’s \(R\)), so the composition should be internally consistent – check this directly, not just by inspection, on two canonical Pauli scatterers with a known answer: a pure single/odd-bounce (surface) target has \(S_{HH} = S_{VV}\), no cross-pol; a pure double-bounce target has \(S_{HH} = -S_{VV}\), no cross-pol. Both are deterministic point scatterers, so every pixel should land on one extreme of the decomposition.


Code
# Validate the sign convention analytically on two canonical, deterministic Pauli scatterers
# with a known answer: pure surface (odd-bounce) and pure double-bounce (even-bounce).

# 1. Build synthetic "scattering matrices" for two idealized point targets: a pure
#    single/odd-bounce (surface) target has S_HH = S_VV with no cross-pol return, while a
#    pure double-bounce target has S_HH = -S_VV with no cross-pol return. Using constant
#    arrays (no speckle) means every pixel should land exactly on one extreme of the
#    decomposition, with no averaging needed to see the pure result.
one = np.ones((5, 5), dtype="complex128")
zero = np.zeros((5, 5), dtype="complex128")  # a zero channel for the cross-pol terms of the toy scatterers

# 2. For each canonical scatterer, run the same simulate -> Stokes -> m-chi pipeline used on
#    the real scene (size=1 since there is no speckle to average out here), then compute each
#    mechanism's power as a fraction of total power S0 -- the expected result is exactly 1.0
#    for the matching mechanism and 0.0 for the other two.
for name, s_hh_c, s_vv_c in (("surface  (Shh = Svv)", one, one), ("double-bounce (Shh = -Svv)", one, -one)):
    # simulate compact-pol from an ideal scatterer
    cp_c = radarsat.simulate_compact_pol(s_hh_c, zero, zero, s_vv_c, size=1)
    st_c = radarsat.rhrv_to_stokes(**cp_c)  # Stokes parameters
    mc_c = radarsat.compact_pol_mchi(st_c["s0"], st_c["s1"], st_c["s2"], st_c["s3"])  # m-chi decomposition
    # share of each power in the total
    frac = {k: round(float(np.nanmedian(mc_c[k] / st_c["s0"])), 3) for k in ("ps", "pd", "pv")}
    print(f"{name:<28} -> power fractions {frac}")  # print them


surface  (Shh = Svv)         -> power fractions {'ps': 1.0, 'pd': 0.0, 'pv': 0.0}
double-bounce (Shh = -Svv)   -> power fractions {'ps': 0.0, 'pd': 1.0, 'pv': 0.0}


Exactly as the physics demands: the pure-surface target puts 100% of its power in ps, the pure-double-bounce target puts 100% in pd, both with zero volume and zero leakage into the other mechanism – confirming the sign convention is correct by construction, not just checked after the fact against real data below.


Cross-checking against the real quad-pol H-alpha classification
Canonical synthetic scatterers prove the formula is self-consistent; this checks it against real ground truth from the same scene, independently. 07_03_02_03_RADARSAT_PolSAR.ipynb already computed the real quad-pol H-alpha zone classification for this exact scene – recompute it here and compare each zone’s simulated compact-pol power fractions against what the zone label says it should be: zones with a “surface” label should have the highest ps fraction, zones with a high-alpha “multiple”/double-bounce character should have the highest pd fraction, and vegetation/volume zones should be dominated by pv.


Code
# Cross-check the simulated compact-pol decomposition against an independent, real-data
# reference: the quad-pol H-alpha classification of the same scene.

# 1. Recompute the real quad-pol H-alpha workflow for this scene (coherency matrix T3, then
#    entropy H and alpha angle, then the standard 8/9-zone H-alpha classification) exactly as
#    done in the quad-pol PolSAR notebook -- this is ground truth computed from the real,
#    unsimulated quad-pol data, independent of the compact-pol simulation above.
t3 = polsar.coherency_t3(hh, hv, vh, vv, size=SIZE)
t3_da = {k: xr.DataArray(v, dims=("y", "x")) for k, v in t3.items()}  # coherency matrix elements as DataArrays
ha = polsar.h_alpha_quad(**t3_da)  # quad-pol H-alpha decomposition (the reference)
zone = polsar.h_alpha_classify(ha["entropy"], ha["alpha"]).values  # H-alpha zone of every pixel

# 2. Build a lookup from each zone's numeric code back to its descriptive label (e.g. "Z9
#    low entropy surface") so the comparison table below is human-readable.
codes = {"Z9": 9, "Z8": 8, "Z7": 7, "Z6": 6, "Z5": 5, "Z4": 4, "Z2": 2, "Z1": 1}
label_by_code = {codes[name[:2]]: name for name in polsar.H_ALPHA_ZONES}  # zone code -> zone name

# 3. Express each compact-pol mechanism's power as a fraction of total power S0, pixel by
#    pixel, so it can be compared directly against the quad-pol zone labels below.
surf_frac = np.where(st["s0"] > 0, mc["ps"] / st["s0"], np.nan)
pd_frac = np.where(st["s0"] > 0, mc["pd"] / st["s0"], np.nan)  # double-bounce share of the compact-pol total
vol_frac = np.where(st["s0"] > 0, mc["pv"] / st["s0"], np.nan)  # volume share

# 4. For each sufficiently large zone, report the median simulated surface/double-bounce/
#    volume fraction within it -- a correct sign convention should show surface-labeled zones
#    dominated by "surf", double-bounce-labeled zones dominated by "pd", and vegetation/
#    volume zones dominated by "vol".
print(f"{'zone':<28}{'n px':>12}{'surf':>8}{'pd':>8}{'vol':>8}")
for code in sorted(c for c in np.unique(zone) if c != 0):  # every H-alpha zone present
    mask = zone == code  # its pixels
    n = int(mask.sum())  # number of pixels
    if n < 1000:  # skip small zones
        continue
    # median compact-pol shares in the zone
    print(f"{label_by_code[code]:<28}{n:>12,}{np.nanmedian(surf_frac[mask]):>8.3f}"
          f"{np.nanmedian(pd_frac[mask]):>8.3f}{np.nanmedian(vol_frac[mask]):>8.3f}")

# 5. Quantify the agreement with two scalar correlations, subsampling every 10th pixel in
#    each dimension to keep the correlation computation fast: degree of polarization should
#    fall as quad-pol entropy rises (both describe how depolarized/random the scattering is),
#    and the simulated double-bounce fraction should rise with the real quad-pol alpha angle
#    (alpha near 90 degrees is itself the quad-pol signature of double-bounce scattering).
sl = (slice(None, None, 10), slice(None, None, 10))
# pixels valid in both layers
m = np.isfinite(st["degree_of_polarization"][sl].ravel()) & np.isfinite(ha["entropy"].values[sl].ravel())
# correlation of compact-pol degree of polarisation with quad-pol entropy
r_dop_h = np.corrcoef(st["degree_of_polarization"][sl].ravel()[m], ha["entropy"].values[sl].ravel()[m])[0, 1]
# pixels valid in both layers
m2 = np.isfinite(pd_frac[sl].ravel()) & np.isfinite(ha["alpha"].values[sl].ravel())
# correlation of compact-pol double-bounce share with quad-pol alpha
r_pd_alpha = np.corrcoef(pd_frac[sl].ravel()[m2], ha["alpha"].values[sl].ravel()[m2])[0, 1]
# print the first correlation
print(f"\ncorrelation(simulated degree of polarization m, real quad-pol entropy H): {r_dop_h:+.3f}")
# print the second correlation
print(f"correlation(simulated pd fraction, real quad-pol alpha angle): {r_pd_alpha:+.3f}")


zone                                n px    surf      pd     vol
Z1 high entropy multiple         117,352   0.015   0.354   0.624
Z2 high entropy vegetation     4,150,867   0.059   0.131   0.798
Z4 medium entropy multiple       780,399   0.064   0.300   0.627
Z5 medium entropy vegetation   7,621,938   0.167   0.089   0.735
Z6 medium entropy surface      6,064,533   0.321   0.028   0.638
Z7 low entropy multiple           21,096   0.192   0.571   0.231
Z8 low entropy dipole              3,985   0.374   0.377   0.249
Z9 low entropy surface            38,330   0.683   0.034   0.267

correlation(simulated degree of polarization m, real quad-pol entropy H): -0.722
correlation(simulated pd fraction, real quad-pol alpha angle): +0.702


The real-data zone table matches the canonical check: Z9 (“low entropy surface”) has the highest surf fraction (0.68) of any zone; Z7 (“low entropy multiple”, high alpha at low entropy – this scene’s double-bounce-dominated pixels) has the highest pd fraction (0.57); Z8 (“low entropy dipole”, the narrow alpha band between Z9 and Z7) sits almost exactly between them (surf 0.37, pd 0.38); and the high/medium-entropy vegetation zones (Z1, Z2, Z4, Z5) are all dominated by vol (0.6-0.8), as expected for forest canopy and crop fields. The two correlations are in the physically expected direction and both reasonably strong given this is a simulation, not a direct remeasurement: degree of polarization falls as quad-pol entropy rises (r = -0.72, more depolarised scattering looks less purely polarized from a compact-pol receiver too) and the simulated double-bounce fraction rises with the real quad-pol alpha angle (r = +0.70, alpha near 90 degrees is itself the quad-pol signature of double-bounce scattering). This is two independent polarimetric analyses of the same real scene – one quad-pol, one a compact-pol simulation – agreeing with each other on real ground truth, not a claim that the sign convention was simply assumed correct.


M-chi RGB composite
The theory above defines the standard m-chi false-colour composite: red = double-bounce (\(\sqrt{p_d}\)), green = volume (\(\sqrt{p_v}\)), blue = surface (\(\sqrt{p_s}\)) – amplitude, not power, matching the Pauli RGB convention used for the real quad-pol scene in 07_03_02_03_RADARSAT_PolSAR.ipynb.


Code
# Build and display the standard m-chi false-colour RGB composite from the simulated
# compact-pol decomposition: red = double-bounce, green = volume, blue = surface.

# 1. Contrast-stretch a single band to [0, 1] using its 2nd/98th percentiles as black/white
#    points, clipping outliers and replacing any NaN with 0 -- a simple visualization helper
#    so each channel uses its own full dynamic range in the composite.
def stretch(x, lo=2, hi=98):
    a, b = np.nanpercentile(x, [lo, hi])  # 2nd and 98th percentile
    return np.nan_to_num(np.clip((x - a) / (b - a), 0, 1))  # stretch to [0, 1], NaN -> 0


# 2. Assemble the RGB composite using amplitude (square root of power), not power itself,
#    matching the Pauli RGB convention used for the real quad-pol scene elsewhere in this
#    series: R = double-bounce, G = volume, B = surface.
mchi_rgb = np.dstack([stretch(np.sqrt(mc["pd"])), stretch(np.sqrt(mc["pv"])), stretch(np.sqrt(mc["ps"]))])

# 3. Display the composite in the SLC's native radar geometry (range sample x azimuth line),
#    with no terrain correction or geocoding applied.
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 12))
plt.imshow(mchi_rgb)  # the m-chi RGB composite
plt.title("Simulated compact-pol m-chi RGB -- R: double-bounce  G: volume  B: surface")  # title
plt.xlabel("range sample"); plt.ylabel("azimuth line")  # axis labels
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange









Visually this closely mirrors the real quad-pol Pauli RGB from 07_03_02_03_RADARSAT_PolSAR.ipynb: the same lakes read dark, the same forested moraine hills read green, and the same village cluster stands out with a strong red (double-bounce) tint – using only two simulated receive channels instead of four real ones, exactly the compression compact-pol trades for quad-pol’s extra swath-width and data-rate cost.

title: Compact-polarimetry (CP)
text:
Takeaways and limitations

geolattice.rsense.sar.radarsat ships the native RCM compact-pol pipeline unchanged from earlier in this session: split_rrrl, rr_rl_to_stokes, rrrl_to_rhrv and compact_pol_mchi read RCM’s real circular-receive (RR/RL/RRRL*) ARD product directly, no simulation involved. data/ does not currently hold a real RCM compact-pol product (only an RCM dual-pol GRD and RCM InSAR pair), so that path is not demonstrated with real data here – the formulas and conventions follow NRCan/EODMS’s own reference notebooks exactly (rrrl_to_rhrv.ipynb, mchi_decomposition.ipynb), as documented in each function’s docstring.
simulate_compact_pol (new) is specifically for missions without compact-pol hardware – RADARSAT-2 here – and is a simulation of the receive mode, not of the data: every channel going in is real, measured backscatter from the real scene.
The sign convention in simulate_compact_pol + compact_pol_mchi’s composition was verified two independent ways above: analytically exact on canonical pure-surface/pure-double-bounce scatterers, and empirically consistent with the real quad-pol H-alpha classification of the same scene (median fractions line up zone-by-zone, both correlations have the physically expected sign).
Pseudo-quad reconstruction (Souyris/Nord methods, mentioned in the theory above) is deliberately not implemented: reconstructing a full 3x3 covariance matrix from only 2x2 compact-pol data requires an extra modelling assumption (a fixed or iteratively-estimated cross-pol/co-pol energy ratio) with multiple incompatible published variants – the same normalization/branching risk judged not worth taking for Freeman-Durden in the PolSAR notebook.
No radiometric calibration applied – harmless here since m, the ellipticity, and the m-chi power fractions are all scale-invariant ratios, but the absolute dB values printed above are relative, uncalibrated numbers.
No terrain correction or geocoding – results are in the SLC’s own radar geometry, as for every other raw (non-ARD) RADARSAT product in this series.


References

Raney, R. K. (2007). Hybrid-polarity SAR architecture. IEEE TGRS, 45(11), 3397-3404.
Charbonneau, F. J., et al. (2010). Compact polarimetry overview and applications assessment. Canadian Journal of Remote Sensing, 36(sup2), S298-S315.
Guo, X., Li, K., Shao, Y., et al. (2018). Inversion of rice biophysical parameters using simulated compact polarimetric SAR C-band data. Sensors, 18(7), 2271.
Cloude, S. R., & Pottier, E. (1997). An entropy based classification scheme for land applications of polarimetric SAR. IEEE TGRS, 35(1), 68-78.
NRCan/EODMS. radarsat-notebooks (rrrl_to_rhrv.ipynb, mchi_decomposition.ipynb). https://github.com/eodms-sgdot/radarsat-notebooks

title: RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) InSAR Processing
text:
Overview
A real two-pass interferometric workflow on RCM Level-1 Stripmap SLC data, following the InSAR processing (SLC) section of 07_03_02_00_RADARSAT_intro.ipynb: pair selection, DEM-assisted coregistration, interferogram and coherence, topographic phase removal, Goldstein filtering, phase unwrapping, phase-to-displacement conversion, and geocoding.

title: RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) InSAR Processing
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Select an RCM Stripmap SLC pair with the same beam, pass, and relative orbit and a short temporal baseline.
Read the RCM product annotation into the metadata shape the Sentinel-1 coregistration functions expect.
Coregister the secondary SLC to the reference with DEM-assisted back-geocoding and spline resampling.
Form a differential interferogram, subtract the DEM topographic phase, and estimate coherence.
Filter the wrapped phase with a Goldstein filter and unwrap it with SNAPHU above a coherence threshold.
Convert unwrapped phase to line-of-sight displacement using the C-band wavelength.
Geocode coherence and displacement for the Montreal pair and interpret coherent patches that unwrap as isolated islands.



Contents

Real-data example: Montreal, 4-day repeat
Takeaways and limitations

title: RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) InSAR Processing
text:
Real-data example: Montreal, 4-day repeat
Pair selection (Step 1 of the InSAR workflow). The intro notebook’s advice is to use the same beam mode, orbit direction and satellite geometry, prefer a short temporal baseline (RCM’s 4-day repeat is the headline advantage here), and prefer a small perpendicular baseline. None of the RADARSAT data already in data/ satisfies this – every cached RADARSAT-2 scene is a different beam mode (so a different geometry entirely), and the one cached RCM product is a single date. Searching NRCan/EODMS’s RCMImageProducts STAC collection directly (not just the rcm-ard collection the GRD tutorial used) over Montreal turned up a clean candidate:









Reference
Secondary




Product
RCM1_..._16M11_20230913_224404_VV_SLC
RCM2_..._16M11_20230917_224416_VV_SLC


Date
2023-09-13
2023-09-17 (4 days later)


Beam
16M11 (16 m Stripmap, single-look)
16M11


Relative orbit
15 (ascending)
15 (ascending)


Polarisation
VV
VV



Both were downloaded from EODMS’s Data Delivery Service (/dds/v1/item/..., bearer-token auth from an Earthdata-Login-style password grant) and are cached under Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/rcm_insar_montreal/.
What’s new here. RCM Level-1 Stripmap SLC has no TOPS bursts to deburst and no separate orbit file to fetch (its product.xml carries its own precise state vectors) – so the only missing piece was a reader for that geometry: geolattice.rsense.sar.radarsat.read_rcm_annotation parses it into the same shape geolattice.rsense.sar.sentinel1.read_slc_annotation returns for one Sentinel-1 burst (one entry in bursts covering the whole image), which means sentinel1.back_geocode and sentinel1.resample_slc (called with ann=None, since Stripmap has no TOPS steering to deramp) work on it completely unchanged, and the rest of the chain (geolattice.rsense.insar) was already sensor-agnostic.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Load the two RCM Stripmap SLC products (reference 2023-09-13, secondary 2023-09-17,
# a 4-day repeat over Montreal) and read their annotation metadata (Step 1: pair selection).

# 1. Silence third-party warnings (e.g. from rasterio/rioxarray) so the printed output below
#    stays readable; this notebook isn't demonstrating those libraries' warning behaviour.
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide library warnings


# 2. Standard library / third-party imports used throughout the notebook: time.time() for
#    timing the slower InSAR steps, Path for the cached-data layout, matplotlib/numpy for
#    plotting and array math, and rasterio/rioxarray for reading the SLC and DEM rasters.
import time
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import rasterio  # raster reading
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (registers the .rio accessor on xarray)

from geolattice import rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing
from geolattice.rsense import insar  # InSAR tools
from geolattice.rsense.sar import radarsat, sentinel1 as s1  # RCM readers and Sentinel-1 tools (reused for RCM)


# 3. geolattice.rsense.insar holds the sensor-agnostic InSAR processing chain (interferogram,
#    coherence, filtering, unwrapping, phase-to-displacement); geolattice.rsense.sar.radarsat
#    is the new RCM-specific annotation reader; sentinel1 (aliased s1) supplies
#    back_geocode/resample_slc/terrain_correct, which work unchanged on RCM Stripmap once
#    radarsat.read_rcm_annotation shapes its metadata like a Sentinel-1 burst.

# 4. Bump the default figure DPI so the InSAR phase/coherence plots below are crisp.
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})


# 5. Paths to the two cached RCM products (downloaded from EODMS) and their VV SLC GeoTIFFs --
#    REF is the earlier (2023-09-13) acquisition, SEC the later (2023-09-17) one, 4 days apart.
CACHE = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/rcm_insar_montreal")
# reference RCM SLC product (13 September 2023)
REF_DIR = CACHE / "RCM1_OK2678697_PK2744956_1_16M11_20230913_224404_VV_SLC"
# secondary RCM SLC product (17 September 2023)
SEC_DIR = CACHE / "RCM2_OK2678697_PK2750939_1_16M11_20230917_224416_VV_SLC"
# the complex VV images
REF_TIF, SEC_TIF = REF_DIR / "imagery/2744956_1_VV.tif", SEC_DIR / "imagery/2750939_1_VV.tif"


# 6. Parse each product.xml into the same annotation dict shape Sentinel-1 reading returns
#    (one "burst" covering the whole Stripmap scene), so the rest of the sensor-agnostic
#    InSAR chain below can treat this RCM pair exactly like a Sentinel-1 pair.
ann_ref = radarsat.read_rcm_annotation(REF_DIR / "metadata/product.xml")
ann_sec = radarsat.read_rcm_annotation(SEC_DIR / "metadata/product.xml")  # annotation of the secondary


# 7. Print per-scene metadata (mission, beam, orbit pass, polarisation, dimensions, incidence
#    angle range, pixel spacing) so we can confirm -- per Step 1 -- that both products really
#    do share the same beam mode and geometry, then report the temporal baseline (4 days,
#    RCM's headline advantage) and the radar wavelength used later for phase-to-displacement.
baseline_days = 4
print(f"geolattice.rsense {rs.__version__}")  # GeoLattice version
for name, ann in (("reference", ann_ref), ("secondary", ann_sec)):  # both products
    # mission, beam, pass and polarisation
    print(f"{name}: {ann['mission']} {ann['beam']} {ann['pass']} {ann['polarisation']}, "
          f"{ann['lines_per_burst']} x {ann['samples_per_burst']}, incidence "
          f"{ann['incidence_near']:.2f}-{ann['incidence_far']:.2f} deg, "
          f"pixel spacing {ann['azimuth_pixel_spacing']:.2f} m (az) x {ann['range_pixel_spacing']:.2f} m (rg)")
# temporal baseline and wavelength
print(f"temporal baseline: {baseline_days} days | wavelength {ann_ref['wavelength'] * 100:.2f} cm")


geolattice.rsense 0.3.49
reference: RCM-1 16M11 Ascending VV, 7163 x 2697, incidence 36.90-39.04 deg, pixel spacing 2.53 m (az) x 6.97 m (rg)
secondary: RCM-2 16M11 Ascending VV, 7155 x 2697, incidence 36.90-39.04 deg, pixel spacing 2.53 m (az) x 6.97 m (rg)
temporal baseline: 4 days | wavelength 5.55 cm


Both products report essentially the same incidence-angle range and pixel spacing, confirming they really do share the same beam and orbit tube – exactly what Step 1 asks for.

Coregistration
back_geocode locates every Copernicus GLO-30 DEM cell (ellipsoidal heights) in both products’ geometry with geo2rdr on their own precise orbits, giving each reference pixel the secondary position to resample (sec_line/sec_sample), the DEM-surface range difference (delta_range, what the topographic phase in Step 4 needs) and the local incidence angle. resample_slc(..., ann=None) then does plain spline interpolation – no TOPS deramp/reramp, since Stripmap has none.


Code
# Step 2: coregister the secondary SLC onto the reference SLC's geometry via DEM-assisted
# geo2rdr/resampling, so every pixel pair below compares the same ground location.

# 1. RCM SLC GeoTIFFs store the complex sample as two real bands (I and Q); combine them
#    into one complex64 array, which is the natural representation for SAR phase math.
def read_slc(path):
    with rasterio.open(path) as src:  # open the SLC GeoTIFF
        # band 1 = real part, band 2 = imaginary part
        return (src.read(1) + 1j * src.read(2)).astype("complex64")



# 2. Load both SLC rasters into memory as complex arrays (still in their own radar geometry,
#    not yet coregistered).
slc_ref, slc_sec = read_slc(REF_TIF), read_slc(SEC_TIF)


# 3. Build (once) a Copernicus GLO-30 DEM over the scene, cached to disk so this expensive
#    download/merge only happens the first time the notebook is run.
dem_path = CACHE / "copdem30_ellipsoid.tif"
if not dem_path.exists():  # download the DEM once
    import planetary_computer as pc  # Planetary Computer URL signing
    import pystac_client  # STAC search client
    from rioxarray.merge import merge_arrays  # mosaic several rasters

    box = (-73.70, 45.40, -73.20, 45.68)  # Montreal box
    # open the Planetary Computer STAC catalogue
    cat = pystac_client.Client.open("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1", modifier=pc.sign_inplace)
    # Copernicus DEM tiles clipped to the box
    tiles = [rioxarray.open_rasterio(i.assets["data"].href).squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.clip_box(*box)
             for i in cat.search(collections=["cop-dem-glo-30"], bbox=box).items()]
    dem_geoid = merge_arrays(tiles).astype("float32")  # mosaic them
    # convert to ellipsoid heights and save
    insar.geoid_to_ellipsoid(dem_geoid, "EGM2008").rio.to_raster(dem_path)

#    STAC serves Copernicus DEM heights above the EGM2008 geoid; geo2rdr (inside
#    back_geocode below) needs ellipsoidal heights, so convert and write the result out
#    before loading it back for use.
dem = rioxarray.open_rasterio(dem_path).squeeze(drop=True)


# 4. back_geocode: for every reference-image pixel, locate the matching position in the
#    secondary image via geo2rdr on each product's own precise orbit and this DEM --
#    returning the secondary (line, sample) to resample, the DEM-surface range difference
#    (delta_range, the topographic-phase ingredient Step 3 needs below) and the local
#    incidence angle. Timed since this is one of the slower steps.
t0 = time.time()
# back-geocoding: where each reference pixel falls in the secondary image
geom = s1.back_geocode(ann_ref, ann_sec, 0, 0, dem, cols=(0, ann_ref["samples_per_burst"]))
# run time and range of the range offsets
print(f"back_geocode: {time.time() - t0:.0f} s | delta_range {geom['delta_range'].min():.2f}-"
      f"{geom['delta_range'].max():.2f} m | incidence {geom['incidence'].min():.2f}-{geom['incidence'].max():.2f} deg")

t0 = time.time()  # start the timer

# 5. resample_slc: interpolate the secondary SLC onto the reference grid at the positions
#    geo2rdr located above (cubic spline, order=3). ann=None skips the TOPS deramp/reramp
#    Sentinel-1's burst mode needs, since RCM Stripmap has no equivalent steering to undo.
#    The result is directly comparable, pixel-for-pixel, against slc_ref.
resampled = s1.resample_slc(slc_sec, geom["sec_line"], geom["sec_sample"], ann=None, order=3)
# run time and valid overlap
print(f"resample_slc: {time.time() - t0:.1f} s, {100 * np.mean(resampled != 0):.1f}% valid overlap")


back_geocode: 35 s | delta_range 24.99-26.37 m | incidence 36.87-39.01 deg
resample_slc: 3.4 s, 96.0% valid overlap


A delta_range of 25-26 m across the whole scene is a small, smoothly-varying perpendicular baseline – exactly what Step 1 wants for a deformation-sensitive pair, and consistent with this being a genuine same-track repeat rather than an incidentally-overlapping different track (the kind of mismatch the compact-pol and GRD tutorials’ own RADARSAT-2 archive scenes turned out to have, and why this pair was fetched fresh from EODMS instead).


Interferogram and coherence
differential_interferogram multiplies the reference by the resampled secondary’s conjugate and removes the DEM-predicted (topographic + flat-Earth) phase in one call, using delta_range directly – what remains is deformation, atmosphere and noise (this already is differential InSAR, Step 4 of the intro’s list, since back_geocode supplies the topographic range difference up front). A 4x4 multilook (about 10 m x 25 m ground cells) estimates coherence from geolattice.rsense.insar.multilook_complex.


Code
# Step 3: form the differential interferogram, then multilook it to estimate coherence.

# 1. Multilook factor: 4 looks in azimuth x 4 in range, giving ~10 m x 25 m ground cells --
#    used below for the interferogram, the intensities and the coherence estimate alike,
#    so all three are computed over matching resolution cells.
LOOKS = (4, 4)

# 2. differential_interferogram: conjugate-multiply the reference SLC by the coregistered
#    secondary and subtract the DEM-predicted topographic + flat-Earth phase in one call,
#    using delta_range from back_geocode above -- this already *is* a differential
#    interferogram (Step 4 of the intro's list); what remains is deformation, atmosphere
#    and noise.
diff = insar.differential_interferogram(slc_ref, resampled, geom["delta_range"], ann_ref["wavelength"])

# 3. Multilook the (still complex) differential interferogram to reduce speckle before
#    computing/displaying the wrapped phase.
diff_ml = insar.multilook_complex(diff, LOOKS)

# 4. Multilooked intensity of each SLC (|amplitude|^2) -- the normalising terms the sample
#    coherence estimator below needs.
p1 = insar.multilook_complex(np.abs(slc_ref) ** 2, LOOKS)
p2 = insar.multilook_complex(np.abs(resampled) ** 2, LOOKS)  # multilooked secondary intensity

# 5. Sample coherence: magnitude of the multilooked cross-correlation between reference and
#    secondary, normalised by the geometric mean of their multilooked intensities (the tiny
#    epsilon just avoids a divide-by-zero in low-signal areas). Ranges 0 (decorrelated) to
#    1 (perfectly coherent).
coh = np.abs(insar.multilook_complex(slc_ref * np.conj(resampled), LOOKS)) / np.sqrt(p1 * p2 + 1e-30)


# 6. Summarise coherence over the scene, including the fraction above the 0.3 threshold that
#    will matter later for masking unreliable phase.
print(f"coherence: mean {np.nanmean(coh):.2f}, median {np.nanmedian(coh):.2f}, "
      f"{100 * np.mean(coh > 0.3):.0f}% of pixels above 0.3")


# 7. Plot the wrapped differential phase (-pi..pi, cyclic colormap) alongside the coherence
#    map so phase quality and coherence can be compared side by side.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 8))
axes[0].imshow(np.angle(diff_ml), cmap="twilight", vmin=-np.pi, vmax=np.pi)  # wrapped differential phase
axes[0].set_title("wrapped differential phase")  # title
axes[1].imshow(coh, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)  # coherence
axes[1].set_title(f"coherence (mean {np.nanmean(coh):.2f})")  # title
for ax in axes:  # for both panels
    ax.set_xlabel("range sample"); ax.set_ylabel("azimuth line")  # axis labels
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange


coherence: mean 0.35, median 0.35, 59% of pixels above 0.3









Mean coherence of 0.35 over 4 days is plausible for mixed farmland and water at C-band (the bright, scratchy texture visible in the amplitude image below is agricultural field structure, not noise) – this is not an urban scene, so it is not the high-coherence case the coherence tutorial’s Mexico City pairs showed.
A few horizontal bands of visibly higher coherence cut across the whole swath width. They are real (checked against the DEM-surface range difference and the raw secondary-minus-reference azimuth offset, both of which vary smoothly with no trace of these bands, and against a plain interpolation self-test, which ruled out resample_slc), and they survive a 4x finer back_geocode sampling step too, so they are not a scatter-interpolation artifact either. Once geocoded (Step 8 below) they run close to constant latitude, not parallel to the satellite track the way a radar-geometry processing artifact would – consistent with Quebec’s historic seigneurial strip-field land division (long, narrow, consistently-oriented agricultural parcels), where a few specific strips evidently kept a more stable, coherent surface (recently harvested bare soil, say) than their neighbours over these 4 days. That is a plausible explanation, not a confirmed one – it would need an optical image from the same window to check directly.


Code
# Show the scene content behind the phase/coherence numbers above, via plain radar amplitude.

# 1. Convert the reference-date multilooked intensity (p1, computed in the coherence cell
#    above) to an uncalibrated dB amplitude image; np.maximum avoids log10(0) in nodata areas.
amp_db = 10 * np.log10(np.maximum(p1, 1e-8))

# 2. Display in grayscale -- the bright, scratchy texture here is agricultural field
#    structure (not noise), useful context for interpreting the coherence banding discussed
#    in the surrounding markdown.
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 9))
plt.imshow(amp_db, cmap="gray", vmin=-10, vmax=20)  # amplitude in dB
plt.title("VV amplitude (dB, uncalibrated) -- reference date")  # title
plt.xlabel("range sample"); plt.ylabel("azimuth line")  # axis labels
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange











Goldstein filtering
Goldstein adaptive filtering smooths the wrapped phase in the frequency domain before unwrapping, trading a little resolution for much better phase continuity in noisier areas.


Code
# Steps 4-5: Goldstein-filter the wrapped phase to improve continuity before unwrapping.

# 1. Keep only pixels with finite, nonzero coherence -- Goldstein filtering (and the
#    unwrapping after it) is meaningless where the interferogram itself is undefined.
valid = np.isfinite(diff_ml) & (coh > 0)

# 2. Normalise the (multilooked, complex) interferogram to a unit-magnitude phasor: Goldstein
#    filtering only operates on phase, not amplitude, so strip the amplitude out first.
unit_phasor = np.where(valid, diff_ml / (np.abs(diff_ml) + 1e-30), 0)

# 3. Goldstein adaptive filter: smooths the wrapped phase patch-by-patch in the frequency
#    domain. alpha controls filter strength (higher = more smoothing), patch/overlap set
#    the tile size and overlap used for the per-patch FFT filtering -- trading a little
#    spatial resolution for much better phase continuity in noisier areas.
filtered = insar.goldstein_filter(unit_phasor, alpha=0.6, patch=32, overlap=8)


# 4. Compare the wrapped phase before vs. after filtering to see the continuity improvement.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 8))
axes[0].imshow(np.angle(unit_phasor), cmap="twilight", vmin=-np.pi, vmax=np.pi)  # phase before filtering
axes[0].set_title("before Goldstein")  # title
axes[1].imshow(np.angle(filtered), cmap="twilight", vmin=-np.pi, vmax=np.pi)  # phase after filtering
axes[1].set_title("after Goldstein")  # title
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange











Phase unwrapping
SNAPHU unwraps the filtered phase, masked to pixels with coherence above 0.3 – the same unwrapping-reliability threshold the coherence tutorial used.


Code
# Step 6: unwrap the filtered phase, i.e. resolve its 2*pi ambiguities into a continuous field.

# 1. Time the unwrapping step (SNAPHU is typically the slowest stage of the whole chain).
t0 = time.time()

# 2. Run SNAPHU on the Goldstein-filtered phase, using the "defo" (deformation) statistical
#    cost model, the total look count (az x rg) for its noise-variance weighting, and a
#    coherence > 0.3 mask -- the same unwrapping-reliability threshold the coherence
#    tutorial used -- to exclude pixels too decorrelated to unwrap with confidence.
unwrapped = insar.unwrap(filtered, coh, method="snaphu", cost="defo", nlooks=LOOKS[0] * LOOKS[1],
                         mask=(coh > 0.3))

# 3. Report timing and the resulting (now continuous, radian-valued) unwrapped phase range.
print(f"SNAPHU unwrap: {time.time() - t0:.0f} s, phase range {np.nanmin(unwrapped):.1f} to "
      f"{np.nanmax(unwrapped):.1f} rad")


SNAPHU unwrap: 95 s, phase range -155.4 to 49.8 rad




Phase to displacement
d = -(lambda / 4*pi) * delta_phi. At lambda ~ 5.55 cm, one full fringe (2*pi of phase) is about 2.8 cm of line-of-sight motion.


Code
# Step 7: convert unwrapped phase to line-of-sight displacement, d = -(lambda / 4*pi) * delta_phi.

# 1. phase_to_los applies that conversion using the radar wavelength (~5.55 cm here, so one
#    full fringe/2*pi of phase corresponds to ~2.8 cm of LOS motion).
los = insar.phase_to_los(unwrapped, ann_ref["wavelength"])

# 2. Report the full (unmasked) field's range as a baseline -- see the markdown below for
#    why this range is implausibly large and not real ground motion.
print(f"LOS displacement, full unwrapped field: {np.nanmin(los):.3f} to {np.nanmax(los):.3f} m")


# 3. Apply a stricter coherence threshold (> 0.5) than the unwrapping mask used, and blank
#    out everything below it with NaN.
reliable = coh > 0.5
los_masked = np.where(reliable, los, np.nan)  # keep only reliable (coherent) pixels

# 4. Report the coherence-masked range and what fraction of the scene survives the mask.
print(f"LOS displacement, coherence > 0.5 only: {np.nanmin(los_masked):.3f} to {np.nanmax(los_masked):.3f} m "
      f"({100 * np.mean(reliable):.0f}% of the scene)")


# 5. Plot the unmasked vs. coherence-masked LOS displacement maps side by side for comparison.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 8))
axes[0].imshow(los, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-0.1, vmax=0.1)  # all pixels
axes[0].set_title("LOS displacement (m), unmasked")  # title
axes[1].imshow(los_masked, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-0.1, vmax=0.1)  # coherent pixels only
axes[1].set_title("LOS displacement (m), coherence > 0.5 only")  # title
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange


LOS displacement, full unwrapped field: -0.220 to 0.686 m
LOS displacement, coherence > 0.5 only: -0.215 to 0.673 m (22% of the scene)









The unmasked field’s full range (tens of centimetres in places) is not real ground motion – it is a direct illustration of Step 9’s warning and a common InSAR pitfall: at a mean coherence of 0.35, SNAPHU cannot reliably resolve 2*pi ambiguities over large parts of this scene, and wrong integer-cycle jumps (not noise, discrete 2.8 cm-multiple errors) are exactly what produce implausibly large unwrapped values.
Restricting to coherence > 0.5 does not fix this, and the way it fails is itself instructive: the surviving pixels sit almost entirely inside the coherence bands from Step 3, and within each band the displacement comes out as one consistent but implausibly large value (tens of centimetres), not speckle noise. Each coherent band is an island surrounded by decorrelated (masked) pixels, so SNAPHU has no reliable path connecting it back to the rest of the scene’s unwrapping network – it can integrate the right relative phase inside the island but still land on the wrong absolute 2pi count for it as a whole. A per-pixel coherence threshold cannot catch this, because every pixel inside the island genuinely is coherent; what is missing is connectivity* to a reliable reference. This is exactly the problem persistent- scatterer and SBAS methods are built to avoid, by keeping a redundant network of connections between reliable points rather than unwrapping one interferogram’s full 2-D field (07_03_01_05_PSInSAR.ipynb, 07_03_01_06_InSAR_SBAS.ipynb) – not something a single pair can fix.


Geocode
terrain_correct places the multilooked LOS and coherence layers onto the DEM’s own map grid, range-Doppler style, using each row’s zero-Doppler time and the orbit.


Code
# Step 8: geocode the multilooked LOS and coherence layers onto the DEM's own map grid.

# 1. Reconstruct the per-row zero-Doppler azimuth time at full (pre-multilook) resolution,
#    from the reference annotation's single burst start time plus the azimuth time interval
#    (lines_per_burst rows, each one azimuth_time_interval apart).
lpb = ann_ref["lines_per_burst"]
az_time_full = (ann_ref["bursts"][0]["azimuth_time"]  # azimuth time of every line
               + (np.arange(lpb) * ann_ref["azimuth_time_interval"] * 1e9).astype("timedelta64[ns]"))

# 2. Subsample that per-row time to match the 4x azimuth multilooking used for every InSAR
#    product above, truncated to the actual (multilooked) image height.
az_time_ml = az_time_full[::LOOKS[0]][:los.shape[0]]

# 3. Near-range slant range (from the two-way slant-range time, converted with the speed of
#    light) and the multilooked range pixel spacing -- both needed by the range-Doppler
#    terrain correction to map each (line, sample) to a slant range and ground position.
near_range = ann_ref["slant_range_time"] * s1.SPEED_OF_LIGHT / 2
range_spacing_ml = ann_ref["range_pixel_spacing"] * LOOKS[1]  # range pixel size after multilooking


# 4. terrain_correct: range-Doppler project the multilooked LOS displacement and coherence
#    layers from radar (line/sample) geometry onto the DEM's map grid, using each row's
#    zero-Doppler time together with the reference orbit to locate it on the ground.
geo = s1.terrain_correct({"los": los, "coherence": coh}, az_time_ml, near_range, range_spacing_ml,
                         ann_ref["orbit"], dem)

# 5. Apply the same coherence > 0.5 reliability mask used in Step 7, now to the geocoded LOS.
geo_los = geo["los"].where(geo["coherence"] > 0.5)


# 6. Plot the geocoded coherence and masked LOS displacement maps side by side in map
#    projection (UTM 18N) for direct visual comparison against the radar-geometry versions.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 7))
geo["coherence"].plot(ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)  # geocoded coherence
axes[0].set_title("coherence, UTM 18N")  # title
geo_los.plot(ax=axes[1], cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-0.05, vmax=0.05)  # geocoded LOS displacement
axes[1].set_title("LOS displacement (m), coherence > 0.5")  # title
for ax in axes:  # for both panels
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # equal scale
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange









The geocoded coherence map confirms the banding runs close to constant latitude rather than parallel to the satellite’s tilted ground track – the detail that ruled out a radar-geometry processing artifact and pointed toward a real, land-management-linked explanation instead. The geocoded LOS panel shows the unwrapping-island problem from Step 7 in map form: the surviving points cluster almost entirely inside those same bands, each one a uniform, saturated colour – an isolated coherent patch that kept its internal phase relationships but landed on the wrong absolute 2*pi count, not a real, spatially consistent displacement field.

title: RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) InSAR Processing
text:
Takeaways and limitations

Every InSAR workflow step in the intro notebook now has a real implementation exercised on a real RCM pair: radarsat.read_rcm_annotation (Step 1’s product reading, new in this notebook) feeds sentinel1.back_geocode/resample_slc (Step 2) unchanged, and geolattice.rsense.insar’s differential_interferogram/multilook_complex (Step 3-4), goldstein_filter (Step 5), unwrap (Step 6), phase_to_los (Step 7) and sentinel1.terrain_correct (Step 8) needed no RCM-specific changes at all – they were already sensor-agnostic.
Fixed a real latent bug this pair exposed: terrain_correct assumed row azimuth-time always increases with row number (true for every Sentinel-1 product used so far); this RCM product stores rows in decreasing-time order, which silently broke the time-to-row lookup (np.interp needs ascending xp). Fixed by sorting ascending internally when needed – harmless for the existing ascending case, correct for this one.
Scope of read_rcm_annotation: Stripmap beams only (continuous single-beam imaging, as used here). A ScanSAR beam (e.g. the SC30MCP* compact-pol beams the same EODMS search turned up densely over Montreal) packs several sub-beams with their own burst-like timing, which this reader does not parse – a natural next step given how much ScanSAR SLC coverage is actually available.
No time series here (one pair only) – geolattice.rsense.insar.sbas’s network tools from the Sentinel-1 SBAS tutorial apply equally once more RCM dates are coregistered the same way.
The coherence-banding interpretation (Quebec strip-field land management) is a plausible reading of the evidence gathered, not a verified one.


References

Natural Resources Canada / EODMS, RCM Image Products STAC collection (https://www.eodms-sgdot.nrcan-rncan.gc.ca/search/) and Data Delivery Service API.
Small, D. (2011). Flattening gamma: Radiometric terrain correction for SAR imagery. IEEE TGRS, 49(8), 3081-3093.
Goldstein, R. M., & Werner, C. L. (1998). Radar interferogram filtering for geophysical applications. Geophysical Research Letters, 25(21), 4035-4038.
Chen, C. W., & Zebker, H. A. (2002). Two-dimensional phase unwrapping with use of statistical models for cost functions in nonlinear optimization (SNAPHU). JOSA A, 19(5), 1026-1037.

Core concepts

Learning objectives

Identify SLC, GRC, GRD, and geocoded RCM products, and the polarisation, before choosing a workflow.
Sketch the backscatter, compact-pol, and InSAR chains from reading the product through to a map-ready layer.
Calibrate detected GRD with the product LUT and noise XML, and keep sigma0, beta0, and gamma0 distinct.
Form the RH/RV covariance, Stokes parameters, and an m-χ decomposition, and terrain-correct those outputs afterwards.
Run noise removal, calibration, speckle filtering, terrain flattening, and Range-Doppler terrain correction, and do the statistics in linear units.
Coregister an SLC pair, form an interferogram, remove topographic phase, unwrap, and convert phase to line-of-sight displacement.
Call geolattice.rsense.sar.radarsat for compact-pol, GRD calibration, and Stripmap SLC annotation, and open product.xml so the calibration and geometry are available.

title: RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) Processing
text:
Know the product before processing
RCM basics - C-band SAR at 5.405 GHz, so the wavelength λ is about 5.55 cm. - Three satellites, each on a 12-day repeat. Together they give a 4-day exact-repeat orbit. - Right-looking, with ascending and descending passes.
Product levels









Product
Content
Geometry
Use




SLC
Complex (I/Q), amplitude + phase
Slant range
InSAR, polarimetry, CP decomposition


GRC
Complex, multilooked
Ground range
Polarimetry with ground spacing


GRD
Detected amplitude
Ground range (ellipsoid)
Backscatter mapping, classification


GCC / GCD
Complex / detected
Geocoded to ellipsoid (no DEM)
Quick look; still needs terrain correction



Polarization options - Single (HH or VV). - Dual (HH+HV or VV+VH). - Compact-pol (CP: transmit right-circular, receive H and V, giving the channels RH and RV). - Quad-pol, available only in certain modes.
Folder contents - metadata/product.xml holds the orbit state vectors, timing, incidence angles, beam, and the geolocation grid. - imagery/*.tif has one GeoTIFF per channel. - calibration/ holds the lookup tables for σ⁰, β⁰, and γ⁰ (sigma, beta, and gamma nought) and the noise levels.
RCM orbits are precise and already in the metadata. Unlike Sentinel-1, no separate “Apply Orbit File” step is needed.

title: RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) Processing
text:
Overall workflows
Backscatter workflow (GRD):
Read product.xml → Subset AOI → Thermal noise removal → Radiometric calibration
→ (Multilook) → Speckle filter → Terrain flattening → Terrain correction (RTC)
→ Linear→dB → Masking/QC → Stack & analyse
Compact-pol workflow (SLC/GRC):
Read → Calibrate (complex) → Build 2×2 covariance [C2] → Boxcar/Refined-Lee polarimetric filter
→ Stokes parameters → m-χ / m-δ decomposition (or pseudo-quad reconstruction)
→ Terrain correction → Classification
InSAR workflow (SLC pairs or stacks):
Coregister (DEM-assisted) → Interferogram + coherence → Topographic phase removal
→ Goldstein filter → Phase unwrapping (SNAPHU) → Phase→displacement → Geocode
→ Time series (SBAS/PS, e.g. MintPy)

title: RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) Processing
text:
RADARSAT processing functions in GeoLattice
The mission-specific API is in geolattice.rsense.sar.radarsat (source: radarsat.py). It currently focuses on RCM compact-polarimetry, RCM Level-1 GRD radiometric calibration, and reading metadata for Stripmap SLC interferometry. Use the existing sensor-generic SAR/InSAR tools for shared operations such as multilooking, speckle filtering, SLC coregistration/resampling, and interferogram formation. These helpers do not perform a full end-to-end processor, DEM-based terrain correction, phase unwrapping, or time-series inversion.

RCM compact-polarimetry







Function
Purpose and result




split_rrrl(rrrl)
Splits an RCM-ARD rrrl two-band asset into its real and imaginary arrays (bands 0 and 1).


rr_rl_to_stokes(rr, rl, rrrl_re, rrrl_im)
Converts the RCM-ARD circular receive channels and complex cross term into Stokes parameters s0-s3 and degree of polarization.


rrrl_to_rhrv(rr, rl, rrrl_re, rrrl_im)
Converts RCM-ARD circular-basis products into the equivalent RH/RV 2×2 covariance components c11, c22, c12_re, and c12_im. The output can be used with compatible dual-pol covariance tools.


rhrv_to_stokes(c11, c22, c12_re, c12_im)
Computes Stokes parameters and degree of polarization from an RH/RV covariance matrix.


compact_pol_mchi(s0, s1, s2, s3)
Computes RCM-convention m-χ surface (ps), double-bounce (pd), and volume (pv) powers from Stokes inputs. The documented RCM sign convention matters when interpreting classes.


simulate_compact_pol(s_hh, s_hv, s_vh, s_vv, size=7)
Simulates right-circular-transmit, linear-receive compact-pol data from RADARSAT-2 (or other) quad-pol complex channels. It averages the resulting covariance over the requested window; this is a simulation, not a native RADARSAT-2 compact-pol acquisition.


gamma0_to_sigma0(gamma0, ratio)
Converts RCM-ARD gamma0 to sigma0 using the product’s per-pixel gamma_to_sigma_ratio layer.





RCM Level-1 GRD radiometric calibration







Function
Purpose and result




read_rcm_lut(xml_path)
Parses a lutSigma, lutBeta, or lutGamma calibration XML file, returning the range-axis sample positions, offset, and gain values.


interpolate_rcm_lut(lut, width)
Interpolates the sparse range-only gain values to one gain per image column.


read_rcm_noise_levels(xml_path, cal_type="Sigma Nought")
Reads the selected calibration type’s per-beam NESZ segments from the RCM noise XML. Choose the type matching the LUT being used.


interpolate_rcm_noise(segments, width)
Interpolates and joins those per-beam noise segments over the image columns.


calibrate_rcm(dn, gain, offset=0.0, noise_db=None, floor=1e-6)
Converts detected DN to calibrated linear backscatter using (DN² + offset) / gain, optionally subtracts the matching NESZ in linear units, sets zero DN to missing, and applies a small nonnegative floor. Select sigma0, beta0, or gamma0 LUT consistently with the intended output.



Use the calibration LUT and matching noise calibration from the same product and polarization. The mission-specific module handles LUT/noise interpretation; generic functions in geolattice.rsense.sar.sentinel1 can then be used for operations such as multilooking and dB conversion. Terrain flattening and DEM-based terrain correction require an appropriate external workflow.


RCM Stripmap SLC annotation for InSAR
read_rcm_annotation(xml_path) extracts the timing, range sampling, wavelength, pixel spacing, incidence limits, and orbit state vectors from an RCM Level-1 Stripmap SLC product.xml. It returns an annotation dictionary shaped for the sensor-generic Sentinel-1 back_geocode and resample_slc routines. It supports a single continuous Stripmap image, not ScanSAR burst/sub-swath geometry. RCM’s precise state vectors are included in the product metadata, so this workflow does not require a separate orbit-file download.


Example call patterns
from geolattice.rsense.sar import radarsat

# RCM-ARD compact-pol assets (rrrl is the real/imaginary two-band asset)
rrrl_re, rrrl_im = radarsat.split_rrrl(rrrl)
stokes = radarsat.rr_rl_to_stokes(rr, rl, rrrl_re, rrrl_im)
scattering = radarsat.compact_pol_mchi(
    stokes["s0"], stokes["s1"], stokes["s2"], stokes["s3"]
)

# Level-1 GRD: use the matching calibration LUT and noise XML
lut = radarsat.read_rcm_lut(lut_xml)
gain = radarsat.interpolate_rcm_lut(lut, width=dn.shape[-1])
noise = radarsat.read_rcm_noise_levels(noise_xml, cal_type="Sigma Nought")
noise_db = radarsat.interpolate_rcm_noise(noise, width=dn.shape[-1])
sigma0 = radarsat.calibrate_rcm(
    dn, gain, offset=lut["offset"], noise_db=noise_db
)

# Stripmap SLC: supply the parsed annotation to shared coregistration tools
annotation = radarsat.read_rcm_annotation(product_xml)
The names rr, rl, rrrl, dn, and the XML paths above stand for arrays/assets and metadata belonging to the selected product. Check the product’s polarization basis, calibration type, pixel units, supported beam mode, and function docstrings before applying these examples.


Backscatter workflow, step by step
Step 1, Read and subset - Open product.xml in SNAP, not the TIFF. The TIFF alone has no radar geometry. - Subset to your AOI immediately. RCM scenes are large, and every later step scales with the number of pixels.
Step 2, Thermal noise removal - The sensor adds a noise floor, the NESZ (noise-equivalent sigma zero). It is roughly −20 to −25 dB, depending on beam. - Low-backscatter targets sit near this floor: calm water, smooth roads, and especially cross-pol HV over bare soil. - Subtracting the noise level from the calibration/ folder prevents false brightness and visible beam seams.
Step 3, Radiometric calibration - This converts digital numbers (DN) into physically meaningful backscatter:
σ⁰ (or β⁰, γ⁰) = (DN² + B) / A

A is the range-dependent gain from lutSigma, lutBeta, or lutGamma. It is interpolated across columns from pixelFirstLutValue and stepSize.
B is the offset.
Which one to choose:

β⁰ is radar brightness in slant geometry. It is the required input for terrain flattening.
σ⁰ is normalized to the ellipsoid ground area. It is fine for flat terrain.
γ⁰ is normalized to the area perpendicular to the beam. It is less incidence-angle dependent.

For complex data (SLC), calibrate I and Q separately so the phase is preserved: divide by √A.

Step 4, Multilooking (optional) - This averages pixels in range and azimuth to get roughly square ground pixels. - It reduces speckle, at the cost of resolution. - An example is averaging 2×2 on 16 m data to get a clean 30 m product.
Step 5, Speckle filtering - Speckle is multiplicative noise inherent to coherent imaging.








Filter
Character
When




Boxcar
Simple mean, blurs edges
Polarimetric matrices, large homogeneous areas


Lee / Refined Lee
Adaptive, preserves edges
General land mapping (default choice)


Gamma-MAP
Statistical model
Agriculture, forests


Lee Sigma
Preserves point targets
Urban, ships


Multi-temporal (Quegan)
Uses the stack over time
Time series; best detail retention




Use a 5×5 or 7×7 window.
Do not filter before InSAR coregistration, because it destroys phase.
Avoid heavy filtering before ship or point-target detection.

Step 6, Radiometric terrain flattening - Slopes facing the sensor appear bright, and slopes facing away appear dark, purely from geometry. - Terrain flattening (Small 2011) uses a DEM to compute the true illuminated area. It converts β⁰ into terrain-flattened γ⁰ (γ⁰_T). - It is essential in hilly or mountainous areas and for comparing ascending with descending passes. - In flat agricultural plains it changes little.
Step 7, Terrain correction (geocoding / orthorectification) - Range-Doppler terrain correction uses the orbit, timing, and a DEM to place each pixel at its true map location. This removes foreshortening displacement. - Settings: - DEM: Copernicus GLO-30. SRTM 1-sec also works; use a local LiDAR DEM if available. - Resampling: bilinear for intensity. Nearest neighbour for masks or classes. - Output pixel size: match the beam mode (e.g., 30 m for 30M CP). - Projection: UTM or a national grid. - Also export the layover/shadow mask, the local incidence angle, and the projected local incidence angle. They are critical for quality control and as model covariates.
Step 8, Convert to dB - dB = 10·log₁₀(σ⁰) - Do statistics (averaging, filtering) in linear units, and use dB only for display and for ML features. Averaging dB values biases the result.
Step 9, Quality control - Mask pixels flagged as layover or shadow. - Mask pixels near the noise floor. - Mask image edges that have no-data artifacts. - Check radiometric stability against known stable targets. Urban areas and dense forest should stay near-constant over time.
Compact-polarimetry (CP) Compact-polarimetry (CP) is a SAR mode where the radar transmits a circularly polarized wave (commonly RH or LH) and receives two orthogonal linear polarizations (Horizontal, RH and Vertical, RV). This enables the construction of a 2×2 complex covariance matrix, capturing much of the information of full quad-pol but at the cost and coverage of dual-pol.

The radar records complex scattering coefficients: SRH and SRV (where RH = Received Horizontal, RV = Received Vertical, both after transmitting Right-Circular polarization).
The covariance matrix [C2] is formed as:
C₂ = | <|S_RH|²>      <S_RH S_RV*>   |
     | <S_RV S_RH*>   <|S_RV|²>      |
or, in markdown math: \[
\mathbf{C}_2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \langle |S_{\mathrm{RH}}|^2 \rangle & \langle S_{\mathrm{RH}} S_{\mathrm{RV}}^* \rangle \\
  \langle S_{\mathrm{RV}} S_{\mathrm{RH}}^* \rangle & \langle |S_{\mathrm{RV}}|^2 \rangle
\end{bmatrix}
\] where ⟨·⟩ indicates spatial averaging (speckle filtering).
From this, you compute Stokes parameters:

\(S_0 = \langle |S_{\mathrm{RH}}|^2 \rangle + \langle |S_{\mathrm{RV}}|^2 \rangle\) (total intensity)
\(S_1 = \langle |S_{\mathrm{RH}}|^2 \rangle - \langle |S_{\mathrm{RV}}|^2 \rangle\)
\(S_2 = 2 \, \operatorname{Re}(\langle S_{\mathrm{RH}} S_{\mathrm{RV}}^* \rangle)\) (real part)
\(S_3 = \pm 2 \, \operatorname{Im}(\langle S_{\mathrm{RH}} S_{\mathrm{RV}}^* \rangle)\) (imaginary part; sign depends on handedness convention)

The degree of polarization is:
\[
m = \frac{\sqrt{S_1^2 + S_2^2 + S_3^2}}{S_0}
\] This describes how “purely” the scene scatters polarization (low m = depolarized, e.g., vegetation).
The ellipticity angle (\(\chi\)) (indicates even vs. odd bounce) is:
\[
\sin 2\chi = -\frac{S_3}{m S_0}
\] Negative means odd-bounce dominant (e.g., double-bounce in urban or flooded areas).
The relative phase (\(\delta\)) between RH and RV is:
\[
\delta = \arctan\left(\frac{S_3}{S_2}\right)
\]

m-χ decomposition: This produces an RGB visualization to distinguish scattering types: - Red channel (Double-bounce): $ $ - Green channel (Volume): $ $ - Blue channel (Surface): $ $
Thus, compact-pol SAR enables physically interpretable, information-rich products using rigorous polarimetric math.


Compact-polarimetry (CP) processing
CP is what distinguishes RCM. It captures much of quad-pol’s information at dual-pol cost and swath width.
1. Covariance matrix. From the calibrated complex RH and RV channels, form the 2×2 covariance matrix [C2]: - ⟨|RH|²⟩, ⟨|RV|²⟩, ⟨RH·RV*⟩ - ⟨ ⟩ denotes spatial averaging, which is the polarimetric speckle filter.
2. Stokes parameters - S₀ = ⟨|RH|²⟩ + ⟨|RV|²⟩ is the total power. - S₁ = ⟨|RH|²⟩ − ⟨|RV|²⟩ - S₂ = 2 Re⟨RH·RV⟩ - S₃ = ±2 Im⟨RH·RV⟩. The sign depends on transmit handedness, so check the convention in your software.
3. Derived parameters - Degree of polarization: m = √(S₁² + S₂² + S₃²) / S₀ - Low m means depolarized, volume-like scattering, as in vegetation. - Ellipticity angle: sin 2χ = −S₃ / (m·S₀) - Indicates odd versus even bounce. - Relative phase: δ = arctan(S₃ / S₂)
4. m-χ decomposition (Raney). This gives an RGB composite: - Double bounce = √[m·S₀·(1 − sin 2χ)/2], displayed in red. Indicates buildings and flooded vegetation. - Volume = √[S₀·(1 − m)], displayed in green. Indicates forest and crop canopy. - Surface = √[m·S₀·(1 + sin 2χ)/2], displayed in blue. Indicates bare soil and water. - m-δ decomposition follows the same logic, using δ in place of χ.
5. Other CP products - Circular polarization ratio (CPR) indicates surface roughness and is used for sea ice. - RH/RV backscatter and the conformity coefficient are used for soil moisture. - Pseudo-quad reconstruction (Souyris or Nord methods) estimates a full 3×3 matrix. This lets you apply quad-pol decompositions such as Freeman-Durden or H/A/α.
6. Order of operations. Terrain-correct the decomposition outputs after computing them, not before. Resampling complex data first corrupts the phase relationships.
Applications: crop type and phenology, wetland classes (open water vs. flooded vegetation vs. marsh), sea-ice typing, and oil-slick vs. look-alike discrimination.


InSAR processing (SLC)
1. Pair or stack selection - Use the same beam mode, orbit direction, and satellite geometry. - Prefer short temporal baselines. RCM’s 4-day repeat is a major advantage for coherence. - Prefer small perpendicular baselines for deformation work.
2. Coregistration - Use DEM-assisted coregistration to sub-pixel accuracy, about 0.1 pixel.
3. Interferogram formation - Multiply one image by the complex conjugate of the other. - Remove flat-earth phase. - Estimate coherence (0 to 1), which measures phase reliability.
4. Topographic phase removal - Subtract the DEM-simulated phase. What remains is differential InSAR (DInSAR), containing deformation, atmosphere, and noise.
5. Goldstein adaptive filtering - Reduces phase noise before unwrapping.
6. Phase unwrapping - Use SNAPHU, exported from SNAP and re-imported. - Wrapped phase cycles through −π to π. Unwrapping converts it into a continuous phase.
7. Phase to displacement - d = −(λ / 4π)·Δφ - With λ ≈ 5.55 cm, one fringe is about 2.8 cm of line-of-sight (LOS) motion.
8. Geocode, then time-series analysis - Run SBAS or Persistent Scatterer analysis in MintPy, which reads SNAP outputs, or in StaMPS. - These separate deformation from atmospheric noise.
9. Decomposition - Combine ascending and descending LOS results to estimate vertical and east-west motion.
Applications: subsidence, landslides, infrastructure monitoring, permafrost, and coherence-based change or damage maps.


Downstream analysis







Task
Typical method




Flood mapping
Threshold low γ⁰ in VV/HH or CP (Otsu, split-based), plus a HAND (height above nearest drainage) mask


Change detection
Log-ratio or difference of dB images; coherence drop


Ship detection
CFAR (constant false alarm rate) on unfiltered HH or HV, land-masked


Crop classification
Multi-temporal γ⁰ + CP features + local incidence angle → Random Forest, XGBoost, or temporal deep learning


Soil moisture
Change detection on a time series, or a water-cloud model with a vegetation correction


Biomass / forest
Volume-component and cross-pol backscatter saturate early at C-band; combine with L-band





Tools
ESA SNAP - Full GUI and the gpt command line. - Native RCM reader, calibration, CP tools, InSAR, and terrain correction. - Build the chain in the Graph Builder and batch it.
Python - esa_snappy or subprocess + gpt for automation. - rasterio, xarray, and rioxarray for arrays. - sarsen for radiometric terrain correction (RTC). - scikit-image for Otsu thresholding. - MintPy for InSAR time series.
Other options - NRCan RCM CEOS-ARD: already calibrated, noise-corrected, and terrain-corrected compact-pol at 30 m over Canada. You can skip steps 1 to 8 entirely. - Commercial alternatives: PCI Catalyst, GAMMA, and SARscape.


Common pitfalls

Opening the TIFF instead of product.xml, which loses calibration and geometry.
Averaging or filtering in dB instead of linear units.
Terrain-correcting complex data before polarimetric or InSAR steps.
Skipping terrain flattening in hilly terrain, then attributing slope effects to land cover.
Mixing beam modes, incidence angles, or ascending and descending passes in one time series without normalization.
Ignoring the noise floor in cross-pol channels over smooth surfaces.

title: Sentinel-1 Based Indices
text:
Overview
They help researchers characterize the Earth’s surface, monitor vegetation and agricultural fields, detect flooding, assess soil moisture conditions, map wetlands, and measure changes in land cover.
Unlike optical satellites such as Sentinel-2 and Landsat, Sentinel-1 uses radar signals, so it can collect observations during both day and night and through clouds. This makes it particularly useful in tropical and monsoon regions such as Bangladesh, where persistent cloud cover often limits optical satellite observations.
One important distinction: Sentinel-1 does not have a single universally accepted set of indices comparable to NDVI for optical imagery. Instead, researchers calculate several radar backscatter metrics, polarization ratios, polarimetric features, and temporal change indicators, depending on the application and the available data.
