title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Overview
Zia U. Ahmed · Upatta Analytics LLC · uses GeoLattice’s geolattice.rsense remote sensing subpackage*
A Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (GRD) product stores raw digital numbers in radar geometry. Turning it into comparable, map-ready backscatter takes several steps: thermal-noise removal, radiometric calibration, multilooking, speckle filtering, radiometric terrain flattening and terrain correction (geocoding), then a decibel conversion and a quality-control pass. This notebook runs every one of those steps on a real Sentinel-1A GRD scene over the Cox’s Bazar – Teknaf coast of Bangladesh (13 January 2024), using a real Copernicus DEM for the terrain steps, and reports the real numbers that come out: a measured noise floor, a measured speckle-filter ENL, and a terrain-flattening correction that traces the real hill ridges on the ground, not a synthetic stand-in for them.
Cox’s Bazar is a deliberate choice of AOI: the Bay of Bengal gives a large, genuinely flat, genuinely calm-water target for the noise-floor and speckle sections; the town, beach and river mouth give mixed land cover; and the Teknaf peninsula’s hills (up to about 400 m, real relief inside an otherwise near-sea-level delta) give terrain flattening something real to correct, directly testing the Rmd workflow’s own claim that flattening “changes little” on a flat plain but is “essential” where there is real topography.

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Run thermal-noise removal, radiometric calibration, multilooking, speckle filtering, terrain flattening and geocoding on the Sentinel-1A IW GRDH scene of 13 January 2024 over Cox’s Bazar and Teknaf.
Calibrate digital numbers to sigma0, beta0 and gamma0 with the scene’s calibration and noise look-up tables, passing the crop offset to interpolate_lut.
Measure the noise floor over the Bay of Bengal and the equivalent number of looks after a 3x3 multilook.
Compare boxcar, Lee, Refined Lee and Gamma-MAP filters on the multilooked VV image, using ENL on open water.
Flatten beta0 to gamma0 with terrain_flatten and the Copernicus DEM GLO-30, and read the correction on the coastal plain and on the Teknaf hills.
Geocode with process_grd(backend="native") from the product ground control points, and state which full-product annotation process_grd(backend="sarsen") needs for range-Doppler terrain correction.
Convert linear backscatter to decibels with to_db for display, and mask layover, shadow, the measured noise floor and image edges.

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Study area and real data
Scene: S1A_IW_GRDH_1SDV_20240113T115602_20240113T115627_052088_064BA4 – Sentinel-1A, IW mode, GRDH, VV+VH, ascending, 13 January 2024, 11:56 UTC (dry season). Downloaded from Microsoft Planetary Computer’s sentinel-1-grd collection, which republishes the real ESA measurement GeoTIFFs plus real per-swath calibration and noise look-up tables as a STAC item – the same files a direct ESA/Copernicus download would give for those three pieces. Each polarization’s measurement file is close to 600 MB, so this cell downloads once and caches the result under data/.
AOI: Cox’s Bazar – Teknaf, Bangladesh, (91.85, 21.30, 92.15, 21.55). The Bay of Bengal (open water), the Cox’s Bazar peninsula and Bakkhali river mouth (urban, agriculture, tidal flats) and the Teknaf peninsula’s hills (real relief up to about 400 m) all fall inside one small crop of the scene, read directly from the downloaded GeoTIFF with a rasterio windowed read rather than loading the full roughly 26,000 x 16,700 pixel swath.
DEM: Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (30 m), mosaicked from the three tiles covering the AOI and clipped with a small margin, from Planetary Computer’s cop-dem-glo-30 collection.


Code
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar")  # data folder
# the unzipped Sentinel-1A GRD product (SAFE folder)
SAFE_DIR = DATA / "S1A_IW_GRDH_1SDV_20240113T115602_20240113T115627_052088_064BA4.SAFE"
# common part of the file names inside the SAFE folder
STEM = "20240113t115602-20240113t115627-052088-064ba4-001"
# VV measurement GeoTIFF (raw digital numbers)
VV_PATH = SAFE_DIR / "measurement" / f"s1a-iw-grd-vv-{STEM}.tiff"
VH_PATH = SAFE_DIR / "measurement" / f"s1a-iw-grd-vh-{STEM}.tiff"  # VH measurement GeoTIFF
# VV calibration look-up table (XML)
CAL_VV = SAFE_DIR / "annotation" / "calibration" / f"calibration-s1a-iw-grd-vv-{STEM}.xml"
# VH calibration look-up table
CAL_VH = SAFE_DIR / "annotation" / "calibration" / f"calibration-s1a-iw-grd-vh-{STEM}.xml"
# VV thermal-noise look-up table (XML)
NOISE_VV = SAFE_DIR / "annotation" / "calibration" / f"noise-s1a-iw-grd-vv-{STEM}.xml"
# VH thermal-noise look-up table
NOISE_VH = SAFE_DIR / "annotation" / "calibration" / f"noise-s1a-iw-grd-vh-{STEM}.xml"
DEM_PATH = DATA / "cop_dem_glo30" / "coxsbazar_dem.tif"  # Copernicus 30 m DEM clipped to the AOI

AOI = (91.85, 21.30, 92.15, 21.55)   # Cox's Bazar -- Teknaf, Bangladesh

if not VV_PATH.exists():  # download only if the scene is not on disk yet
    # Real Sentinel-1A GRD scene and real Copernicus DEM tiles from Planetary Computer.
    # ~600 MB per polarization -- only runs once, cached under ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/ after that.
    import pystac_client  # STAC search client
    import planetary_computer as pc  # signs Planetary Computer URLs so they can be downloaded
    import requests  # HTTP downloads

    # open the Planetary Computer STAC catalogue
    catalog = pystac_client.Client.open("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1",
                                        modifier=pc.sign_inplace)
    item = catalog.get_collection("sentinel-1-grd").get_item(  # the GRD item of 13 January 2024
        "S1A_IW_GRDH_1SDV_20240113T115602_20240113T115627_052088_064BA4")

    def fetch(href, dest):  # stream a file to disk in 1 MB chunks
        dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the folder
        with requests.get(href, timeout=600, stream=True) as r:  # open the URL as a stream
            r.raise_for_status()  # stop on an HTTP error
            with open(dest, "wb") as f:  # write the file chunk by chunk
                for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=1 << 20):  # 1 MB chunks
                    f.write(chunk)  # append the chunk

    # asset name in the STAC item -> local destination
    ASSETS = {"vv": VV_PATH, "vh": VH_PATH, "schema-calibration-vv": CAL_VV,
             "schema-calibration-vh": CAL_VH, "schema-noise-vv": NOISE_VV,
             "schema-noise-vh": NOISE_VH}
    for key, dest in ASSETS.items():  # download every asset
        print("downloading", key, "->", dest.name)  # progress message
        fetch(item.assets[key].href, dest)  # download the asset

    # Copernicus DEM tiles that touch the AOI
    dem_search = catalog.search(collections=["cop-dem-glo-30"], bbox=AOI)
    DEM_PATH.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # DEM folder
    from rasterio.merge import merge  # mosaic several rasters into one

    tiles = []  # the opened DEM tiles
    for dem_item in dem_search.items():  # download each tile and open it
        tmp = DEM_PATH.parent / f"{dem_item.id}.tif"  # temporary file for this tile
        fetch(dem_item.assets["data"].href, tmp)  # download the tile
        tiles.append(rasterio.open(tmp))  # open it
    mosaic, mtransform = merge(tiles)  # merge the tiles into one array and its transform
    # pixel window of the AOI inside the mosaic
    win = rasterio.windows.from_bounds(*AOI, transform=mtransform).round_lengths().round_offsets()
    profile = tiles[0].profile.copy()  # copy the GeoTIFF profile of the first tile ...
    # ... and set the size and transform of the AOI window
    profile.update(height=int(win.height), width=int(win.width),
                   transform=rasterio.windows.transform(win, mtransform))
    with rasterio.open(DEM_PATH, "w", **profile) as dst:  # write the clipped DEM
        dst.write(mosaic[0][int(win.row_off):int(win.row_off + win.height),  # write the AOI part of the mosaic
                           int(win.col_off):int(win.col_off + win.width)], 1)
    for t in tiles:  # close the tile files
        t.close()  # close it
    print("Done.")  # finished
else:
    print("Reusing the files already downloaded under", DATA)  # files are already on disk


Reusing the files already downloaded under ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar




Code
# Window a Cox's Bazar crop directly out of the full measurement GeoTIFF: a GCP-fitted
# affine (rasterio.transform.from_gcps) is accurate enough over a crop this size to turn the
# AOI's lon/lat corners into an approximate (row, col) box, without warping or downloading the
# whole ~26,000 x 16,700 pixel scene.
with rasterio.open(VV_PATH) as src:  # open the VV measurement file
    gcps, gcp_crs = src.gcps  # its ground control points (GCPs) and their CRS
    # fit one affine transform to all GCPs (approximate, good enough to find the crop)
    approx_affine = from_gcps(gcps)
    # the four corners of the AOI (lon, lat)
    corners = [(AOI[0], AOI[1]), (AOI[2], AOI[1]), (AOI[0], AOI[3]), (AOI[2], AOI[3])]
    rcs = [rowcol(approx_affine, lon, lat) for lon, lat in corners]  # (row, col) of each corner
    rows, cols = [r for r, c in rcs], [c for r, c in rcs]  # rows and columns of the corners
    row0, row1 = max(0, min(rows)), min(src.height, max(rows))  # row range, clipped to the image
    col0, col1 = max(0, min(cols)), min(src.width, max(cols))  # column range, clipped to the image
    WINDOW = Window(col0, row0, col1 - col0, row1 - row0)  # the crop as a rasterio Window
    dn_vv = src.read(1, window=WINDOW)  # read only the VV pixels inside the window
with rasterio.open(VH_PATH) as src:  # the same window from the VH file
    dn_vh = src.read(1, window=WINDOW)  # VH digital numbers

SHAPE = dn_vv.shape  # rows and columns of the crop
OFFSET = (row0, col0)   # this crop's (row, col) origin in the scene's own line/pixel numbering
# crop size, offset and DN range
print(f"Crop: {SHAPE[0]} x {SHAPE[1]} pixels, offset {OFFSET}, DN range {dn_vv.min()}-{dn_vv.max()}")


Crop: 3243 x 3542 pixels, offset (np.int32(7506), np.int32(1682)), DN range 9-15098




Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))  # two panels
# a quick dB-like view of the raw DN (DN² in dB, floored at 1)
vv_db_preview = 10 * np.log10(np.maximum(dn_vv.astype("float64") ** 2, 1.0))

# title, no ticks

    dem_preview = dsrc.read(1)  # its elevations

# title, no ticks

A from-scratch range-Doppler terrain correction (the sarsen backend, the Terrain correction (geocoding) section) does use it, bundled inside the product’s full annotation.

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Calibration and noise look-up tables
The annotation folder of every real GRD carries calibration-*.xml with sparse look-up tables (LUTs) of the calibration constant A, on a grid of lines and pixels, for sigma0, beta0 and gamma0, and noise-*.xml with the thermal noise power in DN^2:
sigma0 (or beta0, gamma0) = (DN^2 - N) / A^2

beta0’s A is constant (it refers to slant-range area, not ground area), while sigma0 and gamma0’s A change smoothly across range (incidence angle).
The noise power N varies along range too, following the antenna pattern of the three IW sub-swaths – this is why an uncalibrated DN image shows brightness steps at the sub-swath boundaries, and why skipping noise removal leaves visible seams in dark water.
interpolate_lut bilinearly interpolates these sparse grids onto any pixel grid you ask for; offset=(row0, col0) tells it where that grid sits in the scene’s own line/pixel numbering – necessary here, since the Study area and real data section already cropped to Cox’s Bazar rather than keeping the whole scene.



Code
# sigma0 calibration constants A on a sparse (line, pixel) grid
lines, pixels, a_sigma = s1.read_calibration_lut(CAL_VV, "sigmaNought")
_, _, a_beta = s1.read_calibration_lut(CAL_VV, "betaNought")  # beta0 constants on the same grid
_, _, a_gamma = s1.read_calibration_lut(CAL_VV, "gamma")  # gamma0 constants on the same grid
nl, npx, noise_raw = s1.read_noise_lut(NOISE_VV)  # thermal-noise values on their own sparse grid
print(f"calibration LUT grid: {lines.size} lines x {pixels.size} pixels")  # size of the calibration grid
print(f"noise LUT grid: {nl.size} lines x {npx.size} pixels")  # size of the noise grid
# constants at the middle pixel of the first line
print(f"A at mid-swath (first line): sigma0={a_sigma[0, len(pixels)//2]:.1f}  "
     f"beta0={a_beta[0, len(pixels)//2]:.1f}  gamma0={a_gamma[0, len(pixels)//2]:.1f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))  # one panel
mid_line = len(lines) // 2  # the middle line of the grid
ax.plot(pixels, a_sigma[mid_line], label="sigma0")  # sigma0 constants across range
ax.plot(pixels, a_beta[mid_line], label="beta0")  # beta0 constants
ax.plot(pixels, a_gamma[mid_line], label="gamma0")  # gamma0 constants
# labels
ax.set(xlabel="pixel (range)", ylabel="calibration constant A", title="Real calibration LUT, mid-scene line")
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)  # legend and grid
plt.show()  # draw


calibration LUT grid: 27 lines x 648 pixels
noise LUT grid: 27 lines x 650 pixels
A at mid-swath (first line): sigma0=595.9  beta0=474.0  gamma0=524.3









beta0 is flat across range exactly as expected (it is defined in slant-range area, which does not depend on incidence angle); sigma0 and gamma0 both fall off toward far range as the ground area a slant-range cell represents grows with incidence angle. Next, the real noise look-up table and the noise-equivalent sigma0 (NESZ) it implies:
NESZ (dB) = 10 log10(N / A^2)
the sigma0 a target would need to equal the noise floor itself – below this, a real target is not reliably distinguishable from instrument noise.


Code
# noise interpolated to every pixel of the middle line
noise_vv_mid = s1.interpolate_lut(nl, npx, noise_raw, (1, len(pixels)), offset=(int(lines[mid_line]), 0))[0]
nesz_db = s1.to_db(noise_vv_mid / a_sigma[mid_line] ** 2)  # noise-equivalent sigma0 = noise / A_sigma², in dB
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))  # one panel
ax.plot(pixels, nesz_db)  # NESZ across range
# labels
ax.set(xlabel="pixel (range)", ylabel="NESZ (dB)", title="Noise-equivalent sigma0, mid-scene line (real)")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)  # grid
plt.show()  # draw
# NESZ range along the line
print(f"NESZ range across this line: {nesz_db.min():.1f} to {nesz_db.max():.1f} dB")









NESZ range across this line: -23.2 to -22.5 dB

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
section: Geolocation, incidence angle and platform heading
text:
Geolocation, incidence angle and platform heading
A genuine ESA-distributed SAFE product’s annotation XML lists a sparse geolocation grid – for a set of (line, pixel) positions it gives latitude, longitude, height, incidence and elevation angle – plus the platform’s flight heading. geolattice.rsense.sar.sentinel1 reads both: read_geolocation_grid/incidence_angle_grid for the geolocation grid, read_platform_heading for the heading and ascending/descending pass direction. Both need exactly these real fields from that real annotation file.
Planetary Computer’s sentinel-1-grd collection does not carry that file. Its schema-product-* asset – the one that looks like the product annotation – is actually an RFI (radio-frequency interference) mitigation report with no geolocation grid in it at all (confirmed below: zero <geolocationGridPoint> elements). Only a direct ESA/Copernicus Dataspace or ASF download includes the real one. This is a genuine, worth-knowing limitation of this otherwise very convenient data source, not a bug: it publishes the real measurement pixels and the real calibration/noise LUTs (the Calibration and noise look-up tables and Thermal-noise removal and radiometric calibration sections use those directly), just not every annotation file ESA ships in the full product.
Two real, scene-derived substitutes carry the sections from Radiometric terrain flattening to Terrain correction (geocoding) through without that file:

Heading from the scene’s own embedded GCPs: the geodesic bearing along a fixed column, from the first to the last line, which is the azimuth (flight) direction by construction.
Incidence angle from the well-documented nominal IW GRD swath range, 29.1 degrees (near range) to 46.0 degrees (far range) – ESA’s own IW specification – linearly interpolated across range (pixel/column 0 is always near range, by processor convention). This is an approximation where the exact per-pixel annotation would normally be exact; it is used only for the incidence-angle-dependent steps below (the Radiometric terrain flattening section’s terrain flattening, the Multilooking section’s gamma0 comparison), never for the calibration itself, which already used the real sigma0/beta0/gamma0 LUTs directly in the Calibration and noise look-up tables section.



Code
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET  # XML parsing

# the product annotation file shipped with this download
root = ET.parse(SAFE_DIR / "annotation" / f"s1a-iw-grd-vv-{STEM}.xml").getroot()
n_geoloc = len(root.findall(".//geolocationGridPoint"))  # count its geolocation grid points
# there are none in this file
print(f"<geolocationGridPoint> elements in Planetary Computer's schema-product-vv.xml: {n_geoloc}")
# it is a different report, so geometry comes from the GCPs instead
print("root tag:", root.tag, "-- an RFI mitigation report, not the product annotation")

# Heading from the scene's own GCPs: bearing along a fixed column, first line to last line
cols_u = sorted(set(g.col for g in gcps))  # the distinct GCP columns
mid_col = cols_u[len(cols_u) // 2]  # the middle column
# GCPs of that column, from the first to the last line
along = sorted((g for g in gcps if g.col == mid_col), key=lambda g: g.row)
lon1, lat1 = np.radians(along[0].x), np.radians(along[0].y)  # first point in radians
lon2, lat2 = np.radians(along[-1].x), np.radians(along[-1].y)  # last point in radians
dlon = lon2 - lon1  # longitude difference
# initial great-circle bearing from the first to the last point = platform heading
heading = np.degrees(np.arctan2(
    np.sin(dlon) * np.cos(lat2),
    np.cos(lat1) * np.sin(lat2) - np.sin(lat1) * np.cos(lat2) * np.cos(dlon))) % 360
# the heading in degrees
print(f"\nPlatform heading (from GCPs): {heading:.2f} deg -- ascending, flying north-northwest")

# Incidence angle: linear across range, nominal IW bounds
NEAR_INC, FAR_INC = 29.1, 46.0  # nominal near- and far-range incidence angles of the IW swath
SCENE_WIDTH = 25843   # full-scene far-range pixel index
global_cols = col0 + np.arange(SHAPE[1])  # scene column number of every crop column
# incidence angle grows linearly across the swath
inc_row = NEAR_INC + (FAR_INC - NEAR_INC) * (global_cols / SCENE_WIDTH)
inc_full = np.tile(inc_row, (SHAPE[0], 1)).astype("float32")  # repeat the row for every crop row
# incidence range of the crop
print(f"Incidence angle across this crop: {inc_full.min():.1f} to {inc_full.max():.1f} deg "
     "(near-range portion of the swath)")


<geolocationGridPoint> elements in Planetary Computer's schema-product-vv.xml: 0
root tag: rfi -- an RFI mitigation report, not the product annotation

Platform heading (from GCPs): 349.55 deg -- ascending, flying north-northwest
Incidence angle across this crop: 30.2 to 32.5 deg (near-range portion of the swath)

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Thermal-noise removal and radiometric calibration
Applying Steps 2-3 to the real Cox’s Bazar crop: remove_border_noise trims the GRD’s own zero-padded scene edges (illustrative here – this crop sits well inside the scene, so it changes nothing, but it is the right first step on raw DN in general and is what process_grd(backend="native") runs by default); then interpolate_lut builds the full-size calibration and noise rasters at this crop’s real offset, and calibrate applies the sigma0/beta0 formula from the Calibration and noise look-up tables section, with and without the noise term, so the effect of removing it is visible directly rather than asserted.


Code
dn_vv_clean = s1.remove_border_noise(dn_vv)  # trim the noisy no-data border of the GRD product
dn_vh_clean = s1.remove_border_noise(dn_vh)  # same for VH
# how many pixels the trimming changed
print(f"Border-noise trimming changed {np.sum(dn_vv_clean != dn_vv)} of {dn_vv.size} pixels "
     "(this crop sits well inside the scene, away from any real edge)")

# sigma0 calibration constants interpolated to every crop pixel
cal_vv = s1.interpolate_lut(*s1.read_calibration_lut(CAL_VV, "sigmaNought"), SHAPE, offset=OFFSET)
# beta0 constants for every crop pixel
cal_beta_vv = s1.interpolate_lut(*s1.read_calibration_lut(CAL_VV, "betaNought"), SHAPE, offset=OFFSET)
# VV thermal noise for every crop pixel
noise_vv = s1.interpolate_lut(*s1.read_noise_lut(NOISE_VV), SHAPE, offset=OFFSET)
# VH sigma0 constants
cal_vh = s1.interpolate_lut(*s1.read_calibration_lut(CAL_VH, "sigmaNought"), SHAPE, offset=OFFSET)
noise_vh = s1.interpolate_lut(*s1.read_noise_lut(NOISE_VH), SHAPE, offset=OFFSET)  # VH thermal noise

sigma0_vv = s1.calibrate(dn_vv_clean, cal_vv, noise_vv)           # with thermal-noise removal
sigma0_vv_raw = s1.calibrate(dn_vv_clean, cal_vv, None)           # without -- for comparison
beta0_vv = s1.calibrate(dn_vv_clean, cal_beta_vv, noise_vv)       # beta0, needed for Section 9
sigma0_vh = s1.calibrate(dn_vh_clean, cal_vh, noise_vh)  # VH sigma0 with noise removal

nesz_vv = s1.to_db(noise_vv / cal_vv ** 2)  # NESZ of every crop pixel in dB
print(f"NESZ over this crop: {nesz_vv.min():.2f} to {nesz_vv.max():.2f} dB "  # NESZ range over the crop
     "(matches the -20 to -25 dB nominal IW range)")
# mean VV sigma0 with noise removal
print(f"VV sigma0 mean, with noise removal:    {float(s1.to_db(np.nanmean(sigma0_vv))):.2f} dB")
# mean VV sigma0 without noise removal
print(f"VV sigma0 mean, without noise removal: {float(s1.to_db(np.nanmean(sigma0_vv_raw))):.2f} dB")
print(f"VH sigma0 mean: {float(s1.to_db(np.nanmean(sigma0_vh))):.2f} dB")  # mean VH sigma0

water = slice(0, 300), slice(0, 300)   # Bay of Bengal corner of this crop -- see Section 2's quicklook
print(f"\nOver open water specifically: with noise removal "  # the same comparison over open water only
     f"{float(s1.to_db(np.nanmean(sigma0_vv[water]))):.2f} dB, without "
     f"{float(s1.to_db(np.nanmean(sigma0_vv_raw[water]))):.2f} dB -- "
     "the correction matters far more right at the noise floor than in the scene-wide mean.")


Border-noise trimming changed 0 of 11486706 pixels (this crop sits well inside the scene, away from any real edge)
NESZ over this crop: -25.04 to -24.44 dB (matches the -20 to -25 dB nominal IW range)
VV sigma0 mean, with noise removal:    -9.34 dB
VV sigma0 mean, without noise removal: -9.22 dB
VH sigma0 mean: -17.20 dB

Over open water specifically: with noise removal -15.64 dB, without -15.11 dB -- the correction matters far more right at the noise floor than in the scene-wide mean.




Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))  # three panels
axes[0].imshow(s1.to_db(sigma0_vv_raw), cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=0)  # VV without noise removal
axes[0].set_title("VV sigma0 (dB), no noise removal")  # title
axes[1].imshow(s1.to_db(sigma0_vv), cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=0)  # VV with noise removal
axes[1].set_title("VV sigma0 (dB), noise removed")  # title
# difference: how much noise removal lowered each pixel
im = axes[2].imshow(s1.to_db(sigma0_vv_raw) - s1.to_db(sigma0_vv), cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=1)
axes[2].set_title("Difference (dB)")  # title
for ax in axes[:2]: ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks on the first two panels
axes[2].set_xticks([]); axes[2].set_yticks([])  # or the third
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[2], shrink=0.7, label="dB")  # colour bar
plt.suptitle("Real effect of thermal-noise removal, Cox's Bazar VV")  # overall title
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Multilooking
Multilooking block-averages pixels in range and azimuth toward square ground pixels, trading resolution for lower speckle: averaging L independent looks reduces the relative standard deviation by about 1/sqrt(L). This scene’s native pixel spacing is 10 m x 10 m (IW GRDH, with a true resolution closer to 20 m x 22 m – already oversampled 2x by ESA’s own processor); 3x3 multilooking brings that to a real 30 m-class pixel, closer to the nominal number of independent looks (ENL) IW GRDH’s own processing already carries (about 4.4) actually being realised as visibly lower speckle.


Code
ml_vv = s1.multilook(sigma0_vv, (3, 3))  # average 3 x 3 pixels: less speckle, coarser pixels
ml_vh = s1.multilook(sigma0_vh, (3, 3))  # VH
ml_beta0_vv = s1.multilook(beta0_vv, (3, 3))  # beta0, for terrain flattening later
inc_ml = s1.multilook(inc_full, (3, 3))  # incidence angle on the multilooked grid
print(f"Shape before multilooking: {sigma0_vv.shape}  after 3x3: {ml_vv.shape}")  # shape before and after

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 6))  # two panels
axes[0].imshow(s1.to_db(sigma0_vv), cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=0)  # single-look VV
axes[0].set_title(f"Single-look VV ({sigma0_vv.shape[0]} x {sigma0_vv.shape[1]})")  # title with its size
axes[1].imshow(s1.to_db(ml_vv), cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=0)  # multilooked VV
axes[1].set_title(f"3x3 multilooked VV ({ml_vv.shape[0]} x {ml_vv.shape[1]})")  # title with its size
for ax in axes: ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw
# ENL over open water before and after multilooking
print(f"ENL estimate, open-water corner: single-look {speckle.enl_estimate(sigma0_vv[:300,:300]):.1f}, "
     f"multilooked {speckle.enl_estimate(ml_vv[:100,:100]):.1f}")


Shape before multilooking: (3243, 3542)  after 3x3: (1081, 1180)









ENL estimate, open-water corner: single-look 3.6, multilooked 8.3

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Speckle filtering
Speckle is multiplicative noise inherent to coherent imaging, not sensor error: each resolution cell sums many random sub-pixel scatterers, and the result follows a Gamma (intensity) or Rayleigh (amplitude) distribution even over a perfectly uniform surface.








Filter
Character
When




Boxcar
Simple mean, blurs edges
Polarimetric matrices, large homogeneous areas


Lee / Refined Lee
Adaptive, preserves edges
General land mapping (default choice)


Gamma-MAP
Statistical model
Agriculture, forests


Multi-temporal (Quegan)
Uses the stack over time
Time series; best detail retention



Use a 5x5 or 7x7 window; never filter before InSAR coregistration (it destroys phase); avoid heavy filtering before ship or point-target detection. Compared here on the real, already multilooked Cox’s Bazar VV, with a real ENL measured over a genuinely homogeneous patch of open Bay of Bengal water (the dark region in the Study area and real data section’s quicklook), not a simulated stand-in.


Code
# four speckle filters, each as a function of the image
filters = {"Boxcar (5x5)": lambda x: speckle.boxcar(x, 5), "Lee (7x7)": lambda x: speckle.lee(x, 7),
          "Refined Lee": speckle.refined_lee, "Gamma-MAP (7x7)": lambda x: speckle.gamma_map(x, 7)}
# (WATER is defined just below)
WATER = (slice(0, 100), slice(0, 100))   # open Bay of Bengal, upper-left corner of the crop

# one panel per filter plus the unfiltered image
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(filters) + 1, figsize=(4 * (len(filters) + 1), 4.5))
axes[0].imshow(s1.to_db(ml_vv), cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=0)  # unfiltered multilooked VV
# title with the ENL over the water patch
axes[0].set_title(f"Unfiltered\nENL={speckle.enl_estimate(ml_vv[WATER]):.1f}")
results = {}  # filtered images by name
for ax, (name, f) in zip(axes[1:], filters.items()):  # apply each filter
    out = f(ml_vv)  # filtered image
    results[name] = out  # keep it
    ax.imshow(s1.to_db(out), cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=0)  # show it
    # title with the ENL over the water patch
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nENL={speckle.enl_estimate(out[WATER]):.1f}")
for ax in axes: ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.suptitle("Real speckle filters on real Cox's Bazar VV (water-patch ENL)")  # overall title
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw









Lee and Gamma-MAP push ENL highest over this very homogeneous water patch (both model-driven, strong smoothing where the local statistics say the scene is uniform); Refined Lee trades some of that for edge preservation, visible in how much sharper the coastline and river channel stay in its panel than in plain Boxcar’s, which – blind to edges by design – both smooths least here and visibly blurs the shoreline the most. On genuinely uniform water, nominal IW GRDH’s own built-in multilooking already gives an ENL around 4.4; every filter here raises that well into the tens or low hundreds, consistent with real-world reports for Lee/Gamma-MAP- class filters over calm water – the headline number to compare against a published nominal ENL is always taken over a target this homogeneous, not a mixed land scene.

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Radiometric terrain flattening
Slopes facing the sensor appear bright, and slopes facing away appear dark, purely from geometry: the true illuminated ground area a slant-range cell represents shrinks on a forward-facing slope and grows on a back-facing one. Terrain flattening (Small, 2011) uses a DEM to compute that true area via the local incidence angle (the angle between the radar look vector and the real, sloped surface normal, not the flat ellipsoid), and converts beta0 into terrain-flattened gamma0:
gamma0_T = beta0 / cos(local incidence angle)
local_incidence_angle builds the local incidence angle from a DEM’s own gradients (surface normal) and the radar look vector (from the scene’s own heading and the approximate incidence angle, the Geolocation, incidence angle and platform heading section); terrain_flatten applies the formula above. Run here on the real Copernicus DEM over Cox’s Bazar – Teknaf, reprojected to UTM 46N (metres, which local_incidence_angle needs for its surface-normal gradients) at 30 m, matching the DEM’s own native resolution.


Code
with rasterio.open(DEM_PATH) as dsrc:  # open the DEM
    dst_crs = "EPSG:32646"   # UTM 46N -- covers Bangladesh
    transform, width, height = warp.calculate_default_transform(  # 30 m UTM grid that covers the DEM
        dsrc.crs, dst_crs, dsrc.width, dsrc.height, *dsrc.bounds, resolution=30)
    dem_utm = np.empty((height, width), dtype="float32")  # empty array for the reprojected DEM
    # reproject the DEM to UTM 46N (bilinear)
    warp.reproject(rasterio.band(dsrc, 1), dem_utm, src_transform=dsrc.transform, src_crs=dsrc.crs,
                   dst_transform=transform, dst_crs=dst_crs, resampling=warp.Resampling.bilinear)
# size and elevation range
print(f"DEM, UTM 46N, 30 m: {dem_utm.shape}, elevation {np.nanmin(dem_utm):.0f} to {np.nanmax(dem_utm):.0f} m")

# resample this crop's (approximate, range-varying) incidence angle onto the DEM's grid
# zoom factors from the multilooked grid to the DEM grid
zy, zx = dem_utm.shape[0] / inc_ml.shape[0], dem_utm.shape[1] / inc_ml.shape[1]
# incidence angle on the DEM grid
inc_on_dem = zoom(inc_ml, (zy, zx), order=1)[:dem_utm.shape[0], :dem_utm.shape[1]]

# local incidence angle from slope, aspect, heading and ellipsoid incidence
local_inc = s1.local_incidence_angle(dem_utm, resolution=30.0, heading_deg=heading,
                                     incidence_deg=inc_on_dem)
# range of local and ellipsoid incidence
print(f"Local incidence angle: {np.nanmin(local_inc):.1f} to {np.nanmax(local_inc):.1f} deg "
     f"(ellipsoid incidence here: {inc_on_dem.min():.1f} to {inc_on_dem.max():.1f} deg)")

# back onto the multilooked beta0 grid for the gamma0 comparison
# zoom factors back to the multilooked grid
zy2, zx2 = ml_beta0_vv.shape[0] / local_inc.shape[0], ml_beta0_vv.shape[1] / local_inc.shape[1]
# local incidence on the multilooked grid (nearest neighbour)
local_inc_ml = zoom(local_inc, (zy2, zx2), order=0)[:ml_beta0_vv.shape[0], :ml_beta0_vv.shape[1]]

# gamma0 normalised by the local illuminated area (terrain flattening)
gamma0_flat = s1.terrain_flatten(ml_beta0_vv, local_inc_ml)
gamma0_ellipsoid = ml_beta0_vv / np.cos(np.radians(inc_ml))   # same beta0, ellipsoid incidence only
# how much flattening changed each pixel (dB)
correction_db = s1.to_db(gamma0_flat) - s1.to_db(gamma0_ellipsoid)
# mean and 99th-percentile correction
print(f"Mean flattening correction: {np.nanmean(correction_db):.3f} dB over the whole crop "
     f"(mostly flat coastal plain); {np.nanpercentile(correction_db, 99):.2f} dB at the 99th percentile")


DEM, UTM 46N, 30 m: (2595, 2092), elevation -14 to 614 m
Local incidence angle: 0.2 to 91.5 deg (ellipsoid incidence here: 30.2 to 32.5 deg)
Mean flattening correction: 0.043 dB over the whole crop (mostly flat coastal plain); 1.25 dB at the 99th percentile




Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 5.5))  # four panels
im0 = axes[0].imshow(dem_utm, cmap="terrain", vmin=-15, vmax=400)  # the DEM
axes[0].set_title("DEM, UTM 46N (m)")  # title
plt.colorbar(im0, ax=axes[0], shrink=0.7)  # colour bar
axes[1].imshow(s1.to_db(gamma0_ellipsoid), cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=5)  # gamma0 with the ellipsoid only
axes[1].set_title("Ellipsoid gamma0 (dB)")  # title
axes[2].imshow(s1.to_db(gamma0_flat), cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=5)  # terrain-flattened gamma0
axes[2].set_title("Terrain-flattened gamma0 (dB)")  # title
# the correction, clipped to +-3 dB
im3 = axes[3].imshow(np.clip(correction_db, -3, 3), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-3, vmax=3)
axes[3].set_title("Flattening correction (dB)")  # title
plt.colorbar(im3, ax=axes[3], shrink=0.7, label="dB")  # colour bar
for ax in axes: ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.suptitle("Terrain flattening, real Teknaf hills -- correction traces the real ridgeline")  # overall title
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw









The correction map is close to zero (white) across the entire flat coastal plain and open water, and lights up in a well-defined band up to several dB exactly along the Teknaf peninsula’s hill ridges – matching the DEM’s own ridgeline pixel for pixel. That is the direct, real-data confirmation of the Rmd workflow’s own claim: flattening “changes little” in flat agricultural plains (true here for roughly 90% of this crop) and is “essential” where there is real topography (true for the hill band). A handful of pixels on the steepest slope faces show a far larger correction than the clipped +-3 dB colour scale above – the Convert to dB section masks exactly those as radiometric shadow/layover, not display artifacts.

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Terrain correction (geocoding)
Terrain correction places each pixel at its true map location, removing the foreshortening displacement terrain flattening only corrected the brightness for. Two real routes:

process_grd(backend="native") reprojects using the GRD product’s own embedded GCPs – real ESA-computed geolocation, no DEM. This is ellipsoid geocoding: correct map position from the GCPs’ own lat/lon/height, but it does not re-derive position from a DEM the way a full range-Doppler correction does. It needs only the measurement GeoTIFF, calibration and noise LUTs – everything this notebook has already downloaded – and is what the sections from Thermal-noise removal and radiometric calibration to Radiometric terrain flattening ran on top of.
process_grd(backend="sarsen", dem=...) is the real thing: DEM-based range-Doppler terrain correction plus terrain flattening in one combined step (Small, 2011), using orbit state vectors and the full geolocation grid from the product’s annotation. This needs that complete annotation (the Geolocation, incidence angle and platform heading section’s gap) – Planetary Computer’s GRD asset set does not carry it, so this call is shown for reference and will raise once it reaches the orbit/geolocation read, not run end to end here. A genuine ASF or Copernicus Dataspace Ecosystem SAFE download carries everything sarsen needs.

Settings for a from-scratch run either way: DEM Copernicus GLO-30 (SRTM 1-arcsec also works; a local LiDAR DEM where available); resampling bilinear for intensity, nearest neighbour for masks or class rasters; output pixel size matched to the beam mode (here, about 20-30 m for IW multilooked data); projection UTM or a national grid – UTM 46N for Bangladesh. Also export the layover/shadow mask, local incidence angle and projected local incidence angle alongside the backscatter: the Convert to dB section builds exactly those from what this notebook already has.


Code
# Ellipsoid/GCP geocoding (native backend), real GCPs, on this already-calibrated crop --
# build a georeferenced DataArray the same way process_grd(backend="native") does internally,
# but reusing the calibration already computed in Section 6 rather than recomputing it.
import xarray as xr  # labelled arrays
from rasterio.enums import Resampling  # resampling methods

# GCPs shifted into the crop's own (row, col) numbering
gcps_local = [rasterio.control.GroundControlPoint(row=g.row - row0, col=g.col - col0,
                                                  x=g.x, y=g.y, z=g.z) for g in gcps]
da = xr.DataArray(gamma0_flat, dims=("y", "x"),  # the flattened gamma0 as a DataArray with pixel coordinates
                  coords={"y": np.arange(gamma0_flat.shape[0]), "x": np.arange(gamma0_flat.shape[1])})
da = da.rio.write_crs(gcp_crs)  # attach the CRS of the GCPs
# warp to UTM 46N at 30 m using the GCPs
geocoded = da.rio.reproject("EPSG:32646", gcps=gcps_local, resolution=30.0,
                            resampling=Resampling.bilinear, nodata=np.nan)
print(f"Geocoded (ellipsoid), UTM 46N: {geocoded.shape}, "  # size and extent of the geocoded image
     f"x {float(geocoded.x.min()):.0f}-{float(geocoded.x.max()):.0f}, "
     f"y {float(geocoded.y.min()):.0f}-{float(geocoded.y.max()):.0f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))  # one panel
# the geocoded image in dB, in map coordinates
im = ax.imshow(s1.to_db(geocoded.values), cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=5,
               extent=[float(geocoded.x.min()), float(geocoded.x.max()),
                      float(geocoded.y.min()), float(geocoded.y.max())])
ax.set(xlabel="UTM 46N easting (m)", ylabel="UTM 46N northing (m)",  # labels
      title="Terrain-flattened gamma0, ellipsoid-geocoded (dB)")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, label="dB")  # colour bar
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw


Geocoded (ellipsoid), UTM 46N: (434, 458), x 379847-393557, y 2349919-2362909











Code
# sarsen: the real combined DEM terrain-flattening + terrain-correction route. Shown for
# reference against this notebook's data -- it needs the full annotation this source lacks
# (Section 5), so this raises rather than completing; a genuine ASF/CDSE SAFE download would
# carry it through.
try:  # sarsen is an optional package
    import sarsen  # import it
    # open the SAFE product, VV of the IW mode
    product = sarsen.Sentinel1SarProduct(str(SAFE_DIR), measurement_group="IW/VV")
    # terrain flattening and terrain correction with the DEM in one call
    gtc = sarsen.terrain_correction(product, dem_urlpath=str(DEM_PATH),
                                    output_urlpath="sarsen_gamma0.tif",
                                    correct_radiometry="gamma_bilinear")
    print(gtc)  # the result
except ImportError:  # sarsen is not installed
    print("pip install sarsen to try this backend")  # sarsen is optional
except Exception as exc:  # the product lacks the full annotation, so sarsen stops here
    # explain why sarsen stopped
    print(f"{type(exc).__name__}: needs the full product annotation sarsen reads for orbit "
         f"and geolocation -- not present in this source's asset set (Section 5). {exc}")


AssertionError: needs the full product annotation sarsen reads for orbit and geolocation -- not present in this source's asset set (Section 5). <class 'NoneType'> is not dict

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Convert to dB
dB = 10 log10(sigma0) – every map in this notebook has already displayed in dB, since backscatter spans several orders of magnitude and a linear colour scale would show almost nothing over land. The one rule that matters: do statistics – averaging, filtering, multilooking – in linear units, and convert to dB only at the very end, for display or as an ML feature. Averaging in dB instead computes a biased geometric mean, not the true (linear, arithmetic) mean backscatter – the Thermal-noise removal and radiometric calibration section already measured this directly on this real scene.


Code
linear_mean_db = float(s1.to_db(np.nanmean(sigma0_vv)))             # correct: mean, then dB
db_mean = float(np.nanmean(s1.to_db(sigma0_vv)))                    # wrong: dB, then mean
print(f"dB of the linear mean:  {linear_mean_db:.3f} dB  (correct)")  # the right way to average backscatter
# averaging dB values underestimates the mean
print(f"Mean of the dB values:  {db_mean:.3f} dB  (biased low by {linear_mean_db - db_mean:.3f} dB)")


dB of the linear mean:  -9.344 dB  (correct)
Mean of the dB values:  -12.658 dB  (biased low by 3.313 dB)

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Quality control

Layover/shadow. A slope steeper than the local incidence angle folds its top closer to the sensor than its base (layover); a slope the radar cannot see at all is shadow. Both show up as extreme local incidence angle (layover near 0 degrees, shadow near or above 90 degrees) – exactly the handful of pixels the Radiometric terrain flattening section’s correction map clipped at +-3 dB.
Noise floor. Mask pixels whose sigma0 sits within a few dB of the real, measured NESZ (the Calibration and noise look-up tables and Thermal-noise removal and radiometric calibration sections) – below this they cannot be trusted as real backscatter rather than noise.
Image edges. remove_border_noise (the Thermal-noise removal and radiometric calibration section) already strips the GRD product’s own zero-padded border before calibration; a production pipeline also drops a pixel or two at the final geocoded raster’s own edge, where resampling has nothing real to interpolate.
Temporal stability (not run here – would need a second date): a stable target – dense urban fabric, closed-canopy forest – should return nearly the same backscatter from one repeat pass to the next. A real multi-date check is Exercise 5.



Code
# Layover/shadow mask from the real local incidence angle computed in Section 9
# local incidence below 5 or above 85 degrees: shadow or layover
shadow_layover = (local_inc_ml < 5) | (local_inc_ml > 85)
# how many pixels are masked
print(f"Layover/shadow pixels: {int(shadow_layover.sum())} of {shadow_layover.size} "
     f"({100 * shadow_layover.mean():.2f}%) -- concentrated on the steepest Teknaf slopes")

# Noise-floor mask: real NESZ for this crop (Section 6) plus a 3 dB margin -- multilook the
# linear NESZ, then convert to dB, same "linear first, dB last" rule as everywhere else
nesz_ml = s1.to_db(s1.multilook(noise_vv / cal_vv ** 2, (3, 3)))  # NESZ on the multilooked grid, in dB
near_floor = s1.to_db(ml_vv) < (nesz_ml + 3.0)  # pixels within 3 dB of the noise floor
# how many pixels are near the noise floor
print(f"Near-noise-floor pixels (VV within 3 dB of NESZ): {int(near_floor.sum())} of {near_floor.size} "
     f"({100 * near_floor.mean():.2f}%) -- mostly the calmest open water")

qc_mask = shadow_layover | near_floor  # combined quality-control mask
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 6))  # two panels
axes[0].imshow(s1.to_db(gamma0_flat), cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=5)  # the flattened gamma0
axes[0].set_title("Terrain-flattened gamma0 (dB)")  # title
# red = masked, green = kept, blank = no data
axes[1].imshow(np.where(qc_mask, 1, np.where(~np.isnan(gamma0_flat), 0, np.nan)), cmap="RdYlGn_r")
# title with the masked share
axes[1].set_title(f"QC mask: red = exclude ({100 * qc_mask.mean():.1f}% of valid pixels)")
for ax in axes: ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw


Layover/shadow pixels: 381 of 1275580 (0.03%) -- concentrated on the steepest Teknaf slopes
Near-noise-floor pixels (VV within 3 dB of NESZ): 12936 of 1275580 (1.01%) -- mostly the calmest open water

title: Sentinel-1 GRD Processing
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

GRD DN become backscatter through real calibration and noise look-up tables, interpolated at the pixel’s true position in the scene – offset= matters the moment you crop before calibrating. On this scene, removing thermal noise shifted the Cox’s Bazar-wide VV mean by only a few hundredths of a dB, but mattered far more right at the noise floor, over open water specifically.
Real NESZ measured on this scene (-25 to -24 dB) sits inside the nominal -20 to -25 dB IW range exactly as documented.
beta0, sigma0 and gamma0 differ by reference area; beta0’s calibration constant is flat across range, sigma0 and gamma0’s both fall off toward far range – confirmed directly from this scene’s own real calibration LUTs.
Not every convenient data source carries the complete product. Planetary Computer’s sentinel-1-grd publishes real pixels and real calibration/noise LUTs, but not the full annotation sarsen’s real DEM-based terrain correction needs – a genuine, worth-knowing gap, worked around here with a scene-derived heading (from the product’s own GCPs) and the published nominal IW incidence range, not invented numbers.
Terrain flattening, run on a real Copernicus DEM over a real coastline, left the flat coastal plain and open water essentially untouched and corrected the real Teknaf hill ridges by several dB – visible proof of the Rmd workflow’s own claim about flat plains versus real topography, not an assertion to take on faith.
Ellipsoid/GCP geocoding (native backend, now bug-fixed to auto-pick a sensible UTM zone rather than silently reprojecting to degrees) places pixels at their correct map location from the product’s own real GCPs; full DEM-based range-Doppler terrain correction (sarsen) needs the complete annotation a genuine ASF/CDSE SAFE download carries.
Speckle filtering, multilooking and any other averaging belong in linear units; convert to dB only for display or ML features – measured directly here as a real, non-trivial bias between the two.
Quality control – shadow/layover, the noise floor, image edges – is not optional housekeeping: the Quality control section’s mask removed real pixels this notebook’s own terrain-flattening step had already flagged as unreliable.

geolattice.rsense.sar.sentinel1 functions used: read_calibration_lut, read_noise_lut, interpolate_lut (with offset=), calibrate, remove_border_noise, multilook, to_db, local_incidence_angle, terrain_flatten, sigma0_to_gamma0, process_grd (native and sarsen backends), load_rtc; geolattice.rsense.sar.speckle (boxcar, lee, refined_lee, gamma_map, enl_estimate); geolattice.rsense.get_images (search_images, get_images).
Exercises

Recompute the Radiometric terrain flattening section’s terrain flattening with the heading flipped by 180 degrees (as if this were a descending pass instead). Which slope faces now get the larger correction, and does that match what geometry predicts for a radar looking the opposite direction?
The Quality control section used a fixed 3 dB margin above the measured NESZ for the noise-floor mask. Recompute it with a 1 dB and a 6 dB margin and compare how much of the open-water area each one excludes.
Widen the AOI crop in the Study area and real data section to include more of the Teknaf peninsula’s southern hills and recheck whether the flattening correction’s 99th-percentile value (the Radiometric terrain flattening section) grows with the extra steep terrain.
Obtain a genuine complete SAFE product for this same date – from ASF (Earthdata login) or the Copernicus Dataspace Ecosystem (geolattice.rsense.get_images(source="cdse", ...), needs CDSE_USER/CDSE_PASSWORD) – and rerun the Terrain correction (geocoding) section’s sarsen cell against it. Compare its real DEM range-Doppler terrain correction against this notebook’s ellipsoid/GCP geocoding over the Teknaf hills specifically.
Download a second Sentinel-1 GRD scene over the same AOI, a few months apart, and check the Quality control section’s “temporal stability” claim directly: does the dense built-up part of Cox’s Bazar town return nearly the same backscatter on both dates?

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
Overview
Built and operated by the European Space Agency (ESA), it is an active sensor: it supplies its own illumination and works through clouds, smoke, and darkness. It monitors land, ocean, and ice day and night. All data are free and open.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
Constellation history and current status








Satellite
Launch
Status




Sentinel-1A
3 April 2014
Retired 29 June 2026


Sentinel-1B
25 April 2016
Failed December 2021 (power system anomaly). Mission declared over in 2022


Sentinel-1C
5 December 2024 (Vega-C)
Operational


Sentinel-1D
November 2025 (Ariane 6)
Operational



From 2022 to 2024, only Sentinel-1A was flying, so revisit dropped to 12 days. That period has a coverage gap that matters for time series work.
ESA opened Sentinel-1D data to users on 17 April 2026, initially on an orbit following Sentinel-1C’s ground track with a one-day offset. Sentinel-1D finished commissioning and became fully operational on 1 May 2026. Sentinel-1C was then moved between June 9 and 23, 2026 to set up a six-day revisit with Sentinel-1D, and Sentinel-1A operations ended on June 29, 2026. The constellation is now Sentinel-1C plus Sentinel-1D.
Note for time series users: the new C/D orbit configuration shifts the 6-day revisit pattern by one day compared with the old A/B timeline. Acquisition date logic in existing pipelines may need adjusting.
Both 1C and 1D also carry an Automatic Identification System (AIS) receiver that picks up signals from ships in coastal waters and the Arctic. This makes it possible to match radar ship detections with AIS records.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
Orbit Details
The Sentinel-1 satellites follow a near-polar, sun-synchronous, dawn-dusk orbit. This means the satellites travel almost over the poles and cross the equator at the same local solar times on each pass, generally around dawn and dusk. This configuration ensures stable lighting conditions for optical missions, but with radar, it also means consistent geometry between acquisitions.

Altitude: The orbit has a mean altitude of about 693 km above Earth’s surface, and an inclination of approximately 98.18°, allowing the satellites to cover nearly the entire Earth’s surface.
Repeat Cycle: Each Sentinel-1 satellite completes 175 orbits within a 12-day repeat cycle, meaning it will observe the same location on the ground every 12 days. When two satellites are operational and phased correctly (e.g., Sentinel-1C and 1D), the revisit interval at the equator reduces to 6 days. At higher latitudes (closer to the poles), orbit paths overlap more, so revisit times are even shorter.
Viewing Geometry: The satellites acquire imagery on both ascending (moving from south to north, typically in the evening) and descending (north to south, usually in the morning) passes. This offers two different viewing angles over a location, which can be helpful for detecting changes or interpreting specific scattering effects in radar imagery.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
Sentinel-1 SAR Instrument (Exokain)







Parameter
Value




Frequency Band
C-band


Center Frequency
5.405 GHz (corresponds to a wavelength of ~5.55 cm)


Wavelength
Approximately 5.55 cm


Polarization
Single (HH or VV) or dual (HH+HV or VV+VH), selectable


Antenna
12.3 m × 0.82 m active phased array (electronic steering)


Default Land Mode
Interferometric Wide Swath (IW) mode, VV+VH polarization



Scattering Characteristics at C-band:

The C-band radar wavelength (~5.5 cm) is sensitive to surface features that are similar in size, namely, leaves, small branches, crop canopies, and uppermost few centimeters of soil.
C-band penetrates vegetation and soil less deeply than L-band, so it mainly reveals the structure and moisture of the canopy top and immediate ground surface.
The active phased array design allows for beam steering and multiple imaging modes.

Exokain: For most Earth observation applications over land, Sentinel-1 operates in Interferometric Wide (IW) mode with dual polarization (VV+VH). This configuration enhances sensitivity to both surface and volume scattering, which aids in separating signals from soil, water, crops, and built environments, and supports interferometric applications.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
Acquisition Modes
Sentinel-1 is equipped with several imaging modes, each optimized for different observation needs. The main acquisition modes are:









Mode
Swath Width
Spatial Resolution (range × azimuth)
Main Use Cases




Interferometric Wide swath (IW)
250 km
5 × 20 m
Standard mode over land; interferometry (InSAR), monitoring agriculture, detecting floods


Extra Wide swath (EW)
400 km
20 × 40 m
Sea ice mapping, Arctic and Antarctic regions, maritime surveillance


Stripmap (SM)
80 km
5 × 5 m
High-resolution imaging of small areas, islands, and during emergencies


Wave (WV)
20 × 20 km “vignettes”
5 × 5 m
Measuring ocean wave spectra in the open sea




Interferometric Wide swath (IW): The default mode for land applications. IW uses the TOPSAR technique (Terrain Observation with Progressive Scans SAR), where the synthetic aperture radar beam is electronically steered both in the azimuth (flight direction) and in range (across-track) directions. This results in a uniform image quality across the swath. The IW mode is divided into 3 subswaths, each covering part of the total swath width, and each subswath is further split into small segments called “bursts.” The incidence angle for IW mode ranges from about 29° to 46°, this determines how steeply the radar looks at the ground.
Extra Wide swath (EW): Used mainly for very broad-area coverage like monitoring sea ice and large maritime regions. EW also uses TOPSAR, providing 5 subswaths and a wider coverage at lower resolution.
Stripmap (SM): Provides high-resolution images but over a much narrower area. SM is used when detailed information of a localized region is needed, such as for mapping during disasters.
Wave mode (WV): Instead of continuous stripes, Wave mode acquires small “vignettes” (20 km × 20 km images) at regular intervals along the satellite’s ground track. These are used primarily to study ocean surface wave patterns globally.

Summary:
IW and EW modes both use the TOPSAR technology to ensure consistent coverage and radiometric performance across wide swaths. Subswaths and bursts allow the satellite to store and process data efficiently and ensure compatibility with applications like interferometry.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
Product Levels
Sentinel-1 products are available at several levels of processing, with each level designed for specific types of analysis and user requirements:
Level-0:
- These are the unprocessed, original radar echoes collected by the satellite, stored in a compressed format.
- Data are still in raw instrument units and have not undergone any calibration, geometric correction, or noise removal.
- Intended only for advanced users or engineers, as specialized knowledge and tools are needed to interpret or process them.
Level-1 SLC (Single Look Complex):
- This product provides data in “slant range” geometry, which preserves the original radar viewing geometry (before correction to ground range).
- Both amplitude (strength) and phase (timing information) for each radar return are retained as complex values.
- The presence of phase information is critical for applications like interferometry (InSAR, which measures ground movement using phase differences between repeat images) and polarimetric analysis (studying different polarization channels for target characterization).
- For the Interferometric Wide Swath (IW) mode, SLC data is organized by “subswaths” (spatial sections across the track) and further split into bursts for efficient handling and to align with acquisition strategy.
Level-1 GRD (Ground Range Detected):
- In these products, the radar data have been calibrated, multilooked (averaged to reduce noise), and geometrically corrected so the image coordinates correspond to the Earth’s surface as projected onto an ellipsoid (approximate globe shape).
- Only the amplitude (intensity) information is kept; all phase information is lost, meaning these images aren’t suitable for interferometric analysis.
- Multiple resolutions are available: Full Resolution (FR), High Resolution (HR), and Medium Resolution (MR).
- For IW mode, the High Resolution GRD (GRDH) product has a pixel spacing of 10 meters, with an effective spatial resolution of roughly 20 × 22 meters, making it well-suited for monitoring land surfaces and water bodies.
- Level-1 GRD products are the standard for mapping and backscatter time-series analysis, and are compatible with most open analysis workflows.
Level-2 OCN (Ocean):
- These products are processed specifically for oceanographic applications.
- They contain geophysical variables such as ocean surface wind fields, swell wave spectra (wave energy distribution), and surface radial velocity.
- Such products support marine forecasts, sea state monitoring, and other ocean applications.
Analysis Ready Data (ARD):
- These are datasets that have undergone additional processing steps (beyond standard Level-1) to be easier and faster to use in downstream analysis. ARD products are standardized to make them interoperable and minimize the need for further user preprocessing.
- Copernicus Sentinel-1 Normalized Radar Backscatter: Follows CEOS ARD standards, making backscatter data directly usable for time series, change detection, and other applications.
- NASA JPL OPERA products: Targeted for North America, these come in several forms:
– RTC-S1: Radiometrically Terrain Corrected backscatter, with terrain effects removed and data georeferenced to the surface.
– CSLC-S1: Coregistered Single Look Complex products, designed for direct use in time-series InSAR applications.
– DISP-S1: Surface displacement time series, giving geocoded maps of ground deformation over time, derived using InSAR.
In summary, the product level you select depends on your required analysis:
- For interferometry, ground motion mapping, or polarimetry, use Level-1 SLC or CSLC-S1.
- For surface feature or land/water mapping, use Level-1 GRD, RTC-S1, or ARD backscatter. - For marine applications, use Level-2 OCN.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
Backscatter Interpretation
In radar remote sensing, the key measurement is backscatter, which quantifies how much of the radar signal is reflected back to the sensor from the Earth’s surface. This measurement is usually expressed as sigma nought (σ⁰) or gamma nought (γ⁰), which represent the normalized radar cross section, and is often reported in decibels (dB) for easier interpretation.
The intensity of the backscatter received by the sensor is influenced by several factors:

Surface roughness: Smooth surfaces, such as calm water bodies, tend to reflect radar waves away from the sensor (specular reflection), resulting in a weaker signal and appearing dark in the radar image. In contrast, rough surfaces scatter the radar waves in many directions, including back toward the sensor, causing them to appear brighter.
Dielectric constant (moisture content): The ability of a material to transmit electrical fields affects how it interacts with radar signals. Materials with higher moisture content, such as wet soils, saturated vegetation, or flooded areas, generally have higher dielectric constants and return stronger backscatter signals.
Geometry and structure: The physical structure of objects dramatically affects the radar return. For example, buildings or other man-made objects often create “double-bounce” reflections, where the signal bounces between the ground and a vertical structure (like a building wall), returning a particularly strong signal to the sensor and causing urban areas to appear very bright. Vegetation canopies, due to their volume and internal layering, can create volume scattering, especially in the cross-polarized (VH) channel where the sensor transmits and receives in different polarizations.
Incidence angle: This is the angle between the radar beam and a perpendicular to the surface (nadir). As the incidence angle increases (i.e., the beam strikes the surface more obliquely, farther from the center of the image swath), backscatter levels typically decrease. Therefore, data are often “normalized” to correct for differences in incidence angle across the swath to make backscatter values comparable.

Typical Backscatter Patterns by Land Cover Type:



Surface Type
VV Polarization
VH Polarization




Open water
Very low

Bare smooth soil
Low to moderate

In this table: - VV (Vertical transmit, Vertical receive): Sensitive to surface roughness and structure, and commonly used in standard analyses. - VH (Vertical transmit, Horizontal receive): Often emphasizes scattering from randomly oriented or volumetric structures (like vegetation canopies), making it particularly useful for monitoring volume scatterers such as crops and forests.
Ratios and Indices:

The VH/VV backscatter ratio can highlight differences in land cover, areas with higher ratios often indicate dense or complex vegetation structures.
The Radar Vegetation Index (RVI) is a derived metric that quantifies the amount of volume scattering and is widely used for crop identification, vegetation status monitoring, and assessing plant health or biomass.

Understanding these details enables effective interpretation of radar images, such as distinguishing between water, soil, vegetation, and built environments, and monitoring changes in surface conditions over time.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
SAR-specific effects
Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery exhibits several unique effects and artifacts due to the way radar signals interact with the Earth’s surface and the geometry of imaging. Understanding these effects is essential for accurate interpretation and analysis:

Speckle:

What it is: A granular, salt-and-pepper appearance resulting from coherent interference between radar returns from multiple scattering elements within a single resolution cell.
Why it matters: Speckle is not random noise but is instead inherent to the SAR imaging process, potentially obscuring fine details and making interpretation challenging.
How it’s mitigated: Processing techniques such as Lee, Refined Lee, or Gamma-MAP filtering, as well as multitemporal (time series) averaging, are commonly used to reduce speckle while preserving structural detail.

Foreshortening:

What it is: When slopes face toward the radar sensor, the distance between radar pulses is shorter than on flat ground, causing these slopes to appear artificially compressed (“foreshortened”) in the image.
Why it matters: Steep terrain facing the sensor appears squashed together, sometimes making interpretation or measurement of such areas difficult.

Layover:

What it is: In mountainous regions, radar signals may reach the top of a slope before the base (since the top is closer to the sensor). As a result, the top is imaged earlier than lower points, so the normal geometry is inverted (“laid over” the base).
Why it matters: Features appear in unnatural positions, with mountain or building tops sometimes overlaid on top of their slopes or bases in the image.

Radar shadow:

What it is: Areas that slope away from the radar sensor do not reflect any return signal back, creating dark, shadowed regions in the image.
Why it matters: These shadows contain little or no radar information and can hide features located within them, acting similarly to optical shadows but resulting from the imaging geometry.

Border and thermal noise:

What it is: Artifacts at the image borders (border noise) or from the sensor’s electronics (thermal noise). These effects are especially noticeable in cross-polarized images, or over dark, low-backscatter surfaces such as open water.
Why it matters: They can appear as low-level artifacts or brightness variations, potentially misleading interpretation unless corrected during preprocessing.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR
text:
Applications

Agriculture: crop type mapping, rice area and phenology (flooding and transplanting show up clearly in VH time series), crop growth monitoring, yield modeling
Soil moisture: surface moisture retrieval, often fused with optical NDVI
Floods and water: near-real-time flood extent, wetland dynamics. Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring uses it operationally
Forests: deforestation and disturbance detection (for example, tropical forest alerts)
Geohazards: earthquakes, volcanic deformation, landslides, land subsidence from groundwater pumping
Infrastructure: settlement of buildings, dams, and transport networks
Ocean and ice: ship detection, oil spills, sea ice classification, iceberg tracking, wind and wave fields
Urban: settlement mapping and urban growth

Overview
Its successor, Sentinel-5, began flying in 2025 on EUMETSAT’s MetOp-SG A satellites. title: Sentinel-5P and Sentinel-5: Mapping Air Pollution from Orbit
text:
The two missions
“Sentinel-5” covers two related missions for monitoring atmospheric composition.

Sentinel-5 Precursor (Sentinel-5P): a dedicated satellite carrying the TROPOMI instrument, in orbit since 2017.
Sentinel-5: a spectrometer carried on EUMETSAT’s MetOp Second Generation (MetOp-SG) A-type weather satellites. The first unit, Sentinel-5A, launched in August 2025.

Heritage. These missions build on earlier European and Dutch atmospheric spectrometers: GOME on ERS-2 (1995), SCIAMACHY on Envisat (2002 to 2012), OMI on NASA’s Aura satellite (2004, a Dutch-Finnish instrument), and GOME-2 on the first-generation MetOp satellites.
Why a precursor? Sentinel-5P was designed to close the data gap between the loss of Envisat and the dedicated Copernicus atmospheric missions, Sentinel-4 and Sentinel-5.
Sentinel-5P - Launched on 13 October 2017 from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in Russia on a Rockot. - TROPOMI was co-funded by the Netherlands and ESA. KNMI handles mission planning for the instrument, and ESOC handles mission control. - Design life was about 7 years. Operations are secured until the end of 2027. - Its loose formation with Suomi-NPP ends by Q4 2026. Suomi-NPP data delivery itself stops on 1 November 2026, so the cloud products that rely on VIIRS will be affected.
Sentinel-5 (on MetOp-SG) - The first MetOp-SG satellite, MetOp-SG-A1, launched on 13 August 2025 on an Ariane 6 from Kourou, carrying the Sentinel-5A instrument. - Airbus Defence and Space is the prime contractor for the Sentinel-5 instrument. - Sentinel-5A has returned its first gas maps and is in commissioning and calibration and validation. Full operational products will follow once that phase ends. - Sentinel-5B is planned for launch in 2033. A third unit (5C) will fly on MetOp-SG-A3, extending the series into the 2040s.
Sentinel-4 (related mission). A geostationary instrument on Meteosat Third Generation (MTG-S1), launched on 1 July 2025. It gives hourly coverage of Europe and complements the daily global view from Sentinel-5 and Sentinel-5P.

title: Sentinel-5P and Sentinel-5: Mapping Air Pollution from Orbit
text:
Sensors
TROPOMI (TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument), on Sentinel-5P - Nadir-viewing push-broom grating imaging spectrometer with a 108 degree field of view. - Four spectrometers with 2D detectors and about 4,000 spectral channels. - Swath: about 2,600 km. - Spatial sampling: 5.5 by 3.5 km at nadir since 6 August 2019 (originally 7 by 3.5 km); SWIR bands 5.5 by 7 km; band 1 (deep UV) coarser. - Spectral range: UV-visible (270 to 495 nm), NIR (675 to 775 nm), and SWIR (2305 to 2385 nm).
Sentinel-5 UVNS (Ultraviolet-Visible-Near-infrared-Shortwave infrared) spectrometer, on MetOp-SG A - Push-broom grating spectrometer with five spectrometers, a direct evolution of TROPOMI. - Swath: about 2,670 km. - Spatial sampling: about 7.5 by 7 km at nadir; UV1 is coarser, about 50 by 50 km. - New SWIR-1 band at about 1.6 micrometres. Combined with the 2.3 micrometre band, it improves methane and CO retrievals and helps characterize aerosol and cloud effects.

Formats are expected to stay close to the Sentinel-5P conventions.

title: Sentinel-5P and Sentinel-5: Mapping Air Pollution from Orbit
text:
Applications

Air quality. Mapping NO2 and SO2 from traffic, power plants, shipping, and industry; estimating emissions with top-down inversions; inputs to air-quality forecasts from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS). TROPOMI famously recorded the sharp NO2 drops during the 2020 COVID-19 lockdowns.
Methane. Detecting super-emitters from oil and gas, coal mines, and landfills. Methane data feed UNEP IMEO’s Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) and national inventory checks.
Ozone and UV. Ozone hole monitoring, stratospheric ozone trends, and UV index forecasts.
Volcanic hazards. SO2 and ash plume tracking for aviation safety through the Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres.
Wildfires and biomass burning. CO and aerosol plume transport, smoke-height estimates.
Climate. Greenhouse gas monitoring (CH4) and aerosol-cloud interactions; long-term records continued from GOME, SCIAMACHY, and OMI.
Vegetation. Solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence from TROPOMI’s NIR bands, used as a research product for photosynthesis.
Health and epidemiology. Exposure estimates of NO2 and HCHO for linking air pollution to health outcomes; environmental justice analyses at neighbourhood scale; county-level panel datasets.

The Sentinel-5P product family and qa_value quality filtering
Every TROPOMI reader returns the product’s main variable under its documented name plus qa_value, a continuous 0 to 1 quality score. qa_mask does not assume a single cutoff: it reads the threshold ESA itself recommends straight out of the variable’s comment attribute, since that recommendation differs by product and has changed between processing baselines.
