title: Sentinel-5P and Sentinel-5: Mapping Air Pollution from Orbit
section: Boundaries, regional segments and the clip-then-resample workflow
text:
Boundaries, regional segments and the clip-then-resample workflow
A STAC search over a whole country’s bounding box returns every regional segment that intersects it. For a small city-sized area, one segment (about five minutes of orbit) is always enough; for a larger area such as the whole of Bangladesh or New York State, the satellite can need two adjacent segments to cover the full north-south extent in a single overpass, as the Case study B: New York State under Canadian wildfire smoke, 15 July 2026 section finds. The filter that keeps a single-segment download small, excluding the whole orbit duplicate by its scanline count (s5p:shape[0] < 1000), still applies here and is just as necessary: skip it and every download balloons to the full ~600 MB orbit file. The one exception is methane, which, depending on the exact day and AOI, sometimes has no small regional segment at all and needs the whole orbit granule regardless – download_segments below falls back to it automatically when that happens.
Three steps turn a downloaded segment into a clean 1 km map:

Clip. Keep only swath pixel centres that fall inside the exact administrative boundary polygon (shapely.contains_xy), not just the bounding box – a country or state is never a rectangle. Two adjacent segments can repeat one scan line at their shared boundary; average duplicate geolocations before fitting anything, rather than letting the same site enter the interpolator twice.
Project. Reproject the clipped points into a local projected CRS (metres), since a thin plate spline measures distance between points and a degree of longitude is not a fixed distance except exactly at the equator.
Resample. Fit scipy.interpolate.RBFInterpolator with kernel="thin_plate_spline" on the projected points, and evaluate it on a regular 1 km grid built from the boundary’s own projected bounds. neighbors=25 makes this a local thin plate spline, using only each target cell’s nearest control points rather than solving one global system – the only way this stays fast with tens of thousands of 1 km target cells. Pixels outside the exact boundary are masked back out to NaN after interpolation, so the TPS surface fitted from points near the border never leaks into a neighbouring country or state in the final map.



Code
# Load both administrative boundaries and keep a geographic polygon (for clipping swath
# points) plus a projected polygon (for the 1 km grid) for each area of interest.

# Boxes are a little larger than the outline so a STAC search still returns segments that only graze the border.
BD_BBOX = (88.0, 20.5, 92.7, 26.7)     # Bangladesh, with a small margin (west, south, east, north)
NY_BBOX = (-79.76, 40.49, -71.85, 45.02)  # New York State, with a small margin

# Bangladesh boundary
bd_boundary = gpd.read_file("../../../../Data/00_shared/vector_data/Bangladesh/Shapefiles/bd_boundary_GCS.shp")
ny_boundary = gpd.read_file("../../../../All Data/NY_STATE_BD.shp")  # New York State boundary

# A thin plate spline measures distance, so both areas need a metre-based coordinate system.
BD_CRS = "EPSG:32646"                 # UTM zone 46N, metres -- spans Bangladesh with little distortion
NY_CRS = ny_boundary.crs              # already NAD83 Conus Albers (EPSG:5070), metres

# geo: polygon in EPSG:4326, tested against swath longitudes and latitudes.
# proj: the same polygon in the local projected CRS, used to build and mask the 1 km grid.
AOI = {
    "bangladesh": {"geo": bd_boundary.geometry.iloc[0],
                  "proj": bd_boundary.to_crs(BD_CRS).geometry.iloc[0], "crs": BD_CRS},
    "ny": {"geo": ny_boundary.to_crs(4326).geometry.iloc[0],
          "proj": ny_boundary.geometry.iloc[0], "crs": NY_CRS},
}
# Area is reported from the projected polygon, where .area is in square metres.
print("Bangladesh area:", f"{AOI['bangladesh']['proj'].area / 1e6:,.0f} km2")
print("New York area:  ", f"{AOI['ny']['proj'].area / 1e6:,.0f} km2")  # area of New York State


Bangladesh area: 140,052 km2
New York area:   127,188 km2



Collection names, product settings and downloads
Each gas needs a STAC collection prefix, the asset key inside that item, and the reader, variable, unit conversion and colour scale used everywhere below. download_segments fetches the short regional file for one gas and one day, and falls back to the full orbit only when no regional segment exists.


Code
# Map each gas to its STAC names, store the reader and plotting settings, and define the download.

# Collection ids look like "S5P_L2_NO2____...". The prefix is enough to keep one gas out of a mixed search.
GAS_COLLECTION_PREFIX = {"no2": "S5P_L2_NO2", "so2": "S5P_L2_SO2", "co": "S5P_L2_CO_",
                         "ch4": "S5P_L2_CH4", "hcho": "S5P_L2_HCHO", "aer_ai": "S5P_L2_AER_AI"}
# Asset key inside the STAC item. The aerosol index uses a hyphen, unlike the other five.
GAS_ASSET_KEY = {"no2": "no2", "so2": "so2", "co": "co", "ch4": "ch4", "hcho": "hcho", "aer_ai": "aer-ai"}
MAX_SCANLINES = 1000   # excludes the whole orbit duplicate; keeps the regional segment(s)

# reader/var: how to open the file and which data variable to keep.
# convert: optional unit change; None leaves the file's native units.
# floor_zero: the colour scale stays at or above zero for quantities that cannot be negative.
PRODUCTS = {
    "no2": dict(reader=s5p.read_no2, var="nitrogendioxide_tropospheric_column",
               convert=s5p.molecules_per_cm2, cmap="inferno", unit="molecules/cm2",
               floor_zero=True, label="NO2 tropospheric column"),
    "so2": dict(reader=s5p.read_so2, var="sulfurdioxide_total_vertical_column",
               convert=s5p.dobson_units, cmap="viridis", unit="DU",
               floor_zero=True, label="SO2 total column"),
    "co": dict(reader=s5p.read_co, var="carbonmonoxide_total_column",
              convert=None, cmap="magma", unit="mol/m2",
              floor_zero=True, label="CO total column"),
    "ch4": dict(reader=s5p.read_ch4, var="methane_mixing_ratio_bias_corrected",
               convert=None, cmap="cividis", unit="ppb",
               floor_zero=False, label="CH4 bias-corrected mixing ratio"),
    "hcho": dict(reader=s5p.read_hcho, var="formaldehyde_tropospheric_vertical_column",
                convert=None, cmap="YlOrBr", unit="mol/m2",
                floor_zero=True, label="HCHO tropospheric column"),
    "aer_ai": dict(reader=s5p.read_aerosol_index, var="aerosol_index_354_388",
                  convert=None, cmap="RdBu_r", unit="index",
                  floor_zero=False, label="UV absorbing aerosol index"),
}

# download every segment of a product that covers the box on a date
def download_segments(gas, bbox, date, out_dir):
    """Download every regional segment of `gas` that intersects `bbox` on `date` (falling back
    to the whole orbit granule when no regional segment exists), skipping files already on
    disk. Returns the list of local paths."""
    # One calendar day. limit=1000 is high enough that a country-sized box is not truncated.
    search = CATALOG.search(collections=["sentinel-5p-l2-netcdf"], bbox=bbox,
                            datetime=f"{date}T00:00:00Z/{date}T23:59:59Z", limit=1000)
    # A bbox search returns every gas. Keep only the collection prefix for this one.
    items = [it for it in search.items() if it.id.startswith(GAS_COLLECTION_PREFIX[gas])]
    # Prefer the short regional segments. shape[0] is the along-track scanline count.
    small = [it for it in items if it.properties.get("s5p:shape", [9999])[0] < MAX_SCANLINES]
    # Methane sometimes has no regional segment; fall back to the full-orbit granule.
    chosen = small if small else items
    dest_dir = out_dir / gas  # folder for this product
    dest_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)  # create it
    paths = []  # paths of the downloaded files
    for it in chosen:  # every chosen segment
        dest = dest_dir / f"{it.id}.nc"  # local file
        # Skip the HTTP request when a previous run already saved this granule.
        if not dest.exists():
            # Stream in 1 MB chunks so a large orbit file is not held entirely in memory.
            with requests.get(it.assets[GAS_ASSET_KEY[gas]].href, timeout=300, stream=True) as r:
                r.raise_for_status()  # stop on an HTTP error
                with open(dest, "wb") as f:  # write the file ...
                    for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=1 << 20):  # ... in 1 MB chunks
                        f.write(chunk)  # append the chunk
        paths.append(dest)  # remember the path
    return paths  # the downloaded files




Reading, clipping and resampling
read_clip_points keeps the quality-filtered pixel centres that fall inside the administrative boundary and averages any duplicate location where two segments overlap. tps_resample fits a local thin plate spline in the projected coordinate system and evaluates it on a 1 km grid. process_gas runs that sequence for one product, and plot_grid draws the result with robust colour limits so a few overshoot pixels do not stretch the scale.


Code
# Helpers that turn downloaded segments into a boundary-clipped 1 km map.

def read_clip_points(reader, var, paths, boundary_geo, convert=None, min_qa=None):
    # quality-filtered swath points inside a boundary
    """Read one or more Sentinel-5P segments, mask by qa_value, optionally convert units,
    concatenate, and keep only the pixel centres that fall inside `boundary_geo` (EPSG:4326).
    Adjacent segments can share one scan line at their boundary -- duplicate geolocations are
    averaged rather than left as two separate control points at the same site."""
    lons, lats, vals = [], [], []  # longitude, latitude and value of all files
    for p in paths:  # every file
        ds = reader(p)  # read it
        # qa_mask reads the recommended cutoff from the file unless min_qa overrides it.
        valid = s5p.qa_mask(ds["qa_value"], min_qa=min_qa)
        clean = ds[var].where(valid)  # values that pass the quality test
        if convert is not None:  # a unit conversion is given
            clean = convert(clean)  # apply it
        # Ravel keeps one row per swath pixel so later steps can treat the scene as points.
        lons.append(ds.longitude.values.ravel())
        lats.append(ds.latitude.values.ravel())  # latitudes
        vals.append(clean.values.ravel())  # values
    lon, lat, val = np.concatenate(lons), np.concatenate(lats), np.concatenate(vals)  # all files together
    # Drop pixels the quality mask or the retrieval itself set to NaN.
    ok = np.isfinite(val)
    lon, lat, val = lon[ok], lat[ok], val[ok]  # keep finite values
    # contains_xy tests the exact polygon, so pixels in the bounding box but outside the border go.
    inside = shapely.contains_xy(boundary_geo, lon, lat)
    lon, lat, val = lon[inside], lat[inside], val[inside]  # keep points inside the boundary
    # Two adjacent segments can repeat one scan line. Average those duplicates before fitting.
    dedup = (pd.DataFrame({"lon": lon, "lat": lat, "val": val})
            .groupby(["lon", "lat"], as_index=False)["val"].mean())
    return dedup["lon"].to_numpy(), dedup["lat"].to_numpy(), dedup["val"].to_numpy()  # one value per location


# resample scattered points onto a regular grid with a thin plate spline
def tps_resample(lon, lat, val, boundary_proj, dst_crs, res_m=1000.0, neighbors=25):
    """Thin plate spline resample of clipped, quality-filtered swath points onto a regular
    `res_m` grid covering `boundary_proj`'s own bounds (already in `dst_crs`, metres), masked
    back to the exact boundary. Returns (x centres, y centres, 2D grid)."""
    # Project the control points into metres. A degree of longitude is not a fixed distance.
    transformer = pyproj.Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", dst_crs, always_xy=True)
    x, y = transformer.transform(lon, lat)  # points in the projected CRS
    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = boundary_proj.bounds  # bounds of the boundary
    xs = np.arange(minx, maxx, res_m)  # x coordinates of the grid
    ys = np.arange(maxy, miny, -res_m)   # descending: row 0 is the northern edge
    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)  # grid of x and y
    # neighbors=25 keeps the spline local: each cell uses only its nearest control points.
    interp = RBFInterpolator(np.column_stack([x, y]), val, kernel="thin_plate_spline", neighbors=neighbors)
    # interpolated values at every grid cell
    pred = interp(np.column_stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()])).reshape(gx.shape)
    # geometry_mask with invert=True is True inside the polygon. Everything else becomes NaN,
    # so the fitted surface does not leak across the border.
    transform = Affine(res_m, 0, minx, 0, -res_m, maxy)
    # cells inside the boundary
    mask = rasterio.features.geometry_mask([boundary_proj], out_shape=gx.shape, transform=transform, invert=True)
    pred = np.where(mask, pred, np.nan)  # NaN outside it
    # Shift from cell edges to cell centres so the map extent lines up with the grid.
    return xs + res_m / 2, ys - res_m / 2, pred


def robust_vlim(grid, low=1, high=99, floor_zero=False):  # colour limits from percentiles
    """2nd-98th-percentile colour limits -- keeps a handful of TPS overshoot pixels near sparse
    edges from stretching the whole colour scale. `floor_zero` additionally clips the lower
    limit at 0 for quantities (columns, mixing ratios) that cannot be physically negative."""
    vmin, vmax = np.nanpercentile(grid, [low, high])  # low and high percentiles
    return (max(vmin, 0.0) if floor_zero else vmin), vmax  # optionally start at zero


MIN_TPS_POINTS = 20   # below this, a 1 km surface is not a resampling, it is an extrapolation

def process_gas(gas, paths, aoi, min_qa=None):  # read, quality-filter, clip and resample one product
    """Full pipeline for one product: read, qa-mask, clip, dedupe, then TPS-resample to 1 km.
    Returns (lon, lat, val, gx, gy, grid); grid is None when too few points survive clipping."""
    spec = PRODUCTS[gas]  # settings of this product
    lon, lat, val = read_clip_points(spec["reader"], spec["var"], paths, aoi["geo"],  # the clipped points
                                     convert=spec["convert"], min_qa=min_qa)
    # Too few points would let the spline invent a smooth surface across the whole area.
    if lon.size < MIN_TPS_POINTS:
        return lon, lat, val, None, None, None  # too few points: no grid
    gx, gy, grid = tps_resample(lon, lat, val, aoi["proj"], aoi["crs"])  # resample to 1 km
    return lon, lat, val, gx, gy, grid  # points and grid


def plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, grid, spec, title):  # draw one gridded product
    """Draw one resampled grid with robust colour limits and a colourbar in the product's units."""
    vmin, vmax = robust_vlim(grid, floor_zero=spec["floor_zero"])  # robust colour limits
    # extent is the projected cell-centre range; origin="upper" matches the north-to-south rows.
    im = ax.imshow(grid, cmap=spec["cmap"], extent=[gx.min(), gx.max(), gy.min(), gy.max()],
                   origin="upper", vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)
    ax.set_title(title)  # title
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.75, label=spec["unit"])  # colour bar with units
    return im  # the image

title: Sentinel-5P and Sentinel-5: Mapping Air Pollution from Orbit
section: Case study A: Bangladesh, dry season, 15 January 2025
text:
Case study A: Bangladesh, dry season, 15 January 2025
15 January 2025 falls in the dry season described in earlier Sentinel sensor notebooks: low rainfall, brick kiln operation, and stagnant air that traps pollution close to the surface. It also happens to be a day when a single regional segment already spans the entire country for every product except methane (checked directly against the STAC search below, not assumed) – the simplest possible case to start with, one download per product.


Code
# Download every Bangladesh product for 15 January 2025, or reuse files already on disk.

DATE_BD = "2025-01-15"
BD_OUT = DATA / "s5p_bangladesh_2025_01_15"  # folder for the Bangladesh downloads

# NetCDF files of every gas already on the local drive
local = {gas: sorted((BD_OUT / gas).glob("*.nc")) for gas in PRODUCTS}

if all(local.values()):  # every gas downloaded before
    SEGMENTS_BD = local  # use the local drive
    print("Reading the files already downloaded under", BD_OUT)  # say so
elif ONLINE:  # something is missing: download (download_segments skips files already saved)
    SEGMENTS_BD = {gas: download_segments(gas, BD_BBOX, DATE_BD, BD_OUT) for gas in PRODUCTS}
else:  # offline: use whatever is on disk
    SEGMENTS_BD = local
    print("Offline: reusing the files already downloaded under", BD_OUT)  # say so

# One line per gas: how many files the search kept, and their names.
# Bangladesh is usually one regional file each, except methane.
for gas, paths in SEGMENTS_BD.items():
    # product, number of files and names
    print(f"{gas:7s} {len(paths)} file(s): " + ", ".join(p.name for p in paths))


no2     1 file(s): S5P_L2_NO2____20250115T063914_20250115T064414_37609.nc
so2     1 file(s): S5P_L2_SO2____20250115T063914_20250115T064414_37609.nc
co      1 file(s): S5P_L2_CO_____20250115T063914_20250115T064414_37609.nc
ch4     1 file(s): S5P_L2_CH4____20250115T053913_20250115T072044_37609.nc
hcho    1 file(s): S5P_L2_HCHO___20250115T063914_20250115T064414_37609.nc
aer_ai  1 file(s): S5P_L2_AER_AI_20250115T063914_20250115T064414_37609.nc



Nitrogen dioxide
NO2 comes mostly from combustion: traffic, power generation, brick kilns and industry. It is short lived, hours to a day, so a map reflects local emissions far more than regional transport.


Code
# Run the full NO2 pipeline for Bangladesh and map the 1 km surface.

# Filled in by run_bd as each product is processed, so the six-panel figure can reuse them.
bd_grids = {}   # gas -> (gx, gy, grid)
bd_points = {}  # gas -> (lon, lat, val), the clipped control points behind each grid

def run_bd(gas):  # process one Bangladesh product and keep the results
    """Clip and resample one Bangladesh product, store the points and the grid, and return both."""
    lon, lat, val, gx, gy, grid = process_gas(gas, SEGMENTS_BD[gas], AOI["bangladesh"])  # points and grid
    bd_points[gas] = (lon, lat, val)  # store the points
    bd_grids[gas] = (gx, gy, grid)  # store the grid
    return lon, lat, val, gx, gy, grid  # return everything

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, no2_bd = run_bd("no2")  # nitrogen dioxide
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 7))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, no2_bd, PRODUCTS["no2"], f"Bangladesh NO2, {DATE_BD}")  # the NO2 map
plt.show()  # draw
# The count is swath pixels inside the border. The mean is taken over the 1 km grid, NaNs ignored.
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(no2_bd):.3e} molecules/cm2 over the country")









3260 clipped control points -> mean 2.780e+15 molecules/cm2 over the country




Sulphur dioxide
SO2 mostly traces heavy industry, power generation from fuel oil or coal, and the traditional fixed-chimney brick kilns common across central Bangladesh, which burn low grade coal and biomass. Anthropogenic SO2 columns are small and noisy; never clip negative values before averaging, since they are retrieval noise distributed around zero, not real negative mass.


Code
# Run the SO2 pipeline for Bangladesh and map the total column in Dobson units.
# Negative retrieval noise is kept in the grid; floor_zero only holds the colour scale at zero.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, so2_bd = run_bd("so2")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 7))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, so2_bd, PRODUCTS["so2"], f"Bangladesh SO2, {DATE_BD}")  # the SO2 map
plt.show()  # draw
# number of points and mean SO2
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(so2_bd):.4f} DU over the country")









3206 clipped control points -> mean 0.0002 DU over the country




Carbon monoxide
CO comes from incomplete combustion: vehicles, brick kilns, cooking fires and crop residue burning. It lives long enough, weeks, to carry a regional background signal on top of local emissions, and its SWIR retrieval is markedly less cloud-sensitive than NO2 or SO2’s UV-visible bands.


Code
# Run the CO pipeline for Bangladesh, map the column, and convert the country mean to ppb.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, co_bd = run_bd("co")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 7))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, co_bd, PRODUCTS["co"], f"Bangladesh CO, {DATE_BD}")  # the CO map
plt.show()  # draw
# co_mixing_ratio turns mol/m2 into a mixing ratio. 101325 Pa is standard sea-level pressure.
xco = s5p.co_mixing_ratio(np.nanmean(co_bd), 101325.0)
# number of points and mean CO
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(co_bd):.4f} mol/m2, "
     f"about {float(xco):.0f} ppb assuming sea level pressure")









748 clipped control points -> mean 0.0532 mol/m2, about 149 ppb assuming sea level pressure




Methane
Methane is the most demanding of these six products to retrieve: its SWIR band needs a genuinely clear, low-aerosol, high-reflectance scene. Bangladesh’s dry season haze works against it even on an otherwise clear day, so expect noticeably fewer qa_value-passing pixels than the other five products – a real limitation of the instrument and the atmosphere, not a processing bug.


Code
# Run the methane pipeline for Bangladesh and map the bias-corrected mixing ratio.
# Fewer control points than the other gases is expected: the SWIR retrieval rejects hazy pixels.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, ch4_bd = run_bd("ch4")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 7))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, ch4_bd, PRODUCTS["ch4"], f"Bangladesh CH4, {DATE_BD}")  # the methane map
plt.show()  # draw
# number of points and mean CH4
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(ch4_bd):.1f} ppb over the country")
print("Enhancement above a clean background (~1900 ppb) is consistent with the delta's dense "  # interpretation
     "rice paddies, cattle and wetlands rather than with any single city.")









443 clipped control points -> mean 1956.4 ppb over the country
Enhancement above a clean background (~1900 ppb) is consistent with the delta's dense rice paddies, cattle and wetlands rather than with any single city.




Formaldehyde
HCHO is a proxy for volatile organic compound emissions: biomass burning, vehicle exhaust, industrial solvents and biogenic emissions from vegetation all contribute, so unlike NO2 it does not read as purely anthropogenic.


Code
# Run the formaldehyde pipeline for Bangladesh and map the tropospheric column.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, hcho_bd = run_bd("hcho")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 7))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, hcho_bd, PRODUCTS["hcho"], f"Bangladesh HCHO, {DATE_BD}")  # the formaldehyde map
plt.show()  # draw
# number of points and mean HCHO
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(hcho_bd):.3e} mol/m2 over the country")









3217 clipped control points -> mean 2.168e-04 mol/m2 over the country




UV absorbing aerosol index
The aerosol index is not a concentration – it compares the observed UV reflectance against what a clean Rayleigh atmosphere would produce. A positive value flags UV-absorbing aerosol such as smoke, dust and haze; a negative value usually indicates clean air or cloud.


Code
# Run the UV aerosol-index pipeline for Bangladesh and map it.
# Positive values flag absorbing aerosol (smoke, dust, haze); negative values are cleaner air or cloud.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, ai_bd = run_bd("aer_ai")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 7))  # one panel
# the aerosol index map
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, ai_bd, PRODUCTS["aer_ai"], f"Bangladesh UV aerosol index, {DATE_BD}")
plt.show()  # draw
# number of points and mean index
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(ai_bd):.3f} over the country")









3260 clipped control points -> mean -0.361 over the country




A six-pollutant snapshot of Bangladesh
Putting all six products side by side, each already clipped and resampled to the same 1 km grid, gives one picture of what dry season Bangladesh carries in a single overpass.


Code
# Draw all six Bangladesh products on one figure, reusing the 1 km grids stored in bd_grids.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 9))
for ax, gas in zip(axes.ravel(), PRODUCTS):  # every product
    gx, gy, grid = bd_grids[gas]  # its grid
    plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, grid, PRODUCTS[gas], PRODUCTS[gas]["label"])  # draw it
plt.suptitle(f"Bangladesh, {DATE_BD}: six pollutants at 1 km (thin plate spline resampled)")  # overall title
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

section: Case study B: New York State under Canadian wildfire smoke, 15 July 2026
text:
Case study B: New York State under Canadian wildfire smoke, 15 July 2026
In mid-July 2026, smoke from wildfires burning in Canada drifted south over the northeastern United States, including New York State. The same six-product pipeline built in the Boundaries, regional segments and the clip-then-resample workflow and Case study A: Bangladesh, dry season, 15 January 2025 sections applies unchanged – download, clip to the exact state boundary, resample to 1 km – the only difference is what the pollutants show: a transient smoke plume rather than Bangladesh’s steady anthropogenic emissions. New York State’s larger north-south extent also means every product here needs two adjacent regional segments, not one, to cover the whole state in a single overpass, exactly the case download_segments and read_clip_points were built to handle.


Code
# Download every New York product for 15 July 2026, or reuse files already on disk.
# This state usually needs two adjacent regional segments per gas to cover its full north-south extent.

DATE_NY = "2026-07-15"
NY_OUT = DATA / "s5p_ny_2026_07_15"  # folder for the New York downloads

# NetCDF files of every gas already on the local drive
local = {gas: sorted((NY_OUT / gas).glob("*.nc")) for gas in PRODUCTS}

if all(local.values()):  # every gas downloaded before
    SEGMENTS_NY = local  # use the local drive
    print("Reading the files already downloaded under", NY_OUT)  # say so
elif ONLINE:  # something is missing: download (download_segments skips files already saved)
    SEGMENTS_NY = {gas: download_segments(gas, NY_BBOX, DATE_NY, NY_OUT) for gas in PRODUCTS}
else:  # offline: use whatever is on disk
    SEGMENTS_NY = local
    print("Offline: reusing the files already downloaded under", NY_OUT)  # say so

for gas, paths in SEGMENTS_NY.items():  # every product
    print(f"{gas:7s} {len(paths)} file(s): " + ", ".join(p.name for p in paths))  # number of files and names


no2     2 file(s): S5P_L2_NO2____20260715T181011_20260715T181511_45362.nc, S5P_L2_NO2____20260715T180511_20260715T181011_45362.nc
so2     2 file(s): S5P_L2_SO2____20260715T181011_20260715T181511_45362.nc, S5P_L2_SO2____20260715T180511_20260715T181011_45362.nc
co      2 file(s): S5P_L2_CO_____20260715T181011_20260715T181511_45362.nc, S5P_L2_CO_____20260715T180511_20260715T181011_45362.nc
ch4     2 file(s): S5P_L2_CH4____20260715T181011_20260715T181511_45362.nc, S5P_L2_CH4____20260715T180511_20260715T181011_45362.nc
hcho    2 file(s): S5P_L2_HCHO___20260715T181011_20260715T181511_45362.nc, S5P_L2_HCHO___20260715T180511_20260715T181011_45362.nc
aer_ai  2 file(s): S5P_L2_AER_AI_20260715T181011_20260715T181511_45362.nc, S5P_L2_AER_AI_20260715T180511_20260715T181011_45362.nc



Nitrogen dioxide
NO2 is short lived and mostly local (traffic, power generation), so it is not expected to track a smoke plume the way the next five sections’ aerosol- and combustion-linked products do – a useful contrast against the UV absorbing aerosol index section’s aerosol index.


Code
# Run the full NO2 pipeline for New York and map the 1 km surface.
# NO2 is short lived, so this map should reflect local emissions more than the smoke plume.

ny_grids = {}   # gas -> (gx, gy, grid); grid is None when too few points survive
ny_points = {}  # gas -> (lon, lat, val), kept so a failed resample can still report a count

def run_ny(gas, min_qa=None):  # process one New York product and keep the results
    """Clip and resample one New York product. min_qa overrides the file's recommended cutoff."""
    # points and grid (optionally with a stricter quality cutoff)
    lon, lat, val, gx, gy, grid = process_gas(gas, SEGMENTS_NY[gas], AOI["ny"], min_qa=min_qa)
    ny_points[gas] = (lon, lat, val)  # store the points
    ny_grids[gas] = (gx, gy, grid)  # store the grid
    return lon, lat, val, gx, gy, grid  # return everything

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, no2_ny = run_ny("no2")  # nitrogen dioxide
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, no2_ny, PRODUCTS["no2"], f"New York NO2, {DATE_NY}")  # the NO2 map
plt.show()  # draw
# number of points and mean NO2
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(no2_ny):.3e} molecules/cm2 over the state")









7502 clipped control points -> mean 2.450e+15 molecules/cm2 over the state




Sulphur dioxide
Wildfire smoke is not a major SO2 source (biomass burning releases far more CO, HCHO and aerosol than sulphur), so this product mainly tests whether the pipeline still behaves normally on a smoke day – a near-zero, noisy signal here is the expected result, not a failure.


Code
# Run the SO2 pipeline for New York. A near-zero, noisy column is the expected smoke-day result.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, so2_ny = run_ny("so2")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, so2_ny, PRODUCTS["so2"], f"New York SO2, {DATE_NY}")  # the SO2 map
plt.show()  # draw
# number of points and mean SO2
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(so2_ny):.4f} DU over the state")









2348 clipped control points -> mean -0.0308 DU over the state




Carbon monoxide
CO is one of the two most reliable smoke tracers in this product set: biomass burning is a major incomplete-combustion source, and CO’s multi-week lifetime lets it accumulate across an entire smoke plume rather than marking only its freshest edge.


Code
# Run the CO pipeline for New York, map the column, and convert the state mean to ppb.
# Biomass burning is a large CO source, so this map should rise with the smoke plume.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, co_ny = run_ny("co")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, co_ny, PRODUCTS["co"], f"New York CO, {DATE_NY}")  # the CO map
plt.show()  # draw
xco = s5p.co_mixing_ratio(np.nanmean(co_ny), 101325.0)  # column -> dry-air mixing ratio at sea-level pressure
# number of points, mean column and mixing ratio
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(co_ny):.4f} mol/m2, "
     f"about {float(xco):.0f} ppb assuming sea level pressure")









2265 clipped control points -> mean 0.1314 mol/m2, about 368 ppb assuming sea level pressure




Methane: a second data availability case study
The Methane section showed methane struggling under Bangladesh’s ordinary dry season haze. Thick wildfire smoke is a far more extreme version of the same obstacle: TROPOMI’s SWIR CH4 retrieval needs a clear, high-reflectance scene, and a heavy smoke plume is neither. Check the raw qa_value coverage before even trying to resample, rather than silently handing a 5-point “map” to a thin plate spline and letting it extrapolate a smooth-looking fiction across the whole state.


Code
# Count methane pixels over New York that pass qa_value before trying to resample.
# A thin plate spline on a handful of points would draw a smooth map that the data do not support.

for p in SEGMENTS_NY["ch4"]:
    ds = s5p.read_ch4(p)  # read the methane file
    # Pixel centres inside the state polygon, not merely inside the search bounding box.
    inside = shapely.contains_xy(AOI["ny"]["geo"], ds.longitude.values.ravel(), ds.latitude.values.ravel())
    qa_in_state = ds["qa_value"].values.ravel()[inside]  # quality values of pixels over the state
    print(f"{p.name}: {inside.sum()} pixels over New York, "  # pixels and quality per file
         f"mean qa_value {qa_in_state.mean():.3f}, {(qa_in_state >= 0.5).sum()} pass qa >= 0.5")

# process_gas returns grid=None (and gx is None) when fewer than MIN_TPS_POINTS survive.
lon, lat, val, gx, gy, ch4_ny = run_ny("ch4")
# too few points to grid
print(f"\n{lon.size} control points survive clipping -- below MIN_TPS_POINTS={MIN_TPS_POINTS}, "
     "so no 1 km surface is fitted" if gx is None else f"{lon.size} control points, mean {np.nanmean(ch4_ny):.1f} ppb")


S5P_L2_CH4____20260715T181011_20260715T181511_45362.nc: 2560 pixels over New York, mean qa_value 0.005, 2 pass qa >= 0.5
S5P_L2_CH4____20260715T180511_20260715T181011_45362.nc: 1300 pixels over New York, mean qa_value 0.009, 3 pass qa >= 0.5

5 control points survive clipping -- below MIN_TPS_POINTS=20, so no 1 km surface is fitted


A handful of pixels pass quality filtering out of several thousand in the search area – the same mechanism as the Methane section, far more pronounced. Smoke scatters and absorbs enough SWIR radiance that the retrieval algorithm itself flags most of the scene as unreliable; the gap in The A six-pollutant snapshot of New York under smoke section’s combined figure is this finding stated plainly, not a plotting error.


Formaldehyde
HCHO is the second strong smoke tracer here: biomass burning releases volatile organic compounds directly, and sunlight breaks many of them down into HCHO within hours, so a fresh plume shows up clearly.


Code
# Run the formaldehyde pipeline for New York. Fresh smoke should raise the tropospheric column.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, hcho_ny = run_ny("hcho")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))  # one panel
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, hcho_ny, PRODUCTS["hcho"], f"New York HCHO, {DATE_NY}")  # the formaldehyde map
plt.show()  # draw
# number of points and mean HCHO
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(hcho_ny):.3e} mol/m2 over the state")









3816 clipped control points -> mean 4.522e-04 mol/m2 over the state




UV absorbing aerosol index
This is the cleanest single signal of smoke in the whole product set. Wildfire smoke is a textbook UV-absorbing aerosol, and Bangladesh’s dry season values in the UV absorbing aerosol index section (roughly -1 to +1) give a useful sense of scale for how extreme a true smoke event reads by comparison.


Code
# Run the UV aerosol-index pipeline for New York and report the mean and the maximum.
# Wildfire smoke is strongly UV-absorbing, so the maximum is the clearest plume signal.

lon, lat, val, gx, gy, ai_ny = run_ny("aer_ai")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))  # one panel
# the aerosol index map
plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, ai_ny, PRODUCTS["aer_ai"], f"New York UV aerosol index, {DATE_NY}")
plt.show()  # draw
print(f"{lon.size} clipped control points -> mean {np.nanmean(ai_ny):.3f}, "  # number of points and mean index
     f"max {np.nanmax(ai_ny):.3f} over the state")









7613 clipped control points -> mean 5.353, max 9.805 over the state




A six-pollutant snapshot of New York under smoke
The same combined layout as the A six-pollutant snapshot of Bangladesh section, with one difference: the Methane: a second data availability case study section found too few quality-passing methane pixels under this much smoke to fit a 1 km surface at all, so that panel reports the finding in text instead of drawing a fabricated map.


Code
# Six-panel New York figure. A product with too few points gets a text note instead of a map.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 9))
for ax, gas in zip(axes.ravel(), PRODUCTS):  # every product
    gx, gy, grid = ny_grids[gas]  # its grid
    if grid is None:  # not enough points to grid
        # ny_points[gas][0] is the longitude array, so its length is the surviving point count.
        n = ny_points[gas][0].size
        # explain in the panel
        ax.text(0.5, 0.5, f"{PRODUCTS[gas]['label']}\n\nonly {n} qa-passing points\nunder heavy smoke\n"
               "(< MIN_TPS_POINTS) --\nno 1 km surface fitted",
               ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, transform=ax.transAxes)
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
        for spine in ax.spines.values():  # keep the panel frame
            spine.set_visible(True)  # visible
    else:
        plot_grid(ax, gx, gy, grid, PRODUCTS[gas], PRODUCTS[gas]["label"])  # draw the grid
# overall title
plt.suptitle(f"New York State, {DATE_NY}: six pollutants at 1 km under Canadian wildfire smoke")
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

title: Sentinel-5P and Sentinel-5: Mapping Air Pollution from Orbit
section: Checking processing consistency across combined downloads
text:
Checking processing consistency across combined downloads
check_processing_consistency reads only global attributes, so it is cheap to run before trusting a result built from more than one file. Bangladesh needed only one file per product, trivially self-consistent; New York’s two adjacent regional segments per product are exactly the case worth checking – read_clip_points already concatenated them into one set of control points on the assumption that they share a processing baseline. Confirm that assumption here, after the fact, rather than take it on faith.


Code
# Confirm that the New York segments combined for each gas share one processing baseline.
# check_processing_consistency reads global attributes only, so it stays cheap even for a full orbit.

for gas, paths in SEGMENTS_NY.items():
    consistency = s5p.check_processing_consistency(paths)  # processor versions of the files
    # An empty flag means the files agree. Any other flag is a processor or pixel-size mismatch.
    bad = consistency[consistency["flag"] != ""]
    status = "OK" if bad.empty else f"{len(bad)} file(s) flagged"  # OK, or the number of flagged files
    # summary per product
    print(f"{gas:7s} {len(paths)} segment(s), processor {consistency['processor_version'].unique().tolist()}: {status}")
# Show the last gas (methane) in full: filename, processor version, pixel-size era, and flag.
consistency[["path", "processor_version", "pixel_size_era", "flag"]].assign(
    path=lambda d: d["path"].map(lambda p: Path(p).name))

title: Sentinel-5P and Sentinel-5: Mapping Air Pollution from Orbit
text:
Summary, exercises and references
Key ideas

Sentinel-5P’s TROPOMI measures NO2, SO2, CO, CH4, HCHO, ozone, aerosol and cloud from a single instrument, daily, at 5.5 by 3.5 km, with a swath wide enough to cover a whole country or state in one or two regional segments rather than a tile mosaic.
Always filter by qa_value. The right threshold differs by product and is written into the variable’s own metadata, not fixed across the mission.
Clip to the exact administrative boundary polygon, not just its bounding box, and average any duplicate geolocations where adjacent regional segments overlap, before fitting anything.
A thin plate spline, fitted in a projected (metres) CRS and evaluated on a regular 1 km grid, turns a sparse, irregular swath into a usable dense raster where simple cell averaging would leave most cells empty – at the cost of some overshoot near sparse edges, handled here with robust percentile colour limits rather than the raw data range.
Bangladesh’s six products, mapped on an ordinary dry season day, each tell a related but distinct story: NO2 and SO2 mark combustion point sources, CO carries a longer-lived regional background, CH4 reflects the delta’s agriculture more than any city, and aerosol index gives a clean single number for the dry season haze.
The same pipeline applied to New York under Canadian wildfire smoke shows CO, HCHO and especially aerosol index responding strongly to a transient plume that NO2 and SO2, both tied to local anthropogenic sources, do not track.
A genuine data availability limit, methane’s retrieval collapsing under heavy smoke, is a real scientific finding worth reporting plainly (the Methane: a second data availability case study section), not a bug to paper over with a misleading extrapolated map.
Check processing consistency across any files a single analysis combines, including two regional segments of the same overpass, not only a multi-date time series.

geolattice.rsense.atmosphere.sentinel_5p functions used: read_no2, read_so2, read_co, read_ch4, read_hcho, read_aerosol_index, qa_mask, molecules_per_cm2, dobson_units, co_mixing_ratio, check_processing_consistency.
Exercises

Repeat the Case study A: Bangladesh, dry season, 15 January 2025 section for a different single day in December 2024 or January 2025 and compare the NO2 and aerosol index means against 15 January 2025 – is this date typical of the dry season, or unusually clean or polluted?
New York’s state boundary clips tightly around a smoke plume that almost certainly extended well into neighbouring Vermont, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania. Download the same date for one neighbouring state (reusing AOI, download_segments and process_gas unchanged) and check whether the aerosol index gradient in the UV absorbing aerosol index section continues smoothly across the border.
tps_resample uses neighbors=25. Rerun the Nitrogen dioxide section with neighbors=10 and neighbors=60 and compare the resulting NO2 maps – what changes, and why does a local thin plate spline behave differently from a global one as neighbors grows?
Use read_so2 with layer_height="7km" on the New York SO2 files to check whether any residual SO2 signal in the Sulphur dioxide section is more consistent with a different plume height assumption than the default boundary-layer column.
Pick a second wildfire smoke date within a few days of 15 July 2026 (the Boundaries, regional segments and the clip-then-resample workflow section’s download_segments function works for any date) and build a small two-date CO and aerosol index comparison to see whether the plume was strengthening or weakening over New York.

Overview
With Sentinel-2A, 2B and 2C in orbit, any location is imaged every 2-5 days. This module works with a real two-and-a-half-year Sentinel-2 time series.

title: Sentinel-2: Red Edge, 10 m and Five-Day Revisits
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Know the MSI bands, resolutions and the L1C/L2A product levels (including the 2022 offset).
Turn an array time series into a georeferenced xarray cube with geolattice.rsense band names.
Mask clouds with s2cloudless probabilities and with the L2A Scene Classification Layer.
Use red-edge indices (NDRE, CIre, MTCI, IRECI, S2REP) and understand why they help.
Build per-class temporal profiles, smooth them and extract crop phenology.
Know when to use Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel (HLS) data.
Estimate LAI, FAPAR, FCOVER, canopy chlorophyll and canopy water content with the Copernicus BioPAR service, and read the season from the maps and profiles.

title: Sentinel-2: Red Edge, 10 m and Five-Day Revisits
text:
The Copernicus mission
Sentinel-2 belongs to the European Union’s Copernicus Programme, which began in 1998 as GMES (Global Monitoring for Environment and Security) and was renamed Copernicus in 2012. The programme aims to provide accurate, timely information for managing the environment, understanding and mitigating climate change, and supporting civil security. ESA defines and develops the space and ground segments. - Mission goal. The objectives include operational continuity with the SPOT and Landsat missions and data for services such as forest monitoring, land cover change detection, and disaster management. - Launch timeline - Sentinel-2A launched on 23 June 2015, Sentinel-2B on 7 March 2017, and Sentinel-2C on 5 September 2024, all on Vega rockets from French Guiana. - Sentinel-2C flew on the 22nd and final first-generation Vega rocket. - Sentinel-2C finished commissioning in late December 2024. It was cross-calibrated against Sentinel-2A in tandem, and it took over 2A’s operational role on 21 January 2025. Sentinel-2A was then moved to an in-orbit standby position. - Sentinel-2D is planned for launch in 2028. - A Sentinel-2 Next Generation mission is being designed for the 2030s.

title: Sentinel-2: Red Edge, 10 m and Five-Day Revisits
text:
Platforms

Constellation. Two satellites are operational at any time (currently 2B and 2C). They share one orbit, positioned 180° apart to optimise coverage and revisit time.
Spacecraft. The satellites use the AstroBus-L bus. Each has a launch mass of about 1,140 kg, 1,700 W of power, and a design life of 7 years. The nominal lifetime is about 7.25 years, with a possible 2-year extension.
Orbit. Sun-synchronous at about 786 km altitude, crossing the equator at 10:30 local time on the descending node.
Swath. 290 km.
Revisit time

About 10 days with one satellite.
About 5 days at the equator with two satellites.
About 2 to 3 days at mid-latitudes, where adjacent orbits overlap.

Coverage. Systematic global coverage of land surfaces from 56° S to 84° N, plus coastal waters.

title: Sentinel-2: Red Edge, 10 m and Five-Day Revisits
text:
The MultiSpectral Instrument

Each satellite carries one MSI, a passive optical push-broom sensor with 13 spectral channels spanning the visible/near-infrared (VNIR) and shortwave infrared (SWIR).
The MSI has two focal planes, one for VNIR and one for SWIR, with 12 staggered detector modules across the swath.
Radiometric resolution. 12-bit.
Spatial resolution. 10 m, 20 m, or 60 m, depending on the band.
Red-edge bands. Three red-edge bands (B5 to B7) are the MSI’s distinguishing feature compared with Landsat. They make it especially sensitive to chlorophyll content and vegetation stress.

Tiling. Products come as 100 × 100 km tiles on the MGRS grid (UTM/WGS84), with tile IDs such as T18TVN.
Format. SAFE folder structure with JPEG2000 band files. Cloud providers also host Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) versions.

Processing baseline 04.00 (January 2022). A radiometric offset was added. Convert digital numbers with: reflectance = (DN − 1000) / 10000. Mixing older and newer data without correcting for this causes artificial jumps in time series. Google Earth Engine’s “HARMONIZED” collections apply the correction for you.

title: Sentinel-2: Red Edge, 10 m and Five-Day Revisits
text:
Applications

Agriculture

Crop type mapping, phenology, and yield estimation
Nitrogen and water stress detection (red-edge bands)
Field boundary delineation

Forestry. Deforestation and degradation monitoring, forest health, biomass.
Land cover and land use. Change detection, urban expansion, impervious surfaces.
Water. Inland and coastal water quality (chlorophyll-a, turbidity), surface water extent, flood mapping.
Disasters. Burn area and severity, flood and landslide mapping, Copernicus Emergency Management Service.
Soil and geology. Digital soil mapping covariates, soil organic carbon proxies, mineral mapping.
Snow, ice, and glaciers. Snow cover and glacier extent.
Environment and health. Urban heat and greenness exposure, habitat and biodiversity mapping, methane plume detection (large point sources, using the SWIR bands).
Machine learning. Benchmark datasets such as EuroSAT, BigEarthNet, and SEN12MS, and foundation models such as Prithvi and SatMAE variants.

# code setup for Sentinel-2 analysis 

from pathlib import Path

# The notebook's data folder: ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical/ next to this notebook, found from here or from the repository root.
DATA = next((p for p in (Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"))
             if p.is_dir()), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"))
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create the data folder if needed

# Base URL for downloading OpenGeo datasets (such as raster/land cover layers)
GH = "https://github.com/opengeos/datasets/releases/download"

# Define the path to a shapefile with New York counties.
# Tompkins County (Ithaca's county) is extracted as a GeoDataFrame for spatial reference.
COUNTIES = Path("../../../../Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/NY_County_GCS.shp")
tompkins = gpd.read_file(COUNTIES)  # all New York counties
tompkins = tompkins.loc[tompkins["COUNTY"] == "Tompkins County"].copy()  # keep Tompkins County
print("Tompkins County bounds:", tuple(round(v, 3) for v in tompkins.total_bounds))  # its bounds

# URL for the 2021 US National Land Cover Database (NLCD) at 90 m resolution.
NLCD_URL = f"{GH}/raster/nlcd_2021_land_cover_90m.tif"

# Mapping from NLCD class codes to human-readable labels and colors (for display/visualization).
NLCD_CLASSES = {
    11: ("Open water", "#466b9f"), 21: ("Developed, open", "#dec5c5"),
    22: ("Developed, low", "#d99282"), 23: ("Developed, medium", "#eb0000"),
    24: ("Developed, high", "#ab0000"), 31: ("Barren", "#b3ac9f"),
    41: ("Deciduous forest", "#68ab5f"), 42: ("Evergreen forest", "#1c5f2c"),
    43: ("Mixed forest", "#b5c58f"), 52: ("Shrub/scrub", "#ccb879"),
    71: ("Grassland", "#dfdfc2"), 81: ("Pasture/hay", "#dcd939"),
    82: ("Cultivated crops", "#ab6c28"), 90: ("Woody wetlands", "#b8d9eb"),
    95: ("Herbaceous wetlands", "#6c9fb8")
}

def nlcd_for(template, name="nlcd_tompkins"):  # NLCD land cover on the grid of another raster
    """
    Given a template raster (usually with a spatial grid you want to match),
    this function loads the NLCD 2021 land cover data for that area, aligns it to the template's grid,
    and saves a local copy as needed for faster future access.
    
    - Downloads NLCD for the required window if not already cached.
    - Uses rasterio and rioxarray for efficient clipping and reprojection.
    - Writes the (clipped) result to disk and loads the data (as int16, with 0 as nodata).
    - Final output matches the spatial grid and projection of 'template'.
    """
    cache = DATA / f"{name}.tif"  # cached local window
    if not cache.exists():  # read the remote file only if no cache exists
        import rasterio, rioxarray  # raster readers
        from rasterio.warp import transform_bounds  # reproject a bounding box
        # Set up a rasterio environment variable needed for GDAL over URLs
        with rasterio.Env(GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN="EMPTY_DIR"):
            # Open the NLCD raster file for remote access
            src = rioxarray.open_rasterio("/vsicurl/" + NLCD_URL)
            # Calculate the bounding box of the template in NLCD's CRS
            b = transform_bounds(template.rio.crs, src.rio.crs, *template.rio.bounds())
            # Extract the required window and load it into memory
            win = src.rio.clip_box(*b).squeeze("band", drop=True).load()
        # Save the temporary, clipped tile locally for later reuse
        rs.write(win, cache, cog=False)
    # Load the cached data, squeeze singleton bands, and set 0 as nodata
    win = rs.read(cache, masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.write_nodata(0)
    # Reproject the land cover raster to match the template's grid and nodata
    out = win.rio.reproject_match(template, resampling=Resampling.nearest, nodata=0)
    # Ensure proper integer type and nodata is set for further use
    return out.astype("int16").rio.write_nodata(0)


def local_scenes(folder, files=()):
    """Scene folders already downloaded under `folder` that contain every file in `files`."""
    folder = Path(folder)
    if not folder.is_dir():  # nothing downloaded yet
        return []
    return sorted(p for p in folder.iterdir() if p.is_dir() and all((p / f).exists() for f in files))

Product levels

L1C: top-of-atmosphere reflectance, orthorectified, 100 × 100 km tiles (MGRS grid).
L2A: bottom-of-atmosphere (surface) reflectance from Sen2Cor, plus the Scene Classification Layer (SCL), aerosol and water-vapour maps.

Both store reflectance × 10,000. Since processing baseline 04.00 (25 January 2022) a BOA_ADD_OFFSET of −1000 is added, so reflectance = (DN − 1000) / 10,000 for newer scenes. Forgetting this makes every post-2022 scene look 10 % brighter. rs.optical.scale handles it automatically from the acquisition date:


Code
# Example: demonstrate how Sentinel-2's processing baseline affects reflectance scaling
# Two observation dates are given: one before and one after the processing baseline change.
# "demo" is a small xarray.Dataset with a single band ("B04": red) and two reflectance values.
# We use rs.optical.scale() to convert digital numbers (with offset/scale) to reflectance for each date.
# The effect is shown using print, so users see the scaled reflectance for both baselines:
t = pd.to_datetime(["2021-08-01", "2023-08-01"])  # Before and after baseline 04.00 (Jan 2022)
demo = xr.Dataset(  # the same DN under two processing baselines
    {"B04": (("time", "x"), np.array([[1800], [2800]], dtype="uint16"))},
    coords={"time": t}
)
print("Same surface, two processing baselines:")  # heading
# Scale reflectance appropriately for each date; print B04 (red) reflectance, rounded to 3 decimals
reflectance = rs.optical.scale(demo, sensor="sentinel2")["B04"].to_series().round(3)
print(reflectance)  # reflectance after removing the right offset

text:
Loading Sentinel-2 L2A from the cloud
rs.optical.load_sentinel2 searches Planetary Computer (or Earth Search), loads bands lazily at 10 m, applies the scale factor and offset, masks clouds with SCL, and renames bands to canonical names. It needs internet access and the optional odc-stac package. The download section below uses the other route, geolattice.rsense.get_images, to download real GeoTIFFs for Tompkins County that the rest of this notebook analyses.


Code
# This code demonstrates how to lazily load Sentinel-2 data from the cloud using rs.optical.load_sentinel2,

# includes several bands of interest, automatically applies scaling/offset corrections,

section: Building a Sentinel-2 cube from files
text:
Building a Sentinel-2 cube from files
geolattice.rsense.get_images searches a STAC catalogue and downloads just the bands we need as AOI-clipped GeoTIFFs. Tompkins County straddles two Sentinel-2 MGRS tiles (18TUN and 18TUM), so each date needs mosaicking; the red-edge, narrow-NIR and SWIR bands are native 20 m and need resampling onto the 10 m grid before they can share a Dataset with the 10 m bands.

Downloading and Preparing Sentinel-2 Files for a Data Cube


Code
# Define the dates we want to use for our Sentinel-2 image time series.
TARGET_DATES = [
    "2025-01-27", "2025-03-18", "2025-03-27", "2025-04-17", "2025-05-12", "2025-05-26",
    "2025-06-03", "2025-07-06", "2025-07-23", "2025-08-02", "2025-08-22", "2025-09-03",
    "2025-09-11", "2025-10-01", "2025-10-16", "2025-11-20"
]

# Specify the list of desired Sentinel-2 bands, including the Scene Classification Layer (scl).
S2_BANDS = [
    "blue", "green", "red", "rededge1", "rededge2", "rededge3",
    "nir", "nir08", "swir16", "scl"
]

# Set output directory for storing image files.
S2_OUT = DATA / "s2_tompkins_2025"

if local_scenes(S2_OUT, [f"{b}.tif" for b in S2_BANDS] + ["item.json"]):  # downloaded before
    print("Reading the Sentinel-2 scenes already downloaded under", S2_OUT)  # use the local drive
elif ONLINE:  # not on disk yet: download when online
    # Search for Sentinel-2 L2A images using a STAC API for Tompkins AOI.
    # Criteria: images from 2025, up to 40% cloud cover, and maximum 250 hits.
    found = search_images(
        aoi=tompkins,
        dates=("2025-01-01", "2025-12-31"),
        source="planetary",
        collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
        cloud=40,
        limit=250,
        quiet=True
    )

    # Sentinel-2 data is organized by MGRS tiles. To build a cube, we want one image
    # per (date, tile) combination. If there's more than one per combo (e.g., due to reprocessing),
    # keep only the one with the "largest" (most recent) id.
    latest = {}  # key=(date, tile) -> id of latest processing
    for item in found.items:  # every found item
        d = item.datetime.date().isoformat()  # its date
        if d not in TARGET_DATES:  # skip dates that are not wanted
            continue  # Skip images outside our target dates
        key = (d, item.properties.get("s2:mgrs_tile"))  # (date, tile)
        # Only keep one per date/tile; pick newer (larger id) if multiple exist
        if key not in latest or item.id > latest[key]:
            latest[key] = item.id  # the newest processing run for this date and tile

    # Now, extract just the unique latest scene ids we need to download for our dates/tiles.
    ids = sorted(latest.values())

    # Download the images (clipped to AOI, for selected bands) into our output folder.
    # Only the needed scenes are fetched, and bands are organized by date/tile.
    saved = get_images(
        S2_OUT, search=found, ids=ids, bands=S2_BANDS,
        mode="clip", quiet=True
    )

    # Print a summary of what was downloaded:
    # Number of successful image downloads, how many dates covered, number of failures, and which tiles were involved.
    print(
        f"{len(saved.scenes)} scenes downloaded across {len(TARGET_DATES)} target dates "
        f"({len(saved.failures)} failures), tiles {sorted({k[1] for k in latest})}"
    )
else:
    # If we are offline, we can't download new Sentinel-2 data,
    # so just report reusing whatever is already in our expected output folder.
    print("Offline: reusing the scenes already downloaded under", S2_OUT)

Reading, Grouping, and Mosaicking Sentinel-2 Bands into a Data Cube


Code
# Construct 3 lists of bands for Sentinel-2:
BANDS_10M = ["blue", "green", "red", "nir"]  # Bands available at 10 meter resolution
BANDS_20M = ["rededge1", "rededge2", "rededge3", "nir08", "swir16"]  # Bands at 20 meter resolution
ALL_BANDS = BANDS_10M + BANDS_20M  # All bands together

# Group all downloaded Sentinel-2 scenes by date.
by_date = defaultdict(list)
for scene_dir in sorted(p for p in S2_OUT.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):  # every downloaded scene folder
    item = json.loads((scene_dir / "item.json").read_text())  # its metadata
    # Grouping by only the date part (YYYY-MM-DD) of the scene timestamp
    by_date[item["properties"]["datetime"][:10]].append(scene_dir)

# Will store reprojected AOI and cube variables:
tompkins_utm = None
cube_vars = {b: [] for b in ALL_BANDS}  # Holds arrays for each band across dates
scl_list, times = [], []  # Store scene classification (SCL) arrays and date list

# For each date, process all covering tiles:
for d in sorted(by_date):
    tile_arrays = {b: [] for b in ALL_BANDS}  # Holds arrays for each band for each tile
    tile_scl = []  # Holds SCL rasters for all tiles for the date
    for td in by_date[d]:  # every tile of this date
        # Read the red band at 10 m: this will set the reference grid
        red10 = rs.read(td / "red.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)
        # Once, project the AOI to the same CRS as the images
        if tompkins_utm is None:
            tompkins_utm = tompkins.to_crs(red10.rio.crs)  # the county in the image CRS (done once)
        # Read all 10m bands directly
        for b in BANDS_10M:
            # 10 m bands are read as they are
            tile_arrays[b].append(rs.read(td / f"{b}.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True))
        # Read all 20m bands and resample them to match 10m resolution
        for b in BANDS_20M:
            arr = rs.read(td / f"{b}.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)  # a 20 m band
            # resampled onto the 10 m grid (bilinear)
            tile_arrays[b].append(arr.rio.reproject_match(red10, resampling=Resampling.bilinear))
        # Read SCL (scene classification: cloud, shadow, etc.) and resample via nearest neighbor (since it's categorical)
        scl = rs.read(td / "scl.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)
        tile_scl.append(scl.rio.reproject_match(red10, resampling=Resampling.nearest))  # categorical

    # Mosaic the reprojected bands across all tiles for the given date, then clip to AOI
    clipped = {b: rs.clip(rs.mosaic(tile_arrays[b]), tompkins_utm) for b in ALL_BANDS}
    for b in ALL_BANDS:  # every band
        cube_vars[b].append(clipped[b])  # Add this date's mosaic to the dataset
    # Do the same for scene classification layer
    scl_list.append(rs.clip(rs.mosaic(tile_scl), tompkins_utm))
    # Keep track of the timestamp corresponding to this date
    times.append(pd.Timestamp(d))

# Build a time index using all collected dates
time_idx = pd.DatetimeIndex(times).rename("time")
# Assemble the final xarray Dataset with dimensions: (time, y, x, bands)
s2 = xr.Dataset({b: xr.concat(cube_vars[b], dim=time_idx, join="outer") for b in ALL_BANDS})
# Add the scene classification ("scl") as a variable, handling slight shape differences (some tiles may be missing)
s2["scl"] = xr.concat(scl_list, dim=time_idx, join="outer")
# Write CRS spatial reference (derived from the first red band)
s2 = s2.rio.write_crs(cube_vars["red"][0].rio.crs)
# Annotate dataset with sensor name
s2.attrs["pyrsense:sensor"] = "sentinel2"
# Print a summary with identified sensor and band mapping info
print("Sensor detected:", rs.optical.guess_sensor(s2), "| red band ->",
      rs.optical.bands.resolve_band_name(s2, "red"), "| red-edge 1 ->",
      rs.optical.bands.resolve_band_name(s2, "rededge1"))
# Display xarray summary
s2

Map the clearest summer scene beside NLCD land cover


Code
# Map the clearest summer scene beside NLCD land cover, and count pixels by class.

# 1. Get the land cover classification (NLCD) raster for the AOI, using the first (earliest) available image in the time series
nlcd = nlcd_for(s2["red"].isel(time=0))

# 2. Flatten the NLCD array, map each pixel value to its class name using NLCD_CLASSES,
#    and count the number of pixels per class (for summary table)
counts = pd.Series(nlcd.values.ravel()) \
            .map(lambda c: NLCD_CLASSES.get(c, ("No data",))[0]) \
            .value_counts()

# 3. Find which dates are in summer (June, July, August)
is_summer = s2["time"].dt.month.isin([6, 7, 8]).values

# 4. For each date, compute the fraction of clear (usable) pixels based on the scene classification (SCL) layer
clear_frac = rs.optical.s2_scl_mask(s2["scl"]).mean(("y", "x")).values

# 5. Select the clearest summer date index (with maximum clear pixel fraction)
#    (If no summer images are clear, uses -1 as a placeholder)
summer = int(np.argmax(np.where(is_summer, clear_frac, -1)))      

# 6. Plot two side-by-side maps:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))

#    a. True color RGB of Sentinel-2 for the clearest summer date
rs.viz.plot_rgb(
    s2.isel(time=summer),
    ["red", "green", "blue"],
    ax=axes[0],
    title=f"True colour, {pd.Timestamp(s2.time.values[summer]):%d %b %Y}",
    p=(1, 99)
)

#    b. Land cover map from NLCD, showing classes present in this AOI
rs.viz.plot_raster(
    nlcd.where(nlcd > 0),  # mask out "no data"
    ax=axes[1],
    categorical={k: v for k, v in NLCD_CLASSES.items() if k in np.unique(nlcd.values)},
    title="NLCD 2021 land cover"
)

# 7. Remove x/y axis ticks for clarity
for a in axes: 
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks

# 8. Adjust layout and display plots
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()  # draw

# 9. Return/display a table summarizing the pixel counts per NLCD class
counts.to_frame("pixels").T

title: Sentinel-2: Red Edge, 10 m and Five-Day Revisits
section: Spectral signatures of the land-cover classes
text:
Spectral signatures of the land-cover classes
Plotting mean reflectance by class across the 9 downloaded bands (on the clearest summer date) shows the features each band captures: the chlorophyll absorption at 665 nm, the steep red edge between 705 and 783 nm, the NIR plateau and the SWIR water absorption.


Code
# This section plots the mean spectral reflectance for each major land cover class across all bands
# for the clearest summer date in the Sentinel-2 image collection. This visualizes the "spectral signatures" 
# of land cover types by showing how they reflect different wavelengths of light.

# Define the central wavelength in nanometers for each band to use as the x-axis
CENTER_NM = {
    "blue": 490, "green": 560, "red": 665,
    "rededge1": 705, "rededge2": 740, "rededge3": 783,
    "nir": 842, "nir08": 865, "swir16": 1610
}

# Scale the raw image data to surface reflectance, select the clearest summer date.
try:
    # reflectance of the chosen summer date
    refl_raw = rs.optical.scale(s2[ALL_BANDS], sensor="sentinel2").isel(time=summer)
except Exception as e:
    raise RuntimeError(f"Error scaling reflectance data: {e}")  # stop with a clear message

# Get the wavelengths (x-axis) corresponding to the bands
wl = np.array([CENTER_NM[b] for b in ALL_BANDS])

# Create a figure for plotting
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))

# For each NLCD class...
for code, (name, color) in NLCD_CLASSES.items():
    # Check that the nlcd raster has "values" attribute
    if not hasattr(nlcd, 'values'):
        raise AttributeError("Expected attribute 'values' in 'nlcd'.")  # stop with a clear message
    # Create a mask for pixels that match this class code
    m = (nlcd.values == code)
    n_pixels = m.sum()  # Count matching pixels
    if n_pixels < 5000:  # too few pixels of this class
        continue  # Skip small classes
    spec = []  # mean reflectance per band
    # For each band, compute the mean reflectance value for this class
    for b in ALL_BANDS:
        band_values = refl_raw[b].values[m]  # values of this band in this class
        # Remove NaN values to avoid warnings or empty means
        band_values = band_values[~np.isnan(band_values)]
        if band_values.size == 0:  # no valid values
            spec.append(np.nan)  # store NaN
        else:
            spec.append(float(band_values.mean()))  # store the mean
    # Plot the spectral signature for this class
    ax.plot(
        wl, spec, marker="o", color=color, 
        label=f"{name} ({int(n_pixels)} px)", lw=2
    )

# Highlight the red-edge region on the spectrum
ax.axvspan(700, 790, color="red", alpha=0.08, label="red-edge region")

# Set axis labels and plot title
ax.set(
    xlabel="Wavelength (nm)",
    ylabel="Surface reflectance",
    title=f"Mean spectra, {pd.Timestamp(s2.time.values[summer]):%d %b %Y}"
)

# Show a legend and display the plot
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

title: Sentinel-2: Red Edge, 10 m and Five-Day Revisits
text:
Red-edge indices
Chlorophyll pigments in plant leaves absorb red light very efficiently, which means the amount of reflected red light becomes very low once a canopy is dense. This causes the classic NDVI index (which uses red and near-infrared bands) to ‘saturate’: above a certain leaf density, increases in chlorophyll or biomass no longer result in higher NDVI values, limiting its usefulness for monitoring differences among dense canopies.
Sentinel-2, however, includes several intermediate ‘red-edge’ bands positioned between the red and NIR regions of the spectrum. These red-edge bands lie on the steep transitional slope between strong red absorption (due to chlorophyll) and high NIR reflectance (from leaf structure). The precise position and slope of this ‘red-edge’ feature are sensitive to changes in chlorophyll content and canopy nitrogen, even after NDVI has already saturated. Therefore, indices that use red-edge bands continue to capture meaningful variation in vegetation condition where NDVI no longer does.
Sentinel-2’s unique band configuration thus enables a number of red-edge-based vegetation indices, making it possible to monitor plant health, chlorophyll, and nitrogen status in much greater detail in dense vegetation areas such as forests or advanced crop stages.

text:
Temporal profiles and phenology
Averaging masked NDVI and NDRE per land-cover class through time reveals each class’s seasonal rhythm. With only 16 real acquisitions across the year the series is far sparser than eo-learn’s 68-date Slovenia patch, so no regridding to a dense regular calendar is attempted; Whittaker smoothing and the phenology metrics run directly on the actual, irregular acquisition dates.


Code
# This block generates time series plots of mean NDVI and NDRE values for each land cover class with sufficient area.
# 1. Create a figure with two subplots (for NDVI and NDRE), stacked vertically and sharing the x-axis (time).
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 7), sharex=True)

# 2. Loop through each NLCD (land cover) class. Each class has a code, a readable name, and a color for plotting.
for code, (name, color) in NLCD_CLASSES.items():
    # Create a mask (boolean array) where the land cover map 'nlcd' matches the current class code.
    m = (nlcd == code)
    # If there are fewer than 5000 pixels of this class, skip it (to only plot major classes).
    if int(m.sum()) < 5000:
        continue
    # For the two indices (NDVI and NDRE), loop through subplots and calculate the class mean time series.
    for ax, idx in zip(axes, ["NDVI", "NDRE"]):
        # Calculate the mean value of the index at each timepoint, using only pixels of this class.
        prof = vi[idx].where(m).mean(("y", "x"))
        # Identify timepoints where at least 50% of the class area has valid data (not cloud/shadow).
        ok = vi[idx].where(m).count(("y", "x")) > 0.5 * int(m.sum())
        # Plot the mean time series for this class at the OK timepoints.
        ax.plot(pd.to_datetime(s2.time.values)[ok.values], prof.values[ok.values], "o-", ms=4,
                color=color, label=name)
# 3. Label y-axes and add gridlines for readability.
for ax, idx in zip(axes, ["NDVI", "NDRE"]):
    ax.set_ylabel(idx)  # y label
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)  # grid
# 4. Add a legend and title to the first axis. Tighten the layout and display the figure.
axes[0].legend(ncol=4, fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title("Class mean profiles (dates with > 50 % of the class clear)")  # title of the top panel
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw










Phenology mapping and metrics by land cover


Code
# This block estimates phenology metrics (seasonal vegetation timing) for a spatial window centered on the AOI, then summarizes results by land cover class.

# 1. Choose a smaller spatial window (4 km × 4 km, at 10 m resolution) for demonstration and faster processing:
ndvi = vi["NDVI"]
ny, nx = ndvi.sizes["y"], ndvi.sizes["x"]     # Get the full image dimensions.
cy, cx = ny // 2, nx // 2                     # Compute the center pixel coordinates.
window = dict(  # a zoom window
    y=slice(cy - 200, cy + 200),              # Select 400×400 pixels (roughly 4 km × 4 km) around center.
    x=slice(cx - 200, cx + 200)
)
ndvi_win = ndvi.isel(**window).load()         # Subset and load NDVI data for the window.
nlcd_win = nlcd.isel(**window)                # Subset land cover map to same window.

# 2. Smooth temporal NDVI curves at each pixel using Whittaker smoothing:
smooth = rs.timeseries.whittaker(ndvi_win, lmbda=5)

# 3. Extract phenology metrics from each pixel’s smoothed NDVI time series:
#    - 'sos' = start of season (green-up DOY)
#    - 'pos' = peak-of-season DOY
#    - 'eos' = end of season DOY
#    - 'amplitude' = difference between peak and base NDVI
pheno = rs.timeseries.phenology(
    smooth,
    threshold=0.4,         # For determining green-up/down
    min_amplitude=0.1      # Ignore pixels with very little seasonal change
)

# 4. Plot spatial maps of selected phenology metrics for the window:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
for ax, k, cm in zip(  # the panels: layer, title and colour map
    axes,
    ["sos", "pos", "amplitude"],                    # Show start, peak, and amplitude
    ["viridis", "plasma", "YlGn"]
):
    rs.viz.plot_raster(  # map the layer
        pheno[k], ax=ax, cmap=cm,
        title={
            "sos": "Start of season (DOY)",
            "pos": "Peak (DOY)",
            "amplitude": "NDVI amplitude"
        }[k]
    )
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

# 5. Summarize the median phenology metrics by land cover class (in the window).
#    Groups all pixels by their class, then aggregates median sos/pos/eos/amplitude per class.
pd.DataFrame({
    k: pd.Series(pheno[k].values.ravel()).groupby(
        pd.Series(nlcd_win.values.ravel()).map(
            lambda c: NLCD_CLASSES.get(c, ("other",))[0]   # Get readable class name or "other"
        )
    ).median()
    for k in ["sos", "pos", "eos", "amplitude"]
}).round(1)

text:
Monthly composites
rs.RasterCube wraps the cube for period selection and temporal resampling. With only one or two clear dates per month in the real 2025 series, a monthly “composite” is mostly a single clear scene rather than a multi-observation median, and February has no acquisition in our 16-date set at all. Computed on the same 4 km x 4 km window as the Temporal profiles and phenology section to keep the resample fast.


Code
# --- Monthly Composites Processing and Visualization ---

# 1. Select the six main bands of interest and extract them from the cleaned Sentinel-2 dataset
#    (within the region/window defined by 'window'). Load the data for use.
win_ds = clean[["blue", "green", "red", "rededge1", "nir", "swir16"]].isel(**window).load()

# 2. Wrap the windowed dataset in a RasterCube, specifying that the sensor is Sentinel-2.
cube = rs.RasterCube(win_ds, sensor="sentinel2")

# 3. Select the data covering the 2025 calendar year, and resample using a monthly window
#    ("1MS" = Month Start frequency), computing the median for each month.
monthly = cube.sel_period("2025-01-01", "2025-12-31").resample("1MS", "median")

# 4. Set up a grid of subplots to display one image for each month (2 rows x 6 columns).
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(16, 5.5))

# 5. For each available median monthly composite in the year, plot an RGB image using
#    "nir", "red", and "green" bands (false color composite to highlight vegetation).
#    The percentile scaling (p=(1, 99)) is used to stretch contrast.
for ax, (t, img) in zip(axes.ravel(), monthly.ds.groupby("time")):
    rs.viz.plot_rgb(  # the composite
        img.squeeze("time"),
        ["nir", "red", "green"],
        ax=ax,
        title=f"{pd.Timestamp(t):%b}", # Month abbreviation
        per_band=False,
        p=(1, 99)
    )
    ax.set_xticks([])  # no x ticks
    ax.set_yticks([])  # no y ticks

# 6. If there are fewer than 12 months with data, any remaining empty axes are hidden.
for ax in axes.ravel()[monthly.ds.sizes["time"]:]:
    ax.axis("off")  # hide unused panels

# 7. Set a title, adjust layout, and display the figure.
plt.suptitle("2025 monthly median composites (colour infrared), 4 km window")
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

# 8. Print the summary of the monthly composites RasterCube.
print(monthly)

# 9. Print a list of months in which there was no clear (cloud-free) Sentinel-2 observation.
print(
    "Months with no clear observation:",
    [f"{pd.Timestamp(t):%b}" for t, v in zip(monthly.times, monthly.valid_fraction().values) if v == 0]
)
