title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
text:
What makes an image “optical”
An optical sensor records electromagnetic energy with lenses or mirrors and detectors, in the part of the spectrum where the Sun provides the illumination:








Region
Wavelength
What the sensor records




Visible (VIS)
0.40-0.70 µm
Reflected sunlight; what our eyes see


Near infrared (NIR)
0.70-1.3 µm
Reflected sunlight; strongly reflected by leaves


Shortwave infrared (SWIR)
1.3-2.5 µm
Reflected sunlight; sensitive to water in leaves and soils, and to minerals


Thermal infrared (TIR)
8-14 µm
Energy emitted by the surface (usually treated separately as thermal remote sensing)



Optical remote sensing is passive: the sensor only listens. Two consequences follow. Images exist only in daylight (except thermal and night-light sensors), and clouds block the view, because cloud droplets scatter visible and infrared light strongly. Radar (chapter 07_03) is the active, cloud-penetrating complement.
What an optical sensor measures in each band is the radiance reaching it. After calibration and atmospheric correction this becomes the surface reflectance, the fraction of sunlight the surface reflects, and the shape of reflectance across bands (the spectral signature) identifies materials (notebook 07_01_00, the How optical sensors form an image and Commercial optical data sections).

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
section: How optical sensors form an image
text:
How optical sensors form an image

The imaging chain
Light from the ground passes through a telescope (mirrors or lenses), is split into wavelength bands by filters, prisms or gratings, and falls on detectors that convert photons into electrons. The electronics amplify and digitize the signal into digital numbers (DN). Detector materials depend on the wavelength:

Silicon (CCD or CMOS) for visible and NIR light, up to about 1 µm.
InGaAs or HgCdTe for SWIR.
HgCdTe or microbolometers for thermal infrared.



Scanning geometries








Design
How the image is built
Examples




Whiskbroom (across-track scanner)
A rotating mirror sweeps a few detectors from side to side while the satellite moves forward
Landsat 1-7 (MSS, TM, ETM+), MODIS, AVHRR


Pushbroom (along-track scanner)
A long line of thousands of detectors images a whole row at once; the orbit motion adds rows
Landsat 8/9 OLI, Sentinel-2 MSI, SPOT, Pléiades, WorldView


Frame camera (area array)
A 2-D detector takes a snapshot of a rectangle, like a phone camera
PlanetScope, SkySat, most UAV cameras



Pushbroom sensors have no moving parts and dwell longer on each ground point, so they give a higher signal-to-noise ratio than whiskbrooms. Very-high-resolution satellites add time delay integration (TDI), summing the signal of successive detector rows as the image moves across them, to collect enough light for pixels under a metre.


Panchromatic, multispectral and hyperspectral








Type
Bands
Typical use




Panchromatic
One broad band (about 0.45-0.80 µm)
The sharpest detail; combined with multispectral bands by pan-sharpening


Multispectral
4-15 broad bands
Land cover, vegetation, water: most operational mapping


Superspectral
15-40 narrower bands
MODIS, Sentinel-3 OLCI: ocean colour, atmosphere


Hyperspectral
100-400 contiguous narrow bands
Minerals, pigments, water quality, crop traits (EnMAP, PRISMA, EMIT)



Each band is defined by its spectral response function, the sensitivity of the detector at each wavelength. Two sensors with “red” bands of different widths and centres record different values over the same surface, which is why data from different sensors must be harmonized before they are combined (for example the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 product).

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
section: Image quality: resolution, geometry and radiometry
text:
Image quality: resolution, geometry and radiometry

Ground sampling distance and swath
The ground sampling distance (GSD) is the distance between pixel centres on the ground. For a detector of pitch \(p\), a telescope of focal length \(f\) and an orbit altitude \(H\), looking straight down (nadir),
\[\text{GSD} = \frac{p\,H}{f} = H \cdot \text{IFOV},\]
where IFOV is the instantaneous field of view of one detector (in radians). The swath is the width imaged on the ground, roughly GSD × number of detectors across track. With a fixed number of detectors, a finer GSD means a narrower swath, and a narrower swath means a longer time before the satellite passes over the same place again.
Viewing angle. Commercial satellites point their telescope off nadir to image a target sooner. At an off-nadir angle θ the across-track GSD grows roughly as \(\text{GSD}_0/\cos^2\theta\) and the along-track GSD as \(\text{GSD}_0/\cos\theta\), and tall objects lean (relief displacement). “0.3 m” imagery is 0.3 m only near nadir.
GSD is not resolution. Optical blur, detector size, satellite motion and atmospheric scattering spread each point over neighbouring pixels. The modulation transfer function (MTF) measures how much contrast survives at each spatial frequency. As a rule of thumb, an object must span two to three pixels to be reliably identified.


Radiometric quality

Quantization (radiometric resolution): Landsat 8 records 12 bits (4,096 levels), Landsat 9 and many commercial sensors 11-14 bits.
Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR): how far the signal stands above detector and electronic noise. It is critical over dark targets such as water, where most of the signal is atmosphere.
Calibration: on-board lamps, solar diffusers, lunar views and ground “pseudo-invariant” desert sites keep DNs traceable to radiance over a mission’s lifetime.



Orbits and revisit
Most land-imaging satellites fly sun-synchronous polar orbits at 450-800 km, crossing the equator at the same local solar time on every pass (about 10:00-10:30 for Landsat and Sentinel-2), so illumination is comparable between dates. The repeat cycle is the time to return to exactly the same orbit track (16 days for one Landsat); the revisit time is how often a place can be imaged at all, which pointing and constellations shorten (daily or better for PlanetScope and the WorldView fleet). Geostationary weather satellites (GOES, Himawari, Meteosat) stare at one hemisphere every 5-15 minutes, at 0.5-2 km pixels.
The chart below places common optical sensors on the two axes that define most choices. Values are approximate nadir figures for the main multispectral product.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# This cell prepares the notebook. Every later code cell reads images, builds
# tables or draws plots, so the libraries are imported once, here.
#
# 1. Show matplotlib figures inside the notebook, and hide warnings that are
#    not errors.
# 2. Import NumPy (arrays), pandas (tables), xarray (labelled rasters),
#    GeoPandas (the class-point shapefile), rasterio (windowed GeoTIFF reads)
#    and matplotlib.
# 3. Import `geolattice` and `geolattice.rsense` as `rs`. `rs` is the remote-sensing
#    toolbox used below: `rs.read`, `rs.viz`, `rs.optical`, `rs.classify`.
# 4. Silence harmless GDAL messages about unusual TIFF tags, set a slightly
#    sharper plot style, and print the package versions and the compute
#    backend (`cpu` or a GPU name).

%matplotlib inline
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide library notices; real errors still print

import os  # environment variables
import time                       # used later to time the live Sentinel-2 / Landsat download
from pathlib import Path          # file paths that work on any operating system

import numpy as np                # numeric arrays: pixel blocks, percentiles, masks
import pandas as pd               # small tables: sensors, bands, class signatures
import xarray as xr               # multi-band images with coordinates
import geopandas as gpd           # read the land-cover point labels (a shapefile)
import rasterio                   # open GeoTIFFs and read a downsampled preview
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.rsense as rs         # optical helpers used in every hands-on section

# Commercial TIFFs often carry non-standard tags. GDAL prints a notice for each
# one. Sending that log to /dev/null keeps the notebook output to the numbers
# we actually print. This does not change the pixel values.
rasterio.Env(CPL_LOG="/dev/null").__enter__()
# figure resolution and a light grid
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3})
# versions and backend
print("geolattice", geolattice.__version__, "| geolattice.rsense", rs.__version__, "| backend:", rs.get_backend())

# This cell compares optical sensors by pixel size and revisit. That trade-off
# is the point of the section above: a finer pixel usually means a narrower
# swath, so the satellite takes longer to see the same place again. Many small
# satellites (a constellation) are how commercial missions break that trade-off.
#
# 1. Build a table with one row per mission:
#    - sensor name
#    - multispectral ground sampling distance (GSD) in metres, at nadir
#    - typical revisit in days
#    - whether the archive is open or commercial
# 2. Scatter pixel size (x) against revisit (y). Both axes are logarithmic, so
#    1 m, 10 m and 100 m are evenly spaced and the coarse daily sensors and the
#    fine sensors fit on one figure.
# 3. Open missions are green circles; commercial missions are red squares.
# 4. A few names would land on top of each other, so `offsets` nudges those labels.

sensors = pd.DataFrame([
    # name, multispectral GSD (m), revisit (days), access
    # Coarse, near-daily, open: whole-Earth monitoring.
    ("MODIS (Terra/Aqua)", 250, 1, "open"), ("VIIRS", 375, 1, "open"), ("Sentinel-3 OLCI", 300, 1.5, "open"),
    # Medium resolution, open: the workhorses for land cover and change.
    ("Landsat 8/9", 30, 8, "open"), ("Sentinel-2A/B/C", 10, 5, "open"), ("HLS (Landsat + Sentinel-2)", 30, 2.5, "open"),
    ("CBERS-4 MUX", 20, 26, "open"), ("NAIP (US aerial)", 0.6, 730, "open"),
    # Fine pixels and a short revisit, sold rather than given away.
    ("PlanetScope", 3, 1, "commercial"), ("SkySat", 0.5, 1, "commercial"), ("SPOT 6/7", 6, 1, "commercial"),
    ("Pléiades 1A/1B", 2, 1, "commercial"), ("Pléiades Neo", 1.2, 1, "commercial"),
    ("WorldView-3", 1.24, 1, "commercial"), ("GeoEye-1", 1.65, 2, "commercial"),
], columns=["sensor", "gsd_m", "revisit_days", "access"])

# Nudge only the names that would collide. The pair is an offset in points
# (positive x is right, positive y is up). Names not listed get a small default.
offsets = {"SkySat": (-10, 10), "WorldView-3": (-30, 22), "Pléiades Neo": (-4, -16), "Pléiades 1A/1B": (14, 20), "GeoEye-1": (-62, 8),
           "PlanetScope": (2, -16), "SPOT 6/7": (2, 10), "MODIS (Terra/Aqua)": (-40, -16), "VIIRS": (4, 8)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.8))  # one panel
# Plot the two access classes separately so each gets its own colour, marker and legend entry.
for acc, mk, col in [("open", "o", "#1b7837"), ("commercial", "s", "#b2182b")]:
    s = sensors[sensors.access == acc]  # sensors of this access class
    # pixel size against revisit time
    ax.scatter(s.gsd_m, s.revisit_days, marker=mk, s=60, color=col, label=acc)
    for _, r in s.iterrows():  # label each sensor
        # textcoords="offset points" places the label relative to the dot, not in data units.
        # A short grey stem is drawn only for the labels we moved, so you can see which dot they belong to.
        ax.annotate(r.sensor, (r.gsd_m, r.revisit_days), xytext=offsets.get(r.sensor, (5, 3)), textcoords="offset points",
                    fontsize=8, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.5, color="grey") if r.sensor in offsets else None)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")  # log scales: 0.5 m and 375 m both stay readable
ax.set_xlabel("Multispectral pixel size at nadir (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("Revisit (days)")  # axis labels
ax.set_title("Spatial versus temporal resolution of optical sensors (approximate)")  # title
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # legend, arrange and draw









Open missions sit to the right (10 m and coarser) and trade detail for free, systematic, global coverage. Commercial constellations fill the lower left: fine pixels and frequent revisits, achieved with many satellites and agile pointing, at a price. NAIP shows that aerial programmes can be both open and very fine, but only every few years and only for one country.


Where the bands are
Band sets differ between sensors. Commercial sensors often add a coastal/aerosol band (water penetration, haze), a yellow band and one or two red-edge and NIR bands. The chart shows nominal band centres and widths from the operators’ specifications.


Code
# This cell draws where each sensor's bands sit along the spectrum.
# A band is a slice of wavelengths: a centre (nm) and a width (nm). Each

    ("WorldView-2/3 (MS)", "Coastal", 427, 50), ("WorldView-2/3 (MS)", "Blue", 482, 60), ("WorldView-2/3 (MS)", "Green", 547, 70),
    ("WorldView-2/3 (MS)", "Yellow", 604, 40), ("WorldView-2/3 (MS)", "Red", 660, 60), ("WorldView-2/3 (MS)", "Red edge", 723, 40),

palette = {"Coastal": "#542788", "Coastal blue": "#542788", "Blue": "#2166ac", "Green": "#1b7837", "Green I": "#5aae61",

The open missions are the only ones in this chart with SWIR bands (WorldView-3 also has a separate 3.7 m SWIR instrument, sold as its own product). SWIR is what separates moisture conditions, burned areas, snow from cloud, and many minerals, so even users of commercial imagery often add Landsat or Sentinel-2 for those questions.

Analysis-ready data (ARD) are surface reflectance on a fixed grid, with per-pixel quality flags, so users can stack dates without re-processing. The Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) defines ARD standards (CEOS-ARD); Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 and Sentinel-2 L2A meet them.
Commercial products are often delivered as DN or scaled radiance with the calibration coefficients in a metadata file (for Maxar, absCalFactor and effectiveBandwidth per band in the .IMD file). Without that file the values can only be used relatively, as in the Hands-on: a commercial 8-band image section.

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
text:
Limitations of optical data

Clouds. About two-thirds of the Earth is cloud-covered at any time, and the tropics and monsoon regions much more in the wet season. Usable observations are far fewer than revisits.
Cloud shadows, haze and smoke darken or brighten pixels without hiding them, which makes them harder to detect than thick cloud.
Illumination. Low sun in winter and at high latitudes, terrain shading on slopes facing away from the sun, and no data at night.
Viewing and sun geometry (BRDF). The same field looks different from different angles; wide-swath and pointing sensors need BRDF normalization (for example nadir BRDF-adjusted reflectance, NBAR).
Mixed pixels. Every pixel coarser than the objects in it records a blend (the Hands-on: pixel size and mixed pixels section).
Sensor differences. Band positions, calibration and processing differ, so mixing sensors needs harmonization.

The usual remedies are per-pixel cloud masks (Landsat QA_PIXEL, Sentinel-2 SCL), cloud-free compositing, combining sensors (HLS), and adding radar, which sees through clouds.

Weaknesses: cost, licences that restrict sharing and derived products, smaller footprints (5-20 km scenes), shorter archives, and sometimes less rigorous radiometric calibration, which complicates time series.
Ways to use commercial data at low or no cost:

Disaster programmes. The International Charter “Space and Major Disasters” and Maxar’s Open Data Program release imagery after major disasters.
Research programmes. NASA’s Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition (CSDA) programme buys commercial data for NASA-funded researchers; ESA’s Third Party Missions programme offers commercial data for research proposals; Planet runs an education and research programme.
Tropical forest basemaps. Norway’s International Climate and Forest Initiative (NICFI) has funded free monthly PlanetScope basemaps of the tropics for forest monitoring.
Marketplaces such as UP42, SkyWatch and Apollo Mapping sell scenes from several operators, often with small minimum orders.

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
text:
Choosing data and getting access
Start from the question, not the satellite:

What is the smallest object or change that matters? Pick a pixel size two to three times finer than it (the Ground sampling distance and swath section).
How often must you look, and when? Crop growth needs weekly data in the growing season; floods need data within days; urban change may need one image a year.
Which spectral information is needed? Red edge for crop nitrogen and stress, SWIR for moisture, burn and minerals, many narrow bands for pigments or minerals.
How large is the area and how long the period? Large areas and long time series favour open data and cloud processing; small sites and single dates can afford commercial imagery.
What can be shared? Open data allow redistribution; commercial licences usually do not.

A common, economical design combines them: open data for the large area and the time series, commercial imagery for training and validation samples, small priority sites or crisis dates.

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
section: One scene from each commercial sensor
text:
One scene from each commercial sensor
Dataset are available for download in GeoLattice Data Folder. We will use one scene from each satellite in /Commercial_images. Multispectral scenes are natural colour (red, green, blue). WorldView-1 has no multispectral bands, so that panel is the panchromatic image in grey. The long side of each panel is 420 pixels, read from the GeoTIFF without loading the whole file. Black is outside the scene. Each band is stretched from the 2nd to the 98th percentile so dark water and bright ground both stay visible.


Code
# Preview one real scene from each commercial sensor in Commercial_images/.
# Full scenes are huge (often hundreds of megabytes). We never load a whole
# file: each panel is a small natural-colour, or grey panchromatic, preview.
#
# 1. `read_preview` opens the GeoTIFF and asks rasterio to resample it on the
#    way in, so the long side of the array is `max_px` pixels (420 here).
# 2. `to_display` stretches each band from the 2nd to the 98th percentile.
#    That keeps dark water and bright ground both visible. Values outside the
#    scene (0 or the fill 65535) are painted black.
# 3. Band index tuples differ by product, because the files do not store bands
#    in the same order:
#    - 8-band WorldView: coastal, blue, green, yellow, red, ... so red/green/blue
#      are bands (5, 3, 2). Rasterio band numbers start at 1.
#    - 4-band files here: blue, green, red, near infrared, so red/green/blue
#      are bands (3, 2, 1).
#    - WorldView-1 has no colour bands, so we read the single panchromatic band.
#    - KOMPSAT stores red, green and blue in three separate files.
# 4. Draw the previews on a 3 × 6 grid. The Apollo Mapping entry is only a
#    pointer to a free poster; there is no local file for it.

COM = Path("../../../../Data/00_shared/data_remote_sensing/Commercial_images")

def read_preview(source, bands, max_px=420):  # read a small preview of a scene
    """Read red, green and blue, or one panchromatic band, with the long side at max_px.

    source is one GeoTIFF, or a list of single-band files already in red, green, blue order.
    KOMPSAT stores each band in its own file.
    """
    # A single path is one multi-band file. A list is one file per colour (KOMPSAT).
    paths = [source] if isinstance(source, Path) else list(source)
    with rasterio.open(paths[0]) as ds:  # open the first file to get its size
        # Scale factor from the full image down to a preview. out_hw is (rows, cols).
        scale = max(ds.height, ds.width) / max_px
        # preview size (rows, cols)
        out_hw = (max(1, round(ds.height / scale)), max(1, round(ds.width / scale)))
    if len(paths) == 1:  # one file holds all bands
        with rasterio.open(paths[0]) as ds:  # open it
            # Read only the requested band numbers, already resampled to out_hw.
            # Bilinear is a smooth preview; it is not the resampling you would use for analysis.
            data = ds.read(list(bands), out_shape=(len(bands), *out_hw),
                           resampling=rasterio.enums.Resampling.bilinear)
    else:
        planes = []  # one file per band
        for path in paths:  # every band file
            with rasterio.open(path) as ds:  # open it
                planes.append(ds.read(1, out_shape=out_hw,  # read it at preview size
                                       resampling=rasterio.enums.Resampling.bilinear))
        data = np.stack(planes)  # shape (3, rows, cols), already in red, green, blue order
    return data.astype("float32")  # as floats

def to_display(data):  # stretch an image for display
    """Stretch each band to the 2nd-98th percentile. A single band is drawn in grey."""
    image = np.zeros(data.shape[1:] + (3,), np.float32)  # an RGB image matplotlib can draw
    grey = data.shape[0] == 1  # one band means panchromatic: copy it into R, G and B
    for i in ([0] if grey else range(3)):  # one band (grey) or three (colour)
        band = data[0 if grey else i]  # the band to stretch
        # Ignore nodata. 0 is outside the scene; 65535 is a common integer fill value.
        valid = np.isfinite(band) & (band > 0) & (band < 65535)
        if int(valid.sum()) < 20:  # too few valid pixels: leave it black
            continue
        # Percentiles ignore the darkest and brightest 2%, which are usually outliers.
        lo, hi = np.percentile(band[valid], (2, 98))
        stretched = np.clip((band - lo) / max(hi - lo, 1), 0, 1)  # stretch to [0, 1]
        stretched[~valid] = 0  # black outside the scene
        if grey:  # single band:
            image[:] = stretched[..., None]  # copy it into all three channels
        else:
            image[..., i] = stretched  # colour channel
    return image  # the display image

# Each entry is (panel title, file or list of files, band numbers).
# Band numbers are 1-based, which is what rasterio expects.
# 8-band WorldView order is coastal, blue, green, yellow, red, so red/green/blue are bands 5, 3, 2.
# The 4-band files here are blue, green, red, near infrared, so red/green/blue are bands 3, 2, 1.
k3 = COM / "KOMPSAT/KOMPSAT3_SanFrancisco_7_13_2013_Bundle"
k3a = "KOMPSAT/K3A_20160824180916_07825_00026235_L1R"  # folder of the KOMPSAT-3A sample
scenes = [  # title, file(s) and band numbers of every sample scene
    # 8-band WorldView: pick red, green, blue out of coastal/blue/green/yellow/red/...
    ("WorldView-3\nNamibia, 2015",
     COM / "World_View/Namibia_WV3_SWIR_MS_Bundle_Sample/054265823020_01/054265823020_01_P001_MUL/15MAR16092139-M2AS-054265823020_01_P001.TIF", (5, 3, 2)),
    ("WorldView-2\nSydney, 2011",
     COM / "World_View/WV2_8band_Bundle_Sydney_Australia/052783824080_01_P001_MUL/11APR03001446-M2AS_R1C1-052783824080_01_P001.TIF", (5, 3, 2)),
    ("WorldView Legion\nBakersfield, 2024",
     COM / "World_View/Bakersfield_CA_8band_LG02/050246255010_01/050246255010_01_P001_MUL/24SEP22184516-M2AS-050246255010_01_P001.TIF", (5, 3, 2)),
    # 4-band blue, green, red, NIR.
    ("WorldView-4\nNew York, 2017",
     COM / "World_View/056965205010_01/056965205010_01_P001_MUL/17APR18154116-M2AS_R1C1-056965205010_01_P001.TIF", (3, 2, 1)),
    # Panchromatic only: one band, drawn in grey by to_display.
    ("WorldView-1\nBoulder, 2010",
     COM / "World_View/052987795060_01/052987795060_01_P001_PAN/10JUN22181146-P2AS-052987795060_01_P001.TIF", (1,)),
    ("GeoEye-1\nCape Town, 2013",
     COM / "GeoEye/053413654010_01/053413654010_01_P001_MUL/13JUL31084528-M2AS-053413654010_01_P001.TIF", (3, 2, 1)),
    ("QuickBird-2\nJaipur, 2013",
     COM / "Quickbird/053398467010_01/053398467010_01_P001_MUL/13SEP18045419-M2AS-053398467010_01_P001.TIF", (3, 2, 1)),
    ("IKONOS-2\nSão Paulo, 2002",
     COM / "IKONOS/po_1462947_0000000/po_1462947_bgrn_0000000.tif", (3, 2, 1)),
    ("SPOT 6\nAbu Dhabi, 2013",

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
text:
Hands-on: a commercial 8-band image
The GeoLattice data folder includes an 8-band Maxar (DigitalGlobe) multispectral image of a coastal area of southern Bangladesh, taken in March, at 1.2 m. Its eight bands match the WorldView-2/3 multispectral set (coastal, blue, green, yellow, red, red edge, NIR1, NIR2), and it is delivered as digital numbers without the calibration file. A 9-class land-cover map and labelled polygons come with it.


Code
# Load the local 8-band commercial image of southern Bangladesh (March) and
# check what kind of file it is before we interpret the colours.
#
# 1. Point at the MARCH folder and name the eight bands in WorldView-2/3 order:
#    coastal, blue, green, yellow, red, red edge, NIR1, NIR2.
# 2. `rs.read` opens the GeoTIFF as an xarray DataArray with those band names,
#    plus the map coordinates stored in the file.
# 3. This file stores no-data as the integer 65536 (one more than a 16-bit
#    maximum, because the file is int32). `where` turns those pixels into NaN,
#    then we cast to float so later division (NDVI) is safe.
# 4. Print the coordinate system, the pixel size in metres, the shape, and the
#    ground size in kilometres. Then print the longitude and latitude of the
#    upper-left corner, and a small table of min / median / max digital numbers.

DG = Path("../../../../Data/00_shared/data_remote_sensing/Commercial_images/World_View/DG_MARCH")
WV_BANDS = ["coastal", "blue", "green", "yellow", "red", "rededge", "nir", "nir2"]   # WorldView-2/3 order
wv = rs.read(DG / "DG_MAR.tif", band_names=WV_BANDS)  # read the 8-band WorldView image with band names
wv = wv.where(wv < 65536).astype("float32")                     # 65,536 marks no-data in this int32 file
# rio.resolution() is (x size, y size). y is negative when rows run north to south, so we take abs.
print("CRS:", wv.rio.crs, "| pixel:", tuple(round(abs(r), 2) for r in wv.rio.resolution()), "m",
      "| size:", wv.shape, f"= {wv.rio.width * 1.2 / 1000:.1f} × {wv.rio.height * 1.2 / 1000:.1f} km")
# Reproject the northwest 2×2 pixels to longitude/latitude just to say where the scene sits.
# rio.bounds() is (left, bottom, right, top). Taking the first two values gives the
# southwest corner of that tiny crop, which is still the upper-left of the full scene.
lon, lat = rs.reproject(wv.isel(band=0, x=slice(0, 2), y=slice(0, 2)), "EPSG:4326").rio.bounds()[:2]
print(f"Upper-left corner near {lat:.3f}°N, {lon:.3f}°E")  # location of the upper-left corner
# to_dataset makes each band a variable, which is what the next cells index by name.
# drop spatial_ref so describe() summarises pixel values, not the CRS coordinate.
wv.to_dataset(dim="band").drop_vars("spatial_ref").to_dataframe().describe().loc[["min", "50%", "max"]].round(0)

Code
# Draw the same 8-band image three ways. `rs.viz.plot_rgb` picks three bands,
# stretches them, and paints them as red, green and blue on screen. The screen
# colours are a choice; they are not the wavelengths the sensor measured.
#
# Left: natural colour. Red light goes to the red channel, green to green, blue
# to blue, so the picture looks like a photograph.
# Middle: classic false colour. NIR1 (strongly reflected by leaves) is painted
# red, so growing vegetation comes out red and water stays dark.
# Right: a vegetation-contrast composite. NIR2, the red-edge band and yellow
# separate crops, trees and bare soil that look similar in natural colour.

ds = wv.to_dataset(dim="band")  # one variable per band name, so plot_rgb can ask for "nir" or "red"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5.4))  # three panels
# natural colour
rs.viz.plot_rgb(ds, ("red", "green", "blue"), ax=axes[0], title="Natural colour (red, green, blue)")
# false colour
rs.viz.plot_rgb(ds, ("nir", "red", "green"), ax=axes[1], title="False colour (NIR1, red, green)")
# NIR2, red edge, yellow
rs.viz.plot_rgb(ds, ("nir2", "rededge", "yellow"), ax=axes[2], title="NIR2, red edge, yellow")
for a in axes:  # for every panel
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # hide pixel indices; the map grid is the same in every panel
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









The scene is a dry-season landscape in the Ganges delta:

Water. A large turbid river crosses the lower right. Narrow tidal channels meander through the image, and fishponds sit among the settlements.
Settlements. Villages and homestead gardens with dense tree cover line the channels and embankments: dark green in natural colour and red in the false-colour image.
Fields. Most fields are pale pink to grey, meaning fallow or harvested in March. Blocks of bright red in the false-colour image are fields with an actively growing dry-season crop.

At 1.2 m, field boundaries, single rows of trees, footpaths and the road crossing the image diagonally are all distinct. In the third composite, built from bands that only some sensors have (NIR2, red edge, yellow), vegetation is orange and the bare fields are pale.
The labelled sample points give each class’s mean digital number in every band. Because these are DNs, not reflectance, the curves can be compared with each other but not with the reflectance signatures of notebook 07_01_00.


Code
# Spectral signatures: the average digital number of each land-cover class in
# every band. A signature is the shape of that line. Water drops in the NIR;
# vegetation dips in the red and jumps at the red edge; bare soil stays bright
# and fairly flat. Those shapes are what a classifier uses.
#
# 1. Read the point shapefile and drop Class_ID 0 (unassigned duplicate points).
# 2. `rs.classify.extract_samples` looks up the pixel under each point and
#    returns a table of band values (X) and the class id of each point (y).
# 3. Average the digital numbers by class name, and add a column with how many
#    points went into each average.
# 4. Plot mean DN against the WorldView band-centre wavelengths (nm).

labels = gpd.read_file(DG / "Label_March.shp")
labels = labels[labels.Class_ID > 0]                              # Class_ID 0 rows are unassigned duplicates
X, y = rs.classify.extract_samples(ds, labels, "Class_ID")          # one row per point: the pixel under that point
# Class_ID -> a cleaned class name ("Water / River", "Crop", ...).
names = labels.drop_duplicates("Class_ID").set_index("Class_ID")["Class"].str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True)
# Group the sample pixels by class name and take the mean DN in each of the 8 bands.
sig = X[WV_BANDS].groupby(pd.Series(y, index=X.index).map(names)).mean()
sig.insert(0, "sample points", pd.Series(y).map(names).value_counts())  # number of sample points of each class
display(sig.round(0))  # show the table

# Nominal WorldView-2/3 multispectral centres, same order as WV_BANDS.
centres = [427, 482, 547, 604, 660, 723, 824, 914]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.8))  # one panel
for cls, row in sig[WV_BANDS].iterrows():  # every class
    ax.plot(centres, row.values, marker="o", lw=1.8, label=cls)  # its mean spectrum
# band names and centre wavelengths on the x axis
ax.set_xticks(centres); ax.set_xticklabels([f"{b}\n{c}" for b, c in zip(WV_BANDS, centres)], fontsize=8)
# labels and title
ax.set_ylabel("Mean digital number"); ax.set_title("Class signatures in the 8-band commercial image")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # legend, arrange and draw

The signatures show the classes the image can separate:

Water/River is the only class whose NIR values fall far below the visible bands (NIR1 257, NIR2 138).
Crop, Vegetation and “Water H” show the vegetation shape: a dip in the red (240-290), a steep rise through the red edge and a NIR1 peak (680-765). “Water H” behaves like vegetation, not water. Together with its name, this suggests floating water hyacinth, which covers many ponds and channels in Bangladesh.
Built-up, fallow, ploughed land and roads are bright and flat across the visible bands, with weaker NIR.

NIR2 is lower than NIR1 for every class. Two likely reasons: the NIR2 band spans the 940 nm water-vapour absorption feature, and DNs of different bands are not on a common scale. Only calibrated reflectance would show which effect dominates here.
Some labels rest on few samples (“Fallow wet” has a single point), so treat those curves with caution.

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
section: Hands-on: pixel size and mixed pixels
text:
Hands-on: pixel size and mixed pixels
How much of this landscape could a coarser sensor see as pure pixels? The 1.2 m land-cover map lets us answer exactly. We aggregate it to the pixel sizes of PlanetScope (3.6 m, the nearest multiple of 1.2 m to 3 m), Sentinel-2 (10.8 m), Landsat (30 m) and MODIS (250.8 m), and count the coarse pixels in which one class covers at least 90% of the area. Those are pure pixels; the rest are mixed, and any classifier can only label them by their dominant class.


Code
# How many pixels stay "pure" when we coarsen this 1.2 m land-cover map to the
# pixel size of a coarser sensor? A coarse pixel is pure when one class covers
# at least 90% of the fine cells inside it. Everything else is mixed: the
# satellite records a blend, and a classifier can only assign the dominant class.
#
# 1. Read the 1.2 m label raster, keep class codes 1-9, and snap it onto the
#    same grid as the WorldView image (nearest neighbour, so class codes are
#    not averaged into fake fractional classes).
# 2. `purity(L, f)` cuts the map into blocks of f × f fine pixels.
#    f = 1 is the original 1.2 m map, f = 3 is 3.6 m, f = 9 is 10.8 m,
#    f = 25 is 30 m, and f = 209 is 250.8 m (1.2 × 209).
# 3. For each block, find the class with the largest share. The block is pure
#    when that share is at least 90% and almost every fine cell is valid.
# 4. Build a table: percent of pure pixels overall, and the same percent inside
#    the crop, fallow, road and river pixels (classes 2, 3, 6 and 9).

lab = rs.read(DG / "Label_MARCH.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True)
# Finite and in 1..9: drop the raster's own nodata and any stray codes.
# reproject_match aligns the labels to the image grid without changing class integers.
lab = lab.where(np.isfinite(lab) & (lab >= 1) & (lab <= 9)).rio.reproject_match(wv.isel(band=0), resampling=rasterio.enums.Resampling.nearest)
L = lab.values  # the label array
classes = np.arange(1, 10)  # the nine class codes
# share of each class at 1.2 m
print("Land-cover shares at 1.2 m:", {names[c]: f"{np.nanmean(L == c) * 100:.1f}%" for c in classes})

def purity(L, f, threshold=0.9):  # which coarse pixels are pure for a block size f
    # Trim the edges so the array divides evenly into f × f blocks.
    H, W = (L.shape[0] // f) * f, (L.shape[1] // f) * f
    # reshape -> (n_block_rows, f, n_block_cols, f), then swap so each block is contiguous,
    # then flatten the f × f cells of each block into one length-f*f axis.
    blocks = L[:H, :W].reshape(H // f, f, W // f, f).swapaxes(1, 2).reshape(H // f, W // f, f * f)
    valid = np.isfinite(blocks).sum(-1)  # how many fine cells in the block are real labels
    # share[..., c] is the fraction of valid cells equal to class c.
    share = np.stack([(blocks == c).sum(-1) for c in classes], -1) / np.maximum(valid, 1)[..., None]
    ok = valid > 0.9 * f * f            # ignore blocks that are mostly outside the map
    dominant = share.argmax(-1) + 1     # class codes are 1-9; argmax is 0-8
    pure = share.max(-1) >= threshold   # True where one class covers >= 90%
    return ok, pure, dominant  # the three arrays

rows = []  # one row per simulated sensor
# block sizes that mimic each sensor's pixel size
for name, f in [("Commercial VHR (1.2 m)", 1), ("PlanetScope-like (3.6 m)", 3), ("Sentinel-2-like (10.8 m)", 9),
                ("Landsat-like (30 m)", 25), ("MODIS-like (250.8 m)", 209)]:
    ok, pure, dom = purity(L, f)  # purity at this block size
    # number of coarse pixels and the share that is pure
    row = {"sensor": name, "pixels": int(ok.sum()), "pure pixels (%)": round(float(pure[ok].mean()) * 100, 1)}
    for c in [2, 3, 6, 9]:                                          # crop, fallow, road, river
        m = ok & (dom == c)  # coarse pixels whose dominant class is c
        # purity per dominant class
        row[f"pure, {names[c]}"] = round(float(pure[m].mean()) * 100, 1) if m.any() else np.nan
    rows.append(row)  # store the row
mix = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("sensor")  # as a table
mix  # show it

Code
# Map the dominant class at four pixel sizes, and paint mixed pixels light grey
# so you can see where a coarser sensor stops resolving this landscape.
#
# At 1.2 m every labelled cell is shown in its own class colour (the map is the
# reference, so nothing is called mixed). At 10.8 m, 30 m and 250.8 m we reuse
# `purity` from the previous cell: the colour is still the dominant class, but
# any block below the 90% rule is covered with light grey.

from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap, BoundaryNorm
# Nine class colours, in Class_ID order 1..9. BoundaryNorm puts each integer in its own bin.
cmap = ListedColormap(["#e41a1c", "#4daf4a", "#d9c27b", "#a6761d", "#80b1d3", "#666666", "#1b7837", "#377eb8", "#08306b"])
norm = BoundaryNorm(np.arange(0.5, 10.5), cmap.N)  # map class codes 1-9 to colours
grey = ListedColormap(["#d0d0d0"])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 5))  # four panels
# four pixel sizes
for a, (title, f) in zip(axes, [("1.2 m", 1), ("10.8 m", 9), ("30 m", 25), ("250.8 m", 209)]):
    # f = 1: show the original labels. f > 1: one colour per coarse block.
    ok, pure, dom = purity(L, f) if f > 1 else (np.isfinite(L), np.ones_like(L, bool), L)
    show = np.where(ok, dom, np.nan).astype(float)  # NaN outside the map, so those cells stay blank
    a.imshow(show, cmap=cmap, norm=norm, interpolation="nearest")  # the dominant class of each coarse pixel
    if f > 1:  # coarse pixel sizes only
        # Second image, drawn on top: grey only where the block exists and is mixed.
        a.imshow(np.where(ok & ~pure, 1.0, np.nan), cmap=grey, alpha=0.75, interpolation="nearest")
    a.set_title(f"{title}" + (" (light grey = mixed)" if f > 1 else " (land-cover map)"), fontsize=10)  # title
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
# one colour bar for all panels
cb = fig.colorbar(plt.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=norm, cmap=cmap), ax=axes, ticks=classes, shrink=0.8)
cb.ax.set_yticklabels([names[c] for c in classes], fontsize=8)  # class names on it
plt.show()  # draw









This landscape is fine-grained: fields, homestead tree belts, channels and roads are a few metres to a few tens of metres across. Even at 3.6 m, 58% of pixels are mixed. At Sentinel-2’s 10.8 m only 30% are pure, at Landsat’s 30 m 15%, and at MODIS scale none: every 250 m pixel blends several classes.
Narrow features disappear first. Roads are 7% pure at 3.6 m, 1.5% at 10.8 m and 0% at 30 m. The river is the most robust class, still 43% pure at 30 m, because its main channel is wide.
Two caveats. The 1.2 m map is a classification supplied with the image, not field truth. The blocks are exact aggregates rather than real sensor footprints, which also blur across pixel edges (MTF), so real sensors look slightly worse. The lesson for sensor choice: in smallholder landscapes like this one, 10-30 m data describe proportions of land cover per pixel rather than individual fields.

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
section: Hands-on: open Sentinel-2 and Landsat over the same place (live)
text:
Hands-on: open Sentinel-2 and Landsat over the same place (live)
Open archives cover this site too. get_images searches Microsoft Planetary Computer for the clearest March scene from Sentinel-2 L2A and Landsat 8/9 Collection 2 Level-2, clips red and near infrared to the commercial image footprint (mode="clip"), and we compare NDVI at the three resolutions. The dates differ from the commercial image, so compare detail, not crops.


Code
# Read the clearest open scene over this same footprint and compare it with
# the commercial image. Scenes already downloaded into ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical/optical_compare are
# read from disk. A scene that is not there yet is downloaded, which needs the
# network; offline, the missing scene is skipped and the rest of the notebook
# still runs.
#
# 1. Test the catalogue, and turn the WorldView image bounds into a longitude /
#    latitude box. That box is the search area.
# 2. Ask `get_images` for March 2024, cloud cover under 10%, and only the
#    clearest scene. `bands=["red", "nir"]` and `mode="clip"` mean we download
#    two bands, already cut to the box, not the whole satellite scene.
#    One search is Sentinel-2 L2A (10 m). The other is Landsat Collection 2
#    Level-2 (30 m).
# 3. `rs.optical.scale` turns the stored integers into surface reflectance.
#    Sentinel-2 L2A also needs a small offset (`boa_offset=-1000`) before the
#    usual scale factor; Landsat's scale is applied with the default.
# 4. NDVI = (NIR − red) / (NIR + red). Store the date, the scene cloud
#    percent and the NDVI grid so the next cell can plot them.

from datetime import date
import json  # read the scene metadata (item.json)

from geolattice.network import is_online  # internet check
from geolattice.rsense.get_images import get_images  # one-call search and download

# The notebook's data folder: ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical/ next to this notebook, found from here or from the repository root.
DATA = next((p for p in (Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"))
             if p.is_dir()), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"))

def local_scenes(folder, files=()):
    """Scene folders already downloaded under `folder` that contain every file in `files`."""
    folder = Path(folder)
    if not folder.is_dir():  # nothing downloaded yet
        return []
    return sorted(p for p in folder.iterdir() if p.is_dir() and all((p / f).exists() for f in files))


ONLINE = is_online(rs.access.CATALOGS["planetary-computer"])  # can Planetary Computer be reached?
bbox = tuple(wv.rio.transform_bounds("EPSG:4326"))  # (west, south, east, north) in degrees
# status and AOI
print("Planetary Computer reachable:", ONLINE, "| AOI (lon/lat):", tuple(round(v, 4) for v in bbox))

OUT = DATA / "optical_compare"  # where the clipped GeoTIFFs are stored
open_imgs = {}  # NDVI and metadata per open sensor
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
# key is the panel name, sensor is what rs.optical.scale expects, kwargs go to get_images.
jobs = [
    ("Sentinel-2 L2A, 10 m", "sentinel2", dict(
        out=OUT / "s2", dates=("2024-03-01", "2024-03-31"), collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
    )),
    ("Landsat C2 L2, 30 m", "landsat", dict(
        out=OUT / "ls", dates=("2024-03-01", "2024-03-31"), collection="landsat-c2-l2",
    )),
]
for key, sensor, kwargs in jobs:  # every sensor
    local = local_scenes(kwargs["out"], ["red.tif", "nir.tif", "item.json"])  # scenes already on disk
    if local:  # downloaded before: read it from the local drive
        scene_dir = local[0]  # the scene folder
        props = json.loads((scene_dir / "item.json").read_text())["properties"]  # its catalogue record
        scene = {"id": scene_dir.name, "datetime": props.get("datetime"), "cloud": props.get("eo:cloud_cover")}
        print(f"{key}: reading {scene_dir}")  # where it comes from
    elif ONLINE:  # not on disk yet: download it
        saved = get_images(  # download the clearest March scene, clipped to the AOI
            bbox=bbox, source="planetary", cloud=10, clearest=True,
            bands=["red", "nir"], mode="clip", quiet=True, **kwargs,
        )
        if not saved.scenes:  # nothing found
            print(f"{key}: no scene"); continue  # skip this sensor
        # saved.scenes[0] is the catalogue record (id, date, cloud). The pixels
        # are GeoTIFFs in the first subfolder of saved.out.
        scene, scene_dir = saved.scenes[0], next(p for p in saved.out.iterdir() if p.is_dir())
    else:  # offline and not on disk
        print(f"{key}: offline and not downloaded yet, skipped"); continue
    ds = xr.Dataset({  # red and NIR as a Dataset
        "red": rs.read(scene_dir / "red.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True),
        "nir": rs.read(scene_dir / "nir.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True),
    })
    # Sentinel-2 surface reflectance is stored with an offset; Landsat is not.
    scaled = rs.optical.scale(ds, sensor=sensor, boa_offset=-1000 if sensor == "sentinel2" else None)
    ndvi = (scaled.nir - scaled.red) / (scaled.nir + scaled.red)  # NDVI from reflectance
    # acquisition date
    when = date.fromisoformat(str(scene["datetime"])[:10]) if scene.get("datetime") else None
    cloud = scene.get("cloud")  # scene cloud cover
    open_imgs[key] = {"date": when, "cloud": cloud, "ndvi": ndvi}  # store the result
    # report it
    print(f"{key}: {scene['id']}, {when}, scene cloud {float(cloud or 0):.1f}%, AOI grid {tuple(ndvi.shape)}")
print(f"Reading and downloading took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")  # run time

Code
# Put the commercial NDVI next to the open NDVI from the previous cell.
# The point of the figure is spatial detail, not the crop calendar: the open
# scenes are a different March than the commercial image.
#
# The commercial NDVI is computed from digital numbers, not reflectance. DN in
# this file is roughly proportional to radiance, so the *pattern* (high over
# leaves, low over water) is meaningful, but the numeric NDVI is not comparable
# to the scaled Sentinel-2 and Landsat values. Those two are real reflectance NDVI.
# If the download was skipped, only the commercial panel is drawn.

# `ds` is the 8-band WorldView dataset from the composite cell (wv.to_dataset).
# The download cell also uses the name `ds` inside its loop. If that cell has
# already run, re-run the composite cell first so this line still sees the
# commercial bands, not the last Landsat or Sentinel-2 scene.
wv_ndvi = (ds["nir"] - ds["red"]) / (ds["nir"] + ds["red"])          # DN-based: relative values only
# One panel for the commercial image, then one panel per open scene that was actually downloaded.
panels = [("Commercial 8-band, 1.2 m (DN-based NDVI)", wv_ndvi)] + [(f"{k}, {v['date']}", v["ndvi"]) for k, v in open_imgs.items()]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(panels), figsize=(6 * len(panels), 5.2))  # one panel per image
axes = np.atleast_1d(axes)  # a single panel comes back as one Axes, not a list
for a, (title, da) in zip(axes, panels):  # every panel
    rs.viz.plot_raster(da, ax=a, cmap="RdYlGn", title=title)  # brown = low NDVI, green = high NDVI
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
if open_imgs:  # only if open scenes were downloaded
    # Date, how many pixels fell inside the AOI, and the median NDVI of those pixels.
    display(pd.DataFrame({k: {"date": v["date"], "pixels in AOI": int(v["ndvi"].notnull().sum()),
                              "median NDVI": round(float(v["ndvi"].median()), 3)} for k, v in open_imgs.items()}).T)

Sentinel-2 still shows individual fields, tree belts and the main channels. Landsat shows the river and the broad pattern of green and fallow land, but the narrow channels and roads have merged into their surroundings, exactly as the mixed-pixel analysis predicted.
The two open sensors, two days apart, agree on the median NDVI (0.398 and 0.413) because both are surface reflectance. The commercial NDVI covers a lower, narrower range (about −0.15 to 0.55) because it is computed from uncalibrated DNs that still contain atmospheric path radiance. Its pattern is valid, but its values cannot be compared with the open data until the image is calibrated. The images are also from different years, so field-by-field differences are expected.

title: Introduction to Optical Satellite Images
text:
Summary, exercises and references
Key ideas

Optical sensors are passive: they record reflected sunlight in the visible, NIR and SWIR, and need daylight and clear skies.
Pushbroom and frame designs dominate modern sensors; panchromatic bands give detail, multispectral and hyperspectral bands give identity.
Pixel size, swath and revisit trade off against each other; off-nadir viewing, MTF and SNR decide what a pixel really shows.
Open data (Landsat, Sentinel-2, MODIS, HLS) are free, calibrated, global and long; commercial data add sub-metre detail, tasking and daily revisits at a cost and with licence limits.
Analysis-ready surface reflectance is the starting point; commercial DNs need their calibration metadata.

What the data showed

The 8-band commercial image, 11-bit DNs at 1.2 m, separates water, vegetation (including probable water hyacinth) and bright bare or built surfaces. Its yellow, red-edge and NIR2 bands add information that broad 4-band sensors lack.
In this fragmented delta landscape only 30% of 10 m pixels and 15% of 30 m pixels are pure; narrow roads vanish entirely at 30 m.
Free Sentinel-2 and Landsat scenes of the same site, two days apart, agree on median NDVI (0.40 and 0.41); uncalibrated commercial DNs do not give comparable values.

Exercises

Compute the GSD of a sensor with 10 µm detectors and a 1.0 m focal length at 500 km altitude. What is its across-track GSD at 30° off nadir?
Recompute the mixed-pixel table with a purity threshold of 75% instead of 90%. Which classes change most?
Using the class signatures of the Hands-on: a commercial 8-band image section, which single band ratio best separates “Crop” from “Vegetation”? Test it with a histogram.
(Online) Repeat the Hands-on: open Sentinel-2 and Landsat over the same place (live) section for a wet-season month (July or August). How many clear Sentinel-2 scenes are there, and why?
Write a short data plan for monitoring rice fields in a 50 × 50 km district for three seasons: which open and commercial data would you use, at what dates, and why?

References

Lillesand, T., Kiefer, R.W. & Chipman, J. (2015). Remote Sensing and Image Interpretation, 7th ed. Wiley.
Jensen, J.R. (2016). Introductory Digital Image Processing: A Remote Sensing Perspective, 4th ed. Pearson.
Schowengerdt, R.A. (2007). Remote Sensing: Models and Methods for Image Processing, 3rd ed. Academic Press.
Wulder, M.A. et al. (2019). Current status of Landsat program, science, and applications. Remote Sensing of Environment 225, 127-147.
Drusch, M. et al. (2012). Sentinel-2: ESA’s optical high-resolution mission for GMES operational services. Remote Sensing of Environment 120, 25-36.
Claverie, M. et al. (2018). The Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 surface reflectance data set. Remote Sensing of Environment 219, 145-161.
Operator specifications: USGS Landsat Missions, ESA Sentinel-2 User Guide, Maxar, Airbus Defence and Space, and Planet product documentation.

title: Data Discovery and Access
text:
Overview
The hard part is no longer getting data but finding the right scenes and loading only the pixels you need. This module covers the modern, cloud-native way to do that: STAC catalogs, Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs read over HTTP, and lazy data cubes with Dask, plus the main providers (Microsoft Planetary Computer, AWS Earth Search, NASA Earthdata, Copernicus Data Space, ASF and Google Earth Engine), all through geolattice.rsense.access.

Setup and connectivity check
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Setup for data discovery and access.
#
# 1. Import the pieces a catalogue search needs: JSON, the clock, HTTP, dates,
#    and Shapely geometries (box, Point, shape).
# 2. Import the usual array and vector stack, plus geolattice.rsense.
# 3. Create outputs/ for the local STAC catalog and the simulated cube.
# 4. Print versions and the active compute backend.

%matplotlib inline
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import importlib.util          # test whether an optional package is installed
import json  # read STAC JSON
import os  # environment variables (credentials)
import time  # timing
import urllib.request  # check whether a server can be reached
from datetime import datetime, timezone  # dates with time zones
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
from shapely.geometry import box, Point, shape  # geometry helpers

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing subpackage

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
OUT = Path("outputs"); OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # folder for the files written in this notebook
# versions and backend
print("geolattice", geolattice.__version__, "| geolattice.rsense", rs.__version__, "| backend:", rs.get_backend())

Code
# Point at the local files the offline sections use, and confirm they exist.

# Live catalogue calls can be skipped when the network is down. The Landsat
# scene, its MTL file, the four DEM tiles and the county shapefile are what
# the local STAC catalog and the Dask example are built from.

DATA = Path("../../../../Data")
L8_DIR = DATA / "00_shared" / "data_remote_sensing" / "LC08_20150706_subset"  # the Landsat 8 subset folder
L8_FILE = L8_DIR / "multi_band.tif"  # multi-band Landsat GeoTIFF
L8_MTL = L8_DIR / "LC08_L1TP_015030_20150716_20170226_01_T1_MTL.txt"  # its metadata (MTL) file
DEM_TILES = sorted((L8_DIR / "DEM_TILES").glob("Onondaga_DEM*.TIF"))  # DEM tiles of Onondaga County
COUNTIES = DATA / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA" / "NY_County_GCS.shp"  # New York county boundaries
# check that every local input exists
print("local files present:", all(p.exists() for p in [L8_FILE, L8_MTL, COUNTIES, *DEM_TILES]))


local files present: True




Code
# Decide what this machine can do before any live search.
#
# 1. reachable() tries to open a URL and returns False on any failure, so a
#    missing network does not crash the notebook.
# 2. ONLINE is True only when Planetary Computer's STAC API answers.
# 3. HAVE records which optional clients are installed (pystac-client,
#    planetary-computer, odc-stac, earthaccess, asf_search, earthengine).
#    Later cells check these flags and print a skip message instead of failing.

def reachable(url, timeout=8):
    try:
        urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout)  # try to open the URL
        return True  # the server answered
    except Exception:
        return False  # no connection

ONLINE = reachable(rs.access.CATALOGS["planetary-computer"])  # can the Planetary Computer STAC API be reached?
HAVE = {m: importlib.util.find_spec(m) is not None  # which optional access packages are installed
        for m in ["pystac_client", "planetary_computer", "odc", "earthaccess", "asf_search", "ee"]}
# odc.stac lives inside the odc namespace package
HAVE["odc.stac"] = HAVE.pop("odc") and importlib.util.find_spec("odc.stac") is not None
print("Planetary Computer reachable:", ONLINE)  # online status
print("Optional packages:", HAVE)  # optional packages
if not ONLINE:  # offline
    # explain what will be skipped
    print("Running offline: live sections will be skipped, local sections run normally.")

title: Data Discovery and Access
text:
Areas of interest
Every search starts with where and when. rs.access.aoi_to_geojson normalizes any AOI (a vector file path, GeoDataFrame, Shapely geometry, GeoJSON dict or a (west, south, east, north) bounding box) into WGS 84 GeoJSON for the catalog APIs. Our study area is the city of Syracuse and Onondaga Lake, inside Onondaga County, New York.


Code
# Turn many kinds of "where" into one GeoJSON geometry.
#
# A STAC search needs a geometry. aoi_to_geojson accepts all of these and
# returns a GeoJSON geometry dict in longitude/latitude:
#   - a (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) tuple
#   - a GeoDataFrame, including one that is still in UTM
#   - a path to a GeoJSON file
#   - a Shapely geometry (here a point buffered by 0.05 degrees)
#   - a polygon read from the county shapefile
# The print shows the geometry type and the first vertex, so you can see that
# the projected copy was converted back to degrees.

bbox = (-76.30, 42.98, -76.05, 43.15)                                  # Syracuse and Onondaga Lake, lon/lat
# the box as a one-row GeoDataFrame
syracuse = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"name": ["Syracuse"]}, geometry=[box(*bbox)], crs=4326)
syracuse_utm = syracuse.to_crs(32618)                                  # a projected copy
syracuse.to_file(OUT / "syracuse_aoi.geojson", driver="GeoJSON")  # save it as GeoJSON
county = gpd.read_file(COUNTIES).query("COUNTY == 'Onondaga County'")  # Onondaga County from the county file

for label, aoi in [("bbox tuple", bbox), ("GeoDataFrame (UTM)", syracuse_utm),  # several ways to give an AOI
                   ("file path", str(OUT / "syracuse_aoi.geojson")),
                   ("shapely point", Point(-76.15, 43.05).buffer(0.05)), ("county polygon", county)]:
    g = rs.access.aoi_to_geojson(aoi)  # convert each to a GeoJSON geometry in lon/lat
    # type and first vertex of the result
    print(f"{label:20s} → {g['type']:12s} first vertex {np.round(np.asarray(g['coordinates'][0][0]).ravel()[:2], 4).tolist()}")

GeoDataFrame (UTM)   → Polygon      first vertex [-76.05, 42.98]
file path            → Polygon      first vertex [-76.05, 42.98]
shapely point        → Polygon      first vertex [-76.1, 43.05]
county polygon       → Polygon      first vertex [-75.9902, 43.1855]


Dates are given as a (start, end) tuple or a STAC interval string such as "2025-06-01/2025-08-31". Keep AOIs as files (GeoJSON or GeoPackage) in your project so every notebook uses the same study area.

title: Data Discovery and Access
section: STAC hands-on: build, search and load your own catalog
text:
STAC hands-on: build, search and load your own catalog
STAC (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog) describes geospatial data with four objects:

Catalog: a container of links (like a folder).
Collection: a catalog plus shared metadata such as licence and spatial/temporal extent (for example, “Sentinel-2 Level-2A”).
Item: one scene or tile with a footprint geometry, a datetime and properties such as cloud cover.
Asset: a file belonging to an item (each band, the QA layer, a thumbnail), with its URL.

A search filters items by collection, footprint and date (plus property queries), then you load the assets you need. To see every piece working without internet, we turn the local Landsat 8 scene into four NDVI tiles and publish them as a STAC catalog with rs.scale.export_stac.


Code
# Build a small STAC catalog from local Landsat NDVI tiles.
#
# STAC is the JSON description catalogues use: a Collection of Items, each Item
# pointing at a file plus the time and place it covers. This cell makes one.
#
# 1. Calibrate the Landsat DNs to top-of-atmosphere reflectance, as in the
#    raster/vector notebook.
# 2. Split the scene into a 2 × 2 grid of NDVI GeoTIFFs.
# 3. export_stac writes a Catalog and a Collection. Every tile gets the same
#    acquisition time and the scene's cloud cover, plus platform and product tags.

mtl = rs.optical.parse_mtl(L8_MTL)
dn = rs.read(L8_FILE, band_names=["blue", "green", "red", "nir"])  # Landsat DN with band names
# DN -> top-of-atmosphere reflectance, band by band
landsat = xr.concat([rs.optical.toa_reflectance(dn.sel(band=n), mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_MULT_BAND_{b}"],
                                                mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_ADD_BAND_{b}"], mtl["SUN_ELEVATION"])
                     for n, b in {"blue": 2, "green": 3, "red": 4, "nir": 5}.items()], dim="band")
landsat = landsat.rio.write_crs(dn.rio.crs)  # attach the CRS
# acquisition time (UTC) from the metadata
acquired = datetime.fromisoformat(f"{mtl['DATE_ACQUIRED']}T{mtl['SCENE_CENTER_TIME'][:8]}").replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)

H, W = landsat.shape[1:]  # image size
tile_dir = OUT / "tiles"; tile_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # folder for the tiles
files = []  # paths of the tiles
for i, (r0, r1) in enumerate([(0, H // 2), (H // 2, H)]):  # two row halves ...
    for j, (c0, c1) in enumerate([(0, W // 2), (W // 2, W)]):  # ... and two column halves
        # NDVI of this quarter
        ndvi_tile = rs.optical.index(landsat.isel(y=slice(r0, r1), x=slice(c0, c1)).to_dataset(dim="band"), "NDVI")
        p = tile_dir / f"ndvi_lc08_20150716_r{i}c{j}.tif"  # its file name
        rs.write(ndvi_tile, p)  # save it
        files.append(p)  # remember the path
# write a STAC catalogue describing the four tiles
cat_path = rs.scale.export_stac(files, OUT / "stac", collection_id="onondaga-ndvi",
                                description="NDVI tiles from Landsat 8 OLI, 16 July 2015, Onondaga County NY",
                                datetimes=[acquired] * len(files),
                                properties={"platform": "landsat-8", "product": "NDVI",
                                            "eo:cloud_cover": mtl["CLOUD_COVER"]})
print("Catalog written to", cat_path, "| acquired", acquired)  # where the catalogue is


Catalog written to outputs/stac/catalog.json | acquired 2015-07-16 15:44:48+00:00




Code
# Open the catalog just written and list its items.
#
# pystac reads the JSON. A Catalog contains Collections; a Collection contains
# Items. Each Item has an id, a datetime, a bounding box, a CRS and one or
# more assets (the actual files). This is the same structure a remote STAC API
# returns for a search hit.

import pystac

catalog = pystac.Catalog.from_file(str(cat_path))  # open the catalogue
collection = next(catalog.get_children())  # its first collection

Searching means keeping the items whose footprint intersects the AOI and whose datetime falls in the window. Public APIs do this server-side; for a static catalog we filter in Python. Then we load the matching assets and mosaic them.


Code
# Search the local catalog the same way a STAC API search works, then load the hits.
#
# search_static keeps an item only when two things are true:
#   - its footprint intersects the AOI
#   - its datetime falls inside the requested window
# July 2015 should hit the tiles that touch Syracuse. August 2015 should hit none,
# because every tile is dated 16 July.
#
# The hits are then read, mosaicked (they are adjacent quarters of one scene)
# and clipped to the AOI. The left map is the search picture: footprints, the
# county, and the red AOI. The right map is the NDVI that search returned.

def search_static(items, aoi, start, end):
    geom = shape(rs.access.aoi_to_geojson(aoi))  # the AOI as a shapely geometry
    t0, t1 = pd.Timestamp(start, tz="UTC"), pd.Timestamp(end, tz="UTC")  # start and end as UTC timestamps
    # items that overlap the AOI and fall in the date range
    return [it for it in items if shape(it.geometry).intersects(geom) and t0 <= pd.Timestamp(it.datetime) <= t1]

hits = search_static(items, bbox, "2015-07-01", "2015-07-31")  # search July 2015
print("Items intersecting the Syracuse AOI:", [h.id for h in hits])  # the matches
# August 2015 has none
print("Items in the wrong month:", len(search_static(items, bbox, "2015-08-01", "2015-08-31")))

# read the matching tiles
arrays = [rs.read(Path(h.assets["data"].get_absolute_href())).squeeze("band", drop=True) for h in hits]
ndvi_mosaic = rs.mosaic(arrays, "first").squeeze()  # mosaic them
ndvi_aoi = rs.clip(ndvi_mosaic, syracuse)  # clip to the AOI
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))  # two panels
footprints = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"id": [it.id[-4:] for it in items]},  # item footprints as polygons
                              geometry=[shape(it.geometry) for it in items], crs=4326)
footprints.boundary.plot(ax=axes[0], color="k")  # their outlines
county.boundary.plot(ax=axes[0], color="grey", lw=0.8)  # county outline
for _, r in footprints.iterrows():  # each footprint
    # label it with the end of its ID
    axes[0].annotate(r.id, (r.geometry.centroid.x, r.geometry.centroid.y), ha="center")
syracuse.plot(ax=axes[0], color="tab:red", alpha=0.4)  # the AOI in red
axes[0].set_title("Item footprints, county outline and search AOI (red)")  # title
# the clipped NDVI
rs.viz.plot_raster(ndvi_aoi, ax=axes[1], cmap="RdYlGn", title="Loaded, mosaicked and clipped NDVI")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


Items intersecting the Syracuse AOI: ['ndvi_lc08_20150716_r0c0', 'ndvi_lc08_20150716_r0c1', 'ndvi_lc08_20150716_r1c0', 'ndvi_lc08_20150716_r1c1']
Items in the wrong month: 0









The Syracuse AOI lies exactly where the four tiles meet (the corner at about −76.20°, 43.02°), so all four items intersect it and are mosaicked. A search window in August returns nothing, because every item is dated 16 July 2015. The clipped mosaic has no seams: Onondaga Lake is strongly negative, downtown Syracuse and the highways are low, and the parks, wooded ravines and farmland around the city are green.

section: Searching public STAC catalogs and reading COGs over HTTP (live)
text:
Searching public STAC catalogs and reading COGs over HTTP (live)
rs.access.stac_search queries a STAC API. For Planetary Computer, asset URLs are signed automatically, so they can be read without an account. Below we look for Sentinel-2 L2A scenes over Syracuse in summer 2025 with less than 20 % cloud cover.


Code
# Live search: Sentinel-2 Level-2A over Syracuse, summer 2025, cloud cover under 20%.
#
# stac_search sends the AOI, the date window and the cloud limit to the catalogue
# and returns STAC Items. Nothing is downloaded yet: only the metadata.
# The table keeps a shortened id, the date, cloud percent and the MGRS tile
# (Sentinel-2's 100 km grid square). If the network or pystac-client is missing,
# the cell prints a skip message and leaves s2_items empty for the cells below.

if ONLINE and HAVE["pystac_client"]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    # Sentinel-2 L2A scenes over the AOI, June-August 2025, up to 20 % cloud
    s2_items = rs.access.stac_search("sentinel-2-l2a", aoi=bbox, dates=("2025-06-01", "2025-08-31"), max_cloud=20)
    # one row per scene: ID, date, cloud cover and tile
    table = pd.DataFrame([{"id": it.id[:44] + "…", "date": it.datetime.date(), "cloud %": round(it.properties["eo:cloud_cover"], 1),
                           "MGRS tile": it.properties.get("s2:mgrs_tile")} for it in s2_items]).sort_values("date")
    # number of scenes, run time and tiles
    print(f"{len(s2_items)} scenes found in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; tiles: {sorted(table['MGRS tile'].unique())}")
    display(table)  # show the table
else:
    s2_items = []  # nothing found
    # offline or missing package
    print("Offline or pystac-client missing: skipped. Online this lists matching Sentinel-2 scenes "
          "with dates, cloud cover and MGRS tile.")

The search returned 23 Sentinel-2 L2A items on 12 dates in about 3 seconds. Two MGRS tiles (18TUN and 18TVN) cover the AOI, and two relative orbits (R054 and R097) image it, so most dates have two items. The cloud percentage is for the whole 110 × 110 km tile, not the AOI. A “20 % cloud” scene can be clear over Syracuse or not, which is why per-pixel masks (SCL) still matter. The clearest date was 2 August 2025, with 0.5% and 0.2% cloud on the two tiles.
Each item lists its assets: one COG per band plus the scene classification (SCL), a true-colour visual image and metadata files.


Code
# From those search results, pick the clearest day and see what a scene contains.
#
# The clearest item is the one with the lowest eo:cloud_cover. Other items from
# the same date are the neighbouring MGRS tiles needed to cover the AOI.
# Listing asset keys shows the band files you can open (B04 is red). The href is
# a URL; the part before "?" is the Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF itself.

if s2_items:
    # the date of the least cloudy scene
    clear_day = min(s2_items, key=lambda it: it.properties["eo:cloud_cover"]).datetime.date()
    same_day = [it for it in s2_items if it.datetime.date() == clear_day]  # all scenes of that date
    # the date and its tiles
    print(f"Clearest date: {clear_day}; scenes that day: {[it.properties['s2:mgrs_tile'] for it in same_day]}")
    a = same_day[0].assets["B04"]  # the red band asset of the first scene
    print("Assets:", ", ".join(same_day[0].assets))  # all asset names
    # title, media type and URL of the red band
    print("B04:", a.title, "|", a.media_type, "|", a.href.split("?")[0][:110], "…")
else:
    same_day = []  # nothing to use
    print("Skipped (no search results).")  # explain


Clearest date: 2025-08-02; scenes that day: ['18TVN', '18TUN']
Assets: AOT, B01, B02, B03, B04, B05, B06, B07, B08, B09, B11, B12, B8A, SCL, WVP, visual, safe-manifest, granule-metadata, inspire-metadata, product-metadata, datastrip-metadata, tilejson, rendered_preview
B04: Band 4 - Red - 10m | image/tiff; application=geotiff; profile=cloud-optimized | https://sentinel2l2a01.blob.core.windows.net/sentinel2-l2/18/T/VN/2025/08/02/S2C_MSIL2A_20250802T154951_N0511_ …


Because each asset is a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF, rs.read can open it straight from its URL with Dask chunks. Clipping to the AOI before computing means GDAL fetches only the internal tiles that overlap Syracuse, a few megabytes instead of the 10,980 × 10,980-pixel band. The AOI crosses two MGRS tiles, so we read both scenes from the clearest day and mosaic them.
Sentinel-2 L2A products processed since 25 January 2022 (processing baseline 04.00) store reflectance as DN + 1000 scaled by 10,000. rs.optical.scale removes that offset; forgetting it biases every index.


Code
# Read only the AOI out of the Sentinel-2 COGs, then scale and compute NDVI.
#
# A Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF can be windowed over HTTP. chunks plus clip_box
# ask for the pixels inside the AOI and leave the rest of the tile on the server.
#
# 1. Project the AOI into the scene CRS and, for red (B04), NIR (B08) and the
#    visual overview, read each same-day tile and mosaic the pieces.
# 2. rs.optical.scale converts the integers to surface reflectance and removes
#    the Sentinel-2 baseline offset (boa_offset=-1000). Ignoring that offset
#    shifts NDVI; the two medians show by how much.
# 3. Draw the true-colour visual asset (scaled from 0-255) beside the NDVI.

if same_day:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    # EPSG code of the scenes
    crs = same_day[0].properties.get("proj:epsg") or same_day[0].properties.get("proj:code")
    aoi_native = syracuse.to_crs(crs).total_bounds  # AOI bounds in the scenes' CRS
    layers = {}  # one mosaic per band
    for band in ["B04", "B08", "visual"]:  # red, NIR and the true-colour image
        # read each scene lazily and keep only the AOI
        parts = [rs.read(it.assets[band].href, chunks={"x": 1024, "y": 1024}).rio.clip_box(*aoi_native) for it in same_day]
        layers[band] = rs.mosaic([p.compute() for p in parts], "first")  # load and mosaic
    # number of files read and run time
    print(f"Read {3 * len(same_day)} clipped COGs in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; "
          f"AOI grid {layers['B04'].shape[-2:]} at 10 m, {sum(v.nbytes for v in layers.values()) / 1e6:.0f} MB in memory")
    # red and NIR as a Dataset
    s2 = xr.Dataset({"B04": layers["B04"].squeeze(), "B08": layers["B08"].squeeze()})
    s2 = s2.assign_coords(time=pd.Timestamp(clear_day))  # add the date
    # DN -> reflectance, removing the 1,000 offset of newer products
    s2_sr = rs.optical.scale(s2, sensor="sentinel2", boa_offset=-1000)
    s2_ndvi = rs.optical.index(s2_sr, "NDVI", sensor="sentinel2")  # NDVI with the offset handled
    # NDVI without removing the offset (wrong)
    naive = rs.optical.index(s2 / 10_000, "NDVI", sensor="sentinel2")
    # the difference the offset makes
    print(f"Median NDVI: {float(s2_ndvi.median()):.3f} with the offset removed, "
          f"{float(naive.median()):.3f} if it is ignored")

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))  # two panels
    vis = layers["visual"].transpose("y", "x", "band").values  # true-colour image as (y, x, band)
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = layers["visual"].rio.bounds()  # its extent
    axes[0].imshow(np.nan_to_num(vis / 255.0), extent=[xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax])  # show it
    axes[0].set_title(f"Sentinel-2 true colour (visual asset), {clear_day}")  # title
    rs.viz.plot_raster(s2_ndvi.rio.write_crs(crs), ax=axes[1], cmap="RdYlGn", title="NDVI, 10 m")  # NDVI map
    for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
else:
    # offline
    print("Skipped (offline). Online this reads only the AOI from the Sentinel-2 COGs and maps NDVI.")


Read 6 clipped COGs in 38.8 s; AOI grid (1918, 2063) at 10 m, 79 MB in memory
Median NDVI: 0.671 with the offset removed, 0.440 if it is ignored









Reading the red, NIR and true-colour assets from both tiles, clipped to the AOI, took 25-40 seconds on this connection (it varies from run to run). It produced a 1,918 × 2,063 grid at 10 m (79 MB in memory), although each full band is 10,980 × 10,980 pixels. Only the internal COG tiles overlapping Syracuse were fetched.
The 10 m image resolves individual streets, the runways of Syracuse Hancock International Airport and the lakeshore far better than the 30 m Landsat scene of the STAC hands-on: build, search and load your own catalog section.
The offset matters. With the +1000 offset removed, the median NDVI is 0.671. Ignoring it gives 0.440, a 34% underestimate that would look like a real vegetation change.
For whole time series, rs.access.stac_load turns the search results into a lazy xarray Dataset (one variable per band, dimensions time × y × x) using odc-stac, which handles reprojection to a common grid and grouping by day.


Code
# Build a lazy time × y × x cube from the search hits.
#
# stac_load (via odc-stac) stacks every item onto one grid at 20 m, keeping
# red, NIR and the scene-classification layer. chunks makes the result a Dask
# array: the print shows the shape, but no pixel has been downloaded until
# something calls .compute(). Without odc-stac, or without search results, the
# cell explains what was skipped.

if s2_items and HAVE["odc.stac"]:
    # a lazy cube of all scenes on a 20 m grid
    cube_s2 = rs.access.stac_load(s2_items, bands=["B04", "B08", "SCL"], aoi=bbox, resolution=20,
                                  chunks={"x": 1024, "y": 1024})
    print(cube_s2)  # show its structure
    # nothing has been downloaded yet
    print(f"Lazy size: {cube_s2.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB across {cube_s2.sizes['time']} dates: nothing downloaded yet")
elif s2_items:  # odc-stac missing
    # how to install it
    print("odc-stac is not installed: install it with  pip install 'geolattice[rsense-access]'  to build lazy "
          "time × y × x cubes from search results.")
else:
    print("Skipped (offline).")  # offline


odc-stac is not installed: install it with  pip install 'geolattice[rsense-access]'  to build lazy time × y × x cubes from search results.

Even without odc-stac, the same searches show what each sensor offers for the AOI:


Code
# Ask the same question of four sensors: how many scenes cover this AOI and season?
#
# One AOI (Syracuse), one window (June-August 2025), four collections.
# Sentinel-2 and Landsat are filtered to cloud cover under 20%. MODIS 8-day
# composites and Sentinel-1 radar have no optical cloud field, so that filter
# is omitted. MODIS items store a start/end interval rather than a single
# datetime, so the date falls back to start_datetime.

if ONLINE and HAVE["pystac_client"]:
    rows = []  # one row per sensor
    # several collections to search
    for name, col, kw in [("Sentinel-2 L2A", "sentinel-2-l2a", {"max_cloud": 20}),
                          ("Landsat 8/9 C2 L2", "landsat-c2-l2", {"max_cloud": 20}),
                          ("MODIS MOD09A1 (8-day)", "modis-09A1-061", {}),
                          ("Sentinel-1 RTC", "sentinel-1-rtc", {})]:
        # search this collection
        found = rs.access.stac_search(col, aoi=bbox, dates=("2025-06-01", "2025-08-31"), **kw)
        # number of items found
        rows.append({"sensor": name, "collection": col, "items, Jun-Aug 2025": len(found),
                     "distinct dates": len({pd.Timestamp(it.datetime or it.properties["start_datetime"]).date()
                                            for it in found})})   # MODIS items carry a start/end interval
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("sensor"))  # show the table
else:
    print("Offline: skipped.")  # offline
