The MODIS row shows why you should check a catalogue’s completeness. The 10 items are five 8-day composite periods, each from both Terra (MOD09A1) and Aqua (MYD09A1), and they all start between 25 May and 26 June. When this notebook was run, Planetary Computer’s modis-09A1-061 collection had no composites for this tile between 26 June and 25 November 2025. The search was correct; the archive had a gap. Before concluding that “nothing happened” in a period, confirm that the data exist.


Code
# One-call loaders: search, scale, mask and stack in a single function.
#
# load_sentinel2 returns a time series of reflectance bands at 20 m.
# composite("median") collapses that series into one cloud-resistant image.
# MNDWI on the composite highlights water.
#
# The same pattern then opens a Landsat series, a MODIS series and a
# Sentinel-1 RTC series. Only the shapes are printed. odc-stac has to be
# installed; otherwise the cell says how to add it.

if ONLINE and HAVE["odc.stac"]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    # load Sentinel-2 surface reflectance for the summer
    s2 = rs.optical.load_sentinel2(bbox, ("2025-06-01", "2025-08-31"), max_cloud=30,
                                   bands=["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir16"], resolution=20)
    comp = s2.rs.composite("median").compute()  # median composite
    # number of scenes and run time
    print(f"Loaded and composited {s2.sizes['time']} scenes in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))  # two panels
    rs.viz.plot_rgb(comp, "true_color", ax=axes[0], title="Sentinel-2 summer median, Syracuse")  # true colour
    # MNDWI water index
    rs.viz.plot_raster(comp.rs.index("MNDWI"), ax=axes[1], cmap="Blues", title="MNDWI (water)")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

    # Landsat red and NIR, 2024-2025, at 60 m
    landsat_ts = rs.optical.load_landsat(bbox, ("2024-01-01", "2025-12-31"), bands=["red", "nir"], resolution=60)
    # MODIS red and NIR, 2025
    modis_ts = rs.optical.load_modis(bbox, ("2025-01-01", "2025-12-31"), bands=["red", "nir"])
    # Sentinel-1 RTC backscatter, July 2025
    s1 = rs.sar.load_rtc(bbox, ("2025-07-01", "2025-07-31"), polarizations=("vv", "vh"), orbit="descending", resolution=40)
    # every loaded dataset
    for name, d in [("Landsat 8/9", landsat_ts), ("MODIS 8-day", modis_ts), ("Sentinel-1 RTC", s1)]:
        # dates, grid size and variables
        print(f"{name:15s} {d.sizes['time']:3d} dates, grid {d.sizes['y']}×{d.sizes['x']}, vars {list(d.data_vars)}")
elif ONLINE:  # online but odc-stac missing
    # how to install it
    print("odc-stac is not installed, so the one-call loaders are skipped. Install the extra with\n"
          "    pip install 'geolattice[rsense-access]'\n"
          "and rerun: this cell then builds a cloud-free Sentinel-2 median and loads Landsat, MODIS and "
          "Sentinel-1 time series for the AOI.")
else:
    print("Offline: skipped.")  # offline

title: Data Discovery and Access
text:
Lazy loading with Dask
Whether data come from a catalog or a local file, the pattern is the same: open lazily with chunks, describe the computation, and compute only the result. Here the local Landsat file stands in for a remote COG.


Code
# A lazy Dask pipeline on the local Landsat file.
#
# chunks of 512 × 512 keep the read as a task graph. index() builds NDVI from
# the DNs without loading them: fine for showing the mechanics, not a physical
# NDVI, because the DNs have not been calibrated.
#
# clip to the Syracuse box, then mean().compute(), forces Dask to run. Only the
# chunks that overlap the AOI are read from disk. The task-graph size printed
# first is the plan; the mean is the result.

lazy = rs.read(L8_FILE, band_names=["blue", "green", "red", "nir"], chunks={"x": 512, "y": 512})
ndvi_lazy = rs.optical.index(lazy.to_dataset(dim="band"), "NDVI")              # DN-based, for illustration
# chunk size and number of tasks in the Dask graph
print("Chunks:", ndvi_lazy.data.chunksize, "| tasks in graph:", len(ndvi_lazy.data.__dask_graph__()))
print("Nothing computed yet:", type(ndvi_lazy.data).__name__)  # still a Dask array: nothing computed

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
# clip and average, then compute
aoi_mean = float(rs.clip(ndvi_lazy.rio.write_crs(lazy.rio.crs), syracuse).mean().compute())
# result and run time
print(f"Mean (DN-based) NDVI over the Syracuse AOI: {aoi_mean:.3f} (computed in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s, "
      "reading only the chunks that overlap the AOI)")


Chunks: (512, 512) | tasks in graph: 129
Nothing computed yet: Array
Mean (DN-based) NDVI over the Syracuse AOI: 0.379 (computed in 0.17 s, reading only the chunks that overlap the AOI)


The NDVI here is computed from raw DNs, which is fine for showing the lazy mechanics but not for analysis: DNs carry an additive offset, so DN-based NDVI differs from the reflectance-based values of the STAC hands-on: build, search and load your own catalog section. Always scale to reflectance first.

title: Data Discovery and Access
section: Data cubes with RasterCube and Zarr
text:
Data cubes with RasterCube and Zarr
A data cube stacks images of the same grid through time. RasterCube is a thin wrapper around an xarray Dataset (time, y, x) that adds construction from files, period selection, temporal resampling and Zarr persistence; cube.ds is always a plain Dataset.
We only have a single-date Landsat scene, so to practise the mechanics we simulate a two-year monthly NDVI series from the real July NDVI: each pixel greens up in spring and browns down in autumn, with the peak a little later on the higher southern hills, a smaller seasonal swing for dense forest, a winter low for everything, and random cloud gaps. The values are illustrative; the workflow is identical for a real Sentinel-2 or Landsat cube from the One-call loaders (live) section.


Code
# Simulate two years of monthly NDVI and open the files as a RasterCube.
#
# There is no local time series on disk, so this cell builds a plausible one
# from the July Landsat NDVI and the DEM:
#   - coarsen by 4 makes 120 m pixels, small enough to store 24 dates easily
#   - the seasonal peak is mid-July, up to two weeks later on the higher ground
#   - vegetated pixels (high July NDVI) swing the most; water and city swing least
#   - about 15% of pixels are punched out as cloud (NaN) at random
# RasterCube.from_files stacks the GeoTIFFs on a time axis. Displaying cube
# shows that stack without extra plotting.

base = rs.optical.index(landsat.coarsen(x=4, y=4, boundary="trim").mean().to_dataset(dim="band"), "NDVI")
base = base.rio.write_crs(landsat.rio.crs)                                     # 120 m July NDVI
dem = rs.mosaic([rs.read(p).squeeze("band", drop=True) for p in DEM_TILES])  # mosaic of the DEM tiles
elev = dem.astype("float32").rio.reproject_match(base).values  # elevation on the NDVI grid
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)  # random generator
dates = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=24, freq="MS") + pd.Timedelta("14D")  # 24 monthly dates (mid-month)
peak_doy = 197 + (np.clip(elev, 100, 650) - 100) / 550 * 14         # mid-July, up to two weeks later on the hills
amp = np.clip(base.values - 0.25, 0.1, 0.6)                          # vegetated pixels swing most, water and city least
paths = []  # file paths of the monthly images
for t in dates:  # every date
    phase = np.cos(2 * np.pi * (t.dayofyear - peak_doy) / 365.25)    # +1 at the peak, −1 in midwinter
    # seasonal NDVI that varies with elevation, plus noise
    img = base.values - amp * (1 - phase) / 2 + rng.normal(0, 0.02, base.shape)
    clouds = rng.random(base.shape) < 0.15  # random 15 % cloud cover
    p = OUT / "cube" / f"ndvi_{t:%Y%m%d}.tif"; p.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # file name and folder
    # save the month with clouds as NaN
    rs.write(base.copy(data=np.where(clouds, np.nan, img).astype("float32")).rename("ndvi"), p)
    paths.append(p)  # remember the path
cube = rs.RasterCube.from_files(paths, dates, band_names=["ndvi"])  # build a cube from the files and dates
cube  # show it

Code
# Three time-axis operations on the cube.
#
# sel_period keeps June, July and August across both years.
# resample("QS-DEC", "median") builds seasonal medians. "QS-DEC" means quarters
# that start in December, so winter is Dec-Feb rather than Jan-Mar.
# valid_fraction is the share of finite pixels on each date (the rest are the
# cloud holes written above). head() shows the first few dates only.

summer = cube.sel_period("2024-01-01", "2025-12-31", months=[6, 7, 8])
seasonal = cube.resample("QS-DEC", "median")  # seasonal (quarterly) median composites
# number of summer scenes and composites
print("Summer scenes:", len(summer.times), "| seasonal composites:", len(seasonal.times))
cube.valid_fraction().to_series().round(3).head()  # share of valid pixels in the first dates

Code
# Extract a time series at three named points and map one seasonal composite.
#
# The cube is in the Landsat CRS, so longitude/latitude have to be transformed
# before they can index it. plot_timeseries draws one line per point.
# isel(time=2) is one seasonal median (the third quarter in the resampled cube).

from pyproj import Transformer
to_cube = Transformer.from_crs(4326, cube.crs, always_xy=True)  # lon/lat -> cube CRS
# three points in lon/lat
lonlat = {"Syracuse (downtown)": (-76.147, 43.048), "Green Lakes State Park (forest)": (-75.970, 43.058),
          "Highland Forest (upland, 400 m)": (-75.935, 42.855)}
pts = {k: to_cube.transform(*v) for k, v in lonlat.items()}  # the points in the cube CRS
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.6))  # two panels
# NDVI time series at the points
rs.viz.plot_timeseries(cube["ndvi"], pts, ax=axes[0]); axes[0].set_title("Simulated monthly NDVI at three points")
seasonal["ndvi"].isel(time=2).plot(ax=axes[1], cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0, vmax=0.85)  # one seasonal composite
# title, no ticks
axes[1].set_title(f"Seasonal median starting {seasonal.times[2]:%b %Y}"); axes[1].set_xticks([]); axes[1].set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









The simulated series behave as designed:

The forest points (Green Lakes and Highland Forest) cycle between about 0.25 in winter and 0.6 in July.
Downtown Syracuse stays between 0.1 and 0.2 all year.
Gaps are the simulated cloud masks. About 66% of each date is valid: 77% of pixels lie inside the county, and 15% of those are clouded.

The June-August 2024 seasonal median map is the July NDVI pattern again: lakes, city and highways low, everything else green. Real cubes from the One-call loaders (live) section work exactly the same way.
Large cubes belong in Zarr: chunked, compressed and readable in parallel from disk or cloud storage. rs.scale.to_zarr_cube writes with sensible chunks (512 × 512 pixels, full time) and can append new dates as they arrive, the usual pattern for monitoring systems.


Code
# Save the cube as Zarr, in two appends, and read it back.
#
# A Zarr store can grow along time. The first call writes year 1 (dates 0-11).
# The second appends year 2 on the time dimension. open_cube reopens the store
# lazily. The last line checks that the values, including the cloud NaNs, match
# the cube still held in memory.

store = OUT / "ndvi_cube.zarr"
rs.scale.to_zarr_cube(cube.ds.isel(time=slice(0, 12)), store)               # first year
rs.scale.to_zarr_cube(cube.ds.isel(time=slice(12, 24)), store, append_dim="time")   # append second year
z = rs.scale.open_cube(store)  # open the saved Zarr cube
# size, chunks and CRS
print("Zarr cube:", dict(z.sizes), "| chunks:", z["ndvi"].data.chunksize, "| CRS:", z.rio.crs)
# same values as the in-memory cube
print("Identical to the in-memory cube:", bool(np.allclose(z["ndvi"].values, cube["ndvi"].values, equal_nan=True)))

title: Data Discovery and Access
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

STAC organises imagery as catalogs, collections, items and assets; search by collection, AOI, date and properties, then load only the assets and pixels you need.
Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs can be read straight from their URLs; clipping before computing fetches only the overlapping internal tiles.
Check product conventions such as the Sentinel-2 +1000 offset before computing indices.
The loaders of geolattice.rsense combine search, lazy loading, scaling, cloud masking and band naming in one call (extra rsense-access).
Keep credentials in environment variables; Planetary Computer and Earth Search need none.
Work lazily with Dask, store cubes in Zarr, and publish your own products as STAC.

Exercises

(Online) Repeat the Sentinel-2 search for your own AOI and plot cloud cover against date. How many scenes pass a 10 % threshold?
(Online) Search the same AOI with catalog="earth-search" and compare the item count and asset names with Planetary Computer.
Filter the local catalog by its eo:cloud_cover property in search_static.
(Online) Read the SCL asset for the clearest day and mask clouds and water before computing the NDVI median.
Resample the simulated cube to annual maxima and map the year-to-year difference.
(Online, Earthdata account) Search HLS for your AOI with rs.optical.load_hls(..., product="both") and count how many more observations you get than with Landsat alone.

Next: The companion notebook (09_01_04) maps every get_images call. The optical notebooks (07_02) then begin with MODIS, the daily global workhorse.

Overview
This module sets up the tools used for the rest of the course and introduces the building blocks every remote sensing workflow in Python relies on: NumPy arrays, labelled xarray objects, georeferencing with rioxarray, vector data with GeoPandas, lazy computation with Dask, and the CPU/GPU backend of GeoLattice’s remote sensing toolkit, geolattice.rsense.

Build and reproject vector data with GeoPandas and Shapely.

text:
Installing the environment
GeoLattice needs the compiled GDAL and PROJ libraries, with Python GDAL bindings that match the installed GDAL. Install those first (conda-forge or your system package manager), then install GeoLattice from its repository with the extras you need.
Option A: conda / mamba (recommended). Compiled geospatial libraries install most reliably from conda-forge. Save this as environment.yml next to your GeoLattice clone:
name: geolattice
channels: [conda-forge]
dependencies:
  - python=3.11
  - gdal
  - rasterio
  - rioxarray
  - geopandas
  - xarray
  - dask
  - jupyterlab
  - pip
  - pip:
      - -e "./GeoLattice[rsense,rsense-access,rsense-classify,rsense-viz,rsense-scale]"
then run mamba env create -f environment.yml and mamba activate geolattice.
Option B: pip. With GDAL already installed, from the root of the GeoLattice repository:
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e ".[rsense,rsense-access,rsense-classify,rsense-viz,rsense-scale]" jupyterlab
or build and install a wheel (python -m build, then pip install "dist/geolattice-0.3.9-*.whl[rsense]").
The remote sensing extras of GeoLattice are:







Extra
Adds




rsense
Core: xarray, rioxarray, rasterio, scikit-image, geopandas


rsense-access
STAC, Planetary Computer, odc-stac, earthaccess


rsense-sar, rsense-insar
ASF search and sarsen; HyP3 SDK and h5py


rsense-lidar, rsense-uav
laspy and cloth-simulation filter; pyodm (OpenDroneMap)


rsense-classify, rsense-xai
scikit-learn and XGBoost; SHAP


rsense-dl
PyTorch, TorchGeo, segmentation-models-pytorch, Lightning


rsense-gee, rsense-viz
Earth Engine API and xee; matplotlib and leafmap


rsense-scale, rsense-apps
Dask distributed, Zarr, pystac; Streamlit templates


rsense-gpu
CuPy for CUDA 12


rsense-all
Every group except rsense-gpu



GPU (optional, NVIDIA). Add CuPy (and optionally cuCIM) matching your CUDA version:
pip install -e ".[rsense-gpu]"
pip install --extra-index-url=https://pypi.nvidia.com cuml-cu12   # GPU machine learning (optional)
Google Colab. Upload or clone the GeoLattice repository into the session, then run !pip install -e "./GeoLattice[rsense,rsense-viz]" in the first cell. Choose Runtime → Change runtime type → GPU and add the rsense-gpu extra to use the GPU.
If import geolattice fails with libgdal.so... cannot open shared object file or No module named '_gdal', the GDAL bindings do not match the GDAL library; the Troubleshooting section of the GeoLattice README explains the fix.

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
text:
Checking the installation and hardware
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Setup for the Python geospatial environment notebook.
#
# 1. Show plots inside the notebook, and hide noisy UserWarnings from matplotlib
#    and the geospatial libraries.
# 2. Import the core stack: NumPy (arrays), pandas (tables), xarray (labelled
#    arrays), GeoPandas (vector data) and matplotlib (plots).
# 3. Import geolattice and the remote-sensing package geolattice.rsense as rs.
# 4. Set a sharp figure style, then print the package versions so the run is
#    reproducible.

%matplotlib inline
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import time                 # used later to time CPU vs GPU work
from pathlib import Path    # file and folder paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing subpackage

# figure resolution and a light grid
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3})
print("geolattice", geolattice.__version__, "| geolattice.rsense", rs.__version__)  # versions


geolattice 0.3.49 | geolattice.rsense 0.3.49


rs.info() reports library versions and every compute device geolattice.rsense can see. Include it in bug reports. (The key pyrsense_backend keeps the name used by PyRSense, from which geolattice.rsense was ported.)

# Inspect the current geolattice.rsense environment.

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
section: CPU and GPU backends in geolattice.rsense
text:
CPU and GPU backends in geolattice.rsense
geolattice.rsense runs the same code on the CPU (NumPy) or an NVIDIA GPU (CuPy). You choose the backend once; every native algorithm then computes on it:

rs.set_backend("auto") picks CUDA if available, then Apple MPS (deep learning only), then CPU.
rs.set_backend("cuda:1") selects a specific GPU.
with rs.device("cuda"): ... switches temporarily.
On a machine without CUDA, requesting "cuda" falls back to the CPU with a warning instead of crashing, so notebooks run anywhere. Asking for a GPU index that does not exist on a CUDA machine is a configuration error and raises ValueError.



Code
# Choose the array backend, then temporarily override it.
#
# geolattice.rsense runs the same functions on NumPy (CPU) or CuPy (NVIDIA GPU).
# rs.set_backend("auto") picks CUDA when a GPU is available, otherwise CPU.
#
# 1. Turn auto mode on and print whether array math will use the GPU.
# 2. rs.device("cpu") is a context manager: code inside the block runs on the
#    CPU, then the previous backend is restored. The print after the block
#    should match the print before it.
# 3. Asking for a device that does not exist (cuda:7) raises ValueError, or a
#    fallback warning on a CPU-only machine. Catch that so the notebook continues.

backend = rs.set_backend("auto")
# the backend and whether array maths runs on the GPU
print("Active backend:", backend, "| array math on GPU:", backend.array_gpu)

with rs.device("cpu") as b:  # temporarily switch to the CPU backend
    print("Inside a CPU block:", b)  # the backend inside the block
print("After the block:", rs.get_backend())  # back to the previous backend

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:  # record warnings instead of printing them
    warnings.simplefilter("always")  # record every warning, even repeated ones
    try:
        with rs.device("cuda:7"):  # ask for a GPU that does not exist
            pass
    except ValueError as err:
        print("Requesting cuda:7 →", err)  # the error message
    for w in caught:                                   # on a CPU-only machine: the fallback warning
        print("Warning:", str(w.message)[:90], "...")  # the first 90 characters of each warning


Active backend: cuda:0 | array math on GPU: True
Inside a CPU block: cpu
After the block: cuda:0
Requesting cuda:7 → cuda:7 requested but only 1 CUDA device(s) found


rs.to_device() and rs.to_cpu() move NumPy arrays, DataArrays and Datasets between host and GPU memory; coordinates stay on the host. Native functions return results in the same memory space as their input, so you can keep CPU data and still get GPU speed by changing only the backend.


Code
# Move an array between host (CPU) memory and device (GPU) memory.
#
# 1. Build a small random float32 cube: 4 bands × 512 × 512 pixels.
# 2. rs.to_device sends it to the active backend. On a GPU machine that is CuPy;
#    on CPU it stays NumPy. rs.to_cpu always brings it back to NumPy.
# 3. memory_report() summarises device memory use.
# 4. recommend_chunks suggests Dask chunk sizes for a much larger cube
#    (10 dates × 20,000 × 20,000), aiming for about 128 MB per chunk.

arr = np.random.default_rng(0).random((4, 512, 512), dtype=np.float32)
on_dev = rs.to_device(arr)  # move the array to the active device (a no-op on the CPU)
# module of the array before and after copying back to the CPU
print(type(on_dev).__module__, "→", type(rs.to_cpu(on_dev)).__module__)
print("Memory:", rs.backend.memory_report())  # memory available on the device
# chunk sizes Dask should use for a large cube
print("Suggested Dask chunks for a 10-date 20,000 × 20,000 cube:",
      rs.backend.recommend_chunks((10, 20_000, 20_000), "float32", target_mb=128))


cupy → numpy
Memory: {'backend': 'cuda:0', 'host_total_gb': 132.3, 'host_free_gb': 116.96, 'gpu_free_gb': 16.51, 'cupy_pool_used_gb': 0.004}
Suggested Dask chunks for a 10-date 20,000 × 20,000 cube: (10, 1536, 1536)


On this machine "auto" selected the NVIDIA GPU (cuda:0), so the rest of the notebook runs on it wherever geolattice.rsense computes. rs.to_device turned the NumPy array into a CuPy array and rs.to_cpu brought it back. On a CPU-only machine the same cells run unchanged and report cpu.
Array computations use float32 by default, which halves memory compared with float64 and is ample for reflectance and backscatter. rs.backend.set_precision("float64") switches it if needed.

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
text:
NumPy: images are arrays
A single-band image is a 2-D array (rows × columns); a multispectral image is 3-D (bands × rows × columns). Most remote sensing operations are array operations: arithmetic between bands, boolean masks and statistics. Here we build a tiny synthetic 4-band “scene” with a lake and a field to practise.


Code
# Build a tiny synthetic 4-band reflectance image (blue, green, red, NIR).
#
# A real satellite image is just a numeric array. This one is 100 rows by 120
# columns so the later steps are easy to see.
#
# 1. mgrid makes row and column index grids.
# 2. A circle becomes a lake and a rectangle becomes a crop field. Every other
#    pixel is bare soil. Each surface gets its own reflectance in the four bands,
#    plus a little Gaussian noise.
# 3. The top-left 5×5 pixels are set to NaN, which is how rasters mark missing data.
# 4. Print the shape and the NIR mean, ignoring those NaNs.

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
rows, cols = 100, 120  # image size
yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:rows, 0:cols]  # row and column index of every pixel
lake = (yy - 40) ** 2 + (xx - 35) ** 2 < 15 ** 2          # circle: a lake
field = (yy > 55) & (xx > 60)                             # rectangle: a crop field

# reflectance per band for background soil, lake and field (blue, green, red, nir)
soil, water, crop = [0.08, 0.12, 0.16, 0.25], [0.06, 0.05, 0.03, 0.01], [0.04, 0.08, 0.05, 0.45]
img = np.empty((4, rows, cols), dtype=np.float32)  # empty 4-band image
for b in range(4):  # each band
    # water, crop or bare soil value plus a little noise
    img[b] = np.where(lake, water[b], np.where(field, crop[b], soil[b])) + rng.normal(0, 0.01, (rows, cols))
img[:, :5, :5] = np.nan                                # a patch of missing data

print("shape (bands, rows, cols):", img.shape, "| dtype:", img.dtype)  # shape and data type
print("NIR mean, ignoring NaN:", round(float(np.nanmean(img[3])), 3))  # mean NIR, ignoring missing values


shape (bands, rows, cols): (4, 100, 120) | dtype: float32
NIR mean, ignoring NaN: 0.279




Code
# Band math and a simple water mask on the synthetic image.
#
# NDVI = (NIR − red) / (NIR + red). Vegetation is high (the crop), water is
# negative (the lake), soil sits in between.
#
# 1. Pull red (band index 2) and NIR (band index 3) and compute NDVI element-wise.
# 2. Treat NDVI < 0 as water and compare that count with the true lake area.
# 3. Draw three panels: a brightened RGB, the NDVI map, and the boolean water mask.

red, nir = img[2], img[3]
ndvi = (nir - red) / (nir + red)                       # element-wise band math
water_mask = ndvi < 0                                  # boolean mask
# detected water pixels vs the true lake size
print(f"Water pixels: {water_mask.sum()} (true lake area: {lake.sum()})")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.8))  # three panels
# imshow expects (row, col, band), so move the band axis from the front to the end.
# Multiplying by 4 just brightens dark reflectance for display.
axes[0].imshow(np.clip(img[[2, 1, 0]].transpose(1, 2, 0) * 4, 0, 1)); axes[0].set_title("RGB (×4 brightened)")
# NDVI with a colour bar
im = axes[1].imshow(ndvi, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=-0.5, vmax=0.9); axes[1].set_title("NDVI"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1])
axes[2].imshow(water_mask, cmap="Blues"); axes[2].set_title("NDVI < 0 (water)")  # the water mask
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


Water pixels: 636 (true lake area: 697)









Two habits avoid most beginner bugs: convert integers to float before division (integer DNs overflow or truncate), and use NaN-aware functions (np.nanmean, np.nanpercentile) when images contain missing data.


Code
# Show why remote-sensing math should use float, not integer digital numbers.
#
# Landsat DNs are often stored as uint16 (0 to 65,535). Adding two large uint16
# values wraps around instead of overflowing to a bigger number. Casting to
# float32 first gives the true sum. The same trap appears in radiance and
# reflectance scaling, so convert to float before any band math.

dn = np.array([60000, 50000], dtype=np.uint16)
# uint16 wraps around on overflow; float does not
print("uint16 sum overflows:", dn + dn, "| as float:", dn.astype(np.float32) + dn)


uint16 sum overflows: [54464 34464] | as float: [120000. 100000.]

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
text:
Xarray: arrays with coordinates
Raw arrays lose track of where and when each pixel is. xarray attaches named dimensions and coordinate labels, so you select by map coordinates or dates instead of indices. A DataArray is one labelled array; a Dataset is a collection of DataArrays sharing coordinates, a natural fit for one variable per band. geolattice.rsense is built on xarray.


Code
# Wrap the NumPy image as an xarray DataArray with real map coordinates.
#
# A plain array only knows "row 10, column 20". xarray also stores what those
# axes mean: band name, easting and northing.
#
# 1. Build 10 m pixel centres. Easting increases to the right. Northing
#    decreases as you go down the image, which is how map coordinates work.
# 2. Attach band names (blue, green, red, nir) and a units/sensor label.
# 3. Displaying scene prints the dimensions, coordinates and attributes.

x = 400_000 + 10 * (np.arange(cols) + 0.5)          # 10 m pixels, UTM easting
y = 4_700_000 - 10 * (np.arange(rows) + 0.5)        # northing decreases down the image
scene = xr.DataArray(img, dims=("band", "y", "x"),  # the array as a labelled DataArray: band, y and x
                     coords={"band": ["blue", "green", "red", "nir"], "y": y, "x": x},
                     name="reflectance", attrs={"units": "reflectance", "sensor": "synthetic"})
scene  # show it

# Compute spectral indices with rs.optical.index on the band Dataset.
#
# The function looks up each index formula from the canonical band names
# (red, nir, and so on). Here we ask for NDVI, NDWI and SAVI, then take the

rs.optical.index(ds, ["NDVI", "NDWI", "SAVI"]).mean().to_pandas().round(3)


NDVI    0.295
NDWI   -0.364

xarray shines with time series. We simulate a season of NDVI for this scene, with a growing crop field, and use label-based time selection, resampling and grouping.


Code
# Build a small NDVI time cube and summarise it.
#
# 1. Dates every 5 days from April through October. A Gaussian bump centred on
#    day-of-year 200 stands in for crop green-up and senescence. Field pixels
#    follow that curve; everywhere else stays near 0.12 (soil), plus noise.
# 2. resample(time="1MS") collapses the 5-day series to monthly means.
# 3. Average the cube over the field and plot that series next to the July map.

dates = pd.date_range("2026-04-01", "2026-10-31", freq="5D")
doy = dates.dayofyear.values  # day of year of each date
season = 0.15 + 0.65 * np.exp(-((doy - 200) / 35.0) ** 2)                 # crop green-up and harvest
# crop NDVI follows the seasonal curve, the rest stays near 0.12, plus noise
ndvi_t = np.where(field, season[:, None, None], 0.12) + rng.normal(0, 0.02, (len(dates), rows, cols))
# the time series as a DataArray (time, y, x)
cube = xr.DataArray(ndvi_t.astype("float32"), dims=("time", "y", "x"),
                    coords={"time": dates, "y": y, "x": x}, name="ndvi")

monthly = cube.resample(time="1MS").mean()  # monthly means
# mean NDVI of the crop field on each date
field_series = cube.where(xr.DataArray(field, dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": y, "x": x})).mean(("y", "x"))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.8))  # two panels
# the field's time series
field_series.plot(ax=axes[0], marker="o", ms=3); axes[0].set_title("Mean NDVI of the crop field")
monthly.sel(time="2026-07").squeeze().plot(ax=axes[1], cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0, vmax=0.9)  # the July mean map
axes[1].set_title("July mean NDVI")  # title
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
text:
Rioxarray: georeferencing
Coordinates alone don’t say which coordinate system they are in. rioxarray adds the .rio accessor (loaded automatically by geolattice.rsense), which stores the CRS and exposes the affine transform, bounds and resolution, and powers reprojection, clipping and writing.


Code
# Attach a coordinate reference system with rioxarray.
#
# Coordinates alone do not say which system they are in. rio.write_crs tags the
# array as EPSG:32618 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 18N). It does not warp the pixels.
#
# Then print four things rioxarray can now answer: the CRS, the pixel size,
# the geographic bounds, and the affine transform that maps pixel index to
# map coordinates.

scene = scene.rio.write_crs("EPSG:32618")             # WGS 84 / UTM zone 18N
print("CRS:        ", scene.rio.crs)  # coordinate reference system
print("Resolution: ", scene.rio.resolution())  # pixel size
print("Bounds:     ", scene.rio.bounds())  # extent
print("Transform:\n", scene.rio.transform())  # affine transform (pixel -> map)


CRS:         EPSG:32618
Resolution:  (10.0, -10.0)
Bounds:      (400000.0, 4699000.0, 401200.0, 4700000.0)
Transform:
 | 10.00, 0.00, 400000.00|
| 0.00,-10.00, 4700000.00|
| 0.00, 0.00, 1.00|


The affine transform maps pixel (column, row) to map (x, y): \(x = a\,col + b\,row + c\), \(y = d\,col + e\,row + f\). Here \(a = 10\) m, \(e = -10\) m (rows go south) and \((c, f)\) is the upper-left corner.

#
# 1. Four Onondaga County DEM tiles, used for the mosaic in the next cell.
# 2. One Landsat 9 Level-2 NIR band (SR_B5), used later for the lazy-read demo.
# 3. Print the file names and how large the Landsat band is on disk.

DATA = Path("../../../../Data/00_shared/data_remote_sensing")

         / "LC09_L2SP_138043_20221216_20221223_02_T1_SR_B5.TIF")

# Read the DEM tiles and mosaic them onto one grid.
#
# 1. rs.read opens each GeoTIFF. squeeze drops a length-1 band dimension so the
#    result is a 2-D elevation map.
# 2. Print each tile's shape and bounds, which should meet at shared edges.
# 3. rs.mosaic merges them. Then report the mosaic CRS, shape, resolution in
#    degrees, the elevation range, and a UTM zone that would suit this area.

tiles = [rs.read(p).squeeze("band", drop=True) for p in DEM_TILES]
for p, t in zip(DEM_TILES, tiles):  # each tile
    print(f"{p.name}: shape {t.shape}, bounds {[round(v, 3) for v in t.rio.bounds()]}")  # its shape and bounds

dem = rs.mosaic(tiles)                                     # merge the four tiles onto one grid
print("\nMosaic CRS:", dem.rio.crs, "| shape:", dem.shape,  # CRS and shape of the mosaic
      "| resolution (deg):", [round(r, 6) for r in dem.rio.resolution()])
print(f"Elevation range: {float(dem.min()):.0f}-{float(dem.max()):.0f} m")  # elevation range

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
text:
GeoPandas and Shapely: vector data
Field plots, administrative boundaries and training samples are vector data. GeoPandas is pandas with a geometry column; Shapely provides the geometry operations. We create three sites inside the Onondaga DEM, reproject them to UTM so distances are in metres, and buffer them.


Code
# Vector workflow: study sites as points, then project, buffer and sample elevation.
#
# 1. Three sites are stored as longitude/latitude points (EPSG:4326).
# 2. estimate_utm_crs picks a local UTM zone. Buffering by 5,000 only means
#    5 km after that reprojection, because degrees are not metres.
# 3. Distance between Syracuse and Green Lakes is then a straight line in metres.
# 4. Sample the DEM at each original lon/lat point (nearest pixel) and drop the
#    buffer column so the table stays compact.

sites = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"site": ["Syracuse", "Onondaga Lake", "Green Lakes State Park"],
     "landcover": ["urban", "lake", "forest and meromictic lakes"]},
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy([-76.147, -76.205, -75.970], [43.048, 43.090, 43.058]), crs=4326)
utm = rs.core.estimate_utm_crs(sites)  # UTM zone for the sites
sites_utm = sites.to_crs(utm)  # reproject to metres
sites_utm["buffer_5km"] = sites_utm.buffer(5_000)          # 5 km, because the CRS is in metres
print("Projected CRS:", sites_utm.crs)  # the projected CRS
print("Distance Syracuse → Green Lakes State Park: "  # a distance in kilometres
      f"{sites_utm.geometry.iloc[0].distance(sites_utm.geometry.iloc[2]) / 1000:.1f} km")
# Sample elevation in geographic coordinates: the DEM itself is still lon/lat.
sites_utm["elevation_m"] = [float(dem.sel(x=pt.x, y=pt.y, method="nearest")) for pt in sites.geometry]
sites_utm.drop(columns="buffer_5km")  # show the table without the buffer column

# Map the DEM with the study sites and their 5 km buffers.
#
# imshow needs an extent (left, right, bottom, top) so the axes are longitude
# and latitude rather than pixel index. The buffers were built in UTM, so they
# are projected back to EPSG:4326 before drawing. Site names are offset a few
# points up and to the right of each marker.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5.5))
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = dem.rio.bounds()  # extent of the DEM
im = ax.imshow(dem.values, cmap="terrain", extent=[xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax])  # the DEM in map coordinates
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Elevation (m)", shrink=0.8)  # colour bar

sites.plot(ax=ax, color="red", markersize=40)  # the sites
for _, r in sites.iterrows():  # each site
    # its name
    ax.annotate(r.site, (r.geometry.x, r.geometry.y), xytext=(5, 5), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("Study sites and 5 km buffers on the Onondaga County DEM")  # title
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude"); ax.set_ylabel("Latitude")  # axis labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









The four tiles share one grid, so rs.mosaic joins them into a 443 × 534 DEM covering 108-623 m, from the Onondaga Lake shore up to the hills of the southern county. The site elevations sampled from it are plausible: Onondaga Lake 110 m, Syracuse 121 m and Green Lakes 145 m. rs.core.estimate_utm_crs chose UTM zone 18N (EPSG:32618) for the area, so distances (14.5 km from Syracuse to Green Lakes) and the 5 km buffers are in metres. Buffering in degrees would give ellipses whose size depends on latitude.

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
section: Dask and tiled processing for large rasters
text:
Dask and tiled processing for large rasters
A single Sentinel-2 tile is about 10,980 × 10,980 pixels per band; a multi-year stack quickly exceeds memory. Two tools keep memory bounded:

Dask splits arrays into chunks and builds a lazy task graph; nothing is computed until you call .compute(). Pass chunks= to rs.read to get Dask-backed data.
rs.apply_tiled runs a function tile by tile with an overlap (“halo”) so moving-window filters have no seams, either looping on the active backend or via Dask’s map_overlap.



Code
# Lazy (Dask) read of a large Landsat 9 band.
#
# chunks={"x": 1024, "y": 1024} tells rasterio/Dask to keep the file as a grid
# of blocks. Nothing is read from disk until .compute().
#
# 1. Open the NIR band and print the Dask array (a plan, not the pixels).
# 2. Report how many pixels that is, and how much RAM a full float32 load would take.
# 3. Ask for min, mean and max. Only the chunks needed for those reductions are read.
#    Time that step.

lazy = rs.read(L9_B5, chunks={"x": 1024, "y": 1024}).squeeze("band", drop=True)
print(lazy.data)                                         # a Dask array: nothing loaded yet
# size of the lazily opened image
print(f"{lazy.size / 1e6:.1f} million pixels, {lazy.nbytes / 1e6:.0f} MB as float32 once loaded")
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
# statistics are only planned, not computed yet
stats = {"min": lazy.min(), "mean": lazy.mean(), "max": lazy.max()}
stats = {k: float(v.compute()) for k, v in stats.items()}  # compute them now
# the results and the run time
print({k: round(v, 1) for k, v in stats.items()}, f"computed in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")


dask.array<getitem, shape=(5565, 5571), dtype=float32, chunksize=(1024, 1024), chunktype=numpy.ndarray>
31.0 million pixels, 124 MB as float32 once loaded
{'min': 7483.0, 'mean': 15626.6, 'max': 27451.0} computed in 0.73 s




Code
# Compare a whole-image filter with the same filter run in tiles.
#
# 1. Load a 2048 × 2048 window. SciPy's uniform_filter smooths that whole array
#    on the CPU (a 9×9 moving average).
# 2. rs.apply_tiled runs the same filter in 512-pixel tiles with a 4-pixel
#    overlap, using SciPy or CuPy to match the active backend.
# 3. Compare the interior, dropping the overlap, and print the largest difference.
#    A correct tiled run should agree with the full-array result.

from scipy.ndimage import uniform_filter

block = lazy.isel(y=slice(1500, 3548), x=slice(1500, 3548)).load()             # a 2048 × 2048 window
full = uniform_filter(block.values, 9)                                          # whole array, SciPy on CPU
smooth = lambda b: rs.backend.ndimage(b).uniform_filter(b, 9)                   # SciPy or CuPy, matching b
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
# apply the filter tile by tile, with a 4-pixel overlap
tiled = rs.apply_tiled(block, smooth, tile=512, overlap=4)
# run time and result type
print(f"Tiled on backend {rs.get_backend()} in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s; result type:",
      type(tiled.data).__module__)
inner = (slice(4, -4), slice(4, -4))                                            # drop the overlap border
# difference between the whole-image and tiled results
diff = np.abs(rs.to_cpu(tiled).values[inner] - full[inner])
print("Max difference between whole-image and tiled result:", float(np.nanmax(diff)))  # the largest difference


Tiled on backend cuda:0 in 0.03 s; result type: numpy
Max difference between whole-image and tiled result: 0.00390625


With a 4-pixel halo (the radius of a 9×9 window) the tiled result matches filtering the whole image. The largest difference is 0.004 on values near 15,000, a relative difference of about 3 × 10⁻⁷, which is float32 rounding: the GPU sums the window in a different order. Only one 512 × 512 tile (plus halo) is processed at a time, which keeps big rasters within GPU memory.
The lambda uses rs.backend.ndimage(b), which returns scipy.ndimage for NumPy blocks and cupyx.scipy.ndimage for CuPy blocks. Because apply_tiled passes GPU blocks when the backend is CUDA, the same function works on either backend. The input was a NumPy-backed DataArray, so the result came back in host memory.

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
text:
Benchmarking CPU (and GPU) performance
Here we time the Refined Lee speckle filter of geolattice.rsense (see the radar notebooks, 07_03) on a synthetic SAR image. When a CUDA GPU is present the second timing runs on the GPU with no code change; otherwise the cell reports that no GPU is present.


Code
# Benchmark a SAR speckle filter (refined Lee) on CPU versus GPU.
#
# 1. Synthetic gamma-distributed backscatter mimics multi-look radar intensity
#    on a 2048 × 2048 grid.
# 2. timed() runs the function once as a warm-up (GPU kernels compile on the
#    first call), then averages several repeats. If the result is a CuPy array,
#    the clock waits until the GPU has actually finished.
# 3. Always time the CPU. If CUDA is available, also time the GPU with data
#    starting on the host (transfers included) and with data already on the device.
# 4. Compare CPU and GPU pixel values. Tiny differences are normal; large ones are not.
# 5. With no GPU, print a skip message instead of failing.

sar = (0.1 * rng.gamma(4.4, 1 / 4.4, (2048, 2048))).astype("float32")

def timed(fn, *a, repeat=3):  # average run time of a function
    fn(*a)                                    # warm-up (GPU kernels compile on first call)
    t = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    for _ in range(repeat):  # run it several times
        out = fn(*a)  # call it
    if type(out).__module__.startswith("cupy"):  # GPU results are computed asynchronously
        import cupy  # CuPy
        cupy.cuda.Device().synchronize()       # wait for queued GPU work before stopping the clock
    return (time.perf_counter() - t) / repeat  # mean time per run

with rs.device("cpu"):  # on the CPU
    t_cpu = timed(rs.sar.refined_lee, sar)  # time the Refined Lee filter
print(f"Refined Lee on 2048 × 2048, CPU: {t_cpu:.2f} s")  # CPU time
if "cuda" in rs.available_backends():  # only when a CUDA GPU is available
    with rs.device("cuda"):  # on the GPU
        t_gpu = timed(rs.sar.refined_lee, sar)  # NumPy input and output (includes copying)
        t_gpu_dev = timed(rs.sar.refined_lee, rs.to_device(sar))  # data already on the GPU
    # speed-up including transfers
    print(f"GPU, NumPy in and out (includes transfers): {t_gpu:.3f} s → {t_cpu / t_gpu:.0f}× faster")
    # speed-up without transfers
    print(f"GPU, data already on the device:            {t_gpu_dev:.3f} s → {t_cpu / t_gpu_dev:.0f}× faster")
    with rs.device("cpu"):  # on the CPU
        ref = rs.sar.refined_lee(sar)  # reference result
    with rs.device("cuda"):  # on the GPU
        gpu = rs.to_cpu(rs.sar.refined_lee(sar))  # GPU result, copied back
    d = np.abs(ref - gpu)  # absolute differences
    # how close the two results are
    print(f"|CPU − GPU|: 99.99th percentile {np.percentile(d, 99.99):.1e}, maximum {d.max():.3f}; "
          f"pixels differing by more than 0.001: {int((d > 1e-3).sum())} of {d.size:,}")
else:
    # no GPU available
    print("No CUDA GPU detected: run this notebook on a GPU machine or Colab GPU to compare.")


Refined Lee on 2048 × 2048, CPU: 1.65 s
GPU, NumPy in and out (includes transfers): 0.021 s → 81× faster
GPU, data already on the device:            0.021 s → 78× faster
|CPU − GPU|: 99.99th percentile 2.5e-07, maximum 0.017; pixels differing by more than 0.001: 2 of 4,194,304


On this laptop (NVIDIA RTX A5500, 16 GB) the GPU ran Refined Lee about 80 times faster than the CPU (0.02 s against about 1.7 s for a 2048 × 2048 image). Moving the 16 MB image to and from the GPU added almost nothing at this size. Speed-ups depend on the algorithm, the image size and the hardware, so time your own workloads.
The two backends agree to float32 rounding: 99.99% of pixels differ by less than about 3 × 10⁻⁷. A handful of pixels (two or three of 4.2 million, varying between runs) differ by up to about 0.02, most likely where two edge directions are almost equally strong and rounding picks a different side. Expect differences of this kind whenever results are compared across devices.

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
text:
Organising a project
A predictable layout makes analyses reproducible and easy to share:
my-rs-project/
├── environment.yml        # exact environment (conda) or requirements.txt (pip)
├── data/
│   ├── raw/               # downloads, never edited
│   ├── interim/           # intermediate products (Zarr cubes, masks)
│   └── processed/         # final rasters/vectors (COG, GeoPackage)
├── notebooks/             # exploration, numbered 01_, 02_, ...
├── src/                   # reusable functions
├── outputs/figures/
└── README.md              # what, why, how to rerun
Good habits: record versions with geolattice.__version__ and rs.info(); fix random seeds; keep raw data read-only; save outputs as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF (rs.write) or Zarr; and store AOIs as GeoPackage or GeoJSON, never as hard-coded numbers scattered through notebooks.

title: The Python Geospatial Environment
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

Images are arrays; xarray adds coordinates, rioxarray adds the CRS, GeoPandas handles vectors.
GeoLattice installs on top of GDAL/PROJ; remote sensing features come from the rsense extras.
geolattice.rsense selects CPU or GPU with one call and falls back safely when no GPU exists, so code stays portable. Functions return results in the memory space of their input.
Dask makes computations lazy; rs.apply_tiled processes huge rasters in seamless tiles.

Exercises

Add a second field to the synthetic scene with a different planting date and plot both NDVI curves.
Use cube.groupby("time.month").max() to make a monthly maximum-NDVI composite.
Buffer the three Onondaga sites by 10 km, compute their areas in km², and explain why you must reproject before buffering.
Reproject the DEM mosaic to the suggested UTM zone with rs.reproject and compare its resolution in metres with the 0.0011° of the tiles.
Read the Landsat 9 band with three different chunk sizes and time lazy.mean().compute(). What chunk size is fastest on your machine?
Time the Benchmarking CPU (and GPU) performance section with repeat=10 and a 4096 × 4096 image. How does the GPU speed-up change with image size?

Next: Notebook 09_01_02 works with real rasters and vectors: formats, reprojection, clipping, mosaicking, zonal statistics and visualization.

title: GeoLattice: Remote Sensing
text:
Remote sensing measures the Earth without touching it. Optical sensors record reflected sunlight in a few broad bands or hundreds of narrow ones, radar sends its own microwaves and works through cloud and at night, LiDAR times laser pulses to map terrain and trees in three dimensions, and drones fly the same field every week. Turning those measurements into crop maps, flood extents, forest loss, field boundaries or the water a crop uses is the work of this chapter.
These 152 notebooks are chapter 09 of the GeoLattice tutorials. They cover data access, optical, radar, UAV, hyperspectral and LiDAR data, texture analysis, super-resolution, image classification, object detection, foundation models, the surface energy balance and soil moisture, and finish with seventeen capstone projects, using geolattice.rsense with real imagery from Bangladesh, the United States and around the world.

title: GeoLattice: Remote Sensing
text:
GeoLattice
GeoLattice is a Python library for geospatial analysis that brings vector and raster processing, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics, spatial databases, web and cloud GIS and remote sensing together under one import. It is built on GDAL, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely and xarray, so its functions take and return objects these libraries already use: GeoDataFrames, xarray DataArrays and Datasets, NumPy arrays and GDAL-readable files.



Package
geolattice


Repository
github.com/zia207/GeoLattice


Python
3.10 or newer


License
MIT


Author
Zia Ahmed, Upatta Analytics



GDAL and PROJ must be installed first, with Python GDAL bindings that match the GDAL library (conda or your system package manager). Then install the remote sensing option, or the full set for the deep-learning notebooks:
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]"
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[all]"                # adds PyTorch and torchgeo for deep learning
GPUs, large vision models and foundation models have their own extras (rsense-gpu, rsense-vision, rsense-foundation, rsense-uav-dl), which a plain install leaves out.
The chapter uses six imports:
import geolattice.rsense as rs
import geolattice.rsense.classify.image_classification as ic
import geolattice.rsense.foundation_models as fm

Overview
Every technique in this course, from NDVI to InSAR, rests on a handful of physical ideas. This module builds them up from the physics, surveys the branches and applications of the field, introduces the remote sensing toolkit of GeoLattice (geolattice.rsense), and tests each idea on real Landsat 8 and Sentinel-2 data from the GeoLattice data folder in DropBox.

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Define remote sensing and describe the chain from energy source to information product.
Place optical, thermal and microwave sensors on the electromagnetic spectrum, and use Planck’s and Wien’s laws to explain why the Sun dominates reflected wavelengths and the Earth dominates thermal wavelengths.
Explain how the atmosphere scatters and absorbs radiation, and how energy interacts with the surface (reflection, absorption, transmission, emission).
Name the main branches of remote sensing (by energy source, spectral region, platform and spectral resolution) and their typical applications.

Extract and interpret spectral signatures of water, vegetation and built surfaces.
Explain spatial, spectral, temporal and radiometric resolution, and see their effect on data.

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
text:
What is remote sensing?
Remote sensing is the acquisition of information about an object or area from a distance, typically from aircraft, drones or satellites, by measuring electromagnetic radiation that the object reflects, emits or scatters back. A sensor never touches the surface: it records a number, and the science of remote sensing is turning that number into a physical quantity (reflectance, temperature, backscatter, height) and then into information (land cover, crop health, flood extent, ground motion).

The remote sensing process
Every remote sensing system, from a smartphone camera to a radar satellite, follows the same chain (Lillesand, Kiefer & Chipman, 2015; Jensen, 2007):








Step
What happens
Example




A. Energy source
The Sun (passive) or the sensor itself (active) illuminates the target
Sunlight; a radar pulse


B. Path to the target
Radiation passes through the atmosphere and is partly scattered and absorbed
Blue light scattered by air molecules


C. Interaction with the target
The surface reflects, absorbs, transmits and emits energy depending on its properties
Leaves reflect near-infrared strongly


D. Path to the sensor
The returning signal crosses the atmosphere again
Haze adds “path radiance”


E. Recording
The sensor converts radiance into digital numbers
12-bit Landsat OLI counts


F. Transmission and processing
Data are downlinked, calibrated, geolocated and corrected
Level-1 → Level-2 products


G. Interpretation and analysis
Physical values become information
NDVI, land-cover maps, change maps


H. Application
Information supports a decision
Irrigation scheduling, disaster response





A short history







Year
Milestone




1858
Gaspard-Félix Tournachon (“Nadar”) takes the first aerial photograph, from a balloon over Paris


1909 to 1918
Aerial photography from aircraft; systematic military reconnaissance in World War I


1940s
Radar and colour-infrared film developed during World War II


1960
TIROS-1, the first weather satellite; the term “remote sensing” is coined (Evelyn Pruitt, U.S. Office of Naval Research)


1972
Landsat 1 (ERTS-1) begins the longest continuous record of Earth’s land surface


1978
Seasat, the first civilian spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR)


1999
Terra/MODIS, daily global multispectral observation; IKONOS, first commercial sub-metre satellite


2014 to 2017
Copernicus Sentinel-1 (SAR) and Sentinel-2 (multispectral) with free and open data


2018 to 2019
GEDI and ICESat-2 bring spaceborne lidar for forest structure and elevation


2020s
Small-satellite constellations, hyperspectral missions (EnMAP, EMIT, PRISMA) and L-band SAR (NISAR)



The open-data policies of Landsat (2008) and Copernicus (2014) turned remote sensing into a data-science discipline: petabytes of analysis-ready imagery are now searched through STAC catalogues and processed in the cloud, which is the workflow geolattice.rsense is built for.

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
text:
Physical principles

The electromagnetic spectrum
EM energy travels as waves; the wavelength λ and frequency ν are linked by the speed of light, \(c = \lambda \nu\), and each photon carries energy \(E = h\nu = hc/\lambda\). Shorter wavelengths therefore mean more energetic photons.
Remote sensing uses several broad regions of the spectrum:









Region
Wavelength
What sensors measure
Examples




Visible (VIS)
0.4 to 0.7 µm
Reflected sunlight
Landsat B2 to B4, Sentinel-2 B2 to B4


Near infrared (NIR)
0.7 to 1.3 µm
Reflected sunlight; very bright for leaves
Landsat B5, Sentinel-2 B8


Shortwave infrared (SWIR)
1.3 to 3 µm
Reflected sunlight; sensitive to water content and minerals
Landsat B6 to B7, Sentinel-2 B11 to B12


Mid-wave infrared (MWIR)
3 to 8 µm
Mixed reflected and emitted energy; very hot targets
MODIS fire bands (3.9 µm)


Thermal infrared (TIR)
8 to 14 µm
Energy emitted by the surface (temperature)
Landsat B10 to B11, MODIS LST


Microwave
1 mm-1 m
Active radar echoes or passive emission
Sentinel-1 (C-band, 5.6 cm), NISAR (L-band, 24 cm)





Code

# This code creates a visual representation of the regions of the electromagnetic (EM) spectrum
# that are used in remote sensing, and highlights the typical wavelength ranges and sensor channels.
# Here is what each part does:

# %matplotlib inline: ensures that plots display inline when using a Jupyter Notebook.

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)      # Suppress UserWarnings (usually from matplotlib)

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

# Set figure display parameters for clarity in the notebook.
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 110,    # Higher DPI for sharper figures
    "axes.grid": True,    # Show grid by default
    "grid.alpha": 0.3     # Light grid lines
})

# Define the major EM spectrum regions used in remote sensing as a list of tuples:
# Each tuple = (region_name, wavelength_start [m], wavelength_end [m], color_as_hex)
regions = [
    ("UV", 1e-8, 4e-7, "#7b3294"),
    ("Visible", 4e-7, 7e-7, "#ffd92f"),
    ("NIR", 7e-7, 1.3e-6, "#e66101"),
    ("SWIR", 1.3e-6, 3e-6, "#b2182b"),
    ("MWIR", 3e-6, 8e-6, "#d6604d"),
    ("TIR", 8e-6, 1.4e-5, "#f4a582"),
    ("Far IR", 1.4e-5, 1e-3, "#fddbc7"),
    ("Microwave", 1e-3, 1.0, "#4393c3"),
]

# Create a figure and axes object for the plot.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 2.4))

# Plot each region as a colored band (axvspan) and add its label:
for name, a, b, col in regions:
    ax.axvspan(a, b, color=col, alpha=0.8)                       # Fill band for each spectrum region
    # Place region name at geometric mean (center in log space); vertical if narrow region
    ax.text(np.sqrt(a * b), 0.5, name, ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=9, rotation=90 if b / a < 3 else 0)

# Add annotations for notable remote sensing satellite sensors and their wavelengths:
for label, wl in [
    ("Sentinel-2 B4\n665 nm", 665e-9),
    ("Landsat B10\n10.9 µm", 10.9e-6),
    ("Sentinel-1\nC-band 5.6 cm", 0.0556),
]:
    # Draw an arrow and label at the corresponding wavelength
    ax.annotate(
        label, (wl, 1.0), xytext=(wl, 1.55), ha="center", fontsize=8,
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->")
    )

# Final plot settings:
ax.set_xscale("log")                                   # X axis as log scale (for wavelength)
ax.set_xlim(1e-8, 1)                                   # Range: 10 nm to 1 m
ax.set_ylim(0, 2)                                      # Unused y scale, for display
ax.set_yticks([])                                      # Hide y-axis ticks
ax.set_xlabel("Wavelength (m)")                        # Label x-axis
ax.set_title("Regions of the EM spectrum used in remote sensing")  # Set plot title
ax.grid(False)                                         # Remove default grid (already colored regions)
plt.tight_layout()                                     # Adjust layout to fit
plt.show()                                             # Display the plot











Code
# This code calculates and prints the wavelength (λ), frequency (ν), and energy per photon for different types of electromagnetic radiation relevant to remote sensing.
# Physical constants:
h = 6.626e-34  # Planck constant in joule-seconds (J·s)
c = 2.998e8    # Speed of light in meters per second (m/s)

# List of named wavelengths in meters for common remote sensing wavebands:
bands = [
    ("Blue light", 0.49e-6),      # Visible blue
    ("NIR", 0.86e-6),             # Near-infrared
    ("Thermal IR", 10.9e-6),      # Thermal infrared
    ("C-band radar", 0.0556),     # Microwave (C-band radar)
]

# Calculate and print properties for each wavelength:
for name, wl in bands:
    frequency = c / wl                # Frequency in Hz
    photon_energy = h * frequency     # Photon energy in joules
    # wavelength, frequency and photon energy of each region
    print(f"{name:13s} λ = {wl:9.3e} m   ν = {frequency:9.3e} Hz   photon energy = {photon_energy:9.3e} J")


Blue light    λ = 4.900e-07 m   ν = 6.118e+14 Hz   photon energy = 4.054e-19 J
NIR           λ = 8.600e-07 m   ν = 3.486e+14 Hz   photon energy = 2.310e-19 J
Thermal IR    λ = 1.090e-05 m   ν = 2.750e+13 Hz   photon energy = 1.822e-20 J
C-band radar  λ = 5.560e-02 m   ν = 5.392e+09 Hz   photon energy = 3.573e-24 J


A blue photon carries about 100,000 times more energy than a C-band radar photon. That is why optical detectors count photons with semiconductors while radar receivers measure the amplitude and phase of a wave, and why microwave radiation passes through clouds that block visible light.


Blackbody radiation: why the Sun and the Earth shine in different bands
Every object above absolute zero emits radiation. For an ideal emitter (a blackbody) the spectral radiance at temperature \(T\) follows Planck’s law:
\[B_\lambda(T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \, \frac{1}{e^{hc/(\lambda k_B T)} - 1}\]
Two consequences follow:

Wien’s displacement law: the wavelength of peak emission is \(\lambda_{max} = 2898\,\mu m\,K / T\).
Stefan-Boltzmann law: the total emitted power grows as \(M = \varepsilon\sigma T^4\), where \(\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}\,W\,m^{-2}K^{-4}\) and \(\varepsilon \le 1\) is the emissivity. Real surfaces are grey bodies with \(\varepsilon\) between about 0.9 (dry soil) and 0.99 (water), which is why thermal remote sensing must correct for emissivity.

Comparing the Sun (≈5,778 K) with the Earth’s surface (≈300 K) explains the split between reflective and emissive remote sensing.


Code
# This code compares the blackbody radiation curves (spectral radiance) of the Sun and the Earth,
# and illustrates why they emit at very different wavelengths.

# Boltzmann constant in J/K
kB = 1.381e-23

# Define a range of wavelengths in meters: from 0.1 µm to 100 µm (for plotting)
wl = np.logspace(-7, -4, 2000)  # 1e-7 m = 0.1 µm, 1e-4 m = 100 µm

# Planck's law: returns spectral radiance B_lambda for wavelength(s) wl [m] and temperature T [K]
def planck(wl, T):
    # The formula returns radiance in W m⁻² sr⁻¹ m⁻¹
    return 2 * h * c**2 / wl**5 / (np.exp(h * c / (wl * kB * T)) - 1)

# Get the radiance curves for the Sun (5778 K) and the Earth (300 K)
# The Sun's radiance is scaled to represent the apparent radiance at Earth's distance (by solid angle factor)
sun = planck(wl, 5778) * (6.96e8 / 1.496e11) ** 2     # (Sun radius / Earth-Sun distance)^2
earth = planck(wl, 300)  # Planck curve of the Earth's surface at 300 K

# Plot both curves on a log-log plot (wavelength in microns)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
# sunlight on log-log axes (wavelength in µm)
ax.loglog(wl * 1e6, sun, label="Sunlight at the top of the atmosphere (5,778 K)")
ax.loglog(wl * 1e6, earth, label="Earth's surface (300 K)")  # Earth emission

# Highlight important spectral regions for remote sensing
# Visible window
ax.axvspan(0.4, 0.7, color="gold", alpha=0.2, label="Visible")
# Thermal IR "window" (where Earth's emission escapes to space most easily)
ax.axvspan(8, 14, color="tomato", alpha=0.15, label="Thermal window 8–14 µm")

ax.set_ylim(1e3, 1e8)  # radiance range shown
ax.set_xlabel("Wavelength (µm)")  # x label
ax.set_ylabel("Spectral radiance (W m⁻² sr⁻¹ m⁻¹)")  # y label
ax.legend(fontsize=8)  # legend
ax.set_title("Planck curves: reflected sunlight vs emitted Earth radiation")  # title
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

# Compute and print the wavelength of peak emission (Wien's law) and total radiated power (Stefan–Boltzmann law)
for name, T in [("Sun", 5778), ("Earth", 300), ("Forest fire", 1000)]:
    peak = 2898 / T  # Wien's law: peak wavelength in µm
    total = 5.67e-8 * T**4  # Stefan–Boltzmann law: total emittance in W/m²
    # peak wavelength (Wien) and total emitted power (Stefan-Boltzmann)
    print(f"{name:12s} T = {T:5d} K  → peak emission at {peak:6.2f} µm,  σT⁴ = {total:12,.0f} W/m²")

# Find the wavelength where Sun and Earth radiance curves cross (emitted power equal)
crossover = wl[np.argmin(np.abs(np.log(sun) - np.log(earth)))] * 1e6  # Convert to µm
print(f"Sunlight and Earth emission are equal near {crossover:.1f} µm")  # where the two curves cross









Sun          T =  5778 K  → peak emission at   0.50 µm,  σT⁴ =   63,196,527 W/m²
Earth        T =   300 K  → peak emission at   9.66 µm,  σT⁴ =          459 W/m²
Forest fire  T =  1000 K  → peak emission at   2.90 µm,  σT⁴ =       56,700 W/m²
Sunlight and Earth emission are equal near 4.6 µm


Interpretation. Sunlight peaks around 0.5 µm (green light) and dominates below about 4 µm, so optical sensors in the VIS, NIR and SWIR measure reflected solar energy. Beyond roughly 4 µm the Earth’s own emission takes over, so thermal sensors measure temperature. A forest fire at 1,000 K peaks near 2.9 µm and radiates more than 100 times as much power per square metre as the ground around it, which is why fire products use mid-infrared bands.


The atmosphere: scattering, absorption and windows
Radiation crosses the atmosphere twice in passive optical remote sensing (Sun → surface → sensor). Two processes change it on the way.
Scattering redirects radiation. Its strength depends on the size of the particle relative to the wavelength:









Type
Particles
Wavelength dependence
Visible effect




Rayleigh
Gas molecules (≪ λ)
\(\propto \lambda^{-4}\)
Blue sky; haze strongest in blue bands


Mie
Aerosols, smoke, dust (≈ λ)
roughly \(\lambda^{-1}\) to \(\lambda^{0}\)
Hazy, washed-out images


Non-selective
Cloud droplets, ice (≫ λ)
none
White clouds



Scattered light that reaches the sensor without touching the surface is path radiance. It brightens dark targets, especially in the blue, and lowers image contrast. Atmospheric correction (the Processing levels: from DN to physical units section) removes it.
Absorption removes energy at specific wavelengths: ozone (O₃) in the ultraviolet, water vapour (H₂O) near 0.94, 1.14, 1.38, 1.87 and 2.7 µm and above 5 µm, carbon dioxide (CO₂) near 2.0, 4.3 and 15 µm, and oxygen (O₂) at 0.76 µm. The spectral regions where the atmosphere is mostly transparent are the atmospheric windows, and sensor bands are placed inside them:







Window
Used by




0.3 to 1.3 µm (VIS-NIR)
All multispectral sensors


1.5 to 1.8 µm and 2.0 to 2.4 µm (SWIR)
Landsat B6/B7, Sentinel-2 B11/B12


3.5 to 4.2 µm (MWIR)
Fire detection (MODIS, VIIRS)


8 to 14 µm (TIR), split by ozone at 9.6 µm
Landsat B10/B11, ECOSTRESS


> 1 cm (microwave)
Radar; almost unaffected by clouds



The opposite trick is also useful: bands placed inside an absorption feature measure the absorber itself. Landsat 8 band 9 (1.37 µm) sits in a strong water-vapour band, so the ground is invisible and only high cirrus clouds appear bright.
The code below compares the relative strength of Rayleigh scattering across the Landsat 8 reflective bands. The Physics in the data: the Sun’s spectrum and atmospheric scattering section tests this \(\lambda^{-4}\) law on a real image.


Code
# This cell shows why blue light is scattered much more than red light.
#
# Rayleigh scattering (molecules in clear air) gets weaker as wavelength gets longer.
# The strength scales as 1 / wavelength^4. Dividing each Landsat band by the red band
# and raising that ratio to the power -4 answers: "how many times more does this band
# scatter than red?"
#
# 1. Store the centre wavelength (micrometres) of each Landsat 8 reflective band.
# 2. Compute the Rayleigh ratio relative to the red band.
# 3. Show both numbers side by side. Coastal and blue come out several times stronger
#    than red; the SWIR bands barely scatter at all.

oli = pd.Series({"coastal (B1)": 0.443, "blue (B2)": 0.482, "green (B3)": 0.561, "red (B4)": 0.655,
                 "nir (B5)": 0.865, "swir16 (B6)": 1.609, "swir22 (B7)": 2.201}, name="centre_um")
# (λ_band / λ_red) ^ -4. A value of 4 means "scattered four times as much as red".
rayleigh = (oli / oli["red (B4)"]) ** -4
# band centres and their relative Rayleigh scattering
pd.DataFrame({"centre (µm)": oli, "Rayleigh scattering relative to red": rayleigh.round(2)})

Blue light is scattered about three times more strongly than red, and the coastal/aerosol band almost five times more. SWIR bands are nearly free of molecular scattering, which is why SWIR composites look sharp even on hazy days.


Energy-matter interactions at the surface
Radiation reaching the surface is split three ways. By conservation of energy, at each wavelength
\[E_I(\lambda) = E_R(\lambda) + E_A(\lambda) + E_T(\lambda),\]
the incident energy equals the reflected, absorbed and transmitted parts. Dividing by \(E_I\) gives the reflectance, absorptance and transmittance, which sum to one. Remote sensing of reflected energy measures the spectral reflectance
\[\rho(\lambda) = \frac{E_R(\lambda)}{E_I(\lambda)},\]
and the curve of \(\rho\) against wavelength is the material’s spectral signature (the Spectral signatures from real images section). Kirchhoff’s law links absorption and emission: a surface in thermal equilibrium emits as well as it absorbs at each wavelength (\(\varepsilon_\lambda = \alpha_\lambda\)), so for an opaque surface \(\varepsilon_\lambda = 1 - \rho_\lambda\). That is why water, a poor reflector in the thermal infrared, is an almost perfect emitter.
The geometry of reflection matters too:

A specular surface (calm water, smooth roofs) reflects like a mirror. It looks either very dark or, at the mirror angle, dazzlingly bright (sun glint).
A Lambertian (perfectly diffuse) surface reflects equally in all directions, so its radiance does not depend on viewing angle. Most land surfaces are treated as approximately Lambertian.
Real surfaces lie in between. Their directional behaviour is described by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF): forests look brighter with the Sun behind the observer (the “hot spot”) because shadows are hidden.

For microwaves the controlling properties are different: surface roughness relative to the wavelength, dielectric constant (mainly moisture) and geometry (corner reflectors in cities, volume scattering in canopies). The radar notebooks (07_03) develop these for SAR.


Radiometric quantities and the radiative transfer equation









Quantity
Symbol
Unit
Meaning




Radiant flux
Φ
W
Energy per unit time


Irradiance
E
W m⁻²
Flux arriving on a surface


Exitance
M
W m⁻²
Flux leaving a surface


Radiance
L
W m⁻² sr⁻¹ µm⁻¹
Flux per area, per solid angle, per wavelength: what a sensor measures


Reflectance
ρ
,
Ratio of reflected to incident flux (0 to 1)



For a Lambertian surface the radiance reaching a sensor at the top of the atmosphere is
\[L_{sensor}(\lambda) = \frac{\rho(\lambda)\,E_{sun}(\lambda)\cos\theta_s\,T_{\downarrow}(\lambda)\,T_{\uparrow}(\lambda)}{\pi\,d^2}
+ L_{path}(\lambda),\]
with exo-atmospheric solar irradiance \(E_{sun}\), solar zenith angle \(\theta_s\), Earth-Sun distance \(d\) (astronomical units), downward and upward atmospheric transmittances \(T\), and path radiance \(L_{path}\). Setting \(T = 1\) and \(L_{path} = 0\) and solving for \(\rho\) gives the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance
\[\rho_{TOA} = \frac{\pi\,L_{sensor}\,d^2}{E_{sun}\cos\theta_s}.\]
Estimating \(T\) and \(L_{path}\) (from radiative transfer models, or from dark objects in the image) gives surface reflectance, the starting point of most analysis. The Physics in the data: the Sun’s spectrum and atmospheric scattering section uses this equation to recover the solar spectrum from a real Landsat metadata file.

Most land-imaging satellites fly sun-synchronous polar orbits, crossing the equator at the same local time on every pass (about 10:00 to 10:30 for Landsat and Sentinel-2), so illumination is comparable between dates.


By spectral resolution

Panchromatic: one broad band (for example Landsat 8 band 8, 15 m), finest spatial detail.
Multispectral: a few broad bands (Landsat, Sentinel-2).

Related disciplines
Photogrammetry measures geometry from overlapping images (digital surface models, orthomosaics; the basis of UAV mapping). Geodesy and GNSS provide the positioning that georeferences every pixel. Geographic information science combines remote sensing layers with other spatial data, which is what the rest of GeoLattice does.

text:
Remote sensing in GeoLattice: geolattice.rsense
GeoLattice bundles a complete remote sensing toolkit in the subpackage geolattice.rsense. Rasters are xarray objects with a coordinate reference system (through rioxarray), and every array operation can run on the CPU (NumPy) or on an NVIDIA GPU (CuPy) through one backend switch. Install it with
pip install "geolattice[rsense]"          # core: xarray, rioxarray, rasterio, scikit-image
pip install "geolattice[rsense-all]"      # data access, SAR, InSAR, lidar, UAV, ML, DL, XAI, viz, scaling
and import it as import geolattice.rsense as rs. Heavy optional dependencies (PyTorch, Earth Engine, PDAL, …) are imported only when a function needs them.







Submodule
Purpose




backend
Choose CPU or GPU (set_backend), move arrays (to_device, to_cpu), precision and memory


core
Read and write rasters (GeoTIFF, COG, NetCDF, HDF, Zarr, SAFE), reproject, clip, mosaic, tile, zonal statistics, data cubes and point clouds


access
Search and download data: STAC (Earth Search, Planetary Computer), Google Earth Engine, ASF (SAR), Copernicus Data Space (CDSE), NASA Earthdata


optical
Sensor loaders (Landsat, Sentinel-2, HLS, MODIS), scaling, cloud masks, 100+ spectral indices, compositing, radiometric and atmospheric correction, land surface temperature, spectral unmixing


sar
Sentinel-1 calibration, speckle filters, multilooking, dB conversion, PolSAR decompositions, change detection, flood, ship and oil-spill mapping


insar
Interferograms, filtering, phase unwrapping, atmospheric correction, SBAS time series, line-of-sight to vertical motion; HyP3, ISCE and MintPy interfaces


uav
OpenDroneMap processing, radiometric calibration, canopy height and cover, plant counting, thermal water stress


lidar
Point-cloud I/O, ground classification, DTM/DSM/CHM, terrain derivatives, tree detection, forest metrics, GEDI and ICESat-2


timeseries
Smoothing (Savitzky-Golay, Whittaker), harmonic fits, phenology, anomalies, drought indices, BFAST-style monitoring, CCDC


classify
Pixel classifiers, clustering, object-based image analysis, change detection, accuracy assessment (Olofsson area estimates)

Deep learning: tile datasets, U-Net and detection models, training, inference, TorchGeo and foundation-model adapters

STARFM spatiotemporal fusion, optical-SAR and lidar-optical fusion

Explainable and trustworthy ML: permutation and SHAP importance, spatial cross-validation, area of applicability, conformal prediction

RGB composites, stretches, raster, time-series and point-cloud plots, interactive maps

Streamlit app templates (change viewer, flood mapper, index explorer)



geolattice.rsense also registers an .rs accessor on every xarray object, so common steps chain naturally, for example ds.rs.scale().rs.mask_clouds().rs.index("NDVI").

Code
# This block of code dynamically inspects all public functions and classes in the submodules of `geolattice.rsense`
# and summarizes them in a pandas DataFrame. It then prints a summary table of the counts of functions and classes per submodule.

# List of submodules in geolattice.rsense to inspect
SUBMODULES = [
    "backend", "core", "access", "optical", "sar", "insar", "uav", "lidar",
    "timeseries", "classify", "dl", "fusion", "xai", "viz", "scale", "apps"
]

rows = []  # one row per public function or class

# For each submodule, import it, retrieve its public API, and extract all functions/classes with their descriptions
for sub in SUBMODULES:
    # Dynamically import the submodule
    mod = importlib.import_module(f"geolattice.rsense.{sub}")
    # Get the list of public names, preferring __all__ if present, else all non-private attributes
    public_names = getattr(mod, "__all__", [n for n in dir(mod) if not n.startswith("_")])

    for name in public_names:  # every public name of the submodule
        obj = getattr(mod, name, None)  # the object behind the name
        # Only process functions and classes
        if not (inspect.isfunction(obj) or inspect.isclass(obj)):
            continue
        # Only include objects declared in geolattice.rsense (skip re-exported names from other libraries)
        if not getattr(obj, "__module__", "").startswith("geolattice.rsense"):
            continue
        # Extract the first line of the object's docstring as its description
        doc = (inspect.getdoc(obj) or "").split("\n")[0]
        rows.append({  # one row: submodule, name, kind and description
            "submodule": sub,
            "name": name,
            "kind": "class" if inspect.isclass(obj) else "function",
            "description": doc
        })

# Create a DataFrame to organize the API entries
api = pd.DataFrame(rows)

# Print the total number of discovered public API entries
print(f"{len(api)} public functions and classes in geolattice.rsense")

# Group the DataFrame by submodule, aggregating counts of functions and classes, and display as a transposed table
print(
    api.groupby("submodule", sort=False)
       .agg(
           functions=("kind", lambda k: int((k == "function").sum())),
           classes=("kind", lambda k: int((k == "class").sum()))
       ).T
)

# This code demonstrates how to inspect and list the custom accessor methods available for xarray's
# Dataset and DataArray objects in the geolattice.rsense module.

import xarray as xr  # xarray is a package for N-dimensional labeled arrays (useful for remote sensing).

# Import custom accessors for xarray, which add "rs" property to xarray objects for remote sensing methods.
from geolattice.rsense.accessor import RSDataArrayAccessor, RSDatasetAccessor

# Get a list of all public (non-private) methods provided by the RSDatasetAccessor (xarray.Dataset.rs)
ds_methods = [m for m in dir(RSDatasetAccessor) if not m.startswith("_")]

# Get a list of all public (non-private) methods provided by the RSDataArrayAccessor (xarray.DataArray.rs)
da_methods = [m for m in dir(RSDataArrayAccessor) if not m.startswith("_")]

# Print available methods for the custom accessors attached to Dataset and DataArray
print("Dataset.rs   :", ", ".join(ds_methods))
print("DataArray.rs :", ", ".join(da_methods))  # the methods the .rs accessor adds to a DataArray

DataArray.rs : apply_tiled, clip, cloud_mask, composite, index, mask_clouds, reproject, scale, sensor, to_cpu, to_device, with_sensor, write, zonal_stats
