Setup and data
This module uses three scenes from the GeoLattice data folder in Dropbox









Dataset
Folder
Contents
Used for




Landsat 8 OLI/TIRS Level-1
Landsat8_RAW/
Collection 1 L1TP subset (16 × 15 km), path 16 / row 30, acquired 2016-09-27: farmland between Canandaigua and Seneca lakes in the Finger Lakes region of New York (42.84°N, 77.13°W; UTM 18N, 30 m); bands 1 to 11, quality band and the MTL.txt metadata file
Radiometric calibration, spectral indices, thermal infrared, scattering


Sentinel-2 MSI
Sentinel_2/
10 bands resampled to 10 m over a 2.1 × 1.7 km area in Amherst, near Buffalo, New York (43.00°N, 78.81°W; UTM 17N), values are reflectance × 10,000; 108 labelled ground-truth polygons (GroundTruth_data.shp)
Spectral signatures, red edge, spatial resolution


Landsat 9 OLI-2 Level-2
LC09_L2SP_138043_20221216_20221223_02_T1/
Collection 2 surface reflectance, path 138 / row 43, 2022-12-16, northwestern Bangladesh (window centred near 24.58°N, 88.96°E)
Scaling Level-2 products



Getting more data. The PyGIS Explorer app lets you draw an area of interest, search a catalogue and download the scenes you select from Earth Search (AWS), Microsoft Planetary Computer, Copernicus Data Space (CDSE), NOAA Digital Coast and USGS 3DEP lidar. The same searches are available in code through rs.access.stac_search, rs.access.stac_load, rs.access.cdse_search and rs.access.earthdata_search (notebook 09_01_03).
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Import necessary libraries
from pathlib import Path
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data

# Set the base data directory
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/00_shared/data_remote_sensing")

# Set the directory and ID string for the Landsat 8 imagery (Level 1 product)
L8_DIR = DATA / "Landsat8_RAW"
L8_ID = "LC08_L1TP_016030_20160927_20170220_01_T1"  # Landsat 8 scene ID

# Parse the Landsat metadata file using the 'parse_mtl' function from rs.optical

# Define the path to the Sentinel-2 data folder
S2_DIR = DATA / "Sentinel_2"

# Dictionary mapping Sentinel-2 band filenames to canonical band names
S2_BANDS = {
    "B2": "blue",
    "B3": "green",
    "B4": "red",
    "B5": "rededge1",
    "B6": "rededge2",
    "B8": "nir",
    "B8A": "nir08",
    "B11": "swir16",
    "B12": "swir22"
}

# Read each specified band into an xarray Dataset:
# - For each key:value pair (e.g., "B2": "blue") in S2_BANDS,
#   read the .tif file for that band from disk.
# - Remove any singleton (single-length) "band" dimension for a 2D array.
# - Scale the raw integer data to reflectance by dividing by 10,000.
# - Store each band as a variable with its canonical name in the Dataset.
s2 = xr.Dataset({
    name: rs.read(S2_DIR / f"{b}.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True) / 10000
    for b, name in S2_BANDS.items()
})

# Sentinel-2 GeoTIFFs carry no coordinate system metadata,
# so we assign the correct UTM 17N CRS (EPSG:32617) from documentation
s2 = s2.rio.write_crs("EPSG:32617")

# Load land use class information from a CSV, setting Class_ID as the index
# Resulting Series maps integer IDs to land use names
classes = pd.read_csv(S2_DIR / "Landuse_ID.csv").set_index("Class_ID")["Landuse"]

# Load ground truth polygons from a shapefile and set CRS to match the imagery
gt = gpd.read_file(S2_DIR / "GroundTruth_data.shp").set_crs("EPSG:32617")

# Filter out any polygons whose Class_ID does not exist in the land use mapping
# and create a copy to retain independence from the original DataFrame
gt = gt[gt["Class_ID"].isin(classes.index)].copy()

# Add a "Landuse" column to the polygons by mapping their Class_ID to descriptive names
gt["Landuse"] = gt["Class_ID"].map(classes)

# Print size information for the image data and the polygon counts per land use class
print(dict(s2.sizes), "| polygons per class:", gt["Landuse"].value_counts().to_dict())

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
section: Where satellite bands sit on the spectrum
text:
Where satellite bands sit on the spectrum
Sensors sample the spectrum in discrete bands. The central wavelengths below come from the official sensor specifications. Sentinel-2 adds three narrow red-edge bands (705 to 783 nm) that Landsat lacks; these respond strongly to chlorophyll content.


Code
# Create a DataFrame describing the reflective bands for three satellite sensors:
# Landsat 8/9 OLI, Sentinel-2 MSI, and MODIS. Each row contains:
# - the sensor name
# - the band name as used by the sensor
# - the center wavelength for that band (in nanometers)
# - the wavelength width of the band (in nanometers)
# - the canonical name used by geolattice.rsense for that band
bands = pd.DataFrame([
    # sensor, band, centre (nm), width (nm), canonical name used by geolattice.rsense
    ("Landsat 8/9 OLI", "B1", 443, 16, "coastal"), 
    ("Landsat 8/9 OLI", "B2", 482, 60, "blue"),
    ("Landsat 8/9 OLI", "B3", 561, 57, "green"), 
    ("Landsat 8/9 OLI", "B4", 655, 37, "red"),
    ("Landsat 8/9 OLI", "B5", 865, 28, "nir"), 
    ("Landsat 8/9 OLI", "B6", 1609, 85, "swir16"),
    ("Landsat 8/9 OLI", "B7", 2201, 187, "swir22"),
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B1", 443, 20, "coastal"), 
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B2", 490, 65, "blue"),
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B3", 560, 35, "green"), 
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B4", 665, 30, "red"),
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B5", 705, 15, "rededge1"), 
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B6", 740, 15, "rededge2"),
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B7", 783, 20, "rededge3"), 
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B8", 842, 115, "nir"),
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B8A", 865, 20, "nir08"), 
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B11", 1610, 90, "swir16"),
    ("Sentinel-2 MSI", "B12", 2190, 180, "swir22"),
    ("MODIS", "b3", 469, 20, "blue"), 
    ("MODIS", "b4", 555, 20, "green"), 
    ("MODIS", "b1", 645, 50, "red"),
    ("MODIS", "b2", 858, 35, "nir"), 
    ("MODIS", "b5", 1240, 20, "swir12"),
    ("MODIS", "b6", 1640, 24, "swir16"), 
    ("MODIS", "b7", 2130, 50, "swir22"),
], columns=["sensor", "band", "centre_nm", "width_nm", "canonical"])

# Make a bar plot showing where these reflective bands are located on the spectrum for each sensor.
# Each horizontal bar represents a spectral band, its width equals the band wavelength range,
# and color corresponds to the canonical band name.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.6))
colours = {  # colour of each canonical band name
    "coastal": "#542788", "blue": "#2166ac", "green": "#1b7837", "red": "#b2182b",
    "rededge1": "#d6604d", "rededge2": "#f4a582", "rededge3": "#fdae61", "nir": "#7f3b08",
    "nir08": "#b35806", "swir12": "#8c510a", "swir16": "#636363", "swir22": "#252525"
}

# Group each sensor's bands and plot them row-by-row, coloring by canonical.
for i, (sensor, grp) in enumerate(bands.groupby("sensor", sort=False)):
    for _, b in grp.iterrows():  # each band of that sensor
        # Draw each band as a horizontal bar at the sensor's row with band width and centered at the central wavelength.
        ax.barh(i, b.width_nm, left=b.centre_nm - b.width_nm / 2, height=0.6, color=colours[b.canonical])
        # Place the band name just above the bar.
        ax.text(b.centre_nm, i + 0.38, b.band, ha="center", fontsize=7)

# Set axis labels and limits.
ax.set_yticks(range(3))
ax.set_yticklabels(bands.sensor.unique())  # sensor names on the y axis
ax.set_xlabel("Wavelength (nm)")  # x label
ax.set_xlim(400, 2350)  # visible to shortwave infrared
# title
ax.set_title("Reflective bands of Landsat 8/9, Sentinel-2 and MODIS (colour = geolattice.rsense canonical name)")
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw









geolattice.rsense refers to bands by these canonical names (blue, red, nir, swir16, …) so the same index formula works for every sensor. It translates each product’s own names (B04, SR_B4, sur_refl_b01) automatically:


Code

# a human-readable string listing all native band names for that sensor, joined by " / ".

# Finally, display the table, filling any missing bands with an en dash.

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
text:
Spectral signatures from real images
A spectral signature is how reflectance changes with wavelength for a material:

Water reflects a little blue and green light and absorbs almost all NIR and SWIR, so it is dark beyond the visible.
Healthy vegetation absorbs blue and red light for photosynthesis, reflects some green, and reflects NIR very strongly because of the internal structure of leaves. The sharp rise between red and NIR is the red edge. Leaf water absorbs in the SWIR.
Built surfaces and bare soil have flatter spectra that rise gradually with wavelength.


Sentinel-2 signatures from ground-truth polygons
rs.classify.extract_samples collects the reflectance of every pixel inside the labelled polygons. Their class means give real surface-reflectance signatures with the red-edge bands.


Code
# Extract per-pixel spectral data and class labels from Sentinel-2 and ground-truth polygons
X, y = rs.classify.extract_samples(s2, gt, "Class_ID")

# Define the mapping from canonical band names to their wavelength (nm) for Sentinel-2
S2_NM = {
    "blue": 490,
    "green": 560,
    "red": 665,
    "rededge1": 705,
    "rededge2": 740,
    "nir": 842,
    "nir08": 865,
    "swir16": 1610,
    "swir22": 2190
}

# For each land cover class, compute the mean reflectance in each band:
# - Select only those columns in X that correspond to canonical bands defined in S2_NM.
# - Map each pixel label 'y' to its human-readable class name using 'classes'.
# - Group the reflectance samples by class name and compute the mean for each band.
sig_s2 = X[list(S2_NM)].groupby(pd.Series(y, index=X.index).map(classes)).mean()

# Print the number of pixels in each class to inform how many samples contributed to each signature
print("pixels per class:", pd.Series(y).map(classes).value_counts().to_dict())

# Show the class mean spectral signatures, rounded to 3 decimal places
sig_s2.round(3)

# This code plots the mean spectral reflectance signatures for different land cover classes
# from Sentinel-2 satellite data, using samples labeled in the ground truth.

# Create a new figure and axes for the plot, with specified size
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.8))

# Define plot color and marker styles for each class
style = {
    "Water": ("#2166ac", "o"),
    "Tree/bushes": ("#1b7837", "s"),
    "Grass": ("#7fbc41", "^"),
    "Building": ("#b2182b", "D"),
    "Parking/road/pavement": ("#636363", "v")
}

# Iterate over each class and its mean reflectance values
for cls, row in sig_s2.iterrows():
    # Get color and marker for this class, or use default if not specified
    col, mk = style.get(cls, ("k", "o"))
    # Plot signature: wavelength vs. mean reflectance for this class
    ax.plot(list(S2_NM.values()), row.values, marker=mk, color=col, lw=2, label=cls)

# Highlight the red-edge region in the spectrum
ax.axvspan(690, 760, color="#fdae61", alpha=0.2, label="red edge")

# Set axes labels
ax.set_xlabel("Wavelength (nm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Surface reflectance")  # y label

# Add plot title
ax.set_title("Sentinel-2 spectral signatures, Buffalo NY (class means of ground-truth pixels)")

# Add legend with smaller font size
ax.legend(fontsize=8)

# Adjust layout and display the plot
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()  # draw









These are surface-reflectance signatures from 1,497 labelled pixels, and each follows the textbook shape:

Vegetation. Trees and grass absorb red light (reflectance 0.03 to 0.05) and reflect strongly in the NIR (0.26 and 0.38). The red edge is visible in the two red-edge bands: grass rises from 0.105 at 705 nm to 0.275 at 740 nm and 0.383 at 842 nm. Grass is brighter than the tree canopy in the NIR because tree crowns contain shadows. Both drop in the SWIR, where leaf water absorbs.
Water (one pond, 53 pixels) is dark in the NIR and SWIR (about 0.02). Its green peak (0.10) is higher than the blue, which suggests algae or suspended sediment rather than clear water.
Buildings are bright and nearly flat from blue to NIR (0.36 to 0.43): light-coloured flat roofs. Roads and parking lots are flat and dark (0.10 to 0.17).



Landsat 8 scene: colour composites
The Landsat 8 Level-1 file stores digital numbers. We first convert the reflective bands to top-of-atmosphere reflectance with the coefficients from the MTL file (the details are in The Processing levels: from DN to physical units section), then display a natural-colour composite (red, green, blue) and a false-colour composite (NIR, red, green), in which vegetation appears red.


Code
# Select all reflective bands to process from the Landsat 8 band mapping.
# Bands 1-7 and 9 are reflective (the rest are thermal or non-optical), so we keep those.
REFLECTIVE = {b: n for b, n in L8_BANDS.items() if b <= 7 or b == 9}

# For each reflective band, convert the digital number (DN) data to top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance.
# This uses the multiplicative and additive calibration coefficients from the MTL metadata file,
# as well as the sun elevation angle. The resulting reflectance arrays are combined into an xarray Dataset.
toa = xr.Dataset({
    name: rs.optical.toa_reflectance(
        dn[name],
        mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_MULT_BAND_{b}"],
        mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_ADD_BAND_{b}"],
        mtl["SUN_ELEVATION"]
    )
    for b, name in REFLECTIVE.items()
}).rio.write_crs(dn.rio.crs)  # Set the coordinate reference system to match the original data

# Create a single figure with 3 subplots, arranged in one row.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5.4))

# Display three types of RGB composites using the reflectance data:
# 1. A true-color (natural color) composite: (red, green, blue)
rs.viz.plot_rgb(toa, "true_color", ax=axes[0], title="Natural colour (red, green, blue)")

# 2. A false-color composite, showing NIR, red, and green (vegetation shows up as red).
rs.viz.plot_rgb(toa, ("nir", "red", "green"), ax=axes[1], title="False colour (NIR, red, green)")

# 3. A SWIR composite: SWIR2, NIR, and red (useful for soil and moisture contrasts).
rs.viz.plot_rgb(toa, ("swir22", "nir", "red"), ax=axes[2], title="SWIR composite (SWIR2, NIR, red)")

# Remove axis tick marks for cleaner visual appearance.
for a in axes:
    a.set_xticks([])  # no x ticks
    a.set_yticks([])  # no y ticks

# Optimize layout and display the figure.
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()  # draw









The subset is a patchwork of farm fields photographed in late September. In the false-colour image, growing crops, pasture and woodlots are red; harvested or bare fields are cyan and grey; small towns and roads are bluish grey. In the SWIR composite, vegetation is green and bare soil is magenta, because dry soil is bright in the SWIR while leaf water absorbs there.


Spectral indices
Spectral indices turn these contrasts into single numbers. NDVI, \((NIR - Red)/(NIR + Red)\), is high for vegetation; NDWI, \((Green - NIR)/(Green + NIR)\), is positive for open water; and NDBI, \((SWIR1 - NIR)/(SWIR1 + NIR)\), is high for built-up and bare surfaces. geolattice.rsense registers more than a hundred indices:

# Print the total number of registered indices

# Summarize the registered indices by their domain (e.g., vegetation, water, urban, etc.)
# Show a table with the counts for each domain
catalog.groupby("domain").size().sort_values(ascending=False).to_frame("count").T

# - NDWI: Normalized Difference Water Index, highlights water
# - NDBI: Normalized Difference Built-up Index, highlights built-up and bare surfaces
vi = rs.optical.index(toa, ["NDVI", "NDWI", "NDBI"])

for a, (name, cmap) in zip(  # each panel with an index and its colour map

    "Harvested / bare fields (NDVI < 0.3)": (vi["NDVI"] < 0.3) & (vi["NDWI"] <= 0),
    "Farm ponds (NDWI > 0)": vi["NDWI"] > 0,

# Add the percentage of the scene that each class represents

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
section: Physics in the data: the Sun’s spectrum and atmospheric scattering
text:
Physics in the data: the Sun’s spectrum and atmospheric scattering
Two theoretical results from the Physical principles section can be checked against the Landsat scene.

The solar spectrum hidden in the metadata
The MTL file gives two linear conversions for each band: DN to radiance (\(L = M_L\,DN + A_L\)) and DN to reflectance without the sun-angle term (\(\rho' = M_\rho\,DN + A_\rho\)). Both describe the same pixel, so the radiative transfer equation of the Radiometric quantities and the radiative transfer equation section, \(\rho' = \pi L d^2 / E_{sun}\), lets us solve for the exo-atmospheric solar irradiance each band sees:
\[E_{sun} = \frac{\pi\,L\,d^2}{\rho'}.\]
Planck’s law for a 5,778 K Sun predicts the same quantity: \(E_\lambda = \pi B_\lambda(T)\,(R_{sun}/d_{AU})^2\).


Code
# --- Explanation of the code below ---
# The following code section computes and compares the exo-atmospheric solar irradiance values used in a Landsat 8 scene's metadata (the MTL file)
# to theoretical values computed from Planck's law for a blackbody at the Sun's temperature (~5,778 K).
# This checks how closely the calibration metadata matches the physical solar spectrum.

# 1. Define the center wavelengths (in microns) for each OLI/Landsat 8 band.
OLI_CENTRE = {
    "coastal": 0.443,
    "blue": 0.482,
    "green": 0.561,
    "red": 0.655,
    "nir": 0.865,
    "swir16": 1.609,
    "swir22": 2.201,
}

# 2. Get the Earth-Sun distance for the day of imaging, from the MTL metadata.
d = mtl["EARTH_SUN_DISTANCE"]

# 3. Recover E_sun (exo-atmospheric solar irradiance) for each band using metadata calibration coefficients.
esun = {}
for b, name in REFLECTIVE.items():  # every reflective band
    if name not in OLI_CENTRE:  # skip bands without a centre wavelength
        continue
    # Choose any digital number (DN) value (here 20,000) since the ratio is linear; it cancels out.
    dn_ref = 20000.0
    # Compute radiance at the top of atmosphere using radiometric rescaling.
    L = mtl[f"RADIANCE_MULT_BAND_{b}"] * dn_ref + mtl[f"RADIANCE_ADD_BAND_{b}"]
    # Compute reflectance without correcting for sun angle.
    rho = mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_MULT_BAND_{b}"] * dn_ref + mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_ADD_BAND_{b}"]
    # Rearranged radiative transfer equation gives E_sun.
    esun[name] = np.pi * L * d**2 / rho
# Store these values in a pandas Series.
esun = pd.Series(esun, name="E_sun from MTL (W m⁻² µm⁻¹)")

# 4. Compute the theoretical solar irradiance at each band's wavelength using Planck's law (blackbody at 5,778 K).
#    - Converts wavelengths to meters, applies πB_λ(T), multiplies by the (Sun radius/distance)^2 solid angle, and scales units.
planck_esun = pd.Series(
    {
        n: np.pi * planck(OLI_CENTRE[n] * 1e-6, 5778) * (6.96e8 / 1.496e11) ** 2 * 1e-6
        for n in esun.index
    },
    name="Planck 5,778 K (W m⁻² µm⁻¹)",
)

# 5. Create a DataFrame summarizing the band center wavelengths, MTL irradiance, Planck prediction, and their ratio.
cmp = pd.concat(
    [pd.Series(OLI_CENTRE)[esun.index].rename("centre (µm)"), esun, planck_esun],
    axis=1,
)
# how close the metadata irradiance is to the Planck prediction
cmp["ratio MTL / Planck"] = cmp.iloc[:, 1] / cmp.iloc[:, 2]

# 6. Display the DataFrame, rounded for neatness.
display(cmp.round(3))

# 7. Plot comparison of the MTL (metadata) and theoretical (Planck) exo-atmospheric solar irradiances across wavelengths.
wl_um = np.linspace(0.3, 2.5, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))  # one panel
# Plot the Planck blackbody curve (in solar units).
ax.plot(
    wl_um,
    np.pi * planck(wl_um * 1e-6, 5778) * (6.96e8 / 1.496e11) ** 2 * 1e-6,
    label="Planck, 5,778 K blackbody",
)
# Plot the actual band center values derived from the MTL.
ax.plot(
    cmp["centre (µm)"], cmp.iloc[:, 1], "o", ms=8, label="Landsat 8 bands (from the MTL file)"
)
ax.set_xlabel("Wavelength (µm)")  # x label
ax.set_ylabel("Solar irradiance (W m⁻² µm⁻¹)")  # y label
ax.set_title("Exo-atmospheric solar irradiance")  # title
ax.legend()  # legend
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

The irradiance implied by the metadata peaks in the blue band at 2,020 W m⁻² µm⁻¹ and falls to 80 W m⁻² µm⁻¹ at 2.2 µm. That is the solar spectrum, recovered from two lines of calibration coefficients. The 5,778 K blackbody reproduces its shape to within 2 to 18%, with a peak near 0.5 µm as Wien’s law predicts. The real Sun is not a perfect blackbody: its photosphere emits from different temperatures at different wavelengths, and absorption lines are averaged over each band. That is why measured solar spectra, not Planck curves, are used in calibration.


Rayleigh scattering in the darkest pixels
The darkest pixels of a scene reflect almost nothing at the surface, so most of their TOA signal is atmospheric path radiance. If molecular (Rayleigh) scattering dominates, the dark-object reflectance should fall steeply with wavelength. The dark object subtraction method (DOS1, Chavez 1996; rs.optical.dos1) uses exactly this signal for a first-order atmospheric correction.
The method needs genuinely dark targets in every band it corrects: deep clear water or deep shadow. This farmland subset has no lake, and in the visible bands the darkest pixels are dense crops and woodland, which absorb blue and red light for photosynthesis. In the NIR and SWIR the same vegetation is bright, so the darkest pixels there are not dark at all. We therefore test the scattering law on the visible bands only.


Code
# Select the four visible Landsat 8 (OLI) bands by name.
vis = ["coastal", "blue", "green", "red"]

# For each band, calculate the 0.1th percentile of Top-Of-Atmosphere (TOA) reflectance values,
# representing the darkest pixels (potentially shadow or water). Store these in a pandas Series.
dark = pd.Series(
    {b: float(np.nanpercentile(toa[b].values, 0.1)) for b in OLI_CENTRE},
    name="dark-object TOA reflectance (0.1th percentile)"
)

# Fit a straight line in log-log space (power-law) to the relationship between wavelength and
# dark-object reflectance across the visible bands, to see how reflectance falls off with wavelength.
# This gives a slope which, for pure Rayleigh scattering, should be -4.
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(
    np.log([OLI_CENTRE[b] for b in vis]),
    np.log(dark[vis].values),
    1
)
# slope of the fitted power law
print(f"Power-law fit over the visible bands: dark reflectance ∝ λ^{slope:.2f}  (pure Rayleigh: λ^-4)")

# Plot the results:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))

# Plot the measured dark-object (0.1th percentile) reflectances vs wavelength for the visible bands,
# using a log-log scale.
ax.loglog([OLI_CENTRE[b] for b in vis], dark[vis].values, "o-", label="darkest 0.1% of pixels")

# Create an array of wavelengths between the blue and red bands (in microns).
lam = np.linspace(0.43, 0.68, 50)

# Plot the theoretical Rayleigh scattering line (λ^-4) normalised to the blue band.
ax.loglog(
    lam,
    dark["blue"] * (lam / OLI_CENTRE["blue"]) ** -4,
    "--",
    label="λ⁻⁴ through the blue band"
)

ax.set_xlabel("Wavelength (µm)")  # x label
ax.set_ylabel("TOA reflectance")  # y label

# Plot the fitted power-law line using the computed slope, again normalised to the blue band.
ax.loglog(
    lam,
    dark["blue"] * (lam / OLI_CENTRE["blue"]) ** slope,
    ":",
    label=f"fitted λ^{slope:.2f}"
)

ax.set_title("Path radiance in the darkest pixels (visible bands)")  # title
ax.legend()  # legend
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

# Apply the Dark Object Subtraction (DOS1) atmospheric correction to all OLI bands.
corrected = rs.optical.dos1(toa[list(OLI_CENTRE)])

# Construct a dataframe comparing the dark-object and median reflectance before and after correction.
pd.DataFrame({
    "TOA dark object": dark,
    "after DOS1": pd.Series({b: float(np.nanpercentile(corrected[b].values, 0.1)) for b in OLI_CENTRE}),
    "median TOA": pd.Series({b: float(toa[b].median()) for b in OLI_CENTRE}),
    "median after DOS1": pd.Series({b: float(corrected[b].median()) for b in OLI_CENTRE})
}).round(4).T

Across the visible bands the dark-object reflectance falls as \(\lambda^{-2.75}\): from 0.105 in the coastal band to 0.035 in the red. That is steeper than aerosol (Mie) scattering alone, but shallower than the pure Rayleigh \(\lambda^{-4}\). Two reasons:

Aerosols add a flatter component.
The darkest pixels here are vegetation, not water, so they still carry some surface reflectance.

DOS1 removes most of this haze. It lowers the median blue reflectance from 0.096 to 0.027 and the coastal band from 0.118 to 0.023, which are typical surface values for vegetated land. In the NIR it subtracts 0.019, but the darkest NIR pixels in this scene are ponds and vegetation rather than haze, so that correction removes real signal. In the SWIR it changes almost nothing.
DOS is therefore a quick fix for the visible bands when a scene has dark targets. Level-2 surface reflectance (the Level-2 surface reflectance section) is the better starting point.

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
text:
The four resolutions
Every sensor is a compromise between four kinds of resolution:










Resolution
Question it answers
Landsat 8/9
Sentinel-2
MODIS




Spatial
How small an object can be seen?
30 m (15 m pan, 100 m thermal)
10, 20, 60 m
250, 500, 1000 m


Spectral
How many bands, and how narrow?
11 bands
13 bands
36 bands


Temporal
How often is a place revisited?
16 days (8 with both)
5 days (two satellites)
1 to 2 days


Radiometric
How finely is brightness quantized?
12-bit (Landsat 9: 14-bit), stored 16-bit
12-bit
12-bit



Improving one usually costs another: MODIS sees the whole planet daily because its pixels are large, while Sentinel-2’s 10 m pixels need five days to cover the globe.

Spatial resolution
We simulate coarser sensors by block-averaging the 10 m Sentinel-2 image to 30 m (Landsat) and 250 m (MODIS). Each coarse pixel is a mixture of everything inside it: a mixed pixel.


Code
# Create a figure with 3 horizontal subplots, sized appropriately for display.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.6))

# Loop through each subplot axis and corresponding coarsening factor:
# f = 1 shows the original 10m Sentinel-2 image,
# f = 3 simulates Landsat resolution (~30m, by averaging 3x3 blocks),
# f = 25 simulates a coarse MODIS-like pixel (~250m, by averaging 25x25 blocks).
for a, f in zip(axes, [1, 3, 25]):
    if f == 1:  # first panel
        # No coarsening; use original image.
        img = s2
    else:
        # Coarsen image by the given factor, trimming edges,
        # then take mean for each coarse pixel and restore CRS info.
        img = s2.coarsen(x=f, y=f, boundary="trim").mean().rio.write_crs(s2.rio.crs)
    # Plot the image in false color (NIR, red, green), set the subplot title
    # with the simulated pixel size and dimensions.
    rs.viz.plot_rgb(
        img, ("nir", "red", "green"), ax=a,
        title=f"{10 * f} m pixels ({img.sizes['x']} × {img.sizes['y']})"
    )
    # Remove x/y axis ticks for clean output presentation.
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])

# Adjust subplot layout for clarity and show the figure.
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()  # draw









At 10 m the interchange, individual buildings, parking lots and the pond in the upper left are sharp. At 30 m (Landsat) the pond and the main roads remain, but buildings merge with the lawns around them. At 250 m (MODIS) the whole 2 km area is only 48 mixed pixels: one darker pixel hints at the pond, and the land cover can only be described as fractions.


Spectral resolution
Spectral resolution decides which materials can be told apart. Trees and grass are both green vegetation; the table compares how far apart their mean signatures are in each band, relative to the variation within the classes (a simple separability measure, \(|\mu_1 - \mu_2| / \sqrt{(s_1^2 + s_2^2)/2}\)).


Code
# Create a new pandas Series that maps numeric class labels y to their descriptive class names using the 'classes' dictionary, and index it with the same indices as X.
lab = pd.Series(y, index=X.index).map(classes)

# Split the DataFrame X into two groups: one for samples labeled as "Tree/bushes" and another for samples labeled as "Grass".
a = X[lab == "Tree/bushes"]
b = X[lab == "Grass"]  # grass pixels

# Calculate the separability between the "Tree/bushes" and "Grass" classes for each Sentinel-2 band.
# For each band:
#   1. Compute the difference in mean values between the classes.
#   2. Take the absolute value of the difference.
#   3. Divide by the pooled standard deviation (the square root of the average variance of the two classes).
# This gives a measure of how distinct the two classes are in each band.
sep = (
    (a[list(S2_NM)].mean() - b[list(S2_NM)].mean()).abs()
    / np.sqrt((a[list(S2_NM)].var() + b[list(S2_NM)].var()) / 2)
).rename("tree vs grass separability")

# Format the results to two decimal places, convert to a single-row DataFrame, and display.
sep.round(2).to_frame().T

In the visible bands trees and grass are barely separable (0.56 in blue, 0.63 in red): both absorb for photosynthesis. Separability rises to 2.0 to 2.4 in the red-edge and NIR bands, where canopy structure differs. It is highest in SWIR1 (3.9), which responds to leaf water and shadow. The narrow red-edge band at 740 nm (2.38) separates them better than the broad NIR band (2.04). An RGB camera would struggle to tell these two classes apart; a multispectral sensor with red-edge and SWIR bands does not.


Radiometric resolution
Radiometric resolution is the number of distinct brightness levels, \(2^{bits}\). Landsat 8 records 12 bits (4,096 levels) and stores them as 16-bit integers scaled to 0 to 65,535. Fewer levels cause visible banding, most of all in dark, low-contrast targets such as water.


Code
# Loop over typical radiometric resolutions (number of bits per pixel)
for bits in (1, 4, 8, 12, 16):
    # For each bit depth, print the corresponding number of brightness levels
    print(f"{bits:2d}-bit → {2**bits:6,d} levels")

# Extract the digital number (DN) values for the NIR (near-infrared) band
nir_dn = dn["nir"].values

# Filter out any invalid (non-finite) pixel values
valid = nir_dn[np.isfinite(nir_dn)]

# Print the range of NIR DN values and how many unique values are present
print(
    f"NIR DN range in this subset: {valid.min():.0f}–{valid.max():.0f}; "
    f"distinct values: {np.unique(valid).size:,}"
)

# Quantize NIR DN values to different bit depths (simulating reduced radiometric resolution).
# This is done for 2, 4, and 8 bits as examples, using simple linear scaling.
q = {
    bits: np.floor((nir_dn - valid.min()) / (valid.max() - valid.min() + 1) * 2**bits)
    for bits in (2, 4, 8)
}

# Visualize the quantized images
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.6))
for ax, (bits, arr) in zip(axes, q.items()):  # each bit depth with its quantised image
    ax.imshow(arr, cmap="gray")  # show it in grey
    ax.set_title(f"NIR quantized to {bits} bits ({2**bits} levels)")  # title with the number of levels
    ax.set_xticks([])  # no x ticks
    ax.set_yticks([])  # no y ticks
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw


 1-bit →      2 levels
 4-bit →     16 levels
 8-bit →    256 levels
12-bit →  4,096 levels
16-bit → 65,536 levels
NIR DN range in this subset: 5290–27590; distinct values: 14,190











Temporal resolution
Temporal resolution cannot be seen in a single scene, but it decides what can be monitored. Crop growth needs observations every few days to weeks, floods need hours to days, and cloud cover reduces the usable revisit: the full Landsat scene used here was 18.8% cloudy (this subset happens to be clear), and in humid regions a 16-day revisit often yields only one or two clear views a month. Combining sensors (Landsat + Sentinel-2 in the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 product, rs.optical.load_hls), adding SAR, or fusing coarse daily data with fine sparse data (rs.fusion.starfm) are the usual remedies. The time-series notebooks (07_06) cover time-series analysis.

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
text:
Passive and active sensors
Passive sensors record natural energy: reflected sunlight (optical) or emitted heat (thermal). Everything in the sections from Spectral signatures from real images to The four resolutions is passive.
Active sensors send their own pulse and time the echo:

Radar (SAR) transmits microwaves that pass through clouds and work at night, which is why Sentinel-1 is the workhorse for flood mapping in the monsoon. It measures backscatter, usually expressed in decibels (dB).
Lidar transmits laser pulses and records return times, giving precise 3-D point clouds of terrain and vegetation structure.

Radar backscatter spans several orders of magnitude, so it is usually shown in decibels, \(\sigma^0_{dB} = 10 \log_{10}(\sigma^0)\):


Code
# Define typical radar backscatter (sigma0, linear scale) for various surfaces
surfaces = {
    "Calm water": 0.001,
    "Bare field": 0.03,
    "Grassland": 0.08,
    "Forest": 0.15,
    "Urban corner reflector": 2.0
}

# Convert linear sigma0 values to decibel (dB) using the SAR utility function
# This helps visualize the large dynamic range in radar backscatter for each surface type
db = rs.sar.to_db(np.array(list(surfaces.values())))

# Create a DataFrame showing both the original (linear) and dB-scaled sigma0 values for easy comparison
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "sigma0 (linear)": list(surfaces.values()),
        "sigma0 (dB)": db.round(1)
    },
    index=surfaces.keys()
)

section: Processing levels: from DN to physical units
text:
Processing levels: from DN to physical units
Raw sensor counts pass through a chain of corrections before analysis:








Level
Content
Example




L0
Raw instrument data
Downlinked telemetry


L1
Calibrated, geolocated radiance or TOA reflectance (as DN with scale factors)
Landsat Collection 1/2 Level-1, Sentinel-2 L1C


L2
Geophysical variables: surface reflectance, surface temperature, backscatter
Landsat C2 Level-2, Sentinel-2 L2A, MOD09


L3
Gridded, composited or aggregated products
MOD13 16-day NDVI


L4
Model outputs that combine data
GPP, soil moisture analyses



For Landsat Level-1 the conversions use coefficients from the scene’s metadata (*_MTL.txt):

Radiance: \(L_\lambda = M_L \cdot DN + A_L\) (rs.optical.radiance)
TOA reflectance: \(\rho = (M_\rho \cdot DN + A_\rho) / \sin(\theta_{SE})\), with sun elevation \(\theta_{SE}\) (rs.optical.toa_reflectance)
Brightness temperature (thermal bands): \(BT = K_2 / \ln(K_1/L_\lambda + 1)\) (rs.optical.brightness_temperature), the inverse of Planck’s law for the band.


Reflective bands


Code
# This block retrieves the calibration coefficients for each reflective band (used to convert between DN, radiance, and TOA reflectance),
# and then summarizes the typical values for each band over the scene.

# Collect the multiplicative/additive coefficients ("M" and "A") for both reflectance ("rho") and radiance ("L")
# from the metadata (MTL) file for each reflective band. These are necessary for conversions:
# - between digital number (DN) and top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance
# - between DN and radiance.
# The coefficients are organized into a DataFrame for easy viewing.
coef = pd.DataFrame({
    name: {
        "M_rho": mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_MULT_BAND_{b}"],   # reflectance gain
        "A_rho": mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_ADD_BAND_{b}"],    # reflectance offset
        "M_L": mtl[f"RADIANCE_MULT_BAND_{b}"],        # radiance gain
        "A_L": mtl[f"RADIANCE_ADD_BAND_{b}"]          # radiance offset
    }
    for b, name in REFLECTIVE.items()
}).T
display(coef)  # show the calibration coefficients

# For a subset of common bands, compute and summarize the central tendency of their DN, radiance, and TOA reflectance values.
# This illustrates the typical pixel values encountered in this scene after calibration.
rows = []
for name in ["blue", "red", "nir", "swir16"]:  # four representative bands
    # Find the band number in L8_BANDS that matches the band name
    b = next(k for k, v in L8_BANDS.items() if v == name)
    # Convert DN to radiance using the calibration coefficients from the metadata
    rad = rs.optical.radiance(
        dn[name],
        mtl[f"RADIANCE_MULT_BAND_{b}"],
        mtl[f"RADIANCE_ADD_BAND_{b}"]
    )
    # Gather median values for DN, radiance, and TOA reflectance for this band
    rows.append({
        "band": name,
        "median DN": float(dn[name].median()),
        "median radiance": float(rad.median()),
        "median TOA reflectance": float(toa[name].median())
    })

# Display the results as a DataFrame (bands as index), rounding for clarity.
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("band").round(3)

Thermal band: brightness temperature
Band 10 (10.9 µm) records emitted radiance. Inverting Planck’s law with the band constants \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) from the MTL file gives the brightness temperature: the temperature a blackbody would need to produce the measured radiance. Correcting for emissivity (estimated from NDVI, rs.optical.emissivity_ndvi) turns it into land surface temperature (rs.optical.landsat_lst, optical notebooks 07_02).


Code
# Calculate at-sensor radiance for thermal Band 10 using the calibration coefficients from the MTL metadata
rad10 = rs.optical.radiance(
    dn["tir1"],                     # Digital numbers (DN) for thermal infrared band (Band 10)
    mtl["RADIANCE_MULT_BAND_10"],   # Radiance multiplicative scaling factor from metadata
    mtl["RADIANCE_ADD_BAND_10"]     # Radiance additive scaling factor from metadata
)

# Convert the radiance to brightness temperature (in Kelvin) using Planck's law and sensor-specific constants
bt = rs.optical.brightness_temperature(
    rad10,                          # at-sensor radiance for Band 10
    mtl["K1_CONSTANT_BAND_10"],     # K1 constant from metadata
    mtl["K2_CONSTANT_BAND_10"]      # K2 constant from metadata
)

# Convert brightness temperature from Kelvin to Celsius, and assign the coordinate reference system
bt_c = (bt - 273.15).rio.write_crs(dn.rio.crs)

# Display the K1 and K2 constants for reference
print(f"K1 = {mtl['K1_CONSTANT_BAND_10']}, K2 = {mtl['K2_CONSTANT_BAND_10']}")

# Set up a figure with two panels: map and histogram
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1]})

# Show the brightness temperature map on the left, colored by temperature
rs.viz.plot_raster(
    bt_c, ax=axes[0], cmap="inferno",
    title="Band 10 brightness temperature (°C), 2016-09-27"
)
axes[0].set_xticks([]); axes[0].set_yticks([])  # no ticks on the image panel

# Plot a histogram of brightness temperature for each land cover class on the right
lc = masks  # Dictionary mapping class names to boolean masks
for name, m in lc.items():  # each land-cover class and its mask
    v = bt_c.where(m).values.ravel()  # Extract temperature values where mask is True
    axes[1].hist(  # histogram of its brightness temperatures
        v[np.isfinite(v)], bins=60, alpha=0.6, density=True, label=name
    )
axes[1].set_xlabel("Brightness temperature (°C)")  # x label
axes[1].set_ylabel("density")  # y label
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)  # legend

# Adjust layout and display the plots
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# Summarize the results: For each land cover class, report the median brightness temperature (°C) and pixel count
pd.DataFrame({
    name: {
        "median BT (°C)": float(bt_c.where(m).median()),
        "pixels": int(m.sum())
    }
    for name, m in lc.items()
}).T.round(1)

On this late-September morning (scene time 15:51 UTC, about 11:50 local), harvested and bare fields were the warmest surfaces, with a median brightness temperature of 22.8 °C. Dense vegetation was 2.7 °C cooler (20.1 °C), because transpiring leaves spend energy evaporating water. The farm ponds (19.6 °C, 129 mixed pixels) were among the coolest. The map is blockier than the reflective bands because TIRS measures at 100 m and the product is resampled to 30 m.
Brightness temperature is not yet land surface temperature. It ignores emissivity, which here is below 1, and atmospheric absorption, so it usually underestimates the true surface temperature by a few degrees.


Level-2 surface reflectance
Most analysis today starts from Level-2 surface reflectance, which is already corrected for the atmosphere. These products are stored as scaled integers, and rs.optical.scale applies the right factors per sensor (for Landsat Collection 2: \(DN \times 2.75\times10^{-5} - 0.2\)). We read a 600 × 600 pixel window from the Landsat 9 Level-2 scene.


Code
# Define the directory and scene ID for the Landsat 9 Level-2 Surface Reflectance product.
L9_DIR = DATA / "LC09_L2SP_138043_20221216_20221223_02_T1"
L9_ID = "LC09_L2SP_138043_20221216_20221223_02_T1"  # the scene ID

# Define a window to select a 600x600 pixel subset from the full scene
win = dict(y=slice(2400, 3000), x=slice(2400, 3000))

# Read each required surface reflectance band file (bands 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) from disk,
# drop the redundant 'band' dimension, select the chosen window,
# and load all pixel values into memory.
l2 = xr.Dataset({
    f"SR_B{b}": rs.read(L9_DIR / f"{L9_ID}_SR_B{b}.TIF", masked=False, chunks={})
                  .squeeze("band", drop=True)
                  .isel(**win)
                  .load()
    for b in (2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
})

# Convert the raw digital numbers (DNs) in l2 to surface reflectance values 
# using the correct scaling for Landsat Collection 2.
sr = rs.optical.scale(l2, sensor="landsat")

# Print which sensor was recognized and used for scaling (metadata compatibility).
print("sensor recognised as:", sr.attrs.get("pyrsense:sensor"))

# Build and display a DataFrame summarizing, for each band:
# - the median raw DN value (from the original data)
# - the median surface reflectance (after scaling)
# and round the numbers to four decimal places for clarity.
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "DN (median)": {v: float(l2[v].median()) for v in l2.data_vars},
        "surface reflectance (median)": {v: float(sr[v].median()) for v in sr.data_vars}
    }
).round(4)

rs.viz.plot_rgb(
    sr,
    ("SR_B5", "SR_B4", "SR_B3"),

plt.tight_layout()

# median value and the range from 5th to 95th percentile (to summarize variability).
print(
    f"NDVI median {float(ndvi_l9.median()):.2f}, 5th–95th percentile "
    f"{float(ndvi_l9.quantile(0.05)):.2f} to {float(ndvi_l9.quantile(0.95)):.2f}"
)

rs.optical.scale recognised the Collection 2 band names and converted, for example, a median DN of 9,869 in the blue band to a surface reflectance of 0.071. No sun-angle or metadata file is needed, because the atmospheric correction was done by USGS.
The 18 × 18 km window in northwestern Bangladesh was imaged in December, in the dry season. A meandering river runs from the upper left to the lower right. Green vegetation along its floodplain and in the west has NDVI 0.5 to 0.65, while the dry fallow and harvested land to the east and south has NDVI 0.1 to 0.3 (median 0.29 over the window).

title: Remote Sensing Fundamentals
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

Remote sensing turns measured radiance into physical quantities and then into information, through a chain of source, atmosphere, target, sensor and processing.
Optical sensors (0.4 to 3 µm) measure reflected sunlight; thermal sensors (8 to 14 µm) measure emitted energy; radar and lidar supply their own illumination.
The atmosphere scatters (Rayleigh ∝ λ⁻⁴) and absorbs; sensors look through its windows, and atmospheric correction removes path radiance.
Spectral signatures (water, vegetation, built surfaces) are the basis of every spectral index and classifier.
Spatial, spectral, temporal and radiometric resolution trade off against each other.
Analysis-ready data are Level-2 surface reflectance, surface temperature or calibrated backscatter in physical units.
geolattice.rsense covers the whole workflow, from data access to deep learning, on CPU or GPU.

What the data showed

Sentinel-2 ground truth reproduced the textbook signatures, including the red edge (grass: 0.105 → 0.275 → 0.383 from 705 to 842 nm).
The Landsat 8 metadata alone recovered the solar spectrum, within 2 to 18% of a 5,778 K blackbody.
Path radiance in the visible bands fell as λ^−2.75, between Rayleigh and aerosol scattering. DOS1 removed most of it, but should not be trusted in bands without dark targets.
Bare fields were 2.7 °C warmer than transpiring vegetation in brightness temperature.
Red-edge and SWIR bands separated trees from grass four to six times better than the visible bands.

Exercises

Use planck() to find the peak wavelength of a 600 K lava flow. Which Landsat band would detect it best?
Add the Sentinel-2 signature of a sixth material by digitising a polygon (for example a sports field or a parking lot) and passing it to rs.classify.extract_samples.
Compute "SAVI", "MNDWI" and "NBR" for the Landsat 8 scene with rs.optical.index and compare their maps with NDVI and NDWI.
Repeat the Rayleigh scattering in the darkest pixels section on band 9 (cirrus, 1.37 µm). What do its brightest pixels show, and why?
Compute the brightness temperature from band 11 and compare it with band 10 over the vegetation and the harvested fields. The difference is the basis of split-window LST algorithms.
Use the PyGIS Explorer app or rs.access.stac_search to find a recent cloud-free Sentinel-2 L2A scene of your area, and plot its spectral signatures.

References

Chavez, P.S. (1996). Image-based atmospheric corrections, revisited and improved. Photogrammetric Engineering & Remote Sensing 62(9), 1025 to 1036.
Jensen, J.R. (2007). Remote Sensing of the Environment: An Earth Resource Perspective, 2nd ed. Pearson.
Lillesand, T., Kiefer, R.W. & Chipman, J. (2015). Remote Sensing and Image Interpretation, 7th ed. Wiley.
Schott, J.R. (2007). Remote Sensing: The Image Chain Approach, 2nd ed. Oxford University Press.
U.S. Geological Survey (2019). Landsat 8 (L8) Data Users Handbook, version 5.0. LSDS-1574.
European Space Agency (2015). Sentinel-2 User Handbook. ESA Standard Document.

Code
# Summarise three different rasters in one table.
#
# describe() pulls the facts you need before trusting a file: how many bands,
# the shape, the in-memory dtype, the no-data flag, the CRS, the pixel size,
# the bounds, and what fraction of pixels are finite (not NaN).
#
# The three columns are the Landsat cube, one DEM tile, and the Sentinel-2 red
# band. squeeze drops a length-1 band axis so a single-band file is 2-D.

def describe(da, name):
    return pd.Series({  # summary of one raster as a table column
        "bands": da.sizes.get("band", 1),
        "rows × cols": f"{da.rio.height} × {da.rio.width}",
        "dtype (in memory)": str(da.dtype),
        "no-data": da.rio.encoded_nodata if da.rio.encoded_nodata is not None else da.rio.nodata,
        "CRS": str(da.rio.crs),
        "resolution": tuple(round(abs(r), 6) for r in da.rio.resolution()),
        "bounds": tuple(round(b, 4) for b in da.rio.bounds()),
        "valid pixels (%)": round(float(np.isfinite(da.values).mean()) * 100, 1),
    }, name=name)

dem_tile = rs.read(DEM_TILES[0]).squeeze("band", drop=True)  # one DEM tile as a 2-D DataArray
s2_red = rs.read(S2_DIR / "B4.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True)  # the Sentinel-2 red band
# the three summaries side by side
pd.concat([describe(landsat_dn, "multi_band.tif"), describe(dem_tile, DEM_TILES[0].name),
           describe(s2_red, "Sentinel_2/B4.tif")], axis=1)

Things to notice:

Landsat (multi_band.tif) stores DNs as float32, with the most negative float32 value (about −3.4 × 10³⁸) as no-data. After masking, 77% of pixels are valid: the scene was clipped to the county outline, and everything outside it is no-data.
The DEM tile is in geographic coordinates (degrees). Only 71% of its pixels are valid for the same reason: it is clipped to the county.
The Sentinel-2 band has no CRS. Its coordinates are numbers without a reference system, so it cannot be overlaid on anything until we assign one (the Coordinate reference systems and reprojection section).
The three files use three different CRS situations and pixel sizes. Before combining them we must bring them onto a common grid.



Code
# Peek at how each GeoTIFF is stored on disk.
#
# The in-memory array hides details that matter for fast or cloud reads:
# the driver, the on-disk dtype, whether the file is tiled, the compression,
# the overview (pyramid) levels, and any TIFF tags. rasterio.open reads only
# that header. Overviews are the reduced-resolution copies a COG uses when you
# zoom out.

for path in [L8_FILE, DEM_TILES[0], S2_DIR / "B4.tif"]:
    with rasterio.open(path) as src:  # open the file
        # format, data type and tiling of the file
        print(f"{path.name:18s} driver {src.driver}, dtype {src.dtypes[0]}, tiled {src.profile.get('tiled')}, "
              f"compression {src.profile.get('compress')}, overviews {src.overviews(1)}, tags {src.tags()}")


multi_band.tif     driver GTiff, dtype float32, tiled False, compression lzw, overviews [], tags {'AREA_OR_POINT': 'Area'}
Onondaga_DEM0.TIF  driver GTiff, dtype float32, tiled True, compression lzw, overviews [], tags {'DataType': 'Generic', 'AREA_OR_POINT': 'Area'}
B4.tif             driver GTiff, dtype float32, tiled False, compression lzw, overviews [], tags {}


The Landsat bands are still raw digital numbers (DN). As in notebook 09_01_00, the MTL metadata file converts them to top-of-atmosphere reflectance, which is what indices need:


Code
# Convert Landsat digital numbers to top-of-atmosphere reflectance.
#
# The pixels in the file are DNs, not reflectance. The MTL text file stores the
# gain, bias and sun elevation that turn DN into TOA reflectance:
#     reflectance = (M * DN + A) / sin(sun elevation)
#
# 1. parse_mtl reads that text file into a dictionary.
# 2. toa_reflectance applies the formula to each band. Band numbers follow the
#    Landsat 8 naming (blue is band 2, nir is band 5).
# 3. concat stacks the four bands back into one cube and copies the CRS.
# 4. The median of each band is a quick sanity check: TOA reflectance of land
#    should sit between 0 and 1, not in the thousands.

mtl = rs.optical.parse_mtl(L8_MTL)
# acquisition date, cloud cover and sun angle
print("Acquired", mtl["DATE_ACQUIRED"], "| cloud cover", mtl["CLOUD_COVER"], "% | sun elevation",
      round(mtl["SUN_ELEVATION"], 1), "°")
band_no = {"blue": 2, "green": 3, "red": 4, "nir": 5}  # band name -> Landsat 8 band number
# DN -> top-of-atmosphere reflectance, band by band
landsat = xr.concat([rs.optical.toa_reflectance(landsat_dn.sel(band=n), mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_MULT_BAND_{b}"],
                                                mtl[f"REFLECTANCE_ADD_BAND_{b}"], mtl["SUN_ELEVATION"])
                     for n, b in band_no.items()], dim="band").rio.write_crs(landsat_dn.rio.crs)
# median reflectance of each band
landsat.to_dataset(dim="band").median().to_pandas().round(3).rename("median TOA reflectance").to_frame().T

title: Raster and Vector Data Essentials
section: Raster formats: COG, NetCDF, Zarr and HDF
text:
Raster formats: COG, NetCDF, Zarr and HDF








Format
Best for
Notes




GeoTIFF / Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF (COG)
Single images, sharing, web maps
A COG is a tiled GeoTIFF with internal overviews, so software can read just the part it needs over HTTP. rs.write writes COGs by default.


NetCDF
Climate and gridded science data, time series
Self-describing, CF conventions; one file holds many variables.


Zarr
Large multi-dimensional cubes, cloud storage
Chunked and parallel; ideal for Dask and object storage.


HDF4 / HDF5
NASA products (MODIS, GEDI, ICESat-2)
Many layers per file; read them with rs.core.read_hdf.


JPEG2000 (JP2), SAFE
Sentinel-2/Sentinel-1 distribution
rs.core.read_safe indexes a .SAFE folder.



Let’s write the Landsat NIR reflectance band in three formats and compare file sizes and read-back fidelity. The source GeoTIFF is striped (not tiled) and has no overviews, so it is not cloud-optimized; rs.write fixes that.


Code
# Write the NIR band three ways and check that each round-trip is exact.
#
# The same array can live in a Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF, a NetCDF file, or a
# Zarr store. What changes is the on-disk layout, not the values.
#
# 1. Cast NIR to float32 and write all three formats.
# 2. size_mb handles both a single file and a Zarr directory (many small files).
# 3. Read each format back and compare values (NaNs count as equal) and the EPSG code.

nir = landsat.sel(band="nir", drop=True).astype("float32")

rs.write(nir, OUT / "nir_cog.tif")                                  # COG, DEFLATE compression
nir.to_dataset(name="nir").to_netcdf(OUT / "nir.nc")  # save as NetCDF
rs.core.write_zarr(nir.rename("nir"), OUT / "nir.zarr")  # save as Zarr

def size_mb(p):  # size of a file or folder (MB)
    p = Path(p)  # as a Path
    # sum of all files when it is a folder
    return (sum(f.stat().st_size for f in p.rglob("*") if f.is_file()) if p.is_dir() else p.stat().st_size) / 1e6

back_cog = rs.read(OUT / "nir_cog.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True)  # read the COG back
back_nc = rs.core.read_netcdf(OUT / "nir.nc", "nir")  # read the NetCDF back
back_zarr = rs.core.read_zarr(OUT / "nir.zarr")["nir"]  # read the Zarr back
pd.DataFrame({  # size of each format and whether the data survived the round trip
    "size (MB)": [nir.nbytes / 1e6, size_mb(OUT / "nir_cog.tif"), size_mb(OUT / "nir.nc"), size_mb(OUT / "nir.zarr")],
    "identical values": ["n/a", bool(np.allclose(back_cog, nir, equal_nan=True)),
                         bool(np.allclose(back_nc, nir, equal_nan=True)), bool(np.allclose(back_zarr, nir, equal_nan=True))],
    "CRS preserved": ["n/a", back_cog.rio.crs.to_epsg(), back_nc.rio.crs.to_epsg(), back_zarr.rio.crs.to_epsg()],
}, index=["in memory", "COG", "NetCDF", "Zarr"]).round(2)

Code
# Confirm the GeoTIFF written above is actually cloud-optimized.
#
# A COG is tiled (here, square internal blocks) and carries an overview pyramid.
# Those two facts are what let a later reader fetch one window, or a zoomed-out
# view, without scanning the whole file.

with rasterio.open(OUT / "nir_cog.tif") as src:
    # internal block size and overview levels of the COG
    print("COG internal tiling:", src.block_shapes[0], "| overview levels:", src.overviews(1))


COG internal tiling: (512, 512) | overview levels: [2, 4]


All three formats read back identical values and keep the CRS (EPSG:32618). For this reflectance band, Zarr was the smallest (7.0 MB against 12.1 MB in memory), the COG came next (9.3 MB), and NetCDF was written uncompressed (12.1 MB) because no compression was requested. Floating-point reflectance compresses less than integer DNs or elevations would. The COG is internally tiled in 512 × 512 blocks with overviews at 2× and 4×; the original multi_band.tif had neither.

title: Raster and Vector Data Essentials
text:
Coordinate reference systems and reprojection
A CRS defines how coordinates relate to places on Earth.

Geographic CRSs (EPSG:4326) use degrees of latitude and longitude. A degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles, so they are poor for measuring distances and areas.
Projected CRSs such as UTM use metres on a flat grid with small distortion within each 6° zone.
Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) is designed for web maps; it stretches distances and areas by \(1/\cos(\text{latitude})\).

rs.core.estimate_utm_crs finds the right UTM zone; rs.reproject warps a raster. Our three rasters show the three situations you meet in practice: Landsat is already in UTM, the DEM is geographic, and the Sentinel-2 files have no CRS at all.


Code
# Pick a projected CRS, and see what Web Mercator does to pixel size.
#
# 1. estimate_utm_crs suggests a UTM zone from the data's own footprint.
#    The Landsat scene and the DEM tile can land in the same zone.
# 2. The DEM is stored in degrees. At Syracuse's latitude, one degree of
#    longitude is shorter than one degree of latitude, so a "square" geographic
#    pixel is not square on the ground.
# 3. Reprojecting the 30 m Landsat pixels to EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator) inflates
#    the reported pixel size by about 1/cos(latitude). Those units are Mercator
#    metres, not ground metres.

lat = 43.05                                                           # Syracuse
# UTM zone for the Landsat scene
print(f"UTM zone suggested for the Landsat scene: EPSG:{rs.core.estimate_utm_crs(landsat)}")
# UTM zone for the DEM tile
print(f"UTM zone suggested for the DEM tile:      EPSG:{rs.core.estimate_utm_crs(dem_tile)}")
# ground size of a geographic (degree) pixel at this latitude
print(f"One DEM pixel: {abs(dem_tile.rio.resolution()[0]) * 111_320 * np.cos(np.radians(lat)):.0f} m east-west × "
      f"{abs(dem_tile.rio.resolution()[1]) * 110_574:.0f} m north-south at {lat}°N")

landsat_wm = rs.reproject(landsat, "EPSG:3857", resampling="bilinear")  # Landsat in Web Mercator
# Web Mercator enlarges distances by 1 / cos(latitude)
print(f"\nWeb Mercator scale factor at {lat}°N: {1 / np.cos(np.radians(lat)):.3f}")
# resolution after reprojection
print("Landsat reprojected to Web Mercator: resolution", tuple(round(abs(r), 1) for r in landsat_wm.rio.resolution()),
      "'metres' for 30 m ground pixels")


UTM zone suggested for the Landsat scene: EPSG:32618
UTM zone suggested for the DEM tile:      EPSG:32618
One DEM pixel: 92 m east-west × 125 m north-south at 43.05°N

Web Mercator scale factor at 43.05°N: 1.368
Landsat reprojected to Web Mercator: resolution (41.1, 41.1) 'metres' for 30 m ground pixels


Both rasters belong in UTM zone 18N, which the Landsat file already uses. The DEM’s “square” 0.00113° pixels are rectangles on the ground: 92 m east-west but 125 m north-south at 43°N, because meridians converge toward the pole. In Web Mercator the same 30 m Landsat pixels become 41.1 “metres” wide (30 × 1.368). Any area measured in EPSG:3857 here would be overstated by a factor of 1.37² ≈ 1.87.
Assigning a missing CRS. The Sentinel-2 files store coordinates but no CRS. Reprojecting or overlaying them is impossible until we assign the CRS, which must come from documentation (here, the metadata of the ground-truth shapefile says UTM zone 17N). Assigning (write_crs) only labels the coordinates; reprojecting (rs.reproject) changes them.


Code
# Fix a missing CRS, then check the scene really sits in western New York.
#
# This Sentinel-2 GeoTIFF was saved without a CRS tag, so rio.crs is None.
# write_crs only attaches the label EPSG:32617 (UTM zone 17N). It does not move
# the pixels. Reprojecting to longitude/latitude afterwards is the check: the
# centre should fall near Buffalo, not on the equator or in another UTM zone.

print("CRS as read:", s2_red.rio.crs)
s2_red = s2_red.rio.write_crs("EPSG:32617")  # attach the correct CRS (overwrites a missing or wrong one)
lon_lat = rs.reproject(s2_red, "EPSG:4326")  # reproject to longitude/latitude
print("After write_crs:", s2_red.rio.crs, "| centre:",  # the CRS and the image centre
      tuple(round(float(v), 4) for v in (lon_lat.x.mean(), lon_lat.y.mean())), "(lon, lat)")


CRS as read: None
After write_crs: EPSG:32617 | centre: (-78.8061, 43.0007) (lon, lat)


Choosing a resampling method matters:

nearest: keeps original values; required for categorical data (land cover classes, QA bits, masks).
bilinear / cubic: smooth interpolation for continuous data (reflectance, elevation).
average: correct when aggregating to coarser pixels (e.g. 10 m → 500 m).

The example classifies the DEM into three elevation zones (a land-cover-like map) and reprojects it to UTM at 30 m. Bilinear resampling invents classes that don’t exist.


Code
# Show why a categorical raster must use nearest-neighbour resampling.
#
# Elevation is a continuous number, so averaging neighbouring pixels (bilinear)
# is reasonable. A class code is not. Bilinear resampling invents values such
# as 1.4, which is not a class.
#
# 1. Mosaic the DEM tiles and bin elevation into classes 1, 2 and 3.
# 2. Reproject a small window to UTM at 30 m, once with nearest and once with bilinear.
# 3. Nearest keeps the original integers. Bilinear produces many fractional values.

dem_all = rs.mosaic([rs.read(p).squeeze("band", drop=True) for p in DEM_TILES])   # Section 6 explains mosaics
# three elevation classes, NaN where the DEM has no data
classes = xr.where(dem_all > 400, 3, xr.where(dem_all > 250, 2, 1)).where(dem_all.notnull())
# as floats with a CRS, and a small window
classes = classes.astype("float32").rio.write_crs(4326).isel(y=slice(250, 330), x=slice(200, 310))
near = rs.reproject(classes, 32618, resolution=30, resampling="nearest")  # reprojected with nearest neighbour
# reprojected with bilinear interpolation
bil = rs.reproject(classes, 32618, resolution=30, resampling="bilinear")
# nearest keeps the class values
print("Unique values, nearest :", np.unique(near.values[np.isfinite(near.values)])[:10])
# bilinear invents values between classes
print("Unique values, bilinear:", np.unique(bil.values[np.isfinite(bil.values)]).size, "distinct values (invalid classes!)")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))  # two panels
# nearest result
near.plot(ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", add_colorbar=False); axes[0].set_title("nearest (correct)")
# bilinear result
bil.plot(ax=axes[1], cmap="viridis", add_colorbar=False); axes[1].set_title("bilinear (wrong for classes)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


Unique values, nearest : [1. 2. 3.]
Unique values, bilinear: 8282 distinct values (invalid classes!)









To combine rasters, put them on the same grid (CRS, resolution, extent and alignment). reproject_match warps one raster onto another’s grid in a single step. Here the DEM is matched to the 30 m Landsat grid so pixels line up one-to-one.


Code
# Put the DEM onto the Landsat grid so the two layers share every pixel.
#
# reproject_match warps the DEM to the Landsat CRS, resolution and extent.
# Bilinear is appropriate because elevation is continuous. The transforms are
# then identical, which means NDVI and elevation can be paired pixel by pixel
# with no further resampling.

from rasterio.enums import Resampling
# resample the DEM onto the Landsat grid
dem_on_landsat = dem_all.astype("float32").rio.reproject_match(landsat, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)
print("Landsat grid:", landsat.shape[1:], "| DEM matched:", dem_on_landsat.shape,  # both grids now match
      "| same transform:", landsat.rio.transform() == dem_on_landsat.rio.transform())


Landsat grid: (1853, 1630) | DEM matched: (1853, 1630) | same transform: True


Matching a 120 m DEM to a 30 m grid does not add detail: bilinear interpolation only smooths between the original elevations. Resampling changes the grid, never the information content.

title: Raster and Vector Data Essentials
text:
Clipping, masking and windowed reads
Clipping cuts a raster to a polygon; masking sets pixels outside it (or failing a condition) to NaN; windowed reading loads only a block of a large file. Our study areas are the Onondaga County boundary from the New York counties layer and a box around the city of Syracuse and Onondaga Lake.


Code
# Load county polygons and a simple box, then clip rasters to them.
#
# 1. Read the New York county shapefile and keep Onondaga County.
# 2. Build an AOI rectangle around Syracuse and Onondaga Lake. box() takes
#    (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in longitude/latitude.
# 3. Compare the county area computed from the geometry (after projecting to
#    UTM metres) with the square-mile column already in the attribute table.
# 4. rs.clip cuts the DEM to the county and to the AOI, and cuts Landsat to
#    the AOI after the box is reprojected into the Landsat CRS.

counties = gpd.read_file(COUNTIES)
onondaga = counties[counties["COUNTY"] == "Onondaga County"]  # the Onondaga County polygon
aoi = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"name": ["Syracuse and Onondaga Lake"]},  # a box around Syracuse and Onondaga Lake
                       geometry=[box(-76.30, 42.98, -76.05, 43.15)], crs=4326)
print(f"Onondaga County: {onondaga.to_crs(32618).area.iloc[0] / 1e6:,.0f} km² "  # county area in km²
      f"(attribute table: {onondaga['SQUARE_MIL'].iloc[0]:.1f} mi² = {onondaga['SQUARE_MIL'].iloc[0] * 2.58999:,.0f} km²)")

dem_county = rs.clip(dem_all, onondaga)  # DEM clipped to the county outline
dem_aoi = rs.clip(dem_all, aoi)  # DEM clipped to the AOI box
landsat_aoi = rs.clip(landsat, aoi.to_crs(landsat.rio.crs))  # Landsat clipped to the AOI (in Landsat's CRS)
# sizes of the clipped rasters
print("DEM clipped to county:", dem_county.shape, "| DEM clipped to AOI:", dem_aoi.shape,
      "| Landsat clipped to AOI:", landsat_aoi.shape)


Onondaga County: 2,095 km² (attribute table: 807.8 mi² = 2,092 km²)
DEM clipped to county: (442, 534) | DEM clipped to AOI: (150, 220) | Landsat clipped to AOI: (4, 639, 687)




Code
# Draw the clipped DEM, a conditional mask, and a false-colour Landsat view.
#
# where(elevation > 400) keeps highland pixels and sets the rest to NaN, so the
# middle map shows only the higher ground. The right panel is NIR-red-green:
# vegetation comes out red. The county outline and the red AOI box sit on the
# left map so you can see how the two clip geometries relate.

mask_high = dem_county.where(dem_county > 400)            # mask by a condition
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.4))  # three panels
# county DEM and outline
dem_county.plot(ax=axes[0], cmap="terrain"); onondaga.boundary.plot(ax=axes[0], color="k", lw=0.8)
# AOI outline and title
aoi.boundary.plot(ax=axes[0], color="red"); axes[0].set_title("DEM clipped to Onondaga County (red: AOI)")
mask_high.plot(ax=axes[1], cmap="terrain"); axes[1].set_title("Elevation > 400 m only")  # only the high ground
# Landsat false colour of the AOI
rs.viz.plot_rgb(landsat_aoi.to_dataset(dim="band"), ("nir", "red", "green"), ax=axes[2],
                title="Landsat false colour, clipped to the AOI")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









The county area computed from the polygon in UTM (2,095 km²) matches the attribute table (807.8 mi² = 2,092 km²) to within 0.2%, a good check that the reprojection is right. The DEM shows the county’s two landscapes: the flat Ontario lake plain in the north (110-150 m), around Onondaga Lake and Syracuse, and the dissected Appalachian Plateau in the south, where hills above 400 m are cut by deep north-south glacial valleys. In the false-colour clip, the city and its roads are cyan-grey, Onondaga Lake is black, and Syracuse’s airport is visible to the northeast.
For files larger than memory, read only what you need. rasterio windows load a pixel block directly, and rs.read(..., chunks=...) gives a lazy array where slicing touches only the required chunks.


Code
# Read only the window you need, instead of the whole Landsat band.
#
# 1. Project the AOI into the Landsat CRS and clip the in-memory NIR band to it.
#    clip_box snaps the request to whole pixels.
# 2. from_bounds turns those map bounds into a rasterio window (pixel rows and
#    columns). read(4, window=...) pulls band 4 of the file, which is NIR,
#    and only that block.
# 3. The printed sizes show the I/O saving. allclose confirms the window matches
#    the in-memory clip, including NaNs.

from rasterio.windows import from_bounds

bounds_utm = aoi.to_crs(landsat.rio.crs).total_bounds  # AOI bounds in Landsat's CRS
clip_dn = landsat_dn.sel(band="nir").rio.clip_box(*bounds_utm)          # in-memory clip, snapped to pixels
with rasterio.open(L8_FILE) as src:  # open the file
    # pixel window of the clipped area
    win = from_bounds(*clip_dn.rio.bounds(), transform=src.transform).round_offsets().round_lengths()
    block = src.read(4, window=win, masked=True).filled(np.nan)            # band 4 of the file = NIR
    print("Window:", win, "→ array", block.shape,  # the window and the array read from it
          f"({block.nbytes / 1e6:.1f} MB instead of {src.width * src.height * 4 / 1e6:.1f} MB per band)")
# reading the window gives the same pixels as clipping
print("Matches the clip:", block.shape == clip_dn.shape and np.allclose(block, clip_dn.values, equal_nan=True))


Window: Window(col_off=535, row_off=449, width=689, height=639) → array (639, 689) (1.8 MB instead of 12.1 MB per band)
Matches the clip: True

title: Raster and Vector Data Essentials
text:
Mosaicking
Large study areas span several scenes or tiles. rs.mosaic merges rasters onto one grid, reprojecting if needed. Where tiles overlap, first / last give priority by order, while min, max or mean combine the values. The four Onondaga DEM tiles are adjacent quarters of the county; we merge them and check the result against the complete county DEM stored separately in Data/00_shared/raster_data/USA/Onondaga_DEM.tif.


Code
# Mosaic the four DEM tiles and check the result against a reference file.
#
# rs.mosaic(..., "first") keeps the first tile's value where tiles overlap.
# The reference Onondaga_DEM.tif is the same mosaic prepared ahead of time.
# Comparing the affine transform (to a tiny tolerance) and the values confirms
# the merge did not shift or resample the grid.
#
# The figure shows the tiles in map order: northwest, northeast, southwest,
# southeast: then the merged grid. File order on disk is not map order.

tiles = [rs.read(p).squeeze("band", drop=True) for p in DEM_TILES]
print("Tile shapes:", [t.shape for t in tiles])  # shapes of the four tiles
merged = rs.mosaic(tiles, "first")  # mosaic them, keeping the first value where tiles overlap
# the county DEM shipped as one file
full = rs.read(DATA / "00_shared" / "raster_data" / "USA" / "Onondaga_DEM.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True)
print("Mosaic shape:", merged.shape, "| reference shape:", full.shape)  # shapes of both
# the mosaic is on the same grid as the reference
print("Same grid (to 1e-9°):", np.allclose(tuple(merged.rio.transform())[:6], tuple(full.rio.transform())[:6], atol=1e-9),
      "| identical values:", bool(np.allclose(merged.values, full.values, equal_nan=True)))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(17, 3.2))  # five panels
order = [2, 3, 0, 1]                                         # show tiles in map order: NW, NE, SW, SE
for a, i in zip(axes[:4], order):  # each tile
    # show it
    a.imshow(tiles[i].values, cmap="terrain", vmin=100, vmax=620); a.set_title(DEM_TILES[i].name, fontsize=9)
axes[4].imshow(merged.values, cmap="terrain", vmin=100, vmax=620); axes[4].set_title("Mosaic")  # the mosaic
for a in axes:  # every panel
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

title: Raster and Vector Data Essentials
text:
Raster algebra: indices and terrain
Band math produces new information layers. geolattice.rsense handles band lookup, NaN, division by zero and GPU execution. Here we compute NDVI from the Landsat reflectance and slope, aspect and hillshade from the DEM matched to the same grid.


Code
# Derive NDVI, slope, aspect and hillshade on the shared Landsat grid.
#
# NDVI comes from the optical bands. Slope, aspect and hillshade come from the
# DEM that was warped onto that same grid, so all four maps line up.
# Hillshade uses a sun in the northwest (azimuth 315°) at 45° above the horizon,
# which is the usual choice for a readable shaded relief. The colorbar is turned
# off because hillshade is a display layer, not a measurement to read off a scale.

ls = landsat.to_dataset(dim="band")
ndvi = rs.optical.index(ls, "NDVI")  # NDVI from the Landsat bands
slope = rs.lidar.slope(dem_on_landsat)  # slope from the DEM
aspect = rs.lidar.aspect(dem_on_landsat)  # aspect from the DEM
# hillshade, sun from the north-west at 45 degrees
hill = rs.lidar.hillshade(dem_on_landsat, azimuth=315, altitude=45)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 13))  # 2 x 2 panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(ndvi, ax=axes[0, 0], cmap="RdYlGn", title="NDVI")  # NDVI
rs.viz.plot_raster(slope, ax=axes[0, 1], cmap="magma", title="Slope (degrees)")  # slope
rs.viz.plot_raster(aspect, ax=axes[1, 0], cmap="twilight", title="Aspect (degrees from north)")  # aspect
rs.viz.plot_raster(hill, ax=axes[1, 1], cmap="gray", title="Hillshade", colorbar=False)  # hillshade
for a in axes.ravel(): a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









NDVI is high almost everywhere in mid-July. The exceptions are water (Onondaga, Otisco and Skaneateles lakes, and water along the northern county edge), the city of Syracuse, and roads. Slope picks out the steep sides of the southern valleys.
The hatched, faceted texture in the aspect and hillshade maps is an artifact, not terrain. The DEM pixels are about 92 × 125 m, and bilinear interpolation onto the 30 m grid creates flat planes between the original elevations. Each plane has a constant aspect and a uniform shade. Resampling a coarse DEM to a fine grid changes the grid, not the information: for real 30 m terrain derivatives, use a 30 m (or finer) DEM.
Because both layers are on one grid, they can be analysed together. How does vegetation greenness change with elevation across Onondaga County?


Code
# Relate NDVI to elevation by binning the paired pixels.
#
# Both rasters share the Landsat grid, so flattening them into two columns does
# not mix locations. dropna removes pixels missing from either layer.
#
# 1. Cut elevation into 25 m bins and, inside each bin, compute the median NDVI,
#    the 25th and 75th percentiles (the interquartile range), and the pixel count.
# 2. Drop bins with 500 pixels or fewer so a thin tail does not dominate the line.
# 3. Plot the median and the shaded interquartile range.
# 4. Separately, look at pixels with NDVI < 0 (water) and where their elevations cluster.

df = pd.DataFrame({"elev": dem_on_landsat.values.ravel(), "ndvi": ndvi.values.ravel()}).dropna()
df["band"] = pd.cut(df.elev, bins=range(100, 650, 25))  # 25 m elevation bands
# NDVI statistics per elevation band
prof = df.groupby("band", observed=True).ndvi.agg(["median", lambda s: s.quantile(0.25), lambda s: s.quantile(0.75), "size"])
prof.columns = ["median", "q25", "q75", "pixels"]  # column names
prof = prof[prof.pixels > 500]  # keep bands with enough pixels
mid = [iv.mid for iv in prof.index]  # middle of each band
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))  # one panel
# interquartile range as a shaded band
ax.fill_between(mid, prof.q25, prof.q75, alpha=0.3, label="interquartile range")
ax.plot(mid, prof["median"], marker="o", label="median NDVI")  # median NDVI
# labels, grid and legend
ax.set_xlabel("Elevation (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("NDVI"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("NDVI by elevation band, Onondaga County, 16 July 2015")  # title
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
water = df[df.ndvi < 0]  # water pixels
print(f"Water pixels (NDVI < 0): {len(water):,}; their elevations cluster at",  # at which elevations they lie
      ", ".join(f"{v:.0f} m" for v in np.percentile(water.elev, [10, 50, 90])), "(10th, 50th, 90th percentile)")
# the three most common elevation bands of water
print(water.groupby("band", observed=True).size().sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).rename("water pixels").to_string())
prof.round(3)  # show the profile table

title: Raster and Vector Data Essentials
text:
Vector-raster interaction
Three operations connect vector and raster data:

Point extraction: values at sample locations (field plots, weather stations).
Zonal statistics: summaries of raster values inside polygons (fields, watersheds, counties).
Rasterization: burning polygons into a raster grid (training labels, masks).



Code
# Sample raster values at point locations.
#
# The five sites start as longitude/latitude. They are reprojected into the
# Landsat CRS so .sel can use the same x/y coordinates as the rasters.
# Wrapping the coordinates in DataArrays with a "site" dimension samples every
# point in one call. method="nearest" picks the pixel whose centre is closest.

sites = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"site": ["Syracuse (downtown)", "Onondaga Lake", "Green Lakes State Park", "Highland Forest", "Skaneateles Lake"]},
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy([-76.147, -76.205, -75.970, -75.935, -76.420],
                                [43.048, 43.090, 43.058, 42.855, 42.920]), crs=4326).to_crs(landsat.rio.crs)
xs = xr.DataArray(sites.geometry.x.values, dims="site")  # site x coordinates
ys = xr.DataArray(sites.geometry.y.values, dims="site")  # site y coordinates
# DEM value at each site (nearest pixel)
sites["elevation_m"] = dem_on_landsat.sel(x=xs, y=ys, method="nearest").values.round(0)
sites["ndvi"] = ndvi.sel(x=xs, y=ys, method="nearest").values.round(3)  # NDVI at each site
sites.drop(columns="geometry")  # show the table without geometry

For zonal statistics we buffer each site by 3 km and summarise NDVI and elevation with rs.zonal_stats, which accepts percentiles (p90) as well as the usual statistics.


Code
# Zonal statistics: summarise each raster inside a 3 km buffer.
#
# A point sample is one pixel. A zone is every pixel inside a polygon.
# buffer(3000) is 3 km because the sites are already in a metre-based CRS.
# rs.zonal_stats returns one row per polygon. NDVI is summarised with mean,
# standard deviation, the 90th percentile and the pixel count. Elevation is
# summarised with min, mean and max. The geometry column is dropped before the
# merge so the table is just numbers.

zones = sites[["site", "geometry"]].copy()
zones["geometry"] = zones.buffer(3000)  # 3 km buffer around each site
# NDVI statistics in each buffer
z_ndvi = rs.zonal_stats(ndvi.rename("ndvi"), zones, stats=["mean", "std", "p90", "count"])
# elevation statistics in each buffer
z_elev = rs.zonal_stats(dem_on_landsat.rename("elev"), zones, stats=["min", "mean", "max"])
# both tables joined by site
z_ndvi.drop(columns="geometry").merge(z_elev.drop(columns="geometry"), on="site").round(2)
