The point values and the 3 km zone summaries tell different stories:

Onondaga Lake. The point is water (NDVI −0.22), but the 3 km zone mixes lake and shore, so its mean is 0.26 and its standard deviation 0.39, the largest of the five.
Skaneateles Lake. The same applies: the zone is about half water.
Syracuse. Downtown has intermediate NDVI (0.43 at the point, 0.46 in the zone), with street trees and parks between buildings.
Green Lakes State Park and Highland Forest. These forested sites have the highest means (0.72 and 0.74). Highland Forest is also the highest and most varied in elevation (285-562 m).

Each zone contains about 31,370 pixels, close to the area of a 3 km circle in 30 m pixels. Highland Forest has about 290 fewer valid NDVI pixels, because part of its buffer crosses the county line, where the Landsat file has no data.


Code
# Rasterize the buffers so each pixel carries a zone id.
#
# rasterio.features.rasterize burns vector polygons into the NDVI grid.
# Zone 1, 2, 3... are written as integers; pixels outside every buffer stay 0.
# The expected count for one circle is π r² / pixel area, with r = 3000 m and
# 30 m pixels. The figure lays those zone ids over the hillshade.

from rasterio.features import rasterize
# burn the buffers into a raster: zone number per pixel
burned = rasterize(((g, i + 1) for i, g in enumerate(zones.geometry)), out_shape=ndvi.shape,
                   transform=ndvi.rio.transform(), fill=0, dtype="int16")
# pixels per zone
print("Pixels per zone:", {s: int(n) for s, n in zip(zones.site, np.bincount(burned.ravel())[1:])},
      f"| a 3 km circle holds π·3000²/30² ≈ {np.pi * 3000**2 / 900:.0f} pixels")
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = hill.rio.bounds()  # extent of the hillshade
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 8))  # one panel
ax.imshow(hill.values, cmap="gray", extent=[xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax])  # hillshade background
# zones in colour
ax.imshow(np.where(burned > 0, burned, np.nan), cmap="tab10", alpha=0.8, extent=[xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax])
sites.plot(ax=ax, color="k", markersize=10)  # the sites
for _, r in sites.iterrows():  # each site
    # its name
    ax.annotate(r.site, (r.geometry.x, r.geometry.y), xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8, color="w")
ax.set_title("Rasterized 3 km zones over hillshade"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # title, no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

title: Raster and Vector Data Essentials
text:
Visualization and contrast stretching
Satellite values rarely fill the display range, so images look dark or washed out without a contrast stretch. rs.viz.rgb builds composites from preset band combinations and supports several stretches:

percentile (default 2-98 %): robust to outliers; the usual choice.
minmax: full data range; sensitive to a few extreme pixels.
std: mean ± n standard deviations.
equalize: histogram equalization; maximizes contrast but distorts colours.



Code
# Compare four ways to stretch a true-colour image for display.
#
# Satellite reflectance rarely fills 0-1, so an unstretched RGB looks dark or
# washed out. rgb(..., method=...) rescales values for drawing only:
#   minmax: stretch from the minimum to the maximum (a few bright roofs dominate)
#   percentile: ignore the darkest and brightest tails
#   std: stretch around the mean by a number of standard deviations
#   equalize: spread values so each brightness level is used about equally
# The underlying reflectance array is not changed.

scene = ls.rio.clip_box(*aoi.to_crs(landsat.rio.crs).total_bounds)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 4.6))  # four panels
for a, m in zip(axes, ["minmax", "percentile", "std", "equalize"]):  # four contrast stretches
    # natural colour with that stretch
    rs.viz.plot_rgb(rs.viz.rgb(scene, "true_color", method=m), ax=a, title=f"stretch = {m}")
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









minmax leaves the image nearly black, because a few very bright roofs set the maximum. percentile (2-98%) gives a natural-looking image. std is greyer and lower in contrast. equalize maximizes contrast everywhere but gives water and the city a purple cast, so it is useful for interpretation but not for presentation.
The Sentinel-2 scene stores reflectance ×10,000. Scaling it to 0-1 lets us compute indices correctly and compare composites at 10 m resolution:


Code
# Build a Sentinel-2 dataset from separate single-band GeoTIFFs.
#
# Each file is one band stored as digital numbers. Dividing by 10,000 converts
# those integers to surface reflectance (the Sentinel-2 scaling). The files have
# no CRS tag, so EPSG:32617 is attached from the scene documentation.
# The three panels are natural colour, false colour (vegetation in red), and NDVI.

S2_BANDS = {"B2": "blue", "B3": "green", "B4": "red", "B8": "nir"}
# Sentinel-2 bands as reflectance (DN / 10,000)
s2r = xr.Dataset({name: rs.read(S2_DIR / f"{b}.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True) / 10_000
                  for b, name in S2_BANDS.items()}).rio.write_crs("EPSG:32617")
s2_ndvi = rs.optical.index(s2r, "NDVI")  # NDVI
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_rgb(s2r, "true_color", ax=axes[0], title="Natural colour")  # natural colour
rs.viz.plot_rgb(s2r, ("nir", "red", "green"), ax=axes[1], title="False colour (NIR-R-G)")  # false colour
rs.viz.plot_raster(s2_ndvi, ax=axes[2], cmap="RdYlGn", title="NDVI")  # NDVI
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw











Code
# Save the products this notebook computed.
#
# NDVI and hillshade go out as GeoTIFFs (rs.write keeps the CRS and transform).
# The site points go out as a GeoPackage, which holds the geometry and the
# elevation/NDVI columns sampled above. The print lists everything now in outputs/.

rs.write(ndvi, OUT / "ndvi_onondaga_utm.tif")
rs.write(hill.astype("float32"), OUT / "hillshade_onondaga_utm.tif")  # save the hillshade as GeoTIFF
sites.to_file(OUT / "sites.gpkg", driver="GPKG")  # save the sites as GeoPackage
print(sorted(p.name for p in OUT.iterdir()))  # list the output folder


['hillshade_onondaga_utm.tif', 'ndvi_onondaga_utm.tif', 'nir.nc', 'nir.zarr', 'nir_cog.tif', 'sites.gpkg']

title: Raster and Vector Data Essentials
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

Always inspect CRS, resolution, data type and no-data before analysis. A missing CRS must be assigned from documentation before anything else.
Use COG for sharing single rasters, Zarr for large cubes, NetCDF for gridded science data.
Reproject to a projected CRS for distances and areas; use nearest for classes and bilinear/average for continuous data; put layers on one grid with reproject_match.
Clip and read windows to stay within memory; mosaic tiles with explicit overlap rules.
Zonal statistics and point extraction link rasters to field data and administrative units.

Exercises

Reproject the Landsat reflectance to Web Mercator with nearest and cubic resampling and compare NDVI histograms with the original UTM NDVI.
Clip the Landsat scene to a polygon around Onondaga Lake and estimate the lake area from NDVI < 0 pixels (in km²). Compare with the published area (about 12 km²).
Mosaic the four DEM tiles with "mean" after making them overlap by 20 pixels and adding +10 m to one tile. Where does the seam appear?
Compute zonal statistics of slope for the five sites. Which is steepest?
Make an “agriculture” composite of the Sentinel-2 scene using other bands (for example B11, B8, B2) and different stretches, and describe what each reveals.
Use the county layer to clip the Landsat scene to the neighbouring Madison or Cayuga County. What happens, and why?

title: Getting Access to Remote Sensing Images
text:
Overview
The catalogues are public. The hard part is knowing which catalogue holds which kind of image, and which GeoLattice call talks to it.
This notebook is that map. It uses geolattice.rsense.get_images, the same search and download path as PyGIS Explorer, and shows the two other doors in the library: lazy cloud cubes (geolattice.rsense.access and the one-call loaders) and a GeoTIFF you already have (geolattice.rsense.read). The examples use a small area around Ithaca, New York, plus Landsat, UAV and lidar files that ship in the GeoLattice data/ folder.
Notebook 09_01_00 covers the physics. Notebook 09_01_03_data_discovery_and_access goes further into STAC items, Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs and data cubes. The sensor modules after that assume you can already get the image.
If import geolattice fails, finish notebook 09_01_01_the_python_geospatial_environment and come back.

title: Getting Access to Remote Sensing Images
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Choose among the three GeoLattice doors: download files, open a lazy cube, or read a local raster.
Match an image type (optical, radar, lidar, aerial, thermal, atmospheric) to a source and a collection.
Build an area of interest from a bounding box or a vector file.
Search a catalogue and read the scene list before any download.
Write a get_images call that clips the bands you need, and know when the product is always a whole file.
Open a GeoTIFF that is already on disk.

Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Setup for getting access to remote-sensing images.
#
# 1. Import Path, pandas, GeoPandas and matplotlib, plus a small HTTP helper
#    used to test whether a catalogue is reachable.
# 2. Import geolattice.rsense twice: as rs for the lower-level readers, and as gi
#    for the high-level search/download API in geolattice.rsense.get_images.
# 3. Print the package versions. Later cells add the data paths and the
#    online/offline flag.

%matplotlib inline
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings

import importlib.util  # check whether optional packages are installed
import urllib.request  # check whether a server can be reached
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing subpackage
from geolattice.rsense import get_images as gi  # one-call search and download of satellite images

# figure resolution and a light grid
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3})
print(f"geolattice {geolattice.__version__} | geolattice.rsense {rs.__version__}")  # versions


geolattice 0.3.10 | geolattice.rsense 0.2.0.dev0




Code
# Locate the local files and check what this machine can reach.
#
# 1. The Ithaca AOI is a GeoJSON polygon. UAV mosaics and lidar LAZ tiles are
#    files you already have, used in the last section. outputs/images is where
#    a download would be written.
# 2. reachable() probes Earth Search. ONLINE is False when that call fails, and
#    the live searches below then skip instead of raising.
# 3. HAVE records optional packages (pystac-client, earthaccess, laspy, ...).
#    get_images itself does not need all of them; the lower-level STAC and
#    lidar cells do.

DATA = Path("../../../../Data")
AOI_FILE = DATA / "00_shared" / "data_remote_sensing" / "Data_Ithaca" / "Sentinel_2" / "aoi.geojson"  # Ithaca AOI polygon
UAV_DIR = DATA / "00_shared" / "data_remote_sensing" / "UAV"  # drone (UAV) mosaics
LIDAR_DIR = DATA / "00_shared" / "data_remote_sensing" / "Data_Ithaca" / "Lidar"  # lidar tiles
OUT = Path("outputs/images")  # where downloaded images are saved

print("AOI file:   ", AOI_FILE.exists(), AOI_FILE.name)  # is the AOI file there?
print("UAV mosaics:", len(list(UAV_DIR.glob('*.tif'))) if UAV_DIR.exists() else 0)  # number of UAV mosaics
print("Lidar tiles:", len(list(LIDAR_DIR.glob('*.laz'))) if LIDAR_DIR.exists() else 0)  # number of lidar tiles


def reachable(url, timeout=8):  # can a URL be opened within the timeout?
    try:
        urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout)  # try to open it
        return True  # the server answered
    except Exception:
        return False  # no connection


ONLINE = reachable("https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1")  # is the Earth Search STAC API reachable?
HAVE = {  # which optional packages are installed
    name: importlib.util.find_spec(name) is not None
    for name in ("pystac_client", "planetary_computer", "odc", "earthaccess", "asf_search", "ee", "laspy")
}
print("Earth Search reachable:", ONLINE)  # online status
print("Optional packages:", HAVE)  # optional packages
if not ONLINE:  # offline
    # explain what still runs
    print("Running offline. Catalogue, AOI and local files still run. Live searches will be skipped.")

The catalogue inside get_images
The names above are COLLECTIONS in geolattice.rsense.get_images. The next cell builds a table from that object: every source, every collection, and the bands get_images downloads when you omit bands. An empty band list means the product is a whole file (a SAFE archive, a coastal photo, a LAZ tile, a NetCDF).

# Build a table of every collection get_images knows about.
#
# list_collections() groups collection ids by catalogue (earth-search, planetary,
# cdse, noaa, usgs). For each one this loop records:
#   - the short source id and the human catalogue name
#   - the collection id and its product label
#   - the bands get_images downloads if you do not pass bands=[...]
#   - whether a login is required
# Most STAC catalogues can be searched with no account. Copernicus is the
# exception: search is public, but downloading a SAFE file needs a CDSE login.

LOGIN = {
    "earth-search": "none",
    "planetary": "none",
    "cdse": "search is public; download needs a CDSE account",
    "noaa": "none",
    "usgs": "none",
}

rows = []  # one row per collection
for source, collections in gi.list_collections().items():  # every catalogue and its collections
    for collection in collections:  # every collection
        bands = gi.default_bands(collection, source)  # its default bands
        rows.append({  # one row: catalogue, collection and bands
            "source": source,
            "catalogue": gi.SOURCE_LABELS[source],
            "collection": collection,
            "product": gi.COLLECTION_LABELS.get(collection, collection),
            "default_bands": ", ".join(bands) if bands else "(whole file)",
            "login": LOGIN[source],
        })

catalogue = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # as a table
# number of collections and catalogues
print(f"{len(catalogue)} collections across {catalogue['source'].nunique()} catalogues")

title: Getting Access to Remote Sensing Images
text:
Search before you download
search_images returns a SearchResult. It holds the scene list and the original catalogue items, and it writes nothing. Read scenes first: each entry has an id, a time, cloud cover when the sensor reports it, and a platform.
clearest=True keeps the scene with the lowest cloud cover. ids= keeps only the scenes you name. limit caps the list (the default is 50).
The cells below search July 2024 over the Ithaca polygon. NAIP and lidar ignore a single month: NAIP returns the newest year that covers the area, and lidar is searched across 2018-2024 because a county is flown every few years, not every week.


Code
# Two helpers so a failed catalogue does not stop the rest of the searches.
#
# scene_frame turns a FoundScenes result into a tidy table: one row per scene,
# with the family name you passed in, the catalogue, the collection, the id,
# the date, cloud percent and the platform. An empty result becomes a single
# note row so the table still shows that the search ran.
#
# safe_search calls gi.search_images when ONLINE is True. quiet=True stops the
# progress log. Any exception is caught and printed, and an empty frame is
# returned, so one timeout does not abort the notebook.

def scene_frame(found, family):
    """One row per scene, plus a note row when the catalogue returns nothing."""
    if found is None:  # no search result
        return pd.DataFrame()  # empty table
    rows = []  # one row per scene
    for scene in found.scenes:  # every scene
        when = scene.get("datetime") or ""  # its date, if any
        rows.append({  # one row of scene properties
            "family": family,
            "source": found.source,
            "collection": found.collection,
            "scene_id": scene.get("id"),
            "date": str(when)[:10],
            "cloud_pct": None if scene.get("cloud") is None else round(float(scene.get("cloud")), 1),
            "platform": scene.get("platform") or "",
        })
    if not rows:  # nothing found
        rows.append({  # a note row instead
            "family": family,
            "source": found.source,
            "collection": found.collection,
            "scene_id": " ".join(found.notes) or "(no scenes)",
            "date": "",
            "cloud_pct": None,
            "platform": "",
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)  # the table


def safe_search(family, **kwargs):  # search one image family without stopping on errors
    if not ONLINE:  # offline
        print(f"offline, skipped {family}")  # say so
        return pd.DataFrame()  # empty table
    try:
        found = gi.search_images(aoi=AOI_FILE, quiet=True, **kwargs)  # search the catalogue for the AOI
        print(f"{family:22} {found}")  # summary of the result
        return scene_frame(found, family)  # the scenes as a table
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"{family:22} {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")  # report the error
        return pd.DataFrame()  # empty table




Code
# Search several optical collections over Ithaca and stack the hits in one table.
#
# Every entry is (label, keyword arguments for search_images). The arguments
# that change from row to row are the catalogue (source), the collection, the
# date window, the cloud limit and how many scenes to keep (limit).
# NAIP has no date filter here: the search returns the latest aerial photos
# that intersect the AOI. Copernicus is the same Sentinel-2 archive as Earth
# Search, reached through a different catalogue.

optical = [
    ("Sentinel-2 L2A", dict(
        source="earth-search", collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
        dates=("2024-07-01", "2024-07-31"), cloud=20, limit=8)),
    ("Landsat 8/9 L2", dict(
        source="planetary", collection="landsat-c2-l2",
        dates=("2024-06-01", "2024-08-31"), cloud=40, limit=6,
        platforms="Landsat 8 and 9")),
    ("MODIS NDVI/EVI", dict(
        source="planetary", collection="modis-13Q1-061",
        dates=("2024-06-01", "2024-08-31"), limit=4)),
    ("HLS Sentinel-2", dict(

Radar scenes have no eo:cloud_cover, so clearest=True is the wrong filter. Constrain the orbit and the polarization instead: s1_orbit="ascending" or "descending", and s1_polarization="VV+VH" (or "VV", "HH", "HH+HV"). A time series of backscatter should stay on one orbit direction, because the two looks are not the same geometry. Over Ithaca in July 2024 the ascending passes intersect the polygon and the descending passes do not. An empty list means that orbit misses the polygon. Search the other direction.
Sentinel-5P is one collection and many gases. s5p_product selects the gas: L2__NO2___, L2__O3____, L2__CO____, L2__CH4___, and the others listed in gi.S5P_PRODUCTS. The file is NetCDF, so get_images saves the whole product rather than a map clip.
Lidar returns a tile of points. The id is the LAZ name. Tiles are large (often tens to a few hundred megabytes), so search, then pass ids= for the one tile you want.

title: Getting Access to Remote Sensing Images
text:
Download with get_images
get_images searches and writes files. Pass search= a SearchResult you already trust, or pass the same aoi and dates you used to search.
Arguments that change what lands on disk:







Argument
Effect




bands
Asset names to keep. Defaults come from default_bands (red, green, blue, near infrared, and SCL for Sentinel-2)


mode="clip"
Read the area out of each Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF. This is the default


mode="full"
Save the whole asset


stack=True
Also write stack.tif from red, green, blue and near infrared. Only for mode="clip"


clearest=True
Download the least cloudy scene only


ids=
Download these scene ids and ignore the rest


limit
How many scenes to consider


workers
Parallel downloads. The default is 4



Copernicus SAFE products, NOAA photos, USGS LAZ tiles and NetCDF collections are always whole files. mode is ignored for them. NAIP is always a clip of red, green, blue and near infrared.
Set DOWNLOAD = True in the next cell when you want files under outputs/images/. Left as False, the cell only prints the plan. A Sentinel-2 clip of five bands over this polygon is a few megabytes. A lidar tile is not.


Code
# Prepare download calls, and do not download unless DOWNLOAD is set to True.
#
# search_images only lists scenes. get_images searches and writes files.
# Leaving DOWNLOAD = False makes the notebook safe to re-run: it prints the
# arguments and stops. Set it to True to clip the clearest July 2024 Sentinel-2
# scene (red, green, blue, nir and the scene-classification layer) to the AOI
# and stack those bands in one file.
#
# recipes holds the same kind of call for Landsat, MODIS vegetation indices,
# HLS, NAIP, Sentinel-1, Sentinel-5P, USGS lidar, and a Copernicus SAFE zip.
# The Copernicus recipe needs CDSE_USER and CDSE_PASSWORD because it downloads
# a full product, not a clipped COG window.

DOWNLOAD = False  # True writes files under outputs/images/

# The clearest Sentinel-2 scene in July 2024, clipped to the Ithaca polygon.
sentinel2_call = dict(
    out=OUT / "sentinel2",
    aoi=AOI_FILE,
    dates=("2024-07-01", "2024-07-31"),
    source="earth-search",
    collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
    cloud=20,
    bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir", "scl"],
    mode="clip",
    stack=True,
    clearest=True,
    limit=8,
)

# Other products. Uncomment a block inside the DOWNLOAD branch, or call get_images yourself.
recipes = {
    "landsat": dict(
        out=OUT / "landsat", aoi=AOI_FILE,
        dates=("2024-06-01", "2024-08-31"),
        source="planetary", collection="landsat-c2-l2",
        platforms="Landsat 8 and 9", cloud=40,
        bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir", "lwir11", "qa_pixel"],
        mode="clip", clearest=True, limit=6,
    ),
    "modis_vi": dict(
        out=OUT / "modis_vi", aoi=AOI_FILE,
        dates=("2024-06-01", "2024-08-31"),
        source="planetary", collection="modis-13Q1-061",
        bands=["ndvi", "evi", "red", "nir"],
        mode="clip", limit=1,
    ),
    "hls": dict(
        out=OUT / "hls", aoi=AOI_FILE,
        dates=("2024-07-01", "2024-07-31"),
        source="planetary", collection="hls2-s30", cloud=30,
        bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir", "fmask"],
        mode="clip", clearest=True, limit=4,
    ),
    "naip": dict(
        out=OUT / "naip", aoi=AOI_FILE,
        source="earth-search", collection="naip",
        bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir"],
        limit=1,
    ),
    "sentinel1": dict(
        out=OUT / "sentinel1", aoi=AOI_FILE,
        dates=("2024-07-01", "2024-07-31"),
        source="planetary", collection="sentinel-1-rtc",
        s1_polarization="VV+VH", s1_orbit="ascending",
        bands=["vv", "vh"], mode="clip", limit=1,
    ),
    "sentinel5p": dict(
        out=OUT / "sentinel5p", aoi=AOI_FILE,
        dates=("2024-07-01", "2024-07-03"),
        source="planetary", collection="sentinel-5p-l2-netcdf",
        s5p_product="L2__NO2___", limit=1,
    ),
    "lidar": dict(
        out=OUT / "lidar", aoi=AOI_FILE,
        dates=("2018-01-01", "2024-12-31"),
        source="usgs", collection="lidar-lpc", limit=1,
    ),
    # Copernicus writes a full SAFE zip and needs CDSE_USER / CDSE_PASSWORD.
    "copernicus_s2": dict(
        out=OUT / "cdse_s2", aoi=AOI_FILE,

        source="cdse", collection="SENTINEL-2", product_type="S2MSI2A",

print("Sentinel-2 call:")  # header
for key, value in sentinel2_call.items():  # every argument of the Sentinel-2 call
    print(f"  {key}: {value}")  # print it
print("Other recipes ready:", ", ".join(recipes))  # the other prepared recipes

section: Lazy cubes, without saving a file
text:
Lazy cubes, without saving a file
get_images writes files you can archive, open in a GIS, or hand to someone else. When the next step is a calculation in Python, a lazy cube reads the window you need and leaves the rest in the cloud.
rs.access.stac_search asks a STAC catalogue (Planetary Computer, Earth Search, USGS Landsat, Copernicus, NASA LPCLOUD) and returns items. rs.access.stac_load turns those items into an xarray dataset, one variable per band, reading only the window over your area. That path needs the rsense-access extra:
pip install "geolattice[rsense-access]"
The one-call loaders wrap search, load, scale and cloud masking:
s2 = rs.optical.load_sentinel2(AOI_FILE, ("2024-07-01", "2024-07-31"), max_cloud=20)
landsat = rs.optical.load_landsat(AOI_FILE, ("2024-06-01", "2024-08-31"), max_cloud=30)
modis = rs.optical.load_modis(AOI_FILE, ("2024-06-01", "2024-08-31"))
rtc = rs.sar.load_rtc(AOI_FILE, ("2024-07-01", "2024-07-31"), orbit="ascending")
load_hls reads the NASA copy of Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 and needs an Earthdata login. load_sentinel2(..., catalog="earth-search") reads the AWS copy instead of Planetary Computer.
The next cell searches Planetary Computer for Sentinel-2 when pystac-client is installed. It does not load pixels. Notebook 09_01_03 loads them, signs Planetary Computer URLs, and builds a cube.


Code
# The lower-level search, for when you want the STAC Items themselves.
#
# get_images hides the catalogue response. rs.access.stac_search returns the
# pystac Items, which is what you need for stac_load or a custom reader.
# This call asks Planetary Computer (not Earth Search) for up to five
# Sentinel-2 scenes. odc-stac is required to turn those items into a cube;
# without it the cell only lists ids, cloud cover and dates.
# get_images in the previous cell does not need pystac-client for every source.

if ONLINE and HAVE["pystac_client"]:
    items = rs.access.stac_search(  # search Planetary Computer for Sentinel-2 items
        "sentinel-2-l2a",
        aoi=AOI_FILE,
        dates=("2024-07-01", "2024-07-31"),
        max_cloud=20,
        catalog="planetary-computer",
        limit=5,
    )
    print(f"{len(items)} Sentinel-2 item(s) from Planetary Computer")  # number of items
    for item in items:  # every item
        props = item.properties  # its properties
        # ID, cloud cover and date
        print(f"  {item.id}  cloud={props.get('eo:cloud_cover')}  {str(props.get('datetime'))[:10]}")
    if not HAVE["odc"]:  # odc-stac missing
        # explain what is skipped
        print("odc-stac is not installed, so stac_load and the one-call loaders are not run here.")
        print('Install them with: pip install "geolattice[rsense-access]"')  # how to install it
else:
    missing = "the network" if not ONLINE else "pystac-client"  # what is missing
    print(f"STAC search skipped ({missing} is unavailable).")  # explain
    print("get_images in the previous sections does not need pystac-client.")  # get_images works without it

title: Getting Access to Remote Sensing Images
text:
Files you already have
A path is enough once the image is local. rs.read opens a GeoTIFF, a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF, a JPEG2000 or a NetCDF subdataset as an xarray array. A URL works too, including /vsicurl/ and s3:// paths that GDAL can see.
The next cell downloads a fresh clip for Tompkins County, the county that contains Ithaca, New York. The boundary comes from Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/NY_County_GCS.shp. get_images reads one MODIS 16-day vegetation composite (modis-13Q1-061) over that county and writes GeoTIFFs under outputs/images/modis_tompkins/. The product is 250 m and carries NDVI, red, near infrared and blue. It has no green band, so the color panel is near infrared, red and blue. Stored values are integers; multiply by 0.0001 to get NDVI and reflectance. Pixels outside the county boundary are left empty.


Code
# Download one MODIS vegetation scene and clip it to Tompkins County.
#
# This is the end-to-end path: a county polygon in, a north-up NDVI map out.
# Offline, it stops after printing the county bounds.
#
# 1. Keep the Tompkins County polygon (Ithaca sits inside it) and ask get_images
#    for one MOD13Q1 / MYD13Q1 scene: blue, red, NIR and NDVI, clipped to the county.
# 2. modis_band reads each GeoTIFF, drops the fill value (stored integers at or
#    below -2000) and multiplies by the product scale factor 0.0001.
# 3. county_mask clips again to the polygon, in the sinusoidal CRS the file uses.
# 4. Reproject NDVI to UTM zone 18N so the county is north-up, and warp the other
#    bands onto that same grid.
# 5. stretch() maps each band's 2nd-98th percentile onto 0-1 for display.
#    This collection has no green band, so the colour view is NIR, red, blue.
#    Pixels outside the county are painted white. The second panel is NDVI.

COUNTIES = DATA / "00_shared" / "vector_data" / "USA" / "NY_County_GCS.shp"
tompkins = gpd.read_file(COUNTIES)  # all New York counties
tompkins = tompkins.loc[tompkins["COUNTY"] == "Tompkins County"].copy()  # keep Tompkins County
print(  # its bounds
    "Tompkins County, Ithaca, NY bounds (min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat):",
    tuple(round(float(v), 3) for v in tompkins.total_bounds),
)

modis_out = OUT / "modis_tompkins"  # output folder for the MODIS clip

if not ONLINE:  # offline
    print("Offline: the MODIS clip was not downloaded.")  # say so
else:
    saved = gi.get_images(  # search, clip and save one MODIS vegetation scene
        modis_out,
        aoi=tompkins,
        dates=("2026-08-01", "2026-09-15"),
        source="planetary",
        collection="modis-13Q1-061",
        bands=["blue", "red", "nir", "ndvi"],
        mode="clip",
        limit=1,
        quiet=True,
    )
    scene = saved.scenes[0]  # the downloaded scene
    scene_dir = saved.out / scene["id"]  # its folder
    print(saved)  # summary of the download
    print("scene:", scene["id"], "date:", str(scene["datetime"])[:10])  # scene ID and date

    def modis_band(name):  # read one band, mask fill values and apply the scale factor
        """MOD13Q1 / MYD13Q1 integers, scale factor 0.0001. Fill values stay empty."""
        da = rs.read(scene_dir / f"{name}.tif").squeeze(drop=True).astype("float32")  # read as floats
        return da.where(da > -2000) * 0.0001  # fill values (<= -2000) -> NaN, then scale

    blue, red, nir, ndvi = (modis_band(name) for name in ("blue", "red", "nir", "ndvi"))  # the four bands
    tompkins_sin = tompkins.to_crs(ndvi.rio.crs)  # the county in the file's sinusoidal CRS

    def county_mask(da):  # clip a band to the county polygon
        return da.rio.clip(tompkins_sin.geometry, tompkins_sin.crs, drop=True)  # clip and drop the outside

    blue, red, nir, ndvi = (county_mask(da) for da in (blue, red, nir, ndvi))  # clip all four bands
    # The MODIS grid is sinusoidal. Put the county north-up before drawing it.
    ndvi = ndvi.rio.reproject("EPSG:32618")
    # the other bands onto the NDVI grid
    blue, red, nir = (da.rio.reproject_match(ndvi) for da in (blue, red, nir))
    # grid size and NDVI range
    print("clip:", dict(ndvi.sizes), "NDVI", round(float(ndvi.min()), 2), "to", round(float(ndvi.max()), 2))

    def stretch(values):  # 2-98 % stretch to [0, 1]
        data = np.asarray(values, dtype="float32")  # as a float array
        lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(data, (2, 98))  # percentile limits
        return np.clip((data - lo) / (hi - lo + 1e-6), 0, 1)  # stretch and clip

    # This collection has no green band. Near infrared, red and blue is the color view.
    false_color = np.dstack([stretch(nir.values), stretch(red.values), stretch(blue.values)])
    outside = ~np.isfinite(ndvi.values)  # pixels outside the county
    false_color[outside] = 1  # paint them white
    ndvi_show = np.ma.masked_where(outside, ndvi.values)  # hide them in the NDVI panel
    when = str(scene["datetime"])[:10]  # the scene date

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6))  # two panels
    axes[0].imshow(false_color, interpolation="nearest")  # the false-colour image
    # title
    axes[0].set_title(f"Tompkins County, Ithaca, NY\nMODIS 13Q1, {when}\nnear infrared, red, blue (250 m)")
    im = axes[1].imshow(ndvi_show, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0.2, vmax=0.9, interpolation="nearest")  # NDVI
    axes[1].set_title("NDVI, Tompkins County\nscale factor 0.0001")  # title
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1], fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)  # colour bar
    for ax in axes:  # for both panels
        ax.set_axis_off()  # no axes
    plt.tight_layout()  # arrange

title: Getting Access to Remote Sensing Images
text:
Summary and exercises
Key ideas

geolattice.rsense.get_images searches and downloads Sentinel-2, Landsat, MODIS, HLS, NAIP, Sentinel-1, Sentinel-3, Sentinel-5P, NOAA coastal photos and USGS lidar. list_collections(), bands_for() and default_bands() are the names the functions accept.
Search with search_images and read the scene list. Download with get_images once the list is the one you want.
mode="clip" reads your area out of a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF. Copernicus, NOAA, lidar and NetCDF products are whole files.
rs.access and rs.optical.load_sentinel2, load_landsat, load_modis, load_hls, plus rs.sar.load_rtc, skip the local copy and return a lazy cube.
rs.read opens a GeoTIFF you already have: a Landsat subset, a UAV mosaic, or a commercial sample.

Exercises

Change the cloud limit on the Sentinel-2 search to 5 percent. How many July 2024 scenes remain over this polygon?
Search Landsat 5 as well as Landsat 8 and 9 (platforms="Landsat 4-9" is the built-in choice, or pass a list). Which mission appears in 2024?
Call gi.default_bands for modis-15A2H-061 and hls2-l30. Which names would you pass as bands for leaf area, and which for a Landsat-like HLS scene?
Search Sentinel-1 twice, once ascending and once descending, and compare the scene times. Pick one direction before you build a backscatter series.
Set DOWNLOAD = True for the Sentinel-2 recipe only, then open stack.tif with rs.read and compare it with the 2015 Landsat subset.

Next: The optical notebooks (07_02) begin with MODIS, the daily global workhorse. The optical modules (07_02) then cover Landsat and Sentinel-2. Radar, UAV and lidar each have their own folder after that.

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Overview
Haze, terrain shading, clouds, mismatched resolutions and small geometric offsets all bias results. This module works through the main corrections with real data and, wherever possible, measures how well each one works.

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Follow the radiometric chain DN → radiance → TOA → surface reflectance, and apply DOS1.
Estimate sun geometry from an image and correct terrain illumination (cosine, C, Minnaert, SCS+C).
Compare cloud-free compositing methods on a real Sentinel-2 series.
Pan-sharpen and evaluate the result with Wald’s protocol and ERGAS.
Detect and correct sub-pixel misregistration.
Estimate sub-pixel land-cover fractions with linear spectral unmixing, and validate them.

text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)  # hide routine library warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)  # e.g. "mean of empty slice" in all-NaN areas

import json  # read JSON metadata
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import rasterio  # raster reading
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
from rasterio.enums import Resampling  # resampling methods

import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing tools

rasterio.Env(CPL_LOG="/dev/null").__enter__()  # silence GDAL log messages for the whole session
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution




Code
from pathlib import Path  # file paths
import urllib.request  # download files over HTTP

# The notebook's data folder: ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical/ next to this notebook, found from here or from the repository root.
DATA = next((p for p in (Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"))
             if p.is_dir()), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"))
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed
GH = "https://github.com/opengeos/datasets/releases/download"  # base URL of the opengeos datasets release
RAW = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com"  # base URL for raw GitHub files
# the eo-learn test patch (Sentinel-2 time series)
EOP = f"{RAW}/sentinel-hub/eo-learn/develop/example_data/TestEOPatch"
URLS = {  # file name -> download URL
    # Landsat 9 C2 L2 surface reflectance, 8 July 2024, Las Vegas (90 m, 7 bands)
    "landsat_las_vegas.tif": f"{GH}/raster/landsat_las_vegas.tif",
    # Landsat annual composites over Pucallpa, Peru (SWIR1, NIR, Red, Green; 8-bit)
    **{f"pucallpa_{y}.tif": f"{RAW}/opengeos/data/main/landsat/{y}.tif" for y in range(1985, 2021, 5)},
    # ECOSTRESS L2T land surface temperature (70 m), southern California, 1 April 2023
    "ecostress_lst.tif": f"{GH}/raster/ECOv002_L2T_LSTE_26860_001_10SGD_20230401T203733_0710_01_LST.tif",
    # Landsat 7 composite + 90 m DEM, central Sierra Nevada (same grid family as Part I)
    "landsat.tif": f"{GH}/raster/landsat.tif",
    "dem_90m.tif": f"{GH}/book/dem_90m.tif",
    "cog.tif": f"{GH}/raster/cog.tif",
    # Real Sentinel-2 L1C time series (eo-learn TestEOPatch, Slovenia, 68 dates, 13 bands)
    "s2_bands.npy": f"{EOP}/data/BANDS-S2-L1C.npy",
    "s2_clp.npy": f"{EOP}/data/CLP.npy",
    "s2_clm.npy": f"{EOP}/mask/CLM.npy",
    "s2_lulc.npy": f"{EOP}/mask_timeless/LULC.npy",
    "s2_dem.npy": f"{EOP}/data_timeless/DEM.npy",
    "s2_timestamps.json": f"{EOP}/timestamps.json",
    "s2_bbox.geojson": f"{EOP}/bbox.geojson",
}

def fetch(name):  # download helper
    """Download a tutorial dataset once and return its local path."""
    path = DATA / name  # local path
    if not path.exists():  # download only if missing
        print(f"Downloading {name} ...")  # progress message
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(URLS[name], path)  # copy the URL to the local path
    return path  # the local path

NLCD_URL = f"{GH}/raster/nlcd_2021_land_cover_90m.tif"  # NLCD 2021 land cover (90 m), read remotely
NLCD_CLASSES = {11: ("Open water", "#466b9f"), 21: ("Developed, open", "#dec5c5"),
                22: ("Developed, low", "#d99282"), 23: ("Developed, medium", "#eb0000"),
                24: ("Developed, high", "#ab0000"), 31: ("Barren", "#b3ac9f"),
                41: ("Deciduous forest", "#68ab5f"), 42: ("Evergreen forest", "#1c5f2c"),
                43: ("Mixed forest", "#b5c58f"), 52: ("Shrub/scrub", "#ccb879"),
                71: ("Grassland", "#dfdfc2"), 81: ("Pasture/hay", "#dcd939"),
                82: ("Cultivated crops", "#ab6c28"), 90: ("Woody wetlands", "#b8d9eb"),
                95: ("Herbaceous wetlands", "#6c9fb8")}

def nlcd_for(template, name="nlcd_window"):  # NLCD land cover on the grid of another raster
    """NLCD 2021 land cover on the grid of `template`.

    Reads only the needed window of the 200 MB CONUS COG over HTTP (cloud-native), then
    nearest-neighbour resamples it onto the template grid. Cached in ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical/.
    """
    from rasterio.enums import Resampling  # nearest-neighbour resampling for classes
    cache = DATA / f"{name}.tif"  # cached local window
    if not cache.exists():  # only read the remote file once
        import rasterio, rioxarray  # raster readers
        from rasterio.warp import transform_bounds  # reproject a bounding box
        with rasterio.Env(GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN="EMPTY_DIR"):  # do not list the remote folder (faster)
            src = rioxarray.open_rasterio("/vsicurl/" + NLCD_URL)  # open the remote GeoTIFF lazily
            # bounds of the template in the NLCD CRS
            b = transform_bounds(template.rio.crs, src.rio.crs, *template.rio.bounds())
            win = src.rio.clip_box(*b).squeeze("band", drop=True).load()  # read only that window
        rs.write(win, cache, cog=False)  # cache it
    # read the cached window; 0 = no data
    win = rs.read(cache, masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.write_nodata(0)
    # resample onto the template grid (nearest)
    out = win.rio.reproject_match(template, resampling=Resampling.nearest, nodata=0)
    return out.astype("int16").rio.write_nodata(0)  # as 16-bit integers with 0 as no-data

y = max(p[1] for p in bb) - 10 * (np.arange(b.shape[1]) + 0.5)  # y coordinates of pixel centres

                coords={"time": times, "y": y, "x": x}).rio.write_crs(32633)

from scipy.ndimage import binary_dilation  # grow masks by a few pixels
# clear = cloud probability below 0.4, cloud edges included
clear = xr.DataArray(~np.stack([binary_dilation(p > 0.4, iterations=2) for p in clp]),
                     dims=("time", "y", "x"), coords=s2[["B02"]].coords)
s2c = s2.where(clear)  # cloudy pixels -> NaN
print(s2.sizes)  # dimensions

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Radiometric correction and DOS1
The chain from raw counts to surface reflectance:

DN → radiance: L = M·DN + A (gain/offset from metadata): rs.optical.radiance
Radiance → TOA reflectance: divide by solar irradiance and sun angle: rs.optical.toa_reflectance
TOA → surface reflectance: remove atmospheric scattering and absorption with a radiative transfer model (6S, LaSRC for Landsat, Sen2Cor for Sentinel-2).

Agencies now distribute surface reflectance, so step 3 is usually done for you. When it isn’t (historical archives, commercial imagery), Dark Object Subtraction (DOS1) is a robust first-order correction: the darkest pixels in each band should be nearly black, so any excess brightness is atmospheric path radiance.


Code
# the least cloudy July or August date
k = int(np.argmin(np.where(times.month.isin([7, 8]), clp.mean((1, 2)), 9)))
toa = s2.isel(time=k)[["B02", "B03", "B04", "B08"]]  # top-of-atmosphere blue, green, red and NIR of that date
dos = rs.optical.dos1(toa, percentile=0.5)  # dark-object subtraction (DOS1) using the 0.5th percentile
# darkest values before and after
tab = pd.DataFrame({"TOA dark (0.5th pct)": [float(np.nanpercentile(toa[v], 0.5)) for v in toa.data_vars],
                    "after DOS1": [float(np.nanpercentile(dos[v], 0.5)) for v in toa.data_vars]},
                   index=["blue", "green", "red", "NIR"]).round(4)
tab["path radiance removed"] = (tab.iloc[:, 0] - tab.iloc[:, 1]).round(4)  # the path radiance that was removed
tab  # show the table









TOA dark (0.5th pct)
after DOS1
path radiance removed




blue
0.0650
0.01
0.0550


green
0.0483
0.01
0.0383


red
0.0268
0.01
0.0168


NIR
0.1418
0.01
0.1318







Look at the NIR row: DOS1 removed 0.13 of “path radiance” from NIR, far more than from blue. That is physically impossible (scattering falls with wavelength). The method assumes every band contains a truly dark object; in this 1 km² of forest and meadow there is no water or deep shadow, so the darkest NIR pixels are still vegetation. The fix is to apply DOS only to bands where dark objects exist (here the visible bands) and leave NIR unchanged.


Code
# DOS1 on the visible bands only, NIR unchanged
dos = rs.optical.dos1(toa[["B02", "B03", "B04"]], percentile=0.5).merge(toa[["B08"]])
ndvi_toa = rs.optical.index(toa, "NDVI")  # NDVI from TOA reflectance
ndvi_dos = rs.optical.index(dos, "NDVI")  # NDVI after DOS1
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))  # three panels
# TOA true colour
rs.viz.plot_rgb(toa, ["B04", "B03", "B02"], ax=axes[0], per_band=False, title="TOA (hazy blue cast)")
# after DOS1
rs.viz.plot_rgb(dos, ["B04", "B03", "B02"], ax=axes[1], per_band=False, title="After DOS1 (visible bands)")
axes[2].hist(ndvi_toa.values.ravel(), 60, histtype="step", label="TOA", lw=2)  # NDVI histogram, TOA
axes[2].hist(ndvi_dos.values.ravel(), 60, histtype="step", label="DOS1", lw=2)  # NDVI histogram, DOS1
axes[2].set(xlabel="NDVI", title="Scattering lowers NDVI"); axes[2].legend()  # labels, title and legend
for a in axes[:2]: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks on the images
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
# mean NDVI before and after
print(f"Mean NDVI: TOA {float(ndvi_toa.mean()):.3f} → DOS1 {float(ndvi_dos.mean()):.3f}")









Mean NDVI: TOA 0.734 → DOS1 0.849


Scattering is strongest at short wavelengths (blue > green > red), so DOS1 removes most from blue. Because path radiance inflates red while NIR is almost unaffected, TOA NDVI is biased low and the correction raises it. Always compare indices across dates on surface reflectance, not TOA, and sanity-check any image-based correction against physics.

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Topographic correction
On slopes facing the sun, pixels receive more light than on slopes facing away, so the same forest looks brighter or darker depending on aspect. The local illumination is
\[\cos i = \cos\theta_z \cos s + \sin\theta_z \sin s \cos(\phi_a - a)\]
(θz sun zenith, φa sun azimuth, s slope, a aspect). We use the Sierra Nevada Landsat composite and a 90 m DEM, both reprojected to UTM so slopes are computed in true metres (Web Mercator would stretch distances by ~26 % at this latitude and flatten the slopes).


Code
# the Landsat 7 image with band names
img = rs.read(fetch("landsat.tif"), band_names=["blue", "green", "red", "nir"])
# zero = no data; reproject to UTM 11N at 180 m
img = img.where(img > 0).rio.reproject("EPSG:32611", resolution=180, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)
img = img.where(img > 0) / 255.0  # DN (0-255) -> 0-1
dem = rs.read(fetch("dem_90m.tif")).squeeze("band", drop=True).astype("float32")  # the DEM as floats
# average the DEM onto the image grid
dem = dem.rio.reproject_match(img.isel(band=0), resampling=Resampling.average)
dem = dem.where(dem > -100)  # mask invalid elevations
ds = img.to_dataset(dim="band").rio.write_crs("EPSG:32611")  # bands as variables, with the CRS
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_rgb(ds, "false_color", ax=axes[0], title="Landsat 7 colour infrared")  # colour infrared
# hillshade
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem), ax=axes[1], cmap="gray", title="Hillshade of the DEM", colorbar=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


Downloading landsat.tif ...
Downloading dem_90m.tif ...









This is a five-year composite, so there is no single sun position in the metadata. We can estimate it from the image: for a given azimuth and elevation, compute cos i and find the geometry that best explains the brightness pattern of vegetated pixels.


Code
ndvi = ds.rs.index("NDVI")  # NDVI
veg = (ndvi > 0.3) & dem.notnull()  # vegetated pixels with elevation
nir = ds["nir"].values  # NIR as an array
best = (-1, None)  # best (correlation, (azimuth, elevation)) so far
grid = []  # every tested sun position
for az in range(90, 241, 10):  # sun azimuths 90-240 degrees
    for el in range(30, 76, 5):  # sun elevations 30-75 degrees
        # cosine of the solar incidence angle for this sun position
        ci = rs.lidar.illumination(dem, az, el).values
        m = veg.values & np.isfinite(ci) & np.isfinite(nir)  # vegetated, valid pixels
        r = np.corrcoef(ci[m], nir[m])[0, 1]  # correlation between illumination and NIR
        grid.append((az, el, r))  # store it
        if r > best[0]:  # strongest correlation so far
            best = (r, (az, el))  # keep this sun position
r_best, (SUN_AZ, SUN_EL) = best  # the best sun position
# correlations as an elevation x azimuth table
g = pd.DataFrame(grid, columns=["az", "el", "r"]).pivot(index="el", columns="az", values="r")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.5))  # one panel
im = ax.imshow(g, origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap="viridis",  # the correlation surface
               extent=[g.columns.min() - 5, g.columns.max() + 5, g.index.min() - 2.5, g.index.max() + 2.5])
# the best position and a colour bar
ax.plot(SUN_AZ, SUN_EL, "r*", ms=14); plt.colorbar(im, label="corr(cos i, NIR)")
ax.set(xlabel="Sun azimuth (°)", ylabel="Sun elevation (°)",  # labels and title
       title=f"Estimated sun position: azimuth {SUN_AZ}°, elevation {SUN_EL}° (r = {r_best:.2f})")
plt.show()  # draw









The estimate (a south-east, fairly high sun) is consistent with mid-morning summer acquisitions of Landsat at 37-38° N. Now we apply the four correction methods and measure how much illumination dependence remains, using vegetated pixels only to fit the empirical coefficients.


Code
cos_i = rs.lidar.illumination(dem, SUN_AZ, SUN_EL)  # solar illumination with the estimated sun position
results = {"original": ds}  # uncorrected image
for method in ["cosine", "c", "minnaert", "scs+c"]:  # four topographic correction methods
    # correct the image, fitting on vegetation only
    results[method] = rs.optical.topographic_correction(ds, dem, SUN_AZ, SUN_EL, method=method, mask=veg)

ci = cos_i.values  # illumination as an array
m = veg.values & np.isfinite(ci)  # vegetated, valid pixels
aspect = rs.lidar.aspect(dem).values  # aspect in degrees
north = m & ((aspect > 315) | (aspect < 45)) & (rs.lidar.slope(dem).values > 15)  # steep north-facing slopes
south = m & (aspect > 135) & (aspect < 225) & (rs.lidar.slope(dem).values > 15)  # steep south-facing slopes
rows = {}  # statistics per method
for name, r in results.items():  # every method
    v = r["nir"].values  # its NIR band
    ok = m & np.isfinite(v)  # valid pixels
    # illumination correlation and north/south contrast
    rows[name] = {"corr(cos i, NIR)": np.corrcoef(ci[ok], v[ok])[0, 1],
                  "NIR south/north slope ratio": np.nanmean(v[south]) / np.nanmean(v[north]),
                  "NIR CV (vegetated)": np.nanstd(v[ok]) / np.nanmean(v[ok])}

A good correction drives the correlation with cos i towards zero and the south/north ratio towards 1 without inflating variability. All four methods help. The empirical C and Minnaert corrections remove the illumination effect almost completely; the cosine method and SCS+C leave part of it. The cosine method has no fitted coefficient: it assumes surfaces reflect equally in all directions and ignores diffuse skylight, which is why it is known to over-correct poorly lit slopes. Which empirical method wins varies by scene and land cover, so measure it as done here rather than assuming.

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Cloud-free compositing
Composites merge several cloud-masked dates into one image. Methods trade cleanliness against spectral consistency (whether all bands of a pixel come from the same date). We composite the 2016-2017 summer (June-September) Sentinel-2 dates with each method in rs.optical.composite.


Code
season = s2c.sel(time=s2c.time.dt.month.isin([6, 7, 8, 9]))  # cloud-masked summer dates
season = season[["B02", "B03", "B04", "B05", "B08", "B11", "B12"]]  # bands used for compositing
print(f"{season.sizes['time']} summer dates, mean clear fraction "  # number of dates and mean clear share
      f"{float(clear.sel(time=season.time).mean()):.0%}")
# compositing methods and their options
methods = {"median": {}, "mean": {}, "percentile": {"q": 25}, "max_index": {"index": "NDVI"},
           "median_nearest": {}, "bap": {"target_doy": 200}}
comps = {m: rs.optical.composite(season, m, **kw) for m, kw in methods.items()}  # build every composite


32 summer dates, mean clear fraction 60%




Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(14, 9))  # 2 x 3 panels
for ax, (m, c) in zip(axes.ravel(), comps.items()):  # every composite
    # true colour with a 1-99 % stretch
    rs.viz.plot_rgb(c, ["B04", "B03", "B02"], ax=ax, per_band=False, p=(1, 99), title=m)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









To compare quantitatively we use three checks: residual haze/cloud (share of pixels with TOA blue reflectance > 0.12, well above clear vegetation even with haze in this scene), gaps (pixels with no value), and spectral realism: the distance of each composite pixel’s spectrum to the nearest real clear observation of that pixel. Per-band statistics (median, mean, percentile) mix dates, so their spectra need not match any real observation; selection methods keep real spectra.


Code
obs = np.stack([season[v].values for v in season.data_vars], -1)        # (t, y, x, b)
rows = {}  # statistics per method
for m, c in comps.items():  # every composite
    comp = np.stack([c[v].values for v in season.data_vars], -1)       # (y, x, b)
    d = np.sqrt(np.nansum((obs - comp[None]) ** 2, -1))  # spectral distance of each date to the composite
    d[np.all(np.isnan(obs), -1)] = np.nan  # NaN where a pixel was never clear
    # residual haze and distance to the observations
    rows[m] = {"residual haze/cloud (blue > 0.12)": float(np.nanmean(c["B02"].values > 0.12)),
               "gaps": float(np.isnan(c["B04"].values).mean()),
               "distance to nearest real spectrum": float(np.nanmean(np.nanmin(d, 0))),
               "mean NDVI": float(rs.optical.index(c, "NDVI").mean())}

Max-NDVI favours the greenest date (often mid-summer) and so biases vegetation upward, which is fine for vegetation mapping but not for soils or change detection. BAP balances date proximity, distance from clouds and greenness, choosing more consistent dates. Median-nearest is robust to residual cloud and keeps real spectra, making it a good general default.

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Pan-sharpening and Wald’s protocol
Landsat 8/9 have a 15 m panchromatic band alongside 30 m multispectral bands. Pan-sharpening injects the pan detail into the colour bands. To evaluate it we use Wald’s protocol: degrade everything by the resolution ratio, sharpen the degraded data, and compare with the original, which serves as ground truth.
Our scene is at 90 m, so we simulate a 90 m pan band from the visible bands (OLI’s pan covers 500-680 nm), degrade the multispectral bands to 270 m, sharpen back to 90 m, and score against the true 90 m bands with RMSE, correlation and ERGAS (lower is better; < 3 is good).


Code
ls = rs.read(fetch("landsat_las_vegas.tif"),  # a Landsat scene of Las Vegas
             band_names=["coastal", "blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir16", "swir22"], as_dataset=True)
# mask zero red, clip to small positive values and set the CRS
ls = ls.where(ls["red"] > 0).clip(min=1e-4).rio.write_crs(32611)
ls.attrs["pyrsense:sensor"] = "landsat"  # record the sensor
sub = ls.isel(x=slice(300, 750), y=slice(150, 600))                        # 450 × 450 px, city centre
truth = sub[["red", "green", "blue"]]  # the reference (true) RGB at 90 m
# synthetic panchromatic band: weighted sum of blue, green and red
pan = (0.25 * sub["blue"] + 0.4 * sub["green"] + 0.35 * sub["red"]).rio.write_crs(32611)
ms_coarse = truth.coarsen(x=3, y=3, boundary="trim").mean()  # multispectral degraded 3x (270 m)
ms_coarse = ms_coarse.drop_vars("spatial_ref").rio.write_crs(32611)   # drop the stale 90 m transform
# resolutions of the two inputs
print("MS degraded to", ms_coarse.rio.resolution(), "| pan at", pan.rio.resolution())

def ergas(fused, ref, ratio):  # ERGAS: relative error across bands, scaled by the resolution ratio
    # relative RMSE of each band
    terms = [(np.sqrt(np.nanmean((fused[b].values - ref[b].values) ** 2)) / np.nanmean(ref[b].values)) ** 2
             for b in ref.data_vars]
    return 100 / ratio * np.sqrt(np.mean(terms))  # ERGAS formula

# baseline: bilinear upsampling without the pan band
out = {"bilinear (no pan)": xr.Dataset({b: ms_coarse[b].rio.reproject_match(pan, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)
                                        for b in truth.data_vars})}
for method in ["brovey", "ihs", "hpf"]:  # three pan-sharpening methods
    # fuse the coarse bands with the pan band
    out[method] = rs.optical.pansharpen(ms_coarse, pan, method=method)
scores = {}  # scores per method
for name, f in out.items():  # every result
    f = f.assign_coords(x=truth.x, y=truth.y)  # same coordinates as the reference
    scores[name] = {"ERGAS": ergas(f, truth, 3),  # ERGAS and other scores
                    "RMSE (red)": float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean((f["red"] - truth["red"]) ** 2))),
                    "corr (red)": float(xr.corr(f["red"], truth["red"]))}
pd.DataFrame(scores).T.round(4)  # show the table

# images and titles

        ("HPF", out["hpf"])]
for ax, (t, d) in zip(axes, show):  # every panel

All three sharpening methods beat plain upsampling by a wide margin. Brovey and IHS score best here, partly because our simulated pan band is an exact weighted sum of the visible bands; a real pan band has a broader response, which usually costs Brovey colour fidelity. HPF injects detail more conservatively. Remember that Wald’s protocol assumes the quality ranking is scale-invariant, a reasonable but untestable assumption.

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Co-registration
Images from different dates or sensors can be offset by a fraction of a pixel to a few pixels. Unnoticed, this creates false change along every edge. rs.optical.coregister estimates the translation by sub-pixel phase correlation and resamples the image to match.
First a controlled test: shift a real Sentinel-2 band by a known amount and recover it.


Code
from scipy.ndimage import shift as nd_shift  # shift an image by a sub-pixel amount
ref = s2["B08"].isel(time=k)  # the NIR band of the clear date
true_shift = (1.6, -2.3)                                   # rows, cols (pixels)
# a copy shifted by a known amount
moved = ref.copy(data=nd_shift(ref.values, true_shift, order=3, mode="nearest"))
# estimate the shift and correct it (1/50 pixel precision)
fixed, info = rs.optical.coregister(moved, ref, upsample=50)
inner = (slice(6, -6), slice(6, -6))  # interior pixels (edges are affected by the shift)
# applied vs estimated shift
print(f"Applied shift: {true_shift} px → estimated correction: ({info['dy']:.2f}, {info['dx']:.2f}) px")
# mean difference to the reference before and after
print(f"Mean |difference| to reference: before {np.nanmean(np.abs(moved.values - ref.values)[inner]):.4f}, "
      f"after {np.nanmean(np.abs(fixed.values - ref.values)[inner]):.4f}")


Applied shift: (1.6, -2.3) px → estimated correction: (-1.58, 2.26) px
Mean |difference| to reference: before 0.0390, after 0.0077




Code
# Real data: how well are clear Sentinel-2 dates aligned with each other?
clear_dates = [i for i in range(len(times)) if clp[i].mean() < 0.05][:12]
rows = []  # offsets of every clear date
for i in clear_dates[1:]:  # every clear date except the reference
    # estimate its offset against the reference date
    _, inf = rs.optical.coregister(s2["B08"].isel(time=i), s2["B08"].isel(time=clear_dates[0]),
                                   apply=False, upsample=50)
    # offset in metres (10 m pixels)
    rows.append((times[i].date(), round(inf["dy"] * 10, 2), round(inf["dx"] * 10, 2)))
off = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["date", "dy (m)", "dx (m)"])  # as a table
print(f"Reference date {times[clear_dates[0]].date()}; median |offset| = "  # reference date and median offset
      f"{np.median(np.hypot(off['dy (m)'], off['dx (m)'])):.1f} m")

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Linear spectral unmixing
A 90 m pixel in a city mixes roofs, roads, trees, lawns and soil. Linear unmixing models each pixel spectrum as a fraction-weighted sum of pure endmember spectra. We take endmembers from the image, guided by NLCD: vegetation (greenest pixels), impervious (high-intensity developed, low NDVI), soil (barren/shrubland, low NDVI) and water (Lake Mead).


Code
nlcd = nlcd_for(ls["red"])  # NLCD land cover on the Landsat grid
nd = ls.rs.index("NDVI")  # NDVI
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # random generator

def sample(mask, n=150):  # random sample of up to n pixels from a mask
    rr, cc = np.nonzero(mask.values)  # rows and columns of the mask pixels
    idx = rng.choice(rr.size, min(n, rr.size), replace=False)  # random indices
    return pd.DataFrame({"x": ls.x.values[cc[idx]], "y": ls.y.values[rr[idx]]})  # their map coordinates

pure = {  # masks of pure pixels for each endmember
    "vegetation": nd > float(nd.quantile(0.998)),
    "impervious": (nlcd == 24) & (nd < 0.12),
    "soil": nlcd.isin([31, 52]) & (nd < 0.1),
    "water": (nlcd == 11) & (ls["nir"] < 0.02),
}
# sample points of all classes
pts = pd.concat([sample(m).assign(cls=k) for k, m in pure.items()], ignore_index=True)
pts = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pts, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(pts.x, pts.y), crs=32611)  # as a GeoDataFrame
bands6 = ["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir16", "swir22"]  # the six reflective bands
E = rs.optical.endmembers_from_samples(ls, pts, "cls", bands=bands6)  # mean spectrum of each class = endmembers
wl = [482, 562, 655, 865, 1609, 2201]  # band centre wavelengths (nm)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))  # one panel
for kname, spec in E.items():  # every endmember
    ax.plot(wl, spec, "o-", label=kname, lw=2)  # its spectrum
# labels, title, legend and draw
ax.set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Surface reflectance", title="Image endmembers"); ax.legend(); plt.show()











Code
frac = rs.optical.unmix(ls, E, bands=bands6, method="scls")  # sum-to-one constrained unmixing
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 4))  # four panels
# three fractions and the residual error
for ax, kname, cm in zip(axes, ["vegetation", "impervious", "soil", "rmse"], ["Greens", "Reds", "YlOrBr", "magma"]):
    # map each layer (fractions clipped to 0-1)
    rs.viz.plot_raster(frac[kname].clip(0, 1) if kname != "rmse" else frac[kname], ax=ax, cmap=cm,
                       vmin=0, vmax=1 if kname != "rmse" else None, title=kname)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw











Code
# Fully constrained (non-negative, sum-to-one) unmixing on a subset, compared with SCLS
sub_ds = ls.isel(x=slice(400, 520), y=slice(250, 370))
# fully constrained unmixing (non-negative, sum to one)
fc = rs.optical.unmix(sub_ds, E, bands=bands6, method="fcls")
sc = rs.optical.unmix(sub_ds, E, bands=bands6, method="scls")  # sum-to-one constrained only
# share of negative fractions in each
pd.DataFrame({m: {"negative fractions": float((f[list(E)].to_array() < 0).mean()),
                  "mean RMSE": float(f["rmse"].mean())} for m, f in [("SCLS", sc), ("FCLS", fc)]}).T.round(4)

df = pd.DataFrame({"code": nlcd.values.ravel(), "impervious": frac["impervious"].clip(0, 1).values.ravel(),

title: Preprocessing of Optical Images
text:
Summary, exercises and references
Key ideas

Indices and multi-date comparisons need surface reflectance; DOS1 is a quick fallback.
Terrain illumination can dominate brightness in mountains; empirical C/SCS+C corrections work best, and the sun position can even be estimated from the image.
Compositing methods differ in cleanliness and spectral realism; selection methods (median-nearest, BAP) keep real spectra.
Evaluate pan-sharpening with Wald’s protocol and ERGAS rather than by eye.
Check co-registration before change detection, especially across sensors.
Unmixing turns mixed pixels into interpretable sub-pixel fractions; validate them.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.optical.dos1, rs.lidar.illumination/hillshade/slope/aspect, rs.optical.topographic_correction, rs.optical.composite, rs.optical.pansharpen, rs.optical.coregister, rs.optical.endmembers_from_samples, rs.optical.unmix.
Exercises

Fit the topographic C coefficient per land-cover class instead of for all vegetation. Does SCS+C improve further?
Add a 30th-percentile composite and a bap composite with target_doy=240. How do haze and NDVI change?
Repeat the Wald test with a 1:2 ratio (180 m) instead of 1:3. Does the ranking change?
Co-register a Landsat 9 scene to a Sentinel-2 scene of the same area (notebook 07_01_03 loaders).
Add a “dark impervious” (asphalt) endmember and see whether the soil/roof confusion drops.

Overview
This module covers the Landsat archive, Collection 2 products, scale factors, QA decoding, composites, spectral indices, surface temperature, and two real multi-decade change analyses.

Core concepts

Learning objectives

Know the Landsat missions, sensors, band layouts and Collection 2 processing levels.
Apply Collection 2 Level-2 scale factors for reflectance and surface temperature.
Decode QA_PIXEL bit flags and build cloud masks.
Make and interpret natural- and false-colour composites.
Compute, compare and validate spectral indices for vegetation, water and built-up land.
Understand land surface temperature retrieval and analyse a real LST product.
Analyse multi-decade change from real Landsat time series in the Pucallpa and Bangladesh delta capstones.

title: Landsat: Half a Century of Earth Observation
text:
The program
Landsat is a joint NASA and USGS program:

NASA builds and launches the satellites.
USGS operates them, processes the data, and maintains the archive at the EROS Center in Sioux Falls, South Dakota.
First satellite. Landsat 1 was launched on 23 July 1972 as ERTS-1 (Earth Resources Technology Satellite) and was renamed Landsat in 1975.
Commercialization period (1985 to 1992). Operations moved to a private company, EOSAT. Scene prices rose to several thousand dollars, which sharply limited use. The Land Remote Sensing Policy Act of 1992 returned Landsat to government management.
Open data policy (2008). USGS made the entire archive free. This changed land-change science: downloads went from a few thousand scenes a year to millions, and global wall-to-wall analyses became possible.
Collections.

Collection 1 was released in 2016.
Collection 2, released in December 2020, is the current standard. It improved geolocation and added global Level-2 surface reflectance and surface temperature.

Recent milestones

Landsat 7 acquired science data until 19 January 2024 and was decommissioned on 4 June 2025, after 26 years in orbit.
Landsat 7 had already moved to a lower orbit (697 km) in 2022. This made room for Landsat 9 to join Landsat 8 at 705 km.
Over its lifetime, Landsat 7’s ETM+ sensor acquired more than 3.3 million scenes.

Landsat Next (future).

Planned as a constellation of three spacecraft launched together no earlier than 2030, with better spatial, spectral, and temporal resolution than Landsat 8 and 9.
Planned specifications include a 6-day revisit (versus 8 days for Landsat 8 and 9 in tandem) and about 15 times more data than Landsat 9.
The FY2026 President’s Budget restructured the mission. USGS and NASA are now looking for more affordable approaches to Landsat data continuity.
Congress’s FY2026 appropriations language differs from the budget request, so the final design and schedule remain uncertain.

title: Landsat: Half a Century of Earth Observation
text:
Sensors

Return Beam Vidicon (RBV), Landsat 1 to 3. A television-camera system with three broad visible/NIR channels. It was secondary to the MSS and is rarely used today.
Multispectral Scanner (MSS), Landsat 1 to 5.

4 bands: green, red, and two NIR.
About 79 m resolution, resampled to 60 m.
6-bit radiometry.

Thematic Mapper (TM), Landsat 4 to 5.

7 bands, adding blue, SWIR, and thermal.
30 m resolution (thermal 120 m).
8-bit radiometry.

Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), Landsat 7.

TM bands plus a 15 m panchromatic band; thermal at 60 m.
Landsat 7 was the first Landsat with an onboard data recorder.
SLC-off gaps: after the Scan Line Corrector failed in 2003, each scene has wedge-shaped strips of missing data and keeps roughly 78% of its pixels. Gap-filling or compositing is needed.

Operational Land Imager (OLI), Landsat 8, and OLI-2, Landsat 9.

Push-broom design, which gives a better signal-to-noise ratio than the older whisk-broom scanners.
9 bands, including new coastal/aerosol and cirrus bands.
Narrower NIR band that avoids the 825 nm water-vapour absorption feature.
Radiometry: OLI collects 12-bit data; OLI-2 transmits 14-bit data.

Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS), Landsat 8, and TIRS-2, Landsat 9.

2 thermal bands at 100 m, resampled to 30 m.
TIRS on Landsat 8 suffers stray light, which makes Band 11 less reliable. TIRS-2 has improved baffling.

title: Landsat: Half a Century of Earth Observation
text:
Data products

Level-1 (top of atmosphere)
Processing levels: - L1TP: precision terrain-corrected using ground control points and a DEM. The best quality. - L1GT: systematic terrain correction only. - L1GS: systematic correction only.
Quality tiers: - Tier 1: meets geometric accuracy requirements and is suitable for time-series analysis. - Tier 2: lower geometric accuracy or heavy cloud. - Real-Time: available within hours, later reprocessed into a tier.


Level-2 science products
Surface Reflectance (SR) - Algorithms: LaSRC for Landsat 8/9; LEDAPS for Landsat 4 to 7. - Scaling: reflectance = DN × 0.0000275 − 0.2
Surface Temperature (ST) - Single-channel algorithm, using Band 10 on Landsat 8/9. - Scaling: temperature (K) = DN × 0.00341802 + 149.0
Quality bands - QA_PIXEL: CFMask cloud, shadow, snow, and water bitmask. - QA_RADSAT: saturation flags. - SR_QA_AEROSOL: aerosol level (Landsat 8/9).


Analysis-ready data and Level-3 products

U.S. ARD: tiled at 5,000 × 5,000 pixels on the Albers grid for the conterminous U.S., Alaska, and Hawaii.
Level-3 products:

Burned Area
Dynamic Surface Water Extent (DSWE)
Fractional Snow Covered Area
Provisional Actual Evapotranspiration




Format and harmonized data

Format: Collection 2 products are delivered as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) with MTL metadata in text, XML, and JSON, plus STAC records.
Harmonized data: NASA’s Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) combines Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 at 30 m for a revisit of about 2 to 3 days.

title: Landsat: Half a Century of Earth Observation
text:
Applications

Long-term land change. The 50+ year record is Landsat’s unique strength. Examples:

Hansen Global Forest Change (Global Forest Watch)
USGS Annual NLCD and LCMAP
JRC Global Surface Water

Agriculture

Crop type and cropland extent mapping
Irrigation mapping
Field-scale evapotranspiration (OpenET uses Landsat thermal data)

Forestry. Deforestation, disturbance and recovery (LandTrendr, CCDC algorithms), insect damage.
Water

Surface water dynamics and reservoir and lake monitoring
Water quality (turbidity, chlorophyll)
Glacier and ice-sheet change

Urban and climate

Urban expansion and impervious surfaces
Urban heat islands (thermal bands)
Land surface temperature trends

Disasters. Fire burn severity (MTBS in the U.S. uses NBR/dNBR), flood extent, volcanic and landslide mapping.
Geology and soils. Mineral and lithology mapping (SWIR), soil mapping covariates, erosion and desertification.
Environment and health

Greenness and heat exposure metrics for epidemiology
Vector habitat mapping
Wetland and mangrove change

Machine learning. Long, consistent time series support temporal deep learning and change detection. Landsat is also used in foundation-model pretraining, often together with HLS.

                22: ("Developed, low", "#d99282"), 23: ("Developed, medium", "#eb0000"),
                24: ("Developed, high", "#ab0000"), 31: ("Barren", "#b3ac9f"),

                43: ("Mixed forest", "#b5c58f"), 52: ("Shrub/scrub", "#ccb879"),
                71: ("Grassland", "#dfdfc2"), 81: ("Pasture/hay", "#dcd939"),
                82: ("Cultivated crops", "#ab6c28"), 90: ("Woody wetlands", "#b8d9eb"),
                95: ("Herbaceous wetlands", "#6c9fb8")}

def nlcd_for(template, name="nlcd_window"):  # NLCD land cover on the grid of another raster
    """
    NLCD 2021 land cover on the grid of `template`.

    Reads only the needed window of the 200 MB CONUS COG over HTTP (cloud-native), then
    nearest-neighbour resamples it onto the template grid. Cached in ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical/.
    """
    from rasterio.enums import Resampling  # nearest-neighbour resampling for classes
    cache = DATA / f"{name}.tif"  # cached local window
    if not cache.exists() or os.path.getsize(cache) == 0:  # read the remote file only if no cache exists
        import rasterio, rioxarray  # raster readers
        from rasterio.warp import transform_bounds  # reproject a bounding box
        with rasterio.Env(GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN="EMPTY_DIR"):  # do not list the remote folder (faster)
            src = rioxarray.open_rasterio("/vsicurl/" + NLCD_URL)  # open the remote GeoTIFF lazily
            # bounds of the template in the NLCD CRS
            b = transform_bounds(template.rio.crs, src.rio.crs, *template.rio.bounds())
            win = src.rio.clip_box(*b).squeeze("band", drop=True).load()  # read only that window
        rs.write(win, cache, cog=False)  # cache it
    else:
        print(f"Found {cache.name} locally; using cached version.")  # cache found
    # read the cached window; 0 = no data
    win = rs.read(cache, masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.write_nodata(0)
    # resample onto the template grid (nearest)
    out = win.rio.reproject_match(template, resampling=Resampling.nearest, nodata=0)
    return out.astype("int16").rio.write_nodata(0)  # as 16-bit integers with 0 as no-data

title: Landsat: Half a Century of Earth Observation
text:
Scale factors
Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 data is distributed as unsigned 16-bit digital numbers (DNs). These DNs require scaling to retrieve physical values:

For surface reflectance bands (e.g., blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR), the reflectance is calculated as:

Reflectance = DN × 0.0000275 − 0.2
Valid range: DN values 7,273 to 43,636 map to surface reflectance values of 0 to 1.

For the surface temperature band (thermal infrared, typically B10), the conversion to Kelvin is:

Surface temperature (K) = DN × 0.00341802 + 149.0

A DN value of 0 indicates a fill value (nodata; these pixels should be ignored).

The scaling function rs.optical.scale automatically detects the relevant bands within the dataset. It applies the appropriate equation to each band, converting raw DNs to meaningful physical units (reflectance, temperature), while keeping non-spectral bands like qa_pixel unmodified. In this notebook, we use it to scale the real (unmodified) DNs downloaded in the Loading Landsat data section to obtain correctly calibrated surface reflectance and temperature data.


Code
# This block scales the raw digital number (DN) values for each physical band in the Landsat scene
# to meaningful physical units (reflectance or temperature), then summarizes the values for a sample pixel.

# 1. Convert the DN values in 'ls_dn' to scaled reflectance and temperature values, producing a new xarray Dataset.
ls = rs.optical.scale(ls_dn, sensor="landsat")

# 2. Choose a specific pixel position (y=700, x=800) in the image for sampling.
px = dict(y=700, x=800)

# 3. Select all bands except 'qa_pixel' (i.e., only the bands with physical meaning).
phys_bands = [b for b in LS_BANDS if b != "qa_pixel"]

# 4. For each physical band, extract at that pixel:
#    - The original DN value (integer read directly from the file)
#    - The scaled value (rounded to 4 decimals), in physical units
#    - The units (from array metadata; reflectance or Kelvin)
#    These are assembled into a pandas DataFrame for easy inspection.
pd.DataFrame({
    "stored DN": [int(ls_dn[b].isel(px)) for b in phys_bands],
    "scaled": [round(float(ls[b].isel(px)), 4) for b in phys_bands],
    "units": [ls[b].attrs.get("units") for b in phys_bands],
}, index=phys_bands)

Atmospheric correction can push very dark surfaces (deep water, shadow) slightly below zero. Negative values make ratio indices explode (e.g. NDVI = −500 when NIR ≈ −0.001), so we clip reflectance to a small positive floor before computing indices.


Code
# Count and display the number of negative reflectance pixels for each physical band except 'lwir11' (thermal IR).
# Negative reflectance values can occur due to atmospheric correction artifacts.
neg = {b: int((ls[b] < 0).sum()) for b in phys_bands if b != "lwir11"}
# Only print bands where negative pixels exist.
print("Negative reflectance pixels (real scene):", {b: n for b, n in neg.items() if n})

# Clip all reflectance bands to a minimum value of 1e-4 and maximum of 1.0,
# to avoid extreme values in index calculations. The thermal band is left unclipped.
ls = ls.clip(min=1e-4, max=1.0)
ls["lwir11"] = rs.optical.scale(ls_dn, sensor="landsat")["lwir11"]   # Restore thermal band to original, in Kelvin (K).

# Set a sensor attribute for documentation and future reference.
ls.attrs["pyrsense:sensor"] = "landsat"

# Display the constants used to convert thermal band B10 (Landsat 9) DN values to Kelvin,
# which can be useful for reference or further processing.

A handful of values account for most pixels in real scenes. Let’s decode them, including the ones that actually occur in our downloaded scene.


Code
# This block decodes the most common QA_PIXEL bit patterns found in Landsat scenes and summarizes
# which quality flags (cloud, shadow, water, etc.) are set for those values. It also flags which codes
# are actually present in our particular scene.

# 1. Prepare an array of typical QA_PIXEL values observed in real scenes.
codes = xr.DataArray(
    np.array([1, 21824, 21952, 22080, 22280, 23888, 30048, 54596, 55052], dtype="uint16"),
    dims="value"
)

# 2. Decode the individual boolean flags (fill, cloud, shadow, snow, water, etc.) using their bit positions.
flags = {
    name: rs.optical.decode_bits(codes, bit).values
    for name, bit in landsat.QA_BITS.items()
}

# 3. Decode the quality confidence for selected features (cloud, shadow, snow, cirrus).
# These are stored as 2 bits each; decode_bits(..., 2) decodes 2-bit fields.
conf = {
    f"{n}_conf": rs.optical.decode_bits(codes, b, 2).values
    for n, b in [("cloud", 8), ("shadow", 10), ("snow", 12), ("cirrus", 14)]
}

# 4. Compile the information into a single DataFrame.
qa_table = pd.DataFrame({**flags, **conf}, index=codes.values)

# 5. For each code, indicate if it would be marked as "usable" (clear land/water) by the default mask.
qa_table["usable (default mask)"] = rs.optical.landsat_qa_mask(codes).values

# 6. Check which codes from the list are actually present in the current scene.
real_codes, real_counts = np.unique(ls_dn["qa_pixel"].values, return_counts=True)
# does the code occur in this scene?
qa_table["present in our scene"] = [int(c) in real_codes for c in codes.values]

# 7. Display the summary DataFrame.
