text:
Colour composites
Assigning different bands to red, green and blue highlights different surface properties. rs.viz.plot_rgb has presets and applies a 2-98 % percentile stretch per band.


Code
# Define a dictionary of RGB composite presets, mapping internal preset names
# to readable descriptions showing which bands will be mapped to RGB.
presets = {
    "true_color": "Natural colour (R, G, B)",
    "false_color": "Colour infrared (NIR, R, G)",
    "agriculture": "Agriculture (SWIR1, NIR, B)",
    "swir": "SWIR (SWIR2, NIR, R)",
    "urban": "Urban (SWIR2, SWIR1, R)",
    "water": "Land/water (NIR, SWIR1, R)",
}

# Create a 2x3 grid of subplots to display all six composites side by side.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 7))

# Loop over both the axes and the preset-composite pairs.
# For each subplot, plot the Landsat RGB composite image using the current preset,
# set the subplot title to the readable description,
# and remove axis ticks for a cleaner display.
for ax, (preset_name, title) in zip(axes.ravel(), presets.items()):
    rs.viz.plot_rgb(ls, preset_name, ax=ax, title=title)  # the composite with this preset
    ax.set_xticks([])  # no x ticks
    ax.set_yticks([])  # no y ticks

# Adjust layout so plots do not overlap and display the figure.
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()  # draw









Irrigated parks and golf courses glow red in colour infrared; Lake Mead is black in the land/water composite because water absorbs NIR and SWIR; the urban composite separates roofs and pavement (purple-grey) from desert soils (tan).

section: Validating index-based water and built-up maps
text:
Validating index-based water and built-up maps
Thresholded indices, such as MNDWI (for mapping water) and combinations like NDBI > 0 & NDVI < 0.2 (for mapping built-up areas), provide simple, rapid classification maps of land cover. However, these “quick maps” can be misleading if not validated against reliable, independent reference data, since threshold choices may not generalize across regions or conditions. To assess the accuracy of these index-based classifications, we compare their results with the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) 2021, which serves as ground truth. The NLCD data is accessed in the form of a cloud-optimized GeoTIFF directly from the web, and for efficiency, only the section corresponding to the Las Vegas area (the current scene) is downloaded and used for validation.


Code
# This code section validates simple water and built-up area maps based on thresholded spectral indices, 
# by comparing them to reference data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD).

# 1. Load the NLCD reference data for the same area as the current Landsat scene (las vegas).
nlcd = nlcd_for(ls["red"])

# 2. Define reference masks from NLCD classes: 
#    - water: class 11
#    - built-up: classes 22, 23, 24 (various types of developed/urban land)
water_ref = nlcd.isin([11])
built_ref = nlcd.isin([22, 23, 24])  # reference built-up area: NLCD developed low, medium and high

# 3. Threshold the remotely sensed indices to create binary water and built-up predictions.
#    - For water: Use the MNDWI index, classifying as water where MNDWI > 0 (literature-based threshold).
#      (Otsu's method is mentioned, but avoided here because water is extremely rare in this desert area.)
water = vi["MNDWI"] > 0.0

#    - For built-up: Common rule combines a high NDBI (Normalized Difference Built-up Index) 
#      and a low NDVI (to exclude vegetated/non-urban areas).
built = (vi["NDBI"] > 0) & (vi["NDVI"] < 0.2)

# 4. Restrict evaluation to valid pixels (NLCD value > 0)
valid = nlcd > 0

# 5. For both water and built-up, compare the predictions to the NLCD reference and compute accuracy metrics.
rows = {}
for name, pred, ref in [  # each prediction compared with the reference
    ("Water (MNDWI > 0)", water, water_ref),
    ("Built-up (NDBI > 0 & NDVI < 0.2)", built, built_ref)
]:
    # Compute an accuracy report: overall accuracy, kappa statistic, user's (precision) and producer's (recall) accuracy for the "positive" class.
    r = rs.classify.accuracy_report(ref.values[valid.values], pred.values[valid.values], labels=[False, True])
    pc = r["per_class"].loc[True]  # scores of the "built-up" class
    rows[name] = {  # one row of scores
        "overall accuracy": r["overall_accuracy"],
        "kappa": r["kappa"],
        "user's acc. (class)": pc.users_accuracy,
        "producer's acc. (class)": pc.producers_accuracy
    }

# 6. Print statistics about reference pixels:
print(
    f"Water reference pixels: {int(water_ref.values[valid.values].sum())} of {int(valid.sum())} "
    f"({float(water_ref.values[valid.values].mean()):.2%})"
)

#    Also, print the median NDBI for built-up ("developed") and for shrub/barren desert in the area 
#    (to help explain misclassification results).
print(
    f"Median NDBI: developed: {float(vi['NDBI'].where(built_ref).median()):.3f}, "
    f"shrub/barren desert: {float(vi['NDBI'].where(nlcd.isin([31, 52])).median()):.3f}"
)

# 7. Display accuracy metrics in a DataFrame.
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)

# the agreement/disagreement between built-up predictions and the NLCD reference,
# and the remotely sensed water prediction (MNDWI > 0).

# 1. Set up a figure with 3 side-by-side axes.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.5))

# 2. Plot the original NLCD land cover map for the valid pixels.
#    The legend only includes mapped NLCD class codes that actually appear in our subset.
rs.viz.plot_raster(
    nlcd.where(valid),
    ax=axes[0],
    title="NLCD 2021",
    categorical={k: v for k, v in NLCD_CLASSES.items() if k in np.unique(nlcd.values)}
)

# 3. Plot a map showing, pixel by pixel, where the built-up mask and NLCD agree or disagree,
#    for valid pixels only. `agree` codes: 
#    0: both non-built,
#    1: missed (NLCD built-up but not by index), 
#    2: false alarm (index only), 
#    3: agree built.
agree = (built.astype(int) * 2 + built_ref.astype(int)).where(valid)
rs.viz.plot_raster(  # map of the layer
    agree,
    ax=axes[1],
    title="Built-up: index vs NLCD",
    categorical={
        0: ("both non-built", "#f0f0f0"),
        1: ("missed (NLCD only)", "#2b83ba"),
        2: ("false alarm (index only)", "#fdae61"),
        3: ("agree built", "#d7191c")
    }
)

# 4. Plot the predicted water map using MNDWI > 0 as threshold, on valid pixels.
rs.viz.plot_raster(
    water.astype(int).where(valid),
    ax=axes[2],
    title="Water (MNDWI > 0)",
    categorical={
        0: ("land", "#e8e2d0"),
        1: ("water", "#2166ac")
    }
)

# 5. Remove axis ticks for a cleaner look, lay out, and show the plot.
for a in axes:
    a.set_xticks([])  # no x ticks
    a.set_yticks([])  # no y ticks
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw









Water scores 98.9% overall accuracy, but its kappa is only 0.10 and user’s accuracy (precision) just 5%, open water is under 0.1% of this scene, so even a tiny false-positive rate swamps the true water pixels in absolute terms. Overall accuracy alone is misleading for a rare class; check precision and kappa too. The built-up rule fails outright (kappa below zero): in this desert, bare soil has a higher NDBI than the city (compare the medians printed above with the NDBI map in the Spectral indices section), so the rule flags much of the desert as built-up while missing most of the city. NDBI was designed for humid regions where non-urban land is vegetated. This is why index thresholds, and even standard auto-thresholding methods like Otsu, must be validated locally; the classification chapter, 07_08 replaces them with a trained classifier.

title: Landsat: Half a Century of Earth Observation
text:
Land surface temperature
Thermal sensors measure radiance, which converts to brightness temperature (BT) with the Planck constants K1 and K2. BT assumes a blackbody; real surfaces emit less (emissivity ε < 1), so the land surface temperature is higher than BT:
\[\mathrm{LST} = \frac{BT}{1 + (\lambda BT / \rho)\ln\varepsilon}, \qquad \rho = hc/k = 14388\ \mu m\,K\]
ε can be estimated from NDVI (Sobrino et al. 2004). Collection 2 ST_B10 already contains LST computed this way with ASTER-based emissivity. Let’s see how much the emissivity correction matters across Las Vegas for a uniform 310 K brightness temperature:


Code
# This code demonstrates how surface emissivity corrections affect Land Surface Temperature (LST) estimates.
# 1. Estimate the land surface emissivity using NDVI, following Sobrino et al. (2004).
emis = rs.optical.emissivity_ndvi(vi["NDVI"])

# 2. Create a synthetic brightness temperature (BT) array, setting all pixels to 310 K.
bt = xr.full_like(vi["NDVI"], 310.0)

# 3. Compute the land surface temperature using the single channel method, accounting for emissivity.
#    The wavelength is set to 10.904 μm, matching Landsat 9 Band 10.
lst = rs.optical.lst_single_channel(bt, emis, wavelength=10.904)

# 4. Plot the estimated emissivity and the difference between LST and BT.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
# emissivity estimated from NDVI
rs.viz.plot_raster(emis, ax=axes[0], cmap="cividis", title="Emissivity from NDVI")
# how much emissivity changes LST for a fixed brightness temperature
rs.viz.plot_raster(lst - bt, ax=axes[1], cmap="inferno", title="LST - BT (K) for BT = 310 K")

plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

# 5. Print the thermal constants (K1, K2) for Landsat 9 Band 10, which are required for LST calculations from radiance.
print("Landsat 9 B10 thermal constants (K1, K2):", landsat.THERMAL_K["landsat-9"]["B10"])









Landsat 9 B10 thermal constants (K1, K2): (799.0284, 1329.2405)


Ignoring emissivity would underestimate desert surface temperatures by about 2 K and water by under 1 K. Next we analyse a real LST product: an ECOSTRESS scene over Santa Barbara County on California’s Central Coast, combined with NLCD land cover for the same window.

# 1. Read the ECOSTRESS land surface temperature (LST) image and remove the singleton "band" dimension for a simplified 2D array.
eco = rs.read(fetch("ecostress_lst.tif")).squeeze("band", drop=True)

# 2. Convert the LST data from Kelvin to Celsius, renaming the variable accordingly for clarity.
eco_c = (eco - 273.15).rename("LST (°C)")

# 3. Load the NLCD (National Land Cover Database) land cover classification corresponding to the spatial extent of the ECOSTRESS data.
lc_eco = nlcd_for(eco, name="nlcd_ecostress")

# 4. Set up a side-by-side plot with two subplots.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# 5a. Display the ECOSTRESS LST (in Celsius) in the first subplot using the "inferno" colormap.
rs.viz.plot_raster(eco_c, ax=axes[0], cmap="inferno", title="ECOSTRESS LST, 1 Apr 2023 (°C)")

# 5b. Display the land cover classification in the second subplot.
#     Only show categories that are present in the data, using their categorical labels.
rs.viz.plot_raster(
    lc_eco.where(lc_eco > 0),
    ax=axes[1],
    title="NLCD 2021",
    categorical={k: v for k, v in NLCD_CLASSES.items() if k in np.unique(lc_eco.values)}

# 6. Remove axis ticks for a cleaner presentation.
for a in axes:
    a.set_xticks([])  # no x ticks
    a.set_yticks([])  # no y ticks

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()  # draw

Found nlcd_ecostress.tif locally; using cached version.











Code
# 1. Flatten the ECOSTRESS LST and NLCD arrays and create a DataFrame with these values.
#    Rows with missing (NaN) values are dropped.
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "lst": eco_c.values.ravel(),    # Land Surface Temperature values (in °C)
    "code": lc_eco.values.ravel()   # Land cover code values
}).dropna()

# 2. Remove rows where the land cover code is not positive (e.g., background or unclassified).
df = df[df.code > 0]

# 3. Create a new column mapping each land cover code to its class name.
#    NLCD_CLASSES[c][0] gives the human-readable class label.
df["class"] = df.code.map(lambda c: NLCD_CLASSES[c][0])

# 4. Calculate summary statistics for LST, grouped by land cover class: 
#    - count: number of pixels
#    - median: median LST for the class
#    - std: standard deviation of LST for the class
#    Keep only classes with at least 2,000 pixels, then sort by median LST.
stats = df.groupby("class")["lst"].agg(["count", "median", "std"]).query("count > 2000")
stats = stats.sort_values("median")  # coolest classes first

# 5. Create a horizontal bar plot of the median LST (with standard deviation as error bars)
#    for each land cover class.
ax = stats["median"].plot(
    kind="barh",
    xerr=stats["std"],
    figsize=(8, 4.5),
    color="C3"
)
ax.set(xlabel="Median LST (°C) ± 1 std", title="Surface temperature by land cover")  # labels and title
plt.show()  # draw

# 6. Compare the median surface temperature for two groups:
#    - Developed (medium/high intensity): NLCD codes 23, 24
#    - Forest and agriculture: NLCD codes 41, 42, 43 (forest), 81, 82 (agriculture)
#    Print their median LST and the difference.
dev = df[df.code.isin([23, 24])].lst.median()
veg = df[df.code.isin([41, 42, 43, 81, 82])].lst.median()  # median LST of forest and agriculture
# urban heat island: the difference
print(f"Developed (medium/high) {dev:.1f} °C vs forest/agriculture {veg:.1f} °C -> difference {dev - veg:.1f} °C")









Developed (medium/high) 30.9 °C vs forest/agriculture 23.2 °C -> difference 7.7 °C


On this spring afternoon developed land is the hottest class, several degrees warmer than cropland, shrubland and forest, and the ocean is coolest: a clear surface urban heat island. Compare this with Las Vegas, where the desert around the city can be as hot as, or hotter than, the irrigated city itself.

title: Landsat: Half a Century of Earth Observation
text:
Summary, exercises and references
Key ideas

Landsat offers 30 m imagery back to 1984 (TM) and 1972 (MSS), free and consistently calibrated.
Use Collection 2 Level-2: apply DN × 0.0000275 − 0.2 for reflectance and decode QA_PIXEL.
Band numbers differ between sensors; canonical names make code sensor-independent.
Indices are fast but correlated; validate thresholded maps against reference data, and watch overall accuracy on a rare class, which can look good while precision and kappa are poor.
Surface temperature depends on emissivity; land cover strongly controls LST.
Multi-decade series reveal land-use change, but per-date classification is noisy; animating the raw composites is often more convincing than any single derived map.
MSS, TM, ETM+ and OLI can all be mosaicked into one time series by sticking to the bands they share (red, green, NIR) and reprojecting every scene to one common grid.

geolattice.rsense functions used: geolattice.rsense.get_images.get_images/search_images, rs.optical.load_landsat, rs.read, rs.optical.scale, rs.optical.decode_bits, rs.optical.landsat_qa_mask, rs.viz.rgb/plot_rgb/plot_raster, .rs.index, rs.optical.list_indices/register_index, rs.classify.accuracy_report, rs.optical.emissivity_ndvi/lst_single_channel, rs.RasterCube, rs.reproject.

title: Sentinel-3: Ocean Colour, Surface Temperature and Altimetry
text:
The mission
Sentinel-3 is the Copernicus mission for global ocean, land, ice, and atmosphere monitoring. It measures: - Sea surface temperature, ocean colour, and sea level - Land cover and other environmental indicators for climate monitoring - Heritage. Sentinel-3 continues observations from earlier ESA and French missions: - Envisat (2002 to 2012): MERIS (ocean colour), AATSR (surface temperature), and RA-2 (altimetry) - ERS-1 and ERS-2: ATSR series - SPOT-VEGETATION and PROBA-V: vegetation monitoring, continued through Sentinel-3’s synergy products - Development. ESA develops the satellites on behalf of the European Commission. Thales Alenia Space is the prime contractor. - Operations split - EUMETSAT flies the satellites and produces the marine products. - ESA produces the land products. - Launch timeline - Sentinel-3A launched on 16 February 2016 on a Rockot from Plesetsk, Russia. - Sentinel-3B launched on 25 April 2018, also on a Rockot. - Sentinel-3C launched on 15 September 2026 on a Vega C from Kourou (mission VV30), sharing the ride with ESA’s FLEX fluorescence satellite. It returned its first images in late September 2026 and is currently in commissioning. - Sentinel-3D is planned for 2028. - A next-generation mission is planned for the 2030s: Sentinel-3 Next Generation Optical, plus a separate topography mission.

title: Sentinel-3: Ocean Colour, Surface Temperature and Altimetry
text:
Platforms

Constellation. Two satellites operate together. Sentinel-3A and 3B fly in the same orbit about 140° apart. Sentinel-3C will join them and eventually take over from 3A.
Spacecraft. About 1,150 kg each, with a design life of about 7 years and fuel for roughly 12.
Orbit

Sun-synchronous at about 815 km altitude.
Equatorial crossing at 10:00 a.m. local time (descending node). The early-morning crossing reduces cloud and sun-glint effects over the ocean.
27-day repeat cycle, which is set by the altimetry ground track.

Revisit with two satellites

OLCI: less than 2 days globally, and about daily at mid-latitudes.
SLSTR: about daily in the dual view, and better than daily in the nadir view.
Altimetry: 27-day repeat. With two satellites, the tracks are interleaved, which gives a denser spatial grid of measurements.

title: Sentinel-3: Ocean Colour, Surface Temperature and Altimetry
text:
Sensors
Each satellite carries four main instrument packages.
1. Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI) - Push-broom imaging spectrometer that succeeds MERIS. - 21 bands from 400 to 1020 nm. - Resolution: 300 m in Full Resolution (FR) mode; 1.2 km in Reduced Resolution (RR) mode. - 1,270 km swath from 5 cameras. The view is tilted 12.6° westward to reduce sun glint.
2. Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR) - Dual-view conical scanner that succeeds AATSR. - 9 spectral bands plus 2 dedicated fire channels. - Resolution: 500 m in the visible/SWIR; 1 km in the thermal infrared. - Two views of each location: - Nadir view with a 1,400 km swath - Oblique (backward) view with a 740 km swath - Combining the two views gives very accurate atmospheric correction for sea surface temperature, accurate to about 0.3 K.
3. Synthetic Aperture Radar Altimeter (SRAL) - Dual-frequency radar altimeter (Ku-band at 13.575 GHz and C-band at 5.41 GHz). - Operates in SAR (delay-Doppler) mode with about 300 m along-track resolution, which makes it suitable for coastal zones, rivers, lakes, and sea ice.
4. Supporting packages - Microwave Radiometer (MWR). Measures at 23.8 and 36.5 GHz to correct the altimeter for atmospheric water vapour (wet troposphere correction). - Precise Orbit Determination (POD). GNSS receiver, DORIS, and a laser retroreflector, giving orbits accurate to the centimetre for sea-level measurement.

Swath products
GeoLattice provides reader, flag-decoding and swath-to-grid regridding functions for Sentinel-3’s OLCI, SLSTR, SRAL and Synergy products through geolattice.rsense.optical.sensors.sentinel3. Help on function decode_flags in module geolattice.rsense.optical.sensors.sentinel3:

decode_flags(flag: 'xr.DataArray') -> 'dict[str, xr.DataArray]'
    Every named bit of a Sentinel-3 flag variable, read from its own metadata.
    
    Uses the variable's ``flag_masks`` and ``flag_meanings`` attributes (CF convention),
    never a hardcoded bit position, since the bit layout differs by product and baseline.

Help on function flag_mask in module geolattice.rsense.optical.sensors.sentinel3:

flag_mask(flag: 'xr.DataArray', exclude: 'Iterable[str]', *, match: 'str' = 'exact') -> 'xr.DataArray'
    Boolean validity mask (``True`` = usable) excluding the named flags.
    
    ``match="exact"`` requires the flag meaning to equal an entry in ``exclude``;
    ``match="contains"`` excludes a flag if any entry in ``exclude`` is a substring of its
    name (handy for SLSTR, whose per-channel flags are named e.g. ``cloud_in``).

section: Downloading a real OLCI water product
text:
Downloading a real OLCI water product
Western Lake Erie develops seasonal harmful algal blooms (HABs) most summers, driven by agricultural runoff into the Maumee River. We search Planetary Computer’s sentinel-3-olci-wfr-l2-netcdf collection for two late-summer 2023 dates and download the real product files for each: the default water variables, the WQSF quality flag, and the pixel geolocation (geo_coordinates.nc), reproducing the structure of an extracted .SEN3 folder on disk so the reader functions below work exactly as they would on a manually downloaded product. One date also gets three OLCI reflectance bands (Oa10, Oa11, Oa12) for the Terrestrial chlorophyll indices, in and out of their domain section.


Code
# Define the geographical bounding box for the area of interest: Western Lake Erie open water.
ERIE_BBOX = (-83.35, 41.38, -82.55, 41.85)  

# List of dates we want to download Sentinel-3 OLCI water products for.
OLCI_DATES = ["2023-09-05", "2023-09-19"]

# Key OLCI water variables to extract for analysis.
WATER_VARS = ["chl_oc4me", "chl_nn", "tsm_nn", "trsp", "iop_nn"]

# OLCI reflectance bands (used in later sections, only required for the first date).
OA_BANDS = ["oa10", "oa11", "oa12"]                 

# Output directory where downloaded data will be stored.
S3_OUT = DATA / "s3_erie_2023"

# scene folders that already hold every water variable plus the flags and geolocation
erie_local = local_scenes(S3_OUT, [f"{v}.nc" for v in WATER_VARS] + ["wqsf.nc", "geo_coordinates.nc"])
if len(erie_local) >= len(OLCI_DATES):  # one folder per date is on disk
    print("Reading the OLCI scenes already downloaded under", S3_OUT)  # use the local drive
elif ONLINE:  # not on disk yet: download when online
    # Search the Planetary Computer STAC catalog for Sentinel-3 OLCI L2 water products
    # over the given bounding box and date range.
    search = CATALOG.search(
        collections=["sentinel-3-olci-wfr-l2-netcdf"],
        bbox=ERIE_BBOX,
        datetime="2023-09-01/2023-09-20",
        limit=20
    )
    # Index the search results by their observation date.
    items = {it.datetime.date().isoformat(): it for it in search.items()}
    for i, d in enumerate(OLCI_DATES):  # every OLCI date
        it = items[d]  # Get search item for target date.
        scene_dir = S3_OUT / it.id  # Create a separate folder for each product.
        scene_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)  # its folder
        # Create a mapping of asset keys to their destination filenames for water variables.
        assets = {f"{v.replace('_', '-')}": f"{v}.nc" for v in WATER_VARS}
        # Always add quality flags and geolocation files.
        assets.update({"wqsf": "wqsf.nc", "geo-coordinates": "geo_coordinates.nc"})
        # For the first date, also download the reflectance bands.
        if i == 0:
            # the reflectance NetCDF of every band
            assets.update({b: f"Oa{b[2:]}_reflectance.nc" for b in OA_BANDS})
        # Download each asset file if it's not already present.
        for key, fname in assets.items():
            dest = scene_dir / fname  # local file
            if dest.exists():  # skip files already downloaded
                continue  # Skip if already downloaded.
            r = requests.get(it.assets[key].href, timeout=60)  # download the asset
            r.raise_for_status()  # Raise an error on connection/HTTP failure.
            dest.write_bytes(r.content)  # Write the file to disk.
        # Print confirmation after downloading each product.
        print(d, it.id, "downloaded")
else:
    # If not downloading (e.g. offline), notify about reusing existing data on disk.
    print("Offline: reusing the scenes already downloaded under", S3_OUT)

text:
Reading and masking OLCI L2 water data
read_olci_water opens the five default water variables plus WQSF and geolocation, and renames each from its real file variable name (CHL_NN, KD490_M07, …) to the documented canonical name. olci_water_mask then builds a validity mask from WQSF.


Code
# List all subdirectories in the output directory, which each correspond to a downloaded Sentinel-3 scene.
scene_dirs = sorted(p for p in S3_OUT.iterdir() if p.is_dir())

# Read the OLCI water data from the first available scene directory using the provided helper.
ds0 = s3.read_olci_water(scene_dirs[0])

# Display the names of the variables contained in the dataset.
print("Variables:", list(ds0.data_vars))

# Print the size (number of elements) for each dimension in the dataset to show its shape.
print("Shape:", dict(ds0.sizes))


Variables: ['chl_oc4me', 'chl_oc4me_err', 'chl_nn', 'chl_nn_err', 'tsm_nn', 'tsm_nn_err', 'trsp', 'trsp_err', 'iop_nn', 'iop_nn_err', 'wqsf']
Shape: {'rows': 4091, 'columns': 4865}


WQSF’s default exclusion list includes a LAND flag, appropriate for open ocean, where it reliably separates water from coastline. Over a turbid, algae-rich inland lake like western Lake Erie it misfires: the land/water discrimination algorithm reads the lake’s high-sediment, high-chlorophyll reflectance as land far more often than it should. Checking the flag breakdown inside our own AOI shows this directly.


Code
# Extract longitude and latitude arrays from the dataset.
lon, lat = ds0["longitude"].values, ds0["latitude"].values

# Create a boolean mask for all pixels that fall within the defined Lake Erie bounding box (ERIE_BBOX).
in_bbox = (
    (lon >= ERIE_BBOX[0]) & (lon <= ERIE_BBOX[2]) &  # longitude between min and max
    (lat >= ERIE_BBOX[1]) & (lat <= ERIE_BBOX[3])    # latitude between min and max
)

# Decode the WQSF flags for quality and validity assessment, resulting in a dictionary of boolean arrays (one per flag).
flags = s3.decode_flags(ds0["wqsf"])

# For each flag, compute the fraction of AOI pixels where that flag is set (True). This builds a breakdown of flag prevalence.
breakdown = pd.Series({
    name: float(arr.values[in_bbox].mean())  # Average flag value within AOI; gives fraction set.
    for name, arr in flags.items()
}).sort_values(ascending=False)

# Print the total number of AOI pixels and show the flag breakdown for flags with >1% occurrence (rounded to 0.1%).
print(f"{int(in_bbox.sum())} pixels inside the Lake Erie AOI; flag fraction set:")
breakdown[breakdown > 0.01].round(3)  # flags that affect more than 1 % of pixels

# LAND is set on ~99% of in-lake pixels here -- a known issue over turbid Great Lakes
# water, not a bug in the flag decoding. Drop it from the exclusion list for this AOI, keeping
# every other quality flag (cloud, invalid, saturated, glint, ...) that genuinely means bad data.
# The default mask for OLCI water pixels excludes (masks out) pixels flagged as 'LAND', which is useful for open-ocean scenes.
# However, over Lake Erie, the 'LAND' flag tends to be incorrectly set for turbid water due to high sediment/chlorophyll.
# Here, we build a custom exclusion list that keeps all default quality flags except 'LAND':
ERIE_EXCLUDE = [f for f in s3.OLCI_WFR_DEFAULT_EXCLUDE if f != "LAND"]
print("Exclusion list for this AOI:", ERIE_EXCLUDE)  # flags excluded for this AOI

# Apply the custom exclusion list to mask out only truly bad data, not 'LAND', for this Area of Interest (AOI).
valid0 = s3.olci_water_mask(ds0["wqsf"], exclude=ERIE_EXCLUDE)

# Calculate and print the fraction of AOI pixels inside the Lake Erie bounding box that are considered valid (not masked).
print(f"Valid fraction inside the AOI: {float(valid0.values[in_bbox].mean()):.1%}")

title: Sentinel-3: Ocean Colour, Surface Temperature and Altimetry
section: Chlorophyll retrieval: log back-transform and swath-to-grid
text:
Chlorophyll retrieval: log back-transform and swath-to-grid
OLCI’s neural-network chlorophyll product (chl_nn) is stored log10-scaled: average the raw values and you get a biased (too-low) mean. log_to_linear reverses the transform, and swath_to_grid then resamples the per-pixel swath coordinates onto a regular longitude/latitude grid over our AOI, the last step of the workflow, run only once after masking and unit conversion so no cloud edge gets interpolated across.


Code
# Function to generate a gridded chlorophyll-a map for Lake Erie from a Sentinel-3 OLCI scene.
def erie_chl_map(scene_dir):
    # Read OLCI L2 water data from the given scene directory (swath-form, not gridded)
    ds = s3.read_olci_water(scene_dir)
    # Create a mask of good-quality water pixels, using a custom exclusion list for the AOI
    valid = s3.olci_water_mask(ds["wqsf"], exclude=ERIE_EXCLUDE)
    # Convert log10-scaled chlorophyll to linear mg/m³ values, masking out invalid pixels
    chl = s3.log_to_linear(ds["chl_nn"]).where(valid)
    chl.name = "chl_nn"  # its name
    # Resample swath pixels onto a fixed lat/lon grid over the area of interest (Lake Erie)
    return s3.swath_to_grid(chl, ds["longitude"], ds["latitude"], resolution=0.005, bounds=ERIE_BBOX)

# Function to parse the sensing start date from a Sentinel-3 product folder name.
def scene_date(folder):
    # date of a Sentinel-3 product from its ID
    """Sensing start date from a Sentinel-3 product ID, e.g. '..._20230919T153401_...' -> '2023-09-19'."""
    # Folder names have format ..._YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS_...: extract YYYYMMDD and reformat
    stamp = folder.name.split("_")[4]            # 'YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS'
    return f"{stamp[:4]}-{stamp[4:6]}-{stamp[6:8]}"  # as YYYY-MM-DD

# For every downloaded scene, compute a masked, gridded chlorophyll-a map,
# and associate it with its acquisition date (string) in a dictionary.
chl_maps = {scene_date(d): erie_chl_map(d) for d in scene_dirs}

# Print summary statistics for each mapped scene:
# - the date
# - fraction of non-missing pixels (valid fraction)
# - mean chlorophyll-a value in valid pixels (mg/m³)
# - max chlorophyll-a value (mg/m³)
for label, grid in chl_maps.items():
    vf = float(np.isfinite(grid.values).mean())  # valid share of the gridded image
    print(label, "valid frac:", round(vf, 3),  # report it
         "mean chl-a:", round(float(np.nanmean(grid.values)), 2) if vf > 0 else None,
         "mg/m3, max:", round(float(np.nanmax(grid.values)), 1) if vf > 0 else None)

text:
Mapping a harmful algal bloom


Code
# Create a figure with two side-by-side subplots to compare two chlorophyll-a maps
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))

# Loop over each subplot axis, and each (date label, gridded chlorophyll data) pair in chl_maps
for ax, (label, grid) in zip(axes, chl_maps.items()):
    # Determine the extent (bounding box) of the grid for proper map display
    extent = [float(grid.x.min()), float(grid.x.max()), float(grid.y.min()), float(grid.y.max())]
    # Display the gridded chlorophyll-a data as an image with a color map and set color limits
    im = ax.imshow(
        grid.values,
        cmap="turbo",         # Use 'turbo' color map for vivid visualization
        vmin=0, vmax=50,      # Color bar scale: 0 to 50 mg/m³ chlorophyll-a
        extent=extent,
        origin="upper"
    )
    # Set title with formatted date
    ax.set_title(f"{pd.Timestamp(label):%d %b %Y}")
    # Add a colorbar to the plot for chlorophyll concentration
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.85, label="chlorophyll-a (mg/m3)")

# Add a main title for the figure describing the dataset and algorithm used
plt.suptitle("Western Lake Erie chlorophyll-a, OLCI NN algorithm")
# Adjust layout to prevent overlap and display the plot
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()  # draw









The 5 September pass has the better swath coverage of the two and shows the bloom’s real shape: chlorophyll concentrated along the southwestern shoreline near the Maumee River mouth (Toledo, Ohio) at 15-30+ mg/m³, fading to under 5 mg/m³ in the clearer open water to the northeast, exactly where western Lake Erie’s blooms are known to originate. The 19 September pass only grazes the AOI along its orbital track, leaving most of the frame empty; a small AOI near the edge of even OLCI’s 1270 km swath is not guaranteed full coverage on every pass.

print(
    f"Mean {float(np.nanmean(lst_grid.values)):.1f} C, "
    f"range {float(np.nanmin(lst_grid.values)):.1f} to {float(np.nanmax(lst_grid.values)):.1f} C"
)









Mean 30.5 C, range 22.3 to 35.9 C


This overpass crosses the valley at roughly 10 pm local time, not midday. SLSTR, like most polar orbiters, has fixed day and night equator-crossing times rather than a choice of local time. A nighttime LST composite is still useful: the urban-versus-desert temperature contrast at night is often a cleaner signal of the urban heat island than the daytime image, since built surfaces release stored daytime heat slowly while the surrounding desert cools fast.

section: Active forest fires in western Canada
text:
Active forest fires in western Canada
SLSTR’s Level-2 fire product (SL_2_FRP) is a table of actively burning pixels, one row per fire, with fire radiative power (FRP) in megawatts. FRP is the rate at which those pixels were releasing energy at the time of the overpass. Mapped together, they are the active fire area.
Mid-May 2023 was the early peak of that year’s Canadian wildfire season. Alberta declared a provincial state of emergency on 6 May, and large fires were burning in the boreal forest of west-central Alberta and northern Saskatchewan. This section downloads every SLSTR FRP scene that intersects those two provinces on 16 May 2023, keeps the pixels classified as vegetation fires, and maps them.
Two details of FRP_in.nc matter before frp_to_points returns one row per fire:

The file mixes a one-dimensional fire table (dimension fires) with a two-dimensional flag image (rows by columns). Pass only the fire-table variables. Sending the whole dataset through to_dataframe tries to align those two grids.
classification is a bit mask. Bit value 1 is vegetation_fire. The same mask also carries onshore gas flares, offshore flares, volcanoes and industrial sources. Alberta has persistent industrial hot spots, so the vegetation bit is what keeps this a forest-fire map. This product generation has no FRP_MWIR_confidence column for frp_to_points to filter on, so the classification mask does that job.

Neighbouring orbits, and the day and night overpasses, can see the same 1 km pixel more than once. After clipping to the provinces we keep the strongest FRP in each 0.01 degree cell (about 1 km, the SLSTR fire grid). aggregate_frp then sums those pixels onto a 0.2 degree grid so the burning area is readable at provincial scale. Black rings mark pixels with FRP of at least 150 MW.


Code
# Alberta and Saskatchewan: the frame of the map below.
CANADA_BBOX = (-120.2, 49.0, -101.3, 56.8)
FRP_DAY = "2023-05-16"  # the day of the fire scenes
FRP_OUT = DATA / "s3_frp_canada_2023"  # folder for the FRP scenes

if local_scenes(FRP_OUT, ["FRP_in.nc"]):  # downloaded before
    print("Reading the FRP scenes already downloaded under", FRP_OUT)  # use the local drive
elif ONLINE:  # not on disk yet: download when online
    # Neighbouring orbits plus the day and night passes all cross this box,
    # so one calendar day is more than one scene.
    search = CATALOG.search(
        collections=["sentinel-3-slstr-frp-l2-netcdf"],
        bbox=CANADA_BBOX,
        datetime="2023-05-16T00:00:00Z/2023-05-17T00:00:00Z",
        limit=40,
    )
    n_scenes = 0  # number of scenes downloaded
    for it in search.items():  # every found item
        # keep only that day and items with an FRP file
        if it.datetime.date().isoformat() != FRP_DAY or "frp-in" not in it.assets:
            continue
        scene_dir = FRP_OUT / it.id  # its folder
        scene_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)  # create it
        dest = scene_dir / "FRP_in.nc"  # local file
        if not dest.exists():  # download only if missing
            r = requests.get(it.assets["frp-in"].href, timeout=120)  # download it
            r.raise_for_status()  # stop on an HTTP error
            dest.write_bytes(r.content)  # save it
        n_scenes += 1  # count it
        print(it.id, "downloaded")  # progress
    print(n_scenes, "scenes for", FRP_DAY)  # total
else:
    print("Offline: reusing the scenes already downloaded under", FRP_OUT)  # offline

Code
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import contextily as cx  # web-map basemaps
from shapely.geometry import box  # rectangle geometry
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm  # logarithmic colour scale

frames = []  # fire points of every scene
for scene in sorted(p for p in FRP_OUT.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):  # every FRP scene folder
    ds = s3.read_slstr_frp(scene)  # read the fire radiative power product
    # Skip scenes whose swath missed every fire, and drop the 2-D flag image
    # so the table stays one row per fire.
    if ds.sizes.get("fires", 0) == 0:
        continue
    # variables with one value per fire
    fire_vars = [name for name in ds.data_vars if ds[name].dims == ("fires",)]
    frames.append(s3.frp_to_points(ds[fire_vars]))  # fires as points

if not frames:  # no fires found
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"No FRP scenes with fires under {FRP_OUT}")  # stop with a clear message

# all fires as one GeoDataFrame
fires = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True), geometry="geometry", crs=4326)

# Bit 1 of classification is vegetation_fire. Gas flares and industrial
# sources use other bits and stay out of this map.
veg = fires[(fires["classification"].astype(int) & 1) != 0].copy()
west, south, east, north = CANADA_BBOX  # the study box
veg = veg.cx[west:east, south:north].copy()  # keep fires inside it

# Repeated views of the same ~1 km pixel: keep the strongest FRP.
veg["gx"] = (veg.geometry.x // 0.01) * 0.01
veg["gy"] = (veg.geometry.y // 0.01) * 0.01  # 0.01 degree grid row
# keep the strongest fire per grid cell
veg = veg.sort_values("FRP_MWIR", ascending=False).drop_duplicates(["gx", "gy"])

RES = 0.2  # degrees, about 15-20 km, readable on a provincial map
grid = s3.aggregate_frp(veg, resolution=RES, agg="sum")  # total FRP per grid cell
cells = gpd.GeoDataFrame(  # the cells as polygons
    {"FRP_MWIR": grid.to_numpy()},
    geometry=[box(gx, gy, gx + RES, gy + RES) for gy, gx in grid.index],
    crs=4326,
)
cells = cells[cells["FRP_MWIR"] >= 50]  # cells with at least 50 MW
hot = veg[veg["FRP_MWIR"] >= 150]  # single fires of at least 150 MW

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 7.2))  # one panel
cells.to_crs(3857).plot(  # the cells in Web Mercator, coloured by FRP
    ax=ax,
    column="FRP_MWIR",
    cmap="YlOrRd",
    norm=LogNorm(vmin=50, vmax=float(cells["FRP_MWIR"].max())),
    alpha=0.62,
    legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"label": "Summed FRP (MW)", "shrink": 0.62},
)
hot.to_crs(3857).plot(  # the hottest fires on top
    ax=ax, facecolor="none", edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.6, markersize=16, zorder=3
)
frame = gpd.GeoSeries([box(west, south, east, north)], crs=4326).to_crs(3857)  # the study box in Web Mercator
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = frame.total_bounds  # its bounds
ax.set_xlim(minx, maxx)  # x extent
ax.set_ylim(miny, maxy)  # y extent
# The default OpenStreetMap tile server blocks this client. Esri's street map
# still carries the town names used to read the clusters.
cx.add_basemap(ax, source=cx.providers.Esri.WorldStreetMap, attribution_size=6)
ax.set_axis_off()  # no axes
ax.set_title("Active vegetation fires, Alberta and Saskatchewan, 16 May 2023")  # title
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

print(  # summary of the fires
    f"{len(frames)} scenes with fires, "
    f"{len(veg)} vegetation-fire pixels after removing repeats, "
    f"strongest pixel {float(veg['FRP_MWIR'].max()):.0f} MW"
)









14 scenes with fires, 6440 vegetation-fire pixels after removing repeats, strongest pixel 1556 MW


On 16 May 2023 the active vegetation pixels sit in the boreal forest. One cluster runs through west-central Alberta, from the country north of Grande Prairie through Fox Creek toward Whitecourt. The other is in northern Saskatchewan, around Buffalo Narrows, La Loche and La Ronge. The prairie from Red Deer south through Medicine Hat and Regina is quiet on this date. The colour scale is logarithmic, so fires of a few hundred megawatts and the largest cell sums (well above 10,000 MW) can be read on the same map. A dark cell is a sum of FRP over about 0.2 degrees: one intense fire, or many neighbouring pixels. The black rings are the individual pixels at or above 150 MW inside that area.

section: Terrestrial chlorophyll indices, in and out of their domain
text:
Terrestrial chlorophyll indices, in and out of their domain
geolattice.rsense registers two indices built on OLCI’s red-edge bands: MCI, designed for turbid and coastal waters (so appropriate for Lake Erie), and OTCI, the terrestrial chlorophyll index, designed for vegetated land. Both run on the same three bands (oa10, oa11, oa12); only one of them is appropriate for a lake scene.

cat = rs.optical.list_indices().set_index("name").loc[["MCI", "OTCI"], ["long_name", "bands", "reference"]]

Code
# Explanation:
# The code below selects a specific OLCI (Ocean and Land Colour Imager) scene by date, reads critical bands and chlorophyll from the data, applies a water mask to exclude unwanted pixels, then computes two chlorophyll indices—MCI (Maximum Chlorophyll Index) and OTCI (OLCI Terrestrial Chlorophyll Index). Finally, it prints summary statistics for both indices.
#
# 1. OLCI scene folders are labeled alphabetically by satellite, not by date. To get the scene from "2023-09-05", it searches scene_dirs for that date (using scene_date).
oa_scene = next(d for d in scene_dirs if scene_date(d) == "2023-09-05")

# 2. Reads OLCI water product data for the selected scene. Only the neural-network chlorophyll ('chl_nn') and three red-edge bands ('oa10', 'oa11', 'oa12') are loaded.
refl_ds = s3.read_olci_water(oa_scene, variables=["chl_nn", "oa10", "oa11", "oa12"])

# 3. Applies a water mask to the three red-edge bands (excluding features defined in ERIE_EXCLUDE),
#    resulting in a cleaned reflectance dataset used for index calculation.
clean_refl = refl_ds[["oa10", "oa11", "oa12"]].where(
    s3.olci_water_mask(refl_ds["wqsf"], exclude=ERIE_EXCLUDE))

# 4. Computes the MCI and OTCI indices using the cleaned reflectance data.
mci = clean_refl.rs.index("MCI")
otci = clean_refl.rs.index("OTCI")  # OLCI Terrestrial Chlorophyll Index

# 5. Prints basic statistics:
#    - For MCI: mean value and data range (minimum to maximum), ignoring any missing values (NaN).
#    - For OTCI: mean, median, and range (rounded for clarity), ignoring missing values.
print(f"MCI:  mean {float(mci.mean(skipna=True)):.4f}, "
     f"range {float(mci.min(skipna=True)):.4f} to {float(mci.max(skipna=True)):.4f}")
print(f"OTCI: mean {float(otci.mean(skipna=True)):.2f}, "  # its statistics
     f"median {float(otci.median(skipna=True)):.2f}, "
     f"range {float(otci.min(skipna=True)):.0f} to {float(otci.max(skipna=True)):.0f}")


MCI:  mean -0.0006, range -0.0376 to 0.0854
OTCI: mean 0.26, median 0.04, range -3070 to 3313


MCI stays in a small, physically sensible range. OTCI does not: its formula divides by oa11 - oa10, the slope across vegetation’s red edge, which is well-behaved over leaves but near zero (and noisy in sign) over water, since open water has no red-edge feature at all. A handful of near-zero denominators blow the statistic up to thousands in either direction. This is not a bug in the formula, it is what happens when an index built on one physical assumption (a reflecting canopy) is pointed at a target where that assumption does not hold. The general lesson from the SLSTR land surface temperature section of the Sentinel-2 notebook (NDVI saturating over dense canopy) in reverse: here the index is undefined-feeling rather than insensitive, which can be the more dangerous failure mode, since it still returns a number.

title: Sentinel-3: Ocean Colour, Surface Temperature and Altimetry
text:
Summary, exercises and references
Key ideas

Sentinel-3 bundles four instruments (OLCI, SLSTR, SRAL, MWR) covering ocean colour, surface temperature, fire and sea-surface height, each with its own NetCDF product family and flags.
Every quality flag follows the same CF flag_masks/flag_meanings convention; decode it from the variable’s own metadata rather than a hardcoded bit position.
Real product files do not always use the lowercase, stem-matching variable names their own documentation suggests: trsp.nc holds KD490_M07, rc_gifapar.nc holds two bands, not one. Check against a real download rather than trusting an assumed name.
A standard ocean flag (LAND) can misfire over turbid inland water; know your AOI before you trust a default exclusion list.
Log-scaled products (chlorophyll, TSM) must be back-transformed before averaging or mapping.
Resample swath data to a grid once, at the end, after masking and unit conversion.
An index is only as good as the physical assumption behind it; pointed outside its domain, it can fail by returning an extreme, confident-looking number rather than an obviously missing one.
SLSTR FRP is a table of burning pixels, not a raster. Keep the vegetation-fire bit of classification before treating a hotspot as a forest fire, and collapse repeated views of the same pixel before summing.

geolattice.rsense functions used: geolattice.rsense.optical.sensors.sentinel3.read_olci_water, olci_water_mask, read_slstr_lst, slstr_lst_mask, read_slstr_frp, frp_to_points, aggregate_frp, decode_flags, flag_mask, log_to_linear, kelvin_to_celsius, swath_to_grid, rs.optical.list_indices, .rs.index.
Exercises

Use read_olci_land to retrieve FAPAR (gifapar) and OTCI over a real vegetated AOI (for example, farmland away from open water) and confirm OTCI behaves sensibly there.
Build a short chlorophyll time series over a full bloom season (June-October) and locate its peak, mirroring the phenology work in the optical chapter’s (07_02) MODIS and Sentinel-2 notebooks.
Repeat the Active forest fires in western Canada section for a later date in the 2023 season (for example 15 August) and compare where the vegetation fires sit. Split Day_night before the 1 km collapse and see which pass detects more pixels.
Compare chl_oc4me (open-ocean algorithm) and chl_nn (neural-network algorithm) over the same Lake Erie scene. Which handles this turbid water better?

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
What is SAR
RADAR stands for RAdio Detection And Ranging. A radar image is made by an active sensor. The sensor sends out microwave pulses, usually looking sideways from an aircraft or satellite, and records the energy that bounces back, called backscatter. Each pixel stores the strength (amplitude) of that echo. In complex data it also stores the phase, and the echo’s timing fixes the pixel’s position.
Optical images record reflected sunlight. Radar is different in a few ways:

Day and night, all weather. Microwaves pass through cloud, smoke, haze, and light rain, and the sensor provides its own illumination.
It sees physical and electrical properties, not color. Brightness depends on surface roughness, geometry, moisture (dielectric constant), and structure.
Wavelength sets how far the signal penetrates:

X-band (~3 cm) mostly interacts with leaves and surface detail.
C-band (~5.6 cm) reaches into crop canopies.
L-band (~23 cm) and P-band (~70 cm) penetrate forest canopy and dry soil.

Polarization describes the transmit and receive orientation (HH, VV, HV, VH). Each combination responds to different scattering mechanisms.

Buildings, flooded forest, ships



Two other features are typical of radar images:

Speckle is a granular “salt-and-pepper” noise that comes from coherent imaging.
Geometric distortions affect steep terrain. These are foreshortening, layover, and radar shadow.

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Types of radar images
1. Real Aperture Radar (RAR / SLAR) - This is early side-looking airborne radar. - Resolution is limited by the physical length of the antenna, so it is coarse at long range. - Today it is mainly of historical interest. It was used for regional mapping in cloudy tropics, such as Brazil’s RADAM project.
2. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) - SAR uses the platform’s motion and signal processing to simulate a very long antenna. This gives fine resolution regardless of altitude. - Common products: - SLC (Single Look Complex): amplitude plus phase, in slant-range geometry. It is the input for interferometry and polarimetry. - GRD (Ground Range Detected): amplitude or intensity only, multilooked, and projected to ground range. This is the standard “radar picture,” for example Sentinel-1 GRD. - Imaging modes trade coverage against resolution: - Spotlight: finest detail, smallest area. - Stripmap: a balance of the two. - ScanSAR / TOPS: wide swath, coarser resolution. - Applications: flood mapping, oil spill and ship detection, sea-ice monitoring, land cover classification, and deforestation alerts.
3. Polarimetric SAR (PolSAR) - Images are acquired in single-, dual-, or quad (full) polarization. - Quad-pol data can be split into scattering mechanisms using decompositions such as Pauli, Freeman-Durden, or H/A/α. - Applications: crop type mapping and crop growth stage, forest biomass, wetland classification, soil moisture retrieval, and urban structure.
4. Interferometric SAR (InSAR) - InSAR uses the phase difference between two SAR images of the same area taken from slightly different positions or at different times. - Products: - Interferogram: colored fringes, where each fringe is one cycle of phase. - Coherence image: shows how stable the surface was between the two dates. - DEM: for example SRTM and TanDEM-X. - Differential InSAR (DInSAR) and time-series methods (PS-InSAR, SBAS) measure ground motion at millimeter to centimeter scale. - Applications: - Earthquake and volcano deformation. - Land subsidence from groundwater pumping or mining. - Landslides. - Stability of infrastructure such as dams, bridges, and railways. - Glacier flow. - Coherence-based damage and change mapping.
5. Polarimetric Interferometric SAR (PolInSAR) and Tomographic SAR (TomoSAR) - PolInSAR combines polarimetry and interferometry. TomoSAR uses many passes to resolve vertical structure. - Applications: forest canopy height, 3D forest structure, biomass, and 3D urban reconstruction. These are mainly done with P- and L-band, as in the ESA BIOMASS mission.
6. Multi-temporal SAR stacks - A dense time series is built from repeat passes. Sentinel-1, for example, revisits every 6 to 12 days. - Applications: - Crop phenology and planting or harvest detection, such as rice mapping in monsoon Asia. - Change detection. - Flood progression. - Near-real-time disaster response.
7. Other radar imaging systems - Weather (Doppler) radar is ground-based (e.g., NEXRAD). Its reflectivity and velocity images show rainfall intensity, storm structure, and tornado signatures. - Ground-Penetrating Radar (GPR) produces subsurface profiles called radargrams. Uses include utility location, archaeology, soil horizons, and pavement inspection. - Radar altimetry and scatterometry are mostly profiles or coarse grids rather than fine images. They measure sea surface height, ice sheet elevation, and ocean wind vectors. - Bistatic and multistatic SAR use separate transmitter and receiver. TanDEM-X uses this configuration for single-pass DEM generation.

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Applications by sector

Agriculture:

Crop type mapping and acreage, especially in cloudy seasons.
Rice monitoring.
Soil moisture.
Crop growth and biomass indicators.

Forestry: deforestation detection, biomass, and canopy height.
Hydrology: floods, wetlands, soil moisture, and snow.
Geohazards: earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides, and subsidence.
Oceans and cryosphere: oil spills, ship detection, sea ice, waves and winds, and glacier dynamics.
Urban and infrastructure: urban growth and building deformation monitoring.
Defense and security: surveillance and maritime domain awareness.

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
How a radar image works
The diagram below shows a side-looking SAR acquisition: the satellite moves along azimuth, illuminates a ground swath with a short physical antenna, and a long synthetic aperture is formed by combining echoes from many positions. Range is across-track.



Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) – Side View



Azimuth: flight direction along the satellite track
Range: direction perpendicular to the flight path (across the swath)
Real aperture: short physical antenna on the satellite
Synthetic aperture: long effective antenna formed by combining echoes from many positions along the track
Processing chain: transmit pulse → receive echoes at many positions → record amplitude and phase → focus / match-filter → high-resolution image

title: SAR Fundamentals
section: The basic principle: radar is an active sensor
text:
The basic principle: radar is an active sensor
A radar satellite transmits microwave pulses toward the Earth and measures a portion of the energy scattered back toward its antenna. Unlike an optical sensor, it does not need sunlight, and microwave observations can generally be acquired through clouds.
The basic sequence is:
Transmit → interact with the surface → scatter → receive the echo → process the signal → form an image.
A SAR pixel is not a conventional photograph of an object. It represents a measurement derived from the returned electromagnetic signal, after radar focusing and image processing.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, Circle, Polygon
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (12, 6), "font.size": 11})




Code
# Figure 1: satellite transmission and return echo
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))
ax.set_xlim(0, 12); ax.set_ylim(0, 7); ax.axis("off")

# Earth surface
ax.fill_between([0, 12], [1.1, 1.1], [0, 0], color="#9caa75", alpha=.8)
ax.plot([0, 12], [1.1, 1.1], lw=3, color="black")
ax.text(10.7, .55, "Earth's surface", ha="center", weight="bold")

# Satellite
sat = FancyBboxPatch((1.0, 5.2), 1.8, .8, boxstyle="round,pad=.12", fc="#c7d5e8", ec="#23395d", lw=2)
ax.add_patch(sat)
ax.text(1.9, 5.6, "SAR satellite", ha="center", va="center", weight="bold")
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((.2,5.35),.65,.5,fc="#426b9a",ec="black"))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((2.95,5.35),.65,.5,fc="#426b9a",ec="black"))
ax.plot([1.9, 2.35], [5.2, 4.65], color="black", lw=2)
ax.add_patch(Polygon([[2.15,4.65],[2.55,4.65],[2.35,4.25]], closed=True, fc="#777777", ec="black"))

# Target
ax.add_patch(Circle((7.5,1.12),.13,color="#6b4f2a"))
ax.text(7.5,.45,"Target on ground",ha="center")

# Transmit and return paths
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((2.4,4.35),(7.35,1.35),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=18,lw=2.5,color="#d97706"))
ax.text(4.2,3.35,"Transmitted microwave pulse",rotation=-31,color="#9a4d00",ha="center")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((7.65,1.4),(2.55,4.55),connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-.18",arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=18,lw=2.5,color="#1677b8"))
ax.text(5.0,2.15,"Returned backscatter (echo)",rotation=29,color="#125b8b",ha="center")

ax.text(9.2,5.5,"The sensor measures the\nreturned signal's amplitude\nand phase.",ha="center",va="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=.5",fc="#f3f4f6",ec="#555"))
ax.set_title("Figure 1. Active radar remote sensing: transmit and receive",fontsize=15,weight="bold")
plt.show()










Two-way travel time and slant range
The radar pulse travels from the antenna to the target and then back to the antenna. If the measured round-trip time is (t), the slant range is:
\[
R = \frac{c\Delta t}{2}
\]
where \(c \approx 3 \times 10^8\) m/s is the speed of light. The division by two is necessary because the measured time includes both the outgoing and returning paths.
For example, a round-trip time of approximately 4.67 milliseconds corresponds to a slant range of about 700 km.


Code
c = 299_792_458  # speed of light, m/s
round_trip_time = 4.67e-3
slant_range = c * round_trip_time / 2
print(f"Slant range: {slant_range/1000:,.1f} km")


Slant range: 700.0 km

title: SAR Fundamentals
section: How microwave energy interacts with Earth’s surface
text:
How microwave energy interacts with Earth’s surface
The returned signal depends on surface roughness, dielectric properties (including moisture), geometry, wavelength, polarization, and incidence angle. Four scattering mechanisms are especially useful when interpreting SAR.


Code
# Figure 2: four simplified scattering mechanisms
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 8))
titles = ["A. Specular reflection (smooth surface)", "B. Diffuse scattering (rough surface)",
          "C. Volume scattering (vegetation)", "D. Double-bounce scattering (trunk + water)"]

for ax, title in zip(axes.flat, titles):
    ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 6); ax.axis("off")
    ax.plot([0.5,9.5],[1,1],color="#6b7280",lw=2)
    ax.set_title(title,weight="bold")

# specular
ax=axes[0,0]
ax.plot([1,9],[1,1],color="#2563eb",lw=5)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((3,5),(5,1.25),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=15,color="#d97706",lw=2))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((5,1.25),(7.5,5),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=15,color="#d97706",lw=2))
ax.text(5,.35,"Smooth water / surface",ha="center")
ax.text(7.4,4.7,"Reflected away",ha="center",color="#9a4d00")

# diffuse
ax=axes[0,1]
rng=np.random.default_rng(4)
x=np.linspace(.8,9.2,35); y=1+0.18*np.sin(x*4)+0.08*rng.normal(size=len(x))
ax.plot(x,y,color="#8b6b45",lw=2)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((4,5),(5,1.4),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=15,color="#d97706",lw=2))
for end in [(3,3.7),(5.5,4.3),(7.4,3.1),(6.2,2.7)]:
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((5,1.4),end,arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=13,color="#1677b8",lw=1.5))
ax.text(5,.35,"Rough soil / uneven surface",ha="center")

# volume
ax=axes[1,0]
ax.plot([1,9],[1,1],color="#6b7280",lw=2)
for xx,hh in [(2,2.8),(3.3,3.6),(4.6,2.7),(6,3.5),(7.4,2.9),(8.4,3.4)]:
    ax.plot([xx,xx],[1,hh],color="#477a45",lw=3)
    ax.add_patch(Circle((xx,hh),.38,color="#78a96b",alpha=.8))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((4.8,5.5),(5.4,3.6),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=15,color="#d97706",lw=2))
for start,end in [((5.4,3.6),(4.5,4.8)),((5.4,3.6),(6.4,4.7)),((4.5,4.8),(3.8,3.7))]:
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(start,end,arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=12,color="#1677b8",lw=1.5))
ax.text(5,.35,"Leaves, branches, stems",ha="center")

# double bounce
ax=axes[1,1]
ax.plot([1,9],[1,1],color="#2563eb",lw=5)
ax.plot([6,6],[1,4.6],color="#7c5b3f",lw=7)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((3.1,5.2),(5.8,1.2),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=15,color="#d97706",lw=2))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((5.8,1.2),(6,4.3),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=15,color="#d97706",lw=2))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((6,4.3),(3.3,5.4),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=15,color="#1677b8",lw=2))
ax.text(3.1,.35,"Water",ha="center"); ax.text(7.2,3.7,"Tree trunk / wall",ha="center")
fig.suptitle("Figure 2. Conceptual radar scattering mechanisms",fontsize=16,weight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()










Specular reflection
A smooth surface can reflect most incident energy away from the sensor. Calm open water therefore often appears dark in SAR imagery.


Diffuse or surface scattering
A rough surface redirects energy in many directions. Some energy returns to the sensor, often producing a stronger response than a smooth surface.


Volume scattering
Microwave energy interacts with components inside vegetation, such as leaves, branches, and stems. Multiple scattering events can contribute to the returned signal.


Double-bounce scattering
A signal can reflect between two approximately perpendicular surfaces, such as water and a vertical tree trunk or building wall. Flooded vegetation and some urban targets can therefore produce strong returns.
Important: These are simplified physical models. Real pixels often contain mixtures of scattering mechanisms.

title: SAR Fundamentals
section: SAR image geometry: range, azimuth, and incidence angle
text:
SAR image geometry: range, azimuth, and incidence angle
A side-looking SAR image has two principal image directions:

Range: across-track direction, approximately from near range to far range.
Azimuth: along-track direction, parallel to the satellite’s flight path.

The incidence angle is measured between the incoming radar beam and the surface normal (a line perpendicular to the local surface).


Code
# Figure 3: range/azimuth geometry
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12,6))
ax.set_xlim(0,12); ax.set_ylim(0,7); ax.axis("off")
ax.fill_between([0,12],[1.1,1.1],[0,0],color="#a6b77b")
ax.plot([0,12],[1.1,1.1],color="black",lw=2)
# satellite and orbit direction
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((1,5.4),1.6,.65,boxstyle="round,pad=.1",fc="#c7d5e8",ec="#23395d"))
ax.text(1.8,5.72,"Satellite",ha="center",va="center",weight="bold")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((.6,6.35),(3.2,6.35),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=16,lw=2,color="#1677b8"))
ax.text(1.9,6.55,"Flight direction (azimuth)",ha="center",color="#125b8b")
# radar beam and ground points
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((2.3,5.35),(7.5,1.2),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=17,lw=2.5,color="#d97706"))
ax.text(4.7,3.6,"Range direction",rotation=-38,color="#9a4d00")
ax.scatter([4.4,7.5,10.2],[1.1,1.1,1.1],s=70,c=["#3b82f6","#16a34a","#ef4444"])
ax.text(4.4,.55,"Near range",ha="center"); ax.text(7.5,.55,"Target",ha="center"); ax.text(10.2,.55,"Far range",ha="center")
# normal and angle
ax.plot([7.5,7.5],[1.1,4.0],ls="--",color="#555")
ax.text(7.7,3.1,"Surface normal",rotation=90,va="center")
ax.text(6.4,2.1,"Incidence angle θ",rotation=0,ha="center")
ax.set_title("Figure 3. SAR image geometry: range and azimuth",fontsize=15,weight="bold")
plt.show()

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
How synthetic aperture radar works
A satellite moves along its orbit while repeatedly transmitting pulses. A ground target is observed from multiple positions along the flight path. The processor combines the phase history of these echoes to focus the target in azimuth.
This is called a synthetic aperture: the motion of the platform is used to synthesize the effect of a much longer antenna.
The simplified diagram below shows a target being illuminated from several successive satellite positions.


Code
# Figure 4: synthetic aperture concept
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12,6))
ax.set_xlim(0,12); ax.set_ylim(0,7); ax.axis("off")
positions=[1.5,3.5,5.5,7.5,9.5]
for i,x in enumerate(positions):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x-.45,5.4),.9,.45,boxstyle="round,pad=.06",fc="#c7d5e8",ec="#23395d"))
    ax.text(x,5.62,f"P{i+1}",ha="center",va="center",fontsize=9)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x,5.35),(6,1.3),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=12,
                                 lw=1.3,color="#d97706",alpha=.75))
ax.scatter([6],[1.15],s=120,c="#dc2626",zorder=5)
ax.text(6,.55,"Same ground target",ha="center",weight="bold")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((1.2,6.25),(10,6.25),arrowstyle="-|>",mutation_scale=16,lw=2,color="#1677b8"))
ax.text(5.6,6.5,"Satellite motion along track",ha="center",color="#125b8b")
ax.text(6,3.3,"Echoes from multiple\npositions are combined\ncoherently by SAR processing",
        ha="center",va="center",bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=.5",fc="#f3f4f6",ec="#555"))
ax.set_title("Figure 4. Synthetic aperture: combining observations along the orbit",fontsize=15,weight="bold")
plt.show()

title: SAR Fundamentals
section: How a SAR image is organized
text:
How a SAR image is organized
A focused SAR image is a two-dimensional array. Its rows and columns correspond to azimuth and range samples (the exact orientation depends on the product convention and display).
A simplified image grid:


Code
# Figure 5: synthetic SAR image with range and azimuth axes
rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
h,w = 180,260
img = rng.normal(0.25,0.06,(h,w))
# create illustrative regions: water, fields, urban strip, vegetation
img[:, :55] *= .18
img[35:125, 65:150] += .16
img[20:160, 175:220] += .28
img[75:105, 220:255] += .08
img = np.clip(img,0,1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12,5))
ax.imshow(img,cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=.75,aspect="auto")
ax.set_xlabel("Range direction  →  (near range to far range)")
ax.set_ylabel("Azimuth direction  ↓  (along-track)")
ax.set_title("Figure 5. Example of a synthetic grayscale SAR-like image (not real satellite data)")
ax.text(25,18,"Dark water",color="white",ha="center",bbox=dict(fc="black",alpha=.55,ec="none"))
ax.text(108,55,"Agricultural fields",color="white",ha="center",bbox=dict(fc="black",alpha=.55,ec="none"))
ax.text(197,35,"Bright urban area",color="white",ha="center",bbox=dict(fc="black",alpha=.55,ec="none"))
plt.show()

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
SAR brightness and backscatter
A SAR display often uses grayscale intensity. Dark pixels generally represent lower returned power; bright pixels represent higher returned power. Brightness is not a unique land-cover label: the same surface type can look different as moisture, roughness, incidence angle, polarization, and geometry change.








Surface or target
Common interpretation
Important qualification




Calm open water
Often dark
Wind, waves, and nearby structures can brighten it


Bare soil
Variable gray
Strongly affected by roughness and moisture


Crops
Variable
Depends on crop growth stage, water, and polarization


Forest
Often moderate
Can be bright or dark depending on structure and wavelength


Buildings
Often bright
Orientation and shadowing matter


Flooded vegetation
Sometimes bright
Double-bounce can increase the return




Backscatter in decibels
For a calibrated backscatter coefficient (^0):
\[
\sigma^0_{dB}=10\log_{10}(\sigma^0)
\]
A negative dB value is normal. For example, a linear value of 0.01 becomes -20 dB.


Code
linear_backscatter = np.array([0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3])
db = 10 * np.log10(linear_backscatter)
for x, y in zip(linear_backscatter, db):
    print(f"σ⁰ = {x:0.3f}  ->  {y:6.2f} dB")


σ⁰ = 0.001  ->  -30.00 dB
σ⁰ = 0.003  ->  -25.23 dB
σ⁰ = 0.010  ->  -20.00 dB
σ⁰ = 0.030  ->  -15.23 dB
σ⁰ = 0.100  ->  -10.00 dB
σ⁰ = 0.300  ->   -5.23 dB




Code
# Figure 6: linear backscatter to dB conversion
x = np.logspace(-3,0,300)
y = 10*np.log10(x)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9,5))
ax.plot(x,y,lw=2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Linear backscatter coefficient (σ⁰)")
ax.set_ylabel("Backscatter (dB)")
ax.set_title("Figure 6. Conversion from linear backscatter to decibels")
ax.grid(True,alpha=.3)
plt.show()

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Wavelength and radar bands
The relationship between wavelength \(\lambda\), frequency \(f\), and the speed of light \(c\) is:
\[
\lambda = \frac{c}{f}
\]
Longer wavelengths generally interact with larger vegetation components and can penetrate farther into some vegetation canopies than shorter wavelengths. This is not a guarantee of penetration to the ground: canopy density, water content and structure all matter.

X-band

Wavelength: about 2.5–3.75 cm (often ~3 cm)
Frequency: 8–12 GHz
Penetration: very low — mainly canopy surface and fine roughness
Best for: high-resolution urban mapping, infrastructure, ships, ice/snow surfaces, damage assessment
Common satellites: TerraSAR-X, TanDEM-X, COSMO-SkyMed, ICEYE, Capella



C-band

Wavelength: about 3.75–7.5 cm (commonly ~5.6 cm)
Frequency: 4–8 GHz
Penetration: limited — upper canopy and agricultural soil moisture
Best for: agriculture, flood mapping, land cover, InSAR deformation, sea ice and oceans
Common satellites: Sentinel-1, RADARSAT-2, RADARSAT Constellation, Gaofen-3



L-band

Wavelength: about 15–30 cm (commonly ~23–24 cm)
Frequency: 1–2 GHz
Penetration: high — canopy volume, trunks, sometimes ground; dry soil and sand
Best for: forest biomass and structure, deformation under vegetation, soil moisture in vegetated areas
Common satellites: ALOS-2 (PALSAR-2), SAOCOM, NISAR (L-band); P-band (e.g. BIOMASS) penetrates even deeper



Comparison









Feature
X-band (~3 cm)
C-band (~6 cm)
L-band (~23 cm)




Penetration
Very low
Limited
High


Main interaction
Canopy surface
Upper canopy
Volume + ground


Resolution potential
Highest
High
Moderate


Sensitivity to biomass
Low
Moderate
High


Best environment
Urban, bare surface
Agriculture, floods
Forests, dense vegetation



Rule of thumb: see the surface clearly → X-band; all-rounder → C-band; look into or through vegetation → L-band.


Code
# Figure 7: approximate radar band wavelengths
bands = {"X band": 0.03, "C band": 0.056, "L band": 0.23, "P band": 0.70}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10,4.8))
names=list(bands.keys()); vals=list(bands.values())
bars=ax.bar(names,vals)
ax.set_ylabel("Approximate wavelength (m)")
ax.set_title("Figure 7. Approximate wavelengths of common SAR bands")
ax.grid(axis="y",alpha=.25)
for b,v in zip(bars,vals):
    ax.text(b.get_x()+b.get_width()/2,v+.015,f"{v*100:.1f} cm",ha="center")
plt.show()












Radar bands X, C and L: wavelength and penetration

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Polarization
Polarization describes the orientation of the transmitted and received electric field (VV, VH, HH, HV).



Radar polarization: VV, VH, HH and HV













Polarization
Transmit
Receive
Type
Main interaction
Typical appearance




VV
Vertical
Vertical
Co-polarized
Surface scattering (soil, water, roads)
Bright on smooth surfaces


HH
Horizontal
Horizontal
Co-polarized
Surface + double-bounce (buildings, trunks)
Bright on man-made structures


VH
Vertical
Horizontal
Cross-polarized
Volume scattering (vegetation, forests)
Brighter in forests and crops


HV
Horizontal
Vertical
Cross-polarized
Volume scattering (same as VH)
Similar to VH



Co-polarized channels (VV and HH) send and receive in the same orientation. They respond strongly to surface scattering; HH is especially sensitive to double-bounce.
Cross-polarized channels (VH and HV) send in one orientation and receive in the perpendicular orientation. Energy is rotated by multiple scattering in volumes, so forests and dense crops appear brighter.
Practical use: VV for soil moisture, water and agriculture; HH for urban structure; VH/HV for vegetation density. Many missions acquire dual or quad polarisation so these channels can be combined.

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Typical SAR image processing workflow
A Sentinel-1 workflow commonly includes the following steps. The exact sequence depends on the product, application, and software.

Select data: Choose acquisition dates, orbit direction, mode, and polarization.
Apply orbit information: Improve the satellite’s position and velocity metadata.
Remove thermal noise: Reduce instrument-related noise where appropriate.
Radiometric calibration: Convert digital measurements to a calibrated backscatter quantity such as (^0), (^0), or (^0).
Speckle filtering (optional): Reduce granular speckle while balancing detail preservation.
Terrain correction: Account for terrain-related geometric distortions using a DEM.
Geocoding: Place the image into a map coordinate reference system.
Convert to dB (often for display/analysis): Apply (10_{10}) to power backscatter.
Analyze: Classify water, monitor crops, estimate change, or study surface properties.

Important: Speckle filtering and dB conversion are not substitutes for radiometric calibration or terrain correction.


Code
# Figure 9: processing workflow
steps = [
    "Sentinel-1\nGRD / SLC",
    "Orbit\ninformation",
    "Thermal-noise\nremoval",
    "Radiometric\ncalibration",
    "Speckle\nfiltering*",
    "Terrain\ncorrection",
    "Geocoded\nbackscatter",
    "Analysis:\nflood / crops / change"
]
fig, ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(14,3.8))
ax.set_xlim(0,14); ax.set_ylim(0,3); ax.axis("off")
for i,s in enumerate(steps):
    x=.2+i*1.72

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Application: detecting floods with Sentinel-1
Open water often appears dark in SAR because a smooth water surface reflects much of the radar energy away from the sensor. A simple change-detection measure is:
\[
\Delta VV = VV_{flood} - VV_{pre-flood}
\]
A large negative change can indicate newly inundated smooth surfaces. But this is not a universal flood rule: flooded vegetation may brighten due to double-bounce scattering, and wind-roughened water may be bright.
A robust flood workflow should consider: - Pre-flood and flood-season images with comparable acquisition geometry. - VV and VH channels. - Permanent water masks. - Terrain and slope. - Vegetation and urban areas. - Temporal consistency and validation data.


Code
# Figure 10: illustrative pre-flood and flood images
rng=np.random.default_rng(8)
base=np.clip(rng.normal(.48,.10,(150,220)),0,1)
pre=base.copy()
# river channel
for r in range(150):
    c=int(35+0.35*r+12*np.sin(r/15))
    pre[r,max(0,c-7):min(220,c+7)] = .10
flood=base.copy()
for r in range(150):
    c=int(35+0.35*r+12*np.sin(r/15))
    flood[r,max(0,c-18):min(220,c+18)] = .08
# some bright flooded vegetation patches
flood[45:95,135:165] = np.clip(flood[45:95,135:165]+.28,0,1)

fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,3,figsize=(14,4.5))
axes[0].imshow(pre,cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=1); axes[0].set_title("Pre-flood (illustrative)")
axes[1].imshow(flood,cmap="gray",vmin=0,vmax=1); axes[1].set_title("Flood period (illustrative)")
change=flood-pre
im=axes[2].imshow(change,cmap="RdBu_r",vmin=-.6,vmax=.6); axes[2].set_title("Flood minus pre-flood")
for ax in axes: ax.axis("off")
fig.colorbar(im,ax=axes[2],fraction=.046,pad=.04,label="Illustrative intensity difference")
fig.suptitle("Figure 10. Conceptual SAR flood change example — simulated data, not Sentinel-1",fontsize=14,weight="bold")
plt.show()










Why flooded vegetation can be different
Open water may have low backscatter, but water beneath upright stems, trunks, or buildings can create double-bounce paths. The resulting return may be stronger than before flooding. This is why flood mapping in wetlands, mangroves, and crop fields should not rely exclusively on a single low-backscatter threshold.

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Quick knowledge check
Answer these questions after reviewing the notebook.

Why does calm open water often appear dark in a SAR image?
What is the difference between range and azimuth?
Why is SAR called a synthetic aperture?
What does a negative backscatter value in dB mean?
Why can flooded vegetation become brighter instead of darker?
What is the difference between VV and VH polarization?
Why is terrain correction important?


Suggested answers

Smooth water often reflects energy away from the antenna, producing a weak return.
Range is across-track; azimuth is along-track.
The platform’s motion allows the processor to combine echoes from multiple positions, synthesizing a longer aperture.
It means the linear backscatter coefficient is between zero and one; this is normal for many calibrated SAR measurements.
Double-bounce scattering between water and vertical vegetation structures can strengthen the return.
VV is vertical transmit/vertical receive; VH is vertical transmit/horizontal receive.
Terrain can distort the apparent location and shape of features; a DEM helps correct geometry and geolocate pixels.

text:
SAR in GeoLattice: geolattice.rsense.sar
GeoLattice puts its radar toolkit in geolattice.rsense.sar, which maps to the source package src/rsense/sar/. Import it as part of the remote-sensing namespace:
import geolattice.rsense as rs
from geolattice.rsense import sar          # or: from geolattice.rsense.sar import to_db, process_grd, ...
Install the SAR extras with the remote-sensing stack:
pip install "geolattice[rsense]"       # core raster + optical + SAR helpers
pip install "geolattice[rsense-all]"   # SAR, InSAR, lidar, UAV, ML/DL, viz, scaling
The package is organised around the jobs you actually do with radar data:







Job
What geolattice.rsense.sar provides




Read and calibrate
Sentinel-1 GRD/SLC helpers (process_grd, read_grd_subset, calibrate, to_db / from_db), RCM Level-1 readers, NISAR HDF5 readers


Clean the image
Speckle filters (boxcar, lee, refined_lee, gamma_map, multitemporal), multilooking, border-noise removal


Geometry
Incidence grids, terrain flattening / correction, layover–shadow masks, TOPS burst handling for InSAR prep


Polarimetry
Dual-pol features, H/A/α, Stokes, m-χ / m-δ, compact-pol conversion for RCM


Change and applications
Log-ratio and omnibus change, flood / rice / ship / oil-spill maps, dual-pol vegetation indices


Mission-specific
sentinel1, radarsat, nisar, plus ship detection with AIS matching

text:
Microwave bands, penetration and roughness
Longer wavelengths penetrate deeper into vegetation, dry soil and snow, and “see” surfaces as smoother. The Rayleigh criterion calls a surface smooth (mirror-like, dark) when its height variation is below λ / (8 cos θ).

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Imaging geometry
SAR looks sideways. Range (across-track) resolution comes from pulse bandwidth and is finer in ground range at steeper incidence; azimuth (along-track) resolution comes from synthesising a long antenna, ideally half the physical antenna length, independent of range.


Code
c = 299_792_458.0  # speed of light (m/s)
bw = 56.5e6                                   # Sentinel-1 IW range bandwidth (Hz), sub-swath IW1
slant_res = c / (2 * bw)  # slant-range resolution = c / (2 x bandwidth)
inc = np.array([30, 35, 40, 45])  # a range of incidence angles (degrees)
# ground-range resolution = slant-range resolution / sin(incidence)
pd.DataFrame({"incidence (°)": inc, "slant-range resolution (m)": round(slant_res, 2),
              "ground-range resolution (m)": (slant_res / np.sin(np.radians(inc))).round(2)})
