Because the image is built from distance to the sensor, terrain distorts it:

Foreshortening: slopes facing the radar are compressed (bright, narrow).
Layover: if a slope is steeper than the incidence angle, its top is closer to the radar than its foot and is imaged before it.
Shadow: slopes facing away, steeper than 90° − θ, receive no signal.

Let’s trace these along a real west-east profile across the Sierra Nevada escarpment, with the radar looking east (ascending pass) at 35°.


Code
# simulated scene (elevation, land cover) and the Landsat image of the same area
scene, optical = sim.study_area(fetch("landsat.tif"), fetch("dem_90m.tif"))
row = int(np.nanargmax(np.nanstd(scene.elevation.values, axis=1)))       # most rugged row
z = scene.elevation.isel(y=row).values.astype(float)  # elevation profile along that row
x = (scene.x.values - scene.x.values[0]).astype(float)  # distance from the first pixel along the row (m)
ok = np.isfinite(z); x, z = x[ok], z[ok]  # keep only valid elevations

# slant range, layover and shadow along a terrain profile for one incidence angle
def profile_geometry(x, z, theta_deg):
    th = np.radians(theta_deg)  # incidence angle in radians
    r = x * np.sin(th) - z * np.cos(th)          # slant-range coordinate (far-field)
    p = x * np.cos(th) + z * np.sin(th)          # constant along a beam line
    layover = np.r_[False, np.diff(r) < 0]  # layover where slant range decreases as ground distance increases
    # shadow where the terrain is hidden behind earlier terrain along the beam
    shadow = np.r_[False, p[1:] < np.maximum.accumulate(p)[:-1]]
    return r, layover, shadow  # return the three arrays

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 6.5))  # terrain (top) and slant range (bottom)
for th, ls in [(20, ":"), (35, "-"), (45, "--")]:  # three incidence angles, each with its own line style
    r, lay, sh = profile_geometry(x, z, th)  # geometry for this angle
    if th == 35:  # draw the terrain and its distortions only once, for 35 degrees
        axes[0].plot(x / 1000, z, "k-", lw=1)  # terrain profile
        axes[0].plot(x[lay] / 1000, z[lay], "r.", ms=4, label="layover")  # layover points in red
        axes[0].plot(x[sh] / 1000, z[sh], ".", color="grey", ms=4, label="shadow")  # shadow points in grey
    # slant range against ground distance, with the layover and shadow shares
    axes[1].plot(x / 1000, (r - r[0]) / 1000, ls, label=f"θ = {th}°: {lay.mean():.1%} layover, {sh.mean():.1%} shadow")
# labels and legend of the top panel
axes[0].set(ylabel="Elevation (m)", title="Real terrain profile (radar looking east, θ = 35°)"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].set(xlabel="Ground distance (km)", ylabel="Slant range (km)",  # labels of the bottom panel
            title="Where slant range decreases with ground distance, the image folds over (layover)")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # legend, arrange and draw









Steep incidence (20°) causes much more layover; shallow incidence (45°) causes more shadow. Sentinel-1 IW spans roughly 30-46°, a compromise. In mountains, combining ascending and descending passes (looking east and west) fills many gaps.

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Speckle
Each resolution cell holds many scatterers whose echoes add with random phases. Their sum is a random walk in the complex plane, so even a perfectly uniform field shows grainy brightness: amplitude follows a Rayleigh distribution and intensity an exponential distribution, with standard deviation equal to the mean. Speckle is therefore multiplicative, not additive noise.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # random generator with a fixed seed
N, pixels = 50, 200_000  # 50 scatterers per pixel, 200,000 pixels
# each pixel sums 50 echoes with random phase: fully developed speckle
field = (np.exp(1j * rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, (pixels, N))) / np.sqrt(N)).sum(1)
amp, inten = np.abs(field), np.abs(field) ** 2  # amplitude and intensity of the summed field

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.8))  # three panels
# the running sum of one pixel's echoes in the complex plane (a random walk)
axes[0].plot(np.cumsum(np.exp(1j * rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, N))).real,
             np.cumsum(np.exp(1j * rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, N))).imag, "-o", ms=2)
axes[0].set(title=f"Random walk of {N} scatterer echoes", aspect="equal")  # title and equal axes
axes[1].hist(amp, 100, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="simulated")  # histogram of the simulated amplitude
# compare with the theoretical Rayleigh distribution
a = np.linspace(0, 3.5, 200); axes[1].plot(a, stats.rayleigh(scale=np.sqrt(0.5)).pdf(a), "k", label="Rayleigh")
axes[1].set(title="Amplitude", xlabel="|E|"); axes[1].legend()  # labels and legend
axes[2].hist(inten, 100, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="simulated")  # histogram of the simulated intensity
# compare with the theoretical exponential distribution
i = np.linspace(0, 6, 200); axes[2].plot(i, stats.expon().pdf(i), "k", label="exponential")
# the ratio std/mean is 1 for single-look intensity
axes[2].set(title=f"Intensity (std/mean = {inten.std() / inten.mean():.2f})", xlabel="|E|²"); axes[2].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









Multilooking averages L independent looks, reducing the relative standard deviation to 1/√L. The averaged intensity follows a Gamma distribution, and the equivalent number of looks ENL = mean² / variance measured over a homogeneous area tells you how much speckle remains.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))  # one panel
x = np.linspace(0, 3, 300)  # normalised intensity axis
for L in [1, 4, 16]:  # average 1, 4 and 16 independent looks
    # group the pixels in sets of L and average each set
    looks = inten[: pixels // L * L].reshape(-1, L).mean(1)
    # histogram with the estimated equivalent number of looks (ENL)
    ax.hist(looks, 120, density=True, histtype="step", lw=1.5, label=f"L = {L}: ENL = {rs.sar.enl_estimate(looks):.1f}")
    ax.plot(x, stats.gamma(L, scale=1 / L).pdf(x), "k:", lw=1)  # theoretical gamma distribution for L looks
# labels
ax.set(xlim=(0, 3), xlabel="Normalised intensity", title="Multilooking narrows the distribution (dotted: Gamma pdf)")
ax.legend(); plt.show()  # legend and draw

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Real Sentinel-1 backscatter
This real VV image (20 m, already terrain-corrected and in dB) comes from the pyroSAR test data. SAR intensities span several orders of magnitude, so they are usually displayed in decibels, dB = 10·log10(σ⁰), but averaged and filtered in linear units: averaging dB values gives the geometric mean and biases results low.


Code
# real Sentinel-1 VV backscatter in dB, as a 2-D DataArray
db = rs.read(fetch("s1_vv_db.tif")).squeeze("band", drop=True)
db = db.where(db > -60)  # mask no-data values
lin = rs.sar.from_db(db)  # dB -> linear power
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(db, ax=axes[0], cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=0, title="VV (dB)")  # the image in dB
# the same image on a linear scale
rs.viz.plot_raster(lin, ax=axes[1], cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=0.3, title="VV (linear)")
# histogram of the dB values
axes[2].hist(db.values.ravel(), 100, color="C0"); axes[2].set(xlabel="dB", title="Histogram in dB")
for a in axes[:2]: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks on the two images
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
# averaging in dB is not the same as averaging linear power
print(f"Mean of dB values: {float(db.mean()):.2f} dB | dB of the linear mean: {float(rs.sar.to_db(lin.mean())):.2f} dB")









Mean of dB values: -12.12 dB | dB of the linear mean: -10.11 dB




Code
# ENL in the most homogeneous 15 × 15 window (lowest coefficient of variation)
w = 15  # window size (pixels)
best = (np.inf, None)  # (lowest coefficient of variation, position) found so far
L = lin.values  # linear backscatter as an array
for r in range(0, L.shape[0] - w, 5):  # slide the window every 5 rows ...
    for c in range(0, L.shape[1] - w, 5):  # ... and every 5 columns
        blk = L[r:r + w, c:c + w]  # the 15 x 15 block
        if np.isnan(blk).any():  # skip blocks with missing values
            continue
        cv = blk.std() / blk.mean()  # coefficient of variation of the block
        if cv < best[0]:  # keep the most homogeneous block
            best = (cv, (r, c))  # keep its CV and position
r, c = best[1]  # its top-left corner
# ENL of that block
print(f"Most homogeneous window at row {r}, col {c}: ENL = {rs.sar.enl_estimate(L[r:r + w, c:c + w]):.1f}")
# for comparison
print("Nominal ENL of Sentinel-1 IW GRDH: 4.4 (this product was further multilooked and resampled to 20 m)")

A simulated Sentinel-1 view of Long Valley
The simulator places a radar over the real terrain of Mono Lake, Long Valley caldera and the Sierra Nevada crest. Compare the optical image with simulated VV and VH, and see where geometry makes SAR unusable.

incidence = sim.incidence_grid(scene.elevation)                  # 30° (west) → 46° (east), looking east
# local incidence angle and layover and shadow masks from the DEM
local_inc, layover, shadow = sim.local_geometry(scene.elevation, incidence)
# simulated VV backscatter with speckle
vv = sim.speckle(sim.backscatter(scene.landcover, local_inc, "VV", incidence=incidence), seed=1)
# simulated VH backscatter with speckle
vh = sim.speckle(sim.backscatter(scene.landcover, local_inc, "VH", incidence=incidence), seed=2)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 10))  # 2 x 3 panels
# the real Landsat image in colour infrared
rs.viz.plot_rgb(optical, ["nir", "red", "green"], ax=axes[0, 0], title="Landsat colour infrared (real)")
# the land-cover classes the simulation uses
rs.viz.plot_raster(scene.landcover.where(scene.landcover > 0), ax=axes[0, 1], title="Land cover (from Landsat)",
                   categorical={1: ("Water", "#2166ac"), 2: ("Forest", "#1b7837"), 3: ("Shrub/grass", "#a6d96a"),
                                4: ("Bare/rock", "#bababa")})
# local incidence angle
rs.viz.plot_raster(local_inc, ax=axes[0, 2], cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=0, vmax=90, title="Local incidence angle (°)")
# simulated VV in dB
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.sar.to_db(vv), ax=axes[1, 0], cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=0, title="Simulated VV (dB)")
# simulated VH in dB
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.sar.to_db(vh), ax=axes[1, 1], cmap="gray", vmin=-32, vmax=-8, title="Simulated VH (dB)")
# 0 = usable, 1 = layover, 2 = shadow
geo = (layover.astype(int) + 2 * shadow.astype(int)).where(scene.landcover > 0)
rs.viz.plot_raster(geo, ax=axes[1, 2], title="Geometric distortion",  # geometric distortion map
                   categorical={0: ("usable", "#f0f0f0"), 1: ("layover", "#d7191c"), 2: ("shadow", "#2c7bb6")})
for a in axes.ravel(): a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
# share of layover and shadow pixels
print(f"Layover: {float(layover.mean()):.2%} of pixels, shadow: {float(shadow.mean()):.2%}")









Layover: 0.41% of pixels, shadow: 0.01%


Slopes facing the radar (west-facing) are bright and compressed; lakes are black; forest stands out in VH because volume scattering depolarises the signal. Geometry, not land cover, dominates the brightness in the mountains, which is why terrain correction (see the Sentinel-1 GRD notebook) comes first.

title: SAR Fundamentals
text:
Summary, exercises and references
Key points

Wavelength controls penetration and apparent roughness (Rayleigh criterion).
SAR images are formed in slant range; terrain causes foreshortening, layover and shadow.
Brightness reflects scattering mechanism, geometry and moisture; VH highlights volume scattering.
Speckle is multiplicative; ENL measures it; filter and average in linear units, display in dB.
geolattice.rsense.sar (src/rsense/sar) covers Sentinel-1, RCM and NISAR processing, speckle, polarimetry, change detection and applications.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.read, rs.sar.to_db/from_db, rs.sar.enl_estimate, rs.viz.plot_raster, rs.lidar.slope/aspect (inside the simulator); geolattice.rsense.sar.sentinel1’s read_geolocation_grid, read_platform_heading and load_rtc; geolattice.rsense.get_images’s search_images and get_images.
Exercises

Recompute the profile in the Imaging geometry section for a radar looking west (descending). Which slopes now suffer layover?
Change the simulator’s incidence range to 20-30° and compare layover and shadow fractions.
Estimate ENL in three homogeneous windows of the real image and explain any differences.
Using the Rayleigh criterion, at what wavelength would a 2 cm-rough field look smooth at 40°?
From the src/rsense/sar module table, name the submodule you would use for (a) refined Lee filtering, (b) RCM compact-pol m-χ, and (c) NISAR GCOV indices.
In the visual walkthrough, explain why calm open water is dark in SAR while flooded vegetation can be bright.

Core concepts

Learning objectives

Select scenes with one product type, orbit direction, relative orbit, mode, and polarisation, and a temporal baseline that fits the application.
Apply the GRD chain from precise orbits and noise removal through calibration, speckle filtering, terrain correction, and conversion to dB.
Coregister a GRD time series, apply a multitemporal speckle filter, and compute temporal features in linear units.
Prepare IW SLC data with TOPSAR-Split, an orbit file, back-geocoding, and enhanced spectral diversity.
Explain how DInSAR removes topographic phase, and how coherence, SBAS, and persistent scatterers use a stack differently.
Outline dual-pol decomposition, the EW sea-ice workflow, ship detection, and Level-2 ocean products.
Match a monitoring goal to a product and workflow, and name the GeoLattice functions for search, GRD preprocessing, RTC, and interferograms.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
Before processing: selecting scenes

Pick the product type

GRD (Ground Range Detected): Provides backscatter intensity data, useful for general land cover classification, crop mapping, flood detection, and ship/oil spill monitoring. It contains magnitude information only, not phase.
SLC (Single Look Complex): Contains both amplitude and phase information, required for applications like interferometry (InSAR for surface deformation), coherence analysis (change or stability detection), and advanced polarimetric decompositions. SLCs have finer spatial detail but require more complex processing, larger storage, and precise co-registration.

Keep geometry consistent

Orbit direction: Use only ascending or only descending orbit scenes for a time series to ensure consistent viewing geometry. Mixing can cause undesirable geometry-related differences in backscatter.
Relative orbit (track): Use the same relative orbit number (track) when building multi-date stacks or time series, as this guarantees a nearly identical ground swath.
Acquisition mode: Use the same imaging mode. Interferometric Wide (IW) mode is standard for land; Extra Wide (EW) for sea ice; Stripmap (SM) for some specific sites.
Frame/Burst alignment (for SLC): For InSAR processing, ensure the scenes have the same burst/frame coverage and length to avoid edge artifacts or missing areas.

Check polarization:

VV+VH (vertical transmit/vertical receive + vertical transmit/horizontal receive): Most common dual-pol for land surfaces, offering more information for crop types and land cover.
HH+HV (horizontal transmit/horizontal receive + horizontal transmit/vertical receive): Used mainly in polar or maritime regions, sensitive to sea ice and ocean phenomena.
Choose scenes with the same polarization(s) to facilitate comparison and stacking.

Check temporal baseline:

Coherence and InSAR applications: Select pairs with the shortest possible time interval (6 or 12 days for Sentinel-1, depending on location and date). Shorter baselines minimize surface changes that corrupt interferometric phase and maximize the likelihood of high coherence.
Time series analysis: Consistent and regular revisit intervals improve quality and robustness of temporal statistics/results.

Download precise orbit files (POEORB):

These files contain high-precision satellite position data, essential for accurate geocoding and InSAR. They are made available about 20 days after data acquisition.
For near-real-time applications, use restituted orbits (RESORB), which are less accurate but available within hours. For any scientific or mapping application, always rerun processing with POEORB as soon as they are published.

Get a DEM (Digital Elevation Model):

A DEM is required for terrain correction and interferometric processing. The Copernicus DEM (GLO-30, 30m resolution) is currently the global standard, offering high accuracy and seamless coverage. It is freely available and recommended.
SRTM 1 arc-second (30m): Also works well for many areas, especially between latitudes 60°N and 56°S. For the best results in mountainous or non-SRTM regions, use GLO-30 or, if available, local high-resolution DEMs.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
GRD Backscatter Workflow (σ⁰ or γ⁰)
This workflow outlines the main steps needed to process Sentinel-1 GRD (Ground Range Detected) data in order to generate backscatter images. Backscatter (σ⁰ or γ⁰) gives information about how much of the radar signal is reflected from the ground back to the satellite, which is crucial for many land applications.
The process begins by reading the raw radar data and applying precise satellite position corrections. Next, it removes different types of noise, including instrument (thermal) noise and unwanted border artifacts. Afterward, the data is calibrated to turn raw digital numbers into physically meaningful backscatter values (σ⁰ or β⁰).
In areas with hills or mountains, terrain-flattening optionally adjusts for the effects of slope on the radar signal, producing γ⁰ backscatter that is normalized to local ground surface. To improve image quality, a speckle filter is applied to reduce radar “graininess” without losing important detail.
Terrain correction then geocodes the image, aligning it with a real-world map projection and using a digital elevation model (DEM) to account for topography. Finally, the backscatter data is converted into decibel (dB) scale for easier interpretation and analysis, and subsets can be made for the area of interest.
This workflow ensures that the resulting images accurately reflect surface properties, are spatially consistent, and are ready for further analysis in GIS or remote sensing studies.
Used for: land cover, crop mapping, soil moisture, forest monitoring, flood mapping.








Step
SNAP operator
Purpose and Mathematical Details




1
Read
Load the GRD .SAFE or .zip file, this contains the observed radar intensity data in Digital Numbers (DN) for each pixel.


2
Apply-Orbit-File
Refine the satellite’s known position by applying precise orbit corrections, to improve geolocation (coordinate mapping of radar returns).


3
ThermalNoiseRemoval
Remove additive instrument noise from the image, especially affecting cross-polarization (VH), typically by subtracting a noise floor estimated from calibration. If \(I_{\text{raw}}\) is the raw intensity and \(N\) is the thermal noise, then \(I_{\text{clean}} = I_{\text{raw}} - N\).


4
Remove-GRD-Border-Noise
Mask out low-intensity scenes and artifacts typically present at the scene edges after focusing, often by thresholding the pixel intensity.


5
Calibration
Convert DN to backscatter coefficient (\(\sigma^0\) or \(\beta^0\)). If \(DN\) is the digital number and \(CF\) is the calibration factor, \(\beta^0 = DN^2 \times CF\). \(\sigma^0\) is normalized radar cross section per unit ground area. Calibration ensures results can be physically interpreted and compared across scenes.


6
Terrain-Flattening (optional)
In hilly terrain, radar backscatter is affected by local slope. Convert \(\beta^0\) to \(\gamma^0\) to correct for this: \(\gamma^0 = \frac{\beta^0}{\cos \theta_{local}}\), where \(\theta_{local}\) is the local incidence angle (angle between radar and terrain normal). This produces estimates of radar backscatter as if the surface were flat, reducing topographic effects.


7
Speckle-Filter
Apply spatial filters (e.g., Refined Lee, Lee Sigma, Gamma-MAP) to reduce speckle noise, which is multiplicative. For example, the Lee filter’s output at a pixel is: \(I_{\text{filt}} = W \cdot I_{\text{mean}} + (1-W) \cdot I_{\text{orig}}\), where \(W\) is a weighting function based on local mean and variance, and \(I_{\text{orig}}\) is the original intensity.


8
Terrain-Correction
Geocode the raster, mapping radar image coordinates to map grid coordinates (e.g. UTM/WGS84) using a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) and Range-Doppler method, with pixel values resampled to a consistent ground resolution (typically 10 m). This ensures each pixel covers an equal-sized area on the ground.


9
LinearToFromdB
Convert the calibrated linear backscatter to decibel (dB) scale for analysis by \([\text{dB}] = 10 \times \log_{10}(\sigma^0)\), where \(\sigma^0\) is the backscatter coefficient. The dB scale emphasizes relative differences and compresses dynamic range.


10
Subset / Write
Clip the image (spatial subset) to the Area of Interest (AOI) and export data layers as GeoTIFF for mapping and GIS analysis.



Notes - For terrain flattening, always calibrate to \(\beta^0\) (not \(\sigma^0\)), since \(\beta^0\) is the radar reflectivity per slant range pixel, and only then apply the terrain-flattening correction to obtain \(\gamma^0\) for slope normalization. - If multitemporal speckle filtering will be done later, skip single-date speckle filters here, multitemporal approaches reduce noise while preserving temporal signal. - For all mathematical operations (averaging, composing, ratios, e.g. \(r = \frac{VH}{VV}\)), use the linear (not dB) backscatter values throughout the workflow. Only convert to dB after all calculations to avoid bias, since \(10\log_{10}(\text{mean}(x)) \neq \text{mean}(10\log_{10}(x))\). - Statistical and band derivations after terrain correction (e.g., band ratio \(VH/VV\) or Radar Vegetation Index \(RVI = \frac{4 \cdot VH}{VV + VH}\)) should be computed using the linear backscatter values (not dB).

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
Multitemporal GRD time series workflow
Used for: crop phenology, rice mapping, change detection, and deforestation monitoring using multi-temporal Sentinel-1 GRD data.
Multitemporal GRD analysis leverages the temporal dimension to investigate surface change and seasonal dynamics. Each step is critical to ensuring spatial and radiometric consistency throughout the time series, enabling reliable extraction of temporal features per pixel.

Run steps 1 to 5 of the GRD workflow on each scene:

Steps include: reading data, applying precise orbit files, removing thermal noise, masking border noise, and calibrating to backscatter coefficients (β⁰ or σ⁰) for each image.

All images should be from the same acquisition geometry (same Sentinel-1 satellite, track, frame, and orbit direction) to ensure spatial alignment and comparable incidence angles.

Coregister the stack:

Temporal co-registration ensures all images align perfectly at the pixel level over the time series.

Use SNAP CreateStack operator for precise co-registration of all scenes (can also terrain-correct each image to the same projected grid, which is often sufficient for land cover analysis).

Apply multitemporal speckle filtering:

Use SNAP’s Multi-Temporal-Speckle-Filter (e.g., Quegan filter) to reduce speckle while preserving both spatial structures and the temporal signature in each pixel.

Multitemporal filters outperform single-image filters by averaging over time, assuming temporal consistency of underlying signals.

Terrain correction on common grid:

Apply terrain correction to all images so they are geocoded to a consistent map grid (such as UTM), using a DEM (e.g., Copernicus GLO-30).

This step compensates for geometric distortions due to topography and ensures that multi-date stacking and later spatial analysis are reliable.

Convert to dB:

Transform the calibrated, terrain-corrected backscatter from linear power (\(\sigma^0\) or \(\gamma^0\)) to decibel scale: [dB] \(= 10 \log_{10}(\sigma^0)\) per pixel.

dB values are easier to interpret for change detection, providing an intuitive measure of relative differences.

Build a data cube:

Stack all the processed images into a multi-temporal data cube, such as an xarray.DataArray, where the time dimension indexes dates of acquisition and spatial dimensions cover the Area of Interest.

This enables pixelwise analysis across time and facilitates downstream feature extraction and modeling.

Extract temporal features per pixel:

Calculate statistics such as mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and percentiles for each pixel across the time axis.

Application-specific features include, for example, the date of minimum VH (useful for rice transplanting/flood detection), amplitude of seasonal change, and the speed or slope of temporal backscatter increase.

Optional smoothing:

To further reduce residual noise in the temporal signal, apply temporal smoothing filters (e.g., Savitzky-Golay filter or a running mean) to each pixel’s time series.

This is especially useful before extracting features sensitive to noise, such as change point detection.

Classification or modeling:

Use the extracted temporal features as input variables for land cover classification or change detection models.

Common algorithms include Random Forest, XGBoost, or, for time series sequence modeling, deep learning approaches like LSTM or Transformer architectures.

Validation:

Assess the accuracy of classification or change maps using ground truth from field surveys, agricultural records, or high-resolution reference imagery.


Rice mapping tip:
- Rice transplanting causes a sudden decline in VH backscatter (flooded, bare soil; often below −20 dB), followed by a progressive increase as plants grow and scatter more radar energy. Detecting this sharp VH minimum and subsequent rise is a robust temporal indicator for paddy rice phenology.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
section: SLC preprocessing (common steps for all phase-based work)
text:
SLC preprocessing (common steps for all phase-based work)
Sentinel-1 IW SLC (Single Look Complex) data are divided into 3 subswaths (IW1, IW2, IW3), and each subswath contains about 9 bursts. Each burst is an individual segment of data acquired in time and must be handled separately to avoid introducing artifacts, especially in phase analysis (e.g., for InSAR).

SLC Preprocessing Steps









Step
SNAP operator
Purpose
Mathematical/Technical Explanation




1
TOPSAR-Split
Select subswath(s), polarization(s), and only the bursts covering your AOI (area of interest)
Isolates subsets of data: If \(S(t, s)\) is the signal as a function of time \(t\) and subswath \(s\), this step selects \(S(t, s_{\mathrm{desired}})\) and spatially subsets by burst to your AOI.


2
Apply-Orbit-File
Applies precise orbital information
The satellite’s actual position and velocity can be denoted by \(\vec{r}(t), \vec{v}(t)\). This step refines the navigation metadata so pixel geolocation produces correct phase and amplitude geometry, reducing errors \(\Delta \vec{r}\) introduced by the predicted orbit. Accurate orbits are crucial because any orbital error \(\delta \vec{r}\) leads to phase errors \(\Delta \phi \approx -\frac{4\pi}{\lambda} (\delta \vec{r} \cdot \hat{l})\) where \(\lambda\) is radar wavelength and \(\hat{l}\) is the look vector.


3
Back-Geocoding
Coregisters secondary (slave) image to reference (master) using precise orbits and a DEM (Digital Elevation Model)
Each SLC pixel in the reference image has coordinates \((x^{(ref)}_i, y^{(ref)}_i)\); the secondary needs to be resampled so corresponding pixels align spatially. Formally, find a mapping \(T\) such that \((x^{(slave)}_j, y^{(slave)}_j) \to (x^{(ref)}_i, y^{(ref)}_i)\). Back-geocoding thus matches each pixel in the slave to the reference, correcting for geometry and topography to minimize spatial misalignment, which is critical for consistent phase comparison.


4
Enhanced-Spectral-Diversity (ESD)
Fine azimuth (along-track) coregistration; essential for TOPS to avoid phase jumps at burst boundaries
TOPS mode SLCs are acquired by rotating the beam during acquisition, which can create phase discontinuities at burst edges if bursts are not precisely aligned. Spectral diversity uses the overlap regions between bursts to estimate and correct small coregistration errors. The phase correction, \(\phi_{\text{corr}}\), is estimated using the difference between overlapping burst spectra, minimizing phase discontinuities by adjusting the azimuth alignment, i.e., \(\phi_{\text{ESD}} = \arg \left ( \sum_{k} S_1(k) S_2^*(k) \right )\), where \(S_1(k)\) and \(S_2(k)\) are the Fourier components in the overlap and \(^*\) denotes complex conjugation.



After these 4 preprocessing steps (TOPSAR-Split, Apply-Orbit-File, Back-Geocoding, and ESD), the coregistered SLCs are ready for advanced SAR processing, such as interferometry (measuring displacement/deformation from phase \(\phi\)), coherence (computing temporal or spatial correlation), or polarimetry (analyzing scattering mechanisms by different polarizations).

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
section: Differential InSAR (DInSAR) Workflow: DInSAR vs. InSAR
text:
Differential InSAR (DInSAR) Workflow: DInSAR vs. InSAR
What is DInSAR and how does it differ from conventional InSAR?

InSAR (Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar): Uses the phase difference \(\Delta\phi\) between two Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images acquired from slightly different viewpoints (typically a short time apart, or in a “single-pass” configuration) to map topography. This “topographic phase” encodes the surface elevation.
DInSAR (Differential InSAR): Measures surface deformation over time by comparing two SAR images acquired at different times (from slightly different orbital positions). DInSAR removes the constant topographic phase (using a DEM or a third SAR acquisition, see below), so the remaining phase reflects only surface movement (deformation), atmospheric delays, and noise.

Key difference:
- InSAR measures topography; DInSAR measures temporal ground motion by removing topographic contribution.
Mathematical details
The observed interferometric phase at a pixel can be modeled as:
\(\displaystyle \phi_{\text{total}} = \phi_{\text{flat}} + \phi_{\text{topo}} + \phi_{\text{disp}} + \phi_{\text{atm}} + \phi_{\text{noise}}\)
where: - \(\phi_{\text{flat}}\): flat-earth phase (due to imaging geometry) - \(\phi_{\text{topo}}\): phase due to surface elevation (topography) - \(\phi_{\text{disp}}\): phase due to displacement (the signal DInSAR seeks) - \(\phi_{\text{atm}}\): phase delays from atmosphere - \(\phi_{\text{noise}}\): decorrelation and noise
In conventional InSAR, the primary outcome is \(\phi_{\text{topo}}\) (topography).
In DInSAR, we wish to compute \(\phi_{\text{disp}}\) (displacement), which requires removing both \(\phi_{\text{flat}}\) and \(\phi_{\text{topo}}\) (using accurate orbits and a DEM).
The line-of-sight (LOS) displacement \(d_{\text{LOS}}\) is related to unwrapped phase as:
\(\displaystyle d_{\text{LOS}} = -\frac{\lambda}{4\pi} \, \phi_{\text{unwrapped}}\)
where: - \(\lambda\) is the radar wavelength (here, \(\approx 5.55 \,\text{cm}\) for Sentinel-1), - \(\phi_{\text{unwrapped}}\) is the phase after flattening, topography removal, and phase unwrapping.
Example: For Sentinel-1, one full fringe (phase cycle of \(2\pi\)) corresponds to \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\), so \(\approx 2.8\) cm of LOS motion.
DInSAR Workflow Steps with Explanations








Step
SNAP operator
Mathematical/Technical Purpose




1 to 4
(SLC preprocessing)
See earlier: split SLC, orbit refinement, coregistration, spectral diversity to align images and ensure pixel correspondence. (Math: aligns \(S_1(x, y)\) to \(S_2(x, y)\) for pixelwise phase difference).


5
Interferogram
Compute complex interferogram: \(I = S_{\mathrm{ref}} \cdot S^{*}_{\mathrm{sec}}\); phase \(\phi = \arg(I)\). Remove \(\phi_{\text{flat}}\) for proper phase referencing; compute coherence as \(|\langle S_{\mathrm{ref}} S^{*}_{\mathrm{sec}}\rangle|/(\sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}\sigma_{\mathrm{sec}})\) to assess reliability.


6
TOPSAR-Deburst
Combine individual bursts into a continuous SLC grid (needed for Sentinel-1 IW mode, preserves phase consistency across bursts).


7
TOPSAR-Merge (if needed)
Mosaic subswaths if AOI spans multiple sub-images.


8
TopoPhaseRemoval
Subtract computed topographic phase \(\phi_{\text{topo}}\) using a DEM and precise baseline; isolates \(\phi_{\text{disp}}\).


9
Multilook
Spatial averaging to reduce speckle and yield near-square pixels (e.g., \(4 \times 1\) looks combines pixels in range and azimuth).


10
Goldstein-Phase-Filtering
Apply adaptive filtering to smooth random phase noise while preserving deformation signals.


11
SNAPHU export → unwrapping → import
“Unwrap” phase so \(\phi \in \mathbb{R}\), not just \([-\pi, \pi]\). (Mathematically, integrate phase jumps to reconstruct continuous phase field.)


12
Phase-To-Displacement
Apply \(d_{\text{LOS}} = -(\lambda/4\pi)\phi_{\text{unwrapped}}\) to convert phase into meters of surface motion.


13
Terrain-Correction
Map output to geographic coordinates (orthorectification).



Quality checks and best practices - Coherence masking: Exclude pixels with low coherence (typically $<$0.3), as noisy or rapidly changing ground conditions cause decorrelation. - Baseline control: Use pairs with low perpendicular baseline to reduce spatial decorrelation and minimize topographic errors. - Atmospheric effects: Compare phase with topography and/or meteorological data to spot and correct for stratified atmospheric delays. - Multi-track processing: To resolve 2D or 3D motion, combine DInSAR from ascending/descending passes; invert for up-/east-/north-components.
Summary Table, InSAR vs. DInSAR:
| | InSAR | DInSAR | |–|——-|——–| | Main Output | Surface elevation (DEM) | Surface deformation (displacement map) | | Removes topography? | No | Yes, using DEM or 3-image stack | | Key Math | \(\phi \approx \phi_{\text{flat}} + \phi_{\text{topo}}\) | \(\phi_{\text{disp}} = \phi - \phi_{\text{flat}} - \phi_{\text{topo}}\) | | Typical application | DEM generation | Monitoring earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides, urban subsidence |
References:
- Massonnet & Feigl, “Radar interferometry and its application to changes in the Earth’s surface,” Rev. Geophys., 1998.
- ESA Sentinel-1 InSAR Guide.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
Interferometric Coherence Workflow
Interferometric coherence is a measure of how similar two radar images (SLCs, or Single Look Complex data) are when observed at two different times. It quantifies, on a pixel-by-pixel basis, the degree to which ground features remain unchanged (“correlated”) versus altered between the two acquisitions.
The coherence workflow typically involves preparing the SLC data (splitting bursts, aligning the images, correcting orbits), then computing the local similarity using a mathematical formula that compares the two radar signals over a small neighborhood or moving window. This results in a new image showing, for each pixel, how stable or reliable the radar signal is between the two dates, a value from 0 (completely different, very unstable or changed ground) to 1 (identical, extremely stable).
Coherence maps are crucial for applications such as change detection, damage assessment after disasters, monitoring subsidence, or even tracking agricultural activity, because areas that experience change (like plowed soil, flooded fields, or collapsed buildings) will show a marked drop in coherence, while unchanged ground remains highly coherent.
Applications: Crop harvesting and tillage detection, urban mapping, flood extent in built-up areas, earthquake damage mapping, and more.
The interferometric coherence \(\gamma\) quantifies the similarity (correlation) between two complex SAR images (typically Single Look Complex, SLCs) acquired at different times. Coherence is computed as:
\[
\gamma = \frac{|\langle S_{\text{ref}} S^*_{\text{sec}} \rangle|}{\sqrt{ \langle |S_{\text{ref}}|^2 \rangle \langle |S_{\text{sec}}|^2 \rangle }}
\]
where: - \(S_{\text{ref}}\) is the reference complex SAR image, - \(S_{\text{sec}}\) is the secondary image, - \(S^*_{\text{sec}}\) is the complex conjugate of the secondary image, - \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) denotes spatial averaging over a moving window (e.g., 10 pixels in range × 3 pixels in azimuth).
The denominator normalizes the correlation (so that \(0 \leq \gamma \leq 1\)): - \(\gamma=1\) indicates perfect correlation (no change, very stable scatterers). - \(\gamma=0\) indicates complete decorrelation (temporal, volume, or geometric change).
Step-by-step workflow:

SLC preprocessing: Split subswaths, apply precise orbits, perform back-geocoding, and (with Sentinel-1 IW data) Enhanced Spectral Diversity (ESD) to align the images and ensure pixel correspondence. Mathematically, this ensures that \(S_{\text{ref}}(x, y)\) and \(S_{\text{sec}}(x, y)\) represent the same ground location.
Coherence operator: Calculate \(\gamma\) for each pixel using a moving window (typically \(10 \times 3\) pixels) as above. Spatial averaging both improves the stability of \(\gamma\) and mitigates speckle noise, but at a loss of spatial detail.
TOPSAR-Deburst: For Sentinel-1 IW, SLC data are collected in bursts; de-bursting stacks them together, ensuring continuity of phase and coherence across burst boundaries.
TOPSAR-Merge (if applicable): If the Area of Interest (AOI) spans multiple sub-swaths, these are mosaicked into one continuous image.
Multilook (optional): Further spatial averaging (“looks”) can be applied to reduce speckle and improve radiometric quality. Mathematically, multilooking performs local averaging of both amplitude and phase, which reduces the variance of the coherence estimate while degrading resolution.
Terrain Correction: The resulting coherence (and other SAR products) are geocoded via orthorectification, mapping image coordinates to map coordinates using a DEM and the satellite’s geometry.
Build coherence time series: By pairing consecutive SLC scenes (e.g., 6 or 12 days apart for Sentinel-1), and repeating the above, a time series \(\gamma(t)\) can be assembled for each pixel/patch. Time variations in \(\gamma\) can then be interpreted for land cover change, agricultural practices, surface stability, or post-disaster damage.

Physical interpretation: - \(\gamma \approx 1\): Very stable scatterers (e.g., buildings, rocks), little or no phase change. - \(\gamma \ll 1\): Significant decorrelation due to rapid ground cover change (e.g., vegetation growth, plowing, flooding, snow, or urban destruction).
Practical note: A sharp drop in coherence over urban/built-up regions after an earthquake often indicates structural damage, as randomization of scatterers causes decorrelation.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
InSAR Time Series (SBAS and PS-InSAR)
Purpose: Detect and quantify long-term surface motions (e.g., subsidence from groundwater withdrawal, mining, or infrastructure shifts) with millimeter-per-year (mm/yr) accuracy.
Data Requirement: At least 20 Sentinel-1 SLC (Single Look Complex) scenes acquired from the same satellite track, spanning a year or longer. These images provide phase information essential for temporal analysis.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
SBAS (Small Baseline Subset) Method
The SBAS method is a popular InSAR (Interferometric SAR) time series technique designed to track slow, long-term ground movements, such as subsidence, uplift, or landslide, with high accuracy. It works by carefully selecting pairs of radar images that are close together in both acquisition time and satellite position (“small baselines”), which helps to minimize errors from atmospheric variations and differences in imaging geometry. By analyzing a large set of these tightly spaced interferograms over time, SBAS can create displacement time-series for every pixel, helping scientists monitor ground deformation at millimeter precision over years.
1. Download SLC Data: Obtain \(N\) SLC images \(\{S_1, S_2, \dots, S_N\}\) and the corresponding precise orbit ephemerides.
2. Coregistration: All SLCs are geometrically aligned (coregistered) to a common reference date (say, \(S_{ref}\)) so that pixels correspond spatially: \(S_k(x, y)\) aligns to ground location \((x, y)\) across all \(k\).
3. Interferogram Network Construction:
Form a set of interferometric pairs \((i, j)\) such that both their temporal baseline \(\Delta T_{ij}\) and perpendicular spatial baseline \(\Delta B_\perp^{ij}\) are below chosen thresholds. The network is typically sparse to avoid large decorrelation.
4. Interferogram Generation & Unwrapping:
For each selected \((i, j)\): - Compute the wrapped phase difference: \[
  \phi_{ij}(\mathbf{r}) = \arg\left[ S_i(\mathbf{r}) S_j^*(\mathbf{r}) \right]
  \] where \(*\) denotes complex conjugate. - Apply filtering and unwrap phases in space to obtain \(\tilde{\phi}_{ij}(\mathbf{r})\).
5. Network Inversion for Displacement:
For a stack of \(N\) images, each interferogram measures relative phase changes: \[
  \tilde{\phi}_{ij} (\mathbf{r}) = \phi_j(\mathbf{r}) - \phi_i(\mathbf{r}) + \delta_{ij}(\mathbf{r})
  \] where \(\delta_{ij}\) encompasses atmospheric, orbital, and noise contributions. Solve the system of equations (one per interferogram) for the phase (displacement) at each acquisition, often via least-squares or singular value decomposition (SVD) inversion. The phase is related to displacement as: \[
  d_k(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\lambda}{4\pi} \, \phi_k(\mathbf{r})
  \] where \(\lambda\) is the radar wavelength.
6. Atmospheric Delay Correction:
Remove atmospheric artifacts by estimating \(\delta_{ij}\) (with external models, e.g. GACOS or ERA5, or spatial filtering).
7. DEM Error Correction:
The measured phase comprises a DEM error term; estimate a constant DEM offset for each pixel or scene and subtract it.
8. Velocity and Displacement Time Series:
The per-date displacement estimates \(d_k(\mathbf{r})\) yield a time series for every ground pixel; from the linear fit, estimate velocity: \[
  v(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{d_{N}(\mathbf{r}) - d_1(\mathbf{r})}{T_{N} - T_1}
  \] where \(T_k\) is the time of scene \(k\).
9. Reference Point Calibration:
Remove residual phase bias by “zeroing” the displacement to a non-moving reference pixel or calibrate against a GNSS station.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
Persistent Scatterer (PS) InSAR
PS-InSAR stands for “Persistent Scatterer Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar.” It’s an advanced technique that uses a stack of SAR images to precisely measure ground movement at individual, stable point scatterers (such as buildings, rocks, or other objects that remain consistent over time) with millimeter accuracy.
The method works by analyzing changes in the phase of reflected radar signals across many satellite passes, focusing only on those locations (“persistent scatterers”) that behave very consistently over time. By looking at these stable reflection points, PS-InSAR can filter out much of the noise and atmospheric effects that limit conventional InSAR, allowing for long-term ground deformation time series, even in areas with lots of vegetation or urban development.

Coregistration: All Single Look Complex (SLC) images \(S_k\) (\(k=1\dots N\)) are coregistered to a common reference scene \(S_{ref}\), so that pixels correspond spatially across the stack: \(S_k(x, y)\) refers to the same ground location \((x, y)\) in all scenes.
Forming Interferograms with a Common Reference: For each subsequent SLC image \(S_k\) (\(k \neq ref\)), form the interferogram with respect to the reference: \[
I_k(\mathbf{r}) = S_k(\mathbf{r}) S_{ref}^*(\mathbf{r})
\] where \(\mathbf{r}\) denotes pixel location, and \(^*\) denotes the complex conjugate. This yields \(N - 1\) interferograms, all referenced to the same epoch.
Selection of Persistent Scatterers: For each pixel, compute the amplitude dispersion index: \[
D_{amp}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\sigma_A(\mathbf{r})}{\mu_A(\mathbf{r})}
\] where \(\sigma_A\) is the standard deviation and \(\mu_A\) is the mean of the amplitude time series at \(\mathbf{r}\). Pixels with \(D_{amp}\) below a threshold (commonly \(0.25\)) are considered Persistent Scatterers (PS). Alternatively, phase stability or spectral tests can be used.
Parameter Estimation for PS Points: For each PS pixel, the unwrapped interferometric phase \(\tilde{\phi}_k(\mathbf{r}_{PS})\) (relative to the reference) is modeled as: \[
\tilde{\phi}_k(\mathbf{r}_{PS}) = \phi_{disp}(t_k) + \phi_{DEM} + \phi_{atm}(t_k) + \phi_{noise}(t_k)
\]

\(\phi_{disp}\): phase due to displacement (to be estimated, typically linear in time for velocity, plus possible nonlinear components).
\(\phi_{DEM}\): phase due to DEM errors (constant per pixel).
\(\phi_{atm}\): atmospheric phase (varies per image).
\(\phi_{noise}\): residual noise. Parameter estimation is commonly done by time series analysis (e.g., Least Squares, SVD). The linear component yields mean velocity: \[
v_{PS} = \frac{\lambda}{4\pi} \cdot \text{slope}\left[\tilde{\phi}_k\right]
\] where \(\lambda\) is radar wavelength.

Result: Output is a set of point-wise displacement time series \(d_k(\mathbf{r}_{PS})\) and mean velocities \(v_{PS}\) for each detected persistent scatterer.

Tools: ISCE2 topsStack + MintPy (SBAS for area-based, PS for point-based), SNAP → StaMPS (PS-InSAR), ASF HyP3 + MintPy (cloud), Dolphin (phase linking), NASA OPERA DISP-S1 (North America ready-made).

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
Dual-Pol Polarimetric Decomposition (SLC)
Dual-pol polarimetric decomposition is a technique used to extract detailed information about the physical and structural properties of the Earth’s surface from Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data, specifically when only two polarization channels- usually VV (vertical transmit, vertical receive) and VH (vertical transmit, horizontal receive) -are available.
In polarimetric SAR (PolSAR), each pixel of an image can contain complex information (amplitude and phase) about how radar signals interacted with the Earth’s surface. Dual-pol decomposition focuses on mathematically analyzing the relationships between the two available polarimetric channels (VV and VH), allowing us to infer land cover characteristics, detect and classify vegetation, map wetlands, and even gauge crop or forest structure.
The process involves creating a \(2\times2\) complex covariance matrix (\(\mathbf{C}_2\)) at each pixel by combining the VV and VH channels. This matrix encodes both the intensity and the correlation between the two polarizations. Polarimetric decomposition methods (such as H/α decomposition) then analyze the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of this matrix to derive physically-interpretable parameters: entropy (\(H\)), which measures randomness or heterogeneity of scattering; anisotropy (\(A\)), which contrasts the strengths of different scattering mechanisms; and the mean alpha angle (\(\alpha\)), which indicates the dominant type of scattering (surface, volume, or double-bounce) at that location.
By applying dual-pol decomposition to Sentinel-1 SLC data, we can generate thematic maps that highlight differences in land cover, identify flooded areas, monitor vegetation change, or characterize surface structure, all using only the information in the VV and VH channels. This enables many advanced remote sensing applications even when full quad-polarimetric data is not available.
Used for: land cover classification, vegetation structure, wetland mapping.
The following workflow enables extraction of physical and structural properties of the scene using only the two dual-polarization channels (VV and VH) available in Sentinel-1 SLC data:

TOPSAR-Split: Split both VV and VH polarization channels from the SLC product, so that \(S_{VV}(x, y)\) and \(S_{VH}(x, y)\) are available for all pixels \((x, y)\).
Apply-Orbit-File: Apply precise orbit information to correct satellite position and timing.
Calibration with complex output: Perform radiometric calibration to obtain calibrated backscatter values while preserving both amplitude and phase (complex values) of \(S_{VV}\) and \(S_{VH}\) for each pixel.
TOPSAR-Deburst: Merge burst-wise SLC slices into a single, seamless scene for further processing.
Polarimetric-Matrices (C2 covariance matrix): For dual-pol (VV,VH), form the \(2 \times 2\) complex covariance (C2) matrix for each pixel: \[
\mathbf{C}_2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
  \langle S_{VV} S_{VV}^* \rangle & \langle S_{VV} S_{VH}^* \rangle \\
  \langle S_{VH} S_{VV}^* \rangle & \langle S_{VH} S_{VH}^* \rangle
\end{bmatrix}
\] where \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) denotes local multilook or averaging.
Multilook: Spatial averaging (multilooking) improves radiometric quality and reduces speckle, so all covariance/clutter statistics are estimated over a \(n \times m\) pixel window: \[
\langle S_{ij} S_{kl}^* \rangle = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N S_{ij}^{(n)} \left(S_{kl}^{(n)}\right)^*
\]
Polarimetric-Speckle-Filter (e.g. Refined Lee): Apply a polarimetric-adapted speckle filter to the C2 matrix to suppress noise while preserving polarimetric information.
Polarimetric-Decomposition → H-Alpha dual-pol: Perform eigenvalue/eigenvector decomposition of the (filtered) C2 matrix for each pixel, yielding the polarimetric entropy \(H\), anisotropy \(A\), and alpha angle \(\alpha\):

Let \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\) be the normalized eigenvalues of \(C_2\) (\(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 1\)), then:

Entropy: \[
H = -\sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \log_2 \lambda_i
\]
Anisotropy: \[
A = \frac{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}
\]
Alpha angle: Weighted mean of scattering angle, from the eigenvector orientations; in dual-pol: \[
\alpha = \sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \alpha_i
\] where \(\alpha_i\) is derived from the eigenvector corresponding to \(\lambda_i\). These parameters help distinguish different scattering mechanisms (e.g. surface, volume, dihedral) via physical interpretation.


Terrain-Correction: Geocode the results into map coordinates accounting for local terrain/topography.
Feature extraction and classification: The derived features \(H\) (entropy), \(A\) (anisotropy), \(\alpha\) (alpha angle) at each pixel are used as inputs to a classification algorithm (e.g., Random Forest, SVM, or unsupervised clustering) for land cover or structure identification.


Note: Since Sentinel-1 only acquires VV and VH, the C2 (dual-pol) and its associated decompositions (H-Alpha dual-pol) are used, rather than full quad-pol decompositions (e.g., Freeman-Durden, Yamaguchi) which require HH and HV as well.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
EW mode sea ice workflow

Read EW GRDM (Ground Range Detected Medium resolution) bands (HH, HV):

Obtain two polarization channels: \(S_{HH}\) and \(S_{HV}\), where \(S_{pq}\) denotes the complex SAR signal for transmit \(p\) and receive \(q\) polarization.

Apply Orbit File:

Refine the satellite’s position and velocity by incorporating the precise orbit ephemeris. This improves geolocation accuracy of each pixel.

Thermal Noise Removal:

Remove additive noise from each pixel, especially important for the HV channel over sea ice. For each pixel: \[
S_{corr} = S_{raw} - N_{thermal}
\]
Where \(S_{raw}\) is the observed signal, \(N_{thermal}\) the estimated thermal noise, and \(S_{corr}\) the corrected value.

Radiometric Calibration to \(\sigma^0\):

Convert DN (digital number) to calibrated backscatter coefficient \(\sigma^0\): \[
\sigma^0 = \mathrm{CF} \cdot |S_{corr}|^2
\]
Where \(\mathrm{CF}\) is a calibration factor (depends on the product and sensor).

Incidence Angle Correction:

EW mode has a large incidence angle range (\(\theta \approx 19^\circ\) to \(47^\circ\)). Correct \(\sigma^0\) to a reference angle \(\theta_{ref}\) (e.g., \(35^\circ\)): \[
\sigma^0_{ref} = \sigma^0_{obs} + f(\theta_{ref}) - f(\theta_{obs})
\]
Where \(f(\theta)\) models the angular dependence, often empirically fit as \(f(\theta) = a\,\theta + b\,\theta^2\).

Speckle Filtering:

Apply a spatial filter (e.g. Lee or Frost) over a moving window of \(n \times m\) pixels to suppress speckle: \[
\hat{\sigma}^0_{i,j} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N \sigma^0_{i_k,j_k}
\]
Where \(\hat{\sigma}^0_{i,j}\) is the filtered backscatter at \((i,j)\).

Ellipsoid/Terrain Correction (Geocoding):

Map the image to a cartographic projection (e.g., polar stereographic projection, EPSG:3413), correcting for topography: \[
(x,y)_{\text{map}} = f(\text{lat}(\text{range}, \text{az}), \text{lon}(\text{range}, \text{az}))
\]

Texture Feature Extraction (GLCM) and Band Ratios:

Compute statistical texture features from the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM), e.g. contrast, entropy: \[
\text{Contrast} = \sum_{i,j} (i-j)^2 \, \text{GLCM}(i,j)
\]
Calculate backscatter ratios: \[
R = \frac{\sigma^0_{HH}}{\sigma^0_{HV}}
\]

Classification of Ice Types:

Use extracted features \([\sigma^0_{HH}, \sigma^0_{HV}, R, \text{Texture}_1, ...]\) as input vectors \(\vec{x}\) to a classifier: \[
\text{Class} = \mathrm{ML\,or\,CNN}(\vec{x})
\]
Output categories: open water, new ice, first-year ice, multi-year ice.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
Ship detection workflow (GRD)

Preprocessing of GRD data:

Apply precise orbit file corrections to improve geolocation accuracy.
Radiometrically calibrate the data to convert pixel values to backscatter coefficients (sigma0).
Generally avoid strong speckle filtering at this stage to preserve small ship targets, as aggressive filtering can mask point-like objects.

Land-Sea Masking:

Mask out land areas using a detailed coastline shapefile or a Digital Elevation Model (DEM).
This focuses subsequent detection steps over the sea and prevents false positives from bright land targets.

Adaptive Thresholding (CFAR - Constant False Alarm Rate):

For each pixel, compute a local background mean or statistical distribution (in a moving window).
Set a threshold based on the background, flagging pixels significantly brighter than their surroundings as potential ship candidates.
Variants include CA-CFAR (cell-averaging), OS-CFAR (ordered statistics), etc.

Object Discrimination:

Group connected detected pixels into distinct objects (“blobs”).
Remove objects that are smaller than the expected ship size (likely noise) or larger than a plausible ship (likely land, islands, or bright artifacts).
Additional metrics such as shape, orientation, and backscatter amplitude can be used to further refine detections.

Exporting Results:

Extract the geolocated positions and estimated sizes/shapes of all detected ships.
Output may be provided in vector format (e.g., GeoJSON, shapefiles, or CSV with coordinates, bounding boxes, and ancillary info).

(Optional) Matching with AIS (Automatic Identification System) Records:

Some Sentinel-1 missions (C and D) carry AIS receivers, which can record transmitted vessel locations.
Match detected objects with AIS records based on time and proximity to validate detections, annotate ship identities, or assess non-cooperative traffic.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Processing
text:
Level-2 OCN (Ocean) Products
Sentinel-1’s Level-2 Ocean (OCN) products are derived data outputs generated and preprocessed by ESA, removing the need for users to perform their own processing beyond data extraction and interpretation. These products are distributed in NetCDF format and contain geolocated, value-added physical measurements ready for analysis.
The main Level-2 OCN products include:

OWI (Ocean Wind Fields):

Provides estimates of ocean surface wind speed (in m/s) and wind direction (in degrees) at each measurement cell.
Useful for marine meteorology, weather forecasting, and hazard monitoring.
Includes quality flags, uncertainty metrics, geolocation, and time stamps for each wind vector cell.
Generated from both Interferometric Wide (IW) and Extra Wide (EW) modes, and covers most open ocean areas observed by Sentinel-1.

OSW (Ocean Swell Spectra):

Contains estimates of ocean swell parameters, such as swell height, period, and direction, derived from SAR wave mode (WV) and stripmap mode (SM).
Data is typically provided as wave spectra (energy density as a function of frequency and direction), allowing reconstruction of dominant wave fields and their long-distance propagation.
Used for oceanography, coastal studies, and maritime safety assessments.

RVL (Radial Surface Velocity):

Delivers measurements of the radial component (towards or away from the sensor) of surface water velocity.
Derived using Doppler centroid estimations from the SAR signal.
Valuable for tracking surface currents, ocean circulation patterns, and rapidly changing conditions such as tides or river plumes.


These Level-2 products are accompanied by detailed metadata, including timestamps, quality indicators, source orbit details, and processing history, ensuring traceability and scientific utility.

text:
Sentinel-1 Processing with GeoLattice
Below are short descriptions of commonly-used functions for processing Sentinel-1 imagery:

search_sentinel1(): Searches for Sentinel-1 data by specifying criteria such as date range, area of interest, polarization, and product type.
download_sentinel1(): Downloads Sentinel-1 products from various repositories (e.g., ASF, Copernicus Open Access Hub) using product IDs or metadata.
preprocess_grd(): Performs preprocessing of Sentinel-1 GRD data, such as radiometric calibration, geocoding, and terrain correction.
rtc_processing(): Generates Radiometrically Terrain Corrected (RTC) products from GRD data, removing terrain-induced distortions.
insar_coregister(): Coregisters a stack or pair of Sentinel-1 SLC images, aligning them for interferometric processing.
generate_interferogram(): Generates interferograms from coregistered SLC pairs to map phase differences due to ground deformation.
time_series_insar(): Processes a stack of SLC images to generate time series of ground displacement (for example, using MintPy or Dolphin).
visualize_sar(): Loads and displays Sentinel-1 SAR products in analysis-ready formats, such as amplitude, coherence, or displacement.
apply_speckle_filter(): Reduces speckle noise in SAR imagery using spatial filtering techniques.
export_geotiff(): Saves Sentinel-1 processed products (RTC, interferogram, etc.) to GeoTIFF format for further geospatial analysis.

These functions may be accessible via packages like geolattice-sentinel1, pyroSAR, sarsen, or custom scripts, depending on the workflow.

The 2017 clearing and the processing chain
In the weeks after 25 August 2017, more than 700,000 Rohingya refugees crossed from Myanmar into Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Kutupalong and Balukhali, modest existing camps, grew within months into the world’s largest refugee settlement. The reserve-forest hillsides around them were cleared for shelters, firewood and footpaths faster than almost any other land-cover change this notebook series has looked at. The AOI below covers Camp 4 Extension, Camp 18 and the Balukhali/Moragachhtola area, matching the screenshot used to define it.
Section 10 of Notebook 07_02_05 followed this clearing with Sentinel-2 and met the limit of optical monitoring: the influx began in the June-October monsoon, when the AOI is almost always under cloud. Radar sees through cloud. This notebook builds a multitemporal Sentinel-1 GRD time series for 2017 from the raw GRD products, scene by scene, and turns it into a deforestation map:

Planetary Computer holds 48 GRD scenes over the AOI for 2017 on two relative orbits:

Descending track 77: 20 Sentinel-1A scenes and one Sentinel-1B scene, all VV+VH, from 3 January to 29 December.

title: Sentinel-1 Multitemporal GRD Time Series: Deforestation around the Rohingya Camps (2017)
section: GRD steps on every scene: calibrated windows
text:
GRD steps on every scene: calibrated windows
Notebook 07_03_01_01 took one GRD scene through the full chain. Here the same steps run on every scene, but only on the AOI. read_grd_subset locates the AOI in each scene’s radar geometry with the scene’s own ground control points (GCPs), reads just that window from the remote Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF (about 0.6 MB instead of ~600 MB per polarisation), and applies thermal-noise removal and calibration to sigma0 with the scene’s own calibration and noise look-up tables, sampled at the window’s true position in the scene.


Code
def read_scenes():  # read and calibrate every scene
    scenes, rows = {"vv": [], "vh": []}, []  # calibrated windows per polarisation, and a log
    for it in items:  # loop over the scenes
        t0 = time.perf_counter()  # time each scene
        for pol in ("vv", "vh"):  # both polarisations
            # read only the window around the AOI, calibrate to sigma0 and remove thermal noise
            scenes[pol].append(rs.sar.read_grd_subset(
                pc_href(it.assets[pol].href), pc_href(it.assets[f"schema-calibration-{pol}"].href),
                pc_href(it.assets[f"schema-noise-{pol}"].href),
                bounds=BOUNDS, margin=40))
        # window size and run time
        rows.append({"scene": it.id, "window (rows x cols)": "x".join(map(str, scenes["vh"][-1]["window"][2:])),
                     "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1)})
    return scenes, pd.DataFrame(rows)  # return the scenes and the log as a table

stack_file = CACHE / f"grd_sigma0_track{TRACK}_2017.nc"  # the processed stack is cached as NetCDF
if stack_file.exists():  # reuse it when present
    print("Reusing", stack_file)  # the cached stack will be loaded instead
    scenes = None  # the individual scenes are not needed then
else:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    scenes, read_log = read_scenes()  # read and calibrate all scenes
    # total run time
    print(f"{len(items)} scenes x 2 polarisations read and calibrated in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")
    display(read_log.head(3))  # first three rows of the log
    s = scenes["vh"][0]  # the first VH scene
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6))  # two panels
    # VH sigma0 in dB, still in radar geometry
    ax[0].imshow(rs.sar.to_db(s["data"]), cmap="gray", vmin=-25, vmax=-5)
    # title and axis labels
    ax[0].set_title(f"VH sigma0 (dB), {times[0]:%d %b %Y}, radar geometry"); ax[0].set_xlabel("range (pixel)"); ax[0].set_ylabel("azimuth (line)")
    # histogram of the VH values
    ax[1].hist(rs.sar.to_db(s["data"][np.isfinite(s["data"])]).ravel(), bins=80, color="0.4")
    # label and title
    ax[1].set_xlabel("VH sigma0 (dB)"); ax[1].set_title(f"window {s['window'][2]} x {s['window'][3]} at line {s['window'][0]}, pixel {s['window'][1]}")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


Reusing ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/s1_rohingya_2017/grd_sigma0_track77_2017.nc


In radar geometry the image is mirrored and skewed relative to a map: a descending pass flies south and looks west, and pixels are spaced in slant-range time and azimuth time, not metres on the ground. The next step puts every date on the same map grid.

title: Sentinel-1 Multitemporal GRD Time Series: Deforestation around the Rohingya Camps (2017)
text:
Co-register the stack
SNAP’s CreateStack co-registers images of one track to a master. The simpler route the workflow allows, and the one used here, is to geocode every scene directly onto one common grid: then all dates land on identical pixels by construction. create_stack builds a north-up 10 m UTM grid over the AOI and warps each scene onto it with the GCPs surrounding its window. To check the result, each date is registered against the stack’s temporal mean: a perfectly co-registered stack gives offsets of zero.


Code
if stack_file.exists():  # cached stack
    stack = xr.open_dataset(stack_file).load()  # load it into memory
    stack = stack.rio.write_crs(CRS)  # attach the CRS
else:
    # resample every scene onto one 10 m UTM grid and stack them along time
    stack = xr.Dataset({pol: rs.sar.create_stack(scenes[pol], times, bounds=BOUNDS, crs=CRS, resolution=RES, name=pol)
                        for pol in ("vv", "vh")})
    # record where the data came from
    stack.attrs.update({"source": "Planetary Computer sentinel-1-grd", "track": TRACK, "calibration": "sigma0, noise removed"})
    # save the stack (without the CRS helper variable)
    stack.drop_vars("spatial_ref", errors="ignore").to_netcdf(stack_file)
# dimensions, CRS and units
print(dict(stack.sizes), "| CRS", stack.rio.crs, "| units:", stack.vh.attrs.get("units"))

mean_vv = rs.sar.to_db(stack.vv.mean("time"))  # temporal mean of VV in dB, the registration target
# shift of each date against the mean (within 5 pixels)
offsets = [rs.sar.estimate_offset(rs.sar.to_db(stack.vv.isel(time=k)), mean_vv, max_shift=5, smooth=5)
           for k in range(stack.sizes["time"])]
# offsets as a table
co = pd.DataFrame(offsets, columns=["dy", "dx", "correlation"], index=times.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
# range of offsets and correlations
print(f"offsets of each date against the temporal mean: dy in {sorted(co.dy.unique())}, dx in {sorted(co.dx.unique())}; "
      f"correlation {co.correlation.min():.2f}-{co.correlation.max():.2f}")


{'time': 19, 'y': 377, 'x': 382} | CRS EPSG:32646 | units: linear
offsets of each date against the temporal mean: dy in [np.int64(0)], dx in [np.int64(-1), np.int64(0), np.int64(1)]; correlation 0.63-0.74


The stack holds 19 dates on one 377 × 382 grid of 10 m pixels. Registered against the stack’s own temporal mean, every date has a north-south offset of 0 and an east-west offset of at most one pixel (10 m), with correlations of 0.63 to 0.74 (speckle keeps single dates from correlating more closely). The dates are co-registered with each other to within a pixel. Whether the stack sits in the right place on the ground is a different question, answered in Step 3.
The classes used to check the processing (and, in Step 8, to train and test the models) come from the Sentinel-2 reference of Notebook 07_02_05 on the same grid:

title: Sentinel-1 Multitemporal GRD Time Series: Deforestation around the Rohingya Camps (2017)
text:
Multitemporal speckle filter
A single-image filter (Lee, Refined Lee, Gamma-MAP; Notebook 07_03_01_01) estimates each pixel from its neighbours in one image, so it must trade speckle for spatial detail. The Quegan and Yu (2001) multitemporal filter also uses the other dates:
J_k(x) = E[I_k](x) / N · Σ_i I_i(x) / E[I_i](x)
where E[·] is a local spatial mean. Each date keeps its own local level E[I_k], while the speckle pattern, which is independent between dates, averages out over the N ratios, reducing it by up to √N. We compare it with a single-date Lee filter of the same 7 × 7 window on a homogeneous patch of stable forest (Equivalent Number of Looks, ENL = mean² / variance: higher is smoother) and on how well each preserves the mean backscatter and edges.


Code
def s2_ndvi(day, grid):  # Sentinel-2 NDVI of one date, used as an independent reference
    "Cloud-masked Sentinel-2 NDVI of one date on the radar grid (two MGRS tiles mosaicked)."
    # the Sentinel-2 folders of that date
    dirs = [p for p in S2_DIR.iterdir() if p.is_dir() and json.loads((p / "item.json").read_text())["properties"]["datetime"][:10] == day]
    layers = {}  # one layer per band
    for band in ("red", "nir", "scl"):  # red, NIR and the scene classification layer (SCL)
        # each tile reprojected onto the radar grid (nearest for classes, average for reflectance)
        tiles = [rioxarray.open_rasterio(p / f"{band}.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True).rio.write_nodata(0)
                 .rio.reproject_match(grid, resampling=Resampling.nearest if band == "scl" else Resampling.average)
                 for p in dirs]
        cube = xr.concat(tiles, "tile")  # stack the tiles
        # mosaic: maximum over tiles, ignoring zeros
        layers[band] = cube.max("tile") if band == "scl" else cube.where(cube > 0).max("tile")
    red, nir = layers["red"] / 1e4, layers["nir"] / 1e4               # 2017: processing baseline < 04.00, no offset
    # NDVI, kept only where SCL says vegetation, bare soil or water (classes 4-6)
    return ((nir - red) / (nir + red)).where(layers["scl"].isin([4, 5, 6]))

grid = stack.vh.isel(time=0)  # the radar grid (first date)
# median NDVI of two dry-season dates before the influx
ndvi_before = xr.concat([s2_ndvi(d, grid) for d in ("2017-01-09", "2017-02-08")], "t").median("t")
# median NDVI of two dates at the end of 2017
ndvi_after = xr.concat([s2_ndvi(d, grid) for d in ("2017-11-20", "2017-12-15")], "t").median("t")
forest_before, forest_after = (ndvi_before > 0.5).values, (ndvi_after > 0.5).values  # forest = NDVI above 0.5
observed = np.isfinite(ndvi_before.values) & np.isfinite(ndvi_after.values)  # pixels seen in both periods
labels = np.full(grid.shape, -1)  # -1 = unlabelled
labels[observed & ~forest_before] = 0                                  # non-forest already in Jan-Feb 2017
labels[observed & forest_before & forest_after] = 1                    # forest, both periods
labels[observed & forest_before & ~forest_after] = 2                   # forest cleared during 2017
CLASSES = {0: "non-forest", 1: "stable forest", 2: "cleared forest"}  # class codes -> names
px_ha = RES * RES / 1e4  # hectares per pixel
# area of each class
print({CLASSES[k]: f"{(labels == k).sum() * px_ha:.0f} ha" for k in CLASSES}, f"| unlabelled {np.mean(labels < 0):.1%}")


{'non-forest': '276 ha', 'stable forest': '465 ha', 'cleared forest': '561 ha'} | unlabelled 9.6%




Code
# Lee filter applied to each date on its own
lee_single = xr.apply_ufunc(lambda a: np.asarray(speckle.lee(a, 7)), stack.vh, input_core_dims=[["y", "x"]],
                            output_core_dims=[["y", "x"]], vectorize=True)
# Quegan multitemporal filter: uses all dates together
quegan = rs.sar.multitemporal_speckle_filter(stack, spatial="boxcar", size=7)

# the most homogeneous 21 x 21 patch of stable forest
from scipy.ndimage import uniform_filter  # moving-window mean
share = uniform_filter((labels == 1).astype(float), 21)  # share of stable-forest pixels in each 21 x 21 window
# centre of the window with the most stable forest
cy, cx = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(np.where(np.isfinite(stack.vh.isel(time=0)), share, 0)), share.shape)
patch = (slice(cy - 10, cy + 11), slice(cx - 10, cx + 11))  # the 21 x 21 patch around it
rows = []  # one row per filter
# the three versions of the stack
for name, img in [("unfiltered", stack.vh), ("Lee 7x7, single date", lee_single), ("Quegan multitemporal 7x7", quegan.vh)]:
    # mean ENL over the dates in the forest patch
    enl = np.mean([speckle.enl_estimate(img.isel(time=k).values[patch]) for k in range(img.sizes["time"])])
    # ENL, mean backscatter and edge strength
    rows.append({"filter": name, "ENL on stable forest (mean over dates)": enl,
                 "mean VH (dB of linear mean)": float(rs.sar.to_db(np.nanmean(img.values))),
                 "edge strength (mean |gradient|, dB/pixel)": float(np.nanmean(np.abs(np.gradient(rs.sar.to_db(img.mean("time").values))[1])))})
filt = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("filter")  # as a table
display(filt.round(2))  # show it

k = int(np.argmin(np.abs(times - pd.Timestamp("2017-11-23"))))  # the date closest to 23 November 2017
zoom = (slice(80, 260), slice(80, 260))  # a 180 x 180 pixel zoom
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))  # three panels
# one panel per version
for a, (name, img) in zip(ax, [("unfiltered", stack.vh), ("Lee 7x7, single date", lee_single), ("Quegan multitemporal 7x7", quegan.vh)]):
    # the zoom of this version on that date, with title
    a.imshow(rs.sar.to_db(img.isel(time=k).values)[zoom], cmap="gray", vmin=-22, vmax=-8); a.set_title(f"{name}, VH {times[k]:%d %b %Y}"); a.set_axis_off()

The single-date Lee filter smooths more, but it erases spatial detail: the mean gradient falls from 0.68 to 0.27 dB per pixel. The Quegan filter more than doubles the ENL while keeping almost all of the edges, the shelters, paths and clearing boundaries this study is about. title: Sentinel-1 Multitemporal GRD Time Series: Deforestation around the Rohingya Camps (2017)
section: Terrain correction to a common grid
text:
Terrain correction to a common grid
The stack is co-registered with itself (Step 1), but is it in the right place on the ground? Geocoding from GCPs places each pixel using the GCPs’ heights, interpolated between points about 20 km apart, rather than a DEM, and the camps sit on hills. Full terrain correction (range-Doppler with a DEM) needs the orbit state vectors and the complete product annotation, which Planetary Computer’s GRD files do not carry (Notebook 07_03_01_01, Section 5). Planetary Computer does publish the same acquisitions already terrain-corrected with a DEM, as RTC gamma0. We use it as the geometric reference: measure where the GCP-geocoded stack sits relative to it and to the Sentinel-2 reference, then register the stack to it.


Code
# cached Planetary Computer RTC (terrain-corrected gamma0) stack
rtc_file = CACHE / f"rtc_gamma0_track{TRACK}_2017.nc"
if rtc_file.exists():  # reuse it when present
    rtc = xr.open_dataset(rtc_file).load()  # load it
else:
    # RTC scenes of the same track and period
    rtc_items = sorted([i for i in pc_catalog().search(collections=["sentinel-1-rtc"], bbox=list(BOUNDS),
                                                       datetime=f"{ROH_DATES[0]}/{ROH_DATES[2]}").items()
                        if i.properties["sat:relative_orbit"] == TRACK], key=lambda i: i.datetime)
    x, y = stack.x.values, stack.y.values  # the GRD stack's grid coordinates
    # load VV and VH on that grid, one image per day
    rtc = odc.stac.load(rtc_items, bands=["vv", "vh"], crs=CRS, resolution=RES, x=(x.min() - 5, x.max() + 5),
                        y=(y.min() - 5, y.max() + 5), groupby="solar_day").interp(x=x, y=y, method="nearest")
    rtc = rtc.where(rtc > 0)  # zero means no data
    rtc["time"] = pd.to_datetime(rtc.time.values)  # plain datetime values
    rtc.drop_vars("spatial_ref", errors="ignore").to_netcdf(rtc_file)  # cache the stack
# confirm the RTC dates match the GRD dates
print(f"RTC: {rtc.sizes['time']} dates on the same grid; dates match the GRD stack: "
      f"{bool((pd.to_datetime(rtc.time.values).normalize() == times.normalize()).all())}")

dem_file = CACHE / "copdem30_stack_grid.nc"  # the DEM on the stack grid, cached like the stacks
if dem_file.exists():  # reuse it when present
    dem = xr.open_dataarray(dem_file).load()  # load it
else:
    # Copernicus 30 m DEM tiles over the AOI
    dem_items = list(pc_catalog().search(collections=["cop-dem-glo-30"], bbox=list(BOUNDS)).items())
    # load the DEM onto the stack grid
    dem = odc.stac.load(dem_items, bands=["data"], crs=CRS, resolution=RES, x=(stack.x.min().item() - 5, stack.x.max().item() + 5),
                        y=(stack.y.min().item() - 5, stack.y.max().item() + 5)).data.isel(time=0).interp(x=stack.x, y=stack.y)
    dem.drop_vars(["spatial_ref", "time"], errors="ignore").to_netcdf(dem_file)  # cache it
slope = np.degrees(np.arctan(np.hypot(*np.gradient(dem.values, RES))))  # slope in degrees from the DEM gradient
# elevation and slope ranges
print(f"terrain: {float(dem.min()):.0f} to {float(dem.max()):.0f} m, median slope {np.nanmedian(slope):.0f} deg, 95th percentile {np.nanpercentile(slope, 95):.0f} deg")

grd_mean = rs.sar.to_db(quegan.vh.mean("time"))  # mean VH of the filtered GRD stack, dB
rtc_mean = rs.sar.to_db(rtc.vh.mean("time"))  # mean VH of the RTC stack, dB
# three comparisons: GRD vs RTC, and each against Sentinel-2 NDVI
checks = {"GCP-geocoded GRD stack vs RTC": (grd_mean, rtc_mean),
          "GCP-geocoded GRD stack vs Sentinel-2 NDVI (Jan-Feb)": (grd_mean, ndvi_before),
          "RTC vs Sentinel-2 NDVI (Jan-Feb)": (rtc_mean, ndvi_before)}
# offset and correlation of each pair (search within 30 pixels)
reg = pd.DataFrame([dict(zip(["dy (rows)", "dx (cols)", "correlation"], rs.sar.estimate_offset(a, b, max_shift=30)), comparison=n)
                    for n, (a, b) in checks.items()]).set_index("comparison")
# offsets in metres
reg["offset (m)"] = [f"{abs(r['dy (rows)']) * RES} N-S, {abs(r['dx (cols)']) * RES} E-W" for _, r in reg.iterrows()]
reg  # show the table

# the GRD stack before and after registration, and the RTC
for a, img, title in [(ax[1], grd_mean, "GRD stack, GCP geocoding"), (ax[2], rs.sar.to_db(stack_tc.vh.mean("time")), "GRD stack, registered"),
                      (ax[3], rtc_mean, "RTC (DEM terrain-corrected)")]:
    a.imshow(img, cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=-10); a.set_title(f"{title}\nmean VH 2017 (dB)")  # mean VH in dB

The terrain is low but rugged: 0 to 44 m, with a median slope of 9° and 5% of slopes above 23°. The registration checks:



Comparison
