title: NISAR RSLC: Range-Doppler Single Look Complex Processing
section: Load the AOI and locate its radar-coordinate window
text:
Load the AOI and locate its radar-coordinate window
The metadata geolocation grid is a sparse set of tie points at multiple terrain heights. For this quick look, the zero-metre ellipsoidal-height slice is used to find the image window intersecting the AOI bounds. The window is padded by two tie-point intervals so that interpolation near the AOI edge has neighboring samples. The exact AOI polygon is applied again after geocoding.


Code
# Load the AOI, then use the sparse NISAR geolocation grid to find the radar-coordinate
# (line/sample) window of the full-resolution image that covers the AOI.

# 1. Load the AOI polygon and make sure it is in geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326) to
#    match the lon/lat tie points stored in the geolocation grid.
aoi = gpd.read_file(AOI_PATH)
if aoi.crs is None:  # assume WGS 84 when the file has no CRS
    aoi = aoi.set_crs("EPSG:4326")  # set it
aoi_ll = aoi.to_crs("EPSG:4326")  # the AOI in longitude/latitude
min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat = aoi_ll.total_bounds  # its bounding box

GEO = "/science/LSAR/RSLC/metadata/geolocationGrid"  # HDF5 path of the geolocation grid
SWATH = "/science/LSAR/RSLC/swaths/frequencyA"  # HDF5 path of the frequency-A swath
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:  # open the RSLC file
    swath = f[SWATH]  # the swath group
    geo = f[GEO]  # the geolocation group
    n_lines, n_samples = swath["HH"].shape  # image size
    # 2. The geolocation grid stores tie points at several terrain heights above the
    #    ellipsoid; pick the slice closest to zero metres for this quick-look workflow.
    heights = geo["heightAboveEllipsoid"][:]
    height_index = int(np.argmin(np.abs(heights)))  # the grid layer closest to zero height
    tie_lon = geo["coordinateX"][height_index, :, :]  # longitude of every tie point
    tie_lat = geo["coordinateY"][height_index, :, :]  # latitude of every tie point
    tie_range = geo["slantRange"][:]  # slant range of the tie-point columns
    scene_range = swath["slantRange"][:]  # slant range of the image columns
    valid_ranges = swath["validSamplesSubSwath1"]  # valid range samples of each line

    # 3. Find which tie points fall inside the AOI's lon/lat bounding box. These are
    #    coarse, sparse grid points, so this only approximately brackets the AOI.
    intersects = (
        np.isfinite(tie_lon) & np.isfinite(tie_lat)
        & (tie_lon >= min_lon) & (tie_lon <= max_lon)
        & (tie_lat >= min_lat) & (tie_lat <= max_lat)
    )
    tie_rows, tie_cols = np.where(intersects)  # tie points that fall inside the AOI
    if tie_rows.size == 0:  # none: the AOI is outside the scene
        raise ValueError("The AOI does not intersect the RSLC geolocation grid")  # stop with a clear message

    # 4. Convert the matching tie-point row/column indices into full-resolution
    #    line/sample pixel indices, padding by two tie-point intervals on each side so
    #    later interpolation near the AOI edge has neighboring samples to draw on.
    tie_line_to_pixel = np.linspace(0, n_lines - 1, tie_lon.shape[0])
    # first image line of the AOI window (with a margin)
    row_low = max(0, int(np.floor(tie_line_to_pixel[max(0, tie_rows.min() - 2)])))
    # last image line
    row_high = min(n_lines, int(np.ceil(tie_line_to_pixel[min(tie_lon.shape[0] - 1, tie_rows.max() + 2)])) + 1)
    # tie-point column -> image sample
    tie_sample_to_pixel = np.interp(tie_range, scene_range, np.arange(n_samples))
    col_low = max(0, int(np.floor(tie_sample_to_pixel[max(0, tie_cols.min() - 2)])))  # first image sample
    # last image sample
    col_high = min(n_samples, int(np.ceil(tie_sample_to_pixel[min(tie_lon.shape[1] - 1, tie_cols.max() + 2)])) + 1)

# 5. Report the AOI bounds, the chosen height slice, and the resulting radar window so
#    we know up front how much of the ~2.9 billion-sample scene will actually be read.
print(f"AOI bounds (longitude, latitude): {min_lon:.5f}, {min_lat:.5f}, {max_lon:.5f}, {max_lat:.5f}")
print(f"Zero-height geolocation slice: {heights[height_index]:.0f} m")  # height of the grid layer used
print(f"Radar window: lines {row_low:,}:{row_high:,}, samples {col_low:,}:{col_high:,}")  # the radar window
print(f"Window size: {row_high-row_low:,} x {col_high-col_low:,} single-look samples")  # its size

# 6. Plot the (subsampled) tie-point coverage against the AOI boundary as a sanity
#    check that the AOI truly falls within the scene footprint before reading pixels.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
# tie points (every eighth)
ax.scatter(tie_lon[::8, ::8], tie_lat[::8, ::8], s=2, color="0.65", label="NISAR geolocation ties")
aoi_ll.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="red", linewidth=1.5, label="AOI_coastal")  # the AOI outline
# labels and title
ax.set(xlabel="Longitude", ylabel="Latitude", title="NISAR tie-point coverage and coastal AOI")
ax.legend()  # legend
ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")  # equal scale
plt.show()  # draw

Zero-height geolocation slice: 0 m
Radar window: lines 2,563:33,720, samples 12,034:45,411
Window size: 31,157 x 33,377 single-look samples

title: NISAR RSLC: Range-Doppler Single Look Complex Processing
section: Stream and multilook the complex RSLC
text:
Stream and multilook the complex RSLC
The code below calculates mean(|S|²) over 64 × 64 blocks. It limits working memory by reading a few multilooked output rows at a time. NISAR’s validSamplesSubSwath1 start/end indices are used to ignore samples outside the valid range swath. This is a block-averaged intensity product; it does not average complex phase and should not be used as an SLC interferogram input.


Code
# Stream the AOI window of the complex HH/HV arrays in bounded chunks and compute
# multilooked linear beta0 power (mean of |S|^2), honoring the valid-sample range mask.

LOOKS = (64, 64)  # (azimuth lines, range samples)
OUTPUT_ROWS_PER_CHUNK = 4  # multilooked rows computed per read

# multilooked power of a radar window, read chunk by chunk from the HDF5 file
def read_multilooked_power(dataset, valid_sample_dataset, window, looks=LOOKS,
                           output_rows_per_chunk=OUTPUT_ROWS_PER_CHUNK):
    """Stream a radar-window block average of complex SLC power."""
    # 1. Unpack the window and derive how many complete multilook blocks fit in it,
    #    trimming the window so every output pixel is backed by a full look x look block.
    line0, line1, sample0, sample1 = window
    look_az, look_rg = looks  # azimuth and range looks
    out_lines = (line1 - line0) // look_az  # output lines
    out_samples = (sample1 - sample0) // look_rg  # output samples
    line1 = line0 + out_lines * look_az  # trim the window to whole looks
    sample1 = sample0 + out_samples * look_rg  # trim the window to whole looks
    output = np.full((out_lines, out_samples), np.nan, dtype="float32")  # output array
    sample_indices = np.arange(sample0, sample1)  # image sample numbers of the window

    # 2. Process a few multilooked output rows at a time (output_rows_per_chunk) so only
    #    a small slab of the multi-gigabyte complex HDF5 dataset is held in memory at once.
    for out0 in range(0, out_lines, output_rows_per_chunk):
        count = min(output_rows_per_chunk, out_lines - out0)  # output rows in this chunk
        raw0 = line0 + out0 * look_az  # first input line of the chunk
        raw1 = raw0 + count * look_az  # last input line of the chunk
        # 3. Read this chunk's raw complex samples and convert to linear power |S|^2
        #    (real^2 + imag^2); this is the single-look beta0-proportional power.
        block = dataset[raw0:raw1, sample0:sample1]
        # power = real² + imaginary²
        power = block.real.astype("float32") ** 2 + block.imag.astype("float32") ** 2
        # 4. Mask out samples outside the valid range swath for each line, using NISAR's
        #    per-line validSamplesSubSwath1 start/end indices, so invalid fill data does
        #    not get averaged into the multilooked power.
        valid = valid_sample_dataset[raw0:raw1]
        valid_pixels = (  # mask of samples inside each line's valid range
            (sample_indices[None, :] >= valid[:, 0, None])
            & (sample_indices[None, :] <= valid[:, 1, None])
        )
        power[~valid_pixels] = np.nan  # invalid samples -> NaN
        # 5. Reshape into (output_rows, look_az, output_cols, look_rg) blocks and average
        #    only the finite (valid) samples in each look x look block, leaving a block
        #    NaN only if it contains no valid samples at all.
        blocks = power.reshape(count, look_az, out_samples, look_rg)
        finite = np.isfinite(blocks)  # finite values in each look block
        totals = np.where(finite, blocks, 0).sum(axis=(1, 3))  # sum of the finite values per block
        counts = finite.sum(axis=(1, 3))  # number of finite values per block
        output[out0:out0 + count] = np.divide(  # mean power per block
            totals, counts, out=np.full_like(totals, np.nan), where=counts > 0
        )
    return output  # the multilooked power

# 6. Snap the AOI window from Step 2 down to a whole number of 64x64 look blocks so the
#    multilooked output arrays below have well-defined, consistent dimensions.
window = (row_low, row_high, col_low, col_high)
n_lines_ml = (row_high - row_low) // LOOKS[0]  # multilooked lines
n_samples_ml = (col_high - col_low) // LOOKS[1]  # multilooked samples
row_high = row_low + n_lines_ml * LOOKS[0]  # trim the window to whole looks
col_high = col_low + n_samples_ml * LOOKS[1]  # trim the window to whole looks
window = (row_low, row_high, col_low, col_high)  # the final window

# 7. Stream and multilook the HH and HV complex arrays over the trimmed window. Each
#    call only ever touches the AOI window, never the full ~2.9 billion-sample scene.
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:
    swath = f[SWATH]  # the swath group
    valid_samples = swath["validSamplesSubSwath1"]  # valid range samples of each line
    # HH beta0 (uncalibrated power), multilooked
    beta0_hh_values = read_multilooked_power(swath["HH"], valid_samples, window)
    beta0_hv_values = read_multilooked_power(swath["HV"], valid_samples, window)  # HV beta0, multilooked

# size of the multilooked arrays
print(f"Multilooked arrays: {beta0_hh_values.shape[0]:,} x {beta0_hh_values.shape[1]:,}")
print(f"HH beta0 valid fraction: {np.isfinite(beta0_hh_values).mean():.1%}")  # valid share of HH
print(f"HV beta0 valid fraction: {np.isfinite(beta0_hv_values).mean():.1%}")  # valid share of HV

HH beta0 valid fraction: 100.0%
HV beta0 valid fraction: 100.0%

title: NISAR RSLC: Range-Doppler Single Look Complex Processing
section: Incidence-angle correction, filtering, and dB display
text:
Incidence-angle correction, filtering, and dB display
NISAR RSLC samples are calibrated to beta-nought. The approximate ellipsoid sigma-nought is beta0 × sin(incidence angle). Both beta0 and sigma0 are kept in linear power for filtering; dB conversion is only for visualization. Terrain-flattened gamma0 is not computed here.


Code
# Interpolate the incidence-angle grid onto the multilooked pixel locations, convert
# beta0 to an ellipsoid sigma0 approximation, Lee-filter the linear power, and display in dB.

# 1. Build coordinate-mapping arrays that translate multilooked (azimuth, range) pixel
#    centers into fractional tie-point grid indices, so the sparse incidence-angle grid
#    can be interpolated onto the exact multilooked sample locations.
geo_line_positions = np.linspace(0, image_shape[0] - 1, tie_lon.shape[0])
geo_sample_positions = tie_sample_to_pixel  # tie-point column positions in image samples
# image line at the centre of each multilooked row
ml_lines = row_low + (np.arange(n_lines_ml) + 0.5) * LOOKS[0]
# image sample at the centre of each multilooked column
ml_samples = col_low + (np.arange(n_samples_ml) + 0.5) * LOOKS[1]
# multilooked rows -> fractional tie-point rows
tie_line_coords = np.interp(ml_lines, geo_line_positions, np.arange(tie_lon.shape[0]))
# multilooked columns -> fractional tie-point columns
tie_sample_coords = np.interp(ml_samples, geo_sample_positions, np.arange(tie_lon.shape[1]))
# fractional tie-point coordinates of every multilooked pixel
sample_grid = np.meshgrid(tie_line_coords, tie_sample_coords, indexing="ij")

# 2. Read the incidence-angle tie points at the same zero-height slice used for the AOI
#    window, then bilinearly interpolate them onto the multilooked grid built above.
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:
    geo = f[GEO]  # the geolocation group
    incidence_ties = geo["incidenceAngle"][height_index, :, :]  # incidence angle at the tie points

# incidence angle of every multilooked pixel (bilinear)
incidence_deg = map_coordinates(incidence_ties, sample_grid, order=1, mode="nearest")
# 3. Wrap the multilooked HH/HV beta0 power arrays as labeled xarray DataArrays so
#    azimuth/range coordinates and units/polarization metadata travel with the data.
coords = {"azimuth": ml_lines, "range": ml_samples}
beta0_hh = xr.DataArray(beta0_hh_values, dims=("azimuth", "range"), coords=coords,  # HH beta0 as a DataArray
                        name="beta0_hh", attrs={"units": "linear beta0", "polarization": "HH"})
beta0_hv = xr.DataArray(beta0_hv_values, dims=("azimuth", "range"), coords=coords,  # HV beta0 as a DataArray
                        name="beta0_hv", attrs={"units": "linear beta0", "polarization": "HV"})
# 4. Approximate ellipsoid sigma0 as beta0 * sin(incidence angle); this is a geometric
#    approximation, not a terrain-flattened radiometric correction.
sigma0_hh = beta0_hh * np.sin(np.deg2rad(incidence_deg))
sigma0_hv = beta0_hv * np.sin(np.deg2rad(incidence_deg))  # sigma0 = beta0 x sin(incidence)
sigma0_hh.name, sigma0_hv.name = "sigma0_hh", "sigma0_hv"  # names
sigma0_hh.attrs["units"] = sigma0_hv.attrs["units"] = "linear sigma0"  # units

# 5. Apply GeoLattice Lee speckle filtering to the linear sigma0 power (never to dB values),
# which preserves the physical units while suppressing multiplicative speckle noise.
sigma0_hh_lee = xr.DataArray(rs.sar.lee(sigma0_hh.values, size=5), dims=sigma0_hh.dims,
                            coords=sigma0_hh.coords, name="sigma0_hh_lee")
# Lee speckle filter (5 x 5)
sigma0_hv_lee = xr.DataArray(rs.sar.lee(sigma0_hv.values, size=5), dims=sigma0_hv.dims,
                            coords=sigma0_hv.coords, name="sigma0_hv_lee")
# 6. Convert the filtered linear sigma0 to dB only for visualization; downstream
#    quantities (Step 5 geocoding) continue to use the linear arrays, not these dB ones.
hh_db = rs.sar.to_db(sigma0_hh_lee)
hv_db = rs.sar.to_db(sigma0_hv_lee)  # filtered HV in dB

# 7. Display HH and HV side by side, stretching each image independently between its
#    2nd and 98th percentile dB values so both channels show useful contrast.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))
for ax, image, title in (  # the three images with their titles
    (axes[0], hh_db, "HH sigma0, Lee filtered (dB), September 22nd, 2026"),
    (axes[1], hv_db, "HV sigma0, Lee filtered (dB), September 22nd, 2026"),
):
    low, high = np.nanpercentile(image.values, [2, 98])  # 2-98 % stretch limits
    shown = ax.imshow(image, cmap="gray", vmin=low, vmax=high, interpolation="nearest")  # show the image
    # title and axis labels
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Range sample (multilooked)", ylabel="Azimuth line (multilooked)")
    fig.colorbar(shown, ax=ax, shrink=0.75, label="dB")  # colour bar
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw









The contrast stretch above uses the valid-pixel 2nd and 98th percentiles for display only. It does not alter the underlying linear beta0 or sigma0 arrays.

title: NISAR RSLC: Range-Doppler Single Look Complex Processing
section: Interpolate the quick look to a map grid
text:
Interpolate the quick look to a map grid
The sparse NISAR geolocation tie points are linearly interpolated to the multilooked sample locations at zero metres ellipsoidal height. GeoLattice nisar.geocode_l1 then interpolates the quick-look sigma0 layers to a 200 m UTM grid. Finally, the exact GeoJSON polygon is used to clip the result to the study area.


Code
# Interpolate tie-point lon/lat onto the multilooked grid, project to UTM, geocode the
# filtered sigma0 quick looks to a 200 m grid, and clip to the exact AOI polygon.

# 1. Interpolate the sparse lon/lat tie points onto the multilooked sample locations
#    (same index grid used for the incidence angle in Step 4) to get a map coordinate
#    for every multilooked pixel.
tie_x = map_coordinates(tie_lon, sample_grid, order=1, mode="nearest")
tie_y = map_coordinates(tie_lat, sample_grid, order=1, mode="nearest")  # latitude of every multilooked pixel
# 2. Project those geographic coordinates into the local UTM zone (46N covers coastal
#    Bangladesh) so the geocoded quick look has a metric, map-projected grid.
to_utm = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", "EPSG:32646", always_xy=True)
map_x, map_y = to_utm.transform(tie_x, tie_y)  # longitude/latitude -> UTM

# 3. Use GeoLattice's nisar.geocode_l1 to resample the irregularly-spaced radar-coordinate
#    sigma0 quick looks onto a regular 200 m UTM grid, using the per-pixel map_x/map_y
#    coordinates computed above.
MAP_RESOLUTION_M = 200
geo_hh = nisar.geocode_l1(  # geocode HH onto a UTM grid
    sigma0_hh_lee, map_x, map_y, epsg=32646, resolution=MAP_RESOLUTION_M
)
geo_hv = nisar.geocode_l1(  # geocode HV onto a UTM grid
    sigma0_hv_lee, map_x, map_y, epsg=32646, resolution=MAP_RESOLUTION_M
)
# 4. Clip the geocoded grids to the exact AOI polygon (reprojected to UTM), rather than
#    the coarser radar-window bounding box used earlier, to remove the extra padding.
aoi_utm = aoi.to_crs("EPSG:32646")
geo_hh = geo_hh.rio.clip(aoi_utm.geometry, aoi_utm.crs, drop=True, all_touched=True)  # clip HH to the AOI
geo_hv = geo_hv.rio.clip(aoi_utm.geometry, aoi_utm.crs, drop=True, all_touched=True)  # clip HV to the AOI
# 5. Convert the clipped linear sigma0 grids to dB for the final map display.
geo_hh_db = rs.sar.to_db(geo_hh).rename("sigma0_hh_db")
geo_hv_db = rs.sar.to_db(geo_hv).rename("sigma0_hv_db")  # HV in dB

# 6. Plot the geocoded, clipped HH/HV dB quick looks with the AOI boundary overlaid for
#    visual confirmation that the map-projected result matches the requested study area.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))
for ax, image, title in (  # the two images with their titles
    (axes[0], geo_hh_db, "HH sigma0 (dB), UTM 46N, \nSeptember 22nd, 2026"),
    (axes[1], geo_hv_db, "HV sigma0 (dB), UTM 46N, \nSeptember 22nd, 2026"),
):
    # show with a robust stretch
    image.plot.imshow(ax=ax, cmap="gray", robust=True, cbar_kwargs={"label": "dB"})
    aoi_utm.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="cyan", linewidth=0.8)  # AOI outline
    ax.set_title(title)  # title
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # equal scale
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

print(f"Clipped quick-look grid: {geo_hh.sizes['y']:,} rows x {geo_hh.sizes['x']:,} columns")  # grid size
print(f"Map CRS: {geo_hh.rio.crs}; pixel size: {MAP_RESOLUTION_M} m")  # CRS and pixel size









Clipped quick-look grid: 561 rows x 663 columns
Map CRS: EPSG:32646; pixel size: 200 m

title: NISAR RSLC: Range-Doppler Single Look Complex Processing
text:
HH/HV dual-polarization RGB composite
Create a false-color composite from the clipped, geocoded dB quick looks: red = HH sigma0 (dB), green = HV sigma0 (dB), and blue = HH−HV (dB), equivalent to the HH/HV power ratio expressed in decibels. Each channel is contrast-stretched independently between its 2nd and 98th percentiles for display; this RGB is for visual interpretation, not quantitative color measurement.


Code
# Build a false-color RGB composite (R=HH dB, G=HV dB, B=HH-HV dB ratio) from the
# clipped geocoded quick looks, with each channel independently percentile-stretched.

# 1. Pull the dB arrays as plain float32 numpy arrays and derive the third ('blue')
#    channel as the HH-HV difference in dB, equivalent to the HH/HV power ratio.
hh_rgb = geo_hh_db.values.astype("float32")
hv_rgb = geo_hv_db.values.astype("float32")  # HV in dB as an array
ratio_rgb = hh_rgb - hv_rgb  # HH minus HV (dB): the cross-polarisation ratio
valid_rgb = np.isfinite(hh_rgb) & np.isfinite(hv_rgb)  # pixels valid in both

# 2. Helper that linearly stretches one channel's finite pixels between given
#    percentiles into the [0, 1] range expected by matplotlib's imshow for RGB images.
def stretch_rgb_channel(channel, valid_mask, percentiles=(2, 98)):
    values = channel[valid_mask]  # the valid values of the channel
    if values.size == 0:  # no valid values
        raise ValueError("RGB channel has no finite pixels in the clipped AOI")  # stop with a clear message
    low, high = np.percentile(values, percentiles)  # percentile limits
    if high <= low:  # constant channel
        return np.zeros(channel.shape, dtype="float32")  # return zeros
    return np.clip((channel - low) / (high - low), 0, 1).astype("float32")  # stretch to [0, 1]

# 3. Stretch each of the three channels independently (each has its own dB range) and
#    stack them into an (rows, cols, 3) RGB array; zero out any pixel invalid in HH or HV.
rgb = np.stack([
    stretch_rgb_channel(hh_rgb, valid_rgb),
    stretch_rgb_channel(hv_rgb, valid_rgb),
    stretch_rgb_channel(ratio_rgb, valid_rgb),
], axis=-1)
rgb[~valid_rgb] = 0  # no-data pixels in black

# 4. Plot the RGB composite on its UTM map extent, with the AOI boundary overlaid in
#    white for visual reference against the coastline and surface features.
x = geo_hh_db.x.values
y = geo_hh_db.y.values  # northing values
extent = (x.min(), x.max(), y.min(), y.max())  # map extent
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))  # one panel
ax.imshow(rgb, extent=extent, origin="upper", interpolation="nearest")  # the RGB composite
aoi_utm.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=0.8)  # AOI outline
ax.set(xlabel="Easting (m)", ylabel="Northing (m)",  # axis labels and title
       title="NISAR RSLC dual-pol false-color RGB\nR: HH dB | G: HV dB | B: HH/HV dB")
ax.set_aspect("equal")  # equal scale
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

Optionally export the clipped quick looks
Exports are disabled by default. When enabled, the files are small, georeferenced dB quick looks; they are not source-resolution NISAR products and should not be labeled as terrain-corrected RTC.


Code
# Optionally write the clipped, geocoded dB quick looks to GeoTIFFs; disabled by default
# so running the notebook does not silently create output files on disk.

# 1. Flip this flag to True to export; when False (the default) the block below is

if WRITE_OUTPUTS:  # only when output writing is switched on
    # 2. Create the output directory (if needed) and write each polarization's dB
    #    quick look as an LZW-compressed GeoTIFF carrying its UTM georeferencing.

    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create the output folder

    # save HV in dB
    geo_hv_db.rio.to_raster(output_dir / "NISAR_RSLC_HV_sigma0_db_quicklook.tif", compress="LZW")
    print(f"Wrote quick looks to {output_dir.resolve()}")  # where the files were written

title: NISAR RSLC: Range-Doppler Single Look Complex Processing
text:
Interpretation and next steps

Bright HH returns indicate stronger co-polarized backscatter; HV highlights depolarizing vegetation and rough surfaces. Water is typically dark in both channels, subject to wind, incidence geometry, and local conditions.
The beta0-to-sigma0 conversion here is an ellipsoid-incidence approximation. For radiometric terrain correction and map-projected analysis, use the matching NISAR GCOV product or an ISCE3 workflow with a DEM.
The sparse geolocation grid and geocode_l1 interpolation provide an exploratory map only. They do not model terrain-dependent radar visibility, layover, or shadow.
For multi-date deformation, use matched RSLCs and a full InSAR workflow: precise orbit/DEM-assisted co-registration, complex interferogram formation, coherence, phase filtering, unwrapping, referencing, displacement conversion, and terrain-aware geocoding. The outputs in this notebook are intensity quick looks, not phase-preserving SLC data.

title: NISAR GCOV: Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance Processing
text:
Processing overview and limitations
GCOV is a geocoded Level-2 covariance product on a projected map grid. Unlike the complex GSLC, GCOV stores averaged real covariance terms and associated product masks. This scene is on a 10 m EPSG:32646 grid and contains HHHH and HVHV, representing co-polarized and cross-polarized power terms. It does not contain VVVV or the cross-covariance terms needed for full quad-pol analysis.
The AOI subset is read from HDF5 in bounded chunks and block-averaged to approximately 100 m for visualization. The HHHH/HVHV layers are inspected as linear gamma0 covariance terms; the provided rtcGammaToSigmaFactor is applied pixel-by-pixel to derive an approximate sigma0 view. GeoLattice Lee filtering and dB conversion are used for display. This is not a substitute for inspecting calibration, masks, and product specification when doing quantitative analysis.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Import libraries, locate the NISAR GCOV HDF5 scene and the AOI GeoJSON on
# disk, and sanity-check that both files actually exist before any later cell
# tries to open them.

from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd  # vector data (the AOI)
import h5py  # read NISAR HDF5 files
import leafmap  # interactive web maps
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import rioxarray  # registers the .rio accessor
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

from geolattice import rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing
from geolattice.rsense.sar import nisar  # NISAR helpers

# 1. Render figures at a slightly higher DPI than the matplotlib default so
#    the covariance/dB panels later in the notebook are easier to read.
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})

# 2. Resolve the data directory so the notebook runs both from the repo root
#    (e.g. in CI) and from this notebook's own folder (typical interactive
#    use), falling back to a local "../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/NISAR_bd" folder in the latter case.
DATA_RELATIVE = Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/NISAR_bd")
if not DATA_RELATIVE.exists():  # when run from the repository root instead of this folder
    DATA_RELATIVE = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_03_radar/NISAR_bd")  # use the path from the root
DATA_DIR = DATA_RELATIVE  # the data folder

# 3. Point at the specific GCOV granule (frequency-A, dual-pol HH/HV) and its
#    matching AOI polygon, then fail fast with a clear message if either file
#    is missing rather than letting a later cell raise an opaque HDF5 error.
SCENE = DATA_DIR / (
    "NISAR_L2_PR_GCOV_031_069_A_013_4005_DHDH_A_20260922T232058_"
    "20260922T232133_P05023_N_F_J_001.h5"
)
AOI_PATH = DATA_DIR / "AOI_coastal.geojson"  # the coastal AOI polygon
assert SCENE.is_file(), f"NISAR GCOV file not found: {SCENE.resolve()}"  # stop if the GCOV file is missing
assert AOI_PATH.is_file(), f"AOI GeoJSON not found: {AOI_PATH.resolve()}"  # stop if the AOI file is missing

# 4. Echo the resolved paths and the installed GeoLattice version so the notebook
#    output records exactly what was read, which helps with reproducibility.
print(f"GeoLattice remote sensing version: {rs.__version__}")
print(f"GCOV: {SCENE.name}")  # the GCOV file
print(f"AOI:  {AOI_PATH}")  # the AOI file

title: NISAR GCOV: Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance Processing
section: Inspect the product and covariance layers
text:
Inspect the product and covariance layers
GeoLattice reads the product identification metadata and inventories the frequency-A grid. This inventory reports dataset shapes and metadata without loading the multi-gigabyte covariance arrays.


Code
# Inspect the GCOV product identification metadata and the frequency-A grid
# layout without loading the full (multi-gigabyte) covariance arrays.

# 1. Read the product identification group (mission, product type/level,
#    track/frame, orbit direction, zero-Doppler time window, DOI, ...) and
#    print only the keys that are actually present in this granule.
identification = nisar.read_identification(SCENE, "GCOV")
# list the datasets of the frequency-A grid
grid_info = nisar.inspect_hdf5(SCENE, "/science/LSAR/GCOV/grids/frequencyA")

for key in (  # identification fields to show
    "missionId", "productType", "productLevel", "productVersion",
    "trackNumber", "frameNumber", "orbitPassDirection", "lookDirection",
    "zeroDopplerStartTime", "zeroDopplerEndTime", "productDoi",
):
    if key in identification:  # print only the fields that are present
        print(f"{key}: {identification[key]}")  # field name and value

# 2. Open the frequency-A grid group directly with h5py (read-only, closed
#    automatically by the "with" block) to pull out the small, cheap-to-read
#    scalars and 1-D coordinate axes needed for the rest of the notebook:
#    which covariance terms/polarizations exist, the overall raster shape,
#    the projection (EPSG code) and pixel spacing, and the x/y coordinate
#    axes used later to compute AOI row/column windows.
GRID = "/science/LSAR/GCOV/grids/frequencyA"
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:  # open the GCOV file
    grid = f[GRID]  # the frequency-A grid group
    image_shape = grid["HHHH"].shape  # size of the HHHH grid
    # covariance terms in the file (decoded from bytes)
    covariance_terms = [v.decode() if isinstance(v, bytes) else str(v)
                        for v in grid["listOfCovarianceTerms"][:]]
    polarizations = [v.decode() if isinstance(v, bytes) else str(v)  # polarisations (decoded from bytes)
                     for v in grid["listOfPolarizations"][:]]
    epsg = int(grid["projection"][()])  # EPSG code of the map projection

title: NISAR GCOV: Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance Processing
section: Select the AOI and inspect it on satellite imagery
text:
Select the AOI and inspect it on satellite imagery
The GCOV is already geocoded. The AOI is transformed into the product CRS to calculate the exact row/column subset from the coordinate axes. Leafmap displays the supplied polygon over Esri World Imagery as a geographic context check; the subset itself remains based on the GCOV projected grid.


Code
# Load the AOI polygon, convert it into the GCOV map grid's CRS to find the
# exact row/column subset to read, and plot the AOI over satellite imagery
# as an independent visual check that it lands where expected.

# 1. Read the AOI GeoJSON and guard against an empty file. If the file has
#    no CRS defined, assume geographic WGS84 (EPSG:4326) rather than failing
#    on the reprojection below.
aoi = gpd.read_file(AOI_PATH)
if aoi.empty:  # the AOI file has no polygon
    raise ValueError(f"AOI contains no features: {AOI_PATH}")  # stop with a clear message
if aoi.crs is None:  # assume WGS 84 when the file has no CRS
    aoi = aoi.set_crs("EPSG:4326")  # set it

# 2. Keep a lon/lat copy for the Leafmap basemap display, and reproject a
#    separate copy into the GCOV product's own projected CRS (from the
#    "epsg" variable read out of the grid in the previous cell) because the
#    row/column lookup below must be done in the product's native grid, not
#    in geographic coordinates.
aoi_ll = aoi.to_crs("EPSG:4326")
aoi_grid = aoi.to_crs(f"EPSG:{epsg}")  # the AOI in the grid's projection
min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y = aoi_grid.total_bounds  # its bounding box

# 3. Translate the AOI's projected bounding box into GCOV array indices by
#    finding which entries of the x/y coordinate axes fall inside it. This
#    works directly because GCOV is already geocoded onto a regular grid,
#    unlike a range/azimuth radar product that would need resampling first.
row_indices = np.flatnonzero((y_axis >= min_y) & (y_axis <= max_y))
column_indices = np.flatnonzero((x_axis >= min_x) & (x_axis <= max_x))  # columns inside the AOI
if row_indices.size == 0 or column_indices.size == 0:  # no overlap
    raise ValueError("The AOI does not overlap the GCOV map grid")  # stop with a clear message
row_start, row_stop = int(row_indices[0]), int(row_indices[-1] + 1)  # first and last row (+1)
column_start, column_stop = int(column_indices[0]), int(column_indices[-1] + 1)  # first and last column (+1)
# AOI bounds in the grid CRS
print(f"AOI bounds in EPSG:{epsg}: {min_x:.1f}, {min_y:.1f}, {max_x:.1f}, {max_y:.1f}")
# the grid window
print(f"GCOV window: rows {row_start:,}:{row_stop:,}, columns {column_start:,}:{column_stop:,}")
print(f"Window size: {row_stop-row_start:,} x {column_stop-column_start:,} source pixels")  # its size

# 4. Build a quick Leafmap view centered on the AOI, draped over Esri World
#    Imagery, purely as a geographic context check (does the polygon fall
#    where it should on the coast?) - this is independent of, and does not
#    feed into, the GCOV pixel subsetting computed above.
west, south, east, north = aoi_ll.total_bounds
center = ((south + north) / 2, (west + east) / 2)  # map centre (lat, lon)
aoi_map = leafmap.Map(center=center, zoom=8, height="600px")  # an interactive map
aoi_map.add_basemap("Esri.WorldImagery")  # satellite basemap
aoi_map.add_gdf(  # add the AOI polygon
    aoi_ll,
    layer_name="Coastal AOI",
    style={"color": "#ff3b30", "weight": 3, "fillColor": "#ff3b30", "fillOpacity": 0.12},
    hover_style={"color": "#ffff00", "weight": 4, "fillOpacity": 0.2},
    zoom_to_layer=False,
)
aoi_map.add_layer_control()  # layer switcher
aoi_map  # show the map

title: NISAR GCOV: Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance Processing
section: Stream and aggregate the covariance layers
text:
Stream and aggregate the covariance layers
The GCOV scene is large, so this cell reads only AOI rows and columns in bounded chunks. Each output cell aggregates covariance in linear units; dB conversion happens later. The source mask marks valid subswath values from 1 through 254. Values 0 (partially focused/invalid) and 255 (outside the acquisition) are excluded. The RTC factor is applied per source pixel before aggregating sigma0, not after averaging.


Code
# Stream only the AOI rows/columns of the GCOV covariance terms from HDF5 in
# bounded row chunks, mask out invalid/out-of-swath pixels, apply the RTC
# gamma0-to-sigma0 factor per source pixel, and block-average down to a
# coarser display grid - all without ever loading the full scene into memory.

LOOKS = (10, 10)  # 10 m GCOV pixels -> approximately 100 m display cells
OUTPUT_ROWS_PER_CHUNK = 4  # aggregated rows computed per read

# block averages of gamma0, sigma0 and the RTC factor, read chunk by chunk
def stream_gcov_window(grid_group, window, looks=LOOKS,
                       output_rows_per_chunk=OUTPUT_ROWS_PER_CHUNK):
    """Block-average valid dual-pol GCOV gamma0, sigma0, and RTC factor."""
    # 1. Snap the requested window down to a whole number of output blocks
    #    (out_rows x out_columns at the given "looks" factor) so every block
    #    below is uniformly sized; a window smaller than one block is an error.
    row0, row1, col0, col1 = window
    look_y, look_x = looks  # looks in y and x
    out_rows = (row1 - row0) // look_y  # output rows
    out_columns = (col1 - col0) // look_x  # output columns
    if out_rows < 1 or out_columns < 1:  # window smaller than one block
        # stop with a clear message
        raise ValueError("AOI window is smaller than the selected aggregation factors")
    row1 = row0 + out_rows * look_y  # trim to whole blocks
    col1 = col0 + out_columns * look_x  # trim to whole blocks

    # 2. Pre-allocate NaN-filled output arrays for every layer this function
    #    produces, so any output block that ends up with zero valid source
    #    pixels is correctly left as NaN rather than 0.
    names = ("hh_gamma0", "hv_gamma0", "hh_sigma0", "hv_sigma0", "rtc_factor")
    # one output array per layer
    output = {name: np.full((out_rows, out_columns), np.nan, dtype="float32") for name in names}

    # 3. Walk down the output grid a few rows at a time (output_rows_per_chunk)
    #    rather than reading the whole AOI window at once, which keeps peak
    #    memory bounded regardless of how large the AOI is.
    for out0 in range(0, out_rows, output_rows_per_chunk):
        count = min(output_rows_per_chunk, out_rows - out0)  # output rows in this chunk
        source0 = row0 + out0 * look_y  # first source row
        source1 = source0 + count * look_y  # last source row
        row_slice, col_slice = slice(source0, source1), slice(col0, col1)  # row and column slices of the chunk

        # 4. Read this chunk's source pixels for both diagonal covariance
        #    terms, the RTC gamma0-to-sigma0 factor, and the product mask.
        hh = grid_group["HHHH"][row_slice, col_slice]
        hv = grid_group["HVHV"][row_slice, col_slice]  # HV backscatter (gamma0) of the chunk
        # gamma0-to-sigma0 factor of the chunk
        factor = grid_group["rtcGammaToSigmaFactor"][row_slice, col_slice]
        mask = grid_group["mask"][row_slice, col_slice]  # the product's validity mask

        # 5. Build the valid-pixel mask: the GCOV mask convention treats 0 as
        #    partially focused/invalid and 255 as outside the acquisition, so
        #    only values 1-254 denote valid subswath coverage. Also drop any
        #    non-finite values and physically impossible (negative) power.
        valid = (mask > 0) & (mask < 255)
        # drop NaN, non-positive HH and negative HV
        valid &= np.isfinite(hh) & np.isfinite(hv) & (hh > 0) & (hv >= 0)

        # 6. Derive sigma0 from gamma0 by applying the RTC factor per source
        #    pixel (before averaging), since the factor itself varies pixel
        #    to pixel and averaging first would give a biased result.
        blocks = {
            "hh_gamma0": hh,
            "hv_gamma0": hv,
            "hh_sigma0": hh * factor,
            "hv_sigma0": hv * factor,
            "rtc_factor": factor,
        }
        # 7. For each layer, reshape the chunk into (rows, look_y, cols, look_x)
        #    blocks, sum only the valid entries per block, divide by the count
        #    of valid entries, and store NaN for any block with no valid data
        #    at all - i.e. a masked block-average in linear units.
        for name, layer in blocks.items():
            layer_valid = valid & np.isfinite(layer)  # valid values of this layer
            layer_blocks = layer.reshape(count, look_y, out_columns, look_x)  # values grouped into blocks
            # validity grouped into blocks
            valid_layer_blocks = layer_valid.reshape(count, look_y, out_columns, look_x)
            # sum of valid values per block
            totals = np.where(valid_layer_blocks, layer_blocks, 0).sum(axis=(1, 3))
            n_valid = valid_layer_blocks.sum(axis=(1, 3))  # number of valid values per block
            output[name][out0:out0 + count] = np.divide(  # mean per block
                totals, n_valid,
                out=np.full((count, out_columns), np.nan, dtype="float32"),
                where=n_valid > 0,
            )
    return output  # the aggregated layers

# 8. Snap the AOI window from the previous cell down to a whole number of
#    LOOKS-sized output blocks (mirrors the snapping done inside the
#    function) so the output coordinate axes built below line up exactly
#    with the aggregated arrays returned by stream_gcov_window.
n_output_rows = (row_stop - row_start) // LOOKS[0]
n_output_columns = (column_stop - column_start) // LOOKS[1]  # output columns
row_stop = row_start + n_output_rows * LOOKS[0]  # trim to whole blocks
column_stop = column_start + n_output_columns * LOOKS[1]  # trim to whole blocks
window = (row_start, row_stop, column_start, column_stop)  # the final window
with h5py.File(SCENE, "r") as f:  # open the GCOV file
    gcov = stream_gcov_window(f[GRID], window)  # aggregate the AOI window

# 9. Build the coarse output x/y coordinate axes as the mean position of
#    each block of source pixels it was aggregated from, so the downsampled
#    arrays carry geographically meaningful coordinates for later plotting
#    and clipping.
out_x = x_axis[column_start:column_stop].reshape(n_output_columns, LOOKS[1]).mean(axis=1)
# y coordinate of every output row
out_y = y_axis[row_start:row_stop].reshape(n_output_rows, LOOKS[0]).mean(axis=1)
coords = {"y": out_y, "x": out_x}  # coordinates of the output grid
print(f"Aggregated GCOV grid: {n_output_rows:,} rows x {n_output_columns:,} columns")  # grid size
print(f"Valid HH gamma0 fraction: {np.isfinite(gcov['hh_gamma0']).mean():.1%}")  # valid HH share
print(f"Valid HV gamma0 fraction: {np.isfinite(gcov['hv_gamma0']).mean():.1%}")  # valid HV share
print(f"Mean RTC gamma0-to-sigma0 factor: {np.nanmean(gcov['rtc_factor']):.3f}")  # mean gamma0-to-sigma0 factor

title: NISAR GCOV: Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance Processing
text:
Dual-polarization indices and GeoLattice filtering
GeoLattice nisar.gcov_indices computes the HV/HH ratio and dual-pol RVI from linear gamma0 covariance terms. Since this granule has no VVVV term, quad-pol RVI and HH/VV ratio are intentionally not computed. GeoLattice Lee filtering is applied to linear sigma0 quick looks; the filtered layers are converted to dB only for display.


Code
# Wrap the aggregated numpy arrays as labeled xarray DataArrays, compute
# dual-polarization indices from the linear gamma0 covariance terms, apply
# GeoLattice Lee speckle filtering to the sigma0 quick looks, convert to dB for
# display only, and plot a 2x2 panel of covariance/index/RTC layers.

# 1. Attach the shared (y, x) coordinates built in the previous cell to each
#    aggregated layer so downstream operations (indices, filtering, plotting,
#    clipping) all carry consistent geographic coordinates.
hh_gamma0 = xr.DataArray(gcov["hh_gamma0"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hh_gamma0")
# HV gamma0 as a DataArray
hv_gamma0 = xr.DataArray(gcov["hv_gamma0"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hv_gamma0")
hh_sigma0 = xr.DataArray(gcov["hh_sigma0"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hh_sigma0")  # HH sigma0
hv_sigma0 = xr.DataArray(gcov["hv_sigma0"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="hv_sigma0")  # HV sigma0
# the gamma0-to-sigma0 factor
rtc_factor = xr.DataArray(gcov["rtc_factor"], dims=("y", "x"), coords=coords, name="rtc_gamma_to_sigma_factor")

# 2. Compute dual-polarization indices (HV/HH ratio and dual-pol RVI) from
#    the linear gamma0 covariance terms. Because this granule lacks VVVV,
#    only the dual-pol variants are available - quad-pol RVI and HH/VV
#    ratio require a term this scene does not contain.
dual_indices = nisar.gcov_indices(hh_gamma0, hv_gamma0)

# 3. Apply a Lee speckle filter to the linear sigma0 quick looks (not to the
#    raw gamma0 covariance terms), then convert the filtered result to dB
#    purely for display - the filtering and the index computation above
#    both operate on linear power, as speckle statistics assume.
hh_sigma0_lee = xr.DataArray(rs.sar.lee(hh_sigma0.values, size=5), dims=("y", "x"),
                             coords=coords, name="hh_sigma0_lee")
# Lee speckle filter on HV sigma0 (5 x 5)
hv_sigma0_lee = xr.DataArray(rs.sar.lee(hv_sigma0.values, size=5), dims=("y", "x"),
                             coords=coords, name="hv_sigma0_lee")
hh_sigma0_db = rs.sar.to_db(hh_sigma0_lee)  # filtered HH sigma0 in dB
hv_sigma0_db = rs.sar.to_db(hv_sigma0_lee)  # filtered HV sigma0 in dB

# 4. Plot a 2x2 panel: the two diagonal covariance terms in dB (stretched to
#    their own 2nd-98th percentile since no fixed display range applies to
#    dB covariance), the dual-pol RVI on a fixed 0-4 scale, and the RTC
#    gamma0-to-sigma0 factor on a fixed 0-1 scale, since both indices have a
#    physically meaningful range rather than a data-dependent one.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 10))
for ax, image, title, cmap, limits in (  # the panels: image, title, colour map and limits
    (axes[0, 0], rs.sar.to_db(hh_gamma0), "HHHH gamma0 covariance (dB)", "gray", None),
    (axes[0, 1], rs.sar.to_db(hv_gamma0), "HVHV gamma0 covariance (dB)", "gray", None),
    (axes[1, 0], dual_indices["dual_pol_rvi"], "Dual-pol RVI from gamma0", "YlGn", (0, 4)),
    (axes[1, 1], rtc_factor, "RTC gamma0-to-sigma0 factor", "viridis", (0, 1)),
):
    if limits is None:  # no fixed limits: use a 2-98 % stretch
        vmin, vmax = np.nanpercentile(image.values, [2, 98])  # stretch limits
    else:
        vmin, vmax = limits  # fixed limits
    artist = ax.imshow(image, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, origin="upper")  # show the image
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (m)", ylabel="Northing (m)")  # title and axis labels
    plt.colorbar(artist, ax=ax, shrink=0.78)  # colour bar
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw









The covariance and index panels are visualized on the aggregated grid. The RTC factor is a product-provided normalization layer; it is not itself a terrain correction model. Check the GCOV product specification and per-layer metadata before interpreting values across scenes or processing versions.

title: NISAR GCOV: Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance Processing
section: Georeference and clip the outputs to the AOI
text:
Georeference and clip the outputs to the AOI
The GCOV data are already map-projected. Attach the EPSG to the downsampled xarray layers, then clip to the exact supplied GeoJSON polygon using rioxarray.


Code
# Attach the GCOV product's CRS to each aggregated xarray layer and clip
# every layer to the exact AOI polygon (not just its bounding box), then plot
# the clipped HHHH/HVHV covariance panels with the AOI boundary overlaid.

def georeference_and_clip(image):
    # 1. Tell rioxarray which dimensions are x/y, stamp the GCOV grid's EPSG
    #    code onto the array (the data is already projected, so this only
    #    labels it rather than reprojecting), then clip to the AOI polygon's
    #    exact geometry. all_touched=True keeps any output pixel the polygon
    #    boundary passes through, matching the row/column window logic used
    #    when the AOI was first selected.
    return image.rio.set_spatial_dims(x_dim="x", y_dim="y").rio.write_crs(
        f"EPSG:{epsg}"
    ).rio.clip(aoi_grid.geometry, aoi_grid.crs, drop=True, all_touched=True)

# 2. Apply the same georeference-and-clip step to every aggregated layer that
#    later cells need in AOI-clipped form: both diagonal covariance terms,
#    the dual-pol RVI index, the RTC factor, and the Lee-filtered sigma0 dB
#    layers used for the RGB composite in Step 6.
hh_gamma0_aoi = georeference_and_clip(hh_gamma0)
hv_gamma0_aoi = georeference_and_clip(hv_gamma0)  # HV gamma0, clipped to the AOI
rvi_aoi = georeference_and_clip(dual_indices["dual_pol_rvi"])  # dual-pol RVI, clipped
rtc_aoi = georeference_and_clip(rtc_factor)  # RTC factor, clipped
hh_sigma0_db_aoi = georeference_and_clip(hh_sigma0_db)  # HH sigma0 in dB, clipped
hv_sigma0_db_aoi = georeference_and_clip(hv_sigma0_db)  # HV sigma0 in dB, clipped

# 3. Plot the clipped HH and HV gamma0 covariance terms in dB side by side,
#    using xarray's built-in imshow (robust=True stretches to a robust
#    percentile range automatically) with the AOI boundary drawn on top so
#    the clip extent is visually verifiable.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))
for ax, image, title in (  # the panels with their titles
    (axes[0], rs.sar.to_db(hh_gamma0_aoi), "HHHH gamma0 covariance (dB), AOI"),
    (axes[1], rs.sar.to_db(hv_gamma0_aoi), "HVHV gamma0 covariance (dB), AOI"),
):
    # show with a robust stretch
    image.plot.imshow(ax=ax, cmap="gray", robust=True, cbar_kwargs={"label": "dB"})
    aoi_grid.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="cyan", linewidth=0.7)  # AOI outline
    ax.set_title(title)  # title
    ax.set_aspect("equal")  # equal scale
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

print(f"AOI output grid: {hh_gamma0_aoi.sizes['y']:,} rows x {hh_gamma0_aoi.sizes['x']:,} columns")  # grid size
print(f"CRS: {hh_gamma0_aoi.rio.crs}; source pixel spacing: {x_spacing:g} m")  # CRS and pixel spacing

title: NISAR GCOV: Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance Processing
text:
Dual-polarization RGB composite
Display red = HH sigma0 (dB), green = HV sigma0 (dB), and blue = HH−HV (dB), equivalent to the HH/HV ratio in decibels. Each channel is contrast-stretched independently from its 2nd to 98th percentile. This false-color composite is for visual interpretation only.


Code
# Build a false-color dual-polarization RGB composite for visual
# interpretation: red = HH sigma0 (dB), green = HV sigma0 (dB), and
# blue = HH-HV (dB), i.e. the HH/HV ratio expressed in decibels.

# 1. Pull the AOI-clipped, Lee-filtered sigma0 dB arrays out as plain numpy
#    arrays and compute the HH-HV difference, which in dB space is
#    equivalent to the HH/HV linear ratio. Track which pixels are finite in
#    both channels so invalid AOI-edge pixels can be masked out uniformly.
hh_values = hh_sigma0_db_aoi.values.astype("float32")
hv_values = hv_sigma0_db_aoi.values.astype("float32")  # HV in dB
ratio_values = hh_values - hv_values  # HH minus HV (dB)
valid_rgb = np.isfinite(hh_values) & np.isfinite(hv_values)  # pixels valid in both

# stretch one channel to [0, 1] between percentiles of its valid values
def stretch_channel(values, mask, percentiles=(2, 98)):
    # 2. Contrast-stretch one channel independently of the others, using
    #    only the valid (finite) pixels to compute the 2nd/98th percentile
    #    bounds, then clip and rescale to 0-1 for display as an RGB channel.
    #    A degenerate (constant) channel is returned as all zeros rather
    #    than dividing by zero.
    finite_values = values[mask]
    if finite_values.size == 0:  # no valid values
        raise ValueError("RGB channel has no finite data inside the AOI")  # stop with a clear message
    low, high = np.percentile(finite_values, percentiles)  # percentile limits
    if high <= low:  # constant channel
        return np.zeros(values.shape, dtype="float32")  # return zeros
    return np.clip((values - low) / (high - low), 0, 1).astype("float32")  # stretch to [0, 1]

# 3. Stack the three independently stretched channels into an (rows, cols, 3)
#    RGB image (red=HH, green=HV, blue=HH-HV ratio), then force any pixel
#    that was invalid in either source channel to black rather than letting
#    it show a partially-stretched or NaN color.
rgb = np.stack((
    stretch_channel(hh_values, valid_rgb),
    stretch_channel(hv_values, valid_rgb),
    stretch_channel(ratio_values, valid_rgb),
), axis=-1)
rgb[~valid_rgb] = 0  # no-data pixels in black

# 4. Plot the composite using the AOI's own x/y coordinate extent (rather
#    than pixel indices) so it lines up with the AOI boundary overlay, and
#    use "nearest" interpolation to avoid blending real and masked pixels.
x = hh_sigma0_db_aoi.x.values
y = hh_sigma0_db_aoi.y.values  # northing values
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))  # one panel
# the RGB composite in map coordinates
ax.imshow(rgb, extent=(x.min(), x.max(), y.min(), y.max()), origin="upper", interpolation="nearest")
aoi_grid.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=0.8)  # AOI outline
ax.set(xlabel="Easting (m)", ylabel="Northing (m)",  # axis labels and title
       title="NISAR GCOV dual-pol false-color RGB\nR: HH sigma0 dB | G: HV sigma0 dB | B: HH/HV dB")
ax.set_aspect("equal")  # equal scale
plt.tight_layout()  # arrange
plt.show()  # draw

title: NISAR GCOV: Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance Processing
text:
Summary, exercises and references
Summary

NISAR GCOV is a geocoded Level-2 covariance product; this granule uses a 10 m EPSG:32646 grid.
The available terms are HHHH and HVHV, so this scene supports dual-polarization analysis, not full quad-pol decomposition.
The AOI subset is streamed from HDF5, invalid mask values are excluded, and linear covariance and RTC-scaled sigma0 values are aggregated before dB display.
GeoLattice computes the HV/HH ratio and dual-pol RVI and applies Lee filtering to linear power.
Display stretches and the RGB composite are visual aids; they are not calibrated comparisons across scenes.

Conclusion
This notebook demonstrates a memory-bounded GeoLattice workflow for examining NISAR GCOV over the coastal Bangladesh AOI. Because the product is already geocoded, the AOI can be selected directly from its projected coordinate axes. The supplied granule contains only HH and HV diagonal covariance terms; use its matched product documentation and full covariance terms where available before attempting quad-polarimetric interpretation. For rigorous analysis, preserve the native product grid, masks, and metadata and validate whether gamma0 or RTC-scaled sigma0 is appropriate for the application.
Additional resources

NASA NISAR mission data and products
ASF DAAC NISAR dataset information
NISAR product specification documentation
ISCE3 processing framework
GeoLattice user guide
GeoLattice NISAR readers and GCOV utilities

Leafmap is required for the satellite basemap and is available through the optional geolattice[rsense-viz] dependencies. Confirm product version, processing release, covariance-term definitions, mask metadata, and RTC factor conventions before quantitative use.

Ground sampling distance and footprint
For a nadir camera the size of one pixel on the ground is
\[GSD = \frac{\text{sensor width} \times \text{altitude}}{\text{focal length} \times \text{image width (px)}}\]

text:
Overlap, line spacing and trigger distance
Photogrammetry needs every ground point in several images. Forward (front) overlap is set by the distance between exposures along a line, side overlap by the spacing between lines:

line spacing = footprint width × (1 - side overlap)
trigger distance = footprint height × (1 - front overlap)

The LUMS paper flew two missions per date: 6 m for orthomosaics and 10 m for DEMs.

    p = rs.uav.flight_plan(altitude, camera="mini4pro_4k_video", front_overlap=0.8, side_overlap=0.7)
    rows.append({"mission": purpose, "altitude_m": altitude, **{k: round(v, 3) for k, v in p.items()}})

Video-based capture
LUMS recorded 4K video at 24 frames per second, flying at about 1 m/s, and kept every 6th frame. The distance between kept frames is
\[\text{frame spacing} = \frac{\text{speed} \times \text{frame step}}{\text{fps}} = \frac{1 \times 6}{24} = 0.25\ \text{m}\]

title: UAV Fundamentals and Mission Planning
section: Sizing a mission and flight patterns
text:
Sizing a mission and flight patterns
The LUMS field has two 30 m × 10 m plots. The helper below counts lines, images and flight time for a rectangular block flown in parallel lines.


Code
def mission(width_m, length_m, altitude, camera, *, front=0.8, side=0.7, speed=1.0,
            fps=None, frame_step=1, turn_s=8.0):
    """Lines, images and minutes for a block of parallel lines along the long side."""
    p = rs.uav.flight_plan(altitude, camera=camera, front_overlap=front, side_overlap=side,
                           speed_ms=speed, fps=fps, frame_step=frame_step)
    n_lines = int(np.ceil(width_m / p["line_spacing_m"])) + 1  # cover the block edge to edge
    step = p.get("frame_spacing_m", p["trigger_distance_m"])  # video frame or photo trigger spacing
    per_line = int(np.ceil(length_m / step)) + 1
    seconds = n_lines * length_m / speed + (n_lines - 1) * (p["line_spacing_m"] / speed + turn_s)
    return {"altitude_m": altitude, "gsd_mm": 10 * p["gsd_cm"], "lines": n_lines,
            "line_spacing_m": p["line_spacing_m"], "images": n_lines * per_line, "minutes": seconds / 60}

def draw_pattern(ax, width, length, spacing, multi_s=False):
    """Draw a grid (parallel lines, lawnmower) or a multi-S (cross-hatched) pattern."""
    xs = np.arange(0, width + spacing / 2, spacing)
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):  # serpentine along y
        ys = [0, length] if i % 2 == 0 else [length, 0]
        ax.plot([x, x], ys, color="C0", lw=1.2)
        if i < len(xs) - 1:
            ax.plot([x, xs[i + 1]], [ys[1], ys[1]], color="C0", lw=1.2)
    if multi_s:  # a second pass perpendicular to the first
        ys2 = np.arange(0, length + spacing / 2, spacing)
        for j, y in enumerate(ys2):
            xx = [0, width] if j % 2 == 0 else [width, 0]
            ax.plot(xx, [y, y], color="C3", lw=1.0, alpha=0.8)
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0, 0), width, length, fill=False, color="k", lw=1.5))
    ax.set(aspect="equal", xlabel="m", ylabel="m")

sp = rs.uav.flight_plan(10, camera="mini4pro_4k_video", side_overlap=0.7)["line_spacing_m"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 5.5))
draw_pattern(axes[0], 20, 30, sp); axes[0].set_title("Grid (lawnmower)")
draw_pattern(axes[1], 20, 30, sp, multi_s=True); axes[1].set_title("Multi-S / double grid")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









A single grid is enough for orthomosaics over flat fields. A double grid (multi-S, flown again at 90°) adds viewing angles that stabilise SfM camera calibration and reduce the doming that appears in elevation models built without ground control (notebook 09_04_06). It roughly doubles flight time.

title: UAV Fundamentals and Mission Planning
text:
Sun angle, wind and regulations
Sun. Low sun casts long shadows that hide soil and inflate apparent canopy cover; very high sun over water and wet soil (as in flooded rice) gives specular glare. A common rule is to fly within about two hours of solar noon, or under uniform overcast. The function below gives solar elevation from date, time and latitude (NOAA approximation, accurate to well under a degree).


Code
def solar_elevation(when, lat, lon):
    """Solar elevation angle (degrees) for UTC timestamps at a latitude/longitude."""
    t = pd.to_datetime(when)
    doy = t.dayofyear.to_numpy() if hasattr(t, "dayofyear") else t.dayofyear
    hour = t.hour + t.minute / 60
    g = 2 * np.pi / 365 * (doy - 1 + (hour - 12) / 24)  # fractional year (radians)
    decl = (0.006918 - 0.399912 * np.cos(g) + 0.070257 * np.sin(g) - 0.006758 * np.cos(2 * g)
            + 0.000907 * np.sin(2 * g) - 0.002697 * np.cos(3 * g) + 0.00148 * np.sin(3 * g))
    eqt = 229.18 * (0.000075 + 0.001868 * np.cos(g) - 0.032077 * np.sin(g)
                    - 0.014615 * np.cos(2 * g) - 0.040849 * np.sin(2 * g))  # minutes
    solar_time = hour * 60 + eqt + 4 * lon  # true solar time in minutes
    ha = np.radians(solar_time / 4 - 180)  # hour angle
    phi = np.radians(lat)
    cos_z = np.sin(phi) * np.sin(decl) + np.cos(phi) * np.cos(decl) * np.cos(ha)
    return 90 - np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cos_z, -1, 1)))

lat, lon = 31.47, 74.41  # Lahore (LUMS campus), Pakistan, UTC+5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))
for day in ["2025-08-13", "2025-09-17", "2025-10-03"]:
    utc = pd.date_range(f"{day} 00:00", f"{day} 15:00", freq="10min")  # 05:00-20:00 local
    ax.plot(utc.hour + utc.minute / 60 + 5, solar_elevation(utc, lat, lon), label=day)
ax.axhline(30, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1); ax.text(6.2, 31, "30° (long shadows below)", fontsize=8)
ax.set(xlabel="Local time (h, UTC+5)", ylabel="Solar elevation (°)", title="Sun height over the LUMS field")
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); plt.show()









Wind. Sub-250 g drones drift and tilt in gusts, which blurs frames and changes the view angle; keep sustained wind under about half the aircraft’s rated limit for mapping work, and fly lines across the wind where possible so ground speed stays constant.
Regulations. Rules differ by country and change often. In many jurisdictions drones under 250 g face lighter registration requirements, but altitude limits (commonly 120 m above ground), visual line of sight, distance from people and airports, and data-protection rules still apply. Always check the current rules of your aviation authority and get landowner permission before flying.

title: UAV Fundamentals and Mission Planning
section: Sanity-checking GSD on a real frame
text:
Sanity-checking GSD on a real frame
A frame’s GSD can be checked against any object of known size. Rice in the LUMS field was transplanted in rows; at the reported 1.85 mm/px a 3840 × 2160 frame covers about 7.1 m × 4.0 m. Below, one frame is read with that GSD so the axes are in metres, and a 1 m scale bar is drawn. Compare the bar with the plant spacing you expect (about 0.2 m between hills in transplanted rice) to judge whether the stated GSD is plausible.


Code
frame_path = sorted((LUMS / "2025-08-22").glob("*.png"))[0]  # first sample frame of 22 Aug
gsd_m = 0.00185  # 1.85 mm/px reported for the 6 m orthomosaics
img = rs.uav.read_frame(frame_path, gsd=gsd_m)  # (band, y, x) in metres
print(img.sizes, "| footprint:", round(img.sizes["x"] * gsd_m, 2), "m x", round(img.sizes["y"] * gsd_m, 2), "m")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.2))
ext = [float(img.x.min()), float(img.x.max()), float(img.y.min()), float(img.y.max())]
ax.imshow(rs.uav.to_rgb_array(img), extent=ext)
x0, y0 = ext[0] + 0.3, ext[2] + 0.3
ax.plot([x0, x0 + 1.0], [y0, y0], color="white", lw=4)  # 1 m scale bar
ax.text(x0 + 0.5, y0 + 0.08, "1 m", color="white", ha="center", fontsize=11, weight="bold")
ax.set(xlabel="x (m)", ylabel="y (m)", title=f"{frame_path.parent.name}/{frame_path.name} at 1.85 mm/px")
plt.show()

title: UAV Fundamentals and Mission Planning
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

GSD = sensor width × altitude / (focal length × image width). Treat a camera preset as a planning figure and confirm it on a real frame or in the photogrammetry report.
Line spacing and trigger distance follow from the footprint and the overlap. SfM needs on the order of 75 to 85% forward overlap; the LUMS video still overlaps by about 95% at 6 m.
For video, frame spacing = speed × frame step / fps. At 1 m/s and 24 fps, every 6th frame is 0.25 m apart.
A second grid at 90° costs about twice the flight time and gives the extra view angles that reduce doming when there is no ground control.
Fly within about two hours of solar noon, keep the wind well under the aircraft’s mapping limit, and check the current airspace rules before take-off.

GeoLattice functions used: rs.uav.flight_plan, rs.uav.CAMERAS, rs.uav.read_frame.
Exercises

A MicaSense RedEdge-MX must deliver 5 cm GSD. At what altitude must it fly, and how many lines does a 200 m × 150 m field need at 75 % side overlap?
Using mission(), find the fastest speed at which the LUMS 10 m DEM mission keeps at least 85 % forward overlap when every 12th video frame is kept.
Extend solar_elevation to report the time window when the sun is above 45° on 2025-09-17 at the LUMS field.
Pick another frame from a later date. Do plant spacing and the 1 m bar still agree? What would a 10 m flight do to the bar’s length in pixels?

References

Chaudhry, H., Rana, S. and Jaleel, A. (2026). UAV-based crop reconstruction and trait estimation using RGB imagery without external geospatial infrastructure. Computers and Electronics in Agriculture (accepted). Data: CC BY 4.0; code: MIT.
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory. General solar position calculations.
James, M. R. and Robson, S. (2014). Mitigating systematic error in topographic models derived from UAV and ground-based image networks. Earth Surface Processes and Landforms, 39, 1413-1420.

title: Photogrammetry: Orthomosaic, DSM and DTM
text:
Overview
The difference between the surface and the bare ground is the canopy height model (CHM). This notebook explains the SfM steps on real LUMS frames, shows how to run OpenDroneMap (ODM) from Python with rs.uav.run_docker and rs.uav.run_nodeodm, and loads finished products with rs.uav.load_outputs, whether they come from ODM or from commercial software such as Agisoft Metashape (used in the LUMS paper).

title: Photogrammetry: Orthomosaic, DSM and DTM
text:
The SfM pipeline








Step
What happens
What can go wrong




1. Feature detection
Thousands of distinctive points (SIFT, ORB) per image
Few features over uniform water or soil


2. Matching
Same points found in overlapping images; outliers removed with RANSAC
Low overlap, repeated texture (crop rows), wind-moved leaves


3. Bundle adjustment
Camera positions, orientations and lens model solved together with 3-D points
Lens model and camera height trade off: doming


4. Georeferencing
Model scaled and placed with GPS tags, GCPs or RTK
Consumer GPS: metres of absolute error


5. Dense matching
Depth for nearly every pixel: dense point cloud
Thin leaves, moving canopy


6. DSM / DTM
Highest (DSM) or ground-classified (DTM) points gridded
Ground hidden under full canopy


7. Orthomosaic
Images projected onto the DSM and blended
Seams, ghosting on tall plants



Steps 1 and 2 can be demonstrated directly on the data.

title: Photogrammetry: Orthomosaic, DSM and DTM
section: Features and matching on real frames
text:
Features and matching on real frames
The public LUMS sample frames were picked from different parts of the field, so no two of them overlap. To see matching at work, the cell below makes two “views” from one frame: a left window and a right window that share a chosen fraction of their width, with the second view slightly rotated and rescaled as a drone would see it on the next pass. ORB features are then matched and a homography is fitted with RANSAC using rs.uav.estimate_homography.


Code
frame = rs.uav.to_rgb_array(rs.uav.read_frame(sorted((LUMS / "2025-08-22").glob("*.png"))[0], max_dim=1920))
gray = cv2.cvtColor((frame * 255).astype(np.uint8), cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
H_img, W_img = gray.shape

def two_views(img, overlap, width=640, angle=4.0, scale=1.03):
    """Two windows of `width` px sharing `overlap` of their width; the second rotated/scaled."""
    shift_px = int(round(width * (1 - overlap)))
    x0 = (img.shape[1] - width - shift_px) // 2
    a = img[:, x0:x0 + width]
    b_full = img[:, x0 + shift_px:x0 + shift_px + width]
    M = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((width / 2, img.shape[0] / 2), angle, scale)
    b = cv2.warpAffine(b_full, M, (width, img.shape[0]), borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT)
    return a, b

a, b = two_views(gray, 0.75)
orb = cv2.ORB_create(3000)
ka, da = orb.detectAndCompute(a, None); kb, db = orb.detectAndCompute(b, None)
m = sorted(cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_HAMMING, crossCheck=True).match(da, db), key=lambda x: x.distance)[:80]
vis = cv2.drawMatches(a, ka, b, kb, m, None, flags=cv2.DrawMatchesFlags_NOT_DRAW_SINGLE_POINTS)
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4.5)); plt.imshow(vis); plt.axis("off")
plt.title(f"ORB features: {len(ka)} and {len(kb)}; 80 best cross-checked matches shown (75 % overlap)")
plt.show()









Now vary the overlap. The number of RANSAC inliers (matches consistent with one geometric model) collapses as overlap falls, which is why mapping missions plan 75 to 85 % forward overlap.


Code
rows = []
for ov in [0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2]:
    a, b = two_views(gray, ov)
    try:
        _, info = rs.uav.estimate_homography(b, a, method="orb", n_features=3000)
    except RuntimeError as e:  # too few matches
        info = {"matches": 0, "inliers": 0, "rmse_px": np.nan}
    rows.append({"overlap_%": int(ov * 100), **{k: info[k] for k in ("matches", "inliers", "rmse_px")}})
ov_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(ov_tab.round(2))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
ax.plot(ov_tab["overlap_%"], ov_tab.inliers, "o-", lw=2)
ax.set(xlabel="Overlap between views (%)", ylabel="RANSAC inliers", title="Matches available to bundle adjustment")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3); plt.show()

Repeated texture is the other enemy: rice rows look alike everywhere, so a feature can match the wrong row. Lowe’s ratio test (used inside estimate_homography) rejects a match when the second-best candidate is almost as good as the best one, and RANSAC removes the rest.

Ground control: GCP / RTK vs infrastructure-free









Approach

GCPs surveyed with GNSS
1-3 cm
Targets laid and surveyed every flight

2-5 cm

Little doming

metres
None
Doming / bowl and tilt in the DEM



The LUMS study used no GCPs and no RTK. Its orthomosaics are therefore internally consistent but not accurately placed on Earth, and its elevation models carried a dome-shaped error that was removed afterwards with RANSAC plane/polynomial fitting (notebook 09_04_06). For relative traits within a field (counts, cover, height above local ground) this is enough.

title: Photogrammetry: Orthomosaic, DSM and DTM
text:
Running OpenDroneMap from Python
ODM is the open alternative to Agisoft Metashape and Pix4D. GeoLattice drives it two ways:

rs.uav.run_docker(project_dir, options=...) runs the opendronemap/odm image on project_dir/images and writes the products into project_dir.
rs.uav.run_nodeodm(images, out_dir, host=..., port=...) sends images to a NodeODM server (docker run -p 3000:3000 opendronemap/nodeodm), waits and downloads the results. Needs pip install pyodm.

The options mirror ODM’s command-line flags. For the LUMS 6 m frames a sensible start is:


Code
odm_options = {
    "dsm": True, "dtm": True,               # build both elevation models
    "orthophoto-resolution": 0.2,           # cm/px; about the frame GSD at 6 m
    "dem-resolution": 0.6,                  # cm/px; DEMs are noisier, so coarser
    "feature-quality": "high",
    "pc-quality": "high",
    "matcher-neighbors": 16,                # video frames: many close neighbours
    "use-3dmesh": False,                    # 2.5-D mesh is better for flat fields
    "auto-boundary": True,
}
pd.Series(odm_options, name="value").to_frame()

        shutil.copy(f, imgs / f.name)

section: Loading products: ODM layout or explicit paths
text:
Loading products: ODM layout or explicit paths
rs.uav.load_outputs(odm_dir) looks for odm_orthophoto/odm_orthophoto.tif, odm_dem/dsm.tif and odm_dem/dtm.tif. Metashape and Pix4D use other names, so explicit paths can be given instead (or in addition).
So that this section runs without a photogrammetry run, the cell below writes a small set of example products: an orthomosaic made from a LUMS frame, placed in UTM zone 43N at the LUMS field with 1.85 mm pixels, and a DSM/DTM pair built with rs.uav.synthetic_dem, which adds a realistic GCP-free dome and tilt. The DTM is written on a shifted grid of the same size, as happens when two products come from different exports.


Code
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (registers the .rio accessor)
from affine import Affine

crs = "EPSG:32643"  # WGS 84 / UTM 43N (Lahore)
x0, y0 = 437_000.0, 3_481_500.0  # an easting/northing near the LUMS campus (illustrative)

ortho = rs.uav.read_frame(sorted((LUMS / "2025-08-22").glob("*.png"))[0], max_dim=1920)
gsd_o = 0.00185 * 3840 / ortho.sizes["x"]  # GSD after downsizing
ortho = ortho.assign_coords(x=x0 + gsd_o * (np.arange(ortho.sizes["x"]) + 0.5),
                            y=y0 - gsd_o * (np.arange(ortho.sizes["y"]) + 0.5)).rio.write_crs(crs)
ortho_path = OUT / "example_ortho.tif"
ortho.rio.to_raster(ortho_path)

big_dsm, big_chm = rs.uav.synthetic_dem((184, 326), gsd=0.02, doming=0.8, canopy_height=0.5, seed=3)
ground = big_dsm - big_chm  # true (domed) ground surface on the large grid

def place(da):
    """Give a local-grid DataArray UTM coordinates."""
    return da.assign_coords(x=x0 + da.x.values, y=y0 + da.y.values).rio.write_crs(crs)

dsm = place(big_dsm.isel(y=slice(0, 180), x=slice(0, 320)))          # DSM export grid
chm_true = big_chm.isel(y=slice(0, 180), x=slice(0, 320)).values      # truth on the DSM grid
dtm = place(ground.isel(y=slice(2, 182), x=slice(3, 323)))            # DTM export: same size, 3 x 2 px offset
dsm_path, dtm_path = OUT / "example_dsm.tif", OUT / "example_dtm.tif"
dsm.rio.to_raster(dsm_path); dtm.rio.to_raster(dtm_path)
print("DSM origin", float(dsm.x[0]), float(dsm.y[0]), "| DTM origin", float(dtm.x[0]), float(dtm.y[0]))
print("wrote", ortho_path, dsm_path, dtm_path)

title: Photogrammetry: Orthomosaic, DSM and DTM
text:
Canopy height from DSM - DTM
rs.uav.chm_from_surfaces checks CRS and grid alignment (not just the shape) and reprojects the DTM onto the DSM grid when they differ. Subtracting the raw arrays of the shifted pair would mix pixels 6 cm apart.


Code
dsm_r, dtm_r = products["dsm"], products["dtm"]
naive = dsm_r.squeeze().values - dtm_r.squeeze().values  # wrong: ignores the offset
chm = rs.uav.chm_from_surfaces(dsm_r, dtm_r, min_height=0.0)
truth = chm_true
inner = (slice(4, -4), slice(4, -4))  # skip the border the DTM does not cover
err = pd.DataFrame({
    "method": ["raw array difference", "chm_from_surfaces"],
    "RMSE_m": [np.sqrt(np.nanmean((naive - truth)[inner] ** 2)),
               np.sqrt(np.nanmean((chm.values - truth)[inner] ** 2))],
})
display(err.round(3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.6))
ext = [float(dsm_r.x.min()) - x0, float(dsm_r.x.max()) - x0, float(dsm_r.y.min()) - y0, float(dsm_r.y.max()) - y0]
im0 = axes[0].imshow(dsm_r.squeeze(), cmap="terrain", extent=ext); axes[0].set_title("DSM (m): canopy on a dome")
im1 = axes[1].imshow(chm, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=0.8, extent=ext); axes[1].set_title("CHM = DSM - DTM (aligned)")
im2 = axes[2].imshow(naive - truth, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-0.3, vmax=0.3, extent=ext); axes[2].set_title("Error of raw difference (m)")
for ax, im in zip(axes, [im0, im1, im2]):
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8); ax.set(xlabel="m", ylabel="m")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Two points stand out. First, the DSM is dominated by the dome, not the crop: notebook 09_04_06 removes it when no DTM exists. Second, an alignment error of a few centimetres shows up as bands of false height along every plot edge and a tilt-like bias wherever the ground slopes. Here alignment recovers the true heights exactly because the offset is a whole number of pixels; sub-pixel offsets leave a small interpolation error.

title: Photogrammetry: Orthomosaic, DSM and DTM
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Structure-from-Motion matches features across overlapping frames, solves the cameras, and builds a dense cloud, a DEM and an orthomosaic.
Overlap decides whether neighbouring frames match. GCP or RTK fixes where the model sits on the ground.
run_docker and run_nodeodm launch OpenDroneMap. load_outputs opens an orthomosaic, DSM and DTM from ODM or from a Metashape export.
Canopy height is DSM minus DTM (chm_from_surfaces).

GeoLattice functions used: rs.uav.estimate_homography, rs.uav.run_docker, rs.uav.run_nodeodm, rs.uav.load_outputs, rs.uav.chm_from_surfaces, rs.uav.synthetic_dem.
Exercises

Repeat the overlap experiment with method="sift". Does SIFT keep more inliers at 40 %?
Increase angle in two_views to 20°. At what angle does matching fail at 75 % overlap?
Download the 2025-08-13 orthomosaic, set ORTHO_PATH and reload. What is its resolution and does it carry a CRS?
Shift the example DTM by a full 0.5 m and compare the two CHM RMSEs again.

References

Westoby, M. J. et al. (2012). ‘Structure-from-Motion’ photogrammetry: a low-cost, effective tool for geoscience applications. Geomorphology, 179, 300-314.
OpenDroneMap Authors. ODM: a command line toolkit to generate maps, point clouds, 3D models and DEMs from drone images. https://opendronemap.org

title: RGB + NIR Multispectral Analysis
text:
Overview
A two-camera rig brings two problems a single multispectral sensor hides. The cameras see slightly different footprints, so the bands must be co-registered, and they record raw digital numbers (DN), not reflectance, so indices are relative unless the images are calibrated against reference panels. This notebook works through both on the paired Canola, Drybean, Wheat and Lentil-Wheat crop sets, then follows NDVI through the season for each crop.

Explain relative vs calibrated reflectance and apply panel calibration, the empirical line method and irradiance normalisation (rs.uav.panel_calibration, empirical_line, sunshine_normalize).
Build NDVI trajectories across flight dates for four crops.

Load one Canola pair without registration and estimate the homography that maps NIR onto the green band. Its translation terms are the offset in pixels; the diagonal terms are the scale difference between the two lenses.

r = pairs[pairs.session == "canola_06082019"].iloc[5]
raw = rs.uav.load_pair(r.rgb_path, r.nir_path, register=False)
green, nir = raw.sel(band="green").values, raw.sel(band="nir").values
