title: RGB + NIR Multispectral Analysis
text:
Co-registration
rs.uav.coregister(moving, reference) fits the homography (ORB or SIFT features, Lowe’s ratio test, RANSAC), optionally refines it with the Enhanced Correlation Coefficient (ECC) method (kept only if it improves the match), and warps the moving band. load_pair(..., register=True) does the same inside the loader.
Pixel correlation between NIR and green is not a fair score (the bands respond differently to leaves and soil), so alignment is judged by how well their edges coincide: rs.uav.edge_agreement correlates the Sobel edge maps and ignores the empty border a warp leaves behind. coregister uses the same score to validate its own answer: a solution with too few inliers, an implausibly large shift, or edges that agree less than before is rejected and the band is returned unwarped (info["accepted"] is then False).


Code
def edges(a):
    """Gradient magnitude, rescaled to 0-1 (for overlays)."""
    gy, gx = np.gradient(np.nan_to_num(a))
    m = np.hypot(gx, gy)
    return np.clip(m / np.percentile(m, 99), 0, 1)

aligned, reg = rs.uav.coregister(nir, green, method="sift", refine=True)
print({k: (round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in reg.items() if k != "H"})


{'method': 'sift', 'matches': 98, 'inliers': 86, 'rmse_px': 0.557, 'accepted': True, 'reason': '', 'shift_px': 0.521, 'edge_before': 0.472, 'edge_after': 0.547, 'correlation': 0.142}




Code
win = (slice(250, 450), slice(400, 700))  # zoom window (rows, cols)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2))
for ax, band, title in [(axes[0], nir, "before"), (axes[1], aligned, "after")]:
    ax.imshow(np.dstack([edges(band)[win], edges(green)[win], np.zeros_like(green[win])]))
    ax.set_title(f"Edges {title} (NIR red, green green, overlap yellow)"); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









The shift is only a couple of pixels, but the scale term (about 0.7 %) adds up to several pixels at the frame edges, which is where the overlay improves most.
Below, the three methods are compared on three pairs per crop with validation switched off, to see what each would do on its own, and then with validation on.


Code
rows = []
for crop, d in pairs.groupby("crop"):
    for _, rr in d.sample(3, random_state=1).iterrows():
        p = rs.uav.load_pair(rr.rgb_path, rr.nir_path)
        g, n = p.sel(band="green").values, p.sel(band="nir").values
        base = rs.uav.edge_agreement(n, g)
        for method in ["orb", "sift", "ecc"]:
            for validate in [False, True]:
                try:
                    al, inf = rs.uav.coregister(n, g, method=method, refine=(method != "ecc"), validate=validate)
                    rows.append({"crop": crop, "frame": rr.frame, "method": method, "validate": validate,
                                 "edge_gain": rs.uav.edge_agreement(al, g) - base,
                                 "shift_px": float(np.hypot(*inf["H"][:2, 2])), "inliers": inf.get("inliers", np.nan),
                                 "accepted": inf["accepted"], "reason": inf["reason"]})
                except Exception as e:  # e.g. ECC does not converge
                    rows.append({"crop": crop, "frame": rr.frame, "method": method, "validate": validate,
                                 "edge_gain": np.nan, "accepted": False, "reason": f"failed: {type(e).__name__}"})
reg_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)

What the table shows on these crops:

SIFT is the most dependable: it improves edge agreement on nearly every pair.
ORB usually works but occasionally returns a wild homography from a handful of inliers.
ECC alone often fails to converge or drifts, because NIR and green look different; use it only as a refinement step after feature matching.
On some wheat frames every method agrees on a large shift that makes things worse: the regular drill rows look alike, so all three lock onto a neighbouring row. Validation catches this and keeps the unwarped band.

Lentil-Wheat frames have the sparsest canopy and fewest features, so always check inliers and accepted before trusting a registration.

title: RGB + NIR Multispectral Analysis
text:
NDVI, GNDVI and SAVI
With the registered pair, rs.uav.vegetation_indices adds the NIR indices automatically:

NDVI = \((NIR - R)/(NIR + R)\)
GNDVI = \((NIR - G)/(NIR + G)\), more sensitive to chlorophyll in dense canopies
SAVI = \(1.5\,(NIR - R)/(NIR + R + 0.5)\), damps the soil background in sparse canopies

text:
Relative vs calibrated reflectance
The NIR and RGB cameras have different sensitivities, exposure settings and gains. A DN of 150 in NIR is not comparable to 150 in red, so DN-based NDVI is shifted and scaled by an unknown amount, and it shifts again whenever exposure or sunlight changes. Look at the distribution of NDVI medians per Drybean frame: in some sessions most pixels are negative, which real vegetation reflectance would never produce.


Code

meds = []
for _, rr in bean.iterrows():
    p = rs.uav.load_pair(rr.rgb_path, rr.nir_path)
    meds.append({"session": rr.session, "nir_mean_DN": float(p.sel(band="nir").mean()) * 255,
                 "red_mean_DN": float(p.sel(band="red").mean()) * 255,

Calibration converts DN to reflectance. The cell below builds a synthetic example on top of a real pair: the pair is treated as “true” reflectance (scaled to realistic levels), a camera with a different gain and dark offset per band turns it into DN, and two reflectance panels (a 50 % grey and a 5 % black, as on commercial calibration targets) are pasted into the scene. Calibration then has to recover the truth.


Code
true = pair.copy() * xr.DataArray([0.25, 0.30, 0.20, 0.55], dims="band", coords={"band": pair.band})  # reflectance scale
true = true.clip(0, 1)
panels = {"grey": ((20, 70, 20, 70), 0.50), "black": ((20, 70, 90, 140), 0.05)}  # (row0, row1, col0, col1), reflectance
for (r0, r1, c0, c1), rho in panels.values():
    true[:, r0:r1, c0:c1] = rho

gain = {"red": 380.0, "green": 300.0, "blue": 420.0, "nir": 210.0}  # DN per unit reflectance
dark = {"red": 12.0, "green": 10.0, "blue": 15.0, "nir": 22.0}      # dark offset (DN)
dn = xr.Dataset({b: (true.sel(band=b, drop=True) * gain[b] + dark[b]).clip(0, 255) for b in gain})
truth = xr.Dataset({b: true.sel(band=b, drop=True) for b in gain})

grey_dn = rs.uav.panel_dn_from_image(dn, panels["grey"][0])
black_dn = rs.uav.panel_dn_from_image(dn, panels["black"][0])
one_panel = rs.uav.panel_calibration(dn, grey_dn, {b: 0.50 for b in gain})
two_panel, fits = rs.uav.empirical_line(dn, {b: [black_dn[b], grey_dn[b]] for b in gain},
                                        {b: [0.05, 0.50] for b in gain})
print("empirical line fits (gain, offset, r2):", {b: tuple(round(v, 4) for v in f) for b, f in fits.items()})

def ndvi(ds):
    return (ds.nir - ds.red) / (ds.nir + ds.red)

veg = (ndvi(truth) > 0.3).values
res = pd.DataFrame({
    "NDVI mean (vegetation)": [float(ndvi(x).values[veg].mean()) for x in (truth, dn, one_panel, two_panel)],
    "RMSE vs truth": [0.0] + [float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean((ndvi(x) - ndvi(truth)).values ** 2))) for x in (dn, one_panel, two_panel)],
}, index=["true reflectance", "raw DN", "one panel (gain only)", "empirical line (2 panels)"])
res.round(4)

Raw-DN NDVI is biased because NIR and red have different gains and offsets. One panel fixes the gain but not the dark offset; two panels (empirical line) recover the truth. Real panels must be imaged at the flight’s altitude and sun angle, and be large enough to cover many pixels free of their edges.
Changing light. If clouds dim the sun by 30 % halfway through a flight, every DN drops. A downwelling light sensor (DLS) on top of the drone records the irradiance per band, and rs.uav.sunshine_normalize rescales each image to a reference irradiance:


Code
E_ref = {"red": 1.00, "green": 1.00, "blue": 1.00, "nir": 1.00}  # irradiance at panel capture
E_cloud = {"red": 0.70, "green": 0.71, "blue": 0.74, "nir": 0.66}  # under a passing cloud (bluer, less NIR)
dim = xr.Dataset({b: (truth[b] * E_cloud[b] * gain[b] + dark[b]).clip(0, 255) for b in gain})
dim_corr = rs.uav.sunshine_normalize(xr.Dataset({b: dim[b] - dark[b] for b in gain}), E_cloud, E_ref)
dim_corr = xr.Dataset({b: dim_corr[b] + dark[b] for b in gain})  # put the dark offset back
cal_dim, _ = rs.uav.empirical_line(dim, {b: [black_dn[b], grey_dn[b]] for b in gain}, {b: [0.05, 0.50] for b in gain})
cal_fix, _ = rs.uav.empirical_line(dim_corr, {b: [black_dn[b], grey_dn[b]] for b in gain}, {b: [0.05, 0.50] for b in gain})
pd.Series({"cloudy, panel from sunny time": float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean((ndvi(cal_dim) - ndvi(truth)).values ** 2))),
           "cloudy, DLS-normalised first": float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean((ndvi(cal_fix) - ndvi(truth)).values ** 2)))},
          name="NDVI RMSE").round(4).to_frame()









NDVI RMSE

The dark offset is removed before scaling because irradiance only multiplies the signal, not the sensor’s dark current.

    p = rs.uav.load_pair(rr.rgb_path, rr.nir_path, register="sift", refine=False)

    return {"ndvi_veg": float(v.NDVI.where(mask).mean()), "gndvi_veg": float(v.GNDVI.where(mask).mean()),

title: RGB + NIR Multispectral Analysis
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

A two-camera rig does not share one footprint. Register NIR to RGB (coregister) before computing an index, and check the fit with edge agreement.
NDVI, GNDVI and SAVI need NIR. On raw digital numbers they stay relative until a calibration converts them.
A panel, an empirical line and a sunshine correction are the three steps from DN toward reflectance.
Follow NDVI by crop and date only after the pairs that failed registration have been dropped.

GeoLattice functions used: rs.uav.load_pair, rs.uav.coregister, rs.uav.estimate_homography, rs.uav.edge_agreement, rs.uav.vegetation_indices, rs.uav.panel_calibration, rs.uav.panel_dn_from_image, rs.uav.empirical_line, rs.uav.sunshine_normalize, rs.uav.summarize_dates.
Exercises

Register 20 Lentil-Wheat pairs with ORB and with SIFT. How often does validation reject each one, and for which reason?
Add a third panel (20 %) to the synthetic example. Does the empirical line still give r2 close to 1? What happens if the black panel is partly in shadow (add 15 DN)?
Replace NDVI with SAVI in Section 6. Does the soil-adjusted index change the early-season Drybean values more than the late ones?
Compute per-session NIR and red DN means and plot them against NDVI. How much of the NDVI change between dates follows exposure?

References

Gitelson, A. A. et al. (1996). Use of a green channel in remote sensing of global vegetation from EOS-MODIS. Remote Sensing of Environment, 58, 289-298 (GNDVI).
Huete, A. R. (1988). A soil-adjusted vegetation index (SAVI). Remote Sensing of Environment, 25, 295-309.
Smith, G. M. and Milton, E. J. (1999). The use of the empirical line method to calibrate remotely sensed data to reflectance. International Journal of Remote Sensing, 20, 2653-2662.

title: Plant Counting and Size
text:
Overview
Early in the season, before canopies merge, plants can be counted from millimetre-resolution drone imagery. This notebook counts transplanted rice hills in the LUMS frames two ways: a classical approach (local maxima of Excess Green with rs.uav.count_plants), and the deep-learning approach of the LUMS paper (RiceNet density regression with rs.uav.density_count). Both run tile by tile on large images, so the notebook also covers overlapping tiles, cosine-weighted stitching and merging duplicate detections across tiles.

title: Plant Counting and Size
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Detect plants as peaks or blobs of a vegetation index, with distances set in metres.
See how sensitive counts are to the minimum spacing, and choose it from agronomy.
Tile a large image with overlap, stitch tile outputs with cosine weights, and merge duplicate points (sliding_windows, predict_tiled, merge_points).
Estimate per-plant size and assign size classes (size_classes).
Compute plant density per area unit (plants_per_area).
Run RiceNet density counting when its weights are available.

Not in the public release. Counts here are checked by eye and between methods

Classical counting: peaks of Excess Green
Each rice hill is a cluster of green leaves. Smoothing ExG with a Gaussian of a few centimetres merges the leaves of one hill into a single bump; local maxima at least min_distance_m apart above an Otsu threshold become plants. Because the frame is read with its GSD, both distances are given in metres.

section: Large images: tiles, stitching and merging
text:
Large images: tiles, stitching and merging
An orthomosaic can be 30 000 × 20 000 pixels; models run on tiles. rs.uav.sliding_windows yields overlapping windows (LUMS: 1024 px tiles, 128 px overlap).


Code
full = rs.uav.read_frame(frames[3], gsd=GSD)  # full resolution, 3840 x 2160
H, W = full.sizes["y"], full.sizes["x"]
wins = list(rs.uav.sliding_windows(H, W, tile=1024, overlap=128))
print(len(wins), "tiles of 1024 px with 128 px overlap on a", (H, W), "frame")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.6))
ax.imshow(rs.uav.to_rgb_array(full.isel(x=slice(None, None, 4), y=slice(None, None, 4))), extent=[0, W, H, 0])
for r0, c0, h, w in wins:
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((c0, r0), w, h, fill=False, color="yellow", lw=1))
ax.set_title("Overlapping tiles"); ax.axis("off"); plt.show()


15 tiles of 1024 px with 128 px overlap on a (2160, 3840) frame









Stitching. When a tile-wise output depends on the tile (a model’s response near its borders, or any per-tile normalisation), plain averaging leaves visible seams. Cosine (Hann) weights give each tile’s centre full weight and fade towards its borders, so overlaps blend smoothly. The demonstration below uses a deliberately tile-dependent function, ExG rescaled to 0-1 within each tile:


Code
rgb_full = rs.uav.to_rgb_array(full)

def tile_exg(t):
    """ExG rescaled to 0-1 within the tile: a stand-in for a tile-dependent model output."""
    e = 2 * t[..., 1] - t[..., 0] - t[..., 2]
    return (e - e.min()) / (np.ptp(e) + 1e-9)

stitched = {b: rs.uav.predict_tiled(rgb_full, tile_exg, tile=1024, overlap=128, blend=b) for b in ["mean", "cosine"]}
w = rs.uav.cosine_weight(1024, 1024)
seams = sorted({c0 for _, c0, _, _ in wins} | {c0 + w_ for _, c0, _, w_ in wins})  # tile edges along x

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 7), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.2, 1]})
axes[0, 0].imshow(w, cmap="magma"); axes[0, 0].set_title("Cosine (Hann) weight of one tile"); axes[0, 0].axis("off")
axes[0, 1].imshow(stitched["mean"][::4, ::4], cmap="Greens"); axes[0, 1].set_title("Stitched with blend='mean'"); axes[0, 1].axis("off")
band = slice(0, 1024)  # the first row of tiles
for ax, b in [(axes[1, 0], "mean"), (axes[1, 1], "cosine")]:
    prof = stitched[b][band].mean(axis=0)
    ax.plot(prof, lw=0.8)
    for sx in seams:
        ax.axvline(sx, color="r", lw=0.6, alpha=0.6)
    ax.set(title=f"Column mean of the first tile row, blend='{b}' (red: tile edges)", xlabel="column", ylabel="value")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

inner = [sx for sx in seams if 0 < sx < W]
for b in ["mean", "cosine"]:
    prof = stitched[b][band].mean(axis=0)
    print(f"blend={b!r}: mean jump across inner tile edges = {np.mean([abs(prof[sx] - prof[sx - 1]) for sx in inner]):.4f}")









blend='mean': mean jump across inner tile edges = 0.0092
blend='cosine': mean jump across inner tile edges = 0.0018


With blend="mean" the profile steps wherever a tile starts or ends (red lines), because each tile was rescaled differently. Cosine weights fade each tile out towards its edges, so the transition is spread over the overlap and the steps are smoothed out. (RiceNet’s density maps are stitched this way.)
A note on the weight itself: the LUMS script builds it from a cosine over half a period, which makes a ramp that peaks in the tile’s bottom-right corner, not a centred window. GeoLattice uses the full period, as shown in the top-left panel.
Merging points. Plants in an overlap are detected by two tiles. rs.uav.merge_points replaces points closer than a radius with their mean.


Code
def tile_peaks(core_only):
    """ExG peaks per tile, in frame pixels; optionally keep only each tile's core."""
    out = []
    for r0, c0, h, w_ in wins:
        t = full.isel(y=slice(r0, r0 + h), x=slice(c0, c0 + w_))
        p = rs.uav.count_plants(rs.uav.vegetation_indices(t, "ExG"), min_distance_m=0.15, sigma_m=0.03, gsd=GSD)
        rr, cc = p.row.to_numpy() + r0, p.col.to_numpy() + c0
        if core_only:  # the half of each overlap nearest a tile belongs to that tile
            half = 128 // 2
            keep = ((rr >= (r0 + half if r0 > 0 else 0)) & (rr < (r0 + h - half if r0 + h < H else H)) &
                    (cc >= (c0 + half if c0 > 0 else 0)) & (cc < (c0 + w_ - half if c0 + w_ < W else W)))
            rr, cc = rr[keep], cc[keep]
        out.append(pd.DataFrame({"row": rr, "col": cc}))
    return pd.concat(out, ignore_index=True)

all_pts = tile_peaks(core_only=False)
merged = rs.uav.merge_points(all_pts, radius=0.15 / GSD / 2, x="col", y="row")  # half the spacing, in pixels
core = tile_peaks(core_only=True)
core_merged = rs.uav.merge_points(core, radius=0.15 / GSD / 2, x="col", y="row")
whole = rs.uav.count_plants(rs.uav.vegetation_indices(full, "ExG"), min_distance_m=0.15, sigma_m=0.03, gsd=GSD)
pd.Series({"whole frame at once": len(whole),
           "all tile points": len(all_pts), "all tile points, merged": len(merged),
           "tile cores only": len(core), "tile cores, merged": len(core_merged)}).to_frame("count")

Merging alone is not enough: a peak detector also fires on leaves cut by a tile edge, and those half-plants sit too far from the true centre to be merged. Keeping only each tile’s core (dropping detections within half the overlap of an inner edge) removes them, and merging then has little left to do. RiceNet’s density_count uses the same idea (its border argument). Small differences from the whole-frame count remain because Otsu picks a threshold per tile.

title: Plant Counting and Size
text:
Plant size
RiceNet’s second network regresses a size for each plant. A classical stand-in: grow each detected plant into the vegetation mask with a watershed seeded at the peaks, and take each region’s area. rs.uav.size_classes then labels plants small, medium or large by quartiles, as the LUMS maps do.


Code
from scipy import ndimage as ndi
from skimage.segmentation import watershed

mask, cover = rs.uav.canopy_cover(exg)
markers = np.zeros(exg.shape, np.int32)
markers[pts.row.to_numpy(), pts.col.to_numpy()] = np.arange(1, len(pts) + 1)
smooth = ndi.gaussian_filter(np.nan_to_num(exg.values), 0.03 / gsd)
regions = watershed(-smooth, markers, mask=mask.values)
area_px = ndi.sum(np.ones_like(regions), regions, index=np.arange(1, len(pts) + 1))
plants = pd.DataFrame({"row": pts.row, "col": pts.col, "size_px": area_px,
                       "area_cm2": area_px * (gsd * 100) ** 2})
plants["size_class"] = rs.uav.size_classes(plants, col="size_px")
display(plants.groupby("size_class").area_cm2.describe().round(1))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4.6))
axes[0].imshow(np.ma.masked_equal(regions, 0) % 20, cmap="tab20"); axes[0].set_title("Watershed regions (one colour per plant)")
axes[1].imshow(rs.uav.to_rgb_array(img))
for cls, c in [("small", "orange"), ("medium", "yellow"), ("large", "cyan")]:
    d = plants[plants.size_class == cls]
    axes[1].scatter(d.col, d.row, s=25, c=c, edgecolors="k", lw=0.5, label=cls)
axes[1].legend(loc="lower right"); axes[1].set_title("Size classes")
for a in axes: a.axis("off")

RiceNet density counting
RiceNet (Chaudhry et al. 2026, code in code/plant_counting_&_size_estimation/) predicts a density map whose integral is the plant count; peaks of the map are plant centres. The GeoLattice port, rs.uav.density_count, runs it on 1024 px tiles with 128 px overlap, stitches the density with cosine weights, finds peaks (peaks_from_density) and merges duplicates with merge_points. An optional second network gives plant size.

title: Plant Counting and Size
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Before canopies merge, plants are peaks of Excess Green. Set the minimum spacing from how the crop was planted, then check a hand count.
Large frames are counted in overlapping tiles. Cosine weights hide the seams, and merge_points drops detections that were counted twice.
Plant size and plants per square metre turn the points into stand traits.
RiceNet density counts take over when peaks blur together. The windowing around that model is the same tiling machinery.

GeoLattice functions used: rs.uav.count_plants, rs.uav.sliding_windows, rs.uav.predict_tiled, rs.uav.merge_points, rs.uav.size_classes, rs.uav.plants_per_area, rs.uav.density_count, rs.uav.load_ricenet.
Exercises

Count plants by hand in a 1 m × 1 m window of one frame, then pick the min_distance_m that best reproduces your count. Does it transfer to the other frames?
Replace ExG with VARI (clipped to -1..1) in count_plants. Which index gives cleaner peaks in flooded areas?
Run predict_tiled with overlap=0 and overlap=256. How do seams and run time change?
With RUN_DL = True, compute the agreement \(1 - |n_{ExG} - n_{RiceNet}| / n_{RiceNet}\) per frame.

References

Chaudhry, H., Rana, S. and Jaleel, A. (2026). UAV-based crop reconstruction and trait estimation using RGB imagery without external geospatial infrastructure. Computers and Electronics in Agriculture (accepted).
Lempitsky, V. and Zisserman, A. (2010). Learning to count objects in images. NeurIPS.
Lindeberg, T. (1998). Feature detection with automatic scale selection. International Journal of Computer Vision, 30, 79-116 (Laplacian-of-Gaussian blobs).
Beucher, S. and Meyer, F. (1993). The morphological approach to segmentation: the watershed transformation.

title: Panicle Detection with YOLO
text:
Overview
From late September the LUMS frames show pale, cream-coloured panicles above the leaves, and the study counted them with a fine-tuned YOLOv5 detector run in sliding windows (1024 px, stride 512) over the orthomosaic, keeping boxes above 0.7 confidence and merging overlaps with non-maximum suppression (NMS) at IoU 0.4. This notebook builds that pipeline with rs.uav.tiled_detect and friends. A detector is any function tile -> boxes, so the windowing, merging, counting and scoring are first checked on a synthetic scene with known answers and then run on real frames with a simple colour-based candidate detector; the LUMS YOLOv5 weights plug into the same call when downloaded.

title: Panicle Detection with YOLO
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Lay out sliding windows and understand why objects cut by window edges inflate counts.
Merge window detections back into image coordinates with cross-window NMS.
Score detections against reference boxes: precision, recall, F1 and count agreement.
Convert boxes to polygons and compute panicles per m².
Run a YOLO model (ultralytics or YOLOv5) in the same pipeline and prepare a small labelled set for fine-tuning.

text:
Sliding windows
A 3840 × 2160 frame is larger than a detector’s input. detection_windows(H, W, window, stride) lays out windows with stride steps; with stride = window / 2 every object away from the image border falls wholly inside at least one window. The last row and column of windows are shifted back to end exactly at the image edge.


Code
frame = sorted((LUMS / "2025-10-03").glob("*.png"))[1]
img = rs.uav.read_frame(frame, gsd=GSD)
H, W = img.sizes["y"], img.sizes["x"]

print(len(wins), "windows on", (H, W))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.6))
ax.imshow(rs.uav.to_rgb_array(img)[::4, ::4], extent=[0, W, H, 0])
for i, (r0, c0, h, w) in enumerate(wins):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((c0, r0), w, h, fill=False, color=f"C{i % 10}", lw=1.2))

section: Checking the machinery on a scene with known answers
text:
Checking the machinery on a scene with known answers
Before trusting a count, check the windowing on a scene where the right answer is known. The synthetic image below has 64 bright squares of 40 px on a dark background; the “detector” finds bright connected components in a window and returns their boxes with confidence 0.95. Squares cut by a window edge come back as partial boxes.


Code
def square_detector(tile, conf):
    """Toy detector: boxes around bright connected components, confidence 0.95."""
    lab, _ = ndi.label(tile[..., 0] > 128)
    out = [[s[1].start, s[0].start, s[1].stop, s[0].stop, 0.95, 0] for s in ndi.find_objects(lab)]
    return np.array(out, np.float32).reshape(-1, 6)

scene = np.zeros((700, 900, 3), np.uint8)
truth = []
for r in range(30, 680, 90):
    for c in range(30, 880, 110):
        scene[r:r + 40, c:c + 40] = 255
        truth.append((c, r, c + 40, r + 40))
truth = pd.DataFrame(truth, columns=["x1", "y1", "x2", "y2"])
scene_img = rs.uav.as_image(scene)

rows = []
for label, kw in [("no NMS, keep edge boxes", dict(iou=1.01, edge_margin=0)),
                  ("NMS only", dict(iou=0.4, edge_margin=0)),
                  ("NMS + drop edge boxes", dict(iou=0.4, edge_margin=2))]:
    det = rs.uav.tiled_detect(scene_img, square_detector, window=256, stride=128, conf=0.5, **kw)
    rows.append({"setting": label, "detections": len(det), **rs.uav.detection_scores(det, truth, iou=0.5)})

Without NMS every square is counted once per window that sees it. NMS merges full duplicates, but a square cut by a window edge yields a partial box whose IoU with the full box is low, so it survives NMS and inflates the count. Dropping boxes that touch an interior window edge (edge_margin) removes them: the whole object is always found by a neighbouring window when objects are smaller than the overlap (window - stride). For objects larger than the overlap, set edge_margin=0.

title: Panicle Detection with YOLO
text:
Panicle candidates on real frames
Without the trained weights, a simple colour rule stands in for the detector: panicles here are pale cream clusters (bright, low saturation, yellowish hue) above green leaves. The function below finds such pixels, joins them into blobs and returns a box per blob larger than a few square centimetres, with a “confidence” equal to the fraction of candidate pixels in the box (elongated, diagonal blobs fill little of their box, hence the low threshold of 0.15). It also fires on bright leaf midribs and dry leaf tips, so treat its output as candidates; the point is to exercise the pipeline, not to replace a trained model.


Code
def panicle_candidates(tile, conf, min_area_px=400, max_area_px=20_000):
    """Colour-blob stand-in detector: (n, 6) boxes [x1, y1, x2, y2, score, class]."""
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(tile, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV_FULL).astype(np.float32)
    hue, sat, val = hsv[..., 0] * 360 / 255, hsv[..., 1], hsv[..., 2]
    cand = ((val > 180) & (sat > 30) & (sat < 90) & (hue > 35) & (hue < 80)).astype(np.uint8)
    cand = cv2.morphologyEx(cand, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, np.ones((3, 3), np.uint8))  # drop speckle
    n, lab, stats, _ = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(cand, connectivity=8)
    out = []
    for i in range(1, n):
        x, y, w, h, a = stats[i]
        if min_area_px <= a <= max_area_px:
            score = a / float(w * h)  # how much of the box the blob fills
            if score >= conf:
                out.append([x, y, x + w, y + h, score, 0])
    return np.array(out, np.float32).reshape(-1, 6)

section: Preparing a small labelled set for fine-tuning
text:
Preparing a small labelled set for fine-tuning
Detectors transfer poorly between varieties, growth stages and camera heights, so a few hundred labelled panicles from your own fields usually pay off. The LUMS model was fine-tuned from COCO weights. The workflow:

Cut frames into 1024 px tiles (the inference size) and keep tiles with panicles.
Label boxes in a tool such as CVAT or Label Studio, exported in YOLO format: one text file per tile, one line per box: class x_centre y_centre width height, all relative to the tile size.
Write a dataset YAML and train with ultralytics.

The cell below performs step 1 and writes YOLO-format label files from the candidate boxes, purely to show the format; in practice you would correct these pseudo-labels by hand before training.


Code
ds = OUT / "yolo_panicles"
for sub in ["images/train", "labels/train"]:
    (ds / sub).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
n_tiles = n_labels = 0
for r0, c0, h, w in detection_windows(H, W, 1024, 1024):  # non-overlapping tiles for training
    inside = boxes[(boxes.x1 >= c0) & (boxes.x2 <= c0 + w) & (boxes.y1 >= r0) & (boxes.y2 <= r0 + h)]
    if inside.empty:
        continue
    stem = f"{frame.parent.name}_{frame.stem}_{r0}_{c0}"
    cv2.imwrite(str(ds / "images/train" / f"{stem}.jpg"), cv2.cvtColor((rgb[r0:r0 + h, c0:c0 + w] * 255).astype(np.uint8), cv2.COLOR_RGB2BGR))
    xc = ((inside.x1 + inside.x2) / 2 - c0) / w; yc = ((inside.y1 + inside.y2) / 2 - r0) / h
    bw = (inside.x2 - inside.x1) / w; bh = (inside.y2 - inside.y1) / h
    lines = [f"0 {a:.6f} {b:.6f} {c:.6f} {d:.6f}" for a, b, c, d in zip(xc, yc, bw, bh)]
    (ds / "labels/train" / f"{stem}.txt").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    n_tiles += 1; n_labels += len(lines)
(ds / "panicles.yaml").write_text(f"path: {ds.resolve()}\ntrain: images/train\nval: images/train\nnames:\n  0: panicle\n")
print(f"wrote {n_tiles} tiles and {n_labels} boxes to {ds}")
print((ds / "panicles.yaml").read_text())

title: Introduction to Imaging Spectroscopy
text:
Overview

What imaging spectroscopy measures
Light reflected from a surface carries the fingerprint of what it met. Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light, leaf water absorbs near 970, 1200, 1450 and 1940 nm, clays absorb near 2200 nm, carbonates near 2340 nm and iron oxides near 900 nm. Most of these features are 10 to 50 nm wide. A broadband sensor averages them away; a spectrometer with 5 to 10 nm bands resolves them.
Imaging spectroscopy (also called hyperspectral imaging) measures that spectrum for every pixel of an image. The term was coined for NASA’s Airborne Imaging Spectrometer in the early 1980s, and AVIRIS (1987) set the template still in use: about 224 contiguous bands at 10 nm from 400 to 2500 nm.
The key ideas are:

Spectral range: the wavelengths covered. VNIR is about 400 to 1000 nm, SWIR about 1000 to 2500 nm. VNIR-only sensors (DESIS, OHS, PACE OCI) see pigments and water colour; VSWIR sensors (EMIT, EnMAP, PRISMA, Tanager) add the minerals, leaf water, cellulose and greenhouse gases.
Spectral sampling: the spacing between band centres, for example 5 nm.
Spectral resolution: the width of each band’s spectral response function, usually given as the full width at half maximum (FWHM). Sampling a little finer than the FWHM (Nyquist) lets the spectrum be reconstructed without gaps.
Signal to noise ratio (SNR): narrow bands collect few photons, so noise matters much more than in multispectral data. SNR is lowest at the ends of the range and inside absorption bands.

The hyperspectral data cube
Stacking the band images gives a three dimensional cube: two spatial axes and one spectral axis. A Tanager scene is about 426 bands by 700 rows by 800 columns, close to 1 GB as 32 bit floats. Each pixel is a spectrum; each band is an image. Three storage layouts are common: band sequential (BSQ, one image after another), band interleaved by line (BIL) and band interleaved by pixel (BIP). Products arrive as ENVI binary plus header, HDF5 or HDF-EOS5, NetCDF or multiband GeoTIFF.


How imaging spectrometers are built

Whiskbroom scanners sweep a mirror across track and disperse one pixel at a time onto a line detector (AVIRIS Classic, HyMap). Simple optics, but moving parts and short dwell time.
Pushbroom spectrometers image a whole line across track through a slit; a grating or prism spreads it over a 2-D detector (space by wavelength), and the platform’s motion builds the image line by line. Almost all modern sensors (EMIT, EnMAP, PRISMA, Tanager, AVIRIS-NG, HySpex, Specim) are pushbroom. Each detector column has its own response, which causes striping.
Snapshot and tunable filter cameras capture all bands at once or step through filters; they are common in laboratories, microscopes and drones. Filter based satellites such as OHS sit between multispectral and hyperspectral.

Silicon detectors cover the VNIR; mercury cadmium telluride (HgCdTe) detectors, cooled to below about 150 K, cover the SWIR. Two instrument artefacts deserve a name: spectral smile (the band centres shift slightly across the swath) and keystone (a pixel’s footprint shifts slightly with wavelength).


From radiance to reflectance
The sensor measures at-sensor radiance (W m⁻² sr⁻¹ µm⁻¹): sunlight that crossed the atmosphere twice and bounced off the surface, plus light scattered by air and aerosols. To compare pixels, dates and sensors it must be converted to surface reflectance, the fraction of incident light the surface reflects (0 to 1). Atmospheric correction codes such as ISOFIT, ATCOR, FLAASH and the mission processors invert a radiative transfer model per pixel, retrieving water vapour and aerosols on the way.
The atmosphere also leaves its own absorption bands, which mark where surface information is weak or absent:

Airborne systems (AVIRIS-NG, AVIRIS-3, HyMap, HySpex, CASI and SASI), drone cameras (Headwall, Specim, Cubert) and laboratory push broom cameras share the same data model at finer pixels.


Applications

Vegetation: chlorophyll, carotenoids, anthocyanins, leaf water, nitrogen, lignin and cellulose, plant stress and species mapping; LAI and canopy chlorophyll from radiative transfer models such as PROSAIL.
Geology and soils: mineral maps from diagnostic absorption features (clays, micas, carbonates, iron oxides), soil organic carbon and texture, mine waste monitoring.
Water: chlorophyll a, phycocyanin (cyanobacteria), suspended sediment, coloured dissolved organic matter, shallow water bathymetry and benthic habitats.
Snow and ice: grain size, liquid water, light absorbing impurities (dust, algae, soot).
Greenhouse gases: methane and carbon dioxide plumes from oil and gas, coal, landfills and livestock, with source emission rates.
Fire: active fire temperature, burn severity, post fire recovery.
Urban and industry: roofing and paving materials, plastics, impervious surfaces.
Laboratory and industry: food quality and contamination, sorting, pharmaceuticals, art conservation and forensics.

Hyperspectral Imaging with GeoLattice
geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral (imported here as hs) holds every function the chapter uses. Cubes are xarray.DataArray objects with dimensions (band, y, x) and band coordinates wavelength (nm), fwhm (nm) and good (bool). Swath products that are not yet on a map grid use (band, line, sample) in the same way. Readers exist for ENVI, EMIT, EnMAP, PRISMA, Tanager, OHS, AVIRIS and band described GeoTIFFs, and every analysis function (preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, indices, libraries, unmixing, detection, traits) accepts and returns this layout.

title: Introduction to Imaging Spectroscopy
text:
Why narrow bands matter
hs.synthetic_library returns idealised spectra of six materials built from Gaussian absorption features at 1 nm steps. They are teaching spectra, not measurements, but their features sit at the right wavelengths. Below they are convolved with the band responses of Tanager (426 bands, about 5.5 nm FWHM), Landsat 8/9 OLI and Sentinel-2 MSI with hs.resample_spectral, which applies a Gaussian response function for each target band.


Code
lib = hs.synthetic_library(np.arange(400.0, 2501.0, 1.0))  # six idealised spectra at 1 nm
print(lib.names)  # material names

# Treat the library as a tiny cube: bands x 1 row x 6 columns, so every cube function applies.
lib_cube = hs.as_cube(lib.spectra.T[:, None, :], lib.wavelengths)

# Tanager band centres and FWHM, read from one pixel of a surface reflectance file.
sr_agri = next((TANAGER / "agriculture").glob("*/*_ortho_sr_hdf5.h5"))  # agriculture scene
probe = hs.read_tanager(sr_agri, window=(slice(0, 1), slice(0, 1)))  # 1 x 1 pixel read
tan_wl, tan_fwhm = probe["wavelength"].values, probe["fwhm"].values  # band centres and widths
print(f"Tanager: {tan_wl.size} bands, {tan_wl[0]:.1f} to {tan_wl[-1]:.1f} nm, "
      f"FWHM {tan_fwhm.min():.1f} to {tan_fwhm.max():.1f} nm")


['green_vegetation', 'dry_vegetation', 'soil', 'water', 'clay_kaolinite', 'carbonate_calcite']

Code
# How deep does the 2205 nm clay feature look to each sensor? Continuum = straight line
# between the shoulders at 2120 and 2260 nm; depth = 1 - R(band) / R(continuum).
clay = 4  # library column of the clay spectrum
rows = []
for name, s in sims.items():
    wl = hs.wavelengths(s)  # band centres of this sensor
    y = s.isel(x=clay, y=0).values  # clay spectrum at those bands
    inside = (wl > 2120) & (wl < 2260)  # bands within the feature
    if not inside.any():
        rows.append({"sensor": name, "bands in 2120 to 2260 nm": 0, "feature depth": np.nan})
        continue
    cont = np.interp(wl[inside], [2120, 2260], np.interp([2120, 2260], lib.wavelengths, lib.spectra[clay]))
    rows.append({"sensor": name, "bands in 2120 to 2260 nm": int(inside.sum()),
                 "feature depth": float(np.max(1 - y[inside] / cont))})
ref = lib.spectra[clay]  # 1 nm reference
cont = np.interp(lib.wavelengths, [2120, 2260], np.interp([2120, 2260], lib.wavelengths, ref))
win = (lib.wavelengths > 2120) & (lib.wavelengths < 2260)
rows.append({"sensor": "1 nm reference", "bands in 2120 to 2260 nm": int(win.sum()),
             "feature depth": float(np.max(1 - ref[win] / cont[win]))})

The Landsat and Sentinel-2 SWIR2 bands are 175 to 190 nm wide: each sees the whole doublet as one slightly darker value, and the feature depth drops to a fraction of the true depth, too shallow to tell kaolinite from other clays or from dry vegetation. The same happens to the red edge, the leaf water bands and every gas absorption.

section: The GeoLattice cube: a laboratory example
text:
The GeoLattice cube: a laboratory example
The HACARUS dataset stores each band as a separate 8 bit PNG whose file name holds the wavelength (suger_salt_flour_1293nm.png). That is a common pattern for laboratory and drone cameras, and a good way to see how a cube is put together. The scene shows three white powders that look alike to the eye: sugar, salt and flour.


Code
def read_png_cube(folder):
    """Stack the *_<wavelength>nm.png band images of a HACARUS scene into a cube."""
    files = sorted(Path(folder).glob("*nm.png"), key=lambda p: float(re.search(r"_(\d+)nm", p.name)[1]))
    wl = [float(re.search(r"_(\d+)nm", p.name)[1]) for p in files]  # wavelength from each file name
    stack = np.stack([np.asarray(Image.open(p), dtype="float32") for p in files])  # (band, row, col)
    return hs.as_cube(stack, wl, name="dn")  # cube with a wavelength coordinate


ssf = read_png_cube(DATA / "archive/data/sugar_salt_flour")  # sugar, salt and flour scene

The powders swap brightness from band to band. Sugar (upper right) is dark from 1450 nm onward and almost black near 2100 nm, where the O-H and C-H bonds of sucrose absorb. Salt (lower right) is bright except near 1940 nm, where it turns dark: a water absorption, so this salt holds some moisture. Flour (left) stays in between. Their positions follow the dataset’s annotated preview: sugar upper right, flour left, salt lower right. Circular regions of interest give the mean spectrum of each with hs.mean_spectrum.


Code
rr, cc = np.mgrid[:ssf.sizes["y"], :ssf.sizes["x"]]  # row and column of every pixel
rois = {"sugar": (110, 112), "flour": (160, 62), "salt": (190, 117), "tray": (30, 100)}  # (row, col) centres
masks = {k: (rr - r) ** 2 + (cc - c) ** 2 < 12 ** 2 for k, (r, c) in rois.items()}  # 12 px radius discs

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.3), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 2.3]})
axes[0].imshow(hs.band_at(ssf, 1940), cmap="gray")  # a band where the powders differ
for (k, (r, c)), col in zip(rois.items(), ["C0", "C1", "C2", "C3"]):
    axes[0].add_patch(plt.Circle((c, r), 12, fill=False, color=col, lw=2))  # ROI outline
    axes[0].text(c + 14, r, k, color=col, fontsize=9, va="center")
    s = hs.mean_spectrum(ssf, masks[k])  # mean spectrum inside the ROI
    axes[1].plot(s.index, s.values, color=col, label=k)
axes[0].set_title("1940 nm"); axes[0].axis("off")
axes[1].set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Digital number (8 bit)", title="Mean spectra")
axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The spectra confirm the images. Sugar is the darkest powder at every wavelength and falls to almost zero beyond 2050 nm; salt has a sharp drop between about 1880 and 1950 nm and a smaller dip near 1430 nm, both water bands; flour shows a dip near 1930 nm and stays moderately bright beyond 2000 nm. These are raw 8 bit digital numbers, not reflectance: they include the lamp spectrum and the camera response (the hump peaking near 1670 nm in the tray spectrum), and a white reference would be needed to convert them. Even so, the shapes differ clearly, which is all spectral matching (notebook 09_05_06) and target detection (notebook 09_05_08) need.

title: Introduction to Imaging Spectroscopy
text:
Radiance, reflectance and the atmosphere
The same window read from the ortho radiance product shows what the sensor actually measured. Pixels are picked by NDVI computed from two bands: a dense green canopy (high NDVI) and a bare field (low NDVI, bright in the SWIR).


Code
red, nir, swir = (hs.band_at(cube, w) for w in (650, 860, 2200))  # bands nearest 650, 860, 2200 nm
ndvi = (nir - red) / (nir + red)  # normalised difference vegetation index
veg_rc = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(ndvi.where(ndvi < ndvi.quantile(0.999)).values), ndvi.shape)  # dense canopy
soil_score = swir.where(ndvi < 0.2)  # bright SWIR among sparsely vegetated pixels
soil_rc = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmin(abs(soil_score - soil_score.quantile(0.9)).values), ndvi.shape)
print("vegetation pixel (row, col):", veg_rc, "NDVI", round(float(ndvi[veg_rc]), 2))
print("bare soil pixel (row, col):", soil_rc, "NDVI", round(float(ndvi[soil_rc]), 2))

rad_file = next(sr_agri.parent.glob("*_ortho_radiance_hdf5.h5"))  # TOA radiance product
rad = hs.read_tanager(rad_file, window=WIN)  # same window, radiance in W m-2 sr-1 um-1
print(rad.attrs["units"], rad.shape)

bare soil pixel (row, col): (np.int64(195), np.int64(280)) NDVI 0.17
W/(m^2 sr um) (426, 300, 300)




Code
wl = hs.wavelengths(cube)  # band centres (nm)
features = {"O2 760": 760, "H2O 940": 940, "H2O 1140": 1140, "H2O 1380": 1380,
            "H2O 1880": 1880, "CO2 2010/2060": 2035}  # atmospheric absorption features
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(13, 7.5), sharex=True)
for (name, (r, c)), col in zip([("green canopy", veg_rc), ("bare soil", soil_rc)], ["C2", "C5"]):
    axes[0].plot(wl, rad.values[:, r, c], color=col, label=name)  # radiance spectrum
    refl = np.where(cube["good"].values, cube.values[:, r, c], np.nan)  # reflectance, bad bands hidden
    axes[1].plot(wl, refl, color=col, label=name)
for name, w in features.items():
    axes[0].axvline(w, color="0.5", ls=":", lw=1)
    axes[0].text(w, axes[0].get_ylim()[1] * 0.97, name, rotation=90, va="top", ha="right", fontsize=8)
for lo, hi in hs.preprocess.WATER_VAPOUR_RANGES:
    axes[1].axvspan(lo, hi, color="0.92", zorder=0)  # bands dropped as bad
axes[0].set(ylabel="Radiance (W m⁻² sr⁻¹ µm⁻¹)", title="At-sensor radiance")
axes[1].set(ylabel="Surface reflectance", xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", title="Surface reflectance")
axes[0].legend(); axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Radiance follows the solar spectrum: it is largest in the visible and NIR and falls steeply into the SWIR, and the atmosphere cuts deep notches at the oxygen A band, the water vapour bands and the CO₂ pair. Both pixels share those notches, and radiance drops to zero in the opaque windows near 1400 and 1900 nm. After correction the reflectance spectra show the surface. The canopy has the green peak, the red absorption, the steep red edge near 700 nm, a high NIR plateau with dips near 970 and 1200 nm (leaf water) and much lower SWIR reflectance, again because of leaf water. The soil rises from the visible to a plateau of about 0.4 between 1500 and 2200 nm and declines slowly beyond it. title: Introduction to Imaging Spectroscopy
text:
Spectral signatures across Tanager scenes
Each scene contributes one material. A pixel is chosen by a simple rule on a few bands (read with bands= so only seven of the 426 bands are loaded), then the full spectrum is read as the mean of a 3 by 3 pixel window around it.


Code
probe_idx = [hs.band_index(probe, w) for w in (560, 650, 860, 1650, 2200)]  # green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2


def nd(a, b):
    """Normalised difference of two band arrays."""
    return (a - b) / (a + b)


def closest(score, q):
    """(row, col) of the valid pixel whose score is nearest to its q-th quantile."""
    target = np.nanquantile(score, q)
    return np.unravel_index(np.nanargmin(np.abs(score - target)), score.shape)


rules = {  # material: (scene folder prefix, rule returning (row, col))
    "green vegetation": ("agriculture", lambda G, R, N, S1, S2: closest(nd(N, R), 0.995)),
    "bare soil (Permian Basin)": ("energy-mining",
                                  lambda G, R, N, S1, S2: closest(np.where(nd(N, R) < 0.12, S1, np.nan), 0.5)),
    "sea water": ("coastal-water-bodies", lambda G, R, N, S1, S2: closest(np.where(nd(G, N) > 0.3, N, np.nan), 0.5)),
    "snow": ("snow-ice", lambda G, R, N, S1, S2: closest(np.where(nd(G, S1) > 0.8, G, np.nan), 0.5)),
    "urban (roofs and roads)": ("urban",
                                lambda G, R, N, S1, S2: closest(np.where((nd(N, R) < 0.1) & (nd(G, N) < 0), S1, np.nan), 0.5)),
    "burn scar (Franklin Fire)": ("fire",
                                  lambda G, R, N, S1, S2: closest(np.where(N > 0.08, nd(N, S2), np.nan), 0.002)),
    "desert (Syria)": ("GHG-plumes", lambda G, R, N, S1, S2: closest(np.where(nd(N, R) < 0.12, S1, np.nan), 0.5)),
}

sigs, picks = {}, {}
for material, (prefix, rule) in rules.items():
    f = scenes.loc[scenes["folder"].str.startswith(prefix), "sr_file"].iloc[0]  # SR file of the scene
    few = hs.read_tanager(f, bands=probe_idx)  # five bands of the whole scene
    r, c = rule(*few.values)  # pixel chosen by the rule
    win = hs.read_tanager(f, window=(slice(max(r - 1, 0), r + 2), slice(max(c - 1, 0), c + 2)))  # 3 x 3 pixels
    sigs[material] = hs.mean_spectrum(win).where(win["good"].values)  # mean spectrum, bad bands NaN
    picks[material] = (prefix, int(r), int(c))

Each class has its own shape:

Green vegetation has the red edge and the highest NIR to red contrast (NDVI near 0.9).
Bare soil and desert rise steeply through the visible (iron oxides make them red), level off in the SWIR and decline beyond 2200 nm, where clays and carbonates absorb. The Syrian desert is the brightest.
Sea water is dark everywhere and close to zero beyond 700 nm.
Snow is very bright in the visible (0.9 to 1.1; values slightly above 1 come from the viewing geometry and the correction), has ice absorptions near 1030 and 1260 nm and falls to a few percent beyond 1500 nm. Its NDSI is the highest of all classes.
Urban surfaces are flat and moderately bright, a mixture of roofs, asphalt and concrete.
Burn scar pixels are dark in the NIR and relatively bright near 2200 nm, so their burn ratio (NBR) is the lowest.

The rules picked typical pixels, not pure ones: at 30 m most pixels mix several materials, and the urban spectrum in particular is an average of roofs, roads and trees. Spectral matching, unmixing and detection later in the chapter work with exactly these differences in shape.

title: Introduction to Imaging Spectroscopy
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Imaging spectrometers record hundreds of narrow contiguous bands; FWHM, sampling and SNR decide which absorption features can be resolved. Broad multispectral bands average away features such as the 2165 and 2205 nm clay doublet.
A hyperspectral cube is (band, y, x) with a wavelength axis; in GeoLattice every function works on that layout and selects bands by wavelength (band_at, band_index, sel_range).
Sensors measure radiance; surface reflectance requires atmospheric correction. Oxygen, water vapour and CO₂ leave absorption bands, and the opaque water vapour windows are flagged as bad bands.
hs.read_tanager reads Tanager ortho and basic products with subsetting by window, bbox, bands or wavelength; hs.read_tanager_ancillary returns the masks, water vapour, aerosol and geometry.
Vegetation, soil, water, snow, urban surfaces and burn scars have distinct spectral shapes, the basis of every method in this chapter.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: synthetic_library, as_cube, resample_spectral, wavelengths, band_index, band_at, sel_range, mean_spectrum, read_tanager, read_tanager_ancillary, read_ohs, plot_rgb, band_stats, plot_band_stats, spectral_viewer, wavelength_slider, plus the tables preprocess.SENSOR_SRF and preprocess.WATER_VAPOUR_RANGES.
Exercises

Repeat the narrow band comparison for the carbonate spectrum (carbonate_calcite, feature near 2340 nm). Which multispectral band, if any, sees it?
Build cubes for the rice and coffee HACARUS scenes with read_png_cube and plot the mean spectra of two objects in each.
Read the ROCX 2025 scene with bbox= around Lake Ontario’s shore and compare the water spectrum with the Venezuelan sea water spectrum above. What does the difference near 550 to 700 nm suggest?
Read the urban scene with mask_clouds=True and count how many pixels the cloud and cirrus masks remove.
Using rad and cube, divide radiance by reflectance for the canopy pixel. What does the result approximate, and why does it fall to near zero in the opaque water bands?

title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
text:
Overview

Bad bands
Three groups of bands are usually removed: the opaque water vapour windows near 1400 and 1900 nm (and beyond about 2450 nm), the ends of the range where detector response and solar irradiance are low (below about 400 nm), and individual bands that are noisy, saturated or mostly fill. Products often ship a good band list; checking SNR and NaN fractions catches the rest.


Noise and SNR
Noise in imaging spectrometers is a mix of photon (shot) noise, which grows with signal, and detector and readout noise, which does not. Two image based estimates are common: the shift difference method assumes neighbouring pixels share the same signal, so their difference is noise (it overestimates noise in textured scenes); the residual method predicts each band from its spectral neighbours by regression and takes the residual (Roger and Arnold 1996), which is robust to spatial texture.


Striping
Each column of a pushbroom image is seen by one detector element. Small differences in gain and offset between elements show up as along track stripes. Moment matching scales every column to the band’s global mean and standard deviation; it assumes each column sees, on average, the same mix of surfaces, which holds for long swaths.


Masks
Clouds, cloud shadow, water and saturated pixels distort statistics and endmembers. Simple reflectance rules (bright and spectrally flat in the visible for cloud, NDWI for water, dark NIR for shadow) work as a first pass; mission cloud masks, which use the 1380 nm cirrus band and spectral tests, are better when available.


Radiance to reflectance
Physics based atmospheric correction (ISOFIT, ATCOR, FLAASH, the Tanager processor) is the norm. Without it, scene based approximations are still useful:

Empirical line: a linear fit per band between image values and field measured reflectance of at least two targets (dark and bright). Accurate near the targets’ conditions.
Flat field: divide every pixel by the spectrum of a bright, spectrally flat area.
Internal Average Relative (IAR): divide by the scene mean spectrum. Removes the solar and atmospheric shape but leaves the scene average’s own features in every spectrum.



Spectral transforms

Smoothing (Savitzky Golay, moving average, Gaussian) reduces band to band noise at the cost of some spectral resolution.
Derivatives remove baselines and sharpen features: the first derivative peaks at the red edge inflection; the second derivative locates absorption minima.
Normalisation (standard normal variate, vector norm, brightness) removes overall brightness differences caused by illumination and topography, keeping shape.
Continuum removal divides a spectrum by its convex hull, so absorption features become dips below 1 that can be compared across samples (Clark and Roush 1984). Band depth, position, width and asymmetry summarise one feature.



Spectral resampling
Convolving a hyperspectral spectrum with the spectral response functions of a multispectral sensor simulates that sensor. This links field and satellite spectroscopy, creates training data for Sentinel-2 or Landsat models and lets products from different sensors be compared.

Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings

from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
from geolattice.rsense import hyperspectral as hs  # hyperspectral cubes, readers and tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_05_HyperSpectral")  # data folder next to this notebook
TANAGER = DATA / "Tanger"  # Planet Tanager sample scenes
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed


def tanager_file(category, product="sr"):
    """Path of a Tanager product (sr or radiance) for a scene category folder."""
    return next((TANAGER / category).glob(f"*/*_ortho_{product}_hdf5.h5"))


print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__)  # library version used for this notebook

text:
Bad bands
A 200 by 200 pixel window of the agriculture scene (forest, river and fields) is used for most of the notebook.


Code
WIN = (slice(250, 450), slice(300, 500))  # rows and columns
sr = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("agriculture"), window=WIN)  # surface reflectance, all bands
wl = hs.wavelengths(sr)  # band centres (nm)
bad = hs.bad_bands(sr)  # default rules: water vapour windows, < 400 nm, NaN or constant bands, product flags
print("bands:", sr.sizes["band"], "| product flags bad:", int((~sr["good"].values).sum()),
      "| bad_bands flags:", int(bad.sum()))
extra = bad & sr["good"].values  # flagged by bad_bands but good in the product
print("extra bands:", np.round(wl[extra][:6], 1), "...", np.round(wl[extra][-6:], 1))

print("with min_snr=5:", int(noisy.sum()), "bands flagged")
mean = sr.mean(("y", "x")).values  # window mean spectrum
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4))
ax.plot(wl, mean, color="0.3", lw=1, label="window mean")
ax.plot(wl[bad], mean[bad], "o", ms=3, color="C3", label="bad_bands (default)")
ax.plot(wl[noisy & ~bad], mean[noisy & ~bad], "o", ms=3, color="C1", label="added by min_snr=5")
ax.set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Reflectance", title="Bands flagged for removal")

with min_snr=5: 191 bands flagged









clean cube: (350, 200, 200)


The product’s own list removes the two opaque water vapour windows. bad_bands adds the bands below 400 nm and beyond 2450 nm, where the spectrum turns noisy (notebook 09_05_00), and a few at the edge of the 1400 nm window. The SNR threshold is far more aggressive here: it removes the red chlorophyll absorption (about 620 to 700 nm) and nearly the whole SWIR beyond 1970 nm, simply because this forest window is dark there and the simple SNR in band_stats counts forest texture as noise. A threshold of 5 is therefore too strict for this scene; check what a rule removes before applying it.

title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
section: Noise and signal to noise ratio
text:
Noise and signal to noise ratio
Tanager ships a per pixel, per band reflectance uncertainty. Its median over the window is a useful reference for the two image based noise estimates.


Code
unc = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("agriculture"), variable="surface_reflectance_uncertainty", window=WIN)
u = np.nanmedian(unc.values.reshape(unc.sizes["band"], -1), axis=1)  # median uncertainty per band
shift = hs.estimate_noise(sr, method="shift")  # neighbour difference method
resid = hs.estimate_noise(sr.isel(band=np.flatnonzero(sr["good"].values)), method="residual")  # spectral regression
good = sr["good"].values

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.2))
ax.plot(wl, np.where(good, u, np.nan), label="product uncertainty (median)", lw=1.5)
ax.plot(wl, np.where(good, shift, np.nan), label="shift difference", lw=1)
ax.plot(wl[good], resid, label="residual (spectral regression)", lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Noise (reflectance units)", yscale="log",
       title="Per band noise: product uncertainty and image based estimates")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
ratio = pd.Series({"shift / product": np.nanmedian(shift[good] / u[good]),
                   "residual / product": np.nanmedian(resid / u[good])})
ratio.round(2)









shift / product       13.54
residual / product     0.79
dtype: float64


All three curves rise at the edges of the water vapour windows and towards 2500 nm, where the signal is weakest. The shift difference estimate sits more than ten times above the product uncertainty because neighbouring forest pixels genuinely differ (texture counts as noise). The residual method, which uses only spectral neighbours, follows the product’s error model in the SWIR and falls below it in the VNIR, where neighbouring 5 nm bands are so strongly correlated that part of the noise is predictable from them; its median is about 0.8 times the product value. Use the residual method, or the product uncertainty when it exists, to set SNR thresholds or MNF noise models.

title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
text:
Detector striping
Striping is easiest to judge in sensor geometry, where every column is one detector element. Stripes make neighbouring columns differ more than neighbouring rows, so the ratio of the mean absolute difference across track to the mean absolute difference along track is a simple measure: about 1 for an image without stripes, above 1 with stripes. (Comparing column means is not a good check, because moment matching sets them all equal by construction.)


Code
def anisotropy(img):
    """Mean |difference| between neighbouring columns divided by that between neighbouring rows."""
    return float(np.nanmean(np.abs(np.diff(img, axis=1))) / np.nanmean(np.abs(np.diff(img, axis=0))))


swath = hs.read_tanager(DATA / "20250224_145149_32_4001_basic_radiance_hdf5.h5", wavelength_range=(2100, 2300))
swath = swath.rename(line="y", sample="x")  # destripe works on the column (x) axis
ohs = hs.read_ohs(next((DATA / "10m_OH2_Hyperspectral_Sample/Spanish-OHS").iterdir()),
                  bands=[5, 14, 27], window=(slice(1500, 3500), slice(1500, 3500)))  # sensor geometry
ohs = ohs.rename(line="y", sample="x")
rows = []
for name, c in {"Tanager swath (2100 to 2300 nm)": swath, "OHS bands 5, 14, 27": ohs}.items():
    d = hs.destripe(c)  # moment matching per column
    before = np.mean([anisotropy(c.values[b]) for b in range(c.sizes["band"])])  # mean over bands
    after = np.mean([anisotropy(d.values[b]) for b in range(c.sizes["band"])])
    rows.append({"image": name, "anisotropy before": before, "after destripe": after})
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4)









image
anisotropy before
after destripe

1.0755

1
OHS bands 5, 14, 27

Both L1 products are already well calibrated. The Tanager swath has a small across track excess (about 7 percent), which destriping reduces; the OHS bands have none, and destriping changes them very little. Destriping an image that does not need it only risks removing real differences between columns. To see what the method can do, the next cell adds synthetic stripes (a random gain of about 3 percent per column) to the OHS 866 nm band and removes them again.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
clean = ohs.isel(band=[2])  # OHS band 27 (866 nm)
gain = 1 + rng.normal(0, 0.03, clean.sizes["x"])  # one gain per detector column
striped = clean * gain[None, None, :]  # striped copy
fixed = hs.destripe(striped)  # moment matching
med = hs.destripe(striped, method="median")  # median matching
tab = pd.DataFrame({k: {"anisotropy": anisotropy(v.values[0]),
                        "RMSE to clean (DN)": float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean((v.values - clean.values) ** 2)))}
                    for k, v in {"clean": clean, "striped": striped, "destriped (moment)": fixed,
                                 "destriped (median)": med}.items()}).T
display(tab.round(3))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(clean.values, [2, 98])  # common stretch
for ax, (t, v) in zip(axes, [("clean", clean), ("synthetic stripes", striped), ("destriped (moment)", fixed)]):
    ax.imshow(v.values[0, :600, :600], cmap="gray", vmin=lo, vmax=hi)  # 600 x 600 pixel detail
    ax.set_title(t); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









anisotropy
RMSE to clean (DN)




clean
0.996
0.000


striped
1.664
4.765


destriped (moment)
1.000
8.998


destriped (median)
1.069
6.301














The synthetic stripes are obvious and raise the anisotropy from 1.0 to about 1.7. Moment matching brings it back to the clean value and the stripes disappear from the image, but the RMSE against the clean band goes up, not down. Every column is forced to the same mean and standard deviation, yet in this 20 km window some columns genuinely cross more reservoir or more bright fields than others; those real differences are flattened too. Median matching keeps more of them and ends between the two. Destriping removes visible stripes, but it is a cosmetic and statistical correction that can bias absolute values. Apply it to long swath segments, preferably with gains from the instrument’s calibration, and do not apply it to data that show no stripes.

title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
text:
Cloud, water and shadow masks
The fire scene over Malibu has a patch of cloud above the ocean. hs.quality_mask needs only the 450, 560, 650 and 860 nm bands (plus 1380 nm for cirrus), so only those are read.


Code
fire = tanager_file("fire")
probe = hs.read_tanager(fire, window=(slice(0, 1), slice(0, 1)))  # wavelengths only

The thin cloud over the ocean is easy to see in true colour, yet none of the masks flags it. The product’s beta cloud and cirrus masks mark only 36 pixels in the whole scene, and the default rule (blue reflectance above 0.25) marks 94. Under the cloud the rules see pixels that are no longer water (the cloud raises the NIR) but are not bright enough for cloud, so they end up as “other”, fringed by “shadow”. Lowering the blue threshold to 0.10 does not help: it flags the white surf line and beaches instead. The water and shadow rules themselves work (ocean against land, steep shaded slopes in the mountains). Thin cloud over dark water is a known weak point of simple tests; a scene specific rule, such as treating non water pixels inside the open ocean as suspect, works better here. Use product masks where they work, add rules where they do not, and always look at the result.

title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
text:
From radiance to reflectance
The radiance product of the same window is converted with three scene based methods and compared with Planet’s surface reflectance. For the empirical line, two pixels (the darkest and brightest in the NIR) play the role of field targets, with the surface reflectance product standing in for field spectra.


Code
rad = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("agriculture", "radiance"), window=WIN)  # W m-2 sr-1 um-1
nir = hs.band_at(sr, 860).values
dark = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmin(nir), nir.shape)  # darkest NIR pixel (water)
bright = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(nir), nir.shape)  # brightest NIR pixel
targets = {name: ((slice(r - 1, r + 2), slice(c - 1, c + 2)), sr.values[:, r - 1:r + 2, c - 1:c + 2].mean((1, 2)))
           for name, (r, c) in {"dark": dark, "bright": bright}.items()}  # (window, "field" spectrum)
el, coefs = hs.empirical_line(rad, targets)  # per band gain and offset
ff = hs.flat_field(rad, targets["bright"][0])  # divide by the bright target
iar = hs.iar_reflectance(rad)  # divide by the scene mean

good = sr["good"].values & (wl > 400) & (wl < 2450)  # well-behaved bands
truth = sr.values[good].reshape(good.sum(), -1)  # product reflectance, (bands, pixels)
def mean_angle(e, t):
    """Mean spectral angle (degrees) between estimated and true spectra (columns are pixels)."""
    ok = np.all(np.isfinite(e), 0) & np.all(np.isfinite(t), 0)
    cos = (e[:, ok] * t[:, ok]).sum(0) / (np.linalg.norm(e[:, ok], axis=0) * np.linalg.norm(t[:, ok], axis=0))
    return float(np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cos, -1, 1))).mean())


rows = []
for name, est in [("empirical line", el), ("flat field", ff), ("IAR", iar)]:
    e = est.values[good].reshape(good.sum(), -1)
    ok = np.isfinite(e) & np.isfinite(truth)
    rows.append({"method": name, "output": "reflectance" if name == "empirical line" else "relative",
                 "RMSE (reflectance)": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((e[ok] - truth[ok]) ** 2))) if name == "empirical line" else np.nan,
                 "mean spectral angle to product (deg)": mean_angle(e, truth)})

With two targets the line through them fits exactly (the r2 of 1 in the coefficient table is trivial), but it also predicts all other pixels closely: an RMSE below 0.01 and a spectral angle of about 1 to 2 degrees, because the atmosphere over a 6 km window is nearly uniform and one gain and offset per band describe it. Flat field and IAR spectra are only relative and inherit the shape of their reference: divided by a bright vegetated target or by the forest dominated scene mean, the test pixel loses its red edge and looks nearly flat, which shows up as a spectral angle of tens of degrees. These methods are fallbacks when no atmospheric correction is available, for example for laboratory or drone data.

title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
text:
Smoothing, derivatives and normalisation


Code
cl = sr.isel(band=np.flatnonzero(good))  # well-behaved bands only
veg_rc = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(hs.index(cl, "NDVI").values), nir.shape)  # most vegetated pixel
spec = cl.isel(y=[veg_rc[0]], x=[veg_rc[1]])  # 1 x 1 cube keeps every function usable
sm = {m: hs.smooth(spec, method=m, window=9) for m in ("savgol", "moving", "gaussian")}
d1 = hs.derivative(spec, 1, window=9)  # first derivative (per nm)
d2 = hs.derivative(spec, 2, window=11)  # second derivative

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.2))
w = hs.wavelengths(spec)
axes[0].plot(w, spec.values.ravel(), color="0.6", lw=2, label="original")
for m, s in sm.items():
    axes[0].plot(w, s.values.ravel(), lw=1, label=m)
axes[0].set(xlim=(1950, 2450), ylim=(0, 0.12), title="Smoothing (SWIR detail)", xlabel="Wavelength (nm)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].plot(w, d1.values.ravel()); axes[1].set(xlim=(500, 900), title="First derivative", xlabel="Wavelength (nm)")
rep = float(hs.red_edge_position(spec).values.ravel()[0])  # red edge inflection
axes[1].axvline(rep, color="C3", ls="--"); axes[1].text(rep + 5, axes[1].get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, f"red edge {rep:.0f} nm")
axes[2].plot(w, d2.values.ravel()); axes[2].set(xlim=(500, 1300), title="Second derivative", xlabel="Wavelength (nm)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









All three smoothers reduce band to band noise in the far SWIR; Savitzky Golay keeps narrow features best, a moving average flattens them most. The first derivative turns the red edge into a peak whose position, the red edge inflection, is a chlorophyll and stress indicator (notebook 09_05_04). The second derivative marks curvature changes such as the shoulders of absorption features.


Code
import xarray as xr  # labelled arrays, to pick pixels by index

ndvi = hs.index(cl, "NDVI").values  # narrowband NDVI of the window
forest = np.flatnonzero(ndvi.ravel() > 0.85)  # dense canopy pixels
X = cl.values.reshape(cl.sizes["band"], -1)  # (bands, pixels)
order = np.argsort(X[hs.band_index(cl, 860), forest])  # sort canopy pixels by NIR brightness
pick = forest[order[[5, len(order) // 2, -5]]]  # dark, median and bright canopy
trio = xr.DataArray(X[:, pick][:, None, :], dims=("band", "y", "x"), coords={"wavelength": ("band", hs.wavelengths(cl))})

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
for ax, (title, c) in zip(axes, [("original", trio), ("standard normal variate", hs.snv(trio)),
                                 ("vector normalised", hs.normalize(trio))]):
    for i, lab in enumerate(["shaded canopy", "median canopy", "sunlit canopy"]):
        ax.plot(hs.wavelengths(c), c.values[:, 0, i], lw=1, label=lab)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Wavelength (nm)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









Three dense canopy pixels differ mostly in brightness, because of slope and canopy shadow. After the standard normal variate (each spectrum centred and scaled) or vector normalisation the curves almost coincide, leaving only the small differences in shape that carry biochemical information.

title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
text:
Continuum removal and band depth
The Permian Basin scene is bare caliche and sandy soil with oil and gas pads. Clays absorb near 2200 nm (Al-OH) and carbonates near 2340 nm (CO₃). Continuum removal over 2000 to 2450 nm makes both features visible; hs.band_depth maps them.


Code
em = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("energy-mining"), window=(slice(400, 650), slice(350, 600)), wavelength_range=(1950, 2460))
em = em.isel(band=np.flatnonzero(em["good"].values))  # good SWIR bands
em_s = hs.smooth(em, window=7)  # light smoothing helps feature depth on 5 nm bands
cr, hull = hs.continuum_removal(em_s, start=2000, stop=2450, return_hull=True)  # ratio to the convex hull
r0, c0 = 120, 120  # one pixel
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.2))
axes[0].plot(hs.wavelengths(em_s), em_s.values[:, r0, c0], label="spectrum")
axes[0].plot(hs.wavelengths(hull), hull.values[:, r0, c0], "--", label="convex hull")
axes[0].set(title="SWIR spectrum and its continuum", xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Reflectance"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].plot(hs.wavelengths(cr), cr.values[:, r0, c0])
for w, t in [(2200, "Al-OH 2200"), (2340, "CO3 2340")]:
    axes[1].axvline(w, color="0.5", ls=":"); axes[1].text(w + 4, float(cr.values[:, r0, c0].min()), t, fontsize=8)

The continuum removed spectrum shows the clay and carbonate features as shallow dips of 2 to 3 percent; the deepest dip, near 2010 nm, is residual CO₂ absorption from the atmosphere, not a mineral. The depth maps follow the landscape: well pads and roads, built from crushed caliche (calcium carbonate), stand out as a grid of dots and lines in the carbonate map, while the clay map follows field and soil boundaries. title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
text:
Simulating multispectral sensors
hs.resample_to_sensor convolves the cube with Gaussian approximations of a sensor’s band responses and returns a Dataset with canonical band names (blue, red, nir, swir16, …), the same names geolattice.rsense.optical uses.


Code
s2 = hs.resample_to_sensor(sr, "sentinel2")  # simulated Sentinel-2 bands
print(list(s2.data_vars))
ndvi_s2 = (s2["nir"] - s2["red"]) / (s2["nir"] + s2["red"])  # broadband NDVI (B8, B4)
ndvi_hs = hs.index(sr, "NDVI")  # narrowband NDVI from the nearest Tanager bands
ndre_s2 = (s2["nir08"] - s2["rededge1"]) / (s2["nir08"] + s2["rededge1"])  # Sentinel-2 red edge index
ndre_hs = hs.index(sr, "NDRE")  # narrowband NDRE

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
for ax, (a, b, t) in zip(axes, [(ndvi_hs, ndvi_s2, "NDVI"), (ndre_hs, ndre_s2, "NDRE")]):
    x, y = a.values.ravel(), b.values.ravel()
    ok = np.isfinite(x) & np.isfinite(y)
    ax.hexbin(x[ok], y[ok], gridsize=60, bins="log", cmap="viridis")
    lim = [min(x[ok].min(), y[ok].min()), max(x[ok].max(), y[ok].max())]
    ax.plot(lim, lim, "w--", lw=1)
    ax.set(xlabel=f"Tanager narrowband {t}", ylabel=f"simulated Sentinel-2 {t}",
           title=f"{t}: r = {np.corrcoef(x[ok], y[ok])[0, 1]:.3f}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


['coastal', 'blue', 'green', 'red', 'rededge1', 'rededge2', 'rededge3', 'nir', 'nir08', 'watervapor', 'swir16', 'swir22']









Simulated Sentinel-2 NDVI is almost identical to the narrowband NDVI (r = 1.000, on the 1:1 line): red and NIR reflectance are flat enough across the band widths that averaging changes little. NDRE is different. Sentinel-2’s red edge band 5 (704 nm, 15 nm wide) sits on the steep slope of the red edge, and the simulated index runs well above the narrowband version, with more scatter (r = 0.988). Indices built on steep parts of the spectrum change systematically with band width and position. Models trained on hyperspectral data should therefore be applied to multispectral data only after resampling the training spectra, never with the narrowband formulas.

title: Preprocessing Hyperspectral Cubes
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Remove the opaque water vapour bands and the noisy ends of the range; an SNR threshold catches more, at the cost of bands.
Noise estimates differ by method: the residual method is closest to Tanager’s own uncertainty; the shift difference method mistakes texture for noise.
Pushbroom striping lives in sensor geometry. Column moment matching removes visible stripes but can raise absolute error; the Tanager and OHS L1 data here barely need it.
Simple reflectance rules separate water, land and shadow, but neither they nor the beta product mask catch thin cloud over the ocean: inspect masks, do not trust them blindly.
With uniform atmosphere an empirical line from two targets reproduces surface reflectance well; flat field and IAR give only relative spectra.
Smoothing, derivatives, normalisation and continuum removal each bring out different parts of a spectrum; band depth maps turn absorption features into mineral or biochemical maps.
Resampling to a multispectral sensor changes index values; resample before transferring models.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: read_tanager, read_tanager_ancillary, read_ohs, bad_bands, drop_bad_bands, estimate_noise, destripe, quality_mask, empirical_line, flat_field, iar_reflectance, smooth, derivative, red_edge_position, snv, normalize, continuum_removal, band_depth, index, resample_to_sensor, plot_rgb.
Exercises

Run bad_bands(sr, min_snr=...) for thresholds 2, 5 and 10 and count the remaining bands in the VNIR and SWIR.
Destripe the Tanager swath with method="median" and compare the stripe index with moment matching.

title: Narrowband Indices and Vegetation Analysis
text:
Overview

What a leaf spectrum records








Region
Main absorbers
Typical indices




400 to 500 nm
Chlorophyll a and b, carotenoids
SIPI, CRI


500 to 600 nm
Carotenoids, anthocyanins; xanthophyll cycle at 531 nm
PRI, CRI1, ARI1


650 to 690 nm
Chlorophyll (red absorption)
NDVI, MCARI, TCARI


690 to 750 nm
Red edge: slope set by chlorophyll content and canopy structure
NDRE, MTCI, CIred_edge, red edge position


750 to 1300 nm
Leaf structure and canopy LAI (scattering); weak water bands at 970 and 1200 nm
NDVI, MTVI2, WBI, NDWI (Gao)


1300 to 2500 nm
Leaf water; dry matter (cellulose, lignin, protein) near 1730, 2100 and 2300 nm
NDII, MSI, CAI, NDLI, NDNI





Why narrow bands
Broadband NDVI saturates once the canopy closes (LAI above about 3): red reflectance is near zero and NIR is high, so further increases in chlorophyll or leaf area barely change the ratio. Indices built on the red edge, where absorption is weaker, keep responding to chlorophyll at high biomass. Narrow green bands make pigment and photosynthetic efficiency indices possible (PRI tracks the de-epoxidation of xanthophylls under excess light), and narrow SWIR bands separate leaf water from dry matter, the basis of drought stress, fuel moisture and crop residue mapping.


The red edge position
The wavelength of the steepest slope between about 680 and 760 nm, the red edge position (REP), moves to longer wavelengths as chlorophyll increases (a few nm per 10 µg cm⁻²) and to shorter wavelengths under stress or senescence. It is estimated from the maximum of the first derivative or with the four point linear interpolation of Guyot and Baret (1988).


Caveats
Indices respond to everything that changes reflectance at their bands: soil background, canopy structure, view and sun angles, illumination and atmospheric residuals. They are fast and robust proxies, but quantitative retrieval (notebook 09_05_05) needs models and field data.
