title: Narrowband Indices and Vegetation Analysis
text:
Index maps
A 400 by 400 pixel window (12 by 12 km) of the agriculture scene covers forest, fields, the river and a town.


Code
agri = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("agriculture"), window=(slice(150, 550), slice(200, 600)))  # all bands
NAMES = ["NDVI", "NDRE", "MTCI", "PRI", "CRI1", "ARI1", "PSRI", "NDWI_Gao", "NDII", "CAI", "NDLI", "NBR_hs"]
idx = hs.index(agri, NAMES)  # Dataset, one map per index
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(16, 12))
hs.plot_rgb(agri, "true_color", ax=axes[0, 0])
for ax, n in zip(axes.ravel()[1:], NAMES[:11]):
    v = idx[n]
    ax.imshow(v, cmap="RdYlGn" if n not in ("PSRI", "CAI", "ARI1", "CRI1") else "viridis",
              vmin=np.nanpercentile(v, 2), vmax=np.nanpercentile(v, 98))
    ax.set_title(n); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









NDVI, NDRE and MTCI all outline the forest, but with different contrast inside it: NDVI is almost uniform over the closed canopy, while the red edge indices still vary. The water indices (NDWI and NDII) are high wherever leaves are wet and dense, and the town and bare ground stand out as low. The cellulose absorption index (CAI) is nearly uniform over this green wet season landscape and drops only over the river and wet ground, since there is little dry plant matter to detect. PRI, CRI1, ARI1 and PSRI show finer patterns tied to pigments and illumination, and all of them mark the sediment laden river strongly.

title: Narrowband Indices and Vegetation Analysis
text:
How many independent indices?


Code
veg = (idx["NDVI"] > 0.5).values  # vegetated pixels
T = pd.DataFrame({n: idx[n].values[veg] for n in NAMES}).dropna()  # one row per pixel
corr = T.corr(method="spearman")  # rank correlation between indices
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6.5))
im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(NAMES)), NAMES, rotation=60); ax.set_yticks(range(len(NAMES)), NAMES)
for i in range(len(NAMES)):
    for j in range(len(NAMES)):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{corr.iat[i, j]:.1f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7)
ax.set_title(f"Spearman correlation over {len(T):,} vegetated pixels")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8)
plt.show()









Several groups emerge. NDVI, NDII and the burn ratio correlate at 0.8 to 1.0 in this canopy, because greener canopies here are also wetter; the red edge indices NDRE and MTCI form a tight pair (0.9); the anthocyanin and senescence indices (ARI1, PSRI) run against all the greenness indices; PRI, CAI and NDLI are only weakly related to the rest and carry the most independent information. In a model it is better to choose one index per group, or to use the full spectrum (notebook 09_05_05), than to stack a dozen indices that measure the same thing.

Red edge position


Code
rep_d = hs.red_edge_position(agri)  # maximum first derivative, parabolic refinement
rep_l = hs.red_edge_position(agri, method="linear")  # four point linear interpolation

Both methods place the red edge of this canopy near 721 nm, and the spread is small: a few nm across the whole window, close to the 5 nm band spacing. In such a narrow range the two methods agree only moderately (r about 0.64): the derivative method follows the sampled spectrum and is noisier, the linear method assumes a straight red edge between 700 and 740 nm and compresses the range. MTCI, which uses three bands on the red edge, is related to the REP to a similar degree (r about 0.62). Use one method consistently when comparing dates or sites, and expect the REP to be most useful where chlorophyll varies more than in this uniformly green forest.

title: Narrowband Indices and Vegetation Analysis
section: NDVI saturation and red edge indices
text:
NDVI saturation and red edge indices
If NDVI saturates, it should flatten while a red edge index keeps rising as canopy greenness increases. A plot against the red edge chlorophyll index (CIred_edge, a ratio that does not saturate) shows it.


Code
ci = hs.index(agri, "CIred_edge").values  # R800 / R720 - 1
v = veg & np.isfinite(ci)
bins = np.quantile(ci[v], np.linspace(0, 1, 21))  # 20 equal-count bins of CIred_edge
mid = 0.5 * (bins[1:] + bins[:-1])
med = {n: [np.nanmedian(idx[n].values[v][(ci[v] >= a) & (ci[v] < b)]) for a, b in zip(bins[:-1], bins[1:])]
       for n in ["NDVI", "NDRE"]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
for n, m in med.items():
    ax.plot(mid, m, "o-", label=n)
ax.set(xlabel="CIred_edge (bin medians)", ylabel="Index value (median)", title="NDVI flattens, NDRE keeps rising")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
slope = {n: np.polyfit(mid[-8:], np.array(m)[-8:], 1)[0] / np.polyfit(mid[:8], np.array(m)[:8], 1)[0] for n, m in med.items()}
print("slope in the densest 8 bins relative to the sparsest 8 bins:", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in slope.items()})









slope in the densest 8 bins relative to the sparsest 8 bins: {'NDVI': np.float64(0.08), 'NDRE': np.float64(0.38)}


Over sparse vegetation both indices rise with CIred_edge; in the densest canopy NDVI’s slope drops to a small fraction of its initial value, while NDRE keeps a larger share of its sensitivity (compare the two slope ratios printed above). This is the practical reason to use red edge indices for nitrogen and chlorophyll in closed crops and forests.

title: Narrowband Indices and Vegetation Analysis
text:
Three scenes, three seasons
Vegetation from the Chaco in the wet season, Bosnian hills in winter and New York farmland and forest in late summer. Each scene is read with only the bands the indices need (14 bands), and pixels with NDVI above 0.3 are compared; at most 20,000 pixels are sampled per scene.


Code
COMPARE = ["NDVI", "MTCI", "PRI", "NDII", "CAI", "PSRI"]
need = sorted({float(w) for n in COMPARE for w in hs.indices.INDICES[n].wavelengths})  # wavelengths used

for cat_name, label in [("agriculture", "Chaco, Feb (wet season)"), ("natural-lands", "Bosnia, Feb (winter)"),
                        ("ROCX2025", "New York, Sep (late summer)")]:
    c = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file(cat_name), bands=bands)  # whole scene, needed bands only
    d = hs.index(c, COMPARE).to_dataframe()[COMPARE].dropna()  # one row per pixel

    rows.append(d.assign(scene=label))
    print(f"{label}: {len(bands)} bands read, {(d['NDVI'] > 0.3).sum():,} vegetated pixels sampled")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(COMPARE), figsize=(18, 4))
for ax, n in zip(axes, COMPARE):
    ax.boxplot([comp.loc[comp.scene == s, n] for s in comp.scene.unique()], showfliers=False)
    ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3], ["Chaco", "Bosnia", "New York"], rotation=20); ax.set_title(n)

plt.show()
comp.groupby("scene")[COMPARE].median().round(3)

title: Narrowband Indices and Vegetation Analysis
text:
A custom index
hs.register_index adds an index by name, wavelengths and formula; the formula receives one reflectance array per wavelength. Here the green chlorophyll index (Gitelson et al. 2003), CIgreen = R800 / R550 - 1, is added and compared with CIred_edge.


Code
hs.register_index("CIgreen", [800, 550], lambda r800, r550: r800 / r550 - 1,
                  description="Green chlorophyll index", reference="Gitelson et al. 2003")
cig = hs.index(agri, "CIgreen")  # works like any built in index
both = np.isfinite(cig.values) & v
print("CIgreen in catalogue:", "CIgreen" in hs.list_indices(),
      "| Spearman r with CIred_edge:", round(pd.Series(cig.values[both]).corr(pd.Series(ci[both]), method="spearman"), 3))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.8))
for ax, (n, a) in zip(axes, [("CIgreen", cig.values), ("CIred_edge", ci)]):

    ax.set_title(n); ax.axis("off")

Summary and exercises
Key points

Narrowband indices target single absorption features: pigments, red edge, leaf water and dry matter. Defined by wavelength, they run on any imaging spectrometer that covers the bands.
Many indices are strongly correlated; choose one per group or use full spectrum models.
The red edge position and red edge indices respond to chlorophyll where NDVI saturates.
Index distributions separate green, dormant and senescent vegetation between places and seasons.
Custom indices are one line with hs.register_index.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: read_tanager, index, list_indices, available_indices, red_edge_position, register_index, band_index, plot_rgb.
Exercises

Compute hs.index(agri, "PRI", width=10) (averaging bands over 10 nm). Does the map get less noisy?
Map NDNI and NDLI over the agriculture window. Do they show patterns that NDVI does not?
Compute the REP for the ROCX scene and compare the distribution with the Chaco scene.

title: Spectral Libraries and Spectral Matching
text:
Overview

Spectral libraries
A spectral library is a set of reference spectra on a common wavelength grid, with metadata. Major public libraries are:








Library
Content
Range




USGS Spectral Library version 7 (splib07)
Minerals, rocks, soils, vegetation, man made materials, mixtures; also convolved to many sensors
200 nm to 200 µm


ECOSTRESS / ASTER library (JPL)
Minerals, rocks, soils, vegetation, water, snow, man made
0.35 to 15.4 µm


SPECCHIO and EcoSIS
Field and laboratory spectra with metadata, many vegetation datasets
mostly 350 to 2500 nm



Laboratory spectra have higher spectral resolution than any imaging spectrometer, so they must be resampled to the sensor’s bands (convolved with its spectral response functions) before comparison. Image endmembers (spectra taken from the image itself) avoid calibration and atmospheric mismatches but are rarely pure.


Similarity measures
For a pixel spectrum x and a reference s:

Spectral angle mapper (SAM) (Kruse et al. 1993): the angle between the two vectors, arccos(x·s / (|x| |s|)). Insensitive to overall brightness (illumination, topography).
Spectral information divergence (SID) (Chang 2000): a symmetric relative entropy between the spectra normalised to probability distributions. Sensitive to small differences in shape.
SID-SAM: SID multiplied by the tangent of SAM, combining both (Du et al. 2004).
Spectral correlation angle (SCA): based on the Pearson correlation, so insensitive to both gain and offset.
Euclidean distance: sensitive to brightness; useful when absolute reflectance matters.

The pixel is assigned to the most similar reference; a threshold on the best score leaves pixels unclassified when nothing in the library matches, which is how unknown materials show up.


Matching absorption features
Overall shape is dominated by brightness and broad slopes. For minerals, matching continuum removed spectra over the diagnostic window (for example 2000 to 2450 nm) compares the absorption features themselves, the idea behind expert systems such as the USGS Tetracorder.

Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings

from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
from geolattice.rsense import hyperspectral as hs  # hyperspectral cubes, readers and tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_05_HyperSpectral")  # data folder next to this notebook
TANAGER = DATA / "Tanger"  # Planet Tanager sample scenes
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed


def tanager_file(category, product="sr"):
    """Path of a Tanager product (sr or radiance) for a scene category folder."""
    return next((TANAGER / category).glob(f"*/*_ortho_{product}_hdf5.h5"))


print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__)  # library version used for this notebook

import re  # wavelengths from file names
import geopandas as gpd  # labelled points for image libraries
from PIL import Image  # PNG band images
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap  # class colours
from matplotlib.patches import Patch  # legend entries


def read_png_cube(folder):
    """Stack the *_<wavelength>nm.png band images of a HACARUS scene into a cube."""
    files = sorted(Path(folder).glob("*nm.png"), key=lambda p: float(re.search(r"_(\d+)nm", p.name)[1]))
    wl = [float(re.search(r"_(\d+)nm", p.name)[1]) for p in files]
    return hs.as_cube(np.stack([np.asarray(Image.open(p), dtype="float32") for p in files]), wl, name="dn")


def disc(shape, r, c, radius):
    """Boolean disc mask."""
    rr, cc = np.mgrid[:shape[0], :shape[1]]
    return (rr - r) ** 2 + (cc - c) ** 2 <= radius ** 2

For reflectance images with topography and shadow, angle based measures are the usual choice; Euclidean distance is useful when brightness is diagnostic (water against dark asphalt).

section: A laboratory scene: sugar, salt and flour
text:
A laboratory scene: sugar, salt and flour
Small training discs (radius 6 pixels) give one spectrum per class. Larger reference discs around them, excluding the training pixels, are used to score each measure.


Code
ssf = read_png_cube(DATA / "archive/data/sugar_salt_flour")  # (96, 256, 192)
shape = ssf.shape[1:]
centres = {"tray": (30, 100), "sugar": (110, 112), "flour": (160, 62), "salt": (190, 117)}  # (row, col)
train = {k: disc(shape, r, c, 6) for k, (r, c) in centres.items()}
refer = {k: disc(shape, r, c, 16) & ~train[k] for k, (r, c) in centres.items()}  # evaluation pixels
lab_lib = hs.library.from_dict({k: hs.mean_spectrum(ssf, m).values for k, m in train.items()}, hs.wavelengths(ssf))
print(lab_lib, lab_lib.names)

results, maps = [], {}
for m in ["sam", "sid", "sca", "euclidean"]:
    cls = hs.classify_spectral(ssf, lab_lib, measure=m)  # best match per pixel
    maps[m] = cls["class"].values
    correct = sum(int((maps[m][refer[k]] == i).sum()) for i, k in enumerate(lab_lib.names))
    total = sum(int(refer[k].sum()) for k in lab_lib.names)
    results.append({"measure": m, "accuracy on reference discs": correct / total})
pd.DataFrame(results).set_index("measure").round(3)

SAM, SID and SCA classify every reference pixel correctly and give almost identical maps; their only visible error is a strip of “flour” along the dark right edge of the tray. title: Spectral Libraries and Spectral Matching
text:
An unknown material
The second scene holds the same powders plus a small white eraser hidden in the sugar. It is classified with the library from the first scene, so the eraser has no class of its own. A SAM threshold leaves pixels unclassified when even the best match is poor.


Code
con = read_png_cube(DATA / "archive/data/sugar_salt_flour_contamination")  # same camera, another acquisition
sam_con = hs.sam(con, lab_lib)  # angle to each class (radians)
best = sam_con.min("target").values  # best angle per pixel
eraser = disc(con.shape[1:], 110, 118, 7)  # eraser location from the dataset's annotated preview
sugar_ring = disc(con.shape[1:], 110, 118, 25) & ~disc(con.shape[1:], 110, 118, 12)  # sugar around it
print(f"median best angle: eraser {np.degrees(np.median(best[eraser])):.1f} deg, "
      f"surrounding sugar {np.degrees(np.median(best[sugar_ring])):.1f} deg, scene {np.degrees(np.median(best)):.1f} deg")
thr = float(np.quantile(best, 0.99))  # reject the 1 percent worst matching pixels
cls_con = hs.classify_spectral(con, lab_lib, measure="sam", threshold=thr)
rejected = cls_con["class"].values == -1
print(f"threshold {np.degrees(thr):.1f} deg | eraser pixels rejected: {rejected[eraser].mean():.0%} | "
      f"other pixels rejected: {rejected[~eraser].mean():.1%}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.8))
axes[0].imshow(hs.band_at(con, 1940), cmap="gray"); axes[0].add_patch(plt.Circle((118, 110), 9, fill=False, color="r"))
axes[0].set_title("1940 nm (eraser circled)")
im = axes[1].imshow(np.degrees(best), cmap="magma", vmax=np.degrees(np.quantile(best, 0.995)))
axes[1].set_title("Best SAM angle (deg)"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1], shrink=0.8)
axes[2].imshow(np.where(rejected, np.nan, cls_con["class"].values), cmap=cmap, vmin=-0.5, vmax=3.5, interpolation="nearest")
axes[2].set_title("SAM classes, unmatched pixels blank")
for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


median best angle: eraser 6.0 deg, surrounding sugar 3.0 deg, scene 1.9 deg
threshold 9.2 deg | eraser pixels rejected: 30% | other pixels rejected: 0.9%









The eraser’s best match (a median of about 6 degrees) is twice as poor as that of the sugar around it, so the eraser stands out as a bright spot in the angle map, and a threshold that rejects only one percent of the scene rejects about a third of its pixels. The rest of the eraser’s pixels are mixed with sugar at its edge and still match sugar. The other rejected pixels lie along the boundaries between piles, where powders mix. Matching against a library finds the eraser, but crudely. This is the simplest form of anomaly detection, and notebook 09_05_08 develops detectors that do much better.

title: Spectral Libraries and Spectral Matching
text:
Minerals in the Permian Basin
Clays and carbonates are identified by their SWIR absorption features. The energy and mining scene is matched over 2000 to 2450 nm, both on the raw spectra and on continuum removed spectra, against the synthetic clay, carbonate, soil and dry vegetation spectra.


Code
WIN = (slice(400, 650), slice(350, 600))
em = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("energy-mining"), window=WIN, wavelength_range=(2000, 2450))
em = hs.smooth(em.isel(band=np.flatnonzero(em["good"].values)), window=7)  # good SWIR bands, lightly smoothed
em_cr = hs.continuum_removal(em)  # continuum removed image


def cr_library(lib):
    """Resample a library to the image bands and continuum remove it."""
    c = hs.resample_spectral(hs.as_cube(lib.spectra.T[:, None, :], lib.wavelengths), hs.wavelengths(em))
    return hs.SpectralLibrary(hs.wavelengths(em), hs.continuum_removal(c).values[:, 0, :].T, lib.names)


ref = lib_tan.subset(["clay_kaolinite", "carbonate_calcite", "soil", "dry_vegetation"])
syn = hs.classify_spectral(em_cr, cr_library(ref), measure="sam")  # synthetic references
pd.Series(syn["class"].values.ravel()).map(dict(enumerate(ref.names))).value_counts(normalize=True).to_frame("synthetic references")









synthetic references




soil
1.0







With the idealised references almost every pixel goes to one class. The synthetic spectra have deep, clean Gaussian features, while the real features here are 2 to 5 percent deep and sit on a noisy, sloping continuum, so one reference happens to be closest to everything. This is the common failure of matching against references that do not resemble the data, and the reason real libraries (resampled with the sensor’s response functions) or image references are used.
Image references come from the pixels with the strongest features. The band depth maps of notebook 09_05_02 pick the 25 pixels with the deepest carbonate feature (positioned between 2320 and 2365 nm) and the 25 with the deepest clay feature; the scene median stands for background soil.


Code

top_c = np.unravel_index(np.argsort(np.where(real, cd, -1).ravel())[-25:], cd.shape)  # deepest carbonate pixels
top_k = np.unravel_index(np.argsort(kd.ravel())[-25:], kd.shape)  # deepest clay pixels

img_cr = cr_library(img_lib)
cr = hs.classify_spectral(em_cr, img_cr, measure="sam")
crc = cr["class"].values
summary = pd.DataFrame({"fraction": [np.mean(crc == i) for i in range(3)],
                        "median carbonate depth": [np.median(cd[crc == i]) for i in range(3)],
                        "median clay depth": [np.median(kd[crc == i]) for i in range(3)]}, index=img_lib.names)

The carbonate pixels are the well pads and roads built from crushed caliche, a few percent of the window; the clay rich class follows patches of soil, and the rest is background. The continuum removed references show why: the carbonate reference has a clear minimum near 2340 nm, the clay reference near 2205 nm, and the background has weak versions of both. title: Spectral Libraries and Spectral Matching
section: An image library for a city
text:
An image library for a city
Image libraries come from labelled samples. Here 30 pixels per class are chosen by simple index rules (as in notebook 09_05_00) and stored as a GeoDataFrame of points; hs.from_image averages their spectra into a library, which then classifies the whole window with a SAM threshold.


Code
urban = hs.drop_bad_bands(hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("urban"), window=(slice(319, 619), slice(285, 585))))
G, R, N, S1 = (hs.band_at(urban, w).values for w in (560, 650, 860, 1650))
ndvi, ndwi = (N - R) / (N + R), (G - N) / (G + N)
rules = {"water": ndwi > 0.3, "tree and grass": ndvi > 0.75,
         "bright roof": (ndvi < 0.15) & (S1 > np.nanquantile(S1, 0.97)),
         "dark pavement": (ndvi < 0.15) & (ndwi < 0) & (S1 < np.nanquantile(S1[ndvi < 0.15], 0.15)),
         "mixed residential": (ndvi > 0.35) & (ndvi < 0.5)}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pts = []
for label, mask in rules.items():
    r, c = np.nonzero(mask)
    pick = rng.choice(len(r), min(30, len(r)), replace=False)  # 30 random pixels per class
    pts += [{"label": label, "row": int(rr), "col": int(cc), "x": float(urban.x[cc]), "y": float(urban.y[rr])}
            for rr, cc in zip(r[pick], c[pick])]
pts = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pts, geometry=gpd.points_from_xy([p["x"] for p in pts], [p["y"] for p in pts]), crs=urban.rio.crs)
city_lib = hs.from_image(urban, pts, "label", buffer=0)  # mean spectrum per label
print(city_lib, city_lib.names, "| points per class:", pts["label"].value_counts().to_dict())

hs.plot_rgb(urban, "true_color", ax=axes[0])

The class map reproduces the city’s structure: parks and tree lined streets, the large flat roofs of commercial buildings and paved areas stand out from the mixed residential blocks, which cover about 60 percent of the window. Water, although in the library, is not assigned at all. The window holds only a thin strip of river, and water is so dark (1 to 3 percent reflectance) that noise dominates its spectral shape: the water pixels lie a median of about 17 degrees from their own mean spectrum, beyond the 8 degree threshold, so they stay unclassified. Angle measures are a poor choice for very dark targets; a brightness rule or Euclidean distance works better for water. The red dots show where the training pixels came from: because the rules pick extreme pixels for some classes, the library spectra are purer than typical pixels, which is one reason mixed pixels end up in “mixed residential” or unclassified. Unmixing (notebook 09_05_07) models such pixels as mixtures instead.

title: Spectral Libraries and Spectral Matching
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Libraries must be resampled to the sensor; features outside the sensor’s range or narrower than its bands cannot be matched.
SAM, SID and SCA ignore brightness (SCA also offsets); Euclidean distance does not. Angle based measures suit images with shadows and topography.
A library from small training regions classifies a laboratory scene almost perfectly; a threshold on the best score exposes materials missing from the library.
Continuum removal makes matching depend on absorption features, which is essential for minerals.
Image libraries from labelled points map urban surfaces quickly; mixed pixels remain a limitation.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: SpectralLibrary, synthetic_library, library.from_dict, from_image, as_cube, mean_spectrum, sam, spectral_similarity, classify_spectral, continuum_removal, band_depth, resample_spectral, smooth, read_tanager, drop_bad_bands, plot_rgb.
Exercises

Classify the HACARUS rice scene with a library built from training discs on the three rice types and the eraser. Which measure works best?
Repeat the Permian Basin matching with SID and SID-SAM on the continuum removed spectra.
Change the city threshold to 5 and 12 degrees. How does the unclassified fraction change?
Download a few USGS splib07 spectra (for example kaolinite, calcite and montmorillonite, ASCII files of the splib07a set), read them with hs.read_usgs(folder), resample them with lib.resample(cube) and repeat the mineral matching with real references.

title: Target and Anomaly Detection
text: Banner

title: Target and Anomaly Detection
text:
Overview

Background and the Mahalanobis distance
Let μ and Σ be the mean and covariance of the background spectra. A pixel x is unusual when it is far from μ in units of the background spread, measured by the Mahalanobis distance (x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ). Whitening by Σ⁻¹ is what makes hyperspectral detectors powerful: it suppresses directions in which the background naturally varies (brightness, vegetation amount) and amplifies directions in which it does not.


Anomaly detection

RX (Reed and Xiaoli 1990) is the Mahalanobis distance to the global background (global RX) or to a ring of pixels around each pixel, excluding a guard window (local RX). No target spectrum is needed, but every rare material is an anomaly, wanted or not.



Target detection
With a target spectrum t:

Matched filter (MF): (x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (t − μ) / (t − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (t − μ), normalised so that a pure target scores about 1 and the background about 0; for small fractions the score approximates the target abundance.
Adaptive coherence estimator (ACE) (Kraut and Scharf 1999): the squared cosine between the whitened pixel and the whitened target; between 0 and 1 and insensitive to pixel brightness.
Constrained energy minimisation (CEM) (Harsanyi 1993): a filter with unit response to the target and minimum average output, using the correlation matrix (no mean removal).
Orthogonal subspace projection (OSP) (Harsanyi and Chang 1994): projects out a set of known background signatures, then matches the target.



Evaluating detectors
A detector produces a score map; a threshold turns it into detections. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) plots the true positive rate against the false alarm rate over all thresholds, and its area (AUC) summarises it. In practice targets are rare, so what matters is the detection rate at a very low false alarm rate (for example one in a thousand pixels).

title: Target and Anomaly Detection
text:
Detection with GeoLattice
hs.rx (global and local), hs.matched_filter, hs.ace, hs.cem and hs.osp return score maps on the cube grid; a background mask restricts the statistics to chosen pixels and shrinkage stabilises the covariance. hs.detection_roc computes the ROC table with the AUC in its attributes.

Learning objectives

Compute global and local RX anomaly maps and interpret them.
Build a target spectrum from one scene and detect the target in another.
Compare MF, ACE, CEM and OSP and their sensitivity to background statistics.
Implant sub-pixel targets of known fraction and measure detection rates with ROC curves.
Use the matched filter score as an abundance estimate.

title: Target and Anomaly Detection
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings

from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
from geolattice.rsense import hyperspectral as hs  # hyperspectral cubes, readers and tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_05_HyperSpectral")  # data folder next to this notebook
TANAGER = DATA / "Tanger"  # Planet Tanager sample scenes
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed


def tanager_file(category, product="sr"):
    """Path of a Tanager product (sr or radiance) for a scene category folder."""
    return next((TANAGER / category).glob(f"*/*_ortho_{product}_hdf5.h5"))


print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__)  # library version used for this notebook

import re  # wavelengths from file names
from PIL import Image  # PNG band images


def read_png_cube(folder):
    """Stack the *_<wavelength>nm.png band images of a HACARUS scene into a cube."""
    files = sorted(Path(folder).glob("*nm.png"), key=lambda p: float(re.search(r"_(\d+)nm", p.name)[1]))
    wl = [float(re.search(r"_(\d+)nm", p.name)[1]) for p in files]
    return hs.as_cube(np.stack([np.asarray(Image.open(p), dtype="float32") for p in files]), wl, name="dn")


def disc(shape, r, c, radius):
    """Boolean disc mask."""
    rr, cc = np.mgrid[:shape[0], :shape[1]]
    return (rr - r) ** 2 + (cc - c) ** 2 <= radius ** 2


def tpr_at(score, truth, far):
    """Share of target pixels above the threshold that only a fraction `far` of background pixels exceed."""
    s = np.asarray(getattr(score, "values", score), float)
    t = np.asarray(truth, bool)
    ok = np.isfinite(s)
    thr = np.quantile(s[ok & ~t], 1 - far)  # background quantile
    return float(np.mean(s[ok & t] > thr))


GeoLattice 0.3.49

rx_g = hs.rx(con)  # global RX on the first 10 principal components (default)
rx_l = hs.rx(con, mode="local", window=21, guard=7)  # local RX: ring between 7 and 10 pixels
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.8))

        for t, m in [("global RX", rx_g), ("local RX", rx_l)]}

The eraser is the brightest spot in both RX maps, but it has competition. Global RX also lights up the camera’s vertical stripes (column to column differences of the push broom sensor, invisible in the band image but rare in the statistics) and parts of the lower pile. Local RX suppresses the stripes, because neighbouring columns share them, but turns every small irregularity in the powder texture into speckle. Only about a third of the eraser disc is detected at a false alarm rate of 1 percent; part of the disc is mixed border pixels. Neither detector knows what the eraser looks like.

title: Target and Anomaly Detection
section: A target spectrum from another scene
text:
A target spectrum from another scene
The rice scene, taken with the same camera, also contains a small eraser. Its spectrum, the mean of a 3 by 3 window at the local RX peak near the annotated position, becomes the target signature for the other scene. Using a signature from a different acquisition is the realistic case: a library or field spectrum is never measured in the image being searched.


Code
rice = read_png_cube(DATA / "archive/data/rice")
near = disc(rice.shape[1:], 135, 155, 12)  # around the annotated eraser
rxr = hs.rx(rice, mode="local", window=21, guard=7).values
r0, c0 = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(np.where(near, rxr, -np.inf)), rxr.shape)  # strongest anomaly there
target = rice.values[:, r0 - 1:r0 + 2, c0 - 1:c0 + 2].reshape(rice.sizes["band"], -1).mean(1)  # eraser spectrum
sugar_rice = rice.values[:, disc(rice.shape[1:], 110, 120, 20)].mean(1)  # rice B around it, for comparison
print("eraser found at", (int(r0), int(c0)), "in the rice scene")
wl = hs.wavelengths(con)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4))
ax.plot(wl, target, lw=2, label="eraser (rice scene) = target")
ax.plot(wl, sugar_rice, label="rice B (rice scene)")

title: Target and Anomaly Detection
section: Implanting sub-pixel targets in a city
text:
Implanting sub-pixel targets in a city
To measure detection at known fractions, 40 pixels of the Portland window are replaced by linear mixtures of the original pixel and a target: crushed caliche (calcium carbonate) taken from a well pad in the Permian Basin scene, a material absent from the city. The fractions are spread evenly between 2 and 40 percent.


Code
urban = hs.drop_bad_bands(hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("urban"), window=(slice(319, 619), slice(285, 585))))
em = hs.read_tanager(tanager_file("energy-mining"), window=(slice(400, 650), slice(350, 600)))
em = em.sel(band=urban["band"])  # same good bands as the urban cube
cd = hs.band_depth(em, 2340, 2270, 2400)["depth"].values  # carbonate feature depth
r, c = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(cd), cd.shape)  # deepest carbonate pixel: a caliche pad
caliche = em.values[:, r - 1:r + 2, c - 1:c + 2].reshape(em.sizes["band"], -1).mean(1)  # 3 x 3 mean spectrum

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
H, W = urban.shape[1:]
flat = rng.choice(H * W, 40, replace=False)  # 40 random pixels
rows_, cols_ = np.unravel_index(flat, (H, W))
frac = np.linspace(0.02, 0.40, 40)  # known target fractions
implanted = urban.copy()
X = implanted.values
for rr, cc, f in zip(rows_, cols_, frac):
    X[:, rr, cc] = (1 - f) * X[:, rr, cc] + f * caliche  # linear mixture
truth_u = np.zeros((H, W), bool); truth_u[rows_, cols_] = True
print("target pixel from the Permian Basin:", (int(r), int(c)), f"| 2340 nm depth {cd[r, c]:.3f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.8))
ax.plot(hs.wavelengths(urban), caliche, lw=2, label="caliche target")
ax.plot(hs.wavelengths(urban), np.nanmedian(urban.values.reshape(urban.sizes["band"], -1), 1), label="Portland median")
ax.set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Reflectance", title="Target and background"); ax.legend()
plt.show()


target pixel from the Permian Basin: (210, 21) | 2340 nm depth 0.175

text:
Matched filter scores as abundances


Code
mf_by_frac = det["MF"].values[rows_, cols_]  # MF score of each target, in the order of frac
slope, icpt = np.polyfit(frac, mf_by_frac, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
ax.plot(frac, mf_by_frac, "o")
ax.plot([0, 0.4], [0, 0.4], "k--", lw=1, label="1:1")

      f"99.9th percentile {np.nanpercentile(det['MF'].values[~truth_u], 99.9):.3f}")









correlation 0.998 | background MF: median -0.000, 99.9th percentile 0.057


The matched filter score rises linearly with the implanted fraction, so after normalisation it is an abundance estimate, the basis of gas plume retrieval in the next notebook (where the “target” is a methane absorption spectrum and the score becomes a column enhancement). The fit has a slope of 1.00 and no offset. Scatter around the line comes from the background pixel each target was mixed into; the 99.9th percentile of the background score (about 0.06) is the fraction above which a target stands out from all but one in a thousand background pixels.

title: Target and Anomaly Detection
text:
Anomalies in the city
Without implanted targets, what does RX find in Portland?


Code
rx_u = hs.rx(urban, n_components=20)  # global RX on the original window
top = np.argsort(np.nan_to_num(rx_u.values, nan=-1).ravel())[-8:][::-1]  # eight most anomalous pixels
tr, tc = np.unravel_index(top, rx_u.shape)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1, 1.4]})
hs.plot_rgb(urban, "true_color", ax=axes[0]); axes[0].plot(tc, tr, "c+", ms=12, mew=2)
axes[1].imshow(rx_u, cmap="magma", vmax=np.nanpercentile(rx_u, 99.5)); axes[1].set_title("Global RX"); axes[1].axis("off")
for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(tr[:5], tc[:5])):
    axes[2].plot(hs.wavelengths(urban), urban.values[:, a, b], lw=1, label=f"anomaly {i + 1} ({a}, {b})")
axes[2].plot(hs.wavelengths(urban), np.nanmedian(urban.values.reshape(urban.sizes["band"], -1), 1), "k", lw=2, label="median")
axes[2].set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Reflectance", title="Top anomalies"); axes[2].legend(fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The strongest anomalies are a few unusual surfaces: very bright roofs and spectra with unusual SWIR features (roofing materials or coatings) that occur in only a handful of pixels. RX finds them without any prior knowledge, which makes it a good screening tool, but every one of them has to be inspected; a target detector with the right signature is far more selective.

title: Target and Anomaly Detection
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Whitening by the background covariance is what makes hyperspectral detectors sensitive to small targets.
RX needs no signature but flags every rare material; local RX favours small objects in uniform surroundings.
With a target signature, even one from another acquisition, MF, ACE and CEM detect targets far more selectively than RX; OSP depends on how well its undesired signatures describe the background.
Implanted targets of known fraction give honest ROC curves: detection is reliable above a few percent fraction in a city at 30 m, and the matched filter score estimates the fraction.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: rx, matched_filter, ace, cem, osp, detection_roc, nfindr, band_depth, band_at, read_tanager, drop_bad_bands, as_cube, plot_rgb.
Exercises

Estimate the background for the matched filter only from pixels outside the piles (background= mask). Does detection of the eraser improve?
Implant the targets at fractions between 0.5 and 5 percent. At what fraction does the MF detection rate at a false alarm rate of 0.1 percent fall below one half?
Add shrinkage=1e-3 to the matched filter in the city. Why can shrinkage help when the number of pixels is small compared with the number of bands?
Use the snow spectrum from notebook 09_05_00 as the target in the city. What do the strongest detections look like?

text: Banner

title: Thematic Applications Across Tanager Scenes
text:
Overview

Fire and burn severity
Fire removes green leaves (NIR falls), exposes ash, char and soil and dries what remains (SWIR rises). The normalised burn ratio, NBR = (R860 − R2200) / (R860 + R2200), falls from about 0.4 to 0.7 over healthy vegetation to near zero or below over severe burns. With images before and after a fire the difference (dNBR) measures severity; with one post fire image the NBR and the spectra of char and ash still outline the burn. Hyperspectral sensors also see active fires through thermal emission in the SWIR and the potassium emission lines at 766 and 770 nm.


Snow and ice
Snow is the brightest natural surface in the visible and one of the darkest in the SWIR, because ice absorbs strongly beyond about 1400 nm. The normalised difference snow index, NDSI = (R560 − R1650) / (R560 + R1650), separates snow from clouds and other surfaces. Weaker ice absorptions at 1030 and 1260 nm deepen as grain size grows, because light travels farther through ice in larger grains; the depth or area of the 1030 nm feature is a classic grain size proxy (Nolin and Dozier 2000). Impurities (dust, soot, algae) lower the visible reflectance.


Coastal and inland water
Water leaving radiance is a few percent of the total signal, so atmospheric and sun glint correction matter. A common glint correction subtracts the NIR or SWIR reflectance, where water leaving signal is negligible, from every band. Suspended sediment raises red and NIR reflectance (roughly linearly up to tens of g m⁻³); chlorophyll a creates a dip near 670 nm and a peak near 700 nm, which the normalised difference chlorophyll index, NDCI = (R708 − R665) / (R708 + R665), exploits in turbid water (Mishra and Mishra 2012); cyanobacteria add a phycocyanin dip near 620 nm.


Iron oxides and soils
Ferric iron (hematite, goethite) absorbs strongly in the blue and green and weakly near 900 nm, which makes iron rich soils and rocks red or orange. A red to green ratio, or the depth of the 900 nm feature, maps them; ferrous iron (in many silicates) absorbs near 1000 nm.

title: Thematic Applications Across Tanager Scenes
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings

from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
from geolattice.rsense import hyperspectral as hs  # hyperspectral cubes, readers and tools

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_05_HyperSpectral")  # data folder next to this notebook
TANAGER = DATA / "Tanger"  # Planet Tanager sample scenes
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results written by this notebook
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed


def tanager_file(category, product="sr"):
    """Path of a Tanager product (sr or radiance) for a scene category folder."""
    return next((TANAGER / category).glob(f"*/*_ortho_{product}_hdf5.h5"))


print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__)  # library version used for this notebook

from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap  # class colours
from matplotlib.patches import Patch  # legend entries


def bands_near(path, wavelengths_nm):
    """Indices of the Tanager bands nearest to the given wavelengths."""
    probe = hs.read_tanager(path, window=(slice(0, 1), slice(0, 1)))
    return sorted({hs.band_index(probe, w) for w in wavelengths_nm})


def pick(score, mask, q):
    """(row, col) of the pixel in mask whose score is nearest its q-th quantile."""
    s = np.where(mask, score, np.nan)
    return np.unravel_index(np.nanargmin(np.abs(s - np.nanquantile(s, q))), s.shape)


def mean3(cube, rc):
    """Mean 3 x 3 spectrum around (row, col)."""
    r, c = rc
    return cube.values[:, max(r - 1, 0):r + 2, max(c - 1, 0):c + 2].reshape(cube.sizes["band"], -1).mean(1)

title: Thematic Applications Across Tanager Scenes
section: A burn scar on the Malibu coast
text:
A burn scar on the Malibu coast
The Franklin Fire started on 9 December 2024 in the Santa Monica Mountains above Malibu. Six days later Tanager imaged the area. Burned land is found with NBR over the land part of the scene.


Code
fire_f = tanager_file("fire")
fire = hs.read_tanager(fire_f, bands=bands_near(fire_f, [461, 561, 651, 766, 770, 861, 1650, 2200]))  # 8 bands, whole scene
nbr = hs.index(fire, "NBR_hs")  # (R860 - R2200) / (R860 + R2200)
R, G, N, S2 = (hs.band_at(fire, w).values for w in (651, 561, 861, 2200))
land = ((G - N) / (G + N) < 0) & np.isfinite(N)  # not water
burn = land & (nbr.values < 0.05)  # low NBR on land: burned (or bare) ground
px_area = 30 * 30 / 1e6  # km2 per pixel
print(f"land {land.sum() * px_area:.0f} km2 | NBR < 0.05: {burn.sum() * px_area:.1f} km2 | "
      f"NBR on land: median {np.nanmedian(nbr.values[land]):.2f}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5.2))
hs.plot_rgb(fire, (651, 561, 461), ax=axes[0], title="True colour")
hs.plot_rgb(fire, (2200, 861, 651), ax=axes[1], title="SWIR composite (2200, 860, 650 nm)")
im = axes[2].imshow(np.where(land, nbr, np.nan), cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=-0.3, vmax=0.6)
axes[2].contour(burn, [0.5], colors="k", linewidths=0.4); axes[2].set_title("NBR on land, NBR < 0.05 outlined"); axes[2].axis("off")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[2], shrink=0.7)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


land 146 km2 | NBR < 0.05: 23.4 km2 | NBR on land: median 0.29











Code
full = hs.read_tanager(fire_f, window=(slice(0, 400), slice(None)))  # all bands, northern (land) part of the scene
full = hs.drop_bad_bands(full)
nb_full = hs.index(full, "NBR_hs").values
lnd = land[:400]
picks = {"burned (lowest NBR)": pick(nb_full, lnd, 0.01), "low NBR, bright (dry grass or partly burned)": pick(nb_full, lnd, 0.15),
         "unburned chaparral": pick(nb_full, lnd, 0.9), "bare or urban": pick(np.where(nb_full < 0.15, hs.band_at(full, 650).values, np.nan), lnd, 0.98)}
wl = hs.wavelengths(full)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.5))
for name, rc in picks.items():
    s = mean3(full, rc)
    ax.plot(wl, s, lw=1.3, label=f"{name}, NBR {nb_full[rc]:.2f}")
ax.set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Reflectance", title="Spectra across the fire scene"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
print(f"maximum SWIR reflectance on land at 2200 nm: {np.nanmax(S2[land]):.2f} (flames would stand far above any surface)")









maximum SWIR reflectance on land at 2200 nm: 0.47 (flames would stand far above any surface)


Low NBR outlines a compact burn scar in the mountains, which the SWIR composite shows in magenta against the green of unburned chaparral. The 23 km² below the threshold include more than the scar: scattered bare, built up and dry pixels along the coast also fall below 0.05, so the scar itself is smaller. The spectra explain the index. The burned pixel has lost the red edge and NIR plateau of vegetation and is dark and nearly flat, rising only slowly into the SWIR (char and ash), while unburned chaparral keeps a clear red edge. Pixels just below the threshold can still look like dry vegetation (bright, with a weak red edge), and the “bare or urban” spectrum is twice as bright as char in the visible: brightness and shape separate them from char, which a single NBR threshold does not. No pixel on land has SWIR reflectance above about 0.5, so there are no active flames six days after ignition. With an image from before the fire, dNBR would separate burned land from naturally bare ground.

axes[1].set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Reflectance", title="Snow spectra by 1030 nm depth (larger depth: larger grains)")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"1030 nm depth over bright snow: median {np.nanmedian(depth):.3f}, 5 to 95 percent {np.nanpercentile(depth, 5):.3f} to {np.nanpercentile(depth, 95):.3f}")









1030 nm depth over bright snow: median 0.136, 5 to 95 percent 0.100 to 0.144


The scene is 94 percent bright snow over land and sea ice, with about 3 percent dark open water and 2 percent darker ice. NDSI is high over all snow and ice and low over water. The small bright patch classed as “other” has low NDSI although it is bright: a cloud, which unlike snow reflects strongly at 1650 nm.
The 1030 nm depth over bright snow varies only between about 0.10 and 0.14, and its map is dominated by a smooth gradient across the scene and by topographic texture rather than by patches of snow type. The spectra show why: the median pixel is far brighter than the others (reflectance above 1 on a sunlit slope), so illumination and slope change the spectra more than grain size does. Band depth, a ratio to the local continuum, removes much of a brightness change but not the change in path length and diffuse light with slope and sun angle. Ranking grain size from this map would need a terrain illumination correction first, and converting depth to micrometres a snow radiative transfer model.

title: Thematic Applications Across Tanager Scenes
section: Turbid water off the Paraguaná Peninsula
text:
Turbid water off the Paraguaná Peninsula
The coastal scene shows clear Caribbean water, a refinery coast and a pale sediment plume. Water is masked by NDWI, glint is removed by subtracting each pixel’s mean reflectance between 1550 and 1650 nm (where water leaving signal is nil), and two water quality proxies are mapped: red reflectance at 650 nm for turbidity and NDCI for chlorophyll.


Code
cw_f = tanager_file("coastal-water-bodies")
cw = hs.read_tanager(cw_f, wavelength_range=(400, 1700))
cw = cw.isel(band=np.flatnonzero(cw["good"].values))
G, N = hs.band_at(cw, 560).values, hs.band_at(cw, 860).values
water = ((G - N) / (G + N) > 0.2) & np.isfinite(G)  # water by NDWI
glint = hs.sel_range(cw, 1550, 1650).mean("band").values  # SWIR reflectance (glint, residual offset)
cwc = cw - glint  # glint corrected cube
red = hs.band_at(cwc, 650).values  # turbidity proxy
ndci = hs.index(cwc, "Chl_NDCI").values  # (R708 - R665) / (R708 + R665)
print(f"water: {water.mean():.0%} of the scene | SWIR glint over water: median {np.nanmedian(glint[water]):.4f}, "
      f"95th percentile {np.nanpercentile(glint[water], 95):.4f}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 5))
hs.plot_rgb(cw, (651, 561, 461), ax=axes[0], title="True colour")
for ax, (img, t, cmap) in zip(axes[1:], [(glint, "SWIR (1550 to 1650 nm) over water", "magma"),
                                         (red, "Red reflectance after glint correction", "YlOrBr"),
                                         (ndci, "NDCI after glint correction", "viridis")]):
    v = np.where(water, img, np.nan)
    im = ax.imshow(v, cmap=cmap, vmin=np.nanpercentile(v, 2), vmax=np.nanpercentile(v, 98)); ax.set_title(t); ax.axis("off")
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.65)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


water: 41% of the scene | SWIR glint over water: median 0.0168, 95th percentile 0.0227











Code
w = hs.wavelengths(cwc)
picks = {"clearest water": pick(red, water, 0.02), "median water": pick(red, water, 0.5),
         "turbid plume": pick(red, water, 0.99)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.3))
for name, rc in picks.items():
    ax.plot(w, mean3(cwc, rc), lw=1.4, label=f"{name}: R650 {red[rc]:.3f}, NDCI {ndci[rc]:.2f}")
ax.set(xlim=(400, 950), xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Glint corrected reflectance", title="Water spectra"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.axhline(0, color="0.6", lw=0.8)
plt.show()
r_ok = water & np.isfinite(red) & np.isfinite(ndci)
print(f"Spearman r between red reflectance and NDCI over water: {pd.Series(red[r_ok]).corr(pd.Series(ndci[r_ok]), method='spearman'):.2f}")









Spearman r between red reflectance and NDCI over water: -0.34


Over water the SWIR reflectance is small but not zero (about 0.017), and its pattern of wind streaks and wave fields is the sun glint that the correction removes; it is also higher next to the plume and the coast, where adjacency effects from the bright land and sediment add light. After correction the clearest water is blue with a reflectance of a few percent at 450 nm and almost nothing beyond 600 nm, typical of oligotrophic Caribbean water, while the plume raises the green, red and NIR strongly: suspended sediment scatters light at all wavelengths. The NDCI map is the cautionary part. In clear water both its bands are close to zero, so the index is dominated by noise and by the detector stripes; it only becomes meaningful where the water is productive or turbid. Over all water NDCI and red reflectance are weakly negatively correlated (r about -0.34), and in the plume the 708 nm reflectance is set by sediment scattering, not by chlorophyll; separating the two requires bio-optical models or field samples. Red reflectance alone is a robust relative turbidity map; converting it to g m⁻³ needs a calibration such as Nechad et al. (2010).

title: Thematic Applications Across Tanager Scenes
section: Iron oxides in Bosnia and Herzegovina
text:
Iron oxides in Bosnia and Herzegovina
The winter scene of the natural lands collection shows dormant forest and fields and a conspicuous red brown patch. The ferric iron index (R750 / R560) finds such surfaces; the spectra confirm what they are.


Code
nl_f = tanager_file("natural-lands")
nl = hs.read_tanager(nl_f, wavelength_range=(400, 1300))
nl = nl.isel(band=np.flatnonzero(nl["good"].values))
fe = hs.index(nl, "FerricIron").values  # R750 / R560
R, G, B, N = (hs.band_at(nl, w).values for w in (650, 560, 460, 860))
ndvi = (N - R) / (N + R)
red_ratio = R / G  # red to green ratio: iron oxides are red
valid = np.isfinite(fe)
iron = valid & (red_ratio > np.nanpercentile(red_ratio[valid], 99.5)) & (ndvi < 0.3)  # reddest, non vegetated pixels
print(f"iron oxide candidates: {iron.sum():,} pixels ({iron.sum() * 900 / 1e6:.2f} km2)")
rows_, cols_ = np.nonzero(iron)
r0, c0 = int(np.median(rows_)), int(np.median(cols_))  # centre of the candidates
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.3, 1.3, 1.2]})
hs.plot_rgb(nl, (651, 561, 461), ax=axes[0], title="True colour"); axes[0].contour(iron, [0.5], colors="c", linewidths=0.6)
im = axes[1].imshow(red_ratio, cmap="Oranges", vmin=np.nanpercentile(red_ratio, 2), vmax=np.nanpercentile(red_ratio, 99.8))
axes[1].set_title("Red / green ratio (R650 / R560)"); axes[1].axis("off"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1], shrink=0.7)
w = hs.wavelengths(nl)
spec = {"iron oxide candidates": nl.values[:, iron].mean(1),
        "forest (NDVI > 0.5)": np.nanmean(nl.values[:, ndvi > 0.5], 1),
        "other bare ground (NDVI < 0.2)": np.nanmean(nl.values[:, (ndvi < 0.2) & ~iron & valid], 1)}
for n, s in spec.items():
    axes[2].plot(w, s, lw=1.4, label=n)
axes[2].set(xlabel="Wavelength (nm)", ylabel="Reflectance", title="Mean spectra"); axes[2].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
cr = hs.continuum_removal(hs.as_cube(np.array(list(spec.values())).T[:, None, :], w), start=750, stop=1250)
print("depth of the ~900 nm ferric iron feature (continuum removed, 750 to 1250 nm):",
      {n: round(float(1 - cr.values[:, 0, i].min()), 3) for i, n in enumerate(spec)})


iron oxide candidates: 2,391 pixels (2.15 km2)









depth of the ~900 nm ferric iron feature (continuum removed, 750 to 1250 nm): {'iron oxide candidates': 0.146, 'forest (NDVI > 0.5)': 0.064, 'other bare ground (NDVI < 0.2)': 0.055}


The reddest non vegetated pixels form the compact patch seen in the true colour image, and their mean spectrum has what iron oxides predict: low reflectance in the blue and green, a steep rise into the red, and a broad absorption between about 850 and 950 nm whose depth after continuum removal is larger than for other bare ground or forest. Without field knowledge the material can be called iron oxide rich (exposed red soil, weathered rock, tailings or similar), not identified more exactly; matching against laboratory spectra of hematite and goethite would be the next step (notebook 09_05_06).

title: Thematic Applications Across Tanager Scenes
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Burn scars show low NBR and dark, flat char spectra; brightness and shape separate them from bare ground and dry vegetation, and a pre fire image would give burn severity.
NDSI separates snow and ice from water, rock and cloud; the 1030 nm ice absorption is a grain size proxy, but on rugged terrain illumination must be corrected first.
Coastal water needs glint correction; red reflectance maps turbidity, while NDCI is noise in clear water and confounded by sediment in turbid water.
Iron oxide rich surfaces are found with a red to green ratio and confirmed by their 900 nm feature.

geolattice.rsense.hyperspectral functions used: read_tanager, drop_bad_bands, index, band_at, band_depth, sel_range, smooth, continuum_removal, as_cube, plot_rgb.

Use the 1260 nm ice absorption instead of 1030 nm on Baffin Island. Do the two depth maps agree?

title: LiDAR Fundamentals
text: Banner

title: LiDAR Fundamentals
text:
Overview
LiDAR is an active remote sensing technique: the instrument supplies its own light, a short pulse of laser energy, and records the echo. The time the pulse takes to travel to a surface and back gives the distance to that surface. Combined with the exact position and orientation of the instrument at the moment of firing, each echo becomes a point with x, y and z coordinates. A modern airborne survey collects hundreds of thousands to a few million such points every second.
A short history:

1960 to 1970s. The laser was demonstrated in 1960. Within a few years it was used to range the Moon (retroreflectors left by Apollo 11 in 1969) and, in the 1970s, NASA flew airborne laser profilers that measured a single line of heights beneath the aircraft.
1990s. The Global Positioning System (GPS) and accurate inertial measurement units (IMUs) made it possible to know where an aircraft was, and how it was tilted, to a few centimetres and a few thousandths of a degree. Scanning mirrors spread the pulses across a swath, and commercial airborne laser scanning (ALS) was born.
2000s. Full-waveform digitisers recorded the whole returned signal instead of a few discrete echoes. Terrestrial laser scanners (TLS) on tripods and mobile laser scanners (MLS) on vehicles spread to surveying, engineering and forestry. NASA’s ICESat (2003 to 2009) carried the first spaceborne laser altimeter for Earth’s ice and land.
2010s. National programs began mapping whole countries: the USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), the Netherlands’ AHN, England’s Environment Agency survey, Denmark, Spain and many more. Geiger-mode and single-photon systems, which detect individual photons, raised collection rates. ICESat-2 (2018) and GEDI on the International Space Station (2018, science data from 2019) began sampling forests and terrain worldwide.
2020s. Small, cheap sensors on drones (UAV LiDAR) and in phones, and automotive LiDAR for self-driving vehicles, made point clouds a routine data type. Cloud-optimised formats (COPC, EPT) let users stream only the part of a national archive they need.


How LiDAR works
Ranging. A pulse leaves the laser at time \(t_0\), reflects from a surface and returns at \(t_1\). Light travels at \(c \approx 299{,}792{,}458\) m/s, and the pulse covers the distance twice, so the range is
\[R = \frac{c\,(t_1 - t_0)}{2} = \frac{c\,\Delta t}{2}.\]
A target 1,000 m away returns its echo after about 6.7 microseconds. A timing error of 1 nanosecond moves the range by 15 cm, so LiDAR receivers time echoes to a few tens of picoseconds.
Georeferencing. The range alone is a distance along the laser beam. The system turns it into a ground coordinate with three more measurements made at the same instant:

GNSS (GPS and other satellite navigation systems) gives the position of the sensor, usually corrected against a base station on the ground or a precise orbit service.
The IMU gives the attitude of the sensor: roll, pitch and heading.
The scanner reports the angle at which the beam left the instrument.

The point is then \(\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}_{\text{GNSS}} + \mathbf{R}_{\text{IMU}}\,(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{R}_{\text{bore}}\,\mathbf{r}_{\text{scan}}\,R)\), where \(\mathbf{l}\) is the lever arm between the GNSS antenna and the laser, \(\mathbf{R}_{\text{bore}}\) is the small boresight rotation between IMU and laser, and \(\mathbf{r}_{\text{scan}}\) is the unit vector of the beam. Errors in any of these terms (GNSS position, IMU angle, boresight calibration, range) all end up in the point. An angular error of 0.005 degrees at 1,000 m range moves a point by about 9 cm, which is why calibration matters.
Wavelength. Most topographic systems use near-infrared light at 1064 nm (Nd:YAG lasers) or 1550 nm (fibre lasers, safer for eyes at higher power). Vegetation reflects strongly at these wavelengths, while water absorbs them, so lakes appear as holes in the data. Bathymetric LiDAR adds a green 532 nm channel that penetrates clear water and maps the bottom. Automotive and many drone sensors use 905 nm diodes.
Footprint. The beam spreads slightly as it travels. With a divergence of \(\gamma\) radians the footprint diameter at range \(R\) is roughly \(D \approx \gamma R\): 0.25 mrad at 1,000 m gives a 25 cm spot. GEDI’s footprint on the ground is about 25 m wide, ICESat-2’s about 11 to 17 m.
Multiple returns. A footprint can be partly intercepted by leaves and partly continue to the ground. Each surface that reflects enough energy produces a separate echo, so one pulse can give several returns: the first return is usually the top of the canopy or a roof, intermediate returns come from branches and understory, and the last return is often the ground. Every point records its return_number and the number_of_returns of its pulse.
Discrete return versus full waveform. Discrete-return systems detect peaks in the returned signal in real time and keep up to 4 to 15 of them. Full-waveform systems digitise the whole returned energy as a function of time (every nanosecond or so), so the user can extract more returns later and measure the shape of each echo. GEDI is a full-waveform instrument; its products are summaries of the waveform.
Single-photon and Geiger-mode LiDAR. Instead of measuring a strong echo, these detectors are sensitive enough to register single photons. They fire many weak pulses at high rates (tens of kilohertz to megahertz) and build up the surface from photon statistics. ICESat-2’s ATLAS instrument works this way.
Intensity. Each return also records the strength of the echo. Intensity depends on the reflectance of the target at the laser wavelength, the range, the angle of incidence and the fraction of the footprint the target filled. It looks like a near-infrared photograph and helps separate asphalt from grass or paint lines from road, but it is rarely calibrated, so values are not comparable between surveys.
Point density and spacing. Density (points per m²) controls the smallest detail the data can resolve. For one flight line it is approximately
\[\rho \approx \frac{\text{PRF}}{v \cdot W}, \qquad W = 2H\tan(\theta/2),\]
where PRF is the pulse repetition frequency, \(v\) the ground speed, \(W\) the swath width, \(H\) the flying height and \(\theta\) the full scan angle. Overlap between flight lines and multiple returns raise the density further. The nominal point spacing is \(1/\sqrt{\rho}\).


How LiDAR data are acquired
Platforms.









Platform
Typical height or range
Typical density
Typical use




Airborne, fixed wing (ALS)
500 to 4,000 m above ground
2 to 50 points/m²
Regional and national terrain, forestry, floodplains


Airborne, helicopter
100 to 500 m
20 to 200 points/m²
Power lines, railways, corridors


Drone (UAV LiDAR)
30 to 120 m
100 to 1,000+ points/m²
Small sites, forestry plots, construction, mines


Terrestrial (TLS) on a tripod
1 to 1,000 m range
millimetres between points
Forest plots, buildings, cliffs, heritage


Mobile (MLS) on a car, train, boat or backpack
1 to 300 m range
very high along the route
Roads, rail, street furniture, city models


Bathymetric airborne
300 to 600 m
1 to 20 points/m²
Shallow seas, rivers, coastlines


Spaceborne (ICESat-2, GEDI)
about 400 to 500 km
sparse footprints or photon tracks
Global canopy height, ice sheets, sea ice



Scanning mechanisms. An oscillating mirror sweeps the beam from side to side and leaves a zigzag pattern on the ground; a rotating polygon mirror gives parallel lines; a nutating (Palmer) scanner draws ellipses, so each spot is seen from two directions; Risley prisms in small drone sensors produce rosette patterns.
An airborne survey, step by step.

Flight planning. The surveyor chooses flying height, speed, scan angle and pulse rate to reach the required density, and spaces the flight lines so neighbouring swaths overlap (often 20 to 50 %). Calm weather, leaf-off season for terrain mapping or leaf-on for forest structure, and no snow or flooding are chosen where possible.
Ground control. GNSS base stations log positions during the flight, and surveyed check points are placed on open, flat ground for later accuracy testing.
Collection. The aircraft flies the lines while the laser, GNSS and IMU log their data, often together with a camera.
Trajectory processing. GNSS and IMU data are combined in a Kalman filter to give the sensor’s position and attitude for every pulse.
Point generation and calibration. Ranges, scan angles and the trajectory are combined into points. Overlapping flight lines are compared, and boresight and timing offsets are adjusted (strip adjustment) until the lines agree.
Classification. Software and human editors label points as ground, vegetation, buildings, water, noise and so on.
Quality control and delivery. The vertical accuracy is tested against the check points, and the producer delivers tiled point clouds, a digital elevation model (DEM), breaklines around water, intensity images and metadata.

Accuracy. Modern ALS reaches a vertical root mean square error (RMSEz) of about 5 to 10 cm on open hard surfaces. The USGS 3DEP Lidar Base Specification defines quality levels:








Quality level
Aggregate nominal pulse density
Non-vegetated vertical accuracy (RMSEz)




QL0
≥ 8 points/m²
≤ 5 cm


QL1
≥ 8 points/m²
≤ 10 cm


QL2
≥ 2 points/m²
≤ 10 cm


QL3
≥ 0.5 points/m²
≤ 20 cm





Data products and file formats
LAS is the binary exchange format of the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing (ASPRS). A LAS file has a public header (version, point format, number of points, scale and offset, bounds), variable length records (the coordinate reference system and other metadata) and the point records. Coordinates are stored as integers and recovered as \(X = X_{\text{int}} \cdot \text{scale} + \text{offset}\), so a scale of 0.001 means millimetre precision.








LAS version
Year
Main additions




1.0
2003
Point formats 0 and 1 (GPS time)


1.1
2005
File source ID, user data


1.2
2008
Point formats 2 and 3 (RGB colour)


1.3
2010
Point formats 4 and 5 (waveform packets)


1.4
2011 to 2019
Point formats 6 to 10: 15 returns, 256 classes, WKT coordinate systems, NIR channel



Related formats:







Format
What it is




LAZ
Lossless compression of LAS (LASzip), typically 5 to 10 times smaller


COPC
Cloud-Optimized Point Cloud: one LAZ file whose points are arranged in an octree, so a program can read just a region or a coarse level of detail with HTTP range requests


EPT
Entwine Point Tiles: a folder of octree tiles plus a JSON description; the USGS 3DEP archive on Amazon Web Services is published this way


E57
ASTM exchange format for terrestrial scanners, with images and scan positions


PLY, PCD, XYZ
Simple formats used by CloudCompare, MeshLab, Open3D and the Point Cloud Library


LASX
An index file written by ArcGIS next to a LAS file to speed up display; it holds no points



Classification codes. ASPRS defines standard classes for LAS 1.4 (point formats 6 to 10):









Code

64 to 255

Derived rasters. A DEM or DTM (digital terrain model) is the bare-earth surface from ground points. A DSM (digital surface model) is the highest surface, including trees and roofs. The CHM (canopy height model) or nDSM is DSM minus DEM: the height of objects above the ground. Intensity images, point-density grids and hillshades are common quality-control rasters.


Applications

Terrain and water. Bare-earth DEMs for flood modelling and floodplain maps, drainage and culvert mapping, coastal erosion, sea-level-rise exposure, and the hydrologically conditioned elevation data behind national hydrography.
Forestry and ecology. Canopy height, cover, vertical structure and gaps; tree counts and crown sizes; timber volume and aboveground biomass for carbon accounting; habitat models for birds and mammals that depend on canopy layering.
Urban areas and infrastructure. Building footprints, heights and roof shapes for 3D city models and solar potential; power-line clearance and vegetation encroachment; road and railway corridor surveys; bridge and dam monitoring; telecommunication line-of-sight planning.
Geology and hazards. Fault scarps, landslides and debris flows, volcanic deformation and post-event change detection by differencing surveys from different dates.
Archaeology and cultural heritage. Removing vegetation digitally reveals buried walls, roads and field systems, for example the Maya settlements under the Guatemalan rainforest and the medieval cities around Angkor in Cambodia. TLS documents monuments in millimetre detail.
Cryosphere. Ice-sheet and glacier elevation change and sea-ice freeboard from ICESat and ICESat-2.
Agriculture. Field drainage design, land levelling, erosion and orchard canopy structure.
Transport and robotics. LiDAR on cars, robots and drones for navigation, obstacle detection and high-definition maps.
Global carbon. GEDI’s canopy-height and biomass products and ICESat-2’s canopy heights give the first near-global samples of forest structure.



Accessibility







Source
Coverage and notes




USGS 3DEP (The National Map, apps.nationalmap.gov)
Most of the United States; point clouds and 1 m and 1/3 arc-second DEMs; free


USGS 3DEP on AWS (s3://usgs-lidar-public)

Microsoft Planetary Computer

Curated high-resolution topography worldwide, with on-demand processing


NOAA Digital Coast
Coastal topographic and bathymetric LiDAR for the United States


State and provincial programs
For example the NYS GIS Clearinghouse for New York, the source of LiDAR tiles like the ones used here


National programs elsewhere
Netherlands (AHN), England (Environment Agency), Denmark, Finland, Spain (PNOA), Switzerland, New Zealand and others publish national point clouds


NASA Earthdata (search.earthdata.nasa.gov)
GEDI L1B to L4 and ICESat-2 ATL03, ATL06 and ATL08 granules; free login required



Python tools:

laspy reads and writes LAS, LAZ (with the lazrs backend) and COPC.
PDAL runs processing pipelines and reads EPT and many other formats.
h5py reads GEDI and ICESat-2 HDF5 files.
pyproj, rasterio, rioxarray and geopandas handle coordinate systems, rasters and vectors.
geolattice.rsense.lidar wraps all of these in one PointCloud container with readers, filters, ground classification, surfaces, terrain, forest, urban and spaceborne tools.

title: LiDAR Fundamentals
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings (e.g. LAZ backend notices)

import os  # file sizes
import time  # timing
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import rasterio  # raster I/O (used by the plotting helpers)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
from pyproj import CRS, Transformer  # coordinate reference systems

import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing

text:
The LiDAR equations in numbers
The table applies the ranging and footprint equations for an airborne sensor at three flying heights: the round-trip time of a pulse, the footprint for a typical 0.25 mrad beam divergence, and the range error caused by a 1 ns timing error.


Code
C = 299_792_458  # speed of light (m/s)
rows = []  # one row per flying height
for H in (500, 1000, 2000, 4000):  # flying heights above ground (m)

                 "round trip (µs)": round(2 * H / C * 1e6, 2),  # Δt = 2R / c
                 "footprint at 0.25 mrad (cm)": round(0.25e-3 * H * 100, 1),  # D ≈ γ R
                 "range error for 1 ns (cm)": round(C * 1e-9 / 2 * 100, 1)})  # ΔR = c Δt / 2

Flight planning. The next cell writes the density equation as a function and plans a survey. For each flying height it gives the swath width, the spacing between flight lines for 30 % side overlap, the single-pass pulse density and the density once the overlap is counted. The figure shows how density falls with flying height and rises with pulse rate; the dashed lines mark the 3DEP QL2 (2 points/m²) and QL1 (8 points/m²) thresholds.


Code
def flight_plan(H, prf_khz=400, speed_kn=140, fov_deg=40, overlap=0.3):  # density of an ALS survey
    W = 2 * H * np.tan(np.radians(fov_deg) / 2)  # swath width (m)
    v = speed_kn * 0.5144  # ground speed in m/s (1 knot = 0.5144 m/s)
    rho1 = prf_khz * 1e3 / (v * W)  # pulses per m² from one flight line
    return {"swath (m)": W, "line spacing (m)": W * (1 - overlap),  # swath and line spacing
            "pulses/m², one line": rho1, "pulses/m², with overlap": rho1 / (1 - overlap)}  # densities

plan = pd.DataFrame({H: flight_plan(H) for H in (500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000)}).T.round(2)  # five heights
plan.index.name = "flying height (m)"  # label the index
display(plan)  # show the plan

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))  # one panel
Hs = np.linspace(300, 4000, 200)  # flying heights to plot
for prf in (100, 400, 1000, 2000):  # pulse rates (kHz)
    ax.plot(Hs, [flight_plan(h, prf_khz=prf)["pulses/m², with overlap"] for h in Hs], label=f"{prf} kHz")  # density curve
for q, d in (("QL2", 2), ("QL1", 8)):  # 3DEP thresholds
    ax.axhline(d, ls="--", c="grey", lw=0.8); ax.text(3950, d * 1.08, q, ha="right", fontsize=8)  # dashed line and label
ax.set(xlabel="Flying height above ground (m)", ylabel="Pulses per m²", yscale="log",  # axes
       title="Pulse density for a 40° scanner at 140 knots, 30 % side overlap")  # title

title: LiDAR Fundamentals
section: Multiple returns and a simulated full waveform
text:
Multiple returns and a simulated full waveform
A pulse that enters a canopy can return several echoes. The cell below takes the real Madison point cloud (read properly in the Reading a point cloud and fixing units section), picks the 10 m cell with the most canopy returns that still has ground returns, and treats all returns in a 10 m wide circle there as a single footprint. Summing a Gaussian pulse at the height of every return gives an approximate waveform: the returned energy as a function of height. A discrete-return system keeps only the peaks; a full-waveform system keeps the whole curve. The relative heights RH50 and RH98, which GEDI reports, are the heights below which 50 % and 98 % of the energy lies.


Code
pc_ft = rs.lidar.read_las(MADISON)  # the whole Madison cloud (feet, state plane)
z_m = np.asarray(pc_ft.z) * 0.3048006096  # heights converted from US survey feet to metres
r_ft = 5.0 / 0.3048006096  # a 5 m radius (10 m wide) footprint, in feet
cell = pd.DataFrame({"i": (pc_ft.x // (2 * r_ft)).astype(int), "j": (pc_ft.y // (2 * r_ft)).astype(int),  # 10 m cells
                     "z": z_m, "c": pc_ft["classification"]})  # height and class of every point
cell = cell[cell.c != 7]  # drop noise points
cell["h"] = cell.z - cell.groupby(["i", "j"]).z.transform("min")  # height above the lowest point in the cell
stats = cell.groupby(["i", "j"]).agg(ground=("c", lambda c: (c == 2).sum()),  # ground returns per cell
                                     canopy=("h", lambda h: (h > 5).sum()))  # returns more than 5 m up
best = stats[stats.ground >= 5].canopy.idxmax()  # the cell with most canopy returns that still sees the ground
cx, cy = (best[0] + 0.5) * 2 * r_ft, (best[1] + 0.5) * 2 * r_ft  # centre of that cell (feet)
inside = ((pc_ft.x - cx) ** 2 + (pc_ft.y - cy) ** 2 < r_ft ** 2) & (pc_ft["classification"] != 7)  # returns in the footprint
zf = z_m[inside]  # their heights (m)
ground_z = zf[pc_ft["classification"][inside] == 2].mean()  # mean ground height in the footprint
h = zf - ground_z  # height above ground of every return

zz = np.linspace(-2, h.max() + 3, 500)  # heights at which to evaluate the waveform
sigma = 0.6  # width of the outgoing pulse expressed in metres of height
wave = np.exp(-0.5 * ((zz[:, None] - h[None, :]) / sigma) ** 2).sum(1)  # sum of one Gaussian per return
cum = np.cumsum(wave) / wave.sum()  # cumulative energy from the ground up
rh = {p: zz[np.searchsorted(cum, p / 100)] for p in (25, 50, 75, 98)}  # relative heights RH25 to RH98

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5), sharey=True)  # two panels
rn = pc_ft["return_number"][inside]  # return number of each echo
for k, col in zip(range(1, 5), ("#1a9850", "#91cf60", "#fc8d59", "#8c510a")):  # returns 1 to 4
    m = rn == k  # echoes with this return number
    ax[0].scatter(np.random.default_rng(k).uniform(0, 1, m.sum()), h[m], s=12, color=col, label=f"return {k}")  # jittered
ax[0].set(xticks=[], ylabel="Height above ground (m)", title=f"{inside.sum()} discrete returns in a 10 m footprint")  # axes
ax[0].legend()  # legend
ax[1].plot(wave / wave.max(), zz, c="k")  # the waveform
for p, v in rh.items():  # relative heights
    ax[1].axhline(v, ls="--", lw=0.8, c="C3"); ax[1].text(1.02, v, f"RH{p} = {v:.1f} m", va="center", fontsize=8)  # mark
ax[1].set(xlabel="Relative returned energy", xlim=(0, 1.35), title="Simulated full waveform")  # axes
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The first returns (green) sit in the upper canopy, later returns lie lower down and the last ones reach the ground, which forms the strong peak at 0 m. The waveform’s energy is spread through the canopy; RH98 is close to the top of the tallest crown and RH50 shows where the middle of the energy lies. A real waveform also depends on the reflectance of leaves and ground and on the shape of the outgoing pulse, so this is an illustration, not an instrument simulation.

The table shows several things worth knowing:

The 2008 UB tile is LAS 1.0, point format 1 (x, y, z, intensity, returns, scan angle, GPS time). Its coordinates are longitude and latitude, stored with a scale of 10⁻⁷ degrees (about 1 cm). The 2020 Ithaca and the Madison files are LAS 1.4, point format 6, the current standard.

text:
Classification codes
ASPRS_CLASSES in geolattice.rsense.core maps the class codes to names. The cell counts the codes present in each dataset. Producers do not always follow the table: the 2008 UB tiles use code 12 for overlap points (a convention of older LAS versions), and Madison uses code 11 in a way the next sections examine.

def class_counts(path, n=3_000_000):  # class histogram from the first n points of a file

    with laspy.open(path) as r:  # open without reading everything
        c = np.asarray(r.read_points(min(n, r.header.point_count)).classification)  # class codes
    return pd.Series(c).value_counts(normalize=True)  # share of each code

codes.insert(0, "ASPRS name", [ASPRS_CLASSES.get(int(k), "reserved / overlap") for k in codes.index])  # class names

section: Reading a point cloud and fixing units
text:
Reading a point cloud and fixing units
rs.lidar.read_las returns a PointCloud: aligned NumPy arrays for x, y, z and every attribute, plus the coordinate reference system from the file header. This columnar layout is what numerical work needs: selecting, masking and gridding operate on whole arrays at once.


Code
print(pc_ft)  # the Madison cloud read in the waveform section
print("fields:", pc_ft.fields)  # the attributes stored for every point
crs = CRS.from_user_input(pc_ft.crs)  # CRS from the LAS header
print(f"CRS EPSG:{pc_ft.crs}: {crs.name} | horizontal unit: {crs.axis_info[0].unit_name}")  # name and unit


<PointCloud 4,068,294 pts [CPU] fields=['x', 'y', 'z', 'intensity', 'return_number', 'number_of_returns', 'classification', 'scan_angle', 'gps_time', 'user_data', 'point_source_id'] bbox=(2353000.0, 1075500.0, 2358000.0, 1080500.0) crs=2255>
fields: ['x', 'y', 'z', 'intensity', 'return_number', 'number_of_returns', 'classification', 'scan_angle', 'gps_time', 'user_data', 'point_source_id']
CRS EPSG:2255: NAD83 / Mississippi West (ftUS) | horizontal unit: US survey foot


The horizontal coordinates are in US survey feet (Mississippi West state plane), and so are the heights. Mixing feet and metres is the most common silent error in LiDAR work: a “30 m” tree that is really 30 feet tall. The next cell finds the UTM zone of the cloud’s centre with rs.core.utm_epsg, reprojects x and y with rs.lidar.reproject, and converts z from feet to metres.


Code
lon, lat = Transformer.from_crs(pc_ft.crs, 4326, always_xy=True).transform(  # bbox centre to lon/lat
    np.mean(pc_ft.bbox[::2]), np.mean(pc_ft.bbox[1::2]))
utm = rs.core.utm_epsg(lon, lat)  # UTM zone for that location
print(f"centre {lat:.4f}° N, {lon:.4f}° E -> UTM EPSG:{utm}")  # where the data are

xy = rs.lidar.reproject(pc_ft, utm)  # x and y to UTM metres (z is passed through unchanged, still feet)
pc = rs.PointCloud(xy.x, xy.y, np.asarray(pc_ft.z) * 0.3048006096, dict(xy.attrs), utm)  # z feet -> metres
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = pc.bbox  # extent in metres
area = (xmax - xmin) * (ymax - ymin)  # area in m²
print(pc)  # the metric cloud
# summary line
print(f"extent {xmax - xmin:.0f} m x {ymax - ymin:.0f} m | mean density {len(pc) / area:.2f} points/m² | "
      f"elevation {pc.z.min():.1f} to {pc.z.max():.1f} m")  # check the numbers are metric
