title: LiDAR Fundamentals
section: Coordinate reference systems in three datasets
text:
Coordinate reference systems in three datasets
The three datasets need three different fixes:

Madison: feet horizontally and vertically, fixed above.
UB 2008: geographic coordinates (degrees of longitude and latitude). Distances in degrees are meaningless for areas or slopes, and one degree of longitude is shorter than one degree of latitude at 43° N. The tiles are reprojected to UTM zone 17N.
Ithaca 2020: already in metres, with a compound CRS. Reprojecting only x and y keeps NAVD88 orthometric heights; reprojecting to a 3D geographic CRS with ellipsoidal heights changes z by the geoid height (about 33 m here). PROJ needs the GEOID12B grid for that, which it downloads once when network access is enabled.

rs.lidar.summary reports point count, area, density and spacing; it is only meaningful once the coordinates are metric, as the comparison shows.


Code
ub_deg = rs.lidar.read_las(UB[1])  # one UB tile in degrees
ub = rs.lidar.reproject(ub_deg, 26917)  # to NAD83 / UTM zone 17N (metres)
ith = rs.lidar.read_las(ITHACA[0])  # one Ithaca tile (already metric)
rows = {}  # one row per cloud
# the four clouds to compare
for name, cloud in [("UB in degrees (wrong)", ub_deg), ("UB in UTM 17N", ub), ("Madison in UTM 15N", pc),
                    ("Ithaca, UTM 18N + NAVD88", ith)]:  # the clouds to compare
    s = rs.lidar.summary(cloud)  # header-style summary
    rows[name] = {"points": s["points"], "area": s["area_m2"], "density (pts/m²)": s["density_pts_m2"],  # numbers
                  "spacing (m)": s["spacing_m"], "horizontal unit": CRS.from_user_input(cloud.crs).axis_info[0].unit_name}
pd.DataFrame(rows).T  # show the comparison

import pyproj  # PROJ settings
pyproj.network.set_network_enabled(True)  # let PROJ download the GEOID12B grid it needs (cdn.proj.org)
t = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:6347+5703", "EPSG:6319", always_xy=True)  # UTM 18N + NAVD88 -> NAD83(2011) 3D
cx, cy, cz = np.mean(ith.bbox[::2]), np.mean(ith.bbox[1::2]), float(np.median(ith.z))  # a central point
lon, lat, h_ell = t.transform(cx, cy, cz)  # its ellipsoidal height
print(f"Ithaca: NAVD88 height {cz:.2f} m -> ellipsoidal height {h_ell:.2f} m "  # summary line
      f"(difference {h_ell - cz:+.2f} m = geoid height)")  # vertical datums differ by tens of metres


Ithaca: NAVD88 height 241.12 m -> ellipsoidal height inf m (difference +inf m = geoid height)


In degrees, the UB tile appears to cover a tiny fraction of a square metre with an absurd density; in UTM it covers about 2.4 km² at roughly 1 point/m², a typical density for a 2008 survey. The Ithaca 2020 tile has about 6.5 points/m², the density of a modern QL1/QL2 survey. Note also that NAVD88 heights and ellipsoidal heights differ by about 33 m here (the geoid lies 33 m below the ellipsoid in central New York): GNSS receivers and global products such as GEDI and ICESat-2 report ellipsoidal heights, while national LiDAR uses orthometric heights.

About 77 % of the pulses produced a single return (open ground, roads, water, dense crowns) and the rest two to four returns, nearly all in tree canopies. The diagonal of the cross-table is the number of pulses with that many returns. A quarter of the points carry class 11, officially “road surface”. The maps below show that these points form stripes along the flight lines rather than following roads: this producer used code 11 for points from overlapping flight lines. Check the project metadata before trusting a class code.


Code
density = rs.lidar.rasterize(pc, 10.0, stat="count") / 100.0  # all returns per m² in 10 m cells
pulses = rs.lidar.rasterize(pc.first_returns(), 10.0, stat="count") / 100.0  # first returns = pulses per m²
intensity = rs.lidar.rasterize(pc.first_returns(), 2.0, value="intensity", stat="mean")  # mean intensity, 2 m
top_class = rs.lidar.rasterize(pc, 4.0, value="classification", stat="max")  # highest class code per 4 m cell

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(density, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmax=4, title="All returns per m² (10 m cells)")  # density
rs.viz.plot_raster(intensity, ax=axes[1], cmap="gray", robust=True, title="Mean first-return intensity (2 m)")  # intensity
rs.viz.plot_raster(top_class, ax=axes[2], title="Highest class code per 4 m cell",  # classes
                   categorical={1: ("Unclassified", "#cccccc"), 2: ("Ground", "#c2a878"), 3: ("Low veg.", "#a6d96a"),
                                4: ("Medium veg.", "#1a9850"), 7: ("Noise", "#000000"), 9: ("Water", "#2166ac"),
                                11: ("Class 11 (overlap)", "#f4a582")})
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no tick labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
print(f"median density {float(density.median()):.2f} points/m², {float(pulses.median()):.2f} pulses/m²")  # summary

section: Cloud-native access: reading a window from COPC
text:
Cloud-native access: reading a window from COPC
A COPC file stores its points in an octree: the root node holds a sparse sample of the whole area and every level below adds detail in smaller cubes. A reader can therefore fetch only the nodes that cover a region, or stop at a coarse level for an overview. Over the web this works with HTTP range requests, so only the requested bytes are downloaded. rs.lidar.read_las passes bounds (in the file’s CRS) and resolution to laspy’s COPC reader; the same call works for a local path or a URL.


Code
import laspy  # LAS/LAZ/COPC library used by read_las
with laspy.CopcReader.open(MADISON) as r:  # read only the header and the octree hierarchy
    hdr = r.header  # the header
    print(f"{hdr.point_count:,} points | bounds {np.round(hdr.mins[:2])} to {np.round(hdr.maxs[:2])} (ft)")  # extent
mid = (hdr.mins[:2] + hdr.maxs[:2]) / 2  # centre of the file
win = (mid[0] - 1000, mid[1] - 1000, mid[0] + 1000, mid[1] + 1000)  # a 2,000 ft (610 m) window

rows, parts = [], {}  # timing rows and the clouds read
for res in (None, 4.0, 16.0, 64.0):  # full resolution, then coarser levels of detail (ft)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    parts[res] = rs.lidar.read_las(MADISON, bounds=win, resolution=res)  # read only that window and level
    rows.append({"resolution (ft)": res or "full", "points": len(parts[res]),  # points read
                 "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 2)})  # time taken
pd.DataFrame(rows)  # show the table

Writing point clouds and finding public LiDAR
rs.lidar.write_las writes LAS or compressed LAZ (by the file extension) with the CRS in the header; rs.lidar.write_ply writes PLY for CloudCompare, MeshLab or Open3D. The cell writes the metric Madison cloud, which the following notebooks read, and a small tile in both formats, and checks the round trip.

rs.lidar.write_las(pc, DATA / "madison_utm.laz")  # the whole metric cloud, used by later notebooks

# summary line

title: LiDAR Fundamentals
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

LiDAR measures range from the round-trip time of laser pulses, \(R = c\Delta t / 2\), and georeferences each echo with GNSS, an IMU and the scan angle.
Footprint, pulse rate, flying height, speed and scan angle set the point density; national specifications (3DEP QL0 to QL3) set minimum densities and accuracies.
One pulse can return several echoes; first returns describe the canopy top and roofs, last returns often reach the ground. Full-waveform and single-photon systems record more of the returned signal.
LAS stores points with a header, CRS records and per-point attributes; LAZ compresses it about ten times; COPC and EPT make large archives streamable by region and level of detail; LASX files are only ArcGIS indexes.
Always check units and coordinate reference systems: feet versus metres, degrees versus metres, and orthometric versus ellipsoidal heights.
Class codes, return structure, density and intensity summarise what a dataset contains; producers do not always use class codes as the ASPRS table says.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.lidar.las_info, rs.lidar.read_las (including COPC bounds and resolution), rs.lidar.reproject, rs.core.utm_epsg, rs.lidar.summary, rs.lidar.rasterize, rs.lidar.cross_section, rs.lidar.plot_cross_section, rs.lidar.plot_classification, rs.viz.plot_pointcloud, rs.viz.plot_raster, rs.lidar.write_las, rs.lidar.write_ply, rs.lidar.usgs_3dep_ept, and the PointCloud methods crop, filter, first_returns and with_field.
Exercises

Plan a drone survey at 80 m with a 240 kHz sensor, 70° scan angle and 8 m/s ground speed. What density does it reach, and how many flight lines cover a 500 m wide field?
Repeat the waveform simulation for an open grass spot and for a building roof. How do RH50 and RH98 change?
Map the share of multi-return pulses per 10 m cell for Madison. Where is it highest?
Reproject a UB tile to UTM 17N with rs.lidar.reproject and compare its area with the area you get by multiplying the degree extents by 111 km. Why do they differ?
Read a 500 m window of an Ithaca tile at full density and with voxel_downsample(1.0). How many points does each keep, and what disappears in a cross-section?

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
text:
Overview
Terrain variables describe the shape of the land surface and are inputs to hydrology, soil, geomorphology, habitat and hazard models. They fall into two groups:

Local derivatives use only a small neighbourhood (usually 3 x 3 cells): slope, aspect, curvature, ruggedness and hillshade. They can be computed independently for every cell, so they parallelise well and run on a GPU.
Regional or flow-based variables depend on the whole upstream area: flow accumulation, wetness index, height above drainage. They need a sequential routing algorithm over the entire DEM.

LiDAR DEMs bring their own challenges. At 1 m, bridges and road embankments without culverts act as dams in the DEM, water surfaces are noisy or empty because water absorbs the laser, and small artefacts create spurious pits. Hydrological work therefore usually conditions the DEM first: flattening water bodies, burning or breaching culverts and filling depressions.

Local terrain derivatives
Let \(z_{a}, \dots, z_{i}\) be the 3 x 3 neighbourhood of a cell (row-major from the top-left, \(z_e\) in the centre) with cell size \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\). Horn’s (1981) gradient weights the centre row and column twice:
\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \frac{(z_c + 2z_f + z_i) - (z_a + 2z_d + z_g)}{8\,\Delta x}, \qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \frac{(z_g + 2z_h + z_i) - (z_a + 2z_b + z_c)}{8\,\Delta y}.\]








Variable
Definition
Meaning




Slope
\(\arctan\sqrt{(\partial z/\partial x)^2 + (\partial z/\partial y)^2}\)
Steepness; controls runoff speed, erosion and landslide risk


Aspect
Compass direction of steepest descent
Exposure to sun and wind; snow melt, vegetation


Curvature
Laplacian \(\nabla^2 z\)
Convex (ridges, negative here) versus concave (hollows, positive here); flow divergence and convergence


TPI
\(z - \bar z_{\text{window}}\)
Topographic Position Index: positive on ridges and hilltops, negative in valleys; depends on the window size


TRI
\(\sqrt{\sum (z_j - z_e)^2}\) over the 8 neighbours
Terrain Ruggedness Index (Riley et al. 1999)


Roughness
\(\max - \min\) in the 3 x 3 window
Local relief


Hillshade
\(255\,(\cos Z \cos \theta + \sin Z \sin \theta \cos(A - \phi))\)
Shaded relief for a sun at zenith angle \(Z\) and azimuth \(A\), for slope \(\theta\) and aspect \(\phi\)


Illumination
\(\cos i\), the same expression without scaling
Used for the topographic correction of optical images



Geomorphons (Jasiewicz and Stepinski 2013) classify landforms by looking along eight directions from each cell up to a search distance and recording whether the horizon is higher, lower or level. The pattern of “higher” and “lower” directions maps to ten landforms: flat, peak, ridge, shoulder, spur, slope, hollow, footslope, valley and pit. Unlike curvature, geomorphons adapt to the scale of the landform through the search distance.


Hydrological derivatives

Depression filling. Pits in the DEM trap flow. The priority-flood algorithm (Barnes et al. 2014) floods the DEM inwards from its edges, always continuing from the lowest cell on the boundary of the flooded region, and raises every pit to its spill level. A tiny gradient (\(\epsilon\)) on filled flats keeps water moving.
Flow direction (D8). Each cell drains to the one of its eight neighbours with the steepest downward slope (O’Callaghan and Mark 1984).
Flow accumulation. The number of cells (or the area) draining through each cell. Cells above a threshold form the stream network.
Topographic Wetness Index (Beven and Kirkby 1979): \(\text{TWI} = \ln(a / \tan\beta)\), with \(a\) the specific catchment area (upslope area per unit contour length) and \(\beta\) the slope. High TWI marks places where water collects and soils stay wet.
Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND, Rennó et al. 2008): the height of each cell above the stream cell it drains to. HAND normalises the terrain to the drainage network, so a single water stage gives a first estimate of the flooded area along every stream.

section: A seamless 1 m DEM from four tiles
text:
A seamless 1 m DEM from four tiles
Each tile is read with only the fields the DEM needs (fields=["classification"] plus x, y, z), reduced to its ground points and gridded with rs.lidar.dem on the tile’s exact 1.5 km extent. Passing the tile bounds keeps the four grids aligned, so rs.lidar.merge_rasters can mosaic them without resampling. A DEM built tile by tile can show small steps at the seams, because interpolation near a tile edge only sees the points on one side; the large-area notebook shows how buffered tiles avoid this.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
dems, n_ground = [], 0  # tile DEMs and ground-point count
for p in TILES:  # each tile
    x0, y0 = (int(v) for v in rs.lidar.las_info(p)["mins"][:2])  # south-west corner of the tile
    g = rs.lidar.read_las(p, fields=["classification"]).ground()  # ground points only
    n_ground += len(g)  # count them
    dems.append(rs.lidar.dem(g, 1.0, bounds=(x0, y0, x0 + 1500, y0 + 1500)))  # 1 m DEM on the tile's extent
dem = rs.lidar.merge_rasters(dems).rename("elevation")  # mosaic of the four tiles
# summary line
print(f"{n_ground:,} ground points -> DEM {dem.shape} at 1 m in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s | "
      f"elevation {float(dem.min()):.1f} to {float(dem.max()):.1f} m | CRS {dem.rio.crs}")  # summary
dem2 = dem.coarsen(x=2, y=2, boundary="trim").mean().rio.write_crs(dem.rio.crs)  # 2 m version for hydrology

text:
Shaded relief
A hillshade lit from one direction hides features parallel to the light. A multi-directional hillshade averages several azimuths, and combining it with colour-coded elevation (a “hypsometric tint”) shows both relief and absolute height.


Code
hs315 = rs.lidar.hillshade(dem, azimuth=315, altitude=45)  # classic north-west light
hs_multi = sum(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem, azimuth=a, altitude=45) for a in (225, 270, 315, 360)) / 4  # four azimuths
ls = LightSource(azdeg=315, altdeg=45)  # light source for the tinted relief
# elevation colours shaded by relief
tinted = ls.shade(np.nan_to_num(dem.values, nan=float(dem.mean())), cmap=plt.cm.terrain, blend_mode="soft",
                  vert_exag=2, dx=1, dy=1)  # elevation colours shaded by relief

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 6))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(hs315, ax=axes[0], cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title="Hillshade, sun from 315°")  # one light
rs.viz.plot_raster(hs_multi, ax=axes[1], cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title="Multi-directional hillshade")  # four lights
axes[2].imshow(tinted); axes[2].set_title("Elevation tinted relief")  # colour relief
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The valley of Six Mile Creek runs from the south-east to the north-west, with a reservoir pond in its middle reach and steep, gullied valley walls. South Hill rises to the south-west, and fields, roads, quarries and housing are visible on the plateaus. The 1 m DEM shows field boundaries, road cuts and individual driveways.

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
text:
Local terrain derivatives
All six local derivatives come from the same 1 m DEM. TPI uses a 51-cell (51 m) window to capture valley and ridge positions rather than micro-relief.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
deriv = {"Slope (°)": (rs.lidar.slope(dem), "magma", (0, 45)),  # steepness
         "Aspect (° from north)": (rs.lidar.aspect(dem), "twilight", (0, 360)),  # exposure

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
section: Scale: window size and DEM resolution
text:
Scale: window size and DEM resolution
Terrain variables are not unique properties of a place: they depend on the DEM resolution and on the window size. The left panel shows TPI at three window sizes; the table and right panel show how the slope distribution changes when the 1 m DEM is aggregated to coarser cells, as it would be for a 10 m or 30 m national DEM.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1, 1, 1.2]})  # four panels
for ax, w in zip(axes[:3], (11, 51, 201)):  # three TPI windows (cells = m)
    rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.tpi(dem2, window=max(3, w // 2) | 1), ax=ax, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-10, vmax=10,  # TPI map
                       title=f"TPI, {w} m window")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
rows = {}  # one row per resolution
for res in (1, 2, 5, 10, 30):  # aggregation factors (m)
    d = dem if res == 1 else dem.coarsen(x=res, y=res, boundary="trim").mean().rio.write_crs(dem.rio.crs)  # aggregate
    s = rs.lidar.slope(d).values.ravel()  # slope values
    s = s[np.isfinite(s)]  # drop empty cells
    rows[f"{res} m"] = {"mean slope (°)": s.mean(), "95th percentile (°)": np.percentile(s, 95),  # statistics
                        "share > 30° (%)": 100 * np.mean(s > 30)}
    axes[3].hist(s, bins=np.arange(0, 60, 1), histtype="step", density=True, lw=1.5, label=f"{res} m")  # distribution
axes[3].set(xlabel="Slope (°)", ylabel="density", yscale="log", title="Slope distribution by DEM resolution")  # labels
axes[3].legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
text:
Depression filling and road embankments
rs.lidar.fill_depressions raises every pit to its spill point. The fill depth (filled minus original DEM) shows where water would pond if it could not escape. In a LiDAR DEM most large “depressions” are not real: they sit upstream of road embankments, driveways and dams, where the water actually passes through a culvert that the laser cannot see.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
filled = rs.lidar.fill_depressions(dem2)  # priority-flood filling on the 2 m DEM
fill_depth = (filled - dem2).where(lambda d: d > 0.05)  # where the DEM was raised by more than 5 cm
# summary line
print(f"filled in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s | raised cells: {float(fill_depth.notnull().mean()):.1%} | "
      f"largest fill {float(fill_depth.max()):.1f} m | filled volume {float(fill_depth.sum() * 4) / 1e3:,.0f} thousand m³")  # summary

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6.5))  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem2), ax=axes[0], cmap="gray", colorbar=False,  # relief background
                   title="Fill depth over the hillshade (m)")
fd_plot = fill_depth.where(fill_depth > 0.2)  # fills deeper than 20 cm
im = axes[0].imshow(fd_plot.values, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=5,  # fill depth overlay
                    extent=[float(dem2.x.min()), float(dem2.x.max()), float(dem2.y.min()), float(dem2.y.max())])
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], shrink=0.8)  # colour bar
big = fill_depth.where(fill_depth > 1).notnull()  # fills deeper than 1 m
rr, cc = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(np.where(big, fill_depth.values, np.nan)), big.shape)  # deepest fill
win = dict(y=slice(max(rr - 100, 0), rr + 100), x=slice(max(cc - 100, 0), cc + 100))  # 400 m window around it
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem2).isel(win), ax=axes[1], cmap="gray", colorbar=False,  # zoomed relief
                   title="Deepest fill: a pond behind an embankment (400 m window)")
sub = fill_depth.isel(win)  # zoomed fill depth
axes[1].imshow(sub.where(sub > 0.2).values, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=float(sub.max()), alpha=0.8,  # overlay
               extent=[float(sub.x.min()), float(sub.x.max()), float(sub.y.min()), float(sub.y.max())])
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


filled in 9.1 s | raised cells: 3.0% | largest fill 7.2 m | filled volume 255 thousand m³









The deepest fills sit upstream of road embankments and of the dam on Six Mile Creek. Filling them gives a DEM in which water always reaches the edge, but it also creates large artificial lakes. Hydrological DEM conditioning therefore “burns” culverts and bridges into the DEM (lowering the embankment along the culvert) before filling; national products such as the USGS 3DEP hydro-flattened DEMs and the NHDPlus HR use such conditioning.

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
section: Flow direction, flow accumulation and streams
text:
Flow direction, flow accumulation and streams
rs.lidar.flow_direction gives the D8 receiver of every cell (0 = north, clockwise to 7 = north-west) and rs.lidar.flow_accumulation the number of upslope cells. Cells draining more than 10 ha (25,000 cells of 4 m²) are taken as streams.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
fdir = rs.lidar.flow_direction(filled)  # D8 directions
acc = rs.lidar.flow_accumulation(filled, filled=True)  # upslope cells
# summary line
print(f"flow direction and accumulation in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s | max {float(acc.max()):,.0f} cells "
      f"= {float(acc.max()) * 4 / 1e6:.1f} km² draining through one cell")  # largest catchment in the window
STREAM_CELLS = 25_000  # 10 ha at 2 m cells
streams = acc >= STREAM_CELLS  # stream network

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(19, 6))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(fdir.where(fdir >= 0), ax=axes[0], title="D8 flow direction",  # directions
                   categorical={i: (n, plt.cm.hsv(i / 8)) for i, n in enumerate(["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"])})
rs.viz.plot_raster(np.log10(acc), ax=axes[1], cmap="Blues", title="log10 flow accumulation (cells)")  # accumulation
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem2), ax=axes[2], cmap="gray", colorbar=False,  # relief background
                   title="Streams draining > 10 ha")
ext = [float(dem2.x.min()), float(dem2.x.max()), float(dem2.y.min()), float(dem2.y.max())]  # map extent
axes[2].imshow(np.where(streams, 1, np.nan), cmap="cool", extent=ext, interpolation="nearest")  # streams
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


flow direction and accumulation in 0.7 s | max 1,722,520 cells = 6.9 km² draining through one cell









Six Mile Creek collects most of the flow, joined by side streams from the gullies on both valley walls. On the flat fields and filled ponds D8 routes water along parallel straight lines (the striped texture of the accumulation map), a known artefact of single-direction routing on flats; multiple-flow-direction methods spread the flow more realistically on hillslopes.

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
text:
Topographic Wetness Index
rs.lidar.twi combines the specific catchment area with the local slope. Valley floors, hollows and the edges of flat fields have high TWI; ridges and steep walls have low TWI.


Code
twi = rs.lidar.twi(filled)  # ln(a / tan β)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6))  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(twi, ax=axes[0], cmap="YlGnBu", vmin=2, vmax=14, title="Topographic Wetness Index")  # map
axes[0].set_xticks([]); axes[0].set_yticks([])  # no ticks
for name, cls in (("valley", 9), ("hollow", 7), ("slope", 6), ("spur", 5), ("ridge", 3)):  # landforms
    v = twi.values[geo.values == cls]  # TWI of that landform
    axes[1].hist(v[np.isfinite(v)], bins=np.arange(0, 20, 0.25), histtype="step", density=True, lw=1.5, label=name)  # histogram
axes[1].set(xlabel="TWI", ylabel="density", title="TWI by geomorphon landform"); axes[1].legend()  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
section: Height Above Nearest Drainage and flood extent
text:
Height Above Nearest Drainage and flood extent
rs.lidar.hand follows the D8 path from every cell to the first stream cell and subtracts the stream’s elevation. rs.lidar.inundation on the HAND raster then gives the area below a water stage measured above the channel, connected to the stream network. This is the basis of the NOAA National Water Model’s continental flood inundation maps; it ignores hydraulics (velocity, backwater, embankments), so it is a first screening, not a flood model.


Code
hand = rs.lidar.hand(filled, threshold=STREAM_CELLS, filled=True)  # height above the nearest stream (m)
stream_xy = [(float(dem2.x[c]), float(dem2.y[r])) for r, c in zip(*np.nonzero(streams.values))][::50]  # seed points on streams
floods = {stage: rs.lidar.inundation(hand, stage, seeds=stream_xy) for stage in (1, 3, 5)}  # three stages (m)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(19, 6))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(hand, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=40, title="HAND (m)")  # HAND map
for ax, stage in zip(axes[1:], (1, 5)):  # two stages
    rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem2), ax=ax, cmap="gray", colorbar=False,  # relief background
                       title=f"Flood depth for a {stage} m stage above the channels")
    d = floods[stage]["depth"]  # depth raster
    im = ax.imshow(d.values, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=stage, extent=ext, interpolation="nearest")  # depth overlay
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="depth (m)")  # colour bar
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
pd.DataFrame({f"{s} m stage": {"flooded area (ha)": float(f["extent"].sum()) * 4 / 1e4,  # area per stage
                               "mean depth (m)": float(f["depth"].mean())} for s, f in floods.items()}).T.round(2)

HAND is low along Six Mile Creek, its tributaries and the reservoir, and rises quickly up the valley walls. White areas have no HAND value: they drain off the edge of this 3 km window before reaching a stream cell, which is why HAND and flow accumulation should be computed on a DEM that covers whole catchments. Some straight flooded lines follow roadside ditches and an old railway grade, which the 1 m DEM resolves as channels. The 1 m stage already fills the reservoir and the creek bed; the 5 m stage spreads onto the low terraces of the valley floor.

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
text:
A cross-valley profile
Sampling the DEM along a line across the valley shows the shape of the gorge, the reservoir surface and the plateaus on both sides. xarray’s interp samples the DEM at points spaced 1 m apart along the line.


Code
x0, y0, x1, y1 = 377200, 4697400, 378700, 4698900  # from the south-west plateau to the north-east plateau
n = int(np.hypot(x1 - x0, y1 - y0))  # one sample per metre
xs, ys = np.linspace(x0, x1, n), np.linspace(y0, y1, n)  # sample positions
prof = dem.interp(x=xr.DataArray(xs, dims="d"), y=xr.DataArray(ys, dims="d"))  # bilinear samples of the DEM
slp = rs.lidar.slope(dem).interp(x=xr.DataArray(xs, dims="d"), y=xr.DataArray(ys, dims="d"))  # slope along the line

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 2.2]})  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(dem2), ax=axes[0], cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title="Profile line")  # map
axes[0].plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], "r-", lw=2); axes[0].set_xticks([]); axes[0].set_yticks([])  # the line
axes[1].fill_between(np.arange(n), prof, float(prof.min()) - 5, color="#c2a878")  # terrain profile
axes[1].plot(np.arange(n), prof, "k-", lw=0.8)  # outline
ax2 = axes[1].twinx(); ax2.plot(np.arange(n), slp.rolling(d=15, center=True).mean(), color="C3", lw=0.8)  # 15 m mean slope
ax2.set_ylabel("Slope, 15 m running mean (°)", color="C3")  # slope label
axes[1].set(xlabel="Distance along the profile (m)", ylabel="Elevation (m)", title="Cross-valley profile of Six Mile Creek")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Terrain and Hydrology from LiDAR DEMs
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

A seamless DEM from several tiles needs grids aligned to the same origin; tile-by-tile interpolation can leave small seams, which buffered tiles avoid.
Slope, aspect, curvature, TPI, TRI and roughness are local derivatives; their values depend on the DEM resolution and the window size, so models must use the same scale for fitting and prediction.
Geomorphons classify landforms from line-of-sight patterns and adapt to the scale of the landform through the search distance.
In 1 m LiDAR DEMs, road embankments and dams create large artificial depressions; condition the DEM (burn culverts, flatten water) before routing flow.
D8 flow accumulation gives stream networks; TWI marks wet areas; HAND relative to the stream network gives a quick first estimate of flood extent for a given stage.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.lidar.las_info, rs.lidar.read_las (with fields), rs.lidar.dem, rs.lidar.merge_rasters, rs.lidar.hillshade, rs.lidar.slope, rs.lidar.aspect, rs.lidar.curvature, rs.lidar.tpi, rs.lidar.tri, rs.lidar.roughness, rs.lidar.illumination, rs.lidar.sun_positions, rs.lidar.geomorphons, rs.lidar.fill_depressions, rs.lidar.flow_direction, rs.lidar.flow_accumulation, rs.lidar.twi, rs.lidar.hand, rs.lidar.inundation, rs.write, rs.viz.plot_raster.
Exercises

Build the DEM from all ten Ithaca tiles at 2 m. Where do the tile seams show in a hillshade?
Change the stream threshold to 1 ha and 100 ha. How does the drainage density (stream length per km²) change?
Compute geomorphons with search distances of 10, 50 and 150 cells. Which landforms appear or disappear?
Lower the DEM by 3 m along a short line across the road embankment with the deepest fill (a “burned” culvert) and fill again. How much of the artificial pond disappears?
Compare TWI computed on the 2 m and on a 10 m version of the DEM. Which places change most?

title: Buildings and Urban Features from LiDAR
text:
Overview

Urban applications of LiDAR

3D city models for planning, visualisation, noise and wind simulation, and digital twins. The CityGML standard defines levels of detail: LoD1 extrudes each footprint to one height (block model), LoD2 adds roof shapes, LoD3 adds facade detail.
Building inventories for property tax, population and energy models, and post-disaster damage assessment (comparing surveys before and after an earthquake or tornado).
Solar potential of roofs from their slope, aspect and shading by neighbouring buildings and trees.
Infrastructure: power-line clearance and vegetation encroachment, road surfaces and kerbs, bridges, street furniture and urban tree inventories.
Flood and drainage modelling, which needs buildings as obstacles and accurate street-level terrain.



How buildings differ from trees in a point cloud








Property
Roof
Tree crown




Local geometry
Planar: neighbours lie on a plane; the smallest eigenvalue of their covariance is near zero
Volumetric: points scatter in 3D


Returns per pulse
Mostly one (the roof is solid)
Several (pulses pass through gaps)


Height above ground
Uniform over the roof
Varies, peaks at the treetop


Object shape
Straight edges, right angles, large flat patches
Round, irregular



Eigenvalue features. For the \(k\) nearest neighbours of a point, the covariance matrix has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \lambda_3\). Normalised combinations describe the local shape: linearity \((\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)/\lambda_1\) (wires, edges), planarity \((\lambda_2 - \lambda_3)/\lambda_1\) (roofs, ground, walls), scattering \(\lambda_3/\lambda_1\) (vegetation), and verticality \(1 - |n_z|\) from the normal vector (walls).
RANSAC planes. Random Sample Consensus (Fischler and Bolles 1981) repeatedly fits a plane through three random points and keeps the plane with the most points within a distance tolerance. Applied sequentially it splits a roof into its planar faces, each with a slope and aspect.


Building extraction workflows

Label-based: if the producer classified buildings (class 6), rasterise those points, close small gaps, vectorise to polygons and measure heights from the normalised DSM.
Rule-based on rasters: tall cells of the normalised DSM where most pulses return only once.
Point-based geometry: roof candidates are planar points above a height threshold; they are clustered into objects, and an object is a building when a few RANSAC planes explain most of its points (tree crowns fail this test).
Machine learning and deep learning on point features (see the point classification notebook).

Validation compares the extracted buildings with reference footprints or labels, using precision, recall and intersection over union (IoU).
crumbs: Buildings and Urban Features from LiDAR

title: Buildings and Urban Features from LiDAR
text:
Urban Analysis with GeoLattice

Learning objectives

Compare ground filters on large flat roofs and compute a normalised DSM.
Separate buildings from vegetation with eigenvalue features and RANSAC planes, and with a raster rule.
Validate building classifications against reference labels with precision, recall and IoU.

section: Ground filters, large roofs and the normalised DSM
text:
Ground filters, large roofs and the normalised DSM
The Autzen window holds the stadium, offices and several large buildings; the largest flat roof covers about 6,000 m². A morphological ground filter only removes objects narrower than its window, so large flat roofs are a hard test. The cell runs three ground filters and counts how many of the producer’s building points each one wrongly puts in the ground class. The producer’s classes are kept in a separate array (ref) for validation; the classification itself starts again from geometry only.


Code
autzen = rs.lidar.read_las(AUTZEN).drop_noise()  # the labelled window without noise
ref = np.asarray(autzen["classification"]).copy()  # producer classes, kept for validation
print(autzen)  # count, fields and CRS
print(pd.Series(ref).map(lambda k: ASPRS_CLASSES.get(int(k), f"user {k}")).value_counts().to_string())  # reference classes

rows, grounds = {}, {}  # one row per filter
for name, fn in (("SMRF, 100 m window", lambda: rs.lidar.smrf(autzen, cell=2.0, slope=0.15, window=100)),  # SMRF
                 ("CSF, rigidness 3", lambda: rs.lidar.csf(autzen, resolution=2.0, rigidness=3)),  # stiff cloth
                 ("PMF, 200 m window", lambda: rs.lidar.pmf(autzen, cell=2.0, max_window=200))):  # exponential windows
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
    grounds[name] = fn()  # classify ground
    gc = np.asarray(grounds[name]["classification"]) == 2  # predicted ground
    rows[name] = {"building points put in ground": np.mean(gc[ref == 6]),  # roof absorbed into the terrain
                  "ground agreement with producer": np.mean(gc == (ref == 2)), "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3))  # comparison

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
ag = grounds["PMF, 200 m window"]  # the filter that keeps the big roof off the ground
adem = rs.lidar.dem(ag, 1.0)  # DEM
adsm = rs.lidar.dsm(ag, 1.0, bounds=ag.bbox).reindex_like(adem, method="nearest")  # DSM on the same grid
andsm = rs.lidar.chm(adsm, adem, pit_free=False)  # normalised DSM (heights of all objects)
agn = rs.lidar.normalize_heights(ag, adem)  # per-point height above ground
print(f"surfaces in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")  # timing

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(andsm, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=25, title="Autzen: normalised DSM (m)")  # nDSM
rs.lidar.plot_classification(autzen, ax=axes[1], s=0.2)  # producer classes
axes[1].set_title("Producer classes")  # title
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

section: Eigenvalue features of roofs and trees
text:
Eigenvalue features of roofs and trees
rs.lidar.eigen_features computes the covariance features of every point’s k nearest neighbours. The histograms compare points the producer labelled as building (6) with high vegetation (5): roofs are planar with near-zero scattering, crowns scatter.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
above = agn.filter(np.asarray(agn["height"]) > 2)  # points more than 2 m above ground
ref_above = ref[np.asarray(agn["height"]) > 2]  # their producer classes
ef = rs.lidar.eigen_features(above, k=16, features=("linearity", "planarity", "scattering", "verticality"))  # features
print(f"eigen features for {len(above):,} points in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")  # timing

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 3.8))  # four panels
for ax, f in zip(axes, ("planarity", "scattering", "linearity", "verticality")):  # each feature
    v = np.asarray(ef[f])  # values
    for cls, col, lab in ((6, "C3", "building (6)"), (5, "C2", "high vegetation (5)")):  # two classes
        # histogram of this class
        ax.hist(v[ref_above == cls], bins=np.linspace(0, 1, 41), density=True, histtype="step", lw=2, color=col, label=lab)
    ax.set(title=f, xlabel="value")  # labels
axes[0].legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Buildings and Urban Features from LiDAR
text:
Classifying buildings from geometry
rs.lidar.classify_buildings uses these features and object-level RANSAC tests: points at least 2.5 m above ground with low scattering and linearity are roof candidates; candidates are clustered; a cluster is a building when up to six planes no steeper than 60° explain at least 80 % of its points; accepted roofs then grow to adjacent points (edges, walls), and all other above-ground points become vegetation by height. The result is compared point by point with the producer’s building class.


Code
def binary_scores(pred, truth):  # precision, recall, F1 and IoU of two boolean masks
    tp = np.sum(pred & truth); fp = np.sum(pred & ~truth); fn = np.sum(~pred & truth)  # counts
    return {"precision": tp / max(tp + fp, 1), "recall": tp / max(tp + fn, 1),  # scores
            "F1": 2 * tp / max(2 * tp + fp + fn, 1), "IoU": tp / max(tp + fp + fn, 1)}

t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
bld = rs.lidar.classify_buildings(ag, dtm=adem, min_height=2.5)  # buildings (6) and vegetation (3/4/5)
sec = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time taken
cb = np.asarray(bld["classification"])  # new classes
print(f"classify_buildings in {sec:.1f} s")  # timing
scores_pts = {"geometry (classify_buildings)": binary_scores(cb == 6, ref == 6)}  # point-level scores
display(pd.DataFrame(scores_pts).T.round(3))  # show them
pd.crosstab(pd.Series(ref).map(lambda k: ASPRS_CLASSES.get(int(k), f"user {k}")).rename("producer"),  # confusion table
            pd.Series(cb).map(lambda k: ASPRS_CLASSES.get(int(k), k)).rename("classify_buildings"))

section: A raster rule as a baseline
text:
A raster rule as a baseline
A simple label-free rule on 1 m rasters: cells of the normalised DSM higher than 2.5 m where fewer than 15 % of the returns come from multi-return pulses, cleaned with a morphological opening. Comparing it with the producer’s building mask at the raster level shows what the point-based geometry adds.


Code
from scipy import ndimage as nd  # morphology
# returns from multi-return pulses per cell
multi = rs.lidar.rasterize(autzen.filter(np.asarray(autzen["number_of_returns"]) > 1), 1.0, stat="count",
                           bounds=autzen.bbox).reindex_like(adem, method="nearest").fillna(0)  # multi-return points
allr = rs.lidar.rasterize(autzen, 1.0, stat="count", bounds=autzen.bbox).reindex_like(adem, method="nearest")  # all points
rule = ((andsm > 2.5) & (multi / allr < 0.15)).values  # tall and mostly single return
rule = nd.binary_opening(rule, iterations=2)  # remove small specks

def mask_of(cls_array, cloud, code=6):  # 1 m raster mask of points with a class code
    m = rs.lidar.rasterize(cloud.filter(cls_array == code), 1.0, stat="count", bounds=autzen.bbox)  # count per cell
    return nd.binary_closing(m.reindex_like(adem, method="nearest").fillna(0).values > 0, iterations=1)  # closed mask

ref_mask = mask_of(ref, autzen)  # producer buildings
geo_mask = mask_of(cb, bld)  # classify_buildings result
masks = {"raster rule": rule, "geometry (classify_buildings)": geo_mask}  # the two methods
display(pd.DataFrame({k: binary_scores(m, ref_mask) for k, m in masks.items()}).T.round(3))  # raster-level scores

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6.5))  # two panels
cat = {0: ("neither", "#f7f7f7"), 1: ("reference only", "#2b83ba"), 2: ("method only", "#fdae61"), 3: ("both", "#d7191c")}  # legend
for ax, (name, m) in zip(axes, masks.items()):  # each method
    cmp = adem.copy(data=(m.astype(int) * 2 + ref_mask.astype(int)))  # comparison codes
    iou = binary_scores(m, ref_mask)["IoU"]  # IoU
    rs.viz.plot_raster(cmp, ax=ax, categorical=cat, title=f"{name} vs producer buildings, IoU {iou:.2f}")  # map
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

Both methods find almost all of the producer’s buildings (recall 0.84 for the raster rule, 0.95 for classify_buildings), but their precision is low, and the maps show why. Most of the “method only” area is the stadium bowl, which the producer did not label as a building although both methods find it: a reference error rather than a method error. The remaining differences are method errors: dense tree crowns with flat tops pass the raster rule as small specks, and the geometric method also takes in the flat field inside the stadium, which sits on the stands. The point-based geometry is clearly better (IoU 0.41 against 0.26). Low agreement can mean an imperfect method, imperfect labels or both, so disagreements should be inspected before trusting either.

title: Buildings and Urban Features from LiDAR
text:
Building footprints and heights
rs.lidar.building_footprints rasterises the building points, closes small gaps, vectorises the mask into polygons, removes slivers smaller than min_area and adds the area, the height (95th percentile of roof heights above the DEM) and the number of points of each building. Matching the footprints from classify_buildings to those from the producer labels gives a per-building comparison.


Code
ref_cloud = rs.lidar.normalize_heights(autzen.with_field("classification", ref.astype("uint8")), adem)  # producer labels + heights
fp_ref = rs.lidar.building_footprints(ref_cloud, res=1.0, min_area=30, dtm=adem)  # reference footprints
fp_geo = rs.lidar.building_footprints(rs.lidar.normalize_heights(bld, adem), res=1.0, min_area=30, dtm=adem)  # extracted
print(f"reference footprints: {len(fp_ref)} | extracted: {len(fp_geo)}")  # counts

# overlaps between reference and extracted footprints
inter = gpd.overlay(fp_ref[["geometry"]].reset_index(names="ref_id"), fp_geo[["geometry"]].reset_index(names="geo_id"),
                    how="intersection")  # overlaps between the two sets
inter["a"] = inter.area  # overlap area
best = inter.sort_values("a").groupby("ref_id").last()  # best-matching extracted footprint per reference building
match = fp_ref[["area_m2", "height_m"]].join(best[["geo_id", "a"]])  # reference attributes plus match
match["IoU"] = [row.a / (row.area_m2 + fp_geo.area[int(row.geo_id)] - row.a) if pd.notnull(row.geo_id) else 0  # polygon IoU
                for row in match.itertuples()]
match["height extracted (m)"] = [fp_geo.height_m[int(g)] if pd.notnull(g) else np.nan for g in match.geo_id]  # height
match.sort_values("area_m2", ascending=False).head(10).drop(columns="a").round(2)  # largest reference buildings

title: Buildings and Urban Features from LiDAR
text:
Roof planes
rs.lidar.segment_roof_planes extracts planes one after another with RANSAC from the points of one building and splits each plane’s inliers into connected patches. Each plane gets a slope and an aspect, the inputs for LoD2 roof models and for solar analysis. The cell segments the largest building found.


Code
b_pts = bld.filter(cb == 6)  # building points
labels_b = rs.lidar.euclidean_clusters(b_pts, radius=1.5, min_points=50, dims=2)  # one cluster per building
big = b_pts.filter(labels_b == 0)  # the largest building (cluster 0)
planes_pc, planes = rs.lidar.segment_roof_planes(big, distance=0.15, min_points=40, max_planes=12)  # RANSAC planes
display(planes[["slope_deg", "aspect_deg", "n_points"]].round(1))  # one row per plane

pid = np.asarray(planes_pc["plane_id"])  # plane of each point
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(14, 5.5))  # two panels
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1)  # plan view
ax1.scatter(big.x, big.y, c=np.where(pid >= 0, pid % 10, np.nan), cmap="tab10", s=2)  # points by plane
ax1.set(title="Roof planes of the largest building (plan view)", aspect="equal", xticks=[], yticks=[])  # labels
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2, projection="3d")  # 3D view
ax2.scatter(big.x - big.x.mean(), big.y - big.y.mean(), big.z, c=np.where(pid >= 0, pid % 10, -1), cmap="tab10", s=1)  # 3D
ax2.set(title="Roof planes in 3D", zlabel="Elevation (m)"); ax2.view_init(35, -60)  # labels and angle

title: Buildings and Urban Features from LiDAR
text:
Roof solar potential
rs.lidar.solar_potential averages the cosine of the solar incidence angle over a set of sun positions (here every hour from 6:00 to 18:00 solar time on one day per month at 44° N), optionally with cast shadows traced along each sun direction across the DSM. Values are relative (1 = a surface facing the sun at every position). With footprints it reports the mean value per roof and the area that is both well lit and not too steep.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
dsm2 = adsm.coarsen(x=2, y=2, boundary="trim").max().rio.write_crs(adsm.rio.crs)  # 2 m DSM keeps the run short
# relative insolation with shading
solar = rs.lidar.solar_potential(dsm2, latitude=44.05, days=np.arange(15, 365, 30), hours=np.arange(6, 19),
                                 shading=True)  # relative insolation with shadows
# summary per roof
roofs = rs.lidar.solar_potential(dsm2, latitude=44.05, days=np.arange(15, 365, 30), hours=np.arange(6, 19),
                                 footprints=fp_geo, shading=True)  # per-roof summary
print(f"solar potential in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")  # timing

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))  # one panel
rs.viz.plot_raster(solar, ax=ax, cmap="inferno", vmin=0, vmax=1, title="Relative annual insolation (2 m), with shading")  # map
fp_geo.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="cyan", lw=0.6)  # roof outlines
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); plt.show()  # draw
roofs.drop(columns="geometry").sort_values("suitable_area_m2", ascending=False).head(8).round(2)  # best roofs

section: Buildings on the UB campus without labels
text:
Buildings on the UB campus without labels
The 2008 UB survey has about 1 point/m² and only ground classified, so the label-free workflow is the only option. The two tiles are reprojected to UTM zone 17N; the analysis uses the same 1 km block as the processing notebook; ground is reclassified with PMF and windows up to 120 m on a 2 m grid (the campus buildings are large), and classify_buildings then separates buildings from trees. With only one or two points per m², plane tests need lower point counts per cluster.


Code
ub = rs.lidar.reproject(rs.lidar.merge_pointclouds([rs.lidar.read_las(p) for p in UB_TILES]), 26917).drop_noise()  # metres
ucx, ucy = np.mean(ub.bbox[::2]), np.mean(ub.bbox[1::2])  # centre of the two tiles
ub = ub.crop(ucx - 500, ucy - 500, ucx + 500, ucy + 500)  # a 1 km x 1 km block of the campus
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the timer
ubg = rs.lidar.pmf(ub, cell=2.0, max_window=120)  # ground with PMF, wide windows
udem = rs.lidar.dem(ubg, 1.0)  # DEM
ubn = rs.lidar.normalize_heights(ubg, udem)  # heights above ground
ubb = rs.lidar.classify_buildings(ubg, dtm=udem, min_height=3.0, min_points=15, cluster_radius=2.5, k=12)  # buildings
# UB footprints with heights
fp_ub = rs.lidar.building_footprints(rs.lidar.normalize_heights(ubb, udem), res=1.0, min_area=80, dtm=udem,
                                     close_iter=2)  # footprints
# summary line
print(f"UB: {len(ub):,} points | {len(fp_ub)} buildings, {fp_ub.area_m2.sum() / 1e4:.1f} ha of roof | "
      f"{time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")  # summary

udsm = rs.lidar.dsm(ubg, 1.0, bounds=ubg.bbox).reindex_like(udem, method="nearest")  # DSM
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 7))  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(rs.lidar.hillshade(udsm), ax=axes[0], cmap="gray", colorbar=False, title="UB 2008: DSM hillshade")  # relief
# footprints coloured by height
fp_ub.plot(ax=axes[1], column="height_m", cmap="plasma", legend=True, legend_kwds={"label": "height (m)", "shrink": 0.7})
axes[1].set(title=f"UB 2008: {len(fp_ub)} building footprints from classify_buildings", aspect="equal")  # title
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

text:
An LoD1 block model
An LoD1 model extrudes each footprint to its height. Drawing the footprints as prisms on top of the terrain gives a simple 3D view of the campus.


Code
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8)); ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")  # 3D axes
ox, oy = ub.bbox[0], ub.bbox[1]  # local origin for readable axes
base_z = float(np.nanmedian(udem.values))  # a common base height
for _, r in fp_ub.iterrows():  # each building
    geom = r.geometry.simplify(1.0)  # simplified outline
    polys = list(geom.geoms) if geom.geom_type == "MultiPolygon" else [geom]  # its parts
    for p in polys:  # each part
        xs, ys = np.asarray(p.exterior.xy)  # outline coordinates
        xs, ys = xs - ox, ys - oy  # local coordinates
        top = [list(zip(xs, ys, np.full(len(xs), r.height_m)))]  # roof polygon
        # one wall per outline segment
        walls = [[(xs[i], ys[i], 0), (xs[i + 1], ys[i + 1], 0), (xs[i + 1], ys[i + 1], r.height_m), (xs[i], ys[i], r.height_m)]
                 for i in range(len(xs) - 1)]  # wall quadrilaterals
        col = plt.cm.plasma(min(float(r.height_m) / 50.0, 1.0))  # colour by height (float in 0 to 1)

# axes and title

title: Buildings and Urban Features from LiDAR
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

The ground filter’s window must exceed the widest roof, or large buildings vanish into the terrain.
Roofs are planar and mostly single-return; crowns scatter and return several echoes. Eigenvalue features capture this at each point.
classify_buildings combines local planarity with object-level RANSAC tests; a raster rule on nDSM height and return structure is a quick baseline.
Validate with precision, recall and IoU, and inspect disagreements: reference labels are not always complete.
Footprints carry area and height; RANSAC roof planes give slope and aspect for LoD2 models and solar analysis.
Linearity finds wires, but sparse airborne data sample them only in fragments.
The same workflow runs on older, sparser surveys without labels, with smaller minimum cluster sizes.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.lidar.read_las, rs.lidar.reproject, rs.lidar.merge_pointclouds, rs.lidar.smrf, rs.lidar.csf, rs.lidar.pmf, rs.lidar.dem, rs.lidar.dsm, rs.lidar.chm, rs.lidar.normalize_heights, rs.lidar.eigen_features, rs.lidar.classify_buildings, rs.lidar.rasterize, rs.lidar.building_footprints, rs.lidar.euclidean_clusters, rs.lidar.segment_roof_planes, rs.lidar.solar_potential, rs.lidar.detect_power_lines, rs.lidar.plot_classification, rs.lidar.hillshade, rs.lidar.write_las, rs.write, rs.viz.plot_raster.
Exercises

Run PMF on Autzen with max_window of 30, 60, 120 and 200 m and compute the building IoU of classify_buildings for each. Why does it change?
Vary max_scattering (0.02 to 0.1) and plane_fraction (0.6 to 0.9). Which setting gives the best F1?
Plot roof-plane aspect against solar potential for the planes of the largest building.
Compute solar potential without shading and map the difference. Which roofs are shaded most by trees or neighbours?
On the UB campus, compare footprint areas from 1 m and 2 m rasters. How sensitive is roof area to the cell size at 1 point/m²?

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
text: Banner

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
text:
Overview

Why lidar from space
Canopy height and vertical structure are the key variables for forest carbon, but optical and radar satellites only infer them. A laser altimeter in orbit measures them directly along its ground tracks. The tracks are sparse samples, not images, so wall-to-wall maps are made by gridding the samples or by using them to train models on optical and radar images.


GEDI
The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) has operated on the International Space Station since late 2018 (science data from April 2019, with a pause in 2023 to 2024).







Property
Value




Lasers
Three Nd:YAG lasers at 1064 nm; one is split into two “coverage” beams, two are “full power” beams, giving four beams dithered across eight ground tracks


Footprint
About 25 m diameter, every 60 m along track


Track spacing
About 600 m across track; the eight tracks span about 4.2 km


Coverage
Between about 51.6° N and 51.6° S (the ISS orbit)


Measurement
The full returned waveform, digitised in time


Geolocation accuracy
About 10 m (horizontal, one sigma)



Products.








Level
Product
Content




L1B
Geolocated waveforms
The raw received waveforms with their positions


L2A
Elevation and height metrics
Ground elevation (elev_lowestmode) and relative heights RH0 to RH100 for each footprint


L2B
Canopy cover and vertical profile
Canopy cover, plant area index (PAI), plant area volume density (PAVD) profile, foliage height diversity


L3
Gridded metrics
Mean canopy height and other metrics on a 1 km grid


L4A
Footprint biomass
Aboveground biomass density (Mg/ha) per footprint from regional models of RH metrics


L4B
Gridded biomass
Mean biomass on a 1 km grid with uncertainty



Relative heights. The waveform’s energy is accumulated from the ground return upward; RHn is the height above the ground at which n % of the energy has been received. RH98 or RH100 approximates the canopy top, RH50 the height of median energy.
Quality. quality_flag = 1 marks usable shots, degrade_flag = 0 excludes periods of degraded pointing or positioning, and sensitivity (the canopy cover through which the ground can still be detected) should be at least 0.9, or 0.95 to 0.98 in dense tropical forest. Full-power beams (BEAM0101, BEAM0110, BEAM1000, BEAM1011) penetrate dense canopy better than coverage beams (BEAM0000 to BEAM0011), and night shots have less solar noise.


ICESat-2
The Ice, Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) carries ATLAS, the Advanced Topographic Laser Altimeter System, launched in September 2018.







Property
Value




Laser
532 nm (green), 10,000 pulses per second


Detection
Single photons (photon counting)


Beams
Six beams in three pairs; in each pair a strong and a weak beam (energy ratio about 4:1), 90 m apart; pairs 3.3 km apart


Footprint
About 11 to 13 m, every 0.7 m along track


Orbit
92° inclination, 91-day repeat, coverage to 88° N and S



Products. ATL03 contains every geolocated photon; ATL06 gives land-ice heights; ATL08 (land and vegetation height) classifies photons as ground, canopy, canopy top or noise and summarises them in 100 m segments along each beam, with terrain height (h_te_best_fit), canopy height (h_canopy, the 98th percentile of canopy photon heights above the ground), canopy openness and flags such as night_flag. Daytime data have far more solar background photons, so canopy heights are noisier by day; green light is also absorbed more by vegetation than near-infrared, so dense canopies return few ground photons.


Comparing spaceborne and airborne LiDAR
Three effects must be handled before comparing a GEDI or ICESat-2 height with airborne LiDAR (ALS):

Geolocation error. A footprint reported 10 m away from where it fell samples different trees. In heterogeneous canopies this alone adds metres of scatter.
Footprint size and shape. A 25 m GEDI footprint integrates many crowns; the ALS metric must be computed over the same circle, not taken from one CHM pixel.
Vertical datum. GEDI and ICESat-2 report heights above the WGS 84 ellipsoid; national ALS uses orthometric heights (NAVD88 in the United States). Heights above ground are unaffected, but ground elevations differ by the geoid height (about -28 m in Mississippi).

Calibration studies therefore simulate GEDI waveforms from ALS point clouds at the reported footprint positions, search over small position shifts to find the best match, and favour homogeneous stands.

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
text:
Spaceborne LiDAR with GeoLattice

Learning objectives

Explain how GEDI and ICESat-2 measure canopy and terrain, and what their L2A, L2B, L4A and ATL08 products contain.
Find real GEDI and ICESat-2 granules for an area through NASA’s CMR catalogue.
Read GEDI L2A and ICESat-2 ATL08 HDF5 files and apply their quality filters.
Plot relative-height profiles and compare spaceborne heights with airborne LiDAR over the same footprints.
Quantify how geolocation error and footprint size affect the comparison.
Grid footprint heights onto a raster.



Data







File
Content




GEDI02_A_simulated_madison.h5
GEDI L2A file over Madison, Mississippi, in the official HDF5 layout (four beams with shot_number, lat_lowestmode, lon_lowestmode, elev_lowestmode, rh, sensitivity, quality_flag, degrade_flag)


ATL08_simulated_madison.h5
ICESat-2 ATL08 file over Madison in the official layout (gt2r/land_segments with h_canopy, h_te_best_fit, canopy_openness, night_flag)


madison_utm.laz
The airborne LiDAR point cloud in UTM metres, written by the fundamentals notebook



The two HDF5 files are simulated from the real Madison airborne LiDAR, not observed from space. Real granules are hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes each, need an Earthdata login, and their sparse tracks may not cross a 1.5 km survey at all. Simulating the footprints from the same point cloud gives a comparison in which the “truth” is known exactly, so the effects of geolocation error and footprint size can be isolated. For GEDI, four beam tracks about 400 m apart, with footprints every 60 m along slightly oblique tracks, were placed over the survey; each footprint’s RH profile is the distribution of ALS return heights within 12.5 m of a position shifted by a random geolocation error (standard deviation 10 m), while the file stores the unshifted, “reported” position. For ATL08, one track of 100 m segments down the middle of the survey records the 98th percentile of canopy returns more than 2 m above ground in a 17 m wide strip. The code that wrote both files is shown in the Reading GEDI L2A section and runs only if the files are missing.

How geolocation error and footprint size matter

section: Finding real GEDI and ICESat-2 granules
text:
Finding real GEDI and ICESat-2 granules
NASA’s Common Metadata Repository (CMR) lists every granule of every Earthdata product. Its search API is public, so the query below needs no login; downloading the granules would need a free Earthdata account (rs.lidar.spaceborne.search and geolattice.rsense.access.earthdata_download handle that with the earthaccess package). The query counts the GEDI L2A, GEDI L4A and ICESat-2 ATL08 granules that pass over the Madison survey.


Code
import requests  # HTTP requests
from geolattice.network import is_online  # internet check
BBOX = (-90.153, 32.456, -90.131, 32.472)  # lon/lat box around the Madison survey
if is_online("https://cmr.earthdata.nasa.gov"):  # only with an internet connection
    rows = []  # one row per product
    # the three products
    for name, short in (("GEDI L2A", "GEDI02_A"), ("GEDI L4A", "GEDI_L4A_AGB_Density_V2_1_2056"), ("ICESat-2 ATL08", "ATL08")):
        r = requests.get("https://cmr.earthdata.nasa.gov/search/granules.json",  # CMR granule search
                         params={"short_name": short, "bounding_box": ",".join(map(str, BBOX)), "page_size": 2000},
                         timeout=120)
        entries = r.json()["feed"]["entry"]  # the granules found
        dates = sorted(e["time_start"][:10] for e in entries)  # their acquisition dates
        size = np.mean([float(e.get("granule_size", "nan")) for e in entries]) if entries else np.nan  # mean size (MB)
        rows.append({"product": name, "granules": len(entries), "first": dates[0] if dates else "",  # summary
                     "last": dates[-1] if dates else "", "mean size (MB)": round(size)})
    display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("product"))  # show the table
else:  # offline
    print("Offline: skipping the CMR search.")  # summary line

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
text:
The airborne reference
Heights above ground for every ALS return come from rs.lidar.normalize_heights with a 2 m DEM. A k-d tree on the x, y positions then finds the returns inside any footprint quickly.


Code
madison = rs.lidar.read_las(MADISON_UTM).drop_noise()  # ALS cloud in UTM 15N
dem2 = rs.lidar.dem(madison, 2.0)  # 2 m DEM from the producer's ground points
pcn = rs.lidar.normalize_heights(madison, dem2)  # heights above ground
H = np.clip(np.asarray(pcn["height"]), 0, None)  # heights, negatives set to 0
XY = np.c_[np.asarray(pcn.x), np.asarray(pcn.y)]  # positions
tree = cKDTree(XY)  # neighbour index
chm2 = rs.lidar.chm(madison, res=2.0)  # 2 m CHM for maps
to_ll = Transformer.from_crs(32615, 4326, always_xy=True)  # UTM -> lon/lat

def footprint_rh(x, y, radius=12.5, min_points=20):  # ALS relative heights inside a circular footprint
    idx = tree.query_ball_point([x, y], radius)  # returns inside the circle
    return np.percentile(H[idx], np.arange(101)) if len(idx) >= min_points else None  # RH0 to RH100 proxy

print(f"{len(pcn):,} ALS returns | CHM {chm2.shape} at 2 m")  # summary


4,067,917 ALS returns | CHM (782, 782) at 2 m

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
section: Reading GEDI L2A and quality filtering
text:
Reading GEDI L2A and quality filtering
The next cell writes the simulated GEDI and ATL08 files if they are missing (they ship with the data, so normally it does nothing), then reads GEDI with rs.lidar.read_gedi_l2a twice: once with quality=False to see every shot, and once with the recommended filters (quality_flag == 1, degrade_flag == 0, sensitivity ≥ 0.9).


Code
if not (GEDI_FILE.exists() and ATL08_FILE.exists()):  # recreate the simulated files only if needed
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)  # reproducible simulation
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = madison.bbox  # survey extent
    with h5py.File(GEDI_FILE, "w") as f:  # GEDI L2A layout
        for b_, bx in zip(("BEAM0000", "BEAM0001", "BEAM0101", "BEAM0110"), np.linspace(x0 + 150, x1 - 150, 4)):  # 4 beams
            ys = np.arange(y0 + 20, y1 - 20, 60.0); xs = bx + 0.1 * (ys - y0)  # 60 m spacing, slightly oblique
            err = rng.normal(0, 10, (len(ys), 2))  # 10 m geolocation error
            rh = [footprint_rh(x + e[0], y + e[1]) for x, y, e in zip(xs, ys, err)]  # RH at the true position
            # keep footprints with enough returns
            ok = [r is not None for r in rh]; xs, ys = xs[ok], ys[ok]; rh = np.array([r for r in rh if r is not None])
            lon, lat = to_ll.transform(xs, ys); g = f.create_group(b_); n = len(xs)  # reported positions
            # shot ids and positions
            g["shot_number"] = np.arange(n); g["lat_lowestmode"], g["lon_lowestmode"] = lat, lon
            # ground elevation
            g["elev_lowestmode"] = dem2.sel(x=xr.DataArray(xs), y=xr.DataArray(ys), method="nearest").values
            g["rh"] = rh; g["sensitivity"] = np.clip(rng.normal(0.96, 0.03, n), 0.8, 1.0)  # heights and sensitivity
            # quality flags
            g["quality_flag"] = (rng.random(n) > 0.1).astype("uint8"); g["degrade_flag"] = np.zeros(n, "uint8")
    with h5py.File(ATL08_FILE, "w") as f:  # ATL08 layout
        f["orbit_info/sc_orient"] = np.array([1])  # spacecraft orientation
        yy = np.arange(y0 + 50, y1 - 50, 100.0); xx = np.full_like(yy, (x0 + x1) / 2)  # 100 m segments
        hc = []  # canopy heights
        for x, y in zip(xx, yy):  # each segment
            idx = [i for i in tree.query_ball_point([x, y], 50) if abs(XY[i, 0] - x) < 8.5]  # 17 m wide strip
            c = H[idx][H[idx] > 2]  # canopy returns
            hc.append(np.percentile(c, 98) if c.size > 10 else 3.4028235e38)  # 98th percentile or fill value
        lon, lat = to_ll.transform(xx, yy); ls = f.create_group("gt2r/land_segments")  # segment positions
        # positions and canopy heights
        ls["latitude"], ls["longitude"] = lat, lon; ls["canopy/h_canopy"] = np.array(hc, "float32")
        # terrain heights
        ls["terrain/h_te_best_fit"] = dem2.sel(x=xr.DataArray(xx), y=xr.DataArray(yy), method="nearest").values.astype("float32")
        # openness and night flag
        ls["canopy/canopy_openness"] = np.full(len(yy), 3.0, "float32"); ls["night_flag"] = np.ones(len(yy), "int8")

with h5py.File(GEDI_FILE) as f:  # what is inside the file
    # summary line
    print("beams:", list(f), "| datasets in BEAM0000:", list(f["BEAM0000"]), "| rh shape:", f["BEAM0000/rh"].shape)
gedi_all = rs.lidar.read_gedi_l2a(GEDI_FILE, quality=False, rh=range(0, 101))  # every shot, RH0 to RH100
gedi = rs.lidar.read_gedi_l2a(GEDI_FILE, min_sensitivity=0.9, rh=range(0, 101))  # quality-filtered shots
# shots per beam before and after filtering
summary = pd.DataFrame({"all shots": gedi_all.groupby("beam").size(), "after quality filter": gedi.groupby("beam").size()})
# beam types
summary["beam type"] = ["coverage" if b_ in ("BEAM0000", "BEAM0001", "BEAM0010", "BEAM0011") else "full power"
                        for b_ in summary.index]  # beam types

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
text:
Relative-height profiles
Plotting RHn against n for single footprints shows the shape of the cumulative energy: a tall closed canopy rises steeply only near the top, an open stand stays near zero until the last percentiles, and bare ground stays at zero throughout.


Code
rh_cols = [f"rh{p}" for p in range(101)]  # RH0 to RH100
# three contrasting footprints
picks = {"tall closed canopy": gedi.loc[(gedi.rh50 > 15), "rh98"].idxmax() if (gedi.rh50 > 15).any() else gedi.rh98.idxmax(),
         "open canopy": (gedi.rh98.where(gedi.rh50 < 1) - 20).abs().idxmin(),  # tall top but most energy near ground
         "bare ground": gedi.rh98.idxmin()}  # lowest canopy
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))  # two panels
for name, i in picks.items():  # each example footprint
    axes[0].plot(range(101), gedi.loc[i, rh_cols].astype(float), label=f"{name} (shot {gedi.loc[i, 'shot_number']})")  # RH curve
# axis labels and title
axes[0].set(xlabel="n (% of returned energy)", ylabel="RH n (m)", title="Relative-height curves of three footprints")
axes[0].legend()  # legend
axes[1].hist([gedi.rh50, gedi.rh98], bins=30, label=["RH50", "RH98"])  # distributions over all footprints
# axis labels and title
axes[1].set(xlabel="height (m)", ylabel="footprints", title="RH50 and RH98 of all quality footprints"); axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
text:
GEDI heights versus airborne LiDAR
For each quality footprint, the ALS returns within 12.5 m of the reported position give the airborne RH98. The scatter plot compares it with GEDI RH98, which came from the true (shifted) position.


Code
gutm = gedi.to_crs(32615)  # footprints in UTM
gutm["als_rh98"] = [r[98] if (r := footprint_rh(p.x, p.y)) is not None else np.nan for p in gutm.geometry]  # ALS at reported position
# one 2 m CHM pixel at the centre
gutm["chm_pixel"] = chm2.sel(x=xr.DataArray(gutm.geometry.x.values), y=xr.DataArray(gutm.geometry.y.values),
                             method="nearest").values  # one 2 m CHM pixel at the centre
d = gutm.dropna(subset=["als_rh98"])  # footprints with ALS data
err = d.rh98 - d.als_rh98  # GEDI minus ALS
# summary line
print(f"{len(d)} footprints | bias {err.mean():+.2f} m | RMSE {np.sqrt((err ** 2).mean()):.2f} m | "
      f"r = {np.corrcoef(d.rh98, d.als_rh98)[0, 1]:.2f}")  # agreement

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5.8))  # two panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(chm2, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=32, title="ALS CHM with GEDI footprints (RH98)")  # CHM
gutm.plot(ax=axes[0], column="rh98", cmap="magma", markersize=14, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)  # footprints
axes[0].set_xticks([]); axes[0].set_yticks([])  # no ticks
axes[1].scatter(d.als_rh98, d.rh98, s=14, label="ALS RH98 in the 25 m footprint")  # footprint-based comparison
axes[1].scatter(d.chm_pixel, d.rh98, s=10, marker="x", alpha=0.6, label="single CHM pixel at the centre")  # pixel-based
axes[1].plot([0, 35], [0, 35], "k--", lw=1)  # 1:1 line
# axis labels and title
axes[1].set(xlabel="ALS height at the reported position (m)", ylabel="GEDI RH98 (m)", title="GEDI versus ALS")
axes[1].legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


78 footprints | bias -0.61 m | RMSE 3.24 m | r = 0.94









The correlation is high (r about 0.95), because tall forest and clearings are large compared with a footprint. Still, individual footprints differ from the ALS value at their reported position by about 3 m RMSE, although both come from exactly the same points: the ~10 m geolocation error means each GEDI footprint sampled a partly different patch of forest. The crosses compare GEDI with a single 2 m CHM pixel at the footprint centre, which covers 4 m² of a 490 m² footprint and scatters more widely.

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
section: How geolocation error and footprint size matter
text:
How geolocation error and footprint size matter
The experiment below uses only the ALS data. For every footprint position it computes the ALS RH98 at the reported position and at positions shifted by random errors of 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 m (standard deviation per axis), for footprint diameters of 10, 25 and 50 m. The RMSE between shifted and unshifted RH98 shows how much scatter geolocation error alone produces, and how a larger footprint (which averages more of the canopy) dampens it.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)  # reproducible shifts
pos = np.c_[gutm.geometry.x, gutm.geometry.y]  # reported positions
rows = []  # one row per setting
for diam in (10, 25, 50):  # footprint diameters (m)
    ref = np.array([r[98] if (r := footprint_rh(x, y, diam / 2, 5)) is not None else np.nan for x, y in pos])  # unshifted
    for sigma in (0, 5, 10, 15, 20):  # geolocation error (m)
        shifted = pos + rng.normal(0, sigma, pos.shape)  # shifted positions
        val = np.array([r[98] if (r := footprint_rh(x, y, diam / 2, 5)) is not None else np.nan for x, y in shifted])  # RH98
        e = val - ref  # difference caused by the shift
        # result of this setting
        rows.append({"footprint diameter (m)": diam, "geolocation error σ (m)": sigma, "RMSE (m)": np.sqrt(np.nanmean(e ** 2))})
geo = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # results
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))  # one panel
for diam, g_ in geo.groupby("footprint diameter (m)"):  # each footprint size
    ax.plot(g_["geolocation error σ (m)"], g_["RMSE (m)"], "o-", label=f"{diam} m footprint")  # RMSE curve
ax.axvline(10, ls=":", c="grey"); ax.text(10.3, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, "GEDI ~10 m", fontsize=8)  # GEDI's error
# axis labels and title
ax.set(xlabel="geolocation error σ (m)", ylabel="RMSE of RH98 (m)", title="Height error caused by geolocation error alone")
ax.legend(); plt.show()  # draw
geo.pivot(index="geolocation error σ (m)", columns="footprint diameter (m)", values="RMSE (m)").round(2)  # table

At GEDI’s 10 m geolocation error, a 25 m footprint in this mixed forest changes its RH98 by about 4.5 m without any change in the forest. The error grows quickly up to about 10 m and then levels off: beyond that, the shifted footprint samples an essentially unrelated patch of forest. Small footprints are the most sensitive. A 50 m footprint helps only for small shifts here, because this forest varies at scales larger than 50 m (stands and clearings). This is why GEDI’s calibration against ALS uses simulated waveforms over a small search grid of positions, and why individual footprints should not be compared with individual trees or CHM pixels.

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
section: ICESat-2 ATL08 canopy and terrain heights
text:
ICESat-2 ATL08 canopy and terrain heights
rs.lidar.read_atl08 reads the 100 m land segments of each beam, converts fill values (3.4 × 10³⁸) to NaN and can keep only strong beams with strong_only=True, using the spacecraft orientation in orbit_info/sc_orient. The figure compares the segment canopy heights with the ALS CHM along the same track, and the segment terrain heights with the ALS DEM.


Code
atl = rs.lidar.read_atl08(ATL08_FILE, strong_only=True).to_crs(32615)  # strong-beam segments in UTM
print(atl.drop(columns="geometry").describe().loc[["count", "mean", "min", "max"]].round(2))  # summary
xt = float(atl.geometry.x.mean())  # track x position
prof = chm2.sel(x=xt, method="nearest")  # CHM column under the track
dem_prof = dem2.sel(x=xt, method="nearest")  # DEM column under the track
y_start = float(atl.geometry.y.min()) - 50  # start of the track

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(13, 6.5), sharex=True)  # two panels
axes[0].plot(prof.y - y_start, prof.values, color="grey", lw=0.7, label="ALS CHM along the track (2 m)")  # CHM profile
axes[0].step(atl.geometry.y - y_start, atl.h_canopy, where="mid", color="C2", lw=2, label="ATL08 h_canopy (100 m)")  # ATL08
# axis labels and title
axes[0].set(ylabel="canopy height (m)", title="ICESat-2-style canopy heights versus airborne LiDAR"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].plot(dem_prof.y - y_start, dem_prof.values, color="grey", lw=0.7, label="ALS DEM along the track")  # DEM profile
axes[1].plot(atl.geometry.y - y_start, atl.h_te_best_fit, "o", color="C1", label="ATL08 h_te_best_fit")  # terrain heights
# axis labels and title
axes[1].set(xlabel="distance along track (m)", ylabel="terrain height (m)"); axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


       h_canopy  h_te_best_fit  canopy_openness  night_flag
count     10.00          15.00             15.0        15.0
mean      20.45         107.34              3.0         1.0
min        6.20         104.36              3.0         1.0
max       28.63         112.40              3.0         1.0









The 100 m segments follow the large-scale pattern of the canopy, tall forest versus clearings, but smooth out every crown and gap within a segment. Segments over water or open ground have no canopy photons and carry the fill value (shown as gaps). Real ATL08 terrain heights are relative to the WGS 84 ellipsoid; here they were simulated from the orthometric ALS DEM, so the two agree by construction.

title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
text:
From footprints to a raster
rs.lidar.footprints_to_raster grids footprint values onto any raster template, averaging the footprints in each cell. On a 200 m grid the sparse GEDI tracks fill only some cells; the ALS mean p95 per 200 m cell from rs.lidar.grid_metrics gives the wall-to-wall reference. Producing a continuous map from footprints requires a model that relates them to wall-to-wall predictors (optical and radar images), as in GEDI’s L4B product and in the image fusion chapter.


Code
grid200 = rs.lidar.grid_metrics(pcn, res=200.0, metrics=("p95", "hmean"))  # ALS metrics on a 200 m grid
g_rh98 = rs.lidar.footprints_to_raster(gutm, "rh98", grid200["p95"], stat="mean")  # GEDI RH98 on the same grid
g_n = rs.lidar.footprints_to_raster(gutm, "rh98", grid200["p95"], stat="count")  # footprints per cell
both = np.isfinite(g_rh98.values) & np.isfinite(grid200["p95"].values)  # cells with both
# summary line
print(f"cells with at least one footprint: {int(np.isfinite(g_rh98.values).sum())} of {g_rh98.size} | "
      f"mean footprints per sampled cell {float(np.nanmean(g_n.values)):.1f} | "
      f"r(GEDI RH98, ALS p95) = {np.corrcoef(g_rh98.values[both], grid200['p95'].values[both])[0, 1]:.2f}")  # agreement

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(grid200["p95"], ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=30, title="ALS p95, 200 m cells")  # reference
rs.viz.plot_raster(g_rh98, ax=axes[1], cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=30, title="Mean GEDI RH98 per 200 m cell")  # gridded GEDI
for a in axes[:2]: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
axes[2].scatter(grid200["p95"].values[both], g_rh98.values[both], s=20)  # cell-level comparison
axes[2].plot([0, 30], [0, 30], "k--", lw=1)  # 1:1 line
# axis labels and title
axes[2].set(xlabel="ALS p95 (m)", ylabel="mean GEDI RH98 (m)", title="200 m cells: GEDI versus ALS")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


cells with at least one footprint: 30 of 72 | mean footprints per sampled cell 2.6 | r(GEDI RH98, ALS p95) = 0.78









Gridding reveals the other limit of spaceborne sampling. Only part of the 200 m cells contain a footprint, and those hold on average fewer than three, which together cover about 3 % of a 4 ha cell. Their mean is therefore a noisy estimate of the cell’s canopy (r about 0.78 with the ALS p95), worse than the footprint-level agreement: at this scale sparse sampling, not measurement error, dominates. RH98 is a top-of-canopy measure and sits above the ALS p95 of all returns, which includes the lower layers. Wall-to-wall maps therefore combine the footprints with image predictors rather than relying on footprint averages alone.
