title: Spaceborne LiDAR: GEDI and ICESat-2
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

GEDI records full waveforms in 25 m footprints along eight tracks between 51.6° N and S; L2A gives relative heights (RH98 ≈ canopy top), L2B canopy cover and profiles, L4A and L4B biomass.
ICESat-2 counts single green photons in 11 to 13 m footprints along six beams; ATL08 summarises them as terrain and canopy heights in 100 m segments.
Always filter: GEDI quality_flag, degrade_flag and sensitivity (≥ 0.9, higher in dense forest), full-power beams and night shots; ICESat-2 strong beams and night data.
Geolocation error (about 10 m for GEDI) alone causes metres of height scatter in heterogeneous forest; compare footprints with ALS metrics over the same footprint area, not single pixels. Gridded footprint means are limited by how few footprints fall in each cell.
Spaceborne heights are relative to the WGS 84 ellipsoid; check vertical datums before comparing ground elevations with national LiDAR.
Footprints are samples; wall-to-wall maps need gridding plus models with image predictors.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.lidar.read_las, rs.lidar.dem, rs.lidar.chm, rs.lidar.normalize_heights, rs.lidar.read_gedi_l2a, rs.lidar.read_atl08, rs.lidar.grid_metrics, rs.lidar.footprints_to_raster, rs.write, rs.viz.plot_raster; for real data rs.lidar.spaceborne.search, rs.lidar.read_gedi_l2b and rs.lidar.read_gedi_l4a.
Exercises

Read the GEDI file with min_sensitivity of 0.95 and 0.98. How many footprints remain on each beam?
Repeat the geolocation experiment with RH50 instead of RH98. Is the middle of the canopy more or less sensitive to position errors?
For each footprint, search shifts of up to 20 m in 2 m steps for the ALS RH98 closest to the GEDI RH98. What is the distribution of the best shifts, and how does it compare with the simulated 10 m error?
Grid the GEDI footprints at 100 m, 200 m and 500 m. How does the correlation with ALS change?
With an Earthdata login, download one real GEDI L2A granule that crosses your study area and read it with rs.lidar.read_gedi_l2a(path, bbox=...).

title: Texture Analysis
text: Banner

title: Texture Analysis
text:
Overview
Two land patches can have identical mean reflectance (e.g., a smooth lake and a rippled sand dune under the same lighting) yet look completely different because of how their pixel values vary spatially. Texture analysis extracts that difference as quantitative features usable for classification, segmentation, or change detection.
In satellite image analysis it’s especially valuable for: - Separating classes with overlapping spectral signatures (e.g., urban vs. bare soil, different crop types, forest stand types) - SAR imagery, where backscatter alone is noisy (speckle) but the spatial pattern of that speckle is informative (smooth water vs. rough forest canopy vs. textured urban fabric) - Characterizing surface roughness, canopy structure, building density, ice/snow surface type

Statistical Methods
The most widely used family. Based on the statistical distribution of gray-level (pixel intensity) values.
a) First-order statistics (no spatial relationship) Computed directly from the image histogram within a moving window — mean, variance, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, entropy. Fast but ignores where pixels sit relative to each other, so two very differently-patterned textures can give identical first-order stats.
b) Second-order statistics — Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM / Haralick texture) The workhorse of satellite texture analysis. A GLCM tabulates how often pairs of gray levels occur at a specified distance and direction (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°) within a moving window. From that matrix, Haralick (1973) derived features such as:







Feature
What it measures




Contrast
Local intensity variation (edges, roughness)


Correlation
Linear dependency between neighboring pixels


Energy / Angular Second Moment (ASM)
Uniformity — high for smooth, repetitive textures


Homogeneity (Inverse Difference Moment)
Closeness of the distribution to the diagonal


Entropy
Randomness/complexity of the texture


Dissimilarity
Average of absolute intensity differences


Variance
Spread of gray-level values



GLCM texture is heavily used with SAR imagery (e.g., distinguishing forest, cropland, and urban areas by backscatter texture) and in scikit-image’s graycomatrix/graycoprops, ENVI, SNAP, and Orfeo Toolbox.
c) Higher-order statistics - Gray-Level Run Length Matrix (GLRLM): measures runs of consecutive pixels with the same gray level in a given direction - good for directional/linear textures (e.g., furrowed fields, linear building rows). - Gray-Level Size Zone Matrix (GLSZM): measures connected zones of same-intensity pixels regardless of direction — captures texture coarseness/fineness.


Structural (Syntactic) Methods
Texture is treated as a set of primitive elements (texels) arranged according to placement rules - e.g., a regularly spaced row of houses or orchard trees. These methods detect repeating structural elements and their spatial arrangement rules, often via edge detection, morphological operations, or primitive-matching. Well suited to man-made, highly regular patterns (agricultural field rows, building grids) but fragile on natural, less-regular textures like vegetation canopy.


Transform-Based (Spectral) Methods
Texture is analyzed in a transformed domain where repetitive patterns show up as concentrated energy at specific frequencies/scales.

Fourier Transform: converts the image to the frequency domain; periodic textures (row crops, orchard grids) produce distinct peaks in the power spectrum. Sensitive to global periodicity but not localized texture changes.
Wavelet Transform: decomposes the image into multiple scales and orientations simultaneously (multi-resolution analysis), capturing both coarse and fine texture detail — useful because real-world textures (forest canopy, urban fabric) exist at multiple scales at once.
Gabor Filters: a bank of filters tuned to specific frequencies and orientations, modeling how texture varies directionally; widely used for crop row orientation, building facade detection, and as texture features ahead of classification (including as input channels to CNNs).



Model-Based Methods
Texture is assumed to follow a generative statistical/geometric model, and the model’s fitted parameters become the texture features.

Markov Random Fields (MRF): model a pixel’s value as statistically dependent on its neighbors; the fitted dependency parameters describe the texture. Commonly used in SAR/optical segmentation where spatial context regularizes noisy classification.
Fractal models: estimate a fractal dimension describing surface roughness/self-similarity across scales — useful for natural terrain (coastlines, mountain texture, forest canopy roughness) where regular GLCM features struggle.
Autoregressive (AR) models: express each pixel as a linear combination of its neighbors; the regression coefficients describe local texture.



Local Pattern-Based Methods

Local Binary Patterns (LBP): compares each pixel to its immediate neighbors, encoding the pattern as a binary code (brighter/darker than center), then builds a histogram of codes within a window. Computationally cheap, rotation-invariant variants exist, and it performs well for texture classification (e.g., urban building density, impervious surface detection) without needing GLCM’s directional windows.



Deep-Learning-Based Texture Features (modern approach)
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) learn hierarchical texture representations automatically from data rather than hand-crafted statistics. Lower CNN layers tend to capture edge/texture-like features similar to Gabor/LBP responses, while deeper layers capture more abstract structure. Increasingly used for land-cover classification, crop-type mapping, and SAR texture classification where hand-crafted GLCM features previously dominated — though GLCM/LBP features are still commonly fused with CNN features or used standalone for interpretability and lower compute cost.


Optical vs. SAR Texture - a key distinction

Optical imagery: texture mainly reflects true surface structure (canopy gaps, building shadows, field furrows) since the sensor measures reflected sunlight.
SAR imagery: backscatter texture is a mix of real surface roughness and speckle (a multiplicative noise artifact from coherent radar). This makes raw SAR pixel values noisy, but the texture statistics (GLCM contrast/homogeneity, local variance) of speckle patterns are themselves diagnostic — smooth water gives low-variance speckle, rough forest/urban areas give high-variance speckle — which is why GLCM-based texture is a standard companion to backscatter intensity in SAR land-cover classification (relevant to the RADARSAT/NISAR notebooks in this repo).



Common tools for implementing texture analysis

Python: scikit-image (graycomatrix/graycoprops for GLCM, local_binary_pattern for LBP), mahotas, pyradiomics
GIS/remote sensing software: ENVI (texture toolbox), SNAP (GLCM operator for SAR), Orfeo Toolbox (otbcli_HaralickTextureExtraction), Google Earth Engine (glcmTexture())
R: glcm package

Want me to add a worked texture-analysis example (e.g., GLCM on one of the SAR scenes already in this repo) as a notebook cell or a short standalone demo?

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Transform-Based (Spectral) Methods
text:
Overview
Transform- based methods make frequency, orientation and scale explicit by moving the image into another domain: the Fourier domain, a bank of Gabor filters, or a wavelet decomposition. This notebook explains the theory of the three transforms, computes them on the NIR band of a Landsat 9 scene over Las Vegas with geolattice.rsense.texture, maps the dominant orientation of the street grid and the mountain ridges, and tests what transform-based texture adds to spectral information.

Image texture in brief
Spectral values tell us what a pixel is made of; texture tells us how pixel values are arranged around it. Texture is the spatial variation of gray levels inside a neighbourhood and describes properties such as smoothness, coarseness, regularity, directionality and contrast. Haralick, Shanmugam and Dinstein (1973) noted that tone and texture are always present together in an image, but one may dominate the other depending on the scene.
At Landsat’s 30 m resolution many land-cover classes overlap spectrally: urban fabric, bare soil and rock are all bright and dry in an arid scene; crop types or forest stands can share the same NDVI; rough terrain mixes lit slopes and shadow within a few pixels. Texture separates such classes because it responds to pattern, not only to brightness, and texture layers are routinely stacked with bands and indices as predictors in land-cover classification, urban mapping, forest-structure modelling and soil mapping.
Methods are usually grouped into six families. This series covers them in five notebooks:



Notebook
Family
Methods




09_07_01
Statistical and structural texture
First-order statistics, GLCM, GLRLM, edge density, lacunarity


09_07_02
Transform-based (spectral) texture (this notebook)
Fourier power spectrum, Gabor filter bank, Haar wavelets


09_07_03
Local pattern-based texture
Local Binary Patterns (LBP)


09_07_04
Model-based texture
Markov Random Field energy, fractal dimension, autoregressive model


09_07_05
Deep-learning-based texture
Pretrained CNN feature maps



All methods come from geolattice.rsense.texture. Every function accepts a 2-D xr.DataArray (or NumPy array) and returns a georeferenced result with the same shape as the input; inputs with leading dimensions (band, time, polarization) are processed slice by slice, and multi-feature methods return an xr.Dataset with one variable per feature.


Theory: texture as frequency, orientation and scale
1. Fourier power spectrum. The 2-D discrete Fourier transform writes an \(M \times M\) tile \(g(x, y)\) as a sum of sinusoids:
\[F(u, v) = \sum_{x=0}^{M-1}\sum_{y=0}^{M-1} g(x, y)\, e^{-2\pi i (ux + vy)/M}.\]
The power spectrum \(|F(u,v)|^2\) tells how much variance the tile has at each spatial frequency \((u, v)\). The distance from the centre of the (centred) spectrum, \(\rho = \sqrt{u^2 + v^2}\), is the spatial frequency (fine patterns far from the centre, coarse patterns near it), and the angle \(\phi = \arctan(v/u)\) is the orientation of the pattern (perpendicular to the stripes). Summing the power in concentric rings gives a rotation-invariant description of coarseness (Rosenfeld and Troy 1970; Weszka, Dyer and Rosenfeld 1976):
\[E_k = \frac{\sum_{\rho \in \text{ring } k} |F|^2}{\sum |F|^2}.\]
Each tile is multiplied by a 2-D Hann window before the transform, to suppress the artificial edges created by cutting the tile out of the image (spectral leakage).
2. Gabor filters. A Gabor filter is a sinusoid of frequency \(f\) and orientation \(\theta\) under a Gaussian envelope (Gabor 1946; Daugman 1985):
\[h(x, y) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{x'^2 + y'^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\exp\!\left(2\pi i f x'\right),\qquad
x' = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta,\; y' = -x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta.\]
Convolving the image with \(h\) gives a complex response whose energy \(|g * h|^2\) is high where the image contains a pattern of that frequency and orientation. A bank of filters (several \(f\) and \(\theta\)) is a localized Fourier analysis: unlike the global spectrum of a tile, every pixel gets its own frequency-orientation description. Gabor filters resemble the receptive fields of simple cells in the mammalian visual cortex, which is one reason they work well for texture segmentation (Jain and Farrokhnia 1991).
3. Wavelets. The discrete wavelet transform (Mallat 1989) splits an image into an approximation and detail at successive scales. One level of the 2-D Haar transform takes each 2 × 2 block \(\{a, b; c, d\}\) and returns
\[LL = \tfrac{a+b+c+d}{2},\quad LH = \tfrac{a-b+c-d}{2},\quad HL = \tfrac{a+b-c-d}{2},\quad HH = \tfrac{a-b-c+d}{2},\]
each at half the resolution. LL is a smoothed image that feeds the next level; LH and HL hold detail along the two image axes and HH diagonal detail. Level 1 describes 30 m detail, level 2 60 m, level 3 120 m, and so on. The local energy of each subband is a scale- and orientation-specific texture feature.










Transform
Localization
Frequency resolution
Orientation
Cost




Fourier rings
One tile at a time
Fine (many rings)
Averaged out (rings)
Low (FFT)


Gabor bank
Every pixel
Few chosen frequencies
Explicit, chosen angles
Medium (one convolution per filter)


Haar wavelet
Every pixel
Octaves (×2 per level)
2 axes + diagonal
Very low





Applications








Application
Method
Why it works




Row-crop, orchard and vineyard mapping
Fourier rings, Gabor
Planting rows produce a sharp peak at one frequency and direction


Urban structure and building density
Gabor energy, wavelet detail
Street grids repeat at block-scale frequencies in two directions


Ocean waves and swell from SAR
Fourier spectrum
The wave spectrum gives wavelength and direction directly


Geological lineaments and fold belts
Oriented Gabor filters
Ridges, dykes and faults have a preferred strike


Sand-dune morphometry
Fourier spectrum
Dune spacing and crest orientation are spectral peaks


Forest canopy texture
Wavelet energy, Fourier
Crown size sets the dominant scale of variation


Multi-scale land-cover classification
Wavelet energy at several levels
Classes differ at different scales





Learning objectives

Explain how the Fourier power spectrum, Gabor filters and Haar wavelets describe frequency, orientation and scale.
Read a 2-D power spectrum and relate ring energy to texture coarseness.
Compute Fourier ring, Gabor and wavelet texture on Landsat NIR with geolattice.rsense.texture.
Map the dominant orientation and anisotropy of texture with a Gabor bank.
Compare transform-based texture signatures and test what they add to an unsupervised classification.

section: Loading the Landsat bands and the study window
text:
Loading the Landsat bands and the study window
The files hold raw Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (DN). We read them with rs.read, put them in one xr.Dataset, and convert them to surface reflectance with rs.optical.scale, which applies reflectance = DN × 0.0000275 − 0.2 and turns the fill value 0 into NaN.
Window-based texture is easier to see, and much faster to compute, on a smaller area. We work on a 512 × 512 pixel window (15.4 × 15.4 km) on the eastern edge of Las Vegas that contains four very different surfaces:

the regular street grid of the city (west),
the smooth, bare alluvial fan below Frenchman Mountain (centre),
the folded sedimentary ridges of Frenchman Mountain (east),
the vegetated channel of the Las Vegas Wash (south), red in colour infrared.



Code
# 1. Read each band as a 2-D DataArray (drop the singleton "band" dimension).
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/00_shared/data_remote_sensing/landsat9_vegas_20240708/LC09_L2SP_039035_20240708_02_T1")  # Landsat 9 scene, path 39 row 35, 8 July 2024
BANDS = ["blue", "green", "red", "nir"]  # the four bands used in this notebook
# read each band; masked=False keeps the raw digital numbers (DN)
ls_dn = xr.Dataset({b: rs.read(DATA / f"{b}.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)
                    for b in BANDS})  # one variable per band
ls_dn = ls_dn.rio.write_crs(ls_dn["red"].rio.crs)  # store the CRS on the Dataset as a whole

# 2. Scale DN to surface reflectance (fill value 0 becomes NaN) and clip to [1e-4, 1].
# Landsat Collection 2 scale and offset: DN -> reflectance
ls = rs.optical.scale(ls_dn, sensor="landsat").clip(min=1e-4, max=1.0)
# scene size, pixel size and CRS
print(f"{ls.rio.width} x {ls.rio.height} pixels at {ls.rio.resolution()[0]:.0f} m, CRS {ls.rio.crs}")

# 3. Study window (rows/columns in the full scene) and the NIR band used for most texture measures.
WIN = dict(y=slice(500, 1012), x=slice(900, 1412))  # 512 x 512 pixel window (rows 500-1011, columns 900-1411)
sub = ls.isel(WIN)  # all four bands inside the window
nir = sub["nir"]  # the NIR band of the window


1679 x 1512 pixels at 30 m, CRS EPSG:32611




Code
# Where the study window lies, and how it looks in natural colour and colour infrared.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5.5))  # three panels side by side
# full scene, red-green-blue
rs.viz.plot_rgb(ls, "true_color", ax=axes[0], title="Las Vegas, Landsat 9, 8 Jul 2024 (R, G, B)")
# the study window in yellow (x = column 900, y = row 500)
axes[0].add_patch(Rectangle((900, 500), 512, 512, fill=False, ec="yellow", lw=2))
# the window in natural colour
rs.viz.plot_rgb(sub, "true_color", ax=axes[1], title="Study window, natural colour")
# NIR, red, green: vegetation appears red
rs.viz.plot_rgb(sub, "false_color", ax=axes[2], title="Study window, colour infrared (NIR, R, G)")
for a in axes:  # hide the pixel ticks
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Transform-Based (Spectral) Methods
section: Fourier power spectrum and ring energy
text:
Fourier power spectrum and ring energy

Reading a power spectrum: synthetic stripes
Three synthetic 64 × 64 images with stripes of period 16, 8 and 4 pixels, and one with random noise. The spectrum of a stripe pattern is a pair of bright points; their distance from the centre grows as the period shrinks, and they lie on a line perpendicular to the stripes.


Code
# Synthetic textures and their Fourier power spectra.
yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:64, 0:64]  # row and column index of a 64 x 64 grid
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # random generator with a fixed seed
synth = {  # four test images
    "period 16, vertical stripes": np.sin(2 * np.pi * xx / 16),  # brightness varies along x only
    "period 8, diagonal stripes": np.sin(2 * np.pi * (xx + yy) / (8 * np.sqrt(2))),  # varies along x + y
    "period 4, horizontal stripes": np.sin(2 * np.pi * yy / 4),  # varies along y only, at a high frequency
    "random noise": rng.normal(size=(64, 64)),  # no structure at all
}
han = np.outer(np.hanning(64), np.hanning(64))  # 2-D Hann window: tapers the edges to avoid spectral leakage
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(16, 8))  # images (top) and spectra (bottom)
for k, (name, img) in enumerate(synth.items()):  # one column per image
    # power = |FFT|² of the tapered, mean-free image; fftshift puts frequency 0 in the centre
    spec = np.abs(np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft2((img - img.mean()) * han)))**2
    axes[0, k].imshow(img, cmap="gray"); axes[0, k].set_title(name, fontsize=10)  # the image
    # the spectrum on a log scale
    axes[1, k].imshow(np.log10(spec + 1e-6), cmap="magma"); axes[1, k].set_title("log10 power spectrum", fontsize=10)
for a in axes.ravel():  # no ticks
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









Each stripe pattern gives a pair of bright points in the spectrum, on a line perpendicular to the stripes. The period-16 points sit close to the centre; the period-4 points sit far out. Noise spreads its power over the whole spectrum.


Code
# Ring energy of the same images, computed with tx.fourier_texture (32 x 32 tiles, 6 rings).
# mean share of energy in each of 6 frequency rings, per image
ring_tab = pd.DataFrame({name: {k: float(np.nanmean(v)) for k, v in tx.fourier_texture(img, size=32, step=8, n_rings=6).items()}
                         for name, img in synth.items()})  # one column per synthetic image
ax = ring_tab.plot(kind="bar", figsize=(10, 4), rot=0)  # grouped bars: rings on x, one colour per image
ax.set(ylabel="Share of spectral energy", xlabel="Ring (0 = coarsest, 5 = finest)",  # axis labels
       title="Fourier ring energy of synthetic textures")  # and title
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
# show the table
ring_tab.round(3)

Period 16 (2 cycles per 32-pixel tile) falls entirely in ring0, period 8 (4 cycles) mostly in ring1 (the diagonal pattern leaks into ring0), and period 4 (8 cycles) in ring2. Noise spreads across all rings. The rings extend to the corners of the spectrum, beyond the highest frequency along the axes, so ring5 collects only the finest diagonal frequencies and always holds a small share.
Note that the energy fractions include the tile mean (the zero frequency), which always falls in ring0. On real imagery, where most variance is at low frequencies, ring0 therefore holds most of the energy, and the information is in how much energy spills into the outer rings.


Power spectra of real Landsat tiles


Code
# three 40 x 40 pixel sample boxes (rows, columns) in the study window
BOXES = {"Urban grid": (slice(100, 140), slice(40, 80)),
         "Alluvial fan": (slice(300, 340), slice(270, 310)),  # gravel slopes
         "Mountain ridges": (slice(130, 170), slice(400, 440))}  # rugged terrain
# one colour per box
COLORS = {"Urban grid": "#d7191c", "Alluvial fan": "#fdae61", "Mountain ridges": "#2b83ba"}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13, 8.5))  # NIR tiles (top) and their spectra (bottom)
han32 = np.outer(np.hanning(32), np.hanning(32))  # 32 x 32 Hann taper
for k, (name, (ys, xs)) in enumerate(BOXES.items()):  # one column per box
    # the central 32 x 32 pixels of the box
    tile = nir.values[ys.start + 4:ys.start + 36, xs.start + 4:xs.start + 36]
    # power spectrum of the tapered, mean-free tile
    spec = np.abs(np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft2((tile - tile.mean()) * han32)))**2
    axes[0, k].imshow(tile, cmap="gray"); axes[0, k].set_title(f"{name}: NIR, 32 x 32")  # the tile
    ls_ = np.log10(spec + 1e-12)  # log power
    # stretched between the 20th and 99.5th percentiles
    axes[1, k].imshow(ls_, cmap="magma", vmin=np.percentile(ls_, 20), vmax=np.percentile(ls_, 99.5))
    axes[1, k].set_title("log10 power spectrum (mean removed)")  # title
for a in axes.ravel():  # no ticks
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









The urban tile has a cross-shaped spectrum with power along both axes and far from the centre: the north-south and east-west streets repeat every few pixels. The ridge tile has power elongated along the horizontal frequency axis, perpendicular to its north-south ridges, with secondary peaks that mark the ridge spacing. The fan tile’s power is concentrated near the centre: its texture is coarse and weak.


Ring energy maps
tx.fourier_texture(img, size, step, n_rings) slides a size × size tile every step pixels, computes the Hann-windowed power spectrum and returns the share of energy in each of n_rings rings. Tiles of 32 × 32 pixels (960 m) resolve periods between 2 and 32 pixels.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
# 32 x 32 tiles every 4 pixels, energy share in 6 rings
four = tx.fourier_texture(nir, size=32, step=4, n_rings=6)
print(f"fourier_texture: {time.time() - t0:.1f} s ->", list(four.data_vars))  # run time and layer names

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(24, 4.3))  # six panels
for ax, f in zip(axes, four.data_vars):  # one panel per ring
    rs.viz.plot_raster(four[f], ax=ax, cmap="viridis", title=f"Fourier {f}")  # draw the ring energy
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


fourier_texture: 0.8 s -> ['ring0', 'ring1', 'ring2', 'ring3', 'ring4', 'ring5']









ring0 holds more than 99% of the energy on the fan and the ridges, against 97% in the city. The city moves energy into the outer rings: ring2 holds 0.73% of the energy in the urban box against about 0.06% on the fan and the ridges, more than ten times as much.


Code
# Tile size controls the trade-off between frequency resolution and spatial detail.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5))  # three tile sizes
for ax, s in zip(axes, [16, 32, 64]):  # 16, 32 and 64 pixels
    # step = one eighth of the tile, at least 2
    f = tx.fourier_texture(nir, size=s, step=max(2, s // 8), n_rings=6)
    outer = f["ring3"] + f["ring4"] + f["ring5"]  # energy in the three finest rings (fine texture)
    # on a log scale
    rs.viz.plot_raster(np.log10(outer + 1e-8), ax=ax, cmap="viridis", title=f"log10 energy in rings 3-5, tile {s} x {s}")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









16 × 16 tiles give sharp boundaries but noisy values and a coarse frequency resolution; 64 × 64 tiles give stable values but a blocky map in which the city-fan boundary is smeared over 2 km. 32 × 32 is a good compromise for Landsat.

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Transform-Based (Spectral) Methods
text:
Gabor filter bank

The filters
Below are the real parts of the 12 kernels used in this section: 3 frequencies × 4 orientations. Frequency is in cycles per pixel, so f = 0.1 is a 10-pixel (300 m) period, f = 0.25 a 4-pixel (120 m) period and f = 0.4 a 2.5-pixel (75 m) period. In scikit-image, the wave of a filter with θ = 0 runs along the x-axis, so it responds to vertical stripes (north-south streets); θ = 90 responds to horizontal stripes.


Code
from skimage.filters import gabor_kernel  # Gabor kernels from scikit-image
FREQS, THETAS = (0.1, 0.25, 0.4), (0, 45, 90, 135)  # 3 frequencies (cycles per pixel) x 4 orientations (degrees)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(11, 8.5))  # one panel per kernel
for i, f in enumerate(FREQS):  # rows: frequency
    for j, t in enumerate(THETAS):  # columns: orientation
        k = np.real(gabor_kernel(f, theta=np.radians(t)))  # real part of the complex kernel
        # show it with its parameters
        axes[i, j].imshow(k, cmap="RdBu_r"); axes[i, j].set_title(f"f = {f}, theta = {t}", fontsize=9)
        axes[i, j].set_xticks([]); axes[i, j].set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.suptitle("Real part of the Gabor kernels (kernel size shrinks as frequency rises)")  # overall title
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









tx.gabor_texture(img, frequencies, thetas, size) stretches the band to 0-1 (2nd-98th percentile), filters it with every (frequency, θ) pair, and pools the response energy in a size × size window. Each feature is named gabor_f<frequency>_t<theta>.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
# filter energy for every frequency and orientation, averaged in 9 x 9 windows
gab = tx.gabor_texture(nir, frequencies=FREQS, thetas=THETAS, size=9)
# run time and number of features (3 x 4 = 12)
print(f"gabor_texture: {time.time() - t0:.1f} s, {len(gab.data_vars)} features")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(18, 13))  # 3 x 4 panels
for ax, f in zip(axes.ravel(), gab.data_vars):  # one panel per filter
    rs.viz.plot_raster(gab[f], ax=ax, cmap="magma", title=f)  # draw the energy
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


gabor_texture: 1.3 s, 12 features









θ = 0 lights up the north-south streets and θ = 90 the east-west streets; θ = 45 and θ = 135 respond to the diagonal boulevard and the curving Wash. The low-frequency filters (f = 0.1, 300 m period) respond to block-sized patterns and to the broader ridges, which appear in θ = 0 and θ = 45; the high-frequency filters (f = 0.4, 75 m) respond almost only in the city. The fan is dark in every filter.

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Transform-Based (Spectral) Methods
text:
Haar wavelet decomposition

The subbands
First we look at the decomposition itself. tx._haar_step is the internal helper that performs one level of the orthonormal 2-D Haar transform; applying it twice gives the classic pyramid of subbands.


Code
a0 = np.nan_to_num(nir.values, nan=float(nir.mean()))  # the NIR window with NaN replaced by the mean
ll1, lh1, hl1, hh1 = tx._haar_step(a0)  # one Haar step: approximation and three detail bands at half resolution
ll2, lh2, hl2, hh2 = tx._haar_step(ll1)  # a second step on the approximation

def show(ax, a, t, cmap="gray"):  # helper: one panel with a 2-98 % stretch
    # stretch limits, then draw
    lo, hi = np.percentile(a, [2, 98]); ax.imshow(a, cmap=cmap, vmin=lo, vmax=hi); ax.set_title(t, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(17, 9))  # level 1 (top) and level 2 (bottom)
show(axes[0, 0], ll1, f"LL1 approximation {ll1.shape}")  # smoothed image at level 1
show(axes[0, 1], lh1, "LH1 detail (30 m)", "RdBu_r")  # horizontal detail
show(axes[0, 2], hl1, "HL1 detail (30 m)", "RdBu_r")  # vertical detail
show(axes[0, 3], hh1, "HH1 diagonal detail (30 m)", "RdBu_r")  # diagonal detail
show(axes[1, 0], ll2, f"LL2 approximation {ll2.shape}")  # level 2: approximation
show(axes[1, 1], lh2, "LH2 detail (60 m)", "RdBu_r")  # and its three details
show(axes[1, 2], hl2, "HL2 detail (60 m)", "RdBu_r")
show(axes[1, 3], hh2, "HH2 diagonal detail (60 m)", "RdBu_r")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

# Energy budget: the orthonormal transform preserves total energy.
# energy (sum of squares) of each part
e = {"LL2": (ll2**2).sum(), "detail L2": sum((b**2).sum() for b in (lh2, hl2, hh2)),
     "detail L1": sum((b**2).sum() for b in (lh1, hl1, hh1))}  # all level-1 details
tot = sum(e.values())  # total energy of all parts
# shares, and total over the image energy (1 = energy preserved)
print({k: f"{v / tot:.2%}" for k, v in e.items()}, "| total / image energy =", round(tot / (a0[:512, :512]**2).sum(), 6))









{'LL2': '98.23%', 'detail L2': '0.98%', 'detail L1': '0.79%'} | total / image energy = 1.0


LH (differences along rows) highlights north-south structures: north-south streets and the ridges. HL (differences along columns) highlights east-west streets. HH is high where both change, mostly in the city. Note that naming conventions for LH and HL differ between textbooks and libraries; check the orientation on your own data, as here.
The transform is orthonormal, so the total energy is preserved (ratio 1.0). Because the tile mean is in the approximation, 98% of the energy is in LL2 and only about 1.8% in the six detail subbands, and those 1.8% hold all the texture.
tx.wavelet_texture(img, level, size) returns the local mean energy of every detail subband, resampled to full resolution and pooled in a size × size window: LH_L1, HL_L1, HH_L1, LH_L2, …


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
wav = tx.wavelet_texture(nir, level=3, size=9)  # 3 levels; local energy of each detail band in 9 x 9 windows
print(f"wavelet_texture: {time.time() - t0:.2f} s ->", list(wav.data_vars))  # run time and layer names

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(15, 14))  # 3 x 3 panels: level (rows) by orientation (columns)
for ax, f in zip(axes.ravel(), wav.data_vars):  # one panel per layer
    rs.viz.plot_raster(np.log10(wav[f] + 1e-9), ax=ax, cmap="magma", title=f"log10 energy {f}")  # log energy
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # no ticks
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


wavelet_texture: 0.10 s -> ['LH_L1', 'HL_L1', 'HH_L1', 'LH_L2', 'HL_L2', 'HH_L2', 'LH_L3', 'HL_L3', 'HH_L3']









At level 1 the city has 5 to 10 times more detail energy than the fan and the ridges, and the LH/HL pair separates the two street directions. At level 2 (60 m) the folds of Frenchman Mountain appear in LH_L2, because the ridges are wider than one pixel. At level 3 (120 m) the maps become blobby and the contrast between surfaces weakens.

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Transform-Based (Spectral) Methods
text:
Application: orientation mapping
The four orientations of the Gabor bank can be combined into two maps for one frequency:

Dominant orientation: the θ with the highest energy.
Anisotropy: (max − min) / (max + min) of the energies across θ, from 0 (isotropic: equal energy in all directions) to 1 (all energy in one direction).

Orientation is meaningful only where texture is both strong and anisotropic, so the map is masked where energy or anisotropy is low.


Code
f = "0p25"  # use the f = 0.25 filters
# stack the four orientations along a new 'theta' dimension
E = xr.concat([gab[f"gabor_f{f}_t{t}"] for t in THETAS], dim="theta").assign_coords(theta=list(THETAS))
emax, emin = E.max("theta"), E.min("theta")  # strongest and weakest orientation response
aniso = (emax - emin) / (emax + emin + 1e-12)  # 0 = same in every direction, 1 = one direction only
dom = E.argmax("theta").astype(float)  # index of the strongest orientation (0-3)
# keep only strong (above median) and clearly oriented pixels
mask = (emax > float(emax.quantile(0.5))) & (aniso > 0.4)

from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap  # a four-colour map for the orientations
# red, green, blue, orange
ocmap = ListedColormap(["#e41a1c", "#4daf4a", "#377eb8", "#ff7f00"])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 6))  # three panels
rs.viz.plot_rgb(sub, "false_color", ax=axes[0], title="Colour infrared")  # reference image
rs.viz.plot_raster(aniso, ax=axes[1], cmap="viridis", title="Gabor anisotropy, f = 0.25")  # anisotropy
# dominant orientation where the mask is true
im = axes[2].imshow(dom.where(mask), cmap=ocmap, vmin=-0.5, vmax=3.5, interpolation="nearest")
cb = plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[2], ticks=range(4), fraction=0.046)  # colour bar with one tick per orientation
cb.ax.set_yticklabels(["0: N-S stripes", "45", "90: E-W stripes", "135"])  # label the ticks
axes[2].set_title("Dominant Gabor orientation (strong, anisotropic texture only)")  # title
for a in axes:  # no ticks
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw

# Share of masked pixels in each orientation, per box.
tab = {}  # orientation shares per box
for name, (ys, xs) in BOXES.items():  # loop over the boxes
    d = dom.where(mask).isel(y=ys, x=xs).values.ravel()  # orientations of the masked pixels in the box
    d = d[np.isfinite(d)].astype(int)  # drop unmasked pixels
    # share of each orientation
    tab[name] = {f"theta {t}": (d == k).mean() if d.size else np.nan for k, t in enumerate(THETAS)}
    tab[name]["oriented pixels"] = d.size / 1600  # share of the box's 1,600 pixels that are oriented
# show as percentages
pd.DataFrame(tab).map(lambda v: f"{v:.0%}")

On the ridges, 66% respond to θ = 0 and 34% to θ = 45, consistent with ridges that strike between north and north-east. Only 10% of the fan pixels pass the mask: the fan has little oriented texture. # three 40 x 40 pixel sample boxes (rows, columns) in the study window
BOXES = {"Urban grid": (slice(100, 140), slice(40, 80)),
         "Alluvial fan": (slice(300, 340), slice(270, 310)),  # gravel slopes east of the city
         "Mountain ridges": (slice(130, 170), slice(400, 440))}  # rugged terrain
# one colour per box
COLORS = {"Urban grid": "#d7191c", "Alluvial fan": "#fdae61", "Mountain ridges": "#2b83ba"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))  # one panel
# colour infrared background
rs.viz.plot_rgb(sub, "false_color", ax=ax, title="Sample boxes on the study window")
for name, (ys, xs) in BOXES.items():  # draw each box
    # x = column start, y = row start, then width and height
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((xs.start, ys.start), xs.stop - xs.start, ys.stop - ys.start,
                           # outline only, labelled for the legend
                           fill=False, ec=COLORS[name], lw=2.5, label=name))
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # legend, no ticks
plt.show()  # draw











Code
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans  # k-means clustering
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler  # standardise features to mean 0, std 1
from scipy.ndimage import generic_filter  # moving-window filter for the speckle measure

def box_means(ds):  # average feature values per sample box
    """Mean of every variable of `ds` inside each sample box."""
    # rows = features, columns = boxes
    return pd.DataFrame({name: {v: float(ds[v].isel(y=ys, x=xs).mean()) for v in ds.data_vars}
                         for name, (ys, xs) in BOXES.items()})

def plot_signatures(sig, title):  # compare the boxes feature by feature
    """Bar chart of box means, min-max scaled per feature across the three boxes."""
    # scale each feature to 0-1 across the three boxes
    norm = sig.sub(sig.min(axis=1), axis=0).div(sig.max(axis=1) - sig.min(axis=1), axis=0)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(max(7, 0.75 * len(norm)), 4.5))  # width grows with the number of features
    x = np.arange(len(norm))  # one group of bars per feature
    for k, name in enumerate(norm.columns):  # one bar per box, shifted sideways
        ax.bar(x + (k - 1) * 0.27, norm[name], width=0.27, color=COLORS[name], label=name)  # draw the bars
    ax.set_xticks(x, norm.index, rotation=45, ha="right")  # feature names, rotated
    ax.set(ylabel="Relative value (0 = lowest box, 1 = highest)", title=title)  # labels
    ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # legend and draw

def kmeans_map(ds, k=5, n_fit=40000, seed=0):  # unsupervised map from a set of layers
    """Standardize the layers, fit k-means on a random pixel sample and label every pixel."""
    df = ds.to_dataframe(dim_order=["y", "x"])[list(ds.data_vars)]  # pixels as rows, layers as columns
    ok = df.notna().all(axis=1).values  # pixels without missing values
    X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[ok].values)  # standardise so every layer weighs the same
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)  # random sample generator
    # fit on at most 40,000 random pixels (faster)
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=seed).fit(X[rng.choice(len(X), min(n_fit, len(X)), replace=False)])
    lab = np.full(ok.size, np.nan); lab[ok] = km.predict(X)  # label all valid pixels; others stay NaN
    # labels back on the image grid
    return xr.DataArray(lab.reshape(ds.sizes["y"], ds.sizes["x"]), coords={"y": ds.y, "x": ds.x}, dims=("y", "x"))

def speckle(lab):  # how noisy a cluster map is
    """Share of pixels whose label differs from the majority label of their 3 x 3 neighbourhood."""
    a = np.nan_to_num(lab.values, nan=-1).astype(int)  # NaN -> -1 so the labels are integers
    # majority label in each 3 x 3 window
    mode = generic_filter(a, lambda v: np.bincount(v.astype(int) + 1).argmax() - 1, size=3)
    return float((a != mode).mean())  # share of pixels that differ from their neighbourhood majority

def box_purity(lab):  # how uniform each box is in a cluster map
    """Share of each box's pixels that fall in the box's most common cluster."""
    out = {}  # one value per box
    for name, (ys, xs) in BOXES.items():  # loop over the boxes
        v = lab.isel(y=ys, x=xs).values.ravel()  # labels inside the box
        v = v[np.isfinite(v)].astype(int)  # drop missing labels
        out[name] = np.bincount(v).max() / v.size  # share of the most common label
    return out  # dictionary box -> purity

# Spectral layers used as the baseline in every notebook: the four bands and NDVI.
# normalised difference vegetation index
ndvi = ((sub["nir"] - sub["red"]) / (sub["nir"] + sub["red"])).rename("NDVI")
spectral = xr.Dataset({**{b: sub[b] for b in BANDS}, "NDVI": ndvi})  # four bands plus NDVI

# Correlation among the transform features.
tdf = tr_feats.to_dataframe()[list(tr_feats.data_vars)].dropna()  # pixels as rows, features as columns
# rank correlation is robust to the skewed energies
tc = tdf.corr(method="spearman")   # rank correlation: insensitive to the skewed energy values

Gabor energy at f = 0.25 and 0.4 and the level-1 wavelet energies form a tight group (ρ = 0.8 to 0.9): they all measure fine-scale roughness. Gabor anisotropy is independent of everything else.

Does this family add information? A clustering test
Texture is useful only if it carries information that the spectral bands do not. We run k-means with 5 clusters on (a) the four bands and NDVI only and (b) the same spectral layers plus this notebook’s texture features, all standardized. Two numbers summarize the maps:

Speckle: the share of pixels whose cluster differs from the majority of their 3 × 3 neighbourhood (lower = more spatially coherent).
Purity: the share of pixels in each sample box that fall in that box’s most common cluster (higher = the surface is mapped as one unit).



Code
def compare_clusterings(texture_ds, label):  # clustering with and without the texture layers
    """k-means on spectral layers only vs spectral + texture layers; maps, speckle and box purity."""
    k_spec = kmeans_map(spectral)  # five spectral layers
    k_both = kmeans_map(xr.merge([spectral, texture_ds], compat="override"))  # spectral plus texture layers
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 6))  # three panels
    rs.viz.plot_rgb(sub, "false_color", ax=axes[0], title="Colour infrared")  # reference image
    for ax, lab, t in zip(axes[1:], [k_spec, k_both],  # the two cluster maps with their titles
                          ["k-means, spectral only (5 layers)",
                           f"k-means, spectral + {label} ({5 + len(texture_ds.data_vars)} layers)"]):
        ax.imshow(lab, cmap="Set2", interpolation="nearest")  # one colour per cluster
        ax.set_title(f"{t}\nspeckle = {speckle(lab):.1%}")  # title with the speckle share
    for a in axes:  # no pixel ticks
        a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
    return pd.DataFrame({"spectral only": box_purity(k_spec),  # box purity of both maps, as percentages
                         # format each value as a percentage
                         f"spectral + {label}": box_purity(k_both)}).map(lambda v: f"{v:.0%}")

# Energies are heavy-tailed: cluster on their logarithms.
tr_km = tr_feats.copy()  # a copy used only for clustering
for v in tr_km.data_vars:  # every layer except anisotropy (already 0-1)
    if v not in ("Gabor anisotropy",):
        tr_km[v] = np.log10(tr_feats[v] + 1e-9)  # log energy; 1e-9 avoids log(0)
compare_clusterings(tr_km, "transform texture")  # maps, speckle and box purity

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Transform-Based (Spectral) Methods
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Transform-based methods describe texture by frequency (how fine), orientation (which way) and scale (at which resolution).
The Fourier spectrum of a tile shows the period and direction of repeating patterns; ring energy is a rotation-invariant summary of coarseness. Tile size trades frequency resolution against spatial detail.
A Gabor bank gives every pixel its own frequency-orientation description and can map the dominant direction of streets, ridges, crop rows or dunes.
Haar wavelets split detail into octaves of scale and three orientations at almost no computational cost; level 1 captures 30 m detail, level 2 60 m and level 3 120 m.
Most transform energies are strongly skewed; use their logarithms in statistics and models.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.read, rs.optical.scale, rs.viz.plot_rgb, rs.viz.plot_raster, tx.fourier_texture, tx.gabor_texture, tx.wavelet_texture.
Exercises

Add θ = 22.5°, 67.5°, 112.5° and 157.5° to the Gabor bank. Does the orientation map of the ridges become more precise?
Use tx.fourier_texture with 12 rings on 64 × 64 tiles and plot the mean ring spectrum of each sample box. At what period does the city peak?
Compute wavelet texture to level 4 (240 m). At which level do the city and the ridges differ most?
Repeat the orientation mapping on the red band. Are the dominant orientations the same?
Apply tx.gabor_texture to an agricultural Landsat scene with centre-pivot or row crops, and map the row direction of each field.

References

Daugman, J.G. (1985). Uncertainty relation for resolution in space, spatial frequency, and orientation optimized by two-dimensional visual cortical filters. JOSA A, 2(7), 1160-1169.
Gabor, D. (1946). Theory of communication. Journal of the IEE, 93(26), 429-457.
Jain, A.K. and Farrokhnia, F. (1991). Unsupervised texture segmentation using Gabor filters. Pattern Recognition, 24(12), 1167-1186.
Mallat, S.G. (1989). A theory for multiresolution signal decomposition: the wavelet representation. IEEE TPAMI, 11(7), 674-693.
Rosenfeld, A. and Troy, E.B. (1970). Visual texture analysis. Conference Record of the Symposium on Feature Extraction and Selection in Pattern Recognition, IEEE, 115-124.
Weszka, J.S., Dyer, C.R. and Rosenfeld, A. (1976). A comparative study of texture measures for terrain classification. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC-6(4), 269-285.

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Model-Based Methods
text:
Overview
A small number of parameters then summarizes the whole neighbourhood: how strongly a pixel depends on its neighbours, how rough the intensity surface is, how much variation the model cannot explain. This notebook covers three model families (Markov Random Fields, fractals and autoregressive models), explains their theory, computes them on the NIR band of a Landsat 9 scene over Las Vegas with geolattice.rsense.texture, and tests what they add to spectral information.

Image texture in brief
Spectral values tell us what a pixel is made of; texture tells us how pixel values are arranged around it. Texture is the spatial variation of gray levels inside a neighbourhood and describes properties such as smoothness, coarseness, regularity, directionality and contrast. Haralick, Shanmugam and Dinstein (1973) noted that tone and texture are always present together in an image, but one may dominate the other depending on the scene.
At Landsat’s 30 m resolution many land-cover classes overlap spectrally: urban fabric, bare soil and rock are all bright and dry in an arid scene; crop types or forest stands can share the same NDVI; rough terrain mixes lit slopes and shadow within a few pixels. Texture separates such classes because it responds to pattern, not only to brightness, and texture layers are routinely stacked with bands and indices as predictors in land-cover classification, urban mapping, forest-structure modelling and soil mapping.
Methods are usually grouped into six families. This series covers them in five notebooks:



Notebook
Family
Methods




09_07_01
Statistical and structural texture
First-order statistics, GLCM, GLRLM, edge density, lacunarity


09_07_02
Transform-based (spectral) texture
Fourier power spectrum, Gabor filter bank, Haar wavelets


09_07_03
Local pattern-based texture
Local Binary Patterns (LBP)


09_07_04
Model-based texture (this notebook)
Markov Random Field energy, fractal dimension, autoregressive model


09_07_05
Deep-learning-based texture
Pretrained CNN feature maps



All methods come from geolattice.rsense.texture. Every function accepts a 2-D xr.DataArray (or NumPy array) and returns a georeferenced result with the same shape as the input; inputs with leading dimensions (band, time, polarization) are processed slice by slice, and multi-feature methods return an xr.Dataset with one variable per feature.


Theory 1: Markov Random Fields
A Markov Random Field (MRF) models an image as a random field in which the value of a pixel depends only on its neighbours \(\mathcal{N}(s)\) (the Markov property):
\[P\big(g_s \mid g_{S\setminus s}\big) = P\big(g_s \mid g_{\mathcal{N}(s)}\big).\]
The Hammersley-Clifford theorem shows that such a field has a Gibbs distribution
\[P(g) = \frac{1}{Z}\exp\!\big(-U(g)/T\big),\qquad U(g) = \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} V_c(g),\]
where the energy \(U\) is a sum of potentials \(V_c\) over cliques (sets of mutually neighbouring pixels) and \(Z\) is a normalizing constant (Geman and Geman 1984; Cross and Jain 1983). With pair cliques and a quadratic potential (a Gaussian MRF, the continuous analogue of the Ising/Potts model) \(V_{\{s,t\}} = \beta\,(g_s - g_t)^2\). A low energy means the configuration is likely under a smoothness prior; a high energy means neighbours disagree.
Fitting a full MRF (estimating \(\beta\) for several neighbour directions) is expensive. tx.mrf_texture_energy uses the clique energy itself as the feature: the mean squared difference between a pixel and its 4 (first-order) or 8 (second-order) neighbours, averaged over a window. MRFs are the classic prior in unsupervised segmentation of SAR and optical images, where this energy is the quantity the segmentation tries to minimize.


Theory 2: Fractal dimension
Mandelbrot (1982) showed that many natural surfaces are self-similar: they look statistically alike at different magnifications. Pentland (1984) proposed treating an image’s intensity as a 3-D surface \(z = g(x, y)\) and measuring its fractal dimension \(D\). A smooth surface has \(D = 2\); the rougher and more space-filling it is, the closer \(D\) gets to 3. For fractional Brownian surfaces \(D = 3 - H\), where \(H\) is the Hurst exponent.
Differential box-counting (Sarkar and Chaudhuri 1994) estimates \(D\) for an \(M \times M\) tile. The tile is split into \(r \times r\) grid cells, and the intensity axis is scaled to the same range as the spatial axis, so it can be divided into boxes of height \(r\). In each cell the number of boxes needed to cover the surface from its minimum \(l\) to its maximum \(k\) is \(n_r = \lceil k/r \rceil - \lfloor l/r \rfloor + 1\). The total count \(N_r = \sum n_r\) follows a power law
\[N_r \propto r^{-D}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D = \text{slope of } \log N_r \text{ against } \log(1/r).\]


Theory 3: Autoregressive models
A simultaneous autoregressive (SAR) model expresses each pixel as a linear combination of its neighbours plus noise (Kashyap and Chellappa 1983; Mao and Jain 1992):
\[g_s - \mu = \sum_{t \in \mathcal{N}(s)} \theta_t\,(g_t - \mu) + \varepsilon_s,\qquad \varepsilon_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).\]
The coefficients \(\theta_t\) describe the strength and direction of spatial dependence, and \(\sigma^2\) the unexplained variation. tx.autoregressive_texture fits the isotropic one-parameter version \(g_s \approx \rho\,\bar g_{\mathcal{N}_4}(s)\) in every window by least squares:
\[\hat\rho = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}\big(g, \bar g_{\mathcal{N}_4}\big)}{\operatorname{Var}\big(\bar g_{\mathcal{N}_4}\big)},\qquad
\text{residual} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}\big(g - \hat\rho\,\bar g_{\mathcal{N}_4}\big)}{\operatorname{Var}(g)}.\]
Because the neighbour mean \(\bar g_{\mathcal{N}_4}\) averages four pixels, its variance is lower than the variance of \(g\) wherever pixels are only partly correlated, so \(\hat\rho\) is often slightly above 1 on real images. It is best read as a relative measure of spatial coherence; the residual measures how much of the local variation is not explained by the neighbours.


Applications

section: Loading the Landsat bands and the study window
text:
Loading the Landsat bands and the study window
The files hold raw Collection 2 Level-2 digital numbers (DN). We read them with rs.read, put them in one xr.Dataset, and convert them to surface reflectance with rs.optical.scale, which applies reflectance = DN × 0.0000275 − 0.2 and turns the fill value 0 into NaN.
Window-based texture is easier to see, and much faster to compute, on a smaller area. We work on a 512 × 512 pixel window (15.4 × 15.4 km) on the eastern edge of Las Vegas that contains four very different surfaces:

the regular street grid of the city (west),
the smooth, bare alluvial fan below Frenchman Mountain (centre),
the folded sedimentary ridges of Frenchman Mountain (east),
the vegetated channel of the Las Vegas Wash (south), red in colour infrared.



Code
# 1. Read each band as a 2-D DataArray (drop the singleton "band" dimension).
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/00_shared/data_remote_sensing/landsat9_vegas_20240708/LC09_L2SP_039035_20240708_02_T1")  # Landsat 9 scene, path 39 row 35, 8 July 2024
BANDS = ["blue", "green", "red", "nir"]  # the four bands used in this notebook
# read each band; masked=False keeps the raw digital numbers (DN)
ls_dn = xr.Dataset({b: rs.read(DATA / f"{b}.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)
                    for b in BANDS})  # one variable per band

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Model-Based Methods
text:
Markov Random Field energy

A toy check: smooth vs. noisy fields
Three synthetic fields with the same variance: a smooth (strongly correlated) field, a moderately correlated field and white noise. The clique energy rises as spatial dependence weakens.


Code
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter  # smoothing
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # random generator with a fixed seed
fields = {}  # three synthetic surfaces
# smoothing sigma per surface (0 = none)
for name, s in [("smooth (sigma = 6)", 6), ("moderate (sigma = 2)", 2), ("white noise", 0)]:
    f = rng.normal(size=(128, 128))  # white Gaussian noise
    f = gaussian_filter(f, s) if s else f  # smooth it unless sigma is 0
    fields[name] = (f - f.mean()) / f.std()  # standardise to mean 0, std 1

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.3))  # three panels
energy = {}  # mean MRF energy per surface
for ax, (name, f) in zip(axes, fields.items()):  # loop over the surfaces
    ax.imshow(f, cmap="gray"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])  # show the surface, no ticks
    # mean energy with 4 and 8 neighbours
    energy[name] = {f"{n}-neighbour energy": float(np.mean(tx.mrf_texture_energy(f, size=9, neighborhood=n))) for n in (4, 8)}
    # title with the 4-neighbour energy
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nenergy (4-nbr) = {energy[name]['4-neighbour energy']:.3f}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
# show the table
pd.DataFrame(energy).round(3)

Energy rises from 0.06 for the smooth field to 0.15 for the moderately correlated field and 1.99 for white noise.
For unit-variance white noise the expected squared difference between two independent pixels is 2, which is what the 4-neighbour energy returns. Correlated fields have much lower energy.


MRF energy of the Landsat window
tx.mrf_texture_energy(img, size, neighborhood) returns one layer: the mean clique energy in a size × size window, with a 4- or 8-pixel neighbourhood.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
# mean squared difference to the 4 nearest neighbours, in 9 x 9 windows
mrf4 = tx.mrf_texture_energy(nir, size=9, neighborhood=4)
mrf8 = tx.mrf_texture_energy(nir, size=9, neighborhood=8)  # the same with all 8 neighbours
print(f"mrf_texture_energy x2: {time.time() - t0:.2f} s")  # run time

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5))  # three panels
# log energy, 4 neighbours
rs.viz.plot_raster(np.log10(mrf4), ax=axes[0], cmap="magma", title="log10 MRF energy, 4-neighbour")
# log energy, 8 neighbours
rs.viz.plot_raster(np.log10(mrf8), ax=axes[1], cmap="magma", title="log10 MRF energy, 8-neighbour")
# ratio: how much the diagonal neighbours add
rs.viz.plot_raster(mrf8 / mrf4, ax=axes[2], cmap="RdBu_r", title="8-neighbour / 4-neighbour energy")
for a in axes:  # no ticks
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


mrf_texture_energy x2: 0.02 s









MRF energy is about seven times higher in the city than on the fan or the ridges (log10 −2.59 against −3.44 and −3.43), and the Wash stands out as a high-energy line. The 8/4 ratio lies between 1.28 and 1.33 in all three boxes: at 30 m every surface is spatially correlated, so diagonal neighbours are always less similar than direct ones.
Diagonal neighbours are √2 farther away than the four direct neighbours. On a spatially correlated surface they are therefore less similar to the centre, and the 8-neighbour energy is higher than the 4-neighbour energy (a ratio near 1.5 for the smooth toy fields). For independent pixels distance does not matter and the ratio is 1, as for the white-noise field.


Code

for ax, s in zip(axes, [3, 9, 21]):  # 3, 9 and 21 pixels

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Model-Based Methods
text:
Fractal dimension

Differential box-counting step by step
We implement the box count for one 32 × 32 tile in each sample box and fit the log-log line. This is the same calculation tx.fractal_dimension performs for every tile.


Code
def dbc_counts(tile, box_sizes=(2, 4, 8, 16)):  # differential box counting on a square tile
    """Differential box-counting: total box count N_r for each box size r."""
    size = tile.shape[0]  # tile side in pixels
    t = (tile - tile.min()) / max(tile.max() - tile.min(), 1e-9) * size   # intensity scaled to the grid size
    counts = []  # N_r for each box size
    for r in box_sizes:  # loop over box sizes
        n = size // r  # boxes per side
        cells = t[:n * r, :n * r].reshape(n, r, n, r)  # split the tile into n x n blocks of r x r pixels
        lo, hi = cells.min(axis=(1, 3)), cells.max(axis=(1, 3))  # lowest and highest intensity in each block
        # boxes of height r needed to cover the intensity range of each block, summed
        counts.append(np.sum(np.ceil(hi / r) - np.floor(lo / r) + 1))
    return np.array(counts, float)  # N_r as floats

r = np.array([2, 4, 8, 16])  # box sizes
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 4.3))  # three tiles and the fit plot
for k, (name, (ys, xs)) in enumerate(BOXES.items()):  # one tile per sample box
    # the central 32 x 32 pixels of the box
    tile = nir.values[ys.start + 4:ys.start + 36, xs.start + 4:xs.start + 36]
    N = dbc_counts(tile)  # box counts
    D, b = np.polyfit(np.log(1 / r), np.log(N), 1)  # slope of log N_r against log(1/r) = fractal dimension D
    axes[k].imshow(tile, cmap="gray"); axes[k].set_title(f"{name}: D = {D:.3f}")  # the tile with its D
    axes[k].set_xticks([]); axes[k].set_yticks([])  # no ticks
    axes[3].plot(np.log(1 / r), np.log(N), "o", color=COLORS[name])  # the counts
    # the fitted line
    axes[3].plot(np.log(1 / r), D * np.log(1 / r) + b, "-", color=COLORS[name], label=f"{name} (D = {D:.3f})")
axes[3].set(xlabel="log(1 / r)", ylabel="log N_r", title="Box-counting fits")  # labels
axes[3].legend(fontsize=8)  # legend
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw









The log-log points lie almost on straight lines, as the power law predicts. The urban tile is the roughest (D = 2.24), and the fan and ridge tiles are nearly equal (2.16). The lines are close together: fractal dimension differences between surfaces are small at this resolution.


Code
# Fractal dimension of synthetic fractional Brownian-like surfaces with known roughness.
def fbm_surface(h, n=256, seed=0):  # a random surface whose roughness is set by h
    """Spectral synthesis of a fractional Brownian surface with Hurst exponent h (D = 3 - h)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)  # random generator
    # squared spatial frequency of every FFT cell
    k = np.fft.fftfreq(n)[:, None] ** 2 + np.fft.fftfreq(n)[None, :] ** 2
    k[0, 0] = 1  # avoid dividing by zero at frequency 0
    amp = k ** (-(h + 1) / 2)  # amplitude falls with frequency as a power law
    phase = np.exp(2j * np.pi * rng.random((n, n)))  # random phases
    return np.real(np.fft.ifft2(amp * phase))  # inverse FFT gives the surface

rows = []  # one row per Hurst exponent
for h in [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]:  # rough (0.2) to smooth (0.8)
    s = fbm_surface(h)  # the surface
    fd_s = tx.fractal_dimension(s, size=32, step=16)  # D in 32 x 32 tiles every 16 pixels
    # theoretical vs estimated D
    rows.append({"Hurst H": h, "theoretical D = 3 - H": 3 - h, "estimated D (median)": float(np.nanmedian(fd_s))})
# show the table
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)

Box-counting with only four box sizes on 32 × 32 tiles is strongly biased: all three estimates lie between 2.03 and 2.18, far below the theoretical 2.2 to 2.8. The ranking is still correct, and rougher surfaces always get a higher estimate. This is how fractal dimension should be used in practice: as a relative measure of roughness, compared only between estimates made with the same tile and box sizes.


Fractal dimension map
tx.fractal_dimension(img, size, step, box_sizes) estimates D in a size × size tile every step pixels. All box sizes must divide the tile size evenly.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
fd = tx.fractal_dimension(nir, size=32, step=4, box_sizes=(2, 4, 8, 16))  # 32 x 32 tiles every 4 pixels
# 64 x 64 tiles every 8 pixels, one more box size
fd64 = tx.fractal_dimension(nir, size=64, step=8, box_sizes=(2, 4, 8, 16, 32))

# spread of D over the window

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.5))  # two panels
# 32-pixel tiles
rs.viz.plot_raster(fd, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", title="Fractal dimension, 32 x 32 tiles (960 m)")
# 64-pixel tiles

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Model-Based Methods
text:
Autoregressive texture

The model in each sample box
For each box we plot every pixel against the mean of its 4 neighbours and fit the regression line. The slope is ρ and the scatter around the line is the residual.


Code
a = nir.fillna(float(nir.mean())).values  # NIR as an array, NaN -> mean
# mean of the four neighbours (np.roll shifts the image by one pixel)
nbr = (np.roll(a, 1, 0) + np.roll(a, -1, 0) + np.roll(a, 1, 1) + np.roll(a, -1, 1)) / 4

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.5), sharex=False)  # one scatter plot per box
rows = {}  # AR parameters per box
for ax, (name, (ys, xs)) in zip(axes, BOXES.items()):  # loop over the boxes
    x_, y_ = nbr[ys, xs].ravel(), a[ys, xs].ravel()  # neighbour mean (x) and pixel value (y)
    rho = np.cov(y_, x_)[0, 1] / np.var(x_, ddof=1)  # least-squares slope: the AR coefficient
    # share of the variance the model does not explain
    resid = np.var((y_ - y_.mean()) - rho * (x_ - x_.mean())) / np.var(y_)
    # store rho, residual share and correlation
    rows[name] = {"rho": rho, "residual share": resid, "corr(pixel, nbr mean)": np.corrcoef(x_, y_)[0, 1]}
    ax.scatter(x_, y_, s=3, alpha=0.4, color=COLORS[name])  # pixel against neighbour mean
    xx = np.linspace(x_.min(), x_.max(), 2)  # two x values to draw the line
    ax.plot(xx, y_.mean() + rho * (xx - x_.mean()), "k-")  # the fitted line
    ax.set(xlabel="Mean of 4 neighbours", ylabel="Pixel", title=f"{name}: rho = {rho:.2f}")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw
# show the table
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)

The ridges are the most coherent surface: a pixel is almost fully predicted by its neighbours (correlation 0.975, residual share 5%). The fan follows (0.96, 8%), and the city is the least coherent (0.92, 15%). ρ is above 1 in all three boxes (1.04 to 1.14), as explained in the theory section.
tx.autoregressive_texture(img, size) computes ρ and the residual share in every size × size window with box filters (closed form, no loop), so it is fast even on large images.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
ar = tx.autoregressive_texture(nir, size=9)  # rho and residual share in 9 x 9 windows
ar15 = tx.autoregressive_texture(nir, size=15)  # the same in 15 x 15 windows
print(f"autoregressive_texture x2: {time.time() - t0:.2f} s ->", list(ar.data_vars))  # run time and layer names

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 11))  # 2 x 2 panels
rs.viz.plot_raster(ar["rho"], ax=axes[0, 0], cmap="RdYlBu_r", title="AR rho, 9 x 9")  # rho, 9 x 9
# residual share, 9 x 9
rs.viz.plot_raster(ar["residual"], ax=axes[0, 1], cmap="magma", title="AR residual share, 9 x 9")
rs.viz.plot_raster(ar15["rho"], ax=axes[1, 0], cmap="RdYlBu_r", title="AR rho, 15 x 15")  # rho, 15 x 15
# residual share, 15 x 15
rs.viz.plot_raster(ar15["residual"], ax=axes[1, 1], cmap="magma", title="AR residual share, 15 x 15")
for a_ in axes.ravel():  # no ticks
    a_.set_xticks([]); a_.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # arrange and draw


autoregressive_texture x2: 0.09 s -> ['rho', 'residual']









ρ is highest on block-sized city patches and lowest along sharp ridge lines. The residual is high where the simple model fails: isolated bright roofs, the edges of the Wash and the city blocks. A larger window (15 × 15) gives smoother, lower residuals, because more pixels average out local surprises.

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Model-Based Methods
section: Model-based texture of the full scene
text:
Model-based texture of the full scene
MRF energy and the AR model use box filters and run on the whole 1,679 × 1,512 scene in about a second. Fractal dimension loops over tiles; with 32 × 32 tiles every 8 pixels the full scene takes about 20 seconds.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
mrf_full = tx.mrf_texture_energy(ls["nir"], size=9)  # MRF energy of the whole scene
fd_full = tx.fractal_dimension(ls["nir"], size=32, step=8)  # fractal dimension of the whole scene
ar_full = tx.autoregressive_texture(ls["nir"], size=9)  # autoregressive texture of the whole scene
print(f"Full scene, three model-based measures: {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")  # run time

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(20, 6))  # three panels
# log MRF energy
rs.viz.plot_raster(np.log10(mrf_full), ax=axes[0], cmap="magma", title="log10 MRF energy (9x9)")
# fractal dimension
rs.viz.plot_raster(fd_full, ax=axes[1], cmap="viridis", title="Fractal dimension (32x32 tiles)")
# AR residual share
rs.viz.plot_raster(ar_full["residual"], ax=axes[2], cmap="magma", title="AR residual share (9x9)")
for a_ in axes:  # for each panel:
    a_.add_patch(Rectangle((900, 500), 512, 512, fill=False, ec="cyan", lw=1.5))  # mark the study window
    a_.set_xticks([]); a_.set_yticks([])  # no ticks

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans  # k-means clustering
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler  # standardise features to mean 0, std 1
from scipy.ndimage import generic_filter  # moving-window filter for the speckle measure

def box_means(ds):  # average feature values per sample box
    """Mean of every variable of `ds` inside each sample box."""
    # rows = features, columns = boxes
    return pd.DataFrame({name: {v: float(ds[v].isel(y=ys, x=xs).mean()) for v in ds.data_vars}
                         for name, (ys, xs) in BOXES.items()})

def plot_signatures(sig, title):  # compare the boxes feature by feature
    """Bar chart of box means, min-max scaled per feature across the three boxes."""
    # scale each feature to 0-1 across the three boxes
    norm = sig.sub(sig.min(axis=1), axis=0).div(sig.max(axis=1) - sig.min(axis=1), axis=0)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(max(7, 0.75 * len(norm)), 4.5))  # width grows with the number of features
    x = np.arange(len(norm))  # one group of bars per feature
    for k, name in enumerate(norm.columns):  # one bar per box, shifted sideways
        ax.bar(x + (k - 1) * 0.27, norm[name], width=0.27, color=COLORS[name], label=name)  # draw the bars
    ax.set_xticks(x, norm.index, rotation=45, ha="right")  # feature names, rotated
    ax.set(ylabel="Relative value (0 = lowest box, 1 = highest)", title=title)  # labels
    ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # legend and draw

def kmeans_map(ds, k=5, n_fit=40000, seed=0):  # unsupervised map from a set of layers
    """Standardize the layers, fit k-means on a random pixel sample and label every pixel."""
    df = ds.to_dataframe(dim_order=["y", "x"])[list(ds.data_vars)]  # pixels as rows, layers as columns
    ok = df.notna().all(axis=1).values  # pixels without missing values
    X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[ok].values)  # standardise so every layer weighs the same
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)  # random sample generator
    # fit on at most 40,000 random pixels (faster)
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=seed).fit(X[rng.choice(len(X), min(n_fit, len(X)), replace=False)])
    lab = np.full(ok.size, np.nan); lab[ok] = km.predict(X)  # label all valid pixels; others stay NaN
    # labels back on the image grid
    return xr.DataArray(lab.reshape(ds.sizes["y"], ds.sizes["x"]), coords={"y": ds.y, "x": ds.x}, dims=("y", "x"))

def speckle(lab):  # how noisy a cluster map is
    """Share of pixels whose label differs from the majority label of their 3 x 3 neighbourhood."""
    a = np.nan_to_num(lab.values, nan=-1).astype(int)  # NaN -> -1 so the labels are integers
    # majority label in each 3 x 3 window
    mode = generic_filter(a, lambda v: np.bincount(v.astype(int) + 1).argmax() - 1, size=3)
    return float((a != mode).mean())  # share of pixels that differ from their neighbourhood majority

def box_purity(lab):  # how uniform each box is in a cluster map
    """Share of each box's pixels that fall in the box's most common cluster."""
    out = {}  # one value per box
    for name, (ys, xs) in BOXES.items():  # loop over the boxes
        v = lab.isel(y=ys, x=xs).values.ravel()  # labels inside the box
        v = v[np.isfinite(v)].astype(int)  # drop missing labels
        out[name] = np.bincount(v).max() / v.size  # share of the most common label
    return out  # dictionary box -> purity

# Spectral layers used as the baseline in every notebook: the four bands and NDVI.
# normalised difference vegetation index

Does this family add information? A clustering test

title: Texture Analysis of Landsat Imagery: Model-Based Methods
text:
Summary and exercises
Key points

Model-based texture fits a spatial stochastic model and uses its parameters as features.
MRF clique energy measures how strongly neighbours disagree under a smoothness prior; white noise of unit variance has energy 2, correlated surfaces much less.
Fractal dimension measures the roughness of the intensity surface. Box-counting estimates are biased but rank surfaces correctly, so use D as a relative measure.
The AR coefficient ρ measures spatial coherence and the residual share the variation the neighbours cannot explain. ρ slightly above 1 is expected for partly correlated images.
MRF energy and the AR model run on full scenes in about a second, which makes them practical predictors for large-area mapping.

geolattice.rsense functions used: rs.read, rs.optical.scale, rs.viz.plot_rgb, rs.viz.plot_raster, tx.mrf_texture_energy, tx.fractal_dimension, tx.autoregressive_texture.
Exercises

Use more box sizes (2, 4, 8, 16, 32) on 64 × 64 tiles for the synthetic fBm surfaces. Does the estimate get closer to the theoretical D?
Compute MRF energy on NDVI. Which surfaces have the most “texture” in vegetation rather than in brightness?
Extend the AR model to separate horizontal and vertical neighbours (two coefficients). Do the two coefficients differ on the ridges?
Apply the three measures to a Sentinel-1 VV backscatter image in dB. How does speckle affect each one?
Compare the fractal dimension map with a slope map from a DEM of the same area.

References

Geman, S. and Geman, D. (1984). Stochastic relaxation, Gibbs distributions, and the Bayesian restoration of images. IEEE TPAMI, 6(6), 721-741.

title: Image Super-Resolution
text:
Overview
Super-resolution estimates a finer image that is consistent with that coarse observation. The estimate is useful for mapping, and it is under-determined: many different fine images degrade to the same coarse one. This notebook is the map of the subject. It sets out the observation model, the families of methods, the applications, and the shift since about 2021 toward transformers, realistic degradations and diffusion models. The next notebook runs the methods on Landsat 9 and Sentinel-2.
It assumes the optical introduction: ground sampling distance, mixed pixels, and the difference between Landsat and Sentinel-2. No deep-learning library is required here. The hands-on section uses a synthetic 10 m scene so that the true fine image is known.

title: Image Super-Resolution
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Write the blur-downsample-noise model and explain why super-resolution is ill-posed.
Separate interpolation, pan-sharpening, spatiotemporal fusion, multi-frame super-resolution and single-image super-resolution by the extra information each one uses.
Relate classical reconstruction, pansharpening and fusion methods to the deep-learning families that replaced their hand-designed priors.
Name the constraints that dominate remote sensing: spectral fidelity, bandpass differences, the real point-spread function, co-registration and land-cover change.
Match applications to methods, including the failure mode in each application.
Describe recent practice: attention, diffusion, blind degradation, learning without a fine twin, and evaluation that follows the decision the image will support.
Show, on a synthetic scene, that a better interpolator is only a small gain, and that a high-frequency pattern can be almost invisible at 30 m.



Contents

Why spatial resolution runs out
The observation model
Families of methods
Classical methods
Deep learning

title: Image Super-Resolution
text:
Why spatial resolution runs out
The ground sampling distance (GSD) is fixed by detector size, focal length and orbit height, and by how much data the satellite can store and downlink. A finer GSD narrows the swath or shortens the time the detector can collect light. The long, free, frequent records are therefore the coarser ones: MODIS at 250-500 m, Landsat at 30 m since the 1980s, Sentinel-2 at 10, 20 and 60 m since 2015. Commercial satellites resolve 0.3-1 m and cover much less ground, at a cost, and with a short archive.
Three consequences follow for anyone analysing a landscape.

Mixed pixels. A pixel reports the average of everything inside its footprint, weighted by the point-spread function. A 20 m road in a 30 m pixel shifts the spectrum. It does not appear as a road.
The archive is coarse where the record is long. Questions about the 1990s have Landsat, not Sentinel-2. Questions about a cloudy week may have only one clear Landsat scene and several cloudy Sentinel-2 scenes.
Finer pixels are a means. The usual goal is a boundary, an area, an index or a detection. A sharper picture that changes those numbers for the worse is a failed product.

Super-resolution is one way to spend extra information on a finer grid: a sharper band from the same satellite, a finer image from another date, several frames shifted by a fraction of a pixel, or a prior learned from many scenes. It does not repeal the sensor. Structure that the point-spread function averaged away is estimated, and the estimate has to be checked against the decision it will feed.
The Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 product goes the other direction. It matches the two sensors on a common 30 m grid (Claverie et al., 2018). Super-resolution asks for a 10 m grid instead. Harmonization is still required, because the band filters are not the same.

title: Image Super-Resolution
text:
The observation model
For one band, the usual linear model is
\[\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{D}\,\mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{n}.\]
\(\mathbf{x}\) is the fine image we want, \(\mathbf{B}\) applies the point-spread function (optical blur, motion, the detector footprint), \(\mathbf{D}\) samples that blurred image onto the coarse grid, and \(\mathbf{n}\) is noise. In signal-processing notation,
\[\mathbf{y} = (\mathbf{x} * k) \downarrow_{s} + \mathbf{n},\]
where \(k\) is the blur kernel and \(s\) is the scale factor,
\[s = \frac{\mathrm{GSD}_{\mathrm{coarse}}}{\mathrm{GSD}_{\mathrm{fine}}}.\]









Task
Coarse input
Source of finer detail
Scale \(s\)




Landsat multispectral to a Sentinel-2 10 m grid
30 m
Sentinel-2, or a learned prior
3


Landsat pan-sharpening
30 m multispectral
15 m panchromatic band
2


Sentinel-2 20 m bands
20 m
the 10 m bands of the same scene
2

250-500 m

Commercial pan-sharpening

0.3-0.5 m panchromatic
about 4



The same equation is why the problem is ill-posed. \(\mathbf{D}\mathbf{B}\) has a null space. Any pattern that the blur and the sampler average to zero can be added to \(\mathbf{x}\) without changing \(\mathbf{y}\). Inside one coarse pixel, many arrangements of materials share the same average. The Hands-on: a 10 m scene observed at 30 m section builds a pattern of amplitude 0.05 in reflectance that changes the 10 m image by RMSE 0.040 and the 30 m image by RMSE 0.0015.
Something outside \(\mathbf{y}\) has to choose among those explanations:

a sharper image of the same place and time (a panchromatic band, or the 10 m Sentinel-2 bands),
the same place at another time, together with a model of what changed,
repeated looks shifted by a fraction of a pixel,
a prior: edges are sparse, neighbouring pixels in a field share a spectrum, or a network trained on many scenes.

A prior that is wrong produces detail that is plausible and false. In this literature that failure is called hallucination. A road painted in by a generative model where the coarse pixels do not support a road is a hallucination. For a basemap it may be acceptable. For a burned-area or a crop-area number it is not.
The point-spread function is the part practitioners most often get wrong. Computer-vision benchmarks degrade images with bicubic downsampling. A pushbroom satellite is closer to a Gaussian or a measured optical model, followed by the detector integrating over its footprint. A network trained on bicubic blur learns to invert bicubic blur. Applied to Landsat, it leaves real blur in place, or it invents texture to compensate for a kernel it does not have. Estimating \(k\) from the imagery, or training with a kernel close to \(k\), matters as much as the choice of network.

title: Image Super-Resolution
text:
Families of methods
The families differ by what they are allowed to look at, besides the coarse image.









Family
Extra information
What it can recover
Typical remote-sensing use




Interpolation
None
A smooth resampling of the samples already in \(\mathbf{y}\)

Texture and edges that are typical of the training images
A date with no finer reference


Pan-sharpening
A panchromatic band at finer GSD, same time
Real edges, where the pan band sees them
Landsat 15 m, commercial 0.3-0.5 m products


Guided super-resolution

Sentinel-2 20 m and 60 m bands


Spatiotemporal fusion

Multi-frame super-resolution
