Reading the CDL change.

About 76 to 82 % of the pixels change class every year, and almost all of it is the corn ↔︎ soybean rotation (73 to 77 %). The rotation is real, planned and annual: for most applications (yield statistics, nitrogen) it is the change of interest; for land-cover change (cropland lost to development, grassland converted to crops) it is “no change”.
Other change is 2 to 6 % per year, and in 2024 → 2025 92 % of it lies on a field edge (a pixel touching another class): mixed 30 m pixels and slightly different field boundaries in the two years, not land conversion. Only 0.4 % of the pixels show other change inside a field. The 2023 → 2024 and 2024 → 2025 pairs have about twice as much other change as earlier pairs, possibly a change in the CDL production (a 10 m CDL is available from 2024 on).
Sequences: 80 % of the crop pixels follow a strict alternation in 2023 to 2025 (CSC or SCS); 8 % stay corn (corn on corn is a real practice); the rare SSC, CSS and SSS patterns are partly real decisions and partly label noise.
From here on we report every score on all valid pixels and on interior pixels (no class boundary in either year, 70 % of the pixels), where the CDL change is much more reliable.

title: Change Detection: Classical, Post-Classification and Deep Methods on Landsat and Sentinel-2, 2020 to 2025
section: Deep change detection: Siamese, early-fusion and transformer networks
text:
Deep change detection: Siamese, early-fusion and transformer networks
build_change_model(arch, in_channels, num_classes) returns a network with forward(t1, t2) → per-pixel change logits:

Early-fusion U-Net (FC-EF, Daudt et al., 2018): the two images are concatenated as \(2C\) input channels and a single U-Net predicts change. Simple, but the network must learn on its own which channels belong to which date.
Siamese-difference U-Net (FC-Siam-diff): a shared encoder \(f_\theta\) processes each date; the decoder receives the absolute difference of the features at every scale, \(\lvert f_\theta^{(l)}(\mathbf x_1)-f_\theta^{(l)}(\mathbf x_2)\rvert\). Weight sharing makes the two dates comparable by construction.
Siamese-concatenation U-Net (FC-Siam-conc): the same shared encoder, but the features of both dates are concatenated, \([f^{(l)}(\mathbf x_1);f^{(l)}(\mathbf x_2)]\), so the decoder can learn asymmetric (from-to) changes.
BIT-style transformer (after Chen et al., 2021): a shared CNN extracts features; spatial attention compresses each date into a few semantic tokens, \(T=\mathrm{softmax}(A(f))\,f^\top\); a transformer encoder models the joint context of the tokens of both dates; a transformer decoder projects the tokens back onto the pixels, and the absolute difference of the refined features is classified.

PairChipDataset(before, after, masks, normalizer=, transform=) yields {"image": (t1, t2), "mask": change}; the transform (OverheadAugment, dihedral rotations and flips) is applied identically to both dates and the mask. Training uses train_model(task="segmentation") with cross-entropy, ignore_index=-100 for pixels without a reference, and early stopping on the 2023 → 2024 validation pair.
The networks are trained on Sentinel-2 pairs of earlier years, reduced to the six Landsat-equivalent bands, so they can also be applied to the Landsat test pair. The normaliser is fitted on the Sentinel-2 images of 2020 to 2023 only.


Code
# Deep change detection is supervised: it learns from image pairs with change masks. We train on Sentinel-2
# July pairs of earlier years (averaged to 30 m, the six Landsat-equivalent bands) and keep 2024 -> 2025 for test.
PAIRS = {"train": [("2020", "2021"), ("2021", "2022"), ("2022", "2023")], "val": [("2023", "2024")], "test": [("2024", "2025")]}

def change_mask(y1, y2, a1, a2):  # CDL change mask of a pair: 1 changed, 0 unchanged, -100 ignored
    # pixels usable in both years and both images
    ok = (CDL[int(y1)] >= 0) & (CDL[int(y2)] >= 0) & np.isfinite(a1.values).all(0) & np.isfinite(a2.values).all(0)
    return np.where(ok, (CDL[int(y1)] != CDL[int(y2)]).astype("int64"), -100)  # the mask

# per-band z-score from the training-year images
NORM = ic.Normalizer("zscore").fit(np.concatenate([S2[y].values.reshape(len(L_BANDS), -1) for y in ("2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")], 1).T)
SIZE, STRIDE = 64, 32  # 64 px chips, 32 px stride
H, W = REF.shape  # grid size
# every chip corner
starts = [(r, c) for r in range(0, H - SIZE + 1, STRIDE) for c in range(0, W - SIZE + 1, STRIDE)]
def chips(pairs):  # chip pairs and masks of a list of year pairs
    t1, t2, m = [], [], []  # lists
    for y1, y2 in pairs:  # each year pair
        a1, a2 = S2[y1], S2[y2]  # the two images
        cm = change_mask(y1, y2, a1, a2)  # their change mask
        for r, c in starts:  # every chip position
            sl = (slice(r, r + SIZE), slice(c, c + SIZE))  # the window
            if (cm[sl] >= 0).mean() < 0.5:  # skip chips less than half usable
                continue
            # keep both chips and the mask
            t1.append(a1.values[(slice(None),) + sl]); t2.append(a2.values[(slice(None),) + sl]); m.append(cm[sl])
    return np.stack(t1), np.stack(t2), np.stack(m)  # as arrays

CH = {k: chips(v) for k, v in PAIRS.items()}  # chips of every split
for k, (a, b, m) in CH.items():  # each split
    # chip count, size and change share
    print(f"{k:5s}: {len(a):4d} chip pairs of {SIZE} x {SIZE} px ({SIZE * 30 / 1000:.1f} km), change share {(m == 1).sum() / (m >= 0).sum():.1%}")
aug = ic.OverheadAugment(dihedral=True, p=1.0, seed=SEED)            # the same rotation/flip for both dates and the mask
ds_tr = ic.PairChipDataset(*CH["train"], normalizer=NORM, transform=aug)  # training pairs with augmentation
ds_va = ic.PairChipDataset(*CH["val"], normalizer=NORM)  # validation pairs
item = ds_tr[0]  # one item
# its shapes
print("PairChipDataset item:", {k: (tuple(v[0].shape), tuple(v[1].shape)) if k == "image" else tuple(v.shape) for k, v in item.items()})

All four networks reach a validation mean IoU of about 0.78 to 0.80 on the 2023 → 2024 pair. The BIT-style model has a seventh of the parameters of the U-Nets.

Predicting the test pair, and crossing sensors
The networks are applied in the 64 × 64 px tiles they were trained on (50 % overlap, averaged); tiling is necessary for the transformer, whose decoder attends between all pixel positions of its input, which is quadratic in the image size. We predict the Sentinel-2 test pair, and the Landsat test pair in three versions:

raw Landsat reflectance;
cross-calibrated: a linear gain and offset per band fitted on the same-day pair of 10 July 2023 (the approach of harmonised products such as HLS); Sentinel-2 L2A is 10 to 40 % brighter than Landsat Collection 2 in this pair;
histogram-matched onto the Sentinel-2 image of 2023 (a training-year image), with histogram_match.



Code
# change probability for a whole image pair
def predict_full(model, a1, a2, tile=SIZE, stride=SIZE // 2, batch=64):
    """Change probability for a whole image pair, predicted in the 64 x 64 px tiles the models were trained on
    (50 % overlap, overlapping predictions averaged). Tiling also keeps the memory of the transformer bounded:
    its decoder attends between all pixel positions of the input, which is quadratic in the image size."""
    x1 = np.nan_to_num(NORM.transform(a1.values[None], 1))[0].astype("float32")  # normalised first date
    x2 = np.nan_to_num(NORM.transform(a2.values[None], 1))[0].astype("float32")  # normalised second date
    ph, pw = (-(H - tile)) % stride, (-(W - tile)) % stride  # padding to whole tiles
    x1, x2 = (np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (0, ph), (0, pw)), mode="reflect") for x in (x1, x2))  # reflect-pad both
    Hp, Wp = x1.shape[1:]  # padded size
    # tile corners
    pos = [(r, c) for r in range(0, Hp - tile + 1, stride) for c in range(0, Wp - tile + 1, stride)]
    acc, cnt = np.zeros((Hp, Wp), "float32"), np.zeros((Hp, Wp), "float32")  # summed probabilities and counts
    model.to(DEVICE).eval()  # evaluation mode on the device
    with torch.no_grad():  # no gradients needed
        for i in range(0, len(pos), batch):  # batches of tiles
            pb = pos[i:i + batch]  # the batch corners
            # first-date tiles
            t1 = torch.from_numpy(np.stack([x1[:, r:r + tile, c:c + tile] for r, c in pb])).to(DEVICE)
            # second-date tiles
            t2 = torch.from_numpy(np.stack([x2[:, r:r + tile, c:c + tile] for r, c in pb])).to(DEVICE)
            p = torch.softmax(model(t1, t2).float(), 1)[:, 1].cpu().numpy()  # change probability
            for (r, c), pp in zip(pb, p):  # each tile ...
                acc[r:r + tile, c:c + tile] += pp; cnt[r:r + tile, c:c + tile] += 1  # ... added to the sums
    return (acc / cnt)[:H, :W]  # average, cropped to the grid

# Landsat made to look like Sentinel-2 for models trained on Sentinel-2:
#  (b) linear cross-calibration from the same-day pair of 10 Jul 2023 (gain and offset per band, as in harmonised products)
#  (c) histogram_match onto the Sentinel-2 image of 2023
same = np.isfinite(LS["2023"].values).all(0) & np.isfinite(S2["2023"].values).all(0)
# gain and offset per band from the same-day pair
GAIN = {b: np.polyfit(LS["2023"].sel(band=b).values[same].astype("float64"), S2["2023"].sel(band=b).values[same].astype("float64"), 1)
        for b in L_BANDS}
# show them
print("cross-calibration Landsat -> Sentinel-2 (gain, offset):", {b: (round(float(g[0]), 3), round(float(g[1]), 4)) for b, g in GAIN.items()})
def calibrate(a):  # apply the cross-calibration
    # ...
    return a.copy(data=np.stack([np.polyval(GAIN[b], a.sel(band=b).values) for b in L_BANDS]).astype("float32"))
INPUTS = {"Sentinel-2 test pair": (S2["2024"], S2["2025"]),  # four input variants
          "Landsat, raw": (LS["2024"], LS["2025"]),
          "Landsat, cross-calibrated": (calibrate(LS["2024"]), calibrate(LS["2025"])),
          "Landsat, histogram_match to S2 2023": (ic.histogram_match(LS["2024"], S2["2023"]), ic.histogram_match(LS["2025"], S2["2023"]))}
PROB = {}  # change probabilities
for name, m in DEEP.items():  # each deep model
    for inp, (a1, a2) in INPUTS.items():  # each input variant
        PROB[(name, inp)] = predict_full(m, a1, a2)  # predict the whole scene
        score(f"{name} | {inp}", PROB[(name, inp)] >= 0.5)  # score the 0.5 threshold
# scores of the deep models
pd.DataFrame({k: v for k, v in SCORES.items() if k.split(" | ")[0] in DEEP}).T[["precision", "recall", "f1", "iou", "kappa"]].round(3)

Reading the deep results. On the Sentinel-2 test pair all four networks reach F1 ≈ 0.94 to 0.95 for the change class: far above the classical methods (≤ 0.77) and above post-classification (0.91). Applied to raw Landsat, recall drops (F1 about 0.90 to 0.94): the networks have learned Sentinel-2 radiometry. Histogram matching to the Sentinel-2 training distribution recovers almost all of the loss (F1 ≈ 0.94 to 0.95); here matching is the right tool, because the goal is to put a new sensor into the domain the model knows. Linear cross-calibration helps three of the four models but makes the early-fusion U-Net worse: a single same-day pair corrects the sensor, not the seasonal difference between years.

Evaluation: change metrics and area-adjusted change area

change_metrics
For the change class, with \(TP, FP, FN, TN\) counted against the reference,
\[
\text{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\quad \text{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\quad F_1=\frac{2\,\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}}{\text{precision}+\text{recall}},\quad \mathrm{IoU}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP+FN}.
\]
change_metrics also returns overall accuracy and Cohen’s \(\kappa\). All methods are scored on the same pixels: valid in both Landsat and both Sentinel-2 dates and labelled in both CDL years; and separately on the interior pixels of the The CDL as reference: what counts as true change? section.

The ranking is clear: deep change networks (F1 0.90 to 0.95) > post-classification (0.91) > multi-band classical methods with Otsu (0.67 to 0.77) > single-index classical methods (0.54 to 0.60) > ±kσ thresholds (0.10). On interior pixels the deep models reach F1 ≈ 0.99 and post-classification 0.96: most of the remaining disagreement sits on field edges, exactly where the CDL change itself is least reliable (see The CDL as reference: what counts as true change?).


Area-adjusted change area with olofsson
Counting pixels on a change map gives a biased area: the CVA map, which misses half the change, reports about half the change area. Olofsson et al. (2014) correct this with a stratified random sample of reference labels, using the map classes as strata. With \(W_i\) the mapped area share of stratum \(i\), \(n_{ij}\) the sample counts (map class \(i\), reference class \(j\)) and \(n_{i\cdot}\) the sample size of stratum \(i\), the estimated area proportion of reference class \(j\) is
\[
\hat p_{\cdot j}=\sum_i W_i\,\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}},\qquad
\widehat{SE}(\hat p_{\cdot j})=\sqrt{\sum_i W_i^2\,\frac{\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}}\big(1-\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}}\big)}{n_{i\cdot}-1}},
\]
and the area is \(\hat A_j=A\,\hat p_{\cdot j}\) with a 95 % confidence interval \(\pm1.96\,A\,\widehat{SE}\). We draw 500 sample pixels from each map stratum and use the CDL change at those pixels as the reference label (in practice, interpretation of high-resolution imagery or field visits). Because here the CDL is known everywhere, we can check the estimate against the census change area.


Code
# Area-adjusted change area (Olofsson et al. 2014): a map's pixel count is biased by its errors. With a stratified
# random sample of reference labels (strata = mapped change / no change) the error matrix converts map area into an
# unbiased area estimate with a confidence interval. The reference labels here come from the CDL change at the
# sample pixels (in practice: interpretation of high-resolution imagery or field visits).
N_PER_STRATUM = 500
PIX_HA = 0.09  # hectares per 30 m pixel
# the best deep model on the Sentinel-2 pair
best_deep = max([k for k in METHODS if "Sentinel-2 test pair" in k], key=lambda k: SCORES[k]["f1"])
# three maps to assess
cands = {"CVA, 6 bands (Otsu)": next(k for k in METHODS if k.startswith("CVA, 6 bands")),
         "Post-classification (Landsat)": "Post-classification (Landsat RF maps 2024, 2025)",
         f"{best_deep.split(' |')[0]} (Sentinel-2)": best_deep}
true_area = np.nansum(ref[EVAL]) * PIX_HA  # census change area from the CDL
rows = {}  # one row per map
for label, key in cands.items():  # each map
    mp = METHODS[key][EVAL].astype(int)  # its change mask on the evaluation pixels
    rf_ = ref[EVAL].astype(int)  # reference change
    # 500 random pixels per stratum
    idx = np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(mp == s), N_PER_STRATUM, replace=False) for s in (0, 1)])
    cm = classify.confusion_matrix(rf_[idx], mp[idx], labels=[0, 1])           # rows = map, columns = reference
    # area-adjusted estimate
    res = classify.olofsson(cm, {0: int((mp == 0).sum()), 1: int((mp == 1).sum())}, pixel_area=PIX_HA)
    t = res["table"]  # its table
    # mapped and adjusted area, interval and accuracies
    rows[label] = {"mapped change (ha)": t.loc[1, "map_area"], "adjusted change (ha)": t.loc[1, "adjusted_area"],
                   "95 % CI (± ha)": t.loc[1, "area_ci"], "user's acc. (change)": t.loc[1, "users_accuracy"],
                   "producer's acc. (change)": t.loc[1, "producers_accuracy"], "overall acc.": res["overall_accuracy"]}
ol = pd.DataFrame(rows).T  # as a table
# census area and sample size
print(f"reference (CDL) change area over all evaluation pixels: {true_area:,.0f} ha; sample: {N_PER_STRATUM} pixels per stratum")
# does the interval cover the census area?
ol["CI covers the census area"] = (ol["adjusted change (ha)"] - ol["95 % CI (± ha)"] <= true_area) & (true_area <= ol["adjusted change (ha)"] + ol["95 % CI (± ha)"])
display(ol.round(3))  # show it

# A 95 % interval should cover the true area in about 95 % of repeated samples, and a single sample can miss.
# Repeat the stratified sampling 200 times per map and count how often the interval covers the census area.
REPS = 200
cover = {}  # coverage counts
g = np.random.default_rng(1)  # random generator
for label, key in cands.items():  # each map
    mp = METHODS[key][EVAL].astype(int); rf_ = ref[EVAL].astype(int)  # map and reference
    i0, i1 = np.flatnonzero(mp == 0), np.flatnonzero(mp == 1)  # indices of each stratum
    area_map = {0: len(i0), 1: len(i1)}  # stratum sizes
    hits, est = 0, []  # hits and estimates
    for _ in range(REPS):  # 200 repeats
        # a stratified sample
        idx = np.concatenate([g.choice(i0, N_PER_STRATUM, replace=False), g.choice(i1, N_PER_STRATUM, replace=False)])
        # the area estimate of this sample
        t = classify.olofsson(classify.confusion_matrix(rf_[idx], mp[idx], labels=[0, 1]), area_map, pixel_area=PIX_HA)["table"]
        est.append(t.loc[1, "adjusted_area"])  # keep it
        # the interval covered the census area
        hits += abs(t.loc[1, "adjusted_area"] - true_area) <= t.loc[1, "area_ci"]
    # mean, spread and coverage
    cover[label] = {"mean adjusted change (ha)": np.mean(est), "SD across samples (ha)": np.std(est),
                    "CI coverage of the census area": hits / REPS}
print(f"\n{REPS} repeated stratified samples per map:")  # header
print(pd.DataFrame(cover).T.round(3))  # the table

Exercise: the rotation map 2024 → 2025 from Landsat vs from the CDL
Task. Build a rotation map with five classes (corn → soybeans, soybeans → corn, corn → corn, soybeans → soybeans, other) from

On what share of the pixels do the two rotation maps agree? Which rotation classes are most confused?
Is disagreement higher on field edges than inside fields? In small fields than in large ones?
Is it higher near the clouds of the 2024 image? What does that say about the cloud mask?
Is it higher for fields that were corn or soybeans in 2024? Look at the 2024 image of the The data: mid-July Landsat and Sentinel-2 pairs and CDL on one 30 m grid section: why might one crop be harder that year?
Which disagreements are errors of the Landsat maps, which could be errors of the CDL, and which are neither (for example, a field with two crops)?

Hints: boundary() from the The CDL as reference: what counts as true change? section marks field edges; ndi.label gives field sizes; np.isfinite(LS["2024"].values[0]) is the 2024 cloud mask. Try it yourself before reading the solution below.


Code
# One possible solution. Rotation classes from a pair of class maps:
ROT = ["corn → soybeans", "soybeans → corn", "corn → corn", "soybeans → soybeans", "other"]
def rotation(m1, m2):  # rotation class of each pixel from two maps
    r = np.full(m1.shape, 4, "int8")  # "other" by default
    r[(m1 == 0) & (m2 == 1)] = 0; r[(m1 == 1) & (m2 == 0)] = 1  # corn to soybeans; soybeans to corn
    r[(m1 == 0) & (m2 == 0)] = 2; r[(m1 == 1) & (m2 == 1)] = 3  # corn on corn; soybeans on soybeans
    return r  # the classes
# from the Landsat maps and from the CDL
rot_l, rot_c = rotation(MAPS[2024], MAPS[2025]), rotation(CDL[2024], CDL[2025])
ev = EVAL  # evaluation pixels

# agreement share

Discussion of the solution.

The two rotation maps agree on about 79 % of the pixels. The swaps (corn → soybeans, soybeans → corn) agree best (77 to 84 %); “corn → corn” and “soybeans → soybeans” agree least (60 to 68 %), and every CDL class loses 13 to 24 % to “other”, mostly the Landsat maps calling field pixels grass/pasture or wetland/forest.
Disagreement is twice as high on field edges (34 %) as inside fields (16 %): mixed 30 m pixels, and edges that differ slightly between the two years in both products. Inside fields, size matters little in this landscape of large fields.
It is clearly higher within 300 m of a 2024 cloud (28 %): thin cloud, haze and cloud shadow beyond the QA_PIXEL mask change the reflectance, and the Random Forest turns that into a wrong class.
It is higher for fields that were corn in 2024 (25 %, against 17 % for soybeans): in mid-July 2024 the Landsat map confused part of the corn with soybeans or grass (its 2024 accuracy is 0.80, against 0.87 for 2025), which also explains the many corn → corn fields that Landsat calls soybeans → corn.
Whole-field disagreements in the interior are mostly errors of the Landsat maps (one wrong year makes a wrong rotation). Thin lines along roads, drainage ditches and field boundaries are where both products are uncertain, and the CDL is not a better truth there. A few fields are genuinely mixed (a strip of another crop, a replanted part), which neither 30 m map can represent.

title: Change Detection: Classical, Post-Classification and Deep Methods on Landsat and Sentinel-2, 2020 to 2025
text:
Interpretation, caveats and recommended recipe
What the numbers say (Landsat / Sentinel-2 mid-July pair 2024 → 2025; CDL change as reference; 79 % of the pixels change, almost all by rotation):

Check before you compare. The Landsat pair is co-registered to 0.1 px; a deliberate 1-pixel shift is caught by check_coregistration. Raw surface reflectance is already consistent on invariant targets, and histogram_match distorts it when much of the scene really changes.
Thresholds must match the share of change. ±kσ rules assume rare change and fail here (F1 0.10); Otsu works for any share as long as the histogram is bimodal.
Unsupervised spectral change confuses crop swaps with season timing. Classical methods are precise (0.94 to 0.98) but miss 37 to 63 % of the change; multi-band CVA and PCA are better than single indices, and CVA direction separates corn → soybean from soybean → corn, but not from a phenology shift.
Supervised methods know what change means. Post-classification (F1 0.91) gives from-to information but adds the errors of two maps; deep change networks trained on earlier years reach F1 ≈ 0.95 (≈ 0.99 inside fields) and transfer to Landsat after histogram matching to their training domain.
The reference matters as much as the method. Most non-rotation CDL change sits on field edges and is label noise; interior pixels give a much cleaner evaluation.
Report areas from a sample, not from the map. Olofsson’s estimator corrects even a map that misses half of the change; better maps give narrower intervals.

Caveats

CDL is the reference, for both training and testing; the deep models learn its notion of change (including its edge noise), and scores measure agreement with CDL.
Rotation dominates. With 79 % change and almost all of it rotation, the scores mostly reflect corn vs soybeans; a landscape with rare change (urban growth, deforestation) behaves very differently, and there precision of the change class becomes the hard part.
One pair, one date per year. Mid-July images; with August images the corn/soybean contrast and the scores would be higher.
The area sample uses CDL labels, which are known everywhere here; with real reference data the census check is not available, and the reference labels themselves have errors.
Single training runs (one seed); differences between the deep models (≈ 0.01 F1) are within run-to-run variation.

Recommended recipe

Put both dates on one grid; run check_coregistration and fix any shift above about 0.3 px before anything else.
Check radiometry on pseudo-invariant targets; normalise (histogram matching, or a regression on invariant targets) only when it does not remove the change you want to find, and always when crossing sensors.
For a quick unsupervised map, use multi-band CVA or PCA of the difference with an Otsu threshold; use CVA direction to label the type of change.
When labels exist, prefer supervised change: a Siamese-difference U-Net or a BIT-style model trained on earlier date pairs, or post-classification when from-to classes are needed.
Decide what counts as change (here: is rotation change?), and evaluate on a reference that is reliable for that definition (interior pixels, confirmed transitions).
Report change areas from a stratified sample with olofsson, with confidence intervals.


References

Daudt, R. C., Le Saux, B., & Boulch, A. (2018). Fully convolutional siamese networks for change detection. ICIP, 4063-4067.
Chen, H., Qi, Z., & Shi, Z. (2021). Remote sensing image change detection with transformers. IEEE TGRS, 60, 1-14.
Malila, W. A. (1980). Change vector analysis: an approach for detecting forest changes with Landsat. LARS Symposia, 385.
Singh, A. (1989). Digital change detection techniques using remotely-sensed data. International Journal of Remote Sensing, 10(6), 989-1003.
Otsu, N. (1979). A threshold selection method from gray-level histograms. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, 9(1), 62-66.
Olofsson, P., Foody, G. M., Herold, M., Stehman, S. V., Woodcock, C. E., & Wulder, M. A. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment, 148, 42-57.
Boryan, C., Yang, Z., Mueller, R., & Craig, M. (2011). Monitoring US agriculture: the US Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Statistics Service, Cropland Data Layer program. Geocarto International, 26(5), 341-358.

title: Instance Segmentation of Agricultural Fields with Mask R-CNN
text:
Overview
Train and evaluate a geospatial, eight-band Mask R-CNN with GeoLattice using the WorldView-2 field polygons bundled with the image-classification data.
Semantic segmentation assigns a class to each pixel, but does not say which neighboring pixels belong to the same object. Instance segmentation predicts a separate mask for every object and assigns each mask a class and confidence. This notebook learns individual Crop and Fallow field instances from polygon labels, then converts predictions back to map-coordinate vector features.
The example uses WorldView2_BD/Labeled_data/multi.tif (eight multispectral bands) and Labeled_data/aoi_trianing.shp (567 field polygons). The training shapefile has no CRS metadata; its coordinates align with the raster and its associated metadata identifies UTM zone 46N, so the notebook assigns the raster CRS after checking that alignment. These are small, local teaching data, not a regionally representative accuracy benchmark.

title: Instance Segmentation of Agricultural Fields with Mask R-CNN
text:
Core concepts

Learning objectives

Distinguish semantic, object-detection and instance-segmentation outputs.
Convert georeferenced field polygons into per-instance chip masks and Mask R-CNN targets.
Build an eight-band detector with geolattice.rsense.classify.image_classification.
Train with a geographic holdout and evaluate instance-mask AP/IoU.
Convert predicted instance masks to georeferenced polygons with GeoLattice.



Contents

Setup, data paths and compute device
WorldView-2 imagery and field-polygon labels
Instance rasterization, chip sampling and spatial split
Mask R-CNN architecture and objective
GeoLattice model, dataset and training loop
Spatial validation and mask-based metrics
Test-chip predictions and visual inspection
Georeferenced vectors and saved outputs
Interpretation, limitations and recommended recipe



Task and evaluation design
A polygon is one instance; Class_ID supplies its category (1 = Fallow, 2 = Crop). Pixels outside labeled polygons are background. We split the image into contiguous north-to-south bands before making chips: the northern band trains, the middle band validates, and the southern band is held out for testing. Chips do not cross split boundaries. This is more conservative than randomly splitting neighboring chips, although this single small AOI still cannot establish geographic transfer performance.
The primary reported score is mask AP at IoU 0.50, calculated per class with one-to-one matching of predicted and reference masks. We also inspect per-instance mask IoU and vector geometry. Box AP alone is not used as a substitute for mask quality.

WorldView-2 imagery and field-polygon labels
The labeled raster is a compact 760 × 702 pixel, eight-band subset. Band descriptions are not populated in the GeoTIFF, so channels are retained in source order and named B1-B8. The shapefile CRS is absent; the provided raster CRS is used as the label CRS only after confirming the polygon bounds overlap the raster bounds.


Code
with rasterio.open(IMAGE_PATH) as src:  # open the image
    raw = src.read(masked=True).filled(np.nan).astype(np.float32)  # all bands, nodata as NaN
    raster_crs = src.crs  # its CRS
    raster_transform = src.transform  # its transform
    raster_bounds = src.bounds  # its bounds
    raster_nodata = src.nodata  # its nodata value
    height, width = src.height, src.width  # its size
    band_count = src.count  # number of bands
    band_names = [f"B{i}" for i in range(1, band_count + 1)]  # band names B1 to B8
    valid_pixels = np.all(np.isfinite(raw), axis=0)  # pixels with all bands present

if band_count != 8:  # eight bands expected ...
    raise ValueError(f"Expected the eight-band WorldView-2 stack, got {band_count} bands")  # ... or stop
if raster_crs is None:  # a CRS is needed ...
    raise ValueError("The source image needs a CRS for georeferenced instance outputs")  # ... or stop

labels = gpd.read_file(LABEL_PATH)  # read the polygons
if labels.crs is None:  # no CRS ...
    labels = labels.set_crs(raster_crs)  # ... assume the raster CRS
else:
    labels = labels.to_crs(raster_crs)  # otherwise reproject to it
labels = labels.loc[labels.geometry.notna() & ~labels.geometry.is_empty].copy()  # drop empty geometries
labels["Class_ID"] = labels["Class_ID"].astype(int)  # class id as integer
labels = labels[labels["Class_ID"].isin([1, 2])].reset_index(drop=True)  # keep Fallow (1) and Crop (2)

overlap_bounds = (  # labels and raster must overlap
    labels.total_bounds[0] < raster_bounds.right
    and labels.total_bounds[2] > raster_bounds.left
    and labels.total_bounds[1] < raster_bounds.top
    and labels.total_bounds[3] > raster_bounds.bottom
)
if not overlap_bounds:  # they do not ...
    raise ValueError("The polygon labels do not overlap the raster extent; check their CRS")  # ... stop

CLASS_NAMES = {1: "Fallow", 2: "Crop"}  # class names
CLASS_COLORS = {1: "#f2a900", 2: "#37a76f"}
# image size, bands, CRS and nodata
print(f"Image: {width} × {height}, {band_count} bands, CRS={raster_crs}, nodata={raster_nodata}")
print("Label CRS:", labels.crs, "| polygon count:", len(labels))  # label CRS and polygon count
print(labels["Class"].value_counts().rename("polygons"))  # polygons per class

image_da = xr.DataArray(  # the image as a georeferenced DataArray
    raw,
    dims=("band", "y", "x"),
    coords={"band": band_names},

title: Instance Segmentation of Agricultural Fields with Mask R-CNN
section: Instance masks, patch sampling and spatial split
text:
Instance masks, patch sampling and spatial split
Rasterizing each polygon with its own integer identifier produces an instance-ID image, not merely a two-class semantic mask. Each ID retains its field class in class_by_instance; background is zero. Chips are generated within fixed row bands, so no chip can place neighboring train and test rows in the same sample. To avoid counting a field twice in chipwise test metrics, only complete, non-overlapping chips are evaluated; narrow remainder strips at image edges are omitted.


Code
instance_shapes = []  # (geometry, id) pairs
class_by_instance = {}  # instance id -> class id
for instance_id, row in enumerate(labels.itertuples(), start=1):  # each polygon gets an id from 1
    instance_shapes.append((row.geometry, instance_id))  # its geometry and id
    class_by_instance[instance_id] = int(row.Class_ID)  # its class

instance_map = rasterize(  # burn the instance ids into a raster
    instance_shapes,
    out_shape=(height, width),
    transform=raster_transform,
    fill=0,
    dtype="int32",
    all_touched=False,
)
instance_map[~valid_pixels] = 0  # no instance where data are missing
class_map = np.zeros((height, width), dtype=np.uint8)  # class raster
for instance_id, class_id in class_by_instance.items():  # each instance ...
    class_map[instance_map == instance_id] = class_id  # ... paints its class
print("Rasterized instance IDs:", len(np.unique(instance_map)) - 1)  # number of instances
print("Labeled pixels:", int(np.count_nonzero(instance_map)))  # labelled pixels

PATCH = 160  # chip size in pixels
MIN_INSTANCE_PIXELS = 3  # smallest instance kept in a chip
# row bands for train, validation and test
ROW_BANDS = {"train": (0, 320), "validation": (320, 480), "test": (480, height)}

def full_window_starts(start, stop, patch):  # starts of full windows from start to stop
    return list(range(start, stop - patch + 1, patch))  # non-overlapping steps

col_starts = full_window_starts(0, width, PATCH)  # column starts
windows = {name: [] for name in ROW_BANDS}  # chip corners per split
for name, (row0, row1) in ROW_BANDS.items():  # each split
    for r0 in full_window_starts(row0, row1, PATCH):  # each row start
        for c0 in col_starts:  # each column start
            windows[name].append((r0, c0))  # one chip
print({name: len(coords) for name, coords in windows.items()}, "chips")  # chips per split
assert all(r + PATCH <= ROW_BANDS[name][1] and c + PATCH <= width  # every chip lies inside its own band
           for name, coords in windows.items() for r, c in coords)

Code
# Fit radiometric scaling on valid training-band pixels only.
train_valid = np.zeros_like(valid_pixels)
train_valid[:ROW_BANDS["train"][1]] = valid_pixels[:ROW_BANDS["train"][1]]  # valid pixels of the training band
lower = np.array([np.nanpercentile(np.where(train_valid, raw[b], np.nan), 2)  # 2nd percentile per band
                  for b in range(band_count)], dtype=np.float32)
upper = np.array([np.nanpercentile(np.where(train_valid, raw[b], np.nan), 98)  # 98th percentile per band
                  for b in range(band_count)], dtype=np.float32)
upper = np.maximum(upper, lower + 1e-6)  # avoid a zero range
scaled = np.clip((raw - lower[:, None, None]) /  # scale every band to 0 to 1
                 (upper - lower)[:, None, None], 0, 1)
scaled = np.nan_to_num(scaled, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0).astype(np.float32)  # missing values -> 0

class InstanceChipDataset(Dataset):  # chips with instance masks, boxes and classes
    """Mask R-CNN samples: float image [C,H,W] and torchvision instance targets."""
    def __init__(self, coords):  # keep the chip corners
        self.coords = list(coords)  # the list of corners

    def __len__(self):  # number of chips
        return len(self.coords)  # the count

    def __getitem__(self, index):  # one chip and its target
        row0, col0 = self.coords[index]  # its corner
        sl = np.s_[row0:row0 + PATCH, col0:col0 + PATCH]  # its window
        chip = scaled[:, sl[0], sl[1]]  # the scaled bands
        ids = instance_map[sl]  # the instance ids
        masks, classes, boxes = [], [], []  # masks, classes and boxes
        for instance_id in np.unique(ids):  # each instance in the chip
            if instance_id == 0:  # skip the background
                continue
            mask = ids == instance_id  # its mask
            ys, xs = np.where(mask)  # its pixels
            if len(xs) < MIN_INSTANCE_PIXELS:  # skip tiny slivers
                continue
            masks.append(mask.astype(np.uint8))  # keep the mask
            classes.append(class_by_instance[int(instance_id)])  # its class
            boxes.append([xs.min(), ys.min(), xs.max() + 1, ys.max() + 1])  # its bounding box
        if masks:  # any instances ...
            masks = torch.as_tensor(np.stack(masks), dtype=torch.uint8)  # ... masks as a tensor
            boxes = torch.as_tensor(boxes, dtype=torch.float32)  # boxes as a tensor
            classes = torch.as_tensor(classes, dtype=torch.int64)  # classes as a tensor
        else:
            masks = torch.zeros((0, PATCH, PATCH), dtype=torch.uint8)  # empty masks
            boxes = torch.zeros((0, 4), dtype=torch.float32)  # empty boxes
            classes = torch.zeros((0,), dtype=torch.int64)  # empty classes
        target = {  # the torchvision target dictionary
            "boxes": boxes,
            "labels": classes,
            "masks": masks,
            "image_id": torch.tensor([index], dtype=torch.int64),
            "area": masks.flatten(1).sum(1).to(torch.float32),
            "iscrowd": torch.zeros((len(classes),), dtype=torch.int64),
        }
        return torch.from_numpy(chip), target  # chip and target

train_ds = InstanceChipDataset(windows["train"])  # training chips
val_ds = InstanceChipDataset(windows["validation"])  # validation chips
test_ds = InstanceChipDataset(windows["test"])  # test chips
# instances in each training chip
print("Instances per chip (train):", [len(train_ds[i][1]["labels"]) for i in range(len(train_ds))])
print("Train/validation/test chips:", len(train_ds), len(val_ds), len(test_ds))  # chips per split

def detection_collate(batch):  # keep images and targets as tuples
    return tuple(zip(*batch))  # batch -> (images, targets)

BATCH_SIZE = 2 if DEVICE == "cuda" else 1  # batch size (smaller on a CPU)
train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True,  # shuffled training batches
                          collate_fn=detection_collate, num_workers=0)
val_loader = DataLoader(val_ds, batch_size=1, shuffle=False,  # validation batches
                        collate_fn=detection_collate, num_workers=0)
test_loader = DataLoader(test_ds, batch_size=1, shuffle=False,  # test batches
                         collate_fn=detection_collate, num_workers=0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))  # one panel
# the training chip with most instances
sample_index = int(np.argmax([len(train_ds[i][1]["labels"]) for i in range(len(train_ds))]))
sample_image, sample_target = train_ds[sample_index]  # its image and target
ax.imshow(np.moveaxis(sample_image[[3, 1, 0]].numpy(), 0, -1))  # B4, B2, B1 as RGB
# each reference instance
for mask, label in zip(sample_target["masks"].numpy(), sample_target["labels"].numpy()):
    color = CLASS_COLORS[int(label)]  # its class colour
    ax.contour(mask, levels=[0.5], colors=[color], linewidths=1.2)  # its outline

title: Instance Segmentation of Agricultural Fields with Mask R-CNN
text:
Mask R-CNN: architecture and objective
Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN with a parallel mask head. A backbone and feature pyramid produce multi-scale features; the region proposal network (RPN) proposes candidate boxes; RoIAlign samples each proposal without the quantization error of RoI pooling; classification and box-regression heads refine each object; and a small fully convolutional mask head predicts a binary mask for each class and proposal.
For anchor \(a\) and ground-truth box \(b\), the RPN learns objectness and parameterized offsets. The final model minimizes
\[\mathcal L = \mathcal L_{rpn,obj} + \mathcal L_{rpn,box} + \mathcal L_{roi,cls} + \mathcal L_{roi,box} + \mathcal L_{mask}.\]
For a positive proposal assigned to class \(k\), the mask head uses pixelwise binary cross-entropy only for channel \(k\):
\[\mathcal L_{mask} = -\frac{1}{M^2}\sum_{u,v}\left[y_{uv}\log p_{uv,k} + (1-y_{uv})\log(1-p_{uv,k})\right].\]
This class-specific mask prediction keeps overlapping instances distinct. The GeoLattice builder replaces the COCO box and mask classifiers with heads for background, Fallow and Crop and adapts the ResNet input stem to all eight bands.

text:
Build the GeoLattice Mask R-CNN model
build_object_detector("mask_rcnn", ...) delegates construction to GeoLattice’s torchvision detector builder. num_classes includes background, hence three outputs for two field classes plus background. ImageNet/COCO initialization is recommended for this small label set; the adapted first convolution accepts the eight-band input.

section: Train on the spatial training band
text:
Train on the spatial training band
Torchvision detectors consume a list of images and a matching list of targets. The compact loop below is necessary for Mask R-CNN’s detection-specific loss dictionary; model construction, mask-to-vector conversion and export remain GeoLattice APIs. Validation mask AP selects the checkpoint. Reduce EPOCHS if training on CPU.


Code
def mask_iou_matrix(pred_masks, true_masks):  # IoU of every predicted mask with every reference mask
    pred_masks = np.asarray(pred_masks, dtype=bool)  # as booleans
    true_masks = np.asarray(true_masks, dtype=bool)  # as booleans
    if len(pred_masks) == 0 or len(true_masks) == 0:  # none on one side ...
        return np.zeros((len(pred_masks), len(true_masks)), dtype=np.float32)  # ... an empty matrix
    p = pred_masks.reshape(len(pred_masks), -1)  # one row per predicted mask
    t = true_masks.reshape(len(true_masks), -1)  # one row per reference mask
    intersection = p.astype(np.uint32) @ t.astype(np.uint32).T  # pixel intersections
    union = p.sum(1)[:, None] + t.sum(1)[None, :] - intersection  # pixel unions
    return intersection / np.maximum(union, 1)  # IoU

def evaluate_mask_ap(model, loader, iou_threshold=0.5):  # mask AP at an IoU threshold for each class
    """All-point AP with greedy one-to-one matching on mask IoU, per foreground class."""
    model.eval()  # evaluation mode
    records = []  # per-chip predictions and references
    with torch.inference_mode():  # no gradients
        for images, targets in loader:  # each chip
            output = model([images[0].to(DEVICE)])[0]  # predict it
            pred_masks = (output["masks"][:, 0] >= 0.5).cpu().numpy()  # masks above 0.5
            records.append({  # keep predictions and references
                "pred_masks": pred_masks,
                "pred_labels": output["labels"].cpu().numpy(),
                "scores": output["scores"].cpu().numpy(),
                "true_masks": targets[0]["masks"].cpu().numpy().astype(bool),
                "true_labels": targets[0]["labels"].cpu().numpy(),
            })
    class_ap = {}  # AP per class
    for class_id, class_name in CLASS_NAMES.items():  # each class
        # reference instances of this class
        n_true = sum(int(np.sum(r["true_labels"] == class_id)) for r in records)
        if n_true == 0:  # none ...
            class_ap[class_name] = np.nan  # ... AP undefined
            continue
        detections = sorted(  # detections of this class, highest score first
            [(float(score), image_id, mask) for image_id, r in enumerate(records)
             for mask, label, score in zip(r["pred_masks"], r["pred_labels"], r["scores"])
             if label == class_id],
            key=lambda item: item[0], reverse=True,
        )
        matched = {i: set() for i in range(len(records))}  # reference instances already matched
        tp, fp = [], []  # true and false positives
        for score, image_id, pred_mask in detections:  # each detection
            record = records[image_id]  # its chip
            keep = record["true_labels"] == class_id  # references of this class
            gt_masks = record["true_masks"][keep]  # their masks
            ious = mask_iou_matrix(pred_mask[None], gt_masks)[0]  # IoU with each reference
            best = int(np.argmax(ious)) if len(ious) else -1  # best reference
            # good enough and still free ...
            if best >= 0 and ious[best] >= iou_threshold and best not in matched[image_id]:
                matched[image_id].add(best)  # ... mark it matched
                tp.append(1)  # true positive
                fp.append(0)  # not a false positive
            else:
                tp.append(0)  # not a true positive
                fp.append(1)  # false positive
        if not tp:  # no detections ...
            class_ap[class_name] = 0.0  # ... AP is zero
            continue
        recall = np.cumsum(tp) / n_true  # recall curve
        precision = np.cumsum(tp) / np.maximum(np.cumsum(tp) + np.cumsum(fp), 1)  # precision curve
        mrec = np.r_[0.0, recall, 1.0]  # recall padded at both ends
        mpre = np.r_[0.0, precision, 0.0]  # precision padded at both ends
        for j in range(len(mpre) - 2, -1, -1):  # from right to left ...
            mpre[j] = max(mpre[j], mpre[j + 1])  # ... make precision non-increasing
        changes = np.where(mrec[1:] != mrec[:-1])[0]  # points where recall changes
        # area under the precision-recall curve
        class_ap[class_name] = float(np.sum((mrec[changes + 1] - mrec[changes]) * mpre[changes + 1]))
    finite = [v for v in class_ap.values() if np.isfinite(v)]  # defined APs
    return float(np.mean(finite)) if finite else np.nan, class_ap  # mean AP and per-class APs

EPOCHS = 5 if DEVICE == "cuda" else 2  # epochs (fewer on a CPU)
# AdamW on the trainable weights
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad],
                              lr=2e-4, weight_decay=1e-4)
history = []  # per-epoch log
best_state = None  # best weights so far
best_val_ap = -np.inf  # best validation AP so far
for epoch in range(EPOCHS):  # each epoch
    model.train()  # training mode
    loss_sums = {}  # summed losses
    n_batches = 0  # batch count
    started = time.time()  # start the timer
    for images, targets in train_loader:  # each batch
        images = [image.to(DEVICE) for image in images]  # images to the device
        targets = [{k: v.to(DEVICE) for k, v in target.items()} for target in targets]  # targets to the device
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)  # clear gradients
        loss_dict = model(images, targets)  # the five Mask R-CNN losses
        total_loss = sum(loss_dict.values())  # their sum
        if not torch.isfinite(total_loss):  # stop if the loss is not finite ...
            # ... with a clear message
            raise FloatingPointError(f"Non-finite training loss at epoch {epoch + 1}")
        total_loss.backward()  # gradients
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=5.0)  # clip large gradients
        optimizer.step()  # update the weights
        for key, value in loss_dict.items():  # each loss term ...
            loss_sums[key] = loss_sums.get(key, 0.0) + float(value.detach())  # ... added up
        n_batches += 1  # count the batch
    mean_loss = sum(loss_sums.values()) / max(n_batches, 1)  # mean loss per batch
    val_ap, val_by_class = evaluate_mask_ap(model, val_loader)  # validation AP
    history.append({"epoch": epoch + 1, "train_loss": mean_loss,  # log the epoch
                    "val_mask_ap50": val_ap, **{f"val_ap_{k}": v for k, v in val_by_class.items()}})
    if np.isfinite(val_ap) and val_ap > best_val_ap:  # better validation AP ...
        best_val_ap = val_ap  # ... remember it
        best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())  # ... and the weights
    print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:02d}/{EPOCHS} | loss={mean_loss:.3f} | "  # progress line
          f"val mask AP50={val_ap:.3f} | {time.time() - started:.1f}s")

if best_state is not None:  # best weights found ...
    model.load_state_dict(best_state)  # ... restore them
else:
    # otherwise keep the last epoch
    warnings.warn("Validation AP was unavailable; retaining the final epoch weights")
history = pd.DataFrame(history)  # log as a table
history  # show it

section: Held-out spatial evaluation: mask AP and instance IoU
text:
Held-out spatial evaluation: mask AP and instance IoU
The test band is not used for optimization or checkpoint choice. The AP implementation uses confidence-ranked, one-to-one matching within each chip. A match is a true positive only when the predicted and reference binary masks have IoU ≥ 0.50; duplicate matches and unmatched predictions count as false positives. AP is averaged across classes with test references.


Code
# AP at IoU 0.5 on the test chips
test_mask_ap50, test_ap_by_class = evaluate_mask_ap(model, test_loader, iou_threshold=0.50)
print(f"Test mask mAP@0.50: {test_mask_ap50:.3f}")  # headline score
display(pd.DataFrame({"class": list(test_ap_by_class),  # AP per class
                      "mask_AP50": list(test_ap_by_class.values())}))

# IoU of each matched test instance
def test_instance_ious(model, dataset, score_threshold=0.5, iou_threshold=0.5):
    rows = []  # result rows
    model.eval()  # evaluation mode
    with torch.inference_mode():  # no gradients
        for index in range(len(dataset)):  # each test chip
            image, target = dataset[index]  # its image and target
            output = model([image.to(DEVICE)])[0]  # predict it
            pred_masks = (output["masks"][:, 0] >= 0.5).cpu().numpy()  # predicted masks
            pred_labels = output["labels"].cpu().numpy()  # predicted classes
            scores = output["scores"].cpu().numpy()  # confidence scores
            true_masks = target["masks"].numpy().astype(bool)  # reference masks
            true_labels = target["labels"].numpy()  # reference classes
            for class_id, class_name in CLASS_NAMES.items():  # each class
                # confident predictions of this class
                pm = [m for m, lb, sc in zip(pred_masks, pred_labels, scores)
                      if lb == class_id and sc >= score_threshold]
                tm = true_masks[true_labels == class_id]  # references of this class
                ious = mask_iou_matrix(np.asarray(pm), tm)  # IoU matrix
                pairs = []  # all prediction-reference pairs
                for p in range(len(pm)):  # each prediction ...
                    for t in range(len(tm)):  # ... and each reference ...
                        pairs.append((ious[p, t], p, t))  # ... with their IoU
                used_p, used_t = set(), set()  # used predictions and references
                for iou, p, t in sorted(pairs, reverse=True):  # best pairs first
                    if iou < iou_threshold:  # below the threshold ...
                        break
                    if p not in used_p and t not in used_t:  # both still free ...
                        used_p.add(p)  # ... use the prediction
                        used_t.add(t)  # ... and the reference
                        # record the match
                        rows.append({"chip": index, "class": class_name, "mask_IoU": float(iou)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)  # as a table

matched_ious = test_instance_ious(model, test_ds)  # matched test instances
if len(matched_ious):  # any matches ...
    # ... count, mean and median IoU per class
    display(matched_ious.groupby("class")["mask_IoU"].agg(["count", "mean", "median"]))
else:
    # none matched
    print("No test instances passed the score and IoU thresholds; inspect predictions and labels.")

text:
Test-chip predictions: inspect masks, not only scores
The predicted masks are overlaid on a three-band display composite; reference polygon masks are shown separately for comparison. Low scores and partial fields near chip edges are expected in this compact demonstration. A chipwise prediction avoids implying that a seamless scene-wide mosaic has been evaluated.


Code
# draw instance outlines in their class colours
def draw_instance_masks(ax, masks, class_ids, scores=None, threshold=0.5):
    for i, (mask, class_id) in enumerate(zip(masks, class_ids)):  # each mask
        if scores is not None and scores[i] < threshold:  # below the score threshold ...
            continue
        color = CLASS_COLORS.get(int(class_id), "white")  # class colour
        ax.contour(mask.astype(float), levels=[0.5], colors=[color], linewidths=1.2)  # outline

model.eval()  # evaluation mode
preview_ids = list(range(min(3, len(test_ds))))  # first three test chips
# three panels per chip
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(preview_ids), 3, figsize=(13, 4 * len(preview_ids)), squeeze=False)
with torch.inference_mode():  # no gradients
    for row_i, index in enumerate(preview_ids):  # each chip
        image, target = test_ds[index]  # its image and target
        output = model([image.to(DEVICE)])[0]  # predict it
        rgb_chip = np.moveaxis(image[[3, 1, 0]].numpy(), 0, -1)  # B4, B2, B1 as RGB
        pred_masks = (output["masks"][:, 0] >= 0.5).cpu().numpy()  # predicted masks
        pred_labels = output["labels"].cpu().numpy()  # predicted classes
        pred_scores = output["scores"].cpu().numpy()  # confidence scores
        axes[row_i, 0].imshow(rgb_chip)  # image
        axes[row_i, 0].set_title(f"Test chip {index}: image")  # title
        axes[row_i, 1].imshow(rgb_chip)  # image
        # predicted outlines
        draw_instance_masks(axes[row_i, 1], pred_masks, pred_labels, pred_scores, threshold=0.5)
        axes[row_i, 1].set_title("Predicted masks (score ≥ 0.5)")  # title
        axes[row_i, 2].imshow(rgb_chip)  # image
        # reference outlines
        draw_instance_masks(axes[row_i, 2], target["masks"].numpy(), target["labels"].numpy())
        axes[row_i, 2].set_title("Reference instance masks")  # title
        for a in axes[row_i]:  # each panel ...
            a.axis("off")  # ... without axes

text:
Georeferenced instance polygons with GeoLattice
instances_from_detector converts each Mask R-CNN output mask to a polygon using the chip’s own CRS and affine transform. export_vectors writes a GeoPackage. The exported features retain predicted class, confidence and area; they are model proposals and should not be treated as authoritative field boundaries without visual review.


Code
vector_parts = []  # polygons per chip
prediction_rows = []  # raw outputs
model.eval()  # evaluation mode
with torch.inference_mode():  # no gradients
    for chip_index, (row0, col0) in enumerate(windows["test"]):  # each test chip
        chip = torch.from_numpy(scaled[:, row0:row0 + PATCH, col0:col0 + PATCH])  # its scaled bands
        output = model([chip.to(DEVICE)])[0]  # predict it
        prediction_rows.append(output)  # keep the output
        # the matching image window
        chip_da = image_da.isel(y=slice(row0, row0 + PATCH), x=slice(col0, col0 + PATCH))
        chip_da = chip_da.rio.write_transform(  # shift the transform to the chip corner
            raster_transform * Affine.translation(col0, row0)
        )
        vectors = ic.instances_from_detector(  # masks -> georeferenced polygons
            output,
            chip_da,
            score_threshold=0.5,
            mask_threshold=0.5,
            class_names=CLASS_NAMES,
            simplify=0.5,
        )
        if len(vectors):  # any polygons ...
            vectors["chip_id"] = chip_index  # ... tag them with the chip
            vector_parts.append(vectors)  # ... and keep them

if vector_parts:  # polygons found ...
    predicted_fields = gpd.GeoDataFrame(pd.concat(vector_parts, ignore_index=True),  # ... one GeoDataFrame
                                        geometry="geometry", crs=raster_crs)
else:
    predicted_fields = gpd.GeoDataFrame(  # otherwise an empty one
        {"label": [], "class_name": [], "confidence": [], "area": [], "chip_id": []},
        geometry=[], crs=raster_crs,
    )
vector_path = OUTPUT_DIR / "mask_rcnn_test_instances.gpkg"  # output GeoPackage
if len(predicted_fields):  # anything to write ...
    ic.export_vectors(predicted_fields, vector_path, layer="predicted_instances")  # ... export it
    display(predicted_fields.drop(columns="geometry").head())  # first rows
    print(f"Saved {len(predicted_fields)} predicted instances to {vector_path}")  # report
else:
    # nothing written
    print("No instances exceeded the vector-export score threshold; no vector file was written.")

title: Instance Segmentation of Agricultural Fields with Mask R-CNN
text:
Interpretation, caveats and recommended recipe

Instance segmentation is not box detection. Every prediction has a pixel mask; bounding boxes are auxiliary proposal targets. Tree-detection files in this data folder are box annotations and are intentionally not repurposed as instance masks.
The source labels are field polygons. Rasterization introduces grid effects, narrow polygons can disappear at 1.6 m pixels, and neighboring/overlapping annotations may compete for pixels. Inspect the rasterized mask overlay before interpreting scores.
The split is spatial but small. Contiguous row bands reduce direct chip leakage; they do not represent independent farms, seasons or sensors. The test set is one geographic strip.
Eight-band scaling matters. Percentile bounds are fitted from training rows and reused unchanged. For another WorldView-2 scene, repeat radiometric preprocessing consistently and verify band order and calibration.
Model scores are not calibrated confidence. Mask AP at a fixed IoU threshold combines localization and classification; report per-class results and inspect errors, especially touching fields and chip-edge truncation.
Recommended extension: collect spatially independent polygon labels, reserve a separate farm/AOI for final evaluation, compare pretrained and scratch starts, tune score/mask thresholds on validation only, and quantify uncertainty across multiple spatial folds.

The predicted GeoPackage is a reviewable vector product. Keep the raster, transform, CRS, class mapping and preprocessing metadata with any downstream field-area analysis.

Overview
MODIS images the Earth every day but with 500 m pixels; Landsat and Sentinel-2 resolve fields at 10 m to 30 m but revisit every five to sixteen days and lose dates to clouds; Sentinel-1 radar sees through clouds but measures structure and moisture rather than colour; commercial and aerial images (Planet, RapidEye, NAIP) show individual trees and buildings but cover little area and few dates. title: Multi-sensor image fusion
text:
Workflow and GeoLattice functions

Read the local images, download the MODIS 8-day composites, the Sentinel-1 scenes and the CDL for the AOI once with get_images (later runs read them from the local drive), and line up the acquisition dates.
Spatiotemporal fusion: predict Landsat-like 30 m images for 14 and 24 July from the 9 July Landsat image and the MODIS composites with geolattice.rsense.fusion.starfm, and score them against PlanetScope (14 July) and RapidEye (24 July).
Optical-SAR gap filling: cover part of the Sentinel-2 image with a synthetic cloud and fill it from Sentinel-1 (and MODIS) with sar_assisted_gap_fill.
Scale effects: compute vegetation cover from the 0.6 m NAIP image, aggregate it with geolattice.rsense.fusion.upscale, and compare it with what Sentinel-2, Landsat and MODIS pixels see, using geolattice.rsense.fusion.compare.
Multi-sensor classification: map the CDL classes from optical, radar and MODIS time-series features alone, and with early (fuse_early) and late (fuse_late) fusion, on a spatial-block split.
Write the fused products as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs.


Imports, paths, and settings
The cell imports the libraries, finds the repository and the Image_Fusion folder, and defines ensure_download: it reads a product from the local drive when an earlier run has saved it, and otherwise searches Planetary Computer and downloads it with get_images, clipped to the AOI. MODIS 500 m composites come from the modis-09A1-061 collection (Terra only, MOD09A1), Sentinel-1 from the radiometrically terrain-corrected sentinel-1-rtc collection, and the CDL from usda-cdl.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.

from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap  # class colours

from skimage.filters import threshold_otsu  # automatic vegetation threshold
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier  # the classifier

             if (p / "pyproject.toml").exists() and (p / "src" / "rsense").is_dir()), None)

import geolattice.rsense as rs  # GeoLattice remote sensing (fusion, reading, writing)
import geolattice.rsense.classify.image_classification as ic  # fusion helpers, splits and accuracy
from geolattice.rsense.get_images import get_images, search_images  # search and download

if ROOT is None:  # not started inside the repository
    raise FileNotFoundError("Start Jupyter from the GeoLattice checkout or one of its subdirectories")  # stop
# this notebook's folder
NOTEBOOK_DIR = ROOT / "Tutorials" / "notebooks" / "08_remote_sensing" / "09_09_image_classification"
IF = NOTEBOOK_DIR / "../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_09_image_classification" / "Image_Fusion"  # the fusion data folder
OUTPUT_DIR = NOTEBOOK_DIR / "outputs" / "image_fusion"  # products of this notebook
OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed

def ensure_download(folder, collection, dates, bands, id_prefix=None):  # local first, else download once
    out = IF / folder  # where the scenes are kept
    if any(out.glob("*/item.json")):  # downloaded before
        # report the local scenes
        print(f"{folder}: reading {len(list(out.glob('*/item.json')))} scenes from the local drive")
        return out  # nothing to download
    # search the Planetary Computer
    found = search_images(aoi=aoi, dates=dates, source="planetary", collection=collection, limit=50, quiet=True)
    ids = sorted(i.id for i in found.items if id_prefix is None or i.id.startswith(id_prefix))  # scenes to keep
    get_images(out, search=found, ids=ids, bands=bands, mode="clip", quiet=True)  # download, clipped to the AOI

# MODIS band names
MODIS_BANDS = {"sur_refl_b01": "red", "sur_refl_b02": "nir", "sur_refl_b03": "blue", "sur_refl_b04": "green",
               "sur_refl_b06": "swir1", "sur_refl_b07": "swir2"}  # MODIS asset -> band name
# MODIS 8-day reflectance for the summer of 2019
MODIS_DIR = ensure_download("MODIS_MOD09A1_2019", "modis-09A1-061", ("2019-06-15", "2019-08-12"),
                            [*MODIS_BANDS, "sur_refl_state_500m"], id_prefix="MOD09A1")  # Terra 8-day, 500 m
S1_DIR = ensure_download("Sentinel_1_RTC_2019", "sentinel-1-rtc", ("2019-06-20", "2019-08-10"), ["vv", "vh"])  # Sentinel-1 RTC, VV and VH
# CDL 2019 for the AOI

Read every sensor as reflectance
Each product is read as an (band, y, x) array with named bands, scaled to surface reflectance (0 to 1), with no-data and flagged pixels set to missing:

Landsat 8 and Sentinel-2 are already scaled; their clear-sky masks remove the few cloudy pixels.
PlanetScope and RapidEye analytic surface reflectance are stored as reflectance × 10,000.
NAIP is an 8-bit-like digital-number image without radiometric calibration; it is used only for its spatial detail (vegetation versus non-vegetation), never as reflectance.
MODIS MOD09A1 reflectance is scaled by 0.0001; the state quality band removes cloudy, cloud-shadowed and cirrus pixels. Each composite takes, for every pixel, the best observation of an 8-day window starting on its day of year.
Sentinel-1 RTC backscatter (gamma-nought) is converted to decibels.

Two local files need a warning: RapidEye_Rural_AOI_July_14_2019.tif is pixel-for-pixel identical to the 24 July file (the only RapidEye metadata in the folder is for 24 July), so RapidEye is used as one date, 24 July.


Code
def read_img(path, names, scale=1.0, mask=None):  # (band, y, x) reflectance with named bands
    da = rioxarray.open_rasterio(path, masked=True).astype("float32") * scale  # read and scale
    da = da.where(da > 0).assign_coords(band=names)  # zero is no data in these products
    if mask is not None:  # a clear-sky mask (1 = clear)
        m = rioxarray.open_rasterio(mask).squeeze(drop=True)  # the mask
        da = da.where(m == 1)  # keep clear pixels only
    return da  # the image


LS_DIR, S2_DIR = IF / "Landsat8_20190709", IF / "Sentinel_2" / "L2A_T17TQH_20190708"  # local folders
landsat = read_img(LS_DIR / "landsat8_20190709_surface_reflectance_30m.tif",  # Landsat 8, 9 July, 30 m
                   ["coastal", "blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"], mask=LS_DIR / "clear_mask.tif")
s2 = read_img(S2_DIR / "sentinel2_20190708_surface_reflectance_6band_10m.tif",  # Sentinel-2, 8 July, 10 m
              ["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"], mask=S2_DIR / "clear_mask_10m.tif")
planet = {"2019-07-08": read_img(IF / "Planet/July_08_2019/Planet_Rural_AOI_July_08_2019.tif", ["blue", "green", "red", "nir"], 1e-4),  # PlanetScope, 3 m, two dates
          "2019-07-14": read_img(IF / "Planet/July_14_2019/Planet_Rural_AOI_July_14_2019_NAD.tif", ["blue", "green", "red", "nir"], 1e-4)}
rapideye = read_img(IF / "RapidEye/RapidEye_Rural_AOI_July_24_2019.tif", ["blue", "green", "red", "rededge", "nir"], 1e-4)  # RapidEye, 24 July, 5 m


def modis(doy):  # one MOD09A1 composite (start day of year) with its cloud mask applied
    folder = next(MODIS_DIR.glob(f"MOD09A1.A2019{doy:03d}.*"))  # its scene folder
    # the seven MODIS bands
    bands = [rioxarray.open_rasterio(folder / f"{a}.tif", masked=True).squeeze(drop=True) for a in MODIS_BANDS]
    da = xr.concat(bands, dim="band").assign_coords(band=list(MODIS_BANDS.values())) * 1e-4  # reflectance
    # MODIS quality (state) flags
    state = rioxarray.open_rasterio(folder / "sur_refl_state_500m.tif").squeeze(drop=True).values.astype(int)
    clear = ((state & 0b11) == 0) & ((state >> 2 & 1) == 0) & ((state >> 8 & 0b11) == 0)  # no cloud, shadow, cirrus
    return da.where(clear).astype("float32").rio.write_crs(bands[0].rio.crs)  # masked composite


MODIS_DOY = sorted(int(p.name.split(".")[1][5:]) for p in MODIS_DIR.glob("MOD09A1.*"))  # composite start days
mod = {d: modis(d) for d in MODIS_DOY}  # every composite
mod_start = {d: pd.Timestamp("2019-01-01") + pd.Timedelta(days=d - 1) for d in MODIS_DOY}  # first day of each


def s1_db(folder):  # VV and VH backscatter in dB
    # VV and VH as one array
    da = xr.concat([rioxarray.open_rasterio(folder / f"{p}.tif", masked=True).squeeze(drop=True) for p in ("vv", "vh")],
                   dim="band").assign_coords(band=["vv", "vh"])  # linear gamma-nought
    crs = rioxarray.open_rasterio(folder / "vv.tif").rio.crs  # its CRS
    return (10 * np.log10(da.where(da > 0))).astype("float32").rio.write_crs(crs)  # decibels


s1 = {pd.Timestamp(p.name.split("_")[4][:8]): s1_db(p) for p in sorted(S1_DIR.glob("S1A_*"))}  # date -> (band, y, x)
cdl_dir = next(CDL_DIR.glob("cropland_2019*"))  # the CDL scene folder
cdl = rioxarray.open_rasterio(cdl_dir / "cropland.tif").squeeze(drop=True)  # crop codes (EPSG:5070)
cdl_conf = rioxarray.open_rasterio(cdl_dir / "confidence.tif").squeeze(drop=True)  # per-pixel confidence (%)

    "Landsat 8, 9 Jul": landsat.rio.resolution()[0], "Sentinel-2, 8 Jul": s2.rio.resolution()[0],
    "PlanetScope, 8 Jul": planet["2019-07-08"].rio.resolution()[0], "PlanetScope, 14 Jul": planet["2019-07-14"].rio.resolution()[0],

Fusion assumes that what one sensor saw is still there when the other looks. The figure places every acquisition on one time axis: the 8-day MODIS windows as bars, the other sensors as points. title: Multi-sensor image fusion
text:
Spatiotemporal fusion with STARFM

Predict Landsat-like images for 14 and 24 July
STARFM (Gao et al. 2006) predicts a fine image at a date when only the coarse sensor observed. From a fine/coarse pair at t1 (Landsat on 9 July with the MODIS composite of 4 to 11 July) and a coarse image at t2, each fine pixel takes its t1 value plus the coarse-scale change, averaged over spectrally similar neighbours inside a moving window and weighted towards neighbours whose coarse pixel changed little and matched the fine image well. geolattice.rsense.fusion.starfm expects the coarse images already resampled to the fine grid; here MODIS is reprojected onto the 30 m Landsat grid by nearest neighbour, so every 463 m MODIS pixel becomes a block of about 15 × 15 Landsat pixels.
Missing pixels need care: in the current starfm, a missing value anywhere inside a pixel’s 31-pixel window makes that pixel’s prediction missing too, and the 20 to 27 July composite has clouds over part of the AOI. starfm_masked therefore fills missing inputs with the nearest valid value before calling starfm, and masks the prediction again wherever an input was really missing.
Two prediction dates are tested, each against a real fine image the method never saw:

14 July with the MODIS composite of 12 to 19 July; truth: PlanetScope of 14 July;
24 July with the MODIS composite of 20 to 27 July; truth: RapidEye of 24 July.



Code
LS_GRID = landsat.sel(band="red")  # the 30 m target grid
on_ls = lambda da, how: da.rio.reproject_match(LS_GRID, resampling=how)  # put any raster on the Landsat grid
T1_DOY = 185  # MODIS composite of 4-11 July, paired with Landsat of 9 July
# target dates: day of year, name and image
TARGETS = {"2019-07-14": (193, "PlanetScope 14 Jul", planet["2019-07-14"]),
           "2019-07-24": (201, "RapidEye 24 Jul", rapideye)}  # date -> (MODIS composite, truth name, truth image)
coarse = {d: on_ls(mod[d], Resampling.nearest) for d in (T1_DOY, 193, 201)}  # MODIS blocks on the 30 m grid


def fill_nearest(a):  # replace missing pixels with the nearest valid value (window input only)
    miss = np.isnan(a)  # missing pixels
    if not miss.any():  # nothing to fill
        return a  # unchanged
    idx = ndimage.distance_transform_edt(miss, return_distances=False, return_indices=True)  # nearest valid pixel
    return a[tuple(idx)]  # filled copy


def starfm_masked(f1, c1, c2, **kw):  # STARFM on filled inputs, masked where any input was missing
    valid = np.isfinite(f1.values) & np.isfinite(c1.values) & np.isfinite(c2.values)  # real observations
    p = rs.fusion.starfm(*(a.copy(data=fill_nearest(a.values)) for a in (f1, c1, c2)), **kw)  # the fusion
    return p.where(valid)  # no prediction where an input was missing
print({f"A{d}": f"{mod_start[d]:%d %b}-{mod_start[d] + pd.Timedelta(days=7):%d %b}" for d in coarse})  # the three composites and their windows


{'A185': '04 Jul-11 Jul', 'A193': '12 Jul-19 Jul', 'A201': '20 Jul-27 Jul'}




A cross-sensor reference
PlanetScope and RapidEye have other spectral bands and calibrations than Landsat, so their reflectances cannot be compared directly. Each is first averaged onto the 30 m Landsat grid with upscale, and then put on Landsat’s radiometric scale with a pseudo-invariant feature (PIF) normalisation: a straight line per band, fitted between the reference sensor and Landsat on pixels that are not expected to change within two weeks (CDL forest and developed land). Crop fields are left out of the fit, because their change is exactly what STARFM has to predict.


Code
cdl30 = on_ls(cdl, Resampling.nearest).values  # CDL codes on the Landsat grid
PIF = np.isin(cdl30, [121, 122, 123, 124, 141, 142, 143])  # developed and forest: stable over two weeks
truth, pif_fit = {}, {}  # Landsat-scaled reference images and their fits
for date, (_, name, fine) in TARGETS.items():  # each reference image
    # fine image averaged onto the Landsat grid
    agg = xr.concat([rs.fusion.upscale(fine.sel(band=b), LS_GRID, method="mean") for b in ("red", "nir")],
                    dim="band").assign_coords(band=["red", "nir"])  # averaged onto the 30 m grid
    out = []  # normalised bands
    for b in ("red", "nir"):  # each band
        x, y = agg.sel(band=b).values, landsat.sel(band=b).values  # reference and Landsat
        ok = PIF & np.isfinite(x) & np.isfinite(y)  # usable invariant pixels
        slope, icpt = np.polyfit(x[ok], y[ok], 1)  # Landsat = slope * reference + intercept
        # the fit of each sensor and band
        pif_fit[name, b] = {"slope": slope, "intercept": icpt, "PIF pixels": int(ok.sum()),
                            "r": float(np.corrcoef(x[ok], y[ok])[0, 1])}  # the fit
        out.append(agg.sel(band=b) * slope + icpt)  # rescaled band
    truth[date] = xr.concat(out, dim="band")  # the 30 m reference on Landsat's scale

The fits are far from one-to-one (slopes 0.62 to 0.83, intercepts up to 0.12) and the correlations on the stable pixels are 0.82 to 0.90: the two sensors measure the same surfaces on clearly different scales. That spread enters every score below as part of the reference.


Run STARFM and score it
Four predictions of each date are compared with the reference, band by band:

no change: the 9 July Landsat image itself;
MODIS at t2: the coarse composite of the target date, resampled to 30 m (all change, no spatial detail);
Landsat + MODIS change: the 9 July image plus the MODIS difference between the two composites, without STARFM’s neighbour weighting;
STARFM, with a 31-pixel (930 m) window.

All four are scored on the same pixels (where every prediction and the reference exist). The RMSE is reported over all of them and over the 10 % of pixels whose reference changed most since 9 July, where a good fusion method has to beat “no change”.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start the timer
pred, rows = {}, []  # STARFM predictions and scores
for date, (doy, name, _) in TARGETS.items():  # each target date
    for b in ("red", "nir"):  # each band
        f1, c1, c2 = landsat.sel(band=b), coarse[T1_DOY].sel(band=b), coarse[doy].sel(band=b)  # STARFM inputs
        p = starfm_masked(f1, c1, c2, window=31, n_classes=4)  # the fusion
        pred[date, b] = p  # keep it
        ref = truth[date].sel(band=b).values  # the reference
        # candidate predictions for t2
        cands = {"no change (Landsat 9 Jul)": f1.values, "MODIS at t2": c2.values,
                 "Landsat + MODIS change": (f1 + c2 - c1).values, "STARFM": p.values}  # the four predictions
        common = np.isfinite(ref) & np.all([np.isfinite(v) for v in cands.values()], axis=0)  # same pixels for all
        ref = np.where(common, ref, np.nan)  # score on the common pixels only
        change = np.abs(ref - f1.values)  # how much the pixel changed
        big = change >= np.nanpercentile(change, 90)  # the 10 % most changed pixels
        for method, v in cands.items():  # score each
            e = v - ref  # error
            rows.append({"date": date, "band": b, "method": method, "pixels": int(common.sum()),  # one score row
                         "RMSE all": float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean(e ** 2))),
                         "RMSE most changed 10 %": float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean(e[big] ** 2)))})
print(f"STARFM for 2 dates x 2 bands in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")  # run time
METHODS = ["no change (Landsat 9 Jul)", "MODIS at t2", "Landsat + MODIS change", "STARFM"]  # column order
starfm_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot_table(index=["date", "band"], columns="method", values=["RMSE all", "RMSE most changed 10 %"])  # scores as a table
starfm_tab = starfm_tab.reindex(columns=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["RMSE all", "RMSE most changed 10 %"], METHODS]))  # columns in a fixed order
# pixels scored per date and band
print("pixels scored per date and band:", pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby(["date", "band"]).pixels.first().to_dict())
starfm_tab.round(4)  # show it

On 14 July, five days after the Landsat image, STARFM has the lowest error of the four methods in both bands, and on the most-changed pixels it clearly beats “no change”; in the NIR the plain MODIS composite does even better on those pixels, because the largest changes (winter wheat harvest, hay cuts) are wide enough for MODIS to see.           "MODIS 20-27 Jul (input)": ndvi(coarse[201].sel(band="red"), coarse[201].sel(band="nir")),
          "STARFM 24 Jul": ndvi(pred["2019-07-24", "red"], pred["2019-07-24", "nir"]),

title: Multi-sensor image fusion
text:
Optical-SAR gap filling

Fill a synthetic cloud in Sentinel-2 from Sentinel-1
Clouds remove optical observations; radar sees through them. If optical and SAR images are close in time, a model trained on the cloud-free pixels can predict optical reflectance under the clouds from the backscatter. The Sentinel-2 image of 8 July is almost cloud-free, so an elliptical “cloud” covering about a fifth of the AOI is cut out of it on purpose; the real reflectance under it is the truth.
sar_assisted_gap_fill trains a random forest per band on the clear pixels (SAR variables and pixel coordinates as predictors), predicts the masked pixels, and returns a reconstructed flag so that predicted values can never be mistaken for observations. Three predictor sets are compared:

Sentinel-1, 11 July: VV and VH of the scene three days after Sentinel-2;
Sentinel-1, four dates: VV and VH of 29 June, 11 July, 23 July and 4 August, whose change over the season separates crops that look alike on one date;
Sentinel-1, four dates + MODIS: the same plus the cloud-free MODIS composite of 4 to 11 July, a coarse optical view of the same week.



Code
OPT_BANDS = ["red", "nir", "swir1"]  # bands to reconstruct
opt = s2.sel(band=OPT_BANDS).to_dataset(dim="band")  # Sentinel-2 as a Dataset of bands
yy, xx = np.mgrid[:s2.sizes["y"], :s2.sizes["x"]]  # pixel rows and columns
cloud = ((yy - 300) / 140) ** 2 + ((xx - 270) / 170) ** 2 < 1  # synthetic elliptical cloud
cloudy = opt.where(~xr.DataArray(cloud, dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": s2.y, "x": s2.x}))  # cloud cut out
under = cloud & np.isfinite(opt["red"].values)  # pixels to evaluate
print(f"synthetic cloud: {under.sum()} pixels, {under.sum() / np.isfinite(opt['red'].values).sum():.0%} of the clear AOI")  # size of the cloud

S2_GRID = s2.sel(band="red")  # the 10 m grid
sar_vars = {}  # SAR predictors on the Sentinel-2 grid
for d, da in s1.items():  # every Sentinel-1 date
    for p in ("vv", "vh"):  # both polarisations
        # each SAR date on the Sentinel-2 grid
        sar_vars[f"{p}_{d:%m%d}"] = (da.sel(band=p).rio.reproject_match(S2_GRID, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)
                                     .drop_vars("band", errors="ignore"))  # one layer, without its band label
# MODIS bands on the Sentinel-2 grid
mod_vars = {f"modis_{b}": mod[T1_DOY].sel(band=b).rio.reproject_match(S2_GRID, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)
            .drop_vars("band", errors="ignore") for b in OPT_BANDS}  # MODIS 4-11 July on the 10 m grid
PREDICTORS = {"Sentinel-1, 11 July": xr.Dataset({k: v for k, v in sar_vars.items() if k.endswith("0711")}),  # three predictor sets
              "Sentinel-1, four dates": xr.Dataset(sar_vars),
              "Sentinel-1, four dates + MODIS": xr.Dataset({**sar_vars, **mod_vars})}
gap_rows, filled_all = {}, {}  # scores and filled images
for name, feats in PREDICTORS.items():  # each predictor set
    # SAR-assisted gap filling
    filled, r2 = ic.sar_assisted_gap_fill(cloudy, feats.rio.write_crs(s2.rio.crs), model="rf",
                                          n_estimators=100, max_train=30000, seed=SEED)  # fill the cloud
    filled_all[name] = filled  # keep it
    for b in OPT_BANDS:  # score each band under the cloud
        t, f = opt[b].values[under], filled[b].values[under]  # truth and fill
        gap_rows[name, b] = {"RMSE": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((f - t) ** 2))), "R2 under the cloud": float(1 - np.mean((f - t) ** 2) / np.var(t)),  # scores under the cloud
                             "holdout R2 on clear pixels": r2.get(b, np.nan),
                             "flagged reconstructed": int(filled["reconstructed"].values[under].sum())}
for b in OPT_BANDS:  # baseline: fill with the scene mean
    t = opt[b].values[under]  # truth
    gap_rows["scene-mean fill", b] = {"RMSE": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.nanmean(cloudy[b].values) - t) ** 2))),  # the trivial fill
                                      "R2 under the cloud": 0.0, "holdout R2 on clear pixels": np.nan, "flagged reconstructed": 0}
