nd = lambda ds: (ds["nir"] - ds["red"]) / (ds["nir"] + ds["red"])  # NDVI of a Dataset
maps = {"Sentinel-2 8 Jul with the synthetic cloud": nd(cloudy), "filled from Sentinel-1, 11 July": nd(filled_all["Sentinel-1, 11 July"]),  # the four NDVI panels
        "filled from Sentinel-1 four dates + MODIS": nd(filled_all["Sentinel-1, four dates + MODIS"]), "truth": nd(opt)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(19, 5))  # four panels
for a, (t, v) in zip(ax, maps.items()):  # each panel
    a.imshow(v, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0.1, vmax=0.95); a.contour(cloud.astype(int), levels=[0.5], colors="k", linewidths=0.8)  # NDVI and cloud edge
    a.set_title(t, fontsize=10); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])  # title, no ticks

Reading the gap-filling results. Under the cloud, Sentinel-1 of one date is barely better than filling with the scene mean, and in the NIR it is worse (negative R²). Four dates help, and adding the coarse MODIS composite helps most for red and NIR. Yet the hold-out R² that sar_assisted_gap_fill reports on clear pixels is 0.66 to 0.88. Those hold-out pixels lie scattered among the training pixels, and the pixel coordinates are among the predictors, so the model can interpolate from close neighbours, which it cannot do in the middle of a large cloud. The rectangular stripes inside the filled area are the same effect: the random forest splits on the coordinates. Validate gap filling under a realistic cloud, never on a random hold-out alone.

title: Multi-sensor image fusion
section: Scale effects: from NAIP to Sentinel-2, Landsat and MODIS pixels
text:
Scale effects: from NAIP to Sentinel-2, Landsat and MODIS pixels

Vegetation cover at 0.6 m as the reference
A coarse pixel often contains several land covers. The 0.6 m NAIP image of 14 July resolves single trees, roads and farmsteads, so it can tell how much of each Sentinel-2, Landsat or MODIS pixel is vegetated. NAIP is read at 1.2 m (2 × 2 average) to save memory, NDVI is computed from its red and NIR bands, and pixels above an automatic (Otsu) threshold are vegetation. upscale then averages the binary map onto each sensor’s grid: the result is the true vegetation fraction of every coarse pixel. Only coarse pixels at least 95 % covered by NAIP are kept.
Each sensor’s own NDVI is turned into vegetation cover in two ways:

classified: the pixel is vegetation or not (Otsu threshold on that sensor’s NDVI), the usual output of a land-cover map;
fractional: the fractional vegetation cover \((\mathrm{NDVI} - \mathrm{NDVI}_{soil}) / (\mathrm{NDVI}_{veg} - \mathrm{NDVI}_{soil})\), clipped to 0 to 1, with the 2nd and 98th NDVI percentiles of the AOI as the soil and vegetation end-members.

compare gives R², RMSE and bias of each against the NAIP fraction.


Code
naip_path = IF / "HR" / "HR_Rural_AOI_July_14.tif"  # NAIP, 0.6 m, red/green/blue/NIR
with rasterio.open(naip_path) as src:  # read at 1.2 m (2 x 2 average)
    # NAIP at half resolution (block average)
    arr = src.read(out_shape=(src.count, src.height // 2, src.width // 2), resampling=Resampling.average).astype("float32")
    tr = src.transform * src.transform.scale(src.width / arr.shape[2], src.height / arr.shape[1])  # 1.2 m transform
    naip_crs = src.crs  # its CRS
arr[:, (arr == 0).all(axis=0) | (arr >= 256).any(axis=0)] = np.nan  # no data outside the AOI
xs_n = tr.c + (np.arange(arr.shape[2]) + 0.5) * tr.a  # pixel-centre eastings
ys_n = tr.f + (np.arange(arr.shape[1]) + 0.5) * tr.e  # pixel-centre northings
naip_ndvi = (arr[3] - arr[0]) / (arr[3] + arr[0])  # NAIP NDVI (digital numbers, relative only)
veg_thr = threshold_otsu(naip_ndvi[np.isfinite(naip_ndvi)])  # automatic vegetation threshold
# NAIP vegetation mask (missing where NAIP has no data)
veg = xr.DataArray(np.where(np.isfinite(naip_ndvi), (naip_ndvi > veg_thr).astype("float32"), np.nan),
                   dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": ys_n, "x": xs_n}).rio.write_crs(naip_crs)  # 1 = vegetation
covered = veg.notnull().astype("float32")  # 1 where NAIP has data
print(f"NAIP at 1.2 m: {veg.shape}, NDVI threshold {veg_thr:.3f}, vegetation cover {float(veg.mean()):.1%}")  # size, threshold and cover

SENSORS = {"Sentinel-2 (10 m)": (s2.sel(band="red"), s2.sel(band="nir")),  # sensor -> red, NIR
           "Landsat 8 (30 m)": (landsat.sel(band="red"), landsat.sel(band="nir")),
           "MODIS (463 m)": (mod[193].sel(band="red"), mod[193].sel(band="nir"))}  # sensor -> red, NIR
scale_rows, scale_maps = {}, {}  # scores and maps
for name, (red, nir) in SENSORS.items():  # every sensor
    v = ndvi(red, nir)  # its NDVI
    frac = rs.fusion.upscale(veg, v, method="mean")  # true vegetation fraction of each pixel
    full = rs.fusion.upscale(covered, v, method="mean") >= 0.95  # pixels well covered by NAIP
    frac = frac.where(full & v.notnull())  # keep those only
    vv = v.values[np.isfinite(frac.values)]  # NDVI of the kept pixels
    cls = (v > threshold_otsu(vv)).astype("float32").where(frac.notnull())  # classified: 0 or 1
    lo, hi = np.percentile(vv, [2, 98])  # soil and vegetation end-members
    fvc = ((v - lo) / (hi - lo)).clip(0, 1).where(frac.notnull())  # fractional vegetation cover
    scale_maps[name] = (frac, cls, fvc)  # for the figure
    for method, p in (("classified (0 or 1)", cls), ("fractional cover from NDVI", fvc)):  # both methods
        c = rs.fusion.compare(p, frac)  # agreement with the NAIP fraction
        scale_rows[name, method] = {"pixels": c["n"], "true cover": float(frac.mean()), "estimated cover": float(p.mean()),  # agreement with the NAIP fraction
                                    "R2": c["r2"], "RMSE": c["rmse"], "bias": c["bias"]}
pd.DataFrame(scale_rows).T.round(3)  # show it

for r, (name, (frac, cls, fvc)) in enumerate(scale_maps.items()):  # each sensor
    # the three panels
    for c, (t, v) in enumerate((("NAIP vegetation fraction", frac), ("classified", cls), ("fractional cover", fvc))):

Reading the scale results. Classifying each pixel as vegetated or not throws the mixture away: at every resolution its R² against the NAIP fraction is near zero or negative, and at 463 m it is far below zero, even though its scene-wide cover happens to be close. The fractional cover from NDVI follows the NAIP fraction much better (R² 0.27 to 0.42), and its per-pixel error shrinks as the pixels grow (RMSE 0.36 at 10 m, 0.17 at 463 m) because mixtures average out. Most estimates put the cover 6 to 8 points higher than NAIP: NAIP was flown on 14 July, its NDVI comes from uncalibrated digital numbers, and the Otsu threshold is one choice among many, so the reference itself is uncertain by a few points.

title: Multi-sensor image fusion
text:
Multi-sensor classification

Features from three sensor families
The last question is the one this chapter is about: does fusing sensors give a better land-cover map? The 2019 CDL is the reference, on the 30 m Landsat grid, recoded to the eight classes that cover this AOI. Three feature sets describe each 30 m pixel:

optical, one date: the six Landsat reflectances of 9 July and NDVI;
radar time series: Sentinel-1 VV and VH of the four dates (averaged onto 30 m in linear units, then converted to dB);
MODIS time series: NDVI and NIR of the seven 8-day composites, with the cloudy pixels of 20 to 27 July interpolated in time from the neighbouring composites (and the shadowed pixels of the last composite taken from the one before), resampled bilinearly to 30 m.

Early fusion stacks all features into one input (fuse_early stacks the optical and radar arrays, and the MODIS bands are appended); late fusion trains one model per sensor family and averages their class probabilities (fuse_late). The split is by 600 m spatial blocks (spatial_block_split), so test pixels are not neighbours of training pixels.


Code
CLASSES = ["Corn", "Alfalfa/hay", "Soybeans", "Winter wheat", "Forest", "Developed", "Grass/fallow", "Other"]  # 8 classes
# CDL codes of each class
CODES = {0: [1, 12, 13], 1: [36, 37], 2: [5], 3: [24], 4: [141, 142, 143, 190], 5: [121, 122, 123, 124], 6: [176, 61]}
y_map = np.full(cdl30.shape, 7, "int16")  # every other code is "Other"
for k, codes in CODES.items():  # recode the mapped codes
    y_map[np.isin(cdl30, codes)] = k  # paint the class
y_map[cdl30 == 0] = -1  # no data

opt_da = xr.concat([landsat.sel(band=["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"]),  # Landsat bands and NDVI
                    ndvi(landsat.sel(band="red"), landsat.sel(band="nir")).expand_dims(band=["ndvi"])], dim="band")
# Sentinel-1 dB averaged onto the Landsat grid
sar_da = xr.concat([10 * np.log10(on_ls(10 ** (da / 10), Resampling.average)).assign_coords(band=[f"{p}_{d:%m%d}" for p in ("vv", "vh")])
                    for d, da in s1.items()], dim="band")  # radar time series on 30 m (averaged in linear units)
mts = xr.concat([xr.concat([ndvi(mod[d].sel(band="red"), mod[d].sel(band="nir")).drop_vars("band", errors="ignore"),  # (composite, variable, y, x)
                             mod[d].sel(band="nir").drop_vars("band", errors="ignore")], dim="var") for d in MODIS_DOY],
                dim="doy").assign_coords(doy=MODIS_DOY, var=["ndvi", "nir"])  # (composite, variable, y, x) on the MODIS grid

FEATURES = {"optical, 1 date (Landsat)": opt_da, "radar, 4 dates (Sentinel-1)": sar_da,
            "MODIS, 7 composites": mod_da, "early fusion (all)": early}  # feature sets

Reading the classification results. One summer Landsat image is the strongest single source (68 % overall accuracy); the radar time series alone reaches 57 %, and the MODIS time series 48 %, too coarse for fields of a few hectares. Early fusion gives the best map overall (71 %, macro F1 0.60), with the clearest gains for classes that differ in timing or structure rather than colour: forest, alfalfa/hay, grass/fallow and “other”. Late fusion, which averages three models of very unequal quality, gains less. Soybeans are the exception: the single Landsat date separates them best, and every combination dilutes that signal. On the pixels where the CDL itself is confident (80 % or more), every accuracy rises by about ten points, a reminder that part of the remaining error lies in the reference.

title: Multi-sensor image fusion
text:
Interpretation and limitations

STARFM needs coarse change that fine pixels share, and a correct coarse change. It improves on “no change” where whole fields changed between the dates in a way MODIS could see; where change is smaller than a 463 m MODIS pixel, or differs between neighbouring fields inside one MODIS pixel, it can only spread the average change (ESTARFM and FSDAF add spectral unmixing for that case). On 24 July the MODIS NIR change was itself too large, and STARFM passed the error on.
Cross-sensor references carry their own error. PlanetScope and RapidEye were put on Landsat’s scale with a per-band linear fit on stable forest and developed pixels. Their different spectral bands, viewing geometry and residual misregistration remain in the reference, so part of every RMSE belongs to the reference, not to the fusion.
SAR fills patterns, not pigments. Backscatter responds to structure, roughness and moisture rather than leaf colour, so a single radar date explained little of the optical reflectance under the cloud; several dates and a coarse cloud-free optical source (MODIS) explained more. A random hold-out of clear pixels overstated the quality of every fill. Every filled pixel stays flagged as reconstructed.
Pixels mix. A classified coarse pixel is all or nothing; its errors grow with pixel size and cancel only partly over the scene. Fractional estimates are closer to the truth, and a fine reference such as NAIP is the way to check them. NAIP digital numbers are not calibrated, so only NAIP’s spatial pattern was used.
Fusion helped classification, modestly. Early fusion added about three points of overall accuracy and four of macro F1 over the best single sensor, mostly for classes that differ in timing or structure (forest, hay, grass/fallow, other). Late fusion of three models of unequal quality gained less, and soybeans were mapped best by the optical date alone. Late fusion is simpler and copes with a missing sensor; early fusion lets one model use interactions between sensors.
The CDL is a reference, not the truth. Its own accuracy varies by class (its confidence layer is given above); hay, fallow and grass are often confused in the CDL itself.
Data quirks. The two local RapidEye files labelled 14 and 24 July are the same 24 July scene; the PlanetScope image of 14 July is in UTM zone 18N (NAD83) and was reprojected; MOD09A1 composites can mix observations from any day of their 8-day window.


References

Gao, F., Masek, J., Schwaller, M., Hall, F. (2006). On the blending of the Landsat and MODIS surface reflectance: predicting daily Landsat surface reflectance. IEEE TGRS 44(8).
Zhu, X., Chen, J., Gao, F., Chen, X., Masek, J. G. (2010). An enhanced spatial and temporal adaptive reflectance fusion model (ESTARFM). Remote Sensing of Environment 114.
Schott, J. R., Salvaggio, C., Volchok, W. J. (1988). Radiometric scene normalization using pseudoinvariant features. Remote Sensing of Environment 26.
Gutman, G., Ignatov, A. (1998). The derivation of the green vegetation fraction from NOAA/AVHRR data. International Journal of Remote Sensing 19.
Schmitt, M., Zhu, X. X. (2016). Data fusion and remote sensing: an ever-growing relationship. IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Magazine 4(4).
Vermote, E. (2015). MOD09A1 MODIS/Terra Surface Reflectance 8-Day L3 Global 500 m SIN Grid V006/061. NASA EOSDIS LP DAAC.

title: Object Detection in Aerial Imagery
text:
Overview
Image classification assigns one label to a whole image; semantic segmentation assigns a label to every pixel; object detection returns a set of object instances, each with a category, confidence score, and location. Here the objects are swimming pools in small aerial-image tiles. A detector can answer where are the pools and how many are there? rather than only does this tile contain a pool?
This notebook starts with the dataset’s reproducible OpenCV HSV/contour detector, then connects that baseline to GeoLattice’s box geometry, non-maximum suppression (NMS), large-image tiling, detector architectures, and evaluation/training interfaces. The classical detector is useful when pool water has a distinctive colour; it is not a learned CNN and will fail when shadows, roofs, water, or seasonal conditions look similar.

Important data limitation: this folder contains image tiles and a prototype notebook, but no independent, verified pool bounding-box annotations. Consequently, we can inspect predictions and tune a heuristic, but we cannot honestly train a supervised neural detector or report precision, recall, AP, or mAP from this dataset alone. Predictions from the HSV detector are not ground truth for evaluating that same detector. The notebook shows the exact annotation and GeoLattice interfaces needed to continue once labels are added.

section: HSV colour thresholding and contour proposals
text:
HSV colour thresholding and contour proposals
RGB values mix colour and brightness. HSV separates hue \(H\), saturation \(S\), and value \(V\); OpenCV encodes hue on \([0,179]\) and saturation/value on \([0,255]\). A simple pool-water mask is
\[
M(x,y)=\mathbf{1}\{H_{\min}\le H(x,y)\le H_{\max},\;
S(x,y)\ge S_{\min},\;V(x,y)\ge V_{\min}\}.
\]
The starting bounds below are those used in the original sample detector. They are heuristic operating parameters, not fitted model weights. Morphological opening removes isolated specks, and closing fills small gaps:
\[
M\circ B=(M\ominus B)\oplus B,\qquad
M\bullet B=(M\oplus B)\ominus B,
\]
where \(\ominus\) and \(\oplus\) denote erosion and dilation by structuring element \(B\). Connected external contours then provide candidate regions. A contour’s axis-aligned box is \((x_0,y_0,x_1,y_1)\), and the contour fill ratio \(A_c/A_b\) can serve as a rough ranking score, not a calibrated probability.


Code
# OpenCV HSV ranges use H in [0, 179], S/V in [0, 255].
HSV_LOWER = np.array([50, 40, 140], dtype=np.uint8)
HSV_UPPER = np.array([120, 255, 255], dtype=np.uint8)
OPEN_KERNEL = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (3, 3))
CLOSE_KERNEL = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (5, 5))

MIN_CONTOUR_AREA = 80
MIN_BOX_AREA = 250
MAX_BOX_AREA = 25_000

def hsv_pool_proposals(rgb, *, min_contour_area=MIN_CONTOUR_AREA,
                       min_box_area=MIN_BOX_AREA, max_box_area=MAX_BOX_AREA):
    # Return heuristic pool boxes (xyxy pixels), fill-ratio scores, and mask.
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(rgb, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
    mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, HSV_LOWER, HSV_UPPER)
    mask = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, OPEN_KERNEL)
    mask = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, CLOSE_KERNEL)
    contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)

    boxes, scores = [], []
    for contour in contours:
        contour_area = cv2.contourArea(contour)
        if contour_area < min_contour_area:
            continue
        x, y, width, height = cv2.boundingRect(contour)
        box_area = width * height
        if not min_box_area <= box_area <= max_box_area:
            continue
        boxes.append([x, y, x + width, y + height])
        scores.append(contour_area / box_area)
    if not boxes:
        return np.empty((0, 4), dtype=float), np.empty(0, dtype=float), mask
    return np.asarray(boxes, dtype=float), np.asarray(scores, dtype=float), mask

Parameter sensitivity: thresholds are not universal
Raising the minimum contour or box area suppresses speckle but can miss small pools; lowering it increases false positives. A hue/saturation/value threshold that works on one image may fail under haze, shadows, roofs, or a different sensor. The small table below is a proposal-count sensitivity check only. title: Object Detection in Aerial Imagery
text:
Overlapping-window detection and duplicate suppression
Small objects can disappear when a large image is resized to a network’s fixed input size. A sliding-window detector instead runs on overlapping crops, translates local boxes back to the full-image coordinate system, and suppresses duplicate boxes near crop edges. GeoLattice’s detection_tiles generates windows; box_iou and nms implement the standard box overlap and greedy suppression.
For boxes \(A\) and \(B\),
\[
\operatorname{IoU}(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}.
\]
Greedy NMS sorts boxes by score, keeps the highest-scoring box, and removes lower-scoring boxes whose IoU exceeds threshold \(\tau\). The threshold trades duplicate suppression against accidentally merging adjacent pools.


Code
from geolattice.rsense.classify import image_classification as ic

def detect_tiled_hsv(rgb, *, tile=640, overlap=0.20, nms_iou=0.35):
    # Detect in overlapping windows; return full-image xyxy boxes and heuristic scores.
    height, width = rgb.shape[:2]
    windows = ic.detection_tiles(height, width, tile=tile, overlap=overlap)
    all_boxes, all_scores = [], []
    for row, col, window_size in windows:
        crop = rgb[row:min(row + window_size, height),
                    col:min(col + window_size, width)]
        boxes, scores, _ = hsv_pool_proposals(crop)
        if len(boxes):
            boxes[:, [0, 2]] += col
            boxes[:, [1, 3]] += row
            all_boxes.extend(boxes.tolist())
            all_scores.extend(scores.tolist())
    if not all_boxes:
        return np.empty((0, 4), dtype=float), np.empty(0, dtype=float), windows
    boxes = np.asarray(all_boxes, dtype=float)
    scores = np.asarray(all_scores, dtype=float)
    keep = ic.nms(boxes, scores, iou_threshold=nms_iou)
    return boxes[keep], scores[keep], windows

tiled_boxes, tiled_scores, windows = detect_tiled_hsv(sample_rgb)
print(f"{len(windows)} windows -> {len(tiled_boxes)} boxes after NMS")
show_detections(sample_rgb, tiled_boxes, tiled_scores, title="Overlapping-window HSV detections")

text:
Batch results and cautious filename-derived coordinates
We run the same baseline on every JPEG and summarize proposal counts. Names in this sample appear to encode lower-left and upper-right longitude/latitude pairs. The parser below decodes that naming convention and maps pixel boxes to approximate WGS84 polygons by linear interpolation. This is useful for illustration, not a substitute for checking the imagery’s authoritative CRS, image orientation, and georeferencing metadata.
If adjacent images overlap, the same pool may be detected twice. Geographic polygon NMS can merge such duplicate footprints. Counts summed before that step are therefore not necessarily counts of unique real-world pools.


Code
def parse_encoded_coordinate(degrees, fraction):
    sign = -1 if degrees.startswith("-") else 1
    return sign * (abs(int(degrees)) + int(fraction) / (10 ** len(fraction)))

COORDINATE_PATTERN = re.compile(
    r"_(\d{3})_(\d{5})_(-?\d{2})_(\d{5})_"
    r"(\d{3})_(\d{5})_(-?\d{2})_(\d{5})_\d+\.jpg$"
)

def tile_bounds_from_name(path):
    match = COORDINATE_PATTERN.search(Path(path).name)
    if match is None:
        return None
    left = parse_encoded_coordinate(match.group(1), match.group(2))
    lat_a = parse_encoded_coordinate(match.group(3), match.group(4))
    right = parse_encoded_coordinate(match.group(5), match.group(6))
    lat_b = parse_encoded_coordinate(match.group(7), match.group(8))
    return min(left, right), min(lat_a, lat_b), max(left, right), max(lat_a, lat_b)

print("Example encoded bounds (min lon, min lat, max lon, max lat):")
print(sample_path.name, "->", tile_bounds_from_name(sample_path))

title: Object Detection in Aerial Imagery
text:
Detection geometry and model architectures

From boxes to a detection loss
A detector predicts a set of class scores and box coordinates. For a matched object with class \(c\) and ground-truth box \(b^*\), a common objective is
\[
\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{\mathrm{cls}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}(p,c)
+\lambda_{\mathrm{box}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{box}}(b,b^*),
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{box}}=\sum_{q\in\{x,y,w,h\}}\operatorname{SmoothL1}(b_q-b_q^*).
\]
The model must also decide which candidate locations correspond to objects (assignment/matching), and how to handle the many more background locations than pools.


Faster R-CNN: proposals, then refinement
Faster R-CNN is a two-stage detector. A backbone and feature pyramid produce feature maps \(F\). A region proposal network (RPN) predicts objectness \(p_i\) and anchor offsets \(t_i\):
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RPN}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{cls}}}\sum_i
\operatorname{BCE}(p_i,p_i^*)+
\lambda\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{reg}}}\sum_i p_i^*\operatorname{SmoothL1}(t_i-t_i^*).
\]
Proposals are cropped/pooled to a common feature size; a second head predicts the pool/background class and refined box. Region proposals focus computation on likely objects, but add proposal/matching stages and can be slower than one-stage methods.


RetinaNet: dense anchors and focal loss
RetinaNet predicts class probabilities and box offsets at every location and anchor on a feature pyramid. Its focal loss reduces the contribution of easy background examples:
\[
\operatorname{FL}(p_t)=-\alpha_t(1-p_t)^\gamma\log(p_t).
\]
When \(p_t\to1\), the factor \((1-p_t)^\gamma\) suppresses easy examples; hard positives and confusing negatives retain more weight. This addresses the extreme foreground/background imbalance of dense prediction.


FCOS: anchor-free points
FCOS assigns positive feature-map locations inside a ground-truth box. At a positive location \((x,y)\) it regresses distances to the four sides:
\[
(l,t,r,b)=(x-x_0,\;y-y_0,\;x_1-x,\;y_1-y),
\qquad
\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{focal}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GIoU}}.
\]
An optional centerness score downweights low-quality predictions far from the box centre. Removing anchors reduces anchor-scale and aspect-ratio design choices, but point assignment and NMS are still needed.


YOLO: one-stage grid predictions
YOLO-style models predict objectness, box geometry, and class scores in one forward pass over one or more feature scales. For a grid point with centre \((c_x,c_y)\) and stride \(s\), a typical parameterization is
\[
x=c_x+s\,\sigma(t_x),\quad y=c_y+s\,\sigma(t_y),\quad
w=s\,e^{t_w},\quad h=s\,e^{t_h}.
\]
Modern YOLO variants differ in assignment, box loss, and whether heads are anchor-based; the common idea is joint dense prediction followed by confidence filtering and NMS. Ultralytics YOLO weights may require an extra package and a separate annotation/training setup.


Mask R-CNN: boxes plus instance masks
Mask R-CNN adds an FCN mask head to each positive region of Faster R-CNN. For each RoI it predicts a class-specific mask \(M\) with pixelwise binary cross-entropy:
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RPN}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{class}}+
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{box}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}.
\]
Use it when the pool’s outline is required, not just its bounding rectangle. The current dataset has no polygon masks either.


Which detector is a sensible starting point?









Model
Family
Strength
Trade-off




Faster R-CNN
Two-stage, region proposals
Strong general-purpose baseline; explicit proposal refinement
More latency and proposal machinery


RetinaNet
One-stage, anchor-based
Focal loss handles dense foreground/background imbalance
Anchor configuration and matching matter


FCOS
One-stage, anchor-free
Simple point-based box regression
Still needs scale assignment and NMS


YOLO
One-stage, dense
Fast inference and mature deployment ecosystem
Version/weight conventions and training APIs vary


Mask R-CNN
Two-stage, boxes + masks
Instance outline as well as a box
More annotation effort and compute



GeoLattice exposes torchvision Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, FCOS, and Mask R-CNN through build_object_detector; its YOLO path delegates to Ultralytics. On this small-object aerial dataset, crop/window size and verified labels are at least as important as architecture choice.

title: Object Detection in Aerial Imagery
section: Annotation, split design, training, and evaluation
text:
Annotation, split design, training, and evaluation

Why the current images cannot support a valid accuracy score
Supervised object detection requires, for every image, a set of verified boxes and class IDs. A box missed by annotation is counted as a false positive; an omitted pool is counted as a false negative. There are no independent box labels in the supplied folder, so generating labels from the HSV detector and scoring that detector against them would be circular.
Annotate a representative selection of tiles with a tool that exports COCO or another explicit box format. Review difficult cases and include empty-background images. Split by geographic tile/site, not by random boxes or crops: neighboring crops share roofs, lighting, and sometimes the same pool, so a random crop split overstates generalization. Keep a final site-level test set untouched until model selection is complete.


PyTorch target format and GeoLattice hooks
Torchvision-style training batches are (images, targets), where each target has boxes in pixel xyxy coordinates and integer labels (0 is reserved for background; in a two-class model, pool is 1). For each image \(i\):
\[
\texttt{boxes}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{N_i\times4},\quad
\texttt{labels}_i\in\{1,\ldots,C-1\}^{N_i}.
\]
GeoLattice’s train_detection expects a list of image tensors and a list of target dictionaries. The loader needs a custom collate_fn because each image has a different number \(N_i\) of boxes. This code shows the target and collate shapes; it deliberately does not fabricate labels or start training.


Code
def detection_collate(batch):
    # Keep variable-size image and box lists instead of stacking targets.
    images, targets = zip(*batch)
    return list(images), list(targets)

# Example target for a manually annotated tile. Replace these coordinates with reviewed labels.
example_target = {
    "boxes": torch.tensor([[120.0, 210.0, 184.0, 278.0]], dtype=torch.float32),
    "labels": torch.tensor([1], dtype=torch.int64),  # 1 = pool; 0 is background
}
print("boxes:", tuple(example_target["boxes"].shape),
      "| labels:", tuple(example_target["labels"].shape),
      "| device available:", DEVICE)


boxes: (1, 4) | labels: (1,) | device available: cuda




GeoLattice object-detection API: available and used here
GeoLattice already provides object-detection functions in geolattice.rsense.classify.image_classification; a separate object_detection.py module is not needed. This notebook uses detection_tiles, nms, and merge_detections in the runnable HSV baseline. For a trained neural detector, the same module provides build_object_detector and georeferenced tiled inference through detect_objects; it also includes box_iou, mean_average_precision, and count_objects.
The HSV proposals below are not predictions from a GeoLattice neural detector. The pool tiles have no verified boxes, so fitting a pool-specific detector is not possible yet. Once independently labeled examples exist, train a torchvision detector and pass the trained model plus a georeferenced xarray raster to GeoLattice detect_objects. That function handles overlapping windows, global class-wise NMS, and conversion of predicted boxes to map-coordinate polygons.
The code cell smoke-tests the GeoLattice metric API on one deliberately perfect synthetic box. Its score verifies interface behavior only; it is not a score on the pool images.


Code
# Confirm the installed GeoLattice detector API without downloading pretrained weights.

required_detection_api = [
    "build_object_detector", "box_iou", "nms", "mean_average_precision",
    "detection_tiles", "merge_detections", "detect_objects", "count_objects",
]

toy_ground_truth = [{"boxes": np.array([[10, 10, 30, 30]]), "labels": np.array([1])}]

                    "scores": np.array([0.99]), "labels": np.array([1])}]

Constructing a GeoLattice detector after labels exist
The following is a training template, not an executed model result. Once a Dataset reads manually reviewed annotations and returns RGB float tensors in \([0,1]\) plus the target format above, instantiate a GeoLattice detector and pass train/validation loaders. Start with one architecture, keep validation tiles separate by site, and select thresholds/checkpoints on validation only. After training, use ic.detect_objects(model, image_da, ...) on a georeferenced xarray.DataArray/Dataset to obtain map-coordinate boxes.
from geolattice.rsense.classify.image_classification import build_object_detector
from geolattice.rsense.dl.train import train_detection

model = build_object_detector(
    "faster_rcnn", num_classes=2, pretrained=True
)
history = train_detection(
    model, train_loader, val_loader,
    epochs=20, lr=1e-4, device=DEVICE, precision="16" if DEVICE == "cuda" else "32",
)

# image_da must be a georeferenced xarray raster in the model's expected band order.
boxes_gdf = ic.detect_objects(
    model, image_da, tile=640, overlap=128, score_threshold=0.3,
    class_names={1: "pool"}, device=DEVICE,
)
pretrained=True initializes the backbone from torchvision weights; it does not provide pool-specific training. num_classes=2 counts background plus pool. The sample data cannot populate train_loader, so do not run this until independently verified annotations and a dataset class are in place.


Detection metrics: AP and mAP
At IoU threshold \(\tau\), a predicted box is a true positive only when it matches an as-yet-unmatched ground-truth box of the same class with \(\operatorname{IoU}\ge\tau\). Precision and recall along the confidence-ranked list form a curve; average precision integrates its precision envelope. Mean AP averages AP over classes (and, for COCO-style mAP, over thresholds such as \(0.50,0.55,\ldots,0.95\)):
\[
\mathrm{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad
\mathrm{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\qquad
\mathrm{mAP}_{.50:.95}=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{\tau\in\{.50,\ldots,.95\}}
\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\mathrm{AP}_{c,\tau}.
\]
GeoLattice mean_average_precision accepts per-image prediction dictionaries (boxes, scores, labels) and ground-truth dictionaries (boxes, labels). It becomes meaningful only when those ground-truth boxes were labeled independently of the evaluated predictions. Use site-level bootstrap or repeated site holdouts to express uncertainty when the number of independent locations is small.

title: Object Detection in Aerial Imagery
section: Tree detection with annotated aerial-image tiles
text:
Tree detection with annotated aerial-image tiles
Unlike the pool tiles above, Data/08_remote_sensing/08_10_object_detection/Tree_Detection includes bounding-box annotations in YOLO format. We can train a supervised detector and evaluate it on the dataset’s held-out test split. The dataset contains 91 RGB images resized/stretched to 640 x 640, one class (tree), and preassigned train/validation/test folders (64/18/9 images). These are image chips with no geotransform, so detections remain in image-pixel coordinates and cannot be exported as map coordinates without external georeferencing.
GeoLattice already integrates Ultralytics YOLO through ic.build_object_detector("yolo", weights=...). We use its builder to initialize a pretrained YOLOv8 nano model, fine-tune on the supplied labels, and evaluate once on the test split. This is a small demonstration dataset: results are specific to its acquisition and split, and should not be treated as broad geographic validation. Roboflow metadata lists the source as CC BY 4.0; retain attribution to the Tree Counting dataset if redistributing the data or derived work.
For an image of width \(W\) and height \(H\), YOLO stores each box as normalized center and size \((c_x,c_y,w,h)\in[0,1]^4\). Convert to pixel corners by
\[x_0=W(c_x-w/2),\quad y_0=H(c_y-h/2),\quad x_1=W(c_x+w/2),\quad y_1=H(c_y+h/2).\]
The detector jointly predicts class/objectness and box offsets; during evaluation a predicted box is a true positive only when it matches an unmatched reference tree with sufficient IoU. The precision-recall curve yields AP, and AP@0.50 is reported for the single class.


Code
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image
import yaml

TREE_CANDIDATES = [
    Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_10_object_detection/Tree_Detection"),
    Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_09_image_classification/Tree_Detection"),
]
TREE_DATA = next((p for p in TREE_CANDIDATES if p.is_dir()), None)
if TREE_DATA is None:
    raise FileNotFoundError("Could not find ../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_10_object_detection/Tree_Detection from this working directory.")

TREE_SPLITS = {split: TREE_DATA / split for split in ("train", "valid", "test")}
for split, split_dir in TREE_SPLITS.items():
    if not (split_dir / "images").is_dir() or not (split_dir / "labels").is_dir():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Expected images/ and labels/ under {split_dir}")

tree_rows = []
for split, split_dir in TREE_SPLITS.items():
    images = sorted(p for p in (split_dir / "images").iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png"})
    if not images:
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"No tree images found in {split_dir / 'images'}")
    box_total = 0
    class_ids = set()
    for image_path in images:
        label_path = split_dir / "labels" / f"{image_path.stem}.txt"
        if not label_path.is_file():
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"Missing YOLO annotation for {image_path.name}: {label_path}")
        for line_number, line in enumerate(label_path.read_text().splitlines(), start=1):
            parts = line.split()
            if len(parts) != 5:
                raise ValueError(f"Invalid YOLO label {label_path}:{line_number}; expected class cx cy w h")
            class_id = int(parts[0])
            cx, cy, bw, bh = map(float, parts[1:])
            if not (0 <= cx <= 1 and 0 <= cy <= 1 and 0 < bw <= 1 and 0 < bh <= 1):
                raise ValueError(f"Out-of-range normalized box in {label_path}:{line_number}")
            class_ids.add(class_id)
            box_total += 1
    tree_rows.append({"split": split, "images": len(images), "tree boxes": box_total,
                      "class IDs": sorted(class_ids)})

tree_label_path = TREE_SPLITS["train"] / "labels" / f"{tree_sample_path.stem}.txt"
tree_sample_boxes = []
for line in tree_label_path.read_text().splitlines():
    class_id, cx, cy, bw, bh = line.split()
    cx, cy, bw, bh = map(float, (cx, cy, bw, bh))
    h, w = tree_sample.shape[:2]
    tree_sample_boxes.append([w * (cx - bw / 2), h * (cy - bh / 2),
                              w * (cx + bw / 2), h * (cy + bh / 2)])
tree_sample_boxes = np.asarray(tree_sample_boxes, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 4)
show_detections(tree_sample, tree_sample_boxes, title=f"Tree annotations: {tree_sample_path.name}")
print(f"Ground-truth trees in example tile: {len(tree_sample_boxes)}")

ic.build_object_detector returns the Ultralytics model for arch="yolo"; training is delegated to its supported .train method. The dataset YAML is written to a temporary file with explicit absolute paths, avoiding assumptions about how Ultralytics resolves the supplied Roboflow YAML’s relative paths. Training uses the provided train/validation splits; the test split is reserved for the final evaluation cell below. Set TREE_TRAIN_EPOCHS higher for a more complete run. The default is kept modest for a tutorial notebook.

import tempfile

TREE_TRAIN_EPOCHS = 10
TREE_BATCH_SIZE = 8
TREE_DEVICE = 0 if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
TREE_RUNS_DIR = Path("runs/object_detection")
TREE_RUNS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Minimal Ultralytics dataset config with resolved, portable paths for the current machine.
tree_data_config = {
    "path": str(TREE_DATA.resolve()),
    "train": "train/images",
    "val": "valid/images",
    "test": "test/images",
    "names": {0: "tree"},
}
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="geolattice-tree-data-") as temp_dir:
    tree_yaml = Path(temp_dir) / "tree_data.yaml"
    tree_yaml.write_text(yaml.safe_dump(tree_data_config, sort_keys=False))

    tree_model = ic.build_object_detector("yolo", weights="yolov8n.pt")
    tree_train_results = tree_model.train(
        data=str(tree_yaml),
        epochs=TREE_TRAIN_EPOCHS,
        imgsz=640,
        batch=TREE_BATCH_SIZE,
        device=TREE_DEVICE,
        workers=0,
        patience=5,
        max_det=1000,
        project=str(TREE_RUNS_DIR.resolve()),
        name="yolov8n_tree",
        exist_ok=True,
        plots=False,
        verbose=False,
    )
    best_tree_weights = Path(tree_train_results.save_dir) / "weights" / "best.pt"
    if not best_tree_weights.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Training finished without best checkpoint: {best_tree_weights}")

    # Reload the selected checkpoint, then evaluate once on untouched test images.
    tree_detector = ic.build_object_detector("yolo", weights=str(best_tree_weights))
    tree_test_results = tree_detector.val(
        data=str(tree_yaml), split="test", imgsz=640, batch=TREE_BATCH_SIZE,
        device=TREE_DEVICE, workers=0, max_det=1000, plots=False, verbose=False,
    )

print(f"Best checkpoint: {best_tree_weights}")
print(f"Test images: {len(list((TREE_SPLITS['test'] / 'images').glob('*')))}")
print(f"Test mAP@0.50: {tree_test_results.box.map50:.3f}")
print(f"Test mAP@0.50:0.95: {tree_test_results.box.map:.3f}")
print(f"Test precision: {tree_test_results.box.mp:.3f} | recall: {tree_test_results.box.mr:.3f}")

title: Object Detection in Aerial Imagery
text:
Limitations and a practical workflow

What this baseline does and does not establish

The HSV/contour output is a candidate generator, not a trained or validated detector.
Proposal counts depend on colour thresholds, morphology, and contour-size cutoffs; counts are not accuracy.
Filename interpolation produces approximate geographic polygons only if the encoded corners, image orientation, and CRS assumption are correct.
Geographic merging is useful for overlapping images, but cannot resolve an incorrect footprint or a pool missed in every tile.
GPU use matters for neural training/inference; the classical OpenCV pipeline is CPU-friendly.



Recommended next steps

Verify the tile coordinate convention against a trusted map or source metadata.
Manually box pools in a geographically representative subset, including difficult negatives; review annotations independently.
Make train/validation/test splits by non-overlapping sites and report the number of independent sites.
Compare the HSV baseline with a pretrained Faster R-CNN or RetinaNet using identical held-out sites and confidence/IoU conventions.
Report per-site precision, recall, AP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95, plus uncertainty; inspect false positives and missed pools.
If only pool counts are needed, merge overlapping geospatial detections and validate counts per site before scaling.
For tree counting, inspect the held-out test predictions and verify that the chip split separates geographic areas before applying the model elsewhere.

The pool baseline has no independent reference boxes, so it cannot support accuracy claims. The tree model does have held-out annotations and reports test-set metrics, but only nine small chips are in the test split and the supplied split is not demonstrated to be geographically independent; treat its scores as a dataset demonstration, not evidence of transfer to new regions.

title: Field Edge Detection in WorldView Imagery: RGB versus RGB + NIR
text:
What differs from the paper

Image. The shipped scene is an eight-band subset at 1.6 m; the paper reports a 1.24 m WorldView-3 acquisition (18 March 2015). Both are resampled to the 0.5 m label grid.
Split before augmenting. The paper rotated its 51 tiles into 204 and then split them 172 / 8 / 24, so rotated copies of one tile can sit in training and test. Here whole blocks of 2 x 2 tiles are assigned to train, validation or test first, and only training tiles are rotated. This removes that leak, so the test scores here are expected to be lower.
Training budget. The paper trained for 500 epochs, batch size 1, learning rate 1e-4 (TensorFlow 1.14). Here: PyTorch, 60 (SegNet 150) epochs, batch size 4, learning rate 1e-3 (chosen in Learning-rate sensitivity), cosine schedule, best epoch by validation mean IoU.
SegNet settings. With dropout after all ten stages, or with the plain loss, SegNet predicted “non-boundary” everywhere on these 180 training tiles. It uses dropout only at the three deepest encoder and decoder stages (the Bayesian SegNet placement), class-weighted cross-entropy and 150 epochs.
Scored area. Villages, ponds and roads were not digitised. Loss and scores use only pixels inside a digitised field or its boundary band.

# Read the WorldView scene and audit its eight bands.
with rasterio.open(DATA / "multi.tif") as src:
    X8 = src.read().astype("float32")                       # all eight bands: (8, rows, columns)
    TRANSFORM, CRS, NODATA = src.transform, src.crs, src.nodata

fill = X8 == 65535                                         # saturated fill values
# Per band: share of no-data and fill pixels, and the 2nd percentile, median and 98th percentile.
audit = pd.DataFrame({"band": BAND_NAMES,
                      "nodata %": [100 * np.isnan(b).mean() for b in X8],
                      "65535 fill %": [100 * f.mean() for f in fill],
                      "p2": [np.nanpercentile(b[~f], 2) for b, f in zip(X8, fill)],
                      "median": [np.nanmedian(b[~f]) for b, f in zip(X8, fill)],

display(audit.round(1))

BANDS = {"3ch (B, G, R)": [1, 2, 4], "4ch (B, G, R, NIR2)": [1, 2, 4, 7]}   # 0-based: B2, B3, B5, B8

title: Field Edge Detection in WorldView Imagery: RGB versus RGB + NIR
section: The boundary reference on a 0.5 m grid
text:
The boundary reference on a 0.5 m grid
Following section 2.2 of the paper, every field outline is buffered by 0.5 m (a 1 m wide band), burnt into a 0.5 m raster as the boundary class, and the rest of each field is the non-boundary (field) class. The image is resampled to the same 0.5 m grid with bilinear interpolation. This does not add detail; it only puts image and labels on one grid.


Code
# A 0.5 m working grid and the two-class boundary reference.
from rasterio.warp import reproject                        # resample a raster onto another grid

# The paper rasterised the boundaries at 0.5 m, so the image is resampled to the same grid
# (bilinear; resampling adds no detail, it only puts image and labels on one grid).
GSD = 0.5
T05 = from_origin(BOUNDS.left, BOUNDS.top, GSD, GSD)       # transform of the 0.5 m grid (same top-left corner)
H, W = int(round((BOUNDS.top - BOUNDS.bottom) / GSD)), int(round((BOUNDS.right - BOUNDS.left) / GSD))
X05 = np.full((8, H, W), np.nan, "float32")                # empty 0.5 m image, filled band by band
src_img = np.where(fill, np.nan, X8)                       # treat fill values as no-data
for b in range(8):
    reproject(src_img[b], X05[b], src_transform=TRANSFORM, src_crs=CRS, dst_transform=T05, dst_crs=CRS,
              resampling=Resampling.bilinear, src_nodata=np.nan, dst_nodata=np.nan)
ok05 = np.isfinite(X05[1:]).all(0)                         # valid 0.5 m pixels in bands 2-8

# Paper, section 2.2: each field outline is buffered by 0.5 m -> class 1 (boundary);
# the rest of the field -> class 0 here (the paper's "class 2", non-boundary).
# `labelled` marks pixels inside a digitised field or its boundary band; villages, ponds and
# roads that nobody digitised are left out of training and scoring.
BOUNDARY, labelled = ed.rasterize_boundaries(fields, transform=T05, shape=(H, W), buffer=0.5, return_valid=True)
VALID = labelled & ok05                                    # pixels that are labelled and have image data
print(f"0.5 m grid: {W} x {H} pixels | labelled area {VALID.mean():.0%} of the scene | "
      f"boundary pixels {BOUNDARY[VALID].mean():.1%} of the labelled area")

def false_colour(x, bands=(7, 4, 2), lo=None, hi=None):
    """NIR2-red-green false colour (vegetation red), 2-98 % stretch per band."""
    rgb = np.stack([x[b] for b in bands], -1)                          # (H, W, 3)
    lo = np.nanpercentile(rgb, 2, axis=(0, 1)) if lo is None else lo   # per-band 2nd percentile
    hi = np.nanpercentile(rgb, 98, axis=(0, 1)) if hi is None else hi  # per-band 98th percentile
    return np.nan_to_num(np.clip((rgb - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1))

FC = false_colour(X05)
EXT = (BOUNDS.left, BOUNDS.right, BOUNDS.bottom, BOUNDS.top)          # plot extent in map units
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 6.2))
ax[0].imshow(FC, extent=EXT); fields.boundary.plot(ax=ax[0], color="yellow", lw=0.4)
ax[0].set_title("False colour (NIR2-red-green) with the digitised fields (cf. paper Fig. 1)")
lab_img = np.where(VALID, BOUNDARY, np.nan)                            # NaN = not labelled (drawn grey)
ax[1].imshow(lab_img, cmap="gray_r", extent=EXT, interpolation="nearest")
ax[1].set_title("Reference: boundary (black), field (white), grey = not labelled")
ax[1].set_facecolor("0.7")
zoom = (slice(900, 1300), slice(1000, 1400))                           # 400 x 400 pixels = 200 m x 200 m
ax[2].imshow(FC[zoom]); ax[2].contour(BOUNDARY[zoom], levels=[0.5], colors="yellow", linewidths=0.6)
ax[2].set_title("200 m x 200 m zoom: 1 m wide boundary band on 0.5 m pixels")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


0.5 m grid: 2432 x 2246 pixels | labelled area 51% of the scene | boundary pixels 10.5% of the labelled area









Boundaries are only about 10.5 % of the labelled pixels, so a classifier that never predicts a boundary would already be about 89.5 % “accurate”. This is why the paper reports precision, recall and F1 of the boundary class, not overall accuracy.

title: Field Edge Detection in WorldView Imagery: RGB versus RGB + NIR
section: Tiles, a spatial split, normalisation and rotation augmentation
text:
Tiles, a spatial split, normalisation and rotation augmentation

Tiles. 192 x 192 pixels (96 m x 96 m), the paper’s best image size (Table 6). Tiles less than half digitised are dropped.
Split. Neighbouring tiles share fields and bunds, so whole 2 x 2-tile blocks go to one split (about 70 / 10 / 20 % of tiles for train / validation / test). ic.check_split_isolation raises an error if a tile ends up in two splits.
Normalisation. Each band is stretched to [0, 1] between its 2nd and 98th percentiles, computed on training tiles only.
Augmentation. Training tiles are rotated by 90°, 180° and 270° (ed.dihedral_augment), four copies of each tile, as in the paper’s Fig. 3. Validation and test tiles are not augmented.



Code
# Tiles, a spatial split, normalisation and rotation augmentation.

# 192 x 192 tiles (96 m x 96 m) as in the paper; keep tiles at least half labelled.
TILE = 192
LABEL = np.where(VALID, BOUNDARY, 0).astype("int64")                   # 0/1 label, 0 where unlabelled
tiles = ed.tile_pairs(np.moveaxis(X05, 0, -1), LABEL, size=TILE, valid=VALID, min_valid=0.5)
n_tiles = len(tiles["labels"])                                         # tiles: images, labels, valid, origins
print(f"{n_tiles} tiles of {TILE} x {TILE} pixels (paper: 51)")

# Spatial split. Neighbouring tiles share fields, so whole 2 x 2-tile blocks (192 m) go to one
# side. The paper split *after* augmenting (172/8/24 of 204 tiles), which can put rotated
# copies of one tile on both sides; here the split comes first and only training tiles are rotated.
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
block = [tuple(o // (2 * TILE)) for o in tiles["origins"]]             # block (row, col) of each tile
blocks = sorted(set(block))
rng.shuffle(blocks)                                                    # random block order
split_of_block, counts = {}, {"test": 0, "val": 0, "train": 0}
for b in blocks:
    n = block.count(b)                                                 # tiles in this block
    # Fill the test split to 20 % of the tiles first, then validation to 10 %, the rest is training.
    side = "test" if counts["test"] < 0.2 * n_tiles else "val" if counts["val"] < 0.1 * n_tiles else "train"
    split_of_block[b] = side
    counts[side] += n
SPLIT = np.array([split_of_block[b] for b in block])                   # split of every tile
idx = {s: np.flatnonzero(SPLIT == s) for s in ("train", "val", "test")}   # tile indices per split
tile_id = np.array([f"r{r}_c{c}" for r, c in tiles["origins"]])
ic.check_split_isolation(**{s: tile_id[v] for s, v in idx.items()})          # raises if a tile is in two splits
print({s: len(v) for s, v in idx.items()}, "tiles")

# Normalise each band to [0, 1] with its 2nd and 98th percentiles over the training tiles only.
tr_px = tiles["images"][idx["train"]].transpose(1, 0, 2, 3).reshape(8, -1)   # (8 bands, all training pixels)
LO = np.nanpercentile(tr_px, 2, axis=1)[:, None, None]
HI = np.nanpercentile(tr_px, 98, axis=1)[:, None, None]
def normalise(x):
    """(..., 8, H, W) raw reflectance -> [0, 1], NaN -> 0."""
    return np.nan_to_num(np.clip((x - LO) / (HI - LO), 0, 1)).astype("float32")
X_all = normalise(tiles["images"])                       # (N, 8, 192, 192)
Y_all = np.where(tiles["valid"], tiles["labels"], -100)  # -100 = not labelled (ignored in the loss)

# Augment the training tiles with 90, 180 and 270 degree rotations (paper Fig. 3).
Xtr, Ytr = ed.dihedral_augment(X_all[idx["train"]], Y_all[idx["train"]], rotations=(0, 1, 2, 3))
print(f"training set after rotation: {len(Xtr)} tiles; validation {len(idx['val'])}, test {len(idx['test'])}")

# Where the splits are, and one training tile with its four rotations.
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(19, 5.2))
a0 = fig.add_subplot(1, 6, (1, 2))                                    # the map spans two panel widths
a0.imshow(FC); a0.set_xticks([]); a0.set_yticks([])
colours = {"train": "#1b9e77", "val": "#d95f02", "test": "#e7298a"}
for (r, c), s_ in zip(tiles["origins"], SPLIT):
    a0.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((c, r), TILE, TILE, fill=False, ec=colours[s_], lw=1.5))   # tile outline
    a0.text(c + 8, r + 30, s_[:2], color=colours[s_], fontsize=7, weight="bold")         # "tr", "va" or "te"
a0.set_title("192 x 192 tiles: train / val / test (2 x 2-tile blocks)")
i0 = idx["train"][np.argmax(tiles["valid"][idx["train"]].mean((1, 2)))]   # the best-labelled training tile
for k in range(4):
    a = fig.add_subplot(1, 6, 3 + k)
    a.imshow(np.rot90(false_colour(tiles["images"][i0]), k, axes=(0, 1)))   # rotate by k x 90 degrees
    a.set_title(["initial tile", "90 degree rotation", "180 degree rotation", "270 degree rotation"][k]); a.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

title: Field Edge Detection in WorldView Imagery: RGB versus RGB + NIR
text:
Evaluation protocol
For the boundary class, with TP, FP and FN counted over the scored pixels of the tiles (paper Eqs. 1-3):
\[\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \qquad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \qquad F_1 = 2\,\frac{\text{Precision}\cdot\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\]
The same is computed for the non-boundary (field, the paper’s “cropland”) class. AUC, the area under the ROC curve, uses the continuous score and needs no threshold. Every method gives a score per pixel (a probability or an edge strength). It is turned into a boundary map with the threshold that maximises boundary F1 on the validation tiles (ed.select_threshold). The test tiles are scored once, with that threshold.


Code
# Evaluation protocol shared by every method.
SCENE = normalise(X05)                       # (8, H, W) in [0, 1], same normalisation as the tiles
ORIG = tiles["origins"]                      # top-left (row, col) of every tile
TRUTH = tiles["labels"]                      # (N, 192, 192) 0/1
SCORED = tiles["valid"]                      # pixels inside the digitised area

def cut(score2d, which):
    """Tiles of a full-scene score map for the tile indices `which`."""
    return np.stack([score2d[r:r + TILE, c:c + TILE] for r, c in ORIG[which]])

RESULTS, CURVES, SCORES = [], {}, {}         # metric rows, ROC curves and score tiles of every method

def evaluate(name, channels, tile_scores, *, kind, threshold=None, tolerance=0):
    """Pick the threshold on the validation tiles (maximum boundary F1), then score the
    train, val and test tiles. `tile_scores(split)` returns (n, 192, 192) boundary scores."""
    s_val = tile_scores("val")
    if threshold is None:                    # Canny passes a fixed threshold; all others are tuned
        threshold, _ = ed.select_threshold(s_val, TRUTH[idx["val"]], valid=SCORED[idx["val"]], tolerance=tolerance)
    for split in ("train", "val", "test"):
        s = s_val if split == "val" else tile_scores(split)
        SCORES[(name, channels, split)] = s
        # Boundary and field precision, recall, F1 and AUC of this split.
        m = ed.edge_metrics(s, TRUTH[idx[split]], threshold=threshold, valid=SCORED[idx[split]], tolerance=tolerance)
        RESULTS.append({"method": name, "kind": kind, "channels": channels, "split": split, "tolerance_px": tolerance, **m})
        if split == "test" and tolerance == 0:
            # ROC curve on the test tiles, from a random sample of at most 300,000 scored pixels.
            from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve
            ok = SCORED[idx["test"]]
            pick = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(ok.sum(), min(300_000, ok.sum()), replace=False)
            fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(TRUTH[idx["test"]][ok][pick], s[ok][pick])
            CURVES[(name, channels)] = (fpr, tpr, m["auc"])
    return threshold

def table(split="test", tolerance=0, cols=("boundary_precision", "boundary_recall", "boundary_f1",
                                            "field_precision", "field_recall", "field_f1", "auc")):
    # Results of one split and tolerance as a table indexed by kind, method and band set.
    df = pd.DataFrame(RESULTS)
    df = df[(df.split == split) & (df.tolerance_px == tolerance)]
    return df.set_index(["kind", "method", "channels"])[list(cols)].round(3)

print(f"scored pixels: train {SCORED[idx['train']].sum():,}, val {SCORED[idx['val']].sum():,}, test {SCORED[idx['test']].sum():,}; "
      f"boundary share on test {TRUTH[idx['test']][SCORED[idx['test']]].mean():.1%}")

title: Field Edge Detection in WorldView Imagery: RGB versus RGB + NIR
text:
Traditional edge detectors
The paper’s introduction names the classical detectors that preceded learning methods. Each one measures how fast brightness changes:

Roberts: 2 x 2 diagonal differences.
Sobel and Prewitt: 3 x 3 smoothed derivatives in x and y; the gradient magnitude is \(\sqrt{G_x^2 + G_y^2}\).
Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG): \(|\nabla^2 (G_\sigma * I)|\), the second derivative after Gaussian smoothing.
Canny: smoothing, gradient, non-maximum suppression and hysteresis thresholds. It returns thin binary edges, so it has a single operating point instead of a score.

ed.classical_edges runs the detector on every band and keeps the maximum response (a multispectral gradient), so adding NIR2 can only add edges that are visible in that band. None of these methods learns what a field boundary looks like: they respond equally to a bund, a tree crown or a pond shore.


Code
# Traditional edge detectors on 3 and 4 channels.
# name -> (method name in ed.classical_edges, Gaussian smoothing sigma in pixels)
CLASSICAL = {"Roberts": ("roberts", 0.0), "Sobel": ("sobel", 1.0), "Prewitt": ("prewitt", 1.0),
             "Laplacian of Gaussian": ("log", 2.0), "Canny": ("canny", 2.0)}
edge_maps = {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for ch, bands in BANDS.items():
    img = np.moveaxis(SCENE[bands], 0, -1)                   # (H, W, bands) for ed.classical_edges
    for name, (method, sigma) in CLASSICAL.items():
        score = ed.classical_edges(img, method, sigma=sigma)  # edge strength of the whole scene in [0, 1]
        edge_maps[(name, ch)] = score
        # Score the tiles; Canny is binary, so it gets a fixed threshold of 0.5.
        evaluate(name, ch, lambda split, s=score: cut(s, idx[split]), kind="1 classical",
                 threshold=0.5 if method == "canny" else None)
print(f"{len(edge_maps)} edge maps scored in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")
display(table().loc["1 classical"].drop(columns=["field_precision", "field_recall"]))

# The reference and the five 4-channel edge maps in a 200 m x 200 m window.
zoom = (slice(900, 1300), slice(1000, 1400))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(21, 3.9))
ax[0].imshow(FC[zoom]); ax[0].contour(BOUNDARY[zoom], levels=[0.5], colors="yellow", linewidths=0.5); ax[0].set_title("reference")
for a, name in zip(ax[1:], CLASSICAL):
    a.imshow(edge_maps[(name, "4ch (B, G, R, NIR2)")][zoom], cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=1); a.set_title(f"{name} (4ch)")
for a in ax:
    a.axis("off")

title: Field Edge Detection in WorldView Imagery: RGB versus RGB + NIR
text:
Random forest on texture features
The paper’s machine-learning baseline was a random forest with 600 trees and a maximum depth of 30, trained on local binary pattern (LBP) and grey-level co-occurrence (GLCM) texture features. Here the per-pixel features are:

the band values;
a 3 x 3 local standard deviation and the Sobel gradient of each band;
LBP uniformity and entropy, and GLCM contrast, correlation, entropy and homogeneity, all in 7 x 7 windows at the native 1.6 m resolution, computed on the visible-band mean and, for 4 channels, also on NIR2 (geolattice.rsense.texture).

The forest is trained on a balanced sample of 80,000 training-tile pixels.


Code
# Random forest on spectral, gradient and texture features (the paper's baseline).
from rasterio.warp import reproject                       # resample texture layers to 0.5 m
from scipy import ndimage as ndi                          # local filters
from skimage.filters import sobel                         # gradient magnitude
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

def to_05(a):
    """A 1.6 m feature layer -> the 0.5 m grid (bilinear)."""
    out = np.full((H, W), np.nan, "float32")
    reproject(a.astype("float32"), out, src_transform=TRANSFORM, src_crs=CRS, dst_transform=T05, dst_crs=CRS,
              resampling=Resampling.bilinear, src_nodata=np.nan, dst_nodata=np.nan)
    return np.nan_to_num(out)                             # missing values -> 0

# Texture at the native 1.6 m: local binary patterns and grey-level co-occurrence (GLCM)
# contrast, correlation, entropy and homogeneity in 7 x 7 windows (GeoLattice texture module).
t0 = time.perf_counter()
native = normalise(X8[None])[0]                           # (8, 702, 760) in [0, 1]
tex_src = {"gray": native[[1, 2, 4]].mean(0), "nir2": native[7]}   # mean of blue, green, red; and NIR2
TEX = {}
for nm, img in tex_src.items():
    lbp = texture.lbp_texture(img, radius=1, n_points=8, size=7, step=1)        # LBP uniformity and entropy
    glcm = texture.glcm_texture(img, size=7, step=2, levels=32, props=("contrast", "correlation", "entropy", "homogeneity"))
    for k, v in {**lbp, **glcm}.items():
        TEX[f"{nm}_{k}"] = to_05(np.asarray(v))          # e.g. "gray_contrast" on the 0.5 m grid
print(f"texture layers: {len(TEX)} in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")

def rf_features(bands, use_nir_texture):
    """Per-pixel features on the 0.5 m grid: band values, 3x3 local std, Sobel gradient, texture."""
    F = {}
    for b in bands:
        x = SCENE[b]
        F[f"b{b + 1}"] = x                                # the band value
        # Local standard deviation in a 3 x 3 window: sqrt(E[x²] - E[x]²).
        F[f"b{b + 1}_std3"] = np.sqrt(np.maximum(ndi.uniform_filter(x ** 2, 3) - ndi.uniform_filter(x, 3) ** 2, 0))
        F[f"b{b + 1}_sobel"] = sobel(ndi.gaussian_filter(x, 1.0))   # gradient after light smoothing
    F.update({k: v for k, v in TEX.items() if k.startswith("gray") or use_nir_texture})   # NIR texture only for 4ch
    return F

# Train on a balanced sample of training-tile pixels; 600 trees of depth <= 30 as in the paper.
RF = {}
for ch, bands in BANDS.items():
    F = rf_features(bands, use_nir_texture=len(bands) == 4)
    names = list(F)
    stack_tiles = lambda which: np.stack([cut(F[n], which) for n in names], -1)   # (n, 192, 192, f)
    Ft = stack_tiles(idx["train"]); yt = TRUTH[idx["train"]]; okt = SCORED[idx["train"]]
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    # Indices of labelled boundary (pos) and field (neg) pixels; 40,000 of each are drawn.
    pos, neg = np.flatnonzero(okt.ravel() & (yt.ravel() == 1)), np.flatnonzero(okt.ravel() & (yt.ravel() == 0))
    pick = np.concatenate([rng.choice(pos, 40_000, replace=False), rng.choice(neg, 40_000, replace=False)])
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=600, max_depth=30, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED)   # all CPU cores
    rf.fit(Ft.reshape(-1, len(names))[pick], yt.ravel()[pick])
    fit_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
    def rf_scores(split, rf=rf, stack_tiles=stack_tiles):
        # Boundary probability of every pixel of the tiles of one split.
        Fx = stack_tiles(idx[split])
        return rf.predict_proba(Fx.reshape(-1, Fx.shape[-1]))[:, 1].reshape(Fx.shape[:3]).astype("float32")
    cache = {s: rf_scores(s) for s in ("train", "val", "test")}
    evaluate("Random forest", ch, cache.get, kind="2 random forest")
    RF[ch] = {"model": rf, "features": names, "fit_s": fit_s, "scores": cache}
    print(f"{ch}: {len(names)} features, fitted in {fit_s:.0f} s")
display(table().loc["2 random forest"].drop(columns=["field_precision", "field_recall"]))
# The twelve most important features of the 4-channel forest (mean decrease in impurity).
imp = pd.Series(RF["4ch (B, G, R, NIR2)"]["model"].feature_importances_, RF["4ch (B, G, R, NIR2)"]["features"]).sort_values()
imp.tail(12).plot.barh(figsize=(6, 3.6), color="0.4", title="Random forest (4ch): most important features"); plt.show()

title: Field Edge Detection in WorldView Imagery: RGB versus RGB + NIR
text:
The six networks
All six are built by ed.build_edge_model, which accepts in_channels=3 or 4:








Network
Idea
Paper




U-Net
Encoder of 3 x 3 convolutions and max-pools (64 to 1024 filters); the decoder upsamples and concatenates the encoder features at the same scale (skip connections).
Table 2, Fig. 4


SegNet
VGG16 encoder (13 convolutions); the decoder upsamples with the max-pooling indices saved by the encoder, so no upsampling weights are learnt.
Table 3, Fig. 5


FC-DenseNet56/67/103
Dense blocks: each layer receives the feature maps of all previous layers in the block; transition-down and -up between blocks. They differ in depth and growth rate (4, 5 and 4-15 layers per block).
Table 4, Figs. 6-7


FCN-DKConv6
Six 5 x 5 dilated convolutions (dilation 1 to 6) with batch normalisation and leaky ReLU; no pooling, so the resolution never drops.
Table 5



All are trained with pixel-wise cross-entropy (the softmax loss of the paper), Adam with L2 weight decay 1e-4, dropout and a cosine learning-rate schedule. Pixels outside the digitised area carry the label -100 and are ignored by the loss. SegNet is the exception to the shared settings: it has no skip connections, and on this small training set it only learns the thin boundary class with class-weighted cross-entropy and a longer schedule (SPECIAL below).


Code
# The six networks of the paper, built with geolattice.rsense.edge_detectors.
import json                                # store training histories next to the weights

NETS = {                                   # name -> (edge_detectors model name, keyword arguments)
    "U-Net": ("unet_basic", {"base": 64, "depth": 4, "dropout": 0.5}),   # paper Table 2: 64 ... 1024 filters, dropout 0.5
    "SegNet": ("SegNet", {"dropout_p": 0.5}),                           # Table 3: VGG16 encoder, pooling indices, central dropout
    "FC-DenseNet56": ("FC-DenseNet56", {}),                             # Table 4
    "FC-DenseNet67": ("FC-DenseNet67", {}),
    "FC-DenseNet103": ("FC-DenseNet103", {}),
    "FCN-DKConv6": ("FCN-DKConv6", {}),                                 # Table 5: six dilated 5 x 5 convolutions
}
# Build each network once on the CPU to report its size.
arch_tbl = []
for name, (arch, kw) in NETS.items():
    m = ed.build_edge_model(arch, in_channels=4, device="cpu", **kw)
    arch_tbl.append({"network": name, "GeoLattice model": arch, "parameters (4ch)": f"{ic.count_parameters(m):,}"})
display(pd.DataFrame(arch_tbl).set_index("network"))

TRAIN = {"epochs": 60, "batch": 4, "lr": 1e-3, "weight_decay": 1e-4}   # lr confirmed by the sweep below
NET_DIR = OUT / "models"                                               # trained weights are saved here
NET_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# SegNet has no skip connections, and with 180 training tiles it learns to call every pixel
# "non-boundary" under the common settings. It gets class-weighted cross-entropy (boundary weight =
# non-boundary / boundary pixels in the training tiles) and 150 epochs instead of 60.
SHARE = float((Ytr == 1).sum() / (Ytr >= 0).sum())                     # boundary share of labelled training pixels
CLASS_W = torch.tensor([1.0, (1 - SHARE) / SHARE], dtype=torch.float32)
SPECIAL = {"SegNet": {"epochs": 150, "loss": torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=CLASS_W, ignore_index=-100)}}
print(f"boundary share of training pixels {SHARE:.3f}; SegNet boundary weight {CLASS_W[1]:.2f}")

def train_net(name, ch, *, epochs=None, lr=None, batch=None, tag=""):
    """Train one network on one band set (or load it if it was trained before) and return
    (model, history, seconds). Cross-entropy, Adam with L2 weight decay, cosine learning-rate
    schedule; the weights of the epoch with the best validation mean IoU are kept."""
    arch, kw = NETS[name]
    bands = BANDS[ch]
    sp = SPECIAL.get(name, {})                                         # network-specific settings, if any
    epochs, lr, batch = epochs or sp.get("epochs", TRAIN["epochs"]), lr or TRAIN["lr"], batch or TRAIN["batch"]
    pt, js = NET_DIR / f"{name}_{len(bands)}ch{tag}.pt", NET_DIR / f"{name}_{len(bands)}ch{tag}.json"
    model = ed.build_edge_model(arch, in_channels=len(bands), device=DEVICE, **kw)
    if pt.exists():                                                    # trained before: load weights and history
        model.load_state_dict(torch.load(pt, map_location=DEVICE))
        meta = json.loads(js.read_text())
        return model.eval(), meta["history"], meta["seconds"]
    ic.set_seed(SEED)
    # Data loaders: shuffled augmented training tiles, and the validation tiles in order.
    train_dl = ic.as_loader(ic.ChipDataset(Xtr[:, bands], Ytr), batch, shuffle=True, seed=SEED)
    val_dl = ic.as_loader(ic.ChipDataset(X_all[idx["val"]][:, bands], Y_all[idx["val"]]), 8, shuffle=False)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    hist = ic.train_model(model, train_dl, val_dl, task="segmentation", epochs=epochs, loss=sp.get("loss", "ce"),
                          optimizer="adam", lr=lr, weight_decay=TRAIN["weight_decay"], scheduler="cosine",
                          num_classes=2, ignore_index=-100, monitor="val_score", device=DEVICE,
                          seed=SEED, verbose=False)
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), pt)                                 # save weights and history for re-runs
    js.write_text(json.dumps({"history": hist, "seconds": seconds, "epochs": epochs, "lr": lr}))
    return model.eval(), hist, seconds

def net_scores(model, ch, split):
    """Boundary probability of every tile of a split (softmax of class 1)."""
    p = ic.predict_proba_batches(model, X_all[idx[split]][:, BANDS[ch]], batch_size=8, device=DEVICE)
    return p[:, 1].astype("float32")

Learning-rate sensitivity
The paper tuned learning rate, batch size, image size, patch size and dropout (Table 6) and settled on 1e-4 with batch size 1 and 500 epochs. With a 30-epoch budget, the three learning rates compare as follows on the validation tiles:


Code
# Learning-rate sensitivity (cf. paper Table 6), FC-DenseNet56 with 4 channels, 30 epochs.
sweep = []
for lr in (1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4):
    model, hist, sec = train_net("FC-DenseNet56", "4ch (B, G, R, NIR2)", epochs=30, lr=lr, tag=f"_lr{lr:.0e}")

    del model; torch.cuda.empty_cache()                                 # free GPU memory before the next run

Test tiles, boundary class.

All networks except SegNet reach a boundary F1 of 0.41 to 0.46. The random forest reaches 0.36, and the traditional detectors 0.20 to 0.36 (Sobel and Prewitt are best, Canny worst).
With 3 channels the best network is U-Net (0.46). With 4 channels FCN-DKConv6, FC-DenseNet56 and U-Net are tied at 0.45 to 0.46.
SegNet is the weakest network (0.32 and 0.29), below the random forest.
The field (cropland) class is easy for every method: F1 0.88 to 0.95, because it covers about 90 % of the scored pixels.

Training tiles vs test tiles. U-Net drops from F1 0.70 on its training tiles to 0.46 on the test tiles, and the FC-DenseNets from about 0.60 to 0.42. With only 45 training tiles, part of what the networks learn does not carry over to unseen fields.
RGB vs RGB + NIR (last table).

Traditional detectors gain the most. AUC rises by 0.03 to 0.04 for every detector, and F1 by 0.03 to 0.05 (Roberts only +0.005). In the near infrared, the bare or grassy bunds contrast more strongly with the crop.
The random forest gains 0.02 AUC, with F1 unchanged.
The networks gain little and not consistently. AUC changes by -0.001 to +0.021. F1 changes by -0.03 (SegNet) to +0.04 (FC-DenseNet56), and U-Net is slightly lower with NIR. The networks seem to learn the bund pattern from the shape and texture of RGB, so the extra band adds little.

The networks other than SegNet draw thin, mostly continuous lines along the bunds, including on the validation and test tiles. Sobel and the random forest find the same lines but break them up and also respond to texture inside fields. SegNet produces speckle, especially inside the red (densely vegetated) fields.
On the test tile, the networks draw straight lines across the large field where faint bunds are visible in the image but were not digitised. These lines count as false positives, so the precision of the networks is probably understated.


How strict is pixel-exact scoring?
The reference boundary is a 1 m band drawn by hand on a 1.6 m image. A prediction one pixel (0.5 m) to the side counts as both a false positive and a false negative. With a tolerance of 0.5 m or 1 m, a predicted boundary pixel counts as correct when a reference boundary lies within that distance, and vice versa:

title: Field Edge Detection in WorldView Imagery: RGB versus RGB + NIR
section: From boundary probability to field polygons
text:
From boundary probability to field polygons
ed.detect_field_edges runs the best network over the whole scene in overlapping 192 x 192 windows (blended with a Hann weight, so tile seams disappear), thresholds the probability, and turns the connected non-boundary regions into fields (ed.boundary_to_instances), returned as georeferenced polygons with area and perimeter.


Code
# From boundary probability to georeferenced field polygons for the whole scene.
from rasterio.features import rasterize

# Best network by validation boundary F1 (both band sets), applied to the full scene with
# overlapping 192 x 192 windows blended by a Hann weight (ed.predict_boundary_probability,
# called inside ed.detect_field_edges).
val = df[(df.split == "val") & (df.kind == "3 network")].sort_values("boundary_f1", ascending=False)
best_name, best_ch = val.iloc[0][["method", "channels"]]
best_th = float(thr[(best_name, best_ch)])
print(f"best on validation: {best_name}, {best_ch} (val boundary F1 {val.iloc[0]['boundary_f1']:.3f}, threshold {best_th:.2f})")
scene_img = np.moveaxis(SCENE[BANDS[best_ch]], 0, -1)              # (H, W, bands) of the whole scene
t0 = time.perf_counter()
# Probability, threshold, closed regions and polygons of at least 50 m², in map coordinates.
res = ed.detect_field_edges(scene_img, MODELS[(best_name, best_ch)], transform=T05, crs=CRS, threshold=best_th,
                            min_area_m2=50, dilate_pixels=1, tile_size=TILE, overlap=64, batch_size=8, device=DEVICE)
print(f"scene inference + polygons in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s: {len(res.fields)} fields")

# Compare with the digitised fields inside the digitised area: count, size and overlap.
area_poly = fields.union_all()                                     # the digitised area as one polygon
pred = res.fields[res.fields.representative_point().within(area_poly)].copy()   # predicted fields inside it
# Intersections of every digitised field with every predicted field, and their areas.
inter = gpd.overlay(fields[["geometry"]].reset_index(names="ref"), pred[["field_id", "geometry"]], how="intersection")
inter["a"] = inter.area
best_overlap = inter.sort_values("a").groupby("ref").last()       # largest overlap per digitised field
# IoU of each digitised field with its best-overlapping predicted field.
iou = best_overlap.apply(lambda r: r.a / fields.geometry[r.name].union(pred.set_index("field_id").geometry[r.field_id]).area, axis=1)
summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "digitised": {"fields": len(fields), "median area (ha)": fields.area.median() / 1e4, "mean area (ha)": fields.area.mean() / 1e4},
    f"{best_name} ({best_ch.split(' ')[0]})": {"fields": len(pred), "median area (ha)": pred.area.median() / 1e4,
                                               "mean area (ha)": pred.area.mean() / 1e4}}).T
display(summary.round(3))
print(f"digitised fields matched by a predicted field with IoU >= 0.5: {(iou >= 0.5).mean():.0%} "
      f"(>= 0.7: {(iou >= 0.7).mean():.0%}); median best IoU {iou.median():.2f}")

# Save the probability raster and the polygons.
with rasterio.open(OUT / "boundary_probability.tif", "w", driver="GTiff", height=H, width=W, count=1, dtype="float32",
                   crs=CRS, transform=T05, compress="deflate") as dst:
    dst.write(res.probability.astype("float32"), 1)
res.fields.to_file(OUT / "predicted_fields.gpkg", layer="fields", driver="GPKG")

# Probability map, digitised fields and predicted fields side by side.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(19, 6.4))
