text:
Patch features from four encoders
Each model reads the scene through its own contract (norm="model") in chips of its own size, and returns patch features that are averaged to the 640 m grid. The four models are loaded one at a time to keep GPU memory free.


Code
MODELS = ["prithvi-eo-2.0-300m", "ssl4eo-s12-vits16-dino", "satlas-swint-s2-ms", "scale-mae"]  # the encoders


def cell_features(enc, da):  # patch features averaged to the 640 m grid, as (cells, D)
    d = enc.embed_raster(da, dense=True, norm="model", batch_size=8)  # (D, y, x) patch map
    f = int(round(d.sizes["y"] / NY))  # patches per cell side (2 for 320 m patches, 1 for 640 m cells) (2 for 320 m patches)
    if f > 1:  # average f x f patches into one cell
        d = d.coarsen(y=f, x=f, boundary="pad").mean()  # 640 m cells
    return d.values[:, :NY, :NX].reshape(d.sizes["embedding"], -1).T  # (cells, D)


feats, info = {}, []  # features and run information
for n in MODELS:  # every model
    enc = fm.load_model(n, device=DEVICE)  # load once per model
    for k, da in s2.items():  # both dates
        t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
        feats[(n, k)] = cell_features(enc, da)  # (cells, D)
        info.append({"model": n, "date": k, "dim": feats[(n, k)].shape[1], "seconds": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1)})  # record
    del enc; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
cube_bands = {k: np.nan_to_num(da.coarsen(y=CELL, x=CELL, boundary="pad").mean().values[:, :NY, :NX].reshape(10, -1).T)
              for k, da in s2.items()}  # baseline: mean reflectance per cell

title: Prithvi, SSL4EO, SatlasPretrain and Scale-MAE on Sentinel-2
text:
Fine-tuning Prithvi for crop segmentation
fm.segmentation_model builds Prithvi-EO-2.0 with a UperNet decoder through TerraTorch; the decoder upsamples patch features back to pixels. Training chips are 224 pixel windows of the June scene with a stride of 112 pixels, labelled pixel by pixel with the six CDL groups. The western half trains, the eastern half tests, and chips that straddle the dividing line are dropped so no pixel is in both.


Code
X_all = fm.prepare("prithvi-eo-2.0-300m", s2["June"])  # 6 HLS bands, Prithvi statistics
lab_da = cdl.astype("float32").expand_dims(band=["cdl"]).where(cdl >= 0)  # labels as a raster, NaN = none
Xc, cy, cx = fm.chip_raster(X_all, chip_size=224, stride=112)  # (n, 6, 224, 224)
Yc, _, _ = fm.chip_raster(lab_da, chip_size=224, stride=112)  # matching label chips
Yc = np.nan_to_num(Yc[:, 0], nan=-1).astype("int64")  # (n, 224, 224), -1 = ignore
cxs = np.repeat(cx[None], len(cy), 0).ravel()  # chip centre x for every chip
mid = float(np.median(cx))  # dividing line
half = 112 * 20.0  # half a chip in metres
train_idx = np.flatnonzero(cxs + half <= mid)  # chips entirely west
test_idx = np.flatnonzero(cxs - half >= mid)  # chips entirely east
print(len(Xc), "chips |", len(train_idx), "train (west) |", len(test_idx), "test (east)")  # split sizes


156 chips | 72 train (west) | 72 test (east)


One training function serves every model: AdamW (with a five times smaller learning rate for a pretrained encoder that is being fine-tuned), bf16 mixed precision on the GPU, random flips, cross-entropy that ignores unlabelled pixels, and a fixed number of epochs. The test score is the mean intersection over union (mIoU) of the classes present in the test area, and the per-class IoU.


Code
from geolattice.rsense.dl import UNet  # U-Net baseline


def run(model, idx, epochs=20, lr=1e-4, batch=8, out=lambda m, x: m(x), encoder_lr=None):  # train, then score
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)  # same shuffles for every model
    model = model.to(DEVICE)  # move to the GPU
    enc_ids = {id(p) for p in getattr(model, "encoder", torch.nn.Module()).parameters()}  # encoder weights, if any
    head = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad and id(p) not in enc_ids]  # decoder and head
    body = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad and id(p) in enc_ids]  # trainable encoder weights
    groups = [{"params": head, "lr": lr}] + ([{"params": body, "lr": encoder_lr or lr}] if body else [])  # learning rates
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(groups, weight_decay=0.01)  # optimizer
    loss_fn = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=-1)  # skip unlabelled pixels
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
    for ep in range(epochs):  # training epochs
        model.train()  # training mode
        perm = np.random.default_rng(SEED + ep).permutation(idx)  # shuffle the chips
        for i in range(0, len(perm), batch):  # mini-batches
            b = perm[i:i + batch]  # chip indices
            x, y = torch.as_tensor(Xc[b]).to(DEVICE), torch.as_tensor(Yc[b]).to(DEVICE)  # inputs and labels
            if np.random.default_rng(ep + i).random() < 0.5:  # random horizontal flip
                x, y = x.flip(-1), y.flip(-1)  # flip both
            with torch.autocast(DEVICE, dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=DEVICE == "cuda"):  # mixed precision
                loss = loss_fn(out(model, x).float(), y)  # pixel-wise cross-entropy
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()  # update
    secs = time.perf_counter() - t0  # training time
    model.eval(); inter = np.zeros(len(CLASSES)); union = np.zeros(len(CLASSES))  # IoU accumulators
    with torch.no_grad(), torch.autocast(DEVICE, dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=DEVICE == "cuda"):  # inference
        for i in range(0, len(test_idx), batch):  # test chips
            b = test_idx[i:i + batch]  # chip indices
            p = out(model, torch.as_tensor(Xc[b]).to(DEVICE)).argmax(1).cpu().numpy()  # predicted classes
            y = Yc[b]; v = y >= 0  # labels and labelled pixels
            for k in range(len(CLASSES)):  # every class
                inter[k] += ((p == k) & (y == k) & v).sum(); union[k] += (((p == k) | (y == k)) & v).sum()  # counts
    iou = np.where(union > 0, inter / np.maximum(union, 1), np.nan)  # IoU per class
    model.cpu(); torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free the GPU
    return {"mIoU": float(np.nanmean(iou)), **{c: iou[k] for k, c in enumerate(CLASSES)}, "train s": secs}  # scores


def prithvi(frozen):  # Prithvi-EO-2.0 + UperNet, encoder frozen or trainable
    m = fm.segmentation_model(len(CLASSES), backbone="prithvi-eo-2.0-300m")  # TerraTorch encoder-decoder
    for p in m.encoder.parameters():  # encoder weights
        p.requires_grad = not frozen  # freeze or train
    return m


seg_out = lambda m, x: m(x).output  # TerraTorch models return an object with .output
results = {"U-Net from scratch": run(UNet(in_channels=6, classes=len(CLASSES)), train_idx, lr=1e-3),
           "Prithvi frozen + UperNet": run(prithvi(True), train_idx, out=seg_out),
           "Prithvi fine-tuned + UperNet": run(prithvi(False), train_idx, encoder_lr=2e-5, out=seg_out)}  # three models
seg = pd.DataFrame(results).T  # one row per model
seg.round(3)

title: Prithvi, SSL4EO, SatlasPretrain and Scale-MAE on Sentinel-2
text:
Label efficiency
The same frozen Prithvi and the U-Net are trained on 4, 12 and all western chips (chosen at random) and scored on the same eastern chips, with the mean IoU of all classes and the mean IoU of the two main crops.


Code
rows = []  # label efficiency results
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)  # random generator
for n_chips in [4, 12, len(train_idx)]:  # training set sizes
    sub = rng.choice(train_idx, n_chips, replace=False) if n_chips < len(train_idx) else train_idx  # a random subset
    ep = max(20, 20 * len(train_idx) // n_chips // 4)  # more epochs for tiny sets (similar number of updates)
    for name, r in [("U-Net from scratch", run(UNet(in_channels=6, classes=len(CLASSES)), sub, epochs=ep, lr=1e-3)),
                    ("Prithvi frozen + UperNet", run(prithvi(True), sub, epochs=ep, out=seg_out))]:  # both models
        rows.append({"chips": n_chips, "model": name, "mIoU": r["mIoU"], "corn and soybean IoU": (r["Corn"] + r["Soybeans"]) / 2})  # scores

    eff[m].plot(marker="o", logx=True, ax=a); a.set_title(m); a.set_xlabel("labelled training chips (224 px, 20 m)")  # curve

Pretraining does not pay off here, even with few labels. On the two main crops alone the U-Net trained from scratch scores slightly higher than the frozen Prithvi with 4, 12 and 72 labelled chips, and the gap in mean IoU over all classes is larger because of the thin classes. Three reasons are likely. A 224 pixel chip of 20 m data (4.5 km) holds a few dozen fields, so even 4 chips give the U-Net about a hundred fields and 200,000 labelled pixels to learn spectral differences from. Prithvi’s 320 m patches blur field edges and roads. And in June the crops differ mainly in their spectra, which a small network learns quickly. Foundation models earn their place with fewer labelled pixels, objects close to their patch size, other regions and sensors (transfer), or when only embeddings, not training, are affordable. Measure before assuming.

title: Prithvi, SSL4EO, SatlasPretrain and Scale-MAE on Sentinel-2
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

Prithvi, SSL4EO, Satlas and Scale-MAE each need their own bands, units and chip size; embed_raster(norm="model", dense=True) gives comparable patch-feature maps at native resolution.
Late-season corn and soybeans are easy for any input; the early-season scene separates the encoders.
Random cross-validation flatters every input on spatially correlated cells; spatial blocks give the honest estimate.
Clustering embeddings without labels recovers the crop pattern only partly, and how well depends on the encoder and the date.
fm.segmentation_model turns Prithvi into a crop segmenter with a UperNet decoder; freezing the encoder trains fastest, and the label efficiency curve shows where pretraining pays off.



Exercises

Add prithvi-eo-1.0-100m to the probe comparison. Does the smaller, US-only model do worse?
Repeat the probes with the 15 May 2025 date. Which encoder keeps its advantage earliest?
Use 320 m cells (no averaging of ViT patches) for the probes; what changes for Satlas, whose cells are 640 m?
Train the fine-tuned Prithvi with 12 chips. Does unfreezing help or hurt with so few labels?
Replace the UperNet decoder with decoder="FCNDecoder" in fm.segmentation_model and compare speed and mIoU.



References

title: Time in Foundation Models: Prithvi-TL, AnySat, Presto and Galileo
text:
Overview

Pixel time series and image time series
A pixel time series is the sequence of values of one pixel through the season, the input of phenology methods and of Presto. An image time series is a stack of images; models that read it can also use the spatial pattern of each date. Real series are irregular: clouds remove dates, and satellites revisit at different intervals.


How models take time








Mechanism
How it works
Models




3-D patches
a token covers several dates of a 16 x 16 pixel patch
Prithvi-EO (tubelets)


date tokens
the acquisition date (year, day of year) is encoded and added to the tokens
Prithvi-EO-2.0-TL, AnySat, Galileo


location tokens
latitude and longitude are encoded, so the model can learn regional crop calendars
Prithvi-EO-2.0-TL, Presto


temporal attention
tokens of different dates attend to each other, then are pooled over time
AnySat, Galileo, L-TAE heads


per-pixel sequence models
a small transformer reads each pixel’s monthly values from many sensors
Presto



Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M-TL is the same network as Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M plus temporal and location encodings. In TerraTorch both take num_frames; only the TL variant uses temporal_coords and location_coords, which embed_raster(metadata=True) fills from the raster’s dates and coordinates (fm.chip_metadata).


Early-season mapping
Crop maps are most valuable before harvest, for yield forecasts, insurance and markets. The question is not only “how accurate with the whole season?” but “how accurate with the dates available by June, by July?”. Each additional date adds information; a good model uses the early dates well.


Baselines that are hard to beat
NDVI through the season captures green-up timing, the main difference between corn (planted earlier, closes canopy earlier) and soybeans. A random forest on a few NDVI dates is a strong baseline, and any foundation model has to be compared with it.

title: Time in Foundation Models: Prithvi-TL, AnySat, Presto and Galileo
text:
A four-date season
One clear date per month from May to August 2025 is taken from the cube as a (time, band, y, x) DataArray. Corn and soybean cells (640 m, at least 60 % one crop) carry the labels, and 5.8 km blocks define the spatial folds, as in notebooks 09_11_03 to 09_11_05.


Code
series = xr.open_dataarray(CUBE / "s2_20m.nc").sel(time=DATES).load().rio.write_crs("EPSG:32615")  # (4, 10, y, x)
cdl = xr.open_dataset(CUBE / "labels_20m.nc")["cdl"].sel(year=2025).load()  # CDL 2025
NY, NX = -(-cdl.shape[0] // CELL), -(-cdl.shape[1] // CELL)  # cell grid
pad = np.full((NY * CELL, NX * CELL), -1, cdl.dtype); pad[:cdl.shape[0], :cdl.shape[1]] = cdl.values  # padded CDL
blk = pad.reshape(NY, CELL, NX, CELL).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(NY * NX, -1)  # pixels per cell
counts = np.stack([(blk == k).sum(1) for k in (0, 1)], 1)  # corn and soybean pixels
y, purity = counts.argmax(1), counts.max(1) / blk.shape[1]  # label and share
gy, gx = np.divmod(np.arange(NY * NX), NX)  # cell row and column
group = (gy // 9) * 10 + gx // 9  # spatial blocks
ok = purity >= 0.6  # pure corn or soybean cells
print(dict(series.sizes), "|", ok.sum(), "cells:", {"corn": int((y[ok] == 0).sum()), "soybeans": int((y[ok] == 1).sum())})  # summary

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(18, 4.6))  # one panel per date
for a, t in zip(ax, series.time.values):  # every date
    v = series.sel(time=t, band=["red", "green", "blue"]).transpose("y", "x", "band").values  # true colour
    a.imshow(np.clip(np.nan_to_num(v) / 0.15, 0, 1)); a.set_title(str(t)[:10]); a.axis("off")  # one date
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

title: Time in Foundation Models: Prithvi-TL, AnySat, Presto and Galileo
text:
Phenology from NDVI
NDVI per date, averaged over each cell, shows the crop calendar: corn greens up earlier than soybeans, and by August both are at full canopy.


Code
ndvi = ((series.sel(band="nir08") - series.sel(band="red")) / (series.sel(band="nir08") + series.sel(band="red")))  # NDVI per date
nd_cell = ndvi.coarsen(y=CELL, x=CELL, boundary="pad").mean().values[:, :NY, :NX].reshape(len(DATES), -1).T  # (cells, dates)
nd_cell = np.nan_to_num(nd_cell)  # fill rare gaps
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.3))  # one panel
doy = pd.to_datetime(DATES).dayofyear  # day of year
for k, (name, col) in enumerate([("corn", "#e6c229"), ("soybeans", "#2a9d3c")]):  # two crops
    v = nd_cell[ok & (y == k)]  # NDVI series of that crop
    ax.plot(doy, v.mean(0), "o-", color=col, label=name)  # mean
    ax.fill_between(doy, *np.percentile(v, [10, 90], 0), color=col, alpha=0.2)  # 10 to 90 % range
ax.set_xlabel("day of year 2025"); ax.set_ylabel("NDVI (640 m cell mean)"); ax.legend()  # labels
ax.set_title("Crop calendar in the Corn Belt"); plt.show()  # draw









The two crops overlap in May (bare soil), separate in June and July as corn closes its canopy first, and converge again in August. A model using all four dates can use that difference in timing.

title: Time in Foundation Models: Prithvi-TL, AnySat, Presto and Galileo
section: Prithvi with one to four frames
text:
Prithvi with one to four frames
Prithvi-EO-2.0 reads a series as frames of 3-D patches. Here it reads the last T dates up to August (T = 1 is the August date alone, T = 4 is May to August), at native resolution in 224 pixel chips, with patch features averaged over time and to the 640 m grid.


Code
def cells(d):  # (D, y, x) patch map -> (cells, D) on the 640 m grid
    f = int(round(d.sizes["y"] / NY))  # patches per cell side (2 for 320 m patches, 1 for 640 m cells)
    d = d.coarsen(y=f, x=f, boundary="pad").mean() if f > 1 else d  # average 320 m patches into 640 m cells
    return d.values[:, :NY, :NX].reshape(d.sizes["embedding"], -1).T  # (cells, D)


prith, secs = {}, {}  # embeddings and run times
for T in [1, 2, 3, 4]:  # number of frames
    sub = series.isel(time=slice(4 - T, 4))  # the last T dates
    for name in ["prithvi-eo-2.0-300m", "prithvi-eo-2.0-300m-tl"]:  # without and with date/location encodings
        enc = fm.load_model(name, device=DEVICE, num_frames=T)  # Prithvi for T frames
        t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
        prith[(name, T)] = cells(enc.embed_raster(sub, dense=True, norm="model", batch_size=4,
                                                  metadata=name.endswith("-tl")))  # TL also gets dates and coordinates
        secs[(name, T)] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # seconds
        del enc; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
pd.Series(secs).unstack(0).round(1).rename_axis("frames")  # seconds for the scene

text:
Do dates and location help?
Spatial linear probes on every embedding, next to NDVI baselines with the same dates: NDVI values alone with a linear model, and a random forest on NDVI and the ten band means of each date.


Code
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier  # baseline
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_score  # spatial folds

bm = np.nan_to_num(series.coarsen(y=CELL, x=CELL, boundary="pad").mean().values[..., :NY, :NX]
                   .reshape(len(DATES), 10, -1).transpose(2, 0, 1))  # (cells, dates, bands) band means

    rf = RandomForestClassifier(300, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED)  # random forest

    rows.append({"frames": T, "input": "NDVI + bands (random forest)",
                 "F1": cross_val_score(rf, feats[ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok], cv=GroupKFold(5), scoring="f1_macro").mean()})  # RF
    for name in ["prithvi-eo-2.0-300m", "prithvi-eo-2.0-300m-tl"]:  # Prithvi

title: Time in Foundation Models: Prithvi-TL, AnySat, Presto and Galileo
text:
AnySat on the same series
AnySat (Astruc et al. 2025) reads a dictionary of modalities, each with its own dates. For Sentinel-2 it takes a (batch, time, 10, height, width) tensor and the day of year of every date; patch_size is the size of its output patches in metres. AnySat expects Sentinel-2 at 10 m, so the 20 m chips are read as if they were 10 m, a scale mismatch to keep in mind. The tile output is one vector per chip.


Code
z = (series - series.mean(("time", "y", "x"))) / series.std(("time", "y", "x"))  # standardize each band over the season
C, _, _ = fm.chip_raster(z.fillna(0), chip_size=CELL)  # (cells, band, time, 32, 32)
C = np.ascontiguousarray(C.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4))  # (cells, time, band, 32, 32) as AnySat expects
dates = torch.as_tensor(pd.to_datetime(DATES).dayofyear.values - 1).repeat(len(C), 1)  # day of year per chip and date
anysat = fm.load_model("anysat", device=DEVICE, trust_repo=True)  # AnySat from torch.hub
t0 = time.perf_counter(); out = []  # timing and results
for i in range(0, len(C), 64):  # batches of chips
    out.append(anysat.encode({"s2": torch.as_tensor(C[i:i + 64]), "s2_dates": dates[i:i + 64]}, patch_size=40).float().cpu().numpy())  # tile embeddings
E_any = np.concatenate(out); del anysat; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # all chips
print("AnySat:", E_any.shape, f"in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")  # size and time
pd.DataFrame({"F1 (4 dates)": {"AnySat": fm.linear_probe(E_any[ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok])["mean"]["f1_macro"],
                               "Prithvi-EO-2.0-TL": res.loc["prithvi-eo-2.0-300m-tl", 4],
                               "NDVI + bands (random forest)": res.loc["NDVI + bands (random forest)", 4]}}).round(3)  # comparison

AnySat reaches about 0.99 with the four dates, the same level as Prithvi-TL and the random forest, and it embeds the whole scene in about 24 seconds. Its dates are explicit inputs, so it accepts irregular series without resampling them to fixed frames. With the full season every method is near the ceiling here; AnySat’s flexibility matters for longer, irregular and multi-sensor series.

title: Time in Foundation Models: Prithvi-TL, AnySat, Presto and Galileo
section: How early can crops be mapped?
text:
How early can crops be mapped?
The previous tables used the last T dates up to August. Early-season mapping needs the opposite: the first T dates, available by the end of May, June, July and August. Prithvi-TL and the random forest are rerun with growing windows from the start of the season.


Code
rows = []  # early-season results
for T in [1, 2, 3, 4]:  # dates available by May, June, July, August
    sub = series.isel(time=slice(0, T))  # the first T dates
    enc = fm.load_model("prithvi-eo-2.0-300m-tl", device=DEVICE, num_frames=T)  # Prithvi-TL for T frames
    E = cells(enc.embed_raster(sub, dense=True, norm="model", batch_size=4, metadata=True))  # embeddings
    del enc; torch.cuda.empty_cache() if DEVICE == "cuda" else None  # free memory
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(300, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED)  # baseline
    feats = np.c_[nd_cell[:, :T], bm[:, :T].reshape(len(bm), -1)]  # NDVI + bands of those dates
    when = pd.Timestamp(DATES[T - 1]).strftime("%d %b")  # last date used
    rows.append({"by": when, "Prithvi-EO-2.0-TL": fm.linear_probe(E[ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok])["mean"]["f1_macro"],
                 "NDVI + bands (random forest)": cross_val_score(rf, feats[ok], y[ok], groups=group[ok], cv=GroupKFold(5),
                                                                 scoring="f1_macro").mean()})  # both scores
early = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("by")  # by date
ax = early.plot(marker="o", figsize=(7, 4.3)); ax.set_ylabel("macro F1 (spatial 5-fold)")  # curve
ax.set_title("Corn vs soybeans as the season progresses"); plt.show()  # draw

Early in the season the foundation model earns its place. With only the 8 May image, when both crops are bare soil or seedlings, Prithvi-TL reaches a macro F1 of about 0.75 against 0.68 for the random forest. By 22 June it is at about 0.97, while the random forest needs the July image to reach that level. A map of this quality is available about three weeks earlier. From mid-July on both methods agree. Where pretrained features help is exactly where labels and spectral contrast are scarce: here, in the weeks after planting.

Presto (Tseng et al. 2023) is a 0.4 million parameter transformer for single pixels. It reads a year of monthly Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, ERA5 climate, SRTM elevation and dynamic world values, each optional, and returns a 128-value embedding. It is small enough to embed millions of pixels on a CPU, which suits national crop maps. Galileo (Tseng et al. 2025) extends the idea to space and time with many inputs (Sentinel-1 and 2, ERA5, TerraClimate, elevation, night lights) and both global and local masked objectives, in sizes from nano to base.
Both are installed from their repositories (pip install from github.com/nasaharvest/presto and github.com/nasaharvest/galileo) and expect monthly composites per pixel with their own band order and normalization. The GeoLattice workflow is the same as above: build the monthly series with geolattice.rsense.timeseries, embed it with the authors’ model, and evaluate the embeddings with fm.linear_probe and spatial groups. title: Time in Foundation Models: Prithvi-TL, AnySat, Presto and Galileo
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

Time enters foundation models as 3-D patches, date tokens, location tokens, temporal attention or per-pixel sequences; fm.chip_raster and embed_raster accept a (time, band, y, x) series.
Prithvi-EO-2.0 reads one to four frames; the TL variant also takes dates and coordinates, filled by embed_raster(metadata=True) from fm.chip_metadata.
AnySat takes each modality with its own dates and returns tile or patch embeddings.
NDVI phenology with a random forest is a strong baseline for corn and soybeans; foundation model embeddings have to be compared with it under spatial cross-validation.
Accuracy grows as the season progresses; the early-season curve shows when a map becomes usable.
Presto and Galileo are pixel and space-time models run through their authors’ code, then evaluated with the same probes.



Exercises

Replace the four monthly dates with the clearest date of each two-week period and rerun Prithvi-TL with four frames. Does the choice of dates matter more than the model?
Give the TL model a wrong year (2015) in its temporal coordinates. How much does the probe change?
Run AnySat with output="patch" and average its patches per cell, as done for Prithvi.
Add the Sentinel-1 series to AnySat’s input dictionary ("s1" with its own dates). Does radar help in May and June?
Build monthly composites for a whole year with geolattice.rsense.timeseries and plan how you would feed them to Presto.



References

Astruc, G. et al. (2025). AnySat: one Earth observation model for many resolutions, scales, and modalities. CVPR.
Garnot, V. S. F. and Landrieu, L. (2020). Lightweight temporal self-attention for classifying satellite images time series. AALTD.
Szwarcman, D. et al. (2024). Prithvi-EO-2.0. arXiv:2412.02732.
Tseng, G. et al. (2023). Lightweight, pre-trained transformers for remote sensing timeseries (Presto). arXiv:2304.14065.
Tseng, G. et al. (2025). Galileo: learning global and local features in pretrained remote sensing models. arXiv:2502.09356.

title: Foundation Model Embeddings as Covariates: Digital Soil Mapping of SOC
text:
Overview

Covariates in digital soil mapping
The scorpan model (McBratney et al. 2003) predicts a soil property from soil (other properties), climate, organisms (vegetation, land use), relief, parent material, age and n (space). Classical covariates are raster layers that stand for each factor: elevation and slope for relief, precipitation and temperature for climate, NDVI and land cover for organisms, texture for parent material.


Embeddings as learned covariates
An AlphaEarth embedding summarizes a year of optical, radar, lidar and climate observations at a pixel. It already contains much of what the classical covariates represent (vegetation, moisture, terrain texture, land use) and possibly things no single covariate captures. It is also opaque: a dimension has no name, and its relation to soil is learned only through the model fitted on the samples.


Risks

Spatial autocorrelation: nearby samples are similar, so random cross-validation is optimistic; folds must be spatial.
Dimensionality: 64 embedding dimensions for 570 samples invites overfitting; regularization, PCA or tree ensembles help.
Interpretability: importance can be measured, but a dimension must be related to known covariates to be explained.
Area of applicability: predictions far, in covariate space, from every training sample are extrapolations. The dissimilarity index of Meyer and Pebesma (2021) marks them.



Residual structure
If covariates explain the spatial pattern of SOC, the residuals of the model have little spatial structure left: their variogram is flat (pure nugget). If not, regression kriging can add the remaining spatial signal.

section: Three covariate sets under spatial cross-validation
text:
Three covariate sets under spatial cross-validation
Classical covariates, AlphaEarth embeddings, and both together; each with a ridge regression and a random forest, scored with 5-fold cross-validation over spatial blocks (whole blocks are held out). Scores are on log(1 + SOC).


Code
SETS = {"classical (13)": COVS, "AlphaEarth (64)": fm.ALPHAEARTH_BANDS, "both (77)": COVS + fm.ALPHAEARTH_BANDS}  # covariate sets
y = tab["logSOC"].to_numpy()  # target
cv = GroupKFold(5)  # spatial folds
rf = lambda: RandomForestRegressor(500, min_samples_leaf=3, max_features=0.33, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED)  # random forest
rows, oof = [], {}  # scores and out-of-fold predictions
for name, cols in SETS.items():  # every set
    X = tab[cols].to_numpy()  # features
    r = fm.linear_probe(X, y, task="regression", cv=5, groups=groups, alpha=10.0)  # ridge with spatial folds
    p = cross_val_predict(rf(), X, y, groups=groups, cv=cv)  # random forest, out of fold
    oof[name] = p  # keep for residuals
    rows.append({"covariates": name, "ridge R2": r["mean"]["r2"], "random forest R2": 1 - np.sum((y - p) ** 2) / np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2),
                 "random forest RMSE": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y - p) ** 2)))})  # scores
res = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("covariates")  # table
res.round(3)

The classical covariates predict log SOC best (random forest R2 about 0.46), AlphaEarth alone reaches about 0.41, and the two together do not improve on the classical set (0.44). The ridge regression ranks them the same way, lower. With 560 samples over the whole Great Plains, the 13 classical covariates already hold the main drivers of topsoil carbon (vegetation and climate); the embeddings carry much of the same information (see below) plus 64 dimensions’ worth of noise for the model to sort through. Embeddings are not a substitute for well-chosen covariates; they are another set to test.

title: Foundation Model Embeddings as Covariates: Digital Soil Mapping of SOC
text:
How many embedding dimensions matter?
The 64 AlphaEarth dimensions are reduced with principal component analysis, fitted inside each training fold, and a random forest uses the first k components.


Code
from sklearn.base import clone  # fresh models per fold

rows = []  # R2 by number of components
E = tab[fm.ALPHAEARTH_BANDS].to_numpy()  # embeddings
for k in [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]:  # components kept
    pred = np.zeros_like(y)  # out-of-fold predictions
    for tr, te in cv.split(E, y, groups):  # spatial folds
        pca = PCA(k, random_state=SEED).fit(E[tr])  # fitted on training folds only
        m = rf().fit(pca.transform(E[tr]), y[tr]); pred[te] = m.predict(pca.transform(E[te]))  # train and predict
    rows.append({"components": k, "R2": 1 - np.sum((y - pred) ** 2) / np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)})  # score
pcs = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("components")  # table
ev = PCA().fit(E).explained_variance_ratio_.cumsum()  # variance explained
ax = pcs["R2"].plot(marker="o", logx=True, figsize=(7, 4.2), label="random forest R2 (spatial CV)")  # curve
ax.plot([2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64], ev[[1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63]], "s--", label="share of embedding variance"); ax.legend()  # variance
ax.set_xlabel("principal components of AlphaEarth"); ax.set_title("How many dimensions matter?"); plt.show()  # draw
pcs.round(3)

Eight principal components give almost all of the embeddings’ predictive power (R2 about 0.41), and adding more does not help: with 64 components the score even drops slightly. For small soil data sets a handful of components is enough, and fewer dimensions make the model easier to fit and to explain.

title: Foundation Model Embeddings as Covariates: Digital Soil Mapping of SOC
text:
What the embeddings stand for
Permutation importance of the random forest on both sets (fitted on all samples) ranks the covariates and dimensions; each important dimension is then correlated with the classical covariates to see what it tracks.


Code
both = SETS["both (77)"]; Xb = tab[both].to_numpy()  # both sets
model = rf().fit(Xb, y)  # random forest on all samples
imp = permutation_importance(model, Xb, y, n_repeats=10, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)  # permutation importance
ranked = pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=both).sort_values(ascending=False)  # ranked
top_dims = [c for c in ranked.index if c.startswith("A")][:5]  # five most important embedding dimensions
corr = tab[top_dims + COVS].corr(method="spearman").loc[top_dims, COVS]  # rank correlations with classical covariates
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.6]})  # importance and correlations
ranked.head(15)[::-1].plot.barh(ax=ax[0], color=["tab:orange" if c.startswith("A") else "tab:blue" for c in ranked.head(15).index[::-1]])  # top 15
ax[0].set_title("permutation importance (orange = AlphaEarth)")  # title
im = ax[1].imshow(corr, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1); ax[1].set_xticks(range(len(COVS)), COVS, rotation=60, ha="right")  # heat map
ax[1].set_yticks(range(len(top_dims)), top_dims); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8, label="Spearman correlation")  # labels
for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(corr.values):  # values
    ax[1].text(j, i, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7)  # write
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









NDVI and precipitation are by far the most important covariates, followed by a group of AlphaEarth dimensions and silt and clay. The important dimensions are not mysterious: A12 and A22 rise with NDVI and precipitation (Spearman correlations of about 0.45 to 0.60), A01 and A29 fall with them, and A42 follows temperature. They are learned versions of the vegetation and climate gradient that already drives the model, which explains why adding them to the classical covariates adds little here.

title: Foundation Model Embeddings as Covariates: Digital Soil Mapping of SOC
text:
Spatial structure of the residuals
The variogram of log SOC and of the out-of-fold residuals of each random forest, with the same lags. A residual variogram that is flat at the level of its nugget means the covariates captured the spatial pattern; one that still rises with distance leaves structure for regression kriging.


Code
from geolattice.geostatistics import Variogram  # experimental and model variograms

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))  # one panel
series = {"log SOC": y} | {f"residuals, {k}": y - p for k, p in oof.items()}  # target and residuals
fits = {}  # fitted parameters
for (name, z), st in zip(series.items(), ["-", "--", "-.", ":"]):  # every series
    v = Variogram(xy, z, model="spherical", n_lags=15, maxlag=600_000).fit()  # variogram up to 600 km
    lags, gam = np.asarray(v.lags) / 1000, np.asarray(v.experimental)  # lags (km) and semivariance
    ax.plot(lags, gam, "o" + st, ms=4, label=name)  # experimental variogram
    fits[name] = v.fitted_params  # fitted model
ax.set_xlabel("lag (km)"); ax.set_ylabel("semivariance"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Variograms of log SOC and residuals"); plt.show()  # draw

All three models remove much of that structure; the residual variograms are lower and flatter. The classical covariates leave the least structure, AlphaEarth the most, the same order as the cross-validation scores. Some structure remains at all lags below 300 km, so regression kriging of the residuals could still add a little (exercise 2). title: Foundation Model Embeddings as Covariates: Digital Soil Mapping of SOC
section: A SOC map and its area of applicability
text:
A SOC map and its area of applicability
The prediction grid holds the classical covariates at about one million points. AlphaEarth is read once on a 2 km grid in the same Albers projection (EPSG:5070) from the overviews of the public GeoTIFFs (scale=2000 selects them automatically) and joined to the grid points by nearest pixel; the random forest trained on both sets predicts log SOC at every point. The dissimilarity index (DI) measures how far each point is, in weighted covariate space, from the nearest training sample; points with DI above the threshold learned from the training data are outside the area of applicability (AOA).


Code
grid = pd.read_csv(GRID)  # covariates on the prediction grid
grid = grid.rename(columns={"slope_g": "slope", "h_curvatur": "h_curvature"})[COVS + ["x", "y"]].dropna()  # same names as the rasters
cache = OUT / "alphaearth_great_plains_2020_2km.nc"  # cached read
if not cache.exists():  # read once from the public GeoTIFF overviews
    region = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(grid["x"], grid["y"]), crs=soil.crs).total_bounds  # grid bounds (Albers)
    from shapely.geometry import box  # rectangle
    aoi = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[box(*region)], crs=soil.crs)  # the area
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
    fm.alphaearth_to_xarray(aoi, 2020, scale=2000, crs="EPSG:5070").drop_vars("spatial_ref", errors="ignore").to_netcdf(cache)  # 2 km grid
    print(f"read in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")  # timing
aeg = xr.open_dataarray(cache)  # (64, y, x) at 2 km
gx = xr.DataArray(grid["x"].to_numpy(), dims="p"); gy = xr.DataArray(grid["y"].to_numpy(), dims="p")  # grid points
grid[fm.ALPHAEARTH_BANDS] = aeg.sel(x=gx, y=gy, method="nearest").values.T  # nearest 2 km pixel
grid = grid.dropna()  # points with embeddings
grid["SOC_pred"] = np.expm1(model.predict(grid[both].to_numpy()))  # back-transform to kg m-2
from geolattice.rsense.xai.aoa import dissimilarity_index  # AOA
w = pd.Series(np.clip(imp.importances_mean, 0, None), index=both)  # importance weights
di, thr, _ = dissimilarity_index(tab[both], grid[both].to_numpy(), weights=w.to_numpy(), folds=groups)  # DI and threshold
grid["outside_AOA"] = di > thr  # extrapolation
print(f"{len(grid):,} grid points | AOA threshold {thr:.2f} | outside AOA: {grid['outside_AOA'].mean():.1%}")  # summary
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6.5))  # map and AOA
s = grid.sample(min(len(grid), 300_000), random_state=SEED)  # thin for plotting
im = ax[0].scatter(s["x"] / 1000, s["y"] / 1000, c=s["SOC_pred"], s=0.3, cmap="YlOrBr", vmax=np.percentile(s["SOC_pred"], 98))  # SOC map
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], label="predicted SOC (kg m-2)"); ax[0].set_title("SOC, random forest on classical + AlphaEarth")  # labels
ax[1].scatter(s["x"] / 1000, s["y"] / 1000, c=np.where(s["outside_AOA"], "crimson", "lightgray"), s=0.3)  # AOA
ax[1].scatter(xy[:, 0] / 1000, xy[:, 1] / 1000, s=4, c="k"); ax[1].set_title("outside the area of applicability (red), samples (black)")  # samples
for a in ax:  # both panels
    a.set_aspect("equal")  # equal axes
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


1,009,279 grid points | AOA threshold 0.35 | outside AOA: 2.8%









The map shows the broad patterns of Great Plains topsoil carbon: high values in the Colorado and Wyoming mountains and in eastern Kansas, low values on the dry plains of eastern Colorado and across New Mexico. About 3 % of the grid lies outside the area of applicability, mostly in the northern and central Rocky Mountains, where the combination of covariates and embeddings is unlike any sample. Those predictions are extrapolations and should be masked or flagged in any product.

title: Foundation Model Embeddings as Covariates: Digital Soil Mapping of SOC
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

AlphaEarth embeddings at soil samples are a ready-made covariate set; classical covariates, the embeddings, and both together can be compared directly with spatial cross-validation.
Spatial folds, random forests or regularized linear models, and PCA keep 64 dimensions from overfitting 570 samples.
Permutation importance and correlations with classical covariates show what the important embedding dimensions track.
The residual variogram shows how much spatial structure the covariates leave, and so whether regression kriging is worth adding.
The area of applicability marks where the map extrapolates beyond the training data.



Exercises

Use AlphaEarth of 2017 instead of 2020 (the earliest year). Do the scores change?
Add regression kriging: krige the residuals of the best model with geolattice.geostatistics.OrdinaryKriging and add them to the random forest map. Does the spatial CV error drop?
Replace the 5 x 5 spatial blocks with 10 x 10 blocks and with random folds. How much do the scores change?
Average the AlphaEarth embeddings in a 100 m window around each sample instead of taking one 10 m pixel (re-normalise the mean vector). Does it help?
Predict soil texture (silt and clay) from AlphaEarth alone. Which soil property do the embeddings capture best?



References

Brown, C. F. et al. (2025). AlphaEarth Foundations. arXiv:2507.22291.
McBratney, A. B., Mendonca Santos, M. L. and Minasny, B. (2003). On digital soil mapping. Geoderma.
Meyer, H. and Pebesma, E. (2021). Predicting into unknown space? Estimating the area of applicability of spatial prediction models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution.
Hengl, T. et al. (2018). Random forest as a generic framework for predictive modeling of spatial and spatio-temporal variables. PeerJ.

title: Vision-Language Models: Zero-Shot Classification and Text Retrieval
text:
Overview

How CLIP-style models work
CLIP (Radford et al. 2021) trains an image encoder and a text encoder together on image and caption pairs. For a batch of pairs, the model is rewarded when each image’s embedding is most similar (cosine similarity, scaled by a learned temperature) to its own caption’s embedding and not to the other captions. After training, images and text share one space:

zero-shot classification: write one sentence per class (“a satellite image of a river”), embed the sentences, and give each image the class whose sentence is most similar;
text-to-image retrieval: embed a query sentence and rank images by similarity;
image-to-image retrieval: rank images by similarity to an example image.



Remote sensing CLIPs
General CLIP models saw few overhead images. RemoteCLIP (Liu et al. 2024) fine-tunes CLIP on remote sensing captions, many generated from detection and segmentation labels. GeoRSCLIP (Zhang et al. 2024) trains on RS5M, five million remote sensing image-text pairs. SkyCLIP (Wang et al. 2024) uses SkyScript, captions built from OpenStreetMap tags. All read RGB images of about 224 pixels.
Chat models such as GeoChat, EarthGPT, LHRS-Bot and EarthDial go further: a language model reads the image embeddings and answers free-form questions. They are listed in the catalog but are multi-billion-parameter models run through their authors’ code.


Prompts matter
The class sentence is part of the model. “River”, “a satellite image of a river” and “an aerial photo of a winding river” give different text embeddings and different accuracies. Averaging the embeddings of several templates (prompt ensembling) usually helps.


What zero-shot is not
A zero-shot label is a similarity, not a measurement. It works for classes that captions describe often and look distinctive from above; it fails for classes defined by function rather than appearance, for counting, for small objects, for bands other than RGB, and for place names. Every output here is scored against reference labels before it is trusted.

text:
EuroSAT
EuroSAT (Helber et al. 2019) is a standard benchmark of Sentinel-2 patches from 34 European countries. Its RGB version is read directly from the zip archive. A balanced test set of 100 images per class is drawn, and a separate pool of training images is kept for the probes.


Code
zf = zipfile.ZipFile(EUROSAT)  # the archive
files = [n for n in zf.namelist() if n.endswith(".jpg")]  # every image
cls = np.array([n.split("/")[1] for n in files])  # class from the folder name
CLASSES = sorted(PHRASES)  # the 10 classes
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)  # random generator
test_files, pool_files = [], []  # test set and training pool
for c in CLASSES:  # balanced sampling per class
    idx = rng.permutation(np.flatnonzero(cls == c))  # shuffled images of class c
    test_files += [files[i] for i in idx[:100]]; pool_files += [files[i] for i in idx[100:200]]  # 100 test, 100 pool
load = lambda names: [Image.open(zf.open(n)).convert("RGB") for n in names]  # read images
test_img, pool_img = load(test_files), load(pool_files)  # PIL images
y_test = np.array([n.split("/")[1] for n in test_files]); y_pool = np.array([n.split("/")[1] for n in pool_files])  # labels
print(len(files), "images in", len(CLASSES), "classes |", len(test_img), "test |", len(pool_img), "pool | size", test_img[0].size)  # summary

fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 10, figsize=(18, 4))  # two examples per class
for j, c in enumerate(CLASSES):  # every class
    for i in range(2):  # two examples
        ax[i, j].imshow(test_img[CLASSES.index(c) * 100 + i]); ax[i, j].axis("off")  # one image
    ax[0, j].set_title(c, fontsize=8)  # class name
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

Zero-shot classification
fm.zero_shot_classify embeds every image and one sentence per class built from a template, and returns the softmax of the scaled similarities plus the top class. Two models, one template: “a satellite image of {}.” (open_clip first builds the empty network and GeoLattice then loads all 302 weight tensors of the RemoteCLIP or GeoRSCLIP checkpoint into it.)


Code

to_class = dict(zip(names, CLASSES))  # words -> EuroSAT class
zs, t0 = {}, time.perf_counter()  # results and timing
for model in ["remoteclip-vit-b-32", "georsclip-vit-b-32"]:  # two remote sensing CLIPs
    df = fm.zero_shot_classify(test_img, names, model=model, template="a satellite image of {}.", device=DEVICE)  # zero-shot

acc.loc["overall"] = [np.mean(p == y_test) for p in zs.values()]  # overall accuracy

GeoRSCLIP (about 49 % overall) beats RemoteCLIP (about 36 %, close to the figure its authors report for EuroSAT with this encoder), and both are far from the 95 % or more that supervised networks reach on EuroSAT. The matrix shows where GeoRSCLIP fails. It recognises residential areas, highways and water bodies almost perfectly, the classes with a distinctive look and many captions. It confuses classes defined by use rather than appearance: annual cropland and pasture go to herbaceous vegetation, permanent crops (orchards, vineyards) to annual crops, industrial to residential. Dark, uniform forest patches go to “sea or lake”. EuroSAT images are only 64 pixels and are upsampled to 224, so they are much blurrier than the captioned images these models learned from.

title: Vision-Language Models: Zero-Shot Classification and Text Retrieval
text:
Prompt wording and ensembling
The image and text encoders are loaded once with fm.load_model, so many prompts can be tried without re-embedding the images. Each template is scored alone, then all templates are averaged (prompt ensembling).


Code
clip = fm.load_model("remoteclip-vit-b-32", device=DEVICE)  # RemoteCLIP: image and text encoders
pre, tok = clip.extras["preprocess"], clip.extras["tokenizer"]  # image preprocessing and tokenizer


def image_emb(images, batch=128):  # unit-length image embeddings
    out = []  # batches
    for i in range(0, len(images), batch):  # in batches
        x = torch.stack([pre(im) for im in images[i:i + batch]])  # preprocessed tensors
        out.append(clip.encode(x).float().cpu().numpy())  # image embeddings
    E = np.concatenate(out)  # all images
    return E / np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # normalize


def text_emb(sentences):  # unit-length text embeddings
    with torch.no_grad():  # inference
        t = clip.model.encode_text(tok(sentences).to(clip.device)).float().cpu().numpy()  # text embeddings
    return t / np.linalg.norm(t, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # normalize


E_test = image_emb(test_img)  # test images, once
TEMPLATES = ["{}", "a satellite image of {}.", "an aerial photo of {}.", "a remote sensing image of {}.",
             "a low resolution satellite image showing {}.", "a Sentinel-2 image of {}."]  # prompt templates
scores, T_all = {}, []  # accuracies and text embeddings
for t in TEMPLATES:  # every template
    T = text_emb([t.format(n) for n in names])  # one sentence per class
    T_all.append(T)  # keep for ensembling
    scores[t] = np.mean(np.array(CLASSES)[(E_test @ T.T).argmax(1)] == y_test)  # accuracy
ens = np.mean(T_all, 0); ens /= np.linalg.norm(ens, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # averaged class embeddings
scores["ensemble of all templates"] = np.mean(np.array(CLASSES)[(E_test @ ens.T).argmax(1)] == y_test)  # ensemble accuracy
pd.Series(scores, name="accuracy").round(3).to_frame()  # template effects

The bare class words are the worst prompt and “a satellite image of {}.” the best, a spread of six points from wording alone. Averaging all templates does not help here: it lands between the best and the worst single template. Prompt ensembling usually helps when templates are diverse and individually decent; it cannot fix a class whose words the model has not linked to its appearance.

title: Vision-Language Models: Zero-Shot Classification and Text Retrieval
text:
How many labels beat zero-shot?
The same image embeddings feed a logistic regression trained on k labelled images per class from the pool, for k from 1 to 100. Each k is repeated five times with different draws.


Code
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression  # few-shot classifier

E_pool = image_emb(pool_img)  # pool embeddings
rows = []  # few-shot results
for k in [1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100]:  # labels per class
    for rep in range(5 if k < 100 else 1):  # repeated draws
        r = np.random.default_rng(rep)  # draw generator
        idx = np.concatenate([r.choice(np.flatnonzero(y_pool == c), k, replace=False) for c in CLASSES])  # k per class
        clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000, C=10).fit(E_pool[idx], y_pool[idx])  # linear probe
        rows.append({"labels per class": k, "accuracy": np.mean(clf.predict(E_test) == y_test)})  # test accuracy
few = pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("labels per class")["accuracy"].agg(["mean", "std"])  # mean and spread
ax = few["mean"].plot(marker="o", logx=True, figsize=(7, 4.3), label="linear probe on RemoteCLIP embeddings")  # curve
ax.fill_between(few.index, few["mean"] - few["std"], few["mean"] + few["std"], alpha=0.2)  # spread
ax.axhline(scores["ensemble of all templates"], color="k", ls="--", label="zero-shot, prompt ensemble")  # zero-shot level
ax.set_ylabel("EuroSAT test accuracy"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Few labels vs no labels"); plt.show()  # draw

One labelled image per class already beats zero-shot by a wide margin (about 57 % against 36 %), ten per class reach about 84 % and a hundred about 90 %. The image embeddings hold far more class information than the text side can retrieve, which is the practical lesson: zero-shot is for exploring an archive or for classes with no labels at all, and a handful of labels is worth more than any prompt.

title: Vision-Language Models: Zero-Shot Classification and Text Retrieval
text:
Searching an archive with words
DeepGlobe images are 2448 pixels at 50 cm; each of 60 training tiles is cut into 4 x 4 crops of 612 pixels (306 m), giving an archive of 960 crops. Each crop’s reference class is the majority class of its mask when it covers at least half of the crop. Six queries are embedded and the 12 most similar crops are retrieved for each; precision at 12 is the share of retrieved crops whose reference class matches the query.


Code
DG_CLASSES = pd.read_csv(DG / "class_dict.csv")  # class colours
meta = pd.read_csv(DG / "metadata.csv").query("split == 'train'")  # tiles with masks
tiles = meta.sample(60, random_state=SEED)  # 60 random tiles
crops, crop_cls = [], []  # archive images and reference classes
rgb2cls = {tuple(r[["r", "g", "b"]]): r["name"] for _, r in DG_CLASSES.iterrows()}  # mask colour -> class
for _, t in tiles.iterrows():  # every tile
    im = Image.open(DG / t["sat_image_path"]).convert("RGB")  # image
    mk = (np.asarray(Image.open(DG / t["mask_path"]).convert("RGB")) > 128).astype(int) * 255  # mask, clean colours
    for r in range(4):  # 4 x 4 crops
        for c in range(4):  # columns
            box = (c * 612, r * 612, (c + 1) * 612, (r + 1) * 612)  # crop window
            crops.append(im.crop(box).resize((224, 224)))  # resized crop
            sub = mk[box[1]:box[3], box[0]:box[2]].reshape(-1, 3)  # its mask pixels
            names_px, n = np.unique([rgb2cls.get(tuple(p), "unknown") for p in sub[::97]], return_counts=True)  # sampled classes
            crop_cls.append(names_px[n.argmax()] if n.max() >= 0.5 * n.sum() else "mixed")  # majority or mixed
crop_cls = np.array(crop_cls)  # reference classes
E_dg = image_emb(crops)  # archive embeddings
print(len(crops), "crops |", pd.Series(crop_cls).value_counts().to_dict())  # archive summary


960 crops | {'agriculture_land': 636, 'urban_land': 92, 'forest_land': 73, 'barren_land': 58, 'rangeland': 51, 'water': 33, 'mixed': 17}




Code
QUERIES = {"water": "a satellite image of a river or a lake", "forest_land": "a satellite image of a dense forest",
           "urban_land": "a satellite image of a dense town with many buildings",
           "agriculture_land": "a satellite image of farmland with crop fields",
           "barren_land": "a satellite image of bare sand or rock", "rangeland": "a satellite image of grassland and shrubs"}  # text queries
Q = text_emb(list(QUERIES.values()))  # query embeddings
idx, sim = fm.embedding_search(E_dg, Q, k=12)  # top 12 crops per query
prec = {c: np.mean(crop_cls[idx[i]] == c) for i, c in enumerate(QUERIES)}  # precision at 12
base = {c: np.mean(crop_cls == c) for c in QUERIES}  # random retrieval
print(pd.DataFrame({"precision at 12": prec, "share of archive (random)": base}).round(2))  # scores
fig, ax = plt.subplots(len(QUERIES), 6, figsize=(13, 2.3 * len(QUERIES)))  # top 6 per query
for i, (c, q) in enumerate(QUERIES.items()):  # every query
    for j in range(6):  # top hits
        ax[i, j].imshow(crops[idx[i, j]]); ax[i, j].axis("off")  # hit
        ax[i, j].set_title(crop_cls[idx[i, j]], fontsize=7, color="green" if crop_cls[idx[i, j]] == c else "red")  # its class
    ax[i, 0].text(-20, 112, q.replace("a satellite image of ", ""), rotation=90, va="center", ha="right", fontsize=8)  # query
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


                  precision at 12  share of archive (random)
water                        0.08                       0.03
forest_land                  0.50                       0.08
urban_land                   0.83                       0.10
agriculture_land             1.00                       0.66
barren_land                  0.25                       0.06
rangeland                    0.00                       0.05









Text search works for classes with a distinctive look. “A dense town” returns urban crops for 10 of 12 hits against 10 % urban crops in the archive, and “a dense forest” returns forest for half its hits against 8 %. It fails for the rest. The water query returns fields with small ponds and canals, because only 33 crops are mostly water at 306 m. The rangeland query returns nothing labelled rangeland: in DeepGlobe rangeland is defined by use and looks like fallow fields. Agriculture reaches 100 %, but two thirds of the archive is agriculture, so that score means little. Precision must always be read against the share of the class in the archive.

Searching with an example image
An image can be the query too. Here the queries are EuroSAT images (10 m Sentinel-2) and the archive is DeepGlobe (50 cm): a 20 times difference in resolution.

title: Vision-Language Models: Zero-Shot Classification and Text Retrieval
text:
What vision-language models cannot do
A short test of three requests the models are often asked to do: count objects, read infrared, and use place names. Each is scored on images whose answer is known.


Code
# 1. Counting: the probability given to "one", "two" or "many" buildings follows texture, not counts
cnt = text_emb([f"a satellite image with {w} buildings" for w in ["one", "two", "three", "many"]])  # counting prompts
res = E_test[y_test == "Residential"][:50] @ cnt.T  # residential images vs the prompts
print("residential images, chosen count prompt:", pd.Series(np.array(["one", "two", "three", "many"])[res.argmax(1)]).value_counts().to_dict())  # answers

# 2. False colour: the same images shown as NIR-red-green would need infrared bands the model never saw
print("RemoteCLIP input:", fm.model_info("remoteclip-vit-b-32")["inputs"])  # RGB only

# 3. Place names: the same forest images described with two countries
pl = text_emb(["a satellite image of a forest in Germany", "a satellite image of a forest in Brazil"])  # place prompts
f_img = E_test[y_test == "Forest"]  # European forest images
print("European forests matched to 'Germany' vs 'Brazil':", np.bincount((f_img @ pl.T).argmax(1), minlength=2))  # place answer


residential images, chosen count prompt: {'many': 31, 'one': 19}
RemoteCLIP input: RGB 224 px + text
European forests matched to 'Germany' vs 'Brazil': [100   0]



Counting. Every residential image contains dozens of buildings, yet 19 of 50 were matched to “one building”. The similarity follows texture and brightness, not the number of objects.
Bands. The models take RGB only; infrared, the most informative part of the spectrum for vegetation and water, never reaches them.
Places. All 100 forest images were matched to “Germany” rather than “Brazil”. That looks right, but it reflects a learned link between temperate texture and the word, not geolocation: the images come from 34 countries, and none of them is Germany-specific. A place name in a prompt is a stylistic cue, never a location check.

title: Vision-Language Models: Zero-Shot Classification and Text Retrieval
text:
Summary and exercises

Summary

CLIP-style models embed images and sentences in one space; zero-shot classification picks the class whose sentence is most similar to the image.
On EuroSAT, remote sensing CLIPs classify some classes well and confuse others that differ by use rather than appearance; every result needs a reference check.
Prompt wording changes accuracy; averaging several templates is a cheap improvement.
A linear probe on the same image embeddings overtakes zero-shot with a handful of labels per class.
Text search works for visually distinctive classes; image queries work even across a twentyfold change in resolution for some classes.
Counting, non-RGB bands and place names are outside what these models do reliably.



Exercises

Write three alternative phrasings for the two worst classes and find the best one. Is it still best with GeoRSCLIP?
Use remoteclip-vit-l-14 (download about 1.7 GB). Does a larger encoder fix the confusions?
Repeat the few-shot curve with GeoRSCLIP embeddings and with the SSL4EO ResNet-18 on the same RGB images. Which representation is most label-efficient?
Add the query “a satellite image of a road” to the DeepGlobe search. Which class do the hits belong to, and why is the precision hard to define?
Re-run zero-shot on EuroSAT images upsampled from 64 to 224 pixels with nearest neighbour instead of bicubic resampling. Does the interpolation matter?



References

Demir, I. et al. (2018). DeepGlobe 2018: a challenge to parse the Earth through satellite images. CVPR Workshops.

title: Weather and Earth System Foundation Models
text:
Overview

From numerical weather prediction to learned emulators
Numerical weather prediction (NWP) solves the equations of the atmosphere on a grid, step by step, on supercomputers. A learned emulator is trained on decades of reanalysis (ERA5: the best estimate of the past atmosphere, hourly at 0.25 degrees since 1940) to map the state at time t to the state at t + 6 h. Applied repeatedly (an autoregressive rollout) it produces a forecast in seconds on one GPU.









Model
Provider
Architecture
Notable for




FourCastNet
NVIDIA, 2022
Fourier neural operator (v1), spherical FNO (v2)
first competitive learned model; very fast ensembles


GraphCast
Google DeepMind, 2023
graph neural network on an icosahedral mesh
beat ECMWF HRES on most targets at 10 days


GenCast
Google DeepMind, 2024
diffusion model on a mesh
probabilistic ensembles that beat ECMWF ENS


Aurora
Microsoft, 2024
3-D Swin U-Net with Perceiver encoders, 1.3 B parameters
one foundation model fine-tuned for weather, air pollution, ocean waves


Prithvi WxC
NASA and IBM, 2024
2.3 B transformer on MERRA-2
downscaling, gravity waves, fine-tuning tasks



Aurora is a foundation model in the full sense of this chapter: pretrained on more than a million hours of diverse atmospheric data, then fine-tuned for tasks.


What these models predict
Aurora reads four surface variables (2 m temperature, 10 m wind components, mean sea level pressure), five atmospheric variables (geopotential, wind components, temperature, specific humidity) on 13 pressure levels, three static variables (surface geopotential, land-sea mask, soil type) and the two most recent states, 6 hours apart, so it sees the tendency.


How forecasts are scored
The root mean square error (RMSE) against the verifying analysis, weighted by the cosine of latitude so that the crowded grid cells near the poles do not dominate, is the standard score. Persistence (tomorrow equals today) is the simplest baseline; any forecast must beat it.


Links to land applications
Weather drives everything else in this chapter: crop calendars (notebook 09_11_06), drought, evapotranspiration (chapter 08_12) and yield. Learned forecasts are fast enough to run large ensembles for those applications.

title: Weather and Earth System Foundation Models
text:
ERA5 from the cloud
WeatherBench2 publishes ERA5 as a Zarr store on Google Cloud Storage. Opening it reads only the metadata; values are fetched when needed. The forecast starts from the states at 00 and 06 UTC on 1 January 2023 and is verified at 12 and 18 UTC.


Code
era = xr.open_zarr(ERA5, storage_options={"token": "anon"}, consolidated=True)  # lazy, anonymous
print(dict(era.sizes)); print("levels (hPa):", era.level.values)  # archive size and levels
times = pd.to_datetime(["2023-01-01T00", "2023-01-01T06", "2023-01-01T12", "2023-01-01T18"])  # inputs and targets
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
state = era[list(SURF.values()) + list(ATMOS.values())].sel(time=times).load()  # about 1 GB
static = era[list(STATIC.values())].load()  # static fields
print(f"loaded in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s | lat {float(era.latitude[0])} to {float(era.latitude[-1])}")  # timing and orientation

title: Weather and Earth System Foundation Models
text:
Building an Aurora batch
An Aurora Batch holds tensors of shape (batch, history, …) for surface and atmospheric variables, 2-D static fields, and metadata: latitudes (decreasing), longitudes (0 to 360), the time of the latest state and the pressure levels. The history is the 00 and 06 UTC states.


Code
from aurora import Batch, Metadata  # Aurora data structures

def make_batch(i0):  # the states at times[i0] and times[i0 + 1] as an Aurora batch
    sl = slice(i0, i0 + 2)  # two consecutive states
    return Batch(
        surf_vars={k: torch.from_numpy(state[v].isel(time=sl).values[None]) for k, v in SURF.items()},  # (1, 2, lat, lon)
        static_vars={k: torch.from_numpy(static[v].values) for k, v in STATIC.items()},  # (lat, lon)
        atmos_vars={k: torch.from_numpy(state[v].isel(time=sl).values[None]) for k, v in ATMOS.items()},  # (1, 2, level, lat, lon)
        metadata=Metadata(lat=torch.from_numpy(era.latitude.values), lon=torch.from_numpy(era.longitude.values),
                          time=(times[i0 + 1].to_pydatetime(),), atmos_levels=tuple(int(l) for l in era.level.values)))  # metadata

batch = make_batch(0)  # history 00 and 06 UTC
print({k: tuple(v.shape) for k, v in batch.surf_vars.items()}, "|", {k: tuple(v.shape) for k, v in batch.atmos_vars.items()})  # shapes

title: Weather and Earth System Foundation Models
text:
A 6 hour forecast
The full Aurora (1.3 billion parameters, pretrained on ERA5 and other sources) needs more memory than a 16 GB GPU offers at 0.25 degrees: its weights alone take 4.8 GB, and a global forecast step on this machine’s GPU ran out of memory at about 13 GB of activations. It runs on the CPU instead, about six minutes per step with 24 cores. On a GPU with 24 GB or more the same code runs on the GPU in seconds. rollout runs two 6 hour steps at once; the first is the +6 h forecast scored here, the second the +12 h forecast scored further down.


Code
from aurora import AuroraPretrained, rollout  # model and autoregressive rollout

big_gpu = DEVICE == "cuda" and torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory >= 24 * 2**30  # enough GPU memory?
AURORA_DEVICE = "cuda" if big_gpu else "cpu"  # where the full model runs
torch.set_num_threads(os.cpu_count())  # use every core on the CPU
model = AuroraPretrained(autocast=big_gpu)  # 1.3 B parameters (bfloat16 autocast on the GPU)
model.load_checkpoint("microsoft/aurora", "aurora-0.25-pretrained.ckpt")  # pretrained weights (about 5 GB, cached)
model = model.to(AURORA_DEVICE).eval()  # inference mode
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
with torch.inference_mode():  # inference only
    preds = [p.to("cpu") for p in rollout(model, batch, steps=2)]  # +6 h and +12 h
pred = preds[0]  # the +6 h forecast
print(f"Aurora 0.25 pretrained on {AURORA_DEVICE}: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) / 1e9:.2f} B parameters | "
      f"two steps in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s | first forecast valid at {pred.metadata.time[0]}")  # what ran
del model  # free memory
MODEL = "Aurora 0.25 pretrained (1.3 B)"  # label for the figures

title: Weather and Earth System Foundation Models
text:
Scoring against ERA5 and persistence
The forecast valid at 12 UTC is compared with the ERA5 analysis at 12 UTC, and so is persistence (the 06 UTC state). Aurora returns a grid with 720 latitudes (it drops the south pole row), so ERA5 is cut to match.


Code
lat = pred.metadata.lat.cpu().numpy()  # forecast latitudes
w = np.cos(np.deg2rad(lat))[:, None]; w = w / w.mean()  # latitude weights
rmse = lambda a, b: float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean(w * (a - b) ** 2)))  # latitude-weighted RMSE
truth = state.sel(latitude=lat, method="nearest")  # ERA5 on the forecast grid
rows = []  # scores
for k, v in SURF.items():  # surface variables
    f = pred.surf_vars[k][0, 0].float().cpu().numpy()  # forecast
    rows.append({"variable": k, "Aurora +6 h": rmse(f, truth[v].isel(time=2).values), "persistence": rmse(truth[v].isel(time=1).values, truth[v].isel(time=2).values)})  # scores
for k, v, lev in [("z", "geopotential", 500), ("t", "temperature", 850), ("u", "u_component_of_wind", 250)]:  # upper air
    li = list(era.level.values).index(lev)  # level index
    f = pred.atmos_vars[k][0, 0, li].float().cpu().numpy()  # forecast
    rows.append({"variable": f"{k}{lev}", "Aurora +6 h": rmse(f, truth[v].isel(time=2, level=li).values),
                 "persistence": rmse(truth[v].isel(time=1, level=li).values, truth[v].isel(time=2, level=li).values)})  # scores
sc = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("variable"); sc["skill vs persistence"] = 1 - sc["Aurora +6 h"] / sc["persistence"]  # skill score
sc.round(3)

Six hours ahead, Aurora’s errors are a small fraction of persistence’s for every variable: 0.49 K against 2.8 K for 2 m temperature, 32 Pa against 265 Pa for sea level pressure, 24 m2 s-2 against 223 for 500 hPa geopotential. The skill score (1 minus the ratio of the two errors) ranges from about 0.71 for 850 hPa temperature to 0.89 for 500 hPa geopotential. Persistence is a weak baseline at 6 hours, because the daily cycle alone moves surface temperature by several kelvin; the point is that the learned model captures that cycle and the moving weather systems from two input states.


Code
f2t = pred.surf_vars["2t"][0, 0].float().cpu().numpy() - 273.15  # forecast 2 m temperature (C)
err = f2t - (truth["2m_temperature"].isel(time=2).values - 273.15)  # forecast minus ERA5
pers = (truth["2m_temperature"].isel(time=1).values - truth["2m_temperature"].isel(time=2).values)  # persistence error
ext = [0, 360, float(lat[-1]), float(lat[0])]  # map extent
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(12, 14))  # three maps
im = ax[0].imshow(f2t, cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=-40, vmax=40, extent=ext); ax[0].set_title(f"{MODEL}: 2 m temperature, 2023-01-01 12 UTC (+6 h)"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8, label="C")  # forecast
im = ax[1].imshow(err, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-5, vmax=5, extent=ext); ax[1].set_title("forecast minus ERA5"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8, label="K")  # error
im = ax[2].imshow(pers, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-5, vmax=5, extent=ext); ax[2].set_title("persistence minus ERA5"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[2], shrink=0.8, label="K")  # baseline error
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The persistence error map is dominated by the daily cycle: between 06 and 12 UTC the sun rises over Africa and Europe (cold errors there, since persistence keeps the night) and sets over East Asia and Australia (warm errors). Aurora’s error map has none of that pattern. What remains is small-scale noise over land, largest over mountains, deserts and the high latitudes of the northern winter, where surface temperature varies over short distances, and a near-zero error over the oceans.

section: A 12 hour rollout and the Corn Belt
text:
A 12 hour rollout and the Corn Belt
aurora.rollout fed the first forecast back as input, so its second step is a forecast valid at 18 UTC, 12 hours after the last input. The score is computed for the globe and for a box over Iowa (40 to 45 N, 97 to 90 W), the Corn Belt study area of this chapter.


Code
box = (lat >= 40) & (lat <= 45)  # Iowa latitudes
lon = pred.metadata.lon.cpu().numpy(); lbox = (lon >= 263) & (lon <= 270)  # 97 to 90 W in 0..360
rows = []  # rollout scores
for step, p in enumerate(preds, 1):  # each lead time
    f = p.surf_vars["2t"][0, 0].float().numpy()  # forecast
    tgt = truth["2m_temperature"].isel(time=1 + step).values  # ERA5 at the valid time
    per = truth["2m_temperature"].isel(time=1).values  # persistence from 06 UTC
    rows.append({"lead (h)": 6 * step, "Aurora global": rmse(f, tgt), "persistence global": rmse(per, tgt),
                 "Aurora Iowa": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((f - tgt)[np.ix_(box, lbox)] ** 2))),
                 "persistence Iowa": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((per - tgt)[np.ix_(box, lbox)] ** 2)))})  # scores
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("lead (h)").round(2)  # 2 m temperature RMSE (K)

Summary

Learned weather models (FourCastNet, GraphCast, GenCast, Aurora, Prithvi WxC) emulate the atmosphere from reanalysis and forecast in seconds on one GPU.

title: Evapotranspiration and the Surface Energy Balance
text: Banner

title: Evapotranspiration and the Surface Energy Balance
text:
Overview

What evapotranspiration is and why it matters

Evaporation from bare soil, wet leaves and open water, and transpiration, the water plants draw from the root zone and release through their stomata while they take up CO2.
On irrigated farmland ET is the consumptive use of water: the part that does not return to rivers or aquifers. Water rights, groundwater sustainability plans (California’s SGMA), irrigation scheduling and drought monitoring all depend on it.
A field measurement of ET (eddy covariance tower, weighing lysimeter) covers a few hectares at most. Satellite models extend those point measurements to every field.



Two ways to look at ET
The water balance closes the books on water: ET = P + I - R - D - dS (precipitation plus irrigation minus runoff, drainage and the change in soil storage). Most terms are unknown at the field scale. The energy balance closes the books on energy at the surface:
Rn = G + H + LE








Term
Name
Meaning




Rn
net radiation
shortwave from the sun minus what is reflected, plus longwave from the sky minus what the surface emits


G
soil heat flux
energy conducted into the ground


H
sensible heat flux
energy that warms the air above the surface


LE
latent heat flux
energy used to evaporate water; L is the latent heat of vaporization (about 2.45 MJ per kg) and E the evaporation rate



All four are in W m-2. Satellites give Rn (from reflectance and temperature) and G (from Rn and vegetation) quite well. H is the hard part, and LE follows as the residual LE = Rn - G - H. That is why these models are called residual energy balance models.


From watts to millimetres
One kilogram of water per square metre is a layer 1 mm deep, so
ET (mm/h) = 3600 LE / lambda, with lambda = (2.501 - 0.00236 T) 10^6 J kg-1 (T in C).
A latent heat flux of 680 W m-2 held for an hour evaporates 1 mm. Over a day, 1 mm of ET needs 2.45 MJ m-2, an average of 28.4 W m-2 over 24 hours.


Typical midday fluxes










Surface (summer, clear sky)
Rn
G
H

550 to 700

400 to 500

600 to 700

most of the rest



H can be negative over irrigated crops in a desert: hot dry air flowing over a wet field gives up heat to it, and LE can then exceed Rn - G. This advection is common in California and matters in notebooks 05 and 06.


Why thermal images
H = rho cp dT / rah: sensible heat grows with the difference dT between the surface and the air and shrinks with the aerodynamic resistance rah. An evaporating surface spends energy on LE and stays cool, so its dT and H are small. Land surface temperature (LST) from a thermal band is therefore the main signal. Two complications drive the model design:

Radiometric is not aerodynamic temperature. A thermal sensor sees a mix of sunlit soil and canopy, while H responds to the temperature at the height where heat is exchanged (z0h). The difference can be several kelvin over sparse crops.
Air temperature is not known at 30 m. Weather stations are tens of kilometres apart.

SEBAL and METRIC solve both by never using air temperature directly: they assume dT is a linear function of LST and calibrate the line at two anchor pixels, one wet and cool, one dry and hot (notebooks 05 and 06). Two-source models instead split LST into soil and canopy parts (notebook 08).

OpenET



OpenET (Melton et al. 2022) runs six of these models (ALEXI/DisALEXI, eeMETRIC, geeSEBAL, PT-JPL, SIMS and SSEBop) on Landsat for the western United States and publishes their ensemble. Its accuracy assessment against flux towers (Volk et al. 2024) found that the ensemble was among the most accurate estimates over croplands, while single models did better or worse depending on crop and season. This chapter writes each model from its equations so you can see where those differences come from.


From an instant to a season
A Landsat image is a snapshot at about 10:30 to 11:30 local time. Two assumptions carry it to a whole day:

Evaporative fraction EF = LE / (Rn - G) stays constant during the day (SEBAL).
Reference ET fraction ETrF = ET / ETr stays constant, where ETr is the ET of a well watered alfalfa reference computed from weather (METRIC). This also carries the effect of advection and of cloudy afternoons through the reference.

Between clear images, the fraction (not ET itself) is interpolated in time and multiplied by the daily reference ET (notebook 10).

text:
The LST and NDVI scatter
Plotting LST against NDVI gives the characteristic triangle or trapezoid of energy balance studies. Its cool upper right corner holds dense, well watered vegetation (the cold anchor region), its hot lower left corner dry bare soil (the hot anchor region). The upper edge of the cloud, hottest LST for each NDVI, is the dry edge; the cool lower boundary, the wet edge.


Code

LST falls by about 25 K from bare soil (near 60 C) to full cover (near 35 C), and the strong negative correlation (-0.93) is the evaporative cooling the models use. The spread at a given NDVI is just as informative: at NDVI 0.3 the coolest pixels are close to 20 K cooler than the hottest, because a sparse canopy over wet soil evaporates far more than the same canopy over dry soil. NDVI alone (as in crop coefficient methods) cannot see that difference; the thermal band can.

Fallow land and rangeland send most of their available energy into the air as sensible heat; the vegetated crops send most of theirs into evaporation. The darker surfaces also absorb more: net radiation is higher over crops than over bright dry soil, which reflects more sunlight and emits more longwave at its higher temperature. Grapes have a negative mean H (-14 W m-2): on average the vineyards draw heat from the hot air, the advection described in the Overview, and their LE (499 W m-2) is larger than Rn - G. Fallow land still averages about 100 W m-2 of LE: METRIC gives exactly zero ET only to pixels as hot as the hot anchor, and some fields mapped as fallow in the 2024 CDL had a cover crop or were irrigated in another part of the year.

title: Evapotranspiration and the Surface Energy Balance
text:
Summary and exercises

ET is the energy-limited and water-limited loss of water as vapour. Converting with lambda, 680 W m-2 for one hour is 1 mm, and 28.4 W m-2 for a day is 1 mm.
Satellites estimate Rn and G well; the models differ in how they find H, and LE is the residual.
Land surface temperature carries the signal: on 5 July 2024 the fallow median was 9 to 14 K hotter than the crop groups, LST fell by about 25 K from bare soil to full cover, and LST and NDVI had a correlation of -0.93.
Anchor pixels at the cool, dense and hot, bare ends of the LST and NDVI scatter calibrate SEBAL and METRIC.
The instantaneous fraction (EF or ETrF) is carried to a day and a season with reference ET.

Exercises

Repeat the crop group table with the dry edge in mind: for each group, what fraction of pixels has LST within 3 K of the hottest LST for its NDVI bin? What does that say about water stress?
Compute the evaporative fraction LE / (Rn - G) for each group. Which groups exceed 1, and why is that possible?
Load an April scene (sd.load_scene("LC09_L2SP_042035_20240408_02_T1")) and redraw the LST and NDVI scatter. How do the two corners move between spring and midsummer?
Convert the scene mean daily ET to a volume of water in cubic metres for the 28 x 29 km window.

Alfalfa is taller, rougher and has more leaf area, so ETr is typically 15 to 40 % higher than ETo, more in windy, dry weather. METRIC uses ETr because a full-cover, well watered crop in the image rarely evaporates more than about 1.05 ETr, which makes it a natural ceiling for the cold anchor.


The ASCE standardized equation
ASCE-EWRI (2005) fixed the Penman-Monteith equation for the two references into one form:
ETsz = [0.408 Delta (Rn - G) + gamma Cn / (T + 273) u2 (es - ea)] / [Delta + gamma (1 + Cd u2)]

The numerator has a radiation term (energy available) and an aerodynamic term (the drying power of warm, dry, moving air). Net radiation of the reference surface uses albedo 0.23, Rns = 0.77 Rs, and the net longwave Rnl = sigma T^4 (0.34 - 0.14 sqrt(ea)) (1.35 Rs/Rso - 0.35), where Rso is clear-sky radiation from extraterrestrial radiation Ra and elevation. FAO-56 is the daily short reference of this equation; its hourly form uses Cd = 0.34 both day and night.


Weather over irrigated land and over dry land
The equation assumes the weather was measured over a well watered reference. A station or reanalysis grid cell over dry land records hotter, drier air, and the equation then overstates the demand of an irrigated field (Allen 1996; Temesgen et al. 1999). A common diagnostic is the difference between the daily minimum air temperature and the dew point: over a well watered surface the air is near saturation at dawn, so Tmin - Tdew is usually below 2 to 3 C. Larger differences point to arid conditions, and FAO-56 (Annex 6) suggests raising the dew point to Tmin - K0 with K0 of about 2 C before computing reference ET. ERA5 and gridMET grid cells mix irrigated fields with dry rangeland and foothills, so they carry some of this aridity.
