section: Checking the equation with the FAO-56 examples
text:
Checking the equation with the FAO-56 examples
FAO-56 (Allen et al. 1998) works two examples by hand. Example 18 is a daily ETo for Brussels on 6 July (expected 3.9 mm/d), and example 19 an hourly ETo for N’Diaye, Senegal, on 1 October from 14:00 to 15:00 (expected 0.63 mm/h, with the FAO hourly Cd = 0.34 and G = 0.1 Rn). The Senegal hour is centred on 15:30 UTC in this convention.


Code
ex18 = seb.fao56_eto(21.5, 12.3, 1.409, 22.07, seb.wind_2m(10 / 3.6, 10), 100, 50.8, 187)  # Brussels, 6 July
ea19 = seb.actual_vapour_pressure(t_c=38.0, rh=52.0)  # N'Diaye: 38 C, 52 % humidity
ex19 = seb.asce_pm_hourly(38.0, ea19, 2.450, 3.3, 8, 16.217, -16.25, "2026-10-01 15:30", cd=0.34, g_ratio=0.1)  # 14:00 to 15:00
pd.DataFrame({"FAO-56 result": [3.9, 0.63], "seb": [round(float(ex18), 2), round(float(ex19), 3)]},
             index=["Example 18, daily ETo (mm/d)", "Example 19, hourly ETo (mm/h)"])  # comparison

title: Reference ET with the ASCE Standardized Penman-Monteith Equation
text:
One day term by term
5 July 2024, the day of the main Landsat scene, was in a heat wave. The ERA5 daily values at the site go into the equation step by step, so each term can be read off.


Code
d = sd.weather(SITE, "2024-01-01", "2024-12-31")["daily"]  # ERA5 daily for 2024 (cached)
day = d.loc["2024-07-05"]  # the overpass day
tmax, tmin, rs = day.temperature_2m_max, day.temperature_2m_min, day.shortwave_radiation_sum  # C, C, MJ m-2
ea = float(seb.actual_vapour_pressure(t_dew_c=day.dew_point_2m_mean))  # kPa from the mean dew point
u2 = float(seb.wind_2m(day.wind_speed_10m_mean, 10))  # m/s at 2 m
t = (tmax + tmin) / 2  # mean air temperature
P = float(seb.pressure_from_elevation(Z)); gamma = seb.psychrometric_constant(P)  # kPa and kPa/C
delta = float(seb.slope_vapour_pressure_curve(t))  # kPa/C
es = (seb.saturation_vapour_pressure(tmax) + seb.saturation_vapour_pressure(tmin)) / 2  # mean saturation pressure
ra = float(seb.extraterrestrial_radiation_daily(SITE["lat"], 187)); rso = (0.75 + 2e-5 * Z) * ra  # MJ m-2 d-1
rnl = 4.901e-9 * ((tmax + 273.16) ** 4 + (tmin + 273.16) ** 4) / 2 * (0.34 - 0.14 * ea ** 0.5) * (1.35 * min(rs / rso, 1) - 0.35)  # net longwave
rn = 0.77 * rs - rnl  # net radiation of the reference surface
rows = {}  # term table
for ref, cn, cd in [("ETo (grass)", 900, 0.34), ("ETr (alfalfa)", 1600, 0.38)]:  # both references
    den = delta + gamma * (1 + cd * u2)  # denominator
    rad = 0.408 * delta * rn / den  # radiation term, mm/d
    aero = gamma * cn / (t + 273) * u2 * (es - ea) / den  # aerodynamic term, mm/d
    rows[ref] = {"radiation term": rad, "aerodynamic term": aero, "total": rad + aero,
                 "seb.asce_pm_daily": float(seb.asce_pm_daily(tmax, tmin, ea, rs, u2, Z, SITE["lat"], 187,
                                                                reference="tall" if cd == 0.38 else "short"))}  # check
print(f"Tmax {tmax} C, Tmin {tmin} C, Tdew {day.dew_point_2m_mean} C, ea {ea:.2f} kPa, es - ea {es - ea:.2f} kPa, "
      f"u2 {u2:.2f} m/s, Rs {rs} MJ m-2 (Rso {rso:.1f}), Rn {rn:.1f} MJ m-2")  # inputs
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(2)  # mm/d

title: Reference ET with the ASCE Standardized Penman-Monteith Equation
section: Hourly reference ET and the overpass
text:
Hourly reference ET and the overpass
METRIC needs ETr at the moment of the image (to calibrate the cold anchor) and for the whole day (to scale the image). The hourly equation runs on each ERA5 hour; ERA5 hours are averages ending at the time stamp, so the centre of each hour is 30 minutes earlier.


Code
h = sd.weather(SITE, "2024-07-05", "2024-07-05")["hourly"]  # ERA5 hourly, UTC
mid = h.index - pd.Timedelta(minutes=30)  # centre of each hour
ea_h = seb.actual_vapour_pressure(t_dew_c=h.dew_point_2m.values)  # kPa
u2_h = seb.wind_2m(h.wind_speed_10m.values, 10)  # m/s
etr_h = np.array([float(seb.asce_pm_hourly(T, e, r * 0.0036, u, Z, SITE["lat"], SITE["lon"], m, reference="tall"))
                  for T, e, r, u, m in zip(h.temperature_2m, ea_h, h.shortwave_radiation, u2_h, mid)])  # mm/h
eto_h = np.array([float(seb.asce_pm_hourly(T, e, r * 0.0036, u, Z, SITE["lat"], SITE["lon"], m, reference="short"))
                  for T, e, r, u, m in zip(h.temperature_2m, ea_h, h.shortwave_radiation, u2_h, mid)])  # mm/h
scene = sd.load_scene(sd.MAIN_SCENE)  # the overpass time is in the scene attributes
ref = sd.reference_et(scene)  # overpass ETr and daily ETr used by the later notebooks
print(f"sum of 24 hourly ETr {etr_h.sum():.1f} mm, daily equation {rows['ETr (alfalfa)']['total']:.1f} mm | "
      f"sum of hourly ETo {eto_h.sum():.1f} mm, daily {rows['ETo (grass)']['total']:.1f} mm")  # hourly vs daily
print(f"ETr at the overpass ({pd.Timestamp(scene.attrs['datetime']):%H:%M} UTC): {ref['etr_inst']:.2f} mm/h")  # instant value

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))  # one panel
local = mid + pd.Timedelta(hours=SITE["utc_offset"])  # local time
ax.bar(local, etr_h, width=0.03, color="#2166ac", label="ETr (alfalfa)")  # hourly ETr
ax.bar(local, eto_h, width=0.03, color="#92c5de", label="ETo (grass)")  # hourly ETo in front
ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp(scene.attrs["datetime"]) + pd.Timedelta(hours=SITE["utc_offset"]), color="r", label="Landsat overpass")  # image time
ax.set_ylabel("mm/h"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Hourly reference ET, 5 July 2024 (local time)")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


sum of 24 hourly ETr 12.9 mm, daily equation 15.6 mm | sum of hourly ETo 9.7 mm, daily 10.7 mm
ETr at the overpass (18:33 UTC): 0.93 mm/h









The 24 hourly values add up to less than the daily equation gives on this day (12.9 against 15.6 mm for alfalfa). The daily form averages the saturation vapour pressure at Tmax and Tmin, which on a day with a 21 C range overstates the mean deficit because saturation pressure rises steeply with temperature, and it applies daytime constants to the whole day’s mean wind; at night the hourly form uses a much larger Cd and so little ET. ASCE (2005) prefers the sum of hourly values when hourly data exist, while many METRIC applications use the daily form. The chapter uses ERA5 for both the overpass ETr and the daily ETr, so every image is scaled with the same weather source.

title: Reference ET with the ASCE Standardized Penman-Monteith Equation
section: A year of daily reference ET
text:
A year of daily reference ET
sd.daily_reference applies the daily equation to every ERA5 day of 2024 (the same steps as above, vectorized).


Code
era = sd.daily_reference(SITE, "2024-01-01", "2024-12-31", z=Z)  # ETr, ETo, Open-Meteo's ETo, rain
print(f"2024 totals: ETr {era.etr.sum():.0f} mm, ETo {era.eto.sum():.0f} mm (Open-Meteo's own ETo {era.eto_openmeteo.sum():.0f} mm), "
      f"rain {era.precip.sum():.0f} mm")  # annual totals
print(f"April to October: ETr {era.loc['2024-04':'2024-10'].etr.sum():.0f} mm, ratio ETr/ETo {(era.etr / era.eto).loc['2024-04':'2024-10'].mean():.2f}")  # season
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.8))  # one panel
ax.plot(era.etr, color="#2166ac", lw=1, label="ETr (alfalfa)")  # daily ETr
ax.plot(era.eto, color="#92c5de", lw=1, label="ETo (grass)")  # daily ETo
ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.bar(era.index, era.precip, color="#999999", width=1); ax2.set_ylim(60, 0); ax2.set_ylabel("rain (mm)")  # rain from the top
ax.set_ylabel("mm/day"); ax.legend(loc="upper left"); ax.set_title("Daily reference ET from ERA5, Westside 2024")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


2024 totals: ETr 2366 mm, ETo 1706 mm (Open-Meteo's own ETo 1709 mm), rain 320 mm
April to October: ETr 1979 mm, ratio ETr/ETo 1.39









Reference ET follows the sun and the heat: about 1 to 2 mm/d in winter and over 10 mm/d (ETr) in summer, with the early July heat wave standing out. The 320 mm of rain in the ERA5 cell, nearly all between November and April, is a small fraction of the 2,366 mm alfalfa reference demand, so crops on the Westside depend on irrigation. In the irrigation season (April to October) ETr is on average 1.39 times ETo. Open-Meteo’s own grass ETo is computed from hourly values and differs a little from the daily equation used here.

ERA5 and gridMET
gridMET (Abatzoglou 2013) combines PRISM and NLDAS-2 at 4 km and publishes daily ETr and ETo with the ASCE equation. It is the weather behind OpenET. The two products agree on the seasonal cycle but differ day by day.

                      "ETo": seb.compare_to_tower(both["ERA5 ETo"], both["gridMET ETo"])}).T  # both references

title: Reference ET with the ASCE Standardized Penman-Monteith Equation
text:
Aridity of the weather data
Over a well watered surface the dew point at dawn is close to the minimum temperature. The distribution of Tmin - Tdew in summer shows how far the gridded weather is from that state, and the FAO-56 adjustment (Tdew raised to at least Tmin - 2 C) shows what it would change.


Code
summer = d.loc["2024-05":"2024-09"]  # dry season
gap = summer.temperature_2m_min - summer.dew_point_2m_mean  # Tmin - Tdew, C
print(f"ERA5 May to September: Tmin - Tdew median {gap.median():.1f} C, 90th percentile {gap.quantile(0.9):.1f} C")  # aridity diagnostic
tdew_adj = np.maximum(d.dew_point_2m_mean, d.temperature_2m_min - 2.0)  # FAO-56 Annex 6 adjustment, K0 = 2 C
ea_adj = seb.actual_vapour_pressure(t_dew_c=tdew_adj.values)  # adjusted vapour pressure
etr_adj = seb.asce_pm_daily(d.temperature_2m_max.values, d.temperature_2m_min.values, ea_adj, d.shortwave_radiation_sum.values,
                            seb.wind_2m(d.wind_speed_10m_mean.values, 10), Z, SITE["lat"], d.index.dayofyear.values, reference="tall")  # ETr with adjusted humidity
adj = pd.Series(etr_adj, index=d.index)  # as a series
season = slice("2024-04", "2024-10")  # irrigation season
print(f"April to October ETr: {era.etr.loc[season].sum():.0f} mm as measured, {adj.loc[season].sum():.0f} mm with the humidity adjustment "
      f"({100 * (adj.loc[season].sum() / era.etr.loc[season].sum() - 1):.0f} %)")  # effect on the season


ERA5 May to September: Tmin - Tdew median 13.0 C, 90th percentile 20.0 C
April to October ETr: 1979 mm as measured, 1742 mm with the humidity adjustment (-12 %)


A median Tmin - Tdew of 13 C, far above 2 C, says the ERA5 air at this point is much drier than air over an irrigated field. Raising the dew point lowers the season’s ETr by 12 % (1,979 to 1,742 mm). This is an upper bound of the effect: the adjustment assumes a fully irrigated landscape, while the Westside is a mix of irrigated and fallow land. Studies that need absolute accuracy correct gridded weather against local agricultural stations (OpenET bias-corrects gridMET ETo and ETr with station ratios). For METRIC the absolute level matters less than consistency: the cold anchor is calibrated to 1.05 ETr and the image is scaled with ETr from the same source, so a constant bias largely cancels in the fraction and returns only through the daily scaling.

title: Reference ET with the ASCE Standardized Penman-Monteith Equation
text:
Summary and exercises

The ASCE standardized equation gives grass (ETo) and alfalfa (ETr) reference ET from temperature, humidity, radiation and wind; seb.fao56_eto and seb.asce_pm_hourly reproduce the FAO-56 examples 18 (3.9 mm/d) and 19 (0.63 mm/h).
On 5 July 2024, a hot, very dry day, the aerodynamic term contributed more than the radiation term, and ETr exceeded 15 mm.
On 5 July the 24 hourly values summed to 12.9 mm against 15.6 mm from the daily equation; the daily form overstates the deficit on days with a large temperature range.
ERA5 and gridMET agree on the seasonal cycle (R2 0.93 for daily ETr) but ERA5 is hotter, drier and less windy, effects that partly cancel.
Gridded weather over a mix of irrigated and dry land is drier than air over an irrigated field (median Tmin - Tdew of 13 C in ERA5); the FAO-56 dew point adjustment would lower the season’s ETr by up to 12 %.

Exercises

Recompute the 5 July term table with gridMET inputs. Which input changes the aerodynamic term the most?
Use seb.asce_pm_hourly with reference="short" for every hour of July 2024 and compare the monthly sum with the daily equation’s sum. In which weather is the difference largest?
Repeat the aridity adjustment with K0 = 0, 2 and 4 C. How sensitive is the season’s ETr?
Compute the ETr/ETo ratio for every day of 2024 and plot it against wind speed. Why does it rise with wind?

title: Soil Heat Flux, Roughness and Aerodynamic Resistance
text: Banner

title: Soil Heat Flux, Roughness and Aerodynamic Resistance
text:
Overview

Soil heat flux
G is largest over bare, dark, hot soil in full sun and small under a dense canopy, which shades the ground. Satellite models estimate the ratio G/Rn from vegetation and temperature:







Model
Formula




SEBAL (Bastiaanssen 2000)
G/Rn = (Ts - 273.15) (0.0038 albedo + 0.0074 albedo^2) (1 - 0.98 NDVI^4) / albedo


METRIC (Tasumi 2003), LAI of at least 0.5
G/Rn = 0.05 + 0.18 exp(-0.521 LAI)


METRIC, LAI below 0.5
G/Rn = 1.80 (Ts - 273.15) / Rn + 0.084


Water
G/Rn about 0.5 for clear water in midday (heat stored in the water column)



The ratios apply around midday; over a whole day G is close to zero, which is why daily ET uses Rn - G only at the instant of the image.


Wind near the surface
Under neutral conditions wind increases with the logarithm of height:
u(z) = (u* / k) ln((z - d) / zom)
u* is the friction velocity (the shear the surface exerts), k = 0.41 the von Karman constant, zom the momentum roughness length (roughly 1/8 of the canopy height) and d the displacement height (about 2/3 of the canopy height). At a blending height of about 200 m the wind is assumed to be the same over every surface in the scene, so wind measured at one weather station is extended to 200 m with the station’s grass roughness and brought back down over each pixel with that pixel’s zom.


Aerodynamic resistance and the METRIC trick
Heat is carried from the surface by turbulence with a resistance
rah = (ln(z2 / z1) - psi_h(z2) + psi_h(z1)) / (u* k)
SEBAL and METRIC evaluate it between two heights above the zero plane displacement, z1 = 0.1 m and z2 = 2 m, and define dT as the temperature difference between those heights, not between the surface and the air. This sidesteps two unknowns: the roughness length for heat (zoh, much smaller than zom and poorly known) and the difference between radiometric and aerodynamic temperature. The calibration of dT at the anchors (notebook 05) absorbs them.


Stability
When the surface is much hotter than the air, rising warm air enhances turbulence (unstable conditions, typical of dry land at midday): rah falls and H rises. When the surface is cooler than the air (irrigated crops under hot air), turbulence is damped (stable): rah rises. The Monin-Obukhov length
L = -rho cp u*^3 Ts / (k g H)
measures the balance between shear and buoyancy. Negative L is unstable, positive stable, infinite neutral. The corrections psi_m and psi_h follow Paulson (1970) for unstable and Webb (1970) for stable air. Because L depends on H and H on rah, they are solved by iteration.

The wind profile and the blending height

title: Soil Heat Flux, Roughness and Aerodynamic Resistance
text:
Stability: a numerical experiment
The experiment holds the wind (3.1 m/s at 200 m) and roughness fixed and asks: for a given temperature difference dT between 0.1 and 2 m, what is H under neutral assumptions and after the Monin-Obukhov iteration? It repeats the inner loop of seb.sensible_heat_iterative without the anchor calibration. dT stays below 10 K: at the hot anchor of this scene METRIC converges at about 5 K, because H cannot exceed the available energy Rn - G.


Code
def h_iterated(dT, zom, u_blend=u200, t_surface=320.0, pressure=100.5, n_iter=30):  # H for a fixed dT, with stability
    psi_m200 = psi_h2 = psi_h01 = 0.0  # start neutral
    rho = float(seb.air_density(pressure, t_surface - dT))  # air density, kg/m3
    for _ in range(n_iter):  # iterate H, L and the corrections
        ustar = seb.friction_velocity(u_blend, 200.0, zom, psi_m200)  # m/s
        rah_ = seb.aerodynamic_resistance(ustar, z1=0.1, z2=2.0, psi_h_z2=psi_h2, psi_h_z1=psi_h01)  # s/m
        h = rho * seb.CP * dT / rah_  # W/m2
        L = seb.monin_obukhov_length(rho, ustar, t_surface, h)  # m
        pm200, _ = seb.stability_corrections(200.0, L)  # momentum at 200 m (unstable)
        pm2, psi_h2 = seb.stability_corrections(2.0, L)  # heat at 2 m (and momentum at 2 m for stable air)
        _, psi_h01 = seb.stability_corrections(0.1, L)  # heat at 0.1 m
        psi_m200 = np.where(L < 0, pm200, pm2)  # METRIC uses 2 m for the stable momentum term
    return float(h), float(rah_), float(L)  # final values


dts = np.arange(-4, 10.5, 0.5)  # dT from -4 K (stable) to 10 K (strongly unstable)
rows = []  # results
for zom in (0.01, 0.1, 0.4):  # smooth, medium, rough
    for dT in dts:  # every temperature difference
        h_n = 1.15 * seb.CP * dT / float(seb.aerodynamic_resistance(seb.friction_velocity(u200, 200.0, zom)))  # neutral H
        h_s, r_s, L = h_iterated(dT, zom)  # with stability
        rows.append({"zom": zom, "dT": dT, "H neutral": h_n, "H with stability": h_s, "rah": r_s, "L": L})  # one row
exp = pd.DataFrame(rows)  # all cases
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))  # two panels
for zom, c in zip((0.01, 0.1, 0.4), ["#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3"]):  # each roughness
    e = exp[exp.zom == zom]  # its cases
    ax[0].plot(e.dT, e["H neutral"], "--", color=c); ax[0].plot(e.dT, e["H with stability"], "-", color=c, label=f"zom {zom} m")  # H curves
    ax[1].plot(e.dT, e["H with stability"] / e["H neutral"].where(e.dT != 0), color=c, label=f"zom {zom} m")  # ratio

At the dT of a hot anchor (about 5 K), unstable air lowers rah and raises H to about three times the neutral estimate over smooth surfaces, less over rough ones, which are already well mixed. title: Soil Heat Flux, Roughness and Aerodynamic Resistance
text:
Summary and exercises

G/Rn is about 0.3 over hot bare soil and below 0.1 under dense crops; the SEBAL and METRIC formulas differ most over partial canopies.
Wind measured at a station is carried to a 200 m blending height and back down over each pixel’s roughness; an orchard has about 1.75 times the friction velocity of bare soil.
LAI, NDVI and crop-table roughness disagree most over orchards, which LAI and NDVI see as partial canopies.
METRIC’s rah between 0.1 and 2 m avoids the roughness length for heat and the radiometric versus aerodynamic temperature problem; the anchor calibration absorbs them.
Neutral rah between 0.1 and 2 m was 35 to 60 s/m. Stability corrections raise H about threefold at a hot anchor’s dT of 5 K over smooth surfaces and must be iterated.

Exercises

Recompute G with method="bastiaanssen" and method="metric" for the 8 April scene. Where do the two disagree most early in the season?
Double the wind at 200 m and repeat the stability experiment. How does the correction factor change?
Replace the LAI roughness in sd.energy_inputs with the crop table roughness and run sd.run_metric_scene. How much do daily ET maps of orchards change?
Plot the Monin-Obukhov length of the experiment against dT. At what dT does |L| drop below 2 m, the height of z2?

title: METRIC: Internal Calibration against Reference ET
text:
Overview

What METRIC changes








Step
SEBAL
METRIC




Cold anchor
H = 0, LE = Rn - G
ET = 1.05 ETr, H = Rn - G - 1.05 ETr lambda (can be negative)


Hot anchor
LE = 0
ET = ETrF_hot ETr, with ETrF_hot from a daily soil water balance of bare soil (FAO-56 evaporation); 0 after a long dry period


dT calibration
on Ts
on Ts_datum, LST moved to a common elevation with a lapse rate (mountain scenes)


Incoming shortwave
flat ground
slope and aspect of every pixel


Daily ET
EF Rn24
ETrF ETr24


Monthly and seasonal ET

ETrF interpolated between images, times daily ETr (notebook 10)





Why 1.05 ETr at the cold anchor
The alfalfa reference represents a tall, dense, well watered crop. Allen et al. (2007) found that the coolest, fully vegetated fields in an agricultural scene typically evaporate about 5 % more than the reference, because they are slightly rougher, wetter or warmer-surrounded than a reference field. More recent METRIC applications often use 1.0 for the cold anchor and account for the extra 5 % elsewhere; the value is a parameter (etrf_cold).


Why the reference ET fraction carries the day
EF is constant through a day only if the energy partition does not change. In advective regions the afternoon brings hotter, drier air, so ET rises relative to Rn - G and EF increases during the day. ETrF holds better, because the alfalfa reference responds to the same advection. Allen et al. (2007) and many studies since found ETrF from a late morning image to be a good estimate of the 24 hour ratio for irrigated crops.


The hot anchor after rain
A bare field that was wetted by rain in the last days still evaporates. METRIC runs the FAO-56 soil evaporation model (a two stage water balance of the top 10 cm) with daily rain and reference ET to estimate ETrF_hot. In the dry San Joaquin summer the last rain is months back and ETrF_hot = 0.

Daily ET differs much more. This is why scaling with reference ET is preferred for irrigated crops in arid regions, and why eeMETRIC rather than an EF-based daily scaling is part of OpenET. title: METRIC: Internal Calibration against Reference ET
text:
Summary and exercises

METRIC sets the cold anchor to 1.05 ETr and the hot anchor to the ETrF of a soil water balance (zero after two months without rain), so wet fields can evaporate more than Rn - G by drawing heat from the air.
On 5 July 2024 the cold anchor needed 657 W m-2 for evaporation, 52 W m-2 more than its Rn - G; 37 % of the pixels had negative H.
ETrF reads as a crop coefficient: close to 1 for well watered full cover, lower for orchards and near 0 for fallow land.
METRIC’s daily ET was 2.1 to 2.4 times SEBAL’s for every crop group on this advective day, mostly because of the daily scaling with reference ET instead of net radiation.
The calibration changes from image to image (b from 0.17 to 0.71 across six dates); the datum temperature changed daily ET by less than 0.22 mm for 99 % of pixels on this flat valley floor.

Exercises

Rerun METRIC with etrf_cold=1.0. How much does daily ET change, and is the change the same for every crop?
Pretend 10 mm of rain fell two days before the image and set etrf_hot=0.3. Which pixels change most?

title: Two-Source Energy Balance: Separating Soil Evaporation and Transpiration
text:
Overview

Splitting the radiometric temperature
The thermal sensor measures one radiometric temperature Trad. TSEB writes it as an emission- weighted mix of canopy temperature Tc and soil temperature Ts:
Trad^4 = f_theta Tc^4 + (1 - f_theta) Ts^4, with f_theta = 1 - exp(-0.5 Omega LAI / cos(theta_v))
f_theta is the fraction of the view filled by vegetation at view angle theta_v (Landsat looks almost straight down) and Omega a clumping factor (1 for a random canopy, below 1 for rows and orchards).


Splitting net radiation
Net radiation is shared between canopy and soil with an extinction law, Rn_s = Rn exp(-kappa Omega LAI / sqrt(2 cos(theta_s))), Rn_c = Rn - Rn_s, with kappa about 0.45 and theta_s the sun zenith angle. Soil heat flux is a fraction of the soil’s net radiation, G = 0.35 Rn_s.


The Priestley-Taylor start
The canopy is first assumed to transpire at the Priestley-Taylor rate, LE_c = alpha_PT fg Delta / (Delta + gamma) Rn_c with alpha_PT = 1.26 (unstressed). Then:

H_c = Rn_c - LE_c, and Tc follows from H_c = rho cp (Tc - Ta) / rah.
Ts follows from the radiometric split.
H_s = rho cp (Ts - Ta) / (rah + rs), with the soil resistance rs of Kustas and Norman (1999), which depends on the wind near the soil and the temperature difference between soil and canopy.
LE_s = Rn_s - G - H_s.

If LE_s comes out negative, which is impossible during the day, the canopy is stressed: alpha_PT is lowered step by step until LE_s is zero or positive. If it reaches zero, the canopy is not transpiring at all.


Parallel and series networks
In the parallel network (used here) soil and canopy exchange heat with the air above the canopy independently. The series network lets both exchange heat with the air inside the canopy space, which then exchanges with the air above; it is more realistic for dense canopies and needs more resistances. pyTSEB (Nieto et al.) implements both, together with many refinements.


ALEXI and DisALEXI
TSEB needs the air temperature Ta, and it is sensitive to it: an error of 1 K in Ta changes H over a hot surface by tens of W m-2. ALEXI (Anderson et al. 1997) removes that dependence by using the rise in surface temperature between early morning and midday from geostationary satellites, coupled to a model of the growing atmospheric boundary layer. DisALEXI then disaggregates the coarse ALEXI fluxes to Landsat resolution by adjusting the air temperature until the Landsat TSEB fluxes match the ALEXI ones; this is the OpenET member of the family.

Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (registers the .rio accessor)
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

import geolattice  # GeoLattice

Transpiration dominates ET over dense canopies (T/ET of 0.86 for tomatoes at 91 % cover), and soil evaporation takes over as cover falls (0.44 for almonds, 0.31 for pistachios). Field studies with isotopes and sap flow in orchards and vineyards commonly report T/ET of 0.5 to 0.9 depending on cover and irrigation method (drip irrigation wets less soil than sprinklers or furrows). TSEB has no information on how the soil was irrigated: it infers soil evaporation only from the energy left after the soil’s sensible heat. The rangeland and developed land show the weakness: TSEB gives them about 165 W m-2 of soil evaporation, although their soil is dry in July. The soil resistance limits how much sensible heat the hot soil can lose, and the residual becomes evaporation. Soil evaporation is the least certain part of a TSEB result, and orchard T/ET here is likely too low.

title: Two-Source Energy Balance: Separating Soil Evaporation and Transpiration
text:
Summary and exercises

TSEB splits radiometric temperature and net radiation between soil and canopy, starts the canopy at the Priestley-Taylor rate, and lowers it where the soil budget would need negative evaporation.
Soil and canopy temperatures differed by 9 to 18 K within the vegetated crop groups.
Transpiration dominates ET at full cover (T/ET 0.86 for tomatoes) and soil evaporation grows as cover falls; TSEB’s soil evaporation is the least certain part (it gave dry rangeland about 165 W m-2) because it knows nothing about how the soil was wetted.
TSEB agreed with METRIC on the pattern of latent heat (correlation 0.94) but changed the scene mean LE by about 13 W m-2 per kelvin of air temperature, the sensitivity that motivated ALEXI and DisALEXI.
Over tall canopies, reanalysis 2 m air temperature must be treated as air above the canopy, or the aerodynamic resistance is undefined.

Exercises

Rerun TSEB-PT with clumping 1.0 for every pixel. How do orchard T/ET and soil temperature change?
Lower alpha_pt from 1.26 to 1.0 (a stressed canopy). Which crops lose the most transpiration?
Replace the crop table heights with hc = 0.1 + 0.5 * lai and compare LE by crop group.
Run TSEB-PT on the 26 May scene, when many annual crops were young. How does the scene’s T/ET compare with July?

title: From Snapshots to Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use
text:
Overview

Interpolate the fraction, not ET
ET on any day is the product of the crop’s state (how much leaf area, how wet the soil) and the weather of the day. The crop’s state changes slowly over weeks; the weather changes daily. METRIC therefore interpolates ETrF between images and multiplies by each day’s alfalfa reference ET:
ET_day = ETrF_interpolated(day) x ETr(day), ET_season = sum over days
Interpolating ET itself would carry a hot image day’s ET into a cool cloudy week. Linear interpolation is the usual choice; splines can overshoot after a harvest. Long gaps (winter clouds) make the interpolated fraction unreliable, so the interpolation stops beyond a maximum gap.


The hot anchor after rain
In winter, rain wets bare soil and it evaporates for days. METRIC estimates the hot anchor’s ETrF_hot with the FAO-56 two-stage soil evaporation model, a daily water balance of the top 10 to 15 cm of soil:

Rain refills the evaporating layer (depletion De falls).
While De is below the readily evaporable water REW (stage 1), the surface evaporates at the energy-limited rate, Ke = Ke_max.
Beyond REW (stage 2), evaporation falls linearly to zero at the total evaporable water TEW: Kr = (TEW - De) / (TEW - REW), Ke = Kr Ke_max.

ETrF_hot is the Ke of the image date. In the dry summer it is zero.


Crop coefficients from space
ETrF is a crop coefficient on the alfalfa basis. Multiplying by ETr/ETo puts it on the grass basis used by FAO-56 (Kc = ETrF ETr / ETo), so satellite estimates can be compared with the tabulated values that irrigation districts still use for planning. The satellite values include the actual water management (deficit irrigation, weeds, cover crops, harvest dates), which the tables cannot.

section: The hot anchor’s ETrF from a soil water balance
text:
The hot anchor’s ETrF from a soil water balance
The evaporating layer is given a total evaporable water of 25 mm and a readily evaporable water of 9 mm, typical of the clay loams of the Westside (FAO-56 Table 19), and Ke_max = 1.0 on the alfalfa basis. The balance runs daily through 2024 with ERA5 rain and ETr.


Code
def soil_evaporation_ke(rain, etr, tew=25.0, rew=9.0, ke_max=1.0):  # FAO-56 two-stage evaporation of bare soil
    de, out = tew, []  # start dry (fully depleted)
    for p_, e_ in zip(rain.values, etr.values):  # day by day
        de = max(de - p_, 0.0)  # rain refills the layer
        kr = 1.0 if de <= rew else max((tew - de) / (tew - rew), 0.0)  # stage 1 or stage 2
        ke = kr * ke_max  # evaporation coefficient
        de = min(de + ke * e_, tew)  # evaporation depletes the layer
        out.append(ke)  # Ke of the day
    return pd.Series(out, index=rain.index)  # daily Ke


ke = soil_evaporation_ke(rain, ref["etr"])  # daily Ke of a bare field

title: From Snapshots to Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use
text:
Daily ETrF
seb.interpolate_etrf fills each pixel’s days between clear images linearly, stops at gaps longer than 50 days (none exceeds that for most pixels; cloudy pixels of the 10 November image make some longer), and holds the first and last values to the ends of the year.


Code
daily = seb.interpolate_etrf(etrf, start="2024-01-01", end="2024-12-31", max_gap_days=50, extrapolate=True)  # (366, y, x)
print(dict(daily.sizes), f"| pixel-days without a value: {float(daily.isnull().mean()):.2%}")  # coverage
pts = {"almond orchard": (193, 25), "fallow field": (206, 193)}  # the cold and hot anchors of 5 July as examples
pts["tomato field"] = tuple(int(v) for v in np.argwhere((cdl == 54).values & (etrf.sel(time="2024-07-05").squeeze() > 0.9).values)[100])  # a well watered tomato pixel
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4))  # one panel
for name, (iy, ix) in pts.items():  # three pixels
    line = ax.plot(daily.time, daily[:, iy, ix], lw=1.5, label=name)[0]  # interpolated ETrF
    ax.plot(etrf.time, etrf[:, iy, ix], "o", color=line.get_color(), ms=5)  # image values
ax.set_ylabel("ETrF"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Daily ETrF interpolated between 27 Landsat images (dots)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


{'time': 366, 'y': 953, 'x': 926} | pixel-days without a value: 0.01%









The orchard keeps a high ETrF from spring to autumn. The tomato field rises from planting to full cover in early summer and drops at harvest. The fallow field stays low except after winter rains, when its bare soil evaporates. Between images the lines are straight: a harvest that happened a few days after an image appears later and more gradually than it was.

title: From Snapshots to Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use
text:
Rain between images
Straight lines between images carry the soil wetness of an image day across the following weeks: an image taken the day after a storm makes every bare field look wet for a month, and a storm between two dry images is missed. METRIC corrects the uncovered part of each pixel with the daily soil evaporation of the FAO-56 balance (Allen et al. 2007). The soil evaporation seen on the image dates is interpolated too, removed, and replaced by the daily value, weighted by the bare fraction 1 - fc:
ETrF_adj(day) = ETrF_interp(day) + (1 - fc_interp(day)) (Ke(day) - Ke_interp(day))


Code
fc_daily = seb.interpolate_etrf(fc, start="2024-01-01", end="2024-12-31", max_gap_days=50, extrapolate=True, clip=(0, 1))  # daily cover
ke_img = ke.reindex(pd.DatetimeIndex(etrf.time.values))  # Ke on the image dates
days = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31")  # every day of 2024
ke_interp = ke_img.reindex(days.union(ke_img.index)).interpolate("time").ffill().bfill().reindex(days)  # Ke as the images see it
corr = xr.DataArray((ke.reindex(days) - ke_interp).values, coords={"time": days}, dims="time")  # daily minus interpolated soil evaporation
daily_adj = (daily + (1 - fc_daily) * corr).clip(0, 1.3)  # adjusted daily ETrF
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4))  # one panel
iy, ix = pts["fallow field"]  # the fallow pixel
ax.plot(daily.time, daily[:, iy, ix], color="#bbbbbb", lw=2, label="linear between images")  # before
ax.plot(daily_adj.time, daily_adj[:, iy, ix], color="#8c510a", lw=1.2, label="with daily soil evaporation")  # after
ax.plot(etrf.time, etrf[:, iy, ix], "ko", ms=4, label="images")  # image values
ax.set_ylabel("ETrF"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("A fallow field: rain between images"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









After the adjustment the fallow field’s ETrF falls back within days of each storm instead of staying high until the next image, and storms between images appear as short pulses. Vegetated pixels change little, because the correction is weighted by their bare fraction. The rest of the notebook uses the adjusted daily ETrF.

title: From Snapshots to Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use
section: Winter: where METRIC is not reliable
text:
Winter: where METRIC is not reliable
The calibration log shows the winter images (January, February, November and December) with anchors only 5 to 8 K apart and a daily alfalfa reference ET of 1 to 3 mm. On those dates METRIC gives nearly every pixel, fallow land included, a fraction close to or above 1 (the crop coefficient section below lists them). With so little contrast the calibration is poorly constrained, and wet soil after rain makes both anchors evaporate. Operational METRIC work in California concentrates on the growing season for this reason. From November to March this notebook uses a cover-based coefficient instead, in the spirit of SIMS: green cover transpires at the reference rate, bare soil evaporates as the FAO-56 balance allows.
ETrF_off(day) = 0.95 fc(day) + (1 - fc(day)) Ke(day), from November to March
crumbs: Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use

title: From Snapshots to Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use
text:
Monthly and annual ET
Each day’s fraction times that day’s ETr, summed by month and over the year. Three versions of the annual total show the effect of each step.


Code
ke_da = xr.DataArray(ke.reindex(days).values, coords={"time": days}, dims="time")  # daily Ke as a DataArray
off = (daily_adj.time.dt.month <= 3) | (daily_adj.time.dt.month >= 11)  # November to March
etrf_off = (0.95 * fc_daily + (1 - fc_daily) * ke_da).clip(0, 1.05)  # cover-based coefficient
final = xr.where(off, etrf_off, daily_adj)  # METRIC April to October, cover-based in winter
etr_series = ref["etr"]  # daily alfalfa reference ET, mm
annual_linear = seb.seasonal_et(daily, etr_series)  # linear ETrF only
annual_rain = seb.seasonal_et(daily_adj, etr_series)  # with the rain adjustment
annual = seb.seasonal_et(final, etr_series)  # with the winter replacement as well
monthly = seb.seasonal_et(final, etr_series, freq="MS")  # mm per month
season = seb.seasonal_et(daily_adj, etr_series, start="2024-04-01", end="2024-10-31")  # METRIC irrigation season
print(f"window mean annual ET: linear {float(annual_linear.mean()):.0f} mm, rain adjusted {float(annual_rain.mean()):.0f} mm, "
      f"winter replaced {float(annual.mean()):.0f} mm")  # effect of each step
print(f"April to October (METRIC) {float(season.mean()):.0f} mm | alfalfa reference {etr_series.sum():.0f} mm | rain {rain.sum():.0f} mm "
      f"({rain.loc['2024-04':'2024-10'].sum():.0f} mm from April to October)")  # totals
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5.5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.2]})  # map and bars
im = ax[0].imshow(annual, cmap="YlGnBu", vmin=0, vmax=1600); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8, label="mm")  # annual ET map
ax[0].set_title("Actual ET, 2024"); ax[0].axis("off")  # title
mm = monthly.mean(["y", "x"]).to_series()  # window mean per month
ax[1].bar(mm.index.strftime("%b"), mm.values, color=np.where(mm.index.month.isin([1, 2, 3, 11, 12]), "#92c5de", "#2166ac"),
          label="actual ET, window mean (light: cover-based)")  # monthly ET
ax[1].plot(mm.index.strftime("%b"), etr_series.resample("MS").sum().values, "k-o", ms=4, label="alfalfa reference ET")  # reference
ax[1].set_ylabel("mm per month"); ax[1].legend(); ax[1].set_title("Monthly ET, Westside window")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


window mean annual ET: linear 1198 mm, rain adjusted 1167 mm, winter replaced 1102 mm
April to October (METRIC) 865 mm | alfalfa reference 2366 mm | rain 320 mm (38 mm from April to October)









The rain adjustment lowers the window’s annual mean from 1,198 to 1,167 mm and the winter replacement to 1,102 mm. Most of the ET happens from May to September, when the orchards and summer crops are at full canopy, and it stays well below the alfalfa reference because much of the window is fallow or harvested for part of the year.

Crop water use
seb.zonal_et groups the annual ET by CDL class and converts depths to volumes with the pixel area. One acre-foot is 1,233.5 m3.


Code
use = seb.zonal_et(annual, cdl, names=sd.CDL_NAMES, pixel_area=pixel_area, min_count=5000)  # per crop class
use["annual, linear only (mm)"] = seb.zonal_et(annual_linear, cdl, pixel_area=pixel_area, min_count=5000)["mean_mm"]  # before both adjustments
use["season Apr-Oct (mm)"] = seb.zonal_et(season, cdl, pixel_area=pixel_area, min_count=5000)["mean_mm"]  # irrigation season

      f"({annual.sum().item() / 1000 * pixel_area / 1233.5 / 1000:.0f} thousand acre-feet) over {annual.notnull().sum().item() * pixel_area / 1e4:,.0f} ha")  # total volume
fallow_et = float(annual.where(cdl == 61).mean())  # unirrigated fallow land, mm

      f"({float(season.where(cdl == 61).mean()):.0f} mm of it from April to October, when {rain.loc['2024-04':'2024-10'].sum():.0f} mm fell)")  # plausibility

Pistachios and almonds use the most water in total, because they cover the largest area and keep their canopy all season. Per hectare, almonds, grapes, cotton and alfalfa use the most over the April to October season (1,250 to 1,500 mm), pistachios and tomatoes about 1,000 mm. The spread between the 10th and 90th percentiles within each crop shows how much management varies from field to field; it is what makes field-scale ET useful for water accounting.
The water balance check is a warning. Fallow land is not irrigated, so over a year its ET cannot exceed the rain (320 mm) by much; yet it gets 575 mm, and 357 mm of that between April and October, when only 38 mm of rain fell. METRIC gives typical fallow fields an ETrF of about 0.15 to 0.2 in summer, because they are a little cooler than the hot anchor, and multiplied by a reference ET of 10 to 15 mm a day that small fraction adds up. The orchard totals are also higher than the 1,100 to 1,400 mm a year often quoted for mature, fully irrigated almonds in the San Joaquin Valley. Two causes act on every pixel: the ERA5 reference ET is not corrected for aridity (notebook 02 put that effect at up to 12 %), and the 1.05 cold anchor in an advective heat wave. Notebook 11 turns the fallow check into a bias estimate and asks which model and reference ET choices bring the totals down.

title: From Snapshots to Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use
text:
Satellite crop coefficients
The median ETrF of each crop on each image date, converted to the grass basis with that day’s ETr/ETo, gives a seasonal crop coefficient curve. The dashed lines are approximate mid-season values from FAO-56 Table 12 for standard, well watered conditions.


Code
CROPS = {75: "Almonds", 204: "Pistachios", 54: "Tomatoes", 2: "Cotton", 69: "Grapes", 24: "Winter wheat", 61: "Fallow/idle cropland"}  # crops to follow
FAO_MID = {"Almonds": 0.90, "Pistachios": 1.10, "Tomatoes": 1.15, "Cotton": 1.15, "Grapes": 0.85, "Winter wheat": 1.15}  # approximate FAO-56 Kc mid (grass basis)
ratio = (ref["etr"] / ref["eto"]).reindex(etrf.time.values)  # ETr/ETo on each image date
kc = pd.DataFrame({name: [float(etrf.sel(time=t).where(cdl == code).median()) * ratio.loc[t] for t in etrf.time.values]
                   for code, name in CROPS.items()}, index=pd.DatetimeIndex(etrf.time.values))  # satellite Kc per crop and date
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5))  # one panel
for name in CROPS.values():  # every crop
    line = ax.plot(kc.index, kc[name], "o-", ms=4, label=name)[0]  # satellite Kc
    if name in FAO_MID:  # tabulated value
        ax.axhline(FAO_MID[name], color=line.get_color(), ls="--", lw=0.8)  # FAO-56 mid-season
ax.set_ylabel("Kc (grass basis) = ETrF x ETr/ETo"); ax.legend(ncol=4, fontsize=8); ax.set_title("Satellite crop coefficients, 2024 (dashed: FAO-56 mid-season)")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

peak["Winter wheat"] = kc.loc["2024-04-01":"2024-04-30", "Winter wheat"].median()  # wheat peaks in April
display(kc.loc[["2024-01-11", "2024-02-12", "2024-12-04"]].round(2))  # winter images: METRIC fractions near or above 1 everywhere

The winter images show the problem discussed above: every class, fallow land included, has a coefficient of 1.2 to 1.6.

title: From Snapshots to Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use
text:
How many images are enough?
Landsat 8 alone visits every 16 days. Keeping every other image of the April to October season simulates that, and the difference in seasonal ET measures what a sparser record costs.


Code
grow = etrf.sel(time=slice("2024-04-01", "2024-10-31"))  # the 22 growing season images
rows = {}  # one row per experiment
for name, sel in [("all season images", slice(None)), ("every other image (1st, 3rd, ...)", slice(0, None, 2)),
                  ("every other image (2nd, 4th, ...)", slice(1, None, 2)), ("every fourth image", slice(0, None, 4))]:  # experiments
    sub = grow.isel(time=sel)  # chosen images
    d_ = seb.interpolate_etrf(sub, start="2024-04-01", end="2024-10-31", max_gap_days=None, extrapolate=True)  # daily ETrF
    s_ = seb.seasonal_et(d_, etr_series)  # season ET, without the rain adjustment (little rain in this season)
    if name == "all season images":  # the reference
        base = s_  # all images
    diff = s_ - base  # against all images
    rows[name] = {"images": sub.sizes["time"], "window mean (mm)": float(s_.mean()), "mean difference (mm)": float(diff.mean()),
                  "pixels changed by more than 100 mm (%)": 100 * float((np.abs(diff) > 100).sum() / diff.notnull().sum())}  # summary

title: From Snapshots to Seasonal ET and Crop Water Use
text:
Summary and exercises

METRIC on 27 Landsat images of 2024, interpolated in ETrF and multiplied by daily ERA5 alfalfa reference ET, gives daily, monthly and annual ET for every 30 m pixel.
The FAO-56 soil evaporation model gives the hot anchor’s ETrF after rain and, applied between images, keeps wet-soil evaporation from being carried across dry weeks.
On winter images METRIC’s fraction is not meaningful (coefficients of 1.2 to 1.6 for every class); a cover-based coefficient replaced it from November to March.
Satellite crop coefficients matched FAO-56 for tomatoes, cotton and wheat, exceeded it for almonds and grapes, and were far below for pistachios.
A water balance check exposed a positive bias over dry land: fallow fields got 357 mm of ET in a season with 38 mm of rain. Orchard totals are also on the high side.
With every other season image, 2.7 % of pixels changed by more than 100 mm; with every fourth, 17 %.

Exercises

Recompute the season with the humidity-adjusted ETr of notebook 02 (etr_humidity_adjusted). How much of the orchard excess does it remove?
Replace ERA5 ETr with the gridMET ETr saved in notebook 02 (etr_gridmet). How much does the annual total change, and does the crop ranking change?
Compute water use per field instead of per crop: polygonize the CDL tomato fields (geolattice.raster has a polygonize tool) and pass the polygons to seb.zonal_et.
Change TEW and REW of the soil evaporation model to those of a sandy loam (20 and 7 mm). Which winter images change?

title: Soil Moisture: Concepts and Why It Matters
text:
Overview

Ways to express soil water








Quantity
Definition
Units




Gravimetric water content w
mass of water / mass of dry soil
g g-1


Volumetric water content theta
volume of water / volume of soil, theta = w rho_b / rho_w
m3 m-3


Porosity phi
pore volume / soil volume, 1 - rho_b / rho_s
m3 m-3


Degree of saturation s
theta / phi, 0 (dry) to 1 (saturated)
1 or %


Field capacity FC
water held after free drainage, about -33 kPa
m3 m-3


Wilting point WP
water held so tightly that plants cannot extract it, -1500 kPa
m3 m-3


Plant available water PAW
FC - WP
m3 m-3



Satellites and most sensors report volumetric water content. Some products (ASCAT, the ESA CCI ACTIVE record) report the degree of saturation instead, which needs porosity to convert; crop models think in available water between wilting point and field capacity.


Surface and root zone
Microwave sensors see the top few centimetres (about 5 cm at L-band, 1 to 2 cm at C- and X-band), while crops draw water from the top metre. The surface layer reacts to every shower and dries within days; deeper layers respond to the sum of many events. Chapter notebooks 05 and 24 come back to this gap between what is sensed and what matters to plants.


Why it matters

Water cycle: wet soils produce more runoff from the same rain; dry soils store it.
Energy cycle: evaporation from moist soil cools the surface; dry soil heats the air and can intensify heat waves (land-atmosphere coupling).
Carbon cycle: photosynthesis and soil respiration both slow down when water runs short.
Hazards and agriculture: drought, flood potential, landslides, fire danger and crop yield all depend on the water stored in the soil.



Measuring soil moisture in situ








Method
Principle
Footprint




Gravimetric sampling
weigh, oven dry at 105 C, weigh again
a core of a few cm, destructive


Time domain reflectometry (TDR)
travel time of a pulse along rods gives the apparent permittivity; the Topp et al. (1980) equation converts it to theta
about 10 cm around the rods


Capacitance and impedance probes
permittivity from the frequency or impedance of a circuit (USCRN and SCAN use Stevens HydraProbes)
a few cm


Cosmic-ray neutron sensing (COSMOS)
fast neutrons from cosmic rays are slowed by hydrogen in soil water
about 150 m radius, 10 to 50 cm deep


GNSS reflectometry
change of reflected GPS signal with soil permittivity
tens of metres



Point sensors measure a few cubic centimetres; a satellite pixel averages kilometres. This scale gap is the main difficulty of validation (notebooks 21 to 23).

Ten years of soil moisture at five depths
The USCRN sensors report the mean of each hour. Daily means are enough to see the seasons; the missing winter values are frozen soil, when the probes do not measure liquid water.

title: Soil Moisture: Concepts and Why It Matters
section: How a storm wets the profile
text:
How a storm wets the profile
The wettest day of 2024 at the station was 2 July. The hourly record shows how the water entered the profile.


Code
t0 = pd.Timestamp("2024-07-01 12:00")  # before the storm (UTC)
win = uscrn.loc[t0:t0 + pd.Timedelta(days=6)]  # six days of hourly data
rain_start = win.index[win.p_mm > 0.5][0]  # first hour with rain
rows = []  # response of each depth
for d in DEPTHS:  # each sensor
    s = win[f"sm_{d}"]  # hourly series
    before = float(s.loc[:rain_start].iloc[-3:].mean())  # value just before the rain
    peak_t = s.idxmax()  # time of the maximum
    rows.append({"depth_cm": d, "before": before, "peak": float(s.max()), "rise": float(s.max()) - before,
                 "hours_to_peak": (peak_t - rain_start).total_seconds() / 3600})  # rise and delay
resp = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("depth_cm")  # one row per depth
display(resp.round(3))  # response table
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4))  # hourly plot
for d, c in zip(DEPTHS, plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0, 0.9, 5))):  # one line per depth
    ax.plot(win.index, win[f"sm_{d}"], color=c, label=f"{d} cm")  # hourly soil moisture
ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.bar(win.index, win.p_mm, width=1 / 24, color="tab:blue", alpha=0.4); ax2.set_ylabel("rain (mm/h)")  # rain
ax.set_ylabel("soil moisture (m3/m3)"); ax.legend(ncol=5, loc="upper left")  # labels
print(f"rain from {rain_start:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} UTC: {win.p_mm.sum():.0f} mm in the window")  # storm total
ax.set_title("The wetting front of the 2 July 2024 storm"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

About 83 mm fell in two bursts on 2 July and a third on 4 July. Every sensor down to 50 cm rose within the same hour as the rain and peaked about 12 hours after it started, so the water did not move down as a slow front: in this clay-rich soil it bypassed the matrix through cracks and root channels (preferential flow). The size of the rise, however, shrinks with depth, from 0.12 m3 m-3 at 5 cm to 0.06 at 50 cm and almost nothing at 100 cm, which was already near saturation. Between storms the surface layers dry fastest. A satellite sees only the top of this column, which is why its retrievals look much more variable than what a crop experiences.

text:
Two stations, two networks
SCAN Ames lies about 60 km north-west of the USCRN station. Both use HydraProbe sensors but different installations and calibrations.


Code

The two series share the seasonal drying and the largest storms, but their daily correlation is only 0.43 at 5 cm and 0.39 at 50 cm: rain falls differently 60 km apart, the soils differ, and so do the installations. On 11 days the SCAN 5 cm sensor reports more than 0.55 m3 m-3, above any plausible porosity of a loam; these are sensor artefacts (for example water ponding around the probe), and validation in notebook 21 screens such values out. Two stations in one region are not interchangeable at the daily scale, which is the first hint of the point-to-pixel problem.

text:
Water holding limits from texture
Saxton and Rawls (2006) fitted regressions of the water held at -33 and -1500 kPa on sand, clay and organic matter, using about 2,000 US soil samples. sm.saxton_rawls returns wilting point, field capacity, saturation (porosity), plant available water, normal bulk density and saturated hydraulic conductivity. The comparison is instructive. Under the USCRN station the functions give a wilting point of about 0.21 to 0.22 and a field capacity of about 0.38 m3 m-3, but the driest 2 % of days at 5 to 20 cm (0.16 to 0.18) fall below that wilting point: near the surface, evaporation dries the soil beyond the -1500 kPa that plants can reach, and sensor calibration in clay soils adds an offset. title: Soil Moisture: Concepts and Why It Matters
section: Plant available water in the root zone
text:
Plant available water in the root zone
The relative available water (theta - WP) / (FC - WP) is 1 at field capacity and 0 at wilting point. Crops start to close their stomata below about 50 %. Here it is computed for the 10 to 50 cm layer at the USCRN station with the pedotransfer limits of the corresponding SoilGrids depths.


Code
lim = ptf["USCRN Des Moines 17 E"]  # limits under the USCRN station
layer = {10: "5-15cm", 20: "15-30cm", 50: "30-60cm"}  # sensor depth -> SoilGrids layer
raw = sum(sm.soil_water_status(daily[f"sm_{d}"], lim.loc[g, "wilting_point"], lim.loc[g, "field_capacity"])
          for d, g in layer.items()) / 3  # mean relative available water of the three sensors
raw = pd.Series(np.asarray(raw), index=daily.index)  # daily series
season = raw[(raw.index.month >= 5) & (raw.index.month <= 9)].dropna()  # May to September days with data
n_days = season.groupby(season.index.year).size()  # observed days per season
dry = season.lt(0.5).groupby(season.index.year).mean() * 100  # share of observed days below 50 %
dry = dry[n_days >= 100]  # keep seasons with at least 100 of 153 days observed
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3, 1]})  # series and bars
ax[0].plot(raw.index, raw, lw=0.8); ax[0].axhline(0.5, color="tab:red", ls="--", lw=1)  # 50 % line
ax[0].set_ylabel("relative available water"); ax[0].set_title("Root zone (10 to 50 cm), USCRN Des Moines 17 E")  # labels
dry.plot.bar(ax=ax[1], color="tab:orange"); ax[1].set_ylabel("% of May to Sept days below 50 %")  # yearly bars
ax[1].set_xlabel(""); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
print(dry.round(0).astype(int).to_dict(), "| seasons left out (too few days):", sorted(set(n_days.index) - set(dry.index)))  # values









{2015: 0, 2016: 5, 2017: 24, 2018: 25, 2019: 13, 2020: 30, 2021: 49, 2023: 57, 2024: 10} | seasons left out (too few days): [2022, 2025]


The years differ sharply: in 2023 the root zone spent 57 % of the observed growing season days below 50 % of available water, in 2021 49 %, while 2015 and 2016 hardly dropped below it. Seasons with large gaps (the 2022 outage) are left out because a share of a few observed days would be misleading. The chapter’s drought notebook (25) maps these dry seasons across the region from SMAP.

title: Soil Moisture: Concepts and Why It Matters
section: Unit conversions and the Topp equation
text:
Unit conversions and the Topp equation
A gravimetric sample, a degree of saturation from a scatterometer and a TDR reading all describe the same soil water. The Topp et al. (1980) cubic relates the apparent permittivity measured by TDR to volumetric water content for most mineral soils.


Code
rho_b = float(prof["SCAN Ames"].loc["0-5cm", "bdod"])  # SoilGrids bulk density at the surface (g/cm3)
w = 0.20  # a gravimetric sample (g/g)
theta = float(sm.volumetric_from_gravimetric(w, rho_b))  # volumetric water content
phi = float(sm.porosity_from_bulk_density(rho_b))  # porosity from bulk density
print(f"bulk density {rho_b:.2f} g/cm3: w = {w} g/g -> theta = {theta:.3f} m3/m3; "
      f"porosity {phi:.3f}; degree of saturation {float(sm.degree_of_saturation(theta, phi)):.2f}")  # conversions
print(f"an ASCAT-style 62 % saturation is {float(sm.saturation_to_volumetric(62.0, phi)):.3f} m3/m3")  # saturation to volumetric
eps = sm.topp_inverse(np.array([0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45]))  # permittivity of each water content
display(pd.DataFrame({"theta": [0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45], "apparent permittivity": eps,
                      "back with topp": sm.topp(eps)}).round(3))  # round trip

title: Soil Moisture: Concepts and Why It Matters
text:
Summary and exercises

Volumetric water content is the common currency; degree of saturation and relative available water need porosity, field capacity and wilting point, which texture can estimate.
At the Iowa station near-surface soil moisture swings between about 0.16 and 0.41 m3 m-3, while the 100 cm layer stays near 0.48 to 0.52; in situ records have gaps too.
The 83 mm storm of 2 July 2024 reached 50 cm within the hour through preferential flow, but the rise shrank from 0.12 m3 m-3 at 5 cm to almost nothing at 100 cm.
Two stations 60 km apart correlate only at about 0.4 day to day, and one reports values above porosity that need screening.
SoilGrids texture with the Saxton and Rawls functions gives limits of the right magnitude, but the near-surface soil dries below the estimated wilting point and the subsoil is wetter than estimated.
The share of growing season days below 50 % of available water separates drought seasons (2021,

from wet ones.


Exercises

Repeat the storm analysis for the 20 May 2024 event. Is the response faster or slower than in July, and why might the antecedent moisture matter?
Compute the relative available water at SCAN Ames with its own SoilGrids profile. Which station had more stress days in 2023?
Change the organic matter in sm.saxton_rawls from the SoilGrids value to 1 % and to 4 %. How much do field capacity and plant available water change?
Use sm.degree_of_saturation with the pedotransfer saturation to express the USCRN 5 cm record as degree of saturation. What fraction of days is above 0.9?

title: SMAP L3 Enhanced: a Daily Cube and its Climatology
text: Banner

title: SMAP L3 Enhanced: a Daily Cube and its Climatology
text:
Overview

The SMAP product family








Product
Grid
Content




L2_SM_P, L3_SM_P (SPL3SMP)
36 km
single channel retrieval from the radiometer footprint


L2_SM_P_E, L3_SM_P_E (SPL3SMP_E)
9 km
the same retrieval on Backus-Gilbert interpolated Tb


L4_SM (SPL4SMGP)
9 km, 3-hourly
Tb assimilated into a land surface model: surface and root zone


L2_SM_SP (SPL2SMAP_S)
3 and 1 km
SMAP Tb disaggregated with Sentinel-1 backscatter





AM and PM overpasses
SMAP is in a sun-synchronous orbit with a 6 am local descending (AM) and 6 pm ascending (PM) equator crossing. The baseline retrieval uses the AM pass, when the soil, canopy and air temperatures are closest, so the single effective temperature of the model is most valid; the L3 file has both, and the PM group’s variables end in _pm. The swath is 1,000 km wide, so a location is seen two or three times in three days.


Quality flags
retrieval_qual_flag (bits: 0 recommended quality, 1 retrieval attempted, 2 retrieval successful, 3 freeze-thaw retrieval successful; a set bit means “not”) and surface_flag (static and radar water, coastal, urban, precipitation, snow, frozen ground, mountains, dense vegetation) describe each retrieval. The recommended quality mask keeps retrievals whose bit 0 is clear: vegetation water content below 5 kg m-2, little open water and no frozen soil, among other conditions.


Climatology and anomalies
Soil moisture has a strong seasonal cycle. The day-of-year climatology (the mean for each calendar day, smoothed over a 31-day window) is the baseline against which droughts and wet spells are anomalies: anomaly = theta - climatology(doy).

      f"{float(revisit.median()):.0f} days of 153 per cell and season (median)")  # revisit

title: SMAP L3 Enhanced: a Daily Cube and its Climatology
text:
Summary and exercises

SMAP L3 Enhanced over the Midwest box is a cube of about 3,900 days of AM and PM retrievals with their flags and ancillary layers.
Winter retrievals are few (frozen ground, snow); 14 to 29 % of attempted retrievals are not of recommended quality.
With AM first and PM fill, about half of the region has a retrieval on a summer day, and a cell has one on 87 of 153 days of the season.
The smoothed climatology peaks in late March (0.26 m3 m-3) and bottoms out in early August (0.19); 2023 was the driest summer of the record.

Exercises

Use combine="mean" in sm.daily_cube. Where do the AM and PM retrievals differ most, and in which season?
Apply level="strict" in sm.mask_quality. How many more retrievals are removed, and is the 2023 anomaly different?
Plot the vegetation water content (vegetation_water_content) climatology for July. Which parts of the region exceed 5 kg m-2?
Compute the climatology from 2015 to 2020 only and recompute the 2023 anomaly. How sensitive is an anomaly to the reference period?

title: ESA CCI: Long-Term Trends and Anomalies
text:
Overview

Three products








Product
Sensors
Units




PASSIVE
SMMR, SSM/I, TMI, AMSR-E, WindSat, AMSR2, SMOS, SMAP, GPM, FY-3
m3 m-3


ACTIVE
ERS-1, ERS-2 AMI-WS, ASCAT on MetOp-A, B and C
% saturation


COMBINED
both, merged
m3 m-3





How the merging works
Each sensor’s retrievals are rescaled to a common reference (GLDAS Noah land model soil moisture) by CDF matching, so they share one climatology; where several sensors overlap, their values are averaged with weights from triple collocation error estimates (Dorigo et al. 2017; Gruber et al. 2019), giving more weight to the sensor with the smaller error. Each value carries an uncertainty and flags (frozen soil, dense vegetation, no convergence, water).


Sensor eras and trends
The number and quality of sensors change over time: before 1987 only SMMR (every other day, coarse), from 2002 AMSR-E, from 2007 ASCAT, from 2010 SMOS, from 2015 SMAP. Coverage and noise change with them. Trends computed across sensor changes can be artefacts, so the analysis below checks the data density through time and uses robust, rank-based statistics.


Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope
The Mann-Kendall test asks whether later values tend to be larger (or smaller) than earlier ones, using only the signs of all pairwise differences; it makes no assumption about the distribution. Sen’s slope is the median of all pairwise slopes, robust to outliers. Both are applied per cell to annual (or seasonal) means.

Since 1991, 71 % of the cells have a negative Sen’s slope and 23 % a significant drying trend (p < 0.05), concentrated in the west and north-west; no cell has a significant wetting trend. The median slope is small, about -0.003 m3 m-3 per decade. By season the national series dries in the pre-monsoon (-0.006 per decade) and monsoon (-0.005), while the dry Rabi season gets slightly wetter (+0.003), all significant at 5 %. A wetter dry season while the rest of the year dries is what the expansion of groundwater-irrigated Boro rice would produce. These trends are small against the year-to-year variability and comparable with the steps that sensor changes can introduce, so a significant trend in a merged record is a hypothesis to check against independent data (rain gauges, reanalysis, groundwater), not a finding on its own.

title: ESA CCI: Long-Term Trends and Anomalies
text:
Summary and exercises

ESA CCI COMBINED gives 46 years of daily soil moisture over Bangladesh; data density rises from about 35 to 140 valid days per cell and year, and uncertainty halves, as sensors are added.
The national mean is lowest in March and April (about 0.19 m3 m-3) and highest in July (about 0.36).
The national anomaly index ranks the pre-monsoon of 2023 among the driest months on record.
Since 1991 a quarter of the cells dry significantly, mainly in the north-west, while the Rabi season gets slightly wetter; such trends must be weighed against sensor changes in the record.

Exercises

Recompute the trend map from 2007 to 2024 only (dense ASCAT and multi-sensor era). Are the significant cells the same?
Use sm.mask_quality(cci, level="recommended") (flag 0 only). How many monsoon values remain?
Compare the national anomaly index with the annual rainfall of a Bangladesh station from a public source, and compute their correlation.

text: Banner

title: Sentinel-1 Preprocessing for Soil Moisture
text:
Overview

From raw data to gamma0 RTC







Step
What it does




GRD (Ground Range Detected)
amplitude images in radar geometry, multilooked to about 20 m


Orbit correction
precise orbit files fix the geolocation


Thermal noise removal
subtracts the receiver noise, important for low VH backscatter


Radiometric calibration
DN to sigma0 (per unit ground area) or beta0 (per unit slant area)


Terrain flattening
divides by the illuminated area from a DEM: gamma0 RTC (Small 2011)


Geocoding
projects to map coordinates (UTM)


Speckle filtering
reduces the multiplicative noise of coherent imaging



Planetary Computer’s sentinel-1-rtc collection provides gamma0 RTC at 10 m for every Sentinel-1 IW scene over land, produced with the GAMMA software; ASF’s OPERA RTC-S1 and Earth Engine’s COPERNICUS/S1_GRD are alternatives. GeoLattice can also process GRD itself (geolattice.rsense.sar.process_grd).


Geometry: one relative orbit
Backscatter depends on the incidence angle (about 30 to 46 degrees across the IW swath) and on the look direction. Over Iowa each place is seen from two ascending relative orbits (63 and 165) at different angles. Keeping one relative orbit keeps the geometry of every pixel constant in time, so temporal changes reflect the surface, not the viewing angle. Mixing orbits requires an incidence angle normalization (sm.normalize_incidence).


Speckle
SAR images are the coherent sum of many scatterers in each pixel, which produces a granular, multiplicative noise with an equivalent number of looks (ENL) of about 4 for GRD. Spatial filters (boxcar, Lee, refined Lee) blur field boundaries; the multitemporal filter of Quegan and Yu (2001) uses the time series to reduce speckle while keeping spatial detail.


VV, VH and soil moisture
Co-polarized VV backscatter is dominated by surface scattering from the soil and responds most to soil moisture; cross-polarized VH comes mainly from volume scattering in vegetation and tracks biomass. Their ratio (VH/VV, or VH minus VV in dB) is a common vegetation descriptor for retrievals.

text:
Why one relative orbit
The same fields seen from the two orbits on nearby dates differ systematically, because the incidence angle and the look direction differ.


Code
from geolattice.rsense.access import stac_load  # loading
other = 63 if s1.attrs["relative_orbit"] == 165 else 165  # the second orbit
pick = cat[(cat.time.dt.year == 2020) & (cat.time.dt.month.isin([6, 7]))]  # a few summer scenes of both orbits
sub = [i for i in items if pd.Timestamp(i.properties["datetime"]).tz_localize(None) in set(pick.time)]  # their items
raw = stac_load(sub, bands=["vv"], aoi=sd.IOWA_SAR, crs=s1.rio.crs, resolution=50, chunks={"x": 1024, "y": 1024}).load()  # gamma0, linear
raw_db = 10 * np.log10(raw.vv.where(raw.vv > 0))  # dB
orb = xr.DataArray([dict(zip(pick.time, pick.orbit)).get(pd.Timestamp(t), np.nan) for t in raw.time.values], dims="time")  # orbit of each date
mean_by_orbit = {o: float(raw_db.where(orb == o).mean()) for o in (s1.attrs["relative_orbit"], other)}  # scene mean per orbit
print({f"orbit {k}": round(v, 2) for k, v in mean_by_orbit.items()}, "dB mean VV, June to July 2020")  # systematic difference


{'orbit 165': -9.62, 'orbit 63': -10.2} dB mean VV, June to July 2020


The two orbits differ by about 0.6 dB on average over the same fields and weeks, comparable with the change that a few hundredths of m3 m-3 of soil moisture produces. Mixing them without normalization would add a geometry-driven zigzag to every time series.

text:
Speckle filtering


Code
from geolattice.rsense.sar import speckle  # filters
one = raw.vv.isel(time=0)  # one unfiltered scene (linear)
win = dict(x=slice(int(one.sizes["x"] * 0.4), int(one.sizes["x"] * 0.4) + 200), y=slice(int(one.sizes["y"] * 0.4), int(one.sizes["y"] * 0.4) + 200))  # 10 km window
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.6))  # raw, Lee, multitemporal
for a, (name, img) in zip(ax, (("unfiltered", one), ("refined Lee", speckle.refined_lee(one)),
                              ("multitemporal (cube)", 10 ** (s1.vv.sel(time=one.time, method="nearest") / 10)))):  # three versions
    (10 * np.log10(img.isel(**win))).plot(ax=a, vmin=-16, vmax=-4, cmap="gray", add_colorbar=False); a.set_title(name); a.axis("off")  # map
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
for name, img in (("unfiltered", one), ("multitemporal", 10 ** (s1.vv.sel(time=one.time, method="nearest") / 10))):  # ENL of a field
    patch = img.isel(x=slice(200, 220), y=slice(200, 220))  # a 1 km block
    print(f"{name}: ENL estimate {speckle.enl_estimate(patch):.1f}")  # equivalent number of looks









unfiltered: ENL estimate 2.4
multitemporal: ENL estimate 10.3


The unfiltered 50 m image has an equivalent number of looks of only about 2.4 over a field, so a single pixel is very noisy. The refined Lee filter smooths within its 7 x 7 window and blurs the field pattern at this pixel size; the multitemporal filter raises the ENL to about 10 while keeping field boundaries and roads sharp, because it borrows information from the other 78 dates instead of the neighbours.

Summary and exercises

Planetary Computer RTC provides terrain-flattened gamma0 for every Sentinel-1 scene; over central Iowa only Sentinel-1A observed in 2019 to 2021, from two ascending relative orbits, every 12 days each.
Keeping one relative orbit avoids systematic differences of about 0.6 dB between geometries.

title: Water Cloud Model and Surface Scattering Inversion
text: Banner

title: Water Cloud Model and Surface Scattering Inversion
text:
Overview

The Water Cloud Model
For a vegetation descriptor V (NDVI, LAI or vegetation water content) and incidence angle t (Attema and Ulaby 1978):
sigma0 = A V^E cos(t) (1 - tau2) + tau2 sigma0_soil, with tau2 = exp(-2 B V / cos(t))
The first term is the direct backscatter of the canopy, the second the soil backscatter attenuated twice (two-way) by the canopy. The soil term is commonly linear in decibels, sigma0_soil(dB) = C + D theta. A, B, C and D are calibrated per crop against field data; E is often fixed at 1.


Surface scattering models









Model
Type
Inputs
Validity




Oh (1992, 2004)
semi-empirical, from truck-mounted radar
theta (or permittivity), rms height s, angle
ks 0.1 to 6, theta 0.04 to 0.29


Dubois et al. (1995)
semi-empirical
permittivity, s, angle
ks < 2.5, angle > 30 degrees, NDVI < 0.4


IEM (Fung et al. 1992)
physical, integral equation
permittivity, s, correlation length l, correlation function
ks < 3



They need roughness, which is rarely known; inversion therefore searches soil moisture and roughness together in a look-up table (LUT), and works only on bare or nearly bare fields.


Vegetation descriptors
NDVI from optical images is easy to obtain but saturates in dense canopies and needs a clear day; radar itself offers descriptors such as the cross-polarization ratio VH/VV, which grows with volume scattering and is available on every pass.

Without constraints the corn fit finds almost no soil sensitivity (D of about 1.4 dB per m3 m-3), because the corn samples barely show one; inverting such a model amplifies every 0.1 dB of noise into large soil moisture errors. Bounding D to the physical range moves both crops to the lower bound of 20 dB per m3 m-3 at a small cost in calibration RMSE (1.4 dB).

title: Water Cloud Model and Surface Scattering Inversion
text:
Leave-one-field-out validation
The calibration RMSE flatters the model, because every field helped fit the parameters it is tested on. Leaving out each field in turn, calibrating on the others and inverting the left-out field gives an honest estimate of the retrieval error at a new field. The baseline to beat is simply predicting the mean soil moisture of the campaign.


Code
def loo(desc, bounds=None):  # leave-one-field-out retrieval with a given vegetation descriptor
    out = []  # predictions
    for site in df.site.unique():  # each field in turn
        train, test = df[df.site != site], df[df.site == site]  # split
        p = sm.calibrate_wcm(train.vv_db, train.sm, train[desc], train.incidence, groups=train.crop, bounds=bounds)  # fit on the others
        if test.crop.iloc[0] not in p.index:  # crop not calibrated
            continue
        pred = sm.invert_wcm(test.vv_db.values, test[desc].values, test.incidence.values, p.loc[test.crop.iloc[0]].to_dict())  # invert
        out.append(test.assign(pred=pred, mean_pred=train.sm.mean()))  # keep, with the campaign-mean baseline
    return pd.concat(out)  # all predictions


cv_free, cv = loo("ndvi"), loo("ndvi", BOUNDS)  # unconstrained and constrained
summary = pd.DataFrame({"WCM, unconstrained": sm.validation_metrics(cv_free.sm, cv_free.pred),
                        "WCM, D bounded": sm.validation_metrics(cv.sm, cv.pred),
                        "campaign mean (no satellite)": sm.validation_metrics(cv.sm, cv.mean_pred)}).T  # comparison
display(summary[["n", "bias", "rmse", "ubrmse", "pearson_r"]].astype(float).round(3))  # table
rows = []  # constrained model by crop and period
for key, g in cv.groupby(["crop", "iop"]):  # groups
    m = sm.validation_metrics(g.sm, g.pred)  # retrieval against ThetaProbe
    rows.append({"crop": key[0], "period": key[1], "n": int(m.n), "bias": m.bias, "ubrmse": m.ubrmse, "R": m.pearson_r})  # row

The honest test is sobering. The unconstrained model misses new fields by 0.20 m3 m-3 RMSE; the constrained model by 0.085, with a correlation of 0.22; and simply predicting the campaign mean, with no satellite at all, gives 0.039, because the soil moisture of these fields varied so little in this summer. The model only shows skill in August (R 0.35 over corn and 0.45 over soybean), when the range of conditions between fields was wider, and none in early June.
This is a common outcome of field campaigns, not a failure of the code. The ThetaProbe measures 0 to 5 cm and C-band senses 1 to 2 cm; soil sampling and the radar pass are up to a day apart; a 60 m window at the field centre represents a field only roughly; and roughness, row direction and residue differ between fields in ways the model does not know. Published WCM retrievals over crops reach 0.04 to 0.06 m3 m-3 mainly when parameters are calibrated per field over long time series, which removes the field-to-field differences that dominate here.

text:
Bare-soil models in early June
On the first campaign dates most fields were bare or had small plants (NDVI below 0.4). There the canopy can be neglected and a surface scattering model applies directly.


Code
bare = df[(df.ndvi < 0.4)].copy()  # nearly bare fields
print(f"{len(bare)} samples with NDVI < 0.4")  # sample size
grid_t = np.round(np.arange(0.10, 0.46, 0.01), 2)  # LUT soil moisture
lut = sm.iem_lut(grid_t, [0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0], [4.0, 8.0, 12.0], [34.0, 35.0, 39.0, 44.0, 45.0], freq_ghz=5.405, pol="vv", clay=0.3)  # IEM look-up table

for s_ in (0.7, 1.0, 1.5):  # Oh 2004 for three roughness values
    bare[f"oh_vv_s{s_}"] = sm.oh_model(bare.sm.values, s_, bare.incidence.values)["vv"]  # forward VV

Of the Oh 2004 curves, an rms height of 1.5 cm reproduces the mean early-June backscatter best (-7.7 against -8.2 dB observed), a typical value for tilled fields. The IEM look-up table inversion with roughness as a free parameter, however, does not retrieve the field differences (R -0.16, ubRMSE 0.10 m3 m-3): with a single polarization, a rougher dry field and a smoother wet field have the same VV, and the inversion cannot tell them apart. Multi-polarization or multi-angle data, or roughness measured in the field, are needed for bare-soil inversion.

title: Water Cloud Model and Surface Scattering Inversion
text:
Summary and exercises

SMAPVEX16 gives 135 matched samples of field soil moisture, Sentinel-1 backscatter on three orbits, incidence angle and Sentinel-2 NDVI over 32 corn and soybean fields.
The field soil moisture varied little (standard deviation 0.039 m3 m-3) and VV responded to it only in August; field-to-field roughness dominated in early June.
An unconstrained Water Cloud Model overfits (0.20 m3 m-3 RMSE at new fields); bounding the soil sensitivity to physical values brings it to 0.085, still above the 0.039 of predicting the mean.
The cross-polarization ratio is a usable vegetation descriptor without optical data.
Bare-soil inversion of a single polarization with unknown roughness is ill-posed.
Leave-one-field-out validation, and comparing against a no-skill baseline, are what reveal this; a calibration RMSE alone would have hidden it.

Exercises

Fit the WCM with E free (extend bounds and pass different E values) and compare the cross-validated RMSE.
Use VH instead of VV in the calibration. Is VH a better or worse soil moisture channel under the crops?
Add Dubois (sm.dubois_model with sm.mironov_dielectric) to the bare-soil comparison.
Map soil moisture for the 1 June 2016 pass (orbit 63) with sd.smapvex16_scene("2016-06-01", 63).

title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
text:
Overview

Two rules for any downscaling method

Mass conservation: the 1 km values inside a 9 km cell should average to the 9 km value. Then the method only adds spatial pattern and keeps the level and accuracy of the coarse product.
Beat the baseline: a 1 km map is only useful if it is closer to the truth than the coarse value copied into every sub-cell. Correlating a downscaled map with stations mostly rewards the coarse signal it inherits; what counts is the part it adds.



The six methods









#
Method
Fine-scale information
Idea




0
Baseline
none
copy each 9 km value to its 81 cells of 1 km


1
Regression + smooth interpolation
soil texture, organic carbon, elevation, slope
pooled linear regression of coarse anomalies on aggregated static covariates, applied at 1 km as a zero-mean pattern, added to a mass-preserving (pycnophylactic) smooth surface through the 9 km values


2a
DisPATCh
MODIS LST and NDVI
soil evaporative efficiency (SEE) from the LST-NDVI space; SM = SM_c + SMp (SEE - SEE_c) (Merlin et al. 2012)


2b
OPTRAM
MODIS NBAR SWIR and NDVI
the same linear scheme with the OPTRAM moisture index (Sadeghi et al. 2017) instead of SEE


3
Active-passive (SAR)
Sentinel-1 VV at 50 m
SM = SM_c + beta (sigma - sigma_c) (Das et al. 2014), aggregated to 1 km


4
Machine learning + residual
NDVI, rain, texture, terrain, crops, season
XGBoost trained on coarse cells, applied at 1 km, coarse residual added back


5
Deep learning (U-Net)
the same covariates
a residual U-Net that learns the 1 km correction from SPL2SMAP_S 1 km targets


6
Fusion
methods 1 to 4
weighted mean with weights from each method’s error in the training years





How the methods are judged
The truth at 1 km is unknown. Two imperfect references are used: the SMAP/Sentinel-1 product SPL2SMAP_S at 1 km (an independent algorithm, but sharing SMAP and Sentinel-1 with methods 3 and 5) and the 5 cm sensors of two stations (true points, but not representative of 1 km). For every method:

Within-cell skill: the correlation between the pattern a method adds (method - baseline) and the pattern of the reference (reference - baseline), over all cells and days. Zero means no useful sub-cell information.
Gain over the baseline: 1 - ubRMSD(method) / ubRMSD(baseline) against the reference. Positive means better than copying the coarse value.
Mass conservation error: the mean absolute difference between the 9 km block mean of the 1 km map and the 9 km value.
Availability: the share of cells and days with a value (thermal and SAR methods are gappy).

U-Net and fusion learn from SPL2SMAP_S in 2019 and 2020, so all comparisons with SPL2SMAP_S use 2021 only.
