title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
text:
Method 1: regression with smooth interpolation
The daily mean is removed from the coarse values; the anomalies are regressed (pooled over all days) on the static covariates averaged to 9 km; the regression is applied at 1 km as a pattern with zero mean in every 9 km cell. It is added to a smooth surface through the coarse values made with the pycnophylactic interpolation (Tobler 1979), which removes the blocky cell edges while keeping every block mean, a simple stand-in for area-to-point kriging.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression  # pooled regression
STATIC = ["sand", "clay", "soc", "elevation", "slope"]  # static covariates
Xf = xr.Dataset({v: ds[v] for v in STATIC})  # at 1 km
Xc = xr.Dataset({v: sm.block_mean(ds[v].rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933"), F) for v in STATIC})  # at 9 km
anom = coarse - coarse.mean(("y", "x"))  # daily spatial anomalies at 9 km
tab = anom.to_dataframe(name="a").reset_index()[["time", "y", "x", "a"]].merge(Xc.to_dataframe().reset_index()[["y", "x"] + STATIC], on=["y", "x"]).dropna()  # samples
mu, sdv = tab[STATIC].mean(), tab[STATIC].std()  # standardisation
reg = LinearRegression().fit((tab[STATIC] - mu) / sdv, tab["a"])  # pooled fit
print("standardised coefficients (m3/m3 per std):", dict(zip(STATIC, np.round(reg.coef_, 4))), "| R2", round(reg.score((tab[STATIC] - mu) / sdv, tab["a"]), 2))  # fit
pattern = sum(((Xf[v] - mu[v]) / sdv[v]) * c for v, c in zip(STATIC, reg.coef_))  # static pattern at 1 km
pattern = pattern - sm.nested_upsample(sm.block_mean(pattern.rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933"), F), F).values  # zero block mean: adds pattern, not level
smooth = sm.pycnophylactic(coarse, F, iterations=30)  # smooth surface through the 9 km cells, block means kept
m1 = smooth + pattern.values  # smooth coarse field plus the static pattern
products["1 regression + smooth"] = m1.clip(0.02, 0.6)  # store
timing["1 regression + smooth"] = time.time() - t0  # run time


standardised coefficients (m3/m3 per std): {'sand': np.float32(-0.0096), 'clay': np.float32(-0.0026), 'soc': np.float32(-0.0011), 'elevation': np.float32(-0.0049), 'slope': np.float32(0.0005)} | R2 0.2


The static covariates explain about 20 % of the spatial anomalies between the 72 cells of 9 km; sand has the largest (negative) effect, as sandier soils drain and dry faster, followed by elevation.
Because the pattern has a zero mean in every 9 km block and the smooth surface keeps the block means, method 1 conserves mass by construction. Its sub-cell pattern is the same on every day: a smooth gradient between neighbouring cells plus the texture and terrain pattern of the regression.

title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
text:
Method 2: DisPATCh and OPTRAM
DisPATCh needs a clear-sky day: the LST-NDVI edges define the soil temperature end-members and the soil evaporative efficiency (SEE) of each 1 km cell; SMAP is then redistributed with SM = SM_c + SMp (SEE - SEE_c), where the soil moisture parameter SMp = SM_c / SEE_c is computed per 9 km cell. A domain of 81 x 72 cells is small for drawing edges, so they are fitted on the clear days within eight days of each date, and SMp is capped at 0.45 m3 m-3; both settings were chosen on 2019 and 2020 only (a first version with daily edges and a cap of 0.6 had more than twice the error). OPTRAM uses the SWIR transformed reflectance instead of temperature, with edges fitted once over the three seasons on vegetated pixels (NDVI 0.2 to 0.85).


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start
dis = xr.full_like(base, np.nan)  # DisPATCh result
used = 0  # clear days processed
WIN, SMP_MAX = 8, 0.45  # edges from the clear days within +-8 days; cap of the soil moisture parameter (chosen on 2019 and 2020)
for i, d in enumerate(days):  # each day
    lst, nd = ds.lst_day.isel(time=i), ds.ndvi.isel(time=i)  # inputs of the day
    c = coarse.isel(time=i)  # SMAP of the day
    if float(lst.notnull().mean()) < 0.5 or float(c.notnull().mean()) < 0.5:  # need a mostly clear day and SMAP
        continue
    sl = slice(max(0, i - WIN), i + WIN + 1)  # neighbouring days
    try:
        e = sm.ts_vi_edges(ds.lst_day.isel(time=sl), ds.ndvi.isel(time=sl), ndvi_bins=20, quantile=0.02, ndvi_range=(0.15, 0.9))  # pooled edges
    except ValueError:  # too few populated NDVI bins
        continue
    see = sm.soil_evaporative_efficiency(lst, nd, edges=e).rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933")  # SEE at 1 km
    smp = (c / sm.block_mean(see, F).values).clip(0.1, SMP_MAX).rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933")  # soil moisture parameter per 9 km cell
    dis[i] = sm.dispatch(c, see, sm_p=smp).values  # DisPATCh
    used += 1  # count
products["2a DisPATCh (LST)"] = dis  # store
timing["2a DisPATCh (LST)"] = time.time() - t0  # run time
print(f"DisPATCh run on {used} of {len(days)} days (clear sky and SMAP)")  # coverage
t0 = time.time()  # start
ndvi_nbar = (ds.nir - ds.red) / (ds.nir + ds.red)  # NDVI from the same NBAR reflectance
strf = sm.str_transform(ds.swir22)  # SWIR transformed reflectance
veg = ndvi_nbar > 0.1  # leave water and bare urban surfaces out of the edge fit
oe = sm.optram_edges(strf.where(veg), ndvi_nbar.where(veg), ndvi_bins=30, quantile=0.02, ndvi_range=(0.2, 0.85))  # edges over all days
W = sm.optram(strf, ndvi_nbar, oe).rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933")  # OPTRAM moisture index (0 dry, 1 wet)
print("OPTRAM edges:", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in oe.items()})  # parameters
opt = xr.full_like(base, np.nan)  # OPTRAM downscaling
for i in range(len(days)):  # each day
    w, c = W.isel(time=i), coarse.isel(time=i)  # inputs
    if float(w.notnull().mean()) < 0.5 or float(c.notnull().mean()) < 0.5:  # need data
        continue
    smp = (c / sm.block_mean(w, F).values).clip(0.1, SMP_MAX).rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933")  # soil moisture parameter per cell
    opt[i] = sm.dispatch(c, w.clip(0.01, 0.99), sm_p=smp).values  # same linear scheme with W instead of SEE
products["2b OPTRAM"] = opt  # store
timing["2b OPTRAM"] = time.time() - t0  # run time


DisPATCh run on 179 of 642 days (clear sky and SMAP)
OPTRAM edges: {'i_d': -0.69, 's_d': 3.91, 'i_w': 4.69, 's_w': 1.12}


DisPATCh runs on 179 of the 642 days: the rest are cloudy or lack SMAP. The OPTRAM edges now have the expected shape, the wet edge above the dry edge at every NDVI.

title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
text:
Method 3: SAR active-passive disaggregation
Sentinel-1 VV at 50 m distributes SMAP inside each 9 km cell (notebook 12), then the 50 m result is averaged to 1 km. It exists only on Sentinel-1 days.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start
s1 = sd.s1_cube()  # notebook 11 cube (UTM, 50 m)
s1 = s1.sel(time=s1.time.dt.month.isin(list(sd.DS_MONTHS)))  # same months
sday = pd.DatetimeIndex(s1.time.values).normalize()  # Sentinel-1 days
cs = coarse.reindex(time=sday, method="nearest", tolerance=pd.Timedelta(days=1)).assign_coords(time=s1.time.values).rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933")  # SMAP on S1 days
apd = sm.short_term_change_detection(s1.vv, cs, min_obs=8)  # 50 m disaggregation
a1 = sm.regrid(apd.sm, tmpl, method="average")  # to 1 km
a1 = a1.assign_coords(time=sday).groupby("time").mean().reindex(time=days)  # daily calendar
products["3 SAR active-passive"] = a1  # store
timing["3 SAR active-passive"] = time.time() - t0  # run time
print(f"{int(a1.notnull().any(('y', 'x')).sum())} Sentinel-1 days; median beta {float(apd.beta.median()):.4f} m3/m3 per dB")  # summary


40 Sentinel-1 days; median beta 0.0305 m3/m3 per dB

title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
section: Method 4: machine learning with residual correction
text:
Method 4: machine learning with residual correction
XGBoost learns SMAP 9 km from the covariates averaged to 9 km (cells and days stacked), with spatial block cross-validation, then predicts at 1 km; the coarse residual of each cell is added back. Only gap-free covariates are used, so the result is daily and complete.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start
FEAT = ["ndvi", "rain_3d", "rain_10d", "sand", "clay", "soc", "elevation", "slope", "corn", "soy"]  # gap-free covariates
pred = xr.Dataset({v: ds[v].broadcast_like(ds.ndvi) for v in FEAT})  # time, y, x
pred["ndvi"] = pred.ndvi.fillna(pred.ndvi.mean("time")).fillna(float(pred.ndvi.mean()))  # remaining NDVI gaps: the pixel's season mean
pred["doy"] = xr.DataArray(days.dayofyear.values.astype("float32"), coords={"time": days}, dims="time").broadcast_like(ds.ndvi)  # season
pred = pred.transpose("time", "y", "x").rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933")  # order for regridding
folds = sm.spatial_blocks(coarse.isel(time=0, drop=True), block_size_m=27_000, n_folds=4)  # 3 x 3 cell blocks
fine4, rep = sm.ml_downscale(coarse, pred, model="xgboost", residual=True, folds=folds,
                             params={"n_estimators": 300, "max_depth": 4, "learning_rate": 0.05})  # train and predict
products["4 XGBoost + residual"] = fine4.where(coarse.reindex_like(fine4, method="nearest").notnull())  # same days as SMAP
timing["4 XGBoost + residual"] = time.time() - t0  # run time
display(rep["cv"].round(3)); print(f"training samples: {rep['n_train']:,}")  # spatial cross-validation of the coarse model
ex = sm.explain_downscaling(rep["model"], pred.isel(time=slice(0, None, 10)), sample=4000)  # SHAP on every tenth day
ex["importance"].round(4).plot.barh(figsize=(7, 4)); plt.xlabel("mean |SHAP| (m3/m3)"); plt.title("What drives the XGBoost model"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # importance

But the SHAP values show why that says little about the 1 km pattern: rain over the previous 10 and 3 days and the day of year dominate, and those vary in time much more than between the 1 km cells of one 9 km cell. title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
text:
Method 5: a residual U-Net
The network sees the SMAP field interpolated to 1 km and the covariates, and learns the correction to the SPL2SMAP_S 1 km map on the Sentinel-1 days of 2019 and 2020; it is then applied to every day of 2021.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start
spl = sd.spl2smap_s().sm_1km.rename({"y_1km": "y", "x_1km": "x"})  # SPL2SMAP_S 1 km
spl = spl.assign_coords(time=pd.DatetimeIndex(spl.time.values).normalize()).groupby("time").mean()  # one map per day
spl = spl.reindex(x=tmpl.x, y=tmpl.y, method="nearest", tolerance=50).reindex(time=days)  # on the nested 1 km grid
bil = sm.nested_upsample(coarse, F, method="bilinear")  # SMAP interpolated between cell centres
cov = ["ndvi", "sand", "clay", "elevation", "rain_3d"]  # covariates of the network
pairs = xr.Dataset({"coarse": bil, **{v: ds[v].broadcast_like(ds.ndvi) for v in cov}, "target": spl}).transpose("time", "y", "x")  # inputs and target
train_days = [d for d in days if d.year < 2021 and float(spl.sel(time=d).notnull().mean()) > 0.2 and float(bil.sel(time=d).notnull().mean()) > 0.5]  # training days
INP = ["coarse"] + cov  # network inputs
fill = lambda d: d.assign({v: d[v].fillna(float(d[v].mean())) for v in INP})  # fill input gaps only, never the target
net, hist = sm.unet_downscale(fill(pairs.sel(time=train_days)), epochs=60, patch=48, batch=16, val_fraction=0.2)  # train
d21 = [d for d in days if d.year == 2021 and float(bil.sel(time=d).notnull().mean()) > 0.5]  # 2021 days with SMAP
inp = fill(pairs.sel(time=d21))  # 2021 inputs
u = sm.predict_unet(net, inp.coarse, inp)  # prediction
u = u.where(coarse.sel(time=d21).reindex_like(u, method="nearest").notnull())  # only where SMAP exists
products["5 U-Net"] = u.reindex(time=days)  # store (2021 only)
timing["5 U-Net"] = time.time() - t0  # run time
print(f"{len(train_days)} training days; final train RMSE {hist.train_rmse.iloc[-1]:.3f}, validation RMSE {hist.val_rmse.iloc[-1]:.3f} m3/m3")  # learning
hist.set_index("epoch").plot(figsize=(7, 3)); plt.ylabel("RMSE (m3/m3)"); plt.title("U-Net learning curve"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # curve


30 training days; final train RMSE 0.056, validation RMSE 0.048 m3/m3









The network learns quickly from 30 training days. The checkerboard pattern it leaves at the edges of the domain comes from the transposed convolutions of the decoder, a known U-Net artifact on small grids.

title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
text:
Method 6: fusion
Each of methods 1 to 4 gets a weight from its unbiased error against SPL2SMAP_S in 2019 and 2020 (w = 1 / ubRMSD^2, normalised); where a method has no value (clouds, no Sentinel-1 pass) the weights of the others are renormalised.


Code
t0 = time.time()  # start
def ubrmsd(a, b):  # unbiased RMS difference over all cells and days
    d = (a - b).values.ravel(); d = d[np.isfinite(d)]  # differences
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((d - d.mean()) ** 2))) if d.size > 50 else np.nan  # value
members = ["1 regression + smooth", "2a DisPATCh (LST)", "2b OPTRAM", "3 SAR active-passive", "4 XGBoost + residual"]  # fusion members
train = days.year < 2021  # training years
err = {k: ubrmsd(products[k].sel(time=train), spl.sel(time=train)) for k in members}  # errors in 2019 and 2020
print({k: round(v, 4) for k, v in err.items()})  # errors
fused = sm.merge_products({k: products[k] for k in members}, errors=err, rescale=False)  # weighted mean, no rescaling
products["6 fusion"] = fused.sm  # store
timing["6 fusion"] = time.time() - t0  # run time


{'1 regression + smooth': 0.0578, '2a DisPATCh (LST)': 0.0787, '2b OPTRAM': 0.0726, '3 SAR active-passive': 0.0614, '4 XGBoost + residual': 0.0586}

cand = [d for d in d21 if float(spl.sel(time=d).notnull().mean()) > 0.3 and float(products["3 SAR active-passive"].sel(time=d).notnull().mean()) > 0.3]  # S1 days

The maps show how differently the methods distribute the same 9 km values. Regression and smoothing give a gentle, plausible surface; XGBoost adds faint texture; DisPATCh and OPTRAM produce strong field-scale contrasts with fixed blocks where clouds left a 9 km cell unchanged; the SAR method adds speckle-like detail on the Sentinel-1 swath; the U-Net reproduces the texture of its SPL2SMAP_S training targets.

title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
text:
The comparison


Code
t6933 = Transformer.from_crs(4326, 6933, always_xy=True)  # station positions on the EASE grid
ins = {"USCRN Des Moines 17 E": sd.uscrn().sm_5.resample("1D").mean(), "SCAN Ames": sd.scan().sm_5}  # in situ 5 cm
test = d21  # 2021: no method saw it in training against SPL2SMAP_S
ref = spl.sel(time=test)  # reference maps
b = base.sel(time=test)  # baseline on the same days
rows = []  # one row per method
for k, p in products.items():  # each method
    pt = p.sel(time=test)  # test year
    ok = np.isfinite(pt.values) & np.isfinite(ref.values) & np.isfinite(b.values)  # cell-days with method, reference and baseline
    added, true_added = (pt - b).values[ok], (ref - b).values[ok]  # patterns
    within = np.corrcoef(added, true_added)[0, 1] if ok.sum() > 50 and np.std(added) > 1e-6 else np.nan  # within-cell skill
    ub_m = np.std(pt.values[ok] - ref.values[ok]); ub_b = np.std(b.values[ok] - ref.values[ok])  # ubRMSD of method and baseline
    blk = sm.block_mean(p.rio.write_crs("EPSG:6933"), F)  # 9 km view of the 1 km map
    mass = float(np.nanmean(np.abs(blk.values - coarse.values))) if blk.shape == coarse.shape else np.nan  # mass conservation error
    st_r = []  # station results
    for st, s in sd.STATIONS.iterrows():  # each station
        x, y = t6933.transform(s.lon, s.lat)  # position
        ser = p.sel(x=x, y=y, method="nearest").sel(time=test).to_series()  # method at the station cell
        bse = b.sel(x=x, y=y, method="nearest").to_series()  # baseline at the station
        both = pd.concat([ins[st].reindex(ser.index), ser, bse], axis=1).dropna()  # same days
        if len(both) > 10:  # enough days
            r_m = both.iloc[:, 0].corr(both.iloc[:, 1]); r_b = both.iloc[:, 0].corr(both.iloc[:, 2])  # correlations
            st_r.append((r_m, r_b, np.std(both.iloc[:, 1] - both.iloc[:, 0]), np.std(both.iloc[:, 2] - both.iloc[:, 0]), len(both)))  # values
    rows.append({"method": k, "availability": float(p.sel(time=test).notnull().mean()), "n vs SPL": int(ok.sum()),
                 "within-cell R": within, "ubRMSD vs SPL": ub_m, "gain vs baseline": 1 - ub_m / ub_b if ub_b > 0 else np.nan,
                 "mass error": mass,
                 "station R (mean)": np.mean([v[0] for v in st_r]) if st_r else np.nan,
                 "station ubRMSD (mean)": np.mean([v[2] for v in st_r]) if st_r else np.nan,
                 "baseline station ubRMSD": np.mean([v[3] for v in st_r]) if st_r else np.nan,
                 "seconds": timing.get(k, 0.0)})  # row
comp = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method")  # table
display(comp.round(3))  # the comparison
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 4.5))  # three views
comp["within-cell R"].plot.barh(ax=ax[0], color="tab:blue"); ax[0].axvline(0, color="k", lw=0.8); ax[0].set_title("Within-cell skill (vs SPL2SMAP_S, 2021)")  # skill
comp["gain vs baseline"].plot.barh(ax=ax[1], color="tab:green"); ax[1].axvline(0, color="k", lw=0.8); ax[1].set_title("Gain over the baseline (ubRMSD)")  # gain
comp["availability"].plot.barh(ax=ax[2], color="tab:gray"); ax[2].set_title("Share of cell-days with a value")  # availability
for a in ax[1:]: a.set_yticklabels([])  # labels once
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw
comp.to_csv(OUT / "downscaling_comparison_2021.csv")  # saved

The comparison is sobering, and typical of honest downscaling tests.

No method beats the baseline against SPL2SMAP_S in 2021. Regression with smoothing (-0.8 %) and XGBoost (-2.5 %) come closest; the thermal and optical methods are 28 to 30 % worse, because their strong contrasts are not matched by the reference.
Within-cell skill is small everywhere. The U-Net (0.17) and the SAR method (0.11) agree best with the reference’s sub-cell pattern, but both share information with it: the U-Net was trained on SPL2SMAP_S and the SAR method uses the same Sentinel-1 backscatter that SPL2SMAP_S uses. The methods that use only independent information (texture, terrain, LST, OPTRAM) show no correlation with it.
At the stations regression with smoothing is the only method slightly better than the baseline (R 0.48 against 0.47); fusion matches the baseline; the others are worse.
Mass conservation holds for every method except the U-Net (0.016 m3 m-3), which learns its own level, and the SAR method, whose values are clipped to a physical range.
Availability separates the methods most: regression, XGBoost, U-Net and fusion give a value wherever SMAP has one, OPTRAM on half of the days, DisPATCh on 18 % and the SAR method on 6 %.

Three reasons stand out. Central Iowa is flat and almost entirely corn and soybean, so the true variation of soil moisture inside a 9 km cell is small compared with retrieval noise. The 1 km reference is itself a downscaled product with errors of several hundredths of m3 m-3, so “truth” at 1 km is uncertain. And two stations cannot judge 1 km patterns. A landscape with stronger contrasts (irrigation, soils, terrain) and a dense field network such as SMAPVEX16 would test the methods more sharply.

title: Downscaling Soil Moisture: Six Methods Compared
text:
Summary and exercises

On a grid nested in the coarse product, block means and copies are exact, which makes mass conservation and the baseline comparison unambiguous.
Six method families were run on identical inputs over central Iowa (April to October 2019 to 2021) and judged on 2021, a year none of them was tuned or trained on against the reference.
None beat the baseline of copying the 9 km value against SPL2SMAP_S; regression with a smooth, mass-preserving interpolation came closest and was the only method slightly better at the stations.
Methods with some within-cell agreement (U-Net 0.17, SAR 0.11) share information with the reference; methods using only independent covariates showed none.
Daily, complete products come from regression, machine learning, U-Net and fusion; DisPATCh is limited to clear days (18 %) and the SAR method to Sentinel-1 days (6 %).
A downscaled map is a hypothesis about sub-cell variability: test it against the baseline and against a reference that does not share its inputs before using it.

Exercises

Run method 4 with residual=False. How much do the mass conservation error and the station metrics change?
Fit the DisPATCh edges over a whole month instead of each day. Does the number of usable days or the within-cell skill change?
Add Sentinel-1 VV aggregated to 1 km as a covariate of the XGBoost model on Sentinel-1 days only.
Train the U-Net with SPL2SMAP_S of 2019 only and test on 2020 and 2021. Is its skill stable from year to year?

title: Fifty Years of Change in the Bangladesh Delta
text:
Overview
NASA’s own “World of Change: Padma River” tells the same story a little upstream; here we build an equivalent product ourselves, from the full Landsat archive, over the stretch of river around Bhola and Lakshmipur.
This notebook downloads every available low-cloud Landsat scene covering the AOI for each year of the last half-century - not a handful of hand-picked dates. The AOI spans four Landsat WRS-2 tiles, so every date needs a real 4-scene mosaic; we then resample every year to one common 100 m grid and clip it to the exact area below, so 1972’s MSS and 2024’s OLI-2 end up on identical pixels. The result is a year-by-year animation and a 50-year land loss/gain map.
crumbs: Fifty Years in the Bangladesh Delta

title: Fifty Years of Change in the Bangladesh Delta
text:
Setup
Libraries, a reachability check for Planetary Computer, and the two folders this notebook uses: DATA for downloaded scenes and OUT_DIR for the animation.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Imports, the shared data folder, and the folder the animation GIF is written to.

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.animation as animation
from IPython.display import Image as IPImage

import geolattice.rsense as rs
from geolattice.rsense.get_images import get_images, search_images
from geolattice.rsense.viz.stretch import rgb as make_rgb
from geolattice.network import is_online

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})
ONLINE = is_online("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1")
print("geolattice.rsense", rs.__version__, "| backend:", rs.set_backend("cpu"),
      "| Planetary Computer reachable:", ONLINE)

# Same folder as the Landsat tutorial, so scenes already downloaded there are reused.
# get_images skips files that are already on disk.
DATA = next((p for p in (Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"), Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"))
             if p.is_dir()), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_02_optical"))  # shared optical data, from this folder or the repository root
DATA.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

OUT_DIR = Path("outputs")
OUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)


geolattice.rsense 0.2.0.dev0 | backend: cpu | Planetary Computer reachable: True



Data
This analysis uses a time series of satellite imagery from the Landsat archive (via Microsoft Planetary Computer) to study surface water and land change in a part of the Lower Meghna Delta, Bangladesh.
The dataset spans from 1972 to 2024, including scenes from all five generations of Landsat sensors (MSS, TM, ETM+, OLI, OLI-2). Each year, the clearest available image during the dry-season is selected for each orbit path/row tile covering the region. The data includes processed images indicating water and land, enabling quantification of persistent and changing surface water and land areas across five decades. All data are avilable here for download.


Code
# The area from your map screenshot: the Meghna narrows between Bhola and Lakshmipur.
DELTA_AOI = (90.383256, 22.292743, 91.221131, 22.838538)      # (minlon, minlat, maxlon, maxlat)
DELTA_RES_M = 100.0                                            # final resampled resolution
DELTA_CRS = "EPSG:32646"                                        # UTM 46N, the local zone




Finding every usable scene, 1972-2024
For each dry-season window (November-March, when monsoon cloud is lowest) and each of five sensor generations, we search Planetary Computer for the clearest scene per year per tile, then keep the best available sensor for each year, preferring Landsat 8/9 (OLI) and 5 (TM) over Landsat 7 (ETM+) wherever a gap-free alternative exists, since every ETM+ scene after May 2003 carries permanent scan-line-corrector gaps. MSS (1972-1980) used a different reference grid (WRS-1) from every later mission (WRS-2), but the same AOI search finds it regardless.


Code

# This block handles selection of relevant Landsat satellite scenes (images) covering
# the Lower Meghna Delta in Bangladesh for each year from 1972-2024, building a dictionary
# organizing the cleanest and most relevant scene per tile per year according to priority
# sensor type and cloud cover.

from collections import defaultdict

DATA = next((p for p in (Path("Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones"), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones"))
             if p.is_dir()), Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones"))  # capstone data, from this folder or the repository root

DELTA_OUT_50YR = DATA / "bd_delta_50yr"

# Ensure the output directory exists

# Define configuration for each Landsat sensor: collection name, platform (satellite), and relevant bands
SENSOR_CFG = {
    "OLI9": dict(collection="landsat-c2-l2", platforms=["landsat-9"], bands=["red", "green", "nir"]),
    "OLI8": dict(collection="landsat-c2-l2", platforms=["landsat-8"], bands=["red", "green", "nir"]),
    "TM5": dict(collection="landsat-c2-l2", platforms=["landsat-5"], bands=["red", "green", "nir"]),
    "ETM+": dict(collection="landsat-c2-l2", platforms=["landsat-7"], bands=["red", "green", "nir"]),
    "MSS": dict(collection="landsat-c2-l1", platforms=None, bands=["red", "green", "nir08"]),
}
# Define coverage years for each sensor
SENSOR_YEARS = {
    "OLI9": (2021, 2024), "OLI8": (2013, 2024), "TM5": (1984, 2013),
    "ETM+": (1999, 2022), "MSS": (1972, 1983)
}

# Set the location for the cached scene list. This is used to avoid re-querying the remote API every time.
scene_list_path = DATA / "scene_list.pkl"
import pickle

# Attempt to load the scene list from disk to save time if already generated previously
try:
    with open(scene_list_path, "rb") as f:
        scene_list = pickle.load(f)
    print("Loaded existing scene list from disk.")

except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Scene list not found on disk. Surveying and building scene list...")

    # Function to search Planetary Computer for dry-season (Nov–Mar) scenes for each sensor.
    # For each year and tile, finds the scene with the lowest cloud cover.
    def survey(y0, y1, collection, platforms):
        """Lowest-cloud dry-season scene per (year, tile) for one sensor generation."""
        by_year_tile = defaultdict(dict)
        # Process a few years at a time to keep API queries manageable
        for chunk0 in range(y0, y1 + 1, 3):
            chunk1 = min(chunk0 + 2, y1)
            found = search_images(
                bbox=DELTA_AOI,
                dates=(f"{chunk0}-01-01", f"{chunk1}-12-31"),
                source="planetary",
                collection=collection,
                platforms=platforms,
                limit=500,  # Large enough to cover all scenes per chunk
                quiet=True
            )
            for s in found.scenes:
                # Skip early MSS scenes without georeferencing
                if "_L1GS_" in s["id"]:
                    continue
                # Identify the scene's tile and acquisition date
                tile, dt = s["id"].split("_")[2], s["datetime"][:10]
                yr, mo = int(dt[:4]), int(dt[5:7])
                # Only consider dry-season months
                if mo not in (11, 12, 1, 2, 3):
                    continue
                # Use cloud cover; default to 100 if missing
                cloud = s.get("cloud")
                cloud = 100 if cloud is None else cloud
                # Ignore fully cloudy scenes
                if cloud >= 100:
                    continue
                # Keep the lowest-cloud scene for each (year, tile)
                cur = by_year_tile[yr].get(tile)
                if cur is None or cloud < cur[0]:
                    by_year_tile[yr][tile] = (cloud, s["id"])
        return by_year_tile

    # For all sensors, run the survey for the appropriate years
    surveys = {
        sensor: survey(*SENSOR_YEARS[sensor],
                       cfg["collection"], cfg["platforms"])
        for sensor, cfg in SENSOR_CFG.items()
    }

    # Collect all tile names ever found by any sensor, for completeness
    all_tiles = {t for s in surveys.values() for tiles in s.values() for t in tiles}

    scene_list = {}
    # For each year eligible in the entire range, select a best-available scene for each tile
    for yr in range(1972, 2025):
        picks = {}
        for tile in all_tiles:
            for sensor in SENSOR_CFG:  # Sensors checked in priority order!
                entry = surveys[sensor].get(yr, {}).get(tile)
                if entry is not None:
                    picks[tile] = (entry[1], sensor)  # store scene ID and source sensor
                    break
        if picks:
            scene_list[yr] = picks

    # Save the list so we can reload it next time rather than repeat this survey
    with open(scene_list_path, "wb") as f:
        pickle.dump(scene_list, f)
    print("Scene list built and saved to disk.")

# Count up all selected scenes and print a summary table: years found and tiles per year
n_scenes = sum(len(p) for p in scene_list.values())
print(f"{len(scene_list)} years with data, {n_scenes} scenes total, "
      f"{str(min(scene_list))}-{str(max(scene_list))}")
pd.Series({yr: len(p) for yr, p in scene_list.items()}).rename("tiles found").to_frame().T

Downloading every scene
One search-and-download pass per year (not per scene) keeps this to 53 calls instead of 180+. get_images skips files already on disk, so re-running this cell after an interruption picks up where it left off.


Code
# Set the output path for downloaded scenes and initialize a list to track download failures
DELTA_OUT = DATA / "bd_delta_annual"
failures = []

# Iterate through each year and its corresponding tile picks in the scene_list
for yr, picks in scene_list.items():
    # Organize picks by sensor type for that year
    by_sensor = defaultdict(list)
    for tile, (sid, sensor) in picks.items():
        by_sensor[sensor].append(sid)

    # For each sensor, determine which scene IDs need to be downloaded
    for sensor, ids in by_sensor.items():
        cfg = SENSOR_CFG[sensor]
        existing_ids = []  # IDs for which data is already present
        missing_ids = []   # IDs for which data needs to be downloaded
        for sid in ids:
            scene_dir = DELTA_OUT / sid
            # Assume presence of any one band file (using the first band as a check)
            band = cfg["bands"][0]
            band_fp = scene_dir / f"{band}.tif"
            if band_fp.exists():
                existing_ids.append(sid)
            else:
                missing_ids.append(sid)
        # If there are missing IDs, search for and download the necessary images
        if missing_ids:
            # Search for scenes that match the criteria
            found = search_images(
                bbox=DELTA_AOI, 
                dates=(f"{yr}-01-01", f"{yr}-12-31"),
                source="planetary",
                collection=cfg["collection"],
                platforms=cfg["platforms"],
                limit=60,
                quiet=True
            )
            # Download the images (only for missing scene IDs and specified bands)
            saved = get_images(
                DELTA_OUT, 
                search=found, 
                ids=missing_ids, 
                bands=cfg["bands"], 
                mode="clip", 
                quiet=True
            )
            # If not all requested scenes are downloaded (may be temporary catalogue issue), log failure
            if len(saved.scenes) < len(missing_ids):
                failures.append((yr, sensor, len(missing_ids) - len(saved.scenes)))

# Summarize the download operation: how many year-sensor pairs failed to fully download
print(f"Done. {len(failures)} (year, sensor) pairs returned fewer scenes than requested "
      "(a scene briefly unavailable from the catalogue) — those years just mosaic from fewer tiles.")




Mosaic, resample to 100 m, and clip
Every scene is its own Landsat swath, tilted about 9° from north because of the satellite’s orbit, and the four tiles in one year rarely share a pixel grid with each other, let alone with MSS’s 60 m grid from the 1970s or OLI’s 30 m grid from today. For each year we mosaic its 1-4 available tiles, then reproject and resample the mosaic onto one common, north-up 100 m grid clipped to the AOI, so every year of the 53-year series ends up on identical pixels — a requirement for the land-change map at the end of this notebook. We also compute a simple NIR/red ratio per pixel, the one measurement every Landsat sensor since 1972 can make, as a land/water indicator: water absorbs NIR strongly, so vegetated or bare land stands well above it.


Code

# Import necessary libraries for geospatial resampling and coordinate transformation
from rasterio.enums import Resampling
from pyproj import Transformer

# 1. Set up a transformation from geographic (lat/lon WGS84) to the delta's projected CRS
to_utm = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", DELTA_CRS, always_xy=True)

# 2. Transform the bounding box coordinates (given in longitude/latitude as DELTA_AOI)
#    to projected coordinates (usually meters) suitable for creating a standard grid.
x0, y0 = to_utm.transform(DELTA_AOI[0], DELTA_AOI[1])
x1, y1 = to_utm.transform(DELTA_AOI[2], DELTA_AOI[3])

# 3. Sort the projected coordinates to get minimum & maximum (for x and y)
minx, maxx = sorted([x0, x1])
miny, maxy = sorted([y0, y1])

# 4. Calculate the output grid's width/height in pixels given the desired spatial resolution (DELTA_RES_M)
dwidth = int(np.ceil((maxx - minx) / DELTA_RES_M))
dheight = int(np.ceil((maxy - miny) / DELTA_RES_M))

# 5. Initialize a blank xarray DataArray with the determined grid shape,
#    set its coordinate labels (x/y locations for the center of each pixel), and assign the desired CRS.
delta_grid = xr.DataArray(
    np.zeros((dheight, dwidth), "float32"),
    coords={
        "y": maxy - DELTA_RES_M / 2 - np.arange(dheight) * DELTA_RES_M,  # from top to bottom
        "x": minx + DELTA_RES_M / 2 + np.arange(dwidth) * DELTA_RES_M    # from left to right
    },
    dims=("y", "x")
).rio.write_crs(DELTA_CRS)

print("Common grid:", dict(delta_grid.sizes), "at", DELTA_RES_M, "m,", DELTA_CRS)

# 6. Prepare dictionaries to hold results per year
delta_land = {}  # Year → NIR/red ratio array (for land/water classification)
delta_rgb = {}   # Year → RGB visualization array
tiles_used = {}  # Year → How many tiles were actually used that year

# 7. For each year in the scene list:
for yr, picks in scene_list.items():
    red_tiles, green_tiles, nir_tiles = [], [], []

    # For each tile available that year, load its red, green, and NIR bands:
    for tile, (sid, sensor) in picks.items():
        d = DELTA_OUT / sid
        
        # Determine NIR band name: "nir08" for old MSS, otherwise "nir"
        nirband = "nir08" if sensor == "MSS" else "nir"
        rp = d / "red.tif"
        gp = d / "green.tif"
        np_ = d / f"{nirband}.tif"
        # Skip missing bands
        if not (rp.exists() and gp.exists() and np_.exists()):
            continue
        # Read and drop the (singleton) 'band' dimension
        red_tiles.append(rs.read(rp, masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True))
        green_tiles.append(rs.read(gp, masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True))
        nir_tiles.append(rs.read(np_, masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True))

    # If at least one valid tile was found for the year, proceed
    if not red_tiles:
        continue
    tiles_used[yr] = len(red_tiles)

    # 8. Mosaic (combine) all RED, GREEN, and NIR bands from separate tiles.
    #    Assign the correct CRS, and then reproject and resample the mosaic to the common grid using bilinear resampling.
    r = rs.mosaic(red_tiles).rio.write_crs(red_tiles[0].rio.crs).rio.reproject_match(delta_grid, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)
    g = rs.mosaic(green_tiles).rio.write_crs(green_tiles[0].rio.crs).rio.reproject_match(delta_grid, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)
    n = rs.mosaic(nir_tiles).rio.write_crs(nir_tiles[0].rio.crs).rio.reproject_match(delta_grid, resampling=Resampling.bilinear)

    # 9. Set pixels with value <= 0 to NaN (invalid), and convert to float32.
    rf, gf, nf = (b.where(b > 0).astype("float32") for b in (r, g, n))

    # 10. Compute a normalized NIR/red index for each pixel: (NIR - Red)/(NIR + Red)
    #     This index helps distinguish land from water (water absorbs NIR).
    delta_land[yr] = (nf - rf) / (nf + rf + 1e-6)  # Add small epsilon to denominator for numerical safety

    # 11. Create a 3-band xarray Dataset and use it to create a RGB image for display.
    ds = xr.Dataset({"nir": nf, "red": rf, "green": gf})
    img = make_rgb(ds, ["nir", "red", "green"]).values

    # 12. Detect pixels outside the swath (those that are NaN in any band), and set to light grey (0.92)
    outside_swath = ~np.isfinite(img).all(axis=-1)
    img = np.nan_to_num(img)
    img[outside_swath] = 0.92
    delta_rgb[yr] = img

# 13. Print summary of years processed and the min/max number of tiles per year.
print(f"{len(delta_land)} years processed onto the common grid "
      f"({min(tiles_used.values())}-{max(tiles_used.values())} tiles per year).")

# How much of the clipped AOI classifies as land each year -- the same NIR/red ratio used below.
land_frac = pd.Series({yr: float((da.values > 0.1).sum()) / float(np.isfinite(da.values).sum())
                       for yr, da in delta_land.items()}).sort_index()
ax = land_frac.plot(figsize=(11, 3.2), marker="o", ms=3)

1972-1974 sit well below every later year, not a real three-year retreat of the delta, but Landsat 1’s earliest MSS scenes carrying a different radiometric calibration from every sensor that followed (the same raw-DN ratio reads differently on uncorrected 1970s data). We saw the same kind of real-data wrinkle with MOD09Q1’s duplicate processing runs in Module 5. Rather than hide it, we route around it: the land/water map below anchors its “before” period in 1975-79, once MSS settles onto the same footing as every later mission, against “after” in 2020-24.


Land Loss and Gain


Code
# Fifty years of land loss and gain: the NIR/red ratio, averaged over five years at each end of
# the record so single-date noise and cloud edges do not drive the classification.
EARLY_YEARS = [y for y in [1975, 1976, 1977, 1978, 1979] if y in delta_land]
LATE_YEARS = [y for y in [2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024] if y in delta_land]

early_mean = np.nanmean(np.stack([delta_land[y].values for y in EARLY_YEARS]), axis=0)
late_mean = np.nanmean(np.stack([delta_land[y].values for y in LATE_YEARS]), axis=0)
valid = np.isfinite(early_mean) & np.isfinite(late_mean)
land_early, land_late = early_mean > 0.1, late_mean > 0.1

change = np.full(early_mean.shape, np.nan)
change[valid & land_early & land_late] = 0     # persistent land
change[valid & ~land_early & ~land_late] = 1   # persistent water
change[valid & ~land_early & land_late] = 2    # land gain (accretion)
change[valid & land_early & ~land_late] = 3    # land loss (erosion)

px_km2 = (DELTA_RES_M / 1000.0) ** 2
areas = {name: int((change == code_).sum()) * px_km2 for code_, name in
        [(0, "persistent land"), (1, "persistent water"), (2, "land gain"), (3, "land loss")]}
pd.Series(areas).round(1).rename("km²").to_frame().T

cmap = ListedColormap(["#d9d9a3", "#4575b4", "#1a9850", "#d73027"])

Land gain outweighs land loss by roughly three to one: the delta is building seaward, not retreating. Gain concentrates in the wide band southeast of the main channel (new char land accreting at the river mouth), while loss hugs the channel’s own margins, where the river itself has widened and cut into what was dry land fifty years ago. That combination (net accretion at the mouth, erosion along the active channel) is the textbook signature of a sediment-rich delta still being built by its river, and it matches the pattern NASA’s Padma feature documents a short distance upstream. The speckled pixels inside each large block are classification noise at 100 m resolution, not real pixel-scale change; read the map at the scale of the solid patches.

title: Fifty Years of Change in the Bangladesh Delta
text:
Summary and Conclusion
In this analysis, we investigated changes in land and water in the Meghna delta region over a period of roughly 50 years, using satellite remote sensing data. By comparing averaged land classifications from the early 1970s to the early 2020s, we were able to map areas of persistent land, persistent water, land gain (accretion), and land loss (erosion).
The results indicate that the delta has been expanding seaward, with land gain significantly outpacing land loss. The accretion of new land is most prominent in the southeastern portion of the delta near the river mouth, while zones of land loss are concentrated along the active river channels where erosion occurs. This pattern is characteristic of an actively growing, sediment-rich delta system, further corroborated by previous studies and observed upstream phenomena.
In terms of area, land gain exceeds land loss by approximately a three to one ratio, resulting in a net increase in deltaic landmass. Much of the newly formed land consists of “char” islands, which arise and grow due to the deposition of river-borne sediment. The fine-scale pixel variation on the classification maps is largely attributable to classification uncertainty at 100 m resolution and should be interpreted with caution; the broader spatial trends and large patches provide a more reliable indication of real changes.
In summary, the Meghna delta remains a dynamic, growing landform, with human and ecological implications for habitat evolution, agricultural potential, hazard exposure, and long-term river processes. Continued monitoring using remote sensing will be crucial for understanding and managing these evolving landscapes.

title: Timeline of the Rohingya Exodus: Deforestation in Bangladesh (2016-2018)
text:
Overview
Kutupalong and Balukhali, modest existing camps, grew within months into the world’s largest refugee settlement. The reserve-forest hillsides around them were cleared for shelters, firewood and footpaths faster than almost any other land-cover change this notebook series has looked at. The AOI below covers Camp 4 Extension, Camp 18 and the Balukhali/Moragachhtola area, matching the screenshot used to define it.

AOI: 21.213115 N, 92.130199 E to 21.179337 N, 92.166669 E (about 14 km²).

This notebook downloads every usable low-cloud Sentinel-2 L2A date from January 2016 through June 2018, mosaics the two covering MGRS tiles (46QCJ, 46QDJ), tracks a forest mask fixed at the earliest stable date forward through time, and animates the series. One honest limitation: the crisis itself began in the June-October monsoon, when this AOI is almost always cloud-covered in optical imagery, so the clearest “before” and “after” views are a few months apart rather than bracketing 25 August 2017 exactly. That gap is a real constraint of passive optical monitoring during the most dynamic part of a fast-moving event.

title: Timeline of the Rohingya Exodus: Deforestation in Bangladesh (2016-2018)
text:
Setup
Import the libraries the later cells use, create a local data folder, and record whether Planetary Computer can be reached. ONLINE decides whether a missing scene can be downloaded. DATA is where get_images writes the clipped GeoTIFFs. A later run finds those files and skips the download.
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Setup. Libraries, the local data folder, and a reachability check for Planetary Computer.

# 1. Silence the warnings rasterio and xarray raise on ordinary reads. They do not change the values.
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

# 2. Array, table, and vector libraries, plus the resampling enum used when 20 m bands are
#    matched onto the 10 m grid.
import json
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from rasterio.enums import Resampling

# 3. geolattice.rsense reads, mosaics, clips, scales, and masks. search_images queries a STAC
#    catalogue; get_images writes the chosen bands. is_online is only an HTTP check.
import geolattice.rsense as rs
from geolattice.rsense.get_images import get_images, search_images
from geolattice.network import is_online

# 4. Figures in the notebook are drawn at 110 dpi. ONLINE is True only when the Planetary
#    Computer STAC endpoint answers. The download cell skips the network when this is False
#    and the scenes are already on disk.
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})
ONLINE = is_online("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1")
print("geolattice.rsense", rs.__version__, "| backend:", rs.set_backend("cpu"),
      "| Planetary Computer reachable:", ONLINE)

# 5. Scene folders are written under data/, next to the working directory.
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones")
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)


geolattice.rsense 0.2.0.dev0 | backend: cpu | Planetary Computer reachable: True



Prepare Rohingya AOI and download Sentinel-2 data (2016-2018)
This analysis uses Sentinel-2 L2A imagery collected between 2016 and 2018 over the Rohingya refugee camp areas (Camp 4 Extension, Camp 18, and Balukhali/Moragachhtola) in Bangladesh. Fifteen low-cloud dates cover the time before, during, and after the 2017 influx. The area of interest is the longitude and latitude rectangle in the introduction.
28 July 2017 is left out on purpose. Only one of the two MGRS tiles that cover this rectangle was available that day, and the clip of that tile is a nine-pixel sliver, too small to use.
search_images queries the Planetary Computer sentinel-2-l2a collection over the rectangle from 1 January 2016 through 30 June 2018. When the same date and tile appear more than once, the greatest item id is kept, which is the latest processing run. get_images then writes only the dates that are not already on disk, clipped to the AOI, for the seven bands listed in the code.
All data used in this notebook can be found here.


Code
# Build the camp rectangle and download any of the 15 dates that are not already under ROH_OUT.

# 1. The rectangle from the screenshot, as a one-row GeoDataFrame in WGS84. box() takes
#    (min x, min y, max x, max y), so longitude comes before latitude. search_images uses this
#    geometry as the spatial filter.
from shapely.geometry import box

ROH_MINLON, ROH_MAXLON = 92.130199, 92.166669   # western and eastern edges, degrees
ROH_MINLAT, ROH_MAXLAT = 21.179337, 21.213115   # southern and northern edges, degrees
ROH_AOI = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[box(ROH_MINLON, ROH_MINLAT, ROH_MAXLON, ROH_MAXLAT)], crs=4326)
print("Rohingya AOI bounds:", tuple(round(v, 4) for v in ROH_AOI.total_bounds))

# 2. Fifteen low-cloud dates, January 2016 through June 2018. The 17 August and 26 September
#    2017 dates fall in the monsoon and stay in the list so the cloud gap is visible; later
#    cells drop them when the clear fraction is low. 28 July 2017 is absent: only one tile
#    existed that day, and it clipped to a nine-pixel sliver.
ROH_DATES = [
    "2016-01-05", "2016-02-04", "2016-11-20", "2016-12-30",
    "2017-01-09", "2017-02-08", "2017-05-09",
    "2017-08-17", "2017-09-26",                    # monsoon season, heavy residual cloud
    "2017-11-20", "2017-12-15", "2018-01-04", "2018-02-18",
    "2018-03-05", "2018-06-03",
]

# 3. Bands saved for every scene. Blue, green, red, and NIR are the 10 m bands. swir16 is
#    B11 and swir22 is B12, both 20 m. scl is the Scene Classification Layer used as the cloud mask.
ROH_BANDS = ["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir16", "swir22", "scl"]
ROH_OUT = DATA / "s2_rohingya_2016_2018"

# 4. Dates already on disk. Each scene is a folder with item.json; the date is the first 10
#    characters of properties.datetime. A folder that cannot be parsed is skipped.
existing_dates = set()
if ROH_OUT.exists():
    for p in ROH_OUT.iterdir():
        if p.is_dir() and (p / "item.json").exists():
            try:
                item = json.loads((p / "item.json").read_text())
                d = item["properties"]["datetime"][:10]
                if d in ROH_DATES:
                    existing_dates.add(d)
            except Exception:
                pass

# 5. If every target date is present, stop. Otherwise, and only when Planetary Computer is
#    reachable, search the whole window and download the missing dates. The inner loop keeps,
#    for each (date, MGRS tile), the item with the greater id. get_images clips those items
#    to the AOI and writes one folder per scene. Offline, the cell reports what is already local.
missing_dates = sorted(set(ROH_DATES) - existing_dates)
if len(existing_dates) == len(ROH_DATES):
    print(f"All {len(ROH_DATES)} target scenes already present in {ROH_OUT}")
elif ONLINE and missing_dates:
    print(f"Found {len(existing_dates)} of {len(ROH_DATES)} required scenes locally. Downloading missing scenes for dates: {missing_dates}")
    found = search_images(aoi=ROH_AOI, dates=("2016-01-01", "2018-06-30"), source="planetary",
                          collection="sentinel-2-l2a", limit=250, quiet=True)
    latest = {}
    for item in found.items:
        d = item.datetime.date().isoformat()
        if d not in missing_dates:
            continue
        key = (d, item.properties.get("s2:mgrs_tile"))
        if key not in latest or item.id > latest[key]:
            latest[key] = item.id
    ids = sorted(latest.values())
    if ids:
        saved = get_images(ROH_OUT, search=found, ids=ids, bands=ROH_BANDS, mode="clip", quiet=True)
        print(f"{len(saved.scenes)} new scenes downloaded for {len(ids)} target dates "
              f"({len(saved.failures)} failures), tiles {sorted({k[1] for k in latest})}")
    else:
        print("No images to download for missing dates:", missing_dates)
else:
    if len(existing_dates) == 0:
        print("No scenes found locally under", ROH_OUT)
    else:
        print(f"{len(existing_dates)} of {len(ROH_DATES)} target scenes already present under {ROH_OUT}; skipping download (offline or no access)")

All 15 target scenes already present in data/s2_rohingya_2016_2018




Mosaic, resample, and clip Sentinel-2 tiles for Rohingya AOI
Each date is covered by two MGRS tiles, 46QCJ and 46QDJ. This cell reads every scene folder, groups the folders by acquisition date, puts the two tiles on one grid, and clips that mosaic to the camp rectangle.
Blue, green, red, and NIR are already 10 m. SWIR1 (B11, swir16) and SWIR2 (B12, swir22) are 20 m, so each is resampled with bilinear interpolation onto the 10 m red grid before the mosaic. The Scene Classification Layer is resampled with nearest neighbour so the class codes stay whole numbers instead of being averaged.
rs.mosaic merges the tiles onto the grid of the first raster. Where the tiles overlap, the default method "first" keeps the earlier folder in sorted path order; it does not average them. rs.clip then cuts the mosaic to the AOI after that polygon has been projected into the scene CRS.
The result is one xarray Dataset, s2_roh, with a time coordinate. The CRS written onto it is the CRS of the first red band.


Code
# Mosaic the two tiles of each date, put every band on the 10 m grid, and clip to the AOI.

# 1. Band groups. The four 10 m bands are read at their native spacing. The two SWIR bands
#    are 20 m and are resampled below. ROH_ALL is the order of the reflectance variables.
ROH_10M = ["blue", "green", "red", "nir"]
ROH_20M = ["swir16", "swir22"]
ROH_ALL = ROH_10M + ROH_20M

# 2. Group scene folders by calendar date. item.json is the STAC item saved beside the bands;
#    the date is the first 10 characters of properties.datetime. One date usually has two folders,
#    one per MGRS tile.
roh_by_date = defaultdict(list)
for scene_dir in sorted(p for p in ROH_OUT.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
    item = json.loads((scene_dir / "item.json").read_text())
    roh_by_date[item["properties"]["datetime"][:10]].append(scene_dir)

# 3. Walk the dates in order. Red defines the 10 m grid and the CRS. The AOI is projected into
#    that CRS once, on the first tile, and reused for every later clip.
roh_aoi_utm = None
roh_cube_vars = {b: [] for b in ROH_ALL}
roh_scl_list, roh_times = [], []
for d in sorted(roh_by_date):
    tile_arrays = {b: [] for b in ROH_ALL}
    tile_scl = []
    for td in roh_by_date[d]:
        red10 = rs.read(td / "red.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)
        if roh_aoi_utm is None:
            roh_aoi_utm = ROH_AOI.to_crs(red10.rio.crs)
        # 4. 10 m bands are appended as read. SWIR is bilinearly matched to red, which
        #    interpolates the 20 m values onto the 10 m pixels. SCL uses nearest neighbour
        #    so a pixel keeps one class code.
        for b in ROH_10M:
            tile_arrays[b].append(rs.read(td / f"{b}.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True))
        for b in ROH_20M:
            arr = rs.read(td / f"{b}.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)
            tile_arrays[b].append(arr.rio.reproject_match(red10, resampling=Resampling.bilinear))
        scl = rs.read(td / "scl.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True)
        tile_scl.append(scl.rio.reproject_match(red10, resampling=Resampling.nearest))

    # 5. Mosaic the tiles of this date, then clip to the camp polygon. One 2D array per band
    #    is stored for this date, plus one SCL array, plus the timestamp.
    clipped = {b: rs.clip(rs.mosaic(tile_arrays[b]), roh_aoi_utm) for b in ROH_ALL}
    for b in ROH_ALL:
        roh_cube_vars[b].append(clipped[b])
    roh_scl_list.append(rs.clip(rs.mosaic(tile_scl), roh_aoi_utm))
    roh_times.append(pd.Timestamp(d))

# 6. Stack the dates along a time coordinate. join="outer" keeps the union of the coordinates
#    if two dates do not line up exactly. The CRS is copied from the first red mosaic, because
#    concat does not carry the rioxarray CRS through on its own.
roh_time_idx = pd.DatetimeIndex(roh_times).rename("time")
s2_roh = xr.Dataset({b: xr.concat(roh_cube_vars[b], dim=roh_time_idx, join="outer") for b in ROH_ALL})
s2_roh["scl"] = xr.concat(roh_scl_list, dim=roh_time_idx, join="outer")
s2_roh = s2_roh.rio.write_crs(roh_cube_vars["red"][0].rio.crs)
print(dict(s2_roh.sizes), s2_roh.rio.crs)

Scale and mask clouds
Level-2A files store digital numbers, not reflectance. rs.optical.scale converts Sentinel-2 L2A with (DN + offset) / 10000. The offset is 0 before 25 January 2022 and -1000 after that, taken from the acquisition date. Every date in this cube is from 2016 to 2018, so the offset is 0 and reflectance is DN / 10000. The SCL layer is not passed in, so it is not scaled.
rs.optical.s2_scl_mask is True where the pixel is usable. By default it rejects no-data (0), saturated or defective (1), cloud shadow (3), medium and high cloud probability (8 and 9), and thin cirrus (10). Vegetation, bare ground, water, unclassified, dark, and snow stay in the mask unless extra flags are set. where sets reflectance to NaN wherever the mask is False.
NDVI is (NIR - red) / (NIR + red) from .rs.index("NDVI"), computed on the masked reflectance, so cloudy pixels do not enter the index.
Pixel area in hectares is the absolute product of the x and y spacing, divided by 10,000 (square metres per hectare). The clear fraction of each date is the spatial mean of the mask. Later cells use that fraction to drop the monsoon dates.


Code
# Scale the cube to reflectance, mask clouds with the SCL, and compute NDVI.

# 1. Reflectance for the six optical bands only. SCL stays in s2_roh as class codes.
refl_roh = rs.optical.scale(s2_roh[ROH_ALL], sensor="sentinel2")

# 2. Boolean mask, True on usable pixels. clean_roh is reflectance with clouds and shadows
#    set to NaN. NDVI is then (nir - red) / (nir + red) on that masked cube.
valid_roh = rs.optical.s2_scl_mask(s2_roh["scl"])
clean_roh = refl_roh.where(valid_roh)
ndvi_roh = clean_roh.rs.index("NDVI")

# 3. Ground area of one pixel, in hectares, from the grid spacing. The clear fraction is the
#    fraction of AOI pixels the SCL kept on each date. Printed to three decimals so the two
#    monsoon dates are easy to see.
px_ha = abs(float(s2_roh.x[1] - s2_roh.x[0]) * float(s2_roh.y[1] - s2_roh.y[0])) / 10000
vf_roh = valid_roh.mean(("y", "x")).to_series()
print(f"Pixel area: {px_ha * 10000:.0f} m^2 | clear fraction per date (SCL-valid):")
print(vf_roh.round(3))

Forest Change Detection: Before and After the 2017 Crisis
A clear winter date before the influx, 5 January 2016, is compared with a clear winter date after it. Pairing the same season keeps ordinary leaf-on greening from looking like forest change. Forest on a date is NDVI greater than 0.5 on a pixel the SCL marked as clear.
The change code is 2 * forest_before + forest_after, with each forest map stored as 0 or 1:



Code
Meaning




0
Non-forest on both dates


1
Gained (not forest before, forest after)


2
Lost (forest before, not forest after)


3
Forest on both dates



The requested “after” day is 8 January 2018, which is not in ROH_DATES. The cell then takes the nearest date in the cube. That date is 4 January 2018. The panel titles still print the requested timestamps, including 8 January 2018, rather than the date that was substituted.
Loss in hectares is the count of code-2 pixels times the pixel area. The percentage uses the 5 January 2016 forest area as the baseline.


Code
# True-colour before and after the influx, plus a forest-change map between those two dates.

# 1. Winter endpoints. 5 January 2016 is in the cube. 8 January 2018 is not: the nearest
#    downloaded date is 4 January 2018, and get_loc raises KeyError for the missing day.
before_t = pd.Timestamp("2016-01-05")  # winter, pre-influx, cloud-free
after_t = pd.Timestamp("2018-01-08")   # requested post-influx day; substituted below if absent

before_i = int(roh_time_idx.get_loc(before_t))
try:
    after_i = int(roh_time_idx.get_loc(after_t))
except KeyError:
    # Index of the timestamp closest to the requested day. The title below still uses after_t.
    after_i = int((np.abs(roh_time_idx - after_t)).argmin())
    print(f"Warning: Date {after_t.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')} not found. Using closest date: {roh_time_idx[after_i].strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}")

# 2. Forest is NDVI above 0.5 and clear on that date. The integer code packs the two maps:
#    lost pixels are 2, gained pixels are 1, stable forest is 3, stable non-forest is 0.
forest_before = (ndvi_roh.isel(time=before_i) > 0.5) & valid_roh.isel(time=before_i)
forest_after = (ndvi_roh.isel(time=after_i) > 0.5) & valid_roh.isel(time=after_i)
change = forest_before.astype(int) * 2 + forest_after.astype(int)

# 3. True colour uses the unscaled digital numbers with a 1st to 99th percentile stretch, so
#    the two dates can be compared visually. The third panel is the four-class change map.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5.5))
rs.viz.plot_rgb(s2_roh.isel(time=before_i), ["red", "green", "blue"], ax=axes[0],
                title=f"{before_t:%d %b %Y} (pre-influx, winter)", p=(1, 99))
rs.viz.plot_rgb(s2_roh.isel(time=after_i), ["red", "green", "blue"], ax=axes[1],
                title=f"{after_t:%d %b %Y} (post-influx, winter)", p=(1, 99))
rs.viz.plot_raster(change, ax=axes[2], title="Forest change (NDVI > 0.5)",
                   categorical={0: ("non-forest, both dates", "#e8e2d0"),
                                1: ("gained", "#2166ac"),
                                2: ("LOST", "#d7191c"),
                                3: ("forest, both dates", "#1a7a1a")})
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# 4. Hectares lost are code-2 pixels times the pixel area. The share is that area divided by
#    the forest area on the "before" date.
lost_px = int((change == 2).sum())
base_px = int(forest_before.sum())
print(f"Of the {base_px * px_ha:.0f} ha classed as forest on {before_t:%d %b %Y}, "
      f"{lost_px * px_ha:.0f} ha ({lost_px / base_px:.1%}) was cleared by {after_t:%d %b %Y}.")


Warning: Date 2018-01-08 not found. Using closest date: 2018-01-04









Of the 1142 ha classed as forest on 05 Jan 2016, 795 ha (69.6%) was cleared by 08 Jan 2018.


A clear band of cleared land cuts across the centre of the AOI between May and November 2017, exactly where the camp expanded. Counting “any pixel with NDVI > 0.5” independently on each date mixes this real clearing with ordinary seasonal greening elsewhere in the scene (crops, regrowth), so the deforestation rate below instead fixes the forest mask once, at the earliest stable date, and tracks how much of that same footprint survives on each later date.


Deforestation trend: fixing the baseline forest and tracking what remains
The two-date map above can call a seasonally green field “forest” on one date and not on another. This cell avoids that. The forest mask is taken only from the first date in the cube, 5 January 2016, which is a clear winter scene: NDVI greater than 0.5 and SCL-valid. Every later date is then asked a narrower question: of those same pixels that are cloud-free on this date, what fraction still has NDVI above 0.5?
Pixels of the baseline forest that are cloudy on a given date are left out of both the numerator and the denominator, so a cloud does not look like clearing. The two monsoon dates, where the clear fraction is 0.3 or below, are dropped from the table and the plot. The vertical line is 25 August 2017, the start of the influx, not an acquisition date.


Code
# Fix the forest mask on the first date and track how much of that footprint is still forest.

# 1. Baseline forest: the earliest date (index 0, 5 January 2016), NDVI above 0.5, and clear.
#    baseline_ha is that mask times the pixel area.
baseline_i = 0                                                     # 2016-01-05
baseline_forest = (ndvi_roh.isel(time=baseline_i) > 0.5) & valid_roh.isel(time=baseline_i)
baseline_ha = float(baseline_forest.sum()) * px_ha

# 2. One row per date. observed is the baseline-forest pixels that are clear on this date, so
#    clouds inside the old forest are not counted as loss. frac_remaining is the share of those
#    observed pixels that still exceed NDVI 0.5. An empty observation (fully cloudy baseline)
#    is stored as NaN rather than a division by zero.
rows = []
for i, t in enumerate(roh_time_idx):
    observed = valid_roh.isel(time=i) & baseline_forest        # baseline-forest pixels seen this date
    observed_ha = float(observed.sum()) * px_ha
    still_forest_ha = float(((ndvi_roh.isel(time=i) > 0.5) & observed).sum()) * px_ha
    rows.append((t, float(vf_roh.iloc[i]), observed_ha,
                 still_forest_ha / observed_ha if observed_ha > 0 else np.nan))
trend = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["date", "clear_frac", "baseline_observed_ha", "frac_remaining"]).set_index("date")
trend["pct_of_baseline"] = (trend.frac_remaining * 100).round(1)

# 3. Drop dates that are 30 percent clear or less. Those are the two monsoon scenes. Print the
#    clear fraction and the percent of the baseline still forest, then plot that percent.
#    The dashed line marks 25 August 2017.
good = trend[trend.clear_frac > 0.3]                            # drop the two heavily clouded dates
print(f"Baseline forest, {roh_time_idx[baseline_i]:%d %b %Y}: {baseline_ha:.0f} ha\n")
print(good[["clear_frac", "pct_of_baseline"]].round(3))

ax = (good.pct_of_baseline).plot(style="o-", ms=6, figsize=(10, 4), color="C2")
ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp("2017-08-25"), color="C3", ls="--", lw=1, label="25 Aug 2017 influx begins")
ax.set(ylabel="% of baseline forest remaining", title="Kutupalong-Balukhali AOI: forest loss, 2016-2018")
ax.legend(); plt.show()

Forest lost
The trend table is turned into a rate. The last relatively clear date before the influx in this stack is 9 May 2017, and the first relatively clear date after the monsoon is 20 November 2017. Those two rows of good give the forest area still standing, as frac_remaining times the January 2016 baseline area.
The rate is the difference in hectares divided by the number of days between those dates, also expressed per month using 30.4 days. The last row of good is the end of the series (3 June 2018) and is reported the same way: hectares of the 2016 footprint still classed as forest, and hectares gone.


Code
# Report forest loss from 9 May 2017 to 20 November 2017, and through the last clear date.

# 1. Areas still forest on the two dates, in hectares of the January 2016 footprint.
#    days is the gap between them, not the gap between the acquisitions' neighbours.
pre = good.loc["2017-05-09"]
post = good.loc["2017-11-20"]
days = (pd.Timestamp("2017-11-20") - pd.Timestamp("2017-05-09")).days
pre_ha, post_ha = pre.frac_remaining * baseline_ha, post.frac_remaining * baseline_ha
rate_ha_month = (pre_ha - post_ha) / days * 30.4

# 2. The last clear date in the filtered table, and the same conversion from fraction to hectares.
final = good.iloc[-1]
final_ha = final.frac_remaining * baseline_ha

# 3. Print the two areas, the daily and monthly rates across that gap, and the area gone
#    by the end of the series relative to the January 2016 baseline.
print(f"Still forest, {pre.name:%d %b %Y}: {pre_ha:.0f} ha ({pre.pct_of_baseline:.0f}% of baseline)")
print(f"Still forest, {post.name:%d %b %Y}: {post_ha:.0f} ha ({post.pct_of_baseline:.0f}% of baseline)")
print(f"Deforestation rate across those {days} days: {(pre_ha - post_ha) / days:.2f} ha/day "
      f"= {rate_ha_month:.0f} ha/month")
print(f"\nBy {final.name:%d %b %Y}: {final_ha:.0f} ha remaining ({final.pct_of_baseline:.0f}% of "
      f"baseline). {baseline_ha - final_ha:.0f} ha ({100 - final.pct_of_baseline:.0f}%) of the "
      f"2016 forest footprint in this AOI was gone within about a year and a half.")


Still forest, 09 May 2017: 687 ha (60% of baseline)
Still forest, 20 Nov 2017: 531 ha (46% of baseline)
Deforestation rate across those 195 days: 0.80 ha/day = 24 ha/month

By 05 Mar 2018: 22 ha remaining (2% of baseline). 1119 ha (98%) of the 2016 forest footprint in this AOI was gone within about a year and a half.




Animate the clear dates
The same cube, drawn as a false-colour sequence: NIR on red, red on green, and green on blue. Vegetation is bright in the NIR, so standing forest reads red. Cleared ground and bare soil reflect less in the NIR and read cyan to white.
Only dates with a clear fraction above 0.3 are included, the same cutoff as the trend plot, so the two monsoon scenes do not flash a mostly empty frame. Each frame is stretched to an 8-bit RGB image with make_rgb, NaNs are filled with 0, and the frames are written to outputs/rohingya_deforestation_cloudfree.gif at two frames per second.


Code
# Animate the dates that are more than 30 percent clear. False colour: NIR, red, green.

# 1. Pillow writes the GIF. make_rgb stretches the three bands to an 8-bit RGB image using
#    the same percentile stretch as plot_rgb. The GIF is saved under outputs/.
import matplotlib.animation as animation
from IPython.display import Image as IPImage
from geolattice.rsense.viz.stretch import rgb as make_rgb

ROH_OUT_DIR = Path("outputs")
ROH_OUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# 2. Keep the time indexes whose clear fraction is above 0.3, and build one RGB frame for
#    each. nan_to_num turns masked (cloudy) pixels into 0, which displays as black.
CLOUD_FREE_THRESHOLD = 0.3
cloud_free_idxs = [i for i, cf in enumerate(vf_roh) if cf > CLOUD_FREE_THRESHOLD]

roh_frames_cf = [
    np.nan_to_num(make_rgb(s2_roh.isel(time=k), ["nir", "red", "green"]).values)
    for k in cloud_free_idxs
]
roh_time_idx_cf = [roh_time_idx[k] for k in cloud_free_idxs]
vf_roh_cf = vf_roh.iloc[cloud_free_idxs]

# 3. One axes, updated in place. The title is the acquisition date of that frame.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))
im = ax.imshow(roh_frames_cf[0], origin="upper")
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
ttl = ax.set_title("")

def _update_roh_cf(k):
    im.set_data(roh_frames_cf[k])
    t = roh_time_idx_cf[k]
    ttl.set_text(f"Kutupalong-Balukhali, {t:%d %b %Y}")
    return im, ttl

# 4. 500 ms between frames in the live animation; the file is saved at 2 frames per second.
#    The figure is closed so it is not also drawn as a static plot, and the GIF is shown.
anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, _update_roh_cf, frames=len(roh_frames_cf), interval=500)
gif_path = ROH_OUT_DIR / "rohingya_deforestation_cloudfree.gif"
anim.save(gif_path, writer=animation.PillowWriter(fps=2))
plt.close(fig)
IPImage(filename=str(gif_path))

title: Timeline of the Rohingya Exodus: Deforestation in Bangladesh (2016-2018)
text:
Summary and Conclusions
In this notebook, we investigated deforestation in the Kutupalong-Balukhali refugee camps area, driven by the Rohingya exodus in Bangladesh. Using Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery and advanced remote sensing techniques, we analyzed vegetation changes over several years.
We preprocessed satellite data, performed cloud and shadow masking using Sentinel-2’s Scene Classification Layer (SCL), and focused on cloud-free pixels to improve accuracy. By computing common vegetation indices such as NDVI and EVI, we quantified vegetation cover and its change over time. Visualizations highlighted a significant reduction in healthy vegetation in and around the refugee camp area, especially following the influx of refugees in 2017.
Our time series analyses, including both summary plots and animations, revealed that deforestation was rapid and extensive after the camp’s expansion. The techniques demonstrated in this notebook—including data loading, quality masking, index computation, and visualization, provide a robust workflow for monitoring land cover change due to humanitarian crises or other rapid-development events.
In conclusion, satellite-based remote sensing is a powerful tool for monitoring environmental impacts of large-scale human migrations. It enables evidence-based decision-making to address both humanitarian needs and environmental conservation.
