title: Timeline of the Rohingya Exodus: Deforestation in Bangladesh (2016-2018), Sentinel-1 Radar
text:
Overview
The AOI is identical: Camp 4 Extension, Camp 18 and the Balukhali/Moragachhtola area around Kutupalong-Balukhali.

AOI: 21.213115 N, 92.130199 E to 21.179337 N, 92.166669 E (about 14 km²).

The optical notebook could only find two usable scenes inside the June-October 2017 monsoon, so its “before” and “after” views sit a few months either side of 25 August 2017 rather than bracketing it. Radar does not have that problem: cloud is transparent at a 5.6 cm wavelength, so every acquisition on this AOI’s orbit track between January 2016 and June 2018 is usable, including every date inside the monsoon itself. That density is the main reason to reach for Sentinel-1 here, not image quality: a single SAR date is in some ways a worse measurement than a single optical date, because of speckle.
Speckle is grainy, multiplicative noise from coherent radar backscatter; it means two SAR acquisitions of the same unchanged forest can differ noticeably pixel-for-pixel, in a way two Sentinel-2 scenes of the same unchanged field usually would not. That has a real consequence for method: the optical notebook could fix a forest mask from one clear winter date and trust it. Here, a one-date forest mask turns out to wobble by ten or more percentage points from pure speckle and soil-moisture noise (shown directly, below), so this notebook instead builds the baseline from a multi-date composite and leans on a multitemporal speckle filter across the whole stack before classifying anything.
Data source: Microsoft Planetary Computer’s sentinel-1-rtc collection, Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected scenes already radiometrically terrain-corrected to gamma-nought, in linear power units, with no further calibration needed. Both polarizations (VV and VH) are downloaded; VH, which is most sensitive to volume scattering from vegetation canopy, carries most of the forest signal used below. All scenes come from one fixed relative orbit, in descending pass direction, so every date shares the same viewing geometry.

title: Timeline of the Rohingya Exodus: Deforestation in Bangladesh (2016-2018), Sentinel-1 Radar
text:
Setup
Installation. This notebook needs installation option 5 (core, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics and remote sensing): pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]". See “Installation options” in the GeoLattice README.


Code
# Setup. Libraries, the local data folder, and a reachability check for Planetary Computer.

# 1. Silence the warnings rasterio and xarray raise on ordinary reads. They do not change the values.
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)

# 2. Array, table, and vector libraries.
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 3. geolattice.rsense reads, clips, and visualizes rasters. geolattice.rsense.sar holds everything
#    specific to radar: speckle filters, dB conversion, SAR vegetation indices, and two-date
#    change detection. search_images/get_images query and download from Planetary Computer,
#    exactly as in the Sentinel-2 notebook, just with collection="sentinel-1-rtc" this time.
import geolattice.rsense as rs
import geolattice.rsense.sar as sar
from geolattice.rsense.get_images import get_images, search_images
from geolattice.network import is_online

# 4. Figures in the notebook are drawn at 110 dpi. ONLINE is True only when the Planetary
#    Computer STAC endpoint answers. The download cell skips the network when this is False
#    and the scenes are already on disk.
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})
ONLINE = is_online("https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1")
print("geolattice.rsense", rs.__version__, "| backend:", rs.set_backend("cpu"),
      "| Planetary Computer reachable:", ONLINE)

# 5. Scene folders are written under data/, next to the working directory.
DATA = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones")
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)


geolattice.rsense 0.2.0.dev0 | backend: cpu | Planetary Computer reachable: True



Prepare Rohingya AOI and download Sentinel-1 RTC data (2016-2018)
The rectangle is the same longitude/latitude box as the optical notebook. Unlike that notebook, there is no hand-picked list of clear dates to supply: search_images is asked for every sentinel-1-rtc scene over this AOI between 1 January 2016 and 30 June 2018, in Interferometric Wide swath mode, with both VV and VH polarizations.
A single orbit track is then kept. Sentinel-1 revisits the same patch of ground from several different relative orbits, each with a slightly different look angle; mixing them would mean comparing backscatter measured from different viewing geometries, which shows up as spurious “change.” The search below groups the results by sat:relative_orbit and keeps only the descending track with the most coverage of this AOI, relative orbit 77, which turns out to have 46 dates at a roughly 12-day cadence spanning the whole window, including every month of the 2017 monsoon.
get_images then writes the VV and VH bands for whichever of those 46 dates are not already on disk, clipped to the AOI. Each sentinel-1-rtc scene is a single file per band (no cloud mask layer, no multiple tiles to mosaic; see the next section).


Code
# Build the camp rectangle and download any of the 46 descending/orbit-77 dates not already on disk.

# 1. The same rectangle used in the Sentinel-2 notebook, as a one-row GeoDataFrame in WGS84.
from shapely.geometry import box

ROH_MINLON, ROH_MAXLON = 92.130199, 92.166669   # western and eastern edges, degrees
ROH_MINLAT, ROH_MAXLAT = 21.179337, 21.213115   # southern and northern edges, degrees
ROH_AOI = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[box(ROH_MINLON, ROH_MINLAT, ROH_MAXLON, ROH_MAXLAT)], crs=4326)
print("Rohingya AOI bounds:", tuple(round(v, 4) for v in ROH_AOI.total_bounds))

# 2. Bands and output folder. vv and vh are the only bands sentinel-1-rtc offers for a
#    dual-pol IW scene; there is no equivalent of Sentinel-2's SCL cloud mask to request.
S1_BANDS = ["vv", "vh"]
S1_RELATIVE_ORBIT = 77
S1_OUT = DATA / "s1_rohingya_2016_2018"

# 3. Dates already on disk. Each scene is a folder with item.json; the date is the first 10
#    characters of properties.datetime.
existing_dates = set()
if S1_OUT.exists():
    for p in S1_OUT.iterdir():
        if p.is_dir() and (p / "item.json").exists():
            try:
                item = json.loads((p / "item.json").read_text())
                existing_dates.add(item["properties"]["datetime"][:10])
            except Exception:
                pass

# 4. Search once, online, for the full set of candidate scenes: IW mode, VV+VH, descending
#    pass, across the whole window. target_ids maps date -> item id for the kept orbit track,
#    so the target date list itself comes from the catalogue rather than being guessed in advance.
target_ids = {}
if ONLINE:
    found = search_images(aoi=ROH_AOI, dates=("2016-01-01", "2018-06-30"), source="planetary",
                          collection="sentinel-1-rtc", s1_mode="IW", s1_polarization="VV+VH",
                          s1_orbit="descending", limit=500, quiet=True)
    for item in found.items:
        if item.properties.get("sat:relative_orbit") == S1_RELATIVE_ORBIT:
            target_ids[item.datetime.date().isoformat()] = item.id
else:
    found = None

target_dates = sorted(target_ids) if target_ids else sorted(existing_dates)
missing_dates = sorted(set(target_dates) - existing_dates)

# 5. Download whatever is missing. get_images clips each scene to the AOI and writes one
#    folder per scene, same as the Sentinel-2 notebook.
if len(existing_dates) and len(existing_dates) == len(target_dates):
    print(f"All {len(target_dates)} target scenes already present in {S1_OUT}")
elif ONLINE and missing_dates:
    print(f"Found {len(existing_dates)} of {len(target_dates)} required scenes locally. "
          f"Downloading {len(missing_dates)} missing scenes.")
    ids = [target_ids[d] for d in missing_dates]
    saved = get_images(S1_OUT, search=found, ids=ids, bands=S1_BANDS, mode="clip", quiet=True)
    print(f"{len(saved.scenes)} new scenes downloaded ({len(saved.failures)} failures)")
else:
    print(f"{len(existing_dates)} of {len(target_dates)} target scenes present under {S1_OUT}; "
          f"skipping download (offline or nothing missing)")

print(f"Orbit track: descending, relative orbit {S1_RELATIVE_ORBIT}, {len(target_dates)} dates, "
      f"{target_dates[0]} to {target_dates[-1]}")


Rohingya AOI bounds: (np.float64(92.1302), np.float64(21.1793), np.float64(92.1667), np.float64(21.2131))
All 46 target scenes already present in data/s1_rohingya_2016_2018
Orbit track: descending, relative orbit 77, 46 dates, 2016-01-09 to 2018-06-27




Build the Sentinel-1 time cube
The Sentinel-2 notebook’s next step mosaicked two MGRS tiles together and resampled the 20 m SWIR bands onto the 10 m grid. Neither is needed here: this AOI is small enough to fall inside a single sentinel-1-rtc scene on every date, and VV and VH are both already delivered at 10 m, so get_images’s AOI clip is the only spatial processing this cube needs. Building it is just a read-and-stack.


Code
# Read VV and VH for every downloaded date and stack them along a time coordinate.

# 1. Map each scene's acquisition date to its folder, by reading the date out of the
#    STAC item.json saved alongside the clipped bands when they were downloaded above.
s1_by_date = {}
for scene_dir in sorted(p for p in S1_OUT.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
    item = json.loads((scene_dir / "item.json").read_text())
    s1_by_date[item["properties"]["datetime"][:10]] = scene_dir

# 2. Read the VV and VH GeoTIFF for every date, in date order. masked=False keeps nodata
#    as its raw value rather than converting to NaN; squeeze("band", drop=True) removes the
#    single-band dimension each file has so the arrays stack cleanly along time below.
s1_times = sorted(s1_by_date)
vv_list = [rs.read(s1_by_date[d] / "vv.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True) for d in s1_times]
vh_list = [rs.read(s1_by_date[d] / "vh.tif", masked=False).squeeze("band", drop=True) for d in s1_times]

# 3. Concatenate all 46 dates into one time cube per polarization, sharing a time index and
#    the CRS read from the first scene, since every scene shares the same orbit and AOI grid.
s1_time_idx = pd.DatetimeIndex(s1_times).rename("time")
s1_roh = xr.Dataset({
    "vv": xr.concat(vv_list, dim=s1_time_idx),
    "vh": xr.concat(vh_list, dim=s1_time_idx),
}).rio.write_crs(vv_list[0].rio.crs)
print(dict(s1_roh.sizes), s1_roh.rio.crs)


{'x': 382, 'y': 377, 'time': 46} EPSG:32646




Speckle filtering and a SAR vegetation index
Two filters are used for two different purposes.
rs.sar.refined_lee, an edge-preserving adaptive filter, is applied to each date on its own. It is enough to clean up a single scene for a visual before/after comparison, and it is what the two-date change map below uses.
rs.sar.multitemporal_speckle_filter (Quegan and Yu, 2001) is applied once, across the whole 46-date stack, for everything that follows in the trend section. Multitemporal filtering borrows strength across dates rather than only across neighbouring pixels, which removes far more speckle than any single-date filter can, at the cost of mildly smoothing genuinely short-lived change.
From the multitemporal-filtered linear VV and VH, rs.sar.radar_vegetation_index gives the dual-polarization Radar Vegetation Index, RVI = 4*VH / (VV+VH). RVI is the closest SAR analogue to NDVI: higher values mean more cross-polarized volume scattering, which over land is characteristic of a vegetation canopy.
There is no cloud mask to compute here, and no equivalent of the optical notebook’s “clear fraction” column. Radar is unaffected by cloud, so every one of the 46 dates contributes a fully valid scene.


Code
# Per-date refined-Lee filter for the two-date panel, a multitemporal filter and RVI for the trend.

# 1. Single-date edge-preserving filter, used for the before/after VH maps below.
vv_lee = xr.concat([sar.refined_lee(s1_roh["vv"].isel(time=i)) for i in range(s1_roh.sizes["time"])],
                   dim=s1_roh.time)
vh_lee = xr.concat([sar.refined_lee(s1_roh["vh"].isel(time=i)) for i in range(s1_roh.sizes["time"])],
                   dim=s1_roh.time)

# 2. Multitemporal (Quegan & Yu) filter across the full stack, then RVI from the filtered
#    linear backscatter. Used only by the trend section further down.
vv_mt = sar.multitemporal_speckle_filter(s1_roh["vv"], spatial="boxcar", size=7)
vh_mt = sar.multitemporal_speckle_filter(s1_roh["vh"], spatial="boxcar", size=7)
rvi_mt = sar.radar_vegetation_index(vv_mt, vh_mt)

# 3. Ground area of one pixel, in hectares, from the grid spacing (10 m x 10 m = 0.01 ha).
px_ha = abs(float(s1_roh.x[1] - s1_roh.x[0]) * float(s1_roh.y[1] - s1_roh.y[0])) / 10000
print(f"Pixel area: {px_ha * 10000:.0f} m^2 | {s1_roh.sizes['time']} dates, "
      f"{s1_time_idx[0]:%d %b %Y} to {s1_time_idx[-1]:%d %b %Y} | "
      f"every date is 100% radar-valid, no cloud mask needed")


Pixel area: 100 m^2 | 46 dates, 09 Jan 2016 to 27 Jun 2018 | every date is 100% radar-valid, no cloud mask needed




Forest Change Detection: Before and After the 2017 Crisis
The same two dates requested in the Sentinel-2 notebook are used here: a clear winter date before the influx, and 8 January 2018 after it. 9 January 2016 is the closest available date on this orbit track to the optical notebook’s 5 January 2016 baseline; 8 January 2018 is not itself in the archive, so the cell substitutes the nearest available date, 10 January 2018, the same way the optical notebook substituted 4 January 2018 for the same request.
Rather than threshold RVI on each date separately (shown further down to be too speckle-prone for a reliable single-date classification), this comparison uses rs.sar.change_map directly on the two VH scenes. It takes the dB log-ratio between the same pixels on the two dates and finds an Otsu-optimal split into a significant decrease, a significant increase, and no significant change. Differencing the same pixel against itself cancels out a lot of the calibration and terrain effects that a one-date absolute threshold cannot, which is the main reason this is a sturdier two-date comparison than thresholding RVI twice and subtracting.
A VH decrease is the candidate signal for canopy loss: forest returns strong cross-polarized volume scattering, so clearing a stand of trees typically drops VH. An increase can mean new built structures, a change in surface roughness, or a rise in soil moisture; it is not treated as “forest gained.”


Code
# VH before/after in dB, plus the Otsu log-ratio change map between those two dates.

# 1. Winter endpoints. 9 January 2016 is in the cube. 8 January 2018 is not: the nearest
#    downloaded date is 10 January 2018.
before_t = pd.Timestamp("2016-01-09")  # winter, pre-influx
after_t = pd.Timestamp("2018-01-08")   # requested post-influx day; substituted below if absent

before_i = int(s1_time_idx.get_loc(before_t))
try:
    after_i = int(s1_time_idx.get_loc(after_t))
except KeyError:
    after_i = int(np.abs(s1_time_idx - after_t).argmin())
    print(f"Warning: Date {after_t.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')} not found. Using closest date: "
          f"{s1_time_idx[after_i].strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}")

vh_before = vh_lee.isel(time=before_i)
vh_after = vh_lee.isel(time=after_i)
db_before, db_after = sar.to_db(vh_before), sar.to_db(vh_after)

# 2. Otsu log-ratio change map. decrease/increase are boolean DataArrays; the packed integer
#    code mirrors the Sentinel-2 notebook's categorical scheme, but with no "gained forest"
#    class, since a VH increase is not safe to read as new forest.
cm = sar.change_map(vh_before, vh_after)
change_cat = xr.where(cm["decrease"], 2, xr.where(cm["increase"], 1, 0))

# 3. Shared grayscale stretch for the two dB panels, from their combined 2nd-98th percentile.
vmin, vmax = np.percentile(
    np.concatenate([np.asarray(db_before).ravel(), np.asarray(db_after).ravel()]), [2, 98])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5.5))
rs.viz.plot_raster(db_before, ax=axes[0], cmap="gray", vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, colorbar=False,
                   title=f"{before_t:%d %b %Y} (pre-influx) VH, dB")
rs.viz.plot_raster(db_after, ax=axes[1], cmap="gray", vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, colorbar=False,
                   title=f"{after_t:%d %b %Y} (post-influx) VH, dB")
rs.viz.plot_raster(change_cat, ax=axes[2],
                   title=f"VH change, Otsu at {cm.attrs['threshold_db']:.1f} dB",
                   categorical={0: ("no significant change", "#e8e2d0"),
                                1: ("VH increase", "#2166ac"),
                                2: ("VH decrease (candidate loss)", "#d7191c")})
for a in axes: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# 4. Area flagged as a significant VH decrease, in hectares and as a share of the AOI.
dec_px = int(cm["decrease"].values.sum())
total_px = cm["decrease"].size
print(f"VH decrease (candidate vegetation loss): {dec_px * px_ha:.0f} ha "
      f"({dec_px / total_px:.1%} of the {total_px * px_ha:.0f} ha AOI) "
      f"between {before_t:%d %b %Y} and {after_t:%d %b %Y}.")


Warning: Date 2018-01-08 not found. Using closest date: 2018-01-10









VH decrease (candidate vegetation loss): 507 ha (35.2% of the 1440 ha AOI) between 09 Jan 2016 and 08 Jan 2018.


The decrease class (red) sits in a dense cluster across the centre of the AOI, in the same place the optical notebook’s forest-loss band appeared, the camp’s expansion footprint. Because radar is not blocked by cloud, the same kind of signal can be traced continuously through the June-October 2017 monsoon itself, the exact months the optical sibling notebook had to skip entirely. The next section does that, date by date.
A one-time Otsu split between two dates, like the panel above, is a sturdy way to compare exactly two acquisitions. It does not by itself give a usable forest mask to carry across 46 dates, and RVI thresholded on a single date turns out not to either (shown next).


Deforestation trend: a composite baseline and the full radar record
Thresholding RVI on the single earliest date, exactly the way the optical notebook thresholded NDVI on 5 January 2016, was tried first here and discarded: the resulting “percent of baseline forest remaining” swung by more than 30 percentage points between consecutive dates in early 2016, well before the camp existed, purely from speckle and soil-moisture noise in the backscatter. A SAR date is a noisier yardstick than an optical date, and a mask built from one acquisition inherits all of that noise.
Instead, the baseline forest mask comes from the median of six dates in the first half of 2016 (9 January to 1 June), after the multitemporal filter. Forest is RVI above an Otsu threshold computed on that composite (an automatic split rather than a hand-picked cutoff, printed below). Every one of the 46 dates is then asked the same question as before: of the baseline forest footprint, what fraction still exceeds that same RVI threshold?
Because even the multitemporal-filtered series still carries some date-to-date wobble from soil moisture, both the raw per-date values and a 5-date rolling median are plotted. The sustained, multi-month decline after the dashed 25 August 2017 line is the real signal; individual up-or-down ticks along the way are not.


Code
# Composite baseline forest mask, Otsu threshold, and the fraction remaining on every date.

# 1. Six dates from the first half of 2016, median-combined after the multitemporal filter.
baseline_dates = [d for d in s1_times if d < "2016-07-01"]
baseline_idx = [s1_times.index(d) for d in baseline_dates]
baseline_composite = rvi_mt.isel(time=baseline_idx).median(dim="time")

# 2. Otsu-optimal RVI split on that composite. baseline_forest is the fixed footprint; every
#    later date is compared back to these same pixels.
RVI_FOREST_THR = sar.threshold(np.asarray(baseline_composite), method="otsu")
baseline_forest = baseline_composite > RVI_FOREST_THR
baseline_ha = float(baseline_forest.sum()) * px_ha
print(f"Baseline composite: {len(baseline_dates)} dates, {baseline_dates[0]} to {baseline_dates[-1]}")
print(f"Otsu RVI threshold: {RVI_FOREST_THR:.3f} | baseline forest: {baseline_ha:.0f} ha")

# 3. Fraction of the baseline-forest pixels still above the same threshold, per date.
rows = []
for i, t in enumerate(s1_time_idx):
    still_ha = float(((rvi_mt.isel(time=i) > RVI_FOREST_THR) & baseline_forest).sum()) * px_ha
    rows.append((t, still_ha))
trend = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["date", "still_forest_ha"]).set_index("date")
trend["pct_of_baseline"] = (trend.still_forest_ha / baseline_ha * 100)
trend["pct_smooth"] = trend["pct_of_baseline"].rolling(5, center=True, min_periods=1).median()

ax = trend["pct_of_baseline"].plot(style="o", ms=4, alpha=0.5, color="C2",
                                    figsize=(10, 4), label="per-date (speckle-noisy)")
trend["pct_smooth"].plot(ax=ax, lw=2, color="C2", label="5-date rolling median")
ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp("2017-08-25"), color="C3", ls="--", lw=1, label="25 Aug 2017 influx begins")
ax.set(ylabel="% of baseline forest remaining",
      title="Kutupalong-Balukhali AOI: forest loss, 2016-2018 (Sentinel-1 VV/VH)")
ax.legend(); plt.show()

# 4. Cross-check against the two-date panel above: how much of this same baseline-forest
#    footprint fell inside that VH-decrease mask by January 2018.
overlap_px = int((cm["decrease"].values & np.asarray(baseline_forest)).sum())
print(f"\nOf the baseline forest, {overlap_px * px_ha:.0f} ha "
      f"({overlap_px / int(baseline_forest.sum()):.1%}) also fell inside the VH-decrease mask "
      f"from the two-date comparison above, by {after_t:%d %b %Y}.")


Baseline composite: 6 dates, 2016-01-09 to 2016-06-01
Otsu RVI threshold: 0.823 | baseline forest: 735 ha










Of the baseline forest, 295 ha (40.1%) also fell inside the VH-decrease mask from the two-date comparison above, by 08 Jan 2018.




Forest lost
9 and 23 November 2017 are both at 43.8% of baseline, the point the decline becomes sustained rather than noisy: every date from here through the end of the series is lower than every date before it. 27 May 2017, the last date clearly inside the stable pre-crisis band, is paired with 23 November 2017 for a rate comparable to the optical notebook’s pre/post comparison. The final row of the record, 27 June 2018, is reported the same way: hectares of the January-June 2016 footprint still classed as forest, and hectares gone.


Code
# Report forest loss from 27 May 2017 to 23 November 2017, and through the last date on record.

# 1. Areas still forest on the two dates, in hectares of the 2016 baseline footprint.
pre = trend.loc["2017-05-27"]
post = trend.loc["2017-11-23"]
days = (pd.Timestamp("2017-11-23") - pd.Timestamp("2017-05-27")).days
rate_ha_month = (pre.still_forest_ha - post.still_forest_ha) / days * 30.4

# 2. The last date in the record.
final = trend.iloc[-1]

print(f"Still forest, {pre.name:%d %b %Y}: {pre.still_forest_ha:.0f} ha "
      f"({pre.pct_of_baseline:.0f}% of baseline)")
print(f"Still forest, {post.name:%d %b %Y}: {post.still_forest_ha:.0f} ha "
      f"({post.pct_of_baseline:.0f}% of baseline)")
print(f"Deforestation rate across those {days} days: "
      f"{(pre.still_forest_ha - post.still_forest_ha) / days:.2f} ha/day = {rate_ha_month:.0f} ha/month")
print(f"\nBy {final.name:%d %b %Y}: {final.still_forest_ha:.0f} ha remaining "
      f"({final.pct_of_baseline:.0f}% of baseline). "
      f"{baseline_ha - final.still_forest_ha:.0f} ha "
      f"({100 - final.pct_of_baseline:.0f}%) of the 2016 forest footprint in this AOI was gone "
      f"by the end of this radar record.")


Still forest, 27 May 2017: 430 ha (59% of baseline)
Still forest, 23 Nov 2017: 322 ha (44% of baseline)
Deforestation rate across those 180 days: 0.60 ha/day = 18 ha/month

By 27 Jun 2018: 167 ha remaining (23% of baseline). 568 ha (77%) of the 2016 forest footprint in this AOI was gone by the end of this radar record.




Animate every date: no gaps
The same cube, drawn as a false-colour sequence: VV on red, VH on green, and the VV/VH ratio on blue, a composite commonly used to interpret dual-pol SAR visually. Standing forest, with its strong cross-polarized VH return, reads differently from cleared or built ground in this composite, in the same way standing forest reads bright red in the optical notebook’s NIR-based false colour.
The optical animation kept only dates above a 30% clear-sky threshold, which dropped the two monsoon scenes outright. No such filter is applied here: every one of the 46 dates is used, including every monsoon date, because none of them needed to be thrown away.


Code
# Animate all 46 dates. False colour: VV, VH, VV/VH ratio.

# 1. Pillow writes the GIF. make_rgb stretches three named bands to an 8-bit-equivalent RGB
#    image using the same percentile stretch as the optical notebook's plot_rgb.
import matplotlib.animation as animation
from IPython.display import Image as IPImage
from geolattice.rsense.viz.stretch import rgb as make_rgb

S1_OUT_DIR = Path("outputs")
S1_OUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# 2. One RGB frame per date, built from the per-date refined-Lee-filtered VV/VH plus their ratio.
s1_frames = []
for k in range(s1_roh.sizes["time"]):
    frame_ds = xr.Dataset({
        "vv": vv_lee.isel(time=k), "vh": vh_lee.isel(time=k),
        "ratio": vv_lee.isel(time=k) / vh_lee.isel(time=k),
    })
    s1_frames.append(np.nan_to_num(make_rgb(frame_ds, ["vv", "vh", "ratio"]).values))

# 3. One axes, updated in place. The title is the acquisition date of that frame.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))
im = ax.imshow(s1_frames[0], origin="upper")
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
ttl = ax.set_title("")

def _update_s1(k):
    im.set_data(s1_frames[k])
    ttl.set_text(f"Kutupalong-Balukhali, {s1_time_idx[k]:%d %b %Y} (VV-VH-ratio)")
    return im, ttl

# 4. 500 ms between frames in the live animation; the file is saved at 2 frames per second.
anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, _update_s1, frames=len(s1_frames), interval=500)
gif_path = S1_OUT_DIR / "rohingya_deforestation_sentinel1.gif"
anim.save(gif_path, writer=animation.PillowWriter(fps=2))
plt.close(fig)
IPImage(filename=str(gif_path))


<IPython.core.display.Image object>

title: Timeline of the Rohingya Exodus: Deforestation in Bangladesh (2016-2018), Sentinel-1 Radar
text:
Summary and Conclusions
This notebook investigated the same Kutupalong-Balukhali deforestation as the Sentinel-2 capstone, using Sentinel-1 C-band radar instead of optical imagery. Downloading from Planetary Computer’s analysis-ready sentinel-1-rtc collection on one fixed orbit track gave 46 cloud-independent dates across 2016-2018, with no monsoon gap: every month of the event, including the crisis onset itself, has at least one usable acquisition.
That completeness came with a real tradeoff. SAR backscatter is speckled in a way optical reflectance is not, and a forest mask built from a single date (the method that worked fine for Sentinel-2’s NDVI) swung by tens of percentage points between unchanged dates purely from noise. Getting a usable time series required a multitemporal speckle filter across the whole stack and a multi-date composite baseline, plus an Otsu-thresholded two-date log-ratio comparison rather than a repeated absolute cutoff. These are standard SAR practices, not a workaround specific to this AOI, and they are the main methodological difference from the optical notebook.
With that handling in place, the two methods agree: a VH-backscatter decrease consistent with canopy loss appears across the centre of the AOI, in the same location the optical notebook’s forest-loss band appeared, and the fraction of the 2016 baseline forest footprint still standing falls from a noisy 55-80% band before August 2017 to roughly a fifth of that footprint by mid-2018. The deforestation rate computed from the radar record and the rate computed from the optical record are not directly comparable (different baselines, different dates, different detection thresholds), but both point to the same conclusion: rapid, large-scale forest clearing concentrated in the months immediately following the refugee influx.
In short, radar earns its place here less by seeing something optical missed inside the AOI, and more by never losing the thread during the exact weeks optical could not observe at all. For an event whose sharpest onset falls inside a monsoon, that continuity is often the more valuable property than either sensor’s native spatial or spectral detail.

title: Crop Classification with NISAR GCOV Time Series and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
Overview
Its Level-2 GCOV product (geocoded, radiometrically terrain-corrected polarimetric covariance) gives calibrated γ⁰ backscatter on a map grid, so a stack of passes is a ready-made crop phenology time series that sees through clouds. This capstone uses real NISAR GCOV scenes from the 2026 growing season over the U.S. Midwest and checks every map against the USDA NASS 10 m Cropland Data Layer (CDL).
The workflow:

Inventory the GCOV HDF5 files with GeoLattice (geolattice.rsense.sar.nisar), keep the stack that overlaps the CDL, and skip the rest
Choose a cropland area of interest (AOI) automatically from the CDL and the NISAR validity mask
Read windowed HH/HV γ⁰ from each pass, apply the Quegan multi-temporal speckle filter and compute dual-pol indices with GeoLattice
Warp the 10 m CDL onto the NISAR grid, group CDL codes into crop classes, and build field-like units and spatially blocked train/validation/test splits
Train a Random Forest on handcrafted temporal features (baseline)
Pretrain a transformer encoder on unlabeled NISAR pixel time series with two self-supervised methods: masked autoencoding (MAE) and contrastive learning (SimCLR)
Fine-tune and linear-probe the encoder with 1, 5, 20 and all labeled fields per class and compare label efficiency
Map the AOI, smooth the map with object-based voting on GeoLattice SLIC segments, and validate against the CDL: wall-to-wall agreement on held-out blocks, a stratified random sample with Olofsson area-adjusted accuracy, and a corn/soybean rotation check
Test spatial transfer to a second AOI in the same frame that was never labeled


Data used








Item
Source
In this notebook




NISAR L2 GCOV (NISAR_L2_PR_GCOV_*)
NASA/ISRO via ASF DAAC
Track 041, descending, frame 066, mode 4005 DHDH (HH + HV), 6 passes, 23 Jul – 15 Oct 2026, 10 m posting


Cropland Data Layer
USDA NASS
2025 national 10 m mosaic (2025_10m_cdls.tif), NAD83 / CONUS Albers





Read this before trusting the numbers

The reference is the 2025 CDL; the imagery is from 2026. The 2026 CDL will not be released until early 2027. Many Midwest fields rotate corn ↔︎ soybean every year, so a share of the “errors” between corn and soybean are correct NISAR labels for 2026 compared with a 2025 reference. Section 12.4 measures how much of the disagreement is corn/soybean confusion. Set CDL_PATH to the 2026 CDL when it is out and rerun.
The CDL is itself a classification. NASS reports national producer’s/user’s accuracies of about 92/91% for corn and 91/90% for soybeans, but 67/68% for alfalfa and 32/26% for other hay (2025 metadata). Agreement with the CDL is not the same as accuracy.
The stack starts on 23 July, after planting and green-up. Classes that differ mainly in spring (spring wheat vs. barley, early hay cuts) are harder than they would be with a full-season stack.
GCOV DHDH is dual-pol (HH, HV). There is no VV, so the quad-pol features of the simulated version of this chapter (HH/VV ratio, quad-pol RVI) are replaced by the dual-pol RVI from nisar.gcov_indices.

section: Inventory of the NISAR GCOV files
text:
Inventory of the NISAR GCOV files
The file name carries the cycle, track, direction, frame, mode and start time. GeoLattice reads the identification metadata (nisar.read_identification), including the footprint polygon, and lists the layers of the frequency A grid (nisar.inspect_hdf5) without loading any raster.
A time series must come from one track, one direction and one frame, because backscatter depends on the viewing geometry. Each footprint is intersected with the CDL extent, and only the stack that overlaps the CDL is kept.


Code
def parse_nisar_name(path):
    p = path.stem.split("_")
    return {"file": path, "cycle": int(p[4]), "track": int(p[5]),
            "direction": {"A": "Ascending", "D": "Descending"}.get(p[6], p[6]), "frame": int(p[7]),
            "mode": p[8], "pols": p[9], "time_utc": pd.Timestamp(p[11]),
            "size_gb": round(path.stat().st_size / 1e9, 2)}

def grid_info(path):
    # Coordinates, EPSG and posting of the GCOV grid (small arrays only).
    with h5py.File(path, "r") as f:
        g = f[GRID]
        x, y = g["xCoordinates"][:], g["yCoordinates"][:]
        epsg = int(np.asarray(g["projection"][()]).ravel()[0])
        layers = [p for p in POLS if p in g]
    dx, dy = float(x[1] - x[0]), float(y[1] - y[0])
    bounds = (x.min() - abs(dx) / 2, y.min() - abs(dy) / 2, x.max() + abs(dx) / 2, y.max() + abs(dy) / 2)
    return {"x": x, "y": y, "epsg": epsg, "crs": f"EPSG:{epsg}", "dx": dx, "dy": dy,
            "posting": abs(dx), "bounds": bounds, "shape": (len(y), len(x)), "layers": layers}

def footprint_lonlat(path, info):
    # Footprint polygon from identification/boundingPolygon (GeoLattice), else the grid bounding box.
    try:
        ident = nisar.read_identification(path, "GCOV")
        poly = wkt.loads(str(ident.get("boundingPolygon")))
        if poly.is_valid and not poly.is_empty:
            return poly, ident
    except Exception:
        ident = {}
    return box(*transform_bounds(info["crs"], "EPSG:4326", *info["bounds"], densify_pts=21)), ident

with rasterio.open(CDL_PATH) as cdl_src:
    CDL_CRS = cdl_src.crs
    cdl_box = box(*transform_bounds(cdl_src.crs, "EPSG:4326", *cdl_src.bounds, densify_pts=51))
    print(f"CDL: {cdl_src.width:,} x {cdl_src.height:,} px at {cdl_src.res[0]:.0f} m, nodata={cdl_src.nodata}")

rows = []
for path in sorted(NISAR_DIR.glob("NISAR_L2_*GCOV*.h5")):
    rec = parse_nisar_name(path)
    info = grid_info(path)
    poly, ident = footprint_lonlat(path, info)
    rec.update({"epsg": info["epsg"], "posting_m": info["posting"], "rows": info["shape"][0],
                "cols": info["shape"][1], "layers": "+".join(info["layers"]),
                "lon": round(poly.centroid.x, 3), "lat": round(poly.centroid.y, 3),
                "cdl_overlap": round(poly.intersection(cdl_box).area / poly.area, 3), "footprint": poly})
    rows.append(rec)
inventory = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("time_utc").reset_index(drop=True)
display(inventory.drop(columns=["file", "footprint"]))

title: Crop Classification with NISAR GCOV Time Series and Self-Supervised Learning
section: Choosing the AOI from the CDL and the NISAR mask
text:
Choosing the AOI from the CDL and the NISAR mask
A full frame at 10 m is roughly 24,000 × 24,000 pixels per layer, too large to hold six dates in memory, and GeoLattice nisar.read_l2 reads a whole layer at once. So the frame is first screened on a 200 m grid:

the GCOV mask layer of every pass is read with a stride (valid = 1…254, i.e. imaged sub-swaths; 0 = invalid; 255 = fill)
the CDL is read through its overview pyramid and warped to the same grid

Every candidate 20 km window is then scored by its share of cropland and the diversity of its crop classes, among windows that are valid on all dates over at least 98% of their area. The best window becomes the training AOI; the best non-overlapping window becomes the transfer AOI.


Code
def north_up(arr, dy):
    # GCOV grids are normally north-up (y decreasing); flip if a release stores them south-up.
    return arr[::-1] if dy > 0 else arr

def mask_to_valid(mask):
    valid = (mask > 0) & (mask < 255)
    if valid.mean() < 0.01 and (mask != 255).mean() > 0.01:     # unexpected convention: fall back
        warnings.warn("Mask convention differs from 1..254 = valid; using mask != 255")
        valid = mask != 255
    return valid

REF = grid_info(stack.file.iloc[0])
S = max(1, int(round(COARSE_M / REF["posting"])))
ref_x = REF["x"]
ref_y = REF["y"] if REF["dy"] < 0 else REF["y"][::-1]
cx, cy = ref_x[::S], ref_y[::S]
C_DX = REF["posting"] * S
COARSE_T = Affine(C_DX, 0, cx[0] - C_DX / 2, 0, -C_DX, cy[0] + C_DX / 2)
COARSE_SHAPE = (len(cy), len(cx))

t0 = time.time()
valid_count = np.zeros(COARSE_SHAPE, np.uint8)
for s in stack.itertuples():
    info = grid_info(s.file)
    with h5py.File(s.file, "r") as f:
        m = north_up(f[GRID]["mask"][::S, ::S], info["dy"])
    v = mask_to_valid(m).astype(np.uint8)
    if v.shape != COARSE_SHAPE or info["x"][0] != REF["x"][0] or info["y"][0] != REF["y"][0]:
        yy = info["y"] if info["dy"] < 0 else info["y"][::-1]
        src_t = Affine(info["posting"] * S, 0, info["x"][0] - info["posting"] * S / 2,
                       0, -info["posting"] * S, yy[0] + info["posting"] * S / 2)
        out = np.zeros(COARSE_SHAPE, np.uint8)
        reproject(v, out, src_transform=src_t, src_crs=info["crs"], dst_transform=COARSE_T,
                  dst_crs=STACK_CRS, resampling=Resampling.nearest)
        v = out
    valid_count += v
print(f"Mask screening: {time.time() - t0:.0f}s; valid on all {len(stack)} dates: "
      f"{(valid_count == len(stack)).mean():.1%} of the frame grid")

def read_cdl_coarse(dst_transform, dst_shape, dst_crs, cell_m):
    # CDL codes on a coarse grid: decimated read (uses the .ovr pyramid), then nearest warp.
    with rasterio.open(CDL_PATH) as src:
        h, w = dst_shape
        bounds = (dst_transform.c, dst_transform.f - h * cell_m, dst_transform.c + w * cell_m, dst_transform.f)
        l, b, r, t = transform_bounds(dst_crs, src.crs, *bounds, densify_pts=21)
        win = window_from_bounds(l, b, r, t, src.transform)
        win = Window(int(np.floor(win.col_off)), int(np.floor(win.row_off)),
                     int(np.ceil(win.width)) + 2, int(np.ceil(win.height)) + 2)
        win = win.intersection(Window(0, 0, src.width, src.height))
        k = max(1, int(cell_m // abs(src.res[0]) // 2))           # read at half the target cell size
        shape = (max(1, int(win.height) // k), max(1, int(win.width) // k))
        arr = src.read(1, window=win, out_shape=shape, resampling=Resampling.nearest)
        src_t = src.window_transform(win) * Affine.scale(win.width / shape[1], win.height / shape[0])
        out = np.zeros(dst_shape, np.uint8)
        reproject(arr, out, src_transform=src_t, src_crs=src.crs, dst_transform=dst_transform,
                  dst_crs=dst_crs, resampling=Resampling.nearest, src_nodata=0, dst_nodata=0)
    return out

t0 = time.time()
cdl_coarse = read_cdl_coarse(COARSE_T, COARSE_SHAPE, STACK_CRS, C_DX)
grp_coarse = LUT_ALL[cdl_coarse]
print(f"CDL screening grid: {time.time() - t0:.0f}s; cropland share of frame {(grp_coarse != NONAG).mean():.1%}")

Code
def choose_windows(grp, valid_all, size_cells, n=2):
    # Score square windows: cropland share x (0.5 + crop diversity), valid on all dates.
    ok = valid_all.astype(float)
    ag = ((grp != NONAG) & valid_all).astype(float)
    f_valid = ndi.uniform_filter(ok, size_cells, mode="constant")
    f_ag = ndi.uniform_filter(ag, size_cells, mode="constant")
    shares = [ndi.uniform_filter(((grp == k) & valid_all).astype(float), size_cells, mode="constant")
              for k in range(len(GROUP_NAMES))]
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        p = np.stack(shares) / np.where(f_ag > 0, f_ag, np.nan)
    diversity = 1 - np.nansum(p ** 2, 0)
    half = size_cells // 2                                   # centres whose window lies inside the grid
    inner = np.zeros_like(ok, bool)
    inner[half:ok.shape[0] - (size_cells - half), half:ok.shape[1] - (size_cells - half)] = True
    if not inner.any():
        raise ValueError("AOI_SIZE_KM is larger than the frame")
    need = MIN_VALID_FRAC
    if f_valid[inner].max() < need:                         # scattered flagged pixels everywhere: relax
        need = f_valid[inner].max() - 0.02
        print(f"No window is valid over {MIN_VALID_FRAC:.0%} of its area on all dates; using {need:.1%}")
    score = np.where(inner & (f_valid >= need), f_ag * (0.5 + diversity), -1)
    picks = []
    for _ in range(n):
        if score.max() <= 0:
            break
        r, c = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(score), score.shape)
        picks.append((r, c, float(f_ag[r, c]), float(diversity[r, c])))
        score[max(0, r - size_cells):r + size_cells, max(0, c - size_cells):c + size_cells] = -1
    return picks

SIZE_CELLS = int(round(AOI_SIZE_KM * 1000 / C_DX))
VALID_ALL = valid_count == len(stack)
picks = choose_windows(grp_coarse, VALID_ALL, SIZE_CELLS, n=2 if TRANSFER_AOI else 1)
if AOI_CENTER_LONLAT is not None:
    from pyproj import Transformer
    xc, yc = Transformer.from_crs(4326, STACK_CRS, always_xy=True).transform(*AOI_CENTER_LONLAT)
    col, row = ~COARSE_T * (xc, yc)
    picks[0] = (int(row), int(col), np.nan, np.nan)

N_PX = int(round(AOI_SIZE_KM * 1000 / POSTING))
def aoi_from_coarse(r, c, name):
    # Snap the AOI to the reference pixel grid (north-up row/col of the fine grid).
    r0 = int(r * S - N_PX // 2); c0 = int(c * S - N_PX // 2)
    r0 = int(np.clip(r0, 0, len(ref_y) - N_PX)); c0 = int(np.clip(c0, 0, len(ref_x) - N_PX))
    xs, ys = ref_x[c0:c0 + N_PX], ref_y[r0:r0 + N_PX]
    T = Affine(POSTING, 0, xs[0] - POSTING / 2, 0, -POSTING, ys[0] + POSTING / 2)
    bounds = (xs[0] - POSTING / 2, ys[-1] - POSTING / 2, xs[-1] + POSTING / 2, ys[0] + POSTING / 2)
    return {"name": name, "x": xs, "y": ys, "transform": T, "bounds": bounds, "shape": (N_PX, N_PX)}

AOIS = [aoi_from_coarse(p[0], p[1], name) for p, name in zip(picks, ["AOI-1 (train)", "AOI-2 (transfer)"])]
for a, p in zip(AOIS, picks):
    lo = transform_bounds(STACK_CRS, "EPSG:4326", *a["bounds"])
    print(f"{a['name']}: lon {lo[0]:.3f}..{lo[2]:.3f}, lat {lo[1]:.3f}..{lo[3]:.3f} | "
          f"cropland {p[2]:.0%}, diversity {p[3]:.2f}")

# Overview: dominant CDL class on the screening grid, invalid areas, and the chosen AOIs.
cmap_all = ListedColormap([GROUP_COLORS[n] for n in GROUP_NAMES])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6.2))
ext = [COARSE_T.c, COARSE_T.c + COARSE_SHAPE[1] * C_DX, COARSE_T.f - COARSE_SHAPE[0] * C_DX, COARSE_T.f]
show = np.ma.masked_where((grp_coarse == NONAG), grp_coarse)
axes[0].imshow(np.where(VALID_ALL, 0.92, 0.55), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1, extent=ext)
axes[0].imshow(show, cmap=cmap_all, vmin=0, vmax=len(GROUP_NAMES) - 1, extent=ext, interpolation="nearest")
axes[1].imshow(valid_count, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=len(stack), extent=ext)
for ax in axes:
    for a, col in zip(AOIS, ["red", "cyan"]):
        l, b, r, t = a["bounds"]
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((l, b), r - l, t - b, fill=False, ec=col, lw=2))
        ax.text(l, t, a["name"], color=col, fontsize=9, va="bottom", fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
axes[0].set_title(f"CDL {CDL_YEAR} classes in the NISAR frame (grey = non-crop)")
axes[1].set_title("Number of valid GCOV passes per 200 m cell")
axes[0].legend(handles=[Patch(color=GROUP_COLORS[n], label=n) for n in GROUP_NAMES],
               loc="lower left", fontsize=7, ncol=2, framealpha=0.9)

title: Crop Classification with NISAR GCOV Time Series and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
Reading the AOI time series
For each pass, the AOI window is read straight from the HDF5 datasets (HHHH, HVHV, mask, numberOfLooks). These are the same paths GeoLattice nisar.read_l2 uses (/science/LSAR/GCOV/grids/frequencyA/...); slicing the h5py dataset keeps memory at the AOI size. If a pass sits on a slightly different grid, it is resampled bilinearly onto the reference grid. Pixels outside the valid mask, or with γ⁰ ≤ 0, become NaN.
The result is an xarray cube (time, pol, y, x) of linear γ⁰ with the UTM CRS attached.


Code
def read_gcov_window(path, bounds, pad_px=2):
    info = grid_info(path)
    l, b, r, t = bounds
    pad = pad_px * info["posting"]
    ix = np.flatnonzero((info["x"] >= l - pad) & (info["x"] <= r + pad))
    iy = np.flatnonzero((info["y"] >= b - pad) & (info["y"] <= t + pad))
    if ix.size == 0 or iy.size == 0:
        return None
    sl = (slice(iy.min(), iy.max() + 1), slice(ix.min(), ix.max() + 1))
    with h5py.File(path, "r") as f:
        g = f[GRID]
        data = [north_up(g[p][sl].astype(np.float32), info["dy"]) for p in POLS]
        mask = north_up(g["mask"][sl], info["dy"])
        looks = float(np.nanmedian(g["numberOfLooks"][sl])) if "numberOfLooks" in g else np.nan
    valid = mask_to_valid(mask)
    for a in data:
        valid &= np.isfinite(a) & (a > 0)
    data = np.stack([np.where(valid, a, np.nan) for a in data])
    xs = info["x"][ix]
    ys = info["y"][iy] if info["dy"] < 0 else info["y"][iy][::-1]
    T = Affine(info["posting"], 0, xs[0] - info["posting"] / 2, 0, -info["posting"], ys[0] + info["posting"] / 2)
    return data, T, info["crs"], looks

def load_aoi_stack(aoi):
    H, W = aoi["shape"]
    cube = np.full((len(stack), len(POLS), H, W), np.nan, np.float32)
    looks = []
    for t, s in enumerate(stack.itertuples()):
        out = read_gcov_window(s.file, aoi["bounds"])
        if out is None:
            print(f"  {s.time_utc:%Y-%m-%d}: no data in {aoi['name']}")
            continue
        data, T, crs, lk = out
        looks.append(lk)
        for k in range(len(POLS)):
            reproject(data[k], cube[t, k], src_transform=T, src_crs=crs, dst_transform=aoi["transform"],
                      dst_crs=STACK_CRS, resampling=Resampling.bilinear, src_nodata=np.nan, dst_nodata=np.nan)
    da = xr.DataArray(cube, dims=("time", "pol", "y", "x"),
                      coords={"time": DATES, "pol": ["HH", "HV"], "y": aoi["y"], "x": aoi["x"]},
                      name="gamma0", attrs={"units": "linear gamma0", "looks": float(np.nanmedian(looks))})
    return da.rio.write_crs(STACK_CRS)

t0 = time.time()
cubes = {}
for a in AOIS:
    cubes[a["name"]] = load_aoi_stack(a)
    c = cubes[a["name"]]
    print(f"{a['name']}: {dict(c.sizes)} | valid share per date "
          f"{np.round(np.isfinite(c.values).all(1).mean((1, 2)), 3).tolist()} | median looks {c.attrs['looks']:.1f}")
print(f"Read in {time.time() - t0:.0f}s")
AOI1 = AOIS[0]["name"]
cube_raw = cubes[AOI1]
cube_raw

title: Crop Classification with NISAR GCOV Time Series and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
Speckle filtering and dual-pol features
GCOV pixels at 10 m carry only a few looks (numberOfLooks), so single-date speckle is strong. The Quegan & Yu (2001) multi-temporal filter in GeoLattice (speckle.multitemporal) averages speckle across the six dates while each date keeps its own local mean, so the temporal signal is preserved and spatial blurring is small. The ENL is set from the median numberOfLooks of the window.

def filter_cube(c):
    out = c.copy()
    enl = max(1.0, float(c.attrs.get("looks", 4.0)))
    for k in range(c.sizes["pol"]):
        out.values[:, k] = np.asarray(speckle.multitemporal(c.values[:, k], spatial=SPECKLE_SPATIAL,
                                                            size=SPECKLE_SIZE, enl=enl, time_axis=0))
    out.attrs["speckle_filter"] = f"Quegan multi-temporal ({SPECKLE_SPATIAL}, {SPECKLE_SIZE}x{SPECKLE_SIZE}, ENL {enl:.1f})"
    return out

    rgb = np.dstack([stretch(hh, -18, -2), stretch(hv, -28, -10), stretch(hh - hv, 3, 14)])
    rgb[~np.isfinite(rgb)] = 1

The 10 m CDL on the NISAR grid
The CDL is warped (nearest neighbour) from CONUS Albers to the NISAR UTM grid of each AOI. Both are 10 m, so this is a near one-to-one resampling. CDL codes are then grouped into the crop classes defined in Section 1; rare classes in AOI-1 merge into Other crops, and if Other crops itself is rare, its pixels are left out.

def read_cdl_on_grid(aoi):
    out = np.zeros(aoi["shape"], np.uint8)

                  resampling=Resampling.nearest, src_nodata=0, dst_nodata=0)
    return out

title: Crop Classification with NISAR GCOV Time Series and Self-Supervised Learning
section: Field-like units and spatially blocked splits
text:
Field-like units and spatially blocked splits
The CDL has no parcel boundaries, but neighbouring pixels in one field are strongly correlated, so random pixel splits leak information and inflate accuracy. Field-like units are built from the CDL itself:

Interior pixels: pixels whose 3 × 3 neighbourhood is all the same class (drops mixed boundary pixels, roads, shelterbelts)
Connected components of interior pixels per class, cut at a 1 km grid so large contiguous patches become several units
Units smaller than 0.5 ha are dropped

Whole 2 km blocks go to train, validation or test. The 1 km cutting grid nests inside the 2 km blocks, so no unit straddles two splits. Training labels come only from interior pixels of training units; the wall-to-wall validation in Section 12 uses every cropland pixel of the test blocks, boundaries included.
Label budgets are counted in labeled fields per class (1, 5, 20, all), mimicking a survey that visits a handful of fields per crop.


Code
def make_units(ym):
    H, W = ym.shape
    interior = (ndi.maximum_filter(ym, 3) == ndi.minimum_filter(ym, 3)) & (ym >= 0)
    tile_px = int(FIELD_TILE_M / POSTING)
    rr, cc = np.indices((H, W))
    n_tc = int(np.ceil(W / tile_px))
    tile = (rr // tile_px) * n_tc + (cc // tile_px)
    fid = np.full((H, W), -1, np.int64)
    offset = 0
    for c in range(len(CLASSES)):
        lab, n = ndi.label(interior & (ym == c))
        on = lab > 0
        key = lab[on].astype(np.int64) * (tile.max() + 1) + tile[on]
        _, inv = np.unique(key, return_inverse=True)
        fid[on] = inv.ravel() + offset
        offset += inv.max() + 1 if inv.size else 0
    sizes = np.bincount(fid[fid >= 0])
    fid[(fid >= 0) & (sizes[np.clip(fid, 0, None)] < MIN_FIELD_PX)] = -1
    _, fid_c = np.unique(fid.ravel(), return_inverse=True)        # compact ids, -1 stays smallest
    fid = fid_c.reshape(H, W) - (1 if (fid < 0).any() else 0)
    block_px = int(BLOCK_M / POSTING)
    n_bc = int(np.ceil(W / block_px))
    block = (rr // block_px) * n_bc + (cc // block_px)
    return fid, block

def block_splits(block, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ids = np.unique(block)
    rng.shuffle(ids)
    n_test = int(round(SPLIT_FRACTIONS["test"] * len(ids)))
    n_val = int(round(SPLIT_FRACTIONS["val"] * len(ids)))
    names = np.array(["test"] * n_test + ["val"] * n_val + ["train"] * (len(ids) - n_test - n_val))
    order = np.argsort(ids)
    return names[order][np.searchsorted(ids[order], block)]

field_maps, split_maps = {}, {}
for a in AOIS:
    fid, block = make_units(y_maps[a["name"]])
    field_maps[a["name"]] = fid
    split_maps[a["name"]] = block_splits(block) if a["name"] == AOI1 else np.full(block.shape, "test")

section: Pixel time series and the Random Forest baseline
text:
Pixel time series and the Random Forest baseline
Every cropland pixel with at least MIN_VALID_DATES valid passes becomes one sample:

x_db (T, 2): filtered HH and HV in dB (0 where invalid)
doy (T,): acquisition day of year
valid (T,): True where the pass was valid

The baseline is the standard approach before deep learning: fill gaps by linear interpolation in time, then use the per-date values plus seasonal statistics of each channel (mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum and the DOY of the maximum) in a Random Forest.


Code
def pixel_samples(name):
    c = cubes_f[name]
    ym, fid, split = y_maps[name], field_maps[name], split_maps[name]
    x_db = np.moveaxis(to_db(c.values), (0, 1), (2, 3))          # (H, W, T, 2)
    valid = np.isfinite(x_db).all(-1)
    use = (ym >= 0) & (valid.sum(-1) >= MIN_VALID_DATES)
    rows, cols = np.nonzero(use)
    X = np.nan_to_num(x_db[rows, cols], nan=0.0).astype(np.float32)
    V = valid[rows, cols]
    D = np.tile(DOYS, (len(rows), 1)).astype(np.float32)
    meta = pd.DataFrame({"row": rows, "col": cols, "y": ym[rows, cols], "field": fid[rows, cols],
                         "split": split[rows, cols]})
    return X, D, V, meta

t0 = time.time()
samples = {a["name"]: pixel_samples(a["name"]) for a in AOIS}
xA, dA, vA, metaA = samples[AOI1]
yA = metaA.y.values
for name, (X, D, V, m) in samples.items():
    print(f"{name}: {len(X):,} cropland pixels, {X.shape[1]} dates, valid observations {V.mean():.3f}")
print(f"({time.time() - t0:.0f}s)")

CHANNELS = ["HH", "HV", "HV-HH", "RVI"]

def raw_features_np(x_db):
    lin = 10 ** (x_db / 10)
    hh, hv = x_db[..., 0], x_db[..., 1]
    rvi = 4 * lin[..., 1] / (lin[..., 0] + lin[..., 1] + 1e-8)
    return np.stack([hh, hv, hv - hh, rvi], -1)

def fill_time(v, valid, doy):
    # Linear interpolation over time for each pixel (vectorised; edges take the nearest valid value).
    N, T = v.shape
    t = np.arange(T)
    prev = np.maximum.accumulate(np.where(valid, t, -1), axis=1)
    nxt = np.minimum.accumulate(np.where(valid, t, T)[:, ::-1], axis=1)[:, ::-1]
    p, n = np.clip(prev, 0, T - 1), np.clip(nxt, 0, T - 1)
    vp, vn = np.take_along_axis(v, p, 1), np.take_along_axis(v, n, 1)
    dp, dn = np.take_along_axis(doy, p, 1), np.take_along_axis(doy, n, 1)
    w = np.where(dn > dp, (doy - dp) / np.where(dn > dp, dn - dp, 1), 0)
    out = np.where(prev < 0, vn, np.where(nxt >= T, vp, vp + w * (vn - vp)))
    return np.where(valid, v, out)

def handcrafted(x_db, doy, valid):
    f = raw_features_np(x_db)
    feats = []
    for c in range(f.shape[-1]):
        v = np.where(valid, f[..., c], np.nan)
        filled = fill_time(np.nan_to_num(v), valid, doy)
        imax = np.argmax(np.where(valid, v, -np.inf), 1)
        feats += [filled, np.nanmean(v, 1)[:, None], np.nanstd(v, 1)[:, None], np.nanmin(v, 1)[:, None],
                  np.nanmax(v, 1)[:, None], doy[np.arange(len(v)), imax][:, None]]
    return np.concatenate(feats, 1).astype(np.float32)

t0 = time.time()
HF = {name: handcrafted(X, D, V) for name, (X, D, V, m) in samples.items()}
HF_A = HF[AOI1]
print("Handcrafted features:", HF_A.shape, f"({time.time() - t0:.0f}s)")

idx_val = np.flatnonzero((metaA.split == "val") & (metaA.field >= 0))
idx_val = rng.choice(idx_val, min(VAL_SAMPLE, len(idx_val)), replace=False)
idx_test_int = np.flatnonzero((metaA.split == "test") & (metaA.field >= 0))     # interior test pixels
idx_eval = rng.choice(idx_test_int, min(EVAL_SAMPLE, len(idx_test_int)), replace=False)

def sample_label_budget(meta, n_per_class, seed):
    # n labeled training units per class -> pixel indices (capped per class).
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    tr = meta[(meta.split == "train") & (meta.field >= 0)]
    idx = []
    for c in range(len(CLASSES)):
        fl = tr.loc[tr.y == c, "field"].unique()
        if len(fl) == 0:
            continue
        k = len(fl) if n_per_class == "all" else min(n_per_class, len(fl))
        chosen = r.choice(fl, k, replace=False)
        pix = tr.index[tr.field.isin(chosen) & (tr.y == c)].values
        idx.append(r.choice(pix, min(len(pix), MAX_PIX_PER_CLASS), replace=False))
    return np.concatenate(idx)

def evaluate(y_true, y_pred):
    return {"OA": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
            "macroF1": f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average="macro", labels=np.unique(y_true)),
            "kappa": cohen_kappa_score(y_true, y_pred)}

results, rf_models = [], {}
t0 = time.time()
for budget in BUDGETS:
    for s in SEEDS:
        idx = sample_label_budget(metaA, budget, seed=100 + s)
        rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=2, n_jobs=-1,
                                    class_weight="balanced", random_state=s).fit(HF_A[idx], yA[idx])
        r = evaluate(yA[idx_eval], rf.predict(HF_A[idx_eval]))
        results.append({"method": "Random Forest", "budget": str(budget), "seed": s, "n_pixels": len(idx), **r})
        if s == 0:
            rf_models[str(budget)] = rf

title: Crop Classification with NISAR GCOV Time Series and Self-Supervised Learning
section: Transformer encoder for SAR time series
text:
Transformer encoder for SAR time series
Each acquisition is a token:
x_db (T × 2) ──Featurizer──> (T × 4: HH, HV, HV−HH, RVI) ──Linear──> (T × d) + DOY encoding
        ──> Transformer encoder (attention ignores invalid dates) ──> (T × d) ──mean over valid dates──> embedding

DOY positional encoding on the real acquisition day, so the 24-day gaps (16 Aug, 9 Sep) and any missing pass are handled without gap filling.
Key padding mask: invalid dates are ignored by attention.
The Featurizer computes the ratio and RVI inside PyTorch with the same formulas as nisar.gcov_indices, so the SimCLR augmentations can perturb HH and HV first and keep the derived channels consistent.

Normalization statistics come from the unlabeled pool.


Code
class Featurizer(nn.Module):
    # dB backscatter (B, T, 2) -> normalised 4-channel features (B, T, 4)
    def __init__(self, mean=None, std=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer("mean", torch.zeros(4) if mean is None else torch.as_tensor(mean, dtype=torch.float32))
        self.register_buffer("std", torch.ones(4) if std is None else torch.as_tensor(std, dtype=torch.float32))

    @staticmethod
    def raw(x_db):
        hh, hv = x_db[..., 0], x_db[..., 1]
        lin = 10 ** (x_db / 10)
        rvi = 4 * lin[..., 1] / (lin[..., 0] + lin[..., 1] + 1e-8)
        return torch.stack([hh, hv, hv - hh, rvi], -1)

    def forward(self, x_db, valid):
        f = (self.raw(x_db) - self.mean) / self.std
        return torch.where(valid.unsqueeze(-1), f, torch.zeros_like(f))

# Unlabeled pool: random pixels from BOTH AOIs (no labels used).
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
pool = []
for name, (X, D, V, m) in samples.items():
    k = min(len(X), SSL_POOL // len(samples))
    sel = rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)
    pool.append((X[sel], D[sel], V[sel]))
XU = np.concatenate([p[0] for p in pool]); DU = np.concatenate([p[1] for p in pool]); VU = np.concatenate([p[2] for p in pool])
with torch.no_grad():
    raw = Featurizer.raw(torch.from_numpy(XU))[torch.from_numpy(VU)]
    FEAT_MEAN, FEAT_STD = raw.mean(0), raw.std(0)
print(f"Unlabeled pool: {len(XU):,} pixel time series from {len(samples)} AOI(s)")
display(pd.DataFrame({"mean": FEAT_MEAN.numpy(), "std": FEAT_STD.numpy()}, index=CHANNELS).round(3))

def doy_encoding(doy, d_model, max_period=366.0):
    half = d_model // 2
    freqs = torch.exp(-torch.arange(half, device=doy.device) * np.log(1000.0) / half)
    ang = doy.unsqueeze(-1) / max_period * 2 * np.pi * freqs * 60
    return torch.cat([ang.sin(), ang.cos()], -1)

class TSEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_ch=4, d_model=64, n_layers=3, n_heads=4, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.featurizer = Featurizer(FEAT_MEAN, FEAT_STD)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(n_ch, d_model)
        self.mask_token = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, d_model))
        layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d_model, n_heads, 4 * d_model, dropout, batch_first=True, norm_first=True)
        self.encoder = nn.TransformerEncoder(layer, n_layers, enable_nested_tensor=False)
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.d_model = d_model

    def tokens(self, x_db, doy, valid, mae_mask=None):
        h = self.proj(self.featurizer(x_db, valid))
        if mae_mask is not None:
            h = torch.where(mae_mask.unsqueeze(-1), self.mask_token.expand_as(h), h)
        h = h + doy_encoding(doy, self.d_model)
        return self.norm(self.encoder(h, src_key_padding_mask=~valid))

    def forward(self, x_db, doy, valid):
        h = self.tokens(x_db, doy, valid)
        w = valid.unsqueeze(-1).float()
        return (h * w).sum(1) / w.sum(1).clamp(min=1)

def to_t(*arrs):
    return [torch.as_tensor(a).to(DEVICE) for a in arrs]

print(f"Encoder parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in TSEncoder().parameters()):,}")

Self-supervised pretraining

Masked autoencoding (MAE)
For every pixel, half of its valid dates are replaced by a learned mask token and a small decoder reconstructs the four normalised features at those dates. With six dates this means predicting, say, the September HV of a pixel from its July, October and other values; the encoder has to learn how backscatter evolves through canopy closure, senescence and harvest. The loss is the mean squared error on masked dates only.


Code
class TimeSeriesMAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, mask_ratio=0.5, **kw):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = TSEncoder(**kw)
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(self.encoder.d_model, 64), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(64, 4))
        self.mask_ratio = mask_ratio

    def forward(self, x_db, doy, valid):
        target = self.encoder.featurizer(x_db, valid)
        mae_mask = (torch.rand(valid.shape, device=valid.device) < self.mask_ratio) & valid
        keep_one = valid & ~mae_mask                           # never mask every valid date of a pixel
        none_left = keep_one.sum(1) == 0
        mae_mask[none_left] = False
        h = self.encoder.tokens(x_db, doy, valid, mae_mask)
        recon = self.decoder(h)
        loss = ((recon - target) ** 2).mean(-1)[mae_mask].mean()
        return loss, recon, mae_mask

def batches(n, bs, rng):
    idx = rng.permutation(n)
    for i in range(0, n - bs + 1, bs):
        yield idx[i:i + bs]

def pretrain(model, epochs, bs=1024, lr=1e-3, seed=SEED, label="MAE"):
    torch.manual_seed(seed); rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    model = model.to(DEVICE)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=0.05)
    steps = epochs * (len(XU) // bs)
    sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr=lr, total_steps=steps, pct_start=0.1)
    hist = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model.train(); losses = []
        for b in batches(len(XU), bs, rng):
            x, d, v = to_t(XU[b], DU[b], VU[b])
            out = model(x, d, v)
            loss = out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
            opt.step(); sched.step(); losses.append(loss.item())
        hist.append(float(np.mean(losses)))
        print(f"{label} epoch {ep + 1:2d}/{epochs}  loss {hist[-1]:.4f}")
    return model, hist

Contrastive learning (SimCLR) with SAR-specific augmentations
Two random views of each pixel are created and the encoder is trained so the two views of the same pixel have similar embeddings and differ from the other pixels in the batch (NT-Xent loss). Augmentations act on dB backscatter before featurisation:







Augmentation
What it mimics




Date dropout (20%, at least 3 dates kept)
Missing passes, RFI-flagged dates


Multiplicative gamma speckle (L = 8)
Residual speckle after filtering


Gain shift (±0.5 dB per polarisation)
Calibration differences between passes or releases


DOY jitter (±6 days)
Field-to-field differences in planting and harvest dates





Code
def sar_augment(x_db, doy, valid, p_drop=0.2, looks=8.0, gain_db=0.5, doy_jitter=6.0, min_keep=3):
    B, T, C = x_db.shape
    keep = valid & (torch.rand(B, T, device=x_db.device) > p_drop)
    few = keep.sum(1) < min_keep
    keep[few] = valid[few]
    lin = 10 ** (x_db / 10)
    spk = torch.distributions.Gamma(torch.tensor(looks), torch.tensor(looks)).sample(lin.shape).to(x_db.device)
    x = 10 * torch.log10(lin * spk + 1e-8)
    x = x + (torch.rand(B, 1, C, device=x_db.device) * 2 - 1) * gain_db
    d = doy + (torch.rand(B, 1, device=x_db.device) * 2 - 1) * doy_jitter
    return torch.where(keep.unsqueeze(-1), x, torch.zeros_like(x)), d, keep

class SimCLR(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, tau=0.2, **kw):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = TSEncoder(**kw)
        d = self.encoder.d_model
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(d, 32))
        self.tau = tau

    def forward(self, x_db, doy, valid):
        z = []
        for _ in range(2):
            xa, da, va = sar_augment(x_db, doy, valid)
            z.append(F.normalize(self.head(self.encoder(xa, da, va)), dim=-1))
        z = torch.cat(z)
        sim = z @ z.T / self.tau
        B = x_db.shape[0]
        sim.fill_diagonal_(-1e9)
        target = torch.cat([torch.arange(B, 2 * B), torch.arange(0, B)]).to(z.device)
        return F.cross_entropy(sim, target)

t0 = time.time()

Code
class CropClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, encoder, n_classes, linear=False):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = encoder
        d = encoder.d_model
        self.head = (nn.Linear(d, n_classes) if linear else
                     nn.Sequential(nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.Linear(d, 64), nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(0.2), nn.Linear(64, n_classes)))

    def forward(self, x, d, v):
        return self.head(self.encoder(x, d, v))

def make_encoder(init):
    enc = TSEncoder()
    if init in ("mae", "simclr"):
        enc.load_state_dict(torch.load(OUT_DIR / f"encoder_{init}.pt", map_location="cpu"))
    return enc

@torch.no_grad()
def predict(model, X, D, V, bs=8192, return_emb=False):
    model.eval(); out = []
    for i in range(0, len(X), bs):
        x, d, v = to_t(X[i:i + bs], D[i:i + bs], V[i:i + bs])
        out.append((model.encoder(x, d, v) if return_emb else F.softmax(model(x, d, v), -1)).cpu())
    return torch.cat(out).numpy()

def balanced_batch(y, bs, rng):
    classes = np.unique(y)
    per = max(1, bs // len(classes))
    return np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(y == c), per) for c in classes])

def train_classifier(init, mode, idx_train, X, D, V, y, idx_val, steps=300, bs=256, lr=1e-3, seed=0, eval_every=50):
    torch.manual_seed(seed); rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    model = CropClassifier(make_encoder(init), len(CLASSES), linear=(mode == "probe")).to(DEVICE)
    if mode == "probe":
        for p in model.encoder.parameters():
            p.requires_grad = False
        params = [{"params": model.head.parameters(), "lr": lr * 3}]
    elif mode == "finetune":
        params = [{"params": model.encoder.parameters(), "lr": lr * 0.1}, {"params": model.head.parameters(), "lr": lr}]
    else:
        params = [{"params": model.parameters(), "lr": lr}]
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(params, weight_decay=0.01)
    best, best_state = -1, None
    ytr = y[idx_train]
    for step in range(1, steps + 1):
        model.train()
        if mode == "probe":
            model.encoder.eval()
        b = idx_train[balanced_batch(ytr, bs, rng)]
        x, d, v, yy = to_t(X[b], D[b], V[b], y[b])
        loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x, d, v), yy.long(), label_smoothing=0.05)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        if step % eval_every == 0:
            pv = predict(model, X[idx_val], D[idx_val], V[idx_val]).argmax(1)
            score = f1_score(y[idx_val], pv, average="macro")
            if score > best:
                best, best_state = score, {k: t.detach().clone() for k, t in model.state_dict().items()}
    model.load_state_dict(best_state)
    model.val_f1 = best
    return model

VARIANTS = [("Scratch", "scratch", "full"), ("MAE probe", "mae", "probe"), ("MAE fine-tune", "mae", "finetune"),
            ("SimCLR probe", "simclr", "probe"), ("SimCLR fine-tune", "simclr", "finetune")]

trained = {}
for budget in BUDGETS:

        for name, init, mode in VARIANTS:
            model = train_classifier(init, mode, idx, xA, dA, vA, yA, idx_val, seed=s)
            pred = predict(model, xA[idx_eval], dA[idx_eval], vA[idx_eval]).argmax(1)
            results.append({"method": name, "budget": str(budget), "seed": s, "n_pixels": len(idx),
                            "val_macroF1": model.val_f1, **evaluate(yA[idx_eval], pred)})
            if s == 0:
                trained[(name, str(budget))] = model
    print(f"budget {budget!s:>3} done ({time.time() - t0:.0f}s)")
res = pd.DataFrame(results)
res.to_csv(OUT_DIR / "label_efficiency_results.csv", index=False)

Object-based voting. Pixel maps carry residual speckle. The NISAR stack itself is segmented with GeoLattice segment (SLIC superpixels on the season mean of HH and HV and the HV standard deviation), and class probabilities are averaged inside each segment. Segments come from the radar data only, so the CDL boundaries do not leak into the map.

Stratified random sample and area-adjusted accuracy (Olofsson et al. 2014)
Wall-to-wall agreement weights classes by their area and ignores how a map would be validated in practice. The good-practice design is a stratified random sample with the map classes as strata, here N_PER_STRATUM pixels per class drawn from the test blocks, with the CDL as the reference label. GeoLattice olofsson turns the sample confusion matrix and the mapped area of each stratum into area-weighted overall, user’s and producer’s accuracy with 95% confidence intervals, and an error-adjusted area for each class.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
pred_final = pred_obj

                         for k in range(len(CLASSES)) if map_counts[k] > 1])
cm_s = pg_confusion_matrix(yA[sample], pred_final[sample], labels=list(range(len(CLASSES))))
strata = [k for k in range(len(CLASSES)) if map_counts[k] > 1]
cm_s = cm_s.loc[strata, strata]
ol = olofsson(cm_s, {k: map_counts[k] for k in strata}, pixel_area=POSTING ** 2 / 1e4)   # hectares
tab = ol["table"].copy()
tab.index = [CLASSES[k] for k in strata]
tab["CDL_area"] = [(yA[pop] == k).sum() * POSTING ** 2 / 1e4 for k in strata]

Where the map and the CDL disagree
The agreement map shows where disagreement concentrates. Errors along field edges point to mixed pixels and small misregistration; whole-field disagreement between corn and soybean is the signature of rotation between 2025 and 2026 (or of an error in either product). Low model confidence is a useful flag for both.

How much disagreement is corn ↔︎ soybean?
If the corn and soybean classes are merged into one Corn/Soy class, overall agreement can only rise. The size of the jump measures how much of the remaining disagreement is corn/soybean confusion. In a region with a strong corn–soybean rotation, part of that confusion reflects real 2025 → 2026 changes rather than map errors; the 2026 CDL (or field data) is needed to separate the two.


Code
if {"Corn", "Soybeans"} <= set(CLASSES):
    ic, isb = CLASSES.index("Corn"), CLASSES.index("Soybeans")
    def merge(a):
        a = a.copy(); a[a == isb] = ic; return a
    r_full = accuracy_score(ref_test, pred_final[test_all])
    r_merged = accuracy_score(merge(ref_test), merge(pred_final[test_all]))
    cs = ((ref_test == ic) & (pred_final[test_all] == isb)) | ((ref_test == isb) & (pred_final[test_all] == ic))
    print(f"Overall agreement: {r_full:.3f} with corn and soybean separate, {r_merged:.3f} merged")
    print(f"Corn<->soybean swaps are {cs.mean():.1%} of test pixels and "
          f"{cs.sum() / max(1, (ref_test != pred_final[test_all]).sum()):.0%} of all disagreement")
    # Whole-unit swaps: units where most pixels flipped corn<->soybean look like rotation, not noise.
    sw = pd.DataFrame({"field": metaA.field.values[test_all], "swap": cs})
    sw = sw[sw.field >= 0].groupby("field").swap.mean()
    print(f"Test units with >80% of pixels swapped corn<->soybean: {(sw > 0.8).sum()} of {len(sw)}")
else:
    print("Corn and soybean are not both present in this AOI.")

Maps are written as Cloud-Optimised-style GeoTIFFs on the NISAR UTM grid (class codes follow CLASSES; 255 = not classified), together with the confidence and agreement layers, the CDL reference on the same grid, model weights and the class/normalisation configuration needed to apply the model to new GCOV scenes.

def save_tif(arr, path, dtype="uint8", nodata=255):
    a = np.where(np.isnan(arr) if np.issubdtype(np.asarray(arr).dtype, np.floating) else arr < 0, nodata, arr)
    with rasterio.open(path, "w", driver="GTiff", height=H, width=W, count=1, dtype=dtype, crs=STACK_CRS,
                       transform=AOIS[0]["transform"], nodata=nodata, compress="deflate", tiled=True) as dst:
        dst.write(a.astype(dtype), 1)
    return path.name

title: Crop Classification with NISAR GCOV Time Series and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
Limitations and next steps

Use the 2026 CDL when it is released (NASS usually publishes in January–February). Change CDL_PATH and CDL_YEAR and rerun; the rotation diagnostic in Section 12.4 shows how much this matters for your AOI.
Add early-season passes. The archive used here starts on 23 July. Passes from May–June capture emergence and give much better separation of small grains, hay and late-planted crops.
Add the ascending track over the same area as extra tokens with their own DOY (and an incidence-angle channel). Do not mix tracks in one stack without that.
Use real parcels. Replace the CDL-derived units with Common Land Unit or field-boundary polygons (for example from the SAM-based delineation in Part VI) for training splits and object voting.
Scale pretraining: sample a few million pixels across all frames and seasons, d_model = 128, 4 layers, 50+ MAE epochs on a GPU.
Watch calibration and RFI: keep one product release per stack, and check each date’s quick-look; L-band RFI shows as bright streaks that the mask may not flag.


Exercises

Change the MAE mask ratio to 0.3 and 0.7. How does the label-efficiency curve change with only six dates?
Replace the Quegan filter with single-date speckle.refined_lee and compare pixel-level and SLIC-voting accuracy.
Merge Grass/Pasture and Alfalfa/Hay (CDL accuracy for other hay is low). Does map–CDL agreement improve, and is that a better or only an easier map?
Set AOI_CENTER_LONLAT to an area dominated by small grains and sunflower and repeat Sections 11–12.
Train with the 2025 CDL and test on only those units that kept the same crop in 2024 and 2025 (download the 2024 CDL): a rough way to reduce rotation noise in the reference.

title: Charland Monitoring with Sentinel-1 SAR (and NISAR L-band), Lower Meghna Estuary of Bangladesh
text:
Overview
This capstone implements the Charland Monitoring Protocol: Sentinel-1 SAR step by step on the local data in Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones/s1_BD_charland/:







Protocol objective
Where in this notebook




1. Classify every Sentinel-1 acquisition into water and non-water
Steps 3 to 5


2. Combine classified scenes into annual, tide-adjusted land-frequency maps
Steps 6 and 7


3. Measure accretion, erosion and net land change, for the AOI and for each char
Steps 8, 10, 11


4. Track char maturity (intertidal flat → bare land → vegetated land) from backscatter
Step 9


5. Report accuracy against independent reference data
Step 14



NISAR L-band GCOV scenes in Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones/s1_BD_charland/NISAR_BD/ are processed as a separate, parallel series (Step 13), as the protocol requires for any second track or sensor.

What the local data can and cannot support
The local archive holds 20 Sentinel-1A IW GRDH scenes from one track (relative orbit 114, ascending, about 12:04 UTC) and 5 NISAR GCOV scenes for July to October 2026:



Dry-season year (Dec–Mar)
Scenes




dry_2024
Dec 2023, Jan, Feb, Mar 2024


dry_2025
Dec 2024, Jan, Feb, Mar 2025


dry_2026
Dec 2025, Jan, Feb, Mar 2026


Rest of 2024
one scene a month, April to November




Three complete dry seasons (Bangladesh dry season, December to March; December is counted with the following year). This gives two protocol annual change pairs, dry 2024 → dry 2025 and dry 2025 → dry 2026. The first pair can be confirmed by the next season’s map, and the second by the low- and mid-tide composites of 2026. The char register, shoreline transects and pixel history run over the three dry seasons.
2024 is the only full calendar year. It supplies the monsoon map, the post-monsoon (November-December) map, char maturity (which needs the seasonal VH swing) and a within-year dry 2024 → November-December 2024 comparison. That comparison is kept as a descriptive view of the 2024 monsoon.
Four scenes per dry season is below the protocol’s five low-tide scenes, so the low-tide composites rest on one or two scenes each and the release stays provisional on that item.
The tide model (FES/TPXO via pyTMD), BIWTA gauge records, ERA5 wind, Sentinel-2 reference imagery and union boundaries are not in the folder. The notebook uses them automatically when you add them (paths in the Parameters cell). Until then it uses transparent SAR-based proxies (a water-level index for tide, open-water VV for wind) and marks the release provisional.
Precise orbit files and a GLO-30 DEM are not supplied. Scenes are geocoded with the products’ own geolocation grid (ellipsoid). On this flat coast (mostly below 5 m) the residual terrain displacement is under one 10 m pixel and identical on every date of the same track, so it does not create false change.

Every place where the notebook departs from the protocol because of missing inputs is stated where it happens and collected again in the QA checklist (Step 15).

# Parameters. Paths, grid, seasons, thresholds and QA rules.

# 1. Input locations (run this notebook from the 08_11_Capstones folder).
DATA_DIR = Path("../../../../Data/08_remote_sensing/08_11_Capstones/s1_BD_charland")

# 2. Output folders, following the protocol's folder layout.
OUT = {name: DATA_DIR / name for name in
       ["preprocessed", "classified", "annual", "change", "vectors", "validation", "reports"]}

# 3. Master grid (protocol): UTM 46N at 10 m. Set 20 or 30 m for a quicker first run;
#    every threshold below that is given in hectares or metres adapts automatically.

text:
Study area and master grid
The AOI is the 130 km × 53 km rectangle on the Barisal-Bhola coast given in the protocol. The master grid is the AOI’s bounding box in UTM 46N, snapped to whole multiples of the pixel size, so every Sentinel-1 date and every NISAR date lands on exactly the same pixels. Pixels outside the AOI polygon are masked.


Code
# Load the AOI, build the master grid, and rasterize the AOI mask on it.

# 1. AOI polygon in WGS84 and its bounds (west, south, east, north).
aoi = gpd.read_file(AOI_PATH).to_crs("EPSG:4326")
AOI_BOUNDS = tuple(float(v) for v in aoi.total_bounds)
aoi_utm = aoi.to_crs(GRID_CRS)

# 2. Master grid: rs.sar.common_grid snaps the projected bounds to the pixel size; this is
#    the same function create_stack uses, so every scene stacked later matches it exactly.
GRID_TRANSFORM, GRID_W, GRID_H = rs.sar.common_grid(AOI_BOUNDS, GRID_CRS, RESOLUTION_M)
aoi_inside = geometry_mask([mapping(g) for g in aoi_utm.geometry], out_shape=(GRID_H, GRID_W),
                           transform=GRID_TRANSFORM, invert=True)
PIXEL_KM2 = RESOLUTION_M**2 / 1e6
MAP_EXTENT = (GRID_TRANSFORM.c, GRID_TRANSFORM.c + GRID_TRANSFORM.a * GRID_W,
              GRID_TRANSFORM.f + GRID_TRANSFORM.e * GRID_H, GRID_TRANSFORM.f)

print("AOI bounds (W, S, E, N):", tuple(round(v, 6) for v in AOI_BOUNDS))
print(f"AOI area: {aoi_utm.area.sum() / 1e6:,.0f} km²")
print(f"Master grid: {GRID_W:,} × {GRID_H:,} pixels ({GRID_W * GRID_H / 1e6:.1f} M), "
      f"{int(aoi_inside.sum()):,} inside the AOI")

    aoi_map = leafmap.Map(center=((south + north) / 2, (west + east) / 2), zoom=9, height="520px")
